en: *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats;
translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman during the Northern Liang dynasty.
Translated by Gong Dao Tai and others: What is the "Dharma Supreme in the World" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
Why is it called the "Dharma Supreme in the World"?
Regarding these sections and the meaning of their explanations, the *upadeśa* (expository treatise) should be explained in detail therein.
Question: Who composed this sutra? Answer:
"O Buddha, World-Honored One, it is because the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are profoundly deep and subtle; only the All-Knowing One can exhaustively fathom them. He asked:
Who asked and who answered?
The answer is:
according to some accounts, the Venerable Śāriputra asked and the Buddha answered.
Furthermore, some say that five hundred arhats asked the questions and the Buddha answered;
others say that the devas asked the questions and the Buddha answered;
and still others say that an emanated person asked the questions and the Buddha answered.
Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) ought to be explained in detail, yet there was no one to ask.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested a transformed bhikṣu with shaven hair and beard, wearing a saṃghāṭī robe, his appearance upright and dignified. That [bhikṣu] questioned the Buddha and received his answers, just as in the *Saṃyuktāgama* Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Multitude of Meanings.
Question: If that is so, why is it further stated that Kātyāyanīputra composed [this work]? Answer:
That Venerable One always delighted in receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, and explaining it for others, causing it to spread widely; as his fame accrued to him, it is said that he composed it.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this sūtra was composed by that very Venerable Kātyāyanīputra.
Question: It was said previously that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are exceedingly profound and subtle, such that only an omniscient one can fathom them to the ultimate degree.
How then was the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra able to compose [this treatise]?
The answer is:

That Venerable Kātyāyanīputra also possessed sharp and profound wisdom; he was well-versed in both general and specific characteristics, as well as the literal meaning and the sequence of the teachings. He had mastered the Tripitaka and attained the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, being endowed with the eight liberations. Having abandoned the desires of the three realms, he had acquired the wisdom of aspiration.
Under five hundred Buddhas, he practiced and established this vow:
"May I, in a future age within the bequeathed Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, compose an Abhidharma treatise."
Question: If that is so, what is the Buddha’s Abhidharma? Answer:
In various regions and towns, the World-Honored One taught diverse doctrines for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
The Venerable Kātyāyanīputra established topical headings among those diverse teachings, composed verses, categorized them into chapters (vargas), and compiled them into sections (khandas).

If one explains various dissimilar meanings, the *Saṃyukta-varga* (Miscellaneous Chapter) is established; if one explains the characteristics of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the *Anuśaya-varga* is established; if one explains the characteristics of knowledge (*jñāna*), the *Jñāna-varga* is established; if one explains the characteristics of karma, the *Karma-varga* is established; if one explains the characteristics of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the *Mahābhūta-varga* is established; if one explains the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*), the *Indriya-varga* is established; if one explains the characteristics of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the *Samādhi-varga* is established; and if one explains the characteristics of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the *Dṛṣṭi-varga* is established.
As in the *Dharmapada*, the Blessed One, for the sake of sentient beings, expounded various teachings in many different regions and towns.

After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Venerable Dharmatrāta, from among these various expositions, established the Chapter on Impermanence (*Anityavarga*) for those teachings concerning impermanence, and so on, up to establishing the Chapter on Brahmins (*Brāhmaṇavarga*) for those concerning the meaning of brahmins.
This Kātyāyanīputra was likewise so.
Furthermore, whenever Buddhas appear in the world, they all expound the Tripiṭaka, namely: Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma.
Question: What is the distinction between the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma? Answer:
Some may say that there is no distinction. Why is this?
Because they emerge from the river of the Buddha’s single ocean of wisdom, and because they are spoken through the cause of the great mind of compassion.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are also distinctions.
What are these distinctions?
The names themselves are the distinctions.
That is to say: this is the Sūtra, this is the Vinaya, and this is the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, that which distinguishes the mind is called the Sūtra; that which distinguishes the precepts is called the Vinaya; and that which distinguishes wisdom is called the Abhidharma.

Question: If that is so, then in the Sūtras there is both an analysis of precepts and an analysis of wisdom; in the Vinaya there is both an analysis of the mind and an analysis of wisdom; and in the Abhidharma there is both an analysis of the mind and an analysis of precepts.
What is the distinction between these three collections?
The answer is:
it is based on their predominance.
In the Sūtras, mental phenomena are mostly explained; in the Vinaya, the rules of discipline are mostly explained; and in the Abhidharma, wisdom is mostly explained.
Furthermore, within the Sūtras, that which analyzes the mind is called Sūtra, that which analyzes discipline is called Vinaya, and that which analyzes wisdom is called Abhidharma.
In the Abhidharma, if one distinguishes ethical discipline, it is called Vinaya; if one distinguishes the mind, it is called Sūtra; and if one distinguishes wisdom, it is called Abhidharma.
Within the Vinaya, that which analyzes wisdom is called Abhidharma; that which analyzes discipline is called Vinaya; and that which analyzes the mind is called Sūtra.
Such is the distinction among the Three Piṭakas.

Furthermore, within the Sūtras, one should seek the sequential order: for what reason did the Blessed One speak this, and subsequently speak that? For example, after speaking of faith in the Buddha, one should next have faith in the Dharma; this is the meaning of seeking the sequential order.
Within the Vinaya, one should seek [the meaning] through causes and conditions, such as explaining for what specific event this precept was established.
Within the Abhidharma, one should seek it by way of its characteristics (lakṣaṇa), not by sequential order.
Furthermore, the Sūtras are taught based on power; the Vinaya is taught based on great compassion; and the Abhidharma is taught based on fearlessness.

Furthermore, various miscellaneous teachings are called Sūtra; the extensive exposition of the precepts is called Vinaya; and the explanation of general and specific characteristics is called Abhidharma.

Furthermore, causing those who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them is called Sūtra; causing those who have already planted roots of goodness to bring them to maturity is called Vinaya; and when roots of goodness have matured and one attains right liberation, it is called Abhidharma.

Furthermore, for those who have newly entered the Dharma, it is called Sūtra; for those who have already entered the Dharma and are receiving and upholding the precepts, it is called Vinaya; and for those who have already received the precepts, it is called Abhidharma in order to bring about correct understanding.
The Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma—these are the names for their distinctions. Question:
For what causes and conditions did that Venerable One compose this treatise?
The answer is:
It is for the sake of benefiting others.

If one upholds, recites, masters, explains, and maintains right mindfulness of this [teaching], immeasurable afflictions and various evil deeds will not manifest before them; by diligently practicing this, one is able to enter into the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
For example, it is like a person who, wishing to benefit others, lights a great lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes may see various forms.
That Venerable One was likewise; he composed this sutra for the benefit of others.
The Buddha is likewise; for the benefit of others, he expounds the twelve divisions of the sūtras:
first, the Sūtra (sūtra);
second, the Geya (geya); and so forth.
3. Vyākaraṇa; 4. Gāthā; 5. Udāna;
Sixth, the Nidānas; seventh, the Avadānas; eighth, the Itivṛttakas;
9. Geya; 10. Vyākaraṇa; 11. Avadāna-dharma.
12. Upadeśa. Why is this so?

If there are sentient beings who possess internal causes but lack external conditions, they will ultimately be unable to cultivate superior progress; however, if they encounter external conditions, they will be able to practice.

For example, when lotuses—such as the padma, puṇḍarīka, kumuda, and utpala—are in the water of a pond, they do not open, blossom, or emit fragrance if the sunlight does not shine upon them; yet if the sunlight shines upon them, they open, blossom, and give off fragrance.
It is like various objects within a dark room: if there is no lamp to illuminate them, they can never be seen; yet with a lamp, they are seen.
So it is with sentient beings: although the internal cause exists, if the external conditions are absent, they can never cultivate superior progress;
but if they encounter external conditions, they are able to practice superior progress.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Just as within a dark room, though there may be various objects,
if there is no light of a lamp to illuminate them, those with eyes cannot see them."
If a person possesses wisdom but does not hear the Dharma from others,
that person will ultimately be unable to distinguish the meaning of good and evil.
It is like a person with sight who, by means of a lamp, perceives various forms.
The wise rely on extensive learning to distinguish the meaning of good and evil.
Through extensive learning one comes to know the Dharma; through extensive learning one stays far from evil;
through extensive learning one leaves behind what is meaningless; and through extensive learning one attains Nirvana.
The Buddha’s sūtras also state:
"There are two causes and two conditions for the arising of right view:
first, hearing the Dharma from others; [second, internal reflection]."
2. Inner Right Reflection.
Furthermore, it is said:
There are four qualities in a person that are exceedingly rare:
First, associating with virtuous friends;
second, hearing the Dharma from others;
third, correct internal reflection.
Fourth, practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
It is further said:
"If my disciples listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus, they can sever the five hindrances and fully cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment."
Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the benefit of others, so too did that Venerable One.
Furthermore, it was for the sake of destroying the darkness of ignorance.
Just as a lamp dispels darkness and produces light, so too is it with the Abhidharma: it dispels the darkness of ignorance and brings forth the light of wisdom.
Furthermore, it is intended to make the image of selflessness clearly manifest.

Just as a bright mirror reflects all forms and images, if one can skillfully distinguish general and specific characteristics through the wisdom of Abhidharma, the image of selflessness will naturally manifest.
Furthermore, it is for the sake of crossing the river of birth and death.
For example, just as hundreds of thousands of nayutas of sentient beings rely upon a sturdy ship and, being free from fear, are able to go from this shore to the other shore.

In this same way, hundreds of thousands of nayutas of Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, along with their retinues, likewise rely upon the ship of Abhidharma to be without fear, able to go from this shore to the other shore.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of acting as a lamp for all the Sūtras.
Just as a person holding a torch in the midst of darkness has nothing to fear,
so too does a practitioner holding the torch of Abhidharma have no fear regarding the meanings of all the Sūtras.
Furthermore, for the purpose of examining wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena:
just as a skilled appraiser of jewels can properly distinguish diamonds and other precious gems,
so too does one who possesses such knowledge discern wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena through the wisdom of Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is to manifest to those who study the Abhidharma that Mount Sumeru is unshakable.
Just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, remains firmly established upon the golden wheel of the earth, such that the fierce winds from the four directions cannot shake it.

In this way, the wise person establishes the Sumeru mountain of Abhidharma wisdom upon the golden wheel-ground of ethical discipline; thus, the winds of the four inversions and false views cannot cause it to waver.
Furthermore, for three reasons, the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra composed this sūtra:
first, to increase wisdom; second, to awaken the mind.
Third, for the sake of severing the notions of self and person, the Abhidharma is unsurpassed among all sūtras and śāstras for increasing the wisdom of the practitioner.

To awaken the mind: sentient beings are constantly asleep and lack moments of awakening; they do not know which [defilements] are universal (sarvatraga) and which are non-universal, which have their own realm as their object and are universal, and which have other realms as their object and are universal; which have outflow (sāsrava) as their object, and which have the outflow-free (anāsrava) as their object; which have the conditioned (saṃskṛta) as their object, and which have the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) as their object; how they are subsumed, how they correspond, what constitutes their cause, and what constitutes their condition; and who possesses them and who does not.
The ability to discern such phenomena as distant and near is the power of Abhidharma.

As for the severing of the notions of "self" and "person," that venerable master who composed the Abhidharma-piṭaka never asserted the existence of a self or a person; rather, in every instance, he constantly taught non-self and the absence of a person.
For these and other such reasons, that Venerable One composed the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
It is asked:
what is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the Abhidharma?

Answer: The intrinsic nature of the untainted faculty of wisdom (anāsrava-prajñendriya) comprises one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha). The one element is the dharma-element; the one base is the dharma-base; and the one aggregate is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

If one takes up that which is associated with grasping and included within the commonality, it comprises three elements, two bases, and five aggregates. The three elements are the mind element (*manodhātu*), the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*), and the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*). The two bases are the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*). The five aggregates are form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, a sūtra states:
"This Śakra has long possessed a mind that is upright and free from guile; whatever he asks is for the sake of full understanding and not for the sake of causing disturbance.
I shall allow you to ask whatever you wish regarding the profound Abhidharma."
In this context, what is the profound meaning?
It is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, as it is said in a sutra:
There is a brahmin of the Vatsa clan whose nature is upright and free from deceit; whatever he asks is for the sake of full understanding and not for the sake of causing disturbance.
I shall allow you to ask whatever you wish regarding the profound Abhidharma.
In this context, what is the profound meaning?
It is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*).
Furthermore, there were the brahmin Brahmayu and the ascetic Subhadra, concerning whom it is also said as above.
As the Buddha told the Brahmin Śreṇika:

"My Dharma is extremely profound, difficult to understand and difficult to comprehend, difficult to know and difficult to see; it is beyond the reach of thought, deliberation, or discrimination. Only those with subtle, definitive wisdom can know it; it is not within the reach of your shallow intelligence."
Why is this so? Emptiness is itself non-self, yet you conceive of a self.
Throughout the long night, you have held divergent views, divergent desires, and a divergent mind; for this reason, it is beyond the reach of your shallow wisdom.
In this context, what is the profound meaning?
It is the samādhi of emptiness. It is as it has been said:
that a foolish person who lacks eyes should debate the profound meaning with a senior bhikṣu endowed with wisdom.
In this context, what is the profound meaning?
It is the so-called "decline of the Dharma.
As the Buddha told Ānanda:

This Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is profound, difficult to understand and difficult to comprehend, difficult to know and difficult to perceive. It is beyond the reach of discursive thought and conceptualization; only those with subtle, decisive wisdom can know it, for it is not within the reach of your shallow intelligence.
In this context, what is the profound meaning?
It is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As it is said:
This point is profound, namely dependent origination; this dharma is the cessation of desire, which is nirvāṇa.
What herein is the profound meaning?
It is the nature of quiescence and extinction through causes and conditions.
As it is said: "Because all dharmas are profound, they are difficult to see; because they are difficult to see, they are profound.
In this context, what is profundity?
It is the profound nature of the essence of all dharmas.
Question: What is the essence of Abhidharma? Answer:
The untainted faculty of wisdom (anāsrava-prajñendriya).

By the power of this untainted faculty of wisdom, it causes the wisdom acquired at birth (upapatti-pratilambhikā prajñā) to arise, enabling one to receive, uphold, read, recite, and master the twelve divisions of the scriptures; this is also called Abhidharma.

Furthermore, by the power of the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*), it enables the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) to know general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

it further enables the wisdom of hearing to establish general and specific characteristics; and it enables the wisdom of hearing to sever delusion regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-moha*) and delusion regarding conditions (*ālambana-moha*), so that one is not mistaken regarding phenomena (*dharma*).

Moreover, by the power of the untainted faculty of wisdom, it enables the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*)—such as [the meditations on] impurity (*aśubha*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)—to be called Abhidharma as well.

Furthermore, by the power of the faculty of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*), it can cause the cultivation of the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), "summit" (*mūrdhan*), "patience" (*kṣānti*), and the "supreme mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*); these are also called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, by means of such wisdom as this, the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-jñānendriya*) is further rendered clear and pure;
this is called *abhidharma*. Question: If the untainted faculty of wisdom is the essence of *abhidharma*, why is this sutra also named *abhidharma*?
Answer: Because it contains the Abhidharma in its entirety, it is also called "Abhidharma.
As it is said in various sūtras:
Based on various types of equipment (pariṣkāra), various names are established.
Because they are the equipment for the outflows (āsrava), they are called "outflows," just as it is said that the seven outflows are afflictions (kleśa), are burning, and are suffering.
In reality, there are three outflows (*āsrava*): namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Because they possess defilements (*mala*), they are called "defilements.
As a verse says: "Women are the defilement of the holy life; women bind sentient beings. To practice the holy life through asceticism—"
"It is not because of the purity of water.
A woman is truly not defiled; there are actually three defilements, namely the defilements of greed, hatred, and delusion.
She is called "pleasurable" because she possesses the requisites for pleasure, as the verse says:
"Enjoyment in eating and drinking is pleasant; wearing fine robes is also pleasant; walking meditation in mountain caves is likewise pleasant.
Eating and drinking are not themselves the pleasure; rather, it is the pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) that is truly pleasant.
They are called "proclivities" (anuśaya) because they cause [beings] to be fully bound; as it is said:
"O Bhikṣus! One is bound by form and fettered by form."
Form itself is not a latent tendency (*anuśaya*); in reality, there are seven latent tendencies.
To speak fully of "taste" (*rasa*) is as it is said:
"O Bhikṣu!"
The eye relishes forms; forms are the hook of Māra.
It is not the eye that is the relishing, but craving is the true relishing.
To explain desire in its entirety, it is as follows:
The excellence of the five sensual desires can cause the mind of attachment to increase and become defiled.
Form and the other [objects] are not themselves desire; rather, actual desire is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding the factors of decline, it is said that one declines, as it is stated:
An Arhat with occasional liberation (samayavimukta) may fall away due to five causes and conditions:
first, through the toil of managing affairs;
second, through reciting many scriptures; [and so forth].
Third, litigation;
fourth, traveling far away;
fifth, chronic illness.
Non-undertaking of activities and so forth constitute retrogression; this actual retrogression consists of unwholesome and obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) dharmas.
Regarding the full exposition of karma, it is said:
"O Bhikṣu!"
There are three types of unwholesome mental karma that produce bitter retributive fruits: namely, greed, hatred, and wrong view.
While the essence of greed, hatred, and wrong view is not itself karma, there are actually three types of karma, which are body, speech, and mind.
It is called "retribution" because it is the fullness of retribution; as the Venerable Aniruddha said:
"By the retribution for giving a single meal, I was born seven times in the Heaven of the Thirty-three and seven times in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī."
Food is not a result of birth; that which is a result of birth consists of unwholesome states and wholesome states with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Thus it is taught in various places throughout the sūtras, where various names are used according to various specific contexts.
This is also like that; because it is complete with the Abhidharma, it is called "Abhidharma. Question:
By what meaning is it named "Abhidharma"?
Answer: The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra says:
that which is capable of definitively analyzing and distinguishing the twelve divisions of the scriptures is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is said that the ability to fully comprehend the twelve links of dependent origination is called Abhidharma.
Moreover, the ability to sequentially attain right certainty regarding the Four Noble Truths is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is said that that which can explain and elucidate the practice of the Eightfold Noble Path is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is said that that which can realize Nirvana is called Abhidharma.
The Venerable Bhadanta stated:

The Abhidharma is the systematic compilation, analysis, and explanation of such phenomena as the emergence from afflictions, bondage and liberation, and saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, arranged in sequence through the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

"Whatever practices are undertaken by those seeking liberation, all that has not yet been analyzed is here analyzed—namely, 'this is suffering,' 'this is the cause of suffering,' 'this is the path,' 'this is the fruit of the path,' 'this is the path of preparation,' 'this is the path of non-obstruction,' 'this is the path of liberation,' 'this is the path of excellence,' 'this is the path leading toward the fruit,' and 'this is the attainment of the fruit. This is called Abhidharma."
The Venerable Paśya said:
"This wisdom is ultimate wisdom; this wisdom is the foremost wisdom; this wisdom is unerring wisdom—this is called Abhidharma."
The Abhidharmikas say: that which is able to variously discern, awaken to, and realize all phenomena is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, they say that which can exhaustively fathom the profound nature of phenomena to its very source is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is said that that which can purify the Dharma-eye is called Abhidharma.
Furthermore, it is said that that which reveals and elucidates profound and hidden wisdom is called Abhidharma.

Furthermore, it is said that if a person uses the wisdom of Abhidharma to discern general characteristics and specific characteristics, such that no one can rightfully point out any fault in their exposition, this is called Abhidharma.
The Mahīśāsaka school says:
Just as a lamp can illuminate, it is called *abhidharma*; as it is said, among all forms of illumination, the illumination of wisdom (*prajñā*) is supreme.
The Dharmaguptaka school says:
This dharma is called Abhidharma because it is preeminent; as it is said, "Among all dharmas, wisdom is supreme.
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Among the various dharmas, Nirvāṇa is supreme," and because this dharma is next to that, it is called Abhidharma.
The proponents of the Science of Phonetics (Śabdavādin) say:
the term *abhi* signifies both "removal" (*apoha*) and "selection" (*pariccheda*).
As for "removal," it refers to the fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), entanglements (*paryavasthāna*), and afflictions (*kleśa*).

"Selection" refers to all phenomena such as the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*).

Furthermore, the term *abhi* signifies "superiority" (*adhimāna*); just as one who speaks with superiority is called "one of superior pride," just as one who is superior is called "an eminent person," and just as superior negligence is called "excessive negligence," so too in this sutra, the word for "superiority" is *abhidharma*.

Furthermore, the term *abhi* means "to manifest before. Because all the various factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and other dharmas manifest before one, it is called *Abhidharma*.
Furthermore, the term *abhi* means "veneration. Because this dharma is worthy of respect and honor, it is called *Abhidharma*.
This sutra is titled "The Foundation of Wisdom.
Question: Why is it called "The Foundation of Wisdom"?
Answer: All ultimate knowledges (*paryavasāna-jñāna*) emerge from this sūtra; therefore, it is called the "Foundation.

Furthermore, this sūtra is named the "Abode of the Fulfillment of Knowledge" (*jñānapratiṣṭhāna*); all ultimate knowledges are established by means of this sūtra, and for this reason it is called the "Abode of the Fulfillment of Knowledge."
Question: What benefit does this sutra provide? Answer:

Conforming to liberation and conforming to non-self, they sever the reckoning of self and person, manifesting non-self; they give rise to the intent for awakening in others, producing wisdom, removing delusion, and cutting through the net of doubt. Attaining certainty, turning their backs on the blazing fire of saṃsāra, and heading toward the essential exit, they achieve continuity, delight in tranquility, and bring the wheel of birth and death to rest. Conforming to the dharma of emptiness, they reach the shore of nirvāṇa.
It is able to sever all the divergent views of non-Buddhists and give rise to a heart of joy and aspiration for the Buddha-dharma.
Because this sutra possesses such benefits as these, it is called Abhidharma.
1. The Section on Miscellaneous Matters (Saṃyukta-khaṇḍaka), Chapter 1: The Category of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (Laukikāgra-dharma-varga). First: What are the supreme mundane dharmas?
Question: Why does this sutra first explain the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma)?
Is it explained in direct order or in reverse order?

If explained in sequential order, one should first explain impurity (*aśubhā*), next explain mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), next explain the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), next explain the seven points of proficiency and the three types of contemplation—namely, heat (*uṣmagata*), summit (*mūrdhan*), and patience (*kṣānti*)—and only then should one explain the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

If they were explained in reverse order, one should first explain the fruit of arhatship, next the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), next the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala), next the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala), next the path of seeing (darśanamārga), and only then should the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) be explained.
He asked again:
"Is this taught because it is the initial entry into the Dharma? Or is it taught because of the roots of goodness conducive to penetration? Or is it taught because of the most excellent qualities?
If it were taught because it is the initial entry into the Dharma, one should instead teach [the meditation on] impurity or [the practice of] mindfulness of breathing."

If one were to explain by way of the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), one should first speak of the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*), because the stage of heat is foremost at the beginning; as in the treatise of the Venerable Ghoṣaka, where the stage of heat is explained first.

If one were to speak according to the most preeminent virtues, one should first mention the fruit of Arhatship; for there are such matters as these: when the Buddha was in the world, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana possessed the wisdom of right contemplation, had accomplished immeasurable merit and unimpeded diligence, entered the ocean of Abhidharma, and his mind was without increase or decrease. His realization was boundless, and his discourse was difficult to surpass; among all those who debate on the meaning of the teachings, none could withstand him.
The second Kātyāyanīputra also possesses such wisdom and merit; for what reason did he compose this sūtra by first explaining the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?

Answer: The various masters of the treatises explain the Supreme Mundane Dharma in many different ways. Some say it is not explained according to direct order, nor is it explained according to reverse order; rather, it is simply because that compiler’s intention was such. Following his intention, he composed this sūtra, which does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Therefore, he first explained the Supreme Mundane Dharma.

Some say that the Abhidharma should be sought through its characteristics rather than its sequential order; the Sūtras should be sought for their sequential order; and the Vinaya should be sought for its causal conditions.
If one seeks a sequential order within the Abhidharma-sūtra, the text becomes disordered; therefore, one should not seek such a sequence.
Some say that the World-Honored One stated in a sūtra:

"It is impossible for a person who cannot correctly contemplate the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to give rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)."

It is possible that one who can correctly contemplate the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) will be able to give rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Just as the World-Honored One first taught the Supreme Mundane Dharma in the Sūtras, and the authors of the Śāstras composed their treatises based on those Sūtras, they too should first teach the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
Question: Setting aside the author of the sutra, for what reason did the World-Honored One first teach the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma)? Answer:

The World-Honored One, in order to transform sentient beings, taught the Dharma in successive stages; those who have been transformed have already attained the lower and middle degrees of patience (*kṣānti*), but have not yet attained the higher degree of patience or the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

In order that they may attain it, the World-Honored One taught the correct contemplation and reflection upon the nature and characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); one should know that this is precisely "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), followed by the attainment of this "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*). Therefore, these were explained first.
Some say it is for the purpose of stopping various slanders.

Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there are many slanders, namely: slander regarding its name, slander regarding its essence, slander regarding its realm, slander regarding its manifestation, and slander regarding its retrogression.
Regarding the "denial of the name," some claim that this is the dharma of the stage of nature (*gotrabhūmi*) and not the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Regarding the "denial of the essence," some claim that it is the nature of the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

Regarding those who slander the realms (*dhātu*), some say they are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpa- or ārūpyadhātu*), or bound to all three realms, or that they are unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
One currently experiences slander; this may be due to a succession of many moments of mind rather than a single moment of mind.
Regarding those who regress and experience slander, some say it refers to regressing from the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
In order to cease such various forms of slander, he first spoke of the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, all of saṃsāra is not a solid or stable dharma; it is like refuse and foul mud.
Among these, which is most excellent, which is most firm, and which is like the finest cream?
It is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma); therefore, it is mentioned first.

Furthermore, because it accords with non-self (anātman), this sutra constantly teaches non-self, unlike the external scriptures which teach a self, teach the dharma of desire, teach the dharma of existence, or teach material wealth.
This sutra speaks exclusively of non-self, liberation, and nirvana; this "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) also contemplates non-self.
Because it accords with this sutra, it is therefore taught first.
Furthermore, this sutra is the most supreme among all treatises;
just as the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (laukikāgradharma) are the most supreme among all mundane wholesome dharmas, because this sutra is supreme, its supreme dharma should be explained first.

Furthermore, when one abides in the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), it is said that a true Buddha has appeared in the world, and one is able to attain mastery in the enjoyment of the noble Dharma.
When a Buddha appears in the world, there are two ways in which sentient beings enter the Dharma: first, by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*); [and second, by way of ultimate reality].
2. Reality. Regarding the provisional designation:
one shaves off hair and beard, dons the dharma robes, and leaves the household life out of right faith.

Regarding reality: one gives rise to the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) and is able to enter the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) in successive order.
These pseudo-monks have two faults:
first, breaking the precepts; second, abandoning the precepts.

Those who enter the True Dharma do not have such faults; as true śramaṇas, they enjoy the noble Dharma and attain mastery over it, never regressing or losing it according to their respective capacities.

Furthermore, when one abides in the dharma of the highest mundane state (*laukikāgradharma*), the gate of the noble path—which has been closed since beginningless birth and death—is now finally opened; that which has never before been able to abandon, namely the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), is now finally abandoned; and that which has never before been able to attain, namely the untainted noble path (*anāsravamārga*), is now finally attained. For these reasons, the dharma of the highest mundane state is explained first.

Furthermore, when abiding in the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one relinquishes names and acquires names, relinquishes numbers and acquires numbers, relinquishes realms and acquires realms, and relinquishes natures and acquires natures.
Regarding "relinquishing names and acquiring names": one relinquishes the name of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and acquires the name of a noble one (*ārya*).
The same applies to number, realm, and nature.

Furthermore, when abiding in the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), one attains the mind but not the cause of the mind; one attains clarity but not the cause of clarity; and one attains sensation but not the cause of sensation.
Furthermore, when abiding in those dharmas, one abandons old conditions and attains new conditions; abandons the common and attains the uncommon; abandons the mundane and attains the supramundane.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of severing doubt.

Sentient beings—meaning ordinary worldlings—are said to have a nature that is beginningless and likewise endless; now, by teaching the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), its end is demonstrated.

Furthermore, while abiding in those dharmas, the afflictions of an ordinary worldling, the transformations of an ordinary worldling, and the stubbornness of an ordinary worldling no longer arise at all;
however, the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) may still arise.
Furthermore, while abiding in those dharmas, there is no one who passes away without having attained the noble dharmas;
this is not the case for the stages of Heat (uṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti).

While abiding in those dharmas, there is no one who passes away without having attained the Noble Path (āryamārga); they attain right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) where it was not yet attained, they attain the fruits (phala) where they were not yet attained, they emerge from the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi) and enter the group of right determination (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi), and they go from having no Noble Path to having the Noble Path. It is likewise with going from having no imperturbable purity (aveccappasāda) to having imperturbable purity.
Furthermore, when abiding in these roots of goodness, there is no stagnation;
however, in the stages of Heat, Summits, and Patience, there is stagnation.
Furthermore, while abiding in those dharmas, the foundations of mindfulness practiced by ordinary persons reach ultimate fulfillment.

The others are not so. Furthermore, while abiding in those dharmas, there is the cessation and continuation of both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) minds; that which ceases is the tainted mind, and that which continues is the untainted mind. The others are not so.

Furthermore, just as Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, stands upon a golden wheel and cannot be shaken by the fierce winds from the four directions, so too, when one abides in this Dharma, one cannot be shaken by the perverse winds of the four inversions.
Furthermore, when abiding in that dharma, it demonstrates both the beginning and the end, just as the appearance of dawn marks the end of night and the beginning of day.

It is likewise here: it shows the end of the mundane and the beginning of the noble path. Just as it demonstrates the beginning and the end, so too are the means for crossing over, having crossed, entering, and emerging, as well as the ultimate consummation.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to show that although similar dharmas exist, they possess distinct characteristics.

The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is subsumed under the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); it is able to produce the path that extinguishes suffering. Because it is subsumed under suffering, subsumed under the conventional (*saṃvṛti*), subsumed under birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), subsumed under the various realms of existence (*bhava*), and subsumed by the underlying tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭyanuśaya*), it produces the path that extinguishes suffering;
other [dharmas] are not thus.
Furthermore, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has a mundane nature as its object, yet it is capable of producing supramundane objects; for this reason, it is explained first.

Likewise, [the relationship between] the defiled and the undefiled, the faulty and the faultless, the poisonous and the non-poisonous, the turbid and the non-turbid, the mass of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the absence of such a mass, the mass of inversions and the absence of such a mass, the mass of craving and the absence of such a mass, and the mass of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the absence of such a mass, is also to be understood in the same way.

Furthermore, because the Supreme Mundane Dharmas possess momentum and power, they are capable of performing their function like a strong man; for by abiding within these dharmas, one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, it is for three reasons:
first, for the sake of the meaning of the sūtra;
second, to prevent slander.
Third, because the fruit is attained in this very moment.
The meaning of the sūtra, as explained above, is to stop such slander.

"Attaining the fruit in this very moment" means that immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one can produce the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); this is called the fruit of effort (*prayogaphala*).
For these sequential reasons and conditions, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is explained first.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to explain in reverse order the dharmas attained by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*).
As it is said, from the Supreme Mundane Dharma down to the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), these are called the dharmas of deliverance attained by ordinary persons.
As it is said regarding the twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) and so forth, these are called the afflictive dharmas of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Who is able to know these two kinds of dharmas?
Only the wisdom of non-self (*anātma-jñāna*).
Therefore, in the second chapter it is said:
"Is there a single cognition that knows all phenomena? and so forth, at length.
From what does this cognition of selflessness arise?
Because one awakens to dependent origination,
it is therefore stated in the third chapter: "In the life of a single person,
there are twelve links of dependent origination," and so forth, as explained at length.
The ability to awaken to dependent origination arises from affection and reverence.
Therefore, in the fourth chapter, it is said:
"What is affection?"
What is reverence?
[This is] explained at length.
From what cause does this affectionate reverence arise?
Because of the existence of shame and dread of blame, it is therefore stated in the fifth chapter as follows:
"What is shame?"
What is shame (*hrī*)? ...
[and so on] up to the full exposition.
Who is capable of feeling shame and dread of blame?
Based on the analysis of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is therefore stated in the sixth chapter:
"Regarding arising, abiding, aging, and impermanence within form (*rūpa*), should they be said to be form or non-form?"
...and so forth, as explained at length.
By what means can one understand the characteristics of phenomena?
By abandoning that which is meaningless and cultivating that which is meaningful.
Therefore, it is said in the seventh chapter:
"One should know that the various ascetic practices cultivated by others are devoid of purpose," and so forth, as explained at length.
By what means does one abandon what is purposeless and cultivate what is purposeful?
Based on correct recollection,
it is therefore stated in the eighth chapter as follows:
"What is volition?"
What is recollection? [The text continues] with a detailed exposition.

Because of these various causes and conditions, one wishes to explain in reverse order the dharmas attained by ordinary persons; therefore, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is explained first.
What is the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)?
The answer is:
that which, among all mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*), sequentially attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); this is called the supreme mundane dharma.
Question: Is that which has already attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and that which will attain right determination also the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*)?
Answer: No.
This is also so. If one speaks of the present, it should be understood that one is speaking of the past and the future as well. Question:

Regarding the attainment of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) through the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*): is it attained while [the dharmas] are abiding, or is it attained after they have ceased?
If it were attained while they are abiding, then one would be both an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and a noble one (*ārya*) simultaneously.
If it were attained after they have ceased, why do you not say that one has "already attained" right determination, rather than saying that one "now attains" it?
Answer: It should be said that they have already attained it.
As for why the scriptural text does not say they have already attained it, there are instances where, although attainment has already occurred, the expression "attaining now" is used.
It is as when one asks, "Great King, from where have you come?
This refers to having already come, yet speaks of coming now.
It is the same for one who has already awakened to all sensations, already severed the outflows, and already attained liberation.
Some might say that one should state:
"Attaining right determination immediately [thereafter] is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
The critique says:
What is the difference between attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) without interval and attaining right determination in succession?

Furthermore, some say that although the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen, this supreme dharma (*agradharma*) is determined to serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); therefore, it is said that one now attains right determination.
Some say that attaining right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) sequentially through each of the five faculties is called the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgra-dharma). Question:
Who makes this statement?
Answer: This is the explanation of the old Abhidharma masters. Question:
Why does he say that the five faculties are the supreme worldly dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*)? Answer:
It is not necessarily because he intends for the five faculties to be the supreme worldly dharmas; rather, it is for the purpose of refuting divergent arguments.

The proponents of divergent views, the Vibhajyavādins, state that because the five faculties beginning with faith are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), no ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) possess them at all. Question:
For what reason do they make such a statement?
Answer: He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
When the five faculties are sharp and powerful, fully penetrating and perfected, one is heading toward arhatship;
if one lacks these five faculties, one falls into the category of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Because the Sūtra speaks in this way, it is said that the five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are all untainted (*anāsrava*).
In order to refute such arguments, it is taught that the five faculties, beginning with faith, constitute the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

If these five faculties were untainted (*anāsrava*), then since time immemorial one would never have been able to give rise to even a single thought-moment of the untainted to attain the supreme mundane dharmas; therefore, one should know that the five faculties are not purely untainted.
Furthermore, if the five faculties were untainted (*anāsrava*), it would contradict the Buddha’s authentic scriptures.

As it is said: "If I cannot, regarding the five faculties such as faith, contemplate them as they truly are—in terms of their arising, their cessation, their gratification, their danger, and the renunciation thereof—then I shall not attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," and so on at length; thus, one should not contemplate untainted phenomena by means of such characteristics.
The Vibhajyavādins said: "One should contemplate the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*) by means of such characteristics.
How should they be contemplated?"
As the Sūtra says:
"Those who cannot contemplate the five faculties, such as faith, in accordance with reality, practice the contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
By what means are the five faculties, such as faith, attained?
It is attained by accumulating [merit] through associating with virtuous friends; this is called the contemplation of origination (*samudaya*).
What is the contemplation of cessation (*nirodha*)?
When the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) ceases and the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) arises, this is called the contemplation of cessation.
What is the contemplation of gratification?
This untainted dharma is also a condition for craving; this is called the contemplation of gratification. Question:
Are untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) also bound by craving? Answer: No.
Just as in your doctrine, there are outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) which, though they serve as conditions for latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), do not bind them, so it is with mine.
How does one contemplate their peril?
Because all outflow-free phenomena are devoid of craving, this is called contemplating their peril.
What is the contemplation of relinquishment (*upekṣā*)? When all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are relinquished at the time of nirvāṇa, this is called the contemplation of relinquishment.

To sever such various discourses, it is said that one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in succession through the five faculties; this is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Furthermore, if the five faculties were exclusively untainted (anāsrava), it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said: "With my buddha-eye, I observe that the faculties of sentient beings have superior, middling, and inferior degrees."
The Vibhajyavādins state:
The Buddha’s sūtras declare that those of superior faculties are arhats, those of middling faculties are anāgāmins, and those of inferior faculties are sakṛdāgāmins and srotāpannas.

Pūtimatya said: "If that were so, then the World-Honored One’s not turning the wheel of Dharma would be called 'turning the wheel of Dharma,' for all noble ones would already have filled the world, and the Buddha would have no further need to turn the wheel of Dharma."
The Vibhajyavādins say:

"The reason the World-Honored One spoke of the superior, middling, and inferior faculties of sentient beings was to describe the bases upon which those faculties rely, not to describe the essential nature of the faculties themselves."
Yuktavādin said: "If that were so, it would further contradict this sutra, which states:
'The Brahmin Jātiśroṇa went to where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:'"
"Śramaṇa Gautama! How many faculties (indriya) do you say there are?
The Buddha replied:
There are twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).

Although these are also said to be the bases (*āśraya*) of the faculties, it is impossible that both are equally called "faculties" while one is the basis of a faculty and the other is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of a faculty.
Therefore, the five faculties, such as faith and the others, should be both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*). Question:
How should one interpret the Buddhist sūtras cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
Answer: The five faculties, beginning with faith, are of two kinds:
contaminated (sāsrava) and uncontaminated (anāsrava).
That sutra speaks only of the untainted (anāsrava).
Why is this? It is because the distinctions among noble ones (ārya) are explained by means of their faculties (indriya).
Furthermore, while the five faculties are both with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and without-outflows (*anāsrava*), that sutra speaks only of those without-outflows.
Why is this? Because they take the noble ones (*ārya*) as their counteractive factors (*pratipakṣadharma*), thereby distinguishing the noble ones.
Question: It was stated above that if one lacks the five faculties, one falls into the category of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
How is this to be reconciled? Answer:
Regarding the statement that they "fall into the category of ordinary persons" (*pṛthagjana*), this refers to ordinary persons who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*).
Alternatively, some say it refers to the Vātsīputrīya school's assertion that the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) constitute the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Why is this? Because the five faculties are of a wholesome nature.
Since the five faculties are wholesome, the remaining enumerated factors are also wholesome.
Furthermore, the distinction between noble ones is also established by way of their faculties (*indriya*).
As it is said: "One who possesses sharp and penetrating faculties, who has attained fulfillment, becomes an Arhat," as explained in detail above.
Question: For what reason does the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra cite the tenets established by the Vātsīputrīya school? Answer:

The assertions of that Vātsīputrīya school slightly contradict this sutra, namely: that the five faculties constitute the "highest mundane dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), and that the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is invariably defiled.
For him, the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the truth of suffering in the desire realm constitute the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
There are three kinds of *nirvāṇa*:
that of those in training (*śaikṣa*), that of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
The asuras constitute the sixth realm.
They assert the existence of a self and a person.
Because such groups—whether five or six—contradict this sutra, do not claim that everything taught by those schools is identical to this sutra.
The author of that treatise, in order to refute such a view, subsequently states:

"According to my doctrine, the attainment of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in succession among the various minds and mental factors is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*)."

Question: According to what you have said, if the nature of the five faculties is wholesome while the nature of other mental states and mental factors is not wholesome, they must then be either unwholesome or indeterminate.

If the five faculties are inherently wholesome such that associating with them—even when associated with the unwholesome or the indeterminate—is also called wholesome, then since these five faculties also associate with the unwholesome and the indeterminate, they ought themselves to be unwholesome or indeterminate.

This is not so. Why? Because the faculties and the mind and its mental factors share the same basis, the same mode of activity, the same object of perception, the same fruit, the same support, and the same retribution, collectively accomplishing a single function; yet to claim that their nature is wholesome and thus constitutes "association with the wholesome" is merely a deluded notion.
Some say that those who recite and uphold the Sūtras claim that the five faculties (pañcendriya) constitute the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma). The Venerable Dharmatrāta says:
"The supreme mundane dharma has volition (cetanā) as its essential nature; it is merely a difference in nomenclature."
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"The Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is in its essential nature mind; it is merely a difference in designation. Why is this so?"
The mind of faith is distinct, up to and including the mind of wisdom.
If there were sentient beings who could, at a single moment, sequentially attain right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) by means of these five types of mind, such a thing is impossible;
if they attain right determination one by one in sequence, that is possible.
Question: If that is so, does one attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by means of dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*)? Answer:
"No. Why is this? According to your doctrine, the mind does not associate with the mind;
it takes conditioned phenomena as its object. Because it takes conditioned phenomena as its object, one is able to attain right determination in succession."

My faith is likewise; it does not function as having an object of perception while being dissociated from faith. Because it possesses an object of perception, one successively attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
This applies to wisdom (*prajñā*) as well.
Question: If that were so, there would be a great error. Why is this?

If one could attain right determination through faith alone, without relying on diligence, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom, then those who are indolent, forgetful, distracted, or of poor wisdom should likewise be able to attain right determination in succession; this applies to wisdom as well.
In order to sever such a thought in that person, it is said:
"According to my doctrine, the sequential attainment of right determination regarding all mind and mental factors is the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma' (*laukikāgradharma*)."
According to my own interpretation, it means that which is non-erroneous, conforms to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), accords with the scriptural texts, and aligns with our own intention.
Thus it is said: "When the various minds and mental factors successively attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), this is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*)."
In order to clarify the correct meaning, Kātyāyanīputra states that the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is both a faculty (*indriya*) and not a faculty. Question:
When the highest mundane dharma is present before one, are the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) in the future also cultivated as being that same highest mundane dharma?
Answer: Some say that, according to the original sūtra, it is not the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). Why is this?

The sūtra states that among all mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), those which attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in succession constitute the supreme worldly dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Those [mental states] that are future cannot function in such a succession; therefore, they are not the supreme worldly dharma.
Furthermore, if it were as you claim, it would contradict the original sūtra.
As it is said regarding the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*): one should say it is a single moment of mind, not many moments of mind.
The critique states:
It should be stated thus:
that which is future is also the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Question:
If that which is future cannot act as a *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition), how can it be the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*)?
The answer is:
although that which is future cannot act [as such] in the present, it is capable of acting as a dharma that conforms to and facilitates the sequence.

For example, when a bhikṣu performs the poṣadha ceremony, even if he is not present among the saṃgha, if he grants his consent (*chanda*), it is called "attaining the poṣadha," and the business of the saṃgha is likewise accomplished.
In this same way, that which exists in the future world serves as the attainment of the present, just like one who grants consent;

if there were no attainment of the present within the future world for one who does not grant consent, then the present one could not establish the sequence [of the rite]. One should know that if the sequence is established, it is entirely due to the power of that which is in the future.
Why is this? Because that which is future does not act as an obstacle to the Noble Path.
Furthermore, if that which is future were not the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), it would contradict the scriptural text of the *Jñānaprasthāna* (The Treatise on Knowledge).
Why is this so? Just as a path never before attained now appears before one, so too does one cultivate its corresponding seeds in the future.
If those seeds were not to become the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*) in the future, how could they be called the cultivation of corresponding seeds?
For this reason, that which is future is also the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Question:
If that which is future is the supreme mundane dharma, why does the scriptural text not mention it?
Answer: If they were able to provide the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*), the sūtra would have mentioned them;
since they cannot provide the condition of immediate succession, they are not mentioned.
Furthermore, if it were to circulate through the three periods of time, then one would speak [of it];
however, the future is not so.
Some say that because this dharma arises from causes, is accomplished, and dwells within the body, it is therefore spoken of.
As for those future [dharmas], although they arise from causes and bring about the accomplishment of this dharma, they do not abide within the body;
therefore, they are not mentioned. Question: If that is so, why are they not considered a plurality of minds?
Answer: Here, it is stated that only those present moments capable of accomplishing the task are meant; therefore, it does not refer to a plurality of minds.
Alternatively, some say that it refers to those [moments] which enable cultivation within the future.
It is not so for the future.
Some say: "If a mind is the cause of that [subsequent] mind, and that mind is the effect of this [preceding] mind, it is for this reason that [the relationship] is spoken of;
it is not so for the future."
Some say that [the present] can act as a cause, can grasp a fruit, dwells within the body, and has an object of perception; for these reasons it is so described, whereas the future is not thus.
Some say that there are two meanings of "cultivation" (bhāvanā), and it is for this reason that [the text] speaks [only of certain types].
Regarding those future [dharmas], there is only cultivation by acquisition (pratilambha-bhāvanā) and no cultivation by practice (niṣevaṇa-bhāvanā); therefore, they are not mentioned.
Question: Are the form, mind, and formations dissociated from mind that arise simultaneously with those supreme mundane dharmas themselves considered supreme mundane dharmas?
Answer: No.
Some may say, as stated in the original sutra:
"That is not the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). Why is this so?
Because it cannot serve as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
The critique states:
It should be said that this too is the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: Since that [state] cannot serve as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), why is it called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)? Answer:
Although it cannot serve as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it can conform to the meaning of a sequential condition.

Why is this so? Because it arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the "Highest Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*); they share the same fruit, the same basis, and the same retribution. It is for this reason that it is so described.
Question: If that is indeed the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma), why does the original sūtra not mention it? Answer:
Because it cannot serve as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it is not mentioned.
Alternatively, some say that it is mentioned because, being produced from causes, it accomplishes this dharma and is capable of having an object of cognition (*ālambana*).
Although that [mind] arises from causes and accomplishes this dharma, it cannot possess an object; therefore, it is not mentioned.
Alternatively, some say: if it is associated, it has a basis, has power, has activity, and has an object; for this reason, it is so described.
That is not associated; it has no basis, no power, no activity, and no object. Therefore, it is not so described. Question:
Is that "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgra-dharma) itself considered to be the supreme mundane dharma?
Answer: That is not the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma). Question:
For what reason are arising, abiding, and impermanence considered the "supreme mundane dharmas" (laukikāgradharma), while [the other characteristics] are not?
The answer is:

arising and so forth are a single matter; they share the same fruit as the supreme mundane dharma, they coexist, they are inseparable, they always follow one another, and there is no sequence between them.

If it were so attained, it would not be the case that they share a single fruit, do not function together, are dissociated, do not follow one another, or exist sequentially; nor would they be separable from the dharmas attained, like tree bark separated from a tree. For these reasons, it is not the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).

Question: For what reason is the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya considered to be the fruits of śrāmaṇya themselves, yet the attainment of this "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma) is not itself the supreme mundane dharma?
Answer: It is called the fruit of the śramaṇa because it is attained through accomplishment; thus, attainment itself is the fruit of the śramaṇa.

That which can provide the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and can also accord with the meaning of the condition of immediate succession is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*).

If it were attained, it would not be so; therefore, it is not the "supreme worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), and likewise for the other roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).
Their attainment is not itself a root of goodness conducive to penetration. Why is this?

If "attainment" (prāpti) were identical to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla), then once the fruit of an ārya had been attained, one would have to repeatedly give rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration so that they manifest, because [the fruit] is established through attainment;
yet this is not actually the case. Therefore, attainment is not the roots of goodness conducive to penetration.

Some say that if it arises together with the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), that which is co-nascent is called the supreme mundane dharma, while that which arises later is not; the same applies to the other roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Some say that the acquisition (*prāpti*) of [the aids to penetration] is itself the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), and the acquisition of the remaining roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) is itself those roots of goodness conducive to penetration. Question:
If this were so, then one who has already attained the fruit of an ārya would have to repeatedly arouse the roots of goodness conducive to penetration so that they manifest before them.
Answer: It is either present before one or not present before one. Which is present?
This refers to what is called "attainment" (prāpti).
What does not manifest before one?
It refers to all associated mental factors (saṃprayuktadharma).
The critique says:
One should not speak in such a manner; it is better as previously stated. Question:
How many foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) does the supreme mundane dharma (laukikāgradharma) comprise?
The answer is:
one foundation of mindfulness of dharmas (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) in the present, which has the nature of perishing objects; four in the future.
Question: How many conditions (pratyaya) does the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) possess? Answer:
It serves as four conditions:
as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is the associated and co-existent causes;
as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it acts as the immediate antecedent for the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
The objective condition refers to that which is the focal object of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*);
the dominant condition refers to all other phenomena, excluding its own self-nature, as being the conditions from which those [patience and knowledge] arise.
Regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), there are also four conditions:
the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) consists of the associated and co-existent dharmas;
the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm;
regarding the dominant-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it consists of all phenomena except for its own self-nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, according to another interpretation, what is called the "supramundane supreme dharma" (*lokottara-agradharma*)?
The answer is:
It is the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). Why is this so?
Because it is the seed of the noble path.
Furthermore, some say that the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is [the basis]. Why is this so?
Because it is able to exhaust all fetters and attain the ultimate fruit.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*). Why is this so?
This is because, at the moment one first attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), all other untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) are purified and cultivated.
Furthermore, some say it is right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*). Why is this so?
Because it attains the most excellent right concentration within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, some say that it is *nirvāṇa*. Why is this so?
Because it is the most wondrous and supreme among all dharmas.
Furthermore, some say it is the final mind of an arhat. Why is this?
The final mind of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is called the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*); the final mind of an Arhat is called the "supreme supramundane dharma.
Critique: One should not speak in this way.
Because that final mind of an Arhat is not a supramundane dharma;
thus, what was stated previously is correct. Question:

Is there any "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) that does not serve as the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the "receptivity to the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*)? Answer:
Yes, there is.
The supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) consists of form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and dissociated factors (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*).

Question: Is there any associated factor (*saṃprayuktadharma*) that does not serve as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmakṣānti*)?
Answer: There is.
It refers to that which is cultivated in the future.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"If one attains right determination through faith, this is called the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma' (laukikāgra-dharma) acting as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) for the 'Dharma-patience regarding suffering' (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti);

whereas other minds characterized by diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are also called the 'Supreme Mundane Dharma,' yet they do not act as the immediately preceding condition for the Dharma-patience regarding suffering."
The śramaṇa who propounds the doctrine of resemblance says:
"Feeling (vedanā) acts as the immediate antecedent condition for feeling, but not for perception (saṃjñā) and the other factors; the same applies to the remaining enumerated dharmas.
When mental states arise, they do so upon encountering their respective conditions."

If, through craving for a preceding object, a pleasant feeling arises, there is a desire for what is perceived, which gives rise to perception; there is a desire for what is to be done, which gives rise to volition.
Question: If this is so, there is no sense of a corresponding sequential order.
Answer: There are,
but they do not follow a single, sequential order.

In your doctrine, when beings of the non-percipient realm are born, the mind ceases at birth and arises at death; although these two moments of the perception of "going" are distant, they can still form a sequence.
My doctrine is likewise: for example, when feeling ceases and perception arises, and then feeling arises again, although these stages are distant from one another, they can still form a sequence.
The critique states:
One should not speak in this way.

It is not that mind acts as a sequential condition for mind, nor that feeling acts as a sequential condition for feeling; rather, each individual mental state and its associated mental factors arise one after another, acting as sequential conditions for one another.
If one were to speak thus, it would contradict the scriptural text, which asks:
"What are the mental factors that follow in succession?"
Answer: It refers to the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*).
If that were so, there would be yet another fault.

For example, when one enters the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra by relying on the samādhi with vitarka and with vicāra, the samādhi with vitarka and with vicāra should not serve as the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) for the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, because they are dissimilar;
thus, the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra does not arise from an immediately preceding condition.

If it were likewise when one enters the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought by relying on the samādhi without applied thought and without sustained thought, then there would be no liberation. Why is this?

If a mind associated with desire gives rise only to a subsequent mind associated with desire, then contemplations such as the meditation on impurity and other wholesome minds would have no means of arising; if wholesome minds do not arise, there can be no liberation.
Since there are such faults as those previously mentioned, it is better to follow what was said before.
Why is it called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*)? [Question: Why is it so named?
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:

although the essential nature of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) was previously explained, the reason why it is named the "supreme mundane dharma" had not yet been stated; it is for the purpose of explaining that now.
It is just as when someone is praised by the world as "superior," yet it is not known whether they are called superior on account of their lineage, wealth, power, or retinue;
so it is with this person as well, for whom we now wish to explain why he is named "Supreme in the World."

Regarding the term "foremost": because this mind and its mental factors are the most supreme, the most excellent, the longest, the most venerable, the highest, and the most wondrous among all other phenomena, they are called "foremost" on account of such meanings.
Question: When it is said that this is "foremost," does it mean it is preeminent in all worldly dharmas, or preeminent in some respect?
If it were preeminent in all respects, then it would not surpass the knowledge pertaining to the limit of seeing the truths (*satyadarśana-bhāgīya-jñāna*).

Why is this? Because their wisdom and vision are inseparable from the attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and because the power of their wisdom is preeminent; thus, in all cases of the path of seeing, the power of wisdom is predominant.
Furthermore, they also do not surpass those who have cultivated the refined dhyānas through purification (*viśuddha-bhāvanā-dhyāna*).
Why is this? Because those who cultivate the *saṃskṛta-dhyāna* (conditioned meditations) are not born in the same place as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, they do not surpass all roots of goodness at the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Why is this? Because at the time one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the roots of goodness cultivated thereby are forever free from all defilements and hindrances.

Furthermore, those [roots] are not superior to the samādhi of emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*), the samādhi of wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitā-apraṇihita-samādhi*), or the samādhi of signlessness-of-signlessness (*animittā-animitta-samādhi*).

Why is this? Because even the samādhi of emptiness within emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*) and so forth are disparaged as being untainted (*anāsrava*), let alone those that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
If one were to distinguish degrees of excellence, then the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), and Patience (*kṣānti*) should also be called supreme.
