Answer: It is not so. Why is this?

"Heat" (ūṣmagata) refers to that which belongs to the stages of cultivation and meditative concentration within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), is subsumed under the practice of the noble path, and gives rise to faith, affection, and reverence for the True Dharma and the Vinaya.
That which is the True Dharma (saddharma) is said to be faith conditioned by the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
The Vinaya is said to be faith conditioned by the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasatya).
It is asked:
The "Heat" stage is able to take the Four Truths as its object; why, then, is it said that it only takes faith in the Truths of Cessation and the Path?
The answer is:
some say that because Cessation and the Path are the most excellent among the Truths, this should be answered in detail as was previously done for the "Summits."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are objects worthy of taking refuge, they are so described.

Others say that the True Dharma (*saddharma*) is taught as having faith conditioned by the three truths, while the Vinaya is taught as having faith conditioned by the truth of cessation; this too is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), which is able to take the four truths as its object.
The author of that treatise cites a sūtra as proof, stating:
"The Buddha told the bhikṣus Aśvajit and Pūrṇamāsa:
'I have a Dharma of four lines which I shall now explain to you.'"
"Do you wish to know?
You may ask whatever you desire. The two men said:
"We are now, as it were, unfit vessels; what use is there in knowing this?
and so forth, as explained at length. He asked:
The Buddha knew deeply that this person was incapable of receiving the Dharma; for what reason, then, did he say, "I shall let you have your way"?
The answer is:
some explain that people thought this person had no teacher to instruct him, and therefore committed various evils and brought about his own ruin.
Therefore, the Tathāgata raised his hand and said:
"That which I ought to do, I have now completed; yet you have brought about your own ruin through your own perverse conduct. This is not the fault of my failure to instruct you."
Furthermore, there are those who say that it was in order to stop the slanders of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) that the Tathāgata told them, "You may speak as you please.
Had the Tathāgata not spoken thus to them, the various non-Buddhists would have slandered him in this way:

"How can one who possesses great compassion preach the Dharma and provide instruction to some among his disciples while following their inclinations, yet fail to preach the Dharma or instruct those who do not follow his inclinations?"
If the Tathāgata were to address those people directly, the various non-Buddhists would not give rise to slander.
Furthermore, there are those who say it was in order to stop the lack of faith among the Śākyas.
If the Tathāgata had not informed them, at that time the Śākyas would have conceived a lack of faith, wondering:
"Why does Siddhārtha not preach the Dharma and provide instruction for his own kinsmen?"
Out of envy, they feared that the person might become equal to themselves.
If the Tathāgata were to speak to that person, the Śākyas would then no longer harbor any thoughts of disbelief.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "That person has practiced unwholesome conduct himself; the Tathāgata takes that very person as a witness and says to him:
'Whether you were formerly at home or now have gone forth, it was you who practiced unwholesome conduct; this is not my fault.'"
At that time, the Tathāgata rebuked him directly with gentle words, saying, "Therefore, I tell you: let your mind be as it wishes.

Furthermore, some say that this was for the sake of generating the roots of goodness in that person for the future; the Buddha knew that although this person could not yet be transformed at present, he would certainly give rise to the roots of goodness of repentance in the future.
Why is this? That person thinks: "That Greatly Compassionate One allows me to act according to my own will, yet I do not accept it; this is not the fault of the Tathāgata."
Being able to produce such roots of goodness through repentance, by virtue of these conditions, they will certainly emerge from the evil realms.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: the Buddha knows that when this person’s life ends here, they will necessarily be reborn among the nāgas and undergo great suffering; he then thinks:
"From where did I originally come to be born in this place?"
He realized for himself that he had originally left the household life to enter the Buddha-dharma. Then he thought:
"There is no one to transform me; I should now go and perform acts of harm, destroying the stūpas and various monasteries, and killing the bhikṣus."
At that time, through the supernatural power of the Buddha, an image of the Tathāgata will stand before them and say:
"Aśvajit and Pūrṇamāsa!
I have a Dharma of four lines; do you wish to know it?"
"You should know that this present suffering is your own fault, not my blame.
That which I ought to have done, I have already done; yet you now engage in your own perverse conduct."
Because he wished to stop the dragon’s entanglement of anger and cause him to protect the Buddha-dharma, he said to him, "I shall grant you your wish.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"What is meant by the 'four-line dharma'?"
Answer: Some say it is the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Why is this?
Because those two did not perceive the Truths, they committed these evil deeds.
Furthermore, some say it was the four foundations of mindfulness. Why is this?
Those two committed these evil deeds because of their inverted views.
Furthermore, there are those who say it was the four right efforts (*samyakpradhāna*). Why is this?
Those two individuals committed these evil deeds because they were largely indolent.
Furthermore, there are those who say it was the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Why is this?
Those two individuals were unable to accumulate various virtues and therefore committed these evil deeds.
Furthermore, some say that it was the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*). Why is this so?
Those two individuals committed these evil deeds because of their greedy attachment to gain and offerings.
Furthermore, there are those who say it refers to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya. Why is this?
Those two individuals did not actually attain the status of śramaṇas, yet they claimed, "I have attained the four fruits of the śramaṇa," and thus committed this evil deed.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the four excellences are: first, excellence in knowing the elements (dhātu); second, excellence in knowing the sense bases (āyatana); third, excellence in knowing dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); and fourth, excellence in knowing what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna).
Why is this? Because those two individuals were ignorant of cause and effect, they committed such evil deeds.
Furthermore, there is another explanation, as stated in a verse from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*:
"In the Dharma of the Noble Ones, well-spoken words are supreme; second, one should always speak words of affection and avoid those that are unlovely;
third, one should always speak truthful words and remain free from falsehood; fourth, one should always speak words in accordance with the Dharma and avoid those that are contrary to the Dharma."
These are called the four.
Furthermore, there are those who say, as stated in the *Ekottarika Āgama*:
non-greed, non-anger, right mindfulness, and right concentration—these are called the four.
He spoke thus: "What use have I now for knowing this Dharma?
The World-Honored One replied:
"You foolish people, you have abandoned my Dharma, to the point that not even a slight degree of the 'warmth' stage of dharma remains.
He asked: "Why did those two people speak in such a manner?"
"What use have I now for knowing this Dharma?
He replied:

"Some say that such a person knows for themselves that they are not a vessel for the Dharma; since they are not even a vessel for proceeding toward the good realms, how much less could they be a vessel for proceeding toward Nirvana?"

Furthermore, there are those who say: "Because various evil deeds have repeatedly violated the prohibitions within this body, I know for myself that this body is not a vessel for the Dharma; even if one could cause sprouts to grow from tiles or stones, this body of mine can never give rise to the factors of the Dharma of liberation."
Furthermore, some say it is because that person has already performed determinate karma (*niyata-karman*).

Others say it is because that person is close to the dharma of experiencing the fruit of retribution; the signs of retribution in the evil realms have already appeared before them, such that even water flows from their ten fingers.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha has prophesied that such a person shall attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
They think to themselves:
"Why trouble the Tathāgata by preaching the Dharma for my sake? In this present life, I will ultimately never be able to enter into the state of right determination."
For these and other such reasons, they say:
"What use have we now for knowing this Dharma?
The World-Honored One replied:
Those foolish people who distance themselves from my Dharma do not possess even a slight degree of the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) within my True Dharma and Vinaya.
It is asked:
There are many types of Vinaya; [which one is meant here?]

There is the Vinaya of time, the Vinaya of method, the Vinaya of lineage, the Vinaya of family law, the Vinaya of penalizing offenses, the Vinaya of transgressions, the Vinaya of clarity, the Vinaya of the noble ones, and the Vinaya regarding desire, hatred, and delusion.
In this context, what is meant by "vinaya"?
The answer is:
some say that what is taught here is the noble vinaya (ārya-vinaya).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this section explains the discipline (*vinaya*) regarding desire, hatred, and delusion.
It is asked:
Are all those who have not attained the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) identical to Aśvalāyana and Pūrṇa?
Answer: Not all.
There are generally three kinds of sentient beings:
First, the mind with expectation;
second, the mind free from expectation;
third, the mind that has severed expectation.
Those with a fixed resolve are those who maintain the precepts with purity.
Those who have removed their fixed resolve are Arhats who have completed what was to be done.
Those who have severed their fixed resolve are those who violate the precepts.
Because he lacked both the intention to aspire and the intention to eliminate, but possessed only the intention to sever, the World-Honored One rebuked him.
Other sentient beings who possess the intention to sever are likewise the same as him.
As it is said:
"There is not even the slightest dharma of warmth. Question:
This root of goodness of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is most excellent and subtle, abiding in a state of tranquility; why, then, is it now said to be "small"?
The answer is:
because among the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), it is the most minute, and for that reason it is called small.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because these are produced at the very end of the accumulation of wholesome roots of the view-aggregate, they are called "a small portion of the view-aggregate's wholesome roots"; this refers to ānāpāna, the meditation on impurity, and the four foundations of mindfulness.

These four kinds of roots of goodness—namely, the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma)—are called the factors conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya); they are also called the contemplation of the truths (satyadarśana), the cultivation and purification (parikarman), and the roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).

Regarding the term "penetration-factor" (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*): the untainted noble path is "penetration. These roots of goodness conform to that dharma, serve as its wings, and constitute a portion of the nature of that dharma; therefore, they are called "penetration-factors."
"Contemplating the Truths" means observing and scrutinizing the truths through the modes of impermanence and so forth; thus it is called "contemplating the Truths.
"Cultivating" means cultivating for the sake of seeking the Noble Path and its fruits, so that this body may be cleared of impurities and defects to serve as a vessel for the Dharma.
It is just as a farmer, seeking the fruit of grain, cultivates the field and removes the weeds;
he is likewise so described, and thus it is called "cultivation.
As for the term "wholesome roots," the noble path is called "wholesome" and nirvana is called the "fruit."
These dharmas are the primary foundation upon which that [path] is first established; therefore, they are called "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). Question:
What is the distinction between these roots of goodness, such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and the others?
The answer is:

The stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) can suppress the delusions regarding the supremacy of the truths as objects, and even suppress the delusions within one’s own continuum; therefore, it gives rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Furthermore, some say that the stage of Heat can produce the lower degree of clear insight (*prajñā*) directed toward the truths as objects, and even produce the clear insight directed toward the truths within one’s own continuum; therefore, it gives rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma.

Furthermore, the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) gives rise to inferior faith regarding the truths; the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*) gives rise to middling faith; and the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*) gives rise to superior faith.
Because this faith exists within the body, one is able to give rise to the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).

Furthermore, the stage of Heat (ūṣmagata) brings about satisfaction regarding the aggregates (skandha), and because it brings about satisfaction even within the body, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) arises.

Others say that Heat is the locus where the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) enter; the Summit (mūrdhan) is the locus where Heat enters; Patience (kṣānti) is the locus where the Summit enters; and the Supreme Mundane Dharma is the locus where Patience enters.
In this same sequence, the uninterrupted [attainments] are likewise.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"Of these roots of goodness, two belong to the desire realm, namely, Heat and Summits."
The second is the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), namely patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
The critique states:

one should not speak thus; because these belong to the form realm, they are fixed stages and stages of cultivation, and are dharmas subsumed under that which can practice the noble path (*āryacaryā*).
It is well said thus. Question:
How many kinds of the stage of "Heat" (uṣmagata) are there?
Up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), how many types are there?
The answer is:
some say that the Heat-dharmas (*uṣmagata*) are of three types, namely: the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*), the middle-of-the-low (*mṛdu-madhya*), and the highest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-adhimātra*).
The dharmas of the summit (mūrdhan-dharma) are of three kinds:
medium-low, medium-middle, and medium-high.
Patience (kṣānti) is of two kinds:
There are three grades: lower, middle, and upper.
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) consist of one grade, namely the upper-upper.

Regarding these four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in terms of the three grades: "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) is the lower, "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) is the middle, and "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" are the upper.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) is of two kinds:

namely, the lower-of-the-low (*adhamādhamā*) and the lower-of-the-middle (*adhamamadhyamā*). "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) are of three kinds: namely, the lower-of-the-high (*adhamottamā*), the middle-of-the-low (*madhyamadhamā*), and the middle-of-the-middle (*madhyamadhyamā*).
The Dharma of Patience (kṣānti) is of three kinds:
namely, medium-superior, superior-inferior, and superior-medium.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is of one kind: namely, superior-superior.

Regarding these roots of goodness, expressed in three grades: *uṣmagata* (heat) is the lower; *mūrdhan* (summit) is the lower-middle; *kṣānti* (patience) is the middle-upper; and *laukikāgradharma* (the supreme mundane dharma) is the upper.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says: "Heat is of three kinds:"
The lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low.
Regarding the "summit" (mūrdhan), there are six types:
from the lowest-of-the-low up to the middle-of-the-high.
There are eight types of patience (*kṣānti*):
from the lowest-of-the-low up to the medium-of-the-high.
The single category of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is called the highest-of-the-high.
If expressed in terms of three levels: the single stage of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) is considered "inferior";
the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) has two types, namely "inferior" and "intermediate."
Patience (*kṣānti*) is of three kinds, namely: inferior, middling, and superior;
the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are of one kind, namely the superior. One who attains the Dharma of Heat (*uṣmagata*) also abandons [the previous stages].
There are two kinds of relinquishment:
relinquishment at the time of departing from a realm or stage, and relinquishment at the time of falling back.
Regarding relinquishment at the time of falling back: by committing an act of immediate retribution, one is able to sever the roots of goodness and also fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, what further benefit is there?
It has already become the definitive cause for nirvāṇa, like the method of swallowing a hook and bait.
One also abandons the attainment of the *mūrdhan* stage; there are two kinds of abandonment:
[It is abandoned] at the time of departing from a realm or stage, and at the time of falling away.
As for those who abandon it at the time of falling away, they commit an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*) and likewise fall into the evil destinies.
What further beneficial result could there be?
Furthermore, they do not sever their roots of goodness.
If that were so, would Devadatta not have attained the stage of the "Summit" (mūrdhan)?
As it is said in a verse:
"One who receives offerings without virtue is called a mere ordinary person;
one who forgets all that is wholesome is called 'fallen from the summit.
How should this verse be interpreted?"
Answer: This explains that one may fall away from attainment.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because the World-Honored One is like a crown, one who directs an evil mind toward the Buddha falls into the evil realms; therefore, it is called "falling from the crown."
One who has attained *kṣānti* also relinquishes [the roots of goodness], and there is one way of relinquishing them: at the time of transcending the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*).
When relinquishing those roots of goodness, there is no falling back; one does not commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), nor does one sever the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, what further benefit is there?
One does not fall into the evil realms.

Even the attainment of the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) is abandoned; there is one way it is abandoned: when one leaves the realm (*dhātu*) or the stage (*bhūmi*), it is abandoned without falling back.

Why is this so? Because the nature of these roots of goodness is non-retrogressive; one will not commit an act of immediate retribution, will not sever the roots of goodness, and will not fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, what other beneficial advantages are there?
He attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in succession.
Furthermore, there are those who say that even the "heat" stage (*uṣmagata*) may be relinquished; there are two ways in which it is relinquished:
when one leaves the specific level (*bhūmi*) and when one undergoes regression (*parihāṇi*).
Regarding those who abandon [the path] at the time of regression: even if they commit an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), they still fall into the evil realms.
What further beneficial merit do they possess?
Only that they have not severed their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
If that were the case, Devadatta would not have attained the stage of "warmth" (ūṣmagata).
Why? Because he had severed his roots of goodness (kuśalamūla).
One also relinquishes the attainment of the *mūrdhan* (Summits). There are two kinds of relinquishment:
at the time of leaving the earth element (*bhūmi*) and at the time of falling back (*parihāṇi*).
One who relinquishes it at the time of falling back falls into the evil destinies (*durgati*).
Furthermore, what further benefits are there?
One does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and does not sever the roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*).
One also attains patience (*kṣānti*) and relinquishes it; there is one kind of relinquishment, which occurs at the time of departing from a realm (*dhātu*) or stage (*bhūmi*).
Those roots of goodness do not regress; they do not commit the deeds of immediate retribution, they do not sever their roots of goodness, and they do not fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, what other beneficial qualities are there?
They are not stained by attachment to a self.
Question: If that were so, Śrīgupta, Aṅgulimāla, and Sañjayin Vairaṭīputra would not have attained patience. Why is this?
[The opponent asks: "Because of being stained by attachment to a self.
[The respondent] answers:
"They are not stained by attachment to a self; they merely speak of a 'self' for the sake of philosophical discourse."
Question: Since he engages in competitive debate with the Tathāgata regarding the self (*ātman*), how can it be said that he is not attached to the self? Answer:
Because he has not yet severed the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it may temporarily manifest before him, though this is not an instance of defiled attachment.
The attainment of the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) is also abandoned; they are abandoned when one leaves the realm (*dhātu*) or stage (*bhūmi*). The rest is as previously explained.

The people of the West have composed this treatise to address the following points concerning the "warmth" (*uṣmagata*) roots of goodness: What is their underlying intention? Upon what do they rely? What are their causes? With what phenomena do they take as conditions? What are their fruits? What is their support? What is their retribution? What are their wholesome benefits? How many types of practice do they involve? Do they arise by taking names as conditions, or do they originate by taking meanings as conditions? Are they the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), or the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*)? Are they bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), or are they bound to the form or formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*)? Are they accompanied by vitarka and vicāra (*savitarka-savicāra*), without vitarka but with vicāra (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), or without both vitarka and vicāra (*avitarka-avicāra*)?

Is it associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), or is it associated with the faculties of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) or equanimity (*upekṣendriya*); is it a single mind or many minds; is it subject to regression or non-regression? This applies even up to the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). It is likewise for these.
Question: What is the intended meaning of "heat" (uṣmagata)? Answer:
The intention is that all roots of goodness—from generosity and ethical discipline up to the highest degree of patience—are entirely dedicated toward liberation.
As for what they rely upon, they arise based on the meditative concentrations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-samādhi*).
As for what the causes and conditions are: the previously arisen wholesome roots within one’s own stage (*svabhūmi*) are the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
As for what phenomena they take as objects: they take the Four Noble Truths as their objects. As for what the fruits are:
the "Summits" (*mūrdhan*) are proximate to the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); this is the fruit of effort (*prayoga-phala*).
As for what it relies upon: it relies on its own stage (*svabhūmi*) and similar states; the wholesome dharmas that arise subsequently are its *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit).
As for what its retribution is: it consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
Regarding "what beneficial virtues there are": some say they are the definitive cause of *nirvāṇa*;
others say they are that which does not sever the roots of goodness (*akuśalamūla*).
Regarding "practicing how many practices": practicing the sixteen practices serves as the condition; this is called "arising as a condition."
Regarding that which arises from meaning, it should be said to arise conditioned by meaning.
As for whether it is the wisdom of hearing, reflection, or cultivation, it should be said to be the wisdom of cultivation.
Regarding its connection to the desire, form, or formless realms, it should be said to be connected to the form realm.

Regarding those states that possess both vitarka and vicāra, those that lack vitarka but possess vicāra, and those that lack both vitarka and vicāra, they should be said to consist of the three types of formations (*saṃskāra*).
With which faculties (*indriya*) are they associated?
It should be said that they are associated with the three [faculties], as appropriate for each case.
Regarding whether it is a single mind or many minds, one should say it consists of many minds.
Regarding whether it is subject to regression or non-regression, one should say it is the patience that may regress.
As for its proximity to the "summit" (*mūrdhan*), this is the fruit of effortful application.
What beneficial advantages are there in the *mūrdhan* (Summits)?
Some say that one does not sever the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Others say that one does not commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*). The rest is as explained regarding the *uṣmagata* (Heat).
The Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*) are proximate to Patience (*kṣānti*) as its fruit of effort.
What beneficial advantage does Patience possess?
Possessing this beneficial advantage, one does not fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "One is neither defiled by attachment to a self nor does one regress; the rest is as with the 'Summit' stage.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma takes suffering as its object, and the Receptivity to the Dharma of Suffering is its fruit of effortful application.
What are the beneficial virtues of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*)?

One successively attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and practices the four modes of conduct; it should be said that one’s mind is non-retrogressive in a single moment, while the remaining aspects are as in the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*).

When the stage of the Dharma of Heat (*ūṣmagata*) arises: if one takes the Truths of Suffering, Origination, or the Path as objects, there is one present application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and four future applications of mindfulness are cultivated; there is one present practice (*ākāra*) and four future practices are cultivated, taking those of the same nature and not of a different nature.

If one takes the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) as the object, there is one present application of mindfulness and one future application of mindfulness is cultivated; there is one present practice and four future practices are cultivated.

When increasing the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), if one increases the middle stage by means of the lower stage, or the upper stage by means of the middle stage, and takes the Truths of Suffering, Origin, or Path as objects: the four present applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) manifest successively, and the four future ones [also manifest]; there is one present category and sixteen future categories. If one takes the Truth of Cessation as the object:
the present application of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) manifests, and the four future ones [also manifest]; there is one present category and sixteen future categories.

Question: For what reason, when first producing the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), does one cultivate that which is of the same nature (*sabhāga*) in the future, and not that which is of a different nature?
When increasing the stage of heat, why does one cultivate both that which is of the same nature and that which is of a different nature in the future?
Answer: At the time of initial birth, one attains [the path] by practicing the contemplation of the truths while not yet having obtained those seeds;
at the time of growth, one attains it by practicing the contemplation of the truths while already having obtained those seeds. Therefore, it is practiced fully.

At the moment of first arising at the crown, one contemplates suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; there is one present application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and four future ones, one present mental application (manasikāra) and sixteen future ones.

When increasing, the lower degree increases the middle, and the middle increases the upper. If one takes the truths of suffering, origin, or the path as objects, the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) manifest successively: in the present there is one, and in the future there are four; in the present there is one application (ākāra), and in the future there are sixteen.

If one takes the truth of cessation as the object, in the present there is the single foundation of mindfulness of dharmas, and in the future there are four; in the present there is one application, and in the future there are sixteen.

At the time of the initial arising of patience (*kṣānti*) and during its increase, there is one present foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), namely that of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), and four future ones; there is one present application of mindfulness (*manaskāra*), and sixteen future ones.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:

At the time of the initial patience, if it takes as its object the truths of suffering (*duḥkha*), origin (*samudaya*), or the path (*mārga*), there is one present foundation of mindfulness of phenomena and four future ones; there is one present application of mindfulness and four future ones; these are cultivated as being of the same nature, not of a different nature.

If one takes the Truth of Cessation as an object, there is one application of mindfulness on phenomena in the present and one application of mindfulness on phenomena in the future; there is one path-component in the present and four in the future, cultivated as being of the same nature rather than of different natures.

If, at the time of increase, one takes the truths of suffering, origin, and the path as objects, the four foundations of mindfulness manifest successively: four in the future and one application of mindfulness in the present; sixteen in the future and one application of mindfulness in the present.

If one takes the truth of cessation as the object, there is one foundation of mindfulness in the present (the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena) and four in the future; one application of mindfulness in the present and sixteen in the future.
The critique says:
He should not make such a statement; it is better as previously stated. Question:
For what reason do the applications of mindfulness regarding phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) manifest at all times during the stage of acceptance (kṣānti)?
The answer is:
Just as the applications of mindfulness regarding phenomena manifest at all times during the path of seeing the truths (satyadarśanamārga), so too is it for acceptance.
Question: When increasing patience (*kṣānti*), does one cultivate all sixteen aspects (*ākāra*)? Answer:
"No. Just as the objects of focus are gradually eliminated, so too are the modes of activity (*ākāra*).

If one takes the Four Noble Truths as objects, there are sixteen modes; if one takes three truths as objects, there are twelve modes; if one takes two truths as objects, there are eight modes; and if one takes one truth as an object, there are four modes. When these are combined within the momentum generated by a single patience (*kṣānti*), there are sixteen."
Question: For what reason does the cultivation of the increase of patience consist of sixteen, twelve, eight, or four modes? Answer:

Gradually eliminating the objects of focus and gradually eliminating the spheres of activity, one draws closer to attaining right determination; for this reason, at times one cultivates sixteen aspects, or even as few as four.

When the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) arises, there is one present application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and four future ones; there is one present practice (*carita*) and four future ones.

Question: Since the Supreme Mundane Dharma has previously acquired those seeds through the practice of contemplating the Truths (*satya*), why is it that the cultivation of its homogeneous practice (*samānajātīyacarita-bhāvanā*) is not different from its nature?
Answer: One cultivates this very dharma according to what has been attained by that person.
It is like a person who is naked; there is no clothing left to be taken away.
It is the same for that as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is closest to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*); just as within the Path of Seeing one does not cultivate other practices but cultivates only that which is of the same nature, so too it is with the Supreme Mundane Dharma."
Question: When one generates heat (*uṣmagata*) up to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), is there constant continuity or no continuity? Answer:

Some say that it constantly and continuously takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, just as the fifteen moments of mind within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) constantly and continuously manifest.
When those levels of Heat (ūṣmagata) arise, they also constantly and continuously take the Four Noble Truths as their objects.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this principle is not fixed, being either continuous or non-continuous.
Some may cease by taking warmth as their object while focusing on suffering; others may cease by taking origination, cessation, or the path as their objects.
Question: By correctly contemplating and reflecting upon what dharma can one subsequently generate "warmth" (ūṣmagata)? Answer:

This is the mind of the stage of cultivation and the stage of meditative concentration within the form realm; it possesses weariness and detachment, disdain, yearning and aspiration, and a lack of compliance with the force of birth, being without delight.

When such right reflection occurs, it is followed by the arising of "heat" (ūṣmagata); from heat arises "summit" (mūrdhan); from the summit arises "patience" (kṣānti); from patience arises the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma); and from the supreme mundane dharma, one subsequently attains "right determination" (samyaktva-niyāma).
Question: If this may be so for one who is free from desire, how is it for one who is not? Answer:
The same applies to one who is not free from desire.

For one with the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) belonging to the desire realm, through correct contemplation and reflection taking the practice of asceticism (*duṣkara-caryā*) as its object, the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) arises in succession from that ascetic practice; the rest is as explained above.

Question: Suppose one has produced the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) in previous lives but has not yet produced the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), and then passes away. In this present life, one wishes to produce the stage of "Summit. Will one immediately produce the stage of "Summit," or will one instead give rise to the stage of "Heat" once more?
The answer is:
Some say that if one hears the *mūrdhan* (Summit) Dharma from a teacher in its proper sequence, one proceeds directly from the Summit;
if the teacher does not explain it, one returns to arise from the Foundation (*mūla*).

Question: If that is so, why is it said that "Heat" (ūṣmagata) gives rise to "Summits" (mūrdhan), "Summits" give rise to "Patience" (kṣānti), and "Patience" gives rise to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma)? Answer:
One who speaks thus refers to one for whom [the roots] arise sequentially within a single lifetime;
or, it refers to one who previously attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) in a former life and now brings it forth from its fundamental basis.

Question: If one has previously attained the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) in a former life, and now wishes to produce the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) in this present life, what kind of correct contemplation and reflection should one perform? Answer:
Just as with the correct contemplation of "warmth," so it is with the "summit.
Just as the summit arises, so too does patience arise. Question:
If the dharma of "warmth" (uṣmagata) arises, does it lead to the abandonment of desire?
The answer is:
some say that it does not lead to the abandonment of desire.

Why is this? Because that practitioner delights in [the former], they would rather give rise to the *mūrdhan* (Summits) dharma than fail to produce the *kṣānti* (Patience) of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Furthermore, some say that if the practitioner knows themselves to have the power to produce the *mūrdhan*, they will immediately produce it.
Knowing myself to be powerless and unable to reach the Summit, I desire to attain freedom from desire.
Why is this? If I attain freedom from desire, the place where I am reborn will become even more excellent.
Question: If one gives rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) based on the fundamental stages (*maulabhūmi*), is there retrogression?
Answer: [There is.]
Some say that there is falling back from the stages of Heat and Summits, but not from Patience.
Why? Because these roots of goodness are of a nature that does not fall back.
The critique states:
He should not make such a statement. Why is this?

If one gives rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) based on the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*), one attains right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) in that very lifetime.
Why is this? Because all these roots of goodness are entirely for the purpose of giving rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*).
If one relies on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) stage, this is not fixed.
A question is asked:

If one gives rise to the stage of *uṣmagata* (heat) by relying on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, and likewise gives rise to the stages of *mūrdhan* (summit), *kṣānti* (patience), and *laukikāgradharma* (supreme mundane dharmas), does one attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)?

Answer: Some say that if one relies on the *anāgamya* dhyāna to produce the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the stage of "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The same applies to the first dhyāna through the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one gives rise to the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*) based on the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), one subsequently gives rise to the first dhyāna, as well as Heat, Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), thereby attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The same applies to the intermediate dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one relies on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) dhyāna to produce *uṣmagata* (heat) and *mūrdhan* (summits), and subsequently produces the first dhyāna, followed by the summits, patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
The same applies to the intermediate dhyāna, the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one generates *uṣmagata*, *mūrdhan*, and *kṣānti* by relying on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, one subsequently generates the first dhyāna; from *kṣānti* arises the *laukikāgra-dharma*, whereby one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and this continues likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
This explains the sequential dharma for śrāvakas.
Question: What about the bodhisattva?
The answer is:

According to one view, a bodhisattva relies on the fourth dhyāna to produce the stage of heat (*uṣmagata*), and so forth, up to producing the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), thereby attaining right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that a bodhisattva relies on the first dhyāna to produce the stages of heat, the summit (*mūrdhan*), and patience (*kṣānti*); it is the same for the second and third dhyānas; and within the fourth dhyāna, they produce heat, the summit, patience, and the supreme mundane dharma, thereby attaining right determination.

Question: Just as within the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya), one should not successively produce the lower-superior or the middle-inferior, how is it that a bodhisattva is able to produce them?
The answer is:
It cannot [function] within its own stage, but it can function in other stages.
Furthermore, there are those who say that, in order to avoid such faults, one should state as follows:

If, relying on the first dhyāna, one generates the stage of Heat (uṣmagata) up to the fourth dhyāna; or if, relying on the first dhyāna, one generates the stage of Summits (mūrdhan) up to the fourth dhyāna; or if, relying on the first dhyāna, one generates the stage of Patience (kṣānti) up to the fourth dhyāna; then, immediately thereafter, one generates the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) and attains right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement; it is better as previously stated. Why is this so?

All Bodhisattvas rely entirely upon the fourth dhyāna to give rise to the stage of "heat" (ūṣmagata), and so on, up to the arising of the "supreme mundane dharma" (laukikāgradharma), thereby attaining right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).
Question: How is it for Pratyekabuddhas?
Answer: One should know that when a Pratyekabuddha appears in the world alone, he is like a Buddha.
However, if many appear together, this is not fixed, and they are the same as Śrāvakas.
Just as the kakudha deer is born with a single horn, so too is he.
One who appears alone in the world should be known as being like the Buddha. Question:
Did the Bodhisattva in his previous lives ever produce the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*)?
The answer is:
some say that he did produce them; for it is by the power of these roots conducive to penetration that the Bodhisattva did not fall into the evil realms for ninety-one *kalpas*.
"This is a root of goodness conducive to penetration that belongs to another nature, not one's own nature.
Evaluation: One should not speak thus; rather, one should speak as follows:
A bodhisattva has never produced roots of goodness belonging to the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). Why is this?

All the roots of goodness possessed by a bodhisattva do not pass through successive lifetimes; rather, while sitting cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree, they produce the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhasamjñā*) and so forth, up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Question: It is said that for ninety-one kalpas the Bodhisattva does not fall into the evil realms; is this not the power of patience? Answer:

It is not necessary; for roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) are capable of obstructing the evil realms—whether by the power of giving, the power of morality, impurity-contemplation (*aśubha*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), or the stages of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "Summits" (*mūrdhan*)—and only thereafter does one attain "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"To obstruct the evil realms is not possible without relying on the knowledge of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
What is the meaning of this?"
He says this: "To realize the law of dependent origination is itself the untainted path;
were it not for the power of the untainted path, one could not obstruct the evil realms."
The critique says:
One should not speak in this manner; it is better as previously stated. Why is that?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do so with both precepts and wisdom;
when practicing precepts, they do so with both giving and wisdom;
and when practicing wisdom, they do so with both giving and precepts.
By these causes and conditions, one can obstruct ten billion (*nayuta*) evil destinies, let alone those of the ten places of evil destinies.

All the stages of "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) and "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) possessed by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the Bodhisattva is able to fully generate; thereby they obstruct the evil destinies, yet they do not generate the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
Why is this? Because patience is incompatible with the evil realms.

Although Bodhisattvas remain within saṃsāra for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, they intentionally take birth in the evil realms by means of their power of aspiration; regarding this, the analogy of the fish should be explained.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one gives rise to the forbearance of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas to obstruct the evil realms, but does not give rise to the forbearance of a bodhisattva. Why is this?
Because the attainment of the body of the Way is exceedingly remote [for them].

Those who seek the state of a pratyekabuddha, having given rise to the patience of a pratyekabuddha, are unable to give rise to the patience of the Buddha-seed because they are close to the path of a pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there are those who say that those seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha can indeed give rise to the patience of the Buddha-seed.
The critique says:
One should not speak thus; rather, one should speak as follows:
A person seeking the state of a pratyekabuddha is unable to give rise to the patience that is the seed of buddhahood.
Question: When an ordinary person who has attained *kṣānti* (receptivity) passes away, does he relinquish that *kṣānti*?
If he does relinquish it, why is it that he is not reborn in the evil destinies?
If it were abandoned, why is it that ordinary persons abandon it while noble ones do not?
If it is not abandoned, why is it not mentioned in the *Cariya-khaṇḍa* and the *Mahābhūta-khaṇḍa*?
As it is said: "If one is endowed with the body, one is endowed with bodily action," and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer is:
some say that [it] is relinquished.
Question: If one has relinquished [the unwholesome], why is it that one is not born in the evil realms? Answer:
Some say that it is by the power of those roots of goodness that one does not fall into the evil realms despite having abandoned them;
for there are roots of goodness which, even when accomplished, do not obstruct entry into the evil realms, let alone when they are not yet accomplished.

What is called "attaining goodness at the place of birth" means that even if one's own roots of goodness have not yet been fully realized, they are capable of obstructing the evil realms; how much more so when what is called "patience" (kṣānti) is realized? Therefore, the power of those roots of goodness is able to obstruct the evil realms.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the power of those roots of goodness can cause the afflictions and karma leading to rebirth in the evil realms within one's body to be utterly distanced from it, so that they no longer function within this body.
If one does not practice it, by what means could one fall into the evil realms?

It is like a person who takes a purgative in autumn; the medicine does not remain within that person's body—it either exits together with the illness or is digested within the body itself—yet it is able to eliminate the ailment so that it never arises again.
Thus, by the power of those roots of goodness, the afflictions and karmas that would cause one to fall into the evil realms shall never arise again.

Furthermore, some say that these roots of goodness once resided within that person’s body, like a lion dwelling in its lair; although they do not possess the power of habitual attachment within that body, they are able to ensure that the afflictions and karmas leading to the evil realms no longer function, let alone actually causing a fall into those realms.
It is just as when a lion is in its dwelling: even if the lion has gone out and is not present, no other small beasts can approach it, let alone while it is there.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the wholesome roots dwelling within this body are like long-term residents, whereas the afflictions and karma of the various evil realms dwelling within this body are like guests.
Those who have resided there for a long time possess strong power, whereas newcomers do not.
Furthermore, some say that the practitioner has two types of aspirational intent:
first, the intent to remain far removed from all evils; second, the intent to be deeply attached to wholesome dharmas.
Because they possess these two types of resolute intention (*citta*), they do not fall into the evil realms.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"That practitioner possesses such a resolute intention, such a desire, such forbearance, such approval, such intent, such reverence, such affection, and such delight."

Furthermore, there are those who say that he has already attained cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding those evil destinies; since he has attained cessation not through deliberation regarding all such phenomena, they will never manifest again.

Others say that this practitioner has fallen into the swift current of the river of the Dharma-rain, leaving no room for the commission of further karma leading to evil destinies, and is therefore not reborn in the evil destinies.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because of relying upon the Noble Path.
That practitioner, by relying upon the Noble Path, prevents the afflictions and karma of the evil realms from manifesting within this body, let alone falling into those evil realms.
It is just as when a person, fearing an enemy, takes refuge with a king; that enemy is not even able to look him directly in the face, let alone inflict harm upon him.
Furthermore, there are those who say that by means of these roots of goodness, the practitioner, within his own person, guards the dwelling place where the Noble Path resides.
It is just as when a king’s official first guards the ground where the king dwells; no common people dare to dwell there again.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because those roots of goodness are determined to produce rebirth in the realms of humans and devas, if one performs karma that is fixed for a particular realm, one will necessarily be born in that place.
This is just as when a seat of high status and nobility is already fixed, one should not sit upon any other seat.
In this way, the concentration that serves as the locus for those roots of goodness is likewise so.

Furthermore, some say that by means of right skillful means, the practitioner causes the afflictions and karmic actions of the evil realms to no longer function, let alone being born in those evil realms.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because that practitioner perceives the faults and perils of unwholesome conduct and perceives the benefits of wholesome conduct, he does not engage in unwholesome conduct and thus does not fall into the evil realms.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because one possesses a virtuous and noble intention within this body, one does not commit evil deeds and thus does not fall into the evil realms.

Others say it is because the mind is supple, because one follows the path toward Nirvana, and because the roots of faith are deep and firm; for these reasons, one does not commit evil deeds and does not fall into the evil realms.
Question: If it is abandoned, why is it that ordinary beings abandon it while noble ones do not? Answer:

Those ordinary persons lack the power of the Noble Path as an antidote to sustain and govern themselves; even if they possess an antidotal path to sustain and govern themselves, this path is weak, inferior, not firm, and does not endure for long, and is therefore abandoned at the time of death.

Within the body of a noble one, there exists the untainted path of counteraction by which they maintain themselves; because they abide firmly for a long time through that untainted power of concentration, they do not relinquish it at the time of death.
In this context, the analogy of the combined dyes should be explained.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the mind] does not abandon [its objects]. He asks:
If [the fault] is not abandoned, why are the *Karmaskandhaka* and the *Mahābhūtaskandhaka* not mentioned?
The answer is:
some say that if something should have been explained therein but was not, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvasesa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is also taught in the *Karmaskandha*, specifically within the third phrase, which states that a noble one (*ārya*) is in the womb.
There are two kinds of noble ones:
the noble one by designation (*saṃkhyā-ārya*) and the noble one in the ultimate sense (*tattvārtha-ārya*).

Those who have attained the roots of goodness conducive to penetration are called "saints by designation" (nāma-ārya); those who have attained right determination are called "saints in the ultimate sense" (artha-ārya). Therefore, they too are spoken of in this way.

If a person possesses even a single thought of renunciation, they may still be called a noble disciple (ārya-śrāvaka), let alone one who has attained the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla).
Furthermore, some say that among them, there are those who have abandoned [the world] and those who have not.
Who does not abandon it?

One who does not abandon it is one who, regarding these roots of goodness, constantly applies diligent skillful means—namely, one who employs skillful means, employs them at all times, correctly upholds them, and correctly cultivates them;
those who act contrary to this abandon them.
As it has been heard:
if one constantly applies skillful means toward the roots of goodness and even cultivates them well, one will never abandon them even while passing through birth and death.
For example, when Maitrāyaṇīputra was first born, he immediately spoke these words:
There are two kinds of fetters, and so forth, as explained at length.
As previously heard:

if one does not apply oneself diligently to the roots of virtue, and so on, up to failing to cultivate them well, then even if they have been attained within this body, they will be swiftly abandoned.
Thus one should understand that there is both relinquishing and non-relinquishing.
The critique states:

According to the true meaning, if even ordinary persons who have produced the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) in a particular stage may still relinquish them, how much more so for those born in other stages?

Question: Regarding the statement that the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla) obtain retribution—does this mean they act as the initial karma for producing those bodies consisting of the five aggregates of the form realm (rūpadhātu)? Answer:
Some say that the initial karma is not performed. Why is this?

Because those [roots of goodness] resemble the untainted path and loathe rebirth; thus, other karma performs the initial karma, while those roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) perform only the completing karma before receiving their retribution.
Furthermore, there are those who say that by performing the initial practice, one obtains a physical retribution that is exquisite and conducive to following the Path.
Regarding these roots of goodness, such as "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and so forth, there are seventy-three types; what are their specific characteristics?
The desire realm consists of ten types of beings, namely:
first, ordinary worldlings bound by all fetters; second, those who have eliminated one grade of fetter, up to those who have exhausted all nine grades.

In the first dhyāna there are nine [types of practitioners]: some have eliminated one grade of fetters, up to those who have eliminated all nine grades; thus, in the first dhyāna there is no person bound by all fetters, as this is explained with reference to the desire realm.

In this manner, up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), there are likewise nine types; the same applies to the stages of the summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: Is the "heat" (*uṣmagata*) attained by an ordinary person bound by all fetters [the same] as that which removes one grade of the fetters up to nine grades?
Answer: It is of one kind.

"No. There is a difference between an ordinary person bound by all fetters, a difference between those who have eliminated one grade of fetters, and so on, up to a difference between those who have eliminated nine grades. He asked:
If one falls away from the stage of *uṣmagata* and subsequently gives rise to *uṣmagata* again, is it obtained as something previously attained? Answer: No.
Why is this so? Because they are not obtained repeatedly; they are obtained through effort, as there is no similarity between what precedes and what follows.
Just as when one has relinquished the *prātimokṣa* precepts and receives them again, it is not an attainment of what was previously attained, so too is this case.
As it is with *ūṣmagata*, so it is with *mūrdhan*. Question:
When *ūṣmagata* increases, once the *ūṣmagata* has increased, does one again give rise to the first [stage]?
He replied: "No. Why is that?"
Having attained the superior roots of goodness (*viśeṣa-kuśalamūla*), one has nothing further to rejoice in regarding those previously attained.
The same applies to the stages of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*) and "Patience" (*kṣānti*). Question:
In what place do these roots of goodness arise?
The answer is:
among humans in the desire realm, specifically in the three continents, but not in Uttarakuru.
Question: Are the six heavens of the desire realm unable to produce [them]? Answer:
It cannot.
That which has already arisen previously can arise and manifest in the present. Why is this so?
If there is a fine body and also the correct contemplation that accords with revulsion toward it, then warmth can arise therein; these two conditions are present throughout these three continents.
Question: If there is a fine body, then the devas are superior to humans.
If one adopts a correct contemplation that accords with revulsion, then the path to the evil realms will be overcome.
The answer is:
as previously stated, those who possess both [factors] are capable.
Because heaven and the evil realms do not coexist, one is therefore unable [to attain them]. Question:

The stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) relies upon both male and female bodies. If one attains the stage of Heat while relying on a female body, does one also attain the stage of Heat that relies on a male body within that same self?
Answer: Yes, they are attained.
One should know that the same applies to the stages of *mūrdhan* and *kṣānti*.
Question: If one attains the stage of *uṣmagata* (heat) based on a male body, does one also attain the *uṣmagata* that serves as the basis for a woman within that same body? Answer:
It is not possible.
The same applies to those at the stages of *mūrdhan* (Summits) and *kṣānti* (Patience).

Eunuchs, *paṇḍakas* who possess male organs but lack virility, those who possess female organs but lack femininity, those without organs, and those with both sets of organs cannot generate the four wholesome preparatory dharmas, such as *uṣmagata* (Heat), and so forth.
Wisdom is of three kinds:
wisdom derived from hearing, wisdom derived from reflection, and wisdom derived from cultivation.
The answer is:
Some masters briefly explain the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas).
Furthermore, there are those who, having mastered the recitation of the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, develop a sense of weariness and distress, and they say:
"The essential points taught in the Tripiṭaka are nothing other than these eighteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates."

He then observes the elements (*dhātu*). Having observed the elements, he further analyzes them in three ways: namely, by name, by essential nature (*svabhāva*), and by general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).

"By name" refers to the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) up to the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*). "Essential nature" refers to their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). "General characteristic" refers to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
When observing in this manner, one cultivates this wisdom and further attains concentration of mind, giving rise to a sense of weariness and distress toward this realm.

Furthermore, one briefly contemplates the twelve bases (*āyatana*): the eye element is the eye base, continuing thus up to the tangible element which is the tangible base; the seven consciousness elements are the mind base, and the dharma element is the dharma base.

Furthermore, to briefly enter the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*): therein, the ten material bases (*rūpāyatana*) and the derived matter within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); the base of mind (*manāyatana*) constitutes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*); and the base of mental objects constitutes the [remaining] three aggregates.

Furthermore, the brief summary of the aggregates (skandha) constitutes the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna): the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is the foundation of mindfulness of the body; the aggregate of feeling (vedanāskandha) is the foundation of mindfulness of feeling; the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and the aggregates of perception (saṃjñāskandha) and formations (saṃskāraskandha) are the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).

Furthermore, in the brief contemplation of the aggregates and the truths: the fruit of the five aggregates is the truth of suffering; the causes of the five aggregates are the truth of origination; the cessation of the five aggregates is the truth of cessation; and the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training are the truth of the path.
These Truths further have three aspects: name, essential nature, and general characteristic.
"Name" refers to [the names] from suffering up to the path.

"Essential nature" refers to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). Specific characteristics mean that the sense of being oppressed by formations is the meaning of suffering, up to the sense of the practice of transcendence being the meaning of the path.
Regarding the general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*):
suffering has four aspects—impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self;
origination has four aspects—cause, accumulation, existence, and condition; cessation has four aspects:
Cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation: the Path has four aspects—path, method, track, and vehicle.

When one cultivates this wisdom and subsequently attains meditative concentration, just as when one perceives those Truths, one also contemplates them individually in sequence: the suffering of the desire realm is distinguished by its own specific characteristics; the suffering of the form and formless realms is likewise distinguished, up to the distinct severance of the path of practice for the desire realm, and so on, up to the path of practice for the form and formless realms.
At that time, one contemplates the truths as if contemplating external objects such as a piece of cloth.
When practicing contemplation in this manner, it is called the fulfillment of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Cultivating in this successive manner gives rise to the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); further advancing in cultivation gives rise to the wisdom derived from meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), whereby one is able to practice the noble conduct (*ārya-caryā*).

When one contemplates in this manner, it is called the Dharma of Heat (*uṣmagata*). As these qualities thus successively increase, they give rise to the Peak (*mūrdhan*); from the Peak arises Patience (*kṣānti*); from Patience arises the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). From this, the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, which abandons the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering. Subsequently, the Knowledge of the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) arises. Following this sequence, the Subsequent Knowledge of the Path (*mārge ’nvayajñāna*) arises, whereby one attains the fruit of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Continuing in this order up to the Knowledge of Exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), these are called the successive arising of the wholesome roots and the successive arising of the dharmas.
There are three kinds of roots of goodness:
first, the roots of goodness pertaining to merit;
second, the roots of goodness pertaining to liberation.
Third, the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Regarding the roots of goodness conducive to merit (*puṇyabhāgīya*): these are said to act as the seeds for rebirth in the heavens; or, if born among humans, they cause one to be born into a noble and wealthy family, possessing great power and influence, abundant wealth and treasures, a full retinue of attendants, and a handsome and dignified appearance; they also act as the seeds for becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), Śakra, Māra, or Brahmā.

The roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) refer to those that can act as the seeds of liberation; they are the causes that are certain not to regress and necessarily lead to *nirvāṇa*.
The roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) refer to the stages from "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*).
Question: In what place are the roots of goodness conducive to liberation planted? Answer:
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
within the desire realm, in the human path (*manuṣyagati*), not other paths;
within the human path, in the three continents (*dvīpa*), not in Uttarakuru.
When a Buddha appears in the world, it is not a time when there is no Buddha.
Furthermore, some say that even during a time when there is no Buddha, if one encounters a Pratyekabuddha, one also plants the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
What is its essential nature?
The answer is:
it consists of bodily action, verbal action, and mental action, though mental action predominates.
Is this the group of the five consciousnesses, or is it the mental stage?
The answer is:
it is the mental stage, not the group of the five consciousnesses.
Is this a wholesome state acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśala*) or a wholesome state acquired by birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*)?
The answer is:
it is both a wholesome state acquired through application and a wholesome state acquired by birth.
Is this the wisdom derived from hearing, the wisdom derived from reflection, or the wisdom derived from cultivation?
The answer is:
it is the wisdom derived from hearing and the wisdom derived from reflection; it is not the wisdom derived from cultivation.
By what means does one plant these roots of goodness?
The answer is:
either by means of giving, or by means of ethical discipline, or by means of extensive learning; it is not necessarily fixed to one alone.
Why is this so? There are those who, by giving a single mouthful of food as a gift, are able to plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation;
yet there are those who observe the long fast of the Pañcavārṣika festival, yet are unable to plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
There may be those who observe the one-day fast and are able to plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation;
yet there are those who maintain the precepts for their entire lives, but are unable to plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
There are those who, by reciting and upholding even a single verse, are able to plant the roots of merit conducive to liberation;
yet there are others who, though thoroughly proficient in the words and meanings of the Tripitaka, are unable to plant such roots of merit. This is what is meant.
Therefore, it is not fixed.
Why? Because there are those who plant seeds and those who do not plant seeds.
If one dedicates these matters toward liberation and nirvana with the desire to forever leave behind birth and death, and possesses such a courageous mind, then one is able to plant [the seeds];

if one does not dedicate them toward liberation and nirvana to forever leave behind birth and death, then even if one practices much giving, maintains the precepts for a lifetime, and extensively studies and hears much, one cannot plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation.
There are those who are near and those who are distant. The "near" refers to those who planted the seeds in a previous life, which matured in this life, and will lead to liberation in the next life.

The "distant" refers to those who once planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*), yet after undergoing births for many *nayuta* eons, they have been unable to produce the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

The roots of goodness conducive to liberation attained by śrāvakas can be redirected toward the path of pratyekabuddhas; the roots of goodness conducive to liberation attained by pratyekabuddhas can likewise be redirected toward the path of buddhahood; however, the roots of goodness conducive to liberation planted by a buddha cannot be redirected.
Question: Regarding the contemplation of arising and ceasing, what serves as its skillful means? Answer:

That practitioner sees that in springtime the grasses and trees are green like sapphire-blue lapis lazuli; he sees the swift current of a river with foam clinging to its banks. Having seen this, he reflects:
"These external phenomena have now arisen once again."
If he enters a city or a village and sees men and women singing, dancing, playing, and laughing, he asks them:
"For what reason do you act thus?
They reply:
Within this, sons and daughters are born.
He then reflects: "In this way, these internal phenomena have now arisen once again."

Later, in the autumn season, that practitioner sees how all the grasses and trees are withered by the autumn sun, battered by cold winds, and covered in frost and dew; their branches and leaves fall away, and the rivers run dry.
He further reflected:
"These external phenomena have now likewise ceased.
If I enter a city or a village and see men and women with disheveled hair, raising their hands and wailing in lamentation, he asks them:"
"Why is this so? He replied,
"Because men and women have died here."
He further reflects:
"In this regard, the internal phenomena have now ceased once more.

Having deeply perceived such signs, the practitioner returns to his dwelling place and observes his own body, seeing the marks of impermanence—youth, maturity, and old age—and sequentially contemplates the continuous succession of years, months, days, hours, and nights; this is called skillful means (*upāya*).

Through this process of successive reduction, one eventually contemplates the two moments of a single aggregate—one arising and one ceasing; this is called the fulfillment of the contemplation of arising and ceasing. Question:
Is this contemplation of arising and ceasing a conceptual contemplation or a contemplation of reality?
If this were a meditation based on conceptual construction, how would this verse be reconciled?
As it is said:
"If there is knowledge and vision that can exhaust the outflows, how could they be exhausted if there were no knowledge and vision?"
"If one can contemplate the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, / This is the liberation of the mind from afflictions.
It is not by means of contemplation through false conceptualization that one can sever the afflictions.
If it were not a contemplation of reality, one would not perceive the characteristics of coming and going in conditioned phenomena; yet, conditioned phenomena truly have no coming or going.
Some commentators of the treatises state that this is a conceptual visualization (*vikalpa-bhāvanā*). Question:
If that is so, how is this verse to be reconciled?
Answer: Because there is a successive cause, it is said that they arise from one another in succession, like the principle of descendants.
What is the matter?

The contemplation of conceptualized emptiness (*vikalpa-śūnyatā-bhāvanā*) can give rise to the contemplation of actualized reality (*bhūta-artha-bhāvanā*), and the contemplation of actualized reality can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, it is said that they function as successive causes, like the relationship between father, son, and grandson.
Furthermore, there are those who say this refers to the contemplation of actualized reality itself.
Question: If that is so, then conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no coming or going; yet those practitioners perceive coming and going. Answer:
If the contemplation of arising and ceasing is not yet fulfilled, one perceives all conditioned phenomena as having the characteristics of coming and going;
if it is fulfilled, one perceives all conditioned phenomena as being without the characteristics of coming and going.
It is like a child playing with a single-spoked wheel: when it spins rapidly, it appears stationary; when it spins slowly, its coming and going is perceived.
The analogy of the potter’s wheel is likewise.
Question: Is it by means of a single mind that one perceives arising and ceasing? Or is it that two minds perceive them—one perceiving arising and one perceiving ceasing?
If it is by means of a single mind that one perceives arising and ceasing, how can there be two modes of attention within a single mind?
If there were two moments of attention, it would destroy the principle of a single mind.
Furthermore, how is it perceived?
Is one perceiving arising while it is arising, and then perceiving cessation; or is one perceiving cessation while it is ceasing, and then perceiving arising?
If, when observing the arising of arising, one perceives only arising, this is correct;
if, when observing the arising of arising, one further perceives cessation, this is erroneous.
If, when seeing cessation as it ceases, one sees only cessation, this is correct;
if, when seeing cessation as it ceases, one further sees arising, this is erroneous.
If one were to see the arising of the single mind with the single mind, or see the cessation of the single mind with the single mind, then there would be no contemplation of arising and cessation.
The answer is:
one should speak thus:
With a single mind one perceives arising; with a single mind one perceives cessation.
Question: If this is so, then there would be no contemplation of arising and cessation.
Answer: This explanation refers only to the contemplation of the continuous arising and ceasing throughout the course of a single lifetime;
it does not refer to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Three.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll Four.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Northern Liang Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman.

Translated by Kung Tao-t’ai and others: Section on Miscellaneous Matters (Kṣudraka-vastu), Chapter on the World’s Foremost Dharma (Loka-agradharma), Part Four. Regarding these twenty types of view of a self-entity (satkāya-dṛṣṭi), how many are views of "I" (ātma-dṛṣṭi) and how many are views of "mine" (ātmīya-dṛṣṭi)? [The text continues] at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]

In various places throughout the sūtras, the Blessed One has spoken of twenty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-identity) without providing a detailed analysis. Only in one place in the sūtra does the Venerable Śāriputra provide such an analysis; yet, although he analyzes them, he does not state how many of these twenty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi constitute the view of "I" and how many constitute the view of "mine."
Because those various sūtras do not provide such distinctions, I now wish to distinguish them; therefore, I have composed this treatise.
Furthermore, the Vibhajyavādins maintain this position:
"The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) has no object of perception."
Just as the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes "self" as its object, yet in ultimate reality there is no self—what, then, is its object?

This is like a person who sees a rope and thinks it is a snake, or sees a tree stump and thinks it is a person; [the teaching] is intended to stop such thoughts in those people, and also to demonstrate that the view of a self-body does indeed have an object.
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes the five aggregates as its object; it is merely that the perceived object is different, not that there is no object of perception at all.

It is like the analogy of those people: seeing a rope and perceiving it as a snake, or seeing a stump and perceiving it as a person. In this case as well, the perceived object is different, but it is not that there is no object of perception.
Therefore, this treatise was composed in order to refute the views of others, to manifest one's own doctrine, and to demonstrate the definitive characteristics of phenomena.
Question: Among these twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi (view of a self-existent body), how many are views of "I" and how many are views of "mine"?
Answer: Five kinds are the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), and fifteen kinds are the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*). Question:
