If there are five views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), there should likewise be five views of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*); why, then, are fifteen views of what belongs to the self taught?
The answer is:
the five views of self are taught by way of their objective conditions (*ālambana*), while the fifteen views of what belongs to the self are taught by way of their full enumeration.
Why is this? These fifteen views of self arise because they are fully present; therefore, one should speak of them as a single view of self.
That is to say, among the five views, the view of self should be spoken of as two kinds of "as-self" views.
The view of "mine" should be explained as threefold, namely: the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.
The view of "self" should be explained as sixfold; just as there are views of self and views of mine within the desire realm, so it is likewise in the form and formless realms.

One should say there are nine, namely: from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) in the stage of the desire realm, up to the view of self in the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

One should say there are eighteen, namely: from the view of self and the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*) in the stage of the desire realm, up to the view of self and the view of what belongs to self in the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one were to categorize the modes of activity based on the aggregates (*skandha*) as their object, there would be twenty [types of views].
Without distinguishing the locus from which they arise, one views form as the self, form as distinct from the self, form as belonging to the self, or the self as being within form.

Just as there are four kinds of form (*rūpa*), so it is with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*); thus, these five sets of four amount to twenty.
By further analyzing the twelve bases (*āyatana*) through the condition of formations (*saṃskāra-pratyaya*), there are forty-eight.

One does not discriminate regarding the place of origin, such as seeing the eye-base as being the self, the eye-base as distinct from the self, the eye-base as belonging to the self, or the self as existing within the eye-base.

Just as there are four [aspects] for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), so too there are four for each up to the mental-object-base (*dharma-āyatana*); thus, twelve bases multiplied by four yield forty-eight.
When the elements (*dhātu*) are further distinguished according to their modes of activity (*carita*), there are seventy-two.

One does not discriminate regarding the place of origin, such as: "The eye-element is the self," "the eye-element is distinct from the self," "the eye-element belongs to the self," or "the self exists within the eye-element.
Just as there are four [modes] for the eye-element, so it is for each up to the dharma-element; thus, with eighteen [elements], four [modes] each result in seventy-two.
If one discriminates by way of the aggregates (*skandha*) as objects of perception and discriminates by way of the bases from which they arise, there are sixty-five [views].
As it is said: "Form is the self; feeling is my ornament, feeling is my servant, and feeling is my vessel."
Just as there are three types of feeling, so too are there three each for perception, mental formations, and consciousness; thus, these four sets of three make twelve.
Together with form, there are thirteen; thus, these five categories of thirteen amount to sixty-five.
If one discriminates the sense bases (*āyatana*) as conditions and discriminates the places from which they arise, there are four hundred and eight [conceptions]:
"The eye-base is my form-base; it is my ornament, it is my servant, it is my vessel."

Just as there are thirty-four [factors] for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), so too there are thirty-four for each up to the mental-object-base (*dharma-āyatana*); twelve sets of thirty-four thus amount to four hundred and eighty.
If one discriminates the elements as objects and discriminates the bases from which they arise, there are nine hundred and thirty-six [such views]:
"The eye-element is my form-element; it is my ornament; it is my servant; it is my vessel."
Just as there are fifty-two [factors] in the eye-element, so too up to the dharma-element; with eighteen kinds each having fifty-two, there are nine hundred and thirty-six.
In this way, through the various bodies and their succession of moments, there arise immeasurable views of "I" and "mine.
When one analyzes the formations conditioned by the aggregates (*skandha*) without distinguishing the specific bases from which they arise, there are twenty such views.
Question: For what reason is this view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) called a "seed"? Answer:
These twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* each have their own distinctions; therefore, they are called "types. Question:
For what reason are twenty views of self taught based on the aggregates (*skandha*), rather than based on the elements (*dhātu*) or bases (*āyatana*)?

Answer: Some say that the author of that scripture had such an intention, such a desire, and such an approval; having composed the scripture in accordance with that intention, it does not contradict the characteristics of the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are those who say that [the teaching] is intended to manifest the initial expedient means for entering the Dharma; it is like explaining "view" by means of the aggregates (*skandha*).

One should likewise explain it by means of the elements (*dhātu*) and the sense-bases (*āyatana*), yet because it is not so explained, one should know that this meaning is a statement made with intentional omission (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that this mention of the "viewer" (*draṣṭṛ*) within the aggregates (*skandha*) is precisely what is taught in the Buddha’s sūtras; for the sūtras explain twenty kinds of views of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) based upon the aggregates.
Those who composed the treatises likewise relied on the Buddha’s sūtras to explain these twenty kinds of views of self.
Question: Setting aside the author of the sutra,
for what reason did the World-Honored One, based on the aggregates (*skandha*), teach twenty kinds of views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*)?
The answer is:
For the sake of transforming sentient beings, the Buddha taught twenty kinds of views of self based on the aggregates (*skandha*).

If those to be transformed were to attain liberation by hearing about the elements (*dhātu*) and sense bases (*āyatana*), the World-Honored One would likewise teach views of self based on the elements and sense bases.
Because it is not something that should be heard, it is therefore not taught.

Furthermore, there are those who say: when various views arise, they mostly depend upon the aggregates (*skandha*) and only rarely depend upon the elements (*dhātu*) or bases (*āyatana*); for this reason, the World-Honored One taught views by way of the aggregates, rather than by way of the elements or bases.
If form were the self, what would constitute form? All forms whatsoever—
whether they consist entirely of the four great elements or are derived from the four great elements— are definitively of two kinds:
There are those who exhaust all that exists, and there are those who do not exhaust all that exists.
Regarding those who do not exhaust it: even seeking small things such as dregs or husks constitutes "all that exists."
"Exhaustion" refers to seeking all things, such as dregs and husks, as well as everything that exists.
Here, it specifically refers to the exhaustion of all existing forms (*rūpa*). Question:
Just as I see this as being conditioned by my own realm and not by another realm, how could they possibly see all forms as the self?
The answer is:
they conceive as the self only those things that are within their sphere of activity and their cognitive domain, not all forms.
Regarding "form is different from the self," how is form different from the self?
One reckons these four aggregates as being mutually different from the self.
They conceive this thought:
"This form is mine," as when a person possesses wealth, they are called "wealthy.
Regarding the statement "form belongs to me," how does form belong to me?
One calculates that these four aggregates (skandhas) belong to me through mutual dependence.
Just as when a person has a servant, one says, "The servant belongs to me.
Regarding the self within form (*rūpa*), what is meant by "the self within form"?
It is the successive calculation that this [self] is within form among these four aggregates (*skandha*).
He forms this thought:
"Form is my vessel, just as oil is in sesame seeds, fat is in a lump of meat, ghee is in curd, a sword is in its scabbard, a snake is in its basket, or blood is within the body."
Question: It may be so that feeling (*vedanā*) is the self (*ātman*) and form (*rūpa*) is its equipment, because form is coarse and feeling is subtle.
But as for the claim that form is the self and feeling is its equipment—how can one see coarse form enter into subtle feeling?
The Venerable Paśya said:
"One should not reproach a blind man for falling into a pit, nor should one question a person lacking wisdom regarding their folly.

Furthermore, others say: "He who perceives form as the self and feeling as the possessor of the self—because that person perceives both coarse and subtle forms—he, by perceiving form, dwells within feeling."
The Venerable Sūmī said:
Within this body composed of the four great elements, one is capable of perceiving all tactile sensations; wherever there is contact, sensation arises.
Because sensation arises in every place, it is said that form is enveloped within sensation.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"He perceives feeling as being pervasive throughout the body, such that there is no part from the feet to the head where feeling is not present.
However, he conceives form to be the self, which is not pervasive throughout the body; therefore, he perceives form as residing within feeling."
Question: For what reason are twenty kinds of views regarding the self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*) taught, while the other views are not? Answer:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of the sūtra to be thus, and so forth, as explained at length.

Others say that this is to manifest the initial arising of the preliminary means for entering the Dharma; just as it is said that there are twenty types of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity), there should likewise be forty types of *śīlavrataparāmarśa* (clinging to precepts and observances), and eighty types each for *mithyādṛṣṭi* (wrong view) and *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views).
Regarding that which should have been said but was not: this meaning is an incomplete teaching.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha taught the ten kinds of emptiness as an antidote to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).

The ten kinds of emptiness are as follows: namely, internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, ultimate emptiness, the emptiness of that which has no sphere of activity, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness.
With what phenomena do these ten kinds of emptiness correspond?
They correspond to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Because emptiness corresponds to the view of a self, there are twenty kinds of views of a self; other views are not like this, and therefore they are not mentioned.
Question: Is it possible for the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*) to arise with respect to a single aggregate (*skandha*)?
Answer: [Yes].
It arises.

Just as the view of self arises with respect to the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the view of "mine" arises with respect to the remaining forms; the same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*). Question:
Is it not the case that those who possess the view of self all simultaneously reckon the five aggregates to be the self?
If such were the case, how would the Śaka scripture be reconciled? As it says:
There is only the view of a single self; there are not five views of a self.
To have no five views of a self means to have no reckoning of the five aggregates as being the self. Why is this so?
The view of self (ātmadṛṣṭi) conceives of only a single dharma, whereas the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) are distinct dharmas.
According to those who propound the view of self, there is a single self, a singular person, which is indivisible, indestructible, immutable, and eternal.
If it were non-existent, how would one reconcile the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra*,
which says: "O Śramaṇa Gautama!"?
"Form is the self; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the self.
He replied:
"There is not a single instance where one considers the five aggregates as the self at once."
Question: If that is so, how is the *Satyaka-nirgrantha-sūtra* to be reconciled? Answer:
Because his prideful mind was heavy, he spoke in such a manner.
Furthermore, there are those who say that he did not believe in the Buddha, yet possessed internal knowledge and vision, and wished to test whether the Tathāgata truly knew or not.
Therefore, they intentionally utter irrational speech.

Next, they see the Tathāgata’s various marks of discourse: his jaw is like that of a lion, his fangs are sharp and pointed, he has forty teeth in his mouth, and he emits the Brahma-voice; having heard this, those people harbor fear and trepidation, and thus utter irrational speech.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because they perceive the Tathāgata’s majestic power to surpass that of Brahmā and Śakra— being difficult to approach and difficult to associate with—
they speak in a manner contrary to reason on account of such majestic power.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it was because of the intimidation of celestial deities that those people were made to speak words contrary to reason.
Others, who have faith in the Buddha, think:
"Why does this wicked person continue to harass the Tathāgata for so long?"
Therefore, through intimidation, one can cause that person to utter speech that is contrary to reason.
Furthermore, there are some who say that at certain times they conceive of the five aggregates as the self.
Question: If that is so, how do you explain what is stated in the Śaka scriptures? Answer:
That person regards these five aggregates as a single, unified collection.
Question: If that is so, then by what means is it considered a "collection"?
The answer is:
If one reckons the internal bases as the self, then one takes the external bases as its equipment;
if one reckons the external bases as the self, then one takes the internal bases as its equipment.
Question: Is there anyone who perceives atoms and conceives of them as a self?
If such a person exists, then this would be a view of non-self (anātman-dṛṣṭi), not a view of self (ātman-dṛṣṭi).
If [the self] does not exist, how then is the Śaka scripture to be reconciled? For it says:
"Although the five great atoms have distinct characteristics, they are the self and are eternal."
If one says that [the self] is impermanent, this is irrational.
[The opponent] asks:
How can that scripture be reconciled, given that I perceive atoms with my own eyes?
The answer is:

This treatise establishes that the view of extremes takes atoms as its object; since this point is established, one should know that the view of self also takes atoms as its object—this point is likewise established.
Answer: There is no one who perceives a subtle atom (*paramāṇu*) and conceives it as a self (*ātman*). Question:
If that is so, how then are the Śaka scriptures to be reconciled?
The answer is:
what is taught in those scriptures does not accord with the principles of the True Dharma.

Furthermore, there are those who say that some perceive atoms and reckon them to be the self; others perceive through inference, seeing that objects have no substantial reality, yet giving rise to the notion of "objects" at the time of their arising.
The critique says:
one should not speak thus; what was said previously is correct.
Question: Is there anyone who gives rise to the view of a self apart from the five aggregates?
If there is, how is this sūtra to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who give rise to the view of self, they all perceive the five aggregates of clinging.
If there were none, how could a sixth view of self possibly exist?"
Answer: There is no arising of the view of self apart from the five aggregates. Question:
If that is so, how can there be a sixth view of self?
The answer is:

volition (*cetanā*) is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*); when a view of self arises with respect to this volition, and views of "mine" (*mamakāra*) arise with respect to the remaining aggregates of formations, this is precisely the sixth view of self.

The Buddhist sūtras state that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of the sixty-two views; other sūtras further state that whatever views any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas may give rise to all rely upon two extremes: either annihilationism (uccheda) or eternalism (śāśvata).
What is the difference between these two sūtras?
The answer is:
because it explains how all views are produced, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is said to be the root.
Because it guards and nurtures all views, this is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, others say that because it can give rise to all views, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is said to be the root.
To cause various views to arise and function is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"If one who practices the meditative absorption of the 'all-encompassing earth' (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana*) forms this thought:"
"Earth is myself, and I am earth; they are neither separate nor different. This is the case for all other spheres as well. Question:

One who attains the meditative concentrations of all spheres must necessarily be free from desire for the third dhyāna. If such a person perceives earth as the self, it should be understood that this is the view of a self in relation to the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the fourth dhyāna, perceiving the earth of the fourth dhyāna as the self.
If the dharmas of the *sarvatragatadhi* (universal concentration) take the desire realm as their object, how is this not contradictory?
The answer is:
herein, what is not fixed is spoken of as fixed, just as one who is not a śramaṇa is called a śramaṇa.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because it is spoken of by its original name, it is like a king who, though he has lost his throne, is still called "king.
A practitioner who originally attained this meditative concentration may later lose it, yet they are still said to have "attained concentration" based on that original attainment.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because the practitioner’s concentration is too rapid, they lose it; having given rise to the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) within that concentration, they abandon that view and regain that concentration.

Just as Devadatta was swift in meditative concentration, he used his supernormal powers to transform his own body into the likeness of a prince; he played, turning and rolling upon King Ajātaśatru’s lap, and further manifested his features so that King Ajātaśatru would know him to be the Venerable Devadatta.
When he was being fashioned as a statue of the Crown Prince, King Ajātaśatru took him up, fondled and kissed him, and spat into his mouth; out of greed for offerings and gain, he then swallowed it.
For this reason, the World-Honored One spoke to him, saying:
"You are a corpse; you are one who eats saliva.
If you were free from desire when swallowing saliva, then you would have been free from desire at the time when, as a prince, you were being fondled by King Ajātaśatru."

Furthermore, there are those who say that the view of self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes the stage of the fourth dhyāna as "self," and that all the universal bases (sarvatra-dhātu-samādhi) likewise take the stage of the fourth dhyāna as their object. Question:
If this is so, do the universal bases not take the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as their object?
Answer: The concentration of all places takes both the desire realm and the fourth dhyāna as its objects. Question:
If all the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are entirely white, how is it that they perceive distinctions such as blue, yellow, and red?
The answer is:

those things belonging to the category of sentient beings (*sattvasaṃkhyāta*) are entirely white in color; it is things not belonging to the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*) that possess colors such as blue, yellow, and red.
The critique says:
One should not speak thus. Why is that?
If the view of self were a factor that is invariably associated and co-existent with all [mental states], such a fault would indeed follow.
What, then, are those factors that are invariably associated and co-existent with all [mental states]?

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that slightly takes the desire realm as its object and slightly takes the form realm as its object is not a "concomitant" (*sahabhū*) factor associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) in all instances; nevertheless, a single person may receive two names: they are called one who holds the view of a self-identity because they conceive of a self, and they are called one who has attained concentration because they have attained concentration.

The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes the stages within the fourth dhyāna as its object, while all meditative attainments (samāpatti) take the desire realm (kāmadhātu) as their object; these do not occur simultaneously.
Therefore, this treatise has already provided a thorough resolution.
"Perceiving the impermanent as permanent," and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is:

These various wrong views act as a great bondage for sentient beings within the cycle of birth and death, they cause great ruin and affliction, and they serve as a great hidden trap. This is just like a person in the world who is bound, afflicted, or trapped; if one does not see such a person, one cannot avoid them from afar, but if one sees them, one is then able to avoid them from a distance. This explanation applies extensively to these various wrong views as well.
In this context, wrong view should be investigated through two aspects:
first, by its essential nature (*svabhāva*), and second, by its antidote (*pratipakṣa*),
as treated in the *Jñāna-vastu* and the *Dṛṣṭi-vastu*.
As stated in the *Upāyikā-śāstra*, therein wrong view is also investigated by means of two matters:
first, its essential nature (*svabhāva*), and second, its antidote (*pratipakṣa*). As it is said in the *Upāyikā-śāstra*:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! You are an illusion.

The Way of the World-Honored One has already transcended illusion; this false view that slanders the Way is its essential nature, and the severance of such views through the realization of the Way is its antidote."
Furthermore, it is said:
"This one is an Arhat; why do you begrudge him the name 'Arhat'?
The path of the World-Honored One has already transcended stinginess; the nature of this wrong view is to slander the path, and its antidote is the vision that severs [such views].

As stated in the *Gāthāpraśnasaṃgraha* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, one should investigate wrong views by means of their origin, which involves three factors: namely, the origin, the essential nature, and the antidote.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one should not investigate the three aspects of wrong view—namely, its origin, its essential nature, and its antidote;
for if one were to investigate wrong view, it would be like rebuking ignorance by asking, "Why are you ignorant?"
Furthermore, there are those who say that wrong views should be investigated through three aspects: namely, their origin, their essential nature, and their antidote.

If one can investigate wrong views through these three aspects, then even an ordinary person bound by all fetters will not have the faults of wrong views manifest before them; they will be like a noble one who, having severed all wrong views through the untainted path, ensures they never arise again.
For example, in the past, when the Dharma Master Dharmatrāta was in Kaśmīra, he gathered with a great assembly of practicing bhikṣus in one place to discuss various views.
Someone spoke as follows:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"It is truly rare that a noble one can sever so many faults and afflictions such that wrong views and evil conduct never manifest again.
At that time, the Dharma Master Dhava was in this assembly and spoke these words:
"When a noble one severs all wrong views through the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) so that they never manifest again, what marvelous thing is there in that?"
As I now abide on the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), if one seeks out wrong views by means of these two matters, it is impossible for them to persist for long within *saṃsāra*.
Even if they were to persist for a long time in *saṃsāra*, they would no longer manifest; for this reason, one should seek out wrong views by means of three matters.
Regarding those who hold the view of permanence toward what is impermanent: what is impermanent?
The answer is:
all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Question: By what means do those various non-Buddhists claim that [the self] is eternal? Answer:
One perceives the continuity of similar forms, and the various mental factors (citta-dharma) remember what was previously done, enabling one to recite and uphold various treatises.
How does one perceive the continuity of similar forms?
If the form seen yesterday is similar to that seen today, one might think:
"The form of childhood is the very same as the form of old age.
How, then, can mental phenomena remember what was done in the past?
Just as what was done yesterday is remembered today, so too all that was done previously is remembered at a later time.
One who is able to recite and uphold the sūtras and śāstras—just as one who read little in youth is able to recite it until old age—forms this thought:
"The mind that recites today is the very same mind that read in the past."
For this reason, he conceives of permanence; to conceive of the impermanent as permanent is an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
There are two kinds of extreme views:
that of annihilationism and that of eternalism.
This explains the essential nature of the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); its antidote is the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*).
Since this view arises conditioned by suffering, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
It is like dew upon the grass, which dries up when the sun shines.
It is the same for that [view]: when suffering is seen, that view is abandoned.
Furthermore, some say that the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) are its antidotes.

When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) arise, one abandons this false conceptualization, the inverted and perilous view of annihilationism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi).

Question: In well-spoken teachings as well, it is said that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and that their characteristics are eternally abiding; yet, why is this not considered a wrong view?
Why is it that within a poorly taught doctrine, if one speaks of such characteristics, it constitutes a false view?
The answer is:

Some may say that although a well-taught doctrine speaks of the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics that are eternally abiding and unconditioned; [in the poorly taught doctrine, this is not so].
Within the poorly taught Dharma, there is always something to be done at all times.
Furthermore, regarding those who teach: in the well-taught Dharma, one teaches the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) without doing so repeatedly;
whereas in the poorly taught Dharma, one teaches the nature of phenomena by doing so repeatedly.
Furthermore, there are those who say that within well-expounded teachings, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is described as being born by birth, aged by aging, and destroyed by impermanence;
whereas within poorly expounded teachings, it is not born by birth, and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say that while the nature of the Dharma is taught within the well-expounded Dharma and belongs to various causes and conditions,
the Dharma they themselves teach does not belong to causes and conditions.
Furthermore, there are those who say that what is taught in the well-expounded Dharma corresponds to arising and ceasing;
That is not the case.

Furthermore, there are those who say that within the well-expounded Dharma, the teaching arises from causes, is capable of producing effects, and belongs to a multitude of conditions; because of these various causes and conditions, although the well-expounded Dharma speaks of an eternally abiding essence, it does not fall into false views, whereas those who expound poorly fall into false views.
Question: What is the meaning of "extreme view" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)? Answer:
To grasp at the extreme of annihilation and to grasp at the extreme of permanence is the meaning of "extreme views" (antagrāhadṛṣṭi).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told Kātyāyana:
If one observes with right wisdom that the world is a collection and declares it to be non-existent, then [the cycle] no longer proceeds.
To say it is "non-existent" is the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Seeing this existence perish and the future body arise, one forms this thought:
When these sentient beings die here and are born there, is this not annihilation?
Furthermore, Kātyāyana!
If one observes with right wisdom that the world is subject to cessation, the claim that "the world exists" no longer arises.
To say that there is something existing in the world is the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
Knowing that these aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) continue in a successive succession, one forms this thought:
"These phenomena (*dharma*) all have arising and ceasing; they are not eternal."

Furthermore, one who gives rise to the view of a self is already marginal, base, and contemptible in the eyes of the world; how much more so for one who calculates the self as being subject to annihilation or permanence.
Others say that because this view practices the extremes (*antagrāha*), it is called "practicing the extremes" in two senses:
first, practicing the extreme of permanence; second, practicing the extreme of annihilation.
Based on these meanings, it is called the "view of extremes" (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Question:
Since the true meaning of permanence is the extinction of nirvāṇa, why is the view that perceives impermanence as permanent not called a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: To say that all things are non-existent is called false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
This, however, does not state that all things are non-existent; rather, it further affirms their existence. Therefore, it is not a false view.
Regarding those who commonly perceive the impermanent as permanent, what is meant by "permanent"?
The answer is:
the nirvana of cessation.
Question: For what reason do those non-Buddhists claim that nirvāṇa is impermanent? Answer:
They take the four formless absorptions as liberation and nirvana:
the first is called "the bodiless," and the second is called "the boundless mind."
The third is the Pure Aggregate;
the fourth is the World Stūpa.

That which is bodiless is the concentration of the sphere of infinite space; that which is infinite mind is the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness; the Pure Aggregate is the concentration of the sphere of nothingness; and the World Stūpa is the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

They say this: "Just as this nirvāṇa, though long-lasting, must eventually return, one should know that the nirvāṇa spoken of by the Śākyas will likewise return; for this reason, they say that nirvāṇa is impermanent."
The view that what is impermanent is permanent is, by its very nature, a false view; it is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), which serves as its antidote.
Because this view arises due to the cessation [of its cause], it is abandoned through the vision of cessation.
"Like dew upon the grass," and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
Is there a wrong view that can contemplate this practice of impermanence?
If they do exist, how is the *Pakaraṇa-sūtra* to be reconciled?
For it says: "In what way does the latent tendency of wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya) function?"
Answer: To slander that there are no causes and no actions is called the latent tendency of false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya*). Why is this not mentioned here?
If it were non-existent, how would this passage be explained?
For example, it says:
"To view the permanent as impermanent is a false view, abandoned by the vision of cessation."
Answer: There is this wrong view that perceives permanence in what is impermanent. Question:
If that is so, why does the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* not mention it?
The answer is:
that treatise does not exhaustively describe the characteristics of the practice of wrong views.
There are inherent characteristics of various fetters that are not fully explained therein;
furthermore, even those who maintain other views are all included within what has been stated.
Just as one who slanders by saying there is no cause should be known to be slandering the [Truth of] Origination;
so too, one who slanders by saying there is no action should be known to be slandering the [other] three Truths.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who slanders by saying there is no cause is, in fact, slandering the three Truths.
To slander by saying "there is no action" is said to be slandering the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that no wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) can slander the statement that the permanent is impermanent.
[The opponent] asks:
If this is so, how then is this passage to be interpreted?
The answer is:
Nirvana possesses the characteristic of permanence.
If one says that there is no nirvāṇa, this is likewise a slander against the characteristic of permanence.
It is just as if someone were to slander a person by saying they have no fingers, while also slandering the visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility upon which those fingers depend;
it is the same in this case.

Furthermore, there are those who say that while the non-Buddhists claim the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are eternal, the Śākyas claim that *nirvāṇa* is eternal but is not an aggregate. They argue:
"Apart from the aggregates, nothing else exists that is eternal."
For this reason, would it not be a denial of *nirvāṇa*?
"To view suffering as pleasure," and so forth, as explained at length.
What is meant by suffering?
The five aggregates of clinging are truly suffering.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists claim that suffering is pleasure?
The answer is:
It is called "pleasure" because it is a pleasure for a short duration.
It is like a person finding pleasure in rest after extreme exertion, pleasure in coolness during heat, pleasure in warmth during cold, or pleasure in obtaining food and drink when hungry and thirsty.
For this reason, it is said that the aggregates are pleasant.

As it is taught, regarding inferior phenomena as supreme is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), which is its intrinsic nature; its antidote is the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana*).
Question: To view suffering as pleasure is called the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa). For what reason is it not called clinging to views when one views the impermanent as permanent? Answer:
Those who perceive the impermanent as permanent regard both superior and non-superior phenomena as being of one essence.
Although their own phenomena are said to be permanent, they are not superior, such as when one calculates [them to be] like space or cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
To view suffering as pleasure and to regard inferior phenomena as supreme is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*);
to view the impermanent as permanent is not so named.
Furthermore, some say that because there is great suffering within the aggregates (*skandha*), one regards minor suffering as pleasure.
Because one equates this minor pleasure with nirvāṇa, it is called the "clinging to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
To perceive the impermanent as permanent is an error, for within the aggregates (skandhas) there is not even the slightest permanence that could be considered equivalent to the permanent.
Why is this? Because for even a single moment there is no further abiding; it is a phenomenon subject to dispersal and extinction.
As it is said:
What is the phenomenon at the time of cessation?
The answer is:
present phenomena.
For this reason, to perceive the impermanent as permanent is called an extreme view (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), not a dogmatic adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
This applies extensively to cases such as perceiving what is pleasant as suffering, and so forth.
What is the true meaning of "pleasure"?
Pleasure is the cessation of all things, which is nirvāṇa. For what reason do those non-Buddhists regard nirvāṇa as suffering?
The answer is:
Just as when a person has one sense organ impaired, they consider it suffering, they think to themselves:
"If the impairment of a single organ is already considered suffering, how much more so when many organs are impaired?"
For this reason, that which is pleasant in the Dharma is regarded as suffering. The Venerable Sūmīta said:
"If even a single faculty remaining is a cause of suffering, how much more so when many faculties remain—would they not be causes of suffering?"
If the sense-faculties cease, there is liberation.
To perceive suffering within the bliss of nirvāṇa is the nature of wrong view; seeing cessation and abandoning it is its antidote.
This view arises dependent upon cessation and is abandoned by seeing cessation, like dew on the grass; this is explained at length.
It is asked:
For what reason is the view that *nirvāṇa* is suffering called a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and not a view of the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*)?
As it is said:
"The Truth of the Path is also happiness, because it leads to happiness.
The answer is:
The Path has two aspects:
the aspect of suffering and the aspect of happiness.
Because the Path can lead to a state of happiness, it is called the aspect of happiness.
Because it is impermanent, suffering is called a "portion of suffering";
Nirvana is not twofold but consists of pure bliss.
To slander this is wrong view; the Truth of the Path is not like that.
Furthermore, there are those who say that, as explained in the *Dṛṣṭivarga*, there are two kinds of happiness:
first, conventional happiness (*saṃketa-sukha*), and second, happiness of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-sukha*).
What was stated above regarding "being able to reach the state of happiness" refers to conventional happiness, not the happiness of ultimate meaning.
Furthermore, because of the bliss of nirvāṇa, the Path is designated as bliss.
Question: Is there any wrong view that can take nirvāṇa as its object and regard it as suffering?
If they do exist, how is the *Pakaraṇa-sūtra* to be reconciled?
For it says: "In what way does the latent tendency of wrong view (mithyādṛṣṭi-anuśaya) function?"
Answer: Regarding those who slander [the truth] by asserting that there is no cause and no action, and so forth as explained at length—
it should be understood as it was explained above in the section on "permanently conceiving what is impermanent."
Regarding "seeing the impure as pure," what is meant by "impure"?
The answer is:
all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are impure due to two reasons:
First, by means of afflictions; second, by means of objects.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists perceive the impure as pure?
The answer is:

Fools, regarding their conduct, perceive it as pure because of its occasional purity—such as through grooming the nails, teeth, hair, and skin, or by massaging the body and bathing—and on account of these matters, they view it as pure.
If there were even the slightest element of purity within these phenomena, that estimation would not be a false view;
however, because of perverted perception, one estimates that excrement, urine, intestines, the stomach, and so forth are pure, and thus it is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, one should know that tainted formations (*sāsrava-saṃskāra*) are impure phenomena (*aśubha-dharma*) by means of two points:
first, they arise from afflictions (*kleśa*); second, they arise from sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).
As it is said:

Regarding this teaching as supreme is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Its antidote (*pratipakṣa*) is the abandonment through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*), and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
We clearly see excrement, urine, mucus, and saliva flowing out; how can they be said to be pure?
The answer is:
They assert this:
although that which flows out is impure, the place from which it flows out is pure.
It is like the flower of the kiṃśuka tree, which is colored like flesh; when the flowers are in full bloom, a jackal sees them and thinks to itself:
"Just as I do now, I shall surely eat meat."
Dwelling for a long time beneath a tree, he once smelled a flower that had fallen to the ground and realized it was not flesh.
He then thought to himself:
"Although this fallen one is not flesh, those remaining upon the tree must surely be flesh."
Those non-Buddhists are also like this: although that which flows forth from them is not pure, the source from which it flows forth must necessarily be pure.
Question: Just as within the well-expounded Dharma it is also said that wholesome actions with outflows are pure, yet they are not wrong views; [is this not the case here?]
Is that statement itself a false view?
The answer is:
when there is even a slight mark of purity, one perceives a slight purity.
Question: What is the characteristic of purity? Answer:
Being unmixed with afflictions and moreover being contrary to afflictions, it is therefore not a false view.
Within those poorly taught doctrines, to equate impure phenomena with the pure phenomena that accord with ultimate reality is called a false view.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in well-expounded teachings, purity is attained through virtuous conduct; therefore, it is not wrong view.
They claim that because one regards virtuous and non-virtuous conduct, the unwholesome roots, the afflictions, and inverted wrong views as purity, it is called "wrong view."
Question: If contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are impure because they are mixed with afflictions (*kleśa*),
how can it be said that there are three kinds of purity?
Answer: According to the ultimate meaning, all contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) are entirely impure; they are spoken of as pure only by way of conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
What is meant by "conventional designation"?

Because it arises from the wholesome roots of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and because it can also counteract phenomena such as desire, it is called a "provisional designation" (*prajñapti*).
Regarding the "pure view of the impure," this view is of two kinds, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is purification?
The answer is:
the Path and the fruit of the Path.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists say that the Path of Cessation is impure?
The answer is: they speak thus:
According to the true meaning, all afflictions are impure phenomena; since the Path is able to sever them, the Path is also impure because it can sever all afflictions.
Because Nirvana arises from an impure path, it is also impure.
It is just as when a knife cuts an impure object, the knife becomes impure;
and when that impure knife cuts other objects, it causes those other objects to become impure as well.
Furthermore, it is like washing an impure object with water: the water becomes impure;
if one uses this water to wash other objects, those objects become impure.
In the same way, when the path cuts off all afflictions, the path itself becomes impure.
If one considers that this path gives rise to nirvāṇa, that too is impure.

To say that the path is impure is a view whose intrinsic nature is false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); its antidote is the abandonment [of such views] through the realization of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
If one says that cessation is impure, this view is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), which is its intrinsic nature; the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana*) is its antidote.
Wrong views are abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana*), because they arise with the path as their object.

When the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) and the receptivity to the knowledge of the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) arise, the abandonment of views regarding cessation and the abandonment of false views are likewise.
"One who sees a self where there is no self," and so forth, as explained at length.
What is meant by "selflessness"?
The answer is:
all phenomena (dharmas) are without self.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists perceive me?
The answer is:
because they are ignorant of the dharmas of deportment regarding coming and going.
They speak thus:
"If there were no self, who would come and who would go? Who would stand and who would sit? Who would bend and who would stretch?
It is because the self exists that one is able to come, go, stand, sit, bend, and stretch."
Furthermore, if there were no self, then there would be no seeing, hearing, smelling odors, knowing tastes, feeling tangibles, or recollecting.
Since these things exist, one must know that there is a self.

That which perceives a self where there is no self is called the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); this is its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
This view arises taking suffering as its object, and so forth, as explained at length.
There are two kinds of "self":
first, the nominally designated self; second, the conceptualized personal self.
If one conceives of the nominally designated self, it does not constitute wrong view.
If one calculates in terms of a self and what belongs to a self (*pudgala-ātman*), this is a false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*). Question:
In this context, only the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) is mentioned; why is the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīyadṛṣṭi*) not mentioned?
The answer is:
"The view of self is of the nature of perversion, whereas the view of 'mine' is not of the nature of perversion.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the view of self is the root.
If one speaks of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), one should know that this also includes speaking of the view of what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that because the view of self exists, the view of what belongs to the self comes to exist; thus, if one speaks of the view of self, one should know that this also includes speaking of the view of what belongs to the self. The same applies to the view of "I" (*ahaṃ-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of "mine" (*mama-dṛṣṭi*).
Question: For what reason is it not said that the view of self regarding what is non-self is called a false view? Answer:
Because there is no self.
Furthermore, some say: if one perceives the absence of self as being without self, this is right view and is not called wrong view.
It is not seeing a non-cause as a cause, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: How is it that they see a cause where there is no cause? Answer:
Because it is caused by erroneous views.
It is like a farmer who plants seeds and reaps a great harvest in autumn. He speaks thus:
All of this is granted by the grace of the goddess Śrī, the goddess Siddhā, and the goddess Śamā.
If a son or daughter is born, they say:
"This is all granted by the god Nanda and the god Nandabala."
If those who are wealthy and noble give birth to sons or daughters, they will say:
"These were all granted by Viṣṇu and Maheśvara. They thus form such false views, reckoning what is not a cause to be a cause;

this is called the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), which is their intrinsic nature, and it is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*). Its remedy is the vision of suffering.
This clinging to precepts and observances arises conditioned by suffering; therefore, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering. Question:
To perceive a cause where there is no cause is also called "denying the cause"; why then is this not considered wrong view?
The answer is:
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra says:
"If one slanders [the existence of] causes, this is called wrong view."
He does not say there is no cause;
because he does not regard what is not a cause as a cause, it is not a false view.
This concerns the views of having a cause and having no cause, and so forth, as explained at length.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists claim there is no cause?
The answer is:
because they observe that all things, both internal and external, possess various characteristics, they speak thus:
Who carved the rivers? Who piled up the mountains? Who fashioned the fine thorns? Who painted the birds and beasts?
Therefore, this verse was spoken:
"Who is able to create the fine thorns, And paint all the various birds and beasts?"
"All these are produced without cause; there is no sovereign being in the world.

This view of both having causes and lacking causes is, by its very nature, wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); it is abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and this is its antidote.
"This view arises conditioned by origination; one sees that origination is abandoned," and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what reason is it said here that the false view which denies causes is abandoned through the vision of origination?

In the *Dṛṣṭivarga*, it is stated that the wrong view which slanders causes (*hetu*) is to be abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).
The answer is:
some say that such was the intention of the one who composed the Sūtra, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say that while this [text] does not explain the meaning of all causes, that [other text] explains the meaning of all causes.

Again, there are those who say that this [text] denies the cause that produces an effect, whereas that which is explained therein denies the cause that produces an effect as well as the cause that does not produce an effect.
If one says that nirvāṇa has no cause, is this not right view? Furthermore, there are those who say:
"In this context, it refers to the denial of the cause of suffering; in that context, it refers to the denial of the cause of neither-suffering-nor-non-suffering."

Furthermore, there are those who say that herein there is no sense of slandering the cause of the Path; therefore, this is not called the wrong view of slandering the Path. Rather, it possesses only the sense of slandering the cause of Origination, and for this reason, it is called the wrong view of slandering Origination.
"There is one who holds the view of non-existence," and so forth, as explained at length.
What is meant by "existence"?
The answer is:
The Four Noble Truths are precisely these.
For what reason do those non-Buddhists claim that there are no truths?
The answer is:
Because they hold the view of a self, they claim that there is no truth; they assert:
"I have no suffering."
This is to slander suffering [by claiming] "I have no cause";
this is to slander the origin [of suffering].
If there were no cessation for me,
that would be to slander cessation;
if there were no cessation, there would be no antidote.
As it is said in the section on wholesome dharmas:
"One gives rise to faith that these aggregates are suffering and non-self; with a mind focused on suffering, one says there is the Truth of Suffering.
One gives rise to faith that this suffering has a cause; with a mind focused on origination, one says there is the Truth of Origination."
If one gives rise to faith through the cessation of suffering, the mind of cessation speaks of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
if one gives rise to faith through the antidote to cessation, the mind of the path speaks of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

To hold the view that what exists is non-existent is called wrong view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*), which is its intrinsic nature; it is abandoned by the vision of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, which serve as its antidotes.
This view arises conditioned by the Four Noble Truths and is abandoned by seeing the Four Noble Truths; this is explained at length. Question:
For what reason does wrong view not take space (*ākāśa*) or cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its object?
Answer: Some say that if a phenomenon is an aggregate (*skandha*), it is the cause of an aggregate, the cessation of an aggregate, or the antidote to an aggregate.

False view, however, takes as its object space (*ākāśa*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); since these are neither the cause of an aggregate nor its cessation or antidote, false view does not take them as its object.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if a phenomenon is suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, or the antidote to suffering, then wrong view does not take it as its object.

This is because wrong view takes as its objects space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which are contrary to the aforementioned [noble truths]; therefore, wrong view does not take them as its objects.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if a dharma is either a defilement or a means of liberation, then wrong view takes as its object space (*ākāśa*) or non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); since this contradicts the previous [explanation], it does not take those as objects.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if a phenomenon is the object of uncontaminated right view, it is also the object of wrong view; however, space and cessation not through deliberation are not objects of right view, nor are they objects of wrong view.
Just as with wrong view and right view, so too should one understand the cases of clarity and lack of clarity, wisdom and lack of wisdom, certainty and doubt, and faith and slander.
Question: If it is said that there is no such thing as space or cessation not due to conditions, what is the object of this mind?
Answer: It is precisely that which takes space (*ākāśa*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its objects. Why is this so?
This lack of profound respect is like slandering the dharmas that constitute the essential means for transcending afflictions. Question:
What kind of wisdom is this?
Answer: This is a non-obscured indeterminate wrong knowledge that is abandoned through contemplation (*cintāmayī-prahāṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "there is the view of existence," there are three kinds of existence: [existence as cause, existence as fruit, and existence as self].
First, existence through mutual dependence;
second, existence as a locus;
third, substantial existence.
Regarding existence through mutual dependence: because of existence there is non-existence, and because of non-existence there is existence.
Regarding existence in a particular location: it means that while it exists in this place, it does not exist in that place.
Regarding "truly existent" (*dravyasat*): this refers to that which truly exists and that which truly does not exist, such as suffering which truly exists and the self which truly does not exist.
Furthermore, there are those who say that existence is of two kinds:
first, substantial existence (*dravyasat*); second, conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*).
That which exists as a substantial entity refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
That which exists as a conventional designation refers to things such as "man" and "woman.
There are two kinds of denial regarding suffering:
First, the denial of the substance; second, the denial of the fruit.
If one denies origination (*samudaya*), one denies both the substance and the cause.
If one denies cessation (*nirodha*), one denies the substance but does not deny the fruit.
If one slanders the Path, one slanders the substance of things but does not slander the cause.
Some teachers, however, claim that this also slanders the cause.
This is explained at length, beginning with the view that there is no action.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
Some say that one should state as follows:
"If there is a view regarding what is non-existent, it should be called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*).
Others say that one should state as follows:
It is non-active yet possesses wisdom. Why is this?
Because it is not the nature of vision.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one should state as follows: "This is not a view. Why is this so?
Because the five views are not mentioned.
As for why they are not mentioned, what is the intention behind this?
The answer is:
Because one intends to engage in a dialogue:
for example, as it is said, "There is no action, yet there is vision. What kind of view is this?
This is called a question.
Answer: This is not a view;
this is what is called an answer.
Although such a case does not actually exist [in this context], there are questions and answers.

For example, within the "Ten Gates," regarding the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*), and untainted unconditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-asamskṛta-dharma*), one also asks how many latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) they are governed by; this too constitutes a question.
The answer is:
"One is not driven by the latent tendencies.
This, too, is an answer.
Just as there may be questions and answers even though such a thing does not exist, so it is here:
questions and answers are posed even though such a thing does not exist.
To view that which is non-existent as existent—what kind of view is this?
Answer: This is not a view; it is false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Question:
What is wrong knowledge?
The answer is:
some say it is a non-obscured indeterminate dharma that is abandoned through cultivation.

It is like perceiving a correct path as a wrong path, or perceiving a wrong path as a correct path; it is like perceiving a man as a woman, or perceiving a woman as a man—such perceptions as these are what is meant.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this wisdom also includes obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) states, namely those associated with pride (*māna*). For example, that Brahmā spoke thus:
"I am Mahābrahmā, the most honored among all Brahmās; I am the creator."
This is false wisdom. Why is this so?
Because there is no mind abandoned through the vision of the truths that could abide and utter such words.
One should state it thus:
It is as previously explained; this is a dharma that is abandoned through contemplation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and is non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Question:
If that were so, it would contradict what is stated in the Jñānavastu:
"What is wrong knowledge? It is defiled wisdom."
Answer: It does not contradict that. Why is this so?
Ignorance is of two kinds: namely, that which pertains to ultimate reality and that which pertains to conventional designations.
That which pertains to ultimate reality is associated with the latent tendency of ignorance; this has been completely severed by all Arhats.

Regarding "provisional names" (*prajñapti*), such as seeing a stump and calling it a person, these exist even among Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; however, only for the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, are both [types of] such things completely exhausted.
There are four inversions, namely: permanence, bliss, purity, and self.
Because they are shrouded by phenomena that appear similar [to reality], one does not know impermanence.
Because they are shrouded by phenomena of pleasing deportment, one does not know suffering.
Because it is covered by skin, one does not know its impurity;
because it is covered by its functions, one does not know its lack of self. Question:
What is the nature of these four inversions?
The answer is:
they are of the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Question: If these are forms of wisdom (*prajñā*), how many among these five views are inversions (*viparyāsa*) and how many are not? Answer:
Two and a half views are inversions, while two and a half views are not inversions. Regarding the two and a half views that are inversions:
they consist of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the eternalist view subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the statement that "two and a half views are not inverted": these are wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) subsumed under the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). Question:
For what reason are two and a half views inverted, while the other two and a half are not?
Answer: It is called "perverted" (viparyāsa) for three reasons:
first, because it functions erroneously; [and so forth].
Second, superimposition (*samāropa*);
third, inversion of nature (*svabhāvaviparyāsa*).
Although the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) functions as an inversion of nature, it is not a form of superimposition.
Why is this? Because it destroys the nature of things.
Although the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) may shift in its activity and increase, its nature is not inverted.
Why is this so? Because there is a slight similarity between them.

It is also taught that there is a path belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) capable of abandoning desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and a path belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) capable of abandoning desire for the form realm.
This is inversion; its intrinsic nature consists of being a self, a thing, a characteristic, a part, and an essence.
Having already explained the reason for its intrinsic nature, we shall now explain for what reason it is called an inversion.
Answer: They are called "perversions" (viparyāsa) because they involve an increase in what is inverted.
These four perversions are abandoned solely through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya).
Why is this? Because they arise conditioned by suffering, they are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Furthermore, these inversions arise conditioned by the fruit; they are abandoned by the wisdom that perceives the fruit.
Furthermore, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is by nature a perversion to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; thus, when the view of a self is abandoned, it is also abandoned.
Furthermore, suffering is coarse; if one errs regarding this coarse suffering, one is censured by the noble ones.
Just as a person who commits an error during the day is censured by others,
if one errs regarding the subtle nature of the three truths, one is not severely rebuked because of that subtlety.
If someone were to commit a transgression during the night, worldly people would not severely rebuke them.
Furthermore, once a practitioner has seen suffering, they will forever be free from a perverted mind.
If a practitioner, having seen suffering, were not to see its origin, such a thing is impossible, for the sake of analytical discernment.
Even if, after seeing suffering, they do not further perceive the remaining truths, should they be asked:
"Are these aggregates permanent or impermanent?"
He would certainly answer:
"It is impermanent; it does not abide for even a single moment.
If one were to ask: "Is it suffering or is it pleasure?"
He would certainly answer:
"It is suffering, like a red-hot iron ball.
If asked whether it is pure or impure?
He would certainly answer:
"It is impure, just like a heap of excrement.
If asked, "Is there a self or is there no self? [he would likewise answer].
He would certainly answer:
"There is no self, because there is no agent.
Since there is neither an agent nor a recipient, it is like grass, wood, or discarded refuse."
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll Four; Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll Five.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others, during the Northern Liang dynasty.
Chapter Two: On Knowledge (Jñāna-varga). Section Two of the *Saṃyukta-skandhaka*: On Knowledge. Is there a single knowledge that knows all phenomena?
Regarding this chapter and the explanation of its meaning, the *upadeśa* (instructional commentary) should be explained here in detail. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others.
For example, the Mahāsāṃghika school asserts as follows:
The essence itself is capable of knowing its own essence; just as a lamp, being of the nature of illumination, can illuminate itself and also illuminate others, so too is that wisdom:
by its very nature as wisdom, it can know itself and also know others.
The Dharmaguptaka school asserts that wisdom can know associated phenomena.
The Mahīśāsaka school asserts as follows:
Wisdom knows the dharmas that are shared. They state this:
there are two kinds of wisdom that arise simultaneously.
One is associated with the mind, and one is not associated with the mind.
Knowledge associated with the mind knows phenomena not associated with the mind; knowledge not associated with the mind knows phenomena associated with the mind.
The Vātsīputrīyas maintain this position:
"It is the person (*pudgala*) who knows, not wisdom (*jñāna*).
This treatise was composed in order to refute such various dissenting views.
Is there perhaps a single wisdom that knows all phenomena? The answer is: No.
If, moreover, there arises this wisdom that all phenomena are without self, what is it that this wisdom does not know?
The answer is:
it does not know its own self-nature.
This constitutes the cessation of the Mahāsāṃghika view;
not knowing [the principle of] correspondence, it constitutes the cessation of the Dharmaguptaka view;
not knowing [the principle of] coexistence, it constitutes the cessation of the Mahīśāsaka view.
By knowing through wisdom rather than through a person, the intention of the Vatsīputrīya school is refuted.
Herein, questions and answers are formulated, as well as objections and resolutions, as it is said:
"Is there a single wisdom that knows all phenomena?"
This is the question. The answer is: "No."
This is the answer.
Furthermore, if this wisdom arises that all phenomena are selfless, what is there that this wisdom does not know?
This is the challenge.
Answer: Not knowing its own essence, not knowing its association, and not knowing its coexistence—this is what constitutes penetration. Question:
Who asked this question?
Who gave this answer?
Some say that the Vibhajyavādins asked and the Puthuvādins answered.
As the Vibhajyavādin asked the Vaitulika:
"Is there a single cognition that knows all phenomena?
The Vaitulika replied:
"No. The Vibhajyavādins further challenge:
"If this wisdom arises [realizing] that all phenomena are without self, what is there that this wisdom does not know?"
Yuktavādin established this thesis:
"One does not know its own essence, one does not know its association, and one does not know its coexistence.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: the disciple asks and the teacher answers.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there is no questioner and no respondent; rather, the author of the sūtra intended this:
suppose someone were to ask, "Is there a single cognition that knows all phenomena?"
I would answer: "No.
They would then raise this objection:
If this wisdom arises [realizing] that all phenomena are without self, what is it that this wisdom does not know? I shall answer:
It does not know its own essence, it does not know its association, and it does not know its coexistence.
In this context, "one wise one" refers to a single momentary cognition; therefore, it is said that such cognition does not know its own self-nature, and so forth, as explained at length.
If one were to ask:
"Among these ten cognitions, is there perhaps even a single cognition that knows all phenomena?"
One may answer thus: "Yes;
it refers to conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
The same applies to the cases of nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, and two.
If one were to ask:
"Within these two types of knowledge, is there perhaps one knowledge that knows all phenomena?
The answer is:
There is; namely, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Is it possible for that very conventional knowledge to know all phenomena?
The answer is: [No].
It is known.

If, in a single moment, conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*)—excluding its own self-nature, its associated factors (*saṃprayukta*), and its co-existent factors (*sahabhū*)—is able to know all other dharmas arising in the subsequent moment, and is able to know the preceding moment’s conventional knowledge along with its associated and co-existent factors, then conventional knowledge, within two moments, can know all dharmas through a single cognition.
The previous statement that "one wisdom does not know" refers to one momentary instance of wisdom.
Question: For what reason does a self-entity not know its own self-entity?
Answer: Some say that all phenomena, excluding their own self-nature, have the sense of arising through conditions in relation to other things;

however, with respect to its own self-nature, there is no increase and no decrease, no harm and no benefit, no nourishment and no destruction, no augmentation and no diminution, and no cause, no condition, and no sequential order.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if an entity were to know itself, it would contradict worldly empirical analogies; just as a fingertip cannot touch itself, as the black pupil of the eye cannot see its own blackness, and as a blade cannot cut itself, therefore an entity does not know itself.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if a self-nature were to know its own self-nature, then there would be no duality of factors.
As the Blessed One said:
"Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms," and so on, up to "mental consciousness arises conditioned by the mind and mental objects."
Furthermore, there are those who say that if a self-essence were to know itself, then the threefold contact would not exist.
As the Blessed One said:
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; these three constitute the threefold contact."
However, since this contact arises, there is no self-essence capable of knowing its own self-essence.
Furthermore, some say that if a self-essence were to know its own self-essence, then false views would not exist.
If wrong view were able to know itself as "I am wrong view," this would then be right view and could not be called wrong view.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if a self-nature knows its own self-nature, then the nature of this wisdom must ultimately be such that it can know itself but cannot know others.
However, because it is able to know others, it does not know its own self-nature.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if the self-nature were to know its own self-nature, then there would be no distinction between the grasper and the grasped.
Just as the grasper and the grasped are related, so too are cognition and its object.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if a self-nature were to know itself, how could it know?
Is it that one knows the self-nature as being the self-nature, and does one know the other-nature in the same way as one knows the self-nature?
Or is it that one knows the other-nature as being the other-nature, and does one know the self-nature in the same way as one knows the other-nature?
If one knows that one's own nature is indeed one's own nature, and if one knows that the nature of another is indeed the nature of another, this is correct;
if one perceives one's own nature as being like the nature of another, this is erroneous.

If this wisdom, when it arises, were able to know its own nature and also know the nature of others, then one wisdom would possess two functional characteristics; if it possesses two functional characteristics, there would be two wisdoms; and if there are two wisdoms, there would be a multiplicity of self-natures.
Question: If a self-nature does not know itself, how is the analogy from the Mahāsāṃghika school to be reconciled? Answer:
This analogy need not necessarily be reconciled. Why is this?
This analogy is not taught within the Sūtras, Vinaya, or Abhidharma; one cannot use a worldly, conventional illustration to challenge the Dharma of the Noble Ones.
The dharmas practiced by the noble ones differ from the dharmas practiced by worldly people.
If one must reconcile this, how should it be reconciled?
The answer is:
One should state the fault in that analogy.
If the analogy has a fault, the phenomenon it illustrates also has a fault.
In what way does the analogy have a fault?
The answer is:
A lamp has no faculties and no mind; it is not included among the category of sentient beings.
Is that wisdom also without faculties and without mind, such that it too is not included among the category of sentient beings?
Furthermore, since a lamp is composed of a multitude of atoms, is that cognition also composed of a multitude of atoms?
If it were not so, then they would not be analogous.
Furthermore, is the essential nature of a lamp to illuminate?
If it is the nature that illuminates, what further thing would there be to illuminate?
If its essential nature were not illumination, it should be darkness, which would mean it lacks the nature of light.
One takes up a lamp for the purpose of dispelling darkness; if the essential nature of the lamp were darkness, there would be the great fallacy of inconsistency.
For what reason are they not known as associated?
The answer is:
because they arise by taking the same single dharma as their object.
These various minds and mental factors arise by taking a single dharma as their common object; because they share this same object, they are unable to take one another as objects.
It is like many people looking up at the sky: they cannot see one another's faces.
So it is with them as well.
Furthermore, if wisdom takes its own associated feeling as its object, does that feeling take itself as its object or another as its object?
If it takes itself as its object, there would be the fault of taking oneself as one's own object.
If it takes another as its object, then it does not share the same object as wisdom.
For what reason does it not know the co-existent dharmas?
The answer is:
Because of proximity.
It is like when one places a copper probe containing añjana ointment upon the eye; because of that proximity, the eye cannot see. Question:
What is meant by "shared dharmas" (*sādhāraṇa-dharma*)?
The answer is:
they are the arising, abiding, and impermanence of those bodily and vocal karmas that have been transformed.
The śramaṇas of the West speak thus:
"What are co-existent dharmas?
The aggregate-body upon which wisdom arises when it is produced is a co-existent dharma."
Question: According to what you have said, the body upon which wisdom arises is a shared phenomenon (*sādhāraṇadharma*).
If that were so, when visual consciousness arises, one would not see the various distinctions of the body’s own forms.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with the other consciousnesses.
They maintain this view:
when the five consciousnesses arise, each is able to take its own support as its object, whereas the mental consciousness cannot.
Question: The mind is able to take all phenomena as its objects.
Your previous statement that it cannot is therefore incorrect.
Furthermore, if it were the case that the body upon which wisdom arises is called a "shared dharma" (sādhāraṇadharma), there would be a great error. How is this known?

For example, when the patience regarding suffering (duḥkhe dharmakṣānti) arises, one does not yet attain certainty regarding one's own body; this is what is meant by attaining a limited degree of certainty regarding suffering.

He speaks thus: "If the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) does not reach final certainty, then with the arising of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), one attains final certainty.

Just as if the patience regarding the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) does not reach final certainty, then with the arising of the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*), one attains final certainty."
If he were also like that,
he should not have made such a statement. Why is this?
The time for attaining certainty regarding the Path is different from the time for attaining certainty regarding Suffering.
Question: What is the meaning of this?

Answer: Just as the wrong view abandoned through the Truth of the Path universally slanders all paths, it is impossible for one to achieve even a slight degree of certainty regarding the path; this is for the sake of making distinctions.
If one attains even a slight degree of certainty regarding the Path, one is able to sever the wrong view that slanders the Path; how much more so if one attains complete certainty?
This applies with the sole exception of the factors that arise simultaneously in association for a single moment.

For example, if one holds the view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), conceiving form as the self, up to conceiving consciousness as the self, and if at the time when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, one does not attain right certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*) with respect to the body that serves as the basis, then the view of a self in the body—which is the object of observation—should not be abandoned.
Why is this? Because through the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), one does not perceive a self, as one perceives the body as the objective support (*ālambana*).
