Just as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) stands at the head of the afflictions to be abandoned through the truth of suffering, if it is not abandoned, the remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*) will not be abandoned; and if the remaining fetters are not abandoned, one will not attain the definitive certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) regarding suffering.
If one does not attain ultimate and correct certainty regarding suffering, one likewise does not attain ultimate and correct certainty regarding the origin, cessation, and path.
For this reason, when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) manifests, one perceives the very basis of existence as suffering and attains correct certainty therein.
How is this known? It is as stated:
that which is the object of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is also the object of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Those supreme mundane dharmas take as their object the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) in their entirety, without exception.
"Is there perhaps a single consciousness that cognizes all phenomena? and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what reason is consciousness (vijñāna) taught immediately after wisdom (jñāna)?
The answer is:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of that sūtra to express it in this way, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that this is the established method of the ancient sūtras and śāstras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Elder Mahākauṣṭhila went to where the Elder Śāriputra was and asked him, saying: "Elder Śāriputra!"
Regarding what was called "wisdom," what constitutes wisdom?
Next, this question is posed:
regarding what was called "consciousness," what constitutes consciousness?
...and so on, as explained at length.
As it is said in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"How does one know the Dharma?"
Next, it is asked: "What is the dharma of consciousness?
Regarding such meanings as these, wisdom (*jñāna*) was explained first, followed by consciousness (*vijñāna*).
As the Venerable Dharmadinnā said:
If one observes by means of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), this matter is certain.
The author of the sūtra also follows the established tradition; therefore, he first mentions wisdom and subsequently mentions consciousness.
Furthermore, there are those who say that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is itself wisdom (*jñāna*), and wisdom is itself consciousness, differing only by one additional character. Why?
*Jñāna* is translated in the Qin language as "wisdom" (*zhì*), and *vijñāna* is translated as "consciousness" (*shí*). The single additional character is precisely *vi*.
In order to sever such misconceptions and explain their distinct meanings, [the Buddha] first spoke of *jñāna* (knowledge) and subsequently spoke of *vijñāna* (consciousness).
Furthermore, some teachers maintain that this is because both are fundamental dharmas.
In the phenomena of growth, consciousness is the root; in the phenomena of cessation, wisdom is the root.
Furthermore, some say that both are primary dharmas.
Just as it is asked in the section on the Dharma of the Path:
"Who is the sovereign? It is wisdom.
So too, within the phenomena of birth and death, who is the sovereign?
This refers to what is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that both [consciousness and wisdom] rely upon the same basis (*dharma*).
For instance, it is said that one relies on wisdom and not on consciousness; yet it is also said that when the five sense-faculties function, they all rely upon mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one speaks of "knowledge" (*jñāna*), one is speaking of enumerated phenomena (*saṃkhyeya-dharma*); that which has not yet been mentioned is solely the mind (*citta*). Therefore, knowledge is spoken of first, followed by the mind.
Furthermore, there are those who say that among the twelve bases (*āyatana*), two bases are capable of cognition: namely, the mind base (*manāyatana*) and the phenomena base (*dharmāyatana*).
If one speaks of "knowledge" (*jñāna*), one refers to the phenomena base; if one speaks of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), one refers to the mind base.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these six consciousnesses each operate within their own respective domains: the eye-consciousness cognizes form, the ear-consciousness cognizes sound, the nose-consciousness cognizes fragrance, the tongue-consciousness cognizes flavor, the body-consciousness cognizes tangibles, and the mental consciousness cognizes only dharmas.
To stop such an intention and because one wishes to state that consciousness (*vijñāna*) is able to take all phenomena as its objects, consciousness is explained immediately after wisdom (*jñāna*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that because wisdom is able to take all phenomena as its objects, consciousness is explained immediately after wisdom.

Furthermore, there are those who claim that wisdom (*jñāna*) can take both general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) as its objects, whereas consciousness (*vijñāna*) takes only specific characteristics as its object.
To refute such a view and to demonstrate that consciousness is indeed capable of taking both general and specific characteristics as its objects, consciousness is mentioned immediately after wisdom.
Furthermore, there are those who say that while cognition (*jñāna*) operates upon both similar and dissimilar objects, consciousness (*vijñāna*) operates only upon similar objects.
To refute such a view and to explain that consciousness also operates upon both similar and dissimilar objects, consciousness is mentioned immediately after cognition.
Furthermore, there are those who say this is intended to refute the position of the Vātsīputrīya school.
They assert that wisdom (*jñāna*) is a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a factor of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
Relying on the Buddha’s sūtras, they speak as follows:
Because consciousness conditions name-and-form, it is known that this is a branch of existence.
What is the noble path?
It is right view through to right concentration; therefore, wisdom is said to be a branch of the path.

In order to stop such a misconception—that both wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are equally factors of the branches of existence (*bhavāṅga*) and equally factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—and because one wishes to explain that wisdom and consciousness are both factors of the path, consciousness is mentioned immediately after wisdom.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is to stop the position of the *dārṣṭāntika* (analogy-maker).
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Wisdom and consciousness are dharmas that arise sequentially; they do not arise simultaneously.
In order to refute their view, it is said as follows:
If this wisdom arises [realizing] that all phenomena are selfless, what is there that this wisdom does not know?
This wisdom must necessarily have a corresponding consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This is because it would otherwise contradict the principle that consciousness and wisdom arise in succession.
Just as wisdom can take all phenomena as its object by way of their selflessness, so too is consciousness; the rest of the text is as explained above.
Is there perhaps a single consciousness that cognizes all phenomena?
Within this, there are also questions and answers, as well as objections and resolutions, which should be explained according to the *Jñānaprasthāna* (Treatise on Knowledge), as it says:
"There is a mode of practice that takes all phenomena as its object and proceeds by way of the mark of selflessness."
Question: In which sūtra is this stated? Answer: [It is stated in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.]
As it is said in verse:
"If one can observe with wisdom That all conditioned phenomena are without self, One will give rise to a mind of weary disenchantment; This is the path that attains purification."
This verse should be understood as teaching that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are without self (*anātman*).
Question: As it is said:
Question: How can that which gives rise to the mind of revulsion take all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) as its object? Answer:

Some say that the first half-verse teaches the practice of the non-self (*anātman*) of all phenomena, while the second half-verse teaches the practice of taking the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) as its object.
Furthermore, some say that the first half-verse refers to the time of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), while the second half-verse refers to the time of seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*).
Others say that this verse sets forth the teaching on the practice of non-self (*anātman*) at the time of taking suffering as the object.
Why is this so? Because untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not phenomena that should be reviled. Question:
If this is so, how is it that this is the practice of the non-self nature of all dharmas?
The answer is:
"All" is of two kinds:
There is "a portion of all" and there is "all of all.
Here, it refers to "a portion of all," not "all of all. Other sūtras also state:
"All things are ablaze. The untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not ablaze; one should know that "all" here refers to a partial enumeration.
That [statement] is likewise: it speaks of "all" as a partial enumeration.
Furthermore, there are those who say that other sūtras also state:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all conditioned phenomena are non-self; nirvāṇa is quiescent.
This sūtra, however, specifically teaches the practice of the non-self of all dharmas.
The commentary states:
For now, let us set aside whether the Buddhist scriptures speak of this or not.
It is well said thus:
There must be a practice that takes all phenomena as being without self as its object. Why is this so?
Because when a practitioner is on the initial stage of practice, such an observation necessarily manifests before them; it is for this reason that it is taught.
Question: Just as empty space can also take all phenomena as its object, why is this not mentioned here? Answer:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of the sūtra to state it thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that when something should have been stated but was not, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete teaching (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that just as with space, there is a reason why it is empty and a reason why it is not empty.
That for which it is empty is, for example, the absence of "other" within "self."
There is that which is not empty because it exists by way of its own nature (*svabhāva*);
however, in the practice of the non-self (*anātman*), there is no such conceptual differentiation. Therefore, the Venerable Vasumitra spoke thus:
"I do not say that all phenomena are entirely empty."
Question: For what reason can the practice of the contemplation of non-self with outflows take all dharmas as its object,
whereas the practice of the contemplation of non-self without outflows takes only suffering as its object?
Answer: Some say that among the practices of contemplation, the practice of the impure (sāsrava) non-self is superior in its functional power;
whereas the practice of the pure (anāsrava) non-self is superior within its own category at the time of attaining right determination (samyaktva-niyāma).

Just as when first practicing contemplation, the practitioner must contemplate that all phenomena are without self; therefore, the force and function of the practice of the "outflow-tainted" (sāsrava) non-self are predominant, enabling it to take all phenomena as its object.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) practice of the non-self (*anātman*) is superior because it is clearly manifest within its own sphere; therefore, it does not take all phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, some say that the untainted practice of non-self is able to counteract the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
Just as the four inversions take [the five aggregates] as their object, that untainted practice of non-self also takes them as its object.
The tainted practice of non-self cannot counteract the four inversions; therefore, it is able to take all phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, some say that the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) contemplation of the truths has limits, whereas the contaminated (*sāsrava*) contemplation of the truths has no limits.
Others say that the uncontaminated serves as the antidote to afflictions (*kleśa*), and that not all phenomena are of the nature of affliction.
The contaminated [state] does not counteract the afflictions; therefore, it can take all phenomena as its object. Question:
Just as the contemplation of the non-self within the contaminated state cannot exhaustively take all phenomena as its object, they form this thought:
"All dharmas are without self; how then is this not a false view?
He replied:
"Some may say that it takes many factors as its object, rather than taking few."
As for those objects that are mostly taken as conditions, they are like the waters of the great ocean;
those few that are not taken as conditions are like a single drop of seawater.
Furthermore, there are those who say that, according to their respective activities and according to their respective spheres, all take their own substance as a condition.
They are associated and co-existent, yet they are not its sphere of activity nor its domain; therefore, it does not take them as objects.
Question: What is the essential nature of the practice of the non-self of all phenomena when taking them as objects?
The answer is:
"Wisdom is its essence and its nature," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained its essence and nature, we shall now explain why it is called the "practice of non-self."
Answer: Because this practice is devoid of a self or phenomena, it is called the "practice of non-self.

Regarding its realm: although there is also a practice of non-self that takes all phenomena as its object within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, it cannot universally take all phenomena as its object.

As for the stage (*bhūmi*), it exists in seven stages: namely, the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the four fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*), and the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); however, these cannot take all phenomena as their object.
Question: How many objects of cognition can it take as its objective support? Answer:

Conditioned by the four formless aggregates (ārūpya-skandha), there are their respective causes, their respective cessations, the portions of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna-pakṣya), subsequent knowledge itself, and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
The various formless realms, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and space—
whether one says that space and sentient beings are identical or distinct— that state of emptiness is capable of being the object of the perception of selflessness (*anātman*).
The sphere of consciousness (vijñānāyatana) also possesses the practice of non-self (anātman), yet it cannot take all phenomena (dharmas) as its object.
Question: How many kinds of phenomena can it take as its object?

Answer: It takes as its object the three formless aggregates (ārūpya-skandha), their respective causes, their respective cessations, the portion of subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) pertaining to them, subsequent knowledge itself, and cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

The three formless attainments, non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the exclusion of all space—these are the objects of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) when its mode of activity is the perception of non-self (*anātman*).
The sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) takes two stages as its objects.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes one stage as its object.
The rest is as explained above.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the practice of the "I-less" (anātman) within the sphere of infinite space can take as its objects the phenomena mentioned above, and furthermore, it takes five stages as its objects.

Cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and the fourth dhyāna—thus, the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) takes four stages as its object.
The sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) takes three stages as its object.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) takes two stages and cessation not through deliberation as its objects.
The critique states: One should not speak in such a manner; it is better as previously stated.

Regarding the body upon which [the mind] depends: it relies on the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the form realm (rūpadhātu). At the initial birth of the body, it relies on the desire realm; subsequently, the body relies on the form realm.

Why is this so? Initially, one is born depending on a body of the desire realm; at the end of life, one is reborn in the form realm, where, depending on a body of the form realm, [the realization] arises again and manifests before one. The practitioner then practices exclusively the contemplation of non-self.
As for "condition," it conditions all phenomena; as for "foundation of mindfulness," it is the foundation of mindfulness that destroys conditioned phenomena;
as for "wisdom," it is equalizing wisdom. As for "associated with samādhi," it is not associated with samādhi.
Regarding association with the faculties (*indriya*), there is association with three faculties, namely: joy (*saumanasya*), pleasure (*sukha*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The third dhyāna is associated with the faculty of pleasure;
the first and second dhyānas are associated with the faculty of joy.
The preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna are associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
In the desire realm, they are associated with two faculties, namely joy (saumanasya) and equanimity. Question:
Just as the faculties of joy and sorrow are associated with and can take all phenomena as their objects, why is it not stated here that they are "associated" [with them]?
The answer is:
because their essential natures are mutually contradictory.
The nature of the practice of non-self is characterized by aspiration and delight, whereas the nature of the faculty of grief is characterized by dejection;
therefore, they do not correspond with one another. As for "the world," it should be said to exist in the past, future, and present.
Regarding those conditioned by the world (*loka*), they are conditioned by the past, future, present, and non-worldly phenomena (*aloka-dharma*).
As for their being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, they should be said to be wholesome.
Regarding those conditioned by the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate, one should say they have three kinds of conditions.
Regarding those bound to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, one should say they are bound to the desire and form realms, as well as the formless realm.

Regarding those conditioned by phenomena associated with the desire, form, and formless realms, one should say they are conditioned by phenomena associated with the desire, form, and formless realms, as well as by unassociated phenomena.
Regarding those that are in training (*śaikṣa*), beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or neither in training nor beyond training, one should say they are neither in training nor beyond training.

Regarding those conditioned by the state of training (*śaikṣa*), the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and that which is neither training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), they should be said to have three kinds of conditions.

Regarding those abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*), those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*), they should be said to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding objects that are abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned, one should say they are conditioned by three kinds [of objects].
Regarding objects as names and objects as meanings, one should say both are conditioned.

Regarding those that take one's own body as their object and those that take another's body as their object, it should be said that they take one's own body and another's body as objects, and also take that which is neither one's own nor another's as an object.
Regarding the wisdom derived from hearing, the wisdom derived from reflection, and the wisdom derived from cultivation, it should be said that these are the three kinds of wisdom.
In the desire realm, there are the wisdoms of hearing and reflection; in the form realm, there are the wisdoms of hearing and cultivation; in the formless realm, there is the wisdom of cultivation.
Regarding those obtained through application and those obtained by birth, one should say that these are obtained through application and these are obtained by birth.
Regarding the wisdom derived from hearing in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it can be said to be both acquired through application (*prayoga-labdha*) and innate (*upapatti-labdha*).
How can it be said to be acquired through application?
The answer is:
Just as in this world one obtains [the result] by cultivating general and specific characteristics, so too does one obtain it upon being born there;
yet if one has not practiced them, one does not obtain it even though born there.
How, then, can it also be said that it is "obtained through birth"?
Answer: Although these are cultivated, they do not arise in those respective realms and thus are not called "attained at birth.
If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the second dhyāna, or dies in the second dhyāna and is reborn in the first dhyāna, would those [attainments] be considered attained?
Answer: Some say that it cannot be attained. Why is this?
Because it is distant.
If one attains cultivation in the second dhyāna, one obtains it upon being born into the first dhyāna.
When one’s life in the first dhyāna ends and one is born into the second dhyāna, all dharmas belonging to the level of the first dhyāna are completely relinquished.
If one dies in the second dhyāna and is reborn again in the second dhyāna, does that person attain it?
Answer: Yes, they do.
If one dies in the desire realm and is reborn in the formless realm, or dies in the formless realm and is reborn again in the formless realm, does that person attain [the fruit]?
The answer is:
some say they do not, because of the distance.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one cultivates [the formless attainments] while in the formless realm itself, one will be reborn in the formless realm.
A question is asked:
Is it an *ārya* (noble one) who can produce this dharma, or is it an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who can produce this dharma?
Answer: Both the noble ones (ārya) and ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are capable of it.
There are two kinds of ordinary persons:
There are ordinary persons of our own school (insiders) and there are ordinary persons of other schools (outsiders).
Which school’s ordinary persons are able to produce this dharma?
The answer is:
Those within our own school are capable of it, as are those of external schools.
Among those within our own school, ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) obtain it both through skillful means and by birth;
among those of external schools, ordinary persons obtain it only by birth.
Furthermore, there are those who say that non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings attain [the path] only in their place of birth, but it does not arise as a manifest presence. Why is this?
Because they cling to a self.
Question: How does the practice of the non-self nature of all phenomena arise and manifest before one? Answer:
When one born in the desire realm gives rise to [a thought] that manifests in the present, it takes all phenomena as its object.
When one born in the desire realm gives rise to a [thought] belonging to the form realm that manifests in the present, it likewise takes all phenomena as its object.
When one is born in the first dhyāna and it is not manifest as an entry into meditative absorption, it takes all phenomena as its object.
When it is manifest as an entry into meditative absorption, it takes as its object everything from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, the second, third, or fourth dhyānas arise and manifest before them; these likewise take as their objects everything from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
If one is born in the second dhyāna and they manifest before one without having entered meditative absorption, they are able to take all phenomena as their objects.
When entering meditative absorption, it manifests taking the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object.

When one is born in the second dhyāna and brings forth the third or fourth dhyānas, these also manifest taking the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their objects.
It is the same for those born in the third and fourth dhyānas.

Within the formless realm, one practices the contemplation of the non-self nature of all phenomena; whether born in the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm, this [contemplation] manifests before them, taking all phenomena as its object, as explained above.
Question: Which has more objects of cognition (ālambana), the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu)? Answer:
Regarding the realm of form (rūpadhātu), if one has not entered meditative absorption, the objects of focus (ālambana) are the same as those in the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
If one has entered meditative absorption, those belonging to the desire realm are more numerous than those belonging to the realm of form. Why is this so?
Because one does not take the form that is co-existent with concentration as its object by itself, one should state this:

when not in meditative absorption, there is no mindfulness of the body that does not take all forms as its object; there is no mindfulness of feelings that does not take all feelings as its object; there is no mindfulness of the mind that does not take all minds as its object; and there is no mindfulness of phenomena that does not take all phenomena as its object.
Question: Regarding the practice of the non-self nature of all phenomena, is it a practice of aspiration or a practice of weary detachment?
If it is a practice of aspiration, how can it take suffering and its origin as its object?
If one is a practitioner of revulsion and detachment, how can they take as an object a dharma that is to be admired?
The answer is: it should be stated thus:
This is a practice of aspiration and delight, not one of aversion and renunciation. Question:
If it is a practice of aspiration and delight, how can it take suffering and its origin as its object?
Answer: Although it takes suffering and its origin as its object, it is nevertheless a practice of aspiration. Why is this so?

Suppose that one contemplates many impure phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and few pure phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), yet because of those pure phenomena, one practices with a sense of joyful aspiration.
It is like placing a single gold coin upon a pile of copper coins; although the copper coins are many, obtaining even a single gold coin gives rise to joyful aspiration.
It is the same in this case.
Question: Does this practice sever the fetters? Answer:
"Not severed. Question:
If the fetters are not severed, what is the purpose of their arising and becoming manifest?
Answer: It is because one wishes to make the mind sharp and intense.
If the mind is sharp and intense, it can enter the Noble Path.
Question: What is the difference between the practice of emptiness (śūnyatā) and the practice of non-self (anātman)? Answer:
The practice of non-self (*anātman*) serves as the antidote to the notion of "I," while the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) serves as the antidote to the notion of "mine" (*mama*).
Furthermore, the practice of non-self serves as the antidote to the five views of self, while the practice of emptiness serves as the antidote to the fifteen views of "mine."
Furthermore, the practice of non-self counteracts one's own views; the practice of emptiness counteracts what one perceives as "mine.
The same applies to attachment to the self and attachment to what belongs to the self.
Furthermore, the aggregates are not the self; this is the practice of non-self.
"I do not enter into the aggregates" is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, seeing that the eye is without self and giving rise to joy and satisfaction is the practice of non-self (*anātman*);
seeing that "I" do not enter into the eye and giving rise to joy and satisfaction is the practice of emptiness.
This applies likewise up to the sense-base of the mind (*manāyatana*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) is the practice of non-self (*anātma-carita*), while the meaning of the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*) is the practice of emptiness (*śūnya-carita*).
Is it possible for two minds to act as causes for one another in succession?
Question: Why was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
This is to stop the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The non-Buddhists assert that the subsequent mind is the cause of the preceding mind.
Why is this so? Just as when water flows, the subsequent water can urge the preceding water to flow swiftly;
so too, when dharmas arise, future dharmas urge the present to flow swiftly, and the present urges the past to flow swiftly.
In this way, future dharmas are the causes of the present, and present dharmas are the causes of the past.
To sever such a misconception, it is clarified that a subsequent mind is not the cause of a preceding mind.
If the subsequent were to be the cause of the preceding, it would contradict the principle of internal and external dependent origination as taught by the Blessed One:
"Ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so on, up to "birth conditions aging and death."
If the subsequent were the cause of the preceding, then ignorance would be the condition for formations, and so on, up to old age and death being the condition for birth.

Just as it is said that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms, if the subsequent were the cause of the preceding, then visible forms should arise conditioned by visual consciousness.
If parents are the cause of a child, then by that same logic, the child should be the cause of the parents.
This contradicts such internal laws of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
How does it contradict external laws of dependent origination?
Just as the seed is the cause of the sprout, and so on up to the flower being the cause of the fruit,
if that were the case, then the sprout should be the cause of the seed, and so on up to the fruit being the cause of the flower.
If the later were the cause of the earlier, there would be further great fallacies. Why is this?
Because one would experience the fruit without having performed the action, and the fruit would be absent despite having already performed the action.
Question: How can one experience the fruit without having performed the action? Answer:
It is as when one first experiences the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome [actions], and only afterwards performs wholesome and unwholesome actions.
One first experiences the fruits of the precepts of restraint and non-restraint, and only thereafter receives the precepts of restraint;
one first experiences the fruit of the Avīci Hell, and only thereafter commits the five heinous crimes.
One first attains the fruit of a wheel-turning sage king, and only thereafter cultivates the karma of a wheel-turning sage king;
one first attains unexcelled, complete, and perfect enlightenment, and only thereafter practices the various pāramitās.
If that were so, one would experience the fruit without having performed the action, and there would be no fruit for actions already performed.
If actions performed were to have no fruit, then there would be no path leading to liberation or deliverance.
If the subsequent [moment] were the cause of the preceding one, there would be such a great error as this.
Furthermore, the reason for composing this treatise is that, as the Mahāsāṃghika school asserts, two minds arise simultaneously.
This treatise is composed in order to stop such views.
Furthermore, some may claim that causes and conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
now, desiring to clarify the intrinsic nature of causes and conditions, this treatise is composed.
Is it possible for two minds to arise such that they are mutually dependent upon one another? The answer is: No.
Why is this so? Because there is not a single person for whom two minds—prior and posterior—arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, there are those who explain that "the former" refers to the fact that among all past minds, no two arise together, while "the latter" refers to the fact that among all future minds, no two arise together; therefore, the answer was given as follows:
In a single person, two minds do not arise simultaneously—before and after.

Furthermore, some say that "prior" excludes the past and "subsequent" excludes the future; thus, "not simultaneous" is intended to clarify that within a single moment of the present, two minds do not arise together.
If one makes this statement—that there is no case where two minds, a preceding and a succeeding one, arise simultaneously—this stops the intention [of those who claim] that two minds arise together.

Next, if one makes this statement—that a future mind is not the cause of the preceding mind—this stops the intention [of those who claim] that the subsequent [mind] acts as the cause for the preceding one.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if one were to assert that not a single person has two minds arising simultaneously at the prior and subsequent moments, this would negate the meaning of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Next, it is stated that the future mind does not act as a cause for the preceding mind.
This stops the notion of a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), an omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), and a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
In this context, the treatise is composed based on five causes; therefore, the answer is "no.
If the treatise were composed based on six causes, one should answer "yes," because there would be a productive cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).

Just as with two minds, so it is with two feelings, two perceptions, two volitions, two contacts, two attentions, two liberations, two mindfulnesses, two concentrations, and two eyes, up to and including two bodies, two life-faculties, and two bodily continuities; in such cases, there is no sense of mutual causality.
"Is it possible for two minds to take each other as their respective objects? and so forth, as explained at length.
[The opponent] asks:
One should not have formulated that argument first; rather, one should have formulated this argument first.
For what reason? Because the two minds—the preceding and the succeeding—of a single person do not arise simultaneously; one should then ask the following question:
"Is it possible for two minds to exist such that they mutually serve as objects for one another in successive succession?"
What is the intention behind not stating what ought to have been stated?
The answer is:
some say that it was the intention of the author of the sūtra to be thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say that treatises are of two kinds:
first, the fundamental; second, the derivative.
Various people raise this question:
Is it possible for two minds to serve as causes for one another?
Is it possible for two minds to serve as objects for one another?
This is the fundamental treatise.
For what reason do the two minds of a single person not arise simultaneously, one after the other?
This is a secondary inquiry (*pārśvika-vāda*).
Therefore, the fundamental [inquiry] was discussed first, followed by this secondary question.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Abhidharma should be sought by way of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) rather than by way of sequential order.
Whether [a characteristic occurs] before or after makes no difference; one need only not contradict its characteristic and should not demand a specific sequence.
Is it possible for two minds to serve as mutual objects of cognition for one another?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
It was previously stated that two minds do not stand in a relationship of mutual causality, which also implies that two minds lack the quality of being mutual objects of cognition (*ālambana*).
To sever such doubts, this treatise is composed:
"Is it possible for two minds to stand in a relationship of mutual objectification?"
Furthermore, there are those who claim that the objects and conditions of perception lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
In order to refute such views and to clarify that these objects and conditions do indeed possess substantial reality, this treatise was composed.
Question: Is it possible for two minds to serve as mutual objects for one another? Answer: No.
There is. Question: If one answers that there is, this statement is sufficient.
Why is this so? As it is said:
"If a phenomenon is an object-condition for a particular consciousness, there is no such case where it would not at some time serve as its object."
For what reason is it further stated:
"If one is born, is there no future mind?
The answer is:
One should not speak in this way.
The reason for speaking thus is that one wishes to benefit the disciples so that when they receive the meaning, it is clear and distinct.
Is it possible for two minds to take each other as their respective objects?
Answer: There is.
If one generates the intention and contemplates that there is no future. Question:
What is this matter?
The answer is:

A wrong view arises, asserting that there is no future; subsequently, another wrong view arises, asserting that there is no past wrong view, and also asserting that there are no past dharmas. This is called two minds taking each other as objects in succession. Following this, a wrong view arises, and the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) further conceives of that past wrong view as a self.
As it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so it is with the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and the reckoning of annihilation or permanence.

The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) reckons the past as supreme and foremost; the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) reckons them as pure and capable of leading to liberation, reckoning them as the vehicle; doubt (*vicikitsā*) and hesitation reckon two paths; perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedanā*) reckon what is pleasant, excellent, and agreeable; hatred (*vyāpāda*) reckons what is unpleasant, not excellent, and disagreeable; and pride (*māna*) reckons oneself as high and exalted.
Regarding that, ignorance is a state of delusion and lack of knowledge; such states as these are called "defiled minds taking one another as objects.
What is a wholesome mind?
The answer is:

Just as right view reckons the past as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, it regards [the past] as having causes, having accumulations, having conditions; as being existent, having its own nature, having causes, and having conditions.
Such cases as these are called instances where a wholesome mind and wrong view serve as mutual objects for one another.
What about the non-obscured neutral mind?
The answer is:
It is neither skillful nor unskillful; this is called the indeterminate mind wherein wrong views mutually condition one another.
If one gives rise to mental volition and reflection, there is the future.
What is this matter?
The answer is:

For example, when right view arises and says that the future exists, and subsequently another right view arises and says that the past exists, as well as saying that past dharmas exist—this is called two minds taking each other as objects in succession.
The view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi) conceives of past right view as a self; this applies likewise even to non-obscured neutral states that take past right view as their object.
If one gives rise to a mental intention, one contemplates that there is no future path.
Question: Why is this treatise composed once again?
Answer: [As follows:]
Previously, the objects of conditioned-outflow minds (*sāsrava-citta*) were explained; now, the objects of uncontaminated minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are to be explained. Question:
What is the nature of this matter?

Answer: If one generates the intention and contemplates that there is no future path, this mind is associated with wrong view; yet, by taking the non-existence of a future path as its object, one subsequently attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Taking past phenomena as conditions, one contemplates them as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; this has accumulation as its cause and conditions.

Herein, the phrase "at a later time" excludes a single moment and excludes continuity; it does not restrict the time, nor restrict the body, nor restrict [the duration] from beginningless time onward.
For what reason is there no fixed time?
The answer is:

some may slander the Path during the first watch of the night and attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) during the middle watch; others may slander the Path during the middle watch and attain right determination during the last watch.

There may be those who slander the Path during the latter part of the night but attain right determination during the day; there may be those who slander the Path during the day but attain right determination at night;
and there may be those who slander the Path for one day and one night, yet attain right determination for one day and one night.
In this same way, one should know that it applies to half a month, a month, a season, a year, and even to a single lifetime.
If one generates a mental intention that possesses only the future path, this mind is associated with right view.
Conditioned by future paths, the subsequent arising of untainted paths occurs.
Taking past right view as an object—viewing it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—one understands that its cause is accumulation and its condition is existence.
In this way, right view takes the future path as its object;
when the future path arises, it in turn takes right view as its object. This is called mutual dependence through succession.
As for "at a later time," it is as stated:

Regarding the statement that one can enter the Noble Path after the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), this excludes [the possibility of doing so] within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
It is not restricted to a continuous stream (*saṃtati*), nor to a specific time, nor to a specific body, nor even to the period since beginningless saṃsāra.
As it is said:
"The three kinds of correct contemplation can lead one to enter the Noble Path; this is not restricted to a single moment, nor even restricted to the period since beginningless saṃsāra."
Just as the two types of knowledge of others' minds also take each other as objects,
a question is asked:
Why has this treatise been composed once again?

Answer: Previously, the phenomena that take one's own body as their object-condition were explained; now, because one wishes to explain the phenomena that take another's body as their object-condition, it is like the mutual cognition of two people’s minds taking each other as object-conditions.
Question: What are the two types of knowledge of others' minds taught here? Answer:

In this context, it is said that the faculties are identical: they are identical as sharp faculties, identical as medium faculties, and identical as dull faculties; they are identical as the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, up to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna; they are identical as being with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); and they are identical as being part of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) or part of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
Question: How do they serve as mutual objects of perception? Answer:
Both take that mind as their object, but do not take what that mind takes as its object.
If they were to take what that mind takes as its object, then they would be taking the mind itself as their object, and could not be said to be "taking another's mind" as their object.
Question: What kind of knowledge of others' minds is being explained here? Answer:
Regarding the statement here concerning the attainment of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*), a question is asked:
"There are also other ways of knowing the minds of others; why are these not mentioned here?"
The answer is:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of that scripture to state it thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that when something which ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete exposition (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that what is spoken of here refers to that which is excellent both in name and in meaning.

Again, there are those who say that it refers to that which is by nature pervasive, or by nature cultivated, or obtained through the abandonment of desire, or which is the fruit of the fourfold or fivefold dhyāna; these are what are spoken of here.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if wisdom knows the minds of others as they truly are without error, it is described in this context.
Because of this matter, the ocean of wisdom is stirred.
Just as two minds take one another as objects in succession, so it is with all numerical dharmas (*saṃkhyā-dharma*).

Furthermore, one should also distinguish the five consciousnesses, their seeds, realms, wholesome states, defiled states, non-obscured neutral states, and those pertaining to deportment (*airyāpathika*) and craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*).
Those five consciousnesses cannot mutually take one another as objects, because each operates within its own respective sphere;
the mental consciousness, however, can mutually take them as objects, because it takes all phenomena as its objects.

The mind abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the mind abandoned through the vision of the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*) can take one another as objects.
The mind abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering and the mind abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) can likewise take one another as objects.
The minds abandoned by the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*) and the minds abandoned by the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) take one another as their objects.

Furthermore, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned by the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) take one another as objects and can also take latent dispositions with uncontaminated objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) as their objects; however, latent dispositions with uncontaminated objects cannot take latent dispositions with contaminated objects as their objects.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflows (*sāsrava*) that take the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) as their object, which are to be abandoned by the realization of the Truth of the Path, mutually condition one another and can also take latent dispositions with no outflows (*anāsrava*) as their objects. However, latent dispositions with no outflows cannot take latent dispositions with outflows as their objects; rather, latent dispositions with no outflows mutually condition one another in relation to the Path.

The wholesome, unwholesome, and obscured-unspecified [states] abandoned through the path of cultivation take as their objects the five types of minds abandoned through the path of cultivation; the remaining [states] abandoned through the path of cultivation take one another as their objects without being abandoned.

Just as the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the patience regarding the origin (*samudaya-kṣānti*), and the knowledge of the origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) can take the five aggregates as their object, so too the path of mind that is to be abandoned takes the path as its object; they mutually serve as objects for one another according to their respective correspondences.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) mutually condition one another.
The unconditioned factors (*apratisaṃyukta-dharma*) of the desire realm mutually condition one another.
There is no mutual conditioning between the desire realm and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The minds of the form realm, the formless realm, and those that are unconditioned (unbound) take one another as objects.
As for the wholesome [minds], they are able to take three types as objects:
the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral.
Defiled [minds] can take three types as their objects:
wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral. Wholesome resultant-neutral minds take three types as their objects: [wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral].
Wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral [dharmas].
There is no reciprocal condition between unwholesome retribution-neutral [dharmas] and neutral [dharmas]. Why is this?
In the mental stage (*manobhūmi*), there is no unwholesome retribution that is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
As it is said: "Is there any karma for which the body experiences the retribution, but the mind does not?
The answer is: [Yes].
There are instances where unwholesome karma and neutral states of deportment take one another as objects.
What is the manner of this?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of deportment (īryāpatha):
first, deportment itself; second, the mind of deportment.
Deportment refers to visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility.
Regarding the "mind of deportment" (*airyāpathika-citta*), it refers to that which can give rise to the mind of deportment.
The four [sensory] consciousnesses are the skillful means for deportment, but they do not give rise to the mind of deportment.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is both the skillful means for deportment and that which gives rise to the mind of deportment.
Those four consciousnesses can take postures as their objects, but cannot take the minds that initiate postures as their objects;
the mental consciousness can take postures as its objects and can also take the minds that initiate postures as its objects.

Furthermore, there are those who say that from a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) further arises, which is able to take the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object; this constitutes a successive mutual conditioning.
Likewise, a neutral mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-avyākṛta*) involves successive mutual conditioning.
What is this matter?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of craftsmanship.
First is craftsmanship (śilpa) and second is the mind of craftsmanship (śilpacitta).
Craftsmanship refers to form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects; the mind of craftsmanship is that which is capable of giving rise to the mind of craftsmanship.
The five consciousnesses are skillful means for craftsmanship, but they do not give rise to the mind of craftsmanship.
The mental consciousness is both a skillful means for craftsmanship and that which gives rise to the mind of craftsmanship.
The five consciousnesses can take craftsmanship as their object, but they cannot take the mind that gives rise to craftsmanship as their object.
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) can take craftsmanship as its object, and it can also give rise to a mind of craftsmanship that takes [the object] as its object.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because of the mind of craftsmanship, a further mental consciousness arises that can take the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object. This is a false view of mutual causal dependence; it either slanders the effect by means of the cause, or slanders the cause by means of the effect, or fails to slander the effect by means of the cause, or fails to slander the cause by means of the effect.
What is denigrating the result by means of the cause?
It is as when one says that these wholesome and unwholesome karmas have no retribution.
What is denigrating the cause by means of the result?
As it is said, for such a person, all retributions received are without cause and without condition.
How could this not be a denial of the cause by means of its fruit?
It would mean that the afflictions of sentient beings are without cause and without condition.
What is denigrating the fruit by means of the cause?
It is as when one says that the past, future, and present do not exist.
This is called denigrating the fruit by means of the cause; it is a false view to be abandoned through the vision of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

First, regarding the statement that two minds are mutually causes for one another and mutually objects for one another: herein, the meaning of two types of conditions is explained, namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Question: For what reason are the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) not mentioned here? Answer:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of that scripture to be thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that when something should have been stated but was not, one should know that this is an incomplete teaching (*sāvasesa-vacana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this meaning is already included within what was previously stated.
How so? If one speaks of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it should be understood that the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*) has already been explained.

Why is this? As it is said that two minds do not stand in a reciprocal causal relationship, one should know that two minds likewise lack the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
If one speaks of the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), one should know that this also refers to the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Why is this so? As it is said that two minds take one another as objects, one should know that these two minds also take one another as objects through their mutual influence.
This is what is meant by having entered into that which was explained therein.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Five (continued) / Volume Six Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others, during the Northern Liang dynasty.
From the *Saṃyukta-khaṇḍaka*, Chapter on Knowledge (2): For what reason do two minds not arise simultaneously in a single person at different times?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
This is a treatise on animals.
Why is this so? Because it was previously stated that two minds cannot serve as causes for one another in succession.
Why is this? Because there is not a single person for whom two minds, preceding and succeeding, arise simultaneously.
Although this has been stated, the reason for it has not yet been explained; wishing now to explain it, this treatise is composed.

Regarding the question of why two minds do not arise simultaneously in a single person before and after one another, the answer is: there is no second sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). This explains that the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) arise in dependence upon sequential conditions; phenomena of the future world arise based on the conjunction with phenomena of the present world, and they do not arise if such conjunction does not occur.
In the present, if there is a sequence with the future, then [the mind] arises; if there is no sequence, it does not arise.
Furthermore, some say: "For what reason do the two minds of a single person—prior and posterior—not arise simultaneously? and so forth, as explained at length.
Answer: It is the natural law of sentient beings that thoughts arise one after another in succession; two cannot exist simultaneously.
Why is this so? Because there is no second sequential condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Furthermore, some say that this refers to the previous [condition] being like two yokes tied together.
For what reason is there no second sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
The answer is:
the minds of sentient beings arise one after another; two [minds] cannot arise simultaneously.
For what reason do the successive moments of mind in sentient beings arise one by one and not as two simultaneously?
The answer is:
there is no second sequential condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). This is called the meaning of answering each other through mutual succession.

Just as there is a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) in the present that gives rise to a single mind in the future, this should be explained by the analogy of many sheep being shut in a garden with their gates constricted at a narrow passage.
Just as sheep emerge one by one from a narrow gate in a sheepfold, so too do those moments of mind and mental factors arise.
A single present moment opens up the succession for a future moment; if there were many moments in the present world, they would open up the succession for many future moments.
Because [the future] does not exist, there is a sequential opening between one present moment and one future moment.
The proponent of the "maker" (kāraka) says:
For what reason do two minds not arise simultaneously?
Answer: Some say that just as the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) lasts for a single moment, the mind that depends upon the life-faculty also lasts for a single moment; therefore, they do not coexist.
Furthermore, some say that just as the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) lasts for a single moment, the mind (*citta*) that relies upon it also lasts for a single moment;
therefore, they do not coexist. Others say that if two minds were to arise simultaneously, the mind would be impossible to discipline.
If even a single mind is now stubborn and difficult to subdue, how much more so when two minds are present?
Furthermore, some say that if two minds arise simultaneously, then there would be both affliction and the way of transcendence at once—one mind afflicted and one mind seeking transcendence.
If that were so, there would be such faults as the absence of liberation, the absence of detachment, and the absence of vehicles.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If two minds arise simultaneously, what prevents there being three?"
If there were three [realms], then a body belonging to the three realms could be received simultaneously.

If a body were received from the three realms at once, the realms would be destroyed; if the realms were destroyed, then a single person would be simultaneously of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. If that were so, there would be no liberation—and so on, as explained at length.
If three minds arise simultaneously, what prevents there being four?

If there were four minds, one could simultaneously receive the bodies of the four modes of birth; if that were so, it would contradict the four modes of birth, as a single body would be both womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born, and thus there would be no liberation—and so on, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If four [elements] arise together, what prevents there being five?
If there were five, one could simultaneously receive the bodies of the five destinies.
If that were so, the five destinies would be destroyed."
If the five destinies were to perish, the body of a hell-being would be identical to the body of a deity, and so forth, as explained at length.
If there are five [aggregates] arising together, what prevents there being six?
If they do exist, then it would be possible for them to simultaneously take as their object the meanings of the six sense bases, and so forth, as explained at length.

If there were no obstruction to the six, then even up to hundreds of thousands [of consciousnesses] could arise simultaneously throughout future ages, arising in a single kṣaṇa and ceasing in a single kṣaṇa.
If this were so, then there would be no future.

Because there is a future, there is a present; because there is a present, there is a past. If there were no future, there would be no present; if there were no present, there would be no past; if there were no past, there would be no conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); and if there were no conditioned phenomena, there would be no unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
If there were neither the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), then all phenomena (*dharma*) would not exist.
Such faults as these would follow; therefore, two minds cannot arise simultaneously. Question:
Just as numerous mental factors arise simultaneously, there are no such faults as those mentioned above.
If two minds were to arise simultaneously in the same manner as these numerous factors, what further fault would there be?

Answer: Just as a single sequential condition (samanantarapratyaya) unites with a future moment of mind, and because of this union with a single moment of mind, the individual moments of mind of sentient beings arise one by one.

Furthermore, there are those who say that, just as the practice of contemplation unifies with the single mind of the future, because of this unification with the single mind, the minds of sentient beings arise one by one.
If two minds were to arise simultaneously, there would have to be two feelings arising simultaneously.
If there were two feelings, then the dharma of the sentient being’s body would be destroyed.
If the dharma of the sentient being’s body were destroyed, then there would be two kinds of bodies.
If there were two bodies, there would be ten aggregates (*skandhas*).
Because such a fault exists, two minds cannot arise simultaneously. Question:
What is the essential nature of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
The answer is as stated in the *Prakaraṇa*:
This refers to all other past and present minds and mental factors (citta-caitasika), excluding the final mind of an Arhat in the past and present.
Furthermore, some say that all past and present minds and mental factors constitute the essential nature of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya).

Question: If that is so, the final mind of an Arhat lacks the status of being an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*); how then can it be called an immediately preceding condition? Answer:
It is not because of a fault in the final mind of an Arhat that subsequent minds do not arise; rather, it is due to other intervening factors that prevent the arising of later minds.
If they were to arise, they would be able to serve as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Question: What are the characteristics of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*)? Answer:

That which is called "essential nature" is itself its characteristic, and that which is called "characteristic" is itself the essential nature; among all phenomena, characteristics cannot be established apart from their essential nature.
The Venerable Sūmīta said: "The meaning of mutual exclusion is the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Others say:
"The meaning of departing from one's starting point through mutual exclusion is the condition of immediate succession."
Furthermore, some say that the meaning of being able to produce the mind is the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
Others say that the meaning of the continuity of the mind is the equal-and-immediate condition.
Still others say that the meaning of being able to apprehend [an object] is the equal-and-immediate condition.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of the mind’s functional momentum is the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*). The Venerable Buddhadeva stated:
"The characteristic of the mind arising in succession is the condition as immediate antecedent."
Furthermore, there are those who say that causing an unarisen moment to arise is the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The Abhidharmikas say: "The dharma of distinct characteristics causing [dharmas] to arise simultaneously is the condition of immediate succession."
Furthermore, there are those who say that a dharma not yet arisen is the equivalent-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) because it resembles itself.
The essential characteristic of the equivalent-immediate condition has already been explained, but its reason for being so named has not yet been stated.
For what reason is it called the "equivalent-immediate condition"?
Answer: The meaning of "equal and immediate" is the condition of sequence. Question:
If that is so, does the mind serve as the immediate antecedent for another mind, but not for the mental factors?
And do the mental factors serve as the immediate antecedent for other mental factors, but not for the mind?

Answer: As it has been said regarding the teachings of those śramaṇas who propound similar doctrines—that mind acts as the immediate antecedent for mind, and feeling acts as the immediate antecedent for feeling—to speak in such a manner involves an error.

Why is this so? Because a mind of greed serves as the immediate antecedent for a mind of greed; likewise, a mind of hatred for a mind of hatred, a mind of delusion for a mind of delusion, a wholesome mind for a wholesome mind, an unwholesome mind for an unwholesome mind, and an indeterminate mind for an indeterminate mind.
If one speaks in this way, then there would be no liberation or nirvana.
Such a way of speaking is excellent; it means that the mind acts as a sequence for the mind, and likewise acts as a sequence for the numerical dharmas.
Numerical sequence serves as the condition for subsequent numbers, and it also serves as the condition for the mind.
A preceding mental aggregate serves as the condition for a subsequent mental aggregate. Question:
If mind acts as the immediate antecedent for mind, then they would be mutually conforming non-calculable dharmas.
If calculable dharmas act as the immediate antecedent for calculable dharmas, then they would be mutually conforming non-minds?
Answer: If it is as the śramaṇas who speak of similar dharmas say—that the mind conforms to the mind and mental factors conform to mental factors—[then this is so].
The critique says:
One should not speak in this way.

It is better to speak thus: namely, that the mind establishes a sequence for the enumerated dharmas (*saṃkhyā-dharma*), and the enumerated dharmas establish a sequence for the mind; the preceding mental aggregate establishes a sequence for the subsequent mental aggregate, being entirely without distinction, just like a heap of beans.
As stated in the *Prakaraṇa*, if a dharma serves as the immediate antecedent for another dharma, is there ever a time when it does not serve as such?
The answer is:
Yes, if that [subsequent] dharma has not yet arisen.
Question: Regarding this statement that [a dharma] has not yet arisen, does it refer to the preceding one or the succeeding one?
Is it the case that, as with a preceding dharma that has not yet arisen, the succeeding dharma is not called "sequential," whereas if it has arisen, it is sequential?

Furthermore, just as when a subsequent dharma has not yet arisen, a preceding dharma is not said to possess "succession" (*anupūrvi*), would it be the case that once it has arisen, it possesses succession?

For example, regarding the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) acting as the immediate precursor to the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*): just as when the Supreme Mundane Dharma has not yet arisen, the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering is not called "succession," would it be the case that once it has arisen, it constitutes succession?

Furthermore, just as when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen, the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukika-agra-dharma*) are not said to have a sequential order; if they have arisen, do they then possess a sequential order?

If a subsequent dharma is not called "sequential" while a preceding dharma has not yet arisen, but it is called "sequential" once it has arisen, this may be so during states of consciousness (*sacittaka*), but how can it be so during states without consciousness (*acittaka*)?

Just as when one enters the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, whether for seven days or more than seven days, the mind that emerges from the attainment and the mind that entered the attainment are called "successive," and the mind of the second moment must necessarily arise.

Why is this? If a phenomenon can act as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for another phenomenon, there is no sentient being, no phenomenon, no incantation, no medicinal herb, no Buddha, no pratyekabuddha, and no śrāvaka who can obstruct this phenomenon and prevent the mind of the second moment from arising.
If that were the case, the two meditative absorptions would lack substantial reality.
Furthermore, if the subsequent dharma has not yet arisen, the preceding dharma cannot be said to possess "succession"; it is only when [the subsequent dharma] arises that there is succession.

If this were the case, then as long as the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) has not yet arisen, the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgra-dharma*) would not be called "sequential" (*anupūrva*).
Why, then, is it said that they have not yet arisen? Some say that one should state: the preceding dharmas, so long as they have not yet arisen, are not called "sequential."
Question: If that is so, it may be thus when there is a mind; but what about when there is no mind? Answer:
As it is when there is a mind, so it is also when there is no mind. What is the matter?

For example, when one enters the attainment of non-ideation (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind that enters that meditative state—specifically at the very first moment—both takes up its fruit (*phala-grahaṇa*) and gives forth its fruit (*phala-dāna*). All subsequent moments, as well as the mind upon emerging from the meditative state, are designated only as taking up their fruit.
It should not be said that the mind which has entered meditative absorption perishes in the past, while the remaining moments of that concentration and the mind that emerges from it—
which exist in the present— bestow the fruit.

Why is this so? Because the meaning of the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantarapratyaya*) does not involve taking the fruit at one time and giving the fruit at another; rather, it takes the fruit at the very same moment it gives it. Question:
If it takes the fruit at the time of giving the fruit, this may be so when there is consciousness; but how is it when there is no consciousness?
The answer is:

as in the case of one who has entered the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) or the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mind that enters that attainment takes the fruit and gives the fruit in the first moment of the attainment; that [mind] ceases and exists in the past.
If one asserts that the remaining moments of concentration and the mind emerging from concentration, when they are present, both take and give their fruit,
then there would be no case where the taking of the fruit occurs at one time and the giving of the fruit at another.
Question: If that were so, then past phenomena would possess some activity. Answer:
Although that which was performed in the past can take up and give forth a fruit, there is no such thing as a "fruit" [in itself].
When one sees forms or even cognizes dharmas in the past, there is no such functional activity; thus, it is impossible for there to be such a thing as giving forth or taking up a fruit.

Furthermore, there are those who say that as long as the subsequent dharma has not yet arisen, the preceding dharma is not termed "sequential" (samanantara); only when the subsequent dharma arises is the preceding dharma termed "sequential. Question:
If this were so, then before the *duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti* has arisen, would the *laukikāgradharma* not be termed "sequential"?
Answer: It may be called "succession" (anuloma), but it is not called a "condition of succession" (anuloma-pratyaya).
If the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) arises, this is called both "succession" and a "condition of succession."

Just as it is with the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), one should know that the same applies to sequence having sequence, continuity having continuity, and dependence having dependence.
Question: Is there a sequential condition in the future world?
If they did exist, all phenomena would already be abiding in succession within the future; thus, the cultivation of correct means would be useless. Why is this so?
If the Noble Path already exists in succession within the future, arising when its time arrives, what further purpose would there be in practicing correct means?
Furthermore, there would be a great error.

Why is this? Because there is no subduing of desire through the arising of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*); likewise, one cannot subdue all afflictions (*kleśa*) through the arising of the contemplation of the antidote (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*). If this were so, there would be no liberation or nirvāṇa; and so on, as explained at length.
If it were non-existent, how would the Sūtra in Eight Parts be reconciled? As it says:
"This person shall not fall into the evil destinies for twelve kalpas, up to twenty kalpas."

How is one to know that the distinctions among the three types of karma result in retribution in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*), in the next life (*upapadyavipāka*), or in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavipāka*)?

For what reason does the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) at all times give rise only to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhadharmakṣānti*), and not to other dharmas such as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
Why is it that the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) gives rise only to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and not to other dharmas?
The answer is:
one should explain it as follows:
In future time, there is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*). Question:
If it does not exist, then the aforementioned faults do not apply.
How is this Eightfold Sūtra to be reconciled?
The answer is:
The World-Honored One, by observing the past and the present, knows the future world through these same characteristics.
What is the matter?
The answer is:
The World-Honored One, observing the past lives, saw that those sentient beings cultivated such karma and did not fall into the evil realms for that many kalpas.
He sees these sentient beings cultivating such karma that for that many eons they shall not fall into the evil realms.
He sees various sentient beings who, having cultivated such karma in past lives, receive such retribution in the present life;
he sees various sentient beings who, having performed karma there, receive either retribution in the next birth or retribution in subsequent births.
He sees sentient beings performing karma here, which may result in retribution in the present life, retribution in the next life, or retribution in subsequent lives.

Furthermore, there are those who say that sentient beings possess certain characteristics (*nimitta*)—mental non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*)—that abide within the bodies of sentient beings. By means of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the World-Honored One is able to know that because these factors exist within the bodies of sentient beings, they will not fall into the evil destinies for such-and-such eons; he directly perceives these characteristics and thereby knows that these sentient beings will receive retribution in the present life, followed by retribution in the next life, and subsequently retribution in later lives.
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement.
To make this claim is to imply that the Tathāgata possesses only the knowledge of inferential signs (*anvaya-jñāna*) and lacks the knowledge of direct penetration (*pratisaṃvid-jñāna*).
It should be stated thus:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses penetrating wisdom that knows the future.

Although future phenomena are disordered and lack a fixed sequence, the Tathāgata, by means of his luminous and pure wisdom, knows those disordered phenomena of the future that lack a fixed sequence; he knows that such-and-such sentient beings, having performed such karma, will not fall into the evil realms for so many kalpas, but will receive retribution in the present life, followed by retribution in the next birth, and further retribution in subsequent lives—all of which is truly without error.
Just as one who knows the method of calculation understands a heap of grain clearly and without error,
how much more so is it with the Tathāgata’s spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*)? Question:

For what reason does the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) give rise immediately to the Patience regarding the Dharma of Suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti), rather than giving rise to other dharmas such as the Knowledge of Exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna)?
The answer is:
this refers to a fixed numerical sequence, whereas the specific characteristics of the phenomena are not fixed.
Why is this so? The dharma-patience regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) exists in the six stages, yet it is not known which stage it belongs to;
the dharma-patience regarding suffering is associated with the three faculties, yet it is not known with which specific faculty it is definitively associated.
When practicing the four practices, one does not know which practice constitutes the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
