Furthermore, if one sees a person whose body is covered in dust and dirt, who is naked, and who has no attendants, one knows that this person possesses a mind of self-contempt. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is well-dressed, clean, and adorned with various ornaments, one knows that this person possesses a mind of desire. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is ill-clad, unclean, and without ornaments, one knows that this person possesses a mind of aversion. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is calm, composed, and free from agitation, one knows that this person possesses a mind of equanimity. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is agitated, restless, and lacking composure, one knows that this person possesses a mind of distraction. Furthermore, if one sees a person whose faculties are dull and whose mind is obscured, one knows that this person possesses a mind of ignorance. Furthermore, if one sees a person whose faculties are sharp and whose mind is clear, one knows that this person possesses a mind of wisdom. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is arrogant, haughty, and full of conceit, one knows that this person possesses a mind of arrogance. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is humble, modest, and free from pride, one knows that this person possesses a mind of humility. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is stingy and greedy, one knows that this person possesses a mind of attachment. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is generous and gives away all possessions, one knows that this person possesses a mind of non-attachment. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is wrathful and prone to anger, one knows that this person possesses a mind of hatred. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is patient, enduring, and free from resentment, one knows that this person possesses a mind of non-hatred. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is deceitful, crooked, and dishonest, one knows that this person possesses a mind of delusion. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is straightforward, honest, and sincere, one knows that this person possesses a mind of non-delusion. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is malicious and harbors ill will, one knows that this person possesses a mind of harmful intent. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is compassionate, kind, and benevolent, one knows that this person possesses a mind of harmlessness. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is lazy and indolent, one knows that this person possesses a mind of sloth. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is diligent, energetic, and resolute, one knows that this person possesses a mind of diligence. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is distracted and lacks mindfulness, one knows that this person possesses a mind of forgetfulness. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is mindful and clearly aware, one knows that this person possesses a mind of mindfulness. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is confused and lacks discernment, one knows that this person possesses a mind of lack of discernment. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is discerning and wise, one knows that this person possesses a mind of discernment. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is scattered and lacks concentration, one knows that this person possesses a mind of lack of concentration. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is concentrated and one-pointed, one knows that this person possesses a mind of concentration. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is agitated and lacks tranquility, one knows that this person possesses a mind of lack of tranquility. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is tranquil and serene, one knows that this person possesses a mind of tranquility. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is restless and lacks stability, one knows that this person possesses a mind of instability. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is stable and firm, one knows that this person possesses a mind of stability. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is unwholesome and acts with evil intent, one knows that this person possesses an unwholesome mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is wholesome and acts with virtuous intent, one knows that this person possesses a wholesome mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is defiled and impure, one knows that this person possesses a defiled mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is pure and stainless, one knows that this person possesses a pure mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is bound by fetters and shackles, one knows that this person possesses a mind of bondage. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is liberated and free from constraints, one knows that this person possesses a mind of liberation. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is lowly and base, one knows that this person possesses a lowly mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is noble and sublime, one knows that this person possesses a noble mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is inferior and common, one knows that this person possesses an inferior mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is superior and distinguished, one knows that this person possesses a superior mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is small-minded and narrow, one knows that this person possesses a small mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is vast and expansive, one knows that this person possesses a vast mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is limited and restricted, one knows that this person possesses a limited mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is immeasurable and boundless, one knows that this person possesses an immeasurable mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is coarse and vulgar, one knows that this person possesses a coarse mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is refined and subtle, one knows that this person possesses a refined mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is dark and obscured, one knows that this person possesses a dark mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is bright and luminous, one knows that this person possesses a bright mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is heavy and burdened, one knows that this person possesses a heavy mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is light and buoyant, one knows that this person possesses a light mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is sinking and submerged, one knows that this person possesses a sinking mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is emerging and rising, one knows that this person possesses an emerging mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is constricted and narrow, one knows that this person possesses a constricted mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is open and spacious, one knows that this person possesses an open mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is turbulent and disturbed, one knows that this person possesses a turbulent mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is calm and peaceful, one knows that this person possesses a calm mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is agitated and frantic, one knows that this person possesses an agitated mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is collected and composed, one knows that this person possesses a collected mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is distracted and wandering, one knows that this person possesses a distracted mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is focused and attentive, one knows that this person possesses a focused mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is heedless and negligent, one knows that this person possesses a heedless mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is vigilant and careful, one knows that this person possesses a vigilant mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is corrupt and degenerate, one knows that this person possesses a corrupt mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is upright and incorruptible, one knows that this person possesses an upright mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is crooked and devious, one knows that this person possesses a crooked mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is straight and honest, one knows that this person possesses a straight mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is deceitful and guileful, one knows that this person possesses a deceitful mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is sincere and guileless, one knows that this person possesses a sincere mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is malicious and treacherous, one knows that this person possesses a malicious mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is benevolent and kind, one knows that this person possesses a benevolent mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is harsh and cruel, one knows that this person possesses a harsh mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is gentle and mild, one knows that this person possesses a gentle mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is fierce and violent, one knows that this person possesses a fierce mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is peaceful and harmonious, one knows that this person possesses a peaceful mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is contentious and quarrelsome, one knows that this person possesses a contentious mind. Furthermore, if one sees a person who is concordant and harmonious,
"The wardens of that hell now intend to kill me.
The commentary states:
One should not speak in this manner.
If this is so, can humans also know [the minds of others], such that it may be called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Such an explanation is preferable.
There are those who, by attaining knowledge at the place of birth, are able to know these matters.
Is it known at the beginning, known at the middle, or known at the end?
Answer: It should be explained in detail as previously stated.
Among animals, there are also those capable of knowing their own past lives, as stated in the Sūtra:
"Sankha! If you are indeed my father, Dutiya, you may ascend this seat."
Even as he was being raised up,
he spoke these words again:
"If you are indeed my father, Dutiya, then you may eat this rice and meat meal."
Even as he ate it,
he spoke again, saying:
"If you are indeed my father, Dutiya, show me the treasure that belongs to me."
Even if he were to show it to him, one would ask:
"When you form such a thought, is it at the beginning, or in the middle, or at the end?"
Answer: All three times are capable [of it].
In which state of mind does one abide?
Answer: One is able to do so while abiding in states of mind that are wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; one is also able to do so through the minds of deportment, craftsmanship, and retribution.
How many lifetimes can one know?
Answer: Some say that one can know a single lifetime—dying there and being born here;
others say that one can know many lifetimes.
How is this known?
It has been heard that once there was a woman who placed her infant in one place and, due to certain circumstances, went elsewhere and was not present.
At that time, a wolf carried off its cub.
People caught hold of it and said to it:
"For what reason are you now carrying away another's child?"
The wolf replied,
"This child's mother is our enemy.
At that time, people asked:
"What enmity is there?
The wolf replied,
"The mother of this child has constantly devoured my children for five hundred lifetimes, and I likewise have constantly killed her children for five hundred lifetimes."
"If he can relinquish his heart of old enmity, I too shall be able to relinquish mine.
At that time, people said to the mother of the boy:
"You should relinquish your heart of enmity."
The child’s mother replied, "I have now abandoned him.
At that time, the wolf observed the mother's mind; although her mouth spoke of abandonment, her heart did not let go, so he immediately took the child's life and departed.
One who is thus able to know the minds of others also recognizes past lives.
At what time does one know this?
The answer is:
One knows [them] in their entirety—beginning, middle, and end.
By abiding in what state of mind does one know this?
The answer is:
It fully knows the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate;
it knows through the mental ground (manobhūmi) and not by the five bodies of sensory consciousness;
it is also able to know the minds of deportment, craftsmanship, and retribution.
Although that sutra does not explicitly state it, the realm of hungry ghosts also possesses this knowledge. How is this known?
It is heard that once there was a woman possessed by a hungry ghost, who then used a mantra to question the ghost, saying:
"Why do you harass this other woman?
The ghost replied to him, "This woman was my enemy; for five hundred lifetimes she constantly killed me, and I likewise [killed her] for five hundred lifetimes."
"I shall sever his life-force.
If he can relinquish his heart of old enmity, I too shall relinquish mine.
At that time, the woman spoke these words:
"I have now abandoned my hostile intent.
When the ghost observed the woman, although she spoke with her mouth of having abandoned it, her mind did not let go.
The ghost immediately severed the root of her life-force and departed, leaving her behind.
At what time is this known?
The answer is:
as explained in detail above.
Regarding the various heavenly realms, there is likewise this attainment of knowledge concerning the place of birth, yet there is no manifest phenomenon that can be described.
At what time is it known?
The answer is:
The detailed explanation is as above.
Within the human realm, there is no such innate knowledge (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*). Question:
Why is it non-existent?
The answer is:
because they are neither vessels nor fields.

Furthermore, among humans there is the wisdom of observing physical signs and the wisdom of discerning the characteristics of speech; these are innate knowledges (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*), and [the former] is obscured by such wisdoms.

Moreover, although humans lack this innate knowledge, they possess superior and sublime forms of it, namely the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*).
Question: How many minds does one know? Answer:
Some say that those in hell know only the minds of hell-beings, those in the animal realm know only the minds of animals, and hungry ghosts know only the minds of hungry ghosts.

Others say that those in hell know the minds of hell-beings; those in the animal realm know the minds of animals and also know the minds of hell-beings; hungry ghosts know the minds of hungry ghosts and also know the minds of hell-beings and animals; while devas know the minds of all five realms.
Question: If animals do not know the minds of devas, how is the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* to be reconciled? As it says:

The Naga King Supratiṣṭhita and the Naga King Elāpattra, knowing what was in the mind of Śakra, vanished from their own abodes and appeared before Śakra in the time it takes a strong man to flex or extend his arm.
Answer: This is inferential knowledge (anumāna-jñāna). How is this known?
When the devas wish to mobilize their armies for battle, the various bones on the back of the Dragon King Supratiṣṭhita naturally produce a sound. He then thinks:
"Now that this sound has issued from my back, I know for certain that the devas will surely engage in battle with the asuras."
Whenever the devas desire to sport, an image of a fragrant hand spontaneously appears upon the back of the Naga King Elāpattra.
He then thinks: "Since an image of a fragrant hand has appeared upon my back, I know for certain that the devas wish to sport in the groves."
Hungry ghosts also possess innate knowledge (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*) that enables them to recognize their past lives.
As a verse says:
"In my former life, I sought wealth and goods, Whether by lawful or unlawful means."
"Others obtain their joy, while now I suffer affliction.
He asked: "At what time was this known?"
Answer: The detailed explanation is as above.
The various devas also possess innate knowledge (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*), by which they are able to recognize their own past lives.
As the verse says:
"Now, in this Jeta Grove, The assembly of noble ones dwells constantly;
The Dharma King is also therein— Now my heart is filled with joy."
Question: At what time is this known? Answer:
The detailed explanation is as above.
Question: For what reason do some people possess the wisdom attained at birth (*upapatti-pratilambhika-jñāna*) that allows them to know their own past lives?
Answer: It is not his vessel; the detailed explanation is as above.
Furthermore, it is because he is obscured by other dharmas, just as when one’s own nature spontaneously recollects the wisdom of a previous birth.

Furthermore, although among human beings there is no innate wisdom for the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), there are those who possess superior and wondrous faculties, namely the supernormal power of recollecting past lives and the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).
As for those who can cause thunder, lightning, wind, and rain to arise, it is only animals that possess this power, and no others.
Within the realm of animals, it is only the nāgas who possess this power, and no others.

Among those animals, the ability to raise winds and cause rain to fall—whether occurring nearby, which is the fruit of their specific function (*karitra-phala*), or occurring at distant locations outside their immediate dwelling, which is the fruit of their majestic power (*adhipati-phala*)—is as described.
Question: Can a single nāga perform such deeds as these?
Answer: Yes.
It can act. Question:
If that is so, why does the sutra speak of them as being different?
As it is said:
"There are some devas who can cause rain, and there are some devas who can cause wind," and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer is:
Because they act according to their respective inclinations, some may desire to manifest as rain, while others may desire to manifest as wind, and so forth, as explained at length.
Due to these differing inclinations, the sūtras present variations in their accounts.
In this manner, for such beings, whatever they desire is immediately fulfilled.
This is the inherent nature of the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*): when a morsel of food is offered to them, it reaches them.

Furthermore, some say that each of the five destinies (*gati*) has its own inherent law; for example, in the retribution of the hells, even when physical form is severed, it continues again—such is the inherent nature of that place of birth.
Among animals, those capable of flying through the air;
among hungry ghosts, those who reach [the donor] when a morsel of food is offered;

among humans, those who possess courage and the power of mindfulness, who are courageous in their holy life (*brahmacarya*), who do not see the fruit but are able to extensively cultivate its causes through the power of mindfulness, who can remember what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago, and who are practitioners of the holy life—such as these are able to attain the roots of goodness conducive to liberation and conducive to penetration, and achieve right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
In the heavens, there are naturally occurring objects that appear according to one's wishes.
In these various realms, each has its own inherent laws regarding the places of birth.
Furthermore, some say that even within specific regions or lands, there are likewise inherent laws regarding the places of birth.
For example, in the land of Kaśmīra during autumn, oxen have their necks bound with garlands of *utpala* flowers; these cannot be obtained by the nobles of other regions.
Or, for example, in the kingdom of Nagara, commoners drink grape wine; this cannot be obtained by the nobles of the eastern lands.
Just as in the East, those of noble and superior status wear silk while commoners wear cotton;
and just as in the North, those of noble and superior status wear cotton while commoners wear silk—
so too, each realm and region has its own natural laws of birth, which can be fulfilled according to one's inclination.
It is the same for those hungry ghosts: when a morsel of food is given to them, it can satisfy their desires at will.
Furthermore, there are people who, throughout the long night, have such desires and such thoughts, and so forth, as explained at length.
That person has had such desires and such thoughts for a long night, and what they thought has now borne fruit.

It is just like a person from a remote village who, for the sake of wealth and reputation, guards his family estate; he amasses many cattle, sheep, clothing, grain, and various tools for his livelihood, yet out of a desire for fame and honor, he does not give them away to others.
Because they did not practice generosity toward others, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Furthermore, some say that there are those whose nature is one of affection for their kinsmen and whom they wish to benefit; for the sake of their kinsmen, they seek wealth through both lawful and unlawful means.
When they do obtain such times, because of their stinginess and attachment, they have no intention to give even to their own kinsmen, let alone to others.

Due to this lack of a mind for giving, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), dwelling in impure filth and latrines on the outskirts of their former homes.
His kinsmen and relatives, giving rise to a mind of suffering and distress, thought to themselves:
"He has accumulated wealth, yet he neither enjoys it himself nor gives it away to others.
Because of this distress, they wished to give him food; thus, they invited their own kinsmen, friends, acquaintances, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas to provide him with food and drink.
At that time, the hungry ghost saw this with his own eyes; regarding the wealth and possessions of his kinsmen, he conceived the notion that they were his own, thinking:
"These riches and goods were accumulated by me, and now I am giving them away to others."
With a heart of great joy, having conceived a mind of faith and reverence toward the field of merit, the volition associated with renunciation immediately increases.
Because such karma can yield its retribution in the present life, the morsel of food he offers reaches him.
Furthermore, there are those who say that when one performed such karma in past lives, the gift reaches [the recipient].
What is the nature of this matter?
The Venerable Sthavira Saṃgharakṣita replied:
Because those hungry ghosts are characterized by stinginess and attachment, they possess perverted perceptions and perverted views.
Due to these perverted perceptions and views, they perceive a river as not being a river, water as not being water, and even fine food and drink as impure.

When those relatives perform acts of giving for this person, if they are able to give rise to faith, they will eliminate their distortions; they will see the river as a river, see the water as water, and see food as food.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are two kinds of hungry ghosts:
first, those who delight in purity;
second, those who delight in impurity.
Those who perceive purity in pleasure, due to their stinginess and attachment, harbor inverted perceptions regarding rivers and the like, as previously described.
Those who perceive impurity in pleasure see rivers as dry and perceive emptiness within full vessels of food and drink.

If relatives and kin perform acts of giving for the sake of such a person, once the hungry ghost has seen this, they will give rise to a mind of joy toward both the objects given and the field of merit; thus, they are able to increase the volition associated with relinquishment.
By means of this karma, one eliminates inverted perceptions.
Regarding "delight in purity": when seeing a river, one sees it as a river; when seeing water, one sees it as water; and when seeing food and drink in a vessel, one sees it as pure food.
Those who delight in impurity see rivers filled with water and, within empty vessels, see them filled with food.
For this reason, it is said that when a morsel of food is offered to a hungry ghost, it reaches him.

Furthermore, there are those who say that those hungry ghosts possessed some slight wholesome conduct in their previous lives and did not give rise to perverted perceptions regarding food and drink; however, because of their stinginess and attachment, their bodies and minds became timid and weak, and due to this timidity and weakness, they were unable to approach those among the hungry ghosts who possess majestic power and virtue.
There may be circumstances where one goes to such a place, yet the heart finds no joy. Why is this?
Because of one's own lowly and base status.
Those hungry ghosts of great majesty possess various kinds of food and drink due to their roots of merit;
however, because this ghost’s body and mind are timid and weak, it does not dare to eat them.

If his kinsmen perform acts of giving on his behalf, the hungry ghost, having seen this, gives rise to a heart of joy toward the gift and the field of merit. By virtue of this heart of faith and delight, he immediately attains a superior body and mind. Because he has attained a superior body and mind, he is able to go before those among the hungry ghosts who possess majestic power; there, giving rise to a heart of joy and a heart of delight, he is able to consume all the food and drink he receives.
For this reason, when food is given to hungry ghosts, it reaches them.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"It is not the case that one person performs the action and another receives the result; rather, when relatives perform acts of giving for the sake of a ghost, if that ghost develops a mind of faith and reverence toward the field of merit and the material goods, they too have a share in the resulting fruit."
For this reason, when food is offered to hungry ghosts, it reaches them; this is not the case for other realms. Question:
When merit is performed for the sake of hungry ghosts, do they receive only food and drink, or is their physical body also enhanced?
Answer: One both obtains food and drink and increases the body.
Obtaining food and drink is as previously described.
How does one augment the body?
One whose body is foul-smelling attains fragrance; one of ugly appearance attains beauty; one with coarse touch attains refinement; and one without majesty attains a majestic body.
Question: Can this retribution also be obtained within other paths? Answer:
If one can give rise to faith, then one will attain it; if one cannot give rise to it, then one will not attain it.
Question: If such matters as these are attained within all the realms of existence, why is it that here only the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) is mentioned, while the other realms are not?
Answer: Because all hungry ghosts, due to hunger and thirst, constantly harbor a longing for food and drink to sustain themselves;
other realms do not necessarily possess such a mind, and therefore it is not mentioned.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because within the realm of hungry ghosts there is always a seeking mind and an expectant mind, offerings made to them reach them.
There are five destinies, namely: hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas.
Question: Regarding the essential nature of the five destinies (*pañca-gati*), are they non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) or are they of three kinds?
If they are neutral, how do you reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇa*?
As it is said:
"The nature of the realms of existence (gati) is that which is driven by all the underlying tendencies (anuśaya).
If there were three [distinct] natures, then the essence of the realms of existence would be destroyed."
What is the nature of the destruction of the realms of existence?
The answer is:

beings in the hells would then necessarily possess the afflictions and karma of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods; and likewise, virtuous Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods would also possess the afflictions and unwholesome karma of beings in the hells.
One should state this:
the essential nature of the destinies is non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Question:
If that were so, how would one reconcile the statement made in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
The answer is:
it should have been stated by that [text] as follows:

The essential nature of the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and humans consists of the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the desire realm and those to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

The essential nature of the celestial realm, which is influenced by these proclivities, consists of the universal proclivities of all three realms and those proclivities to be abandoned through cultivation that influence it.
It should have been stated in this way; what is the intention behind its not being so stated?
The answer is:
it was stated thus because of an error made by the reciter.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind which synthesizes the various realms of existence (*gati*) is severed by the five paths of action, and for this reason, it is driven by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Again, there are those who say that the essential nature of the realms of existence is threefold.
Question: If that is so, how is it that the essential nature of the realms of existence (*gati*) is not destroyed? Answer:
If one speaks of it in terms of what has already been accomplished, it is subject to destruction; if one speaks of it in terms of its present activity, it is not destroyed.
Why is it that speaking of it in terms of its present activity does not result in its destruction?
The answer is:

Just as those in the hells, among animals, or among hungry ghosts possess the afflictions, karma, and virtues of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, yet these do not manifest before them; likewise, those in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin heaven possess the afflictions, karma, and unwholesome states of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, yet these do not manifest before them.
The commentary states:
It should be said that the essential nature of hell is non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
How is this known?
It is as the Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus: "O Elders!"

If the outflows pertaining to hell manifest before one, and one performs bodily, verbal, and mental karma that results in the suffering of hell—namely, the karmic fruits of crookedness, turbidity, and impurity of body, speech, and mind—one is born within the hells.
Having been born, one experiences its retribution—ranging from form up to consciousness; this is called the realm of hell.
Venerable elders!
Apart from these five aggregates, there is no other dharma that can be named the realm of hell.
For this reason, it is known that the essential nature of the destinies (gati) is non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta).
Nevertheless, the five destinies are differentiated by way of karmic retribution; this is the nature of the destinies.
Now it shall be explained why they are called "destinies" (*gati*). What is the reason for calling them "destinies"?
The answer is:
because one goes toward those places of birth and because one goes toward the continuity of birth in those places, they are called "destinies."
The general characteristics of the various realms of existence have already been explained; their individual characteristics shall now be discussed.
What is called the realm of hell?
The answer is:

This is the hell realm; it is that which acts as a companion to hell beings, receives a hellish body, and obtains its location, its essential nature, and its various sense bases. Being born in that place, one obtains non-obscured neutral form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness. This is called the hell destiny.
For what reason is it called *niraya*?
*Niraya* means "non-existence" in the language of Qin. Why is that?
Within that state there is no joy or pleasure; there is no savor, no gladness, no benefit, no delight, no bliss, and no rapturous joy; therefore it is said that they do not exist.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because one performs excessive unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, one is born in that place.
The continuity of birth in that place is called the hell realm (*niraya-gati*).

Furthermore, some say that the "hell realm" (niraya-gati) is a conventional designation (prajñapti) and a conceptual construction; it does not necessarily possess all the meanings implied by its name.
Others say that this realm is base and inferior, and since there is nothing more base or inferior among the five destinies than the hell realm, it is therefore called "base."
Furthermore, there are those who say this leads to downfall.
As a verse states:
"Those who fall into hell Have their bodies entirely suspended upside down."
"Sitting and slandering the noble sages and all those who practice purity,
one’s faculties will be utterly destroyed, like that scorched and rotting fish. Furthermore,
there are those who say that *niraya*— in the language of Qin, "no place of going"— is the name for this state.
Why is this? Those beings born there have no place of departure, no place of reliance, and no place of refuge; therefore, it is called "no place of departure."
Furthermore, for what reason is it called Avīci?

"Avīci" in the language of Qin means "without interval. It is also called "Pure Suffering and Pain," also called "The Body Nailed with a Hundred Stakes," and also called "The Sixfold Contact of Suffering."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because many sentient beings are born there and there is no space to accommodate them, it is called "Avīci" (the Uninterrupted).
This statement should not be made. Why is this so?
Those born in other hells are many, while those born in Avīci are few.
How is this known?
One is born in Avīci by committing superior unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind; yet, there are few sentient beings who commit such superior unwholesome karma of body, speech, and mind.
Just as sentient beings who perform even a small amount of superior wholesome conduct are born in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), so it is with them as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because there is not even a moment of pleasure, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
Question: If that is so, is there an intention (*āśaya*) within the other great hells that serves as an interval for pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*)?
Answer: [No].
Although there is no underlying intention, pleasant sensation is of two kinds:
first, that which is based on conditions;
second, that which is retribution.
In all hells, there is no resultant pleasant feeling (*vipākavedanā*), yet there is a basis for pleasant feeling (*āśrayasukhavedanā*).
Even in the Avīci hell, there is no basis for pleasant feeling either.
How is it known that in the other great hells there is a basis for pleasant feeling?
As stated in the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*:
"In the Saṃjīva Hell, cold winds blow upon the bodies of sentient beings, causing their flesh and blood to be restored."
Or they might raise this cry:
"O living beings! O living beings!"
At that time, the sentient beings are restored to life.
From this fact, it is known that in other hells there is reliance upon pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
In the Avīci hell, such a thing does not occur; therefore, there is no reliance upon pleasant feeling there.

Furthermore, there are those who say that although the bodies of sentient beings born in the Avīci hell are vast, there is no interval or space when they experience suffering and pain; therefore, it is called "Uninterrupted" (Avīci).
Question: Where are the hells located? Answer:
Some say that forty thousand yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa lies the Avīci Hell.
A question is asked:
Do the other hells lie above and below it, or do they lie alongside it?
Answer: Some say that the Avīci Hell is situated in the center, while the other hells surround it on all four sides,
just as a city stands in the middle surrounded by villages.
Question: This Jambudvīpa is seven thousand yojanas in length and breadth, while the various hells beneath it are each vast and extensive.
As a verse says:
"Flames pervade many yojanas; those who see them have their hair stand on end with terror.
All manner of evil beings constantly burn within it, and its blazing intensity cannot be approached."
"Since each of these hells is thus vast and expansive, how can they be contained?
The answer is:

"The configuration of this great earth is broad at the base and narrow at the top, like grain heaped upon the ground; therefore, the Sūtra says that the great ocean gradually widens and becomes increasingly deep."

Furthermore, there are those who say that the Avīci Hell is at the very bottom; above it is the Saṃjīva Hell, then the Kālasūtra Hell, then the Saṃghāta Hell, then the Raurava Hell, then the Mahāraurava Hell, then the Tapana Hell, and finally the Pratāpana Hell.
That Avīci Hell is twenty thousand yojanas in length, breadth, height, and depth, with a circumference of eighty thousand yojanas;
the other various hells are ten thousand nine hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Some say that the other various hells are ten thousand *yojanas* in length and breadth.

Others say that forty thousand *yojanas* beneath Jambudvīpa lies the Avīci hell; the Avīci hell is twenty thousand *yojanas* in length, breadth, height, and depth, with a circumference of eighty thousand *yojanas*.
The Saṃjīva (Fire-Scorching) Hell is five thousand yojanas in length, breadth, and height; likewise, each of the other hells down to the Saṃghāta (Crying-out) Hell is five thousand yojanas.
Thus, these seven hells together measure thirty-five thousand yojanas. The remaining five thousand yojanas consist of:

one thousand yojanas of blue ground, one thousand yojanas of yellow ground, one thousand yojanas of red ground, one thousand yojanas of white ground, five hundred yojanas of chalky soil, and five hundred yojanas of mud.
Each individual hell has sixteen subsidiary hells.
What are these sixteen?
The answer is:
Each individual hell has four gates, and each gate has four subsidiary hells:
first is the Hell of Hot Sand Where One Sinks Up to the Knees;
second is the Hell of Boiling Excrement with Malevolent Worms.
There is the Hell of the Path of Swords, the Hell of the Rain of Sword-leaves, and the Hell of the Forest of Swords; these three constitute the third subsidiary hell.
The fourth is named the Hell of the River of Hot Ashes.
Each of these gates has four types of retinues.
Including the Avīci hell itself along with its retinue, there are seventeen; the same applies to the remaining seven hells, totaling one hundred and thirty-six.
In the various subsidiary hells (*utsada-naraka*), sinners are punished with manifold types of suffering;
in the primary hells (*maula-naraka*), they are punished with a single type of suffering.

Beneath Jambudvīpa there are also primary hells, whereas upon the surface of Jambudvīpa there are only peripheral hells (*prādeśika-naraka*), which may be located on mountains, in valleys, in wildernesses, or in the air.
In Pūrvavideha and Aparagoyānī there are only peripheral hells, but no primary hells.
In Uttarakuru there are neither primary hells nor peripheral hells.
Why is this so? Because that is a pure karmic fruit and retribution. Question:
For what reason is there a primary hell beneath Jambudvīpa, while there is none in other places?
The answer is:
because the cultivation of virtue by the people of Jambudvīpa is intense, and their performance of unwholesome karma is likewise intense.
Therefore, there are actual hells in Jambudvīpa, whereas they do not exist in other places. Question:
If one commits the five acts of immediate retribution or other grave karmas in other regions, in what place will one receive their retribution?
Answer: It is received beneath this Jambudvīpa. Question:
Are these various hell-wardens sentient beings or non-sentient beings?
If they are sentient beings, having themselves committed many unwholesome karmas, where else would they go to undergo this retribution?
If they were not sentient beings, how would one reconcile the verse spoken by Dharmasubhūti? As it says:
"The person who is stubborn and full of anger, Who always delights in committing various evils..."
"Seeing the suffering of others and giving rise to joy, one will become a henchman of Yama after death.
He replied: "Some say that this belongs to the category of sentient beings."
Question: If that is so, where will one receive this retribution for having committed many unwholesome karmas? Answer:
One receives retribution right there. Why is this?

Even those who have committed the deeds of immediate retribution, severed their roots of goodness, and held superior wrong views receive retribution in that very place; how much more so for the hell-wardens themselves?
Furthermore, there are those who say that these are not among the category of sentient beings.

Due to the causal conditions of the karmic offenses of various sentient beings, they are in reality not sentient beings; yet they manifest in the presence of others in the likeness of sentient beings, employing various means to discipline those who have committed offenses.
Question: If that is so, how do you explain the verse by Dharmasubhūti? Answer:
Regarding this composition of prose and verse, it is not necessary that it be entirely comprehensive. Why is this?
In the composition of prose and verse, there may be additions or omissions, and there may be gains or losses.
If one wishes to understand this matter, what is it?
The answer is:
those who, bound by iron chains, are led before King Yama—these constitute the number of sentient beings.
As for the various other instruments used to punish those who have committed sins, they do not belong to the category of sentient beings;
it is well said thus.
What is the form of the sentient beings in hell like?
Answer: Their form is like that of humans.
What are their languages like?
The answer is:

At the beginning, before they have experienced suffering and pain, they speak entirely in noble speech; later, when they experience suffering and pain, although they utter sounds of agony, there is not even a single word that can be distinguished, but only the sounds of being beaten, struck, and torn apart.
What is called the realm of animals?
The answer is:
it is that which belongs to the category of the animal realm, acts as a companion to animals, and so forth, as explained at length.
For what reason is it called the realm of animals?
Answer: Because their forms are horizontal, their movement is also horizontal.
Because their conduct is lateral and their forms are likewise lateral, it is called the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Furthermore, some say that because they commit transgressions of body, speech, and mind, they are born within that path; hence it is called the realm of animals.

Furthermore, some say that "animal" (tiryagyoni) is a designation (*prajñapti*) based on conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); such designations do not necessarily possess all the meanings implied by their names.
Others say it is called the animal realm because it is pervasive; this pervasiveness exists throughout the five destinies.
Among those in the hells, there are those without feet, such as the *Nandika*;
those with two feet, such as the *Kukura* and others;
and those with four feet, such as dogs and the like.
There are those with many feet, such as centipedes and the like.
Among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), there are also those without feet, such as snakes and the like;
there are those with two feet, such as *kukura* and others.
Regarding those with four legs: those possessing majestic power include elephants, horses, and the like; those lacking majestic power consist only of dogs and the like.
Regarding those with many legs: such as centipedes and so forth.
Among human beings, there are also those without feet, such as crawling insects;
those with two feet, such as wild geese and swans;
and those with four feet, such as elephants and horses.
There are those with many feet, such as centipedes and the like.
Among the gods, in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three, there are those with two feet, such as geese, peacocks, and the like;
and those with four feet, such as elephants, horses, and the like.
Regarding those with two legs from above, these include such creatures as geese, peacocks, and other birds.
Question: We have heard that the various heavens above also ride upon elephants and horses; how is it that you now say they do not?

Answer: Due to the causes and conditions of their own meritorious karma, those beings take the forms of elephants, horses, and so forth—which are not classified as sentient beings—to amuse themselves.
Furthermore, there are those who say they are called "animals" (tiryagyoni) because of their blindness and ignorance.
"Blind and dark" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among the five destinies (*pañcagati*), none have more ignorance than animals. Question:
Where exactly do the abodes of animals reside?
The answer is:
their primary abode is within the great ocean, though they also exist on various islands.
What is their form?
The answer is:
their forms are lateral; there are also those whose forms are directed upward, such as the piśācas, the ilūsakas, the andhapūṭakulas, the kiṃnaras, and so forth.
What is speech? The answer is:

At the time when the world was first formed, all sentient beings spoke only the noble language (*ārya-bhāṣā*). Later, due to the faults of food and drink, the degeneration of the age, and the increase of deceitful minds, there arose various kinds of speech, even including those who were unable to speak at all.
What is called the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*)?
The answer is:
it is the category of hungry ghosts, and so forth, as explained at length.
For what reason is it called Pitṛloka?
"Pitṛ" means "grandfather" in the language of Qin.
There are sentient beings who are first born into that realm, and thus it is named "Grandfather."
Furthermore, those beings who are subsequently born in that place and whose continuity is established there are also called "grandfathers" (pitaras).
For this reason, this realm of existence is named "Grandfather.

Others say that because sentient beings have long practiced and extensively spread a mind of stinginess and greed, they are born into that realm; therefore, it is called the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
Furthermore, some say that this is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say they are called "hungry ghosts" (*preta*) because they suffer greatly from hunger and thirst.

Those sentient beings have bellies as vast as mountains and throats like the eye of a needle; for hundreds of thousands of years they have not heard the sound of water, nor have they ever seen it, let alone been able to touch it.
Furthermore, there are those who say they are called "hungry ghosts" (preta) because they are driven about.
They are constantly driven here and there by the various devas; therefore, this realm is called the "realm of being driven."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because they are constantly full of longing for others, they are called "hungry ghosts" (preta).
For such reasons as these, this realm is named the hungry ghost realm.
Question: Where does this realm of rebirth abide? Answer:
Some say that five hundred yojanas beneath Jambudvīpa lies the abode of King Yama, which is his primary residence; there are also such residences on the other continents.
Those who dwell on the islands of Jambudvīpa are of two kinds:
first, those with majestic power;
second, those without majestic power.
Those possessing majesty and virtue dwell beneath various trees in groves of flowers and fruits, or within beautiful mountain forests; some even have palaces situated in the midst of space.
Those lacking majesty and virtue dwell amidst impurities, filth, excrement, and urine.
In Pūrvavideha and Aparagodānīya there are also two kinds:
those with majestic power and those without majestic power.
In Uttarakuru, there are only those with majestic power.

Why is this so? Because that ground is the place of the pure karmic fruition where the Four Great Kings and the Gods of the Thirty-three Heaven dwell; there, only those possessed of majestic virtue reside.

Furthermore, there are those who say that to the west of Jambudvīpa there are five hundred islands; between every two islands there are five hundred cities of hungry ghosts (preta). Of these, two hundred and fifty are inhabited by those with majestic power, and two hundred and fifty are inhabited by those without majestic power.
Therefore, the Cakravartin King Nimi said to his charioteer Mātali:

"I wish to ascend to heaven; you should proceed along this path so that I may see those sentient beings who are undergoing the retribution of evil and those who are undergoing the retribution of goodness."
At that time, the charioteer Mātala followed the king’s instructions and passed by various cities.
At that time, the king saw both the sinful and the meritorious.

Those possessing majesty and virtue were like the sons of gods: they wore celestial crowns upon their heads, were clad in celestial robes, partook of sweet and delicious food and drink, and each sported and enjoyed themselves.

Regarding those who lack majestic power (*avīrya*): they are naked and without clothing, covering themselves with their hair, and subsisting by wandering for alms while holding earthenware vessels in their hands.
What is their physical form like?
The answer is:
Some stand upright, some lean to one side, and some have faces resembling pigs like images painted on a wall.
What do they say? The answer is:
When the world was first formed, all sentient beings spoke entirely in the noble language (ārya-bhāṣā); the rest is as previously explained.
Furthermore, there are those who say that according to the place where one dies, one is reborn in that interval with the original form and the original language of that place.
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement. Why is this?
If one dies in the formless realm and is reborn in this destiny, could they be without form and without speech?
One should say: according to the place of their birth, their form and speech are likewise.
What is the human realm?
The answer is:
it is the portion of humanity, the companionship of humanity, and so forth, as explained at length.
For what reason is it called Manuṣya?
"Manuṣya" means "mind" in the language of Qin.
Long ago, there was a king named Mūrdhaja who ruled over the four continents and addressed all sentient beings, saying:
"In whatever they intend to do, they should reflect well, deliberate well, and maintain right mindfulness.

Then, in accordance with the King's instruction, all sentient beings reflected, deliberated, and maintained mindfulness regarding everything they did; subsequently, there arose various distinct types of skilled craftsmanship and occupations.
Because human beings act according to their prior intentions, they are called "persons" (*pudgala*);
thus, the intention is like the person. Before this name existed, people called one another *tālaśāṭaka* or *apadāta*.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because one is born into that realm by cultivating wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind in the lower [realms], it is called the human realm (*manuṣya-gati*).
Others say that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because pride (*māna*) is predominant.
Among the five destinies (*gati*), none possess a greater abundance of the mind of pride than humans; therefore, this realm is called the human destiny (*manuṣya-gati*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this realm can pacify the mind;
among the five destinies, none is better at pacifying the mind than the human realm. Why is this so?

If a person can attain the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), and can both cultivate and practice the four dharmas such as drawing near to virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), for this reason they are called "human beings."
Question: Where does it abide? Answer:
They dwell within the four continents and also upon the eight great subcontinents. These are:
first, Kaurava;... [and so forth].
The second is named Kālapa;
the third is named Vidika;
the fourth is named Suvídika.
The fifth is named Śaṭha;
the sixth is named Uttaramantriṇa;
the seventh is named Brahmā.
The eighth is named Cāmara.
Those two islands, Kurava and Kaurava, are dependencies of Uttarakuru.
The two islands, Videha and Subvideha, are dependencies of Pūrvavideha.
The two sub-continents of Śāṭha and Uttaramantriṇa are the satellites of Aparagoyānī;
the two sub-continents of Pāra and Cāmara are the satellites of Jambudvīpa.
Furthermore, some say that these two islands are alternative names for Jambudvīpa, and the same applies to the two islands of the other three continents.
Others say that human beings inhabit all of these islands, though their stature is short and small.
Each of these islands has five hundred smaller islands as its satellites; some are inhabited by people, while others are uninhabited.
Question: What is the appearance of these people?
Answer: Its form stands upright.
What are its words?
Answer: When the world was first formed, all spoke the noble language (āryabhāṣā); the rest is as explained above.
What is the realm of the gods (devagati)?
The answer is:
"Divine category, divine companion, attainment of a divine body," and so forth, as explained at length.
By what definition is it called the "divine realm" (*devagati*)?
Answer: Because it is the most excellent among all realms of existence (gati).
In what way is it superior?

That which is called the celestial realm (deva-gati) is so named because there exists therein excellence in sovereignty, excellence in pleasure, excellence in auspiciousness and virtue, excellence in the body, and excellence in physical form; it is due to the presence of such excellences that it is termed the celestial realm.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because one performs superior wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind, one is born within that realm; therefore, it is called the celestial realm (*devagati*).
Others say that this is a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, some say that because the various devas have no day or night and always illuminate themselves with their own radiance, they are called the celestial realm (*deva-gati*).
Others say that because they are born within that celestial realm due to the causes and conditions of virtuous conduct, and constantly engage in play and enjoyment, it is called the celestial realm.
Where do they dwell?
The answer is:
They dwell on the four sides of Mount Sumeru upon the water, encircling Mount Sumeru; extending sixteen thousand yojanas in breadth, there is the abode of the Musala-hasta devas.
Ten thousand yojanas above that, encircling Mount Sumeru and eight thousand yojanas in width, is the abode of the Mālyadhāraṇa (Holding Flower Garlands) devas.
Ten thousand yojanas above that, encircling Mount Sumeru and four thousand yojanas in width, is the abode of the Sadāmada (Ever-Intoxicated) devas.
Twenty thousand yojanas above this, encircling Mount Sumeru and extending two thousand yojanas in width, is the abode of the Four Great Kings.
There are seven kinds of golden mountains, within which lie the cities of the Four Great Kings and the villages of their celestial subjects; it is here that these devas are most numerous below.
Forty thousand yojanas above that, at the summit of Mount Sumeru, lies the city of Sudarśana, ten thousand yojanas in length and breadth; this is the dwelling place of the Trāyastriṃśa devas.
How long and wide is the summit of Mount Sumeru?
The answer is:
it is forty thousand yojanas in circumference.
Forty thousand yojanas above the summit of Mount Sumeru, amidst clouds, dwell the Yāma devas who reside upon the earth.
Following this sequence, up to the Sudarśana devas, all likewise dwell supported by the earth.
From the Suyāma Heaven up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they likewise abide supported by the earth.
What is their measurement? It is equal to the measurement of the summit of Mount Sumeru; from there upward, the measurements up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven are also like this.
As is the uniform measure of the four continents, so too is the uniform measure of the stage of the first dhyāna;
as is the uniform measure of a thousandfold world system, so too is the uniform measure of the stage of the second dhyāna;
as is the uniform measure of a two-thousandfold world system, so too is the uniform measure of the stage of the third dhyāna.
Just as the dimensions of a trichiliocosm are equal, so too are the dimensions of the fourth dhyāna level.

Furthermore, some say that just as the dimensions of the summit of Mount Sumeru are, the dimensions of the Yāma devas are twice as large; likewise, up to the Paranirmita-vaśavartin devas, they increase in size by double each time.
Just as the dimensions of a thousandfold world system are, so too are the dimensions of the first dhyāna.
As is the measure of a two-thousandfold world system, so too is the measure of the second dhyāna;
as is the measure of a three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system, so too is the measure of the third dhyāna.

However, the measure of the fourth dhyāna stage is immeasurable and boundless; therefore, for one who gives rise to the view of self within the fourth dhyāna stage, that view is difficult to sever and difficult to abandon.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the spatial dimensions of the fourth dhyāna stage are not fixed.
If various devas are born within that dhyāna, they possess as many palaces and abodes as there are;
yet when their lives end, these abodes vanish. Therefore, they are not fixed.
The commentary says:
It is as previously stated that it is excellent; that ground is immeasurable and boundless. Question:
That stage of the fourth dhyāna is not reached by the three calamities; how, then, could it not be permanent?
The answer is:
it is not permanent, because it falls under the category of momentariness (*kṣaṇika*).
What is the form of the various devas? Answer:
Their forms stand upright.
What is speech? The answer is:
it consists entirely of noble speech (*ārya-vāk*).
Having already explained the various reasons for the different realms of existence, we shall now further explain the reasons concerning the asuras. Why are they called asuras?
The answer is:
Asuras are celestial beings; because they are not celestial beings, they are called asuras.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "asura" means "handsome"; because they are not handsome, they are called asuras.
How is this known?

When the world was first formed, the asuras first resided upon the summit of Mount Sumeru. Subsequently, when the devas of the Ābhāsvara Heaven reached the end of their lives, they were reborn on the summit of Mount Sumeru; there, palaces also appeared spontaneously. The asuras, giving rise to great anger, immediately fled from them.
In this manner, there were celestial palaces of the second heaven, extending successively until they completely filled the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The asuras gave rise to great wrath, abandoned the summit of Mount Sumeru, and retreated to dwell below.
Because of hatred, one's physical form is not upright; for this reason, it is called "not upright. Question:
In what place does it abide?
Answer: Some say that within Mount Sumeru there are hollow spaces, like a great city inside an overturned precious vessel, where the asuras dwell.

Question: If that is so, how is it that the various nāgas see the asura armies—clad in armor of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal, and holding in their hands bows, arrows, and various weapons—emerging from the asura city?
This statement is well-explained;
as it is said:
the asura spoke, saying:
"The great ocean where I dwell has a single uniform salty taste.
How is this statement to be reconciled?
The answer is:
The inhabitants of the various Aśura villages dwell in the great ocean, while the Aśura kings reside on Mount Sumeru.
Furthermore, some say that the Aśuras dwell in the waters of the great ocean upon a ground made of gold; upon this ground there is a golden terrace, five hundred yojanas in length and breadth.
Above it is a city where various asuras dwell.
It is asked:
If this is so, this sūtra is well-explained, as it says:
The asuras said: "We dwell in the great ocean, which has a single uniform salty taste;
this statement is well-founded."
As it is said:
"The armies of the asuras emerged from the city," and so forth, in detail.
How is this to be reconciled?
Answer: The devas see them because they station dragons within the Golden Mountains to serve as guards.
Furthermore, within the cities of the asuras, there are four kinds of pleasure gardens and groves:
The first is named Joy;
the second is named Delight;
the third is named Great Delight.
In the fourth grove, named Delightful, there are also *citrāpātali* trees.
It is asked:
Are the asuras included within the realm of the devas, or are they included within the realm of the pretas?
If they belong to the realm of devas, why is it that none among them have attained the certainty of right resolve?
If they belong to the realm of hungry ghosts, why do they form intimate friendships with the devas, and why do they further engage in battle with them?
How, then, is this sūtra to be reconciled?
For it says: Śakra made this statement:
"King Vemacitrin, you were originally a deva of this realm.
He replied:
"Some say that he is included within the deva realm."
Question: If that is so, why is there no one who attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*)? Answer:
Because they are shrouded by deceit and crookedness. What is this matter?
The answer is:
Those asuras thought to themselves:
"The Buddha is partial toward the devas. If the Buddha were to teach the four foundations of mindfulness, they would think:
'He is teaching the four foundations of mindfulness for our sake; he must surely be teaching the five foundations of mindfulness for the devas.'"
If the Buddha were to teach them the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, they would think:
"The Buddha has taught us the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment; he must have taught the gods the thirty-eighth factor of enlightenment."
Because they are thus shrouded by a mind of flattery and crookedness, they are unable to attain right certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that such individuals are comprised within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*).
Question: If that is so, why does he maintain close relations with the various devas? Answer:
Because the devas crave beautiful forms, they do not regard them as a matter of lineage; for example, the Apsarā Śaci was peerlessly beautiful, and for this reason Śakra took her as his wife.
It is also like the daughter of the Kinnara King Drumā, named Manoharā, whom the Bodhisattva Sutasoma took as his wife.
The Bodhisattva belonged to the realm of devas, while the Kinnara belonged to the realm of animals; in such cases, it was for the sake of beauty, not for the sake of lineage.
For what reason does he further engage in battle with the various devas?
The answer is:
there are also instances where one who is inferior fights with one who is superior; for example, a servant may also fight and dispute with his master, and a dog may also contend with a human.
That case is also like this.
How, then, is this sūtra to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"King Vemacitrin was originally a deva of this very place.
He replied:
"King Vemacitrin is the father-in-law of Śakra; it is out of respect and reverence that he spoke those words."

Question: Are such beings as the goddesses Bhadranī, Caṇḍakā, Caṇḍalikā, the god Itadīpa, the god Mahākaṇṭha, and others included within the realm of devas, or are they included within the realm of pretas?
If he were included within the realm of the gods (*deva-gati*), why would he seize the vital essence of humans, take their lives, and receive human sacrifices?
If he were included within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*), how could this sūtra be reconciled?
As it is said in verse:
“Uttara is not to be disturbed, nor is Pilindavatsa;
if I have seen the True Dharma, you all shall likewise attain it.”
He replied: "Some say that it is included within the realm of celestial beings. He asked:
If this is so, why do they rob people of their vital energy, take their lives, and receive their sacrificial offerings?
The answer is:
they do not rob people of their vital energy, nor do they take their lives, nor do they receive their sacrificial offerings.
Among the retinue he leads, there are some who rob people of their vital energy, some who take human life, and some who receive offerings from sacrifices.
Furthermore, there are those who say they are comprised within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta).
Question: If that is so, how can the verse previously cited be reconciled? Answer:
Because he possesses faith and an inclination toward the truths, yet has not actually seen the truths and remains deluded regarding them,
by what means could he see them?
How then can one reconcile this with what the deity Mātṛkaṇḍa said?
Answer: These are words of self-exaltation; being deluded regarding the various realms of existence (*gati*), how could one perceive the distinctions between those realms?
It is merely out of self-aggrandizement that such a statement is made.
Just as the wealthy today claim superiority even over their servants, so too it was with them:
though they were merely attendants of the Four Great Kings, they claimed for themselves, "I am a deva; I have been born among the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings."
All the deities who dwell upon the earth are entirely subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
All the *piśāca* deities, *kiṃnara* deities, *hiraṇyakaśipu* deities, *vārūṇī* deities, and *śarabha-kumāra* deities are entirely subsumed within the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*).
Although their forms stand upright, they still possess the characteristics of animals; some have pointed ears, while others wear armor.
All yakṣas, rākṣasas, khaṭvāṅgas, pūtanas, kumbhāṇḍas, and so forth, are entirely subsumed within the realm of hungry ghosts (preta-gati).
As it is said:
"That which is a portion of hell, that which is an associate of hell, and the life-faculty and other formations dissociated from mind—these are called hell-beings."
Some may say that one should not speak in this way, saying:
"That which is obtained in this place, obtained as an essential nature, and obtained through the various sense bases (āyatana) should be called a portion of hell and a companion of hell."
Furthermore, there are those who say that one should explain the reason why:

the attainment of the various *dhātus* refers to what is attained through the spheres (*āyatana*); the attainment of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) refers to the attainment of the aggregates (*skandha*); and the attainment of the various *āyatanas* refers to the attainment of the internal and external spheres.

Question: If it were sufficient to speak merely of the elements (dhātu), aggregates (skandha), and bases (āyatana), why is this further statement made regarding the acquisition of indeterminate (avyākṛta) form up to consciousness by sentient beings born in hell?
Answer: It is for the sake of explaining the fruit of retribution; it is by way of the fruit of retribution that the five destinies are differentiated.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle seven.
The Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Eight.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Northern Liang Indian *bhikṣu* Buddhabhadra.

Translated by Kung Tao-t’ai and others, this is the fourth section of the *Jñāna-varga* within the *Saṃyukta-gaṇḍī*. It states: "One should say that with one eye one sees forms," and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
It is for the purpose of stopping the intent of those who hold combined views. As the Venerable Dharmatrāta said:
It is the consciousness that sees forms, not the eye;
it is in order to stop such a misconception that it is said "the eye sees" and not "consciousness sees.
As the Vātsīputrīyas say:
One sees forms with one eye; it is not that both eyes see simultaneously.
Why is this? Because the images are distant from one another and because of the extreme rapidity [of the process], people say that both eyes see forms at once.

Question: If it is argued that things cannot be perceived simultaneously because they are spatially distant, then the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is also spatially distant [in its various parts], such as the two arms; yet one can simultaneously perceive touch and give rise to body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*). The same should apply to the two eyes.
Therefore, this treatise is composed to refute the views of those who hold such combined positions.
Furthermore, this treatise is composed to sever the doubts of people.

The distance between the two eyes of sentient beings varies: it may be half a finger-width, one finger-width, two, three, or four finger-widths; half a cubit, one cubit, one *hasta*, one *vyāma*; half a *krośa*, one *krośa*, half a *yojana*, one *yojana*, two, three, or four *yojanas*, up to even a hundred *yojanas*.
Just as there are beings within the great ocean whose bodies measure either one hundred yojanas, or one hundred and forty yojanas, or two hundred and ten yojanas;
or just as the beings in the Akaniṣṭha heaven of the Form Realm have bodies measuring sixteen thousand yojanas.
In such beings, the two eyes are situated very far apart.
Given this fact, people give rise to doubt:
do two consciousnesses arise simultaneously in the two eyes, or does each eye have its own single consciousness?

Does each individual consciousness arise one after another within each eye, or does a single consciousness divide into two parts and arise in both eyes, or does it pass through both eyes like a horizontal beam?
If two consciousnesses were to arise simultaneously in both eyes, how could there not be the fault of having two minds at once?
If [a single consciousness] were to arise in one eye and then subsequently arise in the other eye, how could there not be the fault of temporal succession between moments?

If a single consciousness were to divide itself into two parts and reside within the two eyes, how could that single consciousness not be something subject to division? For if it depends upon the body, it is called body-consciousness; if it arises in dependence upon the eye, it is called eye-consciousness.
If it were like a horizontal beam passing through two eye sockets, why would a single consciousness not be both body-consciousness and eye-consciousness?

Yet, the supports for these five consciousnesses are each distinct, and the spheres of their respective objects are also distinct; it is logically impossible for a single consciousness to have two different bases.

Thus, it is not possible for two consciousnesses to arise simultaneously in both eyes; nor can one consciousness arise in one eye and then subsequently arise in the other; nor can one consciousness be divided into two parts to reside in both eyes, as if a horizontal beam were passing through both eyes—all such [theories] are untenable.
It is not that consciousness does not arise based on both eyes, yet it is able to discern forms that are extremely distant and subtle.
All such phenomena are profound, subtle, and difficult to understand.
This treatise is composed in order to explain the profound, subtle, and difficult-to-understand Dharma.
A question is asked:
How can a single consciousness arise in dependence upon two eyes?
Answer: Because it is the support upon which consciousness relies.
Although the two eyes are far apart from each other, they can both serve as the support for a single consciousness, as both are the supports upon which eye-consciousness relies.
Even if there were a hundred eyes serving as the support for a single consciousness, there would be no fault;
it would be just like a hundred crystal vessels: if one looks at them from one side, a hundred reflections appear, and so it would be in this case as well.
"Although these two supports give rise to a single consciousness that operates upon the object, one should say that 'one eye sees forms,' and so forth, as explained at length.
He replied:
"One should say that both eyes see forms."
One should explain the reasons for causing people in the world to develop faith.
Why is it that one should say both eyes see forms, rather than saying one eye sees forms?

For instance, if one eye is closed, pure visual consciousness does not arise; consequently, one cannot perceive objects extensively, and regarding those objects, one’s vision is not clear, not distinct, and not pure.
If both eyes are opened, then the pure eye-consciousness arises, whereby one is able to see objects extensively, with clarity and purity regarding those objects.
Suppose, for instance, that one eye is closed; then the pure eye-consciousness does not arise, nor does one see objects extensively, and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding the statement that "even when both eyes are open, pure consciousness does not arise, nor is the objective field seen extensively," and so forth:

one should not say that color-forms are seen by both eyes; rather, it is by one eye alone that color-forms are seen, whereby impure consciousness arises and the objective field is not seen extensively, and so forth.
If both eyes are opened, the pure visual consciousness arises and is able to see objects extensively, and so forth, as explained at length.
Therefore, one should say that both eyes see forms; one should not say that a single eye sees forms.
"Obstructed" refers to when the eyes are covered by the hand, clothing, leaves, or any other such objects that block vision.
"Impaired" refers to cataracts, red films, eye-clouds, or the growth of white membranes.
"Obscured" means being covered by smoke, dust, or grime.
"Destroyed" means being rotten, infested by insects, fallen, broken, dissolved, dried up, plucked out, or naturally shed.
As it is with the eye and forms, so it is with the ear and sounds, and the nose and odors.
As the basis is pure, consciousness is pure;
as the basis is impure, consciousness is impure.
Regarding the purity of ultimate reality: wholesome consciousness is pure, while defiled consciousness is impure.

There may be cases where the eye is pure but consciousness is impure; there may be cases where consciousness is pure but the eye is impure; there may be cases where both the eye and consciousness are pure; and there may be cases where both the eye and consciousness are impure.
When the eye is pure and consciousness is impure, it is like an eye free from all obstructions and cataracts producing a defiled consciousness.
When consciousness is pure and the eye is impure, it is like an eye with obstructions and cataracts producing a wholesome consciousness.
When visual consciousness is pure, it is like an eye free from obstructions or cataracts producing wholesome consciousness.
When visual consciousness is impure, it is like an eye with obstructions or cataracts producing defiled consciousness.
Question: For what reason do the eyes, ears, and nose each have two locations, while the tongue and body do not? Answer:
These sense faculties thus adorn the body.
To have two tongues would be a base and loathsome thing, causing the world to despise and laugh at one:
"How can this person have two tongues?"
It would be like a venomous snake.
Furthermore, if there were two bodies, it would be a vulgar and contemptible thing, laughed at by the world:
"How can one person have two bodies?"
It is like twin children born together.
A question is asked:
For what reason are there only two eyes, two nostrils, and two ears, rather than more?
Answer: These various faculties serve to adorn the body.
If there were multiple eyes, the details would be as explained above.
Furthermore, there are those who say that having multiple eyes would be of no benefit.
Why is this? For example, when two eyes see forms, the vision is clear; even more than that would be of no further benefit.
Because they are of no benefit, there are only two eyes.
The ears and nose should also be explained in this same way. Question:
Why are the two eyes, two nostrils, and two ears, despite their distinct locations, each designated as one element (dhātu), one base (āyatana), and one faculty (indriya)?
The answer is:

because they function within a single objective field, serve as the support for a single consciousness, and perform a single function, they are each called one element, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Is it the eye that sees form, or is it consciousness that sees, or is it the wisdom associated with consciousness that sees, or is it their conjunction that sees?
If it were the eye that sees, then one should see even when there is no consciousness, and one should also see when it is conjoined with other forms of consciousness.
If it were consciousness that sees, then consciousness would be the nature of seeing, and thus it would also be the nature of consciousness itself.
If it were the wisdom associated with consciousness that sees, then the wisdom associated with the ear-consciousness should likewise see and hear.
If seeing occurs through a combination [of factors], it has never occurred without such a combination.
The answer is:
the eye sees form, but it must necessarily be accompanied by consciousness.
There are two kinds of eyes:
first, the retributive eye;
second, the nurtured eye.
The same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is of three kinds:
that which is nurtured (aupacayika), that which is karmic fruition (vipākaja), and that which is dependent (āśrita).
Fragrance, odor, and tangibility are also like this.
Sound is of two kinds:
that which is nurtured and that which is dependent.
The mind-base (manāyatana) is of three kinds:
resultant (vipāka), dependent (niśraya), and momentary (kṣaṇika).
That which is the mind associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti) is called momentary.
The sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) has four kinds:
resultant (vipāka), dependent (niśraya), momentary (kṣaṇika), and substantial entity (dravya).
As for the substantial entity, it is so called because it consists of both existent and non-existent phenomena.
Question: Is there a case where there is only the eye as retribution (*vipāka*), but no eye as nurtured growth (*aupacayika*)?
And is there a case where there is only the eye as nurtured growth, but not the eye as retribution?
Answer: There are none.
