It is called a "syllable" (vyañjana), and it is called a "syllable-body" (vyañjanakāya), but it is not called a "multiple-syllable-body."

Regarding those four syllables: that which consists of a single syllable is called a "name" (*nāman*); that which consists of two syllables is a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); and the remaining two syllables are a "multiple-name-body" (*anekanāmakāya*). They are not called phrases (*pada*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), or multiple-phrase-bodies (*anekapadakāya*); rather, they are called "syllables" (*vyañjana*), syllable-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*), and multiple-syllable-bodies (*anevyañjanakāya*).

That which consists of two syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*) and a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); it is not called a "multiple-name-body," nor is it called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), or a "multiple-phrase-body. It is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and a "multiple-syllable-body."

That which consists of eight syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*); it is not called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), nor is it called a "multiple name-body. It is called a "phrase" (*pada*); it is not called a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), nor is it called a "multiple phrase-body. It is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and a "multiple syllable-body" (*anekavyañjanakāya*).

Regarding those eight syllables, when they are designated by a single syllable, it is called a "name" (*nāman*), a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), or a "multiple-name-body" (*anekanāmakāya*); it is called a "phrase" (*pada*), but is not called a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) or a "multiple-phrase-body" (*anekapadakāya*); it is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), or a "multiple-syllable-body" (*anekavyañjanakāya*).
The same applies to names consisting of two syllables.

As for names consisting of four syllables, they are called "name" (*nāman*) and "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), but they are not called "multiple-name-body. They are called "phrase" (*pada*), but they are not called "phrase-body" (*padakāya*) or "multiple-phrase-body. They are called "syllable" (*vyañjana*), "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and "multiple-syllable-body" (*anekavyañjanakāya*).

That which consists of sixteen syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*); it is not called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), nor is it called a "multiple name-body. It is called a "phrase" (*pada*) and a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), but it is not called a "multiple phrase-body. It is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and a "multiple syllable-body."

Regarding those sixteen syllables, when one syllable constitutes a name, it is called a "name" (*nāman*), a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), or a "multiple-name-body" (*anekanāmakāya*); it is called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), but not a "multiple-phrase-body" (*anekapadakāya*); it is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), or a "multiple-syllable-body" (*anekavyañjanakāya*).
The same applies to names consisting of two or four syllables.

A name consisting of eight syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*) and a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), but it is not called a "multiple-name-body. It is called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), but not a "multiple-phrase-body. It is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and a "multiple-syllable-body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*).

That which consists of thirty-two syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*); it is not called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), nor is it called a "multiple-name-body" (*bahunāmakāya*). It is called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), or a "multiple-phrase-body" (*bahupadakāya*). It is called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), or a "multiple-syllable-body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*).
Regarding those thirty-two syllables, names consisting of one syllable, two syllables, four syllables, and eight syllables are as previously explained.

That which consists of sixteen syllables is called a "name" (*nāman*); it is called a "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), but not a "multiple-name-body. It is also called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), or a "multiple-phrase-body. It is also called a "syllable" (*vyañjana*), a "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), or a "multiple-syllable-body."
A single syllable has a single name, as explained extensively above.

A single syllable having two names is called "name" (*nāman*) or "name-body" (*nāmakāya*); it is not called a "multiple-name-body," nor is it called a "phrase" (*pada*), a "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), or a "multiple-phrase-body. It is called "syllable" (*vyañjana*) or "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), but it is not called a "multiple-syllable-body."

Regarding the four names for a single syllable: they are called "name" (*nāman*), "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), and "multiple-name-body" (*nāmanekakāya*); they are not called "phrase" (*pada*), "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), or "multiple-phrase-body" (*padanekakāya*); and they are called "syllable" (*vyañjana*), "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and "multiple-syllable-body" (*vyañjanevakāya*).

Regarding the eight names for a single syllable: they are called "name" (nāma), "body of names" (nāmakāya), and "body of multiple names" (anekanāmakāya); "phrase" (pada), not "body of phrases" (padakāya) nor "body of multiple phrases" (anekapadakāya); and "syllable" (vyañjana), "body of syllables" (vyañjanakāya), and "body of multiple syllables" (anekavyañjanakāya).
Regarding the sixteen names for a single syllable, these constitute phrases and collections of phrases, but they are not called "collections of many phrases"; the rest is as explained above.
Regarding the thirty-two names for a single syllable, it is said that all are fully present.
Regarding "two syllables, one name," it is as previously explained.

Regarding "two syllables, two names," these are called *nāman* (name) and *nāmakāya* (name-body); they are not called multiple-name-bodies (*anekanāmakāya*), nor are they called phrases (*pada*), phrase-bodies (*padakāya*), or multiple-phrase-bodies (*anekapadakāya*). They are called phonemes (*vyañjana*), phoneme-bodies (*vyañjanakāya*), and multiple-phoneme-bodies (*anekavyañjanakāya*).
Regarding two characters forming two names, where one character constitutes a name, it is as previously explained.
Regarding four characters forming one name, it is as previously explained.

Regarding four characters forming two names, they are called *nāman* (name) and *nāma-nāmakāya* (name-body); they are not called *anekanāmakāya* (multiple-name-body). They are called *pada* (phrase), but are not called *padakāya* (phrase-body) or *anekapadakāya* (multiple-phrase-body). They are called *vyañjana* (syllable), *vyañjanakāya* (syllable-body), and *anekavyañjanakāya* (multiple-syllable-body).
Regarding those four syllables and two names, where one syllable constitutes a name, it is as previously explained.
Regarding eight syllables constituting one name, it is as previously explained.

Regarding eight syllables constituting two names, they are called "name" (*nāman*) and "name-body" (*nāmakāya*), but they are not called a "multiple-name-body. They are called "phrase" (*pada*) and "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), but they are not called a "multiple-phrase-body. They are called "syllable" (*vyañjana*), "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and "multiple-syllable-body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*).
Regarding those eight syllables and two names, the case where one, two, or four syllables constitute a name is as previously explained.
As for sixteen syllables constituting a single name, it is as previously explained.

Regarding the sixteen syllables that constitute two names: they are called "name" (*nāman*) and "name-body" (*nāmakāya*). They are not called "multiple-name-body. They are also called "phrase" (*pada*), "phrase-body" (*padakāya*), and "multiple-phrase-body" (*bahupadakāya*); as well as "syllable" (*vyañjana*), "syllable-body" (*vyañjanakāya*), and "multiple-syllable-body" (*bahuvyañjanakāya*).
Regarding those sixteen syllables as a single name, or one, two, four, or eight syllables as a name, it is as previously explained.
Question: Does a "name" (nāma) correspond to the location of the body, or does it correspond to the location of speech?
Answer: Some say that "name" (nāma) follows the locus of speech.

Those who maintain this view—that name follows the locus of speech—hold that when one is born within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and utters speech of the desire realm, the speech belongs to the desire realm, the name belongs to the desire realm, and the person belongs to the desire realm; however, the meaning expressed may belong to any of the three realms or may be unconditioned (apratisaṃyukta).

When one born in the desire realm utters speech belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, that speech belongs to the level of the first dhyāna and its name belongs to the level of the first dhyāna; yet the person remains in the desire realm, while the meaning expressed may be bound to any of the three realms or may be unconditioned (unbound).

When born within the first dhyāna, one utters speech belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; that speech belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, its name belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, and the person belongs to the level of the first dhyāna, while the meaning expressed may be bound to the three realms or unbound.

One born in the first dhyāna utters speech belonging to the desire realm; the speech belongs to the desire realm and the name belongs to the desire realm, while the person belongs to the first dhyāna. The meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

When one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna utters speech belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, that speech is of the first dhyāna and its name is of the first dhyāna, while the person is in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna; the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

When one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna utters speech belonging to the desire realm, that speech belongs to the desire realm and its name belongs to the desire realm, while the person remains in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna; the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.
Question: Regarding those who say that names are the locus of speech, is it only the desire realm and the first dhyāna that possess names, or do the remaining three dhyāna stages also have names?
The answer is:
Some say that it does not exist;
others say that it exists but is inexpressible.
The critique says:
One should not speak in this way; it is better as previously stated.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the name] follows the person and the location.

If one were to say that this is called "following the person and the location," then when one is born within the desire realm and utters speech of the desire realm, the speech belongs to the desire realm, the name belongs to the desire realm, and the person belongs to the desire realm; the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

When one born in the desire realm utters speech belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna, that speech belongs to the stage of the first dhyāna, while the name [of the speaker] belongs to the desire realm and the person belongs to the desire realm; the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

One born in the first dhyāna utters speech belonging to the level of the first dhyāna; that speech is the first dhyāna, its name is the first dhyāna, and the person is the first dhyāna. The meaning of what is said is as previously explained.

One born in the first dhyāna utters speech belonging to the desire realm; the speech itself belongs to the desire realm, while the name [of the speaker] belongs to the first dhyāna, as does the person. The meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

If one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna utters speech belonging to the level of the first dhyāna, that speech belongs to the first dhyāna; the designation of the person is according to their respective level, while the meaning of what is spoken is as previously explained.

When one born in the second, third, or fourth dhyāna utters speech belonging to the desire realm, that speech itself belongs to the desire realm; however, the name of the person [uttering it] belongs to that respective level. The meaning of what is said is as previously explained.

Question: If it is said that these names follow the person and the place, then while the names exist in the stages of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, do they exist in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) or not?
Answer: Some say it does not exist;
others say it exists, yet cannot be described.
The critique says:
One should not speak thus; it is better as previously stated. Question:
Is it reckoned as belonging to the category of sentient beings, or is it not?
Answer: It is reckoned as belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Question: Is "name" (nāma) a form of nourishment (aupacayika), a result of maturation (vipākaja), or a basis (niśraya)?
Answer: [It is all three.]
All names are dependent; they are neither nurtured nor retributive. Question:
If names are not retributive, how is this scripture to be reconciled?
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"I also say that it is named as being born from karma.
He replied:
In this context, the fruit of the power of karma is explained as arising from karma, just as performing wholesome karma also gives rise to a good reputation.
Question: Should this reputation be described as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral?
Answer: It should be said that the name is indeterminate (avyākṛta). Question:
Who accomplishes this name?
Is it the speaker, or is it the dharma being spoken?
If it were the speaker, then even one who has severed their roots of goodness speaks wholesome dharmas; could such a person then accomplish goodness?
If one who is free from desire also speaks what is unwholesome, can that which is unwholesome be accomplished?

If it is that which is spoken of as "dharmas," then dharmas not included within the category of sentient beings (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*) and unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are also spoken of as "dharmas"; could these also accomplish a name?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
name is accomplished by the speaker.

Question: If that is so, then since one who has severed the roots of goodness may still speak of wholesome dharmas, and one who is free from desire may still speak of unwholesome dharmas, would it be possible for them to accomplish what is wholesome or unwholesome?
He replied: "No. Why is this so?"
Although they have attained the names of wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, the substance of those names is itself an indeterminate dharma.
A śrāvaka can produce a single utterance with a single mind, yet a single utterance cannot express even a single syllable.
Question: As it is said, "A," is this not a single syllable? Answer:
During that time, many kṣaṇas have already passed.
The Blessed One utters a single word with a single-minded focus, and each word expresses a single syllable.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses speech so swift and light; his vocal sound is faultless, and his eloquence is supreme.
Question: Do dharmas of the past possess the designations "past," "present," and "future"? Answer:
There are past phenomena that possess past names, such as when Vipaśyin Buddha spoke of past phenomena using such names.
There are past phenomena that possess future names, such as when Maitreya Buddha speaks of past phenomena using such names.
If past dharmas possess present names— just as one now speaks of past dharmas using such present names—
is it possible for future dharmas to possess future, present, or past names?
Answer: There are future dharmas that possess future names, such as when Maitreya Buddha speaks of future dharmas using such names.
There are future dharmas that possess past names, such as when Vipaśyin Buddha speaks of future dharmas using such names.
If future dharmas possess present names— just as we now use such names to speak of future dharmas as if they were present—
is it possible for present dharmas to possess present, past, and future names?
Answer: There are present phenomena that possess present names, such as when one uses such-and-such a name to speak of a present phenomenon.
There are present phenomena that possess past names, such as when Vipaśyin Buddha used such-and-such a name to speak of a present phenomenon.
When present phenomena possess future names, it is as when Maitreya Buddha speaks of present phenomena by means of such names.
Just as speech is able to express names, and names are able to manifest meanings.
Question: Do all names fully manifest their meanings? Answer: No.
"All names are capable of manifesting meaning. Question:

If that is so, when such names as "the view of annihilationism or eternalism," "a second head," "a third hand," "a sixth aggregate," "a thirteenth base," or "a nineteenth element" are used to manifest meaning, what meaning do these names manifest?
The answer is:

It reveals the notions of permanence and annihilation held by sentient beings, as well as the notion of a second head, the notion of a third hand, the notion of a sixth aggregate (*skandha*), the notion of a thirteenth base (*āyatana*), and the notion of a nineteenth element (*dhātu*); it reveals such meanings as these.
Question: If all phenomena are revealed as being without self by means of names, what is there that is not revealed? Answer:
Some say that while the associated and coexistent [factors] do not manifest their own intrinsic nature, all other dharmas are manifested.
Others say that, with the sole exception of its own intrinsic nature, all other dharmas are manifested.
Furthermore, there are those who say that, with the exception of four characters—namely, "all phenomena are without self"—all other dharmas are fully revealed.
Others say that all dharmas whatsoever are fully revealed.
Why is this so? It is because, for example, the syllable *ba* manifests the syllable *ba*, and the syllable *sa* manifests the syllable *sa*.
[The interlocutor] asks:
"Is it the names that are more numerous, or is it the meanings?
He replied:
"Some say that the meanings are more numerous."

Why is this? In terms of meaning (*artha*), it comprises seventeen elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of one element; eleven bases (*āyatana*) and a portion of one base; and four aggregates (*skandha*) and a portion of one aggregate. In terms of name (*nāman*), it comprises one element, one base, and a portion of one aggregate.
Furthermore, there are those who say that names are many while meanings are not many. Why is this?
Because a single meaning may have many names.
Just as in the Nigaṇṭha scriptures, various names are distinguished such that a single meaning may have a thousand names.
The critique says:
Such an explanation is excellent.
The meanings are many, but the names are not many. Why is this?
It is because there is no need for further matters; it is simply because the inclusion of the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth is manifold.

In terms of meaning (*artha*), it subsumes seventeen elements (*dhātu*), a portion of one element; eleven bases (*āyatana*), a portion of one base; and four aggregates (*skandha*), a portion of one aggregate. In terms of name (*nāman*), it subsumes one element, one base, and a portion of one aggregate; that name is also a meaning.
If that were so, it would necessarily encompass the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) in their entirety.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because it is spoken as a teaching, the name exceeds the actual meaning. Why is this?
The World-Honored One teaches the Dharma by expressing a single meaning through many names.
If one considers the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas), then the meanings exceed the names. Question:
Is meaning something that can be expressed?
If it could be expressed, then speaking of fire would burn the tongue, speaking of a sword would cut the tongue, and speaking of impurity would defile the tongue.
If it cannot be so described, how can there be perversion?
It would be like seeking an elephant and a horse arriving instead, or seeking a horse and an elephant arriving instead.
How, then, is this sūtra to be reconciled?
As the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Dharma I teach is excellent in its phrasing and excellent in its meaning.
He replied:
One should argue as follows:
the meaning cannot be expressed. Question:
If this is so, how is it that what one seeks is not erroneous?
The answer is:

In ancient times, people established names based on forms; they had such conceptions that when they sought an elephant, the elephant would come and not the horse, and when they sought a horse, the horse would come and not the elephant.
Furthermore, there are those who say that speech can produce names, and names can manifest meanings.
In this way, speech produces the name "elephant," and the name "elephant" can manifest the meaning of an elephant; the same applies to horses and so forth.
Regarding how this sūtra is to be reconciled, the Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra replied:
"Because it speaks of the manifest meaning through its phrasing, it is said to 'speak the meaning.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is for the purpose of refuting the teachings of the non-Buddhists; for what the non-Buddhists teach is either meaningless or possesses very little meaning."
The teachings spoken by the World-Honored One possess both specific meaning and manifold meanings;

therefore, they are called "teachings with meaning. Furthermore, there are those who say that the words and meanings spoken by non-Buddhists are mutually contradictory—words contradicting meanings and meanings contradicting words—whereas the Dharma taught by the World-Honored One has words that do not contradict its meaning, nor does its meaning contradict its words.
Question: What is the distinction between the letter and the meaning? Answer:
The "letter" (vyañjana) is the flavor, and the "meaning" (artha) is that which is flavored. Question:
Is that flavor also flavored by another flavor? Is that flavor also that which is flavored?
Answer: That flavor is also that which is tasted. Question:
If that is so, what is the difference between taste and the object of tasting?
The answer is:
the object of tasting is comprised of a portion of one of the seventeen elements, a portion of one of the eleven bases, and a portion of one of the four aggregates.
Taste is comprised within one element, one base, and one aggregate, and is included in a small portion [of the bases].
Furthermore, some say that the meaning (*artha*) is both material and non-material, while the phrasing (*vyañjana*) is non-material.

As with the material and non-material, so too are they categorized as associated or dissociated, with support or without support, possessing efficacy or lacking efficacy, having activity or lacking activity, and having an object or lacking an object.
The phrasing (*vyañjana*) is dissociated [from the mind] and so forth, up to being without an object (*anālambana*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that while the meaning (*artha*) may be visible or invisible, the phrasing is always invisible.
The meaning (artha) may be with resistance (sapratigha) or without resistance (apratigha), whereas the letter (vyañjana) is without resistance.
The meaning may be with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava), whereas the letter is with outflows.
The meaning may be conditioned (saṃskṛta) or unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), whereas the letter is conditioned.
The meaning may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate, whereas the phrasing is always indeterminate.
The meaning may pertain to the mundane or the supramundane, whereas the phrasing pertains only to the mundane.
The meaning may be bound to the three realms or unbound, whereas the phrasing is bound to the desire and form realms.

The meaning (artha) pertains to that which is in training (śaikṣa), that which is beyond training (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither in training nor beyond training; the phrasing (vyañjana) pertains to that which is neither in training nor beyond training.

The meaning pertains to what is abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya), what is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya), and what is not abandoned; the phrasing pertains to what is abandoned through the path of cultivation.
The meaning may be defiled or non-defiled, while the phrasing is invariably non-defiled.

Just as with being defiled or non-defiled, so it is with having faults or being faultless, black or white, obscured or unobscured, subject to regression or not subject to regression, and having karmic retribution or being without retribution.
The phrasing is that it is non-defiled, up to being without retribution;
this is what constitutes the distinction in meaning.
As the Sūtra says:
What is "name"? The four aggregates are name. Question:

If names are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), for what reason did the Blessed One say that the four aggregates, excluding the aggregate of form, constitute "name" (*nāman*)?
The answer is:

The Buddha taught that all phenomena are divided into two categories: material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and non-material phenomena (*arūpa-dharma*). All material phenomena constitute the aggregate of form, while all non-material phenomena constitute the [remaining] four aggregates.
All names that manifest meaning are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).

There are six kinds of names: namely, those based on qualities (*guṇa*), place of birth (*jāti-sthāna*), time (*kāla*), according to wish (*yathā-icchā*), function (*kriyā*), and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Those who are named for their merit are as follows: one is called a *sūtra*-reciter because they recite the *sūtras*; one is called a holder of the Vinaya (*vinayadhara*) because they recite the Vinaya; one is called an *abhidharma*-master because they recite the *Abhidharma*; and one is called a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) because they have attained the fruit of stream-entry, up to and including one who has attained the fruit of arhatship and is thus called an arhat.
Regarding names based on place of birth: one born in a city is called a "city person," and likewise, one born in whatever country is called a "person of that country.
Regarding names based on time: as when one is a child, one is called a "child," and as when one is old, one is called an "old man."

Regarding names given according to desire: for example, when a child is born, parents give it a name, as do śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas. Regarding names given according to occupation: for example, one who is capable of painting is called a painter, and one who is capable of working with copper and iron is called a smith of copper and iron.
Regarding "characteristics as names": for example, one who holds a staff and an umbrella is called "one who holds a staff and an umbrella.
Furthermore, some say there are four kinds of names, namely: first, *saṃjñā* (perception);
second, *khyāti* (manifestation).
Third, *taddhita*; fourth, *samāsa*.
Regarding "perception as name," it is like a person of high status taking the name of a slave, or a person of lowly station taking the name of a noble.
Regarding names derived from their functions: because they are able to crawl on their bellies, they are called "belly-crawling insects" (*udvijā*).

Regarding names derived from their objects of worship or their origins: for example, one who serves the god Viṣṇu is called a "worshiper of Viṣṇu," and one born from the god Vāsudeva is called a "son of Vāsudeva."
Regarding that which is called a "name" (*nāman*): it is like a cow of variegated color being called a "variegated cow," or like a person who belongs to a king being called a "king's man.
Furthermore, some say that names are of two kinds: namely, those that are innate (*jāti*) and those that are produced (*kṛtaka*).
Names based on birth are, for example, those of the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras.
Names based on action are, for example, the names given by one's parents at the time of birth, or the names given by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "birth as a name" refers to how, at the time of birth, parents bestow a name, and śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas also bestow a name.
As for "acting as a name," it refers to when friends and acquaintances later bestow another name upon him; this is called the second name.
Furthermore, there are those who say that names are of two kinds: namely, those with characteristics (*sanimitta*) and those without characteristics (*animitta*).
Names with characteristics refer to such designations as impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, the aggregates (*skandha*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding names that are signless (*animitta*): such as the names "sentient being," "person" (*pudgala*), "Nara," "Nārāyaṇa," and so forth.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world and establishes names with signs (*sanimitta*), or whether a Buddha does not appear in the world and there are only signless names, [they remain as such].
Furthermore, there are those who say that names are of two kinds: namely, common and uncommon.
An uncommon name is, for example, the names of the Three Jewels and so forth.
A common name refers to all other names.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all names are exclusively common, and there are no names that are not common. Why is this?
Because a single referent can be established by all names, and all referents can be established by a single name.
Furthermore, there are those who say that names are of two kinds: namely, fixed and unfixed.
A fixed name is, for example, Sumeru Mountain, the four continents, and the great ocean; these are fixed names from the time this world was first formed.
Regarding "those not fixed as names," these refer to other such names.
Furthermore, some say there are no fixed names. Why is this so?
In other peripheral regions, Mount Sumeru and the others are given different names.
The critique states:
Such an explanation is excellent; when the world was first formed, it was named Mount Sumeru, and the Great Ocean of the four continents was likewise named accordingly.
Question: When the kalpa comes to an end and all things are dispersed and destroyed, who then creates these names?
Answer: [As explained previously.]
Some say that this name was transmitted by the rishi upon entering a state of meditative concentration;
others say that sentient beings possess the power of causes that enable them to utter this name.
Question: Are these names merely handed down from antiquity, or were they newly composed by someone else? Answer:
When the world was first formed, names such as "Mount Sumeru" and others were already established by common tradition, while other names were not fixed.
Furthermore, some say that there are two kinds of names: namely, those denoting substance (*dravya*) and those denoting activity (*kriyā*).
Names based on things (dravya) are, for example, names such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta.
Names based on actions (kriyā) are, for example, names such as "the agent," "the cutter," "the cooker," or "the reader."
Question: Is there anyone who knows the limit of names? Answer: Yes.
There is; only a Buddha is able to do so, while others have no such knowledge. Why is this?
Because a Buddha is called "Omniscient" (sarvajña) precisely because he can know the limits of all names.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, there is the appearance in the world of the name-body (nāmakāya) and so forth. Question:

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the "name-body" (nāmakāya) and so forth always manifest in the world; why, then, do you say that it is only when a Tathāgata appears in the world that the name-body and so forth appear in the world?

Answer: When it is said that "the group of names and so forth transcends the world," this refers to the names for the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas). These names accord with non-self, accord with liberation, and accord with emptiness; they sever the view of a person and give rise to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅgas); they turn one away from afflictions and toward the essential way out; they cease delusion and produce wisdom; they sever hesitation and produce certainty; they bring weariness toward birth and death and a delight in tranquility; they sever the intent of outsiders and praise the intent of those within the Way. It is for the sake of teaching such groups of names that it is said they appear in the world.

Question: Just as fire is called "fire," is this name a designation for something possessing characteristics (*sanimitta*), or is it a designation for something without characteristics (*animitta*)? Answer:
This is the name for "having characteristics.
As was previously stated, all names that manifest meanings have characteristics; this name itself possesses characteristics. Question:
If that is so, what are the characteristics of fire?
The answer is:
Generally, there are two kinds of meanings:
There are the presence of characteristics and the absence of characteristics. For example, if there is no characteristic of fire outside of fire itself, one says it is "without characteristics.
If a mirage possesses the characteristic of fire, one says it "has the characteristic of fire."
The Buddha’s sūtras have three names for the teaching of the Dharma, namely: past, future, and present.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these three names for the teaching of the Dharma?

Answer: As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, the three types are called "teaching the Dharma" (*dharmadeśanā*); their essential nature (*svabhāva*) comprises the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), the twelve bases (*āyatanas*), and the five aggregates (*skandhas*).

Question: As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*, there are three ways of explaining the Dharma, wherein their essential nature subsumes the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the five aggregates (*skandha*).

That which is spoken is speech, and that which is manifested is name; these should each constitute one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and a portion of one aggregate (skandha). Why, then, do you say they are subsumed within the eighteen elements, the twelve bases, and the five aggregates?
Answer: Some say that it is called "Dharma" because it takes up three kinds [of things], namely the Dharma, its teaching, and its retinue.
What is the meaning of this?
Answer: Speech is able to produce names, and names are able to manifest meanings; therefore, it is said that [speech] and its attendants [constitute the teaching].
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the Dharma is taught for the sake of the three meanings, the three types of names are called "the teaching of the Dharma."

Why is this so? Because both the speaker and the listener do so for the sake of the meaning; it is for this reason that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and bases (āyatanas) are all fully subsumed. Question:
For what reason are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) spoken of as being of three kinds, while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are not?
The Venerable Sūmī replied:
"This sutra is intended to explain conditioned phenomena; it is not possible for conditioned phenomena to constitute a fourth or fifth category of teaching."
Furthermore, there are those who say that this sutra teaches that all dharmas are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and fall within the present world.
Why is this? Because it is by means of present dharmas that one can realize the unconditioned dharma.
For this reason, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are also included within the threefold designation of "teaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) exist, then teaching these three is called "teaching the Dharma."
The three natures are what are called speech, names, and objects.
Although unconditioned phenomena possess objects in relation to speech, they lack both speech and names; therefore, it is said that they do not exist within the teaching of the three names.
Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One say that "the world" is another name for "teaching the Dharma"? Answer:
Some say it is for the purpose of stopping the views of non-Buddhists, as non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the world.

Others say it is for the purpose of refuting the views of those in future ages who claim that the past and future do not exist; therefore, it is said that the "world" consists of these three types, which is called the teaching on time.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) assert as follows:
"If there were no self (ātman), this person’s preaching of the Dharma would ultimately be for nothing.
It is to refute such a view that this statement was made:
Although there is no self, it is spoken of for the sake of the world. Question:
If one speaks of the past, one understands the matters of the future and the present.
If one preaches the Dharma for the sake of the future, one understands the matters of the past and the present;
if one preaches the Dharma for the sake of the present, one understands the matters of the future and the past.
Among these three types of preaching the Dharma, which is the name for this particular preaching of the Dharma?
The answer is:
Some say that such an explanation is a divergent teaching among the three types of teachings on names.
Furthermore, some say that if one explains the past for the sake of understanding future and present matters, then "the past" refers specifically to the past life.
Understanding matters of the future and the present is subsumed within the future and present time periods.
This applies even when speaking for the sake of the present; it is the same for the past and the future.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one makes such a statement, it is a statement regarding the meaning of the three periods of time.
If it concerns the past, it is a statement regarding the meaning of the past.
To understand the future and the present is to state the meaning of the future and the present.
The same applies to the future and the present.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"There are three kinds of what is called 'teaching the Dharma,' with no fourth or fifth."

Question: If it is said that there are three kinds—namely, the teaching of the Dharma, the speaker, and the listener—this is already sufficient regarding the meaning; why then do you further state that there is no fourth or fifth?
The answer is:
"There is no fourth" negates the existence of a fourth time;
"there is no fifth" definitively establishes that there is no fifth time.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "there is no fourth" excludes a fourth time-period, and "there is no fifth" excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Others say that one should speak of four kinds as being the teaching of the Dharma, namely, the Four Noble Truths (*catvāry āryasatyāni*).
"There is no fifth" means there is no fifth truth.
"There is no sixth" excludes space (*ākāśa*) and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Furthermore, some say that there should be five categories for the teaching of the Dharma, namely the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
"Without a sixth" means there is no sixth aggregate (*skandha*).
"Without a seventh" excludes unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Since these are spoken of as names for the three time periods, there is no fourth or fifth.
There should be one kind of discourse on the Dharma, namely, the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), of which there is neither a second nor a third.
Regarding "no second," it means there is no second practice of contemplation.
The phrase "no third" excludes those phenomena not subsumed under the objects of contemplation.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there should be two types of names for the teaching of the Dharma, namely: concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
There is no third [category], meaning there is no second concentration (*samādhi*) nor second wisdom (*prajñā*).
There is no fourth, which excludes those factors not subsumed under concentration and wisdom.
Since these are explained as the "teaching of the Dharma" throughout the three periods of time, there is neither a fourth nor a fifth.
"There is no fourth" excludes a fourth time period.
"There is no fifth" excludes phenomena not subsumed within the three time periods.

By means of such numerical categories, one should explain the three gates of liberation, as well as the four truths, the five aggregates, the six factors conducive to clear knowledge (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā-bhāgīya-saṃjñā*), the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*), the eightfold path (*aṣṭāṅgamārga*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), and the ten qualities of those beyond training (*daśāśaikṣadharma*)."
The ten powers of the Tathāgata should have ten corresponding designations for teaching the Dharma; there is no eleventh or twelfth.
Regarding the absence of an eleventh, it means there is no eleventh power.
The absence of a twelfth [category] excludes those phenomena not subsumed within the ten powers (*daśabala*).
As that same sutra states:
"One should examine a person by four criteria: Is this elder one with whom it is appropriate to speak, or is he one with whom it is inappropriate to speak?"
What are the four? First, not abiding in what is possible or impossible;
second, not abiding in the treatises on knowledge.
3. Not abiding in conceptual discrimination;
4. Not abiding in the traces of the path. Question:
What is the distinction between these four matters?
The answer is:
some say that those who do not abide in the principle of what is possible and what is impossible (sthānāsthāna) do not know what is possible and what is impossible as it truly is.
Those who do not abide in the treatise on wisdom do not know, as it truly is, wisdom and non-wisdom.
Those who do not abide in conceptual discrimination do not know, as it truly is, the conventional truth and the ultimate truth.
One who does not abide in the path to cessation does not know, as it truly is, the path to the origination of this body, nor does he know, as it truly is, the path to the cessation of this body.

Furthermore, some say that one who does not abide in what is possible and what is impossible is as follows: that the eye and visible forms can produce visual consciousness, and so on up to the mind and mental phenomena producing mental consciousness—this is called "the possible."
To not know things as they truly are is called non-abiding.
One who does not abide in the treatises on wisdom does not truly know the ten types of knowledge.
One who does not abide in discrimination does not truly know the sūtras of definitive meaning and those of provisional meaning.
One who does not abide in the tracks of the path does not know the four tracks of the path as they truly are.
Furthermore, it is said that one who does not abide in what is possible and what is impossible is unable to definitively determine for themselves what is possible and what is impossible.
Those who advocate the theory of non-abiding wisdom cannot endure the analytical inquiry and response concerning what precedes and follows.
Those who do not abide in analysis do not know, as it truly is, the distinction between the deceptive and the real.
One who does not abide in the traces of the Path is displeased when others question them according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who does not abide in what is possible and what is impossible does not distinguish between existence and non-existence.
One who does not abide in the treatise on wisdom does not understand the discourse of the wise.
One who does not abide in non-discrimination does not know that the statement "there is no such place" is a provisional designation.
One who does not abide in the tracks of the Path lacks the awakening-intent that accords with reality.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one who does not abide in the principles of what is possible and what is impossible cannot distinguish between their own meaning and the meaning of others in discourse.
One who does not abide in the treatises on knowledge clings to what was previously heard and refuses to relinquish it, yet is unable to investigate the meaning of what is subsequently heard.
Those who do not abide in discernment hear the correct meaning explained by another and give rise to doubt in their minds, like a person who sees ghee and thinks it is cooked rice.
Those who do not abide in the traces of the Path fail to recognize the sequence of what others explain, taking the preceding as the middle and the middle as the subsequent.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who does not abide in the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible cannot discern whether a matter before them is resolvable or irresolvable;
and one who does not abide in wisdom and treatises cannot employ inference and conceptualization to deliberate upon what is being discussed.
"One who does not abide in conceptualization" does not understand the sequence of what was previously and subsequently taught.
"One who does not abide in the tracks of the path" does not comprehend the intent behind another's question.
The Venerable Vāmalakṣa said:
One who does not abide in what is possible and what is impossible cannot definitively state what is taught.
One who does not abide in wisdom and treatises does not know the deceptive and the real.
One who does not abide in discernment is incapable of withstanding the sequential analysis of questions and answers.
"One who does not abide in the path" is one whose mind is not pleased when others discuss the Dharma according to the teaching.
The Venerable Saṃghabhadra says:
"One who does not abide in what is possible and what is impossible" is one who does not understand the meaning of what is possible and what is impossible as taught in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*.
Those who do not abide in the treatise on wisdom do not understand the essential components of the forty-four knowledges and the seventy-seven knowledges.
Those who do not abide in discernment do not understand the means of escape from the afflictions.
One who does not abide in the path of practice does not know, as it truly is, the dharma that is the path to the cessation of form.

Furthermore, one should examine such a person by four criteria: whether this elder should be answered with a definitive response to a question requiring a definitive answer, and whether he is one with whom one may converse, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is a categorical response?
For example, if one asks, "Is the Buddha truly and perfectly awakened?
one should respond categorically: [Yes].
Is this Buddha-dharma good? One should answer with certainty: "Yes."
Is this śrāvaka one who is well-accordant with the assembly?
One should answer decisively: [Yes].
Is it thus:
that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all conditioned phenomena are without self, and nirvana is peace?
One should answer with certainty: yes.
It is so. This is called a categorical response.
A question is asked:
Why is it that for such a question one provides a definitive answer?
The answer is:

because this question is beneficial in meaning, capable of increasing wholesome qualities, furthering the holy life (*brahmacarya*), leading to the penetration of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and enabling the attainment of *nirvāṇa*; therefore, for such a question, one provides a definitive answer.
What is an analytical response? It is answered as follows:
If one were to ask this question:
"Please teach me the Dharma.
He should answer thus: "The dharmas are manifold:

past, future, and present; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, bound to the formless realm, and unbound; those of the learner, those of the non-learner, and those of neither the learner nor the non-learner; and those to be abandoned by the path of seeing, those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, and those not to be abandoned."
Regarding such teachings as these, what dharma is being explained?
One should provide a detailed analytical answer according to the question asked; this is called the "analytical answer" (vibhajya-vyākaraṇa).
What is the "answer by counter-question" (paripṛcchā-vyākaraṇa)?
Answer: As it is said:
"Preach the Dharma for my sake."
One should answer thus:
"Dharmas are also manifold, ranging from those of the past up to those that are non-terminating.
Among these dharmas, which dharma is being spoken of?"
This is called the method of answering by counter-question. Question:
What is the difference between answering by analysis and answering by counter-question?
Answer: If spoken in terms of the response, there is no distinction;
if considered in terms of the question asked, there ought to be a distinction.
Why is this? There are two kinds of questioning:
there is questioning because one wishes to know the meaning, and there is questioning for the purpose of causing vexation.
If one asks for the sake of understanding the meaning and requests that you preach the Dharma for them, one should answer thus:
"The dharmas are manifold; there are dharmas of the past, and so on, up to those that are non-cessation."
Within this Dharma, what Dharma is being taught?
If one says, "Teach me the past dharmas," one should answer as follows:
Past phenomena are also numerous, being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
If one were to say:
"Explain wholesome phenomena to me."
One should answer thus:
"Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are also numerous, ranging from form (*rūpa*) up to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If one were to say this:
If one asks me to explain the category of form-phenomena (*rūpadharma*), one should answer as follows:
"Form is also manifold; it includes [the abstinences] from killing, up to and including non-frivolous speech."
If someone says, "Please teach me the dharma of non-killing," one should answer as follows:
There are three kinds of non-killing, arising from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. For what purpose is this taught?
If one says, "Teach me that which arises from non-greed," [the Buddha] would explain it accordingly.
One should answer thus:
From non-greed there arise two kinds [of karma]:
informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti).
If one asks for the sake of understanding the meaning, one should explain it by analyzing it in its proper sequence.
If one asks for the sake of causing irritation, one should reply:
"The dharmas are also numerous; which dharma do you wish to have explained?"
One should not say:
"There is the past, the future, and so forth, up to the non-interruption.
If one were to speak thus:
If one asks, "Explain the phenomena of the past for me," one should answer:
"The phenomena of the past are also numerous."
One should not say that it is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
If one were to say: "Speak the wholesome dharmas for my sake."
One should answer thus:
"Wholesome dharmas are also numerous.
One should not say "form" up to "consciousness."
If someone were to say,
"Explain form to me," one should answer as follows:
Formative phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are also manifold;
one should not say that they range from non-killing up to non-frivolous speech.
If one were to say this:
"Explain non-killing to me.
One should answer thus:
"Non-killing is also manifold."
One should not say that it arises from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
If one were to say this:
"For me, explain how it arises from non-greed."
One should answer thus:
"They arise from non-attachment and are manifold.
One should not say they are "manifest" (kriyā) or "unmanifest" (avijñapti).
Thus, regarding those who ask out of a desire to provoke or annoy, one should respond in this manner until the questioning is exhausted, or at times answer spontaneously.

Likewise, there are those who ask because they seek the meaning of the wholesome; those who ask to test the depth of another’s awakening; those who ask because they seek the meaning; those who ask out of a desire to disparage others; those who ask out of straightforwardness; those who ask with deceit and crookedness; those who ask because their temperament is weak; and those who ask out of self-reliance on their own intelligence.
If the questioner is weak or timid, one should answer by means of analysis.
If the questioner asks out of pride in their own wisdom, one should answer by means of counter-questions until the inquiry is exhausted, or at times answer directly oneself.
What is the method of setting aside a question?
The answer is:
For example, various non-Buddhists approached the World-Honored One and asked him this:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Is the world eternal or impermanent?
The Buddha said:
This is not something that should be answered.
[The interlocutor] asks:
For what reason did the Buddha not answer when asked whether the world is eternal or non-eternal?
The answer is:
The various non-Buddhists, holding that the person (pudgala) is eternal, went to where the Buddha was and asked this question: "Is the person eternal, or is it impermanent?"
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Ultimately, there is no person.
If he were to answer that there is no person, they would say this:
I do not inquire whether [the self] exists or does not exist.
If one were to answer that there is annihilation or permanence, ultimately there would be no person.
How could there then be annihilation or permanence?
It is like a person asking another,
"O son of good family!
Does the son of a barren woman show reverence and filial piety?"
He thinks to himself:
"A barren woman has no child.
If I were to answer, "A barren woman has no child," he would say this:
I do not inquire whether it exists or not.
If one were to answer that there is reverence and filial piety, then since a barren woman has no child, what reverence or filial piety could there be?
It is the same with that [case].
This inquiry is not based on reality; because it is neither existent nor real, the Buddha did not answer.

One should know that the same applies to whether the world is eternal or non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, neither eternal nor non-eternal; and whether the world is finite, infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite. It should be understood in this same way.
Again, he asked this question:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
Is the soul identical to the body?"
The Buddha said:
"This should not be answered. He asked:
For what reason did the Buddha not answer this question?
The answer is:
various non-Buddhists, holding that the body is the self, went to where the Buddha was and asked such questions as these.
"O Śramaṇa Gautama!
This body is the self," and so forth, as extensively explained.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"There is a body, but no soul.
If I were to answer, "There is a body, but no soul," they would say:
"I am not asking whether it exists or does not exist."
If one were to answer that the self is different from the body, yet ultimately there is no self, how could this body be said to be different?
It is like a person asking another, "O son of good family!"
Are the horns of a rabbit and the horns of an ox equal and similar?
That person thinks thus:
"The rabbit has no horns; the ox has horns."
If I were to answer that the rabbit has no horns while the ox has horns, they would say:
"I am not asking whether they exist or not.
If you say they are equal and similar, yet the rabbit has no horns, how can you say they are equal and similar?
It is the same with this: this inquiry concerns whether something exists or does not exist, whether it is false or true.
Because this inquiry concerns existence or non-existence, falsity or reality, the Buddha did not answer.
"The body is distinct and the spirit is distinct" is likewise so. Again, he asked:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Is the Tathāgata, after death, annihilated or eternal?
and so forth, elaborating in the fourfold manner.
The Buddha said:
This is not something that should be answered.
[The interlocutor] asks:
For what reason does the Buddha not answer?
The answer is:
Because the various non-Buddhists held that the self (ātman) was originally non-existent but now exists, they went to where the Buddha was and asked him this:
"O Śramaṇa Gautama!"
If this self (*ātman*) was originally non-existent and now exists, and having existed, [disappears], is it eternal or is it subject to annihilation?
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Ultimately there is no self; how could it be that what was originally non-existent now exists, or that what has existed [ceases]? This question concerns that which neither exists nor is real."
Because this question and discourse concern that which neither exists nor is real, the Buddha did not answer.
Again, he asked: "Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Is it that one creates [karma] oneself and experiences [the result] oneself?
The Buddha said:
"This is not something to be answered."
Question: For what reason did the Buddha not answer? Answer:
The various non-Buddhists hold that "I" act and "I" experience; yet the World-Honored One constantly teaches non-self.
They further asked:
"O Śramaṇa Gautama!"
"Does one person perform an action and another person experience its result?
The Buddha said:
"This is not a question that should be answered."
Question: For what reason did the Buddha not answer? Answer:
The various non-Buddhists speak thus:
"The Lord God (Īśvara) creates, and the self experiences.
The World-Honored One, however, always teaches that one's own actions bring about their own retribution.
Again he asked this question:
"Śramaṇa Gautama! Is there neither action nor experiencing?"
The Buddha said:
"This should not be answered. He asked:
For what reason did the Buddha not answer?
The answer is:
the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain this teaching:
"Suffering and pleasure do not arise from causes.
The Buddha has always taught that there are causes and conditions.
[The interlocutor] asks:
If the three previous answers corresponded to answering according to the Dharma, why is this called "answering in debate" (*vāda*), even down to a single phrase that is not a formal debate?
The answer is:
although there is nothing further explained, this is the fundamental form of answering in debate.
Why is this? Because their answers correspond to the underlying principle;
they are thoroughly proficient in the principle even without uttering a single word.
If there are those who achieve victory over an opponent through silence alone, how much more so for one who speaks?
I have heard that there was once a great master of treatises named Śātrīra who traveled to the kingdom of Kaśmīra.

At that time, in the Buddha’s Footprint Forest, there was an arhat named Vāśula, who was endowed with the three types of supernormal knowledge (traividya), free from the desires of the three realms, and had thoroughly mastered the Tripitaka; regarding both internal and external scriptures and treatises, there was nothing he did not fully comprehend.
At that time, Śatireka heard that there was a great master of debate in that forest and immediately went to his location.
Having arrived, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Vasula, offered various words of consolation, and sat down to one side.
Then Śāṭhira said to the Venerable Vāsula:
"Who shall establish the gateway of the thesis first? Vāsula replied:
"I am a long-time resident and should establish the framework for the discourse first;
however, since you have come from afar, let you establish the framework first as you please.
Then, Śāṭhira spoke these words:
"All doctrines maintain that there is retribution for actions. When Vāśula heard these words, he sat in silence.
Then, the disciples of Śātīra proclaimed these words:
"The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has now fallen into defeat.
Rising from his seat, he was about to depart when the Venerable Vaśula spoke these words:
"Śāriputra, if your teacher were indeed Śreṇika, he would know this matter himself.
As they proceeded further from that grove, his teacher thought to himself:
"Why does the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas speak these words?"
"If your teacher were indeed Śāṭhira, he would know this matter for himself.
He then immediately recalled:
"I spoke these words:"
"All treatises have retribution;
yet that śramaṇa son of the Śākyas remains silent and says nothing, thereby arguing for me that there is no retribution.
Thus, the śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has already defeated me."
Just as he had thought, he addressed his disciples:
"I shall now go back to offer my thanks.
The disciples said:
"Since you have already achieved victory among the great assembly, why must you go further?
At that time, the teacher spoke again:
"I would rather suffer defeat at the hands of the wise than achieve victory over the foolish."
He immediately returned to Vāsula and spoke these words:
"You are the victor; I have fallen into defeat.
You are now the teacher, and I am the disciple."
If one can achieve victory even by remaining silent in this manner, how much more so by speaking!
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebuked his disciples, saying:
"You foolish people," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has no comparable attachment, no comparable aversion, no comparable pride, and no comparable ignorance.
In the World-Honored One, attachment and aversion have been severed; he is free from both hatred and love, having cut off the very root of all contention and dispute.
Just as the various disciples have the habit-energies of afflictions, so too did Pindola Bharadvaja have the habit-energy of anger; that elder once reviled the goddess of the Ganges, saying:
"Wait a moment, you wretched slave!"
The Elder Ānanda had the habit of attachment because of his affection for the Śākyaputrīyas;
the Venerable Śāriputra had the habit of pride because he neglected providing medicines according to their illnesses.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is forever free from such habitual tendencies. Why is this?
Because he has already abandoned all unskillful habitual tendencies of affliction.
However, the Buddha employs skillful means through speech that resembles affectionate speech, such as saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣu; it is excellent that you have gone forth.
He also employs speech that resembles anger, such as saying: "You are the son of a slave-girl of the Śākya clan; the Śākyas are your masters."
Words resembling pride are, for example, saying: "I have accomplished the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses.
Words resembling ignorance are, for example, saying:
"Great King, from where have you come?"
As it was said to Ānanda:
"Why are there loud and great sounds outside the grove? He asked:
Since the Tathāgata has uprooted the very root of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), why are there such similar expressions?
The answer is:
it is for the sake of protecting the field of those to be converted.
What is this matter?
Herein, the causes and conditions for the schism of the Saṃgha should be explained in detail. Why is this so?
This is because it constitutes the fundamental causal context of this sutra.
When the bhikṣus were corrupted by Devadatta, the Venerable Śāriputra transformed them so that they returned; those bhikṣus felt great shame and were simultaneously filled with doubt, wondering:
"We have been close to Devadatta; will the precepts we have received not be lost?"
With a sense of shame and remorse, he went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed him with words of affection and gentleness, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣu; it is well that you have been able to leave the household life."
When these words were spoken, all those bhikṣus were able to eliminate their shame, remorse, and doubts.
The reason he addressed the Āmbaṣṭha as "son of a slave girl" was that he wished to shatter his heart of arrogance.
Because he has destroyed the mind of pride, his second body was subsequently reborn in the heavens where he beheld the Noble Truths.
As for why it is said that "I have accomplished the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses," it is because those who do not know the Buddha's merits are made to know them.
The reason for asking, "Great King, from where have you come? was to initiate a discourse on the sequential stages of the Dharma.
The reason for asking why there were loud and great sounds outside the grove was to cause Ānanda to develop a mind of serene seclusion and close devotion.
It is for such various causes and conditions that this treatise is composed.
Why did the World-Honored One reprimand his disciples, calling them "fools"?
There are two meanings to this:
First, there is the reproach;
second, the statement that he is a foolish person.
Now, wishing to explain the meaning of "foolish person," I have made this statement.
What is meant by a "deluded person"?
The answer is:
one who gives rise to ignorance regarding the Buddha-dharma.
The Buddha-dharma is what is called the Path (mārga). Question:
How does delusion arise regarding the Path?
The answer is:
It cannot cause the Path to become deluded; it only increases delusion within oneself.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it can indeed cause the Path to become deluded.
Why is this? Because the Path is characterized by detachment, and because one cannot attain mastery over the Path.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "The Buddha taught the Dharma for severing ignorance; yet this person does not sever ignorance regarding this Dharma, but instead increases their ignorance, and thus [the Buddha] made this statement."
Regarding those who give rise to delusion within the Buddha-dharma and harbor non-arising conceptualizations, they cause the Buddha’s skillful means and functional efficacy to bear no fruit.
What is the reason for this?
Just as a woman who does not give birth is said to be "without the portion of childbirth," so too,
one who hears what the Buddha has taught but does not conceive the embryo of the Noble Path is said to be "without the portion of childbirth" within the Buddha's Dharma.
"Without fruit" means there is neither the fruit of reliance nor the fruit of liberation.
"Without attainment" means that within the Buddha-dharma, nothing is attained.

"Without flavor" means that one does not obtain the flavor of renunciation, the flavor of seclusion and tranquility, the flavor of the path, or the flavor of cessation; therefore, it is said to be without flavor.
"Without benefit" means that there is no benefit of virtuous fruit.
It is like a skilled physician who diligently seeks out various medicinal herbs from all four directions to give to a patient, for the purpose of eliminating their illness.
Yet that patient, on the contrary, throws the medicinal herbs into a heap of refuse, thereby giving rise to two faults:
first, his own illness will not be cured;
second, the physician’s efforts will be wasted in vain.

In this way, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, perform hundreds of thousands of millions of various ascetic practices, diligently seeking the medicine of the untainted noble path, and explain it for those who are to be transformed.
Yet those who hear the Dharma but are unable to practice give rise to two faults:
first, they cannot cure the diseases of their own afflictions;
second, they squander the merit and rewards of the practices undertaken by all Buddhas.
Furthermore, one who gives rise to delusion is said to "give rise to delusion" because they render themselves unfit vessels for the Dharma.
Others say that it is called giving rise to delusion because one severs the resolve to attain Buddhahood.
The Buddha’s aspiration is the desire to bring sentient beings to liberation from all suffering.
Because they are unable to cultivate the means for escaping suffering, it is said that they sever the Buddha’s aspiration.
Furthermore, there are those who say that they sever the Buddha-dharma so that it does not continue.

If such a person practices right conduct themselves, they also cause others to practice right conduct; in this way, through successive transmission, they cause many sentient beings to practice right conduct.
If one cannot practice right conduct oneself and also causes others not to practice right conduct, in this way, one successively causes many sentient beings not to practice right conduct.
Such a person cannot benefit even their own body, let alone many others.
Furthermore, there are those who preach that which was originally intended for the purpose of renunciation, yet fail to attain it; this is called the arising of delusion.
Furthermore, within the Buddha’s teachings, those who do not practice according to the sequence of the meaning are called "fools.

In this context, one who takes the Buddha’s words as the practice of the Buddha-dharma should practice according to the sequence of the meaning; yet, because they are unable to do so, they are called fools.
Furthermore, there are those who say that practicing in accordance with what ought to be practiced is called "practice according to the meaning" (*yathārtha-anupūrvakriyā*).
To practice within the Buddha-dharma not in accordance with what ought to be practiced is called "practice not according to the meaning" (*na-yathārtha-anupūrvakriyā*).
"Non-conformity" means not conforming to the Dharma within the Buddha's teachings.
"Lack of sequential practice" means not engaging in continuous practice within the Buddha's teachings.
One who commits various transgressions and evils violates the Buddha-dharma.
One who does not practice according to the Dharma fails to practice the sequential Dharma, which refers to the Noble Path.
Furthermore, some say that one who speaks contrary to the meaning and fails to practice sequentially is unable to practice at all times.
For example, the bhikṣu Vāhaḍa only undertook the practice of not eating at improper times after three months had passed.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one who does not act in accordance with the sequence of the meaning has produced delusion regarding the Buddha-dharma, as this answers the previous statement.
How does delusion arise?
The answer is:
it arises when one practices the precepts of the Buddha's teaching not according to their meaning and sequence, and so on, up to practicing the Dharma not according to the Dharma and its sequence.
For what reason did the Buddha reprimand his disciples?
This answers the meaning previously stated.
The answer is:
The constant instructions of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are like those of a current preceptor or ācārya who, out of a mind of compassion, addresses his disciples as "fools.
The Buddha is likewise; out of compassion and for the sake of their benefit, he speaks of them as "fools."
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly teach and transform beings through four matters:
first, by means of praise;
second, by means of reprimand.
Third, by relying on others;
fourth, by relinquishment.
Regarding "praising," it is like praising Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and others:
Excellent, excellent!
It is well that this bhikṣu can chant the Dharma with such pure and wondrous voice.
As for those who are to be rebuked, it is as in the case of the rebuke of Udāyin and others.
Regarding "due to others": for example, when turning the Wheel of Dharma, he preached the Dharma to the five bhikṣus, causing eighty thousand devas to attain the Way.
Likewise, when King Bimbisāra welcomed the Buddha, he caused eighty thousand humans and devas to attain the Way.
As when Śakra questioned the Buddha, eighty thousand devas likewise attained the Way.
Regarding "relinquishing": this refers to those such as the Brahmin Vatsagotra and others who must be taught through censure; if they are not censured, they will not receive transformation.
For this reason, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, rebukes his disciples.

Just as an ācārya rebukes a disciple living nearby, or an upādhyāya rebukes a co-resident disciple, using words of harsh reproof; yet those upādhyāyas and ācāryas do not do so out of malice, but rebuke them solely because they do not accord with the Dharma.
It is like parents who, seeing their child engage in unwholesome deeds, rebuke them with harsh and cutting words out of a desire to protect them;
yet those parents harbor no ill will.

If the sons should engage in unrighteous acts, their parents would give rise to a mind of suffering and distress, wishing to restrain the sons from such unrighteous acts and rebuking them with harsh and urgent words.

The Buddha is likewise; it is not out of malice that he fails to rebuke those who should be transformed through reprimand—if he were not to rebuke them, those individuals would ultimately never achieve discipline. Therefore, the World-Honored One rebukes them.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the Buddha’s great compassion is profound, he constantly maintains this thought at all times:
"By what skillful means can I bring benefit to sentient beings?"
If the Tathāgata had not rebuked Devadatta, the many other bhikṣus who followed him would have repeatedly harassed the World-Honored One.
If he had addressed the woman Anupamā as "a vessel for such abundant excrement and urine," her lustful mind would have had no way to be stilled.
If he had not reviled Ambaṣṭha by calling him the "son of a slave girl," that man would have had no way to break his arrogance.
If one did not revile their teacher, Vakkali, there would likewise be no means by which they could destroy their pride.
For the sake of increasing merit in such instances, he also rebukes other people.
Furthermore, there are two reasons for rebuking others:
first, for those whose roots of goodness are not yet mature, rebuke causes their roots of goodness to reach maturity;
second, for those whose roots of goodness are already mature but who do not apply skillful means, rebuke causes them to give rise to such means and thereby attain the fruit of the Path.
Question: For what reason is one called a "deluded person"?
Is one called a deluded person because they are born from delusion, or is one called a deluded person because they currently manifest delusion?
If [the body] were produced from ignorance, then even an Arhat would be an ignorant person. Why?
Because the body of an Arhat is produced from ignorance.
If one speaks of a "deluded person" based on the manifestation [of delusion], then only an Arhat can be said to be non-deluded. Why is this?
Because an Arhat does not manifest delusion.
If that were so, how would one reconcile this sutra?
For it says:
"Foolish man, go far away; do not stand before me."
The commentary states:
One should argue as follows:
a person who currently manifests delusion is called a "deluded person."
Question: If that were so, then only the Arhat would be a person free from delusion.
How, then, is this sūtra to be reconciled?
...and so forth, as explained at length. He replied:
This sutra should be stated as follows:
"Go quickly, bhikṣu; do not stand before me.
I have heard that when the Buddha was entering parinirvāṇa, the long-lived devas were displeased by such a thing, saying:
'This bhikṣu of celestial merit and supernormal power now stands before us, obstructing our path and preventing us from seeing the body of the World-Honored One.'"
"This is our final sight of the Blessed One’s body. Why is this?
Because before long, the Blessed One shall enter parinirvāṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devas, addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Go far away; do not stand before me.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: first, one should reprimand those who are to be delivered through reprimand.
If one rebukes an Arhat who has attained further progress, the Buddha likewise rebukes them, saying, "This is a foolish person.
A question is asked:
Since people possess attachment, aversion, pride, views, and delusion, why does he say this is a "foolish person" rather than a "person of attachment" or the like?
Answer: Because delusion (*moha*) pervades all places.
If one practices the delusion of a particular stage, one is then a person of delusion belonging to that stage.
The Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Nine (and Volume Ten) Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty:
The sixth section of the Jñāna-varga within the Saṃyukta-skandhaka, concerning the six causes, explained at length.
The treatise states:
These six causes are not taught in the Buddha’s sūtras; rather, the four conditions are taught in the Buddha’s sūtras. Now, one wishes to explain the conditions by means of the causes.
What is the matter?

The associated cause (*samyuktahetu*) up to the retributive cause (*vipākahetu*) constitute the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*). The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) constitutes the immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*), and the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). Question:
Do causes subsume conditions, or do conditions subsume causes?
Answer: They are mutually inclusive according to their essential natures.
Some teachers say that there ought to be distinctions between them.
What is the distinction?

From the associated cause (*samyuktahetu*) up to the retributive cause (*vipākahetu*), these are causal conditions (*hetupratyaya*). The efficient cause (*kāraṇahetu*) is the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*). The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) are conditions but not causes.
Does the cause include the condition, or does the condition include the cause?
The condition includes the cause, but the cause does not include the condition.
What is it that is not included?
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*) are also taught in the Buddha’s sūtras.
For instance, they are mentioned among the "Six Dharmas" in the *Ekottarika Āgama*; however, because a long period of time has passed, they have been lost.

That venerable Kātyāyanīputra, by the power of his vows and wisdom, observed the sections on the six causes (*ṣaḍ-hetu*) taught within the Buddha’s sūtras, and based upon these six causes, he composed this treatise (*abhidharma*).

I have heard that the *Ekottarika Āgama* originally increased from one dharma up to a hundred dharmas; now only the sections increasing from one dharma up to ten dharmas remain, while all the rest has been lost.
Furthermore, there are many who have lost even a single dharma, and likewise many who have lost up to ten dharmas.
