I have heard that there was once a great virtuous Arhat named Śāṇavāsa, who was the preceptor of the Venerable Jīvaka.

When that Venerable One entered parinirvāṇa, on that very day seventy-seven thousand Jātaka causes and conditions and ten thousand Abhidharma treatises were extinguished and no longer appeared; from that time onward, they were never practiced again.
When a single master of the treatises passes away, there are certain sūtras and śāstras that no longer circulate; how much more so when hundreds or thousands of masters have passed away?
Furthermore, some say that although there is no single sūtra that explains all six causes in their entirety, each individual cause among the six is explained separately throughout various sūtras.
Question: If that is so, in which sūtra is the associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu) taught? Answer: [It is taught in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.]
As it has been said, this is called the fundamental faith of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), which is termed "associated with indestructible wisdom" (*akṣayajñāna-samprayukta*).
This sūtra explains the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*).

As for where the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) is explained, it is as when it is said that conditioned by the eye and visible forms, eye-consciousness arises, and it also gives rise to the co-arising sensations (*vedanā*), perceptions (*saṃjñā*), and so forth.
This sutra explains the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

As for where it explains the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), it is as stated: "This person accomplishes wholesome dharmas and also accomplishes unwholesome dharmas; in this person, the unwholesome dharmas cease and wholesome dharmas arise anew."
This sutra explains the "similar cause" (*sabhāga-hetu*).

As for where the "pervasive cause" (*sarvatraga-hetu*) is explained, it is as stated: "If a bhikṣu has any reflection or any discrimination, this is called the arising of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*)."

Regarding where the retributive cause is taught: it is as when it is said that one who practices and extensively propagates killing will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be born in hell to undergo the retribution for unwholesome deeds.
This sutra explains the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*).
As for where the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is explained, it is as stated: "By means of two causes and two conditions, right view arises," and so forth, as explained at length.
This sutra explains the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Sūtras such as these all explain the six causes.
This *kaṇḍa* (section) analyzes the causes but does not analyze the conditions (*pratyaya*).
In the *Dṛṣṭi-vibhaṅga* (Analysis of Views), conditions (*pratyaya*) are distinguished while causes (*hetu*) are not. Question:
For what reason did that Venerable One compose his treatise based on the six causes?
The answer is:
It is because [the Buddha] intends to eliminate the views of causelessness and false causes by means of these six causes.

Furthermore, some say that the reason the Venerable One composed this treatise based on the six causes was to manifest the four kinds of fruits, as clearly as observing an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of one's hand.
If one speaks of the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), this manifests the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
If one speaks of the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), this manifests the fruit of reliance (*adhipati-phala*).
If one speaks of the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), it manifests the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
If one speaks of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), it manifests the fruit of sovereign power (*adhipati-phala*).
For this reason, the treatise is composed based upon these six causes.
What is the associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*)?
The answer is:

feeling (*vedanā*) is a cause among the associated causes for the phenomena associated with feeling; likewise, the phenomena associated with feeling are causes among the associated causes for feeling.
Question: Why do these dharmas serve as causes for one another? Answer:
Because the nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) is weak and inferior, the meaning of the question is:
"One does not employ perception (*saṃjñā*) regarding phenomena; that which is capable of perceiving and that which is perceived are not grasped.
One should answer as follows:
If it were not thus, other dharmas being separated from one another would be unable to perform any function.
Therefore, the mind and mental factors mutually nourish, mutually augment, and mutually depend upon one another to be able to bear a heavy burden.
Just as two bundles of reeds stand leaning against one another, so it is with many.
Just as a single rope cannot pull a large piece of timber, whereas many ropes can,
so too is this case.
Question: Why is the mind not mentioned? Answer:
Some say that it is because the intention of the author of that sūtra was such, and so forth, as explained at length.

Others say that one should have stated the cause among the associated causes of mind and mental factors, and so forth, as explained at length; since this was not stated, one should know that this teaching is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this passage does not fully explain the meaning of all causes.
If it were to explain them exhaustively, it should have stated:
"What is the associated cause?"
Among the associated causes (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) of mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*),
what is the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)?
It consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
What is the similar cause?
It refers to past and present dharmas.
What is the pervasive cause?
Regarding all pervasive latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the past and present, as well as the factors associated with and co-existent with those latent dispositions:
what is the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*)?
It consists of unwholesome factors and wholesome factors that are tainted (*sāsrava*).
What is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
It is all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*).
Thus should all causes be explained.
If it were not mentioned, one should know that the explanation of the meaning of the various causes would be incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say it has already been explained within the previously discussed factors associated with sensation (*vedanā-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
What is the meaning of this?
It is as stated in the explanation of the "associated cause" (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) among the factors associated with feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
If this is so, why not simply designate it by the name "mind"?
The answer is:
the meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of "conjunction" (samprayoga). This mind is the primary subject, as the verse says: "The mind is the sixth sovereign lord."
Furthermore, there are those who say that they are called "associated" and "dissociated" phenomena because of the mind.
As it is said:
"This is called a phenomenon associated with the mind; this is called a phenomenon dissociated from the mind."

In this way, perception, volition, contact, examination, desire, liberation, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are the causes within the category of associated causes for the factors associated with wisdom; this is explained in detail up to that point.
Question: Why are only the ten universal mental factors (mahābhūmika-dharma) mentioned, and not the other categories of factors? Answer:
Some say that it was the intention of the author of the sūtra to state it thus, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that when something should have been stated but was not, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete teaching (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that [the number] is stated based on what can be found within the various elements (*dhātu*), stages (*bhūmi*), minds (*citta*), and seeds (*bīja*); other numerical factors are not mentioned because they are contrary to the aforementioned cases.
Question: What is the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga)? Answer:
The meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of "conjunction" (samprayoga). Question:
If the meaning of equality is the meaning of conjunction, then regarding these mental factors (caitasika-dharma), they may be more or fewer in number within the mind.

There is an abundance of wholesome minds and a scarcity of defiled minds; an abundance of defiled minds and a scarcity of non-obscured neutral minds; an abundance of minds bound to the desire realm and a scarcity of minds bound to the form realm; an abundance of minds bound to the form realm and a scarcity of minds bound to the formless realm; and an abundance of outflowing (sāsrava) minds and a scarcity of outflow-free (anāsrava) minds.
Regarding this, what is the meaning of "equality" that constitutes the meaning of "correspondence"?
The answer is:
because their essence is equal, the meaning of equality is said to be the meaning of correspondence.
If there were two feelings and one perception within a single moment of mind, this would not be called "equality" (samatā), nor would it have the sense of "association" (samprayoga).
In a single moment of mind, there is only one feeling; the same applies to the remaining factors.
For this reason, the meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, some say that the meaning of "inseparability" is the meaning of "conjunction.
Still others say that the meaning of "non-distinctness" is the meaning of "conjunction."
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "equally experiencing" (*samavedanā*) is the meaning of "associated" (*samprayukta*).
Just as when a cart is being loaded, all its parts are loaded and none remain unladen,
so too when the mind-cart experiences an object, all the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) experience that object equally, with none failing to do so.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "simultaneous reception" (*sahabhū*) is the meaning of "association" (*samprayoga*), because they do not occur sequentially.
It is like a flock of pigeons in autumn: they arrive at the threshing floor at the same time, eat at the same time, and depart at the same time.
In this way, the mind and its mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) arise simultaneously with respect to their object, perform their functions simultaneously, and cease simultaneously.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is the meaning of "association" (samprayoga).
Just as water and milk do not obstruct one another and thus combine, so too these factors (dharma) are associated (saṃprayukta) because they do not obstruct one another.
Furthermore, some say that the meaning of "association" is the sense of mutual affection (*samaprema*).
Just as people who follow one another in mutual accord say they love each other, so too these phenomena (dharma) that follow one another in mutual accord are said to be associated (saṃprayukta).
The Venerable Vāśpa has said:
"There are four things by virtue of which there is the meaning of association, namely: time, basis, activity, and object."
As for "time," it is the same single moment; as for "basis," it is the same basis; as for "practice," it is the same practice; as for "object," it is the same object of practice.
For this reason, it has the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃprayoga*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "a bundle of reeds" is the meaning of conjunction;
just as two bundles or many bundles of reeds abide by depending upon one another.
Because the nature of the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-caitta-dharma*) is weak and inferior, each one individually is unable to produce [an effect] or to grasp conditions.
When the mind conjoins with the ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), it can function within the world, grasp results, cognize objects, and perform actions.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "binding timber" is the meaning of "association.
Just as one pound of hemp cannot bind timber, if many strands are combined to form a rope, then it can bind timber.
Thus, the mental universal factors (*mahābhūmika-dharma*) have been explained at length as above.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "conjunction" (*samprayoga*) is the sense of pulling one another across a river.
"Pulling one another" means reaching out and grasping each other's hands in succession.
It is like a swift river in a mountain valley: a single person cannot cross it;
yet if many people join hands with one another, they can then cross.
In this way, the mind and the great earth are as explained above in detail.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "companionship" (*sahāya*) is the meaning of "association" (*samprayoga*).
For example, on a wilderness road infested with many bandits and wild beasts, a single person cannot pass through;
yet if many people gather together, relying upon one another in succession, they are then able to pass.
Thus, the mind and the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) are explained at length as above.
The Venerable Sthavira Sumati said:
"What is the meaning of 'concomitance' (*samprayoga*)?"
The meaning of mutual production is the meaning of association. Question:
If that is so, when visual consciousness gives rise to mental consciousness, are they associated?
Answer: Their bases are different.
If they shared the same basis and were able to produce one another, that would be the meaning of association (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, the meaning of non-distinction is the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*). Question:
If that is so, are the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) also associated, since they too are not distinct?
The answer is:
The four great elements have no basis of dependence; if they were to have a basis of dependence and yet not be distinct from it, that would be the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*).
Furthermore, the meaning of having an object (*sālambana*) is the meaning of association.
Question: If that is so, do the five consciousnesses also have objects of perception, and are these associated [with mental factors]? Answer:
Their bases are each distinct.
If they share the same basis and the same object, this is the meaning of association (*samprayoga*).
Furthermore, the meaning of having a single common object is the meaning of association.
Question: If that is so, then since visual consciousness and mental consciousness share the same object, are they associated?
Furthermore, we currently observe many people simultaneously giving rise to minds that together perceive the first moon; are these associated?
Answer: Their bases are each distinct.
If they share the same basis and take the same object, this is the meaning of association (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, the meaning of "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is the meaning of "association" (*saṃprayoga*). Question:
If that is so, when life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are conjoined in a single location, is this association?
The answer is:
Those two have no basis.
If there were a basis, there would also be the characteristic of conjunction; this is the meaning of "association" (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, the meaning of "arising simultaneously" is the meaning of "association. Question:
If that is so, does the simultaneous arising of the four great elements constitute association?
Answer: The four great elements have no basis.
If they had a basis, they would arise simultaneously; this is the meaning of association (saṃprayoga).
Furthermore, arising together, abiding together, and ceasing together is the meaning of association (*saṃprayoga*). Question:
If that is so, when the mind turns toward matter or the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), which arise, abide, and cease together with it, would these then be associated?
Answer: There is nothing upon which they depend.
If there were something upon which they depended, then arising, abiding, and ceasing together would constitute the meaning of association.
Furthermore, having the same basis (*āśraya*), the same mode of activity (*ākāra*), and the same object (*ālambana*) constitutes the meaning of association (*samprayoga*). Question:
How is it known that having the same basis, the same mode of activity, and the same object constitutes association?

Answer: Furthermore, how is it known that having the same basis (*āśraya*), the same mode of activity (*ākāra*), and the same object (*ālambana*) does not constitute the meaning of association (*samprayoga*)?
Moreover, the meaning of performing a single function together is the meaning of association.
Question: If that is so, since patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) perform the same function, are they associated (*saṃprayukta*)? Answer:
They do not arise simultaneously.
If they were to arise simultaneously and perform a single function together, that would be the meaning of association (*samprayoga*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
The meaning of "companionship" (sahāya) is the meaning of "association" (samprayoga).

Just as consciousness follows its respective object (ālambana-vastu) and serves as the basis for various numerical designations, association is defined as being distinct from simultaneous arising (sahaja).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"Having the same basis, the same activity, and the same object is the meaning of association. Why is this so?"

Conditioned phenomena are weak in nature, arising through the power of mutual dependence; not a single great earth is seen to exist independently in the world. For this reason, they are said to be "associated" (saṃprayukta).
This associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu) is certain to produce its functional fruit (kāritra-phala) throughout the three periods of time.
What is the co-arising cause (sahabhū-hetu)?
[The passage continues] at length.
Question: What is the difference between the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)? Answer:
Some say: "If there is an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), then there is a co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Is it possible for there to be a co-arising cause that is not an associated cause?
He replied:
There are those that are non-associated co-existent causes (*sahabhū-hetu*). Question: This may be so.

Regarding the distinction between what was asked: within a single moment, sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) have two causes, namely the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*). What is the difference between them?
The answer is:
the meaning of non-separation is the meaning of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the meaning of having a single fruit is the meaning of the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Furthermore, some say that having a single basis (*āśraya*), a single mode of activity (*ākāra*), and a single object (*ālambana*) is the meaning of the associated cause, while having a single birth, a single duration, and a single cessation is the meaning of the co-arising cause.

Furthermore, some say that the meaning of "taking hands to cross a river" is the meaning of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), while the meaning of "crossing by one's own diligent effort" is the meaning of the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Others say that the meaning of "sharing wealth" is the meaning of the associated cause, while the meaning of "being able to initiate" is the meaning of the co-arising cause.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "equality" is the meaning of the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), and the meaning of "non-separation" is the meaning of the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).
What is the co-arising cause?
The answer is:
The mind and the mental factors (*caitta*) are mutual causes within the category of co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*); this is explained at length.
Previously the mind was not mentioned, but it is now discussed.

The mind and the mental factors are mutual causes within the category of co-arising causes; conversely, the mental factors and the mind are mutual causes within the category of co-arising causes; and the mind and the revolving bodily and vocal actions are mutual causes within the category of co-arising causes.
Bodily and vocal karma refers to the precepts of dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) precepts. Question:
Why is it not stated that the turning of bodily and vocal karma by the mind and the mind itself are mutual causes among the co-arising causes?
The answer is:
When that which ought to be explained is not explained, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete teaching (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).
Furthermore, there are those who explain by speaking extensively at the beginning and end, while speaking briefly in the middle.
As has been explained at length previously and concisely hereafter regarding the causes of actions, so it is here as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind does not provide its cause to bodily and vocal karma according to their respective functions; rather, bodily and vocal karma follow the functions of the mind but do not provide their cause to it.

It is as when a king provides food and drink to his retinue for their benefit, yet does not act in accordance with their affairs; while the retinue acts in accordance with the king's affairs, they do not provide him with food and drink for his benefit.
Such are the actions of mind, body, and speech, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say that bodily and vocal actions arise from the mind and belong to the mind; because they arise from the mind, they are co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
Physical and vocal karma cannot give rise to the mind, because the mind does not belong to karma nor is it produced from it; therefore, they are not co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*).
The critique states:
One should not speak in this manner.
This explanation is excellent:
the mind and the bodily and vocal actions that revolve with it arise together as causes.
One should know that the bodily and vocal actions revolving with the mind are the "causes among causes" within the context of those things that arise together with the mind as causes.
Why is this so? Because they share the same fruit and the same activity. Question:
If this is so, why was it not explained?
The answer is:
because it has already been explained extensively above.

Among the co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) of the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), what are these formations dissociated from mind? What is asked here is: which ones are they?
Answer: Some say that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) arises together with the mind, and that arising (*jāti*) is the cause among causes for the mind.

Others say that the mind arises together with its intrinsic nature—namely, birth, aging, duration, and cessation—and that within these co-arising causes, arising is the cause for the mind, whereas aging, duration, and cessation are not.
Why is this so? The meaning of "increasing" is the meaning of "cause," while that [the latter] has the meaning of "dispersing and destroying.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind and birth, etc., are mutually co-arising causes within the category of co-arising causes.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "The mind is the cause among co-nascent causes for the arising and so forth of mental factors; the arising and so forth of the mind are the causes among co-nascent causes for the mind.
The critique states:
One should not speak in this way.
It is well said thus:

the mind is a cause among the co-arising causes for the arising and so forth of mental factors; the arising and so forth of mental factors are likewise causes among the co-arising causes for the mind.
Question: If that is so, how can this teaching be reconciled?
For instance, it is said:
Excluding the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and its arising, aging, abiding, and ceasing, all other truths of suffering (duḥkhasatya) are not co-existent causes (sahabhūhetu) for the view of a self.
The answer is:
it should be stated as follows:

Excluding the arising, aging, abiding, and ceasing of phenomena associated with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), all other remaining truths of suffering are not co-existent causes for the view of a self.
That this was not stated [in the sūtra] should be understood as an incomplete teaching (sāvaśeṣa-vacana).
Furthermore, regarding the cause among co-arising causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*):

those who maintain this teaching state that when the powers of the four great elements are non-partial, the earth element, water element, fire element, and wind element constitute the cause among co-arising causes.
Regarding the four great elements, some teachers maintain that among the co-arising causes, the earth element is the "cause within the cause" for the other three great elements;
whereas when the power of the four great elements is unequal, the earth element is the "cause within the cause" for the other three great elements.
The three great elements are causes for the earth element within the category of co-nascent causes. Why is this so?
Because the earth element possesses multiple entities.
The single entity and the multiple entities are co-arising causes; the multiple entities are co-arising causes for the single entity.
This applies likewise even to the wind element (*vāyudhātu*).
The critique states:
This way of explaining is excellent:

whether the four great elements possess unequal power or equal power, the earth element acts as a co-arising cause for the other three great elements, and the three great elements act as co-arising causes for the earth element.
Why is this so? Because the earth element does not arise from the earth element as its cause in producing derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*). Question:
Is it a cause for that which has already arisen, or is it a cause for that which has not yet arisen?
The answer is:
it is a cause for that which has already arisen, and it is also a cause for that which has not yet arisen.
Why is this so? Because both that which has already arisen and that which has not yet arisen are entirely subsumed within the category of causal conditions.
As it is said in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
What are the phenomena produced from causes? They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
As it has been stated, both that which has arisen and that which has not yet arisen are phenomena produced from causes;
this is likewise the case here.
Question: Do derived forms (bhautika-rūpa) have a co-nascent cause (sahabhū-hetu)?
Answer: Yes.
There is. Why is this so? Because all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) invariably possess a co-arising cause (sahabhūhetu).
Question: Do derived forms (bhautika-rūpa) have a co-arising cause (sahabhū-hetu) with other derived forms?
Answer: Yes.
No. Why is this? Because a self-nature does not act as a co-arising cause for itself.
Furthermore, there are those who say that derived matter acts as a co-arising cause for derived matter.
How is this so? It is like the atoms that arise simultaneously with the eye faculty, which act as mutual co-arising causes for one another.
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement. Why is this?
Resistant derived matter cannot serve as a co-arising cause for other resistant derived matter.

All minds are invariably accompanied by co-arising mental factors, namely the mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*) such as birth (*jāti*) and so forth; however, not all minds are invariably accompanied by mental factors that are themselves minds.
Form has ten aspects, and for this reason it is called "revolving.
What are these ten? First, co-arising;
2. Co-residence; 3. Co-cessation;
4. Sharing a single fruit.
5. Sharing a common basis;
6. Sharing a common retribution;
7. The virtuous sharing with the virtuous;
8. Unwholesome [dharmas] associated with the unwholesome;
9. Indeterminate [dharmas] associated with the indeterminate;
10. Those that fall within the same world-period.
"Sharing one fruit" refers to the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*).
"Sharing one basis" refers to the fruit of reliance (*niśraya-phala*).
"Sharing one retribution" refers to the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
In summary, there are ten matters.
As for the mundane path that severs fetters (*laukika-saṃyojana-prahāṇa-mārga*), there are eight matters, excluding the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Excluding the mundane path that severs fetters, all other wholesome contaminated (*kuśala-sāsrava*) turnings have seven matters, excluding the fruit of liberation (*vimukti-phala*), the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The turning of the untainted path that severs the fetters consists of seven factors, excluding the fruit of retribution, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.

Excluding the turning of the untainted path that severs the fetters, all other untainted turnings consist of six factors, excluding the fruit of liberation, the fruit of retribution, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate.
The turning of unwholesome consciousness involves seven matters, excluding the fruit of liberation, the wholesome, and the indeterminate.
The turning of indeterminate consciousness involves six matters, excluding the fruit of liberation, the fruit of retribution, the wholesome, and the unwholesome.
Therefore, generally speaking, there are ten matters.
Regarding the mind’s revolving around the mental factors (caitta), there are five matters:
first, the common basis (āśraya);
2. common practice; 3. common object; 4. common fruit;
Fifth, common retribution (*sādhāraṇa-vipāka*).
The numerical factors that revolve within the mind likewise possess five aspects.
The mind and the mental revolutions, as well as the form and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*), possess two aspects:
First, the fruit; second, the retribution.
The transformation of matter by the mind and the formations dissociated from the mind share two things with the transformation of the mind:
first, the fruit; second, the retribution.
Question: What is the essential nature of this turning back? Answer:
These are the four aggregates and the five aggregates.
Just as the form realm consists of the five aggregates, the desire realm and the formless realm consist of the four aggregates. Why is this so?
In the desire realm and the formless realm, there is no mental turning of the precepts; this is the essential nature of turning.

Having already explained that "this is the self," "this is the thing," "this is the characteristic," "this is the portion," and "this is the nature," the reason for this essential nature shall now be explained.
Question: What is the meaning of "revolving" (parivarta)? Answer:
The meaning of "conforming" (*anuvartana*) is the meaning of "turning toward" (*parāvṛtti*); the meaning of "attaining a single fruit" is the meaning of "turning toward";
the meaning of "performing a single task together" is the meaning of "turning toward. As it is said: "Just as you do, so shall we also do."
This is the meaning of "revolving. Question:
For what reason do the precepts of the desire realm not revolve with the mind?
The answer is:
It is not its field, not its vessel, and not its ground; because it is not the field, not the vessel, and not the ground.

Furthermore, some say that because the desire realm is not a stage of meditative concentration (*samāhita-bhūmi*), not a stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), and not a stage of freedom from desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*), the precepts therein also do not revolve together with the mind.

The realm of form (rūpadhātu) is the stage of meditative concentration (samāhitabhūmi), the stage of cultivation (bhāvanābhūmi), and the stage of detachment from desire (vītarāgabhūmi); therein, morality (śīla) functions in conjunction with the mind.
Furthermore, the meaning is this:
morality of the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is said to belong to the mind of the desire realm.
"Can you provide protection for me, whether against the breaking of precepts or the arising of afflictions associated with the mind of breaking precepts?
The mind of the desire realm replied,
"I cannot."
He said by way of admonition:
"If you are unable [to do so], why should I comply with you?
It is just as when someone, fearing an enemy, says to another person:
"Can you provide me with protection?
I shall comply with you.
The other person replied:
"No," the man replied. "If you are unable to do so, why should I comply with you?"
It is the same in this case:

the mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can provide protection against the breaking of precepts and the arising of afflictions that lead to such breaking; therefore, those precepts conform to the mind.
Question: Do all wholesome minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possess the form of the transformative precepts (*saṃvṛti-śīla-rūpa*)? Answer: No.
It is not that existence is exhausted.
Within the first dhyāna, there are six types of wholesome consciousness that lack the matter of the non-reverting precepts (*avivartanīya-śīla*):
the three wholesome bodies of consciousness, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*), the wholesome mind at the time of death, and the wholesome mind of active engagement.
In the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, there are two types of wholesome minds that possess the matter of non-retrogressive precepts (*avivartya-śīla*):
the wholesome mind arising from hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) and the wholesome mind at the time of death.
In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no precepts.
Question: For what reason is there no precept in the formless realm? Answer:
"It is not because it is their field," and so forth, as explained at length.
Precepts coexist with form; since there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are no precepts there.
Furthermore, some say that precepts are derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); since there are no four great elements in the formless realm, there are no precepts there.
Question: Are there no untainted (anāsrava) four great elements, and is there also no untainted precept? Answer:
Untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are not untainted by virtue of the four great elements; rather, they are untainted precepts by virtue of the mind.

Furthermore, precepts serve as the antidote to breaking the precepts and to the afflictions that give rise to such breaking; since the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) lacks both the breaking of precepts and the afflictions that give rise to them, there is no precept therein.
Question: For what reason is there neither breaking of the precepts nor the arising of afflictions that break the precepts, nor their antidotes, in the formless realm? Answer:

Breaking the precepts and giving rise to the afflictions that lead to breaking the precepts are dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is extremely remote from the desire realm in four respects: namely, remoteness of basis (*āśraya*), remoteness of objective range (*gocara*), remoteness of object (*ālambana*), and remoteness of antidote (*pratipakṣa*). In this context, "basis" refers to the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

Question: If that is so, since the second, third, and fourth dhyānas lack the counteractive factors for both the transgression of precepts and the afflictions that give rise to such transgressions, do they also lack the materiality of the "turning-back" precepts?
Answer: There are two kinds of remedies: first, the remedy of abandonment;
[second, the remedy of distance].
2. Remedy for Defects. Although the second, third, and fourth dhyānas lack a remedy for abandonment, they possess a remedy for defects.
As the Blessed One said:
When a noble disciple whose mind is liberated through the immovable dharma enters samādhi, they abandon unwholesome states and cultivate wholesome states.
At that time, their body is devoid of unwholesome states; it is for the purpose of counteracting faults that this is said.
In the formless realm, there is neither the antidote that remedies defects nor the antidote of abandonment.
There are two kinds of ethical discipline: first, that which is co-nascent with the Path; [and second, that which is acquired through effort].
2. Co-arising with concentration (*samādhi-sahaja*).

Precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja*) are untainted (*anāsrava*); precepts co-arising with concentration are tainted (*sāsrava*). If they are precepts co-arising with the Path, they are not precepts co-arising with concentration;
if they are precepts co-arising with concentration, they are not precepts co-arising with the Path.
If it is the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is not the morality co-arising with the Path (*mārga*).

Furthermore, some say that the morality co-arising with the Path is untainted (*anāsrava*), whereas the morality co-arising with meditative concentration is both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted; therefore, the Path is placed as the first category.
If there is morality co-arising with the Path, does that person possess morality co-arising with meditative concentration? Answer:
If one possesses morality co-arising with the Path, one also possesses morality co-arising with meditative concentration.
Is there any morality that arises together with meditative concentration (samādhi) but does not arise together with the Path?
Answer: There is;
namely, impure (sāsrava) morality.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the precept co-arising with the Path is untainted (anāsrava), while the precept co-arising with meditative concentration (samādhi) is the fundamental dhyāna; therefore, one should formulate four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
If there is a precept co-arising with the Path, does that person also possess a precept co-arising with meditative concentration?
If there is morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), does that also include morality co-arising with the Path (*mārga*)?
The answer is:
there may be morality co-arising with the Path that is not morality co-arising with meditative concentration; thus, one should elaborate fully upon the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding "precepts co-arising with the Path but not co-arising with meditative absorption," this refers to the untainted (anāsrava) precepts of the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the intermediate dhyāna.
Regarding "precepts co-arising with meditative absorption but not co-arising with the Path," this refers to the tainted (sāsrava) precepts within the fundamental dhyānas.
That which is both path-concomitant precept and concentration-concomitant precept refers to the untainted (anāsrava) precepts within the fundamental dhyānas.

That which is neither path-concomitant precept nor concentration-concomitant precept refers to the tainted (sāsrava) precepts of the preparatory stage (anāgamya) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
Regarding all precepts of the desire realm: if one attains the precepts that arise together with the Path, does one also attain the precepts that arise together with meditative concentration?
And if one attains the precepts that arise together with meditative concentration, does one also attain the precepts that arise together with the Path?
One should formulate four propositions.

Regarding the attainment of morality co-arising with the Path but not co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): this refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire and attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), during the fifteen moments of mind, attains right determination based on the threshold dhyāna (*anāgamya*) while being free from desire through subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

Regarding the noble ones during the fifteen moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*): for those who have abandoned the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are the preparatory paths (*prayogamārga*), the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), and the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

For those who have not yet abandoned the desires and are "liberated through faith" (*śraddhādhimukta*), when they transform their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become "those who see by insight" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), there are the preparatory, non-obstructive, and liberative paths.

When a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire gives rise to the immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), or gives rise to [the meditations on] impurity (*aśubha*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and so forth, they obtain the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*), rather than the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).

Regarding the attainment of precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) rather than precepts co-arising with the mundane path: for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), at the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) when abandoning the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or when abandoning the desires of the first dhyāna—taking the first dhyāna itself as the preparatory means (*prayoga-mārga*) and the final path of liberation; or if one takes the threshold of the second dhyāna as the preparatory means and the final path of liberation, and so on up to the third dhyāna—it is likewise.

When one has detached from the desire of the fourth dhyāna and, taking the fourth dhyāna as the means (upāya), gives rise to supernormal powers (abhijñā) through the path of means (upāyamārga), there are five paths of non-obstruction (ānantaryamārga) and three paths of liberation (vimuktimārga).

When an ordinary person detached from desire gives rise to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), gives rise to the first, second, and third liberations (*vimokṣa*), gives rise to the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), gives rise to the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), gives rise to the meditations on impurity (*aśubhā*) and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), or when, based on dhyāna, one gives rise to the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya kuśalamūla*); and when dying in the formless realm to be reborn in the realm of form, or dying in a higher stage within the realm of form to be reborn in a lower stage—at such times as these, one attains the morality co-arising with concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*), not the morality co-arising with the path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*).

Regarding the morality co-arising with the Path and the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): when a person free from desire attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, the subsequent knowledge of the Path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) attains right determination based on the higher stages. For a noble one (*ārya*) in the fifteen moments of the Path of Seeing, the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding the subsequent knowledge of the Path effects freedom from the desires of the Desire Realm; likewise, the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the nine paths of liberation effect freedom from the desires of the First Dhyāna, and so on, up to the freedom from the desires of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

When a person liberated through faith who is free from desire transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), at the moment of attaining the path of liberation that is the unhindered path leading to the state of one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), there are the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*), nine unhindered paths, and nine paths of liberation. When an Arhat liberated through non-attachment transforms their faculties to attain the immovable state (*akopyadharman*), there are likewise the preparatory path, nine unhindered paths, and nine paths of liberation.

When practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), three minds arise; when manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are five paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and three paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

When noble ones (*ārya*) who have abandoned desire give rise to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the analytical knowledge of non-contention (*araṇā-pratisaṃvid*), the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhi-jñāna*), the half-*mahā-pṛthagjana* [attainments], emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and subtle signs (*sūkṣma-nimitta*)—in such instances as these, one attains the morality co-arising with the path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) and the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*).

Regarding the statement that one does not abandon the precepts co-arising with the Path (mārga-sahaja-śīla) and the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (samādhi-sahaja-śīla), this excludes the aforementioned cases.
If one abandons the precepts co-arising with the Path, does one also abandon the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration?

One should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding the case where one abandons the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) but not those co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*): this refers to one who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, or is sequentially attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*; or one who, being a *śraddhādhimukta* not yet free from desire, transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*); or one who, having attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* as a *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, falls away from the path of superior progress; or one who falls away from the path of superior progress of the fruit of *srotāpanna*. At these times, one abandons the precepts co-arising with the Path, but does not abandon the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration.

Regarding "one abandons the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration but does not abandon the precepts co-arising with the Path": when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who has detached from the desires of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) falls away from that detachment; or when an ordinary person or a noble one (*ārya*) dies in the form realm and is reborn in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), or dies in the form realm and is reborn within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)—at these times, one abandons the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration but does not abandon the precepts co-arising with the Path.

Regarding the relinquishing of both the morality co-arising with the Path and the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*): when one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* or *arhat* based on dhyāna; when one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) becomes liberated by view (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) after abandoning desire; when one who is immovable (*akopyadharman*) falls away from the fruit of *arhat* through the transformation of faculties; or when one falls away from the fruit of *anāgāmin* during the path of superior progress (*viśeṣamārga*)—at these times, one relinquishes both the morality co-arising with the Path and the morality co-arising with meditative concentration.
Regarding "not abandoning the precepts co-arising with the Path" and "not abandoning the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration": these exclude the aforementioned matters.
If one accomplishes the precepts co-arising with the Path, does one also accomplish the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration?
This is elaborated extensively in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case of one who accomplishes the morality co-arising with the Path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) but not the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi-sahaja-śīla*): it refers to a noble being (*ārya*) born within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who has not yet abandoned desire; this is called accomplishing the morality co-arising with the Path but not the morality co-arising with meditative concentration.

Regarding the accomplishment of the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) but not those co-arising with the path (*mārga*): this refers to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have abandoned desire while born within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as those born within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). This is called the accomplishment of the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration but not those co-arising with the path.
Regarding "accomplishing both": this refers to noble ones born within the desire realm who have abandoned the desires of the desire realm, as well as those born within the form realm;

this is called accomplishing both. Regarding "not accomplishing either": this refers to ordinary persons born within the desire realm who have not abandoned desire, and ordinary persons born within the formless realm; this is called not accomplishing either.
If one does not accomplish the precepts co-arising with the Path, does one also not accomplish the precepts co-arising with meditative concentration?
This is explained at length through the formulation of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first proposition becomes the second, the second becomes the first, the third becomes the fourth, and the fourth becomes the third.
There are four kinds of precepts:
first, the precept of attaining liberation; second, the dhyāna-precept; [third, the prātimokṣa-precept; fourth, the natural precept].
Third, untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*);
fourth, precepts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-śīla*).
That which attains the precepts of liberation (*vimukti-śīla*) refers to the precepts of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The precepts of dhyāna are the precepts of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are the precepts co-arising with the Path (*mārga*).
The precepts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-śīla*) are the precepts of dhyāna.
What is the nature of untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*)?

Within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) that abandon the desires of the desire realm, the conventional transformation of matter (*rūpa*) is called the dhyāna-precept (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the precept of abandonment (*prahāṇa-śīla*).

The unconditioned (anāsrava) transformation of matter (*rūpa*) within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) during the abandonment of desire for the realm of desire is called the "unconditioned precept" (*anāsrava-śīla*) or the "precept of abandonment.
Question: Why is the transformation of matter within the nine paths of non-obstruction during the abandonment of desire for the realm of desire called the "precept of abandonment"?

Answer: Because within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) that turn back form during the process of abandoning desire for the realm of desire, these serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) to transgressions of the precepts and the afflictions that give rise to such transgressions.
For this reason, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
If it is a dhyāna-precept, is it also a precept of abandonment?
If it is a precept of abandonment, is it also a dhyāna-precept?
This should be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding "this is the dhyāna-precept, not the abandonment-precept": excluding the transformation of matter within the nine paths of non-obstruction that eliminate desire for the realm of desire, all other mundane transformations of matter are called the dhyāna-precept, not the abandonment-precept.

Regarding "this is the morality of abandonment, not the morality of meditative concentration": the untainted transformation of form within the nine paths of non-obstruction that abandon the desires of the desire realm is called the morality of abandonment, not the morality of meditative concentration.

Regarding "both are": within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for abandoning the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the conventional (*laukika*) matter that turns back is called "both are.

Regarding "neither are": excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) matter that turns back within the nine paths of non-obstruction for abandoning the desires of the desire realm, all other untainted path-turning matters are called "neither are."
If it is untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*), is it also a precept of abandonment (*prahāṇa-śīla*)?
This is to be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is untainted precept but not a precept of abandonment: excluding the untainted derivative matter (*anuparivartin-rūpa*) within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*navānantarya-mārga*) during the separation from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu-vairāgya*), all other untainted derivative matter is called untainted precept that is not a precept of abandonment.

Regarding "this is the morality of abandonment, not the untainted morality": within the nine paths of non-obstruction that abandon the desires of the desire realm, the conventional transformation of matter is called the morality of abandonment, not the untainted morality.

Regarding "both are": the untainted (anāsrava) evolving matter within the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) during the abandonment of desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is called "both are.

Regarding "neither are": with the exception of the mundane (*laukika*) evolving matter within the nine paths of non-obstruction during the abandonment of desire for the desire realm, all other mundane evolving matter is called "neither are."
Question: If these four kinds of precepts are accomplished, how many kinds are accomplished? Answer:

Some may achieve only the precepts of liberation; some may achieve only the dhyāna-precepts; and some may achieve only the untainted (anāsrava) precepts, but there is no one who is said to achieve only the precepts of abandonment.

There may be those who achieve and attain the precepts of liberation and the precepts of dhyāna; however, there are none who achieve and attain only the precepts of liberation and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla), nor are there any who achieve and attain only the precepts of liberation and the precepts of abandonment (prahāṇa-śīla).

There may be those who achieve only the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) and the dhyāna precepts (*dhyāna-śīla*), or those who achieve only the dhyāna precepts and the precepts of abandonment (*prahāṇa-śīla*); however, there are none who achieve only the untainted precepts and the precepts of abandonment.

There may be those who have attained and accomplished the precepts of liberation, the precepts of dhyāna, and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla), yet have not accomplished the precepts of abandonment; there may be those who have attained and accomplished the precepts of liberation, the precepts of dhyāna, and the precepts of abandonment, yet have not accomplished the untainted precepts; however, there are none who have attained and accomplished the precepts of liberation, the untainted precepts, and the precepts of abandonment, yet have not accomplished the precepts of dhyāna.

There may be those who have accomplished the precepts of dhyāna, the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla), and the precepts of abandonment, yet have not accomplished the attainment of the precepts of liberation.
There may also be those who have accomplished all four kinds.

"One who achieves and attains the *vimukti-śīla* (liberation-precept) but not the others" refers to one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) who has received the precepts but has not attained a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

"One who achieves only the *dhyāna-śīla* (meditation-precept) but not the others" refers to an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) bound by all fetters who is born in the desire realm and has not received the precepts, yet has attained a wholesome mind of the form realm; this includes ordinary persons born in the second, third, or fourth *dhyānas*.
Those who possess only untainted (anāsrava) morality and no others are noble ones (ārya) born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).

Those who possess only the morality of liberation (vimukti-śīla) and the morality of meditative concentration (dhyāna-śīla), and no others, are ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) with full fetters (sakalabandhana) born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) who have attained a wholesome mind of the form realm (rūpadhātu).

However, those who have accomplished the dhyāna-precepts and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) include: noble ones (ārya) born in the desire realm who do not receive the [formal] precepts; and noble ones who are still bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana) regarding what is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) in the desire realm, yet are born in the second, third, or fourth dhyānas.

Regarding the statement that "the attainment of the precepts of dhyāna and the precepts of abandonment belongs to none other [than those in the form realm]": this refers to ordinary persons born within the desire realm who have not received the precepts yet are free from the desires of the desire realm, as well as ordinary persons—from those who have abandoned one type of fetter up to nine types—who are born within the first dhyāna.

Regarding those who have attained and realized the liberation-precepts, the dhyāna-precepts, and the untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla), yet do not possess the precepts of cessation: these are noble ones (ārya) born within the desire realm who have received the precepts and remain bound by all fetters regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path in the desire realm.

Regarding the accomplishment of the precepts of liberation, the precepts of meditation, and the precepts of abandonment, yet not the untainted (anāsrava) precepts: this refers to an ordinary person born within the desire realm who, having received the precepts, has abandoned from one type of desire up to nine types.

Those who have accomplished the precepts of dhyāna and the untainted (anāsrava) but have not yet attained liberation—namely, noble ones (ārya) born within the desire realm who have not received the [formal] precepts, as well as noble ones born in the first dhyāna who have abandoned from one type of desire up to nine types—are included therein.
Regarding those who accomplish four types [of restraint]: it refers to noble persons born within the desire realm who have abandoned from one type of desire up to nine types.
Question: Of these four types of restraint, how many follow the movement of the mind, and how many do not follow the movement of the mind?
The answer is:
Three are associated with the revolving of the mind—namely, the dhyāna-precepts, the outflow-free (anāsrava) precepts, and the precepts of abandonment.
One is not associated with the revolving of the mind—namely, the attained liberation-precepts (vimukti-śīla).
Question: For what reason does the attainment of the precept of liberation not revolve with the mind? Answer:
"It is not his field," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the precept of attaining liberation is coarse, while the precept of mental transformation is subtle.
Furthermore, the precept of attaining liberation is heavy, while the precept of mental transformation is light.
Furthermore, the precept of liberation attained through effort arises from conditioned activity, while the precept of mental transformation arises from the mind.
Furthermore, the precept of liberation attained through others arises from another, while the precept of mental transformation arises from oneself.
Furthermore, the attainment of the *vimukti-śīla* (liberation-precept) arises from the harmony and assembly of the community; the *citta-parivartaka-śīla* (mind-turning-precept) is not so.
Furthermore, the attainment of the *vimukti-śīla* is acquired through conventional designation (*prajñapti*); the *citta-parivartaka-śīla* is obtained from the Dharma itself.
Furthermore, the precept-conduct attained through liberation does not reach the mind, whereas the precept-conduct of mental transformation does reach the mind.
Furthermore, the precept-conduct attained through liberation is obscured by the breaking of precepts, whereas the precept-conduct of mental transformation is not obscured by the breaking of precepts.
Furthermore, the precept of liberation is not obscured by the mind’s turning away when it is covered by an evil mind or the intent to kill; the precept of mental turning, however, is so obscured.
Furthermore, the precept of mental turning arises, abides, and ceases simultaneously with the mind, whereas the precept of liberation does not.
Furthermore, the precept of mental transformation shares the same fruit, the same basis, and the same retribution as the mind; the precept of liberation is the opposite of the former.

Moreover, the nature of phenomena is such that if the mind is wholesome, the phenomenon of mental transformation is also wholesome; if the mind is unwholesome or indeterminate, the phenomenon of mental transformation is likewise unwholesome or indeterminate.
The liberation-precepts (*vimukti-śīla*) are wholesome; if they revolve together with the mind, they revolve only with a wholesome mind, for unwholesome and neutral minds should be abandoned.

Furthermore, it is the nature of phenomena that a mind bound to the desire realm revolves with what is bound to the desire realm, a mind bound to the form realm revolves with what is bound to the form realm, a mind bound to the formless realm revolves with what is bound to the formless realm, and an unbound mind revolves with what is unbound.

When the liberation-precept is bound to the desire realm, if it revolves together with a mind bound to the desire realm, it should be abandoned when a mind bound to the form realm, the formless realm, or an unbound mind manifests.

Furthermore, the nature of phenomena is such that the mind in training (śaikṣa) revolves as training, the mind beyond training (aśaikṣa) revolves as beyond training, and the mind that is neither in training nor beyond training revolves as neither in training nor beyond training.

The liberation-precepts are neither-learner-nor-non-learner; if they revolve together with a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, they should be abandoned when a learner or non-learner mind manifests.

Furthermore, it is the nature of phenomena that the mind abandoned by the path of seeing revolves with what is abandoned by the path of seeing; the mind abandoned by the path of cultivation revolves with what is abandoned by the path of cultivation; and the mind not to be abandoned revolves with what is not to be abandoned.

When the liberation-precepts are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), if they revolve together with a mind abandoned through the path of cultivation, they should be abandoned when a mind abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or an uninterrupted mind (*anantarya-citta*) manifests.

Furthermore, if the attained liberation-precepts were to revolve with the mind, they should be cultivated in future lives; if they were cultivated in future lives, there would be no fault, and they should be accomplished in future lives.
Yet, they are not accomplished in future lives.
Furthermore, regarding the attainment of the precept of liberation (vimukti-śīla) by one whose mind is revolving: it should be attained at the time of rebirth within a realm or stage;
or, if one passes away from the form or formless realms and is born into the desire realm, it should be attained at the moment of the continuous mind (pratisaṃdhi-citta).

If such a fault exists, there would be no distinction between three types of persons: namely, those who abide in morality, those who abide in immorality, and those who abide in neither morality nor immorality.
Furthermore, the attainment of the liberation-precepts is relinquished due to four circumstances:
first, at the time of relinquishing the precepts; [the other three being:]...
2. When one transforms into a hermaphrodite;
3. At the time of death;
4. At the time of severing the roots of goodness.
If one were to attain the *vimukti-śīla* (liberation-precept) such that it turns together with the mind, then even these four matters would not necessitate its relinquishment.
Furthermore, once the *vimukti-śīla* is attained, it arises at all times thereafter, including during periods of sleep, insanity, or confusion.
If the liberation-precepts were to revolve together with the mind, they would exist when the mind exists and should be severed when the mind is absent.
Furthermore, if the liberation-precepts were to revolve together with the mind, then there would be no distinction of superior or inferior among those who receive the precepts;
yet, such distinctions do exist.
In order to prevent such faults as these, one attains the liberation-precepts (vimukti-śīla), which do not revolve with the mind.
The "Heat" stage (uṣmagata) involves the revolving of the precepts; this is the antidote for breaking the precepts and abandoning them.

The stage of the Peak (mūrdhan), the stage of Patience (kṣānti), the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma), and the morality that turns toward the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) within the paths of seeing and cultivation—during these times, two kinds of remedies are applied to counteract the breaking of precepts:
the remedy of distancing (dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa) and the remedy of maintenance (dhṛti-pratipakṣa).

The turning-back precept (*parivṛtti-śīla*) of the preparatory path (*prayoga-mārga*) for detachment from the desires of the desire realm serves as the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) toward transgression.

The turning-back precept of the first path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) for detachment from the desires of the desire realm serves as the antidote of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*) and the antidote of maintenance (*dhṛti-pratipakṣa*) toward transgression; it serves as the antidote of severance (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*) and the antidote of abandonment toward the afflictions that give rise to transgression.

The sevenfold path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) is the turning-back precept; it serves as the counteractive of remoteness (*dūrabhāga-pratipakṣa*) and the counteractive of maintenance (*dhāraṇā-pratipakṣa*) for breaking the precepts, and as the counteractive of relinquishment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteractive of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), the counteractive of remoteness, and the counteractive of maintenance for the afflictions that give rise to the breaking of the precepts.

The ninth path of non-obstruction serves as the counteractive treatment for abandonment, the counteractive treatment for distancing, and the counteractive treatment for maintenance regarding the breaking of precepts; it also serves as the counteractive treatment for abandonment, the counteractive treatment for relinquishment, the counteractive treatment for distancing, and the counteractive treatment for maintenance regarding the afflictions that give rise to the breaking of precepts.

Aside from the aforementioned turning-back precepts, all other turning-back precepts serve as the distant-remedy (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*) and the sustaining-remedy (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*) for breaking the precepts and for the arising of afflictions that lead to breaking the precepts.

Question: If it is the dharma-knowledge that turns back the precepts—enabling one to abandon broken precepts and the afflictions that give rise to them—and not the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), why do you say that subsequent knowledge possesses the turning back of precepts?
The Venerable Sūmī replied: "Because it is their cause;

furthermore, because it belongs to them; furthermore, because it continues from them; furthermore, because it arises from them; and furthermore, because this [state] has already established the counteractive dharma."

Why is this? If, when practicing the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one were not to abandon broken precepts and give rise to afflictions associated with breaking precepts, then subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) would have to abandon them.

Furthermore, since the remedies (*pratipakṣa*) for phenomena are manifold, although subsequent knowledge does not perform the remedy of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) or the remedy of severance (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*) regarding broken precepts and the arising of afflictions associated with breaking precepts, it nonetheless performs the remedy of distancing (*dūribhāvapratipakṣa*) and the remedy of maintenance (*dhāraṇāpratipakṣa*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"If dharma-knowledge possessed the discipline of regression and subsequent knowledge possessed the discipline of non-regression, then although there would be a discipline that serves as an antidote, the Blessed One has stated that there is both a discipline that serves as an antidote and a discipline that does not serve as an antidote."
Question: Is the morality of the desire realm greater, or is the morality of the form realm greater? Answer:
Some say that [the karma] of the desire realm is predominant.
Why is this? Because the fundamental action, as well as the preceding and succeeding actions, can be found there.
Furthermore, because both natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and prohibited transgressions (*pratikṣepa-sāvadya*) can be found therein;
although the fundamental nature of karma exists in the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), it cannot be found elsewhere.
The critique states:
One should say this:

although the precepts of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are numerous, those precepts subsumed by the *anāgamya* (threshold) dhyāna are equal in number to those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); the remainder, however, are more numerous. Question:
Which is more numerous: impure precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*) or pure precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*)?
The answer is:
some say that impure precepts are more numerous.
There are two kinds of contaminated (*sāsrava*) precepts:
one kind is slightly present, while uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) precepts are few.
There is one kind of uncontaminated precept, which is also slightly present.
The commentary states:
One should say that untainted (anāsrava) precepts are more numerous.

However, when the turning-back precepts (*parivṛtti-śīla*) of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) are compared with the outflow-tainted precepts (*sāsrava-śīla*), they are equal; for all others, they are greater. Question:

Are the turning-back precepts of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering more numerous, or are the turning-back precepts of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) more numerous?
The answer is:

Some say that the turning-away of the precept of the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is one degree superior to the turning-away of the precept of the forbearance of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
In this manner, they increase successively by degrees of superiority, up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

In the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, it is explained with thorough clarity that the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is superior to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), and so on, up to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) being superior to the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*).
Regarding the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) for detachment from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one unimpeded [concentration] and one liberation (*vimokṣa*) are superior.
In this manner, they become progressively more excellent, up to the ninth liberation.
Why is this? Just as one gradually abandons broken precepts and the afflictions of breaking precepts, so too does that morality gradually increase.
In this manner, progressing step by step, it becomes successively more excellent, up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
The commentary states:
Such an explanation is excellent;

for instance, the precepts of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) are no different from those of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Why is this? Because they are equally produced from the seven wholesome courses of action of body and speech. Question:
If that is so, how is one to reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*?
The answer is:
such a statement was made because [the self] is conceptually superimposed upon that which arises from causes.

Just as the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) arises from the cause of the patience regarding the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmanidhyānakṣānti*) and thereby attains increase, so it is for everything up to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Such precepts as these are entirely the seven wholesome [factors].
Question: Are the Buddha’s precepts more numerous, or the śrāvaka’s precepts more numerous? Answer:
Some may say that the precepts of the śrāvakas are mostly not those of the Buddha. Why is this?
Because the Buddha possesses only the body-precepts of a single realm, whereas the śrāvakas possess the body-precepts of two realms.
The critique says:
One should state that the Buddha's precepts are numerous.
Why is this? Such precepts as the powers, the fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three unique foundations of mindfulness are not possessed by śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Question: When one is born in the desire realm and attains the path of an arhat, how many stages of bodily transformation and precepts does one obtain? Answer:
As the śramaṇas of the West say, one attains the precept of the revolving body across twenty-six stages.
Why is this so? There are three types of stages within the first dhyāna, namely: the Brahmakāyika, the Brahmapurohita, and the Mahābrahmā.
As the śramaṇas of Kaśmīra say:
"One attains the precepts of the transformation of the body through the twenty-five stages. Why is this so?

The first dhyāna has two locations, namely the Brahmakāyika and the Brahmapurohita; since the Mahābrahmā heaven is subsumed within the Brahmapurohita, it is like the relationship between a village and a forest hermitage (āraṇya).
One attains the discipline of the transformation-body of that stage, which is cultivated in future lives but cannot arise as a manifest presence. Why is this?

It is because the retribution-body of that very stage can cause the discipline of the transformation-body of that stage to arise as a manifest presence; whereas the disciplines of the transformation-bodies of all other stages, though accomplished, do not arise as manifest presences.
Those born in the formless realm possess this [precept] but do not manifest it.
Why is this? Because this precept is subsumed within the six stages (bhūmi).

From the preliminary dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, there is no morality within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) itself; that which is subsumed under the lower stages cannot arise as a present manifestation [there]. Question:
Question: Can all those born in the lower stages cause [the dharmas] to arise and manifest in the present?
Answer: Not all of them can so arise.
Why is this? It is because not all meritorious qualities necessarily arise and manifest before one.
If even faults and evils do not all arise and manifest before one, how much less so the various meritorious qualities?
All merits arise from skillful means.

As previously stated, based on the retributive body of a particular stage, one gives rise to the transformative precepts of the body of that stage; there is never a time when the retributive bodies of two stages manifest simultaneously, let alone many.
Therefore, one attains the precept of the twenty-five stages of bodily transformation, which does not arise fully in its entirety before one.

Question: For what reason do the disciples of the World-Honored One who are born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) accomplish the precept co-arising with the Path (mārga-sahaja-śīla), yet do not accomplish the precept co-arising with meditative concentration (samādhi-sahaja-śīla)?

Why is it that an Arhat in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) accomplishes the morality co-arising with the Path (mārga-sahaja-śīla), yet does not accomplish the morality co-arising with meditative concentration (samādhi-sahaja-śīla)?
The answer is:
some say that because worldly morality is a bond and a fettering dharma, for this reason it is not accomplished.
Untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) are not bound; they are not fettering dharmas, and for this reason they are accomplished.
Furthermore, there are those who say that worldly precepts (laukika-śīla) fall within the realms (dhātu) and fall within the stages (bhūmi), and for this reason they are not accomplished.
Although untainted precepts (anāsrava-śīla) exist within the realms (dhātu), they do not fall under the categories of the [three] worlds; therefore, they are fully accomplished. Question:
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess bodily precepts that endure for a hundred years, even up to eighty thousand years.
If one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a body that is a hundred years old, does one also attain the bodily precepts (*kāya-śīla*) of a body that is eighty thousand years old?
If one does attain them, how can this body obtain the precepts belonging to a different body?
If this were not the case, how would one reconcile what is stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are equal"? As it says: "The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are all equal."
One should argue that it is indeed attained. Question:
If this is so, how does this body attain the precepts of body and speech that differ from it?
The answer is:
If one attains the precepts of a different body through this present body, what fault would there be?

Furthermore, if one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* during a hundred-year period, the precepts attained by that body during those hundred years are said to be "attained within the body" and "perfected and manifest in the present."
Regarding the precepts within a different body, they are said to be "attained but not residing in the body," and are said to be "accomplished but not manifest.
