there are superior, middling, and inferior karmas that lead to rebirth among the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin), wherein each respectively receives three kinds of retribution.
It is likewise among the five classes of gods and humans.
Some perform three kinds of karma and are born among the five classes of gods and humans, each receiving three kinds of retribution.
Those who perform three kinds of non-distinct karma in the stage of the first dhyāna are born in the stage of the first dhyāna and receive three kinds of non-distinct retribution.

By performing inferior karma of the second dhyāna, one is born among the Parīttābha devas to receive inferior retribution; by performing middling karma, one is born among the Apramāṇābha devas to receive middling retribution; and by performing superior karma, one is born among the Ābhāsvara devas to receive superior retribution.

By performing inferior karma of the third dhyāna, one is born among the Parīttābha devas and receives an inferior retribution; by performing middling karma, one is born among the Apramāṇābha devas and receives a middling retribution; by performing superior karma, one is born among the Ābhāsvara devas and receives a superior retribution.

By performing inferior karma of the fourth dhyāna, one is born among the gods of No-Obstruction (Avṛha) to receive an inferior retribution; by performing middling karma, one is born among the gods of Merit (Puṇyaprasava) to receive a middling retribution; and by performing superior karma, one is born among the gods of Vast Fruit (Bṛhatphala) to receive a superior retribution.

By practicing the lower perfuming dhyāna, one is born among the Avṛha devas to receive the lower retribution; by practicing the middle perfuming dhyāna, one is born among the Atapa devas to receive the middle retribution; by practicing the superior perfuming dhyāna, one is born among the Sudarśana devas to receive the superior retribution.

By practicing the superior perfuming meditation, one is born among the Sudṛśa devas and receives superior retribution; by practicing the superior and fully perfected perfuming meditation, one is born among the Akaniṣṭha devas and receives superior and fully perfected retribution; by performing non-distinctive karma, one is born in the Sphere of Infinite Space and receives non-distinctive retribution.
Even up to performing non-distinctive karma, one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and receives non-distinctive retribution.

As for unwholesome karma, it creates the locus for receiving a body in hell; being born within hell, one receives the retribution of unwholesome form, mental states and their concomitants, and formations dissociated from mind.
Form consists of nine bases, excluding the sound base.
Mental states and mental factors consist of painful feeling and its associated phenomena.
Mental formations dissociated from mind consist of the life-faculty, the basis of individual existence, acquisition, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence.

Unwholesome karma creates the bases for receiving bodies as animals or hungry ghosts; one is born among animals or hungry ghosts, experiencing the results of wholesome and unwholesome actions: form, mind and mental factors, and formations dissociated from mind.
Matter refers to unwholesome matter, which comprises nine bases (*āyatana*), excluding the sound base.
Mental states and mental concomitants refer to painful feeling and its associated factors.
Mental formations dissociated from mind refer to the life-faculty, the basis for the acquisition of the body, acquisition (*prāpti*), birth, and so forth.
Wholesome form consists of four bases: visible form, odor, flavor, and tangibility.
As for the mind and mental factors, these are pleasant feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and their associated phenomena.
Mental non-associated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) include acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth.

Furthermore, some teachers say that wholesome karma does not produce the material form of a wholesome retribution in the realms of animals or hungry ghosts; however, if it is a retribution at birth (*upapatti-vedanīya*), it produces the mind, mental factors (*caitta*), and mental non-associated formations.
Question: We now see with our own eyes that among animals and hungry ghosts (preta), some have beautiful and exquisite forms, while others have ugly and hideous forms. Answer:
There may be unwholesome karma that has unwholesome karma as its retinue, or wholesome karma as its retinue.
When unwholesome karma constitutes the retinue, one’s physical form and appearance are ugly and coarse;
when wholesome karma constitutes the retinue, the power of that wholesome karma obscures the unwholesome karma, causing the physical form and appearance to be beautiful and sublime.

Beings created by wholesome karma receive bodies in the six heavens of the desire realm; being born in those places, they experience the results of wholesome and unwholesome karma, namely: matter, mental states and their concomitants, and formations dissociated from mind.
Regarding "form" (*rūpa*): the forms that are the result of wholesome karma consist of nine bases (*āyatana*), excluding the base of sound.
Regarding "mind and mental factors": these refer to pleasant feeling, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, and their associated phenomena.

Mental factors dissociated from thought (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) consist of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the basis for the maintenance of the body (*āśrayopādātṛ*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth.
Regarding the matter that is the retribution of unwholesome karma (*akuśala-vipāka-rūpa*), there are four bases (*āyatana*): visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility.
"Mental states and mental concomitants" refers to painful feelings (*duḥkhā vedanā*) and their associated phenomena (*saṃprayuktadharma*).
"Mental formations dissociated from mind" (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*) refers to acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), and so forth.

Furthermore, some say that unwholesome karma does not produce the unwholesome resultant form (*vipākavarṇa*) of humans or the six heavens of the desire realm; however, if it produces a resultant [consciousness], it gives rise to mental states and mental concomitants, as well as mental formations dissociated from mind.
Question: We currently observe that among humans and devas, some have ugly forms and appearances, while others have beautiful and excellent forms and appearances. Answer:
There may be wholesome karma that has wholesome karma as its retinue, or unwholesome karma as its retinue.
When wholesome karma has wholesome karma as its retinue, one’s physical form and appearance are beautiful.
When unwholesome karma serves as its retinue, that unwholesome karma obscures the wholesome karma, causing the physical form and appearance to be ugly.
Regarding the physical form created by wholesome karma and the place where one receives a body in the formless realm: being born therein, one experiences the retribution of wholesome karma. Question:
As for those born among humans who possess both sexual organs (dviliṅga), is this the retribution of wholesome karma or the retribution of unwholesome karma?
The answer is:
A single form is the retribution of wholesome karma;
if a second form arises at an improper time or in an improper place, it is the retribution of unwholesome karma.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the substance of the sense faculties (*indriya*) is the retribution of wholesome karma, while the locations where the faculties reside are the retribution of unwholesome karma. Question:
For what reason does unwholesome karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) receive retribution for one eon (*kalpa*), whereas wholesome karma does not receive retribution for one eon?
Answer: Unwholesome karma possesses its own superior qualities. Why is this so?
Because retribution is received within the five realms of existence,
wholesome karma possesses its own superior qualities. Why is this so?
Because they receive retribution within the three realms,
they themselves possess matters that are superior in both respects. Why is this so?
Because both receive the retribution of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Question:
If that is so, why is it that unwholesome karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) receives retribution for one eon (*kalpa*), while wholesome karma does not?

Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is neither a stage of detachment from desire nor a stage of cultivation. Therefore, unwholesome karma receives retribution for one kalpa, whereas wholesome karma does not.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in the desire realm, the unwholesome roots are powerful and flourishing while the wholesome roots are weak and feeble.
Moreover, in the desire realm, the unwholesome roots constantly increase, whereas the wholesome roots never increase.

Furthermore, the unwholesome roots of the desire realm are long-established, whereas the wholesome roots are adventitious; the long-established possess superior power, while the adventitious are not equal to them.
Furthermore, the unwholesome roots of the desire realm are capable of severing the wholesome roots, whereas the wholesome roots of the desire realm cannot sever the unwholesome roots.

Furthermore, the dharmas of the desire realm do not avoid or obstruct one another; they are like a husband and wife whose deportment knows no inhibition, or like the son of a householder associating with the son of a candāla.

Furthermore, because there is no vessel for retribution, there is nowhere within the entire realm of desire where a vessel can receive the retribution of wholesome karma for the duration of a kalpa. Question:
Are not the four continents, Mount Sumeru, the golden mountains, and so forth, vessels for one kalpa?
Answer: To say they are not "vessels for retribution" means that these four continents, Mount Sumeru, the golden mountains, and so forth, are not themselves the result of wholesome retribution.
Furthermore, if wholesome karma in the desire realm could produce a retribution lasting for one kalpa, by what cause would this be obtained?
There is only the most supreme wholesome karma.
However, this most supreme wholesome karma is attained at the time of detachment from desire, because karma that has detached from desire cannot create a place for receiving a body.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that unwholesome karma receives its retribution within the five destinies.
Question: As the discussion unfolds, one may ask: for what reason do the fruits of wholesome karma not receive retribution within the five destinies? Answer:
It should be answered as previously stated: regarding the wholesome roots of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
In this context, there is only one unique answer:
namely, that the desire realm is a field for unwholesome seeds; it is easy to plant unwholesome dharmas, but difficult [to plant] wholesome dharmas.
Just as weeds grow easily in a field while rice and other crops are difficult to produce, so too the Buddhist sūtras state that karma is the cause of the eye;
the Abhidharma states that the four great elements are the cause of the eye; and yet others say that the eye itself is the cause of the eye.
What is the distinction between these three that have been explained?
The answer is:
because it is a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), the Buddha’s sūtras state that karma is the cause of the eye.

By means of the cause of production, the cause of support, the cause of duration, the cause of growth, and the cause of nourishment—because of these causes such as production—the four great elements are said to be the cause of the eye;
because of the cause of similarity, the eye is said to be the cause of the eye.
Question: If the four great elements are causes of the eye, and the eye itself is also a cause of the eye, why does the Buddha’s sūtra state only that karma is the cause of the eye? Answer:
Karma is the individual karma of sentient beings; it is by virtue of karma that they are born.

Karma is the locus where sentient beings take up the wealth of their fruits; sentient beings are subject to karma, and it is because of karma that there are distinctions among them, namely, the noble and the lowly, the good and the evil.
Furthermore, it is said that due to the various distinctions of karma, its various potencies, and its various causal conditions for action—
and so forth, as explained at length— there are those who say that because of karma, lifespan undergoes increase and decrease, prosperity and decline, and advancement and regression.
Furthermore, some say that it is due to karma that there are the dull-witted and the intelligent.
Others say that it is due to karma that there are differences in the retribution received across the various realms, births, and destinies.
Furthermore, some say that it is because of karma that the seven classes of followers have their sequential distinctions.
Others say that all sentient beings are stamped by karma.
Furthermore, because karma differs, the sense faculties also differ, just as the sprout differs according to the seed.
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:
"If a person practices and extensively propagates the taking of life, they will be born in the hells."
Having passed away from that state and been reborn among humans, their lifespan is short.
It is asked:
Is it by means of the very same karma that led to birth in hell that one obtains a short life upon being reborn among humans?
The answer is:
Some say that by extensively propagating the teaching of killing as it was spoken, one is born in the hells; when life there ends, one is reborn among humans with a short lifespan.
Furthermore, some say that because of the act of killing, one is born in hell due to that karma; because of the skillful means of that karma, one is short-lived upon birth.
Others say that while one is born in hell due to the karma of killing, being short-lived upon birth is its *niṣyanda-phala* (concordant fruit).
Furthermore, there are those who say that when one kills a sentient being, one causes another to undergo two kinds of suffering:
first, causing them to experience physical pain; second, severing their cherished life.
Because one causes suffering to others, one is born in the hells;
because one cuts off the life of that which others cherish, one is short-lived from birth. Question:
If a person has a short lifespan, is this the retribution for wholesome karma or the retribution for unwholesome karma?
The Venerable Sūmīta said:
"It is the retribution for wholesome karma, not the retribution for unwholesome karma."
Why is this so? Because the human life-span and the other eight faculties are the retributions of wholesome karma.

Since wholesome karma produces the retribution of a twenty-year lifespan among humans, the act of killing causes that lifespan to be diminished; what should have been a twenty-year lifespan becomes only ten years, and at ten years, it is severed.
The Buddhist sutras state:
"When the human lifespan is ten years, there will be born sons and daughters with a lifespan of twenty years.
A question is asked: [Why is this so?]
There is no one who accomplishes karma for another, nor is there anyone for whom another performs karma that they themselves receive. Why, then, is it said thus?
The answer is:
those people with a lifespan of ten years subsequently attain a lifespan of twenty years.
Practicing the ten paths of wholesome action in this way results in a lifespan that is tenfold.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

"All karmas have their own fixed retributions; the karma for a ten-year lifespan has a ten-year retribution, and so on up to the karma for an eighty-thousand-year lifespan having an eighty-thousand-year retribution."
Whatever cause one cultivates accordingly, one receives such a retribution.
Question: When human life expectancy is ten years, is abstaining from killing included within the wholesome courses of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*)?
Answer: It is not subsumed under the paths of action.
It is the path of non-action, not a path of action.
Why is this? Because he established this precept:
"One should not take life."
It constitutes neither the path of non-action nor the path of action.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* asks:
"Is there that which does not receive retribution in the present life, but receives it in a future birth or in a subsequent life?"
Answer: There is.

If karma to be experienced in the present life does not manifest and grant its retribution, while karma to be experienced in the next life or karma to be experienced in subsequent lives manifests and grants its retribution, at that time one receives the retribution of karma to be experienced in the next life.
One who has attained arhatship does not fail to receive the retribution of birth;
the same is said regarding subsequent retribution. Question:
Question: Ordinary persons who are training also possess this quality; why then speak only of the arhat? Answer:
It is because the arhat is able to know whether karma is distant or near, and whether it is reversible or irreversible.
Furthermore, there are those who say that for an Arhat, no further existence is received and those various karmas do not arise and manifest before him.
It is like a person wishing to go to another country, only to have a creditor come and demand payment.

It is the same for them: because learners (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) will receive further bodies, they must undergo this retribution; therefore, it is not mentioned [in their case].
Furthermore, some say that if one possesses the personal power to fully understand this karmic retribution, then it is mentioned.
Some maintain this view:
"A single karma traverses all realms of existence;
that which has remaining retribution... Those who hold this position speak as follows:

Regarding the karma created and the retribution received in previous lives by an Arhat, if this retribution remains, they abandon it through the power of cultivating the Path; thus, they relinquish the karmic retribution of human existence pertaining to the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*) and instead receive retribution in a future birth (*upapadyavedanīya*) or subsequent births (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

As for those who receive [the fruit], they are able to initiate this retribution through such conditions; only Arhats are capable of this, whereas those in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are not.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"There are four kinds of persons:"

There are those who die when their lifespan is exhausted but their wealth is not; there are those who die when their wealth is exhausted but their lifespan is not; there are those who die when both their lifespan and their wealth are exhausted; and there are those who die neither when their lifespan is exhausted nor when their wealth is exhausted.

Regarding the first case: suppose there is a person who performs karma that results in a short lifespan and causes it to increase extensively, and likewise performs karma for wealth that causes it to increase extensively; such a person dies when their lifespan is exhausted, but before their wealth is exhausted.

Regarding the second case: suppose there is a person who performs meritorious deeds for wealth and causes them to increase extensively, and likewise performs meritorious deeds for longevity and causes them to increase; yet, his wealth is exhausted while his longevity is not, and he dies.

Regarding the third case: it is like a person who performs both actions that produce meager wealth and actions that produce a short lifespan, causing both to increase; he then dies when his wealth is exhausted and his life has ended.

Regarding the fourth case: it is like a person who extensively cultivates the karma for wealth and the karma for longevity so that both increase; yet, although his wealth is not exhausted and his lifespan is not exhausted, he dies due to other adverse conditions.
The Venerable Maudgalyāyana spoke thus: that there is untimely death is a certainty regarding the cause of retribution; it exists within the three periods of time as its fruit.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Eleven [End] / Fascicle Twelve.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others.
From the *Saṃyukta-kaṇḍa*, Chapter on Knowledge (8): "What is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)? and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose is this treatise composed? Answer:
This treatise is composed to stop the notion that when phenomena arise there is no agent, and also to clarify that when phenomena arise, they are produced by causes.
What is the cause of production?

Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; that consciousness takes the eye as its efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), and likewise takes visible forms, associated and co-existent dharmas, and even the ear, sounds, up to the mind, mental objects, and associated and co-existent dharmas as its efficient causes.
As it is with visual consciousness, so it is with all consciousnesses up to mental consciousness.
One should speak in this manner, and not speak of "form-dharmas" or "formless dharmas. Why is that?
These six pairs of dharmas encompass all dharmas.
Since they have been well-expounded and well-explained, one should speak thus; what is the intention behind not speaking [of them]?
The answer is:
The former is an extensive explanation and the latter is a concise explanation;
the former is a specific explanation and the latter is a general explanation;
the former is analytical and the latter is non-analytical.
The former statement is sequential, while the latter is not sequential.
Question: Why is it not stated in this way?
What is the cause of activity?
The answer is:
because all phenomena would entail the fault of possessing intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If one were to say that all phenomena are produced causes, then their own essence would also be included among all [other phenomena].
To avoid such an error, this statement is not made.
Visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms. Question:
Apart from its own self-nature, all other phenomena are also conditions capable of producing visual consciousness.
Why is it said only that "the eye, conditioned by visible forms, gives rise to visual consciousness"?
The answer is:
because one grasps that upon which visual consciousness relies and that which is the object of visual consciousness.
Furthermore, because the eye and visible forms act as the proximate dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for visual consciousness, it is stated thus.

The eye and visible forms act as the proximate dominant conditions for visual consciousness more effectively than the co-arising factors such as birth (*jāti*) that arise simultaneously with visual consciousness; therefore, this statement is made.
Excluding its own self-nature.
Question: For what reason does the self-nature not act as a causal agent for itself?
The answer is:
"It is not its own field or its own instrument," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all phenomena, excluding their own self-nature, act as conditions for other phenomena.
Within its own essence, it neither harms nor benefits itself; it neither increases nor decreases, neither advances nor recedes.
Furthermore, there is no fault of differentiation in this explanation.

Why is this so? Because the cause is itself the fruit; the act of doing is itself the deed done, and the process of accomplishing is itself the thing accomplished, even unto the point that arising is itself the event of arising.
Furthermore, a self-nature cannot serve as a support for itself.
Furthermore, an entity itself does not act as its own superior.
Moreover, this contradicts phenomena as they are perceived in the world:
it is observed that the eye cannot see itself, a fingertip cannot touch itself, a blade cannot cut itself, and a strong man cannot carry himself.
It is the same in this case as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "non-obstruction" is the meaning of "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
An entity obstructs its own nature; there are two kinds of obstruction:
The first is nominal obstruction; the second is actual obstruction.
Nominal obstruction is, for example, like a person on a bed or a seat.
Actual obstruction is, for example, like a physical body obstructing itself.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if the self-essence were the cause that produces its own effect, it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras; as a sūtra says:
"Ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth, as explained at length.

If an entity were to act as its own cause of production, then ignorance would be conditioned by ignorance rather than by formations, and so on, up to birth being conditioned by birth rather than by aging and death.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Dependent upon the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises."
It should not be that visual consciousness arises conditioned by the eye and visible forms; rather, it should be that visual consciousness arises conditioned by [a preceding] visual consciousness.
Because one wishes to avoid such an error, a thing does not act as a cause for its own self-nature.
The cause of what is produced is itself the sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*).
What is the sovereign condition?
As it is said:
Does this dharma act as a dominant condition for that dharma?
Or is there a time when this dharma does not act as a dominant condition for that dharma? Answer:
"No. [The opponent] asks:
"When a phenomenon arises, with the exception of its own self-nature, all other phenomena serve as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*); through their conjunction, it arises."
There is no time when they are not in a state of conjunction;
why, then, do they not arise repeatedly? The Venerable Sūmīta said:
"When a phenomenon arises, there is a single conjunction; there is neither a second nor a plurality."
At the time of the cessation of dharmas, there is likewise a single unification, without duality or multiplicity.
Furthermore, some say that once a dharma has arisen, many other dharmas arise; those [subsequent] dharmas lack the power to cause it to arise again.
It is like a person who, while falling into one river, wishes to rise up but falls into another;
such is the case here as well. The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
A single combination can produce a single phenomenon; there is no single phenomenon that can produce two fruits.
Question: What is the essential nature of the causal condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*)?
Answer: All dharmas. Question:
What is the meaning of "condition through power"?
The answer is:
the sense of being preeminent is the meaning of "condition through power."
Question: As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*,
what is the object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*)?
What is the condition of sovereign power?
The answer is: all phenomena.
What great superiority does this possess?
The answer is:
whether considered in terms of its objective sphere or its preceding objects, it possesses no great superiority.
If it were by means of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), there would be many superiorities.
If one takes all phenomena as being without self (*anātman*) as the object, what phenomenon would not be taken as an object?
The answer is:
It does not take itself as an object.
Self-nature does not take its associated or co-existent factors as objects.
Who, then, does not exercise sovereign power?
It is solely its own substance.
The causal condition of sovereign power is precisely the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
What is the meaning of "efficient cause"?
Answer: As previously stated, the meaning of non-obstruction is the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Question:

If the meaning of "non-obstruction" is the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), then it is like how the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātv-āyatana*) obstruct the human realm such that other realms cannot arise therein;
or as visual consciousness obstructs its own locus so that other consciousnesses do not arise there;
or as the houses and trees occupying a particular site prevent other houses and trees from arising in that same location.
If this is so, why is the meaning of non-obstruction the meaning of the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*)?
The answer is:
because it is as has been stated, the meaning of non-obstruction is the meaning of the efficient cause.

According to the meaning of these words, when one speaks of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of the human intermediate state, one speaks of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases of other destinies, saying:
"I obstruct the human destiny, but do not obstruct other destinies, so that you may be born in those other destinies."
In this way, visual consciousness says to the other consciousnesses:
"I obstruct the location of the eye-faculty, but do not obstruct other locations, so that you may arise.
It is like one house or tree saying to other houses or trees:
I obstruct this particular location, but do not obstruct other locations, so that you may achieve success.
For this reason, the meaning of "non-obstruction" is the meaning of "efficient cause" (*kāraṇa-hetu*).
When the five aggregates arise, all dharmas act as conditions of empowerment; if there were even a single dharma that did not accord with them, they would not arise.
Question: Just as when a form-dharma arises, all dharmas act as conditions of empowerment.
When formless phenomena arise, do all phenomena also act as a condition of empowerment?
If, when formless phenomena arise, all phenomena act as a condition of empowerment, then when material phenomena arise, do all phenomena also act as a condition of empowerment?
He replied: "No.
If, when the power of form-phenomena acts as a condition, the power of formless phenomena likewise acts as a condition, would it follow that all phenomena are form?"
If, when acting as a dominant condition for formless phenomena, it likewise acts as a dominant condition for material phenomena, would it follow that all phenomena are formless?
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:

when a phenomenon arises, it arises because there is a cause; when it ceases, it ceases because there is a cause. It arises because there is an object-condition; it ceases because there is an object-condition. It arises because there is a causal basis; it ceases because there is a causal basis.
The Dārṣṭāntikas explain it thus: when a phenomenon arises, it arises because there is a cause;

when a phenomenon ceases, it ceases because there is no cause. It arises because there is an object-condition (ālambana); it ceases because there is no object-condition. It arises because there is a causal basis (vastu); it ceases because there is no causal basis.

I do not say that the dharma of cessation has causes and conditions; rather, one should employ an analogy: it is like shooting an arrow into the air—the effort is exerted at the time of its departure, but no effort is exerted at the time of its fall. Who could be said to act as its cause?
It is like a potter’s wheel: when it turns, force is applied; when it stays still, no force is applied. Who acts as the cause for this?
The critique says: one should not speak thus; what was said previously is correct.
Question: If that is so, how can the analogies stated by the Dārṣṭāntikas be reconciled? Answer:
This need not necessarily be reconciled.

Why is this so? This is neither Sūtra, Vinaya, nor Abhidharma; one cannot use worldly analogies to challenge the dharmas of the noble ones (ārya). Worldly dharmas are distinct, and the dharmas of the noble ones are distinct.
If one wishes to understand this, how should one understand it?
The answer is:
that arrow’s falling also has a cause.
What serves as the cause?
When the arrow is in flight, if it is obstructed by various other objects such as shields and causes it to fall, these are its causes.
Even in the absence of such obstructions, the exertion of force at the moment of shooting is its cause.
If there were no impeller, by what means would it fall?
Thus, regarding the rotation of a potter’s wheel, if one were to hold it with the hand or some other object so that it does not turn, that is its cause.
If there were no one to hold it with the hands and so forth, the previous application of force during its rotation would be its cause.
If there were no rotation, by what means could it remain? Question:
“If phenomena have causes for their arising and also have causes for their cessation,” and so forth, as explained at length.
Why is it that they do not cease at the time of arising, nor arise at the time of cessation?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:
The combination at the time of arising is different from the combination at the time of ceasing.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the functioning of conditions is different when a phenomenon arises, and the functioning of conditions is different when a phenomenon ceases.
What is meant by "being different at the time of arising"?
When acting as a condition at the time of arising, it is concordant; when acting as a condition at the time of ceasing, it is non-concordant.
It is just as in foreign lands, where during the summer retreat, people generally carry their robes and bowls from one monastery to another.
At that time, the bandits skillfully observed their signs;
seeing these bhikṣus emerge from the wilderness into inhabited areas, the bandits approached them, paid their respects, and followed after them.
When they arrive at a remote and perilous place where no one dwells, they plunder their robes and bowls and refuse to comply;
it is the same for them. A single dharma acts as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for many dharmas, and many dharmas likewise act as the efficient cause for a single dharma.
Question: When a single dharma acts as a cause for many dharmas, does it give [its causal efficacy] as a single dharma or as many dharmas?
And when many dharmas act as causes for a single dharma, do they give [their causal efficacy] as many dharmas or as a single dharma?
If a single dharma acts as a cause for many dharmas, why is it not a case of a non-unitary cause producing effects?
If many dharmas act as causes for a single dharma, why does that single dharma not produce many effects?
When many dharmas act as a *adhipati-pratyaya* (dominant condition) for a single dharma, how do they so act?
Is it by acting as many [conditions] together, or by acting as a single [condition]?
If they act as a dominant condition for a single dharma by being many, why does it not follow that there are multiple causes for a single effect?
If it were as you say—that one dharma gives [to another]—how could many dharmas constitute a single dharma?
The critique states:
One should speak thus:
A single dharma acts as a condition of power for many dharmas, and many dharmas act as a condition of power for a single dharma. Question:
If this is so, why is it that many do not become one, and one does not become many?

Answer: According to my doctrine, the one also acts as the many and the many also acts as the one; this is by virtue of the meaning of the causal agent, not because there is any difference in the essential nature of the phenomena.
Past phenomena act as the proximate efficient cause for future and present phenomena.
This means that past phenomena say to future and present phenomena:
"If I did not act as your efficient cause, you would be without a cause."
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), there is none that is without a cause.
A present phenomenon acts as the "proximate efficient cause" (*kāraṇahetu*) for past and future phenomena. The meaning is that the present phenomenon says to the past and future phenomena:
"If I did not act as your efficient cause, then you past phenomena would have no fruit, and you future phenomena would have no cause."
Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is none that is without fruit or without cause.

Past phenomena are the causes produced by future and present phenomena; future and present phenomena are the fruits of past phenomena; and future phenomena are the causes produced by past and present phenomena.
Dharmas of the past and present are not the fruit of the future.
Why is this? Because a fruit must either be simultaneous with or subsequent to its cause.
Past and present [dharmas] do not coexist with nor follow after future dharmas.
Present dharmas act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for past and future dharmas, and future dharmas act as the efficient cause for [future] dharmas.
Future dharmas act as fruits for present dharmas, whereas past dharmas are not fruits.
Why is this? Because a fruit-dharma must be either simultaneous with or subsequent to its cause.
Past phenomena do not coexist with, nor do they follow after, present phenomena.
Material phenomena act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) for material phenomena and produce their dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
Form-dharmas act as the produced cause (*kārya-hetu*) and the fruit of sovereign power (*adhipati-phala*) for formless dharmas;
formless dharmas act as the produced cause and the fruit of sovereign power for formless dharmas.
Non-material phenomena act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) for material phenomena.
Likewise, the visible acts as the efficient cause and the dominant fruit for the visible; the visible for the invisible; the invisible for the invisible; and the invisible for the visible.
The same applies to the categories of the resistant and the non-resistant, as well as the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing.
Conditioned phenomena act as the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) and produce the fruit of dominance (*adhipati-phala*) for conditioned phenomena;
however, conditioned phenomena act as the fruit of dominance for unconditioned phenomena, but do not act as the efficient cause for them.
Unconditioned phenomena do not act as the efficient cause for unconditioned phenomena, nor do they act as the dominant fruit [of them].
Unconditioned phenomena act as the efficient cause for conditioned phenomena, but do not act as their dominant fruit.
Question: For what reason do conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) have causes and conditions, while unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) have neither cause nor condition? Answer:

The nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) is weak and inferior, requiring causes and conditions; the nature of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is powerful and robust, not requiring causes and conditions.
Just as a person who is weak and inferior depends on others for their existence, whereas a person who is powerful and robust does not depend on others for their existence, so it is with these two.

Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) require causes and conditions because they have something to be produced; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) do not require causes and conditions because they have nothing to be produced.
It is like a digger requiring a mattock, or a reaper requiring a sickle;
it is the same for those [phenomena].
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) follow the course of the world; because they can take up results and cognize conditions, they require causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya*).
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) do not follow the course of the world, as explained in detail above.
Just as a person traveling a long distance requires provisions, whereas one who does not travel far does not require them, so it is with this case as well.
Furthermore, conditioned phenomena are like a king and his retinue, or like Indra and his retinue; therefore, they require causes and conditions.
Unconditioned dharmas are like a king, whereas conditioned dharmas are like the king’s retinue;
they are like Indra, whereas conditioned dharmas are like Indra’s retinue. Therefore, they do not require causes and conditions.

Question: Regarding the non-arising of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), is it because of an obstruction by the conditioned that they do not arise, or is it because of an obstruction by the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) that they do not arise?
Answer: It is because conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) create obstacles that [a dharma] does not arise; this is not the case for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

The power of unconditioned phenomena does not act as an obstacle to a dharma that is not destined to arise by withholding its conditions; rather, if it is destined to arise, they act as favorable conditions.
It is like the edge of a stagnant pond where wooden mouths of lions or makara fish are carved, through which water flows out.

When the water does not flow, it is not because these mouths create an obstruction; rather, there are other conditions that cause the water not to flow. When the water does flow, they serve as its support;
so it is with this as well.

Question: Unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) and conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma) have two kinds of conditions, namely, the condition as object (ālambanapratyaya) and the condition of sovereign power (ādhipatipratyaya).

When an unconditioned phenomenon acts as a proximate condition of sovereign power for another, does it act toward that which possesses a condition (sapratiyogin), or toward that which lacks a condition (apratiyogin)?
Answer: Some say that it applies to those with conditions (*sappaccaya*) but not to those without conditions (*appaccaya*).
The critique says:
One should not speak in this way.
One should speak thus:
"The conditions for exercising power over others are no different [from the object itself], like a heap of small beans."

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it may or may not bestow [its influence]. If there is a dharma that possesses an object, it bestows it; if there is no dharma that possesses an object, it does not bestow it.

Wholesome dharmas act as the immediate efficient cause (*samanantara-kāraṇa*) for wholesome dharmas; wholesome dharmas act as the immediate efficient cause for unwholesome dharmas; unwholesome dharmas act as the immediate efficient cause for unwholesome dharmas; and unwholesome dharmas act as the immediate efficient cause for wholesome dharmas.

Regarding how wholesome dharmas act as the immediate causal condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for wholesome dharmas: because of wholesome karma, one is born into the family of a great wealthy householder or a merchant leader; since all the members of that household delight in practicing what is wholesome, by virtue of such association, they also come to delight in practicing what is wholesome. This is called wholesome dharmas acting as the immediate causal condition for wholesome dharmas.

Regarding how the wholesome and the unwholesome act as proximate causal conditions: because of wholesome karma, one is born into the family of a king or a great minister; although the members of that family habitually practice various evils, because of one’s close association with them, one also comes to habitually practice various evils. This is called the wholesome and the unwholesome acting as proximate causal conditions.

Regarding how the unwholesome serves as the proximate causal agent for the unwholesome: because of unwholesome karma, one is born into a family of immoral conduct; due to such intimacy, one constantly commits various evils. This is called the unwholesome serving as the proximate causal agent for the unwholesome.

Regarding how the unwholesome serves as the proximate causal condition for the wholesome: because of unwholesome karma, the body gives rise to severe affliction; through this sense of weariness and aversion, one practices the wholesome. This is called the unwholesome serving as the proximate causal condition for the wholesome.

Internal phenomena act as the immediate efficient cause for internal phenomena; internal phenomena act as the immediate efficient cause for external phenomena; external phenomena act as the immediate efficient cause for external phenomena; and external phenomena act as the immediate efficient cause for internal phenomena.
Regarding internal phenomena acting as the immediate efficient cause for internal phenomena: it is like one person being able to provide for many.
Regarding internal phenomena acting as the immediate efficient cause for external phenomena: it is like a person sowing external seeds.
External giving to the external is, for example, like using manure, soil, water, and so forth to nourish crops.
External giving to the internal is, for example, like using food, drink, and so forth to nourish the bodies of sentient beings.

In this manner, the number of sentient beings compared to the number of sentient beings; the number of sentient beings compared to the number of non-sentient things; the number of non-sentient things compared to the number of non-sentient things; and the number of non-sentient things compared to the number of sentient beings, are explained in detail as above.
One realm can nourish five realms, just as many people might eat a single sheep’s carcass; some may perform wholesome deeds while others may perform unwholesome deeds.
Those who perform wholesome deeds can nourish two realms, namely the celestial realm and the human realm.
Those who commit evil deeds nourish the three realms of existence, namely: hell, animals, and hungry ghosts. Question:
If a single person kills a living being, and all sentient beings provide the causal conditions for that act, why is it that some incur the karmic guilt of killing while others do not?
Answer: If one employs the means for killing and the fruit of killing is fulfilled, one incurs the offense of killing;
if one does not employ the means and the fruit of killing is not fulfilled, one does not incur the offense of killing.
Furthermore, if one possesses a malicious mind, one incurs the offense of killing; if one lacks a malicious mind, the intent to kill does not result in the offense of killing.

Question: If a single sentient person’s taking what is not given serves as the contributory cause for all sentient beings, why is it that some incur the offense of taking what is not given while others do not?

Answer: If one employs the means and fulfills the result, one incurs the offense of taking what is not given; if one does not employ the means and does not fulfill the result, one does not incur the offense of taking what is not given.
Furthermore, if one takes another's property with a mind of greed, perceiving it as such, one incurs the offense of taking what is not given; otherwise, one does not.
It is asked:

Since external objects are produced by the power of all sentient beings, why is it that in some cases one incurs the offense of taking what is not given from another, while in other cases one does not?
The answer is:
Regarding those who possess both the fruit of effort and the fruit of power, one incurs the offense of taking what is not given from them.
Regarding those who possess only the fruit of power but lack the fruit of effort, one does not incur the offense of taking what is not given from them.
Furthermore, if one forms the notion that an object belongs to oneself, one incurs an offense against that person;
if one does not form the notion that an object belongs to oneself, one incurs no offense against that person.
Question: What is the difference between the fruit of majestic power (*vaśitā-phala*) and the fruit of functional effort (*prayoga-phala*)? Answer:
The agent is the fruit of effort, while the enjoyer is the fruit of sovereign power.

For example, when a farmer sows, this is the fruit of effort and not the fruit of sovereign power; whereas one who consumes the resulting grain is the fruit of sovereign power and not the fruit of effort.
Question: Just as the four continents, Mount Sumeru, and other external objects arise through the power of the karma of all sentient beings,
why do these things not diminish when some among those sentient beings attain nirvana?
The Venerable Sūmīpa said:
"There are beings from other worlds who come to be born here; because of the power of their karma, [the world] does not diminish."
Furthermore, it arises by the power of the karma of all sentient beings; even if only a single sentient being were to remain, it would not diminish. Why is this so?
Since the majestic power of karma is present within them as well, how much more so for the sake of incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) nayutas of sentient beings?
Just as a person of noble status, by virtue of the majestic power of their karma, produces gardens, groves, pavilions, elephants, horses, and chariots.
In this way, although such things as sentient beings and non-sentient objects do not diminish even when that person dies,
it is the same for him [the deceased] as well. The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
Because of past karma, it does not diminish. Question:
If a Wheel-Turning Sage King rules over the four continents and attains sovereign mastery, what kind of karmic retribution is that?
Answer: This is the retribution for karma that produces the place of birth. Question:
Are there more *kāraṇa-hetu* (efficient causes), or are there more *kāraṇa-phala* (effects produced by efficient causes)?
The answer is:
there are more *kāraṇa-hetu*, not more *kāraṇa-phala*.
Why is this so? Because all phenomena (*dharma*) are the causes of what is produced, and the causes and effects of what is produced are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).
For this reason, such a doctrine is formulated.
Are there any phenomena that are neither causes, nor immediate antecedents, nor objects, nor dominant conditions?
Answer: Yes; for instance, a phenomenon’s own essence [is not related] to itself in these ways.
Does it exist within the substance of another?
The answer is:
yes; conditioned phenomena exist within the unconditioned, and unconditioned phenomena exist within the unconditioned.
The Buddhist scriptures speak of three kinds of majestic power (*prabhāva*): namely, the majestic power of the world, the majestic power of the self, and the majestic power of the Dharma.

As for the majestic power of the world: it is like when a certain affliction arises before one and the objects of that affliction are easily obtained; yet, because of the censure and reproach of worldly people, one does not commit unwholesome deeds.
As for my power, it is like this: even when afflictions manifest before me and their objects are easily encountered, I do not commit evil deeds so that I may not fall into the evil realms.

Regarding the majestic power of the Dharma: suppose there is someone for whom an affliction arises and the object [of that affliction] is easily obtained; because they have heard much of the Dharma, they do not commit evil deeds, and they also do not commit evil deeds so as not to incur the reproach and suspicion of the world.
Question: Why are these three called "majestic power" (vaśitā)? Answer:

Because they can closely give rise to wholesome dharmas, all sentient beings die when their power is exhausted; except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose power is inexhaustible as he enters parinirvāṇa.
Question: Is there increase or decrease in the causal factors that produce [results]? Answer:
There are. For example, when many people are pulling a large timber, some among them exert all the strength of their hands and feet, while others do not exert much effort.
Or, when erecting a great stupa, the ropes used to bind it may be tight in some places and slack in others.
Such as these are called external dharmas having increase and decrease.
For example, when one provides for one's kinsmen and supplies their necessities more excellently than others, this is called internal dharmas having increase and decrease.
If it is a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is also a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and a sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Thus, for each individual condition, there should be four meanings of conditions in succession.
Question: If that is so, how can there be the substance of the four conditions? Answer:
The fourfold [classification] is established by way of their functions, not by way of their substantial entities. What is this process?
For example, as a preceding moment causes a succeeding moment to increase, it is termed "conditioned cause" (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That which precedes acts as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the arising of that which follows; this is called the sequential condition.
That which follows is able to take what precedes as its object; this is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
That which does not create an obstruction for others is the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is like the dharma of a seed; the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the dharma of opening and guiding; the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) is the dharma of grasping a staff; and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is the dharma of non-obstruction.

In brief, "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) carry the meaning of four types of conditions; it is not the case that every single phenomenon arising from causes and conditions possesses all four types of conditions.
Question: What is the distinction between a cause (hetu) and a condition (pratyaya)?
The Venerable Sūmī said:
"The cause is itself the condition.
If this exists, then that exists; thus it is both the cause and the condition."
The Blessed One also said:
"Ānanda, with such causes, such conditions, and such activities, birth becomes the cause of aging and death."

Question: If it is said that "when this exists, that comes to be," such that this is the cause and this is the condition—for example, when a person sees a jar and a cognitive mind arises, is the jar the cause of that cognition?
Answer: It is not because of the existence of the jar that it serves as a cause for cognition. Why is this so?
The cognition of a jar does not arise from the jar alone; it arises only when there is a conjunction.
This conjunction is the condition for cognition, not the jar itself.
Furthermore, some say that the conjunction is the cause, while the object of the conjunction is the condition.
Question: If one [condition] does not act as a cause, do many [conditions] also not act as causes? Answer:
Just as individual phenomena cannot serve as causes, yet when these various phenomena are combined,
they can indeed serve as causes.
What is the nature of this process?
Just as a single individual thing is not called a "conjunction" (saṃghāta), but rather it is called a conjunction because of the gathering of many things;
so it is with that [case] as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say that similarity is the cause (hetu) and dissimilarity is the condition (pratyaya).
"Similarity" refers to, for example, barley being like barley, or fire being like fire.
Question: In what way is barley similar to a barley sprout?
Answer: Generally speaking, barley is the cause of the sprout. Question:
If that were so, would the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), being causes in this general sense, also be the cause of the sprout?
Furthermore, there are those who say that what is proximate is the cause (*hetu*) and what is remote is the condition (*pratyaya*).
Question: If that were so, there would be no distinction between causes (*hetu*) and conditions (*pratyaya*). Why is this?
If the mind arises in succession, is the preceding wholesome mind not the cause, and would it not be called a condition?
Furthermore, some say that what is unique is the cause, while what is shared is the condition.
Question: If that were so, then barley would also be both a sprout and something rotten; would those, too, be conditions?
For example, the eye is the locus for the arising of visual consciousness, not shared with other consciousnesses.
Is that eye also the cause of the visual consciousness?
Furthermore, some say that "arising" is the cause and "following-arising" is the condition. Question:
If that were so, would it not follow that birth is not the condition and that which follows birth is not the cause?
Furthermore, there are those who say that growth by means of one's own substance is the cause, while growth by means of another's substance is the condition.
Question: If that is so, when a present wholesome mind takes wholesome phenomena as its object, is it called only a cause (*hetu*) and not a condition (*pratyaya*)?
The Venerable Buddhadeva replied:
The agent is the cause and the action is the condition.
Furthermore, some say that what is similar is the cause and what is dissimilar is the condition.
Still others say that what is proximate is the cause and what is remote is the condition.
As it is with near and far, so it is with this and that.
This acting cause is definitively the fruit of all phenomena and is the fruit of sovereign power (*adhipatiphala*). Question:
If there is an associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), is there also a co-arising cause (sahabhū-hetu)? Answer:
If there is an associated cause, there is also a co-arising cause.
Is there a co-existent cause that is not an associated cause?
The answer is:
yes, there are non-associated factors that possess a co-existent cause.
If there is an associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), is there also a similar cause (sabhāga-hetu)?
If there is a similar cause, is there also an associated cause?
This should be elaborated at length as a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
There are cases where there is an associated cause but no similar cause: namely, the associated causes of future phenomena.
There are cases where there is a similar cause but no associated cause: namely, the similar causes of non-associated phenomena.
Those that have both an associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) are the associated dharmas that possess a similar cause.
Those that have neither an associated cause nor a similar cause are all things other than those previously mentioned.
If there is an associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), is there also a pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu)?
If there is a pervasive cause, is there also an associated cause?
This should be expanded into four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).

Regarding those that have an associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) but lack a universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*): these are the associated causes of the future, as well as the past and present associated causes that are not universal.
Regarding "the universal cause is not the associated cause": this refers to the universal cause of non-associated phenomena.
Regarding "the associated cause is the universal cause": this refers to the universal cause of associated phenomena.
Regarding those that are neither associated causes nor universal causes: these are all cases except for those mentioned above.
If there is an associated cause, is there also a retributive cause?
If there is a retributive cause, is there also an associated cause?
This is elaborated at length in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is a concomitant cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) but not a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) refers to the concomitant causes that are neutral (*avyākṛta*) or untainted (*anāsrava*).
That which is a retributive cause but not a concomitant cause refers to the retributive causes of dissociated phenomena (*viprayukta-dharma*).
That which is both an associated cause (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) and a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is the associated-retributive cause.
That which is neither an associated cause nor a retributive cause consists of all things other than those mentioned above.
If there is an associated cause (saṃprayuktaka-hetu), is there also a productive cause (kāraṇa-hetu)? Answer:
If there is an associated cause, there is also a productive cause.
Is there that which is a *kṛtaka-hetu* (produced cause) but not a *samprayuktaka-hetu* (associated cause)?
Answer: There is;
namely, all non-associated (*viprayukta*) dharmas that are *kṛtaka-hetus*.
If there is a co-existent cause, is there also a similar cause?
Answer: If there is a similar cause, there is also a co-existent cause.
Is there a co-existent cause that is not a similar cause?
The answer is:
Yes; namely, the co-existent causes of the future world.
If there is a co-existent cause, is there also a pervasive cause?
Answer: If there is a pervasive cause, there is also a co-existent cause.
Is there a co-existent cause that is not a pervasive cause?
Answer: Yes;
there are co-existent causes that are not pervasive causes.
If there is a coexistent cause, is there also a retributive cause?
The answer is:
if there is a retributive cause, there is also a coexistent cause.
Is there a co-existent cause that is not a retribution cause?
Answer: Yes; there is the co-existent cause of the indeterminate and the untainted (anāsrava).
If there is a co-arising cause (sahabhū-hetu), is there also an efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu)? Answer:
If there is a co-arising cause, there is also an efficient cause.
Is there that which is a produced cause (*kṛta-hetu*) but not a co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)? Answer:
Yes; unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are produced causes.
If there is a similar cause, is there also a pervasive cause?
The answer is:
if there is a pervasive cause, there is also a similar cause.
Is there a case where a similar cause exists without being a pervasive cause?
The answer is:
Yes, namely, a similar cause that is not pervasive.
Is there that which is a similar cause and also a retributive cause?
Or is there that which is a retributive cause and also a similar cause?
This should be elaborated extensively as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
There are causes that are similar but not retributive, namely neutral and untainted similar causes.
There are causes that are retributive but not similar, namely retributive causes in the future world.
That which is both a similar cause and a retributive cause refers to past and present retributive causes.
That which is neither a similar cause nor a retributive cause refers to all things other than those already mentioned.
If there is a similar cause, is there also a producing cause? Answer:
If there is a similar cause, there is also a producing cause.
Is there an object-condition (*kṛta-hetu*) that is not a similar-condition (*sabhāga-hetu*)? Answer:
Yes; for example, unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) in the future world serve as object-conditions.
If there is a universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu), is there also a retributive cause (vipāka-hetu)?
If there is a retributive cause, is there also a universal cause?
Thus, one should elaborate the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) at length.
Regarding "all pervasive causes that are not retributive causes": these are the indeterminate pervasive causes.
Regarding "retributive causes that are not pervasive causes": these are the retributive causes of the future world, as well as the past and present retributive causes that are not pervasive.
Regarding "universal causes and retributive causes," this refers to universal retributive causes.
Regarding "neither universal nor retributive causes," this excludes the aforementioned instances.
If there is a pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu), is there also an efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu)? Answer:
If there is a pervasive cause, there is also an efficient cause.
Is there that which is a produced cause (*kṛta-hetu*) but not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)? Answer: Yes;
namely, the produced causes of future, past, and present phenomena that are not pervasive, as well as unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If there is a retributive cause, is there also a creative cause?
Answer: If there is a retributive cause, there is also a creative cause.
Is there that which is a cause of action (*karmahetu*) but not a cause of retribution (*vipākahetu*)?
The answer is:
Yes; namely, neutral (*avyākṛta*) and untainted (*anāsrava*) causes of action.
Question: Of these six causes, how many are material (rūpa) and how many are non-material (arūpa)? Answer:
The second category consists of those that are non-material (*arūpa*), namely the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);
the remainder are both material and non-material.

Just as it is with the material and non-material, so too should one understand the associated and the dissociated, the supported and the unsupported, the functional and the non-functional, the objective and the non-objective, the resistant and the non-resistant, and the visible and the invisible. They are likewise.
Question: Of these six causes, how many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)? Answer:
Two are with outflows (*sāsrava*), namely the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*) and the retributive cause (*vipākahetu*); the remainder are both with and without outflows (*anāsrava*). Question:
Among these six causes, how many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and how many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Answer: The five conditioned factors are the associated cause up to the retributive cause.
First are the conditioned and the unconditioned, which refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Question:
Of these six causes, how many are past, how many are present, and how many are future?
The answer is:
two belong to the past and present, namely the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);
three exist in all three time periods, namely the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
One exists in the three periods of time and yet does not exist within them; this refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*). Question:
Of these six causes, how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
The answer is:
one is unwholesome or neutral, namely the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);
the other is wholesome or unwholesome, namely the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
The remainder are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Question: Of these six causes, how many are bound to the desire realm, and so forth, up to being unbound?

Answer: Two are bound to the three realms, namely the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) and the retribution cause (*vipāka-hetu*); the remainder are either bound to the three realms or unbound. Question:
Regarding these six causes, how many are of the learner (śaikṣa), how many are of the non-learner (aśaikṣa), and how many are neither of the learner nor the non-learner?
The answer is:
two are neither of the learner nor the non-learner, namely, the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu) and the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu).
The remaining ones are of three kinds. Question:

Of these six causes, how many are abandoned by the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya), how many are abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya), and how many are not to be abandoned (aprahātavya)?
The answer is:
one is abandoned by the path of seeing, namely the omnipresent cause;
one is abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, namely the retributive cause.
The remainder are abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned. Question:
Among these six causes, how many are defiled and how many are undefiled?
Answer: One is defiled, namely the omnipresent cause (sarvatraga-hetu);
the others are both defiled and non-defiled.

Just as with the defiled and the undefiled, so too should one understand the faulty and the faultless, the black and the white, the obscured and the unobscured, and the subject to regression and the non-regressive.
Question: Of these six causes, how many have retribution and how many are without retribution? Answer:
One is "with retribution," namely the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*);
the others are both "with retribution" and "without retribution.
The associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) and the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) take their fruit and give their fruit during a single moment in the present life.

The similar cause (sabhāga-hetu), the pervasive cause (sarvatraga-hetu), and the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) take their fruit in the present, while they bestow their fruit in both the past and the present;
they take their fruit in a single moment, yet bestow their fruit over many moments.
Regarding the cause of retribution (*vipāka-hetu*): it takes up its fruit in the present, but bestows its fruit in the past;
it takes up its fruit in a single moment, yet bestows its fruit over many moments.
If a mind possesses latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and those latent dispositions possess that mind, do those latent dispositions then act as latent dispositions upon this mind?
...and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is for the purpose of refuting the arguments of those who maintain that the mind is single-pointed.
They assert as follows:
The mind with latent tendencies and the mind without latent tendencies are in fact one and the same mind. Why is this?
When the noble path arises, it is in conflict with the latent tendencies, but not in conflict with the mind.
It is like the method of sharpening a blade: it is incompatible with the stains, but not incompatible with the blade itself.
It is like the stains on a garment, a vessel, or a mirror: they are incompatible with the cleaning process, but not incompatible with the garment, the vessel, or the mirror.
Thus, when the Noble Path arises, it obstructs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), but does not obstruct the mind.
As long as the Noble Path has not arisen, the mind possesses latent tendencies; once the Noble Path has arisen, the mind is free of latent tendencies.
The proponents of the theory of a self (pudgalavādins) assert:
"It is the person who is bound and the person who is liberated;
it is not the dharmas that are bound or liberated. The Venerable Dharmatrāta asserts as follows:
There are proclivities that are dissociated from the mind and do not take [an object] as their condition. They assert this:

if they function as proclivities through being conditions or through association, then regarding untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), if they were to function as proclivities through association, they would always and constantly be proclivities, for there is no time when they are not associated with the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitasika*).

For these reasons—desiring to refute the positions of others, desiring to manifest one's own position, and desiring to demonstrate a meaning that accords with the characteristics of the Dharma—this treatise is composed.
If the mind possesses latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), there are five types of mind called "possessing latent tendencies":
the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to the mind abandoned through the path of cultivation.
For two reasons, the mind is said to possess latent tendencies: [the presence of the latent tendency itself and its association with the mind].
First, by way of their nature as latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); second, by way of their nature as concomitants (*sahāya*).
Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of suffering and the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are two factors:

The nature of the proclivities (*anuśaya*) and the nature of their associates (*sahāya*); all pervasive proclivities abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) possess the nature of being proclivities, while other proclivities lack both the nature of being proclivities and the nature of being associates.
Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of the origin and the proclivities abandoned through the vision of the origin, there are two factors:

The nature of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the nature of their associates (*sahāya*). All pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering possess the nature of being underlying tendencies; the remaining underlying tendencies possess neither the nature of being underlying tendencies nor the nature of being associates.
Regarding the mind abandoned through the vision of cessation and the underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation, there are two factors:

There is the nature of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) and the nature of companions (*sahāya*). All pervasive latent proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana*) possess the nature of latent proclivities; other latent proclivities possess neither the nature of latent proclivities nor the nature of companions.
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*).
The mind to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation have two natures:

the nature of being an underlying tendency (*anuśaya-bhāva*) and the nature of being its concomitants (*sahabhū-bhāva*). Regarding the universal underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), they possess the nature of being underlying tendencies; other underlying tendencies lack the nature of being underlying tendencies [but possess] the nature of being concomitants.
The mind abandoned through the vision of suffering is associated with both universal and non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*).
The same applies to that abandoned through the vision of origin.
The mind abandoned through the vision of cessation is associated with proclivities having impure objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and proclivities having pure objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*).
The same applies to those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding the mind abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), whether it be defiled or undefiled: when that mind is associated with the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned by the vision of suffering, and those universal proclivities abandoned by the vision of suffering, there are two factors:
the nature of the proclivity itself and the nature of its accompaniments.

The non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering have the nature of being proclivities; the universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of origin have the nature of being proclivities; and the remaining proclivities have the nature of being associated with proclivities.

Regarding the non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the associated mind of those non-universal proclivities, there are two factors:

the nature of being a proclivity and the nature of being an associate (*sahāya*). As for the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), they possess the nature of being proclivities but lack the nature of being associates; all other proclivities are devoid of both.
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the mind associated with the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have outflow-conditions (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as the proclivities themselves that have outflow-conditions and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, there are two factors: the nature of the proclivity (*anuśaya-svabhāva*) and the nature of its accompaniments (*paryavasthāna-svabhāva*).

All pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin possess the nature of being latent dispositions and the nature of being without companions; there are no others that accompany them.

The mind associated with latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the uncontaminated as their object, as well as those latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the uncontaminated as their object, coexist [with such a mind].

Furthermore, latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the contaminated as their object, along with all pervasive latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin, possess the nature of being latent dispositions and the nature of being without companions.
The remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) are entirely absent [in that state]. The same applies to those abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).
As for the defiled mind abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga), it is accompanied by the latent dispositions abandoned through the path of cultivation.

All pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) possess the nature of being proclivities but lack the nature of having companions;
all other proclivities lack both.

Those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*) that are non-defiled minds, as well as proclivities abandoned through the path of cultivation and those pervasive proclivities abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination, possess the nature of being proclivities but lack the nature of having companions.
The remaining latent dispositions (anuśaya) are entirely absent.
Those minds abandoned through the vision of suffering are of ten types: namely, the five minds associated with the [five] views;
the mind associated with doubt; the minds associated with craving, aversion, pride, and the unique ignorance (āveṇikāvidyā).

There are seven types of mind abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya): namely, the minds associated with the two views, doubt, craving, hatred, pride, and the mind associated with non-associated ignorance (āveṇikī avidyā).
The same applies to those abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*).

There are eight types of mind abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*): namely, minds associated with the three views, doubt (*vicikitsā*), craving (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and the mind associated with non-associated ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).

There are five types [of minds] to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path: namely, those associated with craving, aversion, pride, non-common ignorance, and those associated with non-defiled wholesome or neutral states.
