Regarding the mind associated with the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the ignorance associated with that view of a self, there are two aspects:
the nature of a latent tendency (anuśaya) and the nature of an associate (sahāya).

As for the other latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) and all pervasive latent tendencies abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya), they possess the nature of a latent tendency but lack the nature of an associate.
This applies likewise up to the latent tendency of pride abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya-māna-anuśaya*).

Regarding the mind associated with the unique ignorance (*āveṇika-avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, and the latent tendency of unique ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are two factors: the nature of the latent tendency (*anuśaya-bhāva*) and the nature of its associates (*sahāya-bhāva*).

The other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), as well as all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), possess the nature of being latent dispositions but lack the nature of having companions; the other latent dispositions are entirely absent [in them].
The same should be said for those abandoned through the vision of the origin.

The mind associated with wrong view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with that wrong view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, possess two natures:

the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) and the nature of an associate (*sahāya*). The latent tendencies conditioned by outflows (*sāsrava-ālambana-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as all pervasive latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and origin, possess the nature of a latent tendency but lack the nature of an associate.
It should be known that the mind associated with doubt is also like this.

Regarding the mind associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), and the view of grasping at views itself: it is accompanied by ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with the view of grasping at views;

as for the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflow-objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, and all those that are universal (*sarvatraga*), they possess the nature of being latent dispositions but lack the nature of having companions.
The others are entirely absent.
It should be known that craving, hatred, and pride abandoned through the vision of cessation are likewise.

The mind associated with the unique ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation is co-existent with the latent tendency (anuśaya) of the unique ignorance abandoned through the vision of cessation.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take contaminated objects as their conditions and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, as well as all those that are universal, possess the nature of being latent dispositions but lack the nature of having companions;
the other latent dispositions are entirely absent [in this case].
The same should be said for those to be abandoned by the vision of the path.

The mind associated with craving that is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, and the craving itself to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, are co-existent with ignorance associated with craving;
as for the remaining universal proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, they possess the nature of being proclivities but lack the nature of having companions;
all other proclivities are devoid of both.
It should be known that the same applies to anger and pride abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Regarding the mind associated with the non-common ignorance abandoned through the cultivation of the path, and the [factors] co-existent with the non-common ignorance abandoned through the cultivation of the path;

as well as the remaining latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the cultivation of the path and all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*): these possess the nature of being latent dispositions but lack the nature of having a companion.

In all other cases, there are no accompanying proclivities (*anuśaya*). Regarding the non-defiled mind abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), the proclivities abandoned through the path of cultivation, and all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*), they possess the nature of being proclivities but lack the nature of having companions;
in all other cases, there are no accompanying proclivities.
What has been explained is the *Abhidharmasamuccayavibhāṣā*.
If the mind possesses latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), there are five kinds within the three realms;
if the latent dispositions possess the mind, there are likewise five kinds within the three realms.
If there is a latent disposition (anuśaya) in the mind, or if there is a mind possessing latent dispositions, does that latent disposition act as a latent disposition toward this mind?
Answer: Sometimes it acts as a latent disposition, and sometimes it does not.
What are the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*)? The answer is:
those latent dispositions that have not yet been abandoned; by means of those dispositions, this mind possessing latent dispositions is made to possess them.
What does it mean for one not to be driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)? The answer is:
when all underlying tendencies are abandoned, those tendencies do not drive this mind that still possesses underlying tendencies.
Why is this so? Because the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been severed, they act as tendencies; because they have been severed, they no longer act as tendencies. Question:

For what reason is a mind associated with latent dispositions (anuśaya) called "possessing latent dispositions" when those dispositions have not been abandoned, yet it is not so called when they have been abandoned?
Is a mind that is associated [with a defilement] always called "possessing latent dispositions," whether those associated dispositions have been abandoned or not?
The answer is:
It was previously stated that the mind is said to possess latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) for two reasons:
first, by virtue of being of the nature of a latent tendency itself; second, by virtue of being associated with the nature of a latent tendency.
The various underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) together with the mind are called the nature of the underlying tendency (*anuśayatva*), not the nature of an associate (*sahāyatva*).
If those [tendencies] are severed, the meaning of that nature of the underlying tendency is also severed.
There are two aspects to the associated underlying tendency (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*):

There is the nature of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and the nature of their associates (*sahāya*). If one attains the abandonment of the nature of the underlying tendencies, then one abandons the nature of their associates;
if one does not abandon them, one cannot eliminate the nature of the associates of the mind.
Regarding the passage on "removing the grass and bark," the Venerable Vasumitra said:

"The proclivities that function through association cause the mind to be afflicted; those that function through objects likewise cause the mind to be afflicted. There is no distinction between those that are associated with non-affliction and those that are not, yet this is not the case for those that function through objects."
The underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated [with a mind] obscure the mind; those that take it as an object (*ālambana-anuśaya*) do not.
The associated underlying tendencies share the same basis (*āśraya*), the same mental activity (*ākāra*), and the same object (*ālambana*); those that take it as an object do not.
The associated proclivities (anuśaya) arise, abide, and cease simultaneously with the mind; the object-proclivities (ālambanānuśaya) are not so.
Furthermore, they share the same fruit, the same basis, and the same retribution; the object-proclivities are not so.
The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are associated with the mind arise simultaneously with it, whereas those that take the mind as their object do not.
There is no way to remove the latent dispositions associated with the mind, just as one cannot strip away the bark from the *viṃśa* grass.
If a latent disposition causes the mind to be possessed by it, does that mind then possess that latent disposition?
Answer: It may be that it is not different from that, or it may be that it is different from that.
Regarding "it is not different from that," some teachers say it refers to the defiled mind of an ordinary person bound by all fetters.
The critique states:
One should not speak in this manner. Why is that?
This may be so for one who is bound by all fetters; it may also be so for one who is not so bound.
It may be so for a defiled mind; it may also be so for an undefiled mind.
One should speak thus:
If the mind is not severed from the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is said to be "driven by the tendencies," and the mind is termed "possessing tendencies" (*sānuśaya*);
if it is not driven by the tendencies, it is said that the mind is "without tendencies" (*an-anuśaya*).

Regarding "this is that" and "this is different": when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, if the mind takes as its object that which is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering or that which is to be abandoned by the vision of origination—then, if it is "that," it is driven by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of origination;
if it is "different," it is not driven by those [tendencies] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Question: For what reason is it said that [a phenomenon] is "that" when belonging to another category (*anya-jāti*), and "different" when belonging to its own category (*sva-jāti*)? Answer:

Therefore, it was previously stated: even if the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) were identical to the mind that possesses the latent tendency, it would be so because that [mind] is a latent tendency conditioned by and associated with what is to be abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); however, it is said to be distinct because it is not a latent tendency for what is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is "different" because it is placed in a different location.
How is it placed in a different location?
Because it has been severed, it is said to be placed in a different location.
Furthermore, some say that although one originally attained mastery and acted according to one's will, this has now been severed; therefore, it is said to be different.
Others say that because it has now been severed, there is nothing further to be done, just like a dead person; therefore, it is said to be different.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the power of the Noble Path causes that [state] to become different, it is called "different.
A question is asked:
Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is also this state of being that and being different; why is it not mentioned?
Answer: Some say that when something should have been stated but was not, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete explanation (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*). Others say:

if "that" refers to another seed and "this" refers to a different seed, then it is explained in this context; however, regarding what is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), "that" and "this" both refer to their own seeds, and for this reason it was not mentioned.
Question: What is the latent tendency through object-conditioning (*ālambanānuśaya*)?
What is the latent tendency through association (*samprayogānuśaya*)?
The śramaṇas of Kaśmīr maintain this view:

"The various proclivities (anuśaya) follow their respective objects of activity; just as craving (tṛṣṇā) finds delight and satisfaction in its object, so too, it is explained at length, do the other proclivities follow their respective objects of activity."
Regarding the associated latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), they are like those who share the same crime and are bound together.
The śramaṇas of the West maintain this teaching:
the meaning of "binding" is that which acts as a condition for the latent tendencies.
The meaning of "approaching" (*upaga*) is that which is associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). The Venerable Vāhya said:
"For four reasons, the underlying tendencies are called 'that by which one is bound' (*anuśayita*)."
First, falling into an evil state of mind;
second, being like the heat of fire;
third, being like smoke, dust, and grime.
Fourth, this is a reprimand.

Regarding "falling into an evil state of mind": it is like one person committing an evil deed and causing many others to do so as well; because of a single affliction, many minds and mental factors all fall into an evil state of mind.

"Just as fire is hot": just as when an iron ball is heated by fire, whatever vessel it is placed in becomes hot throughout, so too do the afflictions, arising from whichever mental state they originate in, cause that entire state to become heated.
Regarding "like smoke, dust, and grime": just as the places where smoke, dust, and grime adhere are made defiled by them, so too do these various afflictions defile the mind wherever they arise.

Regarding "reproach": just as when a certain bhikṣu commits an evil deed and causes the Saṃgha to reproach him, so too do these messengers cause his mind to experience reproach according to the place where he is reborn.
What are the latent tendencies associated with [the mind]?
Answer: They are those latent tendencies that are activated by taking [the mind] as their object.
The same applies to the latent dispositions associated with mental factors (*saṃprayuktānuśaya*). Question:
Since the latent dispositions associated with mental factors lack an object (*anālambana*), why are they said to be like those that possess an object (*sālambana*)?
Answer: Although the latent proclivities associated with the mind lack an object, they still possess the four faults mentioned above. Question:
Can past and future [defilements] act as conditions? Answer: They can.
If it were not a "causing agent," then when a non-defiled mind is present, there would have to be no "causing agent" at all.
Furthermore, others say that it gives rise to various acquisitions (*prāpti*), just as fire produces smoke.
The arising of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) and their acquisitions (*prāpti*) in the past and future is likewise.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one does not [admit this], it contradicts the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The Buddha told the young bhikṣu Mālakīmāta:
"You do not know the affairs of desire, much less give rise to a mind of desire; yet you are driven by the craving for desire."
Furthermore, there are those who say that, for five reasons, one is driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) regarding the past and the future:
first, not severing their cause;
second, obtaining non-severance; [and so forth].
3. Not transforming the vessel;
4. Not knowing the conditions;
5. Not attaining the remedy.
If there are underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) in the mind, and the mind has underlying tendencies, should those tendencies in this mind be abandoned?

This teaching states that they should be abandoned by means of their objects (*ālambana*). While the underlying tendencies can be suppressed with respect to their objects, the associated (*samprayukta*) underlying tendencies cannot be suppressed, just as one cannot remove the bark from the *vijaṣa* grass.
"If the mind has underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and so forth, as explained at length, how can one sever all underlying tendencies while not severing them with respect to their objects?
One should not say: 'The underlying tendencies are not severed with respect to their objects.'"
Why is this? Because it has already been asked previously.
One should state it as follows:
There are latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have not yet been abandoned and those that should be abandoned. What are those that have not yet been abandoned?
They are the latent tendencies already abandoned, as well as the associated latent tendencies.
How are the latent tendencies abandoned?
Answer: They are abandoned by means of their objects.

Regarding "the meaning previously manifested": this refers to what was stated above, that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) which take objects as conditions (*ālambana*) should be abandoned; now, I shall explain the terminology.
Because these underlying tendencies give rise to faults and afflictions with respect to their objects, they must be subdued within those very objects.
Just as a person who is fond of gambling and delights in entering taverns or brothels can be restrained and subdued,
so too can the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that give rise to faults within their objects be restrained and subdued.
"In this way, do you say that the conditions for the messengers are severed?
This is a definitive statement regarding another.
If one speaks of another's faults without making a definitive statement regarding that other, it conversely produces one's own fault."
He makes this statement.
The reply is:

"If one were to say this—that the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) which are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path have the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object—how would these proclivities be abandoned?"
If one says that these associated proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned, it must first be established:
"The proclivities are abandoned by way of their objects (*ālambana-prahāṇa*), not by way of dissociation (*asamprayoga-prahāṇa*).
If, as has been stated, the proclivities are abandoned by way of their objects, then those proclivities would no longer produce affliction (*ādīnava*) with respect to their objects.
It should be stated as follows:

regarding those latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have the outflow-tainted (sāsrava) as their object and pertain to the cessation of views and the path to cessation, these latent tendencies are to be abandoned.
When these latent tendencies are abandoned, those [other] latent tendencies are also abandoned.
Just as a tree flourishes with its roots, trunk, leaves, and so forth, yet if its root is severed, the trunk and other parts no longer flourish;
it is the same in that case. Question:

If that is so, it was previously established that the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are abandoned through their objects; now, however, it is clarified that the underlying tendencies are abandoned through subsequent objects.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "In this way, are the underlying tendencies abandoned through their objects?"
Answer: It is said that the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) are abandoned when their objects are seen.
If this is the case, how are those proclivities abandoned which have the cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) as their objects and are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)?
If it is abandoned through the vision of suffering or its origin, these latent tendencies (anuśaya) are not abandoned at the time of seeing suffering or its origin.
If they are abandoned through the vision of cessation or the path, these latent tendencies do not take cessation or the path as their object.
One should state it thus:
If the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have the cessation and the path as their objects and are associated with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) are abandoned, those proclivities are also abandoned.
Why is this so? Because the proclivities that have the outflowing (*sāsrava*) as their objects increase by depending upon the proclivities that have the outflow-free as their objects.
If the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object are abandoned, these [tendencies] are also abandoned.
It is like a person who stands supported by timber; if the timber is removed, the person will inevitably fall;
so it is with this case as well.

Question: If that is so, previously it was definitively stated that the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) are severed by means of the object of perception (*ālambana*), whereas now it is clarified that the object is severed by means of the proclivities. Answer:
If that were so, what fault would there be?
All latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are severed when their objects of perception are seen; how much more so when their objective referents (*ālambana*) are severed—how could they not be severed?
It is like fruit on a tree: if the tree is shaken, the fruit falls; how much more so if the roots are cut—how could it not fall?
It is the same for that as well.
Furthermore, there is one who asks: "In this way, are the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) severed by their objects?
He replies:
"All proclivities (anuśaya) are abandoned by the path through having an object.
The critique states:
One should not speak thus.
Why is this so? The World-Honored One has taught:
"This Noble Eightfold Path can sever the suffering of the past, future, and present, such that there will never again be any portion of birth."
Through the cessation and departure from desire, one attains the peace of *nirvāṇa*.

Both the path with objective conditions (*sālambana-mārga*) and the path without objective conditions (*anālambana-mārga*) are capable of severing the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). The Venerable Śamathadeva said:
The various latent tendencies (anuśaya) are abandoned through four matters:
first, by means of the abandonment of the object;
second, by means of the subsequent object.
Third, because they serve as mutual objects for one another;
fourth, because their antidotes have been attained.
As for those abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, these are the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take contaminated phenomena as their objects.
Regarding those whose objects are severed: the proclivities (anuśaya) of one's own realm are severed, and the proclivities that take other realms as their objects are also severed.
Regarding those whose sequential objects are severed: these are the proclivities that take other tainted (sāsrava) phenomena as their objects.
Regarding "those abandoned by means of an antidote": according to whichever antidote is obtained, one thereby abandons those underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Furthermore, some say that the underlying tendencies are abandoned through four matters:
first, they are abandoned by knowing the object (*ālambana*).
2. Abandonment of the object;
3. Abandonment of subsequent objects;
4. Abandonment through the attainment of the antidote—these should also be explained in detail.
If there are underlying tendencies (anuśaya) within the mind, does that mind possess these underlying tendencies?
The answer is:
either they are identical to it, or they are distinct from it.
How is it that these are not distinct?
The answer is:

if the mind is undefiled and is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation, it is an object-condition for the proclivities (*anuśaya*), rather than being driven by the proclivities as associated conditions.
Why is this? Because its essence is without a causal agent (*abhisamskāra*).
That which is "this" and that which is "other" is the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*).
"That which is identical" refers to being driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);
"that which is different" refers to dwelling together without separation. Question:
For what reason are the associated proclivities (saṃprayukta-anuśaya) said to be distinct?
The answer is:
for this reason, it was previously stated as follows:
If it is said that a certain mind is subject to abandonment (*prahātavya*), does that mind possess those proclivities (*anuśaya*)?

Regarding those proclivities described as being subject to abandonment, one should not say that because a mind is described as possessing proclivities, that mind must therefore possess those proclivities which are subject to abandonment.

Regarding those [defilements] that are not to be abandoned: they are associated with the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) as they correspond to them, yet it is not the case that the mind itself possesses the latent dispositions. However, in order to manifest the definitive meaning, it is also said that the mind possesses the latent dispositions.
Furthermore, there are those who say: although those associated latent dispositions cannot be abandoned by the mind, they can be suppressed with respect to their objects.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this was stated because it is the fundamental basis for the theory of the arising of desire.
"That which is identical" refers to the underlying proclivities (*anuśaya*) as conditions; "that which is different" refers to the underlying proclivities through association (*samprayoga*).

Is it possible for the underlying proclivities to be abandoned while wisdom does not perceive their object, yet wisdom perceives the object while the underlying proclivities are not abandoned? One should elaborate upon this extensively by constructing the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding "the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by insight (*prajñā*) do not perceive their objects": when, within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one perceives the suffering and origin of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one abandons the proclivities that have other realms as their objects.

When perceiving cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), one abandons the proclivities associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are to be abandoned by the seeing of cessation and the path, and which take those [truths] as their objects.

When one abandons desire through the path-knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharmajñāna) during the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), one severs the proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Regarding those proclivities that are not severed because they are objects of vision (*darśana-heya*), it should be understood that when one sees the suffering and origin of the form and formless realms, the proclivities of the desire realm that take other realms as their object are severed; when one sees suffering, the proclivities of one's own realm that take their own realm as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of origin are severed; and when one sees cessation and the path, the proclivities conditioned by the outflows (*sāsrava*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path are severed. It should be known that the same applies when one sees origin and abandons the proclivities to be severed by the path of cultivation.

When one becomes free from desire through the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have outflows (*sāsrava*) and take [the truths of] suffering and origin as their objects are abandoned.

When one becomes free from desire through the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), the latent dispositions that take the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their objects are abandoned.

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned by the wisdom that sees their objects: when seeing suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*), they are proclivities with objects belonging to their own realm (*svadhātu*).
When seeing cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*), they are proclivities with untainted objects (*anāsrava*).

During the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), when one becomes free from desire through the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one abandons the proclivities to be abandoned by the path of cultivation. As for those proclivities not abandoned by the wisdom that sees their objects, exclude the aforementioned cases.

Is there a case where, in a single moment, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are abandoned while wisdom does not perceive the object, yet wisdom perceives the object while the latent dispositions are not abandoned? This should be elaborated extensively as a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case where the latent dispositions are abandoned while wisdom does not perceive what is being abandoned: when one has abandoned the first grade of desire up to the point of having abandoned most of it, and the *dharmajñānakṣānti* (receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma) is present, those outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) objects of perception among the latent dispositions to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the desire realm are abandoned.

When wisdom sees its object and the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not severed, it refers to the underlying tendencies associated with the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*) that were previously severed and which take the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object.

When the underlying tendencies are severed and wisdom also sees its object, it refers to the severance of the underlying tendencies associated with the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) that take the outflow-free as their object.

Regarding "the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that do not abandon wisdom and do not perceive their objects": these refer to the previously abandoned latent dispositions with outflow (*sāsrava*) directed toward the objects of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The same fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*) should also be applied to the subsequent patience (*anvayakṣānti*) regarding the Path.
When seeing cessation, one should likewise formulate two sets of four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Is it possible that the wisdom which realizes the body’s cessation does not see cessation, while the wisdom which does not realize the body sees cessation? One should elaborate upon this at length, formulating the four propositions accordingly.

Regarding the first phrase: at the time of seeing suffering (*duḥkha*), one abandons the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering; at the time of seeing the origin (*samudaya*), one abandons the proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of the origin; at the time of seeing the path (*mārga*), one abandons the proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of the path; and during the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), through the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of the origin, the knowledge of the path, and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), one becomes free from desire and abandons the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by cultivation.
The second phrase refers to the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origin, and the vision of the path at the time of seeing cessation.

The third phrase refers to abandoning the proclivities abandoned through the vision of cessation at the time of seeing cessation, and becoming free from desire through the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The fourth alternative consists of excluding all the aforementioned cases.

Is it possible that, in a single moment, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are extinguished and realized by the body, yet not perceived as extinguished by wisdom; while they are perceived as extinguished by wisdom, they are not realized by the body? This should be elaborated extensively as a tetralemma (*catuṣkoṭi*).

When one attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* through the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) regarding the form and formless realms—which are to be manifested as the cessation of the body—are not perceived as being ceased by the wisdom that realizes this cessation.

Regarding those who have seen with wisdom the cessation of the body but have not yet realized it through bodily witness: these are the remaining unabandoned proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm.

Regarding those who have both seen with wisdom the cessation of the body and realized it through bodily witness: these are the proclivities of the desire realm that were previously abandoned as well as those being abandoned now.

Regarding "neither realized through bodily witness nor seen through wisdom as ceasing," this refers to the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the realms of form and formlessness.
What is the consciousness that has the cause of abandonment as its object? This is explained at length, and so forth.
Regarding the consciousness mentioned here, when its object is severed, the cause [of that consciousness] is also severed.
Those who maintain that a seed does not act as a pervasive cause for itself speak of this consciousness as having its object-severance as its cause.
The causes are all severed.
What is the meaning of this?

When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, if the mind has the objects of the truths of origin and suffering as its conditions, this is called the state where the causes are all severed, the objects are all severed, and the consciousness that takes those severed objects as its conditions is also severed.

At that time, the mind abandoned by the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) takes as its object that which is abandoned by the Truth of Origination, and that which is abandoned by the Truths of Cessation, the Path, and the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
This mind has its causes entirely severed, but its objects are not severed.

At this time, the mind abandoned through the Truth of Origination takes as its object that which is abandoned through the Truths of Suffering, Origination, Cessation, the Path, and the Path of Cultivation; while the causes of this mind are entirely abandoned, its objects are both abandoned and not abandoned.

Regarding those who assert that one's own seeds act as the pervasive cause (*vyāpakahetu*) for their own seeds: this implies that the causes of other seeds are severed and the causes of consciousness are severed by conditions.
What is the meaning of this?

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, if the mind is subject to abandonment by the truth of the origin and takes as its object that which is abandoned by the truth of suffering, this is called consciousness whose objects are to be abandoned through the abandonment [of their causes].
Why is this so? That which is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering is its cause and its object.
Since both have been abandoned together, it is called "consciousness whose cause is severed by the severance of its objects."
If discussed in terms of what is abandoned by the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), it is consciousness that takes abandonment as its object-condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).

If discussed in terms of what is abandoned by the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), there are cases where the cause is abandoned but the object-condition is not, and cases where both are abandoned.

At that time, the mind abandoned by the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya) takes as its object that which is abandoned by the Truths of Cessation, the Path, or the Path of Cultivation; thus, while there are factors that are abandoned and those that are not, the objects of cognition are not abandoned.

At that time, the mind abandoned by the Truth of Origination takes as its object that which is abandoned by the Truth of Suffering up to that which is abandoned by the Path of Cultivation; thus, while there are factors that are abandoned and those that are not, the objects of cognition likewise include both the abandoned and the non-abandoned.
Having thus explained the meaning, the textual exposition shall now be set forth. Regarding the question:
"How many underlying tendencies (anuśaya) take the consciousness at the moment of the severance of conditions as their object? The answer is:
19. Is it one mind? Answer: No.

No. For one who has not yet abandoned the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, if the mind has as its object that which is to be abandoned by the truth of origin or that which is to be abandoned by the truth of suffering, this mind is influenced by the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the truth of origin within the desire realm.

Having already abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) but not yet having abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) do those consciousnesses have as their objects?
Answer: Six underlying tendencies to be abandoned by the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*) in the realm of form.
Question: It would also be the same for one who has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
Why, then, is it said that one must abandon desire for the realm of desire?

Answer: In this context, it speaks of the time when [the defilements] are currently manifesting, not the time when the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the form realm are accomplished and manifesting.

One must be free from desire for the desire realm, yet not necessarily free from desire; therefore, it speaks of the time when they are currently manifesting, and does not speak of one who has accomplished freedom from desire for the form realm but has not yet become free from desire for the formless realm.
The commentary states:
One should not say that they have not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm. Why is this?
If the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, it should be known that one has not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
One should state it thus:

"Having abandoned desire for the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen, but the knowledge of origination has not yet arisen," and so forth, as explained at length.
By how many latent dispositions (anuśaya) is that consciousness conditioned? Answer:
By the six latent dispositions to be abandoned through the vision of the truth of origin (samudaya-satya) in the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu).
Question: Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is also consciousness that takes as its object the cause for abandonment (*prahāṇahetu*).
What is the nature of this?

Answer: As above, when the highest-grade driving force (anuśaya) severs the remaining eight types of mind, this is the consciousness that serves as the cause for the severance of the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya). Why is this so?

That which is the highest-of-the-high abandonment (*uttama-uttama-prahāṇa*) is both a cause and an object-condition (*ālambana*), up to the eight kinds of abandonment, while one kind remains unabandoned.
Why is it not stated that these eight kinds [of abandonment] are also both causes and object-conditions for that one remaining kind?
Answer: When that which ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that this meaning is an incomplete teaching (*sāvaśeṣa-vacana*).

Furthermore, there is another explanation: taking other seeds as causes, taking other seeds as conditions, and being a consciousness of other seeds—this is what is taught therein; those three types are all contained within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Although those [factors] are of nine kinds, they are all included within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga); therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Question: For what reason are the various causes explained in their sequential order as proclivities (anuśaya)?
Answer: Because this is the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
One should thoroughly understand the Abhidharma by means of fourteen matters.
What are these fourteen?
They are the six causes, the four conditions, inclusion, association, possession, and non-possession.
To thoroughly understand these fourteen matters is called thoroughly understanding the Abhidharma.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one should thoroughly understand the Abhidharma through seven points:
first, skillfully knowing causes;
second, skillfully knowing conditions.
3. Skillfully knowing general characteristics;
4. Skillfully knowing specific characteristics;
5. Skillfully knowing what is included and what is not included.
Sixth, being skilled in knowing what is associated and what is dissociated;
seventh, being skilled in knowing attainment and non-attainment.
If one is skilled in these seven dharmas, it should be known that one is also skilled in the Abhidharma.
One who is skilled in these seven dharmas is called an Abhidharmika; it does not mean one who merely recites and maintains its texts.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 12; *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 13.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others.

Section 3: Chapter on Persons (Pudgala-varga). Part One. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination for a single person in this life: how many are in the past, how many are in the future, and how many are in the present?
Regarding these chapters and the explanation of their meanings, the *upadeśa* (expository treatise) should be explained here in detail. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is for the purpose of refuting the positions of others.
For example, the Vibhajyavādins assert that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is an unconditioned phenomenon (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Question: For what reason does he say that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)? Answer:
He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear in the world, the Dharma abides in the Dharma-realm.
The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment and manifested it for others, and so forth, as extensively explained.
For this reason, he taught that the principle of dependent origination is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

In order to stop the intention of those who speak thus, [it is said that] the law of dependent origination falls within the world. If it falls within the world, one should know that the law of dependent origination is necessarily conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Why is this? Because there is no unconditioned dharma that falls within the world. Question:
If dependent origination were a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛtadharma*), how would one reconcile that with the sūtra which says:
"Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, phenomena abide in the realm of phenomena," and so forth, as explained at length?
Answer: One should understand the intended meaning of that sutra. Question:
What is the intended meaning of that sutra?
The answer is:
because that sutra explains the definitive nature of cause and effect.

Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, ignorance is always the cause of volitional formations, and volitional formations are always the result of ignorance; and so on, up to birth being the cause of old age and death, and old age and death being the result of birth.
Such is the intended meaning of that sūtra.

If the intended meaning of that sūtra were as you understand it— namely, that whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the earth always possesses the characteristic of solidity, and so on up to the wind always possessing the characteristic of motion—
could the four great elements then be unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, form is always the characteristic of form, and so on up to consciousness being always the characteristic of consciousness;
are these aggregates (*skandhas*) also unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the harītakī fruit, the kañcaka, and the luheṇī medicine are always bitter in taste.
Furthermore, are they unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)?

According to what you have said, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, the four great elements, the aggregates (*skandha*), the *harītakī* fruit, and the *kāyasthagaluhiṇī* medicine and so forth are always conditioned.

Such a law of dependent origination, whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, although it abides within the dharma-realm, must nonetheless be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Therefore, this treatise was composed in order to refute the positions of others, to reveal one’s own position, and to manifest the meaning that accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). [As it is said:
"In the life of a single person," and so forth, as explained at length.
In this context, that Venerable One intends to clarify five points:
first, why he speaks of only one person;
second, what kind of person he is speaking of; [and so forth].
Third, for what reason is this birth taught?
Fourth, what kind of birth is taught?
Fifth, what is taught regarding the present?
The reason for speaking of only one person is to eliminate the fault of textual prolixity.
If one were to speak of all sentient beings, the text would become cumbersome; therefore, to avoid this fault of verbosity, only one person is mentioned.
As it is said regarding one person, so it should be understood for all sentient beings.

To explain what kind of person this is: if a person undergoes the twelve links of dependent origination—just as one ascends a stone or climbs a ladder—and if past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) arise and manifest, they can produce the present consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
If present craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) arise and manifest, they are able to produce future birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Regarding such a person, if past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) arise and manifest, they are able to produce present consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*);
yet if present craving, grasping, and existence do not arise and manifest, they cannot produce future birth and old age and death.

In this context, such a person is not mentioned; rather, it is said here that if there is past ignorance and formations, up to the point where they can produce future birth, aging, and death, then this is what is being discussed.
As stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna*, there are learners (*śaikṣa*) who have accomplished the eightfold path; regarding those, what kind of learner is being described?
The answer is:

one who traverses the various dhyānas and samādhis like climbing a stone or ascending a ladder—first entering the concentration with directed thought and evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra*), then entering the concentration without directed thought and evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra*), then entering the formless concentrations (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), emerging from the formless concentrations to enter the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and emerging from the attainment of cessation so that a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) manifests before them—it is such a person who is described therein.

If one enters a meditative absorption with directed thought and sustained evaluation, and from that absorption arises until entering the attainment of cessation, and then from the attainment of cessation arises such that an untainted mind manifests before one, this is not mentioned therein.

If one enters a meditative concentration with directed thought and sustained thought, and from that concentration arises [a state] up until entering the attainment of cessation, and from the attainment of cessation arises a mind associated with outflows (sāsrava) which is present before one—this is what is explained therein.
It is also as stated in the Sūtra:
"One sees this sister with a handsome appearance; later one sees her emaciated, frail, and aged; later one sees her sick and lying upon a bed; and later one sees that she has died."
After one day, two days, or even up to seven days, at a later time, one again sees her body turn blue, and so on, until the bones and joints are scattered and destroyed.
Regarding the woman mentioned therein, she must pass through these aforementioned stages of events;
if she does not pass through these aforementioned stages of events, she is not described therein.
Regarding the mention of "one person" herein, it refers to one who must pass through the twelve links of dependent origination, as explained in detail above.
As for why this "birth" is mentioned: if one speaks of birth in the present, one should know that the same applies to birth in the past and the future.
Regarding the phrase "for what kind of birth it is taught": this refers to designating a single lifetime as "birth.

Regarding the phrase "what is taught as the present": this refers to the present state of this single lifetime; it does not refer to the present of a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), nor does it refer to the present of time.
Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination for a single person in this life, how many belong to the past?
The answer is:
two—namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). This implies that there is no further experience from a previous life.
Two are in the future, namely birth and old age and death; this means that there is simply the cessation of the occurrence of birth in a future life.
Eight are in the present, from consciousness up to existence; these explain the continuity of cause and effect.

The first two [links] pertain to the past and thus stop the view of eternalism; the next two pertain to the future and thus stop the view of nihilism; the remaining eight pertain to the present and thus reveal the Middle Way. Question:

The past also possesses the twelve links of dependent origination, the future also possesses the twelve links of dependent origination, and the present also possesses the twelve links of dependent origination.
Why is it said that two [factors] belong to the past, two belong to the future, and eight belong to the present?
The answer is:
regarding present phenomena, one infers the effect from the cause and infers the cause from the effect.

Regarding the inference of the effect from the cause in the present: craving, grasping, and becoming in the present are the causes for future birth, aging, and death; birth, aging, and death are their effects.
To infer the cause from the effect: the present effects of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling have as their causes past ignorance and formations.
This statement is made by inferring the effect from the present cause and inferring the cause from the present effect.
Herein, the dependent origination pertaining to sentient beings (*sattvākhya-pratītyasamutpāda*) is explained, as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-sūtra*:
"What is the dharma of dependent origination?"
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Question:
What is the difference between this teaching and that teaching?
The answer is:

this teaching refers to those included within the category of sentient beings, while that teaching refers to both those included within the category of sentient beings and those not included within the category of sentient beings.
This explains dharmas with faculties (*sendriya*), while that explains dharmas with and without faculties (*sendriyānindriya*).
This explains dharmas with mind (*sacittaka*), while that explains dharmas with and without mind (*sacittakācittaka*).
This explains internal dharmas (*ādhyātmika*), while that explains internal and external dharmas (*ādhyātmikabāhya*).
"This text is of provisional meaning (neyārtha), while that text is of definitive meaning (nītārtha)," and so forth, as explained at length.
There are four kinds of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda):
first, the momentary (kṣaṇika);...
Second is continuity;
third is time;
fourth is sequence.
This refers to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), while that refers to a continuum (*saṃtāna*).
This refers to time, while that refers to succession. Question:
Why, in this context, is it said that only those phenomena pertaining to sentient beings constitute dependent origination?
The answer is:
That Venerable composed his treatise based on the Buddha’s sūtras, and within the Buddha’s sūtras, it is taught that dependent origination pertains to sentient beings.
The Buddhist sūtras are the foundation of this treatise; therefore, that Venerable One composed this treatise based upon the sūtras.

Question: Following this line of inquiry, for what reason does the World-Honored One, in his sūtras, speak only of dependent origination pertaining to the category of sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), and not of that which pertains to non-sentient things (*asattvākhya*)?

Answer: The meaning of "limb" (aṅga) is that of being conducive to existence (bhava). Since these limbs are conducive to existence, they are spoken of only as belonging to the category of sentient beings, and not to the category of non-sentient things.

As this sutra explains that the factors of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) pertain to sentient beings, one should know that when other sutras speak of the members of existence (bhavāṅga), they likewise speak of the factors of dependent origination pertaining to sentient beings.
Question: What is the difference between the factors of dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena (pratītyasamutpanna-dharma)?
Answer: Some say there is no distinction. Why is this?
As stated in the *Puggalapaññatti*:
"What is the dharma of dependent origination?
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)."
What are dependently originated phenomena? They are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).

While this meaning is acceptable, one should further seek their specific distinction: the cause is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), while the result is the dependently originated phenomenon (*pratītyasamutpanna*).

Just as with cause and effect, one should know that it is likewise for the object and the subject, the characteristic and the characterized, the establishment and the established, the continuity and the continued, the arising and the arisen, and the grasper and the grasped.
Furthermore, some say that the past is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the future and present are dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Others say that the past is dependent origination and the future is dependently arisen.

Furthermore, there are those who say that ignorance (*avidyā*) is dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*); and so on, up to birth (*jāti*) being dependent origination and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) being dependently arisen.

Again, there are those who say that ignorance is dependent origination and old age and death are dependently arisen, while the remaining ten links are both dependent origination and dependently arisen.

Furthermore, there are those who say that two [factors] in the past are dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), two in the future are dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*), and the remaining members are both dependent origination and dependently arisen.
The Venerable Pūrṇaśa said: "In this regard, one should formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)."

There are cases where something is a dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) but not dependently arisen (pratītyajāta), and cases where something is dependently arisen but not a dependent origination; this is elaborated at length in four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
That which is a dependent origination but not dependently arisen refers to future phenomena.
That which is dependently arisen but not dependently originating refers to the final death-aggregates of Arhats in the past and present.
That which is both dependently originating and dependently arisen refers to all other past and present phenomena, excluding the five aggregates at the death-moment of Arhats in the past and present.
That which is neither dependent origination nor dependently arisen is the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.
As stated in the *Dharmakāya-sūtra*:

"When various ignorances invariably give rise to formative forces (*saṃskāra*), being inseparable and constantly accompanying one another, this is called dependent origination and that which is dependently arisen."

If ignorance does not invariably produce volitional formations, but rather at times they are separated and do not follow one another, this is called dependent arising (*pratītyasamutpāda*) but not dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*).
This should be stated in the same way for everything up to birth, aging, and death.
The Venerable Sūmilā said: "Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is that which arises from causes; the phenomena born from causes are dependently arisen (*pratītyasamutpanna*).
Furthermore, conjunction (*sāmagrī*) is dependent origination; that which is born from conjunction is dependently arisen."
Furthermore, it is the same for that which arises and that which is caused to arise, and for that which is born and that which is caused to be born.
The distinction lies in the terms "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*). Question:
What is the essential nature of this dharma of dependent origination?
The answer is:
its nature consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The five aggregates are the substance of dependent origination; they are its nature, its self, its entity, and its characteristic.
Having already explained the reason for its substantial nature, we shall now explain by what name it is called the "dharma of dependent origination."
Answer: Some say that its essential nature is capable of arising, and because it arises in dependence upon conditions, it is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda).
Others say that because each [phenomenon] arises from distinct conditions, it is called "dependent origination."
Furthermore, there are those who say that because all things arise equally from conditions, they are called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
A question is asked:
Since various phenomena arise from four conditions, or from three conditions, or from two conditions, how can it be said that arising equally from conditions is the meaning of dependent origination?
Answer: Precisely for this reason, that which arises equally from conditions is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
If a phenomenon is to arise from four conditions, it cannot arise from three or two conditions.
That which arises from three conditions cannot arise from two or four conditions;
that which arises from two conditions cannot arise from three or four conditions.
For this reason, arising equally from conditions is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that when a phenomenon arises, with the exception of its own self-nature, all other phenomena provide it with the power of conditions; for this reason, arising equally from conditions is the meaning of dependent origination.

Furthermore, there are those who say that "arising together" (*sahotpāda*) is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as it is said: "The minds of all sentient beings arise together, abide together, and cease together.
Again, there are those who say that because all sentient beings are equal in relation to this condition, it is called the dharma of dependent origination.
Question: Among such sentient beings, some attain parinirvāṇa earlier while others attain parinirvāṇa later; how can they all be identical in relation to this condition?
The answer is:
For one who attains parinirvāṇa earlier, there is little of the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) prior [to that point] and much subsequent to it;
for one who attains parinirvāṇa later, there is much of the dependent origination prior [to that point] and little subsequent to it.
Because of this matter, arising equally from identical conditions is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Herein, when the dharma of dependent origination is explained in terms of time, there are twelve times, twelve links, and twelve sets of five aggregates (*skandha*).

The Venerable Śamatha said: Within a single moment, there are twelve factors of dependent origination. If one kills with a mind of greed, the delusion associated with that [mind] is ignorance; the volition associated with it is formative action; the consciousness associated with it is consciousness; the arising of karmic activity necessarily constitutes name-and-form; the arising of karmic activity necessarily constitutes the six sense bases; the contact associated with it is contact; the feeling associated with it is feeling; the greed itself is craving; the entanglements associated with it are grasping; the bodily and vocal karmic activities are becoming; the arising of these various phenomena is birth; the transformation of these phenomena is aging; and the disintegration of these phenomena is death.

What has been stated here is acceptable; however, what is explained herein concerns dependent origination over twelve periods, consisting of twelve factors and twelve sets of five aggregates, and does not refer to a single moment.

As stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*: "Because of delusion regarding prior objects, craving arises; this delusion is ignorance (*avidyā*), and this craving is volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). The discrimination of prior objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*); the four aggregates co-arising with consciousness are name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the sense faculties that accompany name-and-form are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the conjunction of the six sense bases is contact (*sparśa*); what is further experienced through contact is feeling (*vedanā*); what is enjoyed by feeling is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); the expansion of craving is grasping (*upādāna*); that which can procure future karma is becoming (*bhava*); the growth of the aggregates is birth (*jāti*); the transformation of the aggregates is aging (*jarā*); the disintegration and destruction of the aggregates is death (*maraṇa*); internal fever is sorrow (*śoka*); the utterance of lamentation is weeping (*parideva*); the parching and trembling of body and mind are suffering and affliction (*duḥkha-daurmanasya*). Such matters as these constitute the various calamities of the great aggregate of suffering."
Question: What is the difference between what was stated previously and this present statement? Answer:
What was previously explained refers to a single mind; what is being explained here refers to multiple minds.
What was previously explained refers to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); what follows refers to a multiplicity of continuities (*saṃtāna*).
As it is said in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
What is ignorance? It refers to the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the past.
The commentary states:
One should not speak in this way.
If it were so, all phenomena would be devoid of their own characteristics (svalakṣaṇa).
One should speak as follows:
What is ignorance? It is the time of the various fetters in the past.
What are formations?
Regarding the time of past formations,
what is consciousness?
It is the mind in its continuity along with its attendants.
What is name-and-form (nāmarūpa)?

It is the continuity of what has already been born, wherein the four types of material sense-faculties have not yet arisen and the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are not yet complete; first, the kalala.
2. Arbuda; 3. Nirarbuda; 4. Aṭaṭa;
5. Hahava; 6. Huhuva; 7. Utpala;
8. Padma; 9. Mahāpadma.
Fifth, *pārasika* and so forth—these are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
What are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)?
Once the four types of material sense organs have arisen, the six sense bases are complete.
When these faculties have not yet been able to serve as the basis for contact (*sparśa*), this stage is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). What is contact?

When these faculties have already been able to serve as the basis for contact, but one has not yet distinguished between suffering and pleasure, and is unable to avoid harm—such as fire, poison, weapons, or various impurities—this stage is called contact.
What is feeling (*vedanā*)?
It is that which can distinguish between suffering and pleasure, avoid all harms, refrain from touching fire, poison, or grasping blades, and distance oneself from all impurities;
it is that which can give rise to craving and yet does not incite lustful desire, nor produce attachment to any object—this is called feeling.
What is craving (*tṛṣṇā*)?
When the three aforementioned types of craving are fully present, that state is called craving.
What is grasping (*upādāna*)?
Because of craving for sense objects, one pursues them in the four directions; at that time, it is called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
What is "existence" (*bhava*)?
At the time of such pursuit, one generates bodily, verbal, and mental karma; at that time, it is called "existence."
What is birth? When the present consciousness exists in the future, that moment is called birth.
What are old age and death?
Just as name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling exist in the present, at that time [when they have passed], it is called old age and death.
Furthermore, there are those who say that ignorance is of two kinds:
that which destroys the essence and that which does not destroy the essence.
There are two kinds of formations conditioned by ignorance:
those consisting of volition and those produced by volition.
There are two kinds of consciousness conditioned by formations:
There is that which is accompanied by remorse and that which is not accompanied by remorse.
Consciousness conditioned by name-and-form is of two kinds:
that which is a basis for craving and that which is not a basis for craving.
There are two kinds of conditions for name-and-form (nāmarūpa) as the condition for the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana):
those that are karmic fruition (vipāka) and those that are nurtured (aupacayika).
There are two kinds of conditions for the six sense bases as the condition for contact (sparśa):
There is contact with resistance (pratigha-sparśa) and contact with designation (adhivacana-sparśa).
Conditioned by contact, there are two kinds of feeling:
bodily feeling (kāyika-vedanā) and mental feeling (caitasika-vedanā).
Conditioned by sensation, craving is of two kinds:
there is craving for sensual pleasure and craving for the necessities of life.
Conditioned by craving, grasping is of two kinds:
There is that which arises from views and that which arises from craving.
Conditioned by grasping, there are two kinds of becoming:
that which arises internally and that which arises externally.
There are two kinds of birth conditioned by existence (*bhava-pratyaya-jāti*):
that which occurs in a single moment and that which extends throughout a single lifetime.
There are two kinds of aging conditioned by birth (*jāti-pratyaya-jarā*): [the same two].
There is that which is seen by the eye and that which is seen by wisdom.
Regarding old age as the condition for death, there are two kinds:
momentary death and the death of the entire body.
As it is said that ignorance is the cause of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
A question is asked:
For what reason is it said only that "ignorance conditions volitional formations," rather than saying "ignorance is the cause of volitional formations"?
Answer: Some say that ignorance is also said to have volitional formations as its cause,
as stated in the *Mahānidāna Sūtra*, where the Buddha told Ānanda:
By such causes, such conditions, and such matters, birth becomes the cause of old age and death.
Just as birth is the cause of old age and death, so too is ignorance the cause of volitional formations, and so on.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if one says "ignorance is the cause of volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayaḥ saṃskārāḥ*), one is speaking only of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and not of the other conditions;
if one says "ignorance is the condition for volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), then one is fully explaining all four conditions.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one speaks of ignorance as the cause of formations (*saṃskāra*), one speaks only of defiled formations;
if one speaks of ignorance as the condition for formations, then one speaks of both defiled and non-defiled formations.
Question: For what reason is it said only that "ignorance conditions formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*), and not that "formations condition ignorance"? Answer:
Some say that if one speaks of "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance," one is speaking only of the condition (*pratyaya*) and not the cause (*hetu*).
Furthermore, in this context, when explaining the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), that which arises earlier is ignorance, and that which arises later is volitional formation.
Question: Since ignorance is a condition for all twelve links of dependent origination, why is it said only that "ignorance conditions volitional formations"? Answer:
Furthermore, there are those who say that when something ought to be stated but is not, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Again, there are those who say that conditions (*pratyaya*) are of two kinds: proximate and remote.
If one speaks of ignorance as the condition for volitional formations, one speaks of an immediate condition; if one speaks of other links, one speaks of a remote condition.
Herein, the immediate is spoken of, not the remote.
As it is with the immediate and the remote, so should it be understood regarding this life and other lives.

Furthermore, ignorance acts as a concordant condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), unlike the other links; therefore, it is said that it serves as a condition for volitional formations and not for the other links.

For example, it is said that "volitional formations are the condition for consciousness," and it is also said that "name-and-form are the condition for consciousness," and again, "conditioned by these two, consciousness arises. What is the difference between these three?
The answer is:

Some say that when it is taught that "volitional formations condition consciousness," this refers to the differentiation of karma; when it is taught that "name-and-form conditions consciousness," this refers to the differentiation of the stations of consciousness; and when it is taught that consciousness arises conditioned by these two, this refers to the differentiation of the support and the object.

Furthermore, there are those who say that consciousness conditioned by formations is like the initial grasping; name-and-form conditioned by consciousness is like the guarding; and consciousness arising conditioned by both is like the nurturing.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "The statement that 'volitional formations condition consciousness' explains the initial continuity; the statement that 'name-and-form conditions consciousness' explains what has already been established; and the statement that 'consciousness arises conditioned by the two' explains that once established, it is able to take an object as its cognitive domain."

Furthermore, there are those who say: when it is taught that "volitional formations condition consciousness," one speaks of volitional formations as "name-and-form"; when it is taught that "name-and-form conditions consciousness," one speaks of name-and-form as "name. When consciousness arises conditioned by these two, one speaks of the "basis" and the "conditioned object."

Furthermore, there are those who say: when it is said that "volitional formations condition consciousness," this refers to the consciousness of the woeful realms; when it is said that "name-and-form conditions consciousness," this refers to the consciousness of humans and the six classes of gods of the desire realm; and when it is said that "consciousness conditions name-and-form," this refers to the material consciousness of the form and formless realms.
The Venerable Paśya said:

"Consciousness conditioned by formations is the consciousness of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); consciousness conditioned by name-and-form is the consciousness of the birth-state (*upapattibhava*); and consciousness produced conditioned by these two is the fundamental existence-consciousness (*mūlabhava*)."

Furthermore, there are those who say that when it is taught that "volitional formations condition consciousness" and "name-and-form conditions consciousness," this refers to defiled consciousness; whereas when it is taught that "consciousness arises conditioned by both [name-and-form and volitional formations]," this refers to consciousness that is both defiled and undefiled.
As it is with the defiled and the undefiled, so should one understand the obscured and the unobscured, the faulty and the faultless, and the regressive and the non-regressive.
Question: What is the distinction between consciousness being conditioned by name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and name-and-form being conditioned by consciousness?
The answer is:

It is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) to describe the initial continuity; once name-and-form has conditioned consciousness, it is said to be established as a continuous succession.
Thus, it is said that consciousness conditions name-and-form to describe the initial birth, and that name-and-form conditions consciousness to describe the guarding [of what] has been born.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these [factors] depend on one another in succession, like bundles of reeds standing by leaning against each other;
or like a driver and an elephant, which can reach their destination by depending on one another; or like a boat and a boatman, who reach the far shore by depending on one another.
Question: As in the case of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*), how does consciousness condition name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*)? Answer:
This explains birth from a womb; it does not explain miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
The critique states:
one should say that miraculous birth is likewise so.
In the case of those born by transformation, when the sense faculties have first arisen but are not yet sharp, this is called "consciousness";
later, when they become sharp, it is called "name-and-form.
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases.
Question: Since name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is already included within the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), why is it said that name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases? Answer:

As previously stated, the period when the four types of material sense-faculties have not yet been obtained and the six sense-bases are not yet complete—during the stages of kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā—is called the stage of nāmarūpa.
"Contact is conditioned by the six sense bases. Question:

In this context it is said that contact is conditioned by the six sense bases; elsewhere, however, it is said that contact is conditioned by name-and-form, and again it is said that contact arises conditioned by both.
What is the distinction between these three?
The answer is:
"The six sense bases condition contact" explains the distinction of their supports.
"Name-and-form conditions contact" explains the distinction between the basis and the object.
Why is this so? Because all external phenomena arise through conjunction only by depending upon the internal.
Contact arises conditioned by two; this refers to present contact.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when it is said "contact is conditioned by the six sense bases," it refers to temporal contact (*kāla-sparśa*); when it is said "contact is conditioned by name-and-form," it refers to the essence of contact itself; and when it is said "contact arises conditioned by two," it refers to the threefold contact (*trividha-sparśa*).
"Contact conditions feeling.

Question: Since contact and feeling are associated and co-arising phenomena (*saṃprayukta-sahabhū-dharma*), why is it said that "contact conditions feeling," but not that "feeling conditions contact"?
Answer: Although these are associated and co-existent dharmas, some dharmas are conducive to other dharmas while others are not.
For example, contact is conducive as a condition for feeling, whereas feeling is not conducive as a condition for contact.
Just as a lamp, though arising simultaneously with its illumination, is the cause of the illumination while the illumination is not the cause of the lamp, so it is here.

As previously explained, in this context of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), contact (*sparśa*) belongs to the prior moment and feeling (*vedanā*) belongs to the subsequent moment; therefore, it is said that "contact conditions feeling," but it is not said that "feeling conditions contact" or "feeling conditions craving (*tṛṣṇā*)."
Question: It may be so that craving has pleasant feeling as its condition. Why is this?
Because of the pursuit of suffering sensations in the four directions for the sake of satisfying one's desires, how do these serve as conditions for craving?
The Venerable Sūmīta said:
Painful feeling acts as a condition for craving more so than pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. How is this so?
As the Blessed One said:
Oppressed by painful feeling, one craves pleasant feeling; because one experiences pleasant feeling, one is driven by the underlying tendency of sensual craving.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all three kinds of feeling can serve as conditions for craving.
What is the meaning of this?
The principle states that the pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) speaks thus:
"I can cause the continuity of existence (*bhava-saṃtati*) to arise; because sentient beings crave me, they pursue me in the four directions."
The sensation of suffering speaks thus:
"I too can cause the continuity of existence; being oppressed by me, one pursues objects in the four directions out of a craving for pleasure."
