Regarding neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, it is said:
"If I can cause the continuity of existence to arise even in the presence of painful and pleasant feelings, how much more so in the fourth dhyāna and above, where there is neither pain nor pleasure?"
Furthermore, there are those who say that all three types of sensation can serve as conditions for craving.
As stated in the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra*:
"If one does not know the three sensations as they truly are, craving arises."
Question: How do these three types of sensation act as conditions for craving? Answer:
There are five kinds of craving:
first, craving for pleasure;
second, craving not to be separated from pleasure.
Third, craving for non-arising suffering;
fourth, craving for swift departure from suffering;
fifth, craving for ignorance.
Regarding those who seek pleasure: because they desire that pleasant feelings which have not yet arisen should arise, craving arises.
Regarding those who do not wish to be separated from pleasure: because their minds do not wish to be separated from pleasant feelings that have already arrived, craving arises.
Regarding "not giving rise to craving for suffering": when a painful sensation has not yet arrived, one gives rise to craving with the desire that it not arise.
Regarding "quickly departing from craving for suffering": when a painful sensation has already arisen, one gives rise to craving with the desire that it be quickly extinguished.

Because one desires the arising of feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant when they have not yet arisen, craving arises; because one desires not to lose them once they have arisen, craving arises; and it is also capable of producing deluded craving.
Craving has grasping as its condition. Question:
Between craving conditioned by feeling and the craving within grasping, what is the difference between these two?
The answer is:
The initial arising of craving is called "craving" (tṛṣṇā); when craving increases and expands, it is called "clinging" (upādāna).
Furthermore, some say that the lower stage is called craving, while the higher stage is called clinging.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if craving has feeling as its cause, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling"; if it has craving as its cause, this is called "clinging. Again, there are those who say:
if craving is the fruit of feeling, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling"; if craving is the fruit of craving, this is called "clinging."

Furthermore, there are those who say: if craving arises from feeling, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling"; if craving arises from craving, this is called "clinging. Again, there are those who say:
if craving can produce afflictions, this is called "craving conditioned by feeling"; if craving can produce karma, this is called "clinging."

Question: For what reason is ignorance (*avidyā*) placed at the beginning of the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of past births, while craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is placed at the beginning of the dependent origination of future births? Answer:
Some say that these two fetters are the fundamental proclivities (*anuśaya*): ignorance is the causal condition for the past, and craving is the causal condition for the future.
Furthermore, there are those who say that ignorance has six aspects:
first, it pervades the five types [of afflictions];
second, it pervades the six consciousnesses.
Third, it can give rise to the karma of body and speech;
fourth, it is of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*);
fifth, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, it can act as a firm and powerful expedient.
Sixth, this existence of universal craving (*sarvatraga-tṛṣṇā*) possesses five characteristics as previously described, with the sole exception that it is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) possesses six characteristics, it is placed at the beginning of the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in their prior life.
Because craving has five characteristics, it is placed at the beginning of the teaching on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) for those born later.
Furthermore, others say that ignorance (*avidyā*) is taught first because it possesses three characteristics:
first, it is always the primary leader; [the other two follow].
Second, it is associated with all fetters;
third, it is universal craving (*sarvatraga-tṛṣṇā*).
Because it is preeminent among the phenomena that arise from craving, it is taught last [among the afflictions] but first [among] the factors of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that ignorance has four aspects:

first, it takes both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as its object; second, it takes both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) as its object.
3. It is both universal and non-universal;
4. it can take its own realm and other realms as objects.
Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) takes only the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as its objects; it is not a universal object-taker regarding its own realm for this reason.

Because craving is superior in its capacity to produce future suffering, it is taught at the beginning of the dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) formula, even though it appears later [in the sequence].
Here, the matter is explained briefly by way of its causes; it shall be explained extensively later.
"Dependent on conditions, there is birth. Question:

For what reason, among the three characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), is one factor (*aṅga*) mentioned alone for "birth," while two factors are mentioned together for "aging and death"?
The Venerable Paśya said:
"The Buddha knows the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and none can surpass him," and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, others say that because it follows the specific characteristics of the phenomenon, the power and function of arising are predominant when a phenomenon arises, while the power and function of aging and death are predominant when a phenomenon ceases.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when a phenomenon arises, birth (*jāti*) enables that phenomenon to continue and be established, while aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*) prevents it from continuing and being established.
Question: For what reason is illness (*vyādhi*) not established as a link (*aṅga*) of dependent origination?
Answer: Some say it is because illness lacks the characteristics of a constituent part (*aṅga*).

Others say that if something exists for all sentient beings, at all times, and in all places, it is called a constituent part; illness does not exist for all sentient beings, at all times, and in all places.
As the Venerable Bakula said:
"I have gone forth within the Buddha's Dharma; even at over eighty years of age, I have never experienced even a minor headache, let alone a bodily illness."

If even the sentient beings of this desire realm do not entirely escape the sickness of the body, how much more so for those in the form and formless realms who experience sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction conditioned by old age and death?
Question: Are sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction branches of existence (*bhava-aṅga*) or not?
Answer: No. Why is this so?

Since factors such as sorrow and lamentation have already been established as branches of existence (*bhava*), they scatter and destroy the branches of existence just like frost and hail; therefore, they are not [counted as] branches. Question:

If factors such as sorrow and lamentation scatter and destroy the branches of existence just like frost and hail, and thus serve as conditions for all twelve branches of existence, why is it that only old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are mentioned?
Answer: Some may say that it should be stated thus:
"With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations, and so on, up to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair."
As for the fact that [birth] is not mentioned, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, some say it is because the end reveals the beginning.
Still others say it is because at the time of old age and death, great sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction arise.
Furthermore, there are those who say that at that time, those who practice evil deeds give rise to great terror.
It is asked:
Does ignorance have a cause?
Is old age and death the fruit of existence?
If it is, why are there not thirteen or fourteen links of dependent origination?
If it is not, how is it that ignorance is not a phenomenon without a cause, and old age and death are not phenomena without a fruit?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
ignorance has a cause and old age and death have a fruit, yet these are not included among the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
What is the cause of ignorance?
It is improper mindfulness and reflection.
What is the fruit of old age and death?
This refers to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

Furthermore, some say that ignorance has a cause and old age and death have a fruit; their essence constitutes the "existence" link (*bhava-aṅga*), and it is not the case that they do not exist within the existence link. Therefore, the existence link exists, and it is neither thirteen nor fourteen links.
What is the cause of ignorance?
It is old age and death.
What is the fruit of old age and death?
This refers to ignorance.

Craving and grasping in the present are ignorance in the past; name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling in the present—these four, if occurring in the future, are called old age and death.
Just as it is said that "feeling conditions craving," one should know that it is taught that "ignorance conditions old age and death.
One should know that the twelve links of dependent origination are like the turning of a wheel.
It should be understood that there is a single principle of dependent origination, as it is said:
What is the dharma of dependent origination?
It refers to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, there are two kinds of the dharma of dependent origination, namely: cause and fruit.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), namely: karma, afflictions (kleśa), and substance (vastu).
Formative forces (saṃskāra) and existence (bhava) are karma; ignorance (avidyā), craving (tṛṣṇā), and grasping (upādāna) are afflictions; and the remaining members are substance.
Furthermore, there are four types of dependent origination, namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), birth (*jāti*), and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

The eight members of the present should be subsumed within the four members of the past and future: craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) of the present are subsumed within ignorance of the past; becoming (*bhava*) of the present is subsumed within formations of the past; consciousness (*vijñāna*) of the present is subsumed within birth of the future; and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*) of the present are subsumed within old age and death of the future.
Furthermore, there are five types of dependent origination: namely, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, and old age and death.
The seven factors of the past and present should be subsumed within these five factors of the present and future.

Ignorance in the past is craving and grasping in the present; formations in the past are becoming in the present; consciousness in the present is birth in the future; and name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling in the present are aging and death in the future.
Furthermore, there are six kinds of dependent origination: past causes and effects, present causes and effects, and future causes and effects.
Furthermore, there are seven kinds of dependent origination, namely: ignorance, volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.

The five members of the future and present [lives] should be subsumed within the seven members of the past and present: present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are past ignorance (*avidyā*); present existence (*bhava*) is past formations (*saṃskāra*); future birth (*jāti*) is present consciousness (*vijñāna*); and future aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, there are eight factors of dependent origination, namely from consciousness up to existence (*bhava*).

The four members of the past and future should be subsumed within these eight members of the present: past ignorance (*avidyā*) is present craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*); past formations (*saṃskāra*) are present existence; future birth (*jāti*) is present consciousness; and future aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are present name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*).
Furthermore, there are nine kinds of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as taught in the *Mahānidāna Sūtra*.
Additionally, there are ten kinds of dependent origination, as taught in the *Nagara-upama Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there are eleven kinds of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), as explained in the *Jñānabīja* [Sūtra].
Furthermore, there are twelve kinds of dependent origination, as explained in various places throughout other sūtras regarding the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśabhavāṅga*).

In these twelve links of dependent origination, afflictions serve as the condition for karma; karma serves as the condition for suffering; suffering serves as the condition for suffering; suffering serves as the condition for afflictions; afflictions serve as the condition for afflictions; afflictions serve as the condition for karma; karma serves as the condition for suffering; and suffering serves as the condition for suffering.
As it is said, "ignorance conditions volitional formations"; this is called afflictions serving as the condition for karma.
"Volitional formations condition consciousness"; this is called karma serving as the condition for suffering.
"Consciousness conditions name-and-form," and so on, up to "contact conditions feeling"; this is called suffering serving as the condition for suffering.
Feeling conditions craving; this is called suffering acting as a condition for afflictions.
Craving conditions clinging; this is called afflictions acting as a condition for afflictions.
Clinging conditions existence; this is called afflictions acting as a condition for karma.
With birth as condition, there is existence; this is called karma acting as a condition for suffering.
With birth as condition, there is aging and death; this is called suffering acting as a condition for suffering.
Among these twelve links of dependent origination, two are the continuity [of karma], while the rest are the threefold [suffering].
The second is the continuity, which consists of consciousness and birth.
The third is the division, which is the essence of karma and afflictions.
Karma consists of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*).
The afflictions (*kleśa*) are ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
Their substance (*vastu*) refers to the remaining members.
Just as with karma, afflictions, and substance, one should know that the three accumulations (*trayaḥ samudayāḥ*) and the three paths (*trayo mārgāḥ*) are likewise.
These twelve links of dependent origination are like a tree that has roots, a trunk, flowers, and fruit.

Ignorance and volitional formations are its roots; consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are its trunk; craving, grasping, and becoming are its flowers; and birth, old age, and death are its fruit.
Regarding these twelve links of dependent origination, some possess flowers and fruits, while others lack both flowers and fruits.
Those that possess flowers and fruits refer to ordinary worldlings and those in training.
"One without flowers and without fruit" refers to the Arhat.
Question: Of these twelve links of dependent origination, how many are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) and how many are continuous (*prabandhika*)?
The answer is:
two are momentary, namely consciousness and birth;
the rest are continuous.
Question: Among the twelve links, how many are defiled and how many are undefiled? Answer:

The fifth category consists of those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), namely: ignorance (*avidyā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and birth (*jāti*); the remainder are both defiled and non-defiled (*akliṣṭa*).
The critique states:
when explaining the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of phenomena in this context, one should specify which factors are defiled and which are non-defiled.
Regarding the five periods previously mentioned, if these are mental states and mental concomitants that are defiled, the remainder may be either defiled or non-defiled.
Among these twelve links of dependent origination, how many exist in the desire realm, and how many exist in the form and formless realms?
Answer: Some say that here only those beings born from a net in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are discussed.
Others say that there are twelve links (*dvādaśāṅga*) within the desire realm.
The realm of form (rūpadhātu) has eleven factors, excluding name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and time;
the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) has ten factors, excluding name-and-form, the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana), and time.
Regarding the realm of form, it should be stated as follows:
Consciousness conditions the six sense bases.
Regarding the formless realm, one should state:
consciousness conditions contact.
The commentary states:
It should be said that there are twelve links in the desire realm, and there are likewise twelve links in the form and formless realms.

Question: If there is no name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and no name-and-form or the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how is it that both realms possess the twelve links [of dependent origination]? Answer:
It is like newly born beings in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whose faculties are not yet sharp; this is called the stage of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
Although there is no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is "name"; and although there are no physical sense-faculties, there is the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
He should speak thus: "Consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the mind-base (manāyatana); the mind-base conditions contact.
For this reason, the twelve links of dependent origination exist in all instances.

Similar factors of existence cause similar factors of existence to continue in succession; factors of existence belonging to the desire realm cause factors of existence belonging to the desire realm to continue in succession.
The same applies to the form and formless realms, with the sole exception that at the time of receiving [rebirth], they can cause dissimilar factors of existence to continue in succession.
What is this process? It is as follows:

one born within the desire realm who has not yet abandoned desire gives rise to craving, grasping, and becoming of the desire realm, which manifest before them and create future birth, aging, and death.
In that case, there is one craving, one clinging, and one becoming in the present; and there will be one birth and one aging-and-death in the future.

When one has abandoned desire for the sense realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the first dhyāna, and the craving, clinging, and becoming of the first dhyāna arise before him, creating future birth and aging-and-death: in that case, there are two cravings, two clingings, and two becomings in the present; and there will be two births and two instances of aging-and-death in the future.

In this way, up until one has abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet abandoned desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there arise craving, clinging, and becoming of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception which manifest before one, producing future birth, aging, and death. In that case, there are nine instances of craving, nine instances of clinging, and nine instances of becoming in the present; there will be nine instances of birth and nine instances of aging and death in the future.

That person, having passed away from the desire realm, is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). Having previously given rise to the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, their present craving and grasping constitute past ignorance; their existence constitutes past formations; and their future birth constitutes present consciousness. Their future aging and death constitute the present: name-and-form, mind-contact, and feeling.
As for the various factors belonging to other stages, whether present or future, they are neither past, nor present, nor future. Why is this so?
If cause and effect are established, then there are the past, future, and present; because cause and effect are not established, there is no past, future, or present.

Furthermore, having passed away from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one is reborn in the sphere of nothingness. Previously, one gave rise to craving, grasping, and becoming for the sphere of nothingness in the present; this craving and grasping are past ignorance, and this becoming is past formations. Future birth is present consciousness, and future aging and death are the present [aggregates], namely name-and-form, mind-contact, and feeling.
Regarding the various factors (*aṅga*) of other stages, whether present or future, they likewise do not possess the past, future, or present [in that same way]. Why is this?
Because when cause and effect are established, there are the past, future, and present; because when cause and effect are not established, there is no past, future, or present.

From the end of life in the sphere of nothingness until birth within the desire realm, there is the manifestation of craving, grasping, and becoming pertaining to the desire realm that previously arose. Craving and grasping are past ignorance; becoming is past formations; future birth is present consciousness; and future aging and death are present name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling.
As for the other *dvādaśa-rāśis* (earth branches), if they are present or future, they are not past, future, or present. Why is this?
If cause and effect are established, then there are the past, future, and present; if cause and effect are not established, then there is no past, future, or present.

When one is born in the desire realm and is able to perform karma that increases the various realms of existence, at the time when ignorance is present, there is one member present—namely, ignorance itself—while the remaining members exist in the future.
When ignorance (*avidyā*) conditions the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), there are two members in the present—namely, ignorance and formations—and ten members in the future.

From the time of formations up to the time of consciousness (*vijñāna*), one member is in the present—namely, consciousness—and two members are in the past—namely, ignorance and formations; the remaining members are in the future.

From the time of grasping (*upādāna*) until the time of existence (*bhava*), two links belong to the past, namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*); two links belong to the future, namely birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*); and eight links belong to the present, from consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to existence (*bhava*).
The Venerable Pūrṇaśa further elucidated this meaning:

"If ignorance and formations are in the present, one should know that ten members are in the future; eight are in the immediately following birth—namely, from consciousness up to existence—and two are in the third birth—namely, birth and old age and death."

If birth, old age, and death are present, ten members belong to the past; eight members belong to the immediately preceding life—namely, from consciousness up to existence—and two members belong to the third preceding life—namely, ignorance and formations.
If eight [factors] are present, two are in the past—namely ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*)—and two are in the future—namely birth (*jāti*) and aging-and-death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

Throughout the Buddha’s sūtras, the law of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is taught; at times it is explained in terms of causes, at times in terms of effects, and at times in terms of both causes and effects.
For whom is the cause taught? For whom is the fruit taught? For whom are both taught?
The answer is:
there are generally three kinds of sentient beings who are to be transformed.
There are superior, middling, and inferior faculties.
For those of superior faculties, the cause is taught; for those of middling faculties, both cause and effect are taught; for those of inferior faculties, only the effect is taught.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings—those who are beginners, those who have already studied, and those who have studied for a long time—for whom one should preach according to their needs.
Or there may be sentient beings who are deluded regarding the cause, the result, or both the cause and the result.

If one is ignorant regarding causes, one explains causes; if one is ignorant regarding effects, one explains effects; and if one is ignorant regarding both cause and effect, one explains both cause and effect. Question:

If one explains the fruit of dependent origination for the sake of sentient beings with inferior faculties, and since Bodhisattvas possess the most superior faculties among all sentient beings, for what reason do they contemplate the fruit of dependent origination?
Answer: Some say it is because he contemplates the dharmas in accordance with them. Why is this so?
When the Bodhisattva beholds old age, sickness, and death, he reflects thus:
"By what conditions do these old age, sickness, and death come to be?
[He realizes] they all arise from birth, and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when a bodhisattva sees old age, sickness, and death, he becomes weary of the world and leaves the household life; having left the household life, he then contemplates birth, old age, and death according to his original intention.

Others say that because he accords with and attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), when a bodhisattva attains right determination, he first contemplates the fruit—how much more so, then, would he not first contemplate it before attaining right determination?
Furthermore, there are those who say that, as previously stated, the fruit is taught for the sake of beginners.

A bodhisattva in their final birth is called a beginner; although they have contemplated the law of causes and conditions throughout countless kalpas, when they contemplate it again at this later stage, they must begin once more from the very beginning.
Just as a person who, though having previously climbed a tree many times, must climb it from the root when doing so again later, so too is he.

Furthermore, there are those who say that because he wishes to burn the tree of existence (*bhava-vṛkṣa*) so that nothing remains, he is like a person who first burns the top of a tree with fire until reaching the root before stopping; so too is he.
The Venerable Pāṣa said:
"One is not called of inferior capacity merely because they do not contemplate the causes and conditions of the Bodhisattva.
However, there are two kinds of people:"
There are those who follow the course of views and those who follow the course of craving.
Those who follow the course of views rely on the samādhi of emptiness to attain right determination and contemplate the causes of dependent origination.
Those who follow the course of craving rely on the samādhi of wishlessness to attain right determination and contemplate the fruits of dependent origination.
Although a bodhisattva may follow the course of craving, they are able to rely on the samādhi of emptiness to attain the correct determination that contemplates the fruit of dependent origination.
The bodhisattva loathes the suffering of old age, sickness, and death, and does not give rise to desire or pleasure for any form of birth and death.
Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva not contemplate ignorance and formations? Answer:

Some say that because one has already practiced both extensive and concise contemplation, when one contemplates craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), this is precisely contemplating ignorance (*avidyā*); and when one contemplates existence (*bhava*), this is precisely contemplating volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
"For this reason, it is called 'already previously observed,' and so forth, as explained at length. Question:

If that is so, when one observes old age and death, one is simultaneously observing name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*); and when one observes birth (*jāti*), one is simultaneously observing consciousness (*vijñāna*). Why, then, must one observe them again?
Answer: The former is a brief observation, while the latter is an extensive observation; the former does not involve discrimination, whereas the latter does. Question:
If this is so, since consciousness has neither expansion nor contraction, why is it observed repeatedly?
The answer is:
although there is neither expansion nor contraction, the bodhisattva observes it repeatedly because they fear birth.
Why is this so? Because the bodhisattva, weary of old age, sickness, and death, seeks their root, asking: "From what do these old age, sickness, and death arise?
He knows that they arise from the evolving consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*).
Who creates the continuous stream of consciousness?
It is known to arise from karma.
From whom does karma originate?
One knows that [the body] arises from afflictions.
Upon what do afflictions depend? One knows that they depend upon the physical basis (āśraya).
He further reflects:
"Who created this body?
He knows that it arises from the continuity of consciousness.
The Bodhisattva then reflects:
"It is from the evolving consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) that all faults and afflictions are produced.

For this reason, he contemplates consciousness more deeply than he does the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), because the formative forces lack the sense of expansion or contraction; thus, his contemplation stops at consciousness.
Question: If that is so, ignorance possesses both broad and concise meanings; why then is it not examined? Answer:
Because the meaning of practice is neither extensive nor concise, one does not contemplate it;
yet, one cannot abandon practice to instead contemplate ignorance. Why is this?
One should contemplate the dharma of dependent origination according to its sequential order and not skip over the stages.
Furthermore, some say that when a bodhisattva contemplates the arising of existence through conditions, this is precisely contemplating karma as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*);

if one contemplates formations as the condition for consciousness, this is likewise contemplating karma as name-and-form. If it were thus, there would be no distinction in the contemplation, and moreover, it would not be a contemplation of what is designated as name-and-form.
If one contemplates that name-and-form conditions consciousness, this is contemplating what is called "name-and-form.

Furthermore, some say: if one contemplates the arising conditioned by existence, this is called contemplating a remote condition; if one contemplates formations conditioning consciousness, this is also contemplating a remote condition. Such [contemplation] would be a contemplation without distinction, and moreover, it would not be a contemplation of a proximate condition;
whereas if one contemplates that name-and-form conditions consciousness, this is contemplating a proximate condition.
Just as with "near" and "far," one should know that this body and other bodies are likewise.

Furthermore, some say: if one contemplates dependent origination through existence (*bhava*), one is contemplating the conditions of a prior life; if one contemplates consciousness conditioned by formations (*saṃskāra*), one is also contemplating the conditions of a prior life, and not contemplating the conditions that arise simultaneously.
However, if one contemplates name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness, one is contemplating conditions that arise simultaneously.

Furthermore, there are those who say that consciousness arises from two conditions: namely, arising from a remote condition (*dūre-pratyaya*) and arising from an accompanying condition (*sahāya-pratyaya*).

If one contemplates that it arises with "existence" (*bhava*) as a condition, this is contemplating a remote condition; if one contemplates that consciousness arises with "formative activities" (*saṃskāra*) as a condition, this is likewise contemplating a remote condition. Such an approach constitutes an undifferentiated contemplation and does not constitute contemplating the dharma of the accompanying condition.
If, however, one contemplates that consciousness arises with "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) as a condition, this is contemplating the dharma of the accompanying condition.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is to avoid the fault of infinite regress.

When a Bodhisattva contemplates old age and death, they simultaneously contemplate this body’s name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*); when contemplating birth, they simultaneously contemplate the continuity of consciousness (*vijñāna*) within this body.

If one contemplates name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling, one is contemplating old age and death within the second birth; if one contemplates consciousness, one is contemplating the arising of the body in the second life; if one contemplates ignorance and formations, one is contemplating the third world, or one may also contemplate the fourth world; thus proceeding further and further, it becomes infinite.
In order to avoid such faults, one does not contemplate ignorance and formations. Question:
For what reason does the Bodhisattva contemplate ten links within the section on origination (*pravṛtti*), yet contemplate twelve links within the section on cessation (*nivṛtti*)?

Answer: Because the bodhisattva loathes conditioned activity and delights in quiescent extinction, he contemplates ten aspects within the category of conditioned activity and twelve aspects within the category of quiescent extinction.
As it is said:
"O Bhikṣu! At this consciousness, my mind turns back."
Question: For what reason does the bodhisattva turn back from within the mind of consciousness?
The Venerable Vaspa replied:
Consciousness has its support in that upon which it dwells. What is the support of consciousness?
It is name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
Because name-and-form has not been severed, the process returns as far back as consciousness.
Furthermore, some say it is called "turning back" because it returns by way of conditions;
as it is said: "Consciousness is conditioned by name-and-form," and also, "Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness."
Because consciousness is the condition for name-and-form, it is said that there is "turning back" (pratyudāvartate) within conditions.
Furthermore, others say that because these two dharmas serve as mutual conditions for one another, it is called "turning back" within conditions.

Furthermore, there are those who say it is like a centipede moving along by means of grass: it first places its front legs and then shifts its hind legs; if it reaches the tip of the grass where there is no place to set its feet, it turns back.
That [person] is also like this.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Bodhisattva, weary of old age, sickness, and death, seeks their original source and asks by what cause they arise.
He knows they arise from the evolving consciousness (*saṃtati-vijñāna*), and so on, until he knows that the afflictions depend upon the substance and thus investigates that substance.
Furthermore, based on what does it exist?
One knows that it arises from the consciousness of the continuum. One reflects thus:
All manner of afflictions arise from this.
If one contemplates consciousness as the condition for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), one is contemplating the consciousness that continues this present body;
if one contemplates name-and-form as the condition for consciousness, one is contemplating the consciousness that continued the past body.
For this reason, the meaning explained by the Venerable Pūrṇaśa becomes clear:
when the two links of birth and old age/death are present, ten links exist in the past, eight links exist in the immediately preceding life, and two links exist in the third life prior to that.

If one contemplates this present life, seeing the faults of the past continuity of consciousness, and likewise those of the future continuity of consciousness, the mind of consciousness then turns back.
The Buddha’s sūtras explain the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in various places, using similes such as a lamp, a mass of fire, and a city.
Question: For what reason do the Buddha’s sūtras explain the dharma of dependent origination as being like a lamp, and so forth, up to being like a city?
The answer is:
For those who attain clarity by using a lamp as an analogy for the dharma of dependent origination, the Buddha says it is "like a lamp.
If they attain clear understanding by using a mass of fire or a city as an analogy, the Buddha says it is "like a mass of fire" or "like a city."

Furthermore, there are those who say that among sentient beings within craving and grasping, there are those who possess a small portion, those who possess a medium portion, and those who possess a superior portion.

If it remains in a small portion, it is said to be like a lamp; if it remains in a middle portion, it is said to be like a mass of fire; if it remains in the upper portion, it is said to be like a city.
As the Buddha’s sūtras state: "Ignorance conditions volitional formations," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
This is intended to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
Why is this so? Because both "formative action" (*saṃskāra*) and "existence" (*bhava*) are essentially karma, yet people mistakenly regard them as being one and the same.
Now, wishing to explain the reasons for this and their specific characteristics, I have composed this treatise.
What is meant by "ignorance conditions volitional formations"?
The answer is:
In order to clearly demonstrate, establish, and explain the characteristics of various karmas,
it is shown that even karma created in other lifetimes causes the maturation of its retribution to increase.

Now, having obtained this body, one receives the retribution for those karmas within this very life; this is called "conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*).
Question: What is the difference between "performing" (*karaṇa*) and "accumulating" (*upacaya*)?
Answer: Some say there is no distinction. Why is this?
Because that which is performed is itself growth, and growth is itself what is performed.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there must be a distinction. Why is this so?
Some fall into the evil realms due to a single unwholesome action, while others fall into the evil realms due to three unwholesome actions.
If one commits a single unwholesome action that would lead to rebirth in hell but desists through skillful means, this is called "committed" but not "increased.
If that action reaches completion, it is called both "committed" and "increased."
Regarding the three types of unwholesome conduct that lead to rebirth in hell: if one commits one or two of these acts, it is called "performance" but not "accumulation";
if one completes all three acts, it is called both "performance" and "accumulation."
One should know that wholesome conduct leading to rebirth among humans or devas is likewise.

Furthermore, some say: if one commits an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and should thus fall into hell, yet ceases it while still in the preparatory stage (*prayoga*), this is called "committed" but not "accumulated";
if this karma reaches completion, it is called both "committed" and "accumulated."
If one commits five acts of immediate retribution, one should fall into hell; if one commits one, two, three, or four, this is called "committing" but not "increasing";
if one fully commits all five acts of immediate retribution, this is called both "committing" and "increasing."
The explanation that the ten unwholesome actions lead to rebirth in the evil realms and the ten wholesome actions lead to rebirth among humans or devas is likewise.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one may be born among humans through a single wholesome karma, or born among humans through many wholesome karmas. For example, because a Bodhisattva possesses thirty-two hundred merits, he attains his final body; if he were to possess thirty-one hundred merits, this would be called "performing" [the action] but not "increasing" it.
If he possesses the full thirty-two hundred merits, this is called both "performing" and "increasing" it.
Furthermore, there are those who say that karma is of two kinds:
determinate and indeterminate.
If one performs an indeterminate action, it is called "performed" but not "accumulated."
If one performs a determinate action, it is called "performed" and is also called "increased.

One should know that the same applies to actions that will certainly produce retribution and those that will not certainly produce retribution, as well as those with retribution in the present life, in the next life, in subsequent lives, or those with indefinite retribution.
Furthermore, there are those who say that karma is of two kinds:
karma with skillful means and karma without skillful means.
Karma with skillful means involves both performance and accumulation; karma without skillful means involves performance but no accumulation.
Thus, it should be understood that the same applies to whether an action is performed intentionally or unintentionally, and whether it is done with prior reflection or without reflection.
Furthermore, some say that karma may be created but not fulfilled, or fulfilled but not created, or both created and fulfilled.
If an action is both performed and brought to completion, it is called "done" and also called "increased";
other actions are called "done" but not "increased.
Furthermore, some say that if an unwholesome karma results in the fruit of the evil realms, or if an unwholesome karma results in the fruit of humans or devas.
When unwholesome [karma] results in the fruits of the evil realms, it is called both "committed" (*kṛta*) and "increased" (*upacita*);
when unwholesome [karma] results in the fruits of humans or devas, it is called "committed" but not "increased."

Furthermore, there are those who say that regarding unwholesome karma, there are cases where the intention is corrupted but the preparatory means are not; cases where the preparatory means are corrupted but the intention is not; and cases where both the intention and the preparatory means are corrupted.
If both the mind and the skillful means are impaired, this is called "action" and is also called "increase";
other cases are called "action" but not "increase.

Furthermore, some say there are three types: those with a virtuous mind but incomplete skillful means; those with complete skillful means but an incomplete virtuous mind; and those with both a complete virtuous mind and complete skillful means.
When a wholesome mind is fully endowed with skillful means, it is called both "action" and "growth";
other cases are called "action" but not "growth.

Furthermore, some teachers say that unwholesome karma may involve the destruction of precepts but not of views, the destruction of views but not of precepts, or the destruction of both precepts and views.
One who has impaired precepts and impaired views is said to both "perform" and "increase" [karma];
others are said to "perform" but not to "increase.
The same explanation applies to wholesome karma, as well as to those who possess the fullness of virtue (*śīla-saṃpanna*) and the fullness of view (*dṛṣṭi-saṃpanna*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are wholesome karmas that have wholesome karma as their retinue, and there are wholesome karmas that have unwholesome karma as their retinue.
When wholesome karma has wholesome karma as its retinue, it is called both "action" (*kṛta*) and "increase" (*upacaya*);
when wholesome karma has unwholesome karma as its retinue, it is called "action" but not "increase."
If one speaks of the unwholesome, it is the opposite of what was stated above.

Furthermore, some say that when one performs an unwholesome deed and does not abandon it, does not condemn it, does not reproach it, and does not rely upon its antidote, this is called both "performing" and "increasing.
When one performs an unwholesome deed but abandons it, condemns it, reproaches it, and relies upon its antidote, this is called "performing" but not "increasing."

Furthermore, there are those who say that there are cases where one performs wholesome karma and constantly maintains mindfulness of it, and cases where one performs wholesome karma but does not maintain mindfulness of it.
That which is constantly maintained with mindfulness is called both "performed" and "increased";
that which is not maintained with mindfulness is called "performed" but not "increased."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one commits an unwholesome deed and does not repent it, this is called both "doing" and "increasing";
if one commits an unwholesome deed and repents it, this is called "doing" but not "increasing."

Thus, seeing faults where there are none, or not seeing faults where they exist; confessing one's transgressions to others when one has committed an evil deed, which is practicing according to the Dharma, versus not confessing one's transgressions to others when one has committed an evil deed, which is not practicing according to the Dharma—the same applies to speaking [of such matters].
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one commits an evil deed while knowing that there is retribution for it, this is called "committing" but not "increasing";
if one commits an evil deed without knowing that there is retribution for it, this is called both "committing" and "increasing."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one repeatedly performs an action but does not rejoice in it, this is called "performing" but not "increasing";
if one repeatedly performs an action and rejoices in it, this is called both "performing" and "increasing."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one performs wholesome deeds and frequently gives rise to wholesome thoughts within this body, it is called both "performing" and "increasing";
if one performs wholesome deeds but does not frequently give rise to wholesome thoughts, it is called "performing" but not "increasing."
The same applies to the explanation of unwholesome actions.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if an action is fully completed—just as when the construction of a house is entirely finished—it is called "done" and also called "increased";
if an action is not fully completed, it is called "done" but not called "increased."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if an action performed is praised by one's companions in practice, it is called both "performed" and "increased";
if it is not so, it is called "performed" but not "increased."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one performs a concordant action and obtains a concordant result, this is called both "action" and "growth";
if one performs a concordant action but does not obtain a concordant result, this is called "action" but not "growth."
When one is harmonious and fully accomplishes the ten virtuous actions, one attains the fruits of human and celestial realms.
Furthermore, some say that if a virtuous deed is definitely dedicated toward a specific goal, it is called both "performed" and "increased";
if a virtuous deed is not definitely dedicated, it is called "performed" but not "increased."
The same applies to the definitive dedication of unwholesome karma.
Furthermore, some teachers say that when wholesome karma is obscured by afflictions, it is called "performed" but not "increased";
when it is not obscured by afflictions, it is called both "performed" and "increased."
When unwholesome karma is not obscured by wholesome karma, it is called both "committed" and "increased";
when it is obscured by wholesome karma, it is called "committed" but not "increased."
The distinction lies between "forming" (*abhisamskāra*) and "increasing.
If the retribution of karma is now obtained as this existence, it is called "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance.
One should know that all such past karmas are entirely subsumed within the category of volitional formations.
What is existence conditioned by grasping?

It is when one performs an action and causes it to increase, such that the retribution of that action brings about the continuity of future existence. One should know that all such future actions are entirely subsumed within the category of "existence-constituting karma" (*bhava-aṅga*).
Question: For what reason is past karma called "formations" (saṃskāra) and present karma called "existence" (bhava)? Answer:
Past karma has already been exhausted and spent, already performed and given its fruit; it lacks the power to produce further retribution, as it has already ripened.
It is just like refuse discarded in an open space, which can no longer produce further fruits of retribution.
For this reason, it is called "becoming" (*saṃskāra*).
That which is contrary to the above is called "existence" (*bhava*). Question:
What is the difference between "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" and "existence conditioned by grasping"?
The answer is:
the difference has already been explained.
This is of the past; this is of the present.
This has already yielded its fruit; this has not yet yielded its fruit.
This is old karma; this is new karma.
Question: What you have said may indeed be so; however, one ought to explain the specific characteristics of the conditions (*pratyaya*). Answer:
"Volitional formations have ignorance as their condition" is stated to demonstrate karma, as explained in detail above.
Regarding that karma as a condition, the Blessed One has said it constitutes a single fetter, namely, the fetter of ignorance.
Regarding "clinging as a condition for existence": if one performs an action here, and so forth, as explained at length.
The Blessed One has stated that those actions conditioned by clinging are all the fetters, namely, the various types of clinging.
Question: For what reason is past karmic conditioning called ignorance (*avidyā*), while present karmic conditioning is called all the fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana*)? Answer:
Since all past lives are not directly perceived,
how can they be explained?
The answer is:

What are called the destination (*gati*), birth (*upapatti*), direction (*deśa*), time (*kāla*), the means performed (*upāya*), the place of arising (*utpattisthāna*), and the physical conditions (*kāyapratyaya*).
As for "destination," one does not know from which previous destination one created the karma for this present existence.
As for "birth," one does not know in what state of birth one created the karma for this present existence.
Regarding "direction," one does not know in which direction the karma for this present existence was created.
Regarding "time," one does not know at what time the karma for this present existence was created.
Regarding "the specific act," one does not know whether the karma for this present existence was created through killing, or through beating and binding, or even through meaningless speech.

Regarding "expedient means" (upāya): it refers to performing expedient actions that create karma for future existence, whether directed toward those classified as sentient beings or those not classified as sentient beings.
Regarding "the locus of arising": it refers to creating karma for future existence within the loci of greed, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding the "body," one does not know whether it is for the sake of a male or female body that one creates karma for present existence.

Regarding the "conditions," one does not know whether those conditions pertain to the past, future, or present, or whether they are for the sake of form, sound, odor, taste, or touch that one creates karma for present existence.
Thus, because the past is not directly perceived, it is said that formations have ignorance as their condition.

As explained above regarding the present, everything from the realms of rebirth up to the exhaustion of conditions is directly perceived; therefore, those karmic actions are said to have all fetters as their condition.

Furthermore, there are those who say that past ignorance conditions formations; this refers to what has already been performed as a preparatory means, which has already yielded its fruit but is not intense. Because it is not intense, it is called "ignorance."

Grasping conditions existence; this is present karma that has not yet employed the means of action, has not yet yielded its fruit, and is by nature intense. Because it is intense, it is called grasping.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one does not know whether past karma arose from greed, from hatred, or from delusion; since neither in one’s own person nor in another’s person is there direct perception [of its origin], yet ignorance exists within all phenomena associated with and co-arising with the afflictions, it is for this reason that it is called "ignorance."

Present karma can be perceived directly in both one's own body and the bodies of others, and it can also be known to arise from greed, hatred, delusion, and other afflictions; therefore, it is called "all fetters."

Question: Regarding the karma of all Arhats, is it "volitional formations conditioned by ignorance" (avidyā-pratyaya-saṃskāra), or is it "existence conditioned by grasping" (upādāna-pratyaya-bhava)? Answer:
It is not that formations are conditioned by ignorance, nor is existence conditioned by grasping. Why is this?
Because they do not arise from ignorance, nor do they arise from grasping.
Although the fruit has already been bestowed and the retribution has already matured, one should know that these are entirely subsumed within the "constituent of action" (*saṃskāra-aṅga*).

If the fruit has not yet been bestowed and the retribution has not yet matured, one should know that such karma is subsumed within the "constituent of existence" (*bhava-aṅga*); once it has departed from the constituent of existence, it no longer resides within the constituent of existence.
Question: How many kinds of karma do ordinary persons born within the desire realm create? Answer:
Ordinary persons born in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire can create four kinds of karma—both wholesome and unwholesome.

Those who have already abandoned the desires of the desire realm but have not yet abandoned the desires of the first dhyāna can create the four kinds of wholesome karma of the desire realm and three kinds of karma of the first dhyāna, excluding karma that ripens in the present life.

In this manner, up to the point of being free from desire for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), one can perform the four kinds of wholesome karma of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and can perform the three kinds of karma pertaining to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), excluding karma that ripens in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya).
Ordinary persons born in the first dhyāna who have not yet abandoned desire can produce four types of karma within the first dhyāna.

If they have abandoned desire for the first dhyāna but have not yet abandoned desire for the second dhyāna, they can produce three types of karma within the first dhyāna— excluding karma that ripens upon rebirth—
and three types of karma within the second dhyāna— excluding karma that ripens in the present life.

Having abandoned the desires of the second dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the desires of the third dhyāna, one can produce three types of karma within the first dhyāna—excluding karma to be experienced upon rebirth;
one can produce two types of karma within the second dhyāna—excluding karma to be experienced upon rebirth and karma to be experienced in the present life;
and one can produce three types of karma within the third dhyāna—excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.

Up to the point of being free from desire for the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), one can produce three kinds of karma within the first dhyāna, excluding karma to be experienced upon rebirth (upapadyavedanīya).

Within the third dhyāna and the three formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), one can produce two kinds of karma, excluding karma to be experienced upon rebirth and karma to be experienced in the present life (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya).
One can produce three kinds of karma in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana), excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.
In this way, ordinary persons up to those born in the sphere of nothingness who have not yet abandoned desire can create four kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of nothingness;
those who have already abandoned desire can create three kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of nothingness, excluding karma to be experienced upon rebirth;
they can also create three kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.
Ordinary persons born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception can create four kinds of karma.
Noble ones born in the desire realm who have not yet abandoned desire can create four kinds of karma;

if they have abandoned desire for the desire realm but have not yet abandoned desire for the first dhyāna, they can create two kinds of wholesome karma in the desire realm, excluding karma that results in rebirth in the next life or subsequent lives.
One can produce three kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna, excluding karma that ripens in the present life.
Having abandoned desire for the first dhyāna but not yet having abandoned desire for the second dhyāna, one can produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the desire realm, as previously explained.

If one is of the non-retrogressive type (*aparihāna-dharman*), they can only produce karma of a single kind pertaining to the first dhyāna—namely, karma with indefinite retribution (*aniyata-vedanīya-karman*).
If one is of the retrogressive type (*parihāna-dharman*), they can produce three kinds of karma, excluding karma with immediate retribution (*dr̥ṣṭadharma-vedanīya-karman*);
they can also produce three kinds of karma within the second dhyāna, excluding karma with immediate retribution.
It should be understood that the same applies to the discarding of desire for the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.

One who has not yet discarded desire for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the desire realm, excluding karma that ripens upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*) and karma that ripens in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

If, however, one is of the nature of non-retrogression (*avinipātadharman*), they can create one kind of karma within the fourth dhyāna, namely, karma with indeterminate ripening (*aniyata-vedanīya*).
If one is of the nature of regression (*parihāṇadharman*), one can create three types of karma, excluding karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
One can also create three types of karma in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), excluding karma to be experienced in the present life.
If one creates karma to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapadyavedanīya*), one does not create karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).
If one creates karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karma*), one does not create karma to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya-karma*).

Furthermore, from the point of having abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) but not yet having abandoned desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one can create two types of karma in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as previously explained;

if, however, one is of the nature of non-retrogression (*avinipātadharman*), one can create one type of karma in each of the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), as previously explained.
If one is of the nature of regression (*parihāṇadharman*), one can create three kinds of karma as previously explained;
one can also create three kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as explained in the section on the sphere of infinite space.

When a noble one is born in the first dhyāna but has not yet abandoned the desire for the first dhyāna, they can create three types of karma belonging to the first dhyāna, excluding karma with a subsequent retribution.

Having abandoned the desire for the first dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the desire for the second dhyāna, they can create two types of karma belonging to the first dhyāna— excluding karma with a retribution at birth and karma with a subsequent retribution—
and they can create three types of karma belonging to the second dhyāna, excluding karma with a present retribution.

Having abandoned the desires of the second dhyāna but not yet having abandoned the desires of the third dhyāna, one can create two types of karma of the first dhyāna—excluding karma that ripens in the next life or subsequent lives;
one can create one type of karma of the second dhyāna, namely karma of indeterminate ripening;
and one can create three types of karma of the third dhyāna—excluding karma that ripens in the present life.

Up to the point where one has abandoned desire for the four *dhyānas* but has not yet abandoned desire for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the first *dhyāna*, as previously described;
one can create one kind of karma pertaining to each of the remaining three *dhyānas*, namely, karma with indefinite retribution (*aniyata-vedanīya-karma*);

and one can create two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space, excluding karma that is to be experienced in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya*) or in subsequent lives (*upapadyavedanīya*).

Up to the point where one has abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet abandoned desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one can produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the first dhyāna as previously described;
one can produce one kind of karma pertaining to the remaining three dhyānas and the three formless attainments, namely, karma with indefinite retribution;
and one can produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, excluding karma that is to be experienced in the present life or in subsequent lives.
As it has been said regarding birth in the first dhyāna, one should know that birth in the other three dhyānas is likewise.
The distinction here is that those born in the other three dhyānas, while not yet free from the desires of their own respective stages, are able to produce four kinds of karma.

When a noble one is born in the sphere of infinite space but has not yet abandoned the desires of that stage, they can produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space—excluding karma to be experienced in the next life or subsequent lives.

When they have abandoned the desires of the sphere of infinite space but have not yet abandoned the desires of the sphere of infinite consciousness, they can produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space as previously described;
they can also produce two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite consciousness—excluding karma to be experienced in the present life or subsequent lives.

Up to the point where one has abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet abandoned desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of infinite space as previously described;
one can perform one kind of karma pertaining to the spheres of infinite consciousness and nothingness—namely, karma with indefinite retribution;
and one can perform two kinds of karma pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, excluding karma that yields retribution in the present life or subsequent lives.
The same applies to those born in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Regarding noble beings born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), whether they have abandoned desire or have not yet abandoned it, they can create two kinds of karma for that sphere, excluding karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*).

While abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), they can create twenty-two kinds of karma, which will receive their fixed or unfixed retribution within that intermediate state.

In this way, during the stages of the kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā; as an infant, a child, a youth, a middle-aged person, and an old person—one invariably experiences both determinate and indeterminate retributions.
While abiding in the stage of *kalala*, one is able to create twenty kinds of karma;
upon returning to the stage of *kalala*, one experiences determinate or indeterminate retribution.
This continues until the time of old age, at which point one experiences all determinate and indeterminate retributions.
Up until the time one dwells in old age, one creates two kinds of karma and subsequently receives two kinds of retribution during that same period of old age—namely, fixed and unfixed retribution.

Question: When one creates karma while dwelling in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and receives retribution while dwelling in the state of birth (*upapattibhava*), is this retribution a retribution to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*) or a retribution to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*)?

Answer: It should be said that this is a result experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), and it should not be said to be a result experienced in a future life (*upapadyavedanīya*). Why is this so?
Because the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is precisely the body of this present life.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 13; *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 14.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats and translated by the Northern Liang Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others.
In the "Chapter on Miscellaneous Matters" (Saṃyukta-vastu), within the "Section on Persons": Is it the case that ignorance conditions conduct, while clear knowledge does not?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question:
For what reason is this treatise composed based on ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*)?
Answer: Some say that it is because the intention of the author of the sūtra was such, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that ignorance (*avidyā*) is contrary to knowledge (*vidyā*), and knowledge is contrary to ignorance.
Ignorance (avidyā) acts as the antidote to knowledge (vidyā), and knowledge acts as the antidote to ignorance.
Furthermore, some say that both are primary, both consist of nine types, and both are fundamental.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the root of the formative factors (*saṃskāra*) that arise; clarity (*vidyā*) is the root of the portion of cessation (*śamatha*).
To what extent do the formative factors have ignorance as their condition? This is explained at length.
In various places, the term "formative factors" is explained extensively, such as when it is said: "With ignorance as condition, there are formative factors."
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
"In this context, when speaking of time, the five aggregates are formations (*saṃskāra*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states as follows:
In this context, karma is said to be "formative action" (*saṃskāra*), as when it is said that there is formative action that harms others.
In this context, unwholesome karma is said to be "formative action," as when it is said that there is no formative action that harms others.
In this context, wholesome karma is said to be "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*), just as it is said that one "performs volitional formations of the conditioned.
Just as it is said that one performs a single volitional formation of the conditioned, here it is stated that volition (*cetanā*) is the volitional formation.

As it is said that the five aggregates consist of form, mind, mental factors, formations dissociated from mind, and the unconditioned; herein, the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind is referred to as "formations" (saṃskāra).

As it is said that there are these [aggregates of] form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, herein the five aggregates associated with and dissociated from mind are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
As it is said regarding the three types of formations: namely, those of body, speech, and mind.

Bodily formations refer to inhalation and exhalation; verbal formations refer to vitarka and vicāra; mental formations refer to saṃjñā and cetanā. Among these, it is taught that the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) and a small portion of the other two aggregates constitute formations (saṃskāra).

As it is said that there are three types of formations (*saṃskāra*): those conducive to merit, those conducive to demerit, and those conducive to the imperturbable; herein, wholesome and unwholesome karma are called formations.
As it is said that formations have five defects, herein unwholesome dharmas are called formations, and they are also called painful contact (*duḥkhasparśa*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that herein the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) are called "formations" (*saṃskāra*). It is as when it is said that a wise person does not abandon formations by means of formations;
and as when it is said that all formations are impermanent—herein, the five aggregates of clinging are spoken of as formations.
As it is said that "nirvāṇa is bliss," herein nirvāṇa is described as bliss.
Herein, nirvāṇa refers to the untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) of the analytical dharma (*saṃkhyā-dharma*), not to cessation through analysis (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

As it is said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, all phenomena are selfless, and nirvana is tranquil. In this context, "conditioned phenomena" refers to all conditioned things (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
This sutra also states that all conditioned things are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
If one speaks of similar courses of action, there are eleven types in total:
four in the desire realm—
wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, and unobscured.
The realm of form has three types:
wholesome, obscured, and unobscured.
The same applies to the formless realm, as well as to outflow-free formations.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) do not act as causes for wholesome karma of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but they function as three conditions: namely, the condition of sequence (*anantara-pratyaya*), the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Ignorance acts as four causes for unwholesome karma—namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—and thus functions as four conditions.
Knowledge is not a cause for it, but acts as two conditions: namely, the condition of object and the condition of dominance.
The same applies to the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta) factors of the desire realm.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is not the cause of the non-obscured-unspecified factors of the desire realm; excluding the retribution of ignorance itself, it acts as three conditions: namely, the condition of immediate succession (*anantara*), the condition of object (*ālambana*), and the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati*).
Knowledge (*vidyā*) is not its cause, acting as only one condition: namely, the condition of sovereign power.

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and the retribution of ignorance act as a single cause, namely the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), and act as four conditions, namely the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Wisdom (*vidyā*) is not its cause; it acts as a single condition, namely the sovereign condition.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are not causes for wholesome formations of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); they act as three causes, excluding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Ignorance acts as four causes for obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) formations of the form realm—namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*)—and acts as four conditions.
Knowledge is not their cause, but acts as two conditions: the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the sovereign-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Knowledge and ignorance are not causes for non-obscured formations in the form realm; ignorance acts as three conditions, excluding the causal condition;
knowledge acts as one condition, namely the sovereign condition.
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is also like this.

Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*) and untainted formations (*anāsrava-saṃskāra*), with the exception of the initial illumination, all other untainted formations are not its cause; they act as two conditions, namely the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Illumination (*vidyā*) and its similar counterparts act as three causes—namely the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)—and act as four conditions.

Initially, clear light and ignorance are not causes for one another, yet they act as two conditions: namely, the condition of the object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Ignorance and initial clear light are not causes for one another, yet they act as one condition: the condition of sovereign power.
This is a brief *vibhāṣā*. Is there any formation (*saṃskāra*) that takes ignorance (*avidyā*) as its object but does not take clarity (*vidyā*) as its object?
The answer is: Yes.
There is none.
Why is this? Because there is no practice that has ignorance as its condition and lacks clarity as its condition.
Is there perhaps a case where one practices with ignorance as a condition regarding clarity, yet without a condition regarding ignorance?
The answer is:
this also does not exist.
Why is this? There is no formation that has clarity as its condition and lacks ignorance as its condition.
Is there any formation that has ignorance as its condition and yet possesses clarity as its condition?
The answer is: There is. Why is this so?

Sentient beings have long been such that there are none who do not slander the Path by claiming it is not the Path; yet, at a later time, they perform deeds beneficial to the earth and cause them to increase, and so forth, as explained at length.
The practice of benefiting from the land refers to obtaining fields, gardens, groves, and fruit-bearing trees.
The practice of kingship refers to becoming a king of a border region, such as the King of Mathurā.
Those who practice as a Lesser Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) obtain sovereignty over one quarter of the world, such as King Ghoṣa, King Mūrdhaja, and the Son of Heaven of Qin.
Those who practice as a Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakravartin) obtain sovereignty over the four continents.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who practices as a king will obtain sovereignty over a single region, such as King Ghoṣa, King Mūlaka, and the Son of Heaven of Qin, among others.
The practitioner who is a great king is one who has become the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch and has already ascended the throne, yet the seven treasures have not yet arrived.
The practitioner who is a wheel-turning monarch is one who has already ascended the throne and the seven treasures have spontaneously arrived.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "acting as a lord of the earth" means being honored as the sovereign among all lands;
"acting as a king" means becoming a minor king within the retinue of a universal monarch (cakravartin).
The practitioner who is a great king dwells in the position of the crown prince of a wheel-turning monarch.
The practitioner who is a wheel-turning monarch attains sovereignty over the four continents, and the seven treasures come to him spontaneously.

Because they arise through this succession of causes and conditions, all sentient beings, as well as seeds, medicinal herbs, and trees, are enabled to grow; furthermore, [the king] collects taxes in accordance with the Dharma.
By the power of this karma, all external seeds are enabled to grow and flourish.
This principle shall now be explained in detail.

Just as various non-Buddhists, seeing that lifespans increase and decrease, give rise to a mind of weary detachment; and further, being oppressed by the suffering of encountering the hated, the suffering of parting from the beloved, and the various sufferings of domestic life, they subsequently leave the household life.

Having gone forth, they possess few desires and are content; they practice diligent asceticism and observe difficult precepts, engaging in various forms of austerity in their desire to seek liberation.
