Because they rely on wrong paths, they move further away from the Noble Path. Because they move further away, they cannot attain the Path. Because they do not attain the Path, they give rise to slander, saying: "There is no such thing as the Path."
Although there is liberation, there is no path to it.
If such a path did exist, we would have attained this path through our various ascetic practices.
Since we have not attained it, one should know that there is no path.
They turn back from the practice of the Dharma and think to themselves:
"If even those who have cultivated much merit within the cycle of birth and death still encounter perils and difficulties, how much more so for those who have done nothing?"
"I shall now cultivate the merit of giving.
He then performed a great sacrifice, providing abundant food and drink for many people,
and made this aspiration:
Suppose I were to become a king, even a wheel-turning monarch.

Just as a disciple of the Buddha observes that life has its increases and decreases and thus gives rise to a mind of weary detachment, I too would be oppressed by the suffering of association with the disliked, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the various sufferings of household life, and would consequently go forth into homelessness.

Having gone forth, he diligently applied himself to spiritual practice during both the first and last watches of the night. For one and two weeks, he remained submerged in meditation; throughout that interval, he sat in the full lotus posture, with a meditation-stone placed upon his head, practicing the methods of the meditation-ball and the meditation-staff, constantly dwelling among the rocky crags on mountain peaks and practicing with vigor.
Although one does not attain the Way due to two reasons:
first, the roots of goodness have not yet matured;
second, one practices erroneous expedient means.
Those whose roots of goodness have not yet matured seek liberation beginning with this very body.
Among those who swiftly attain liberation within the Buddha-dharma, there are:
first, those who plant the roots of goodness conducive to liberation within their own bodies;
Second, maturation within the body;
third, attaining liberation within the body.
To seek liberation without having planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation is called "immaturity of the roots of merit."
Those who practice perverse expedients receive erroneous antidotes;
because of this, they are unable to attain the Way. Failing to attain it, they then slander the Way, saying:
"Though there is liberation, there is no Way to it."
"If there were such a thing as [attaining liberation], I should have attained it through my various kinds of diligent ascetic practices.
For this reason, I have now retreated; furthermore, I reflect:
even for one who performs much merit within the cycle of birth and death, it remains perilous and difficult, let alone for one who performs none."

I shall now cultivate meritorious deeds, performing them myself and instructing others to do so; by establishing long fasts, *pañca-vārṣika* assemblies, and dharma-preaching gatherings, I shall provide various foods and drinks to satisfy many people.
He made this vow: "May I become a king, even reaching the rank of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
He attained everything exactly as he had vowed.
If the Path did not exist, wrong view would have no basis for giving rise to slander; because the Path exists, wrong view slanders it. Therefore, the untainted Path acts as the proximate condition.
If wrong view did not slander the Path, the mind associated with generosity would subsequently not arise; thus, the defiled mind acts as a condition for the non-defiled mind.
If there were no mind associated with giving, external seeds would not grow; in this way, internal phenomena act as the proximate condition for external phenomena.
This preceding mind possesses four conditions.

The preceding mind refers to a mind associated with wrong view; that which is associated and co-existent with it is the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*); doubt is the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); the Path is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); and all other dharmas, excluding its own self-nature, are the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
That final mind possesses a single powerful condition.
"The final mind" refers to the mind associated with giving. Question:
For what reason does the preceding mind have four conditions while the subsequent mind has only one?
The answer is:
Some say that this text should be stated as follows:
If the preceding mind has four conditions, the succeeding mind should likewise have four conditions.
That this was not stated despite being thus intended to be said, one should know that this teaching is incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that here [in this context] only proximate conditions (*āsanna-pratyaya*) are being discussed. As stated in the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra*:

"That which does not act as an obstacle to the mind is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); all phenomena that serve as objects are the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*); the mind that has ceased in the preceding moment is the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*); and co-arising phenomena are the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*)."

Thus, all these have been explained as proximate conditions (*āsanna-pratyaya*); one should know that this passage likewise explains proximate conditions. The four conditions of the preceding mind are proximate conditions.

These four conditions of the preceding mind constitute a single condition of sovereign power (*ādhipati-pratyaya*) for the subsequent mind; they are not causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), not sequential conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and not objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Why is this so? Because the preceding mind acts as the causal condition for wrong views.

A mind associated with wrong views does not practice giving; a doubting mind cannot provide the immediately antecedent condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for a mind intent on giving; and a mind fixed upon the [mundane] path does not practice giving.

Question: Just as the substance of a subsequently arising mind exists within four conditions, and the four conditions of a preceding mind serve as the dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the subsequent mind,
why does the substance itself not likewise act as a dominant condition for its own substance?
Answer: Some say that this passage should be stated as follows:
"The four conditions of the preceding mind act as a single dominant condition for the succeeding mind, with the exception of its own self-nature."
As for the fact that it was not mentioned, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvasesa*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "I previously made this statement; herein, I spoke exclusively of proximate conditions."
The subsequent mind is a distant condition (*dūrapratyaya*) for the preceding mind; this constitutes abandoning the distant and taking up the proximate.

Furthermore, there are those who say that since the self-nature (*svabhāva*) has already been excluded [in other contexts], one should still accept and believe the exclusion of its own nature as taught in other treatises (*śāstra*), other daily recitations (*japa*), and other sections (*skandhaka*). How much more so should one accept and believe this very treatise and this very section, which—just like the preceding chapter of the daily recitation—teaches that all phenomena (*dharmas*), excluding their own nature, act as the condition of sovereign power (*ādhipatipratyaya*)?
For this reason, even though it is not explicitly stated here that its own self-nature is excluded, there is no fault.
Is there perhaps a formation that neither takes ignorance as its object nor takes clarity as its object?
Answer: There is none.
There is no activity that does not take ignorance as its object, nor one that does not take clarity as its object.
Furthermore, if one were to explain it separately for each individual dharma, there would be [the following]:
"Is there any volitional formation (*saṃskāra*) that has ignorance (*avidyā*) as its condition but does not have clarity (*vidyā*) as its condition? and so forth, as explained at length.
That which has ignorance as its condition but does not have clarity as its condition refers to the defiled volitional formations that are the retribution of ignorance.
Regarding the retribution of ignorance: ignorance acts as the cause of retribution, whereas clarity is not its cause.
Why is this? Because clarity has no causal significance.

Ignorance acts as four causes for defiled formations: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*);
clear knowledge is not their cause, because it lacks the nature of being a cause [for them].

Regarding "conditioned by clarity (*vidyā*), not conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*"): with the exception of the initial clarity, all other untainted (*anāsrava*) formations take clarity as their three causes—namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
Ignorance is not their cause, because it lacks the sense of being a cause for them.
That there is a condition of ignorance that conditions clarity—this does not exist.
Why is this so? Because there is no instance where formations are conditioned by ignorance and also conditioned by clarity; for they are remote from one another.
As the verse says:
"The distance between space and the great earth is vast; The distance between this shore and that shore of the ocean is likewise vast;
The places where the sun rises and sets are also far apart; But the distance between the True Dharma and the false Dharma is the farthest of all."

"Those that do not take ignorance as a condition and do not take clarity as a condition are all other non-obscured neutral formations (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-saṃskāra*), excluding the retribution of ignorance. What are these? They are:
the retribution of all wholesome formations; unwholesome bodily and vocal karma; and the retributions of birth, subsistence, aging, impermanence, and so forth."

All derived matter (aupacayika-rūpa), as well as other dependent forms, postures (īryāpatha), crafts (śailpasthānika), and supernormal fruits (abhijñā-phala), along with the initial luminous wholesome formations (kuśala-saṃskāra) that are with outflows (sāsrava)—
such dharmas as these do not depend on ignorance (avidyā), nor do they depend on knowledge (vidyā).
Why is this? Because ignorance and clarity are not causes for one another. Question:

If, as in the attainment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), both ignorance (*avidyā*) and knowledge (*vidyā*) are not its cause, why is this not mentioned here?
The answer is:
some say that when something ought to be stated but is not, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that because when one analyzes the factors common to both [the learner and the non-learner] at the initial clarification, they are also included therein.
The critique states:
One should not speak thus; it is better as was stated previously.
Question: What is the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*)? Answer:
"Not knowing, not understanding, and not recognizing" is the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*). Question:
Apart from clarity (*vidyā*), all other phenomena are also characterized by not knowing, not understanding, and not recognizing; are they all, therefore, ignorance?
Answer: If not knowing, not understanding, and not recognizing constitutes the characteristic of delusion (*moha*), then this is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
As for all other phenomena, although they may not be known, understood, or recognized, they lack the characteristic of delusion; therefore, they are not said to be ignorance.
Question: What is the meaning of "clarity" (vidyā)? Answer:
To know, understand, and discern meaning is the meaning of "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*). Question:
Since conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) also knows, understands, and discerns meaning, why is it not called clear knowledge?
Answer: Some say that if one’s knowledge, understanding, and discernment can achieve certainty regarding ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), that is clarity;
for although conventional wisdom (saṃvṛti-jñāna) involves knowledge, understanding, and discernment, it does not attain certainty regarding ultimate truth.
For example, although the knowledge of distant realms (*dūrabhāgajñāna*) may be sharp and intense, it cannot achieve definitive certainty regarding ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Furthermore, some say that if a cognition (*vijñāna*) of understanding and comprehension can definitively ascertain and exhaustively investigate the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) within ultimate truth, it is "clear vision" (*vidyā*);

whereas conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), despite being a cognition of understanding and comprehension, is not clear vision because it cannot definitively ascertain and exhaustively investigate the primary meaning within ultimate truth.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one possesses knowledge, understanding, and discernment capable of severing the afflictions so that they do not arise again, this is "clear vision" (*vidyā*);
because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is contrary to the aforementioned [characteristics], it is not clear vision.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if knowledge, understanding, and consciousness can destroy existence (*bhava*), it is clear vision (*vidyā*);
because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is contrary to this, it is not clear vision.

Again, there are those who say that if knowledge, understanding, and consciousness sever the continuity of the existence of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and the continuity of old age and death, it is clear vision.
Because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is contrary to the aforementioned [supramundane] states, it is not "clear vision" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, some say that if one knows, understands,
and discerns the path that leads to the exhaustion of suffering and its origin, as well as the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and all forms of grasping (*upādāna*), this is clear vision.
Because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is the opposite of the aforementioned [characteristics], it is not "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).

Furthermore, some say that if one’s cognition and understanding are not of the nature of the inversion of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), are not the locus of greed, hatred, or delusion, are unmixed with the defilements of turbidity and poison, do not fall into the various realms of existence (*bhava*), and do not fall within the truths of suffering or its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-satya*), this is clear knowledge;
because conventional wisdom is the opposite of these, it is not clear knowledge.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if one possesses knowledge, understanding, and discernment such that, having known, one no longer lacks knowledge; and if one has attained definitive wisdom so that delusion, doubt, and false views no longer arise—this is *vidyā* (clear vision).
Because conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is contrary to this, it is not *vidyā*.
Furthermore, there are those who say that conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) exists within the category of neither-ignorance-nor-clarity (*naivavidyānāvidyā*). Why is this?
Because it possesses the threefold meaning of being associated with both clarity (*vidyā*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and their combination.
Just as a person who is a friend to someone yet also a friend to that person's enemy is neither called a friend nor an enemy toward the latter;
so it is with this case as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say that its meaning is "clarity" (vidyā) because it is unmixed with ignorance (avidyā).
Because conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is mixed with ignorance (*avidyā*), it is not "clear vision" (*vidyā*).
Furthermore, some say that a portion of conventional knowledge can give rise to the dharma of slandering the Path; regarding this, the analogy of a traitorous minister should be cited.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "the meaning of being able to cure" refers to clarity (*vidyā*).
For example, when a person is possessed by a ghost, they are cured with incantations;
likewise, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are possessed by the ghosts of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and are cured by the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Because that conventional knowledge cannot provide ultimate remedy, it is not "clear vision" (*vidyā*).

Excluding those phenomena that are the causes of the mind and those that are non-mental phenomena, all other phenomena are subsumed within two elements (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate (*skandha*).
What is that? It refers to the mind associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).

As for its inclusion: it is comprised within two elements (*dhātu*), namely the mental-consciousness element (*mano-vijñāna-dhātu*); one base (*āyatana*), namely the mind base (*mana-āyatana*); and one aggregate (*skandha*), namely the consciousness aggregate (*vijñāna-skandha*), excluding the factors that serve as causes for clarity and all other remaining factors.
That which is not subsumed under the category of clear knowledge comprises one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate (skandha).
What is it? It is the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti).

That which subsumes one element (*dhātu*) is the dharma-element; that which subsumes one base (*āyatana*) is the dharma-base; and that which subsumes one aggregate (*skandha*) is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
The same should apply when explaining the various enumerated dharmas such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth. Question:
Are all types of knowledge (vidyā) caused by knowledge?
And if they are causes of knowledge, are they themselves knowledge?
Thus, one should elaborate the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) in full detail.
"That luminosity which does not have luminosity as its cause" refers to the initial luminosity.
"That which has luminosity as its cause but is not luminosity" refers to the factors that arise simultaneously in association with luminosity.
"That which is luminosity and also has luminosity as its cause" refers to all other instances of luminosity, excluding the initial luminosity.
Regarding "that which is not clarity and does not have clarity as its cause," this excludes the aforementioned cases.
Are all instances of clarity causes of clarity?
And if something is a cause of clarity, is it also clarity itself?
This is elaborated at length into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is illumination but does not act as a cause for illumination refers to future illumination.
That which acts as a cause for illumination but is not itself illumination refers to the factors that arise simultaneously with and are associated with illumination.
That which is clarity and also acts as a cause for clarity refers to past and present clarity.
That which is not clarity and does not act as a cause for clarity excludes the aforementioned instances.
There are fifteen attainments of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*):

first, that which is simultaneous with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering; second, that which is simultaneous with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*); and so on, up to that which is simultaneous with the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*).

At the attainment of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), fourteen [attainments] are acquired; thus they decrease successively until, at the stage of the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*), only one is acquired.
Question: Are there any other attainments in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*)?
Answer: Some say there is none. Why is this?
Just as when the path of seeing ceases, its acquisitions (*prāpti*) also cease accordingly;
just as when the sun sets, its light also sets accordingly.
In this way, the sun is like the path of seeing, and the sunlight is like the various acquisitions. If that path ceases, the acquisitions also cease accordingly.
The commentary states:
There should be further attainment, namely that which pertains to future lives.
Herein, only those who are born are discussed; those who are not born are not mentioned.
The *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* has one attainment (*prāpti*); it acts as the cause for the simultaneous arising of the subsequent *kṣāntis*.
This attainment also does not act as a cause for the *kṣāntis* themselves, but serves as the cause for all subsequently arising untainted paths (*anāsrava-mārga*).

There are three types of acquisitions (*prāpti*) that arise simultaneously with the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*): two are acquisitions of the path (*mārga-prāpti*), and one is an acquisition of liberation (*vimukti-prāpti*).

Regarding the two acquisitions of the path: one is the acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmakṣānti-prāpti*), and the second is the acquisition of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna-prāpti*).
Regarding "attainment of liberation," this refers to the liberation from the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering within the desire realm.

In terms of the meaning of "attainment" (*prāpti*), there is no cause for its acquisition; likewise, in terms of the meaning of "acquisition," there is no cause for its relation to that knowledge (*jñāna*).
The acquisition (*prāpti*) that arises simultaneously with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) acts as a similar cause for those three acquisitions.
There are four acquisitions that arise simultaneously with the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*):
three are acquisitions of the path (*mārga-prāpti*), and one is an acquisition of liberation (*vimukti-prāpti*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*) has no cause; likewise, the acquisition of that subsequent patience regarding suffering also has no cause.

Furthermore, the acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and its co-arising acquisitions act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for the four acquisitions.

The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and its co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*) act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for three acquisitions, with the exception of the acquisition of the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
It is on account of this fact that this statement was made.
Is there any case where an outflow-free state (*anāsrava*) from a previous life does not serve as a cause for an outflow-free path (*mārga*) in a subsequent life? Answer: There is.
The superior [attainment] does not serve as a cause for the inferior.
There are six types of possession (*prāpti*) that arise simultaneously with the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*):
four are acquisitions of the path (*mārga-prāpti*), and two are acquisitions of liberation (*vimukti-prāpti*).

The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) has no cause with respect to the six acquisitions; likewise, those six acquisitions also have no cause with respect to the subsequent knowledge of suffering.
The acquisition that arises simultaneously with the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) acts as a similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) for those six acquisitions.

The dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) and its co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*) act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for five acquisitions, with the exception of the acquisition of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
The subsequent-comparison patience (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) and its co-arising acquisitions act as causes for the last three acquisitions, but do not act as causes for the first three acquisitions.
Question: For what reason do [the first three] not act as causes for the attainment? Answer:
For the reasons stated above, the superior path does not act as a cause for that which is inferior. Question:
It may be granted that the path, being inferior, does not act as a cause; however, since the attainment of liberation is superior, why does it not act as a cause?
Answer: Although the attainment of liberation is superior, because it is obtained through the power of the lower path, it does not act as a cause for [subsequent attainments].
In this manner, up to the stage of *mārgānvayakṣānti*, there are twenty-two attainments that arise simultaneously:
Fifteen are acquisitions through the Path (mārga-prāpti), and seven are acquisitions through liberation (vimukti-prāpti).

There is no causal relationship between the patience of subsequent knowledge of the Path (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) and the twenty-two acquisitions; likewise, there is no causal relationship between the twenty-two acquisitions and the patience of subsequent knowledge of the Path.
The patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) and its co-arising acquisitions (*prāpti*) act as similar causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) for twenty-two acquisitions.

This continues up to the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) and its co-arising acquisitions, which act as similar causes for the three subsequent acquisitions, but do not act as causes for the preceding acquisitions.

When the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is present before one, it acts as the cause for all the paths of cultivation to be realized in the future; that is, from the patience regarding the dharma of suffering up to the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*), it acts as their cause.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is present before one, the path being cultivated in the future does not function as its cause. Why is this?
Because until not even a single moment has arisen, how can it be called a fruit?
The commentary states:
It is preferable to say that these are causes because they are both acquired within a single lifetime and because they constitute the superior path.

In this manner, up until the moment the present *mārga-anvaya-kṣānti* (patience of subsequent knowledge of the path) arises, all paths cultivated in the future serve as its cause; furthermore, from the *mārga-anvaya-jñāna* (subsequent knowledge of the path) up to the stage of the Aśaikṣa (Arhat), they all serve as its cause.

Up until the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, all paths cultivated in the future serve as the efficient cause for the exhaustion [of defilements], as do all paths of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
The first arising of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), excluding its own self-nature, acts as a cause for all paths of those beyond training (*aśaikṣamārga*).

The path of one who proceeds by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) acts as a cause for the path of one who proceeds by faith, and also acts as a cause for the path of one who proceeds by dharma (*dharmānusārin*);
however, the path of one who proceeds by dharma acts only as a cause for the path of one who proceeds by dharma.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the path of one who practices through faith serves as a cause for the path of another who practices through faith, but does not serve as a cause for the path of one who practices through the Dharma; for there is no such thing as one who practices through faith becoming one who practices through the Dharma.
The commentary states:
It is well said that these serve as causes for production, because they belong to the same continuum and are moreover the superior path.
The path of one liberated through faith serves as a cause for the path of one liberated through faith, and also serves as a cause for the path of one who has attained vision.
The path of seeing serves as a cause only for the path of seeing.
The occasional path of liberation serves as a cause for the occasional path of liberation and also for the non-occasional path of liberation;
the non-occasional path of liberation serves as a cause only for the non-occasional path of liberation.
The path of seeing acts as a cause for the path of seeing itself, and also acts as a cause for the path of cultivation and the path of no-more-learning.
The path of cultivation acts as a cause for the path of cultivation itself, and also acts as a cause for the path of no-more-learning;
the path of no-more-learning acts as a cause only for the path of no-more-learning.

The path of the śrāvaka serves as the cause for the path of the śrāvaka; the path of the pratyekabuddha serves as the cause for the path of the pratyekabuddha; and the path of the Buddha serves as the cause for the path of the Buddha. These three paths do not act as causes for one another.
The untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) relies both upon the female body and the male body.

Some teachers say that the path relying on the female body serves as the cause for a subsequent path relying on the female body, and the path relying on the male body serves as the cause for a subsequent path relying on the male body.
They should serve as causes for one another, according to the sharpness or dullness of their faculties.
It is well said thus: some speak of a single path, while others speak of many paths.

Regarding the teaching of a single path: it is not said that the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is identical to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); rather, the path of seeing is distinct from the path of cultivation.
The path of seeing is attained by relying on a body in nine locations:
the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
To speak of a single path means that the path of Jambudvīpa extends even up to the path of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven.

To speak of many paths means that the paths of the bodies upon which beings in Jambudvīpa rely are distinct, extending even up to the paths of the bodies upon which beings in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven rely.
Regarding the statement that there are many paths, there are again two kinds. The first is to say:
"If one attains the vision of the path by means of a Jambudvīpa body, this path is called 'attained,' it resides within the body, it is accomplished, and it is also present before one."
Regarding the path that serves as the basis for other bodies: this path is attained, yet it does not reside within the body, is not possessed, and does not manifest.
Second, they state this:
if one attains the Path of Seeing by means of a body in Jambudvīpa, that path is called "attained," it resides within the body, is possessed, and also manifests.
The path of seeing attained by other bodies is not said to be "attained," does not reside within those bodies, is not accomplished, and does not manifest there.
The path of cultivation relies upon a body of the desire realm, as well as upon bodies of the form and formless realms.
Regarding the "single path," the path attained by relying on a body in the desire realm and the path attained by relying on a body in the form or formless realms are, in fact, one and the same path.
Regarding "many paths," the path attained by relying on a body in the desire realm is distinct from the path attained by relying on a body in the form or formless realms.
Regarding the statement that there are two kinds of "attaining the path," the first is as follows:
it is said that one attains the path based on a body belonging to the desire realm; this path is termed "attained," "abiding within the body," "accomplished," and "manifest."
Attaining the Path by means of another body is termed "attainment" (prāpti), but it does not abide within that body; it is accomplished (samanvāgata) but not manifest (saṃmukhībhūta).
Second, it is taught that attaining the Path by means of a body belonging to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) is termed "attainment," and it abides within that body; it is both accomplished and manifest.
Based on others, it exists within the body, is attained, and is present.
Based on other bodies, one attains the Path, yet it is not obtained, does not exist within the body, is not attained, and is not present.
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement.

If that were the case, then after one has attained the fruit based on a body in the desire realm and is subsequently born into the form or formless realms, and having been so born, the noble path arises and becomes manifest—could it then be said that the fruit is attained again?
It is well as previously stated.

The Noble Path relies both upon the female body and the male body; when it is said that there is "one path," this means that the path relying on the female body and the path relying on the male body are one and the same path.
Regarding the statement that there are many paths: the path of the female body is distinct, and the path of the male body is distinct.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of statements regarding these many paths.
The first states:
If the path attained by a female body is such that this path is termed "attained," is present within the body, is accomplished, and is manifest;
whereas the path within a male body is such that this path is termed "not attained," though it is present within the body, accomplished, yet not manifest.
The second person says:
"If the path attained by relying on a female body is called 'attained,' 'abiding within the body,' 'accomplished,' and 'manifest,' then that same path,
when it pertains to a male body, is not attained, does not abide within the body, is not accomplished, and is not manifest."
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement. Why is this?

If one attains the fruit while relying on a female body, and subsequently attains a male body upon which the Noble Path arises and manifests before one, can it be said that the fruit is attained again?
The previous explanation is preferable.
Anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi is attained by relying on a body with a lifespan of a hundred years, and so on, up to a body with a lifespan of eighty thousand years.

What is called "the one path" means that attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* based on a body with a lifespan of one hundred years is identical to attaining it based on a body with a lifespan of eighty thousand years.

Regarding the statement that there are many paths: the path attained by the body at the time of a hundred-year lifespan is different from the path attained by the body at the time of an eighty-thousand-year lifespan.
There are two kinds of what is called "many paths."
The first says:
Based on a body that has lived for a hundred years, one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; this path is called "attained," it resides within the body, it is accomplished, and it is present before one.
In other paths, it is called "attainment" (prāpti), but it does not abide within the body, is not accomplished, and does not manifest before one.
The second type of statement says:
"One attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* with a body that is a hundred years old"; in this case, the path is called "attainment," it abides within the body, is accomplished, and manifests before one.
In other bodies, it is not attained, does not exist within the body, is not accomplished, and does not manifest.
Question: If this is so, all Buddhas are equal; how then is this teaching to be reconciled?
Answer: They are said to be equal for three reasons:
first, because they originally cultivated and accumulated virtuous practices equally; [and so forth].
Second is the accomplishment of the *dharmakāya* and so forth;
third is the benefiting of the world and so forth.
Regarding the cultivation and accumulation of wholesome practices, all Buddhas exhaustively cultivate various skillful means and the four *pāramitās* throughout three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.

Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the Dharma-body and so forth": all Buddhas fully possess the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three unique applications of mindfulness, and they all abide in the highest of superior faculties.
Regarding "benefiting the world" and so forth: it is because one desires to cause immeasurable nayutas of sentient beings and their retinues to all attain liberation and enter nirvana.
For these three reasons, it is called "equal."
Furthermore, there are those who say that their precepts are also equal, because they all abide in the most supreme precepts;
their faculties are also equal, because they all abide in the most supreme faculties;
and their paths are also equal, because they have all fully accomplished the most supreme paths.
The commentary says:
That which was stated previously is preferable. Question:
Is there any single dharma that can cause twenty-four acquisitions (*prāpti*) to arise and manifest within a single moment?
Answer: There is.

If one attains right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) based on the fourth dhyāna and attains the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) within the six stages, the four modes of practice—namely, the mode of impermanence (anitya-ākāra) and so forth—of that stage will manifest before one.

Question: Is it possible that one attains the abandonment of afflictions (kleśa) yet does not relinquish them, or relinquishes them yet does not attain them? This should be elaborated extensively as a fourfold logical analysis (catuṣkoṭi). Regarding "attaining but not relinquishing":

this refers to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) who have become detached from the desires of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), as well as for noble ones (ārya), except at the time of the transformation of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) or the attainment of a fruit (phala-prāpti); all other paths of abandoning the fetters (saṃyojana) fall under this category.

Regarding "abandoning but not attaining": this refers to ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) when they fall back after having abandoned desire; or when they die in the realms of form or formlessness and are reborn in the desire realm; or when noble ones (ārya) die in a lower stage and are reborn in a higher stage, or when they regress from an intermediate fruit.

Regarding "both obtaining and relinquishing": this refers to ordinary persons who, at the end of their lives in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), are reborn in the form realm (rūpadhātu); or those who, at the end of their lives in a higher stage, are reborn in a lower stage of the form or formless realms; as well as noble ones (ārya) at the time of attaining a fruit, at the time of transforming their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti), and at the time of falling away from a fruit.
Regarding that which must necessarily be relinquished, it excludes the aforementioned matters.
Should one say that inhalation and exhalation revolve by depending on the body?
This is explained at length, and so forth.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
As stated in the *Dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra*:
"For what reason, World-Honored One, did you say that inhalation and exhalation are bodily formations (*kāyasaṃskāra*)?
The answer is as follows:
This is a bodily phenomenon; the body is its basis.
It also belongs to the body and turns back in dependence upon the body.
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, and as stated in the *Dhamma-tejina-sūtra*:
"For what reason do inhalation and exhalation not continue in one who has died?
He replied:
"Inhalation and exhalation depend on the power of the mind; because the dead have no mind, inhalation and exhalation do not continue."

One sutra states that [the self] exists by way of the body, while another sutra states that it exists by way of the mind; people claim that both of these sutras are of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and yet also of non-definitive meaning (*neyārtha*).
It is for the purpose of revealing the true meaning of these two sutras that this treatise is composed.
Should it be said that inhalation and exhalation revolve depending on the body,
or should it be said that they revolve depending on the mind? Answer:
It should be said that [the turning] depends on the body or depends on the mind, according to what is appropriate and convenient.
Question: In what way is it according to what is appropriate and convenient?
Answer: Some say that it is like the inhalation and exhalation of an infant, which are few; those of middle age, which are moderate; and those of old age, which are many.
Others say that this is spoken of according to what is appropriate because there are four reasons.
What are the four?
First, dependence on the body;
second, the passage of the wind-ways.
Third, the various apertures open;
fourth, the mind becomes coarse as inhalation and exhalation manifest before it.
These four matters are explained according to what is appropriate and convenient.

If inhalation and exhalation depended solely on the body and not on the mind, then even when one enters the attainment of non-perception or the attainment of cessation, inhalation and exhalation would still continue. Why is this?

In that state as well, there is a body that serves as the basis for inhalation and exhalation, the respiratory passages are open, and all the pores are dilated; yet, because coarse mental states are not present, inhalation and exhalation do not circulate.

If inhalation and exhalation depended solely on the mind and not on the body, then sentient beings in the formless realm would also experience the circulation of inhalation and exhalation; however, because they lack these four factors, it does not circulate there.

If inhalation and exhalation were to depend solely upon the body and mind without conforming to their suitability, this would occur during the period within the egg and so forth—as explained at length.

While within the egg and such states, the body is not a basis for inhalation and exhalation; the channels for wind are not open and the various orifices are not yet developed. Because there exists only the coarse mind belonging to the stage of inhalation and exhalation, [the breath] does not circulate;
if it were to circulate, there would necessarily be agitation.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the *kalala* stage of the egg is soft and thin, inhalation and exhalation do not circulate;
and because the various apertures of the body have not yet opened during the *arbuda* and *peśī* stages, inhalation and exhalation do not circulate.

Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, although there is a body that serves as the basis for inhalation and exhalation and the pathways for wind remain open, the various pores do not open; because of the power of meditative concentration, the entire body becomes completely sealed, and furthermore, the coarse mental states of the level of inhalation and exhalation do not arise, as the mental states of that stage are subtle.
Question: For what reason is it said that one "enters" the fourth dhyāna, rather than being said to "be born" in the fourth dhyāna? Answer:
Some say that it is because the intention of the author of the sutra was such, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that this passage should have been stated thus:
"entering the fourth dhyāna and being born in the fourth dhyāna."
That which is not mentioned should be understood as being stated incompletely, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, if it mentions entering meditative absorption, one should know that it also mentions the place of rebirth.
As the Sūtra says:
"Having previously cultivated this meditative concentration, one is subsequently reborn in that place.
Therefore, the inhalation and exhalation depend on both the turning of the body and the turning of the mind, according to what is appropriate and convenient.
From the Avīci Hell up to the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven, all sentient beings born within this interval possess their sense faculties; this is explained at length.
Here, "possessing complete sense faculties" refers to being endowed with the aforementioned four matters, not the physical faculties such as the eye and so forth.
Question: For what reason do inhalation and exhalation not occur when one enters the fourth dhyāna? Answer:
A coarse mind can give rise to inhalation and exhalation because those mental states and their associated factors (*citta-caitasika*) are subtle.

Furthermore, some say that a restless mind can give rise to inhalation and exhalation; however, this mind is not restless. It is like a person walking on a busy road who raises up dust; it is just like that.
The Venerable Sūmīpa said:
For what reason do inhalation and exhalation not recur when one enters the fourth dhyāna?
Because for one who has entered the fourth dhyāna, all the pores of the body are closed; since there is no basis [for their movement], inhalation and exhalation do not recur.
The Venerable Bāṇḍa said:
"Upon entering the fourth dhyāna, the body does not move; because that mind is unmoving, the body is also unmoving.
Furthermore, others have said: "In the desire realm, because one craves sensory objects, the body and mind become coarse."

In the first dhyāna, because of vitarka and vicāra; in the second dhyāna, because of prīti; in the third dhyāna, because of sukha; and in the fourth dhyāna, because of being forever free from such factors—there is the stage of having exhalation, the stage of having inhalation and exhalation, and the stage of having neither inhalation nor exhalation.
Inhalation comes; exhalation goes.
Inhalation and exhalation exist within four stages.
These four stages are: the desire realm, the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna.
In the five stages, there is no inhalation or exhalation.
These five stages refer to the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments. Question:
When one abides in the stage of inhalation and exhalation, yet a mind belonging to a stage devoid of inhalation and exhalation is present before one, does the inhalation and exhalation cease?
The answer is:
they do not cease.

Question: When one abides in a state that does not involve inhalation and exhalation, yet a mind pertaining to the stage of inhalation and exhalation is present before one, do inhalation and exhalation still occur?
Answer: Yes.
It does not turn back. Question:

If the body abides in the stage of inhalation and exhalation, and the mind of the stage of inhalation and exhalation is present before one, should it be said that the inhalation and exhalation turn back?
Is it because of the body that one turns back, or is it because of the mind?
The answer is:
some say it is because of the body that one turns back.

Regarding those who maintain this view: because it turns back by means of the body, when one is born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), the mind of the desire realm manifests; this body belongs to the desire realm, and inhalation and exhalation also belong to the desire realm. Turning back from the mind of the desire realm, it is precisely this mind that constitutes the object of observation.

When one is born in the desire realm and the mind of the first dhyāna manifests before them, the body belongs to the desire realm and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the desire realm; these are the objects observed by that very mind as it turns back from the first dhyāna.
Question: If that is so, how is this teaching to be reconciled?
As it is said:
The inhalation and exhalation of the desire realm are extinguished within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) of the first dhyāna.
The answer is:
the inhalation and exhalation of the desire realm either turn back from a mind of the desire realm or turn back from a mind of the first dhyāna.
If one turns back from a mind of the desire realm, it ceases; if one turns back from a mind of the first dhyāna, it manifests before one.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "ceasing" refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

When one is born within the desire realm and the mind of the second or third dhyāna manifests before them, the body belongs to the desire realm and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the desire realm; these are the objects observed by that mind as it turns back from the second or third dhyāna mind.

In the first dhyāna, when the mind of the first dhyāna is present, the body belongs to the first dhyāna, and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first dhyāna; turning back from the mind of the first dhyāna, these are precisely the objects of observation for that mind.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, a mind of the desire realm manifests; the body belongs to the first dhyāna, and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first dhyāna. These turn back from the mind of the desire realm and are not the objective sphere perceived by that mind.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, and the minds of the second or third dhyānas manifest before one, the body belongs to the first dhyāna and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first dhyāna; these are the objects of observation for those minds when they turn back from the second or third dhyānas.
When born in the second dhyāna, it is explained according to its characteristics.

When born in the third dhyāna, the mind of the third dhyāna is present; the body belongs to the third dhyāna, and inhalation and exhalation belong to the third dhyāna. Turning back from the mind of the third dhyāna, that very mind is the object of observation.

When one is born in the third dhyāna, a mind of the desire realm manifests; the body belongs to the third dhyāna, and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the third dhyāna. These turn back from the mind of the desire realm and are not the objective sphere perceived by that [desire-realm] mind.

Thus, when the mind of the second dhyāna manifests while one has already attained the first dhyāna, the body belongs to the third dhyāna and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the third dhyāna; these are turned away from the minds of the first and second dhyānas and are not the objects of observation for those minds.
Regarding those who maintain that inhalation and exhalation turn back because of the body: the inhalation and exhalation of the desire realm serve as objects for four types of consciousness;
the inhalation and exhalation of the first dhyāna serve as objects for three types of consciousness;
the inhalation and exhalation of the second dhyāna serve as objects for two types of consciousness.
The inhalation and exhalation of the third dhyāna serves as the objective sphere for that third dhyāna.

Regarding those who maintain this view—that inhalation and exhalation turn back because of the mind—when one is born in the desire realm and a mind of the desire realm is present, the body belongs to the desire realm and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the desire realm; thus, turning back from the mind of the desire realm, they are the objective spheres observed by that very mind.

If the mind of the first dhyāna manifests before one, while the body belongs to the desire realm and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first dhyāna, then upon returning from that first dhyāna mind, these very objects are the spheres of observation for that mind.

If the mind of the second or third dhyāna is present while the body remains in the desire realm, the inhalation and exhalation belong to that second or third dhyāna; when one turns back from the mind of the second or third dhyāna, it is precisely that [breath] which becomes the object of observation for that mind.

When one is born in the first dhyāna, the mind of the first dhyāna is present; the body belongs to the first dhyāna, and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first dhyāna. Turning back from the mind of the first dhyāna, these are precisely the objects observed by that mind.

If a mind of the desire realm is present before one, while the body belongs to the first dhyāna and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the desire realm, then upon turning back from that desire-realm mind, these very [breaths] become the objects of observation for that mind.

If the mind of the second or third dhyāna is present, while the body belongs to the first dhyāna and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the second or third dhyāna, then upon returning from the mind of the second or third dhyāna, that very mind becomes the observed object.
The same applies to those born in the second dhyāna.

For those born in the third dhyāna, when the mind of the third dhyāna is present, the body belongs to the third dhyāna, the inhalation and exhalation belong to the third dhyāna, and that which turns back from the mind of the third dhyāna is precisely the object observed by that mind.

If a mind of the desire realm is present while the body is in the third dhyāna, and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the desire realm, then upon returning from that desire-realm mind, these [breaths] are precisely the objects observed by that mind.

If the mind of the first or second dhyāna is present, while the body belongs to the third dhyāna and the inhalation and exhalation belong to the first or second dhyānas, then turning back from the mind of the first or second dhyāna, these [breaths] are the objects of observation for that mind.

Regarding those who maintain that inhalation and exhalation depend on the turning of the mind: the inhalation and exhalation of the desire realm are the objects of observation for the mind of the desire realm; those of the first dhyāna are for the first dhyāna; those of the second dhyāna are for the second dhyāna; and those of the third dhyāna are for the third dhyāna.
The critique says:
One should not make such a statement; it is better as previously stated. Question:
Are inhalation and exhalation reckoned as belonging to the category of sentient beings, or do they not belong to the category of sentient beings?
The answer is: they are reckoned as belonging to the category of sentient beings.
Question: Is this an internal phenomenon (*adhyātma-dharma*) or an external phenomenon (*bāhya-dharma*)? Answer:
This is an external phenomenon.
Within this body there is also internal wind, yet inhalation and exhalation are external winds.
Are they nourishment, are they a support, or are they karmic retribution?
Answer: This is the basis.
Although this body also possesses winds of nourishment (*āhāra-vāyu*) and winds of karmic retribution (*vipāka-vāyu*), inhalation and exhalation are the primary basis.
As the Sūtra says, the Buddha told Ānanda:
If one can cause the inhalation and exhalation to proceed in continuous succession like the flight of arrows from one notch to the next, this is called "different food.
What is meant by "different food"?
The answer is:

Although one may nourish the human body with the most excellent food and drink, this does not equal the inhalation and exhalation achieved through right application; and as for that which harms the body, nothing is more detrimental than wrong application.
What is the meaning of "the inhalation and exhalation are like the joints of arrows following one another"?
The answer is:
it is like shooting a subsequent arrow at a preceding arrow; this is the meaning of "the joints of arrows following one another."
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "uninterrupted continuity" is the sense of "the succession from one arrow-hole to the next. Question:
Regarding inhalation and exhalation, does inhalation come first, or does exhalation come first?
Answer: Some say that it emerges first; a wind arises at the navel that opens the various orifices, and only then does [the breath] emerge.
Others say that the wind which opens the various orifices is not the inhalation or exhalation.
Once the various apertures have opened, the wind enters first.
Just as when a hungry or thirsty person eats even a small amount of food, it causes the body to grow and flourish;
so too, at the time of death, when the final breath exits and never enters again, it is called "death."
Furthermore, there are those who say that death occurs when the final inhalation enters but no longer emerges.
As it is said:
"May I always obtain inhalation and exhalation."
When entering the fourth dhyāna, the breath goes out; when emerging from the fourth dhyāna, the breath comes in.
As it is said:
"There is ānāpāna, and there is mindfulness of ānāpāna."
What is meant by *āna*? What is meant by *apāna*?
And what is meant by the cultivation of mindfulness of *ānāpāna*?
The answer is:
Inhalation is *āna* and exhalation is *apāna*.
Furthermore, there are those who say that exhalation is *āna* and inhalation is *apāna*.
As it is said:
when a bhikṣu inhales external air, it is called *āna*; when internal air exhales and disperses, it is called *apāna*.
To be able to take that as an object of mindfulness is called *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).
To cultivate and extensively disseminate the dharma associated with mindfulness is called the cultivation of *ānāpānasmṛti*.
Regarding *ānāpānasmṛti*, it is said that there are six matters.
What are the six? First, counting; second, following; third, settling; fourth, observing; fifth, transforming; sixth, purifying.
Regarding counting:
There are five kinds:
first, counting;
second, subtractive counting;
Third, the enumeration of increase;
fourth, the enumeration of aggregates;
fifth, the enumeration of purity.
Counting refers to going from one to two, up to ten.
Decreasing counting refers to going from three down to one.
Increasing counting refers to going from one up to three or four.
Regarding counting the clusters: one observes six inhalations and six exhalations.
Furthermore, there are those who say that counting the clusters means observing the inhalation as exhalation and observing the exhalation as inhalation.
Regarding the counting of purity, one contemplates the five exhalations. Question:
Does one first count the inhalation, or does one first count the exhalation?
Answer: First, one counts the inhalations. Why is this so?
At the time of birth, the breath enters; at the time of death, the breath exits.

One who contemplates in this manner is said to be practicing the method of contemplation that accords with the cycle of birth and death; therefore, one first observes the entering and exiting [of the breath], and so forth, as explained at length.
As for "following" (anugama): when one observes the breath reaching the throat, the mind also follows it there.
When it reaches the heart, the navel, and even down to the toes, the mind likewise follows it there.
As for "stopping" (sthāpanā): when the breath enters and dwells at the throat, the mind also stops and contemplates there.
Thus, with a sincere mind, one practices both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as far as the navel and even down to the toes.
Furthermore, there are those who say that *śamatha* consists of observing the wind abiding within the body, like observing the thread inside a bright pearl.

The practitioner does not merely contemplate wind; because the wind element is [identical in nature to] the other elements, they contemplate the four great elements equally, without making distinctions.
Contemplating these four great elements, one considers what they can produce: one knows that they produce derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Next, one contemplates derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*): upon what does it depend, and what is its function?
One knows that it depends on the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
For this reason, one contemplates the five aggregates.

As for "turning," it means that by turning this contemplation of inhalation, one gives rise to the application of mindfulness of the body; next, one gives rise to the applications of mindfulness of feeling, mind, and phenomena; and subsequently, one gives rise to the stages of heat, summits, patience, and the supreme mundane dharmas.
"Purity" refers to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, some say that all these roots of goodness are portions of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding "reckoning," there are two matters:
First, counting the inhalations and exhalations;
second, being able to relinquish discursive thoughts.
These two matters follow one another:
First, being able to follow the inhalation and exhalation;
second, abandoning thoughts of sensual desire.
There are two matters regarding tranquility (śamatha):
First, being able to abide in stillness at the tip of the nose;
second, not relinquishing samādhi.
There are two matters regarding contemplation:
First, being able to observe the characteristics of arising, abiding, and changing in the inhalation and exhalation;
second, being able to grasp the characteristics of the mind and mental factors.
There are two matters regarding their transformation:
First, the ability to know the aggregates;
second, the ability to enter the noble path.
Purity is of two kinds:
First, it can sever the fetters;
second, it can purify views. Question:
What is the essential nature of *ānāpānasmṛti*?
The answer is:
it is wisdom (*prajñā*), because within this mental complex (*cittapakṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*) is predominant.
It is called *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) because it takes as its object the associated and co-existent dharmas.
Its essential nature in the desire realm consists of four aggregates (*skandha*), while in the form realm it consists of five aggregates.

Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): it exists within five stages—namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna, the threshold of the second dhyāna, and the threshold of the third dhyāna.

As for the body upon which it relies: it relies on a body of the desire realm and also on a body of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); however, at the time of its initial arising, it must necessarily rely on a body of the desire realm.
The essence of the practitioner is not the practice itself.
As for the "object," the object is that which is [the focus].
Regarding the mindfulness of wind, it is not the fundamental application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), but rather a skillful means (upāya) for the application of mindfulness.
If one takes the attendants of the foundations of mindfulness, they constitute the foundation of mindfulness of the body. Why is this?
Because it takes form as its object.
Question: If that is so, why do the Buddhist sūtras state that the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing) is the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*)? Answer:
Because these are skillful means of the foundations of mindfulness, they are called the four foundations of mindfulness. Question:
If that is so, the contemplation of impurity is also a skillful means of the four foundations of mindfulness; why then is it not called the four foundations of mindfulness?
The answer is:
If there are sentient beings who should hear about *ānāpāna* as the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the World-Honored One speaks of it.
If there are sentient beings who should hear about impurity (*aśubha*) as the application of mindfulness and thereby attain awakening, the Buddha likewise speaks of it.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in this sutra it is also stated that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is a foundation of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
As a verse in this sutra says:
“If one is able to contemplate the blue-black color, One is also able to contemplate its putrefaction.”
This is called the application of mindfulness to the body;
when one observes purity and gives rise to a mind of desire, within that there is also feeling—this is called the application of mindfulness to feeling;
when one is able to maintain a mind free from hatred, this is called the application of mindfulness to the mind.
"Furthermore, one cuts off both craving and aversion; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Furthermore, for what reason is ānāpānasmṛti (mindfulness of breathing) said to be a foundation of mindfulness, while the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is not?
The answer is:
Because the contemplation of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) is firm and reliable, whereas the method of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) is not so.
If a practitioner loses mindfulness and afflictions manifest before them, they are able to quickly return to the contemplation [of breathing].
It is just as when a person, out of fear and terror, quickly runs into a city; so it is with him.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) is not shared with non-Buddhists, nor is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) shared with them.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) can increase the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*). Why is this?
Because when performing this contemplation, one necessarily contemplates the bones of male and female bodies.
Mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing) can increase the characteristics of the Dharma. Why is this?
Because it is the root of the samādhi of emptiness; for this reason, the four foundations of mindfulness are taught.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the mindfulness of *ānāpāna* (breathing) takes a proximate object; it is an unmixed contemplation, not a sequential contemplation, not a contemplation based on sentient beings, and does not require much effort, whereas the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is not so.
Therefore, these are called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and not the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*).
As for "the wise one," this refers to the first type of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Regarding "associated with a faculty," it is associated with a single faculty, namely the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
"World" refers to the three periods of time.
"Conditioned by the world" means conditioned by the three periods of time.
"Wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate" refers to what is wholesome.
"Conditioned by the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral" means conditioned by the neutral.
"Bound to the desire, form, and formless realms" means bound to the desire and form realms.
"Conditioned by that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound" means conditioned by that which is bound to the desire and form realms.
Those that are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee refer to what is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Those that take as their object dharmas that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee refer to taking as their object what is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Regarding those abandoned by the path of seeing, those abandoned by the path of cultivation, and those not abandoned: this refers to those abandoned by the path of cultivation.
Regarding those conditioned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation that are not abandoned: this refers to those conditioned by what is abandoned by the path of cultivation.
"To take names as conditions and to take meanings as conditions" means to take meanings as conditions.
"To take oneself as a condition and to take others as conditions" means to take both oneself and others as conditions.
As a verse in the Sūtra says:
"If one is able to fully practice the mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti),
training in it sequentially just as the Buddha has taught. It is asked:
This verse asks: who is fully endowed [with these qualities] and who is not?
The answer is:
some say that it is here stated that the Buddha is fully endowed, whereas the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not.
Furthermore, some say that Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas are complete, whereas Śrāvakas are incomplete.
Others say that those above the stage of Arhat are complete, whereas those who are still in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say that noble ones (ārya) are complete, whereas ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are incomplete.
The critique states:
Such an explanation is excellent.
If one possesses these six matters, it is called "complete"; if one does not possess these six matters, it is called "incomplete.
As stated in the sutra, the Buddha said:
"In the second month, I entered into meditative concentration and manifested such auspicious signs as were appropriate."
What are the auspicious signs?
The answer is:
the World-Honored One himself spreads out a seat and sits upon it, manifesting by transformation a retinue of bhikṣus surrounding him; these are the auspicious signs.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the World-Honored One caused the earth to tremble slightly; when the bhikṣus saw this, they immediately went to where the Buddha was, and this too was an auspicious omen.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:

"If any heterodox practitioners or brahmins come and ask you, 'In these two months, what meditative absorption has the śramaṇa Gautama entered? you should answer them, 'He has entered the ānāpāna-samādhi.'"

Question: Since even the non-Buddhist brahmins do not know the name of the *ānāpāna* concentration, why does the Buddha say this: "If any non-Buddhists come to question you, you should answer that you have entered the *ānāpāna* concentration"?
Answer: It is intended to cause non-Buddhists to give rise to the thought of aspiration.
If non-Buddhists hear the name of the concentration on *ānāpāna*, they will certainly give rise to the thought of aspiration.
"Because they have given rise to the desire for existence and the perception of it, they come to me; by this cause and condition, they shall enter my Dharma.
Thus he spoke. [The interlocutor] asked:

If the World-Honored One enters all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis, why is it said that he enters only the *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) concentration?
The answer is:
because the *ānāpāna-smṛti* concentration stands at the beginning of all meditative absorptions.
As it is said: "One should contemplate the breath as short," and so forth, up to the full explanation. Question:
Does the breath first become short and later long, or does it first become long and later short?
Answer: One first contemplates the short and subsequently contemplates the long.
How is this known?
Answer: As it is said, when the World-Honored One has been in meditative concentration for not long, his inhalations and exhalations move rapidly;
as he remains in concentration for a longer duration, his inhalations and exhalations become settled and stable.

It is like a person carrying a heavy burden through a steep and difficult place; when his body is utterly exhausted, the inhalations and exhalations move rapidly, but when he comes to rest, the inhalations and exhalations become still.
The Buddha is also like this.
When inhaling, he knows the breath pervades the entire body; when exhaling, he likewise knows it pervades the entire body. Question:
If one fixes the mind on the tip of the nose, how does one further know that the inhalation and exhalation pervade the entire body?
The answer is:
the Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra spoke thus:
One thoroughly understands that this body is of an impermanent nature and does not lose mindfulness.
Question: If this is so, would it not be called "arising from meditative concentration"?
Answer: It is not called "arising," because one does not abandon those skillful means.
In this way, one successively contemplates this body as being of the nature of suffering, emptiness, non-self, defilement, and impurity.
If this mindfulness of ānāpāna has not yet been perfected, one fixes the attention on the tip of the nose;
later, once it has been perfected, one contemplates the pores of the body as being like the roots of a lotus, with the wind entering and exiting through them.
Question: If that is so, why is it not called "arising from concentration"? Answer:
Because he does not abandon the mind directed toward his intended goal through skillful means, it is not called "arising from meditative absorption.
The Venerable Bhadanta said:
"When a Bodhisattva contemplates, he first fixes his mindfulness on the openings of the body where the winds enter and exit, ensuring that the mind does not become distracted."
Nor does one abandon the application of skillful means while bringing the bodily formations to rest during inhalation and exhalation, and so forth, as explained at length.
To bring the bodily formations to rest means to cause these inhalations and exhalations to become increasingly subtle and tranquil, or at times not to observe them at all.

Furthermore, there are those who say that observing the breath for a short duration is called entering the first dhyāna; observing the breath for a long duration is entering the second dhyāna; knowing the breath pervades the entire body is entering the third dhyāna; and ceasing the bodily formations of the breath is entering the fourth dhyāna.
These four meanings should also be explained in this way:
"being mindful of joy while breathing in and out" refers to the first and second dhyānas;
"being mindful of pleasure while breathing in and out" refers to the contemplation of that very pleasure.
One who is mindful of mental formations while breathing in and out observes perception and volition.
Furthermore, some say that one who is mindful of mental formations observes the volition of mental karma and the cessation of mental formations.
Inhalation and exhalation cause those mental formations to become increasingly subtle and tranquil, or at times cease to be observed.
"Being aware of the mind during inhalation and exhalation" refers to observing consciousness.

Regarding one who is mindful of the mind of sympathetic joy, the mind of concentration, and the mind of liberation while entering and exhaling, the Tathāgata has no mind of sympathetic joy, no mind of concentration, and no mind of liberation.
One observes the bodhisattva’s original practice: the mind of sympathetic joy, the concentrated mind, and the liberated mind.
Regarding the awakening to impermanent inhalation and exhalation, one observes that these inhalations and exhalations are impermanent.
Being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation that have ceased is the observation of the cessation of past afflictions.
Being mindful of the inhalation and exhalation that are free from desire is the observation of the cessation of future afflictions.
One who is mindful of the cessation of inhalation and exhalation observes the abandonment of present afflictions.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one who is mindful of the impermanence of inhalation and exhalation observes that the mind and mental factors are impermanent.
One who is mindful of the inhalation and exhalation that involve cessation eliminates the fetter of craving and observes the cessation of the remaining fetters.
One who is mindful of the inhalation and exhalation that involve detachment observes the cessation of all afflictions.
The awareness of the cessation of inhalation and exhalation is the observation of the dharma that severs all fetters.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the awareness of impermanence is the observation of the body’s impermanence.
Awakening to abandonment means observing the abandonment of ignorance.
Awakening to detachment from desire means observing detachment from craving for desire.
Awakening to cessation means observing that nirvana is tranquility.
The Venerable Bāḍha said:
"To awaken to impermanence is to contemplate the five aggregates of clinging.
To awaken to cessation is to contemplate that the five aggregates of clinging are empty and selfless."
To awaken to the departure from desire is to contemplate that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering.
To awaken to cessation is to contemplate that the five aggregates of clinging are the dharma of non-arising and quiescent extinction.
"When I have such thoughts and abide in such a way, these are all coarse concentrations; I should instead dwell extensively within subtle concentration.
[He] asked:
"What is subtle concentration?"
Answer: Some say it is the fourth dhyāna;
others say it is the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
At that time during the night, three deities from the desire realm came to where the Bodhisattva was:
first, one of inferior faculties; second, one of middling faculties; and [third, one of superior faculties].
3. Regarding those of superior faculties:
when the devas of inferior faculties see that he has neither inhalation nor exhalation, and that he is motionless and without mental activity, they say:
"This śramaṇa Gautama has now died."
Among them, those of middling faculties see that their bodies are still warm; although a long time has passed, they have not yet decayed or perished, and they say:
"Though we have not died yet, we shall certainly die later."
Those gods of superior faculties, having previously witnessed various Buddhas and their disciples entering the dharma of meditative absorption, speak thus:
"This is not death, nor is it the time for death; rather, one abides in this concentration, for such is the nature of dharmas."
If someone were to ask:
"What is the noble abiding?
What is the celestial abiding?"
What are the Brahma-abodes?
What are the abodes of those in training?
What are the abodes of those beyond training?
How does the Tathāgata abide? One should answer:
"It is through this mindfulness of ānāpāna (mindfulness of breathing)"; to speak thus is called the correct answer.
Question: Since mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti) is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, why is it said that one dwells as a learner or dwells as a non-learner? Answer:

They are called "learner" (*śaikṣa*) and "non-learner" (*aśaikṣa*) because they are attained at the limit of learning and non-learning; they are called "learner" and "non-learner" because they can enter into the dharmas of learning and non-learning.

Furthermore, some say: they are called "noble and pure" (*āryaviśuddha*) because they are free from afflictions; they are called "learner" because they belong to those in training, and they are called "learner" because they can attain the dharmas of learning; they are called "non-learner" because they belong to those beyond training, and they are called "non-learner" because they can give rise to the dharmas of non-learning.
Regarding the dwelling of the Tathāgata: the dwelling of an Arhat is called the dwelling of the Tathāgata.
"Obtaining what has not yet been obtained" refers to superior progress (*viśeṣagamana*).
