"That which has already been obtained" consists of two [aspects]: first, experiencing happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); [and second, the attainment of nirvāṇa].
Second, those who have already reached the immovable state.
Furthermore, some say that they are called "noble abodes" (āryavihāra) because they belong to the noble ones, and they are called "noble abodes" because they can give rise to noble dharmas.
They are called "divine abodes" (devavihāra) because they belong to the gods, and they are called "divine abodes" because they can give rise to gods.
Up to the point that all that belongs to the Tathāgata is called the "abode of the Tathāgata," and because it can give rise to the dharmas of the Tathāgata, it is called the "abode of the Tathāgata.
One who has not yet attained but now attains is the Arhat.
Regarding those who have already attained the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*), there are four kinds of such happiness:
first, the happiness of renunciation (*pravrajyā-sukha*);
second, the happiness of seclusion (*viveka-sukha*).
Third, the bliss of cessation; fourth, the bliss of the three types of enlightenment (*trividha-bodhi*).
As it is said: "Just as sentient beings with form turn their minds in dependence upon the body," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
Just as sentient beings in the desire and form realms turn their minds by relying on form, those in the formless realm lack form; some might therefore claim that their minds turn without any basis.
This treatise is composed in order to bring certainty to such a view.
It is said that there is a basis for this. Question: What is its basis?
Answer: The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the bases of bodily experience (*āśraya*), and other such factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
What is meant by "factors dissociated from mind"?
This refers to the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*), non-accomplishment, and the arising, abiding, aging, and ceasing [of birth]. Question:
Since these also depend on the turning of the mind, why do you speak only of the body?
Answer: It is called "body" because the body is coarse.

The eye-faculty and the immediately preceding moment of consciousness act as the support and the basis for the arising of eye-consciousness; they give rise to the eye-faculty, the four great elements of the body-faculty, the life-faculty, the locus of sensation, acquisition (*prāpti*), birth, duration, decay, and cessation.
Such dharmas as these act as the support (*āśraya*) but do not act as the basis (*āśraya-bhūta*).
The same explanation applies to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the immediately preceding mind (*samanantara-niruddha-citta*) act as both the support and the basis for body-consciousness (*kāya-vijñāna*), giving rise to the body-faculty, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the locus of the body’s experience (*kāyasthāna*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and birth, duration, decay, and cessation (*jāti-sthiti-jarā-anityatā*).
Such dharmas as these act as a support (*āśraya*) but do not act as a basis (*āśrayatva*).

The mind that has just ceased in immediate succession acts as the support and the basis for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). Furthermore, the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the locus of bodily sensation (*kāyasthāna*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), and cessation (*anityatā*) [act as supports].
Such dharmas as these act as the support (*āśraya*) but do not act as the basis (*āśrayatva*).

Furthermore, it is said that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and the immediately preceding consciousness (*samanantara-niruddha-citta*) act as the support and the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). [These also produce] the eye-faculty, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), the four great elements, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the locus of feeling (*vedanā-kāya-sthāna*), acquisition (*prāpti*), birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), decay (*jarā*), and cessation (*anityatā*).
Such dharmas as these act as the support (*āśraya*) but do not act as the basis (*āśrita*).
The same explanation applies to ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, and tongue-consciousness.

The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the immediately preceding mind (*samanantara-niruddha-citta*) act as the support and the basis for body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), giving rise to the body-faculty, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the locus of the body’s experience (*kāyasthāna*), acquisition (*prāpti*), and birth, subsistence, decay, and cessation.
Such dharmas as these act as a support (*āśraya*) but do not act as a basis (*āśraya*).

The mind that has ceased immediately prior acts as the support and the basis for the mental consciousness; the body-faculty produces the body-faculty; the four great elements, visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects; the life-faculty; the locus of the body's experience; acquisition (*prāpti*); and birth, subsistence, decay, and cessation.
Such dharmas as these act as a support (*āśraya*) but do not act as a basis (*niśraya*).

Furthermore, some say that the eye-faculty and the immediately preceding consciousness act as both a support and a basis for visual consciousness, whereas the four co-arising aggregates act as a support but do not act as a basis.
The same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

The mind that has just ceased in immediate succession serves as the support (*āśraya*) and the basis (*niśraya*) for the mental consciousness; the four aggregates (*skandha*) that arise simultaneously serve as the support but do not serve as the basis.
If this is how it is explained for those born in the desire realm and the form realm, what is the case for those born in the formless realm?
The answer is:

the mind that has ceased immediately prior to the mental consciousness acts as its support and its basis; the three aggregates that arise simultaneously act as its support but do not act as its basis.
Question: Is the essence of the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) one or many?
If it were one, why would the life-force not be severed when one’s hands or feet are cut off?
If there were many [lives], why would hands and feet be severed [without dying]? Why is it that there is no life within the hands and feet?
The answer is:
One should say that the substance is in fact one; because a single life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) resides within the body, it is called "possessing life."

Just as there is one who possesses feeling and is thus called "one with feeling," and just as there is one who possesses volition and is thus called "one with volition," so too because there is one mind, it is called "having a mind," and because that single mind has ceased, it is called "mindless."
Thus, because there is one life-force, it is called "possessing life. Question:
If this is so, why does one not die when their hands and feet are severed?
Answer: There are two kinds of bodies upon which life depends:
those that are complete and those that are incomplete.
When the hands and feet are severed, that which was complete ceases, and that which is incomplete continues to arise.
The body, as the basis for completeness, abides in a state of non-arising.
Regarding those who are not complete [in their faculties], they give rise [to consciousness] upon encountering conditions. Question:
For what reason does one not die when the hands or feet are severed, yet die immediately when the head is cut off or the waist is severed?
Answer: When the hands, feet, or other parts of the body are severed, many bases (*āyatana*) are not destroyed or harmed;
however, when the head is severed or the waist is cut, many bases are destroyed or harmed.
Furthermore, when the hands or feet are severed, the causes for the many bases (*āyatana*) are not destroyed, nor are their conditions (*pratyaya*) impaired;

however, when the head is severed or the waist is cut, the causes for the many bases are destroyed and their conditions are broken, causing the many bases to abide in the state of non-arising (*anutpattidharma*).

Furthermore, because the head is the locus where the various sense faculties (indriya) are gathered, and because the waist is the locus where inhalation and exhalation reside, death occurs if these are damaged or destroyed.

As for the limbs such as the hands and feet, they are neither loci where the various sense faculties are gathered nor loci where inhalation and exhalation reside; therefore, one does not die when they are severed.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) consists of multiple dharmas, which differ within the hands and feet, and likewise differ among all other parts of the body. Question:
If this were so, why would there be no life when one’s hands or feet are severed and cast upon the ground?
Answer: The life-force within the hands and feet, although distinct in nature, belongs to the body.
If they were separated from the body, they would no longer belong to the body; therefore, one does not live.
Furthermore, one does not survive because of the absence of the conditions for nourishing the basis [of existence].
What is the locus of the body that is experienced? Answer:

The similar dharmas of sentient beings consist of their shared mode of receiving a body and dwelling place; this is non-obscured neutral (*avyākṛta*), and it is both maturation (*vipāka*) and a basis (*āśraya*).
Regarding maturation, it refers to the similarity among the various realms of existence (*gati*), such as the mutual similarity among sentient beings in the hells.
In this way, it should be understood that other destinies and other births are likewise mutually similar.
As for the "basis," this refers to the similarity of the realms (*dhātu*); for example, the desire realm resembles the desire realm, and the same applies to the form and formless realms.

Just as it is with the similarity of elements (*dhātu*), so too should one explain, according to their respective characteristics, the regions, clans, householders, bhikṣus, brahmins, those in training (*śaikṣa*), and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that "retribution" refers to what is obtained at the time of initial birth,
while "basis" refers to what is obtained at a later time.
It is like a śramaṇa appearing as a śramaṇa, or a brāhmaṇa appearing as a brāhmaṇa.
This resemblance of the dharma is subject to both acquisition and relinquishment.
As for relinquishment, it occurs either at the time of death or due to other circumstances.

Regarding "other circumstances," for example, when one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one relinquishes the resemblance of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) and acquires the resemblance of a noble one (*ārya*).
When an Arhat enters parinirvāṇa, these are relinquished and not attained again.
Furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of dharmas common to sentient beings: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.

The resemblance to the state of an eighth person is wholesome; the resemblance to the state of one who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution is unwholesome; and the resemblance to the states of all other persons is neutral.
Question: Do all those who die here and are born there completely relinquish the place where they received their bodies?
Or, if they completely relinquish the place where they received their bodies, do they all die here and are born there?
This is expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding "dying here and being born there without relinquishing the locus of the body": this refers to dying in hell and being reborn again in hell, and so on, up to dying among the gods and being reborn again among the gods.
Regarding "abandoning the basis of feeling in this life without dying here to be born there," this refers to those who have attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

Regarding "dying here and being born there while also abandoning the basis of feeling," this refers to dying in the hells and being born in other realms, up to dying among the gods and being born in other realms.
"Neither dying here nor being born there, yet not abandoning the place where one receives a body"—this excludes the aforementioned matters.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Volume 14, Postscript after Collation; this volume, line five of the seventeenth sheet.

Desiring to cause immeasurable nayutas of retinues beneath him to all attain liberation and enter the supreme realm of nirvana—where those who originally possessed the capacity to sever craving and cultivate compassion, as well as brothers and sisters, may find peace and happiness beyond compare.
There are four hundred and fifty-five characters in total.
Those which are absent from both the Dan and Song editions not only fail to connect the beginning and end of the text,
but when one examines the flow of the prose, they are clearly inconsistent with the context.
As for the stylistic conventions of composition,
they are not addressed in this treatise;
they were merely added erroneously by the national edition.
Therefore, I do not accept it now.
I only regret that I have not yet ascertained from which sutra this passage originates;
this must await further verification.
I have recorded these thoughts to inform the worthy ones who come after me:
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifteen,
composed by Kātyāyanīputra and explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.

In the "Chapter on Miscellaneous Matters," Section on Human Types, Part Two: Regarding craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), should it be said that it is abandoned through the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) or should it be said that it is abandoned through the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*)?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is from the Buddha’s sutras.
In the sutras, the World-Honored One taught that there are three kinds of craving:
First, craving for sensual pleasure;
second, craving for existence;
third, craving for non-existence.

Although the World-Honored One’s sūtras state that there is no craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), they do not specify whether it is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Since that sūtra serves as the fundamental basis for this treatise, and because what was not stated therein is fully explained here, this treatise has been composed for this purpose.

Question: Regarding craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*), should it be said that it is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) or should it be said that it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*)? Answer:
It should be said that this is abandoned through the path of cultivation. Why is this?
Because there are no such impermanent conditions; that craving is craving for what does not exist.
Question: This [defilement] is also abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); why then is it said to be abandoned only through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)? Answer:
In order to accord with the meaning of the sūtra, as it is said therein:
"Suppose there is someone who, being oppressed by fear and suffering, forms this thought:"
"May I suffer dismemberment and even death;
after death, may I be free from illness and always attain peace and happiness.
The meaning and intent of that sutra state that the place where one receives a body is impermanent, and the craving for that object is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
Because it accords with the meaning of the sūtras, it is said that [craving for existence] is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, some say that craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is either abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) or abandoned through the path of cultivation.
What is abandoned through the path of vision?
The answer is:
craving for non-existence that is to be abandoned by the path of vision, and so forth, as explained at length.
This preceding passage explained the meaning in accordance with the sūtra; now, however, it explains the ultimate meaning.
According to my view, since there is no craving for existence, it should be said that this is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
According to my own interpretation, it accords with the meaning found within the Buddha’s sūtras.
Since those sūtras constitute the foundation of this treatise, for this reason it is stated that "craving for non-existence is abandoned through the path of cultivation."
In this way, do you wish to claim that craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is abandoned through the cultivation of the path?
This is the view of the Vibhajyavādins; "Vibhajyavāda" means "those who argue by making distinctions," and "Saṃyuktavāda" means "those who argue by association."
If one were to state another's fault based on an indeterminate statement, that would be unreasonable; therefore, it is said:
"Do you wish to claim that craving for non-existence (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?"
Yuktavādin replied, "It is so. Vibhajyavādin spoke as follows:

If one were to say this: "Can a stream-enterer give rise to such craving as, 'May I be cut off, destroyed, or even die, so that after death I may be free from illness and always attain peace and happiness'?"
He replied: "No. He asked:
Why is it that a srotāpanna cannot give rise to this craving?
The answer is:
some say it is because a srotāpanna has faith in the Dharma and faith in karma.

Furthermore, some say it is because one has already seen that all phenomena arise from their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and furthermore, because one is able to fulfill the cultivation of the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

Others say that this craving is increased by the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*) and arises based on the view of annihilation; since noble ones (*ārya*) have abandoned the view of annihilation, [craving does not arise].
Furthermore, there are those who say that this craving arises from sequential causes, because those sequential causes have already been severed.
The Venerable Śamatha said:
"The factors to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing are its cause; for the Noble Ones have already abandoned the factors to be abandoned by the Path of Seeing."
The Vibhajyavādins speak thus: "Listen to my challenge;
I shall state the point where you have fallen into contradiction with your own words.
You have said this:"
Craving for non-existence is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
You should also say:
"A stream-enterer can give rise to this craving, thinking: 'May I be cut off and destroyed, even unto death; after death, may I be free from illness and always attain peace and happiness.'"
If one speaks thus, this is not correct. One should not say:
"There is no craving for existence that is abandoned through the cultivation of the path."
If it is said that craving for non-existence is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this is not correct.
If it is said that this craving is abandoned through the path of cultivation, one should not say that a *srotāpanna* does not give rise to this craving.
If a *srotāpanna* does not give rise to this craving, one should not say that this craving is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). Pūrvavādī makes this statement:

"I do not say that all things which are not abandoned necessarily arise and manifest; there are cases where something is not abandoned yet does not arise and manifest, and there are cases where something, though already abandoned, still arises and manifests."
If those that have not been severed were to arise and manifest in the present, there would be no path to liberation. Why is this?

For ordinary persons and those still in training, there are many such factors that remain unsevered in future lives; if these were all to arise and manifest in the present, one could not attain liberation, because the future is infinite.
Such matters are not acceptable to the wise.
Pūrvavādin previously set forth such doctrines in order to point out the faults of others and to establish a refutation.
"In this way, do you intend to suggest that a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) has not yet exhausted their attachment to the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts?
The Vībhajyavādin replied: "It is so."
Pūtimatya further clarified:

"Do you intend for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) to be able to give rise to such craving as to cause me to become the Naga King Elāpattra, the Naga King Sāgara, or King Yama, and to become the most honored among the beings in hell?"
The Vibhajyavādin replied: "No. He asked:
Why does the *srotāpanna* not give rise to such cravings?
The answer is:
they are places where ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are born, not places where noble ones (*ārya*) are born.
Furthermore, some say that fools are born therein because they are wise men;
others say it is because those evil destinies have already attained non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If a dharma has attained cessation through non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it will no longer arise or manifest before one.
Furthermore, there are those who say that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is of two kinds:
first, craving for the place of birth; [second, craving for existence].
2. Attachment to the means of livelihood (*upakaraṇa-tṛṣṇā*).

Although a *srotāpanna* does not give rise to attachment to places of rebirth within the evil realms, they do give rise to attachment to the means of livelihood, such as elephants, horses, and so forth.
Just as Śakra conceived a heart of affection for the blue-clad yakṣa,
[the interlocutor] asked:
"Furthermore, how does it arise within the realm of hell-beings?"
The answer is:
If one's parents have been reborn in hell, and one hears this from a trustworthy person, one then conceives a heart of affection. Upatissa further said:
Listen to my refutation, which exposes your position as contradictory and defeated. You have stated:
"The stream-enterer has not yet exhausted craving for the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts."
One should say this:
"A stream-enterer (srotāpanna) can give rise to this craving, thinking, 'May I become the Naga King Elapatra,' and so forth, as explained at length.
If one were to say this, it would not be correct.

If it were not said that a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) can give rise to this state, then one should also not say that a stream-enterer has not yet exhausted craving for the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts.
[Yet] if a stream-enterer has not yet exhausted craving for the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, [such craving] does not arise and manifest in the present.
This is precisely where you contradict your own statement and fall into defeat. As you have asserted:
"The *srotāpanna* has not yet exhausted craving for the miserable realms (*apāya*), yet it does not arise as a present manifestation."
"What I have taught regarding craving for non-existence is also like this.
Pūrvavādin then challenged the Vibhajyavādin, saying:
"What do you think?"
If one kills one’s father or mother while bound by the *paryavasthānas* (obsessions), are these *paryavasthānas* abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
The Vibhajyavādins replied: "It is so."
Yuktabuddhi asked Vipaśyitabuddhi, who replied: "No.
He then asked:
Why does the Srotāpanna not give rise to these fetters?
The answer is:
some say that it is those who possess a superior evil mind who can give rise to these fetters and kill their parents; since the Srotāpanna possesses a superior wholesome mind, he does not do so.

Furthermore, some say that it is those with an excess of shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*) who can kill their parents, whereas a *srotāpanna* possesses an excess of shame and dread of blame.

Others say that such [killing] is nurtured by the entanglement (*paryavasthāna*) of false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and arises subsequent to false views; since the *srotāpanna* has already severed false views, [this does not apply to them].
Furthermore, there are those who say that the *srotāpanna* has already attained the discipline of non-action; for this reason, he does not give rise to these fetters (*paryavasthāna*).
Puttamāṭika again rebuked Vibhajjavādin, as explained in detail above.
Pudgalavādin further challenged Vibhajyavādin, saying:
"What do you think?
Regarding the craving for non-existence that is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, should this craving be said to be abandoned by the path of cultivation?"
The Vibhajyavādins replied: "It is so.
Those dharmas abandoned through the cultivation of the path are the wholesome dharmas with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*)."
"Non-existence" refers to the severance of the roots of goodness.
Purandara further rebuked Vibhajyavādin, saying:
"What do you think?"
A stream-enterer (srotāpanna) might give rise to this craving:
"Shall I sever my roots of goodness?
To this, the Vībhajyavādins replied:
"No. [The interlocutor] asks:
"For what reason does a srotāpanna not give rise to such craving?"
The answer is:

The noble ones cherish and delight in meritorious qualities; they constantly desire to bring wholesome dharmas to manifestation and do not wish to be separated from them, and for this reason, [unwholesome states] do not arise.
Pudgalavādin again rebuked Vibhajyavādin, as explained in detail above:
"If it is said that all [defilements] which have not been severed necessarily arise and manifest before one, then one must admit the fault [of admitting] that they exist, and so forth."
In the external scriptures, there are three kinds of objections:
the first is called the objection of doubt;
the second is called the objection of overstatement.
The third is the refutation by means of the "overwhelming difficulty.
As stated in the Buddhist sūtras, the World-Honored One also refuted others by means of three kinds of difficulties:
the first is called the "overwhelming difficulty."
The second is the objection regarding the equality of meaning;
the third is the objection regarding the contradiction of one's own words.
Regarding the "superiority through turning" objection, it is as when the Brahmin Dīrghanakha spoke thus:
"I do not tolerate anything at all.
The Buddha asked him a challenging question: "Do you not tolerate even this view?"
Regarding the objection concerning the meaning of "equality," it is as when Pāṭikāputra asked the Buddha:
"Do you know illusion?
The Buddha replied:
Knowing this, Pāṭikāputra said:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is a magician."
The Buddha asked Pāṭaliputra:
"Do you know that in the kingdom of Kośala there is a wicked man named Sarvakṣudraka who practices many evil deeds?
He replied:
"I know. The Buddha said, "You,
too, are one who has practiced many evil deeds."

Regarding the difficulty of contradictory statements: for example, the householder Upāli first stated that bodily karma is weighty, yet later spoke of the evil intent of a rishi, which led to the destruction of the great city of Kaliṅga and others.
In this context, the Audāyī puts the Vibhajyavādins to defeat by challenging them with the meaning of "equality. [The question is:
"Is there any dharma that does not exist?
He replies:
The three realms are impermanent. Question:
Why is this treatise composed?
Answer: It is because one wishes to leave the Vibhajyavādins with nothing further to say.
If this were not stated, the Vibhajyavādins would say:

Although you have subdued me with words, there is no underlying nature of craving that corresponds to the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa), whether it be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) or abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Therefore, that venerable one spoke thus:
"What dharma is there that has no name?
The three realms are impermanent."
Furthermore, there are those who say that one first explains the meaning and intent of the sūtras in accordance with conventional truth, and subsequently explains the ultimate truth.
Again, there are those who say that the Audāyīputra addressed the Vairaṭīputra:

"Although I have subdued you with my words, there is no underlying essence of craving that corresponds to the characteristics of phenomena, whether it be abandoned through the path of seeing or abandoned through the path of cultivation."
Therefore, it is said thus:
What dharma is there that has no name?
The three realms are impermanent.
Question: Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are also impermanent; why are they not mentioned here? Answer:
If a phenomenon is a basis for craving and a focal object of craving, it is explained herein;
since that which is untainted and impermanent is not a basis for craving nor a focal object of craving, it is therefore not explained.
What is the liberation of the mind?
Is it a mind possessed by desire,
or is it a mind free from desire?
...and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is a Buddhist scripture.
Within the Buddhist scriptures it is said:
The mind associated with desire attains liberation; the mind associated with hatred and delusion attains liberation. One does not say:
"Liberation is attained by a mind that possesses desire," or "Liberation is attained by a mind that is free from desire."
...and so forth, as explained at length.
That sūtra is the fundamental basis of this treatise; it shall now be explained in detail.
Furthermore, some say that the nature of the mind is inherently pure, yet it is obscured by adventitious afflictions.
As the Vātsīputrīyas say:
"The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure; because adventitious afflictions arise and obscure the mind, it is impure. Question:
If it were the case that the nature of the mind is inherently pure, yet becomes impure because it is shrouded by adventitious afflictions,
why does one not cause those adventitious afflictions to become pure as well through that inherently pure mind?
If you do not say that it is because the mind is pure that adventitious afflictions are purified, what is the reason?
Furthermore, does the mind arise first and the adventitious afflictions arise later, or do they arise simultaneously?
If the mind arises first and the adventitious afflictions arise later, then the mind would abide waiting for the adventitious afflictions;
only after the adventitious afflictions have arisen would they then obscure the mind.
If one were to speak in this way, then a single mind would abide for two moments.
If they were to exist simultaneously, at what time could one say that the nature of the mind is originally pure?
Furthermore, there would be no future world in which to abide in the mind that is pure by its very nature.

Therefore, in order to refute the positions of others, to manifest one's own position, and also because one wishes to explain the meaning that accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), this treatise is composed.
What is the liberation of the mind?
Is there liberation of the mind from desire, hatred, and delusion?
Or is there liberation of the mind without desire, hatred, and delusion?
He replied:
The mind is liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion. Question:
Since the mind itself is already liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion, what further thing is there to be liberated?
Answer: If spoken of in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), then the mind is called "liberated.
If spoken of in terms of the world or the body, it is not called "liberated."
If the various afflictions are not severed, that mind does not proceed in the world, nor does it attain liberation from the world;
it does not proceed in the body, nor does it attain liberation from the body.
If all afflictions are severed, that mind operates within the world and attains liberation from the world;
it operates within the body and attains liberation from the body.
Furthermore, some say that the mind associated with desire attains liberation, and the mind associated with hatred and delusion attains liberation.
As the Vibhajyavādins say: "A defiled mind is itself a non-defiled mind.
When afflictions have not been abandoned, it is defiled; when afflictions have already been abandoned, it is non-defiled."
It is just as with a vessel that has impurities: before the impurities have been removed, it is called "with impurity"; once the impurities have been removed, it is called "without impurity.
It is the same in this case.
One who speaks in such a manner should be contradicted and rebuked. Why is this?

It is not that his mind is conjoined with or mixed with desire, hatred, and delusion; yet, if desire, hatred, and delusion are not abandoned, this mind cannot be called liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion.
If one wishes to sever desire, hatred, and delusion, this mind is called "liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion.
To realize this meaning, the Buddha’s sūtra is cited; the World-Honored One said in a sūtra:
"The sun and moon have five obscurations; because they are covered by these five obscurations, the sun and moon are not bright and pure."
What are the five? They are "clouds," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Clouds" refers to how, during the summer season, even a few clouds can pervade the entire sky.
"Smoke" is like the smoke from burning grass and trees pervading the void.
"Dust" is like when it does not rain from heaven and the wind stirs up the dust of the earth, which pervades the void.
"Fog" is like the mist rising from the banks of a great river that pervades the void.
Furthermore, there are those who say that in the eastern lands, whether by day or by night, when the sun rises after rain, mist arises from the earth and fills the void.

As for Rāhu, the Asura King, who obstructs them: the sun and moon are the vanguard of the devas; the devas and the asuras are constantly at war, and because of the power and majesty of the sun and moon, the devas always prevail.
Rāhu, the Asura King, first desired to destroy it; however, because of the karmic power of all sentient beings, he was unable to destroy it and instead shielded it with his hand.

In this way, these various obscurations are distant from the sun and moon and not near them; as long as those obscurations have not been removed, the sun and moon do not appear bright and pure amidst them.
If those obscurations are removed, the sun and moon become bright and pure amidst those very obscurations.

In this way, that mind is not associated with or mixed with desire, hatred, and delusion; if desire, hatred, and delusion are not abandoned, that mind is not called "liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion";
if desire, hatred, and delusion are abandoned, that mind is called "liberated from desire, hatred, and delusion."
The World-Honored One stated in a sutra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the one who possesses the foremost great body is Rāhu, the King of the Asuras," and so forth, as explained at length.
There is no sentient being capable of transforming their own body to be as supremely handsome as Rāhula, the King of the Asuras; this refers to a manifested transformation-body, not a physical body.
What is the liberation of the mind? Is it past,
or is it future?
Question: Is it present? Answer:

When the distant future mind arises, that which constitutes the obstacles to liberation for those beyond training (aśaikṣa) refers to the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
If one speaks of the future, then the past and present are excluded.
If one speaks of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), then the mind of one in training (śaikṣa) is excluded. Question:
Question: Since those in training (*śaikṣa*) also attain liberation, why speak only of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?
Answer: Some say it is because they are more venerable and superior.
If one seeks the superior Dharma, the dharma of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*) is superior to the dharma of those still in training (*śaikṣadharma*).
If one seeks the superior person, then the person beyond training is superior to the person still in training.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
If it is manifold, superior, and faultless, this is called liberation.
When one attains the mind of an Arhat (aśaikṣa), then it is manifold, superior, and faultless, and thus liberated.
Furthermore, when the mind attains two kinds of liberation, it is termed "liberated," namely: liberation of the self-nature (*svabhāva-vimukti*) and liberation of the body (*kāya-prāpti-vimukti*).
On account of this matter, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are formulated:

either there is a case where the mind itself attains liberation while the body does not, or there is a case where the body attains liberation while the mind itself does not; thus, the four propositions are elaborated at length.
Liberation of the self-substance but not of the body refers to the mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
Liberation of the body but not of the self-substance refers to the wholesome contaminated (sāsrava) and non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) minds of an Arhat.
That which is both liberated by its own nature and liberated from the body refers to the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is neither liberated by its own nature nor liberated from the body refers to the contaminated minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and all the minds of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Furthermore, it is called liberation because it is unobstructed.
Those in training (śaikṣa) are obstructed by false liberation, whereas those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are not.
Thus, the right liberation of those in training is contrasted with false liberation;
The one beyond training (aśaikṣa) is not like this.
Furthermore, if the mind attains liberation from all fetters (saṃyojana), it is called "liberated.
The mind of one in training (śaikṣa) possesses partial liberation and partial non-liberation.
It is not so for those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, some say that if the mind attains liberation from the five kinds of objects of affliction and attains liberation from the five kinds of conditions, it is called "liberation" (vimukti).
The same applies to the explanations regarding the five kinds of afflictive hindrances and the five kinds of objective hindrances.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one is not bound by the *mālutā* love-creeper, this is called liberation.
Furthermore, if one is able to completely shave the hair of the crown—the basis for existence up to the Peak of Existence—it is called liberation.
Furthermore, if one cuts off the hair of all afflictions within the three realms, it is called liberation.
Furthermore, if that which is deficient in liberation can be made complete, it is called "liberation.

For instance, from the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*) up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), one is said to be incomplete; upon attaining the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), one is said to be complete.
Furthermore, if one attains the bliss of pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and is not obstructed by afflictions (*kleśa*), this is called liberation.
Although those in training (*śaikṣa*) attain the bliss of pliancy, they are obstructed by afflictions;
those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) attain the bliss of pliancy.
They are not obstructed by afflictions.
Furthermore, if one extensively experiences the bliss of tranquility, it is called liberation;
because a practitioner still has tasks to perform, they do not experience the bliss of tranquility extensively.
If one attains the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), having accomplished what was to be done, then one extensively experiences the joy of tranquility.
It is just as a king does not experience joy extensively while his enemies are not yet eliminated, but once his enemies are eliminated, he experiences joy extensively.
It is likewise for one who has accomplished what was to be done, laid down the heavy burden, and has no further desires.
Furthermore, when sentient beings constantly converse with their afflictions, if they attain separation from them and the mind of the Muni is fulfilled, this is called liberation.
Furthermore, if one is freed from the heavy burden of the defiled aggregates, this is called liberation.
Furthermore, if one is freed from the heat of the afflictions regarding the sense bases and attains the cool sense bases, this is called liberation.

Furthermore, if one leaves behind the sense bases (*āyatana*) that serve as the basis for afflictions and attains the sense bases that do not serve as the basis for afflictions, this is called liberation.

Furthermore, if one distances oneself from the multitude of sentient beings possessed of afflictions and establishes oneself within the multitude of sentient beings free from afflictions, this is called liberation.
Furthermore, if one attains the state of being a field of merit for the world, this is called liberation.
As a verse says:
"The lustful mind ruins sentient beings, Just as weeds ruin a fertile field."
"If one gives to those free from desire, one will certainly obtain a great fruit.
Furthermore, if by taking their life one incurs the immediate retribution (ānantarya), this is called liberation.

Furthermore, if one cuts off all attachments, decisively breaches the embankments of the afflictions, eliminates all obstructions, severs the four kinds of nutriment, departs from the four stations of consciousness, destroys the four Māras, and transcends the nine abodes of sentient beings, this is called liberation.

Furthermore, if one practices unmixed meritorious qualities, yet the learner (śaikṣa) still engages in mixed wholesome dharmas and faults—where wholesome conduct and unwholesome conduct, as well as wholesome roots and unwholesome roots, manifest alternately before them.
If one practices only wholesome deeds and the like, and does not practice unwholesome deeds and the like, this is called liberation.
Question: Since all five aggregates attain liberation, why is it said specifically that the mind attains liberation?
Answer: Some say it is because the mind is preeminent.
Herein, one should explain as follows:
As answered in the first chapter:
A question is asked:
Is it that only a single moment of mind attains liberation?
Answer: No. If one speaks of the arising of a single moment of mind, one should know that this fully describes all future minds.
Why is this? Because the future mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) can function within the world. Question:
When one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), does one attain liberation through the cultivation of all the roots of goodness belonging to the three realms that exist in the future?
Answer: Yes, one does.
Why is this? Because it also removes their hindrances. Question:
If one falls away from the fruit of arhatship and subsequently regains the fruit of arhatship, does that past untainted path previously attained constitute liberation for them?
Answer: It is not obtained, because the obstacles have not been eliminated.
This is as explained at length, starting from "the cessation through the path of non-obstruction" (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The path of non-obstruction is the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
Question: Why is it called "diamond-like"?
The answer is:

It is like a vajra, which there is nothing it cannot sever, nothing it cannot destroy, and nothing it cannot pierce—whether iron, ivory, stone, mani-jewels, crystal, or mountains; among such things as these, there is nothing it does not crush and shatter.
That concentration is likewise; it is impossible that all afflictions would not be destroyed by it.
This is spoken of in terms of conceptual analysis: if even an ordinary person bound by all fetters were able to give rise to this concentration, they would be able to sever all afflictions.
Why is this? Because it is the remedial dharma for all afflictions. How is this known?
Answer: When one attains arhatship, one realizes the attainment of liberation from all afflictions abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms.
For this reason, it is known that this concentration is the antidote to all afflictions.

Question: If the essential nature of the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) consists of either the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) or four aggregates, why is it designated simply as "concentration"? Answer:
Because the power of concentration (*samādhi*) predominates, it is called "concentration.

For example, although the essence of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), it is called the "Path of Seeing" because the power of seeing (*darśana*) predominates.

Similarly, although the essential nature of the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) at the edge of the Path of Seeing consists of either the five aggregates or the four aggregates, it is designated as "knowledge" (*jñāna*) because the power of knowledge (*jñāna*) predominates.
Just as the essential nature of the four paths consists of five aggregates or four aggregates, they are called "paths" because the force of the path is predominant.
The essential nature of the diamond-like concentration consists of five aggregates or four aggregates; it is called "concentration" because the force of concentration is predominant.
Question: If that is so, then one discourse gives rise to another.
Why is it that in those cases the fixed momentum (*niyata-vega*) is predominant?

Answer: Some say that because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend, one must establish a firm concentration to settle one's footing and exert great diligence.
Just as when a person wishes to kill an elephant, they must first plant their feet firmly and exert their martial prowess before they can kill it;

so too, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend—it can only be severed after one has first planted their feet firmly and exerted great diligence.
Just as an elephant [is difficult to restrain], so too are the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Furthermore, some say that because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subtle, difficult to know, and difficult to comprehend, one must maintain the mental factors with great effort.
Just as a person who wishes to shoot a single hair must maintain a great degree of mental concentration,
so it is with this case.
Regarding this diamond-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*), if it occurs within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya-dhyāna*), there are fifty-two such diamond-like samādhis.
What is this matter?
The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is accompanied by six knowledges, namely: the four subsequent knowledges (anvaya-jñāna) and two dharma-knowledges (dharma-jñāna).
As for the two dharma-knowledges, they refer to the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna).

Relying on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, one shall attain the fruit of Arhatship through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*). One contemplates the four aspects of suffering and so forth regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
When any one of these aspects manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.

If one contemplates the four aspects of the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the subsequent knowledge of origin, and if even a single aspect manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship.
If the contemplation of the path through the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.

If, through the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena, the four aspects of the cessation of the conditioned phenomena of the desire realm—such as cessation itself—are contemplated, and even if only one such aspect manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.

If one contemplates the path of abandoning the various practices of the desire realm through the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path, and if even a single practice manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship.

If one employs the subsequent knowledge of cessation, they may contemplate the four aspects of the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the first dhyāna; if even one such aspect manifests before them, they shall attain the fruit of arhatship.
In this manner, even up to the observation of the cessations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is likewise.
Thus, there are eight sets of four, totaling thirty-two.

If one observes the path-component of the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) within the nine stages by means of the subsequent knowledge of the path, and if any one of the four aspects—such as the aspect of the path—manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of Arhatship.

There are thirty-two *anvaya-jñānas* of cessation and four *anvaya-jñānas* of the path; together with the sixteen previously mentioned, these are called the fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) based on the *anāgamya-dhyāna*.

In this way, based on the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna, there are likewise fifty-two diamond-like concentrations (vajropama-samādhi).
There are twenty-eight [aspects] regarding the sphere of infinite space.

If one relies on the sphere of infinite space and contemplates the four aspects of suffering and so forth pertaining to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the subsequent knowledge of suffering, when even a single aspect manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship.
If one explains by means of the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), it is also as stated above.

If one contemplates the four aspects—such as the cessation of formations (*saṃskāra*)—in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) by means of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*), it is as previously explained; or one contemplates the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), or the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) through the four aspects such as cessation, as explained in detail above.

If one contemplates the path through the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding the nine stages—specifically the four aspects of the path such as "the path" and so forth—the detailed explanation is as above.

There are sixteen [aspects] for the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) and four for the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*); together with the eight preceding ones, these are called the twenty-eight adamantine concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) based on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

There are twenty-four [factors] in the sphere of infinite consciousness and twenty in the sphere of nothingness; such is the explanation according to what is appropriate, which constitutes the doctrine of one school.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are eighty [factors] in the preparatory stage (anāgamya-dhyāna).
What is the nature of this matter?
The diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) is associated with six knowledges, as explained above.
If one relies on the threshold dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna), one shall attain the fruit of arhatship through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).
One contemplates the suffering of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as previously explained.
If one contemplates the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), it is as previously explained.

If one contemplates the cessation of the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the desire realm through the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), it is as previously explained.
If one contemplates the path that abandons the conditioned phenomena of the desire realm through the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), it is as previously explained.
If one contemplates the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna by means of the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), it is as previously explained.
Or, if one contemplates the cessation of all conditioned phenomena up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), it is also as explained above.

These eight sets of four make thirty-two; the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) likewise has thirty-two, totaling sixty-four. Together with the previous sixteen, these are called the eighty diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*) based on the stage of the threshold (*anāgamya*).
In this way, there are likewise eighty [types] for the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna;
and there are forty for the sphere of infinite space.
If, relying on the sphere of infinite space, one attains the fruit of arhatship through the subsequent knowledge of suffering, it is explained in detail as above.
To speak of it through the subsequent knowledge of origination is also as above.

If one contemplates the cessation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) by means of subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*), there are sixteen instances up to the cessation of all conditioned phenomena in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). There are likewise sixteen instances of subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*); including the eight preceding ones, these are called the forty adamantine-like concentrations (*vajropamasamādhi*) of the sphere of infinite space.
There are thirty-two [types] in the sphere of consciousness and twenty-four in the sphere of nothingness; these should be explained in detail according to their respective characteristics.
The critique states:
it would be better to explain it in this manner:
Based on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, there should be one hundred and sixty-four diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
What is their nature?

If, based on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, one contemplates the suffering of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), the detailed explanation is as above.
If one contemplates the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudayānvaya-jñāna*), the explanation is also as above.
If one contemplates the cessation of the formations of the desire realm by means of the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), the explanation is also as above.
If one contemplates the paths that sever the various formations of the desire realm through the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*), the explanation is as above.

If one contemplates the cessation of the various formations of the first dhyāna through subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), or even up to contemplating the cessation of the various formations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are eight sets of four, totaling thirty-two, as previously explained.

Some contemplate the first dhyāna and also contemplate the second dhyāna; some contemplate the second dhyāna and also contemplate the third dhyāna; some contemplate the third dhyāna and also contemplate the fourth dhyāna; some contemplate the fourth dhyāna and also contemplate the sphere of infinite space; some contemplate the sphere of infinite space and also contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness; some contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness and also contemplate the sphere of nothingness; or some contemplate the sphere of nothingness and also contemplate the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Some contemplate the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, and the third dhyāna; some contemplate the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; some contemplate the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space; some contemplate the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness; some contemplate the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness; and some contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Some contemplate the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; some contemplate the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, and the sphere of infinite space; some contemplate the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, and the sphere of infinite consciousness; some contemplate the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness; and some contemplate the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Some contemplate the first dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite space; some contemplate the second dhyāna up to the sphere of infinite consciousness; some contemplate the third dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness; and some contemplate the fourth dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Some contemplate from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of consciousness; some contemplate from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness; and some contemplate from the third dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Some observe from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness; some observe from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and some observe from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If one contemplates the four aspects of the path, such as the path itself, within the category of subsequent knowledge among the nine stages by means of subsequent knowledge of the path, and if even a single aspect manifests before one, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship.

There are four of these: there are four subsequent knowledges of suffering, four subsequent knowledges of origin, four dharma-knowledges of cessation, and four dharma-knowledges of the path; there are one hundred and forty-four subsequent knowledges of cessation.
Thus, based on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, there are one hundred and sixty-four diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
There are likewise one hundred and sixty-four for each of the first dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, and up to the fourth dhyāna.

There are fifty-two [moments] in the sphere of infinite space; whether relying on the sphere of infinite space or through the subsequent knowledge of suffering, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship.
One contemplates the four aspects of suffering and so forth regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, as explained in detail above.
If one observes the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with the subsequent knowledge of origin, the detailed explanation is as above.

If one observes the cessation of formations in the sphere of infinite space with the subsequent knowledge of cessation, or even observes the cessation of formations in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the detailed explanation is as above.

Some contemplate the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness; some contemplate the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness; some contemplate the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; some contemplate from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of nothingness; some contemplate from the sphere of infinite consciousness up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; and some contemplate from the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. If one contemplates the path and its subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) across the nine stages—namely, the four aspects of the path and so forth belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge—the detailed explanation is as above.

There are four of these: the subsequent knowledge of suffering has four, the subsequent knowledge of origin has four, and the subsequent knowledge of cessation has forty; these are called the fifty-two diamond-like concentrations based on the sphere of infinite space.
There are thirty-six [aspects] regarding the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*).

If one relies on the sphere of consciousness, one contemplates the suffering of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) through four modes by means of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), as explained in detail above.
If one contemplates the four aspects of the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the subsequent knowledge of origin, it is explained in detail as above.

If one contemplates the cessation of formations in the sphere of consciousness by means of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, or even contemplates the cessation of formations in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is explained in detail as above.

If one contemplates the sphere of consciousness and the sphere of nothingness through the knowledge of subsequent cessation, or contemplates the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or perhaps contemplates everything from the sphere of consciousness up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

If one contemplates the nine stages of the path through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), observing the four aspects such as the path itself and so forth, the detailed explanation is as above.

These consist of four [aspects] for the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), four for the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*), and twenty-four for the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*). Thus, based on the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), there are thirty-six adamantine concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).
There are twenty-four [aspects] regarding the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Based on the sphere of nothingness, if one contemplates the suffering of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) through the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*) by means of the four modes, it is explained in detail as above.
If one contemplates the four aspects of the origin of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception by means of the subsequent knowledge of origin, it is explained in detail as above.

If one contemplates the cessation of formations in the sphere of nothingness, or contemplates the cessation of formations in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, by means of the subsequent knowledge of cessation, it is explained in detail as above.

Alternatively, one contemplates the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), as explained in detail above.

If one contemplates the path and its subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) regarding the four aspects of the path and so forth belonging to the nine stages through the subsequent knowledge of the path, it is explained in detail as above.

There are four of these: four subsequent knowledges of suffering, four subsequent knowledges of origin, and twelve subsequent knowledges of cessation; thus, based on the sphere of nothingness, there are twenty-four diamond-like concentrations (*vajropama-samādhi*).

In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one should not speak of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*); among those born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one should not speak of dharma-knowledge; one should not say that being born in a higher stage involves detachment from a lower stage; and except for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one should also not say that being born in a higher stage contemplates the cessation of a lower stage.

The cases of being born in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are explained in the same way as being born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); being born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is explained in the same way as being born in the desire and form realms.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"There are thirteen [types of] diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*)."
What are the thirteen?

They refer to the abandonments of the afflictions of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which comprise four included within the path of non-obstruction and the path of vision, and nine included within the path of cultivation.
Is it that one whose mind is already liberated attains liberation,
or is it that one whose mind is not yet liberated attains liberation?
He replied:
Regarding the statement that "the already liberated mind is said to attain liberation":
since you say that the already liberated mind is said to attain liberation, you should not say that the already liberated mind attains liberation.
Why is this? If one has not yet attained liberation, one cannot say that one "will be liberated";
if one is currently being liberated, one cannot say that one "has already been liberated."
Question: Since the mind has already been liberated, why say that one "attains liberation"? Answer:
For this reason, it was previously stated thus:
if spoken of in terms of afflictions (*kleśa*), it is called "already liberated";
if spoken of in terms of its presence within the body as it functions in the world, it is called "attaining liberation."
I also speak of one who is already liberated as "attaining liberation," and of one who has already completed their task as "having done it.
If one speaks in this way, what fault is there?
The Buddha also speaks of one who is already liberated as "attaining liberation" and of one who has already completed their task as "having done it."
In order to establish this meaning, he cites a Buddhist scripture: "What do you think?
Is the Buddha’s teaching well-spoken or not?"
As it is said in verse:
"If one cuts off desire without remainder, Like a lotus flower in the water;
A bhikṣu abandons this world and the next, Like a snake shedding its skin and departing."
Question: When the Buddha spoke this verse, did he say that what had already been abandoned was abandoned,
or did he say that what had not yet been abandoned was abandoned?
Answer: The Buddha said that having abandoned something, one speaks of "abandoning.
Here, it is said that desire is severed without remainder; thus, he speaks of "having abandoned" as "abandoning."
In this verse, that which has already been abandoned is referred to as "abandoned," and that which has already been accomplished is referred to as "accomplished.
I am likewise; having already attained liberation, I speak of "attaining liberation," and there is no fault in this.
To prove this point, another Buddhist scripture is cited.
As it is said in a verse:
"When pride is exhausted, the mind is naturally settled; With a virtuous mind, one is liberated from everything."
"First, dwelling in tranquility without distraction, one can cross to the other shore beyond death.
He asked: "In this verse, is it said that those who have already crossed are crossing, or that those who have not yet crossed are crossing?"
Answer: Herein, it speaks of having already crossed over the crossing.
When a wholesome mind attains liberation in every respect, it is called "already crossed," yet it is still referred to as "crossing."
As this sutra states: "That which has been crossed over is called 'crossed over'; that which has been done is called 'done.
I am likewise; having attained liberation, I declare that I have attained liberation.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
One practices aversion and the absence of desire; one practices the liberation that is the absence of desire; one practices liberation and nirvana. Question:
Why is this treatise composed?
The answer is:
This is a Buddhist scripture.
The Buddhist scriptures state that one should cultivate weariness toward and freedom from desire, and so forth, as explained at length.
Without making distinctions as to what constitutes "aversion" or "dispassion," and so forth, it is explained at length.
The Buddha’s sūtras are the foundation of this treatise; that which was not stated therein shall now be explained. For this reason, this treatise has been composed.
There are two kinds of cultivation:
first, that which can produce;
second, that which can reach.
As for "that which can produce": it is like practicing aversion, which can produce desirelessness; practicing desirelessness, which can produce liberation.
As for "that which can reach": it is like practicing liberation, which can reach nirvana.
Furthermore, there are those who say that cultivation is of two kinds:
first, conformity; second, accordance.
"Conformity" means that by practicing aversion one attains desirelessness, and by practicing desirelessness one attains liberation.
"Appropriateness" means that by practicing liberation one should attain nirvana.
Question: If it is the nature of habituation, is it also the nature of conditions? Answer:
Whatever has the nature of conditions (pratyaya) has the nature of accumulation (saṃskāra).
Question: Is there anything that has the nature of accumulation but does not have the nature of conditions?
Answer: There is.
This refers to those who attain nirvāṇa through the cultivation of liberation. Although this cultivation lacks the four conditions for reaching nirvāṇa, it is nonetheless able to reach it.
What is meant by "disenchantment"?
The answer is:
it is the unlearned (aśaikṣa) person’s loathing and contempt for the five aggregates of clinging and all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), as explained at length in the original sūtra.

Question: Since this kind of revulsion is both of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), of one in training (śaikṣa), and of neither training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), why is it described as being only that of one beyond training?
Answer: Some say it is because both the name and the meaning are superior.

If one seeks the superiority of the Dharma, then the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are superior; if one seeks the superiority of the person, then the persons who are beyond training are superior.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

Because it is superior due to its abundance and because there is no fault [in this interpretation], only the disenchantment of those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is mentioned, not that of those in training (śaikṣa) or ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana).
Furthermore, others say: because the Blessed One spoke of the root of the supreme Dharma, and those beyond training are the root of the supreme Dharma.
The state beyond training (aśaikṣa) is the root of the supreme Dharma, not the state of one in training (śaikṣa) nor that of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one speaks of the end, one also clarifies the beginning.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if there were no two phenomena in mutual opposition, it should be explained at length as in the case of the one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of revulsion (*nirveda*)?
Answer: Some say that its essence is the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*). Question:
If this is so, then the statement that the nature of revulsion is the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) is well-established.
How, then, is this passage to be reconciled? As it says:
How does one cultivate revulsion to attain freedom from desire?
The answer is:
the roots of goodness consisting of non-desire, non-hatred, and non-delusion that are associated with revulsion.
Question: If that is so, does wisdom then correspond with wisdom? Answer:
This passage should be stated as follows:
"Those wholesome roots associated with disenchantment and characterized by non-desire.
It should not be stated that they are characterized by non-ill will and non-delusion.
Regarding that which should have been stated but was not, one should know that this passage is an expansion added by the reciter.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this "aversion" (nirveda) is a mental factor (caitasika-dharma) associated with the mind.
Question: If that is so, this passage is well-explained.

However, regarding the substance described in the *Dṛṣṭivarga*, which consists of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkhe kṣānti*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe jñāna*), how is that further explained?
Answer: It is stated therein that one develops revulsion because one draws near to, endures, and knows suffering through patience.
Where does one obtain this revulsion?
Answer: At the limit of the patience regarding suffering and the knowledge regarding suffering. Evaluation:
One should not speak in this way.
It is better as previously stated: the essence of revulsion (*nirveda*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
What, then, is mundane revulsion?
Answer: It is that which is associated with impurity.
This is the essence of ānāpāna; it takes suffering and its origin as its object.
The stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), and Patience (kṣānti) are the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (laukikāgradharma); these take suffering (duḥkha) and its origin (samudaya) as their objects.

The conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) at the edge of the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) is associated with compassion (karuṇā). It is associated with the first and second liberations (vimokṣa) and with the first four spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana).
This body is like a disease, like an abscess, like a sore; it is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self, arising from causes, accumulations, conditions, and formative activities.
To speak of it briefly, it possesses such characteristics as these;
were it to be explained in detail, its measure would exceed the four oceans.
Question: If there is revulsion, is its essence that which is to be reviled?
Or, if its essence is that which is to be reviled, is it revulsion itself?
This is elaborated at length in four permutations.
The first permutation refers to the outflow-free (anāsrava) form of revulsion.
The second permutation refers to the essential nature of all other outflowing (sāsrava) states, excluding mundane revulsion.
The third phrase refers to mundane revulsion (*saṃvṛti-nirveda*).
The fourth phrase refers to all other untainted entities (*anāsrava-svabhāva*), excluding untainted revulsion itself. Question:
Regarding the contemplation of the selflessness of all phenomena, is this a contemplation of revulsion or a contemplation of joyful exultation?
The answer is:
This point has already been explained previously within the section on the practice of selflessness.
How does one cultivate revulsion to attain detachment?
The answer is:
that which is associated with revulsion is free from desire; it is the wholesome root of non-desire.
This passage should be stated as follows:
"One should not say that there is no ill-will, nor that there is the absence of ill-will.
Question: [Why is this so?]
What is the essential nature of non-desire?
The answer is:
its essential nature is non-attachment.
How does one attain liberation by practicing desirelessness?
The answer is:
that liberation is associated with desirelessness, and so forth, as explained at length.
Within all dharmas, there are two natures of dharma that constitute liberation:
first, the conditioned;
second, the unconditioned.
The conditioned refers to liberation among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The unconditioned refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Here, only conditioned liberation is discussed; unconditioned liberation is not mentioned.
There are two kinds of conditioned liberation:
first, the defiled; second, the undefiled.
That which is defiled is false liberation;
that which is undefiled is true liberation.
True liberation, moreover, is of two kinds:
The first is with outflows (sāsrava);
the second is without outflows (anāsrava).

That which is with outflows is associated with the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), and associated with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity (maitrī-karuṇā-muditā-upekṣā).
The untainted (anāsrava) is associated with those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Those in training consist of the four candidates for the fruits and those abiding in the three fruits; those beyond training abide solely in the single fruit.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of those beyond training:
First, those liberated in mind at the proper time;
second, those liberated by wisdom not at the proper time.
Those liberated in mind at the proper time refers to the five types of arhats.
Those who possess wisdom-liberation at non-designated times are the immovable arhats.
This refers to attaining liberation through the mind by severing desire; this refers to attaining liberation through wisdom by severing ignorance.

Question: If the severing of desire constitutes liberation through wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*) and the severing of ignorance constitutes liberation through mind (*citta-vimukti*), how can this be reconciled with what is stated in the *Dharmasaṃgraha-śāstra*?
As it is said:
"How does one whose mind has severed desire attain liberation?
The answer is:
The root of goodness that is non-attachment.
How does one attain liberation through the wisdom that severs ignorance?
The answer is:
The non-delusion wholesome root.
