one kind is that which, having attained the path of seeing, is both accomplished within the body and manifested before it.
This very body attains this wisdom, yet it is not accomplished within the body, nor does it manifest before it.
The second body attains conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), which is both accomplished within the body and manifests before it.
If one attains the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) with this very body, it is not accomplished within that body nor does it manifest.
If one attains the Path of Seeing with this very body, it is accomplished within that body and manifests;
yet, having attained this knowledge (jñāna), it is not accomplished within that body nor does it manifest.
When such a body firmly believes in and firmly adheres to the Dharma, [the knowledge] arises and manifests. If this body attains this wisdom, it is accomplished within the body and manifests.
Upon attaining the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), [that wisdom] is not accomplished within the body, nor does it manifest.

If one generates a firm resolve regarding the duration [of life] and possesses firm faith and firm Dharma, one can likewise cause this body to manifest in the present; such a person is one who possesses the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
That which pertains to the desire realm is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), because it is superior, and not the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).
Because the desire realm is not a stage of freedom from desire, not a stage of meditative concentration, and not a stage of cultivation, it does not possess cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
If one were to cultivate it within the desire realm, it would fall under the category of wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*).
If it pertains to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), it is wisdom derived from cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā), not wisdom derived from hearing (śrutamayī) or reflection (cintāmayī). Why is this?

Because it is superior, it is not wisdom derived from hearing; because the realm of form is a stage of freedom from desire (vairāgya-bhūmi), a stage of meditative concentration (samādhi-bhūmi), and a stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-bhūmi), it is not wisdom derived from reflection.
If one wishes to contemplate, it falls within the category of wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).

As for whether it resides in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) or the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñānakāya*), it resides in the stage of the mind (*manobhūmi*), not in the body of the five consciousnesses. Question:
When one attains the fruit of Srotāpanna and abandons the path of vision (darśanamārga), does one also abandon the knowledge of the limits of vision (darśanāntika-jñāna) and so forth?
Answer: One does not abandon them.
Why is this so? Because the timing for abandoning the untainted (*anāsrava*) is different from the timing for abandoning the tainted (*sāsrava*).

Untainted dharmas are abandoned at three times: namely, at the time of falling away (*parihāṇi*), at the time of attaining a fruit (*phalaprāpti*), and at the time of transforming the faculties (*indriyasaṃcāra*).

Defiled dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*) are also relinquished at three times: namely, at the time of falling back (*parihāṇi*), at the time of transcending a stage or realm (*bhūmi-vyutkrānti*), and at the time of severing the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla-ccheda*).
At those times, because one has not fallen back, has not transcended the stage or realm, and has not severed the roots of goodness, they are not relinquished.
Furthermore, the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) and the path of seeing (darśanamārga) are mutually obstructive in two ways:
first, they cannot be accomplished simultaneously;
second, they do not manifest at the same time.

The path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) associated with the limit of the path of seeing (*darśanamārgāntika*) are mutually exclusive in their mode of manifestation; they do not appear simultaneously, though both may be attained together. Question:
If one does not abandon [the conventional knowledge], does it arise and manifest during the path of cultivation?
Answer: It does not arise and manifest before one.
For this reason, it was previously stated as follows:
On the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is obstructed by a single aspect of the path of seeing (darśanamārga); it is accomplished but does not manifest.
Because it does not obstruct accomplishment, it is not abandoned; because it obstructs its own manifestation and proceeding, it does not manifest.
Furthermore, because these are attendants of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and are not separate from it, they do not manifest during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, because they rely upon the bodies of those with firm faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those with firm dharma (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they do not arise and manifest in other bodies.
Furthermore, because it does not depart from the path of progress, it does not manifest in dependence upon another body.
Question: Does this have a karmic retribution, or not?
Answer: There is retribution. Question:
Where does this retribution reside?
The answer is:
if it belongs to the desire realm, the retribution resides in the desire realm;
If it belongs to the form realm, its retribution is in the form realm.
If it is in the first dhyāna, its retribution is in the first dhyāna; likewise, if it is in the fourth dhyāna, its retribution is in the fourth dhyāna.
Question: This may be so for the śrāvakas. Why is that?
Since Śrāvakas must possess bodies within the form realm (rūpadhātu),
how could this be the case for Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas?
The answer is:
They likewise have, during their successive stages as ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), bodies in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that receive retribution. Question:
If this is so, how can it be that the body of a noble one (*ārya*) acts as the cause, while the body of an ordinary person receives the retribution?
The answer is:
If that were so, what fault would there be?
There would be cases where a noble person acts as the cause, yet an ordinary person receives the retribution.
For example, there are two kinds of causes for the evil realms:
first, those abandoned through the path of seeing;
second, the six types of afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Just as there is no fault in an ordinary person receiving retribution for the causes created by the body of a noble one,
so it is in this case as well.

Furthermore, some say that Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even Śrāvakas receive this retribution through the successive transformation of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases (*skandha-dhātu-āyatana*) of their bodies within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The critique says:
One should not speak in this manner.
It is better to speak as follows:
Because these are tainted roots of goodness, it is said that they have retribution;
yet this retribution does not ripen, for there has never been anyone who has experienced it.
When one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), the future cultivation of the roots of goodness of the three realms occurs.
Question: How many are there to be cultivated? Answer:
If one is born in the desire realm and attains arhatship, then the wholesome roots of the three realms are cultivated in the future life.
If one is born in the first dhyāna, then those of eight stages are cultivated.
This continues until, if one is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, then those of a single stage are cultivated.
Question: Are these roots of goodness acquired through birth, or are they produced through effort? Answer:
This is a skillful means, not something acquired by birth; it pertains to those possessing the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.

If it belongs to the desire realm, it is the wisdom of hearing and reflection; if it belongs to the form realm, it is the wisdom of hearing and cultivation; if it belongs to the formless realm, it is the wisdom of cultivation.

Question: If the wisdom of hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*) belongs to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and the wisdom of hearing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) belongs to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*),
then since the wisdom of hearing and reflection is weak and inferior, how can it be cultivated in a future life?
Answer: It is cultivated in the future life through the power of others, not by one's own power.

This is because it pertains to the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), which consists of the sixfold body of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*); it does not pertain to the fivefold body of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*).

Why is this so? Because the wholesome states of skillful means reside in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whereas the innate wholesome states reside in the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*). Question:
If it were restricted solely to the mental level (*manobhūmi*), how would this statement be reconciled?
As it is said:

"The Arhat who has exhausted the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) accomplishes the factors of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*); how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?"
Does it exist, or does it not exist?
If it exists, who exists? In what manner does it exist?
Answer: There is.

If an Arhat first gives rise to a wholesome eye-consciousness that manifests before him, one factor is past, six factors are future, and one factor is present; once it has ceased, he does not relinquish them.
If a wholesome ear-consciousness is present, two are past, six are future, and one is present; once it has ceased, they are not abandoned.
This continues up until when a wholesome mental consciousness is present: six are past and future, and one is present.
How is this to be reconciled?
The answer is:
what is described here refers to the roots of goodness obtained by one who has first attained the pure body of an Arhat; it does not include those [roots] acquired since beginningless saṃsāra.
Furthermore, there are those who say this refers to the six eternally abiding dharmas of an arhat. Question:
What is the essential nature of these six eternally abiding dharmas of an arhat?
Answer: Some say that its essential nature consists of mindfulness and wisdom.
How is this known?
Answer: It is because it relies upon the Buddhist sūtras.
Within the Buddhist sūtras, it is said:
When an Arhat sees forms with the eye, by the power of mindfulness and wisdom he abides in a mind of equanimity, giving rise to neither sorrow nor joy.
This applies extensively to everything up to his cognizing mental phenomena with the mind; it is explained in the same way.

Furthermore, there are those who say: "If one takes the revolving, corresponding, and co-existent entities—which consist of four or five aggregates—to be these six eternal natures," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the nature of its essence, we shall now explain why it is called "eternally abiding" (nitya).
What is the meaning of "eternal abiding"?
The answer is:
Arhats always abide in this dharma and never depart from it; therefore, it is called "constant abiding. Question:
Do all arhats possess this dharma of constant abiding?
Answer: Some say that it is not entirely non-existent.
If an Arhat is one liberated at any time and has attained the knowledge of the lineages (gotrajñāna), for such a person there exists an eternally abiding dharma.
The critique says: It should be stated thus:
all arhats possess them entirely.
Why is this? Because all Arhats always possess mindfulness and wisdom.
As for the realms, they are the desire realm and the form realm.
Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*), there are five stages, namely the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the four dhyānas. Question:
For what reason does one who has attained the fruit of arhatship cultivate the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) of the three realms in the future life, and not at other times?
Answer: An Arhat must necessarily possess the mundane mind that enters and emerges from meditative absorption.
Furthermore, at that time, because the liberation not yet fully attained is brought to fulfillment, it is the liberation of a learner (śaikṣa).
Even up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), it is not called "fulfillment"; only when one attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) is it called fulfillment.
It is just as when a farmer irrigates a field: once one plot is full, he flows water to another plot; but when all the plots are full, he no longer flows water further. It is the same with this.

Furthermore, there are those who say: at this time, the mind attains mastery and the head is bound with the cord of liberation; at this time, the roots of goodness cultivated are like the presentation of offerings to the Dharma.
It is just as when a king ascends the throne and is first bound with the cord, all the common people present precious treasures;
he is likewise so.

Furthermore, at that time, one is able to subdue afflictions never before subdued; because all the various roots of goodness of the "powerful ones" (balavantaḥ) are praised as excellent, they are cultivated.
It is just as when a great multitude gathers in one place: if someone can throw down a wrestler who has never been overthrown, the multitude celebrates with joy;
so it is in this case as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say that at this time one is able to destroy the enemy of afflictions, which had never before been destroyed; thus, one cultivates the various roots of goodness as if welcoming the Dharma.
It is just as when a person who has defeated his enemies returns to his country and many people come out to welcome him;
so it is with him as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say that from time immemorial, throughout the beginningless past, the body of various roots of goodness has been constantly shrouded and submerged by the body of afflictions, such that it cannot liberate itself.

When the afflictions of the desire realm are exhausted, one does not yet attain cessation; even when the eight types of afflictions up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are severed, one still does not attain cessation.
Only when the nine types of afflictions are completely exhausted does one then attain cessation.
It is like the method of binding a roll of silk with nine knots:
if one knot is severed, or even up to the eighth knot, the bundle does not unravel;
only when all nine knots are severed does it finally come apart.
It is the same for him as well.
At that time, the Arhat liberated by occasion cultivates two kinds of wisdom: namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*).
The knowledge of exhaustion operates through fourteen aspects, while the right view of one beyond training operates through sixteen aspects.
If one relies on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, thirty factors are cultivated through *dharmajñāna* and thirty are cultivated through *anvayajñāna*; this remains the same up to the fourth dhyāna.

If one relies on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), thirty factors are cultivated through *anvayajñāna*, not through *dharmajñāna*; this remains the same up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

For an Arhat liberated at any time (asamayavimukta), there are three kinds of wisdom cultivated at that time: namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi).
The knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising possess fourteen aspects (ākāra); the right view of one beyond training possesses sixteen aspects.

If one relies on the threshold dhyāna (anāgamya-dhyāna), there are forty-four cultivations of dharma-knowledge and forty-four cultivations of subsequent knowledge; this remains the same up to the fourth dhyāna.

If one relies on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there are forty-four factors of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) cultivated, but not factors of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*); this is likewise for up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
When all minds have passed away, is every such mind subject to transformation (*vipariṇāma*)?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is to refute the foolish claims within the world that the past,
future, and present do not exist, and that these are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
In order to stop such a misconception and to clarify that past and future phenomena truly exist, this treatise is composed.
Are all those minds that have passed away subject to transformation?
The transformation of the mind is of two kinds:
first, transformation according to the world;
second, transformation of phenomena.
The past defiled mind undergoes two kinds of transformation:
first, transformation according to the world;
second, transformation of phenomena (*dharma-pariṇāma*).
The undefiled mind undergoes only one kind of transformation, namely, transformation according to the world (*loka-vipariṇāma*), and not transformation of the dharma (*dharma-vipariṇāma*).
As for future and present defiled minds, these are transformations of the dharma, not transformations according to the world.
An undefiled mind does not undergo transformation through unrighteousness (*adharma*), nor does it undergo transformation by conforming to the world.
Regarding all minds that have passed away, is every such mind subject to transformation?
Answer: [Not necessarily.]
All minds that have passed away undergo transformation.
If they are defiled, there are two kinds of transformation;
if they are undefiled, there is one kind of transformation, namely, transformation according to the world.
Is there a mind that undergoes transformation which is not of the past? Answer:
There is future and present mind associated with desire and ill-will.
To clarify this meaning, I cite the Buddha’s sūtras as evidence.
As it is said, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a lurking thief were to cut your limbs and joints with a saw, at that time your mind should not change and you should not utter evil words."
If the mind undergoes transformation and the mouth utters evil words, this is your obstacle.
For this reason, a mind associated with anger is called "transformation.
As it is said:
If a bhikṣu’s mind is transformed by lustful desire,
for this reason, a mind associated with desire is called "transformed. Question:

All defiled minds are subject to transformation; why then is it said only that minds associated with desire and ill-will are subject to transformation, while those associated with other underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not?
The answer is:
Some say that this explanation is incomplete, and so forth, as explained at length.
Others say that when one speaks of a mind associated with certain latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) yet does not mention others, one should know that the meaning is still incomplete.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If it is precisely what is taught in the Buddha's sūtras, then it is explained herein.
These two minds are precisely what is taught in the Buddha's sūtras; therefore, they are explained.

Thus, from this discussion, another question arises: For what reason did the Blessed One state that a mind associated with desire and ill-will is subject to change, yet did not state the same for minds associated with other underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Answer: Because desire can transform the body and hatred can transform the objective realm. Why is this so?
If one gives rise to craving toward an object, and all the mind and mental factors race through that objective field, at such a time this body is like an insentient thing.
If one gives rise to anger toward an object, one cannot even turn the face toward it, let alone look directly at it.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these two are capable of transforming the body and transforming the place of birth.

Regarding the mind of desire being able to transform the body: there may be sentient beings who give rise to the fetters of lust, whereby they can transform male forms so that they cease and female forms so that they arise.
There may be sentient beings who give rise to the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*), which can cause a human body to perish and transform it into the body of a snake.
In this context, one should explain the analogy of a non-Buddhist coming to become a bhikṣu.

I have heard that when a Nirgrantha came to the Buddha’s Dharma to seek ordination as a monk, the bhikṣus spoke before that person of the various faults and afflictions within their own [former] evil teachings.
Upon hearing this, that person conceived great hatred toward the Buddha’s Dharma.
Because of that hatred, his human body immediately perished and he was reborn as a snake.
How can it be that the mind of desire is able to transform one's place of birth?
As the Blessed One said, he addressed the bhikṣus:

"There is a class of devas called the 'Lax in Mindfulness' (Smṛti-pramuṣita-vihārin). When these devas indulge in delightful play and experience pleasure, their bodies become weary and their minds lose mindfulness; because they have lost mindfulness, they pass away from that realm."
What is the sphere where ill will arises? The Blessed One has also said:

there are gods with a mind of ill will and malice; when those gods harbor ill will in their hearts, they look at one another with evil eyes. Because they look at one another with evil eyes, their minds of ill will increase further; because their minds of ill will increase further, they pass away from that state.
Hatred can also transform the place of rebirth; for example, if one strikes another with a mind of hatred, that person may die immediately.
Furthermore, some say that desire can transform time, while hatred can transform form.
Regarding the transformation of time: due to desire, there are temporal distinctions such as infancy, youth, manhood, and womanhood. Regarding the transformation of form:
due to hatred, one uses saws to sever the hands, feet, ears, noses, and various other limbs and members of others.
Because these two dharmas can destroy time and destroy form, they are thus taught.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because these two dharmas can give rise to various afflictions such as hatred and attachment, they are thus taught.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these two dharmas are mentioned because they can swiftly cause the physical appearance of the body to change.
If the mind is defiled, does all such a mind undergo transformation?
...and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: Previously, it was stated that the mind undergoes transformation through sensual desire, leading some to claim that only the mind of sensual desire is subject to transformation and not others;
now, this treatise is composed because it is taught that all minds of desire within the three realms are entirely subject to transformation.
If the mind is defiled, is all that mind subject to change?
Answer: If the mind is defiled, all that mind is subject to change.
If it is a past mind, there are two kinds of transformation:
those of the future and the present.
There is one kind of transformation, namely, the transformation of dharmas.
Is there any mind that undergoes transformation yet is not defiled?
The answer is:
Yes; for instance, a past mind that is dissociated from desire, if it is afflicted, undergoes two kinds of transformation.
The non-defiled [state] is of one kind, namely, that which changes according to worldly conditions.
Regarding the future and present minds associated with anger, it is as stated:
"An enemy spy shall saw apart your body," and so forth, as explained at length.
Such a mind undergoes transformation through these phenomena, yet it is not defiled.
Question: When the present mind reaches the past, it is called "transformation"; why is it that when the future mind reaches the present, it is not called "transformation"?
Answer: If a mind that undergoes transformation were not to transform further, it could be called "transformation.
However, because a future mind reaches the present and must again transform as it passes into the past, it is not called "transformation."
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If there is transformation through action and transformation according to the world, this is called 'transformation' (*pariṇāma*).
Although the present mind undergoes transformation according to the world, it lacks transformation through action."
Why is this? Because as long as there is something produced, it must further undergo transformation until it reaches the past.
[The interlocutor] asks:
Why is it called the thief of discursive thought (*vicāra*)?
The answer is:
by day it watches for an opportunity, and by night it steals and plunders.
Question: For what reason is the saw used as a metaphor? Answer:
When a person is cut with a knife, there is pain upon entry but not upon exit; there is pain upon exit but not upon entry.
When a person is cut with a saw, there is pain both upon entry and upon exit; this is used as a metaphor.
If the mind possesses anger, is that entire mind subject to transformation?
Answer: If the mind possesses anger, that entire mind is subject to transformation; as previously stated, all such cases should be explained in full.
Is it the case that all those minds which undergo transformation are free from ill-will?
Answer: Yes.

This includes past minds not associated with ill-will, as well as future and present minds associated with desire; likewise, this applies to all minds associated with the various afflictions (*kleśa*), according to their respective associations.
The Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll Nineteen [and] Scroll Twenty Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Daotai and others, during the Northern Liang dynasty.
From the *Saṃyukta-vastu*, Chapter on Shamelessness and Lack of Remorse, Part Two: Is everything associated with restlessness and remorse?
...and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: The World-Honored One has taught that restlessness (uddhacca) and remorse (kukkucca) constitute a single hindrance (nīvaraṇa).
Some maintain that there is no remorse apart from restlessness, and no restlessness apart from remorse.
This treatise is composed for the sake of establishing the definitive meaning that remorse exists apart from restlessness, and restlessness exists apart from remorse.
Is every instance of restlessness associated with remorse?
...and so on, as explained at length.
Four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) are established.
What is restlessness that is not associated with remorse?
The answer is:
"It is not that at the time of regret the mind does not cease or rest," and so forth, as explained at length. What is that?
The answer is:

All restlessness (*auddhatya*) of the form and formless realms; the four types of restlessness in the desire realm abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the restlessness of the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); and the restlessness associated with desire, ill-will, pride, avarice, and envy on the level of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*)—restlessness such as these is not associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
Why is this? Because within that category, there is no remorse (*kaukṛtya*).
How is it that remorse does not correspond with restlessness (*auddhatya*)?
The answer is:
"Remorse with an undefiled mind," and so forth, as explained at length. What is that?

For example, if a bhikṣu feels remorse out of fear regarding the precepts—whether he fails to report his own transgression or causes another to report it; whether he leaves bedding exposed in an open area, or locks the doors of the restroom himself or causes another to lock them; or if he feels remorse for performing meritorious deeds.

What are these? There is remorse whose cause is unwholesome and which is itself unwholesome; there is remorse whose cause is unwholesome but which is itself wholesome; there is remorse whose cause is wholesome and which is itself wholesome; and there is remorse whose cause is wholesome but which is itself unwholesome.

Regarding the case where there is a cause for regret that is unwholesome and the regret itself is also unwholesome: it is as if someone who has committed an evil deed thinks, "The evil I have done is slight; I ought to do more."

Regarding the unwholesome cause that results in regret despite being wholesome: it is like someone who, having performed a wholesome deed, later regrets it, thinking, "Why did I perform this wholesome deed?
For example, there was a householder who gave food to a pratyekabuddha, but later regretted it, saying:
"I would rather have given this food to my slaves or laborers; what use is it to give it to such a person?"

Regarding the case where there is a cause for regret that is wholesome, and the regret itself is also wholesome: it is, for example, when someone who has performed a wholesome deed later feels regret and says:
"I have performed little wholesome action; I ought to do more."
As the Venerable Aniruddha said:
"If I had known that this Great Virtuous One possessed such majestic power, I would have offered him even more food."

Regarding the wholesome cause of regret for that which is unwholesome: it is, for example, when someone does not transgress a precept but thinks, "I have done such a thing; it was not good. This refers to precepts such as not leaving bedding or mats spread out in an open area.
Among these four types, remorse that arises from a wholesome cause and remorse that arises from an unwholesome cause do not associate with restlessness (*auddhatya*).
How, then, can restlessness associate with remorse?
This refers to remorse with a defiled mind, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Why is it that the question asks about restlessness (*auddhatya*) and remorse (*kaukṛtya*), while the answer speaks of remorse and restlessness?
Answer: This passage should be stated as follows:
"How is restlessness associated with regret?"
"If the mind feels regret and does not cease or rest," and so forth, as explained at length.
Yet, there is no one who speaks [of this]; what is the intention behind this?
The answer is:

This explains that remorse (*kaukṛtya*) associated with an afflicted mind should be understood as occurring at the time of restlessness (*auddhatya*); all other afflicted minds are associated only with restlessness and not with remorse.
Furthermore, some say that both remorse and restlessness are, in their essential nature, hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
One should ask this question:
How is restlessness associated with remorse?
How is remorse associated with restlessness?
How is it that restlessness (*auddhatya*) is not associated with remorse (*kaukṛtya*),
and remorse is not associated with restlessness? With the exception of the aforementioned cases,
for all dharmas that have already been established by name and described, one should formulate the first, second, and third propositions.
That which has not yet been established by name and not yet expressed in speech constitutes the fourth alternative.
"Is it associated with all sleep? and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
The World-Honored One stated that drowsiness (*styāna*) and torpor (*middha*) constitute a single hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Some claim that there is no drowsiness apart from sleep, and no sleep apart from drowsiness.
Now, wishing to explain that there is indeed drowsiness apart from sleep and sleep apart from drowsiness, this treatise is composed for the sake of establishing the definitive meaning.
Is everything associated with sleep?
This should be expanded into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What is sleep that is not associated with *middha* (torpor)?
If the body is heavy when it has not yet moved, this is called the sleep of the fivefold group of consciousnesses;
if the mind is heavy, this is called the sleep of the mental consciousness.
The same applies to the other phrases, such as "the body and mind are dazed."

What is that? It refers to the sleep of all those in the form and formless realms, and the sleep of those in the desire realm when they are not actually asleep; this is called "sleep" that is not associated with "swoon.
What is "swoon" that is not associated with "sleep"?

In a mind that is undefiled, one sleeps in dreams; the body moves, yet the mind is not distracted and does not engage in activity. The five consciousnesses sleep within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
As for "an undefiled mind," this refers to a virtuous mind or a non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*); this is called sleeping without being associated with drowsiness (*middha*).
How are sleep (*middha*) and torpor (*styāna*) associated?
The answer is:
"The torpor of a defiled mind occurs in dreams," and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer to the remaining phrases follows the pattern of the previous discussion on restlessness and remorse.
Regarding sleep (*middha*), should it be said to be wholesome?
[And so forth, as explained at length.]
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
This leads from one discussion to another.
Previously, it was stated that sleep occurs within a mind that is not defiled, and so forth at length; however, it was not stated whether sleep itself is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Because that [work] did not explain it therein, and because one now wishes to explain it, this treatise is composed.
Should sleep be said to be wholesome? ...
[and so on,] up to the full exposition.
Answer: Sleep may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
What is wholesome?
When a wholesome mind sleeps or dreams, this is called "wholesome. Question:

Is this the sleep or dream of a wholesome mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala-citta*), or is it the sleep or dream of a wholesome mind produced through application (*prāyogika-kuśala-citta*)?
Answer: It is innate virtue, not virtue acquired through application. Question:
Which sentient beings sleep within a wholesome mind?
The answer is:
those who are not currently sleeping.
One who practices much that is wholesome, because of practicing much that is wholesome, is also wholesome even during sleep.
Is it not as when a practitioner, while awake, contemplates their meditative object?
If one sleeps while mindful of an object, one will see that very same object within the dream;
it is the same for a donor who recites the sutras.
In this way, such sentient beings sleep with a virtuous mind.
What kind of sentient beings have unwholesome minds while sleeping?
Answer: Those who are not actually asleep.
Those who frequently commit evil deeds are like butchers and hunters who perform unwholesome acts during the day and likewise in their dreams while sleeping.
As it is with butchers and hunters, so it is with thieves and lecherous people.
Such beings sleep with an unwholesome mind.
Which beings sleep with an indeterminate mind?
The answer is:
When not asleep, one mostly engages in indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) activities; likewise, one sleeps with an indeterminate mind and subsequently experiences the retribution of indeterminate matters.

One may also sleep within an indeterminate state of mind, or sleep with a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), and subsequently perform acts of deportment or craftsmanship.
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi) also lie dormant within the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*).

This is as when, in the aggregates of one's previous existence, there has been much cultivation of the wholesome, unwholesome, and unspecified; and one dies with a wholesome, unwholesome, or unspecified mind.
When one is awake, one frequently performs wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral actions; when asleep, one likewise sleeps with a wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral mind.
Regarding the wholesome deeds performed during sleep, should it be said that they increase or that they are transformed?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: It was previously stated, "a wholesome mind sleeps," and so forth at length; however, it was not stated whether the wholesome increase produced by sleep should be said to be diverted or not diverted.
Because that which was not explained therein is now intended to be explained, this treatise is composed.
Regarding whether the wholesome [karma] performed during sleep should be said to increase or to be diverted,
and so forth, it is explained at length.
Some say that "attainment" (prāpti) is an augmentation;
others say that "arising" (utpāda) is an augmentation.
How is it said that attainment is an augmentation?
As stated in the *Samādhivarga*:

"For what reason do ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), when they regress, experience an increase in the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*);
whereas the disciples of the Blessed One (*śrāvaka*), when they regress, experience an increase only in the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation?"
How is it said that birth is a conceptual construction (*samāropa*)? As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) gives rise to craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five factors necessarily arise."
What are the five? First, craving for the realm of desire;
second, the intensification of craving for the realm of desire.
3. Ignorance; 4. augmentation of ignorance;
5. restlessness.
In this context, it is said that wholesome and unwholesome volitions obtain desirable and undesirable fruits; this is termed "augmentation.
Does that augmentation produce a desirable fruit, or does it produce an undesirable fruit?
Answer: If wholesome [karma] produces a desirable fruit, and unwholesome [karma] produces an undesirable fruit,
how is the wholesome increased?
It is as when one gives while dreaming in sleep.
Just as a person constantly practices giving, they also perform that same act while dreaming in sleep;
if they are fond of practicing extensive learning, they also perform that same act while dreaming in sleep.
It is the same for those who read the Sūtras and Abhidharma, or who maintain the precepts well.

If one is fond of practicing meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they will engage in that very practice even during sleep and dreams; just as one who practices the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) sleeps well, this is called "wholesome increase."
What is the augmentation of the unwholesome?
If one performs good or evil deeds, one also carries out those same deeds during sleep and dreams.

For example, a hunter or butcher may dream of committing acts of killing; a thief may dream of seizing another's property; or a lecher may dream of violating another's woman. This is called the augmentation of the unwholesome.
What is the non-virtuous augmentation that is not a non-virtuous augmentation?
It is like a person who is fond of practicing dignified conduct or crafts; when they sleep and dream, they also engage in those activities.
It is like a practitioner who dreams of being a farmer planting crops, or like a copper or iron smith who dreams of working with copper, iron, and so forth.
Question: If wholesome deeds performed during sleep were to increase [in merit], why did the Buddha say that for a fool there is no karmic fruit during sleep?

Answer: Just as a person who is not sleeping can perform tasks such as farming and sowing, whereas they cannot do so because they are asleep, the Buddha says that for such a person there is no karmic fruit.

Likewise, a person who is not sleeping can recite the sutras, cultivate wholesome roots such as the meditation on impurity, give rise to the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), produce the wholesome roots conducive to penetration such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*), and attain the fruits of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*. Because they are asleep, they cannot obtain such fruits; therefore, the Buddha says that for a fool, when he is asleep, there is no karmic fruit.
The Venerable Sūmī said:
Because one obtains little fruit while asleep, the Buddha stated that there is no fruit.
As it is said in the Buddha’s sūtras:
"It would be better to sleep than to give rise to unwholesome thoughts. He asked:
"If sleeping increases what is unwholesome, for what reason did the Buddha say:"
"Is it better to sleep than to give rise to evil thoughts?
He replied:
"Because one frequently gives rise to many evil thoughts when not sleeping, they are fewer while asleep."
For this reason, the Buddha said:
"It would be better to sleep than to give rise to evil thoughts.
A question is asked: [Why is this?]
Can one create karma for rebirth in a place of birth while asleep?
The answer is:
some say that one can indeed create karma for rebirth in the evil realms while asleep.
It refers to such things as the *brahmadika* worm and the *kuñjara* insect, which receive this minute and fragile body.
What dharma is called "dream"?
This is explained at length, and so forth.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
Previously, the events occurring within dreams were explained, but the nature of the dream itself was not yet discussed.
Now, wishing to explain that, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, it is said in the Buddha’s sutras:
"When I was a bodhisattva, I saw five things in a dream.
King Prasenajit saw ten things in a dream.
As Nandaka’s mother, the upāsikā, said to the Buddha:
"My husband has passed away, and he appeared to me in a dream.
As another sutra states in verse:
"One meets with others in a dream, but upon waking, they are no longer seen."
"Of all things that exist, nothing is seen even after death.
Other sūtras also state:
"You should abandon phenomena that are like dreams."
What is the nature of phenomena as being like a dream?
It is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and so forth, as explained at length.
Although the Buddha’s sūtras speak of dreams in various places, they do not provide a detailed analysis.
The Buddhist sūtras are the fundamental basis for this treatise; because that [basis] does not explain certain matters which one now wishes to explain, this treatise has been composed.
Furthermore, there are those who say: the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain that dreams are not real dharmas.
For what reason does he speak thus?
The answer is:
he speaks thus because of worldly conventional reality.
It is like a person who, having eaten and drunk their fill in a dream, finds their sense faculties strengthened, yet upon waking, suffers from hunger and thirst;
or like one who experiences the five kinds of music in a dream, but upon waking, perceives none of it at all.
One dreams of being surrounded by the fourfold army, yet upon waking, one is alone.
For this reason, the dream is not truly existent.
This treatise is composed in order to refute those who speak thus and to clarify that the dream is indeed a real phenomenon.
What dharma is called "dream"?
The answer is:

when one is asleep, the mind and mental factors follow their respective objects; having awakened, one does not forget them and says to others, "I saw such-and-such things in a dream"—this is what is called a dream.
Question: If one does not remember the things seen in a dream after waking up;
or even if one does remember them, does not speak of them to others—is that still considered a dream?
Answer: This, too, is a dream.
What is spoken of herein is the dream of fulfillment.
One who fulfills dreams is one who, having seen something in a dream, does not forget it upon waking and also speaks of it to others.
It is asked:
what is the essential nature of a dream?
The answer is:
Its essential nature is the mind (manas). Why is this so?
By the power of the mind, the mind and its mental factors arise.
Furthermore, some say that the very nature of a dream consists of the mind and its mental factors. Why is this so?
As stated in the original sūtra:
"The mind and mental factors follow their respective objects.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the objects of the mind and mental factors constitute the essential nature of a dream.
Why is this so? As stated in the original sūtra:
"The mind and its mental factors follow their respective objects."
Furthermore, there are those who say that the essential nature of a dream consists of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
Question: Where does the dream exist?
Answer: [Dreams] belong to the desire realm, not the form or formless realms.
Some say that not all beings in the desire realm experience dreams, such as the sentient beings in the hells.
Why is this? Because they are oppressed by suffering, they are unable to sleep.
Furthermore, there are those who say that even in the hells, there are times of sleep.
Why is this so? As it is said regarding the Reviving Hell (Saṃjīva), at times a cold wind blows, and thus they cry out:
"Be alive, living beings! (saṃjīva).
When the living beings revive, they immediately return to life;
because of the cool wind blowing upon them, they obtain a brief sleep.
For this reason, we know that there are also sleep and dreams within the hells;
animals, hungry ghosts, and humans likewise have sleep and dreams. Question:
What kind of person has dreams?
The answer is:
both ordinary worldlings and noble ones dream.
From the stage of the *srotāpanna* up to the *pratyekabuddha*, all are still dreaming; only the Buddhas do not dream. Why is this?
It is because only the Buddhas are free from doubt and have abandoned all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) regarding the lack of skillful means.
Question: Are the things seen in a dream those that have been previously experienced, or are they not? Answer:
"This is a matter that has been experienced, not a matter that has not been experienced. He asked:
"If that is so, when one sees a person with horns in a dream, where was such a horned person ever seen before?"
Answer: This is because it is a confused perception.
One sees a person in one place and sees horns in another; due to this confused perception, one says that one sees a person with horns in a single location.

Furthermore, there are those who say that within the great ocean there are creatures with human forms and horns upon their heads; because he had previously seen them, he now sees them in a dream as well.
It is asked:
regarding the five things the Bodhisattva sees in his dreams, where did he previously see these things?
The answer is:
There are two further kinds: first, that which has been previously seen; [second, that which has not].
Second is "having previously heard.
That which the Bodhisattva dreams is something he has previously heard. Where did he hear it?
The Buddhas of the past taught these five dreams to their disciples; the Bodhisattva heard of them then, and because he had heard of them before, he now sees them in his dreams as well.
Question: Who manifests this dream? Answer:
Some say that these spirits and deities manifest auspicious or inauspicious events.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
dreams are manifested due to five causes.
As the verse says:
"Through the discrimination of a doubting mind, One perceives the causes of habitual tendencies as manifest phenomena;
It is not a person who comes to speak to one, But because of this, five views arise in a dream."
The medical treatises state that there are seven causes for dreams.
As a verse says:
"Whether it be what has been experienced through hearing or seeing, or what is sought after and discriminated,
the awakening to habitual tendencies and various afflictions— it is because of these that one sees seven dreams. Question:
If the present mental consciousness cannot see forms and so forth, how can it be said that in dreams—which belong to the mental stage—one is able to see forms and so forth?
The answer is:
one says "sees" because of perceiving signs of good or bad fortune; the sages' explanations of dreams are likewise thus.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"During sleep, the five consciousnesses do not manifest before one, and thus one cannot see forms and so forth.
As in the dream of the female lay follower Nandakāmātā, it was because the force of her sleep was weak that she was able to see forms and so forth."

Question: Which involves more objects of recollection—the things remembered in dreams, or the things remembered by the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) in the stage of the fourth dhyāna?
Answer: [The latter.]

The objects recalled in dreams are many, whereas the objects recalled by the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) in the stage of the fourth dhyāna are not so numerous. For this reason, it is said:
"Is it possible that one who has not entered dhyāna and has not brought forth the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can nevertheless recollect events from incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeyakalpa*)?"
Answer: There is;
it refers to that which one contemplates within a dream.
Regarding the dream-books spoken by the rishis: if a person sees such things in a dream, there will be such results.
Question: If knowing the affairs of future lives is the domain of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (praṇidhijñāna), how can one know them without having attained that knowledge?
Answer: [As follows].
One is able to know by means of comparing past and present events with future events:
just as various sages had such dreams and experienced such results in the past, so too, given that there is such a dream now, there shall likewise be such a result.
All such [realizations] are known through analogical characteristics (*upamāna*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"One should abandon phenomena that are like dreams and so forth."
What are these phenomena that are like dreams?
The answer is:
they are the five aggregates (skandhas) and so forth.
Question: For what reason is it said that the five aggregates are like a dream? Answer:
Because they do not accord with people's expectations and exist only briefly without enduring for long, it is said that the aggregates (skandhas) are like a dream. Question:
In what place does one sleep?
The answer is:

As previously stated in the sutra, there is sleep within the five realms of existence, there is sleep within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is sleep for those endowed with all sense faculties while in the mother’s womb, and even the Buddha, the World-Honored One, experiences sleep.
Question: As Satyaka Nirgrantha has said, if a person sleeps, that person is also foolish. Why is this so?
Because of this canopy,
how is this to be reconciled?
The answer is:
Not all sleep constitutes a hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*).
Some sleep is a hindrance, while some sleep is not a hindrance.
Sleep that is not a hindrance occurs when the Buddha arises from it to attend to his physical well-being.
As for sleep being an obscuration, the Buddha does not manifest it in the present. Why is this?
Because he has already abandoned all delusion.
There are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*). Do the five hindrances encompass all hindrances?
And so on, as explained at length. Question:
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is:

The Buddha’s sūtras speak of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*), and some claim that there are only these five hindrances and no others. This treatise was written in order to clarify that, in addition to the five hindrances, there is further the hindrance of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
Do the five hindrances encompass all hindrances, or do all hindrances encompass the five hindrances?
The answer is:
all hindrances encompass the five hindrances, but the five hindrances do not encompass all hindrances; this is explained at length.
The "five hindrances" (pañca-nīvaraṇāni) are those that have been explained.
The "all-encompassing hindrance" (sarva-nīvaraṇa) is the sixth, the hindrance of ignorance (avidyā-nīvaraṇa).
This all-encompassing hindrance subsumes the five hindrances because it is the most predominant among them.
The five [aggregates] do not encompass all things because they are incomplete.
It is like using a large vessel to cover a small one—it covers it entirely; yet using a small vessel to cover a large one—it does not cover it entirely.
It is likewise in this case: all [factors] are subsumed within the five, but the five do not subsume everything.
What is not subsumed? It refers to the veil of ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*).
The Buddha said:
"Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, the foolish and small-minded obtain this body; the same is true for those who are intelligent.
A question was asked:

If ignorance (avidyā) is both a hindrance (nīvaraṇa) and a fetter (saṃyojana), and craving (tṛṣṇā) is likewise both a hindrance and a fetter, why is it said only that "ignorance covers" and not that "craving covers"?
Answer: Some say it is because he wishes to manifest various literary styles and various expositions.
If there are various literary styles, the meaning is easily understood.

Furthermore, there are those who say that "covering" (*nīvaraṇa*) has the sense of "obscuring," for there is no fetter that obscures the eye of wisdom of sentient beings as much as ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Binding" (*saṃyojana*) has the sense of "tying," for there is no fetter that binds sentient beings as much as the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
It is like a person who has two enemies: one binds his hands and feet, while the other covers his eyes with dust.
Bound and blind, this person is unable to go anywhere.
In this way, ignorance shrouds the wisdom-eye of sentient beings and they are bound by the fetter of craving, such that they are unable to arise and turn toward *nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka made this statement:
"Because they are shrouded by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving, unwholesome phenomena arise."
Regarding this, it should be stated: first, Ilīma; second, Maśeṣucora. The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"These manifest two gates," and so forth, as explained at length.
As it is said:
"Enveloped by ignorance and bound by the fetter of craving. The same applies to saying "enveloped by the fetter of craving and bound by ignorance.
For this reason, in order to manifest the meaning of these two gates, [the text] explains at length, and so forth.
Question: For what reason is ignorance (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*) not mentioned among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*)? Answer:
The meaning of "covering" (*chādana*) is the meaning of "hindrance" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Among these five factors that cover functional power and so forth, the covering power of ignorance (*avidyā*) is particularly predominant.
Just as the covering power of a single hindrance of ignorance exceeds the combined covering power of all five hindrances.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because the substance of ignorance (*avidyā*) is heavy, it is not established as an "obscuration" (*nīvaraṇa*) among the five obscurations.
[They ask: "Do all obscurations completely cover?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]

Previously, we explained that among the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) mentioned in the Sūtras, there is an "hindrance of ignorance" (*avidyā-nīvaraṇa*) not included therein; now, we wish to explain the Abhidharma doctrine that all afflictions (*kleśa*) without exception are hindrances. Why is this so?
Because all afflictions completely shroud this body,
for this reason the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra asked:
"Are they covered by the hindrances?"
This is expanded into four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What is an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*) but not a covering (*paryavasthāna*)?
It refers to the five obscurations of the past and future.
Why is this so? It is called a "hindrance" (nīvaraṇa) because it possesses the characteristic of a hindrance.
Since the function of past hindrances has already been completed and the function of future hindrances has not yet arisen, they are not termed "obscuration" (paryavasthāna).
What is concealment (*nivaraṇa*) that is not an envelopment (*nīvaraṇa*)?
It refers to whatever other afflictions (*kleśa*), apart from the five envelopments, manifest at present.
Which ones are these?

This refers to all fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the form and formless realms, as well as the views, pride, and ignorance associated with the desire realm that are not subsumed under the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), which manifest at the time when the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are present.
What is meant by "the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) also being coverings (chādana)"?

When the five hindrances manifest in succession: when the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) manifests without sleep, three hindrances are present—namely, sensual desire, torpor (styāna), and restlessness (auddhatya);
when there is sleep, there are four, as the hindrance of torpor (middha-nīvaraṇa) is added.
The same applies to the explanations regarding ill-will (*vyāpāda*), delusion (*moha*), and regret (*kaukṛtya*).
When the hindrance of sleepiness (*middha-nīvaraṇa*) manifests, two hindrances manifest, namely the hindrances of sleepiness and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
When one is actually asleep, three hindrances manifest; that is, the aforementioned ones with the addition of sleep itself.
What is neither an obscuration (*nīvaraṇa*) nor a covering (*paryavasthāna*)?
It is all phenomena other than those mentioned above.

Among all phenomena that have already been established by name and already designated by description, those that have been so established and designated constitute the first, second, and third phrases; those not yet established by name and not yet designated by description constitute the fourth phrase.
What are these? The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) is treated in four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) throughout the three periods of time, those factors not subsumed under the five present hindrances constitute the first, second, and third propositions. All other associated and dissociated formations, the entirety of the [other] four aggregates, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)—such factors as these constitute the fourth proposition.
Question: Just as past afflictions obscure past phenomena, future afflictions obscure future phenomena, and present afflictions obscure present phenomena.
Why is it that only present afflictions are said to be concealment (*nivaraṇa*), while those of the past and future are not?
The answer is:
some say that if the present is mentioned, one should know that the past and future are also thereby mentioned.
Furthermore, some say that present afflictions can obstruct the Noble Path, whereas past and future afflictions cannot obstruct the Noble Path.
Others say that present afflictions can grasp both the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*), whereas those of the past and future cannot.
Furthermore, some say that present afflictions can grasp and yield fruit, whereas past and future ones cannot.
Others say that present afflictions are currently subject to reproach, defiling this body and causing it to fall into improper states, whereas past and future ones are not.
Furthermore, some say that present afflictions can produce worldly delusion as well as delusion regarding objects.
Others say that present afflictions have functional activity.
Furthermore, some say it refers to the present afflictions, their basis, their range of activity, and their objects.
Others say it refers either to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) or to persons (*pudgala*).
If one speaks in terms of phenomena: past phenomena are shrouded by past afflictions; future and present phenomena are shrouded by future and present afflictions.
If speaking in terms of persons, then present afflictions are called "covering" the person.
As people in the world say:
"Who is covered by afflictions?"
This means that those who have not attained liberation are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*).

The aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) of the present are conventionally designated as "person" (*pudgala*), while the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of the past and future are conventionally designated as "phenomenon" (*dharma*). For this reason, it is the afflictions of the present that are called a "shroud," not those of the past or future.
"Is every latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) unwholesome (*akuśala*)?
... [and so on] up to the full exposition. Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
Some say that all fetters and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*).
As the Dārṣṭāntikas say: "All afflictions are exclusively unwholesome. Why is this so?"
Because of a lack of skillful means,

[the author] intends to stop such an interpretation and also wishes to state that the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and their associated ignorance (*avidyā*) in the desire realm, as well as all fetters (*saṃyojana*) in the form and formless realms, are entirely indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that all afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are exclusively unwholesome (*akuśala*), while all afflictions of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

Now, wishing to demonstrate that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and their associated ignorance (*avidyā*) within the desire realm are also indeterminate, and for this reason, desiring to refute the positions of others and to clarify his own position, as well as wishing to explain the meaning of the correspondence of dharma-characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he composed this treatise.
Are all latent tendencies of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) necessarily unwholesome? Answer:
All that is unwholesome consists of the latent tendencies of ignorance bound to the desire realm.
Is there any latent tendency of ignorance in the desire realm that is not unwholesome? Answer: There is.
This refers to the latent tendencies of ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm. Question:
For what reason is the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes in the desire realm not unwholesome (*akuśala*)?

Answer: If its essence is shamelessness and lack of dread, if it is associated with shamelessness and lack of dread, if it arises from shamelessness and lack of dread, and if it is the fruit of reliance upon shamelessness and lack of dread, then it is unwholesome;
because this [state] is the opposite of those, it is not unwholesome.
Furthermore, this dharma does not invariably destroy the resolve for the goal.
How is it that it does not invariably destroy the resolve for the goal?
The answer is:
Because its essence is not characterized by shamelessness, lack of remorse, and so forth.
Furthermore, because this dharma does not obstruct giving, upholding the precepts, cultivating meditative concentration, and so on. Why is this so?

One who calculates based on the view of self practices giving for the sake of my own happiness; one practices ethical discipline for the sake of my being born in a fortunate realm; and one cultivates meditative concentration for the sake of my attaining liberation.
The view of extremes arises following the view of self-identity; its associated ignorance is likewise so.
Furthermore, these two views are deluded regarding their own phenomena and do not oppress others.

Why is this? One who holds the view of self does not speak thus, saying that "the eye can see forms" or "this is visible"; rather, they speak thus: "I am the seer," and "that which is visible belongs to me."
The same applies up to the case of the mind cognizing mental phenomena (*dharmas*).
This view never coerces others; because the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) arises subsequent to the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), its associated ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise so.
Furthermore, because these views cannot produce karmic retribution, the Venerable Vasumitra stated as follows:
"For what reason are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?"
Answer: Because they cannot produce coarse karma of body or speech. Question:
Are there unwholesome afflictions that cannot produce coarse actions of body and speech, yet are nonetheless indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The answer is:
although they do not arise in the present, when they are subsequently increased, they are able to produce coarse actions of body and speech.
The view of a self-identity and the view of extremes can never arise [in them].
Furthermore, these views cannot cause sentient beings to fall into the evil realms. Question:
Are there unwholesome afflictions that do not cause sentient beings to fall into the evil realms? Could these then be considered indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
The answer is:
when unwholesome afflictions subsequently increase in strength, they can cause sentient beings to fall into the evil realms.
Because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) ultimately cannot cause sentient beings to fall into the evil destinies.
Furthermore, these views cannot produce undesirable fruits. Question:
If one is able to obtain future existence, that is precisely the production of an undesirable fruit.
The Blessed One also said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
I do not praise even for the duration of a finger-snap the arising of future existence. Why is this?
Because all existence is suffering.
The same applies to the ignorance that arises in association with the view of extremes following the view of self-identity.
The Venerable Buddhadeva stated:
"These two views are inversions; they give rise to all afflictions and are not a state of security; therefore, they are unwholesome."
If the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) were not unwholesome, what then would be unwholesome?
The Blessed One has also said:
"O bhikṣus!"

If ignorance (*avidyā*) is unwholesome (*akuśala*), then the ignorance that arises in association with the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) following the view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) would likewise be so.
Are all the underlying tendencies of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*) in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*) exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?

Answer: All latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) within the realms of form and formlessness are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*); the detailed explanation is as in the original sūtra. Question:
Why are the afflictions of the form and formless realms indeterminate?
The answer is:

if their nature consists of lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), or even if they are the resultant fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*) of lack of shame and lack of dread, they are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The afflictions of the form and formless realms are the opposite of this, and are therefore not unwholesome.
Furthermore, these afflictions do not invariably destroy the intention for a future life, as was explained above.
Furthermore, because they cannot produce retribution.
Following this line of inquiry, one asks: for what reason do those various afflictions (*kleśa*) not produce retribution?
The answer is:
These afflictions are restrained and held by the fourfold and fivefold samādhis;
just as a venomous snake, when held by a mantra, cannot bite a person, so too it is with these.
Furthermore, because there is no vessel for retribution therein:
if the afflictions of the form and formless realms were to produce retribution, what kind of retribution would they produce?
They would necessarily produce the retribution of suffering.
The retribution of suffering resides in the desire realm; one cannot undergo retribution within the desire realm through the activities of the form or formless realms.
Furthermore, those afflictions do not arise solely from inverted perceptions, but also have some other causes.

Just as in the realm of form and the formless realm, wrong view slanders suffering because there is some slight pleasure therein; likewise, there is also a slight grasping at views regarding excellence as supreme, and a slight grasping at precepts and observances as pure.

Just as the path of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) can purify the desire realm, the path of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) can purify the form realm, and the path of the formless realm can purify the formless realm.
The Venerable Sthavira Sumati said:
For what reason are the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form and formless realms indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
He replied:
"I am unable to produce coarse actions of body or speech," as explained in detail above.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
If the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the form and formless realms were not unwholesome (*akuśala*), what then would be unwholesome?
The Blessed One has also stated that afflictions give rise to karma.
Are all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin necessarily universal (*sarvatraga*)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
This should be understood as previously explained regarding the universal causes (*sarvatragahetu*).
Are all latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin necessarily universal latent tendencies?
Answer: No.
Are all pervasive and exhaustive [defilements] the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin?
Is there perhaps any latent tendency of ignorance abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin that is not pervasive?
Answer: There is.
It is the ignorance that is not associated with the universal proclivities (sarvatraga-anuśaya).
What is it? It is the ignorance associated with desire, hatred, pride, and so forth, explained according to its specific characteristics.
What is the latent tendency of non-associated ignorance?
Answer: It is not said that there is suffering; rather, one cannot endure it and cannot accept it.
The same applies to the other Truths.
This mind is consistently deluded, consistently inferior, and consistently ignorant; therefore, it is called "unshared ignorance" (*āveṇikī avidyā*). Question:
If this is so, why is it not considered a "false view" (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: It is because of wrong view that they slanderously claim there is no suffering; it is not that they do not wish to endure suffering.
This is just as one whose food from the previous day has not been digested hates the consumption of milk; they are exactly like that.
Some may ask: "The essence has already been explained above; what, then, is its activity?
The answer is:
"It is ignorance, darkness, and delusion."
Furthermore, there are those who say that one first explains what is practiced; for example, if suffering is not explained, one will neither endure it nor find it unacceptable.
[The opponent] asks:
"If this is so, how do you reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*?"
As it is said:
"What is that which is driven by the latent tendency of ignorance?
The answer is:
If it is asked whether this refers to ignorance, darkness, and delusion,
the answer is:
that [text] speaks of the activity of ignorance as being inexhaustible, but it does not mention therein the activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that it does not refer to suffering and so forth, but rather refers to the object-condition (*ālambana*) of ignorance (*avidyā*). Question:
In what sense is this "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) meaning?
Answer: The śramaṇas of Kaśmīr explain it thus:
It is called "unshared" (āveṇika) because it does not correspond with the afflictions associated with the four noble truths as their objects.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these latent dispositions (anuśaya) take the Four Noble Truths as their object and are practiced only by ordinary worldlings; therefore, they are called "unshared" (āveṇika).
The Venerable Pārśva has stated:
"They are called unshared because they are not shared with other afflictions."
Why is this? Because they are distinct from the spheres of activity of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and arise without depending upon them;
therefore, they are called "unshared" (*āveṇika*). The Venerable Vāmalaka said:
It is called "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*) because it is distinct from the afflictions and does not share a single mental state with them.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is called "unshared" because it is distinct from the afflictions and does not share the same preparatory application (*prayoga*).
Question: Is non-associated ignorance abandoned by these five [categories of] abandonment, or is it abandoned by the path of seeing?
If it were abandoned by the path of seeing, how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-sūtra*?
As it is said:
"That is the mind associated with uncommon ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*), which is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*). If it is of five kinds, why is it not mentioned here?
Answer: Some say it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Question:
If this is so, how is one to reconcile what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
The answer is:
this passage should be stated as follows:
That is a mind associated with the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) which is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
What is the intention behind not stating what ought to have been stated?
The answer is:
What is taught in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* does not mention the latent tendency of non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā-anuśaya*).
If it arises through its own power and not dependent on another, that is non-common ignorance.
Although it is not associated with afflictions and does not arise through its own power but rather due to another, it is therefore not "unshared" (āveṇika).
Furthermore, there are those who say that this refers to the five kinds of abandonment.
Question: Why is this not explained here? Answer:
Some say that if ignorance takes the Four Noble Truths as its object, it does not associate with other latent tendencies (anuśaya), and is therefore called "unshared" (āveṇika).
There is also ignorance to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya) that does not associate with afflictions, yet does not take the Four Noble Truths as its object.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if it were not associated with the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and were practiced exclusively by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), then it would be so described therein;

however, although that which is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) is not associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*), it is practiced by both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*), and for this reason it is not so described.
Question: At what point in the mind can the latent tendency of non-common ignorance (*āveṇikāvidyānuśaya*), which is abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), be found? Answer:
The ten minor universal afflictions (*upakleśa-mahābhūmika*) of the desire realm,

as well as *śāṭhya* (deceit) and *pramāda* (heedlessness) in the stage of the first dhyāna of the form realm, and those associated with *pramāda* from the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are these [factors].
Question: At what time does it manifest before one? Answer:
If a person gives rise to right view, or if a person gives rise to [wrong] views, once the mind has become weary, there may at times arise such non-specific ignorance (*āveṇikī avidyā*).
Regarding non-specific ignorance, it is not said to be suffering, and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: If wisdom exists within all states of mind, why is it said that one does not accept suffering? Answer:
Because they are shrouded by ignorance, their wisdom is neither clear nor penetrating.
Is there any latent disposition (*anuśaya*) that is not driven by a concomitant latent disposition? Answer: Yes.
There is. It refers to the latent tendency of non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā-anuśaya*) whose objects have already been abandoned.
Is there any latent tendency that is not itself made latent by another latent tendency?
Answer: There is;
it is precisely that which was mentioned previously.
Is there perhaps that which cannot be made to act?
He replied: "There is."
This refers to the latent tendency of non-shared ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā-anuśaya*) which has the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object.
What is the non-shared restlessness-fetter (*asādhāraṇa-auddhatya-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:
There is no [affliction] that is not associated with the entanglement of restlessness. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: It is in order to dispel the doubts of people.

For instance, there is the latent tendency of non-associated ignorance (*asamprayukta-avidyā-anuśaya*) which is not associated with the afflictions, and it is likewise said that there is the entanglement of non-associated restlessness (*asādhāraṇa-auddhatya-paryavasthāna*).
To stop such doubts and intentions, he answers: "There is no [affliction] that is not associated with the fetter of restlessness.
Why is this? Because the latent tendency of ignorance (avidyā-anuśaya) exists in all defiled states of mind.

Furthermore, just as there is a latent tendency of non-associated ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā-anuśaya*) that does not correspond with the afflictions, one might also claim there is a non-associated restlessness (*asādhāraṇa-auddhatya-paryavasthāna*) that does not correspond with the envelopments (*paryavasthāna*).
To eliminate such a doubt, it is answered that there is no such non-associated restlessness.
Why is this so? Because all defiled states of mind possess both torpor (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*).
For this reason, this treatise was composed.

Question: Since drowsiness (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*) pertain to all three realms and are to be abandoned through the five [categories of] abandonment, and since they can be found in all defiled minds of the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*), why is drowsiness not questioned, but only restlessness?
