If one wishes to definitively state that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven lack direct, clear cognition, this is because their knowledge is inferential and based on signs.
Why is this so? Because the wisdom acquired at birth does not know the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
For this reason, this treatise is composed. Question:
If the wisdom acquired at birth cannot know the dharma of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), how do those various devas know it?
Answer: It is known by five reasons.
First, the World-Honored One gave rise to a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*).
Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One give rise to a conventional mind? Answer:
This is because it accords with the World-Honored One’s intention.
Who is able to most perfectly accord with the World-Honored One’s intention?
It is one who is able to sever future existence.
The Blessed One also said:
"If a bhikṣu gives rise to even a slight portion of future existence, I do not praise that person," and so forth, as explained at length.
Because that bhikṣu has severed future existence and thus accords with the Blessed One’s intention, he gives rise to a conventional mind.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one speaks with words to inform others so that those possessing the knowledge of others' minds may understand.
Second, "informing others" means as previously explained.
3. That venerable one also gave rise to a mundane thought.
It was asked:
"For what reason did that venerable one give rise to a mundane thought?"
The answer is:

That venerable one has had his afflictions burning intensely since beginningless time, but now they have become cooled; he has abandoned the burning sense-bases (*āyatana*) and attained the cool sense-bases, abandoned afflicted sentient beings and dwells among pure sentient beings, and having cast off the heavy burden of the defiled aggregates (*skandha*), he has attained the pure aggregates. Because joy has arisen within him, he gives rise to a conventional mind (*laukika-citta*).
4. That venerable one also informed others.
Question: For what reason did that venerable one inform others?

Answer: It is because one wishes to manifest the truthfulness of what is spoken within the present life; furthermore, it causes the donor to give rise to a heart of joy when providing food, drink, clothing, bedding, seats, and medicinal requisites for illness; and it also demonstrates that there is the fruit of actual practice in the house-leaving life. For these reasons, one informs others.
5. Heard from the Mahātejas-deva. Question: Who is this Mahātejas-deva?
Answer: It refers to those who attain arhatship within the heavenly realms. Question:
"Does one know everything?
He replied:
"One knows if the faculties and so forth are equal."
Question: Do the other devas also praise this Dharma?
Answer: Yes.
It is also praised.
[The opponent] asks: If this is so, why is it not mentioned here?
Answer: Some say that this refers to those among the devas who gather frequently.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days, the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven reflect upon whether there are those among humans or devas who practice wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, there are those who say:
among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, some use the pārijātaka tree as a metaphor for an arhat; it is for this reason that he is praised.
Furthermore, some say that when the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven hear that many people practice much goodness, they rejoice; for this reason, they offer praise.
Others say that the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven constantly observe human beings, providing protection to those who practice goodness; for this reason, they offer praise.
Question: Are those who are still training (śaikṣa) also so designated? Answer: Yes.
They also offer praise,
as it is said in the Sūtra:
"If people in the world serve their parents with filial piety, the devas will praise them."
How much more so for those who are still in training?
[The opponent] asks:
If this is so, why is it that only those whose outflows are exhausted (āsravakṣaya) are mentioned, and not those in training?
The answer is:
"Because it is the most excellent," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is a metaphor for when the *pārijātaka* tree is in full bloom during its peak season.

Furthermore, there are those who say that he is praised because one who has exhausted the outflows (āsravakṣaya) is worthy of receiving offerings; because he is unmixed with faults or afflictions; because he is without blame or reproach; and because he is free from resentment.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if there are Arhats in the world, the devas increase and the evil realms decrease; for this reason, they are praised.
It is just as when a wise king governs the country with rectitude, the population flourishes;
so it is with them as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if there are arhats in the world, the number of human beings increases and the host of asuras decreases.
Just as the waters of the great ocean rise when the moon is full, so it is with them.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if there are arhats in the world, then when the devas and asuras wage war, the devas will be victorious.
This is just as we see that when the deva Subāhu (Good Striver) is present, the devas emerge victorious; it is the same in this case as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if there are Arhats in the world, they are praised because the deities born after them possess superior majesty and virtue compared to the deities born before them.
Just as giving rice-water at a crossroads is superior to other forms of giving, so it is in this case.
Furthermore, some say that because there are arhats in the world, one who gives even a small amount of food will be reborn in the heavens; for this reason, it is praised.
Just as Mahākāśyapa offered a single vessel of millet porridge and Aniruddha offered a single meal, so too did he.
Furthermore, some say that because there are Arhats in the world, those who see them can give rise to faith and reverence and thereby attain rebirth in the heavens; for this reason, they are praised.
Just as a frog or a dog that merely breathed upon a caṇḍāla was reborn in the heavens due to its respectful and faithful mind, so too is it in this case.
Furthermore, some say that if there were Arhats in the world, those in the prison of birth and death would obtain a great amnesty.
It is just as when a king fathers a son and grants a general amnesty for the prisons;
it is the same in this case. Furthermore, there are those who say that if there are arhats in the world, they are able to manifest the paths leading to the good and evil realms.
Just as when the sun rises one can see both level ground and treacherous paths, so it is with this.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if there are Arhats in the world, they do not lose their celestial status nor fall into the evil realms; because they return to their celestial status, they are like Śakra, and so it is with them.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If there are arhats in the world, all the world constantly obtains wholesome benefit without a moment's interruption.
It is just as when a good teacher instructs a good disciple, and they constantly obtain wholesome benefit without a moment's interruption; so it is with them as well."
Furthermore, there are those who say: if there are arhats in the world, although they possess celestial pleasures, they are able to renounce them and contemplate the attainment of solitude.
Just as Śakra, the Cakravartin King, and Yama King have thought of leaving the household life, so too are they.

Furthermore, there are those who say: if there were Arhats in the world, all people in the world would hear the jewels of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and they would always be abundant and inexpensive.
Just as a sea vessel carrying treasures makes the whole world abound in them and renders them cheap, so too is it with them.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If there are Arhats in the world, all people in the world experience happiness;
it is just as when there is a time of abundant harvest. He asked:
Is this for the purpose of praising all arhats?
The answer is:
some say that it is indeed for the purpose of praising all arhats.
Why is this? The devas always delight in praising the virtues of others; since it is extremely rare for anyone to have accomplished all such tasks, they all offer praise.
Furthermore, there are those who say that not all arhats necessarily deserve such praise.
If one becomes an arhat and performs deeds that bring renown, thereby causing [virtue] to increase, then people offer praise;
but if one does not perform deeds that bring renown, or even if one does perform them, they do not cause [virtue] to increase, then even one's neighbors remain unaware of it, let alone the devas.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one who is noble and wealthy leaves the household life—as did King Śibī and others—they praise him.
Again, there are those who say that they praise those who are Arhats as described in the sūtras.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one possesses great wisdom and great merit, and is able to cause the hosts of devas to increase and the evil realms to diminish, then such a person should be praised.
Furthermore, there are those who say that if one benefits others without succumbing to weariness or fatigue—such as Śāriputra and others—they praise them.
Again, there are those who say that if one can protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, becoming a refuge for the world, they praise them.
Question: Do the devas know those who possess overweening pride?
Answer: Yes.
If there is one who, out of overweening pride, claims for himself the state of an Arhat, the devas do not know it;
but if one, free from overweening pride, claims for himself the attainment of Arhatship, the devas then know it.
Furthermore, there are those who say: if one possesses deep and profound roots of goodness yet gives rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*), then one does not know;
however, if one gives rise to the impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) bound to the desire realm and thereby gives rise to overweening pride, then one knows.

Just as Śakra, when there is no Buddha in the world, sees someone dwelling in seclusion and free from affairs, he immediately goes to that person's place to observe whether or not that person possesses the marks of one destined to become a Buddha.
If even Śakra is thus, how much more so the other devas—how could they not know?
It is asked:
Do they also know those who violate the precepts?
The answer is:
If one commits a gross transgression, it is known; if one commits a subtle one, it is not known.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
There is subduing through transformation and practice according to the Dharma, and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: The *Cāṇakīya-śāstra* is the fundamental source for this treatise.
It is heard that in the past, there was a great epidemic in the kingdom of Magadha.
During this time of pestilence, many of King Bimbisāra’s ministers and attendants in the kingdom of Magadha died.
Furthermore, it is said that when King Ajātaśatru killed his father, the king, he also killed the father’s surrounding ministers and attendants.
The various assistants and relatives went to invite Ānanda, saying:
"Please inquire of the Buddha on our behalf.
In various villages, there are those who have faith and devotion to the Buddha; after they pass away, the World-Honored One always fully declares the places where they will be reborn."
"In this kingdom of Magadha, I have not been told where my deceased relatives have been reborn.
You should inquire of the World-Honored One on my behalf: where have these people who passed away been reborn?"
At that time, out of affection, Ānanda consented to employ a skillful means.
He went to where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When other people have reached the end of their lives, the World-Honored One has always spoken of the places where they are reborn."
When the minister of the kingdom of Magadha passed away, the Buddha did not declare his place of rebirth.
Because the Buddha did not declare his place of rebirth, the relatives of that man gave rise to grief and affliction, and failed to develop faith and reverence.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will declare his place of rebirth.

It was in the kingdom of Magadha that the World-Honored One attained equal and perfect enlightenment; furthermore, King Bimbisāra has deep faith in the Buddha, has attained the ultimate Dharma, and reverently serves the Saṃgha."
"For this reason, you should explain the places of rebirth for the ministers and attendants of the kingdom of Magadha who have died.
At that time, the World-Honored One silently consented.

He then took his robe and bowl and entered the city of Nadīka to beg for food. Having finished his meal, he returned to the vihāra, washed his feet, and sat upon a seat prepared within the Kuñjaka chamber. With body and mind well-restrained, he entered meditative concentration, desiring to observe the places of rebirth of the royal attendants of Magadha.
Question: The World-Honored One possesses such knowledge and vision that he should know whatever he wishes to observe simply by bringing it to mind.
For what reason, then, does he prepare his seat, and so forth, as explained at length?
Answer: Some say it is because one wishes to explain matters that are profound, difficult to know, difficult to clarify, and difficult to perceive. Why is this so?
Among all the meanings taught in the sutras of the Buddhas, none is more profound than karma.
Although the twelve links of dependent origination are extremely deep, none is more so than two links;
that their essence is karma is indeed profoundly deep.
Among the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the power of knowing the force of karma is the most profound;
among the four inconceivable dharmas, the inconceivability of karma is the most profound;
and among the eight *skandhas*, the *karma-skandha* is the most profound.
For this reason, he prepared the seats, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, some say it was because he wished to wait for those to be converted to assemble.
Others say it was because the *dhyāna-ariṣṭas* had not yet gathered.
If the Śrāmaṇera Cāṇakya hears that the Buddha intends to speak on this matter, he will certainly come to visit the Buddha.
Furthermore, there are those who say that for this reason the Buddha also speaks of the Tathāgata’s eight qualities of reality:
first, the perfection of clarity; [and so forth].
2. Perfection of ethical discipline;
3. Perfection of teaching the Dharma;
4. Clarity regarding the present.
Fifth, skillfully expounding the Path;
sixth, obtaining virtuous companions;
seventh, obtaining virtuous followers.
Eighth, he possesses a mind that seeks to benefit all sentient beings.
This is explained at length as it appears in the sūtra.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this was taught so that Ānanda might hear and retain it without forgetting, thereby further increasing his heart of yearning, reverence, and respect.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because one wishes to sever the mind that treats others with contempt due to their lack of real virtue.
There are some who possess but little knowledge; when others come to question them, they answer those questions out of a sense of disdain and condescension.

The Tathāgata wishes to demonstrate that although I possess the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision such that I know immediately upon reflection, he nevertheless employs intentional skillful means; how much more so would he employ intentional skillful means for those of small wisdom?
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because he wished to manifest the qualities of a wise person.
The World-Honored One has also stated that there are three characteristics of wisdom:
first, thinking what should be thought well; [and so forth].
Second, they speak what is well-spoken;
third, they practice what is well-practiced.

Furthermore, it is said that the various ministers and officials of the kingdom of Magadha, through various causes, various effects, various karmas, and various retributions, are reborn throughout the six heavens of the desire realm.
Because he wished to contemplate this matter thoroughly, he prepared his seat, and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, there is another account stating that when the Buddha was about to enter meditative concentration, Ānanda asked about this matter; the Buddha had not yet replied when he entered concentration.
At that time, in the afternoon, the World-Honored One arose from meditative concentration and sat upon a seat spread before the community of bhikṣus.
Then Ānanda thought to himself:
"Now the World-Honored One’s body and mind are tranquil; this is precisely the right time to ask."
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in Ānanda’s mind, addressed him, saying:

“In this kingdom of Magadha, there are eighty-four thousand ministers and attendants, or even more than that number; some have been tamed by the transformative Dharma, while others have practiced according to the Dharma, severing the three fetters and attaining the stage of Srotāpanna,” and so on, as explained at length.
Question: What is meant by "assisting"? Answer:
Some say they are called "assistants" because they belong to the inner retinue of King Bimbisāra;
others say they are called "assistants" because they constantly attend upon the Triple Gem.
Furthermore, there are those who say this was his name from a previous life. Why is this so?

King Bimbisāra had formerly been a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*). While he was traveling through the air with his fourfold army, the royal wheel-treasure suddenly ceased to move, as described in detail above.
During the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, he even provided for eighty-four thousand royal attendants.
Having made offerings at the Bodhi tree, they departed by different paths.
The Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) at that time was none other than the present King Bimbisāra.
The eighty-four thousand assistants at that time are these very assistants now; therefore, one knows these were their names in a previous life.
Furthermore, there are those who say that these assistants assisted the king in governing two kingdoms, causing them to be prosperous and flourishing.
After their lives have ended, both countries will be left empty; therefore, they are called "auxiliaries" (*bāzuo*).
The Buddhist scriptures state:
among these auxiliaries, some employ transformative methods to subdue others, while others practice according to the Dharma.
Yet, one does not engage in such discrimination.

Since the Buddhist sūtras constitute the fundamental basis for this treatise, and because there are matters not explained in those various sūtras that one now wishes to explain, this treatise has been composed.
What is subduing through transformative teachings?
What is practicing in accordance with the Dharma?
The answer is:

Some say that among the ministers of Magadha, those who perceive the Dharma with a celestial body are called "tamed by transformation," while those who perceive the Dharma with a human body are called "practicing according to the Dharma."

Furthermore, there are those who say that among the ministers and assistants of the Magadha king, those who do not accept the precepts and the vision of the Dharma are called "tamed through the transformative Dharma," while those who accept the precepts and the vision of the Dharma are called "practicing according to the Dharma."

Furthermore, there are those who say that if one also brings these roots of goodness to maturity and thereby attains liberation therein, it is called "subduing through the transformative Dharma" (*dharmavineya*);
one who achieves fulfillment in these three matters is said to be "practicing according to the Dharma."
Thus, in this [stage], one plants the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) and enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) therein;
in this [stage], one plants the roots of goodness for contemplating the truths (*satyadarśana-kuśalamūla*) and enters the path of seeing therein;
in this [stage], one receives the nominal precepts (*prajñapti-śīla*) and attains the ultimate precepts (*bhūta-śīla*) therein.
In this [stage], one attains the precepts of liberation and the precepts of dhyāna; in that [stage], one attains the untainted (anāsrava) precepts.
In this [stage], one trains well in the mind and trains well in the precepts; in that [stage], one trains well in wisdom.
In this [stage], one attains the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala); in this [stage], one cultivates and purifies the roots of goodness; in that [stage], one attains pure vision.
In this context, one attains the five faculties beginning with faith; in that [other] context, one attains indestructible faith—it should be known that it is likewise so.
This is the conversion through the transformative dharma.

Herein, planting the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) means entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) therein; herein, planting the roots of goodness for contemplating the truths means entering the path of seeing therein.

In this context, entering the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is itself the attainment of the true precepts; receiving the conventional precepts (*prajñapti-śīla*) is itself the attainment of the ultimate precepts; attaining the precepts of liberation and meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) is itself the attainment of the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*); training well in the mind and training well in the precepts is itself the training well in wisdom (*prajñā*); attaining the stage of *srotāpanna* is itself the attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna*; attaining the cultivation of the roots of goodness is itself the attainment of pure vision; and attaining the five faculties such as faith is itself the attainment of indestructible faith—it should be understood that it is likewise so in all these cases.
This is practicing in accordance with the Dharma. Question:

For what reason is one who sees the Dharma among the devas called "tamed by the transformative Dharma" (*nairmāṇika-dharma-vinīta*), while one who sees the Dharma among humans is called "practicing in accordance with the Dharma" (*yathādharma-pratipanna*)?
The answer is:

Because they have practiced and studied among human beings, the Noble Path manifests before them; they also recite and study much while simultaneously understanding its meaning. During the first and last watches of the night, they diligently apply skillful means, undertaking the practice for one, seven, six, or seven days. From sunset until sunrise, they sit in the full lotus posture, practicing with diligent vigor, dwelling among mountain caves and rocky crags, with a meditation cushion upon their heads, and employing the methods of dhyāna-balls and dhyāna-staffs.
Only after having performed such forms of diligence as these does the Noble Path manifest before one.

Since this matter does not exist among the gods, if one cultivates such skillful means in this world and is subsequently reborn there, the Noble Path manifests before one without requiring much effort; therefore, it is called "subduing through transformation."
If, among human beings, one cultivates such dharmas as these so that the Noble Path manifests before them, this is called practicing in accordance with the Dharma.
What is excessive desire?
What is lack of contentment?
...and so on, as explained at length. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: These two dharmas have similar modes of operation.
There are those whose nature is characterized by much desire; people of the world say that such a person does not know contentment.
There are those whose nature is one of insatiability; people of the world say such persons have many desires.
Because these two phenomena are similar, worldly people consider them to be one and the same.
Now, wishing to explain their essential natures as well as their distinctions, I have composed this treatise.
What is meant by "having many desires"?
The answer is:
not yet having obtained [objects of] form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch; this refers to householders.
"Robes, food and drink, bedding, and seats—these are for those who have gone forth.
If one desires, constantly desires, or intensely desires [them], and so forth as extensively explained.
As for the householder, they gallop in all directions in pursuit of objects such as forms."
Those who farm seek fields, gardens, groves, cattle, sheep, and various livestock, as well as the necessities for sustaining life such as diverse grains and wheat.
Those who are wealthy and noble seek royal rank, kingdoms, fiefs, and treasures such as elephants, horses, gold, silver, and lapis lazuli.
For a renunciant to seek such necessary items as robes and alms bowls, as well as dwellings, disciples, and followers, is called having many desires.
One who lacks contentment—referring here to a householder—is one who, having already obtained [objects of] form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch, [still craves more].
"Having already obtained robes, food and drink, bedding, and seats for lying down, one is called a renunciant.
One who lacks contentment cannot be satisfied with what has been obtained," and so on, as extensively explained.
Those who live at home are insatiable; if they are not satisfied with one field, they seek a second field.
Being unsatisfied with two fields, they seek many more, yet remain unsatisfied even then.
The same applies to the explanation regarding gardens, groves, cattle, sheep, and other livestock, as well as all articles of livelihood.
As for those who are wealthy and noble, they are never satisfied with a single royal throne and seek a second one.
They are not content with two royal thrones, seeking instead many more;
the same applies to their seeking many precious jewels.
Likewise, a renunciant is not content with one robe and bowl, but seeks two or three.
This applies even to the insatiability of seeking much, and even to the insatiability regarding the necessities of life; the explanation is likewise.
What is the difference between having many desires and being insatiable?
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again? Answer:
These dharmas are similar; although their essential natures have been explained, their distinctions should still be stated.
What is excessive desire?
What is lack of contentment?
Regarding those with many desires: if they have not yet obtained forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, and so forth, as explained at length.
How is it known that they are "many-desired"?
The answer is:
One knows by means of what is sought;
when one applies many skillful means while seeking objects such as form (*rūpa*), one knows by virtue of those many skillful means. Why is this so?
Excessive desire is the cause of many expedient means.

Regarding the insatiable person: having already obtained forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—and so on, as explained at length—they still desire more and seek further. How is it known that this is being insatiable?
The answer is:
If one who has already desired desires again, this must be a case of frequent and manifold seeking; it is known by virtue of this manifold seeking. Why is this so?
"Having already desired and desiring again" is the cause of repeated and manifold seeking.
Furthermore, some say that lack of contentment is the cause and manifold desire is the effect; these two factors manifest one another.
Either the cause is manifested by means of the effect, or the effect is manifested by means of the cause; both of these factors are the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha-akuśalamūla*).
Furthermore, some say that excessive desire resides in the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*), while lack of contentment resides in the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*).
Why is this so? Because the five consciousnesses take present phenomena as their objects, while desire mostly takes future phenomena as its object.
The critique says:
These two dharmas both reside within the sixfold body of consciousness, and both are dharmas of the desire realm.
It is well said thus.
What is "having few desires"?
What is contentment? Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: These two dharmas are similar.
There are those whose nature is one of few desires; worldly people call such persons "contented."
There are those whose nature is contentment, whom people of the world call "having few desires.
Because these two dharmas are similar, the world regards them as one.
Now, wishing to explain their essential natures and also their distinctions, I have composed this treatise.
What is having few desires?
Not obtaining forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, and so forth at length—this refers to householders.
Not obtaining robes, food and drink, and so forth at length—this refers to those who have gone forth.
"If one does not desire, does not constantly desire, and does not excessively desire," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Regarding those living at home who farm and sow, they do not seek out fields and such," and so forth, as explained at length.
Those who are wealthy and noble do not seek royal positions and so forth, as explained at length.
Those who have left the household life do not seek robes, alms bowls, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is contentment?
The answer is:
having already obtained forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles, and so forth as explained at length—this refers to householders.
"Having obtained robes, food, drink, and so forth," and so on at length; this refers to those who have gone forth.
"One who is content may be satisfied with what they receive," and so on at length.
A householder who is content with what he has is satisfied with one field and does not seek a second field;
likewise, he is satisfied with even a single means of subsistence and does not seek a second, and so forth, as explained at length.
Those who possess wealth and nobility are content with a single kingship and do not seek a second;
they are content with two kingships and do not seek many, and so on, as explained at length.
The renunciant is content with one robe and one alms bowl, seeking nothing more than two;
likewise, regarding the requisites for life, they do not seek many, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is the difference between having few desires and being content?
Question: For what reason is this further discussion undertaken?
Answer: These dharmas are similar;
although their essential natures have been explained, their distinctions must still be explained.
"One who has few desires" refers to not yet having obtained forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles, and so forth, as explained at length.
How is it known that this person has few desires?
The answer is:
One knows through non-seeking, because non-seeking is the cause of having few desires.
As for contentment, it refers to having already obtained [objects of] form, sound, smell, taste, and touch, and so forth, as explained at length.
How is it known that this is contentment?
The answer is:
because one does not seek repeatedly, nor does one employ many skillful means.
Not employing many skillful means is the cause of contentment;
this is what is meant by "distinction.
There may be one who has few requests yet possesses great desire, or one who has many requests yet possesses little desire.

One who has few requests but many desires is like one who, having requested and obtained a single *harītakī* fruit, further desires two; this is called having few requests while possessing many desires.

To have many desires yet possess few cravings means, for example, to seek out hundreds of thousands of measures of gold and the necessities of life, and having obtained them, to no longer desire more; this is called having many desires yet possessing few cravings.
There are those who seek much and are thus discontented, and there are those who seek much and yet are contented.

Regarding those who seek much and are discontented: even when they have obtained the necessities of life sufficient to support their bodies, they still continue to seek more; this is called seeking much while being discontented.
One who seeks much yet is content is such that, even when they obtain the necessities of life insufficient for their own needs, they remain content despite seeking further.
Question: Why is it that one asks about having few desires, yet the answer concerns not desiring at all?
As it is said: "not desiring, not constantly desiring, and not excessively desiring.
The answer is:
there are two kinds of material requisites for life:
First, acting in accordance with the Dharma;
second, not acting in accordance with the Dharma.
One who acts in accordance with the Dharma has few desires; one who does not act in accordance with the Dharma is without desire.
Furthermore, there are those who say that objects for sustaining life are of two kinds:
first, those that are appropriate;
second, those that are inappropriate.
That which is appropriate is fewness of desires; that which is inappropriate is the lack of desire [for what is necessary].
Furthermore, there are those who say that receiving things from others is of two kinds:
first, out of delusion; [the second being for the sake of the Dharma].
Second, for the cessation of suffering.
To cease suffering is to have few desires; the foolish do not desire [this].
Furthermore, there are those who say: one does not desire material wealth, but desires the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that all Arhats have forever severed desire for sensory objects; because they feel compassion for sentient beings, they accept what others require—how, then, could they be said to be difficult to satisfy?
"What is meant by 'difficult to sustain'?
and so forth, as explained at length.
[The interlocutor] asks:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
because the spheres of activity of these two dharmas are similar.
There are those whose nature is difficult to satisfy, whom the world says are difficult to nourish;
there are those whose nature is difficult to nourish, whom the world says are difficult to satisfy.
Because these two dharmas are similar, people of the world claim they are one.
Now, wishing to explain their essential natures as well as their distinctions, I have composed this treatise.
What is meant by "difficult to satisfy"? The answer is:
it is drinking much and eating much.
What is meant by "difficult to nourish"?
Answer: It refers to eating and drinking repeatedly. Question:
Why are the distinctions between these two not inquired about?
The answer is: they should indeed be inquired about.
One should speak as follows:
What is the difference between being difficult to satisfy and being difficult to support?
The answer is:
"Eating much is difficult to satisfy; being selective about food is difficult to sustain.
As for the phrase "without inquiry," one should know that this statement is incomplete, and so forth, as explained at length.
What is it to be easily satisfied?
What is it to be easy to support?
Thus it is explained at length.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
This should be understood as explained in the section on why [the bodhisattva] is difficult to satisfy and difficult to nourish.
How, then, is he easy to satisfy?
The answer is:
"Eating little and drinking little" refers to this.
What is meant by "easy to support"?
The answer is:
"Not eating repeatedly" refers to this.
Question: Why is the distinction not asked about here?
Answer: This should be asked.
As stated above, there are those who eat little yet find it difficult to be satisfied, and those who eat much yet find it easy to be satisfied.
Regarding "eating little yet being difficult to satisfy": one should eat only one morsel, yet eats two; this is called eating little while being difficult to satisfy.

Regarding "eating much yet being easy to satisfy": if one needs one *hu* (a measure of grain) to suffice for the body, yet eats no more than that, this is called eating much while being easy to satisfy.
I have heard that there was once a female elephant named Mata who carried the Buddha’s śarīra into the kingdom of Kaśmīra.
By virtue of this root of goodness, she died in Kaśmīra and was reborn among humans.
Thereafter, she left the household life and attained the fruit of Arhatship, consuming one *śī* of rice daily.
When the time came for her to enter *parinirvāṇa*, she addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Assemble, and I shall personally declare the sublime Dharma I have realized."
The bhikṣuṇīs did not believe her words and spoke thus:
"You are a person so easily satisfied; why do you not say for yourself that you have attained the supreme Dharma?"
She spoke again to the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"Do not give rise to lack of faith; since I first took this body, it has always been easy to satisfy.

She also recounted the causes and conditions of her previous lives, saying: "In the past, I was a female elephant. Having cast off that body, I have now obtained this one, which can eat fifteen *sheng* of rice, yet I eat only ten *sheng*," and so on, as explained at length.
Although such individuals eat much, they are easily satisfied.
It has been heard that King Prasenajit was able to eat two *droṇas* of rice and drink two *droṇas* of gruel; this was due to the causal conditions of his past merit.
Because of a single grain of non-glutinous rice and a single stalk of sugarcane, he grew day by day;
due to such food and drink, his body became stout.
With this large body, he went to where the Buddha was.
The Buddha then asked, "Great King, your body is stout; are you not weary?
At that time, King Prasenajit felt shame and spoke to the Buddha in detail about his situation.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"A person should maintain right mindfulness, Knowing moderation in eating;
Thus they shall not encounter painful sensations, Their food will be easily digested, and their life-span increased."
When King Prasenajit heard what the Buddha had said, he gradually reduced his own food intake.
Eventually, at a later time, he ate only one *droṇa* of rice.
Even though he ate such a large amount, he was easily satisfied.
Some who choose their food are difficult to support, while others who choose their food are easy to support.
Those who choose their food and are difficult to support are those who require choice, fine food even though coarse food would suffice for their bodies.
Choosing food that is easy to digest means that coarse food cannot sustain the body; this refers to not selecting fine food.

Alternatively, there may be one who eats frequently but not much because of greed for flavor; or one who eats much and eats frequently without greed for flavor; or one who eats much and eats frequently out of greed for flavor; or one who does not eat much and does not eat frequently due to a lack of greed for flavor.
The first category refers to crows and the like;
the second category refers to elephants, horses, and the like;
the third category refers to wolves, dogs, raccoon-dogs, cats, and the like.
The fourth phrase refers to cases other than those mentioned above. Question:
What is the distinction here?
Answer: Their essential nature is itself differentiation.
As previously stated, those who are difficult to satisfy eat much, while those who are difficult to nourish are selective about their food.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "difficult to satisfy" refers to having many desires, while "difficult to support" refers to lacking contentment.
These two factors are both dharmas of the desire realm and both constitute the unwholesome root of greed; they pervade all six consciousnesses.
"Easy to satisfy and easy to support" refers to the opposite of what was stated above. Question:
What is the distinction between these?
Answer: The essential nature is itself the differentiation.
As stated previously, eating not much is what makes one easy to satisfy; not being selective about food is what makes one easy to nourish.
Furthermore, there are those who say that being easy to satisfy is "having few desires," and being easy to support is "knowing contentment.
These two dharmas both belong to the dharmas of the three realms; they are the root of goodness of non-greed. Because they are the opposites of greed, they pervade all six consciousnesses.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"There are four noble lineages," and so forth, as explained at length. Question:
For what reason did the World-Honored One preach this sutra?
The answer is:
he preached this sutra in order to bring an end to the four kinds of karmic activities.

Regarding the four types of occupations: some take agriculture as their occupation, some take trade as their occupation, some take service to the government as their occupation, and some take noble status as their occupation.
Regarding the "single occupation," it is the occupation of begging.
The World-Honored One preached this sutra in order to bring an end to the practice of four types of occupations and to establish the single occupation.

Furthermore, wishing to manifest what constitutes an occupation and what ought to be done, he stated: "An occupation consists of begging for robes, food and drink, bedding, and seating materials in order to sustain one's life."
That which ought to be done is this: one should delight in severing afflictions and delight in cultivating wholesome dharmas.
Such is that which ought to be done as inexhaustible karma, that which ought to be done as blameless karma, and that which ought to be done as non-harming karma toward others.
The same applies to the explanation regarding what is to be done through the karma of non-Buddhists.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest the Noble Path and the requisites for the Noble Path.
As for the Noble Path, it refers to those who delight in abandonment and delight in cultivation.
The requisites of the noble ones refer to such things as food, drink, clothing, and bedding.
The fruits of the śramaṇa, the equipment of the śramaṇa, the brāhmaṇa, and the equipment of the brāhmaṇa are also like this.
For these reasons, the Buddha taught this sutra.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)?
Answer: It is called the wholesome root of non-attachment because it is the antidote to attachment.
If taken as being associated with and co-existent [with the mind], its nature consists of the four aggregates or the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there are those who say that its nature is non-greed and diligence;
that the first three [factors] are non-greed, while delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation constitute diligence.
The critique states:
One should not speak in this way; it is better as previously stated.
Why is that? Because both delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation are also of the nature of non-attachment.
Question: If that is so, how can there be four? Answer:
There are four [noble lineages] because they are for the purpose of severing the arising of the four kinds of craving.

To sever the craving that arises regarding clothing, the noble lineage of contentment with clothing is taught; to [sever craving] regarding food, the noble lineage of contentment with food is taught; to [sever craving] regarding dwellings and bedding, the noble lineage of contentment with dwellings and bedding is taught; and to [sever craving] for the increase of existence, the noble lineage of contentment with the delight in renunciation and the delight in cultivation is taught. Therefore, the four noble lineages are taught for the purpose of stopping these four kinds of craving.
"This is the essential nature of the noble lineages," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained their essential nature and the reason for it, we shall now explain why they are called "noble lineages.
What constitutes "noble"?
It is called "noble" (ārya) because it is wholesome, and it is called "noble" because it is untainted (anāsrava).
Furthermore, some say it is called "noble" because noble persons practice this dharma.
Others say it is called "noble" because it can produce excellent and pleasing fruits; this explanation refers to the fruit of reliance (niṣyanda-phala).
Furthermore, there are those who explain it as the fruit of retribution: because it can produce excellent and pleasing fruits of retribution, it is called "holy" (*ārya*).
What is meant by "seed"?
It is so called because the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as well as the disciples of those Buddhas, were born from within this; therefore, it is named "seed."
Furthermore, there are those who say that they are called "seeds" because they enable the Buddha-dharma to endure for a long time.
Why is this? Because after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the fact that the path and dharma remain undestroyed for a thousand years is due to the power of these noble seeds.
Just as beams and rafters support a house so that it does not fall into ruin, so too is this [the nature of the seed].
Furthermore, there are those who say that the meaning of "continuity" (*saṃtati*) is the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*).
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the sense of making the Buddha-dharma continue without interruption is the meaning of "seed."
Because there are such noble ones and such lineages, they are called the "noble lineages" (āryavaṃśa). Regarding their realms:
those with outflows (sāsrava) are bound to the three realms, while those without outflows (anāsrava) are unbound.
Question: It may be that there are four kinds [of abodes] in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because of the presence of clothing, food and drink, and bedding and furniture.

But since there is no food or drink in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and neither clothing, food and drink, nor bedding and furniture in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how can there be four [abodes] there?
The answer is:
Although they do not possess such material things, they do possess such meritorious qualities.

Furthermore, some say that because they practiced the dharma of contentment regarding clothing, food and drink, and bedding and seating in this world, they continue to follow these practices even though they have been born in that realm.
The Venerable Sūmī said:
Although he lacks these factors, he possesses their antidotes.
There are many kinds of antidotes: the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇapratipakṣa*), the antidote of disadvantage (*ādhārapratipakṣa*), the antidote of maintenance (*dūrībhāvapratipakṣa*).

In the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there are these four kinds of antidotes (*pratipakṣa*); in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are two kinds, namely the antidote of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*) and the antidote of remoteness (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"There are no outflow-free (*anāsrava*) robes, food and drink, beds, or bedding, yet there are outflow-free noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)."
Although they lack clothing, food and drink, bedding, and seating, they possess the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
As for the stages (*bhūmi*): the contaminated (*sāsrava*) exist in eleven stages, while the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) exist in nine stages.
As for "basis," it is based on the bodies of the three realms; as for "initial," it is based on the desire realm.
As for "practice," one practices the sixteen aspects and also practices other aspects.
As for "object-condition," it takes all phenomena as its object.
Regarding "foundations of mindfulness," these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
Regarding "wisdom," it is associated with the ten knowledges.
Regarding "concentration," it is associated with the three concentrations.

As for the faculties (*indriya*), they are associated with three faculties, namely: the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
As for the time periods (*adhvan*), it exists within the three time periods.
As for the objects of cognition (*ālambana*), it takes the past, future, and present as its objects, and also takes non-temporal phenomena (*adhvavyatirikta-dharma*) as its objects.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object; the unwholesome and the indeterminate take all three types as their objects.
As previously stated, those bound to the three realms are the outflowing (sāsrava) phenomena, while the non-outflowing (anāsrava) are not bound to any realm.
Regarding those conditioned by the bonds of the three realms and those not so bound: they are conditioned by the bonds of the three realms and also conditioned by that which is not bound.

As for those that are *śaikṣa*, *aśaikṣa*, and neither-*śaikṣa*-nor-*aśaikṣa*: these are the three types; those conditioned by the *śaikṣa*, *aśaikṣa*, and neither-*śaikṣa*-nor-*aśaikṣa* all condition these three types.
Regarding those abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, and those not abandoned: these are abandoned by the path of cultivation and are not abandoned.
Regarding those that take as their object [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, and not abandoned: they take all three types as their objects.
Regarding those that take as their object the phenomena of one's own body, another's body, or the non-body: they take three kinds [of objects].
Regarding those that take names as their object and meanings as their object: they take names as their object and meanings as their object. Question:
Is this the mental ground (manobhūmi), or is it the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya)? Answer:
It is the mental ground, not the five groups of sensory consciousness.
Why is this so? Because the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) are dharmas acquired at birth.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is these five groups of consciousness.
Why is this so? Because all wholesome states of mind are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The critique says:
One should not speak in this way; it is better as previously stated.
Is this innate goodness (*upapattipratilambhika-kuśala*) or acquired goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*)?
The answer is:
This is the goodness of skillful means, not the goodness acquired at birth.
Why is this so? Because all goodness derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation is for the sake of liberation; therefore, it constitutes the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say it is innate wholesome [dharma].
The critique states:
one should not make such a statement.
Why is this so? Even down to an ant, if it possesses birth and attains goodness, can that be considered a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa)?
[The interlocutor] asks:

If these are skillful means (*upāya*), then are the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) of the non-Buddhists considered noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)?
He replied: "They are not."
Why is this? As previously stated, the virtues of hearing, reflection, and cultivation lead to liberation; therefore, they are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
Non-Buddhists lack contentment and seek only to increase existence (*bhava*) and the requisites for existence (*bhavopakaraṇa*); therefore, these are not the noble lineages.
Question: Are there not a few desires and contentment within all wholesome states of mind? Why is this so?
Because this refers to the wholesome roots of non-attachment toward desire.
Why, then, is contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) described as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), while having few desires (*alpecchatā*) is not?
The answer is:
Some may say that "few desires" is still a name for desire, and it is also a synonym for "having no desires.
If one speaks of "few desires" while there is still something desired, it cannot be called "having no desires."
Contentment means having no further desires and no other designations; therefore, it is called a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Furthermore, others say that "fewness of desires" refers to desiring little regarding what has not yet been obtained and desiring little regarding the future.
One who is content is content with what has already been obtained and content with the present.
If one can be content with even a small thing obtained in the present, that is exceedingly difficult.
It is not difficult for one who has few desires to remain so while not yet having attained the future status of a Universal Monarch (cakravartin).
However, because contentment is difficult to achieve, these are called the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
Furthermore, there are those who say that having few desires pertains to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while contentment pertains to all three realms.
Again, there are those who say that having few desires is bound to the three realms and not unbound, whereas contentment is both bound to the three realms and also unbound.
The commentary states:
One should not speak in this way.
These two dharmas are both bound to the three realms and are also unbound.
Question: If that is so, doubt arises once again.
Why is it said that contentment (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*), while having few desires (*alpecchatā*) is not?

Answer: It is because [the Buddha] wishes to distinguish [his teaching] from the knowledge of the non-Buddhists that he does not state that "fewness of desires" (alpecchatā) is a noble lineage (āryavaṃśa).
If he were to state that fewness of desires is a noble lineage, the various non-Buddhists would say this:
"We, too, are those who practice the noble lineages. Why is this?
You still wear rag-robes, whereas we do not wear robes at all."
"You still sustain yourselves by begging for alms, whereas we mostly do not eat;
you still sit beneath trees, whereas we sometimes stand with arms raised and feet upturned, never sitting upon beds or seats."
"Do we who practice this Dharma not possess the noble lineages?

Although non-Buddhist brahmins also practice this Dharma, they are never satisfied with existence and its requisites; therefore, because they differ from non-Buddhists, we do not say that 'fewness of desires' constitutes a noble lineage."
Question: For what reason are medicines prescribed according to specific ailments not mentioned among the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa)? Answer:
Some may say that this teaching is included within what has been stated above.
Why is this? Because there are two kinds of medicine according to the illness:
First, those that are edible;
second, those that are inedible.
Those that are edible are included within food and drink; those that are inedible are included within clothing, bedding, and furniture.
Furthermore, there are those who say that what is used by all people at all times is called a "noble lineage" (āryavaṃśa).
Medicine, however, which is administered according to the specific illness, is not used by all people at all times.
As the Venerable Bakula said:

"I have been ordained within the Buddha's Dharma for eighty years; I do not recall this body ever having been ill, even to the point of a headache, nor do I recall ever possessing medicine for an illness, even as much as a single harītakī fruit."
Thus, not all people in the desire realm maintain medicine for their illnesses at all times, much less those in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, if the enjoyment of this dharma leads to negligence, then the ability to relinquish it is called a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Because medicine administered according to the illness cannot cause one to become heedless, it is not called a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*). Question:
Why is the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) attainment of the precepts of liberation called a noble lineage, while the manifest (*vijñapti*) is not?

Answer: Some say that while the manifest action (*vijñapti*) perishes moment by moment, the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) is a continuous succession; this sense of non-interruption is the noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the unmanifest (avijñapti) is acquired simultaneously with the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga), whereas the manifest (vijñapti) is not;
therefore, the unmanifest is the noble lineage (āryavaṃśa). Laypeople possess the four noble lineages, and renunciants likewise possess the four.
Those who live as householders may have the aspiration in their hearts but are unable to act upon it.
I have heard that Śakra sits upon a throne of various flowers, attended by twelve billion celestial maidens and sixty thousand musicians who constantly perform music to entertain him.
Śakra, however, constantly maintains the aspiration for the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) but does not actually practice them.
A renunciant also possesses such an aspiration and likewise practices the noble lineages.
Yet, some renunciants may become unsatisfied with whatever robes, food, drink, and so forth they happen to obtain; this is the practice of the noble lineages.
I have heard that once there was a bhikṣu who, at sunset, went to where the Buddha was staying and requested a room from the Buddha in which to dwell.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Give this bhikṣu a dwelling."
Ānanda gave it to him.
At that time, the bhikṣu said to Ānanda:
"Venerable Sir!"

He purified this chamber, removing tiles, stones, refuse, and the like; he hung silk banners and streamers, scattered various kinds of flowers, burned exquisite incense, spread fine and soft bedding, and arranged comfortable pillows.
At that time, Ānanda went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters in detail.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"As that bhikṣu has said, prepare everything accordingly."
At that time, Ānanda prepared everything for him.

The bhikṣu then entered his room and sat upon his seat; during the first watch of the night, he gave rise to the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), followed by the remaining liberations in succession, exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*) and attaining the fruit of arhatship, while simultaneously manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
At dawn on that day, by means of his supernormal powers, he suddenly departed from that dwelling.
At that time, Ānanda went to that dwelling at dawn; he saw that the door was open, but the bhikṣu was not there.
He immediately went to inform the Buddha and related these matters in detail.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do not harbor any strange thoughts regarding this bhikṣu."

During the first watch of the night, that bhikṣu attained the pure liberation, and so on, until he cultivated and developed the supernormal powers; by means of these supernormal powers, he departed from that room.
Ānanda! That bhikṣu is by nature fond of what is fresh and fine; he has come from among the gods of the *svabhāva-manas* realm to be born here.
If you do not provide him with such fresh and fine dwellings, bedding, and requisites, that bhikṣu will be unable to attain the dharma of further progress.

In this way, although such a renunciant may not know contentment regarding robes, bedding, seats, and lying-down requisites, and may not use them according to what they have obtained, they are nonetheless able to practice the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa).
The Buddhas of the past all praised the rag-robe (pāṃśukūla) but did not permit its wearing; the present Buddha praises the rag-robe and permits its wearing. Question:
For what reason did the Buddhas of the past praise the rag-robe but not permit its wearing, whereas the present Buddha praises it and permits its wearing?

Answer: Some say that in ancient times, people were not characterized by greed or attachment; even if they possessed garments worth hundreds of thousands of taels of gold, their sense of cherishing and attachment was not as great as that of people today for even an ordinary garment.

Furthermore, there are those who say that in ancient times people possessed abundant wealth and many treasures; for them, seeking robes worth hundreds or thousands of taels of gold was not considered difficult.

In contrast, the people of the present day have meager wealth and few treasures; even seeking robes of discarded rags is still difficult to obtain, let alone robes valued at hundreds or thousands of taels of gold.

Furthermore, there are those who say that in ancient times people’s minds were fond of what was fresh and pure; they did not give rise to a sense of respect for coarse or inferior objects, and for this reason, [the Buddha] praised them but did not permit their use.

In this present age, the nature of people’s dispositions favors what is coarse and inferior; they are able to give rise to faith and respect toward those who utilize coarse and inferior things, and for this reason, [the Buddha] both praises and permits their use.

Furthermore, there are those who say that in ancient times the bodies of people were delicate and soft; if they were to use coarse or inferior objects, they would be unable to sustain themselves. For this reason, it was praised [to prohibit] their use.

In the present age, the bodies of people are coarse and robust; they can sustain themselves even with coarse and inferior requisites. For this reason, it is praised that their use [of such items] is permitted.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"Regarding the various objects of ancient times, if they are praised, their use is likewise permitted."
Why is this? Does the Buddha not praise the rag-robe (pāṃśukūla) for no reason—praising it as being light, easy to obtain, and blameless when sought?
The answer is: [No].

Some say that paṃsukūla robes are held in low esteem because few people wear them; they are held in low esteem because they are easy to obtain when sought after; and they are easy to obtain because they can be found everywhere.
Because it is permitted by the Buddha, there is no fault in seeking it.
Furthermore, because this action is itself faultless, there is no fault in seeking it.
Moreover, because it is practiced by the wise, there is no fault in seeking it.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
It is called "light and base" because it is of little value; it is "easily obtained" because it cannot be acquired from another; and there is no fault in seeking it because it is unproduced.
For two reasons, the Buddha spoke of these as the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) regarding contentment:
first, to sever the mind’s attachment to clothing, as in the case of Nanda and others;
second, to praise contentment with clothing, as in the case of Mahākāśyapa and others.
For two reasons, contentment with food is called a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to sever the mind of craving for food, as in the case of Bādarī and others;
second, to praise contentment with food, as in the case of Bakula and others.
For two reasons, one is said to have contentment regarding beds and seats as a noble lineage (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to sever the mind that clings to beds and seats, as in the case of the bhikṣu Mūḍharāja and others. As it is said, the bhikṣu Mūḍharāja addressed the Buddha:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will observe how coarse and wretched my bed and seat are."
The second is to praise contentment with one's seat and bedding, as in the case of Revata and others.
For two reasons, it is said that delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation are noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, to remove the pride and indolence of those such as Channa; and [second, to encourage those who are already diligent].
Second is the praise of those who practice diligence with vigor, such as Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa and others.
One should know that such persons abide in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) by virtue of four matters:
first, they do not delight in talk concerning the acquisition of gain and offerings.
2. Not delighting in associating with those who crave fine food;
3. Not using many articles of livelihood, and whatever one does use must be pure;
4. Regarding various gains and offerings, neither giving rise to hatred nor attachment whether they are obtained or not.
The Buddha’s sutras state that these four noble lineages are supreme, they are the true nature, they are delightful, and they are unmixed.
Within all the world—whether among śramaṇas or brahmins, or even among devas, Māras, or Brahmās—none can rightfully speak of their faults.
Question: In what sense is it "most excellent"? Answer:
Some may say that if one practices this dharma, one will fall among the most excellent of men.
As the Buddha said:
"Of my five hundred disciples, each has a most excellent quality."
If one knows contentment with the necessities of life, the Buddha also praises such a person as being most excellent.
Furthermore, Nirvana is the most excellent; because this Dharma can reach it, it is called "most excellent."
Furthermore, because one is able to know the most supreme Dharma, it is called the "most supreme Dharma.
What is this most supreme Dharma?
It refers to the Buddha or his disciples.
Who is able to know this Dharma?
It is those who practice the noble lineages and cultivate the noble path.
Furthermore, because this Dharma is the most supreme among all roots of goodness that satisfy the mind, it is called "supreme."
Why is this? Because most sentient beings die with their minds not satisfied.
Those who abide in the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) have their minds satisfied at the time of death.
The essence of this Dharma is supreme; it is called "supreme" because it can reach the supreme.
Furthermore, it is so called because it can eliminate the fault of accumulation. Why is this?
Those who are inferior accumulate much; those who are most excellent do not accumulate.
One who dwells in the noble lineages does not accumulate any of the necessities of life.
Even the wealth and treasures of a Wheel-Turning Sage King who rules over the four continents are easily exhausted.

Abiding in the karma of the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa), its application is inexhaustible because it can eliminate the accumulation of phenomena; its essence is supreme because it can reach the most excellent dharma of nirvāṇa, and is therefore called "supreme."
What is this lineage?
The answer is:

as previously stated, because all the Buddhas of the past, numbering as many as the sands of the Ganges River, as well as their disciples, were all born from this lineage, it is called the "ancient lineage."
Furthermore, because it causes the teachings of all Buddhas to perpetually continue without interruption, it is called the "spiritual lineage" (*gotra*).
Others say that because this dharma is able to know the spiritual lineage, it is therefore called the "spiritual lineage."
The Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, possesses the excellent lineage; since only this Dharma can know it, it is therefore called "lineage" (*gotra*).
Why is it called "delightful"?
The answer is:
All cessation-pleasure (*nirodha-sukha*) and cultivation-pleasure (*bhāvanā-sukha*) are joyful through this Dharma;
therefore, it is called "delightful" (*abhiramaṇīya*). Furthermore, this Dharma may also be said to be "knowable. Why is that?
One who practices this dharma can sequentially discern the divisions of the night; therefore, one assumes the full lotus posture at sunset and remains until sunrise before rising.
Furthermore, because this dharma enables one to know the delightful dharma, it is called "the delightful."
Furthermore, because one can enter the womb of the noble Dharma, it is called "most excellent";
because one enters the lineage of wholesome dharmas, it is called "lineage";
and because while abiding in wholesome dharmas one can perceive their flavor, it is called "delightful."
What is meant by "unmixed"?
The answer is:
because it is not mixed with the four kinds of occupations—namely, farming, trade, serving in government office, and noble pursuits. It is unmixed [with these].
Because this karma is purely virtuous and meritorious, it is called "unmixed.
Śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others cannot rightfully speak of its faults, for it is free from the affliction of being mixed with transgressions and does not oppress others.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that my noble disciples have minds free from hatred and attachment.
How are they free from hatred and attachment?"
"Love" refers to craving and aversion.
Because a noble disciple has subdued craving and aversion and is not overcome by them, he is said to be "without hatred or love.
This sutra also states:
There is the joy of abandonment and the joy of cultivation;
what is the difference between these two?
The answer is:
The path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) is the delight in abandonment, and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is the delight in cultivation.
Furthermore, the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is the delight in abandonment, and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) is the delight in cultivation.

As it is with the paths of seeing and cultivation, so it is for patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*); for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*), and the stages of seeing and cultivation—the explanation is likewise.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-two and Fascicle Twenty-three.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty. Chapter 8: The Section on Volition (Cetanā-varga), Part One. What is volition?
"What is mindfulness?
and so forth, as explained at length.
Regarding this chapter and the interpretation of its meaning, an *upadeśa* (expository treatise) should be provided here.
Question: For what purpose is this treatise composed? Answer:
The activities of these two dharmas are similar.
When people of the world see one who has much thought, they say that this person has much memory;
when people of the world see one who has much memory, they say that this person has much thought.
Now, because I wish to explain their essential nature as well as their distinctions,
some may say that these two dharmas are one. Why is this so?
The proponents of the science of phonology (*śabdavādin*) say:
"Thinking" (*cintā*) and "recollection" (*smṛti*) should be one and the same word; it is merely the addition of a long vowel marker (*dīrgha-bindu*) that constitutes the Indian system of writing.
To stop such an interpretation and to explain their distinction, [the author] says:
Furthermore, there are those who say that this is merely another name for the mind.
As the Dārṣṭāntikas say:
volition (*cetanā*) and memory (*smṛti*) are different names for the mind and possess no separate substance.

In order to refute the views of those who speak thus, and because he intends to explain that volition (*cetanā*) and memory (*smṛti*) are mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) each possessing a distinct essence, he composes this treatise.
What is volition (*cetanā*)?
The answer is:
volition is repeated volition, and so forth, as explained at length.
All such expressions as these are names for mental action (*manas-karman*). What is recollection (*smṛti*)?
The answer is:
it is repeated recollection, and so forth, as explained at length.
All such expressions as these are merely different names for wisdom (*prajñā*); what, then, is the distinction between [wisdom] and recollective thought (*smṛti*)?
Question: For what reason is this further discussion undertaken?
Answer: Since these two dharmas are similar, although their essential natures have been explained, their distinctions should also be explained.
What is the difference between volition (*cetanā*) and recollection (*smṛti*)?
Answer: As stated in the original sūtra, volition (*cetanā*) is karma and mindfulness (*smṛti*) is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, the characteristic of performing an action is volition, while the characteristic of knowing and understanding is mindfulness.

Furthermore, because volition (*cetanā*) is distinct from karma, and because mindfulness (*smṛti*) is distinct from wisdom (*prajñā*), there is a distinction between general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) regarding volition and mindfulness. This is what constitutes their differentiation. Question:
If mindfulness is wisdom, there are three types of wisdom, namely: that arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
What is the essential nature of these three?
The answer is:

That which arises from hearing is the wisdom of hearing; that which arises from reflection is the wisdom of reflection; and that which arises from cultivation is the wisdom of cultivation. Furthermore, there are those who say:

if one upholds, recites, contemplates, and examines the twelve divisions of the scriptures, this is the wisdom of hearing; based on this wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection subsequently arises; and based on this wisdom of reflection, the wisdom of cultivation subsequently arises.
"Just as gold is produced from gold ore and a diamond is produced from gold, so too is it in this case.
[The Master] critiques:
"One should not speak thus."
This explanation is excellent:

the upholding, reciting, and contemplative observation of the twelve divisions of the scriptures constitute innate wisdom (*upapatti-pratilambhikā prajñā*); based on innate wisdom, there arises wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī prajñā*); based on wisdom derived from hearing, there arises wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*); and based on wisdom derived from reflection, there arises wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī prajñā*).
Just as a sprout arises depending on a seed, and stems, leaves, and so forth arise depending on that sprout, so it is with this as well.
Question: What is the distinction between these three types of wisdom?
Answer: Wisdom derived from hearing always understands the meaning by relying on names. Why is this so?
The practitioner reflects thus:
"What is the meaning of what the preceptor has taught?
What is the meaning of what is taught in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma?"
This is called the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

As for the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), at times one understands the meaning by relying on the names, and at other times one understands the meaning without relying on the names.
As for the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), at all times one understands the meaning without relying on the names.
It is like three people bathing in a pool of water: the first cannot swim; the second can swim but not well; and the third can swim well.
The one who cannot swim must at all times grasp the grasses and trees along the bank of the pool before he may bathe.
One who can float but is not skilled may, at any time, either grasp the grasses and trees along the bank of the pond or bathe without grasping them.
One who is skilled at floating enters the water to bathe at all times without grasping any grasses or trees.

The wisdom derived from hearing is like the first person bathing; the wisdom derived from reflection is like the second person bathing; and the wisdom derived from cultivation is like the third person bathing.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the wisdom derived from hearing serves as the cause for the [other] three types of wisdom.
The wisdom of reflection serves as the cause for the wisdom of reflection, but it does not serve as the cause for the wisdom of hearing because it is inferior;
nor does it serve as the cause for the wisdom of cultivation because their realms are different.
Cultivated wisdom acts as a cause for cultivated wisdom, but it does not act as a cause for wisdom derived from hearing, because the latter is inferior;
nor does it act as a cause for wisdom derived from reflection, because their respective realms are distinct.

Furthermore, some say that the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) has three types of fruits; the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) has only the fruit of the wisdom of reflection; and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) has only the fruit of the wisdom of cultivation.

Others further say that when the wisdom of hearing is present, it is cultivated only as the wisdom of hearing; when the wisdom of reflection is present, it is cultivated only as the wisdom of reflection.
This cultivation is cultivation by practice (*pratipatti-bhāvanā*), not cultivation by acquisition (*pratilambha-bhāvanā*), because its nature is inferior and does not extend to the future.
When the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) is present before one, all three types of wisdom are cultivated together.
These are the essential natures of the three wisdoms, and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the essential nature [of these practices], we shall now explain why they are called "hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The answer is:
they are called "hearing" because they arise from hearing; they are called "reflection" because they arise from reflection; and they are called "cultivation" because they arise from cultivation.

Regarding the realms: the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) resides in the desire realm; and the wisdom derived from cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*) resides in the form realm and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Question:
Why is there no wisdom derived from cultivation within the desire realm?
Answer: The desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is neither the stage of detachment from desire nor the stage of cultivation.
If one wishes to cultivate [the path] therein, one immediately falls into the sphere of discursive thought.
Why is there no wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*)?
The answer is:

The realm of form is a stage of meditative concentration (*samāhitabhūmi*), a stage of cultivation (*bhāvanābhūmi*), and a stage of freedom from desire (*vairāgyabhūmi*); when one reflects with desire, one immediately falls back into the midst of cultivation.
Furthermore, there are those who say that all three types of wisdom exist within the desire realm.
Question: Which of these is the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā)?

Answer: It refers to the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna) associated with the path of seeing, the samādhi of emptiness-of-emptiness, the samādhi of wishlessness-of-wishlessness, the samādhi of signlessness-of-signlessness, and all the roots of goodness existing at the limit of the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna). Because these are few, they are not mentioned.
The realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) is of two kinds, namely: hearing (*śruta*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is of one kind, namely: cultivation.
