Having observed both the mind and the afflictions, one teaches the remedial methods according to those afflictions.
One must not teach only a small portion; for if one teaches only a small portion, one will be unable to eliminate the disease of the afflictions.
Nor do I speak of many; for if I were to speak of many, it would be a useless teaching from the Tathāgata.
It is like a physician treating a disease: he first examines the illness and its causes, and only then administers the corresponding medicine.
Nor should one administer too little; if one administers too little, the illness will not be cured.
Nor should one administer too much; if one administers too much, its efficacy will be wasted. One must administer the medicine according to what is appropriate for each case;
it is the same with that [the Buddha's teaching].
Furthermore, to speak briefly, one who has severed the three fetters is called a *srotāpanna*;
to speak extensively, one who has severed the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) and immeasurable sufferings is called a *srotāpanna*.
As it is with the brief and detailed explanations, so it is with non-discriminative and discriminative teachings, as well as simultaneous and sequential teachings.

Furthermore, for those of sharp faculties, it is taught that one who has severed the three fetters is called a *srotāpanna*; for those of dull faculties, it is taught that one who has severed eighty-eight fetters and immeasurable sufferings is called a *srotāpanna*.

Just as there are those of sharp faculties and dull faculties, the power of causes and the power of conditions, internal power and external power, the power of internal reflection and the power of external instruction, and quick wisdom and slow wisdom—the same applies to their explanations.
Furthermore, in order to explain the method of easy practice to entice and advance those who are to be transformed— just as one leads another by the hand to make them rise—
one should here relate the parable of the son of the Vṛjis.

I have heard that there was once a son of the Vṛjis who went forth into the Buddha’s Dharma; at that time, the two hundred and fifty precepts had already been established, and noble sons were permitted to practice them according to their own inclination.
Having heard this, that person felt anxiety and concern, thinking:
"Who can guard such precepts?
He then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha's feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The World-Honored One has established two hundred and fifty precepts, intended for sons of noble family to practice according to their inclination.
I am now unable to guard these precepts.
At that time, the World-Honored One displayed a friendly countenance and did not rebuke him, but comforted and exhorted him with gentle and pleasant words:
"Excellent, excellent,
son of the Vṛjis!"
"Are you able to train well in the three trainings?
That is to say, training well in ethical discipline, training well in the mind, and training well in wisdom.
Having heard this, that person gave rise to great joy and spoke these words:
"I am able to skillfully train in these three kinds of precepts.
By training in these three kinds of precepts, I can gradually train in all precepts.

If the Tathāgata were to say that one who has severed the eighty-eight afflictions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing, as well as immeasurable sufferings, is called a *srotāpanna*, then those receiving instruction would feel anxiety in their hearts."

How can one uproot these eighty-eight trees of affliction, cross over the great rivers of the eighty-eight afflictions, dry up the great oceans of the eighty-eight afflictions, shatter the mountains of the eighty-eight afflictions, and cultivate this path of the eighty-eight remedies?
If the Buddha says that severing the three fetters is called becoming a *srotāpanna*, those who receive his transformation will give rise to great joy, thinking:
"If one severs the three fetters, then this is an easy matter.
If one severs the three fetters, then one severs all the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Why is this? Because they are equally abandoned through their respective antidotes.
For this reason, the Dharma of Easy Practice is taught, as explained in detail above.
Furthermore, because he wishes to explain the most preeminent dharmas,
among all the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the path of vision (darśanamārga), these three fetters are the most preeminent.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke as follows:
These three fetters are the most preeminent among all afflictions abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*);
the others arise following them, just as craving, aversion, pride, and so forth arise based on views.

Furthermore, these three fetters are the leaders of all afflictions abandoned by the path of vision; they are like a victorious army that always marches at the front, and it is by their power that the remaining afflictions arise.
Furthermore, these three fetters are enemies of merit.
By "merit" is meant the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
Who, then, are their enemies?
This refers to the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, these three fetters are the proximate antidotes to the three samādhis:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the proximate antidote to the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*); attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is the proximate antidote to the wishlessness samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*); and doubt (*vicikitsā*) is the proximate antidote to the signlessness samādhi (*animitta-samādhi*).
Furthermore, because these three fetters are closely associated with those on the path of seeing and are frequently active, as stated in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*:
"When the practitioner abides in patience (*kṣānti*), view and doubt do not function."
Even if there are those who practice, they likewise do not perceive it, because their wisdom is inferior and their afflictions are subtle.
"Views" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the grasping of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); "doubt" (*vicikitsā*) refers to doubt itself.
Furthermore, these three fetters are difficult to sever, difficult to shatter, and difficult to transcend.
Furthermore, these three fetters possess the faults of intensification, heaviness, and manifold excesses.
What is the fault of intensification regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
The answer is:

The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is the root of the sixty-two views; views are the root of all afflictions (kleśa); afflictions are the root of karma; and karma is the root of retribution (vipāka). Based on retribution, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena arise.
What is the fault of the excessive proliferation of attachment to precepts?
The answer is:
from attachment to precepts arise various forms of false asceticism.
What fault does doubt intensify?
The answer is:
One who doubts harbors hesitation within regarding the past and future lives.
What is this? How does this exist? Who created this?
How is this to be understood?
From where do these sentient beings come?
Upon death, where do they go?
Furthermore, although these three fetters have been abandoned and known, an Arhat still engages in conduct that resembles [the behavior of an ordinary person].

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which is permanently abandoned through the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvayajñānakṣānti*), although it has been abandoned and known, the Arhat still engages in conduct that resembles [that view], making such statements as:

"This is my robe, this is my bowl; this is my fellow resident disciple, this is my attendant disciple; this is my cell, and these are the requisites within my cell. This is similar to calculating a self.

Regarding the clinging to precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*), although it is eternally severed by the patience of conformity to the Path (*mārgānvaya-kṣānti*) and has been both abandoned and known, an Arhat still practices a semblance of such dharmas.

For example, he may wash his hands and feet, dwell in an araṇya, maintain only the three robes, and so forth—extensively practicing the thirteen qualities of purity—and thereby conceive the notion of ultimate purity.
I have heard that although the Venerable Lomasaṅgiya was an Arhat, he nevertheless went daily to the water to bathe, regarding it as a form of purification. I wonder:
since the path of patience has permanently severed [defilements], and though they are severed and known, why does an Arhat still perform such similar practices?
Seeing an object at a distance, one doubts whether it is a person or a tree stump;
seeing two paths, one doubts whether it is the path one intends to take or not the path one intends to take.
Seeing two robes and two alms bowls, he doubts whether they are his own robes and bowls or not his own.
Furthermore, for the sake of severing the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*), the practitioner causes all fetters to be severed that are abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Furthermore, in order to sever the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), the practitioner also perceives and cognizes the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Moreover, these three fetters pertain to all three realms and are also among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*).
Although sensual desire and ill-will are factors of the lower realm (*avarabhāgīya*), they do not extend throughout the three realms.
Although false views regarding extremes, wrong views, the esteeming of views, craving, pride, and ignorance extend throughout the three realms, they are not factors of the lower realm.

Furthermore, regarding the permanent and complete abandonment of the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), it is explained therein that a *srotāpanna* permanently abandons two of these seven underlying tendencies:
namely, the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*) and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*).
Furthermore, regarding the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are abandoned without remainder; this is explained at length.

Among the nine fetters, the *srotāpanna* has permanently abandoned three fetters, namely: the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of attachment (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated as follows:
"This sutra should be stated thus:
'By severing the three fetters, one attains the stage of Srotāpanna.'"
The three fetters are the fetter of views, the fetter of doubt, and the fetter of grasping.
Furthermore, regarding the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), those that are abandoned without remainder, and so forth, as explained at length.
The ten fetters (*saṃyojana*) refer to the five views,
craving, aversion, pride, ignorance, and doubt.
A *srotāpanna* has eternally severed six fetters, namely the five views and doubt.

Among the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), only three are mentioned: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), adherence to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The other three—namely, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), and adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)—are not mentioned.
Why is this so? Because this arises from that. The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) gives rise to the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi), and the view of extremes arises from the view of a self.
The grasping of precepts gives rise to the grasping of views; the grasping of views arises from the grasping of precepts.
Doubt gives rise to false views; false views arise from the view of a self-identity.
The grasping of precepts gives rise to the grasping of views; the grasping of views arises from the grasping of precepts.
Doubt gives rise to wrong view; wrong view arises from doubt.
Having explained that which can produce [wrong view], one should know that this also explains that from which it arises.
Furthermore, this is the manifestation of the initial gateway, the manifestation of the brief exposition, and the manifestation of the initial entry.
These fetters to be abandoned by the path of vision are either abandoned in one way, two ways, or four ways.
If one speaks of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it should be understood that this already refers to those abandoned in one way.
If one speaks of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that two kinds of abandonment have already been explained.

Although there are no further two kinds [of abandonment], the term "two kinds" refers to attachment to precepts and rituals itself; furthermore, the factors associated with and co-arising alongside attachment to precepts and rituals are also called "two kinds."
If one speaks of doubt, it should be understood that the four types of abandonment have already been explained.
Furthermore, the fetters abandoned by the path of seeing are either universal within their own realm or universal within other realms.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), it should be known that this already includes all pervasive factors of its own realm.
If one speaks of attachment to precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa) or doubt (vicikitsā), it should be known that this already includes all pervasive factors of other realms.

Question: For what reason is everything-pervading within one's own realm (*svadhātu*) described as a single fetter (*saṃyojana*), while everything-pervading in another realm (*paradhātu*) is described as two fetters? Answer:
Because those [defilements] with other realms as their object take both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as objects:

if one speaks of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that this already includes the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have the contaminated as their object;
if one speaks of doubt (*vicikitsā*), it should be understood that this already includes the proclivities that have the uncontaminated as their object.

Just as with universal [factors] within one's own realm and universal [factors] within other realms, universal [factors] of one's own stage and universal [factors] of other stages, so too should one understand those conditioned by one's own realm and conditioned by other realms, and those conditioned by one's own stage and conditioned by other stages.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing, some have outflowing objects (*sāsravālambana*) and some have non-outflowing objects (*anāsravālambana*).

If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that this already includes the proclivities (*anuśaya*) with outflowing objects.
If one speaks of doubt (*vicikitsā*), it should be understood that this already includes the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. Question:
Why are two [proclivities] said to have tainted objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and one said to have an untainted object?
Answer: Those with outflows that take objects consist of either taking objects within one's own realm or taking objects in another realm.
If one speaks of the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), it should be understood that this already includes those taking objects within one's own realm.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that this already includes those conditioned by other realms.

Just as with the distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), so too should one understand the distinctions between the mundane (*laukika*) and the supramundane (*lokottara*), the flavorful (*āsvāda*) and the flavorless (*anāsvāda*), the abiding (*sthiti*) and the emerging (*niḥsaraṇa*), the fettered (*saṃyojana*) and the unfettered (*asaṃyojana*), the bound (*bandhana*) and the unbound (*abandhana*), the grasping (*upādāna*) and the non-grasping (*anupādāna*), and the entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and the non-entanglements (*aparyavasthāna*). It should be known that these are all likewise.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), some have conditioned objects (*saṃskṛta-ālambana*) and some have unconditioned objects (*asaṃskṛta-ālambana*).
If one mentions the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that this already includes those with conditioned objects.
If one speaks of doubt, it should be understood that this already includes the unconditioned as an object.
Just as there are conditioned objects and unconditioned objects, so too should it be understood for permanent objects and impermanent objects, and for eternal objects and non-eternal objects.
Furthermore, among the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing, some are of the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi*) and some are not of the nature of view.

If one mentions the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), it should be understood that those which are of the nature of view have already been mentioned.
If one speaks of doubt, it should be understood that this already includes those things which are not of the nature of view (*dṛṣṭi*).

Just as with what is of the nature of view and what is not of the nature of view, so too should one understand the cases of seeing and not seeing, engaging and not engaging, seeking and not seeking, and turning the mind and not turning the mind.
Furthermore, the fetters abandoned through the path of seeing are either unwholesome or indeterminate.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and rituals and doubt, it should be understood that the unwholesome ones have already been explained.
If one speaks of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), it should be understood that this already includes what is indeterminate (avyākṛta).

Just as with the unwholesome and the indeterminate, so too should one understand the cases of those with retribution and those without retribution; those that produce one fruit or two fruits; those associated with shamelessness (āhrīkya) and lack of dread (anapatrāpya), and those dissociated from shamelessness and lack of dread. It should be known that they are likewise.
Furthermore, there are two types of fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing: those that are by nature elated and those that are by nature dejected.
If one speaks of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it should be understood that this already includes those that are elated.
If one speaks of the clinging to precepts and rituals and doubt, it should be understood that this already includes grief.
Furthermore, these three fetters destroy three kinds of bodies:
the view of a self-body destroys the body of morality; the clinging to precepts and rituals destroys the body of concentration; and doubt destroys the body of wisdom.
Furthermore, these three fetters can destroy the Eightfold Noble Path:

the view of a self-body destroys right speech, right action, and right livelihood; attachment to precepts and rituals destroys right mindfulness and right concentration; and doubt destroys right view, right awakening, and right effort.
Furthermore, it is in order to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
People of the world are for the most part deeply attached to the self and what belongs to the self, deeply attached to the auspicious and the inauspicious, and harbor deep-seated hesitation.
The Buddha said:
"If sentient beings practice such dharmas, they are not called srotāpannas;
if they do not practice such dharmas, they are called srotāpannas."
Question: Is one called a *srotāpanna* upon attaining the first path, or is one called a *srotāpanna* upon attaining the first fruit?
If one is called a *srotāpanna* upon attaining the first path, then the "eighth person" (*aṣṭamaka*) should be a *srotāpanna*.
The eighth person is called one of firm faith and firm dharma. Why is this?
Because they have attained the initial path.

If one who has attained the first fruit is called a *srotāpanna*, then at the moment one attains the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path of right determination—whether by abandoning a great portion of desire or by abandoning all desire of the desire realm—one should also be a *srotāpanna*.
Why is this? Because it is the first attainment of the fruit.
He replied:
Some say that one is called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) because they have first attained the Path.
A question is asked:
If that were so, then the "eighth person" (*aṣṭamaka*) should also be a *srotāpanna*.
Why is this? Because it is the first attainment of the Way.
He replied:
One is called a *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer) because they have first attained the Path; one who has attained that Path and necessarily takes the Path as its object is a *srotāpanna*.
Although the eighth person (*aṣṭamaka*) has also first attained the Path, they are not called a *srotāpanna* because they take suffering (*duḥkha*) as their object.

Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because of first attaining the Path; that Path must be a path comprised within the fruit of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and such is the *srotāpanna*.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because of first attaining the Path; that Path must possess three characteristics:
first, the attainment of a path never before attained.
Second, abandoning the path already attained;
third, severing the fetters into a single flavor.
That which is called "attaining the path not previously attained" refers to the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
"Abandoning what was previously attained" refers to the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
"Severing the fetters in a single flavor" means that the fetters to be abandoned by the Path of Vision are all realized as being of one and the same flavor.
Furthermore, because one first attains the Path, one is called a *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterer); that Path necessarily possesses five factors:
First, attaining the path never before attained;
second, relinquishing the path already attained;
third, severing the fetters through realization of a single flavor.
Fourth, one simultaneously attains the eight knowledges;
fifth, one fully cultivates the sixteen aspects.

Furthermore, because one first attains the Path, one is called a *srotāpanna*. While abiding in that Path, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of the Path are forever exhausted without remainder: the fetters consisting of inverted views regarding objects are forever severed; the fetters countered by patience (*kṣānti*) are forever severed; and false views are forever severed.

Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the Path; while abiding in that Path, such a person can engage in conversation and can be designated as having specific characteristics.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the Path; while abiding in that Path, there may still be birth and death.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one is called a *srotāpanna* because of first attaining the fruit.
A question is raised:

If that were so, then at the moment when one has abandoned the majority of desire, exhausted the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the path of right determination (*samyaktva-niyama*), one should be a *srotāpanna*.
Why is this? Because it is the first attainment of the fruit.
He replied:

One is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the fruit; this refers specifically to one who follows the gradual sequence and is still bound by all fetters, rather than one who has attained through the leap-over method (*vyutkrāntaka*).

Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the Path; that is, one who has first attained liberation, first attained crossing over, and is a person who has attained the first fruit.

Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) because they have first attained the fruit; it must not be that one attains the fruit by severing even a single type of fetter through the mundane path.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the fruit; this is the very first of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the fruit; this refers specifically to one who possesses all four stages of the path and four fruits.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* because they have first attained the fruit; this refers to one among the eight types of persons and the four pairs.
Furthermore, one is called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) because they have first attained the fruit; while abiding in that path, they neither abandon the stage nor abandon the path.
Although the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* does not involve abandoning the stage, it does involve abandoning the path.
Why is this so? Because both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) paths are capable of attaining it.

The fruit of *anāgāmin* also involves the destruction of both stages (*bhūmi*) and paths; as for the destruction of stages, it is attained by relying on six stages; as for the destruction of paths, it is because both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths are capable of attaining it.
Although the fruit of arhatship does not destroy the path, it does destroy the stages (bhūmi). Why is this?
Because it is attained by relying upon nine stages.

The stage of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) is also indestructible, and the path is also indestructible. That which is the indestructible stage is attained by relying on the *anāgamya* stage; that which is the indestructible path is attained solely by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), not by means of the tainted path (*sāsravamārga*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that one is not called a *srotāpanna* because of first attaining the Path, nor is one called a *srotāpanna* because of first attaining the fruit; rather, it is because of the fruit of *srotāpatti* itself that such a person is named a *srotāpanna*.
A name is derived from its substance, just as medicinal water is named after the medicine it contains; the same applies to a jar of ghee or a jar of oil.
Question: For what reason is one called a *srotāpanna*?
Answer: "Srotas" means the stream of the noble path, and "āpanna" means to enter; because one enters the stream of the noble path, one is called a srotāpanna. Question:
If this were so, then the Sakṛdāgāmin, the Anāgāmin, and the Arhat would also be called Srotāpanna. Why is this?
Because they too have entered the stream of the Noble Path.
Answer: This is called the "first attainment" because it is the first time one attains the Path;
as for the names of the other fruits, each has its own specific meaning.
"Not falling into the evil destinies" means not falling into the three evil destinies. Question:
Since the Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat likewise do not fall into the evil destinies, why is it said specifically that only the Srotāpanna does not fall into the evil destinies?
Answer: When one should speak but does not, it should be known that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvasesa*).
Furthermore, each fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) has its own specific meaning.
Just as the *srotāpanna* is said to "not fall into the evil destinies" because of the excellence of not falling into the evil destinies,
and the *sakṛdāgāmin* is named "one who comes back once" because of the excellence of coming back once.
The Anāgāmin is called "Non-returner" because they have excelled in not returning to the desire realm;
the Arhat is called "One who no longer undergoes existence" because they have excelled in not undergoing further existence.
Because each of the fruits of śrāmaṇya has its own specific meaning, they are designated according to that meaning. Question:
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) also exist who do not fall into the evil destinies; why are they not mentioned?
Answer: When that which ought to be said is not said, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, it is not mentioned because ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) may either fall into the evil destinies (*apāya*) or not fall into the evil destinies.
The Noble One certainly does not fall into the evil destinies; therefore, this is said.
As for "certainty" (*niyata*), it is called certainty because one dwells in the group of those destined for right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Regarding the meaning of *srotāpanna*, one should say they are "certainly destined for parinirvāṇa."
Why is this? Because there are the causes and conditions for parinirvāṇa.
It is like a fragile earthen vessel thrown from atop a three-story house onto the ground; before it even reaches the earth, one can say with certainty that it will break.
It is the same in this case as well.
For one who has entered the path of ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā-mārga*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) are termed the "path.

Such a person possesses such desire, such resolve, such approval, such delight, and such intention; because they are closely approaching and turning toward that path, it is said that they have "entered the path of ultimate attainment."
Regarding the statement "only seven existences are to be experienced":
a questioner asks,
"Should it not be that fourteen existences, or even twenty-eight existences, are to be experienced?"
If one speaks in terms of the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*) alone, there are seven for humans and seven for devas, which would amount to fourteen.

If one speaks in terms of both the prior existence and the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), there are seven prior existences and seven intermediate existences for devas, and seven prior existences and seven intermediate existences for humans; thus, there should be twenty-eight.
Why are only seven existences (bhava) mentioned?
The answer is:
this is a numerical category of seven; it does not exceed seven.
There are seven [turns] among humans, seven in the heavens, seven in the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*), and seven in the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Other sūtras also state:
"The four truths are proclaimed three times, making twelve aspects; since there are twelve aspects for each truth, there should be forty-eight aspects for the four truths."

If one were to state that there are twelve aspects for each of the three expositions of the Truth of Suffering, and likewise twelve aspects for each of the three expositions up to the Truth of the Path, there would necessarily be forty-eight aspects.
Why, then, is it said that there are only twelve aspects?
This constitutes the twelvefold enumeration of dharmas, as it does not depart from the three turnings and twelve aspects.
Other sūtras also state:
"A bhikṣu who is skilled in the seven points and possesses the threefold contemplation can swiftly exhaust all outflows within the noble Dharma."
It should not be only seven; there should be thirty-five bases of wholesome skill or immeasurable bases of wholesome skill.
Why, then, are only seven bases of wholesome skill mentioned?
The answer is:
This is the method of the sevenfold enumeration, which does not depart from the sevenfold contemplation.
This is because the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) has seven aspects, and so on up to the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha), which likewise has seven aspects.
Other sūtras also state:
“Monks! I shall now speak of two things.
What are these two things?”
The eye and forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena—these are called "two dharmas.
These are not one or two [in the sense of being singular];
rather, they should be six pairs; however, because they are dharmas numbered as twos, they do not depart from duality.
These seven numerical dharmas are not separate from the number seven, and it is likewise as explained in detail above. Question:
For what reason does the srotāpanna undergo exactly seven existences, neither more nor less?
The Venerable Paśya said:
"Whether one increases or decreases regarding the experience of existence, one will in all cases give rise to doubt.
Yet, because of this doubt, one does not contravene the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa)."
Furthermore, there are as many causes for retribution as there are, and one consequently experiences as many fruits of retribution.
Moreover, by the power of karma, one undergoes only seven existences; by the power of the Path, one does not undergo an eighth existence.
It is like a person bitten by a seven-step snake: by the power of his four great strengths he can walk seven steps, but by the power of the venom he does not reach an eighth step.
Furthermore, if one were to undergo an eighth existence, that body would necessarily be devoid of the Noble Path.
If emptiness were devoid of the Noble Path, then what was previously the vision of the Truths would no longer be the vision of the Truths;
what was originally the attainment of right certainty would no longer be the attainment of right certainty;
and what was originally a noble person would no longer be a noble person.
Furthermore, if one were to undergo an eighth existence, then the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, would become outsiders rather than internal kin.
It is just as among worldly people who are related through seven generations; if the eighth generation arrives, they are treated as outsiders.
It is the same in that case.

Furthermore, when abiding in the stage of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), with the exception of the seven rebirths in the desire realm and the rebirths in each individual location of the form and formless realms, all other rebirths attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
If a phenomenon is attained through analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it will never again arise or manifest.
Furthermore, because there are only seven places of rebirth, one undergoes only seven existences.
Regarding the seven places of birth: these refer to humans and the six heavens of the desire realm, which are the birthplaces of a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), and he is born therein.

Furthermore, within those seven existences (*bhava*), he fully cultivates the sevenfold path and permanently eradicates the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Due to these factors, he undergoes only seven more existences, neither more nor less.

Thus, regarding those *srotāpannas* who undergo seven existences—seven existences in the heavens and seven existences among humans—there are nevertheless distinctions among these *srotāpannas*. Some have seven existences in the heavens and six among humans; some have six in the heavens and five among humans; some have five in the heavens and four among humans; some have four in the heavens and three among humans; some have three in the heavens and two among humans; some have two in the heavens and one among humans. Or, there are those with seven existences among humans and six [in the heavens], down to two among humans and one in the heavens; the explanation is likewise for these cases.
Since this passage speaks only of those who possess seven existences, it says that a *srotāpanna* undergoes seven existences. Question:
Does a *srotāpanna* who fully undergoes seven existences experience the seventh existence in the heavens or among humans?
Answer: Some say that one who attains the stage of *srotāpanna* within this very life counts that very life as one of the seven.

Others say that it is not included in the count of seven; rather, according to that calculation, one attains the Path among humans, completes the seven [lifetimes] in the heavens, and attains parinirvāṇa there.
If one attains the fruit in the heavens, one will fulfill seven more existences among humans and then attain parinirvāṇa.
If this is not counted, having attained the fruit among humans, one will again fulfill seven existences among humans and then attain parinirvāṇa.
Having attained the fruit within the heavens, one completes seven more existences within those very heavens and then attains parinirvāṇa.
The critique states:
the initial birth upon attaining the Path should not be counted among the seven existences.
Why is this so? Because at the time of that birth-existence (upapattibhava), one is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) and not a noble one (ārya).
If one were to count them, there would be only twenty-seven existences, not twenty-eight.
If there were only twenty-seven existences, it would contradict the *Prajñapti-śāstra*,
which states:
"The Srotāpanna will necessarily reach the end of suffering after twenty-eight births."
In order to avoid such an error, it is not said that one who has first attained the Path is born within the seven existences (*bhava*). Question:
Does a *srotāpanna* who is to undergo seven existences bring the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) into manifestation during the first six births?
Answer: Some say that it does not arise.
If it were to arise, one would enter parinirvāṇa.
Some say that [the afflictions] arise and manifest before one. Question:
If this is so, why does one not enter parinirvāṇa?
Answer: Because of the power of karma, they do not enter parinirvāṇa. Question:
If one has fulfilled the seventh [stage] at a time when there is no Buddha in the world, can one attain arhatship while remaining a householder?
The answer is: some say that one cannot.
Although the Buddha-dharma does not exist, one must nonetheless leave the household life and receive the dharma-robes among other teachings before one can attain it.
Some, however, say that it may also be attained while remaining at home.
Having attained this, they did not remain at home, but instead went forth in other teachings and received their religious robes.
In this manner, there were five hundred pratyekabuddhas dwelling in the Mountain of the Rishis, who were originally śrāvakas.
Regarding those who move between the heavens and the human realm: it is as if a deity comes among humans, or a human dwells among the deities;
just as people of the world go from a forest to a garden, or from a garden to a forest, so too is it with them.
"Those who are born" refers to those born within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*).
Regarding "those who have attained the end of suffering," a question is asked:
Does the limit of suffering exist within suffering or outside of suffering?
If it were within suffering, one could not call it the "limit" of suffering.
If it were outside of suffering, how would you account for the worldly analogies currently in use?
It is just like a golden tally: it is gold at the beginning, gold in the middle, and gold at the end.
Suffering is also like this: it is suffering at the beginning, suffering in the middle, and suffering at the end.
What is the limit of suffering?
The answer is:
some say that the final aggregates of an Arhat constitute the limit of suffering.
Some may say that the cessation of extinction (*nirodha-nirvāṇa*) is the limit of suffering (*duḥkhānta*).
If one were to say that the final aggregates (*skandha*) of an Arhat are the limit of suffering, one should not speak of them as the "limit of suffering."
Why is this so? Because its very substance is entirely suffering.
He replied:
For this reason, it should be called the "limit of suffering.

Why is that? Because suffering will no longer arise, it will no longer continue in succession with further suffering, and one will no longer create the causes of suffering; therefore, it is called the limit of suffering.
If it is asserted that the cessation of extinction (*nirodha-nirvāṇa*) is the limit of suffering (*duḥkhānta*), how is the worldly metaphor of the golden tally (*suvarṇagaṇḍikā*) to be reconciled?
The answer is:
This need not necessarily be reconciled. Why is this so?
Because these are not Sūtra, Vinaya, or Abhidharma; one cannot use worldly, manifest analogies to challenge the Dharma of the Noble Ones.
Why is this so? Because the dharmas of the noble ones are distinct from the dharmas of the world.
There are three unwholesome roots:
The unwholesome root of greed, the unwholesome root of hatred, and the unwholesome root of delusion.
Question: What is the essential nature of these three unwholesome roots?
Answer: There are fifteen kinds.
The unwholesome root of greed is the craving abandoned by the five types of cultivation in the desire realm; it pervades the six bodies of consciousness.
The unwholesome root of hatred (*dveṣa-akuśalamūla*) is that hatred which is abandoned by the five [categories of] cultivation; it pervades the six groups of consciousness.
The unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*) is the ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned by all four [categories of] abandonment throughout the entire desire realm.
The four types refer to the truths of origination, cessation, the path, and the cultivation of the path.
Regarding the seeds to be abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), they should be analyzed as follows:

there are ten kinds of ignorance (*avidyā*) abandoned by the truth of suffering, namely those associated with the five views, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*), as well as the eight unshared [ignorances]; these constitute the unwholesome roots (*akuśala-mūla*).

The second [category] consists of those that are not unwholesome roots, namely: those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm. Question:
"Root" has the meaning of "cause."

The ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the cause of all unwholesome phenomena; why then is it not designated as a faculty (*indriya*)?
The answer is:
if a phenomenon is unwholesome in its essential nature and serves as the cause for all unwholesome phenomena, it is established as a faculty.

Although the ignorance associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is the cause of all unwholesome states, its essence is not unwholesome because it is neutral (*avyākṛta*). Therefore, the unwholesome root of delusion (*moha-akuśalamūla*) consists entirely of the four types found in the desire realm—namely, those abandoned through the paths of seeing the origin, cessation, and the path, as well as the path of cultivation—and the eight types abandoned through the path of seeing the truth of suffering; these pertain to the ignorance associated with all six groups of consciousness.
These fifteen types constitute the essence of the three unwholesome roots, and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the nature of their essence, we shall now explain why they are called "unwholesome roots" (*akuśalamūla*).
What is the meaning of "unwholesome root" (*akuśalamūla*)?
The answer is:
the sense of producing, the sense of nourishing, and the sense of increasing—this is the meaning of an unwholesome root.

The meaning of sufficiency, the meaning of benefit, the meaning of flourishing, and the meaning of the outpouring of the unwholesome—these constitute the meaning of the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
The Venerable Sūmīta said:
What is the meaning of the unwholesome roots?
He replied:
"The meaning of being an unwholesome cause is the meaning of an unwholesome root.
Furthermore, the meaning of being an unwholesome seed is the meaning of an unwholesome root."
Furthermore, the meaning of initiating what is unwholesome is the meaning of an unwholesome root.

Furthermore, the meaning of that which has already arisen as unwholesome, that which assists in the arising of the unwholesome, and that which increases the unwholesome is the meaning of an unwholesome root.
The Venerable Buddhatīva said:

"The meaning of 'unwholesome root' is that which is the primary source of the unwholesome, that which can produce the unwholesome, that which assists in the production of the unwholesome, and that which increases the unwholesome."

Question: If the meaning of "cause" is the same as the meaning of "unwholesome root," then the five unwholesome aggregates produced in a prior life act as causes for the five unwholesome aggregates produced in a subsequent life; the ten unwholesome karmas produced in a prior life act as causes for the ten unwholesome karmas produced in a subsequent life; and the thirty-four unwholesome latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) produced in a prior life act as causes for the thirty-four unwholesome latent tendencies produced in a subsequent life.
If all such unwholesome dharmas were to be considered unwholesome roots,
what distinguishing characteristics would these three possess to establish them as unwholesome roots?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra replied:
This is the Tathāgata’s teaching with intentional meaning; he spoke these concise and essential words for the sake of those to be converted.
The Venerable Vaśpa said:
"The Buddha definitively knows the roots of phenomena and also knows their power and function, which others do not know."
If a phenomenon possesses the characteristic of an unwholesome root, it is established as an unwholesome root;
if it does not, it is not so established. The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"The Buddha knew that these three phenomena act as causes for unwholesome states, being swift, predominant, and closely associated; therefore, these three are established as unwholesome roots."
Other unwholesome dharmas do not possess these three characteristics; therefore, they are not established as faculties (*indriya*).

Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots serve as the leaders of all unwholesome dharmas, just as a fierce general leads the victorious army at its head; by their power, the other unwholesome dharmas arise.
Furthermore, among all unwholesome dharmas, which are the most preeminent?
These three dharmas are the most preeminent both in name and in meaning among all unwholesome dharmas; therefore, they are established as faculties (indriya).

Furthermore, the unwholesome root of greed is the direct adversary of the wholesome root of non-greed; the unwholesome roots of hatred and delusion are the direct adversaries of the wholesome roots of non-hatred and non-delusion.
Furthermore, these three factors are the enemies of merit.
"Merit" refers to the three roots of goodness.

Moreover, these three unwholesome roots act as the cause, the root, the master, the basis, the function, the power, the condition, the augmentation, the accumulation, and the source of arising for all unwholesome phenomena.
As for being the cause of production, it is like a seed.
As for being the root, it makes [the dharma] firm and stable.
The rest are explained according to their respective characteristics.
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots can sustain unwholesome phenomena because they cause them to arrive, arise, nourish, and increase.
Moreover, when one seeks to abandon the desires of the desire realm, these three unwholesome roots frequently create hindrances and obstructions, like gatekeepers who do not allow people to enter.

Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are characterized by five modes of abandonment, pervade the six groups of consciousness, possess the nature of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), are capable of giving rise to bodily and vocal karma, and involve firm and powerful means at the time of severing the roots of goodness.
The five types of abandonment are those abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Those that pervade the six groups of consciousness are associated with visual consciousness, up to and including mental consciousness.
Regarding the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*): greed is the underlying tendency of sensual desire; hatred is the underlying tendency of aversion;

and delusion is the underlying tendency of ignorance. As for their ability to give rise to bodily and vocal karma: when greed arises, bodily and vocal karma are produced from greed; when hatred arises, bodily and vocal karma are produced from hatred; and when delusion arises, bodily and vocal karma are produced from delusion.
Regarding the firm and powerful means employed when severing the roots of goodness, as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"When the roots of goodness are severed, how are they severed?
By what means are they severed?"
The answer is:
It is like a person for whom lust is predominant, hatred is predominant, or delusion is predominant, who is able to sever the roots of goodness.
The reason five types of severance are mentioned is to eliminate the five views as well as doubt.
The reason it is said that [the latent tendencies] pervade the six groups of consciousness is to eliminate pride.
The reason it is said that they are of the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) is to eliminate the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*). Question:
If wrong view is able to sever the roots of goodness, why are they not established as unwholesome roots?
The answer is:
when the unwholesome roots sever the roots of goodness, their power is superior both at the time of applying the expedient means and at the time the task is accomplished.
Regarding all wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, their application is difficult during the stage of expedient means, but once the task is accomplished, their application becomes easy.
It has been heard that when a Bodhisattva beholds the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death in the world, they first give rise to the irreversible mind of unsurpassed enlightenment.

From this point onward, throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, this mind does not dwell [in attachment] nor does it regress; there is nothing capable of obstructing or hindering it. This mind is extremely difficult to attain;
it cannot be acquired except at the time of attaining the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), when one cultivates the roots of goodness of the triple world for the future.

When wrong view is established, its power and function are predominant, whereas this is not the case when it is merely a non-expedient; therefore, it is not established as an unwholesome root (*akuśalamūla*).
Furthermore, if a phenomenon, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, can produce unwholesome phenomena or assist in their production, it is established as an unwholesome root.
Greed, hatred, and delusion can both produce unwholesome states and assist in their production;
although wrong view assists in the production of unwholesome states, it cannot itself produce them.

Furthermore, there is wrong view that can sever the roots of goodness; by the power of the various unwholesome roots, these unwholesome roots first cause the roots of goodness to become weak, inferior, and thin, rendering them exhausted and devoid of strength, after which the wrong view is able to sever the roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the five types of abandonment establish the unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).

False view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is not among these five types of abandonment, nor does it pervade the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñānakāya*); it resides in the mental ground (*manobhūmi*). Although it is of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma.
Why is this so? Because the mind abandoned through the path of seeing does not arise simultaneously with bodily or vocal karma, and it is not subsumed by any of the unwholesome roots.
The five aggregates of the unwholesome lack these five factors.

The unwholesome aggregate of form is not severed by the five modes of abandonment, does not pertain to the six groups of consciousness, is not of the nature of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma, and lacks firm and powerful skillful means at the time when the roots of goodness are severed.

The unwholesome aggregates of feeling, perception, and consciousness, as well as the aggregate of formations associated with but not subsumed under the afflictions—these, although abandoned by the five paths of cultivation and common to the six groups of consciousness, do not possess the nature of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*). Although they can give rise to bodily and vocal karma, at the time when the roots of goodness are severed, they lack firm and powerful expedients.

The dissociated formations aggregate (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), although abandoned in five ways, does not pervade the six groups of consciousness, is not of the nature of a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma, and lacks firm and powerful means at the time of severing the roots of goodness.

Among the afflictions (*kleśa*), the five views (*dṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are not abandoned by the five [methods], do not pertain to the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya*), and although they possess the nature of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), they cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma.

Why is this so? Because the mind abandoned through the path of seeing does not arise simultaneously with bodily or vocal karma; thus, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, there is no firm and powerful expedient.

Although the five types of pride are abandoned [through the path of cultivation], they do not pertain to the sixfold group of consciousnesses; and although they are of the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) capable of giving rise to bodily and vocal karma, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, there is no firm and powerful expedient.
There are ten kinds of fetters (paryavasthāna):

the fetter of anger, the fetter of concealment, the fetter of drowsiness, the fetter of restlessness, the fetter of sleep, the fetter of remorse, the fetter of envy, the fetter of avarice, the fetter of shamelessness, and the fetter of lack of dread.

Drowsiness, restlessness, lack of shame, and lack of dread—although these four are abandoned through the fivefold abandonment, they do not possess the nature of underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*). Although they can give rise to bodily and vocal actions, they lack firm and powerful means at the time when the roots of goodness are severed.

Although the five types of sleep are abandoned, they do not pertain to the six groups of consciousness, they are not of the nature of latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), and they cannot give rise to bodily or vocal karma; furthermore, at the time of severing the roots of goodness, there is no firm or powerful expedient means [to counteract them].

The remaining envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) are not abandoned through the five types [of abandonment], do not pertain to the six groups of consciousness, and are not of the nature of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). They may occasionally give rise to bodily and vocal karma, yet at the time of severing the roots of goodness, they lack firm and powerful expedients.

Resentment, obstinacy, flattery, deception, arrogance, and harmfulness—these six are the stains of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); they arise dependent upon the latent dispositions and are not themselves fundamental latent dispositions.
Because there are no supreme [unwholesome] objects, they are not established as unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*).
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are said to be the root of karma and the accumulation of karma.
As it is said:

"Kālāma, you should know that greed is the root of the karma of sentient beings and the accumulation of the karma of sentient beings; hatred and delusion are likewise the root of the karma of sentient beings and the accumulation of the karma of sentient beings."
Furthermore, when these three unwholesome roots are exhausted, karma is also exhausted.
As it is said:
"When greed is exhausted, karma is also exhausted; when hatred and delusion are exhausted, karma is also exhausted."
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots arise from one another and assist one another in arising.
As it is said:
from greed arises hatred, from hatred arises greed, and within these two, ignorance also arises.
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots can give rise to the three types of feeling.
As it is said:

"The latent tendency of greed gives rise to pleasant feeling; the latent tendency of hatred gives rise to painful feeling; and the latent tendency of delusion gives rise to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling."
Question: Since these three latent dispositions (anuśaya) all drive the three types of feeling (vedanā), why is this specific statement made? Answer:
This is because they predominate:
greed predominantly conditions pleasant feeling, hatred predominantly conditions painful feeling, and delusion predominantly conditions neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Furthermore, greed arises from pleasant feeling and takes pleasant feeling as its root; yet, by extensively creating evil karma, it gives rise to much suffering.
Hatred arises from painful feeling, taking painful feeling as its root; because one performs much unwholesome karma, much suffering is produced.
Delusion arises from neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, taking neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling as its root; because one performs much unwholesome karma, much suffering is produced.
Furthermore, these three roots of goodness are said to be love and hatred.

Because of love and hatred, sentient beings frequently give rise to disputes and litigation; thus, devas and asuras constantly engage in mutual combat and slaughter, causing the death of many sentient beings.
Loving is greed; hating is anger. Question:
Why is delusion not mentioned here?
The answer is:
This has already been explained within these two points.
If sentient beings possessed wisdom, they would not even contend over the objects of celestial desire when they appear before them, let alone over the evil desires of the human realm.
Furthermore, by means of this present introductory gate, summary, and initial entry,
it is shown that all afflictions arise from three parts:
they arise either from the part of craving, or from the part of aversion, or from the part of delusion.
The Buddhist scriptures state:

"O Brahmins, you should know that if a person afflicts their mind with twenty-one afflictions, even if they practice the pure mind and give rise to pure thoughts, they will still fall into the evil realms."

I have heard that the Venerable Dharmatrāta established all afflictions as three categories—namely, the category of greed, the category of hatred, and the category of delusion—and distinguished them such that "this is the category of greed," "this is the category of hatred," and "this is the category of delusion."

If one speaks of greed, it should be understood that the factors of greed have been spoken of; if one speaks of hatred, it should be understood that the factors of hatred have been spoken of; if one speaks of delusion, it should be understood that the factors of delusion have been spoken of.

Just as with the categories of attachment, aversion, and delusion, one should know that it is likewise with the categories of the side of kin and the side of enemies; the side of those who are neither kin nor enemies; the side of those who have been beneficial and the side of those who have not been beneficial; the side of those who are pleasing and the side of those who are not pleasing; and the side of those who are neither pleasing nor unpleasing.
Furthermore, because the ten unwholesome karmas arise from the three unwholesome roots, one falls into the ten states of unwholesomeness.
How do the three unwholesome roots give rise to the ten unwholesome karmas?
The answer is:
The Buddhist scriptures state:
There are three types of killing—those arising from greed, those arising from hatred, or those arising from delusion.
This applies likewise to all [unwholesome actions] up to and including wrong views.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* also states:
"The three unwholesome roots are the root causes of the ten unwholesome courses of action," as explained in detail above.
How do the ten unwholesome courses of action give rise to the ten places of rebirth for those who commit such acts?
The Buddhist sutras state:
By extensively practicing the karma of killing, one is reborn among hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; the same applies even to wrong views.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* also speaks in this way: "One who cultivates and extensively spreads the superior karma of killing is born in the Avīci Hell;

one whose [karma] is minor and light is born in the Pratāpana Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Tapana Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Raurava Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Mahāraurava Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Saṃghāta Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Kālasūtra Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born in the Saṃjīva Hell; one whose [karma] is lighter is born among animals;
and one whose [karma] is even lighter is born among hungry ghosts. This applies up to and including wrong views; the explanation is likewise for each."
This is called practicing the ten unwholesome karmas and being born in the ten unwholesome realms.
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are said to be internal defilements.
As it is said:
Greed is an internal defilement; hatred is an internal defilement; delusion is an internal defilement.
As with internal defilements, one should know that internal enemies and internal aversions are likewise.
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are also called "increase" and are also called "decrease."
As it is said:
"How does greed increase?
How does hatred increase?"
What is the increase of delusion?
What is the decrease of greed?
What is the decrease of hatred?
What is the diminution of delusion?
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots can act as heavy causes and heavy conditions for one who is falling away.
As it is said:

If a bhikṣu or a bhikṣuṇī knows that their own mind of desire is blazing, their mind of hatred is blazing, and their mind of delusion is blazing, such that they cannot control themselves, that bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī should know: "I am indeed declining in wholesome qualities."
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are called the affliction-obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As it is said:
"What is the affliction-obstruction?"
The answer is:
It is like a person for whom greed is predominant, hatred is predominant, or delusion is predominant; this is called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, these three unwholesome roots are also termed "dust" (*rajas*).
As it is said:
"These are the dust of greed, the dust of hatred, and the dust of delusion.
Just as with filth and impurities, so too should one understand them to be like arrows, fire, thorns, swords, poisons, and diseases.
Question: How do these three unwholesome roots function? Answer:
If the mind possesses greed, it is devoid of hatred;
if the mind possesses hatred, it is devoid of greed;
delusion, however, is present in both.
Why is this? Because their respective modes of conduct differ:
those of a greedy temperament rejoice, while those of a hateful temperament are sorrowful and distressed.
Furthermore, when the mind of desire is predominant, it causes the body to become supple, moist, and nourished;
when the mind of hatred is predominant, it causes the body to become coarse, rigid, and diminished.

Moreover, when one wishes for the body to be supple so as not to harm external objects, the mind of desire acts accordingly; when one wishes for the body to be coarse and rigid so as to be able to harm external objects, the mind of hatred acts accordingly.
How does one wish to make the body supple?
The answer is:
when the mind of desire is present before one, the body itself becomes supple.
What is meant by "not harming previous conditions"?
The answer is:
if one conceives a heart of love for a previous person, one contemplates them day and night without ever reaching satiety.
How does a mind of ill-will cause the body to become coarse and rigid?
The answer is:
when a mind of ill-will is present before one, it causes one's own body to become coarse and rigid.
How can one harm the preceding object-condition?
The answer is:
if one gives rise to a mind of anger toward another person, one may even not wish to look upon them with one's eyes.
These three unwholesome roots are abandoned in five ways and pertain to the six groups of consciousness.
Why are they abandoned in five ways?
If they were to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) rather than the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), then the mind abandoned by the path of cultivation would be without roots.
If that which is abandoned by the path of cultivation were not abandoned by the path of vision, then the mind abandoned by the path of vision would be rootless.
Why is it associated with the six groups of consciousness?
If it resides in the mental ground and not in the five groups of sensory consciousness, then these five types of sensory consciousness would likewise be rootless.
If the five groups of sensory consciousness were not based on the mental ground, this mind of the mental ground would be rootless;
yet all unwholesome minds take this as their root.
A mind associated with unwholesome desire has two roots, namely greed and the associated ignorance.
It is the same for a mind associated with ill will.
A mind associated with delusion, as well as minds associated with other afflictions, have one root; that single root is ignorance.

Question: The term "root" (*mūla*) has many designations; sometimes it is said that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is the root, sometimes it is said that the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) is the root, sometimes it is said that desire (*chanda*) is the root, sometimes it is said that heedfulness (*apramāda*) is the root, and sometimes it is said that the self-substance (*svabhāva*) is the root.
What is the distinction between these names for the faculties?
The answer is:
when "view of self" (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is considered a faculty, it is because by means of this view one calculates "self" and "what belongs to the self," and thereby gives rise to all [other] views.
The World-Honored One is the root because he is the one who teaches.
Although these dharmas—the emergence from and the binding by afflictions, as well as liberation and the increase of tranquility—all proceed from the Buddha; therefore, he is the root.
Desire is the root because it can gather wholesome dharmas. Why is this so?
If there is a mind possessed of desire, one can gather wholesome dharmas; if there is no mind possessed of desire, one cannot gather wholesome dharmas. Therefore, desire is established as the root.
Heedfulness is the root because it is able to protect wholesome dharmas.
One who is heedless cannot protect wholesome dharmas, whereas one who is heedful can protect them; therefore, heedfulness is the root.
Regarding "the essential nature itself is the faculty": because the essential nature does not abandon its own intrinsic nature, the essential nature itself constitutes the faculty.
Question: If that is so, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) would also be faculties by virtue of their own essential nature.
Why is this? Because its intrinsic nature is not abandoned.
He replied:

If, according to this principle, not relinquishing one's own nature constitutes being a root, then unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) would also not relinquish their own essence and thus be roots;
what fault would there be in that? Furthermore, some, wishing to avoid such a fault, assert:
"The own-essence is the root because the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), being the root of its own essence, is able to produce others."
Question: If that were so, then the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) and its attendants would be rootless. Why is this?
Because there is no similar cause.
The answer is:
although it does not arise from a similar cause, it can nevertheless act as a similar cause for others.
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) likewise do not arise from similar causes, nor can they act as similar causes for others.
The critique states:
one should speak thus:
Because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is not abandoned, it is called the "root of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvendriya*).

From the root of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭīndriya*) up to the root of the individual body (*ātmanendriya*), these are termed the "distinctions. *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 25.
The Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle Twenty-Six.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhabhadra during the Northern Liang dynasty.
Translated together with Daotai and others. *Kṣudraka-vastu*, Chapter One on Unwholesome States, Part Two: The Three Outflows (*āsrava*).
Namely, the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*). Question:
What is the essential nature of these three outflows?
The answer is:
there are one hundred and eight kinds.
There are forty-one kinds of outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*):

five kinds of sensual craving, five kinds of ill-will, five kinds of pride, twelve kinds of views, four kinds of doubt, and ten kinds of envelopments (*paryavasthāna*). These forty-one kinds constitute the essence of the outflows of desire.
There are fifty-two kinds of outflows (*āsrava*):

ten kinds of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), ten kinds of pride (*māna*), eight kinds of doubt (*vicikitsā*), and twenty-four kinds of views (*dṛṣṭi*). These fifty-two kinds constitute the essence of the outflows.
There are fifteen kinds of the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*):

five kinds of ignorance in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), five kinds in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and five kinds in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These fifteen kinds constitute the essence of the outflow of ignorance.
These one hundred and eight types constitute the essence of the three outflows (*āsrava*), and are also called the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* also states:
"What is the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*)?"
He replied:
"Excluding the ignorance bound to the desire realm, all other fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, stains, and entanglements bound to the desire realm are called the outflow of desire."
What are the outflows (āsrava)?

With the exception of ignorance (avidyā) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, all other fetters (saṃyojana), bonds (bandhana), latent tendencies (anuśaya), stains (mala), and envelopments (paryavasthāna) bound to the realms of form and formlessness are called the outflows.
What is the outflow of ignorance?
The answer is:
lack of knowledge regarding the three realms is called the outflow of ignorance.
It is well said that the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) is the lack of knowledge regarding the three realms.
If one were to ask: "What is the outflow of ignorance? [the answer would be as follows].
He replied: "It is conditioned by ignorance regarding the three realms.
To speak in this way, however, does not include the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the untainted (anāsrava) as their object.
Why is this so? Because the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that have the untainted as their object do not take the phenomena of the three realms as their object. Question:
Are unwholesome actions of body and speech afflictions (*kleśa*), or are they not afflictions?
If they are afflictions, why are they not mentioned here? If they are not afflictions, how can one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
As it is said:

"The unwholesome dharmas consisting of misconduct of body and speech are fetters (saṃyojana), but they are not latent tendencies (anuśaya) nor bonds (bandhana). They are afflictions (kleśa), but not envelopments (paryavasthāna); they should be abandoned, severed, and known, because they can produce the retribution of suffering."
Some might answer: "It is the essence of affliction.
If that were so, the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* would be well-explained; why, then, is it not mentioned here?
Answer: It should be stated that bodily and verbal misconduct reside within the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).
There are forty-three types of the outflow of desire.
What is the intention behind not mentioning them?
The answer is:

If the nature of a dharma is that of an affliction (*kleśa*), its nature is also that of an entanglement (*paryavasthāna*); therefore, it is said to be included within the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).

Although unwholesome conduct of body and speech is a defilement (*kleśa*), its essential nature is not that of an active obsession (*paryavasthāna*); therefore, it is not said to be included within the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that the essential nature of unwholesome conduct of body and speech is not itself a defilement; for this reason, it is not said to be included within the outflow of desire.
Question: If that is so, how is the statement in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* to be reconciled? Answer:
The text of the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* should state as follows:

"Evil conduct of body and speech is unwholesome; it is not a fetter (*saṃyojana*), not a bond (*bandhana*), not a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), not an affliction (*kleśa*), and not an entanglement (*paryavasthāna*). It should be abandoned, severed, and understood, because it gives rise to the retribution of suffering."
What is the intention behind not mentioning them?
The answer is:
Although bodily and verbal misconduct are not themselves afflictions (*kleśa*), they are said to be afflictions because they are tormented by the afflictions.

Question: If that which is not itself an affliction (*kleśa*) is called an affliction because it is tormented by afflictions, then why is that which is not a fetter (*saṃyojana*) but is bound by fetters not called a fetter?
That which is not a bond is bound by bonds; why is it not called a bond?
That which is not a latent tendency is driven by latent tendencies; why is it not called a latent tendency?
That which is not an entanglement is entangled by entanglements; why is it not called an entanglement?
Answer: When that which ought to be said is not said, one should know that this explanation is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, it is intended to manifest various explanations and various literary expressions.
If the meaning is adorned with various explanations and various phrases, the meaning becomes easy to understand.

Furthermore, it is for the purpose of manifesting two kinds of gates, two kinds of summaries, two kinds of initial entries, two kinds of torches, two kinds of characteristics, two kinds of textual reflections, and two kinds of universal access.

Just as that which is not an affliction but is tormented by afflictions is called an affliction, that which is not a fetter but is bound by fetters is called a fetter, and so on, up to that which is not an entanglement but is entangled by entanglements is called an entanglement.

Just as that which is not a fetter (saṃyojana) bound by a fetter is not called a fetter, and so on, up to that which is not an entanglement (paryavasthāna) entangled by an entanglement is not called an entanglement; likewise, that which is not an affliction (kleśa) afflicted by an affliction should be said to be "non-affliction. Therefore, two types of gates are manifested, even extending to the manifestation of both types being mutually pervasive.
"This is the essence of the outflows," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the nature of their essence, we shall now explain why they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*).
What is the meaning of "outflow"?

The answer is: the meaning of "staying" is the meaning of *āsrava*; the meaning of "soaking" is the meaning of *āsrava*; the meaning of "flowing out" is the meaning of *āsrava*; the meaning of "sustaining" is the meaning of *āsrava*; the meaning of "being within" is the meaning of *āsrava*; the meaning of "intoxication" is the meaning of *āsrava*; and the meaning of "heedlessness" is the meaning of *āsrava*.
Regarding the statement that "the meaning of 'abiding' is the meaning of 'outflows' (āsrava)": who causes sentient beings to abide within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness?
The answer is:
the outflows.

The meaning of "soaking" (*nikṣepa*) is the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*). Just as when seeds are soaked in a mash of grain, their sprouts immediately grow, so too do sentient beings, by soaking the seeds of karma within the mash of afflictions (*kleśa*), produce the sprouts of future existence (*bhava*).

Regarding the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*) as the sense of "leaking": just as water flows from a spring or milk from a breast, so too do the various outflows flow forth from sentient beings through the six sense-gates.

Regarding the meaning of "held" as the meaning of "outflows" (*āsrava*): just as when a person is held by another, they cannot travel freely in the four directions, so too sentient beings, being held by the afflictions (*kleśa*), cannot emerge of their own accord from within the phenomena of birth and death across the various realms, destinies, and modes of existence.

Regarding the meaning of "internal" as the meaning of "outflows" (āsrava): it is like when a human or a ghost is within one's body; consequently, one speaks what should not be spoken, performs what should not be performed, takes what should not be taken, and touches what should not be touched.
Sentient beings are likewise: when the demons of affliction dwell within them, they speak what should not be spoken, do what should not be done, and touch what should not be touched.

Regarding the meaning of "intoxication" as the meaning of "outflow" (*āsrava*): it is like a person who drinks wine made from roots, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, or fruits; they then become intoxicated and deranged, lacking all discernment.
Sentient beings are likewise; having drunk the wine of afflictions, they become devoid of knowledge.
The meaning of negligence is also like this.
Therefore, the meaning of remaining [in saṃsāra] is the meaning of outflow (*āsrava*), up to and including the meaning of negligence being the meaning of outflow.
The proponents of phonology (Śabdavādins) say:
"Āsrava" is termed *ā-rava*; *ā* also signifies "limit" (*pradeśa*), and *rava* also signifies "outflow" (*āsrava*).
As it is said:

The limit of rain extends as far as the city of Bhaṭṭālikā; the limit of giving extends as far as the Caṇḍālas; likewise, the limit of the outflows (āsrava) extends up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).
