because one follows the path as it is attained and causes it to spread extensively, thereby severing all factors of rebirth (*jāti-bhāga*), severing their measure, and severing their seeds; by gradually making them thin, one brings about ultimate abandonment—therefore, it is called "abandoned through the path of cultivation."
Furthermore, there are those who say that the afflictions abandoned through the path of cultivation may also be said to be abandoned through the path of seeing.
Why is this? Because within the path of cultivation, there is likewise "seeing according to reality."

According to my doctrine, one practices and disseminates the path as it has been attained; by severing all factors of rebirth, severing their measure, and severing their seeds, making them gradually attenuated until they are ultimately severed, it is called "severance through the cultivation of the path."
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:
the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is a sharp and intense path; when one takes that as an object, the nine types of afflictions are abandoned simultaneously.
The path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is not a sharp path; it is practiced repeatedly, and the nine grades of afflictions are abandoned over nine occasions.
For example, when using a sharp axe-blade to cut an object, that which is sharp severs it in a single stroke, whereas that which is dull requires repeated blows to sever it.
It is the same for that as well.

Furthermore, if something is abandoned primarily through the path of seeing, it is called abandoned by the path of seeing; if it is abandoned primarily through the path of cultivation, it is called abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if they are abandoned by a path characterized by two aspects, they are said to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); the two aspects refer to the aspect of vision (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*) and the aspect of wisdom (*prajñā-lakṣaṇa*).

If they are abandoned by a path characterized by three aspects, they are said to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); the three aspects refer to the aspect of vision, the aspect of wisdom, and the aspect of knowledge (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by four aspects is called abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), the four aspects are: eye, clarity, awakening, and wisdom;

if that which is abandoned by the path characterized by five aspects is called abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*), the five aspects are: eye, clarity, awakening, wisdom, and knowledge.

Furthermore, that which is abandoned through patience (*kṣānti*) is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while that which is abandoned through knowledge (*jñāna*) is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, the ninefold fetters (*saṃyojana*) that are abandoned simultaneously are abandoned by the path of seeing, whereas those ninefold fetters that are abandoned over nine stages are abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, that which is abandoned by the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); that which is abandoned by the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Furthermore, that which is abandoned at a time like the splitting of a stone is abandoned through the path of seeing; that which is abandoned at a time like the snapping of a tendon is abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, that which is contrary to the initial resolve (*cittotpāda*) is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); that which is contrary to the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Furthermore, that which is abandoned by seeing the truths for the first time is abandoned through the path of seeing; that which is abandoned by re-observing the truths already previously seen is abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, that which is abandoned by means of a single causal path is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); that which is abandoned by means of two causal paths is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Furthermore, that which is abandoned like a strong man wearing armor is abandoned through the path of seeing; that which is abandoned like a footless person walking is abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if at the time of abandonment it is abandoned by that very knowledge, by that which is known by that knowledge, and by the cultivation of that path, it is abandoned by the path of seeing; if at the time of abandonment it is abandoned by another knowledge, by another object of knowledge, and by the cultivation of another path, it is abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if that which is abandoned by one who is still a candidate (pratipannaka) for a fruit is abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga), whereas if it is abandoned by one who has already attained the fruit, it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

Furthermore, that which is abandoned by those of firm faith (śraddhādhimukta) and those who follow the Dharma (dharmānusārin) is abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga); that which is abandoned by those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and those who have realized the body (kāyasākṣin) is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).

Furthermore, if that which is abandoned upon first emerging from the path is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is an abandonment of the path of seeing; if that which is abandoned through repeated emergence from the path is abandoned, it is an abandonment of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Furthermore, if the abandonment is subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, it is an abandonment of the path of seeing; if the abandonment is subsumed within three, two, or one fruit of śrāmaṇya, it is an abandonment of the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, that which arises by taking non-existence as its object is abandoned through the Path of Seeing; that which arises by taking existence as its object is abandoned through the Path of Cultivation.

Furthermore, that which, once abandoned, does not regress is abandoned through the Path of Seeing; that which, once abandoned, may either regress or not regress is abandoned through the Path of Cultivation.

Furthermore, that which, once severed, is neither bound nor fettered again is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); that which, once severed, may still be bound or fettered is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Furthermore, if at the time of severance, patience (*kṣānti*) is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is abandoned by the path of seeing; if at the time of severance, knowledge is the path of non-obstruction and knowledge is the path of liberation, it is abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if at the time of abandonment, wisdom functions as the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), forbearance (*kṣānti*) functions as the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and wisdom functions as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
If desire is abandoned when wisdom functions as the paths of preparation, non-obstruction, and liberation, it is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Furthermore, if one first attains non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), it is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Alternatively, if one first attains non-analytical cessation and later attains analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), or if one first attains analytical cessation and later attains non-analytical cessation, or if one attains both analytical and non-analytical cessation simultaneously, these are abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Furthermore, if at the time of abandonment one cultivates the path by taking a single truth as its object, it is abandoned through the path of seeing; if at the time of abandonment one cultivates the path by taking all four truths as its objects, it is abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, if the fourfold path is cultivated at the time of abandonment, it is abandoned by seeing; if the sixteenfold path is cultivated at the time of abandonment, it is abandoned by cultivation.

Furthermore, if a similar path is cultivated at the time of abandonment, it is abandoned by seeing; if both a similar and a dissimilar path are cultivated at the time of abandonment, it is abandoned by cultivation.

Furthermore, if it is abandoned at the time of [the first] moment and cultivated through one samādhi, it is abandoned by the path of seeing; if it is abandoned at the time of [subsequent] moments and cultivated through three samādhis, it is abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, that which does not arise at the time of abandonment is abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*); that which may or may not arise at the time of abandonment is abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Among these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and so on, up to how many are abandoned by the path of cultivation?

Up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and so on, up to how many are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*)? Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: The preceding section merely explained the intention of the śramaṇa regarding sudden abandonment; it did not restrict itself to the simultaneous realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya), nor did it clarify the gradual realization of the truths.
Now, this treatise is composed because one wishes to restrict the intention regarding simultaneous realization of the truths while also clarifying the gradual realization of the truths.

Furthermore, there are those who say that while the preceding section primarily explains the perspective of those who realize the truths all at once (*sakṛd-darśana*), it also clarifies the sequential realization of the truths (*anupūrva-darśana*), though not in a coarse or explicit manner.

Now, wishing to present this clearly and with sufficient detail for the sake of those who perceive the truths at a single moment, and also to clarify the sequential perception of the truths, I have composed this treatise.
Furthermore, it is intended to manifest the future severance of the seeds of afflictions and the five kinds of remedial methods.
The five kinds of abandonment of afflictions refer to the categories abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The five kinds of remedial dharmas (*pratipakṣa*) refer to the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), which are the remedies for what is abandoned through the vision of suffering; up to the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the path (*mārga-jñāna*), which are the remedies for what is abandoned through the vision of the path; and knowledge (*jñāna*), which is the remedy for what is abandoned through the path of cultivation.
For these reasons, this treatise is composed. Regarding these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*)?
This is explained at length, and so forth.
Answer: One is abandoned through the vision of suffering, namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Question:
Why is it that the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is abandoned only through the vision of suffering?
The answer is:
because it arises conditioned by suffering, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering.
Furthermore, this view arises conditioned by its fruit; when one contemplates the fruit with wisdom, this view is immediately severed.
Moreover, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is of a perverted nature; all perversions are abandoned through the vision of suffering.
When the inversion is abandoned, this view is also abandoned. Why is this?
Because they share the same antidote.

Furthermore, because these afflictions are coarse, they are severed by the first path of non-obstruction; the remaining subtle afflictions are severed later by the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
It is like dust and grime that do not adhere firmly: they fall away as soon as one shakes them off.
If it is firmly adhered, one must use strong lye and exert great effort before it can be cleansed.
It is like a ceramic vessel: if the grease has not penetrated deeply, it is removed by rinsing with water;
if the grease has penetrated deeply, it is removed only after boiling it with hot water.
It is the same for those as well.

Furthermore, because these faculties of view do not penetrate deeply into the plane of their objects (*ālambana-bhūmi*), they are weak by nature due to this lack of penetration; being weak by nature, they are abandoned by the first path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Other afflictive faculties penetrate deeply into the plane of their objects, and thus they are abandoned by subsequent paths of non-obstruction, up to the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).
For example, if the roots of a tree do not penetrate deeply, it can be blown over by even a slight breeze;
however, if its roots penetrate deeply, even a great wind cannot cause it to fall.
It is the same in this case as well. The Venerable Sūmīta said:
"For what reason is the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) abandoned only through the vision of suffering?"
The answer is:
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) takes the five aggregates as its object; when one subsequently perceives the five aggregates as they truly are, this view of a self is severed.
Furthermore, this view arises from the notions of permanence, pleasure, purity, and self; if one perceives the notions of impermanence, suffering, impurity, and non-self, this view is then severed.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "This view arises from one's own body; therefore, it is called 'view of the body' (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
If one perceives that one's own body is without self, this view is then severed."

The clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is either abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) or abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*). Question:
For what reason is the clinging to precepts and observances not abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudayadarśana*) or the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana*)?
Answer: This is for the sake of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The practices of the non-Buddhists are contrary to the path of suffering (duḥkha-mārga), but they are not contrary to the origin (samudaya) or cessation (nirodha) [of suffering].
Why is this so? Because non-Buddhists conceive of the accumulation [of suffering] as being like dirt and conceive of its cessation as being like a bathing place.
For the sake of seeking such a bathing place, they practice various forms of asceticism.
Because of these various ascetic practices, the defilements of the afflictions further stain the mind even more.
It is like a person who, in order to remove dirt, enters turbid water to bathe, only to find that their filth increases all the more.
It is likewise for that [view].
Furthermore, because it arises dependent on suffering, it is abandoned through the vision of suffering; because it arises dependent on the path, it is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Furthermore, that which arises dependent on defilement is abandoned through the vision of suffering; that which arises dependent on purification is abandoned through the vision of the path.

Furthermore, that which is practiced by those of our own school is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), while that which is practiced by those of external schools is abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, regarding what is not a cause, to conceive it as a cause is abandoned through the vision of suffering; regarding what is not the path, to conceive it as the path is abandoned through the vision of the path.
Doubt regarding views (*dṛṣṭi-vicikitsā*) is abandoned through the [paths of] suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. Question:
Why is there no doubt among those [afflictions] abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)?
Answer: If one has not yet perceived its essence, the mind gives rise to hesitation;
once its essence has been perceived, the mind becomes certain. Therefore, there is no doubt regarding that which is abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
The three unwholesome roots and the three outflows are abandoned through the vision of suffering up to the path of cultivation.
In summary, there are five modes of abandonment; that is, there are those abandoned by one, two, four, or five modes.
The other sections are explained in detail as in the original sūtra.
This section is a detailed expository commentary (upadeśa-vibhāṣā). Question:
Why are they called "abandoned by the path of seeing" (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) up to "abandoned by the path of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*)?
The answer is:

those whose objects (*ālambana*) are determinate and whose antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) are determinate are called abandoned by the path of seeing; those whose objects are indeterminate and whose antidotes are indeterminate are called abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, those [defilements] that are determined by their basis (*āyatana*), determined by their object (*ālambana*), or determined by their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) are said to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*). Those that are not determined by their basis, not determined by their object, or not determined by their antidote are said to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, if one employs the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) as antidotes, and so on up to employing the patience regarding the path (*mārga-kṣānti*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) as antidotes, these are called abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
If one employs [subsequent] knowledge (*jñāna*) as the antidote, these are called abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).

Furthermore, that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering is called "abandoned by the vision of suffering"; that which is abandoned through the vision of the path is called "abandoned by the vision of the path"; and that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering, or the vision of origin, or the vision of cessation, or the vision of the path is called "abandoned by the cultivation of the path."

Furthermore, that which is contrary to suffering is called abandoned by the vision of suffering; likewise, up to that which is contrary to the path is called abandoned by the vision of the path; and that which is contrary to the abandonment of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path is called abandoned by cultivation.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Twenty-eight [and] Volume Twenty-nine.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
In the *Khandhaka* on Unwholesome States, Chapter Five: Of these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are not views?
Up to the ninety-eight *anuśayas*, how many are views (*dṛṣṭi*) and how many are not views?
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: Some say that all afflictions are of the nature of views (*dṛṣṭi*). Question:
Why does he speak in this way? The answer is: He speaks thus:
The intensity of one's engagement constitutes the nature of "view. All afflictions are intense in their respective spheres of engagement:

for instance, the view of a self-identity intensely engages with attachment to "I" and "mine"; the view of extremes intensely engages with attachment to annihilationism or eternalism; false views intensely engage with attachment to non-existence; the grasping at views intensely engages with attachment to [one's own view] as supreme; and the grasping at precepts and observances intensely engages with attachment to [them] as pure. Such is the intensity of their engagement.
Craving is likewise so: its activity regarding passionate attachment is intense; and its activity regarding hatred and aversion, pride and self-elevation, and delusion and doubt is also intense.

In order to sever such misconceptions regarding the intent of those who speak thus, and to clarify that among the afflictions there are both those whose nature is "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) and those whose nature is not "view," this treatise is composed.
Of these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are of the nature of "view," and how many are not of the nature of "view"?
Answer: Two are of the nature of views, namely, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the grasping of precepts and rituals (śīlavrataparāmarśa);
one is not of the nature of views.
This refers to doubt.
The detailed explanation of the remaining categories is as set forth in the original sūtra. Question:
Why are they called "views"? The answer is:
this should be explained in detail here, as in the case of the five views and the bases of views.
Regarding these three fetters, how many are with vitarka and vicāra, how many are without vitarka but with vicāra, and how many are without both vitarka and vicāra?

Up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), how many are with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), how many are without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and how many are without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Some say that vitarka and vicāra exist from the desire realm up to the peak of existence, as the Dārṣṭāntikas maintain.
Why do they make this statement?
He relies upon the Buddha’s sūtras, which state:
"Coarseness of mind is vitarka; subtlety of mind is vicāra."
These characteristics of grossness and subtlety can be found from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "The Abhidharmikas speak as follows:"
Regarding the sequential characteristics of the mind, they possess both coarseness and subtlety throughout the three realms.
However, to claim that from the desire realm up to the Brahma world there is always both directed thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) is an incorrect teaching.
This way of speaking is called a false exposition.
You have made this statement:
"Gross mind is *vitarka* (applied thought) and subtle mind is *vicāra* (sustained thought).

This grossness and subtlety of mind can be found even up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); yet you say that *vitarka* and *vicāra* exist only from the Desire Realm up to the Brahma World. Therefore, what you have said is a bad explanation, not a good one; it is poorly grasped, not well grasped.
The Abhidharmikas speak thus:
"What we have taught is well-spoken and rightly upheld, not wrongly upheld. Why is this so?"
I have explained the characteristics of the gross and the subtle through various matters, not by means of a single matter.

For example, it is said that the *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts) are gross and the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) are subtle; herein, it is not said that awakening (*vitarka*) is gross and observation (*vicāra*) is subtle.
Why is this so? Because these two dharmas do not possess the characteristics of vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought).
As it is said that the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) is coarse while the other four aggregates are subtle, so too it is said that both vitarka and vicāra are subtle dharmas.
Why is this so? Because they are subsumed within the same aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Just as it is said that the desire realm is coarse and the first dhyāna is subtle, so too it is said that vitarka and vicāra are coarse and subtle respectively.
Why is this so? Because both the desire realm and the first dhyāna possess vitarka and vicāra.
As it is said that the stage of the first dhyāna is coarse while the stage of the second dhyāna is subtle, it follows that vitarka and vicāra are what is meant by "coarse."
Why is this? Because above the stage of the first dhyāna, there are no longer vitarka and vicāra. Question:
Regarding their statement that there is vitarka and vicāra on the stages of the first dhyāna, how can they further speak of distinctions among the three stages?
The answer is:
They make this assertion as follows:

From the desire realm and the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are three types of phenomena: namely, the wholesome, the defiled, and the non-obscured neutral. Furthermore, the deeply defiled phenomena from the intermediate dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The wholesome and non-obscured neutral dharmas of the intermediate dhyāna are called the stage with vitarka and vicāra.
The wholesome and non-obscured neutral dharmas from the second dhyāna upwards, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, are called the stage without vitarka and without vicāra.
Question: If that is so, how does this accord with the Buddha’s sūtras?
As it is said in a sūtra:
With the subsiding of directed thought and evaluation, one enters the second dhyāna, which is born of concentration and characterized by joy and bliss. He answers thus:
"The cessation of wholesome directed thought and evaluation is not defiled."
Question: If that is so, by reason of what event are wholesome applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*) extinguished without being defiled? Answer:
One should first extinguish the defiled [states], and only later, when departing from a stage, extinguish the wholesome [states].
However, the Dārṣṭāntikas claim that vitarka and vicāra exist in the higher stages.

It should be understood that this teaching is the fruit of ignorance, the fruit of darkness, and the fruit of a lack of diligent application; nevertheless, because vitarka and vicāra exist in the Desire Realm and the First Dhyāna, they [claim this].
Desiring to refute the views of others, and so forth as explained at length, this treatise is composed:

Of these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), how many are without applied thought but with sustained thought (*avitarka-vicāramātra*), and how many are without applied thought and without sustained thought (*avitarka-avicāra*)?
Answer: The three fetters are of three types:
some are with vitarka and vicāra, some are without vitarka but with vicāra, and some are without both vitarka and vicāra.
What is "with vitarka and vicāra"?
The answer is:
those in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
What is "without vitarka but with vicāra"?
The answer is:
that which exists in the intermediate dhyāna.
What is meant by "without vitarka and without vicāra"?
The answer is:
those who abide in the third dhyāna and the four formless attainments (ārūpya).
The other sections are explained at length as in the original sutra. Question:
For what reason is it called "with vitarka and with vicāra"?
Why is it called "without vitarka and with vicāra"?
Why is it called "without vitarka and without vicāra"? Answer:
When it is accompanied by both vitarka and vicāra, associated with both vitarka and vicāra, and when vitarka and vicāra are both present before one, this is called "with vitarka and with vicāra.

If it is not accompanied by vitarka but only accompanied by vicāra, not associated with vitarka but associated with vicāra, and when vitarka has already ceased while vicāra is present before one, this is called "without vitarka but with vicāra."
If it is not accompanied by vitarka and vicāra, nor associated with vitarka and vicāra, and vitarka and vicāra have already ceased, this is called "without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, if there are various reckonings or various observations, this is called "with vitarka and with vicāra."
If one frequently applies attention (*vitarka*) but does not frequently apply observation (*vicāra*), this is called "without vitarka, with vicāra.
If one neither frequently applies attention nor frequently applies observation, this is called "without vitarka, without vicāra.

Regarding these three fetters (*saṃyojana*), how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), how many with the faculty of pain (*duḥkhendriya*), how many with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), how many with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), and how many with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
This applies likewise up to the ninety-eight latent proclivities (*anuśaya*). Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Some say that when dharmas arise, they arise sequentially and not simultaneously, as the Dārṣṭāntikas do.
The Venerable Buddhadeva speaks thus:
When dharmas arise, they arise sequentially; they do not arise simultaneously.
It is just as when many companions pass through a narrow path: they proceed one after another, and cannot do so at once.
If it is already difficult for two persons to proceed together, how much more so for many?
In this way, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) each arise from their own respective causes of arising; for what reason would numerous phenomena of birth arise simultaneously?
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
conditioned phenomena arise through the conjunction of either a single factor itself, or through the conjunction of multiple factors.
That which arises from the conjunction of a single dharma is called "arising from the conjunction of a single dharma" because it arises within a single moment.

That which arises from the conjunction of multiple dharmas is like the arising of each individual numerical dharma; although many such factors are inseparable, it is therefore called "arising from the conjunction of multiple dharmas."

Furthermore, as for the reason for composing this treatise: some explain that the meaning of "mutually acting as causal power" (*anyonya-āśraya-bala*) is the meaning of "association" (*samprayoga*). They state:
if a dharma arises through the mutual causal power of another dharma, this is the meaning of association.
Just as the mind arises by reason of the power of the mind, and the mind is associated with the mind;
so too, the mental factors (caitasika-dharma) arise by reason of the power of the mind, and the mental factors are associated with the mind.
Furthermore, mental factors arise by reason of the power of the mental factors themselves, and the mental factors are associated with one another.
The mind does not arise by way of the power of numerical dharmas; therefore, the mind is not associated with numerical dharmas.

This treatise was composed to stop the views of those who speak thus, and also to clarify that while the mind is associated with numerical dharmas, numerical dharmas are also associated with numerical dharmas, numerical dharmas are associated with the mind, yet the mind is not associated with itself. Thus, this discussion is undertaken.
Furthermore, as for the purpose of composing this treatise: some assert that a self-entity is associated with itself and not with other entities. They argue as follows:
"The meaning of 'mutual respect' (*saṃbhāvanā*) is the meaning of 'association' (*saṃprayoga*); among all phenomena, there is nothing that respects itself more than it respects its own self-entity."
This treatise is composed to refute the views of those who speak thus, and also to clarify the meaning of the association with other dharmas.
Furthermore, the reason for composing this treatise is that some maintain that a self-essence (svabhāva) is neither said to be associated with itself nor said to be dissociated from itself.
They are not called "associated" because all phenomena cannot act as conditions for their own self-nature.
They are not called "non-associated" because the meaning of equality, similarity, and mutual respect is the meaning of association.
Why is this so? Because among all phenomena, there is no respect greater than respecting one's own self-nature.

This is stated in order to refute the views of those who speak thus, and also to clarify that the associated dharmas are not disordered; therefore, it is said at length, beginning with the refutation of others' positions and the desire to reveal one's own position.

Of these three fetters, how many are associated with the faculty of pleasure, how many with the faculty of pain, how many with the faculty of joy, how many with the faculty of grief, and how many with the faculty of equanimity?
Question: Why is it that one asks only about association with feeling (*vedanā*), and not about association with other numerical factors (*dharmas*)? Answer:
The intention of the author of that treatise was thus, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the possession [of a dharma] does not obstruct its acquisition, though it may obstruct its manifestation.
How does it not obstruct acquisition?
Just as a single person may possess five feelings,
how could this obstruct their simultaneous manifestation?
It is impossible for two feelings to manifest simultaneously.
Furthermore, it is because feeling possesses the characteristics of all the sense-faculties within its single essence.
Furthermore, it is because feeling functions like the hub of a wheel within the cycle of dependent origination.
Furthermore, it is because feeling encompasses and enters into all phenomena.
Furthermore, if one does not ask about feeling (*vedanā*), what else might be asked?
If one asks about the eight faculties such as life (*jīvita*) and so forth, they are exclusively dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-dharma*).
If one asks about the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and the five faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, they are exclusively wholesome (*kuśala*).
If one were to ask:

"Why not inquire about the mind-faculty (manas-indriya)?"—it is because it is called a "concomitant dharma" (saṃprayukta-dharma) by virtue of being the mind-faculty, just as it is called a "mind-concomitant dharma" (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) by virtue of being the mind (citta).

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).

The reason for excluding the faculty of suffering is that the faculty of suffering belongs to the level of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*), whereas these two views belong to the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*).

The reason it is not associated with the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is that the faculty of sorrow functions through a mode of dejection, whereas this [state] functions through a mode of exultation.
In general, however, it is associated with three faculties.
These exist within the three realms; specifically, they are in the desire realm.
In the first and second dhyānas, they are associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
In the third dhyāna, they are associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
In the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments, it is associated with one faculty, namely the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Therefore, taken as a whole, it is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Doubt is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
It is not associated with the faculty of suffering because the faculty of suffering belongs to the level of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañcavijñānakāya*).
In summary, it is associated with four faculties.
Doubt exists within the three realms. For those in the desire realm, it is associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of equanimity.
If it is in the first or second dhyāna, it is associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of joy and the faculty of equanimity.
In the third dhyāna, one is endowed with two faculties, namely the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
In the fourth dhyāna and the four formless attainments (ārūpya), one is endowed with a single faculty, namely the faculty of equanimity.
Therefore, in general, it is associated with four faculties (*indriya*).
Question: Why is doubt (*vicikitsā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), whereas in the first and second dhyānas it is so associated?
Answer: Because the objects of operation for doubt and joy in the desire realm are each distinct.
That which is the object of operation for doubt is not the object of operation for joy; that which is the object of operation for joy is not the object of operation for doubt.
Why is this so? Doubtful conduct leads to sorrow and distress, while joyful conduct leads to exultation.
To share the same object is the meaning of association.
Because they are not identical, they do not associate.
The first and second dhyānas both involve the activity of joyful exultation, and therefore they associate.
Furthermore, in the desire realm, joy is coarse while doubt is subtle; a coarse phenomenon does not associate with a subtle phenomenon.
Why is this so? Because the meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga). Question:
What is the coarse meaning of joy (*prīti*)?
The answer is:
sentient beings give rise [to it] when they ought not to do so, and they give rise to it toward objects before them when they ought not to do so.
Why do sentient beings give rise to [thoughts] that should not arise?
Because the nature of sentient beings is suffering.
Why do they give rise to [thoughts] regarding prior objects that should not arise?
When seeing others who are reeling, falling, or erring, one should give rise to compassion and laugh even more loudly.
This is because those in the first and second dhyānas are both subtle, and thus [the laughter] is appropriate for them.

Furthermore, joy (*prīti*) in the desire realm is light and restless, while doubt (*vicikitsā*) dwells in heaviness; that which is light and restless does not correspond with that which dwells in heaviness.
Why is this so? Because the meaning of "equality" (*samatā*) is the meaning of "correspondence" (*samprayoga*).
In the stages of the first and second dhyānas, both are equally predominant; therefore, they are associated.
Furthermore, joy in the desire realm arises from external phenomena, whereas doubt arises from internal phenomena.
Phenomena arising from the external are not associated with phenomena arising from the internal.
Why is this? Because the meaning of "equality" is the meaning of "association."
The first dhyāna and the second dhyāna both arise from within; therefore, they are associated.
Furthermore, joy in the desire realm is adventitious while doubt is an established resident; that which is adventitious is not associated with that which is an established resident.
Why is this so? The meaning of "equality" (samatā) is the meaning of "conjunction" (saṃprayoga).
Since both the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna are equally states of abiding, they are therefore conjoined.
Furthermore, although doubt in the desire realm does not correspond with the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), it does correspond with other feelings (*vedanā*).

Since the joy of the first and second dhyānas is a feeling belonging to that specific level (*bhūmi*), if it were not to correspond with the faculty of joy, this would be termed a "mind-aggregate without feeling" (*avedanakacitta-kalāpa*), which would undermine the nature of the basis (*āśraya*) and undermine the nature of the associated factors (*samprayuktadharma*).

In order to avoid such faults, doubt (*vicikitsā*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*); however, in the first and second dhyānas, doubt is associated with the faculty of joy.
Greed (*lobha*) is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
Why is this so? Those whose temperament is dominated by greed experience elation; those whose temperament is dominated by sorrow and suffering experience dejection.
Hatred is associated with three faculties, excluding the faculty of joy and the faculty of pleasure.
Why is this so? Because the conduct of hatred is characterized by sorrow and distress, while the conduct of joy and pleasure is characterized by exultation.
The outflows of delusion, sensual desire, and ignorance are associated with the five faculties.
Why is this so? Because these three [feelings] pertain to the six groups of consciousness; they proceed with both elation and dejection.
They are associated with the three faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering and the faculty of grief.
Why is this so? Because there is no sorrow or suffering in the form and formless realms.
The meaning of the absence of sorrow and suffering in the form and formless realms shall be explained in detail in the Indriya-varga (The Chapter on Faculties).
With the exception of wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the meaning of the other categories is as explained in the original sūtra.
Wrong view is associated with four faculties, excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
In summary, wrong view is associated with four faculties.

However, as for wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), it exists within the three realms. That which exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is associated with three faculties (*indriya*), excluding the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) and the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
That which exists in the first and second dhyānas is associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
In the third dhyāna, one is associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
In the fourth dhyāna and the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti), one is associated with a single faculty, namely the faculty of equanimity.

Question: Regarding wrong views in the desire realm, which ones are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and which ones are associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*)? Answer:

Suppose there is a person whose nature is not inclined toward giving or toward making offerings, and later, if they associate with those of wrong views and external paths in one place and hear these words:
"There is no giving, no making of offerings, and no retribution for good or evil deeds."
Upon hearing these words, a mind of faith and delight arises, and one then gives rise to a joyful mind, thinking:
"The wholesome deeds I have performed are excellent.
In this way, such wrong view is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).

Suppose there is a person whose nature is to delight in practicing charity and performing sacrifices, but later he happens to meet with those of wrong views and external paths in one place and hears them say:
"There is no giving, no sacrifice, and no retribution for good or evil deeds."
Upon hearing these words, their hearts gave rise to faith and joy, yet they also felt sorrow, thinking:
"The offerings we have made will have been in vain. Why is this?"
Because there is no karmic retribution,
such wrong view is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
This section is a detailed exposition (*vaibhāṣya*) of the *Upadeśa*.
Question: Why is it called "conjunction" (saṃprayoga)?
The meaning of conjunction is explained in detail in the section on the cause of conjunction (*saṃprayuktaka-hetu*) within the *Saṃyukta-vastu* (Miscellaneous Chapter).
Of these three fetters, how many are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and how many are bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: Some say that envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the Brahma world (*brahmaloka*).
Why do they speak in this way?
Answer: He relies on the Buddhist sūtras.
The Buddhist sūtras state:
The Brahmā King said to the assembly of Brahmās:
"We all dwell together here; let us not go to the presence of the śramaṇa Gautama, for we can remain in this very place until our old age and death."
They say: "The Brahmā King spoke these words out of envy and stinginess.
To refute the intent of those who speak thus, and to clarify that envy and stinginess exist only in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), this treatise was composed.
The three fetters are either bound to the desire realm, or bound to the form realm, or bound to the formless realm.
The meaning of this section is explained in detail as in the original sutra. Question:
Why is it called "bound to the desire realm" (kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)?
Why is it called "bound to the form realm" (rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta) or "bound to the formless realm" (ārūpyadhātu-pratisaṃyukta)? Answer:

Because they bind the phenomena of the desire realm, they are called "bound to the desire realm"; because they bind the phenomena of the form and formless realms, they are called "bound to the form and formless realms.
It is just as a cow tied to a pillar is called a "pillar-bound cow"—it is the same in this case.

Furthermore, the sense bases of the desire realm are called "bound to the desire realm" because they are bound by the phenomena of the desire realm; the sense bases of the form and formless realms are called "bound to the form and formless realms" because they are bound by the phenomena of the form and formless realms.
The feet are called afflictions (*kleśa*). As a verse says:
"The Buddha possesses immeasurable practices; Without feet, who could carry him along?"
"Just as a person who has feet is able to travel freely in all four directions,
so too one who has the feet of afflictions is able to traverse the various destinies, births, and the cycle of birth and death."
Furthermore, because afflictions in the desire realm conceive the notion of a dwelling place and the notion of "I," they are called "bound to the desire realm.
Because afflictions in the form and formless realms conceive the notion of a dwelling place and the notion of "I" within those realms, they are called "bound to the form and formless realms."
Attachment to one's dwelling is craving; because of this view, "I exist," and because it is moistened by the craving of the desire realm, one views and calculates "self" and "what belongs to self";
because it is moistened by the craving of the form and formless realms, one views and calculates "self" and "what belongs to self."

Furthermore, it is called "bound to the desire realm" because it can produce the desire for pleasure within the desire realm; it is called "bound to the form and formless realms" because it can produce the desire for pleasure within the form and formless realms.
Pleasure is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and desire is view (*dṛṣṭi*).

Furthermore, it is called "bound to the desire realm" because it is fettered by the phenomena of birth and death in the desire realm; it is called "bound to the form and formless realms" because it is fettered by the phenomena of birth and death in the form and formless realms.

Furthermore, it is called "bound to the desire realm" because it is defiled by the impurities of the desire realm, harmed by their poisons, and afflicted by their calamities; it is called "bound to the form and formless realms" because it is defiled by the impurities of the form and formless realms, harmed by their poisons, and afflicted by their calamities.
Regarding those fetters that belong to the desire realm, do those fetters exist within the desire realm?
There are six types [of such cases]:
first, those where the realm is [the same as] the fetter;...
Second, these are the destinies;
third, these are the persons;
fourth, these are the entrances.
Fifth, it is the outflows (āsrava);
sixth, it is one's own body.
Regarding "it is the realm" (dhātu), as it is said here:
Regarding those fetters that belong to the desire realm, do those fetters exist within the desire realm?
To this it is said: they are designated by the name "dharma-base" (*dharmāyatana*).
Dharmas belonging to the desire realm are called "desire realm," and dharmas belonging to the form and formless realms are called "form and formless realms.
Regarding what it means to belong to these [realms], it is as stated when teaching the gift of Dharma:
"All these beings of the five destinies shall exhaust the suffering of birth and death."
Regarding "a person," it is as stated in the Vinaya:
these two persons are included within the number of the Saṃgha and may be found within the Saṃgha.
Regarding "entering this," it is as stated in the Prakaraṇa:
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
It consists of the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and that which is form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Regarding what constitutes "outflows" (*āsrava*), it is as stated:
What are the outflows (*āsrava*)?
They are the phenomena associated with outflows (*sāsravadharma*). Regarding what constitutes the body, it is as explained in the *Catuḥmahābhūtakāyavarga*:
What is the Great Dharma?
The answer is:
it is one's own body.
Among these six, this treatise is composed based on "existence as a constituent" (*dhātu*) and not on the others.
Within existence, there are four types:
first, existence as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Second, the presence of the vessel;
third, the presence of the sphere of practice;
fourth, the presence of the location.
"Existing as its own substance" means that all dharmas exist within their own respective portions as their own substance, own characteristic, and own nature.
"Existing in a vessel" means existing within a container, such as Devadatta being inside a house.
As it is with "the vessel exists," so too is the meaning of "the range of activity exists" and "the location exists.
In this context, the discussion is conducted by means of these four types of existence (*bhava*), explained according to their characteristics.
Regarding the fetters (*saṃyojana*) that belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): do those fetters exist within the desire realm?
Answer: There are fetters that belong to the desire realm, yet those fetters do not reside within the desire realm;
there are also fetters that reside within the desire realm, yet those fetters do not belong to the desire realm.
Some fetters belong to the desire realm, and those fetters also exist within the desire realm;
some fetters do not belong to the desire realm, and those fetters do not exist within the desire realm.
What are the fetters that belong to the desire realm but do not exist within the desire realm?
The answer is:
He was bound by the fetters.
Māra Pāpīyān, dwelling in the Brahma Heaven, desired to converse with the Tathāgata.
Question: Bound by what fetters is Māra Pāpīyān when he desires to converse with the Tathāgata? Answer:
Because they are shrouded by the obsession of anger, they wish to engage in speech with the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, some say that because they are shrouded by the obsession of envy, they wish to engage in speech with the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there are those who say that because he is shrouded by the fetter of stinginess, he wishes to engage in speech with the Tathāgata.
The critique states:
One should speak thus:
Enshrouded by the ten envelopments (*paryavasthāna*), as each individual envelopment arises and manifests before him, he desires to engage in speech with the Tathāgata.
He asks: "For what reason is he called Māra?"
Answer: He is called Māra because he severs the life-force of wisdom; "Māra" in the language of Qin means "to kill.
Furthermore, he is called Māra because he constantly practices negligence and thereby harms his own self.
Why is he named Pāpīyān?
The answer is:
because he constantly harbors evil intentions, accomplishes evil dharmas, and accomplishes evil wisdom, he is named Pāpīyān; "Pāpīyān" means "evil" in the language of Qin.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
It should be stated that Pāpīyān has transcended. Why is this so?
Because he was born there after passing beyond Pāpīyan— Pāpīyan being translated in the Qin language as "Evil" (è) and *yú* meaning "kingdom"—
he dwells in the Brahma Heaven, desiring to converse with the Tathāgata.
Question: The Māra King dwells in the Brahma Heaven; what does he do there? Answer:
The *Brahmāyuḥ-sūtra* (or *Brahma-māra-sūtra*) is the source for this treatise.
It is heard that once the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Anāthapiṇḍika Monastery.
At that time, there was a Brahmā who, while dwelling in the Brahma-heaven, gave rise to such a wrong view and spoke these words:

"This place is eternal, unceasing, relinquished, transcendent, and the state of quiescent extinction; there is no other state of eternity, non-cessation, relinquishment, transcendence, and quiescent extinction more excellent than this place."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the mind of that Brahmā, vanished from the Jeta Grove as swiftly as a strong man might bend or extend his arm, and suddenly appeared in the Brahma Heaven, staying not far from the Brahmā’s abode.
At that time, Brahmā saw the Tathāgata from afar and immediately invited him, addressing the Buddha:
"Welcome, Great Sage!
This place is eternal, unceasing, relinquished, transcendent, and quiescent; there is nothing else more eternal or superior than this place."
That you have been able to abandon the various afflictions and manifold sufferings of the desire realm to come here is truly a most joyful matter.
You may dwell here in peace and happiness for all time.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the Brahmā, saying:
"This place is impermanent, yet you say it is permanent;
this place is not a state of peace, tranquility, or renunciation, yet you say it is a state of peace, tranquility, and renunciation."
"You speak thus because you are shrouded by ignorance.
You should remember that among the Brahmās of the past, those who fell into the desire realm were like flowers and fruits that have fallen."
At that time, Brahmā again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Welcome, Great Seer!
This place is eternally blissful," as explained in detail above;
The second and third times were also spoken thus.
At that time, the Tathāgata also addressed Brahmā a second and a third time, saying:
"This place is impermanent," and so forth, as extensively explained, ending with "shrouded by ignorance."
"You should remember that among the Brahmās of the past, those who fell into the desire realm were like flowers or fruits falling.
At that time, the Brahmā king thought to himself:
'Now the Tathāgata is difficult to approach and difficult to converse with.'"
However, as for the various Brahma-dharmas, though their minds are tranquil and at ease in the stage of detachment from desire, they cannot compete with the Buddha in debate.
He further thought:
"Māra Pāpīyān is constantly in opposition to the Tathāgata; he must be able to compete with the Buddha in debate."
At that time, Brahmā brought Pāpīyān to the Brahma-heaven and, having transformed it into the ground of the desire realm, settled him there.
Then Brahmā addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Great Seer, you should know that this place is eternal, and indeed there is nothing superior to it."
At that time, the Tathāgata again addressed the Brahma King:
"This place is impermanent," as explained in detail above.
At that time, Pāpīyān said to the Buddha:
"Great Seer!
Do not oppose what the Brahmā King has spoken; always carry out his instructions in accordance with them.
If you were to oppose the words of the Brahmā King, it would be like someone whose house a meritorious deity has entered, yet who drives that deity out with a staff."
"I have no need for you.
If you were to disobey the word of Brahmā, it would be just like this:
it is as if a person were falling from a great height; if they do not support themselves with their hands and feet, they will fall even further."
It is like a person falling from a tree: if they do not firmly grasp a branch, they will suffer pain;
if they firmly grasp a branch, they do not suffer pain.
Such is the case, O Great Sage!
"Do not oppose the words of the Brahma King;
you should carry out exactly what he has said.
He then addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"Great Seer!
Do you not see that the assembly of Brahmās and those like us surround the Brahma King, following his lead and not contradicting his words?
At that time, the World-Honored One had this thought:
Now that this evil Māra has come to create obstacles for me,
having recognized this situation, he immediately addressed Māra, saying:
"You are not Brahmā, nor are you a member of Brahmā's retinue."
"As for what you said regarding the evil Māra obstructing me, it was your very self who did so.
At that time, Pāpīyān thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama now knows the thoughts within my mind."
Filled with fear, he conceived a sense of weary detachment and sat to one side, unable to return.
At that time, Brahmā, by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhibala*), was able to cause Pāpīyas to return to his own palace.
Therefore, that sutra is the very basis for this treatise.
Furthermore, one who is entangled by the fetters (paryavasthāna), upon the end of life in the form realm, arises as an intermediate state being (antarābhava) in the desire realm.
An ordinary person (pṛthagjana), at the end of life in the form realm, is destined to be born in the desire realm.
The intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm manifests while one is within the form realm.
Why is this? Because such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

The place where the aggregates of death cease is precisely where the intermediate state arises, just as the place where a seed ceases must necessarily give rise to a sprout; it is the same in that case.

When one passes from the aggregates of death to the intermediate state, if even a single of the thirty-six proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm manifests before them, it causes the continuity of birth to arise; this is called a "bond" (*saṃyojana*). It is a bond of the desire realm, yet that bond does not reside within the desire realm itself.
In this context, "is" refers to being a constituent element (*dhātu*); "exists" excludes its own self-nature and refers to the existence of the other three [elements].
How can there be a fetter that exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) while that fetter itself is not of the desire realm?
Bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), one who dies in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is born with an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

Whether an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*), upon dying in the desire realm and being born in the form realm, the intermediate state of the form realm remains within the desire realm.
Why is this so? Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharma*).
Where the aggregates of death cease, there the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arises; just as where a seed ceases, there a sprout arises, so it is in that case as well.

When an ordinary person passes from the death-aggregate to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one or another of the thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the form realm manifests, causing the continuity of birth to arise.

When a noble one (*ārya*) passes from the death-aggregate to the intermediate state, one or another of the three proclivities abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the form realm manifests, causing the continuity of birth to arise.
Furthermore, these fetters of the form and formless realms may manifest while one abides in the desire realm;

while abiding in the desire realm, without dying or passing away, these fetters of the form and formless realms may manifest. In the case of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), if any one of the thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*) manifests, or in the case of a noble one (*ārya*), if any one of the three proclivities to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) manifests.
Thus it is said that there are those who practice dhyāna due to craving, those who practice dhyāna due to conceit, those who practice dhyāna due to views, and those who practice dhyāna due to doubt.
These are called fetters belonging to the desire realm, yet those fetters themselves do not belong to the desire realm.
Regarding these three states of existence: what is this state that belongs to the realm and exists within the realm?

It refers to ordinary persons and noble ones who, while bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), pass away from the desire realm and are reborn into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm.
Ordinary persons are unimpeded in being born into the five destinies; noble ones are unimpeded in being born into two destinies.

Whether an ordinary person is born among the gods or among humans, from the time of the death-aggregate until the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), if even a single one of the thirty-six proclivities (*anuśaya*) manifests before them, it causes the continuity of birth to arise.

When a noble one passes from the death-aggregate to the intermediate state (antarābhava), if even one of the four proclivities (anuśaya) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm manifests, it causes the continuity of birth to arise.
Just as it is from the death-aggregate to the intermediate state, so too is it explained for the transition from the intermediate state to the birth-aggregate (upapattibhava).
Furthermore, these fetters (saṃyojana) of the desire realm are bound; while abiding in the desire realm, they manifest before one.

While abiding in the desire realm, without dying or passing away, these fetters of the desire realm arise and manifest before one. For an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), if any one of the thirty-six proclivities (anuśaya) manifests, for a noble one (ārya), any one of the four proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) regarding the desire realm manifests.
This is called a fetter that belongs to the desire realm and also exists within the desire realm.
Herein, "this" refers to the realm itself, and "exists within" refers to the four types of existence.
What is a fetter that neither belongs to the desire realm nor exists within the desire realm?
Bound by the fetters (*paryavasthāna*), one dies in the form realm and is reborn within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the birth-state (*upapattibhava*) of the form realm.
Those who die in the form realm and are reborn in the form realm are both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary persons are born both in higher and lower realms, and in each respective place they have multiple portions of birth;
noble ones are born in higher realms but not in lower ones, and in each respective place they have only one portion of birth.
When an ordinary person passes from the aggregate of death to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one of the thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*) manifests, causing the continuity of birth.
When a noble one (*ārya*) passes through the stage of cultivation, one of the three proclivities to be abandoned by cultivation manifests, causing the continuity of birth.
The explanation from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*) is likewise.

When one dies in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) and is born into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), this applies to both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). Among ordinary persons, there are multiple births in each location; among noble ones, there is only one birth in each location.
When an ordinary person passes from the aggregate of death to the aggregate of birth, thirty-one latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm may manifest, causing the continuity of birth;
for a noble one (*ārya*), three latent dispositions do so.
Those who pass away from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and are reborn again in the formless realm include both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
Among them, ordinary persons are born both in higher and lower realms, having multiple births in each respective place;
noble ones are born only in higher realms and not in lower ones, having only a single birth in each respective place.
When an ordinary person passes from the aggregate of death to the aggregate of birth, thirty-one latent proclivities (anuśaya) may manifest, causing the continuity of existence to arise;
for a noble one (ārya), it is three latent proclivities.

When an ordinary person dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the form realm, from the moment of the death-aggregate until the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), one or another of the thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the form realm manifests, causing the continuity of birth to arise.

Furthermore, this is bound to the form and formless realms; it manifests while abiding in the form realm; one does not die nor pass away while abiding in the form realm; and these [beings] are both ordinary persons and noble ones.
In ordinary persons, thirty-one proclivities (*anuśaya*) manifest; in noble ones (*ārya*), three proclivities manifest.

Such are the explanations regarding those who practice dhyāna through craving, those who practice dhyāna through conceit, those who practice dhyāna through views, and those who practice dhyāna through doubt.
Dwelling in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one neither dies nor passes away, yet gives rise to thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm manifest before oneself;
these include both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*). For an ordinary person, thirty-one underlying tendencies manifest; for a noble one, three.
This is called a fetter that is neither of the desire realm nor located within the desire realm. Why is this?
Because it exists within the form and formless realms.
"That which is this realm" refers to the realm itself; "that which exists therein" refers to the four types of existence (*bhava*).
Are all fetters (*saṃyojana*) both of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and existing within the form realm?
This should be expanded into a full tetralemma (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase of the preceding four phrases becomes this second phrase;
the second phrase of the preceding becomes this first phrase;
the third phrase of the preceding becomes this fourth phrase.
The former fourth phrase becomes this third phrase:
"Are all fetters that belong to the formless realm also located in the formless realm? Answer:
Those fetters that exist in the formless realm are themselves also of the formless realm. Why is this?
Because in the formless realm there are only fetters bound to the formless realm.
Is there any fetter that belongs to the formless realm but does not reside within the formless realm? Answer: Yes.

These are the fetters of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that manifest while one abides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). They manifest without dying or passing away; these fetters of the formless realm manifest for both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
When ordinary persons give rise to thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the formless realm present before them, noble ones [give rise to] three.
Such are those who practice meditation due to craving, due to pride, due to views, or due to doubt.
This is called a fetter that belongs to the formless realm;
this "this" refers to the realm itself,
and it does not reside within the formless realm.
Why is this so? Because they exist within the realms of desire and form.
"Existence" here excludes existence as one's own self-substance; it refers to the other three types of existence.
Are there fetters that are neither of the desire realm nor located within the desire realm?
This should be elaborated at length as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first permutation of the preceding [set] becomes this second permutation here.
The former second line becomes this first line;
the former third line becomes this fourth line;
and the former fourth line becomes this third line.
If the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), are those fetters also not located in the form realm?
One should expand this into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) as explained for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If the various fetters are not of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), are those fetters also not located in the formless realm?
Answer: There are fetters that do not belong to the formless realm, yet those fetters do not exist within the formless realm either.
Is there any fetter that does not exist within the formless realm, yet is not the case that it does not belong to the formless realm?
Answer: There are.

There are fetters that are not of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet which manifest while one dwells in the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* or *rūpadhātu*); while dwelling in the desire or form realms, without dying or passing away, one gives rise to fetters of the formless realm that manifest before one. This applies both to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and to noble ones (*ārya*).
Ordinary persons manifest thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), while noble ones manifest three.
These fetters do not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Why is this so?
Because it exists within the realms of desire and form.
"Existing" here refers to three types of existence, excluding the existence of its own self-substance (*svabhāva*).
It is not that it does not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why is this so? Because it is the fetter of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
This is that which constitutes the realm.
Question: For what reason did that Venerable One establish a "non-statement" (apavāda) and compose this treatise? Answer:
The intention of the author of that treatise was indeed such, as explained at length.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest mastery over discourse.
One who possesses mastery over discourse is able to compose a treatise even by means of what is not a formal sentence.
One who lacks mastery in discourse cannot even compose correct phrases, let alone incorrect ones.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of generating the faculty of discernment in disciples.

If one constructs a treatise using non-sentences (*apada*), it gives rise to the disciples' conceptualization of the characteristics of the Dharma, such that "this may be so" and "that may also be so.

Furthermore, there are cases where one attains growth by employing non-sentences; for example, within the "Chapter on Persons" (*pudgala-varga*), when using correct sentences, it is stated: "That person has four," "That person has three," or "That person has two";
yet when using non-sentences, it is stated: "That person has five," "That person has six," or "That person has four."
For this reason, that venerable one has composed a treatise using what is not a [logical] proposition:
"If a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths does not abandon form, is he bound by form?"
If one is bound by form, is form not abandoned?
This applies likewise up to consciousness. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
Some say that the abandonment of the existence of form (*rūpa-bhava*) occurs through sequential abandonment, abandonment by way of demarcations, and abandonment in discrete segments.
As the foreign Dharma masters have stated:
"Just as with defiled minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), so it is with the ninefold abandonment of form (*rūpa*).

In order to refute the intent of such a statement, and to clarify that defiled minds and mental factors, as well as wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) and non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds and mental factors, are abandoned simultaneously at the final path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), this treatise is composed.
Question: For what reason are the nine types of defiled mind and mental factors, as well as the wholesome, out-flowing, and non-obscured neutral mind and mental factors,
abandoned simultaneously at the final stage of the path of non-obstruction?
The answer is: Wisdom and ignorance are constantly mutually obstructive.

Inferior-inferior wisdom cuts off superior-superior ignorance; inferior-middle cuts off superior-middle; inferior-superior cuts off superior-inferior; middle-inferior cuts off middle-superior; middle-middle cuts off middle-middle; middle-superior cuts off middle-inferior; superior-inferior cuts off inferior-superior; superior-middle cuts off inferior-middle; and superior-superior cuts off inferior-inferior.

Wholesome form and impure, non-obscured indeterminate phenomena do not obstruct clarity, nor do they obstruct ignorance; rather, they serve as the basis and the foundation for both clarity and ignorance.

Just as the light of a lamp does not obstruct the wick, the oil, or the vessel, but rather obstructs darkness, yet the wick, the oil, and the vessel serve as the basis and the foundation for the lamp’s light.

In this way, these wholesome, contaminated, and non-obscured neutral phenomena of the form realm do not conflict with either clarity or ignorance, yet they serve as the basis and the foundation for both clarity and ignorance.
Furthermore, regarding the defiled mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), according to how many types [of seeds] are severed, one does not possess those types.

As for matter (*rūpa*) that is defiled, it is no longer possessed at the time of abiding in the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), and it is finally severed by the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Regarding form that is wholesome, non-obscured-neutral, as well as other wholesome, out-flowing, non-obscured-neutral conditioned phenomena—all these dharmas are abandoned simultaneously at the final path of non-obstruction.

Although [the fetters] have already been known and abandoned, one still continues to possess the desire for the three realms; therefore, in order to refute the positions of others and to manifest his own position, he says, "and so forth," as explained at length.
And he composed this treatise:
"A disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, yet has not yet severed craving for the realm of form," and so forth, as explained at length. He asks:
To avoid what is it said that one is "complete in the vision of the truths" (*dṛṣṭisampanna*)?
To restrain what is it said that one is a "disciple of the Blessed One" (*bhagavacchrāvaka*)?
The answer is:
One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths does so in order to avoid those of firm faith and those of firm dharma.
This is for the sake of regulating ignorant and small-minded worldlings. He asked:
Why are those of steadfast faith and steadfast practice not said to be "fully endowed with the vision of the truths"?
The answer is:
if one is fully endowed with the vision of the Four Noble Truths and has permanently severed wrong views, this is called being "fully endowed with the vision of the truths."

One who possesses firm faith and firm realization of the Dharma, though not yet fully endowed with the vision of the truths, shall become so; though not yet having permanently severed wrong views, shall permanently sever them.
Furthermore, if within one's person there is no fourfold ignorance and delusion, but rather the fourfold wisdom, this is called being fully endowed with the vision of the truths.
This is because one who possesses firm faith and firm realization has not yet abandoned the four kinds of ignorance and delusion, nor has one yet attained the four kinds of knowledge.
Furthermore, if one tears asunder the fourfold net of hesitation and doubt and gives rise to the fourfold certainty, this constitutes the fulfillment of the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Because those who possess firm faith and firm realization have not yet torn apart the fourfold net of hesitation and doubt, nor have they yet fully attained the fourfold certainties.

Furthermore, when one’s person is free from afflictions like frost and hail, as well as wrong views, perversions, and various evil deeds, this is called being complete in the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Because there is no such thing as one who possesses firm faith and firm realization of the Dharma, they are not said to be complete in the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
It is just as a crop is said to be complete when it is free from frost and hail; so too is this case.
Furthermore, if one is able to subdue the realms of the Four Noble Truths, this is called being fully endowed with the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*).
Because those of firm faith and firm dharma have not yet been able to subdue the realms of the Four Noble Truths, they are said to be not fully endowed.
Question: For what reason is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) not called a disciple of the World-Honored One (Bhagavat)? Answer:
If one hears what the Buddha has taught, the mind remains undifferentiated regarding the Four Truths and the Triple Gem.
Ordinary people are not so; they may either believe the Buddha’s words or believe the words of non-Buddhist teachers.
Furthermore, those who do not serve other deities but serve only the Buddha are called disciples of the World-Honored One.
Ordinary persons, however, may serve either the Buddha or Maheśvara and other such deities.
Furthermore, if one possesses indestructible faith in the Buddha, such a person is called a disciple of the World-Honored One.
Because ordinary worldlings lack this indestructible faith in the Buddha, they are not called disciples of the World-Honored One.
