If it does not act as an object, it is a condition by way of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If future or present *satkāyadṛṣṭi* acts as an object toward past *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, it is both a condition by way of being an object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and a condition by way of sovereign power.
If it does not act as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

If past satkāyadṛṣṭi arises by taking future or present satkāyadṛṣṭi as its condition, then future and present satkāyadṛṣṭi act as two conditions for past satkāyadṛṣṭi, namely: the object-condition and the dominant condition.
If past satkāyadṛṣṭi does not take future or present satkāyadṛṣṭi as its object, then future and present satkāyadṛṣṭi act as a single-conditioned force (ekādhipatipratyaya) toward past satkāyadṛṣṭi.
Question: Just as past views of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) have already completed their function and possess no further capacity,
why is this statement made?

If it is an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), does it function as an objective field-condition (*viṣaya-pratyaya*) and a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*); or if it is not an object-condition, is it solely a dominant condition?
The answer is:
When past satkāyadṛṣṭi was in the present, it took future satkāyadṛṣṭi as its object; having taken it as an object, it ceased and fell into the past.
Although it has ceased and fallen into the past and no longer performs any further action, it is described by way of what it previously performed.

The view of a self in the body within the desire realm [acts as] a single condition of sovereign power for the view of a self in the body within the form realm, but it is not a causal condition. Why is this?
Because the grounds and the realms are distinct, their causes are each different.
There is no equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*). Why is this?
Because there is no one who, with an undefiled mind at the end of life, is reborn in a higher plane; thus, there is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Why is this? Because there are no underlying afflictions (*anuśaya*) as objects.
Because there is the object of majestic power (*prabhāva*), they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm with respect to the view of a self-identity in the desire realm: if it functions as a sequential [condition], it is both a sequential condition and a condition by way of sovereign power (*ādhipatya*);
if it does not function as a sequential condition, it is solely a condition by way of sovereign power.

When one dies with a mind associated with the view of a self in the body within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and through a mind associated with the view of a self in the body within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) causes the rebirth-continuum (*pratisaṃdhi*) of a body associated with the view of a self in the form realm, that [desire-realm] view of a self in the body acts as two conditions for it: namely, the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*) and the condition of sovereign power (*adhipatipratyaya*).
The sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is so called because the view of a self-body in the form realm arises immediately after the view of a self-body in the desire realm;
the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is so called because there is no mutual obstruction.
There is no cause or condition. Why is this?
Because the earth and the elements have distinct causes for each.
There is no object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) does not take other realms as its object.

If one were to die with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), yet cause a rebirth continuum through a mind associated with the view of a self-identity belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), then the view of a self-identity of the form realm would be a condition of single power (*ekādhipatipratyaya*) for the view of a self-identity of the desire realm, but it would not be a condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*).
Regarding the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is as explained above.
Body-view (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm is a single condition of sovereign power for body-view in the formless realm.
Body-view in the formless realm is, if considered in sequential order, both a sequential condition (*anuloma-pratyaya*) and a condition of sovereign power for body-view in the desire realm.
If they do not follow a sequential order, there is a single condition of sovereign power (*ekādhipatipratyaya*), as explained in detail above.
The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm is a single condition of sovereign power for the view of a self-body in the formless realm.

Regarding the view of a self-body in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-satkāyadṛṣṭi) in relation to the view of a self-body in the form realm (rūpadhātu-satkāyadṛṣṭi): if they are established in a sequential order, there is a sequential, powerful condition (anupūrvika-ādhipateya-pratyaya);
if they are not established in a sequential order, there is a single powerful condition. The detailed explanation is as above.

Just as the view of a self-in-a-self relates to the view of a self-in-a-self; the view of a self-in-a-self relates to that which is not all-pervasive; that which is not all-pervasive relates to that which is not all-pervasive; and that which is not all-pervasive relates to that which is all-pervasive.
Regarding that which is not universal with respect to all [realms] but is universal within them: it applies from the lower to the higher and from the higher to the lower. Why is this?
Because here, "universal" refers to those universal factors that take other realms as their object.
In brief, there are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), namely: the five views, doubt, attachment, aversion, pride, and ignorance.
Among these ten underlying tendencies, five are universal (*sarvatraga*) and five are not universal.
The five that are universal (sarvatraga) are: wrong view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and rituals, doubt, and ignorance.
The five that are not universal are: the view of a self-identity, the view of extremes, craving, hatred, and pride.

This text explains that while all-pervasive factors take other realms as their object, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are included among those that are not all-pervasive.
Just as the view of a self-identity takes the view of a self-identity as its object, so too does the view of a self-identity take those that are not all-pervasive as its objects.

Just as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) [is not all-pervasive] with respect to the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), with respect to craving (*rāga*), with respect to aversion (*pratigha*), and with respect to pride (*māna*), so too is it called "not all-pervasive" with respect to those that are not all-pervasive.

Regarding that which is not all-pervasive being [non-all-pervasive] with respect to another non-all-pervasive factor: it is like the view of extremes being [non-all-pervasive] with respect to the view of extremes, with respect to craving, with respect to aversion, with respect to pride, and with respect to the view of a self-identity.

Attachment toward attachment, toward aversion, toward conceit, toward extreme views, and toward the view of a self; aversion toward aversion, toward conceit, toward attachment, toward the view of a self, and toward extreme views; conceit toward conceit, toward the view of a self, toward extreme views, toward attachment, and toward aversion—these are called those that are not universal with respect to the non-universal.

That which is not universal does not pervade all; for example, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) does not pervade wrong view, the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), doubt (vicikitsā), or ignorance (avidyā).

As it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so it is for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), hatred (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*); these are called those that are not universal (*asarvatraga*) but are universal (*sarvatraga*) with respect to their objects.
How many conditions does the view of a self-identity have with respect to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*)?
Answer: It may be four, three, two, or one.
What are the four?
For example, when the grasping of precepts and observances arises immediately after the view of a self-identity, it takes that very view of a self-identity as its object.

The previously arisen view of a self-identity serves as the cause-condition, the immediate-condition, the object-condition, and the sovereign-condition for the subsequently arisen grasping of precepts and observances.
Just as there is a moment of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is subsequently followed by a moment of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

If the subsequently arising clinging to precepts takes the previously arisen view of a self-body as its object, then that previously arisen view of a self-body acts as four conditions for the subsequently arising clinging to precepts: namely, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are two causes: namely, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
Regarding the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), it is because [the view of self-identity] arises immediately after the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Regarding the condition of objective domain (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it arises because later-arising grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) takes earlier-arising views as its object.
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): it is like the principle of a seed. Up to the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it refers to the principle of non-obstruction.
Because those born later who hold precepts as a dogma receive the force of the four conditions of their former views, they are able to function in the world; this is explained at length as above.
What are the three?
The answer is:
Just as the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) gives rise to the clinging to precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa) in immediate succession, it does not take that very view of a self as its object.

The previously arisen view of a self serves as the cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya), the immediate-condition (anantara-pratyaya), and the sovereign-condition (adhipati-pratyaya) for the subsequently arisen clinging to precepts and observances; it does not function as the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
Just as there is a moment of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), subsequently there arises in succession a moment of attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Although this attachment to precepts does not take the view of a self-body as its object, it may take the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as its object, or it may take other factors within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are distinct from the view of a self-body.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) from a previous life has three conditions for the arising of the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in a subsequent life; it lacks the condition of an object (*ālambanapratyaya*).
Regarding the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), there are two causes: namely, the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatragahetu*).

Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): it is because the subsequently arising grasping at precepts arises immediately after the previously arisen view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the condition as sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the absence of the condition as object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it is because the subsequently arising grasping at precepts does not take the previously arisen view of a self-identity as its object.

Furthermore, because of the force of three conditions—the grasping at precepts and observances in a future life and the view of a self-identity in a past life—one is able to function in the world, as explained in detail above.
Moreover, there are three conditions, two conditions, and one condition, which are explained in detail as in the case of the view of a self-identity.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the desire realm serves as a single condition of sovereign power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the form realm; the detailed explanation is as above.

The view of a self-identity in the form realm, with respect to the clinging to precepts and observances in the desire realm, constitutes a condition of sequence and sovereign power, provided that it functions as a sequential factor but does not function as its object (*ālambana*).

For example, when one dwelling in the form realm dies with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a mind associated with the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm causes [rebirth] to arise in continuity.

Although the clinging to precepts and rituals in the desire realm does not take the view of a self-identity in the form realm as its object, the view of a self-identity in the form realm possesses a sequential and dominant condition (*anantarya-pratyaya* and *adhipati-pratyaya*) in relation to the clinging to precepts and rituals in the desire realm.
If one acts upon an object without following a sequential order, there is an object-condition and a power-condition.

If one does not die with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity belonging to the form realm, but rather causes a mind associated with the clinging to precepts and rituals of the desire realm to arise in succession, that [mind] takes the view of a self-identity of the form realm as its condition.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm acts as a condition for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm through two conditions:

namely, the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and the condition of power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*). If one establishes them as sequential, object, and power conditions, then they exist as sequential, object, and power conditions.

For example, when one dwelling in the form realm dies with a mind associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), a mind associated with the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm causes rebirth and continuity; that clinging to precepts and rituals in the desire realm then takes the view of a self-identity in the form realm as its object.

The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) has three conditions for the adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): namely, the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*), the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the condition of sovereign power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*).
Regarding the condition of immediate succession: the adherence to precepts and rituals of the desire realm arises immediately after the view of a self-identity of the form realm.

Regarding the condition of objective sphere (*gocara-pratyaya*): it arises because the grasping at precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm conditions the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm.
Regarding the condition of sovereign power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*): it is because there is no mutual obstruction.
Regarding the absence of a causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): it is because the causes differ according to their respective realms and stages (*bhūmi*).
If it does not act as a sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) nor as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it acts as a single dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

If one does not die with a mind associated with the view of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*), but causes a mind associated with the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) of the desire realm (*kāma-dhātu*) to arise in succession, it arises because it does not take the view of self-identity of the form realm as its object.

The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serves as a single condition of sovereign power (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It lacks the condition of cause (*hetupratyaya*), because the realms and stages (*bhūmi*) of the two factors differ.
It lacks the condition of immediate succession (*samanantarapratyaya*), because the clinging to precepts and observances does not arise immediately after the view of a self-body in the form realm.

There is no objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) belonging to the desire realm does not take the body of the form realm as its object, and because they do not obstruct one another.

There is one condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*): the view of a self-identity in the desire realm serves as a single condition of sovereign power for the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the formless realm.
The view of a self-identity in the formless realm [arising] toward the clinging to precepts in the desire realm is explained at length as above.
The view of a self-identity in the form realm [arising] toward the clinging to precepts in the formless realm is explained at length as above.
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) in the formless realm [is related] to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) in the form realm, as explained in detail above.

Just as it is with the view of a self-identity in relation to the clinging to precepts and observances, so too is it said regarding wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
This is called the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) being omnipresent with respect to all [factors].

As for "that which is omnipresent being omnipresent with respect to all," it is like how false view is [omnipresent] with respect to false view, to the grasping at views (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), to the grasping at precepts and observances (śīlavrataparāmarśa), to doubt (vicikitsā), and to ignorance (avidyā).

The grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) [is associated] with the grasping at views, with the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), with doubt (*vicikitsā*), with ignorance (*avidyā*), and with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
The grasping at precepts and observances [is associated] with the grasping at precepts and observances, with doubt, with ignorance, with false view, and with the grasping at views.
Doubt [pervades] doubt, ignorance, wrong view, adherence to views, and adherence to precepts and rituals.
Ignorance [pervades] ignorance, wrong view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and rituals, and doubt. These are called the universal factors that pervade all.

That which is not universal with respect to all [factors] but is universal with respect to some is, for example, the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) with respect to the clinging to precepts and observances; it is likewise with respect to false views, the clinging to views, doubt, and ignorance.

As it is with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), so it is for the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), aversion (*pratigha*), and pride (*māna*); the explanation is likewise.
This is called that which is not universal (*asarvatraga*) among those that are universal (*sarvatraga*).
If one asks about the inclusion of all phenomena (*dharmasaṃgraha*), one should examine them by means of the bases (*āyatana*).
If one asks about wisdom, one should observe it through the truths.
If one asks about consciousness, one should observe it through the elements.
If one asks about afflictions, one should observe them through their seeds.
If one observes in this manner, the essential nature and characteristics of phenomena will be easy to know and easy to see.
Regarding the afflictions mentioned herein, they should be observed by way of their types.
There are five types of phenomena:
The seeds to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to the seeds to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, there are two types:
first, the universal (sarvatraga); [second, the non-universal].
2. Not universal. The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of origin.
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation are of two kinds:
First, those conditioned by outflows (sāsrava);
second, those conditioned by the outflow-free (anāsrava).
The same applies to those abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga-prahātavya).
Those abandoned through the path of cultivation are not universal.

Those abandoned through the vision of suffering are universal. Regarding those abandoned through the vision of suffering that are universal, [the former] serves as the cause-condition, the immediate-condition, the object-condition, and the sovereign-condition.

Regarding causes (*hetu*), there are four types: the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*), all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering give rise, in immediate succession, to all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering take as their object all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering.

Regarding the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): because they do not obstruct one another, all pervasive [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the sovereign condition for those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not all-pervasive.
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are two types of causes: namely, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) and the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Regarding the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), that which is pervasive and to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) arises sequentially from that which is non-pervasive and to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and is not universal (*asarvatraga*) takes as its object those things abandoned through the vision of suffering that are universal.
Regarding the power-condition (*ādhipati-pratyaya*): it is because there is no mutual obstruction.

The universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering are, with respect to the universal [defilements] abandoned through the vision of origin, conditions by way of cause, immediate succession, object, and dominance.
Regarding the condition by way of cause, there is one cause, namely, the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*): all-pervasive [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering arise in immediate succession from all-pervasive [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of origination.

Regarding the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): all-pervasive [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of origination take as their object all-pervasive [defilements] to be abandoned by the vision of suffering.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipatipratyaya*): it is so called because there is no mutual obstruction.

That which is universal (*sarvatraga*) and is to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkhadarśana-prahātavya*) acts as a cause, sequential, and dominant condition toward that which is not universal and is to be abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudayadarśana-prahātavya*), as well as toward that which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*), the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*), and that which is to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). However, it does not act as an object condition (*ālambanapratyaya*).
As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), it is a single cause, namely the omnipresent cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

As for the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the omnipresent [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering arise sequentially as those various underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) take their own category as an object, not another category.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): because they do not obstruct one another.

Those [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not universal (*asarvatraga*) serve as the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate-condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition, and the condition of dominance for other [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not universal.

Regarding causes (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are three types of causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*), that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and is not all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) gives rise, in immediate succession, to that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and is not all-pervasive.

Regarding objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*): those [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not universal (*asarvatraga*) take as their object those [factors] abandoned through the vision of suffering that are not universal.
Regarding conditions by way of power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

That which is abandoned by seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) but is not universal (*asarvatraga*) serves as the cause-condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate-condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the sovereign-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which is abandoned by seeing suffering and is universal.
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there is one cause, namely the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Regarding the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and is not all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) gives rise, in immediate succession, to that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): that which is universal (*sarvatraga*) among those abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) takes as its object those abandoned by the vision of suffering that are not universal.
Regarding the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

That which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) is not universal (*asarvatraga*), whereas that which is abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) is universal. Regarding the sequential, objective, and dominant conditions (*anuloma-ālambana-adhipati-pratyaya*), there is no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*): that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and is not all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*) gives rise in immediate succession to that which is abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and is all-pervasive.

Regarding the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): that which is abandoned through the vision of origination and is all-pervasive takes as its object that which is abandoned through the vision of suffering and is not all-pervasive.
Regarding the condition of power (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is because there is no mutual obstruction.
There is no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Why is this so?
The universal-out-of-scope proclivities (*asarvatraga-anuśaya*) do not act as causes for the seeds of others.

Those abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal-out-of-scope [act] toward those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) that are not universal-out-of-scope, and toward those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*), and those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*). They function as sequential conditions (*anantara-pratyaya*) and conditions of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but they lack causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

As for the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the universal-outflowing [defilements] abandoned through the vision of suffering do not arise subsequently as those various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As for the condition as sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.
It has no causal conditions. Why is this?
Because it does not act as a cause for the seeds of others.
There is no objective realm as a condition.
Why is this? Because it does not serve as an object-condition for other seeds.

The same explanation applies to those abandoned through the vision of suffering—both the universal and the non-universal—as well as those abandoned through the vision of the origin—both the universal and the non-universal.

The latent dispositions (anuśaya) with outflows that have the cessation [of suffering] as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation act as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for those [dispositions] with outflows that have the cessation as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.

As for the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), there are three types of causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

As for the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), it refers to the outflow-tainted proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with the objects of cessation that are abandoned through the vision of cessation; these arise in immediate succession after [the preceding state] as outflow-tainted proclivities associated with the objects of cessation that are abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it refers to the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), which take as their object those same latent proclivities associated with outflows abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Regarding the sovereign-condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the latent tendencies (anuśaya) with outflow that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation: with respect to the latent tendencies with no outflow, they function as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), and the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but not as the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
As for the causal condition, there is one cause, namely, the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects as their conditions and are to be abandoned by the vision of the cessation [of suffering] arise immediately thereafter as latent tendencies that take uncontaminated objects as their conditions.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not mutually obstruct one another.
There are no objects of perception as conditions.
Why is this? Because those underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that take uncontaminated phenomena as their objects are themselves contaminated views to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Regarding the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that have outflows as their object and are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination, they function as sequential conditions, objective conditions, and conditions by way of power, but not as causal conditions.

Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): because the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin arise immediately after the outflow-tainted proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of cessation that have the outflows as their object.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it refers to all pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination, because they take as their object the proclivities with outflows (*sāsrava*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation.
Regarding the power-condition (*ādhipati-pratyaya*): it refers to the fact that they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding those [defilements] that lack an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): because the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*), they do not serve as object-conditions for the non-universal latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) or the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), nor for any of the latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanā*). However, they do possess sequential and powerful conditions (*anupūrva-pratyaya* and *ādhipatya-pratyaya*).

Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects (*sāsrava-ālambana*) and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), subsequently give rise in immediate succession to all latent dispositions—both those to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), as well as those not universally pervasive (*asarvatraga*), and all those to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*) and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it refers to those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that do not obstruct one another.
Regarding the condition of cause (*hetu-pratyaya*): it is as explained above.
Regarding the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it is because those latent tendencies are not all-pervasive (*asarvatraga*).

The latent tendencies (anuśaya) that take the untainted as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation do not have other types [of objects] as their conditions; with respect to those latent tendencies to be abandoned by the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object, they function as causes, immediate antecedents, and dominant conditions, but they do not function as object-conditions.
As for causes, there are three types of causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), and the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*anantara-pratyaya*): the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and which take the untainted as their object arise in immediate succession after other latent dispositions abandoned through the vision of cessation that take the untainted as their object.
Regarding the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the absence of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is because those latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object are themselves tainted (*sāsrava*).

Latent dispositions with an untainted object that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) serve as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the condition of sovereign power for those latent dispositions with a tainted object that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): there is one cause, namely the similar cause (*sabhāga-hetu*). Regarding the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*):

following the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the path of seeing the cessation of suffering that take the uncontaminated as their object, there subsequently arise in sequence the latent tendencies associated with the path of seeing the cessation of suffering that take the contaminated as their object.

Regarding the condition of objective sphere (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it refers to the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with outflow that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation, because they take as their object the latent dispositions without outflow that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation.
Regarding the condition of sovereign power (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it refers to the fact that they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the universal proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), there is no causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) by way of sequence, object, or sovereign power.

As for the condition of sequence (*samanantara-pratyaya*): this is because the proclivities associated with the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) objects abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) arise in immediate succession to the universal proclivities abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin.

Regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it refers to all pervasive underlying tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, because they take as their object the underlying tendencies abandoned through the vision of cessation that have the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object.
Regarding the condition of sovereign power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*): it refers to the fact that there is no mutual obstruction.

Regarding those [defilements] that lack causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): because the outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*), they do not take other categories as their objects.

Regarding the non-universal defilements abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), as well as those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there exist sequential conditions (*anupūrva-pratyaya*) and conditions of power (*ādhipatya-pratyaya*), but no causal conditions and no objective conditions (*viṣaya-pratyaya*).

Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that have the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) as their object and are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), are immediately followed by the proclivities that are not universal (*asarvatraga*) and are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), as well as all proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*) and those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the absence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): because the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that have cessation as their object and are abandoned through the vision [of cessation], being non-outflow (*anāsrava*), are not universal; thus, they do not act as causes for other seeds.

Regarding those [defilements] that do not have objects as their conditions: these are the non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, as well as all proclivities abandoned through the vision of the path and the path of cultivation, because they do not take other categories as their objects.

The same explanation applies to the latent tendencies (anuśaya) with outflow conditioned by the cessation [of suffering] and those without outflow conditioned by the cessation [of suffering], as well as the latent tendencies with outflow conditioned by the path [of seeing] and those without outflow conditioned by the path [of seeing].

Regarding the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they possess the conditions of cause (*hetu*), immediate succession (*anantara*), object (*ālambana*), and dominance (*adhipati*).

As for the causal condition (*hetupratyaya*), there are three types of causes: namely, the associated cause (*samprayuktakahetu*), the co-arising cause (*sahabhūhetu*), and the similar cause (*sabhāgahetu*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation give rise, in immediate succession, to proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Regarding the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): the proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation take as their object the proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

The latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*) have sequential, objective, and dominant conditions in relation to all pervasive latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*), but they lack causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Regarding the condition of immediate succession (*samanantara-pratyaya*): the pervasive proclivities (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin arise immediately after the proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Regarding the condition of object (*ālambana-pratyaya*): the pervasive proclivities to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin take as their objects the proclivities to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the absence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*), they do not act as causes for other seeds.

Regarding the non-universal proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, as well as all proclivities abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path: they possess sequential conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya*) and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), but they lack causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) and objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Regarding the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*): from the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, there subsequently arise in immediate succession the non-universal latent proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, as well as all latent proclivities to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
Regarding the condition of dominance (*adhipati-pratyaya*): it is because they do not obstruct one another.

Regarding the absence of the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*): since the proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*), they do not act as causes for other seeds.
Regarding those without objective conditions (*anālambana*), because those latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*), they do not take other categories as their objects.
Herein, the omnipresent cause (*sarvatragahetu*) should be explained in detail as set forth in the *Jñānavarga* of the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 30 and Fascicle 31.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Dharmabhadra, together with Daotai and others, during the Northern Liang Dynasty.
Chapter Two: Chapter on the Single Path (Ekāyana-varga), Part One. The Nine Fetters (Nava-saṃyojana):

the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the fetter of hostility (*pratigha*), the fetter of pride (*māna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya*).
If a certain place is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
If it is bound by the fetter of aversion, is it also bound by the fetter of craving?
Regarding this chapter and the explanation of its meaning, the *uddeśa* (summary) should be explained here in detail.
There are five kinds of locations:
first, the location of the essential nature;
second, the location of the object-condition.
3. The locus of bondage; 4. The locus of causes;
5. The locus of belonging.
Regarding the locus of the intrinsic nature, as stated in the *Dṛṣṭivarga*:
"If there is something to be known in a particular locus, is there also something to be abandoned in that locus?
If there is something to be abandoned in a particular locus, is there also something to be known in that locus?"
In this context, the essence of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) is designated as the "basis" (*sthāna*).
The *Dṛṣṭi-khaṇḍa* also states: "If one attains that basis, does one accomplish that basis?"
Some say that here, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is called "locus" (*sthāna*).
Others say that here, those phenomena which possess the characteristic of acquisition (*prāpti*) and the characteristic of accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) are called "locus."
Regarding the locus (*sthāna*): as stated in the *Prakaraṇa*, "All phenomena should be known through wisdom according to their respective loci.
What is meant by "locus"?
That which accords with the movement of wisdom, accords with the objects of wisdom, and accords with the sphere of wisdom is called the "locus.
The Sūtra also states:
there are forty-four loci of wisdom and seventy-seven loci of wisdom.
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
"In this context, the intrinsic nature and the locus are being explained. Why is that?"
One contemplates the branches of existence through patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*jñāna*); the essence of this patience and wisdom is called the "locus" (*sthāna*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states: "In this context, it refers to the locus of conditions."
Why is this so? Because it takes conditioned existence (*bhava*) as its object through wisdom and patience, it is called "the basis of objective support" (*ālambanasthāna*).

Regarding the "basis of bondage" (*bandhanasthāna*), as stated here: if there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*rāgasaṃyojana*) in a certain basis, is there also bondage by the fetter of aversion (*pratighasaṃyojana*) in that same basis?
The five kinds of phenomena are called "bases. Why is this so?
Because the five kinds of afflictions are able to bind these five kinds of phenomena.
The five kinds of phenomena refer to those abandoned through the vision of suffering up to those abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Regarding the locus of causal conditions, as stated in the *Prakaraṇa*:
"What are phenomena that possess a locus?"
What is the dharma that has no locus? ...
up to ... what is the dharma that has a cause?
What is the dharma that is without a cause?
Dharmas that have causes are called "dharmas with a locus"; dharmas that lack causes are called "dharmas without a locus.
As it is said:
"The bhikṣu whose mind is tranquil Is able to sever all loci."
"Exhausting the suffering of birth and death, one will not undergo future existence.
Herein, the cause is stated as the locus. Why is this so?
Because there is a cause, there is birth and death; because the cause is severed, birth and death are severed.
Regarding that which belongs to a place, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"One should abandon the mind of attachment to fields, houses, and marketplaces as being one's own."
As a verse says:
"If one does not relinquish fields and wealth, oxen and horses, male and female slaves, and various forms of sensual beauty,
one shall not attain liberation."
As worldly people say:
"This object belongs to me," or "This place belongs to me.
Among these five types of locations, the discussion is conducted based on the location of attachment (*niśraya*), and not based on the other locations.
Furthermore, there are those who say there are five kinds of bases:
first, the base of the elements (dhātu);
second, the base of the sense-spheres (āyatana).
Third, the locus of the aggregates;
fourth, the locus of the world;
fifth, the locus of the moment.
Regarding these ten bases (*āyatana*), the discussion is conducted based on the basis of dependence (*niśraya-āyatana*).
The Vātsīputrīyas assert the following:
"The basis is a conventional designation (*prajñapti-dharma*); it has no fixed intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)."
The fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not mere designations (*prajñapti*), nor are sentient beings (*sattva*) mere designations;
each has its own determinate essence. The Abhidharmikas maintain this view:
the locus (*sthāna*) is not a mere designation, the fetters are not mere designations, but sentient beings are mere designations.
The Dārṣṭāntikas state as follows:

the fetters do not exist as mere designations and yet possess a determinate essence; whereas the locus exists as a mere designation, and sentient beings exist as mere designations while possessing a determinate essence.
Question: For what reason does he say that location is a conventional designation (prajñapti-dharma) and lacks a fixed essence? Answer:
He speaks thus: "Because within the realm of objects there may be desire or the absence of desire.

For example, when others see a beautiful woman, they may give rise to a mind of reverence, or a mind of desire, or a mind of anger, or a mind of compassion, or a mind of revulsion, or a mind of pity, or a mind of equanimity."
One who gives rise to a mind of reverence is like a child seeing his mother;
one who gives rise to a mind of desire is like one with many lustful cravings seeing a lovely form;
one who gives rise to a mind of anger is like enemies meeting one another.
One who gives rise to a mind of affection is like a wife seeing her husband.
One who gives rise to a mind of revulsion is like one practicing the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā).
One who gives rise to a mind of compassion is a person free from desire, who thinks as follows:
Such beautiful forms will soon perish.
One who gives rise to a mind of equanimity attains arhatship.
Because one gives rise to such minds of desire or non-desire toward sense objects, the locus of wisdom is a dharma of mere designation, lacking any fixed essence.
These afflictions pertain to both the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) and the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).

Regarding those that pertain to the five groups of sensory consciousness: past [afflictions] are bound to past locations; present [afflictions] are bound to present locations; future phenomena that are destined to arise are bound to future locations; and those not destined to arise are bound to locations belonging to all three times.
Regarding those that belong to the mental sphere (*manobhūmi*): the past are bound to the three times; the future are also bound to the three times; and the present are also bound to the three times.

Based on the arising of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are bound to form (*rūpa*); those associated factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*) are bound by association (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*).
Those associated phenomena are the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and the mental-object-base (*dharmāyatana*).
This applies likewise up to the proclivities (*anuśaya*) that arise dependent upon body-consciousness.
As for the proclivities that arise dependent upon mind-consciousness, they are bound to the twelve bases; those associated with them are "associated-bound" (*saṃprayukta-bandhana*).

Regarding "associated phenomena" (*saṃprayuktadharma*), these are the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*). To speak in this manner is the *Ekottaravibhāṣā*.
If, in a certain place, there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*rāgasaṃyojana*), is there also bondage by the fetter of aversion (*pratighasaṃyojana*)?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), one is also bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
Is there, however, one who is bound by the fetter of craving but not bound by the fetter of ill-will?
Answer: There are.

Those dharmas of the form and formless realms for which the fetter of craving has not been severed exist within the three realms; they possess five kinds of conditions and are tainted, yet not all-pervasive.
The fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana) exists in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) with five types of conditions; it is associated with outflows (sāsrava) but is not omnipresent (asarvatraga).
If one is bound by all fetters, then in the five locations of the desire realm, one is bound both by the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) and by the fetter of aversion.

If one is bound by the fetter of aversion and also bound by the fetter of craving, yet not by all fetters, then the fetter of craving persists throughout the three realms; therefore, it is appropriate to apply the subsequent phrase.
If a location is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)? Answer:
If there is a location bound by the fetter of aversion, it is also a location bound by the fetter of craving; these are the five types of locations belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of attachment but not bound by the fetter of aversion? Answer: There is.
The fetter of craving for the form and formless realms has not been abandoned.

Regarding "not abandoned," there may be those for whom the fetter of craving for eight stages has not been abandoned, or even those for whom the fetter of craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception has not been abandoned.

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be five kinds of fetters of craving that have not yet been abandoned, or even those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that have not yet been abandoned.

Within that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, regarding those things to be abandoned through the path of cultivation, there may be nine kinds of fetters of craving that have not yet been abandoned, or even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) that have not yet been abandoned.
Because this is stated in general terms, it says "bound to the realms of form and formlessness.

When the fetter of craving for phenomena (*dharmatṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of craving, and not being bound by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
Why is this so? Because in the form and formless realms, there is no fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*). Question:
Why is it that there is no fetter of malice (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*) in the form and formless realms?
The answer is:
because they are not the proper field or vessel for it, and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, because sentient beings weary of and are afflicted by anger, they aspire to be born in the realm of form or the formless realm; if there were the fetter of anger in those realms, they would not cultivate the necessary means for birth therein.
If a dharma exists both in a lower stage and in a higher stage, then there would be no gradual abandonment of dharmas.
If there were no gradual abandonment of dharmas, then there would be no ultimate abandonment of dharmas.
Why is this? Because the dharmas that are abandoned in succession can give rise to the dharmas of ultimate abandonment.
If there were no dharmas of ultimate abandonment, there would be no liberation or transcendence.
In order to avoid such a fault, there is no fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, if there are the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) or the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), then there is the fetter of ill-will.

Why is this so? Because sentient beings give rise to anger toward others due to the faculty of sorrow and the faculty of suffering, whereas in the form and formless realms, these faculties of sorrow and suffering do not exist.

Furthermore, wherever there is a lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and a lack of dread of blame (*anapatrāpya*), there is the fetter of anger; it is because of a lack of shame and a lack of dread of blame that sentient beings give rise to anger, yet in the form and formless realms, there is no lack of shame or lack of dread of blame.

Just as it is with shamelessness and lack of dread, so too should one understand it to be with stinginess, the male and female faculties, the craving for physical food and sexual desire, the five hindrances, and the five sublime sensual pleasures.
Furthermore, where there is the characteristic of enmity and aversion, there is the fetter of ill will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*).

This characteristic of enmity and aversion consists of the nine bases of vexation (*nava āghāta-vastūni*); these do not exist in the form and formless realms. Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka has said:
"Sentient beings give rise to the fetter of ill will because of enmity and aversion; such enmity and aversion do not exist in the form and formless realms."
Furthermore, in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there is an immediate antidote to the fetter of ill-will (vyāpāda-saṃyojana); this immediate antidote is loving-kindness (maitrī).
It is just as there are no clouds or obscurations where the Vairambha wind blows; so it is in that case as well.
If a person is bound by the fetter of craving in a certain state, are they also bound by the fetter of conceit? Answer: It is so.
If one is bound by the fetter of pride, is one also bound by the fetter of craving? Answer: It is so.
Why is this so? Because these two fetters both exist within the three realms and possess five types of conditions, as they are tainted (*sāsrava*) but not omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).

If one is fully bound by the five types of phenomena across the three realms, being bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) entails also being bound by the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*), and being bound by the fetter of conceit likewise entails being bound by the fetter of craving. Therefore, such propositions may be established.
If a location is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of craving exists throughout the three realms; it possesses five types of conditions, is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and is not universal (*asarvatraga*).

The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) within the three realms has five types of objects; these include both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal (*asarvatraga*).

If one is bound by all five types of dharmas within the three realms, one is fettered both by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and by the fetter of ignorance; likewise, if one is fettered by the fetter of ignorance, one is also fettered by the fetter of craving.

If one is not bound by the latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*), then one is long subject to all pervasive [defilements] that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object; therefore, it is possible to apply the "conformity to the preceding clause" (*pūrvapādaka*).
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) in a particular place, is there also bondage by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If there is bondage by the fetter of craving, there is also bondage by the fetter of ignorance.
As for the "locations," these refer to the five types of locations within the three realms.
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: There is.

For one in whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the latent tendencies of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin have not yet been abandoned regarding those phenomena.
When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the fetter of craving and the fetter of ignorance to be abandoned by seeing suffering are severed;
however, the fetter of ignorance to be abandoned by seeing origin remains bound as a condition to those phenomena to be abandoned by seeing suffering.
Why is this? Because the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) is universal (*sarvatraga*),
whereas the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) is not so.
Why is this so? Because the fetter of craving within one's own continuum has already been severed.

The fetter of craving abandoned through the vision of the origin of suffering does not bind by way of an object toward phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, because it is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
It is not bound by association, because it belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
If a place is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of craving exists within the three realms; it has five types of conditions, is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), and is not universal (*asarvatraga*).

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms and possesses four types of conditions. Regarding the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), it is both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal.

If one is bound by all fetters within the five locations of the three realms, one is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and also bound by the fetter of views; likewise, if one is bound by the fetter of views, one is also bound by the fetter of craving.
If one is not bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), then [the other fetters] increase among the five types.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) increases with respect to all pervasive objects and those conditioned by the untainted (*anāsrava*); therefore, four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.
If a state is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
This should be expanded into four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is bound by the fetter of craving but not by the fetter of views: it refers to those for whom the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and who possess factors dissociated from views (*dṛṣṭi-viprayukta-dharma*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) or the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*).

Regarding the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been abandoned, what are those factors associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*) that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*)?
The answer is:

they are precisely those factors associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), craving, hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

Thus, being dissociated from [right] view and bound by the fetter of craving, one forms a connection through the object-condition within one's own group, and forms a connection through the object-condition within another's group.
It is neither bound by association nor by view.
Why is this? Because views are universal (sarvatraga).

Those [afflictions] that take the five kinds [of objects] as their objects have already been abandoned; as for those not yet abandoned, they do not bind by way of taking other factors dissociated from views as their objects. Because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they do not bind through dissociation; furthermore, because they belong to different aggregates, a self-entity does not correspond with itself.

Regarding the fetter of craving for dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation, there are those for whom it has not yet been severed across nine stages, or there are those for whom it remains unsevered even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Regarding the fetter of craving to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be nine types that have not yet been abandoned, or even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade that have not yet been abandoned.

In brief, when the fetter of craving for the phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation has not yet been severed, this is called being bound by the fetter of craving, but not being bound by the fetter of views. Why is this so?
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is universal (*sarvatraga*).
For one who has already abandoned that which takes the five categories as its object, there is no longer any fetter of views to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the craving-fetter (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) associated with the objects of the factors dissociated from views—which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing—has not yet been abandoned.
What are the factors dissociated from views that are abandoned by the path of seeing?
The answer is:
those very factors associated with false view, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and observances, doubt, craving, hatred, pride, and ignorance.

Such dharmas that are dissociated from views are bound by the fetter of craving; they are bound to their own group by the bond of objective condition and the bond of association, and bound to other groups by the bond of objective condition, but they are not bound by the fetter of views.
Why is this so? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is universal (*sarvatraga*).

Those [factors] among the five types that can be taken as objects have already been abandoned; as for those not yet abandoned, they do not bind by way of objectifying those factors because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object. Furthermore, they do not constitute a binding through association (*saṃprayoga*), because they belong to a different aggregate and a self-entity cannot be associated with itself.
Regarding the dharmas to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*), the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) remains unsevered, as previously explained.
For a disciple of the Blessed One who has fully realized the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), the fetter of craving remains unsevered; the detailed exposition is as above.

Regarding those who are bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*): when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the fetter of views to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) remains unsevered.

When the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the fetter of craving to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) is severed, and the fetter of views is also severed.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that is to be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) binds, as its object, those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); it is bound by the fetter of views, but not by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Why is this?

Because the fetter of craving belonging to its own category has already been abandoned, and the fetter of craving belonging to another category does not bind as an object toward phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, since it is not universal (*asarvatraga*).
It is not bound by association, because it belongs to a different aggregate.
Regarding those bound by both: one who is fully fettered is bound by both the factors abandoned through the path of seeing and the factors abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Question: For what reason is one called "bound by all fetters" (sakalabandhana)? Answer:
Bound by five bases and also able to bind five bases, it is therefore called "fully bound.
That which can fetter the five bases refers to the five kinds of severance of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
That which is bound by the five bases refers to the five kinds of dharmas of severance.

For phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) by one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), there is bondage by one type of craving-fetter (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and two types of view-fetter (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
It is the same for those abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
For phenomena associated with views abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), there is bondage by one type of craving-fetter and three types of view-fetter.

Regarding phenomena not associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-viprayukta-dharma*), there is bondage by one type of fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and bondage by two types of fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
The same applies to those abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*).
Regarding phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya-dharma*), there is bondage by one type of fetter of craving and bondage by two types of fetters of views.

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [types of fetters] regarding those phenomena abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, and the vision of the path, as well as those abandoned through the cultivation of the path.

Regarding those abandoned through the vision of origin and those abandoned through the cultivation of the path, one is bound by one type of the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and one type of the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

Regarding phenomena associated with views that are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*): there is bondage by one type of fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and bondage by two types of fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Regarding phenomena dissociated from views: there is bondage by one type of fetter of craving and bondage by one type of fetter of views.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Regarding dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), they are bound only by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and not by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*); therefore, this is not mentioned.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [types of fetters] regarding those factors associated with views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.
Regarding those factors associated with views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation, one is bound by one type of the fetter of craving and one type of the fetter of views.

Dharmas dissociated from views that are abandoned through the vision of cessation are bound only by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); therefore, they are not mentioned [in this context].
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*).

Regarding the phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are bound only by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

As for those not bound by either, these are the phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*) and the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana*) once the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen; they are not bound by either.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, one is unbound from both [types of] phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of origination, and the vision of cessation.
For a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, one is unbound from both [types of] phenomena abandoned through the vision of the path.
Having already become detached from desire, one is unbound to both [the mind and] the phenomena bound to the desire realm.
Having already become detached from the desires of the form and formless realms, one is unbound to both the phenomena bound to the form and formless realms.
Why is this so? If the fetters are severed, their locus is also severed.
Regarding this, the following argument is made:

Is there any dharma associated with views that is abandoned by the path of seeing the cessation [of suffering], which is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), yet is not such that it is not driven by the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*)?
Answer: There is.

One who has severed the six types of desire attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). When the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the six types of factors associated with views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path are bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Why is this? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Those [factors] among the five types that take [the defiled] as their object have already been abandoned; those six types of views that take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object have also been abandoned; the remaining three types have not yet been abandoned.

Regarding the uncontaminated objects of vision (*anāsrava-ālambana-dṛṣṭi*), there is no bond of objectification (*ālambana-bandhana*) toward the six types of already-abandoned phenomena, because they take the uncontaminated as their object.
There is no bond of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because they belong to a different aggregate.

As for the three types of craving-fetters (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) that have not yet been abandoned, they act as bonds of objectification toward the six types of already-abandoned phenomena to be severed by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path; it is not the case that those [phenomena] are not influenced by the underlying tendencies of view (*dṛṣṭy-anuśaya*).

Why is this so? Because the three types of views constitute the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), while the five types of views constitute the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*); this is because among the underlying tendencies of views, one is further driven by the underlying tendencies of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) and attachment to precepts and observances (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*).
As it is with the fetter of craving and the fetter of views, so it is also with the fetter of craving and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).

Why is this so? Just as the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms and has four types of objects of abandonment— being either with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and being either pervasive (*vyāpaka*) or non-pervasive—
the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is likewise.
If a certain location is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of craving exists within the three realms; it is abandoned through five modes and takes contaminated objects as its conditions, but it is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*).
