The fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms and is severed through four kinds of objects. Among the outflowing (*sāsrava*) factors, some are universal (*sarvatraga*) and some are not universal.

If one is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) across the five locations of the three realms while still possessing all bonds (*sakalabandhana*), one is likewise bound by the fetter of grasping.
If one is bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna*), one is also bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

However, if one is not fully bound by the fetter of craving, then [the fetter of grasping] is more extensive than the five types of grasping and more extensive than all pervasive [fetters]. Therefore, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.

Or, one may be bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*); this is elaborated at length as a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*). Regarding being bound by the fetter of craving but not by the fetter of grasping:

it refers to one for whom the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; the fetter of craving regarding the phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharma*) has not been severed; or the fetter of craving regarding the nine stages has not been severed, up to and including the fetter of craving regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) having not been severed.

Regarding the fetter of craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be nine types that have not yet been abandoned, or even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade that have not yet been abandoned.
In brief, the fetter of craving for phenomena to be abandoned by the path of cultivation has not yet been abandoned.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, and the fetter of craving for phenomena to be abandoned by the cultivation of the path has not been severed—

as explained in detail above— a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, yet has not severed the fetter of craving for phenomena to be abandoned by the cultivation of the path, is said to be bound by the fetter of craving, but not bound by the fetter of grasping.
The fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) that takes the five types as its object has already been abandoned. Why is this?
Because the fetter of grasping is universally pervasive (*sarvatraga*).
Those who have already abandoned the five types of objects that can serve as focal points, yet for whom the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) is not abandoned by the path of cultivation:

those who are bound by the fetter of grasping but not by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) are those for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and thus the fetter of grasping pertaining to phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin remains unabandoned.

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, if the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by seeing suffering has been severed, the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) is also severed.

Regarding the fetter of grasping to be abandoned by seeing the origin, its objective tie (*ālambana-bandhana*) is severed by seeing suffering. This is called being bound by the fetter of grasping but not bound by the fetter of craving.

Why is this so? Because the fetter of craving within one's own continuum has already been severed, and the fetter of craving in another's continuum does not act as a causal bond, since it is not omnipresent (*asarvatraga*);
nor is it a bond of association (*saṃprayoga*), because it belongs to a different aggregate (*skandha*).
Regarding those bound by both: dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation that are possessed by all fetters are bound by both.

Dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering that are possessed by all fetters are bound by one type of *anunaya-saṃyojana* (the fetter of attachment) and bound by two types of *parāmarśa-saṃyojana* (the fetters of grasping).
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya*).
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha*) are bound by one type of fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and three types of fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*).
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga*).

Regarding those [factors] abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one is bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and two are bound by the fetters of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*).

When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the factors abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and the path of cultivation are bound by both.

Dharmas abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*) are bound by one type of fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and also bound by one type of fetter of clinging (*upādāna-saṃyojana*).

Dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-prahātavya*) are bound by one type of fetter of craving and two types of fetters of clinging.

Dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering are bound only by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) and not by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*); therefore, they are not mentioned [in this context].

When the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path are bound by both.

The dharmas abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana-prahātavya*) are bound by one type of fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) and one type of fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*).
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana-prahātavya*).
As for the dharmas abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*), they are bound only by the fetter of craving and not by the fetter of grasping; therefore, [the latter] is not mentioned.
When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [fetters] to those phenomena abandoned through the vision of the path.
Those phenomena abandoned through the vision of the path are bound by one type of fetter of craving and one type of fetter of grasping.
Those abandoned through the path of cultivation are explained in detail as above.

Regarding "not bound by either": when the knowledge of origin has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, the factors abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin are not bound by either.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, one is unbound from both [types of] phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation.
For a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, one is unbound from both [types of] phenomena abandoned through the vision of the path.
When sensual craving has been abandoned, one is unbound from both [the fetters] regarding the phenomena bound to the desire realm.
When craving for the form realm has been abandoned, one is unbound from both regarding the phenomena bound to the form realm.
When craving for the formless realm has been abandoned, one is unbound from both regarding all phenomena.
Why is this so? Because if those fetters are severed, their locus is also severed.
If there is a bond of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) bound to a certain locus, is there also a bond of resentment (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) bound to it?
The fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms; it is abandoned through five modes of abandonment, takes contaminated objects as its condition, and is not universal.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) exists within the desire realm; it is abandoned through the path of cultivation, takes contaminated objects as its condition, and is not universal.

If these are the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation by one who is bound by all fetters, then if they are bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), they are also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*); and if they are bound by the fetter of envy, they are also bound by the fetter of craving.

If one is not bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), one remains long within the three realms and undergoes five kinds of severance; therefore, it is appropriate to apply the latter phrase.
If a place is bound by the fetter of craving, is it also bound by the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā*), one is also bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Regarding the dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*), one is bound by one type of the fetter of craving and one type of the fetter of envy.
Is it possible to be bound by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)? Answer:

Regarding the factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga-prahātavya*), the fetter of craving has not yet been abandoned; that is, either the four types of factors to be abandoned by the path of vision have not had their fetter of craving abandoned, or even up to the point where the fetter of craving for those factors to be abandoned by the path of vision has not yet been abandoned.

When the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) for phenomena bound to the form and formless realms has not been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of craving but not being bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*). Why is this?
Because there is no fetter of envy in the form and formless realms; the meaning of the absence of the fetter of envy is as explained above.
As it is with the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), so too is the explanation for the fetter of craving and the fetter of stinginess.
As it is with the section on the fetter of craving, so too is the explanation for the section on the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*). Why is this so?
Both of these exist within the three realms and are abandoned through five modes; they take contaminated objects as their conditions but are not universal.
If a person is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in a particular place, are they also bound by the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) exists in the desire realm; it is abandoned through five modes of abandonment, takes impure objects as its condition, and is not universal.
The fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) exists in the three realms; it is abandoned through five modes of abandonment, takes impure objects as its condition, and is not universal.

If one who is bound by all fetters is connected to the five locations associated with the desire realm, they are bound by the fetter of ill-will and also bound by the fetter of conceit; if they are bound by the fetter of conceit, they are also bound by the fetter of ill-will.

If one is not bound by the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) and remains long within the three realms, it is therefore possible to apply the "conformity with the preceding clause" (*pūrvapada-anuvartana*).
If there is the binding of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in a particular state, is there also the binding of the fetter of pride?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will, one is also bound by the fetter of conceit.
As for their locus, these are the five types of [defilements] to be abandoned within the desire realm.
Is it possible that one is bound by the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:

there are those in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) for whom the fetter of pride has not yet been abandoned; or there are those for whom the fetter of pride in eight stages has not yet been abandoned; or there are even those for whom the fetter of pride up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) has not yet been abandoned.

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are those who are bound by the fetter of conceit abandoned through five types, and there are those who are bound by the fetter of conceit abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Regarding that fetter of conceit abandoned through the path of cultivation, there may be nine types that have not yet been abandoned, or even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade (*mṛdumṛdu*) that have not yet been abandoned.

In brief, when the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) in the form and formless realms has not yet been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of conceit but not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*). Why is this so?
In the form and formless realms, there is no fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*).
The meaning of "in the form and formless realms there is no fetter of ill-will" is as explained above.
If a place is bound by the fetter of ill-will, is it also bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)?

The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) exists in the desire realm; it is abandoned through five modes [of the path of cultivation], takes contaminated objects as its object, and is not universal.
The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) exists in the three realms; it is abandoned through five modes, takes both contaminated and uncontaminated objects as its object, and is universal.

If one who is bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana) resides in any of the five locations within the desire realm, they are bound by the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana) and also bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana); and if they are bound by the fetter of ignorance, they are also bound by the fetter of ill-will.

If one is not liberated from the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*)—being long bound within the three realms and pervading all things—then it is possible to apply the "conformity with the preceding clause" (*pūrvapādaka*).
If there is the binding of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in a certain place, is there also the binding of the fetter of ignorance?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*).
As for the locations, these are the five types of locations bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: Yes.

For instance, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the fetter of ignorance regarding the factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and those to be abandoned by the vision of origin remains unsevered.

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, one is bound by the fetter of ignorance associated with the objects to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the objects to be abandoned through the vision of the origin; this is called being bound by the fetter of ignorance and not being bound by the fetter of ill-will.
Why is this so? Because the seeds of the fetter of ill-will within oneself have already been severed.
As for the seeds planted by others, they do not constitute a non-objective bond regarding what is abandoned through the vision of suffering, because they are not universal.
It is not bound by association, because it belongs to another aggregate.

Regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness, it may be that the fetter of ignorance of the eight stages has not yet been abandoned, or it may be that the fetter of ignorance up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) has not yet been abandoned.

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be five types [of afflictions] that have not yet been abandoned, or even up to those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) that have not yet been abandoned.

Regarding those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be nine types that have not yet been abandoned, or even up to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) grade that has not yet been abandoned.

In brief, when the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) bound to the realms of form and formlessness has not been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of ignorance but not being bound by the fetter of ill-will (pratigha-saṃyojana).
Why is this? Because there is no ill-will in the form realm and the formless realm.
That there is no fetter of ill-will in the form and formless realms is as explained above.
If a certain state is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ill-will exists in the desire realm; it is abandoned in five ways, takes contaminated objects as its object, and is not universal.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms and is abandoned through four modes. It takes as its object all contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena—both those that are universal (*sarvatraga*) and those that are not.

In the case of one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), regarding the five types of abandonment in the desire realm: wherever there is bondage by the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), there is also bondage by the fetter of views; and wherever there is bondage by the fetter of views, there is also bondage by the fetter of malice.

If one is not bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) persists through five types of abandonment, while the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) persists throughout all pervasive [defilements] of the three realms; therefore, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.
If one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), is one not also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
This should be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding being bound by the fetter of ill-will but not by the fetter of views: this refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), for whom the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, [and who possesses] factors associated with the view of cessation and the view of the path belonging to the desire realm that are dissociated from views (*dṛṣṭi-viprayukta-dharma*).

Regarding the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) that has not yet been abandoned, what are those factors associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*)—which are bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) and are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*) or the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), yet are dissociated from [the view of] self?
The answer is:

they are precisely those factors associated with false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the esteeming of precepts and vows (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).

In this state, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned; it is bound by association with the objects of one's own group, but not bound by association with the objects of another's group, and it is not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Why is this so? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).

Those [factors] among the five types that have already been abandoned no longer constitute a bond through being an object for the remaining unabandoned factors that are dissociated from views, because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
It is not bound by association (*saṃprayoga*), because it belongs to a different aggregate and because a self-nature cannot be bound by itself.

Regarding the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) among the factors of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), it may be that nine types remain unsevered, or even down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) grade remaining unsevered.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen, but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) associated with views—which is to be abandoned by the path of seeing and bound to the desire realm—has not yet been severed.
What, then, are those phenomena associated with views that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing and bound to the desire realm?
Answer: It consists of those factors associated with wrong view, adherence to views, adherence to precepts and rituals, craving, hatred, pride, ignorance, and doubt.

In this dharma, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has not yet been abandoned; it functions as a bond through its object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and a bond through association (*samprayoga-bandhana*) within one's own group (*svakāya*), and as a bond through its object toward other groups (*parakāya*). It is not, however, bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*). Why is this so?
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).

Regarding those [factors] among the five types that are capable of being its objects, those already abandoned do not constitute a bond through objectification (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to factors dissociated from views (*viprayukta-dharma*), because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;

nor do they constitute a bond through association (*saṃprayoga-bandhana*), because they belong to a different aggregate (*anya-skandha*) and because it is improper for a self-entity to be associated with itself.

The fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) regarding those dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*) has not been severed; the detailed explanation is as above.

For a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭi-prativedha*), the fetter of ill-will regarding those dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation has not been severed; the detailed explanation is as above.
This is called being bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

As for being bound by the fetter of views but not by the fetter of ill-will: it refers to one who has not yet abandoned sensual desire, for whom the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; thus, regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin, the fetter of views remains unsevered.

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, the fetter of ill-will and the fetter of views to be abandoned by seeing suffering have already been abandoned; however, there remains the connection of the fetter of views to be abandoned by seeing the origin. Thus, regarding phenomena to be abandoned by seeing suffering, one is bound by the fetter of views, but not bound by the fetter of ill-will.
Why is this so? Because the seeds of the fetter of ill-will within oneself have already been severed.

As for those produced by others, they do not constitute a bond through objectification (*ālambana*) regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), because they are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
It is not bound by association, because it belongs to a different aggregate.

Regarding the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) in the form and formless realms that have not yet been abandoned: in some cases, the fetters of views of eight stages have not been abandoned; in others, up to and including the fetters of views of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) have not been abandoned.

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be those who have not yet abandoned four types of fetters of false view, or those who have not yet abandoned the fetters to be abandoned by insight up to those to be abandoned by the path of vision.

In brief, when the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) regarding phenomena associated with the form and formless realms has not been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of views but not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*). Why is that?
In the realms of form and formlessness, there is no fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); the detailed explanation is as above.
What is meant by "bound by both"?
All phenomena in the desire realm that are subject to abandonment through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, while still possessing full bondage, are bound by both.

For those dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) by one who possesses all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), there is bondage by one type of enmity-fetter (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and bondage by two types of view-fetters (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
It is the same for those dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).
Dharmas associated with views that are abandoned through the vision of cessation are bound by one type of fetter of malice and three types of fetters of views.
Dharmas dissociated from views are bound by one type of fetter of malice and two types of fetters of views.
The factors abandoned by the path of seeing are also like this.
As for the factors of the desire realm abandoned by the path of cultivation, they are bound by one type of fetter, resentment (*pratigha*), and two types of fetters, the views (*dṛṣṭi*).

When sensual craving has not yet been abandoned, and the knowledge of suffering has already arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [fetters] to those phenomena associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through the cultivation of the path.
Dharmas abandoned through the vision of the origin (samudaya-darśana-prahātavya) are bound by one type of fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana) and one type of fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana).
Dharmas associated with views abandoned through the vision of cessation (nirodha-darśana-prahātavya) are bound by one type of fetter of aversion and two types of fetters of views.
Regarding phenomena not associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-viprayukta-dharma*), there is bondage by one type of enmity-tie (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and bondage by one type of view-tie (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
It is the same for phenomena abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya-dharma*).
Regarding phenomena abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya-dharma*), there is bondage by one type of enmity-tie and bondage by one type of view-tie.

The phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), but are not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); therefore, they are not mentioned [in that context].

When the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the phenomena associated with the view to be abandoned by the vision of cessation belonging to the desire realm are bound by both.

Regarding the factors associated with views that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation within the desire realm: they are bound by one type of fetter of malice (pratigha-saṃyojana) and one type of fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana).
As for those factors dissociated from views, although they are bound by the fetter of malice, they are not bound by the fetter of views; therefore, this is not mentioned.
The same applies to the dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Although the dharmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are bound by the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), they are not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); therefore, this is not mentioned.

For one who has not yet abandoned desire-attachment, when the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the factors associated with the views to be abandoned by the path of vision that are bound to the desire realm are bound by both; they are bound by one type of enmity-fetter (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and one type of view-fetter (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

Although the factors associated with the desire realm that are abandoned by the path of seeing—specifically those dissociated from views—as well as those abandoned by the path of cultivation, are bound by the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), they are not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); therefore, they are not mentioned [in this context].
This is called being bound by both.

As for those who are not bound: when the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, one is not bound by either [affliction] regarding those phenomena abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination.
The factors dissociated from views that are abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path within the form and formless realms are unbound by both.
The factors abandoned through the cultivation of the path within the form and formless realms are unbound by both.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, one is unbound from both [types of] phenomena in the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, origin, and cessation;
one is also unbound from both the factors associated with the form and formless realms that are dissociated from vision as well as those to be abandoned by cultivation.
For a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, there is no bondage whatsoever to the factors abandoned through the path of seeing.
Likewise, there is no bondage whatsoever to the factors abandoned through the path of cultivation that pertain to the realms of form and formlessness.
Having already become detached from desire, one is unbound by both [the fetters] regarding the dharmas bound to the desire realm.
Having already become detached from the desire for form, one is unbound by both [the fetters] regarding the dharmas bound to the form realm.
Having already become detached from the desire for the formless realm, one is unbound by all [fetters].
Why is this so? Because those fetters are severed, their bases are also severed.
As it is with the fetter of ill-will and the fetter of views, so too is it explained for the fetter of ill-will and the fetter of doubt.

Why is this? Because these two fetters both exist within the three realms, are abandoned through four modes of abandonment, take as their objects both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), and consist of both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal factors.
Question: It may be granted that there is the bondage of the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and thus it makes sense to speak of non-bondage there;

however, since the fetter of malice does not exist within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how can you say that beings in those realms are not bound by the fetter of malice?
Answer: There are two kinds of non-bondage:
first, attaining non-bondage from bondage; [the second is inherent non-bondage].
Second, non-attachment by nature (*prakṛty-ananubaddha*).
Non-attachment pertaining to the desire realm is "attaining non-attachment from what was bound," because of the presence of the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*);
non-attachment pertaining to the form and formless realms is "non-attachment by nature," because of the absence of the fetter of ill-will.
It is also as stated in the Vinaya:
there are two types of persons called "pure and liberated": first, those who have never violated the precepts; [and second, those who have committed an offense but have purified it].
Second, although there have been transgressions, they have been removed according to the Dharma.
One who has never violated the precepts is said to have "arisen from original purity and liberation.
One who, although having committed transgressions, has removed them according to the Dharma, is said to have "arisen from what was not originally pure, yet attained purity and liberation."
It is likewise in this case.
If a place is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ill-will exists in the desire realm; it is abandoned in five ways, takes contaminated objects as its object, and is not universal (*asarvatraga*).

The fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms; it is abandoned in four ways and takes contaminated objects as its condition. It is both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal.

If one is bound by all fetters and is connected to the five bases of the desire realm, then if one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), one is also bound by the fetter of grasping; and if one is bound by the fetter of grasping, one is also bound by the fetter of ill-will.

If one is not bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) persists through five stages of abandonment, while the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) persists throughout the three realms; as these are universal (*sarvatraga*), four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can thus be established.
If a certain state possesses the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), does it also possess the binding of the fetter of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*)?
This should be elaborated at length as a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is bound by the fetter of ill-will but not bound by the fetter of grasping: it refers to one who has not yet abandoned desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), for whom the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen; in such a person, the fetter of ill-will regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya-dharma*) has not been severed—either nine types remain unsevered, or even down to the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) grade remains unsevered.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the fetter of ill-will toward those phenomena of the desire realm associated with the path of cultivation that have not yet been abandoned remains unsevered.

For a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths, when sensual craving has not yet been abandoned, the fetter of ill-will toward those phenomena of the desire realm associated with the path of cultivation that have not yet been abandoned remains unsevered.
This is called being bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) but not being bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*). Why is this?

Because the fetter of grasping is all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*); those who have already abandoned that which takes the five types [of objects] as its cognitive object no longer possess the fetter of grasping among the phenomena to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-dharma*).

One who is bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is one for whom sensual desire has not yet been abandoned; although the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen, the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, and thus the fetter of grasping regarding those phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origin remains unabandoned.

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, the fetters of grasping and hostility to be abandoned by seeing suffering in the desire realm have already been severed, while the fetters of grasping to be abandoned by seeing the origin remain as active bonds.
Dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are bound by the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), but not by the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).

Why is this? Because the seeds of aversion belonging to one's own category have already been severed; as for those belonging to other categories, they do not constitute a binding object-condition (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to what is abandoned through the vision of suffering, because they are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
It is not bound by association, because it belongs to another aggregate.

Regarding the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness that have not yet been abandoned: in some cases, the fetters of grasping of the eight stages have not yet been abandoned; in others, they extend even up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be four types of fetters not yet abandoned, or even as many as one type not yet abandoned.

Generally speaking, when the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness has not been abandoned, this is called being bound by the fetter of grasping and not being bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).
In the form and formless realms, there is no fetter of malice; the detailed explanation is as above.
Regarding those bound by both: the dharmas of the desire realm that are bound by all fetters and are to be abandoned through the path of vision and the path of cultivation are bound by both.

Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) for one who is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*): they are bound by one type of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and two types of the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).

The same explanation applies to those to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).

Regarding the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*): they are bound by one type of fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and two types of fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
The same explanation applies to the phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*).

When sensual desire has not yet been abandoned, and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [fetters] regarding those phenomena of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Those [factors] abandoned through seeing the origin and those abandoned through the path of cultivation are bound by one type of fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and one type of fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*).
Factors of the desire realm abandoned through seeing cessation are bound by one type of fetter of aversion and two types of fetter of grasping.
The same applies to the teachings regarding the phenomena abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Although the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*) are bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), they are not bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); therefore, this is not mentioned.

When sensual craving has not yet been exhausted, and the knowledge of origination has already arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, one is bound by one type of fetter of ill-will and one type of fetter of clinging toward those phenomena associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation.
The same applies to the teachings regarding the dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

As for the dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), although they are bound by the fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), they are not bound by the fetter of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*); therefore, they are not mentioned.

When sensual craving has not yet been abandoned, and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [the fetters] regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by the vision of the path (*darśana-heya*); specifically, one is bound by one type of the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and one type of the fetter of clinging (*parigraha-saṃyojana*).
The dharmas to be abandoned by the path of cultivation are as explained above;
these are called "bound by both.
Regarding those "not bound by either," the detailed explanation is as in the original sūtra.
Up to the point of being free from desire for the formless realm, both are unbound. Why is this?
If those fetters are severed, their basis is also severed.
If a place is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ill-will exists in the desire realm, as explained above.

The fetter of envy exists in the desire realm; it is abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), takes contaminated objects as its object (*sāsrava-ālambana*), and is not universal (*asarvatraga*).

If it is a location in the desire realm that is subject to abandonment through the path of cultivation by one who is bound by all fetters, then if it is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), it is also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*); and if it is bound by the fetter of envy, it is also bound by the fetter of ill-will.

If one is not bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) persists through five types of abandonment; therefore, it is appropriate to apply the latter phrase.
If a particular state is bound by the fetter of ill-will, is it also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?

Answer: If there is a locus where one is bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), there is also a locus where one is bound by the fetter of ill-will (*vyāpāda-saṃyojana*); this refers to the locus of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Is it possible to be bound by the fetter of ill-will without being bound by the fetter of envy?
Answer: There is.

There may be one for whom the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) has not yet been severed; or there may be one for whom four types [of such fetters] have been severed but the fetter of ill-will has not yet been severed; or even one for whom the fetter of ill-will to be abandoned by the path of vision has not yet been severed.

In brief, when the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) has not been abandoned regarding those factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), this is called being bound by the fetter of ill-will but not bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).
Why is this? Because there is no fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
As with the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of stinginess, the explanation for the fetter of ill-will and the fetter of stinginess is likewise.

Why is this? Because these two fetters are both bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), take contaminated objects as their conditions (*sāsravālambana*), and are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
If a place is bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyāsaṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*)?

The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms; it is abandoned through five modes of abandonment, takes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) objects as its conditions, and is both universal (*sarvatraga*) and non-universal.

The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) exists within the three realms; it is abandoned through four modes of abandonment, takes both contaminated and uncontaminated objects as its conditions, and is both universal and non-universal.

If one is bound by all fetters within the three realms at the five points of abandonment, then being bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana), one is also bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana); and being bound by the fetter of views, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
If one is not bound by all fetters (sakalabandhana), yet possesses the long-standing fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) severed in five ways, one may therefore apply the latter clause.
If a person is bound by the fetter of ignorance in a particular location, are they also bound by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana)?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of views, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
As for the locus, it refers to the five types of locations for abandonment within the three realms.
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance but not by the fetter of views?
Answer: There is.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, the fetter of ignorance associated with views—which is to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path—has not yet been severed.
What are those factors associated with views that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path?
The answer is:
they are those factors associated with that very wrong view, the grasping at views, the grasping at precepts and rituals, craving, hatred, pride, doubt, and the unique ignorance.
This dharma is bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), but not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).
Within its own group (*svakalāpa*), it is bound by way of object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and associated-condition (*samprayoga-pratyaya*);
within another group (*parakalāpa*), it acts as an object-condition but is not bound by association, nor is it bound by the fetter of views.
Why is this so? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is universal; those [factors] that take the five categories as their objects have already been abandoned.

As for the remainder that has not yet been abandoned, they are dissociated from the views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana*), and do not constitute a bond through such objects, because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object.
The non-associated fetters [are so called] because they belong to a different aggregate.

Regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), it may be that the fetter of ignorance of the nine stages has not yet been abandoned, or it may be that the fetter of ignorance up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) has not yet been abandoned.

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be those who have not yet severed nine types of fetters of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), or even those who have not yet severed the lowest-of-the-low grade.

In general, when the fetters of ignorance to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) have not been severed, this is called being bound by the fetter of ignorance but not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*).

Why is this so? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is universal; those who have already abandoned the five types [of objects] that it can take as its objective support no longer possess the fetter of views to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

When the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) associated with the factors to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-heya*) has not been abandoned, and the fetter of ignorance regarding the factors to be abandoned by the path of cultivation has also not been abandoned, as explained in detail above.

Regarding a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭi-prativedha*), if the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation has not yet been severed, the detailed explanation is as stated above.
As it is with the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), so too is the explanation for the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).

Why is this so? These two fetters both exist within the three realms and are abandoned through four modes; they take both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena as their objects, and consist of both universal and non-universal [fetters].
If a certain place is bound by the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ignorance exists throughout the three realms, as explained above;
the fetter of grasping also exists throughout the three realms, as explained above.
If one is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), the five points of abandonment are as explained above.
If one is not bound by all fetters, yet the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) persists through the five points of abandonment, for this reason one may apply the latter phrase.
If a person is bound by the fetter of ignorance (avidyā-saṃyojana) in a certain state, are they also bound by the fetter of grasping (upādāna-saṃyojana)? Answer:
If one is bound by the fetter of grasping, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance but not bound by the fetter of grasping? Answer: There is.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, the fetter of ignorance regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by the path of cultivation remains unsevered; the detailed explanation is as above.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the fetter of ignorance regarding the phenomena to be abandoned by the path of cultivation remains unsevered; it is as explained above.

Regarding a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths (*dṛṣṭi-sampanna*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) pertaining to the factors to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) has not yet been severed; this is explained in detail as above.
If one is bound by the fetter of ignorance in a particular state, is one also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) pertains to the three realms, as explained above.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) pertains to the desire realm, as explained above.

If one is bound by all fetters and belongs to the desire realm, where they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), then if one is bound by the fetter of ignorance, one is also bound by the fetter of envy; and if one is bound by the fetter of envy, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.

If one is not bound by all fetters, yet possesses the long-standing fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) within the three realms across five types of abandonment, one may thus correspond to the latter phrase.
If a person is bound by the fetter of ignorance in a particular location, are they also bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of envy, one is also bound by the fetter of ignorance.
As for the locus, it is the locus of the desire realm, which is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of ignorance but not bound by the fetter of envy? Answer: There is.

Regarding the fetters of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are either not yet severed, or four types of the fetter of ignorance are not yet severed, or even up to one type [of the fetter of ignorance] associated with the path of seeing is not yet severed.

Regarding the fetter of ignorance associated with the realms of form and formlessness, it is either not yet abandoned in nine stages, or it is not yet abandoned up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

In that very sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be five kinds of fetters of ignorance that have not been abandoned, or even those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation that have not yet been abandoned.

Regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there may be nine types that have not yet been abandoned, or even those of the lowest-of-the-low grade (*mṛdu-mṛdu*) that have not yet been abandoned.
In summary, the fetter of ignorance pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness (*rūpa-dhātu* and *ārūpya-dhātu*) remains unabandoned.

Regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), the explanation for the fetter of ignorance and the fetter of stinginess is also as stated above. Why is this so?
Because these two fetters both exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as explained above.
If there is a binding by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) in a certain location, is there also a binding by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of views exists in the three realms, as explained above;
the fetter of grasping also exists in the three realms, likewise as explained above.
If one is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), it is as explained above.

If one is not bound by all fetters, yet possesses the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) which persists within the outflows (*sāsrava*), for this reason, one may apply the "conformable to the preceding clause" (*pūrvapādaka*).
If a place is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of grasping?
Answer: If one is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), one is also bound by the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*).
As for the locus, it refers to the five types of loci for abandonment within the three realms.
Is there one who is bound by the fetter of grasping (*upādāna-saṃyojana*) but not bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)? Answer: There is.

When the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) regarding those factors dissociated from views that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path has not been severed.

When the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the fetter of grasping regarding those factors dissociated from views that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path has not been severed.
The detailed explanation is as above.
If a certain place is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*)?
The fetter of views exists within the three realms, as explained above.
The fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) within the three realms is also as explained above.

If one is bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) across the five stages of abandonment in the three realms, then whoever is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is also bound by the fetter of doubt, and whoever is bound by the fetter of doubt is also bound by the fetter of views.

If one is not bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), each [fetter] remains eternally within its own category; therefore, it is possible to formulate four propositions regarding its own fundamental basis.
If a particular locus is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsāsaṃyojana*)?
This is expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding one who is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) but not by the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsāsaṃyojana*): when the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) has not yet arisen, the factors associated with views to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the vision of the path have their fetter of views not yet severed.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the factors associated with views that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path have not yet had their fetter of views severed.
This is called being bound by the fetter of views, but not bound by the fetter of doubt.

Why is this so? Because the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*) is universal (*sarvatraga*); those [aspects] among its five objects that have already been abandoned are no longer bound by way of being an object (*ālambana-bandhana*) with respect to the factors associated with the vision [of the truths], because they take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object;
nor are they bound by way of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*), because they belong to a different category (*nikāya*).

One who is bound by the fetter of doubt but not by the fetter of views is one for whom the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen; such a person has not yet abandoned the fetter of doubt regarding those factors associated with doubt that are to be abandoned through the vision of cessation and the vision of the path.

When the knowledge of cessation has already arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet arisen, the phenomena associated with doubt that are to be abandoned by the vision of the path have not yet had the fetter of doubt severed.
This is called being bound by the fetter of doubt, but not bound by the fetter of views.

Why is this so? Because the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) is universal; those [factors] among the five types that it can take as objects have already been abandoned. As for the remaining unabandoned factors, it does not bind by taking them as objects when they are associated with doubt, because it takes the untainted (*anāsrava*) as its object;
nor does it bind through association, because it belongs to a different category (*nikāya*).
Regarding those bound by both: dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation that are possessed by complete fetters are bound by both.
Dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering that are possessed by complete fetters are bound by two kinds of fetters of views and two kinds of fetters of doubt.
The same applies to the factors abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the path (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding the factors associated with the view that is abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), they are bound by three types of fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and two types of fetters of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
Dharmas associated with doubt are bound by three kinds of fetters of doubt and two kinds of fetters of views.
Dharmas dissociated from the fetter of views and the fetter of doubt are bound by two kinds of fetters of doubt and two kinds of fetters of views.
The same applies to those [defilements] abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [the defilements] abandoned by the vision of origin, cessation, and the path, as well as those abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of the origin has not yet arisen, one is bound by both [fetters] regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, the vision of the origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through the cultivation of the path.
Regarding phenomena to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, one is bound by one type of fetter, the fetter of views, and one type of fetter, the fetter of doubt.
The same applies to those abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*) and those abandoned through the path (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).

Regarding factors associated with the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), they are bound by two types of fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and one type of fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
Dharmas associated with doubt are bound by two kinds of fetters of doubt and one kind of fetter of views.
Dharmas dissociated from both the fetter of views and the fetter of doubt are bound by one kind of fetter of views and one kind of fetter of doubt.
The same applies to the dharmas abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding those who are unbound from both, the detailed explanation is as in the original sūtra.
This continues until, having become free from desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one is unbound from both.
Why is this so? If those fetters are severed, their basis is also severed.
If there is a binding by the fetter of views regarding a certain basis, is there also a binding by the fetter of envy regarding that same basis?
The fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) pertains to the three realms, as explained above.
The fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) pertains to the desire realm; its detailed explanation is as above.

If one is bound by the fetter of views regarding those phenomena of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) that are still possessed by all fetters, then one is also bound by the fetter of envy; and if one is bound by the fetter of envy, one is also bound by the fetter of views.
If one is not bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*) persists throughout the three realms and is abandoned in four ways;
the fetter of envy (*īrṣyāsaṃyojana*) persists as something to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Therefore, four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.
If a particular locus is bound by the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), is it also bound by the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*)?
This is to be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is bound by the fetter of views but not by the fetter of pride: it refers to those factors bound to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) and for which the fetter of views has not yet been severed; or where four types [of such fetters] have not yet been severed, or even up to the point where the fetter of views associated with the path of seeing has not yet been severed.

Regarding the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) bound to the realms of form and formlessness that have not yet been abandoned: in some cases, the fetters of views belonging to eight stages have not been abandoned; in others, they remain unabandoned up to and including the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

In that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there may be four kinds of fetters not yet abandoned, or even those up to the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) not yet abandoned by the path of vision.
This is called being bound by the fetter of views but not being bound by the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*).

Regarding those who are bound by the fetter of envy but not by the fetter of views: it is when sensual craving has not yet been abandoned; the knowledge of origination has already arisen, but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen; and the envy-fetter regarding the factors of the desire realm to be abandoned by the path of cultivation has not yet been severed.

Even for a disciple of the Blessed One who has fully realized the truths, if sensual desire has not yet been abandoned, then regarding the phenomena bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation, the fetter of envy has not yet been abandoned.
This is called being bound by the fetter of envy but not by the fetter of views. Regarding those bound by both:
a person who is fully fettered (sakalabandhana) is bound by both with respect to the dharmas of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

For a person bound by all fetters, there is bondage by one type of *prāpti-bandhana* (thieving-fetter) and two types of *dṛṣṭi-bandhana* (view-fetter) regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

For one who has not yet abandoned desire, when the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there is bondage by both types regarding the dharmas of the desire realm to be abandoned through the path of cultivation: one type of *dṛṣṭi-bandhana* and one type of *prāpti-bandhana*.
Regarding those that are neither bound [to the desire realm] nor [the form realm], the detailed explanation is as in the original sūtra.
Up to the point of being free from craving for the formless realm, both are neither bound.
As it is with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), so it is also for the fetter of views and the fetter of stinginess.
As with the section on the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), so it is with the section on the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
If, in a certain place, there is the binding of the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), is there also the binding of the fetter of doubt?
This should be explained in detail as was done for the fetters of views and grasping.
The same applies to the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
If, in a certain place, there is the binding of the fetter of grasping, is there also the binding of the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*)?
The detailed exposition is as in the original sūtra.
As with the fetter of grasping (*parigraha-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), the explanation for the fetter of grasping and the fetter of stinginess is likewise.
If a place is bound by the fetter of stinginess, is it also bound by the fetter of grasping?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"

Both of these exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), both take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) as their objects, and neither is universal (*sarvatraga*).

Question: Since stinginess (*mātsarya*) arises dependent on others while avarice (*mātsarya*—here referring to *mātsarya* as a distinct mental factor) arises from oneself, why is the answer given as "it is so"?
The answer is:
Envy takes others as its object and arises because of others; it does not take oneself as its object and does not arise because of oneself.
Avarice takes oneself as its object and arises because of oneself; it does not take others as its object and does not arise because of others.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these two dharmas arise both by depending on others and by having others as their cause, and also by depending on themselves and by having themselves as their cause.
A question is asked:
While it may be acceptable that the *kleśa* depends on others and has others as its cause, how can it be said that it also depends on itself and has itself as its cause?
The answer is:
It is like a person who prepares provisions for two bhikṣus; one becomes excellent, while the other does not.
The one for whom it did not become excellent then thinks to himself:
If what I do is not good, it causes what he does to also not turn out well.

Question: It may be acceptable that stinginess arises with oneself as its object and oneself as its cause; however, how can it be acceptable for it to arise with another as its object and another as its cause?
Answer: Stinginess can also arise from others.
For example, there may be someone who, upon seeing another person practicing giving, immediately conceives a stingy mind.
Why does this person give such things to others?
Therefore, these two also arise conditioned by both self and other, and arise caused by both self and other.
If, in a certain state, there is a past fetter of craving, is there also a future fetter of craving?
...and so forth, as explained at length.
There are afflictions of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and afflictions of specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
Afflictions of specific characteristics refer to attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), envy (*īrṣyā*), and avarice (*mātsarya*).

Regarding the general characteristics of the afflictions (*kleśa*), these consist of the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*).
As for the specific characteristics of the afflictions that bind the five locations within the three realms: those existing in the future can bind all three time periods;
those of the past are not fixed—if they were not severed in a previous life, they bind; if they did not arise previously, or if having arisen they have already been severed, they do not bind.
The present [craving] is also indeterminate: if it is present before one, there is bondage; if it is not present before one, there is no bondage.
The fetter of craving binds the five types of locations within the three realms. The future fetter of craving binds the five types of locations across the three times within the three realms.
The past is indeterminate: if it was not severed in a previous life, there is bondage; if it did not arise previously, or if what arose has already been severed, there is no bondage.
The present [fetter] is also indeterminate: if it is manifest, one is bound; if it is not manifest, one is not bound.
As with the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), the same explanation applies to the fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*).

The fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana) binds the five categories [of the desire realm] across the three periods of time; the future fetter of aversion binds the five categories across the three periods of time.

Regarding the past, it is indeterminate: if it was not severed in a previous life, one is bound by it; if it did not arise previously, or if it arose but has already been severed, one is not bound by it.
Regarding the present, it is also indeterminate: if it is manifest before one, one is bound by it; if it is not manifest before one, one is not bound by it.

Regarding the locus of the fetters of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) bound to the dharmas of the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the three periods of time: In the future, the fetters of envy are bound to the locus of the dharmas of the desire realm bound to the three periods of time that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

In the past, it is not fixed: if they were previously produced and not yet abandoned, one is bound; if they were not previously produced, or if those produced have already been abandoned, one is not bound.
In the present, it is also not fixed: if they are currently manifest, one is bound; if they are not currently manifest, one is not bound.
As with the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*), the explanation for the fetter of parsimony (*kadarya-saṃyojana*) is likewise.

Regarding the total-characteristic afflictions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) bound to the three realms, they are abandoned in five ways across the temporal locations; regarding the past total-characteristic afflictions bound to the three realms, they are abandoned in five ways across the three times, and the same applies to the future and present.
This is said to be the *Saptaka-pudgala-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
If there is a past fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) binding a certain locus, is there also a future fetter of craving binding that same locus?
Answer: It is grasped in this way. Why is that?
Having first stated that the future fetter of craving binds the three time periods, [the question is asked:
"If there is the binding by the future fetter of craving, is there also the binding by the past fetter of craving?"

Answer: If that which was previously produced has not been severed, then one is bound; if it was not previously produced, or if what was produced has already been severed, then one is not bound. Question:
If, at the time when the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) of the past is severed, the fetter of craving of the future is also severed at that very same time,
why is it certain for the future world but not so for the past?
And he made this statement:
"If that which arose previously is not severed, then one is bound; if that which arose previously did not arise, or if that which arose has already been severed, then one is not bound?
The foreign Dharma masters speak thus:
If it is said that what was previously produced is not severed and thus remains bound, this refers to the middle fetter;
if what was previously produced does not arise, this refers to the lower fetter;
if that which was produced has already been severed, this refers to the upper fetter.
The śramaṇas of Kaśmīra further state:
"If one says that what was previously born is not severed, then it is bound; this refers to the three kinds of fetters.
If one says that what was previously unarisen does not arise, this refers to the lower fetter."
If it is said that birth has already been severed, this refers to the intermediate fetters (*madhyama-saṃyojana*) and the higher fetters (*ūrdhva-saṃyojana*).
Just as the past higher and intermediate fetters of craving have been severed, so it is with the future.

Regarding the lower fetters of craving for birth, those future fetters of craving bound to the spheres of attachment in the future world constitute the "future binding. In those very same locations, if the past fetters of craving from previous births have not been severed, one is then bound by them.
If it was not previously produced, then that which is produced must be produced in another location.
If it was not previously produced, and if it is produced in another location, then it is produced in that very location.
That which has been born is already severed and thus not bound.
If one is bound by past fetters of craving regarding a certain object, is there also a present fetter of craving regarding that same object?
Answer: Yes.

If it is present now, whether the fetter of craving does not arise, or other fetters arise and are present, or a wholesome or non-obscured neutral mind arises and is present, or there is no mind—therefore, it is said to be "present."
If there is a bond of craving in the present, is there also a bond of craving in the past?
The answer is:
if it was not severed in a previous life, then one is bound.
If that which has not yet arisen does not arise, and that which has already arisen is severed, then one is not bound.
If there is a future fetter of craving (*anāgata-tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) binding a particular state, is there also a present fetter of craving binding it?
Answer: If it is present before one, it is explained in detail as above.
Suppose there is a bond of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) bound in the present; is there also a bond of craving bound in the future?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
It was previously stated:
"The fetter of craving binds dharmas of the three periods of time in the future.
If a certain locus is bound by the past fetter of craving, is it also bound by the future and present fetters of craving?
Answer: That which is future is bound;
as for that which is present, if it manifests before one, it is explained in detail as above.
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) in the future and the present, is there also [bondage] in the past?
The answer is:
if it was not severed in a previous life, then there is bondage.
If that which has not previously arisen, or that which has arisen and been severed, is not bound;

whereas if that which arose previously and was not severed is bound—then wherever there is a bond of future or present craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), if there is also a bond of past craving that arose previously in that same location, one is bound by it.

If the locus of the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) in the future or present is different [from that of the past], then one is not bound by the fetter of craving that has already arisen in the past.
