If it did not previously arise, or if that which arose in that particular locus has been abandoned, then one is not bound.
If a certain state is bound by future fetters of craving, is it also bound by past and present fetters of craving?
Answer: There may be cases where there is binding by future fetters of craving, but none by past or present ones.
There may be the past without the present;
there may be the present without the past;
or there may be both the past and the present.

There are cases where one is bound by the fetter of craving for the future, but not by those of the past or present: if the fetter of craving for a particular object has not yet been abandoned, it is clear that there is binding by the fetter of craving for the future;
if [craving] has not previously arisen or, having arisen, has already been abandoned, it is clear that there is no binding by the fetter of craving for the past;
and if it is not currently manifest, it is clear that there is no binding by the fetter of craving for the present.

Regarding the case where there is a past [bond] but no present one: if, in a given location, the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) produced in a prior birth has not yet been severed, this clarifies that there is a past bond of craving;
since it does not manifest before one, this clarifies that there is no bond of craving in the present.
Regarding the case where there is present [possession] but no past: if one is bound by the fetter of craving in the past, then one is bound by the fetter of craving in the future.
Regarding the case where there is present but no past: if the fetter of craving is manifest in a particular location, this clarifies that there is possession of the fetter of craving in the present;
if it has not previously arisen, or having arisen has been severed, this clarifies that there is no possession of the fetter of craving in the past.
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving in the present, then there is bondage by the fetter of craving in the future.

Regarding those who possess [bondage] in the past and the present: if in a given location there was bondage by the fetter of craving in a prior birth, it is evident that there is bondage by the fetter of craving in the past;
if in a given location the fetter of craving is manifest in the present, it is evident that there is bondage by the fetter of craving in the present.
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) in the past or present, there must necessarily be [bondage] in the future.
If a particular basis (*adhikaraṇa*) is bound by the fetter of craving in the present, does it also possess bondage by the fetter of craving in the past and future?
The answer is:
That which is future is bound.

Regarding that which is past, if it was previously produced and has not been severed, it is bound; if it was not previously produced, or if what was produced has already been severed, it is not bound.
If there is bondage by the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) regarding the past and future, is there also bondage by the fetter of craving regarding the present?
Answer: If it is present before one, it is explained at length as above.
The various specific-characteristic afflictions are briefly explained herein; as with the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), they form six propositions.
The fetters of hostility (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) are not universal (*asarvatraga*).
The sixfold formulation regarding the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) is likewise.
If, in a certain case, there is bondage by the past fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), is there also bondage by the future fetter of views? Answer:
Thus it is.
If there is a future fetter of views, is there also a past fetter of views?
Answer: Yes.
It is so. Why is this? Because it was previously stated as follows:

All general-characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) afflictions (*kleśa*) bind the phenomena of the three periods of time; those of the future and present take all three periods as their objects. A detailed explanation is as given in the original sūtra.
Regarding the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), there are six propositions; herein, the general-characteristic afflictions are explained in brief.
Just as with the fetter of attachment (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), six propositions are formed; so too are the fetters of grasping (*parāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) all-pervasive (*sarvatraga*).
The same applies to the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) when formulated in six propositions.
If, in a certain location, there is bondage by the past fetter of attachment, is there also bondage by the past fetter of aversion (*pratigha*)?
Answer: If that which was previously produced has not been severed, then one is bound; if it was not previously produced, or if what was produced has already been severed, then one is not bound.

Regarding "if that which was previously produced has not been severed, then one is bound": if there is a bond of past craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) at a certain location, then there is also a bond of past previously produced aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) at that same location.
If it has not arisen previously, or if it arises elsewhere, or if that which has arisen has been severed, then one is not bound.
Suppose there is a past bond of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*); is there also a past bond of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:
If that which was previously produced has not been severed, one is bound; if it was not previously produced, or if what was produced has already been severed, one is not bound.

Regarding the case where one is bound because that which was previously produced has not been severed: if there is a bond of past resentment (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) at a certain location, then there is also a bond of past craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) produced earlier at that same location.
If it has not arisen previously, or if it arises elsewhere, or if that which has arisen has been severed, then one is not bound.
If there is a past bond of the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) in a particular location, is there also a future bond of the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: If it is not severed,
how is it that it is not severed?
Answer: One who has not yet abandoned craving for sensual desire.
If there is a future fetter of aversion (pratigha-saṃyojana), is there also a past fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana)?
The answer is:
If that which was previously produced has not been abandoned, one is bound; if it was not previously produced, or if what was produced has already been abandoned, one is not bound.

Regarding the case where one is bound because that which was previously produced has not been abandoned: if a person is bound by the future fetter of malice (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) in a certain location, then in that very same location, they are also bound by the past, previously produced fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*).
If it has not arisen previously, or if it arises in another place, or if that which has arisen has been severed, then one is not bound.
If there is a past bond of the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) in a particular location, is there also a present bond of the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Answer: It is when it manifests before one.
How does it manifest before one?
Answer: If other fetters do not arise, if a wholesome, out-flowing, non-obscured, and indeterminate mind does not arise, or if one is not without mind, this is called being "present before one."
If there is a present bond of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), is there also a past bond of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:
if it arose previously and was not abandoned, then one is bound; if it did not arise previously, or if what arose has been abandoned, then one is not bound. The detailed explanation is as above.
If, in a certain state, there is the bond of past craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), is there also the bond of past and present aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
The answer is:

there may be the bond of past craving without the bonds of past and present aversion; there may be [the bond of past craving] without [the bond of] the present; there may be [the bond of the present] without [the bond of] the past; or there may be both the past and the present.

Regarding those who have the fetter of past craving but do not have the fetter of past or present aversion: if, in a given state, the previously arisen fetter of craving has not been abandoned and thus binds, this clarifies that there is the fetter of past craving.

That in which the previously arisen fetter of ill-will does not arise, and that which has arisen has been abandoned so that one is no longer bound—this clarifies the absence of the past fetter of ill-will.
That it does not manifest in the present clarifies the absence of the present fetter of ill-will.

There may be cases where there is a past [bond] but no present one: if, in a particular location, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) were not severed in a previous birth, then one is bound; this clarifies that there is a binding by the past fetters of aversion and craving.
If there is no present [existence], it clarifies that there is no bondage by the fetter of present ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*).

Alternatively, there may be a case where there is a present [existence] but no past one; if, in a particular location, the previously arisen past fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has not been severed, then one is bound—this clarifies that there is bondage by the past fetter of craving.
If, in that very locus, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) manifests, it is evident that there is a present bondage by the fetter of aversion.
If it has not previously arisen, or if having arisen it has been abandoned, it is evident that there is no past bondage by the fetter of aversion.

There may be those for whom there are past and present [fetters]: if, in a given situation, the past fetters of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) and aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) from previous lives have not been severed, then one is bound; this clarifies that there is bondage by the past fetters of craving and aversion.
If, in that very locus, the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) is present, then it is clear that there is a bond of the present fetter of aversion.
Now, if there is a bond of the past and present fetters of aversion, is there also a bond of the past fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*)?

Answer: If that which arose previously has not been severed, then one is bound; if it did not arise previously, or if what arose has already been severed, then one is not bound, as explained in detail above.
If there is a past fetter of craving (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) binding a particular object, is there also a future or present fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) binding that same object?
Answer: The rest is explained in detail as in the original sūtra; the seven propositions are formulated as in the original sūtra.

As with the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of ill-will (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), so too are the explanations for the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*) likewise.

The distinction herein should be explained: regarding the factors bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), if the previously arisen fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) has not been severed, one is bound by it.
The fetters of craving and pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), and the fetters of craving and ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), are to be explained in detail as in the original sūtra.
If, in a certain state, there is the bondage of past craving (*anuśaya*), is there also the bondage of past views (*dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: If it has not been abandoned.
What is meant by "not abandoned"?
The answer is:
when the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the Path has not yet arisen.
If there is bondage by the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana) belonging to the past, is there also bondage by the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) belonging to the past? Answer:
If it was not severed in a previous birth, then one is bound; the detailed explanation is as above.
If a person is bound by past fetters of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*) in a certain state, is that so?
Answer: Yes, provided they have not abandoned them.
What is meant by "not abandoning"?
The answer is:
the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) has not yet arisen.
If there is a future fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) that binds, is there also a past fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) that binds?
Answer: The detailed exposition is as in the original Sūtra; the formulation of the seven propositions is likewise as in the original Sūtra.

As with the sevenfold formulation regarding the fetter of craving and the fetter of views, so too are the sevenfold formulations for the fetter of craving and the fetter of grasping, and the fetter of craving and the fetter of doubt; the explanation is likewise.
Regarding past craving, past ill-will, and the inquiry concerning past conceit, one should likewise formulate seven propositions.
Some may say that the first of the seven statements should itself consist of seven statements.
Why is this? Because within this context, there is a question regarding each of the seven sets of seven statements.

Answer: Because there are seven sets of seven phrases. For example, having first asked about the past fetters of craving (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*), one next asks about the future fetter of conceit (*māna*), then the present, then the past and present, then the future and present, then the past and future, and finally the past, future, and present.

The fetter of conceit (*māna-saṃyojana*) should also be explained in this same manner: first, having asked about past attachment and aversion, one asks about future conceit as the initial phrase; next, one asks about the present; next, one asks about the past and present; next, one asks about the future and present; next, one asks about the past and future; next, one asks about the past, future, and present; and finally, one asks about the past as the last phrase.

Furthermore, taking past attachment and aversion as the question for present pride as the first phrase, one next asks about the past and the present; then asks about the future and the present; then asks about the past and the future; then asks about the past, the future, and the present; and finally asks about the past as the last phrase.

From the question regarding past desire and hatred with respect to the past, future, and present pride as the first phrase, up to the question regarding past desire and hatred with respect to past pride as the final phrase.
If one were to speak in this manner, there would be seven sets of seven phrases.
If one were to speak in this manner, it would be a waste of effort; it would be of no benefit to the text and of no benefit to the meaning, nor would it constitute seven sets of seven phrases.
If one wishes to provide benefit regarding both the phrasing and the meaning, such that they also constitute seven sets of seven phrases, one should speak as follows:

just as one first asks about past conceit by means of past attachment and aversion to form the initial phrase, so on until one asks about past, future, and present conceit by means of past attachment and aversion to form the final phrase.

One should take future desire and hatred as the question for future conceit to form the first phrase; next, ask about the present; next, ask about the past and present; next, ask about the future and present; next, ask about the past and future; next, ask about the past, future, and present; and finally, ask about the past to form the last phrase.

Furthermore, regarding present craving and hatred, one first asks about present conceit; next, one asks about the past and the present; next, one asks about the future and the present; next, one asks about the past and the future; next, one asks about the past, the future, and the present; next, one asks about the past; and finally, one asks about the future as the last phrase.

...up to using past, future, and present attachment and aversion as questions regarding past, future, and present pride to form the first phrase, and so on, up to using past, future, and present attachment and aversion as questions regarding past, future, and present pride to form the final phrase.
If one speaks in this manner, it will be beneficial for both the phrasing and the meaning, and the seven-times-seven sets of phrases will be established.

Just as with the questions regarding craving, aversion, and conceit forming seven-times-seven sets, so too are the questions regarding ignorance; and even the questions regarding the fetter of stinginess form seven-times-seven sets in the same way.

Setting aside the fetter of craving (*rāga-saṃyojana*), one asks about the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*) by means of the fetters of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*) and pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), forming seven sets of seven questions; this is likewise for all [the remaining fetters] up to the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).

Setting aside ill-will (*vyāpāda*), one asks about the fetters of conceit (*māna*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) in seven sets of seven statements; this is likewise for the fetter of stinginess (*mātsarya*), up to seven sets of seven statements.

This continues until the final fetter of grasping (*parigraha*); likewise, one asks about the fetter of stinginess by means of the fetters of doubt (*vicikitsā*) and envy (*īrṣyā*), forming seven sets of seven statements.

Just as asking about one fetter by means of two fetters results in seven sets of seven phrases, so too, asking about one fetter by means of three, four, five, six, seven, or eight fetters likewise results in seven sets of seven phrases.
Question: Regarding the six [realms] traversed by a single practice, what is the difference between the seven small and the seven great [kalpas]? Answer:
"Name" refers to the specific distinctions.

Furthermore, posing a question using a single line of dharma is called "Single Line"; posing a question using six phrases is called "Traversing Six"; posing a question using seven phrases is called "Small Seven"; and posing a question using two conclusions for one conclusion, up to eight conclusions for one conclusion, is called "Great Seven."
Furthermore, asking about dissimilar dharmas without being restricted by time is called "one practice" (ekāṅga);
asking about similar dharmas while being restricted by time is called "traversing six" (ṣaḍabhisamaya);
and asking about dissimilar dharmas while being restricted by time is called "small seven" (saptaka).
To inquire about one dharma by means of two dharmas, up to inquiring about one dharma by means of eight dharmas, according to worldly convention, is called the "Great Seven.
One practice traverses the six "Small Sevens" and the "Great Seven"; this is termed their differentiation.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 31 [and] Scroll 32. Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.

Within the *Karma-vastu* (Karmavastu), in the chapter on the "Single Practice" (*Ekacaryā*), it asks: How many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are subsumed under the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
Question: [What are they?]
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
Some say that while [the aggregates] encompass their own phenomena and the phenomena of others, they do not encompass themselves.

For example, the Vibhajyavādins, relying on the sūtras spoken by the Buddha using provisional names and relying on conventional linguistic conventions, teach that there are dharmas that subsume themselves and dharmas that subsume others, yet do not subsume themselves.
What are the sūtras spoken by way of conventional designation?
For example, as the Buddha said:
"It is like a bushel that receives and contains pebbles, serving as the support for the pebbles; because the bushel is superior, it encompasses all the pebbles."
He asserts this:

"The category of 'grasping' (saṃgraha) is distinct from the thing grasped (saṃgṛhīta), yet it encompasses the thing grasped; therefore, one knows that a categorizing dharma encompasses other dharmas but does not encompass itself."
Other sūtras also state:
"Among the five faculties, wisdom is the most supreme, and they are subsumed by wisdom.
Since wisdom is distinct from the other four faculties yet is able to subsume them, we know that it subsumes other dharmas.
Other sūtras also state:
For example, the Buddha asked the householder Khadiravaniya,
"How do you maintain your retinue?"
"How, then, does one know that one is gathering a retinue?
The householder replied:
"The World-Honored One has taught the four methods of attraction: giving, kind speech, beneficial action, and cooperation."
One gathers one's retinue by means of the four methods and knows that one has gathered the retinue. They say this:

"The householder, the retinue, and the methods of gathering are each distinct from one another, yet they are able to gather one another; therefore, we know that the method for gathering others does not gather oneself."
Another sutra further states:
Right view, right effort, and right mindfulness are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom; right concentration is subsumed under the aggregate of concentration.
He says this: "It may be granted that right view is wisdom and is subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom;
and that right concentration is subsumed under the aggregate of concentration."

Right awakening and right effort are not of the nature of wisdom; right mindfulness is not of the nature of concentration. Since right awakening and right effort are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom, while right mindfulness is subsumed under the aggregate of concentration, one thereby knows that a factor may be subsumed within another factor.
Regarding the conventions of worldly language, the world likewise speaks thus:
"The doorframe holds the door hinge; thread can hold a garment;
a rope holds a bundle of firewood. Householders also speak thus:
I am able to manage my household wealth, elephants, horses, and servants;
likewise, one who has left the home life says:
"I manage my robes and bowl, as well as all items used by a śramaṇa."

Based on what is taught in such sūtras of provisional names and because of the inclusion of phenomena within conventional language, one knows that while the inclusion of phenomena includes others, it does not include itself; yet, it is also clarified that the inclusion of phenomena includes its own essence.

If the grasping of phenomena were to grasp only others while not grasping its own self-nature, then the self-nature of one phenomenon would be identical to the self-nature of all phenomena; thus, when one phenomenon arises, all phenomena would arise, and when one phenomenon ceases, all phenomena would cease.
Furthermore, there is yet another fault: dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering would then include those abandoned through the path of cultivation.
If dharmas abandoned through the vision of suffering are abandoned, then dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation should also be abandoned.
If that were the case, then subsequent remedies would be rendered useless.
To avoid such a fault, it is said that the encompassing of phenomena encompasses their own intrinsic nature but does not encompass other phenomena.

Question: If the inclusion of dharmas (dharmasaṃgraha) includes only its own dharma and does not include others, how do you explain the sūtras cited by the Vibhajyavādins and the conventions of worldly language?
The answer is:
That sutra is of provisional meaning (neyārtha), it is a conventional designation (prajñapti), and it possesses an underlying intention (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita).
The question is:
How is it that this sutra is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), is a mere designation (*prajñapti*), and possesses an underlying intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)?
The answer is:
as the sutra says:

The *nakṣatra* (constellation) receives and contains the *nakṣatra-putra* (child of the constellation); that which can contain the *nakṣatra-putra* is here said to be "support" (*āśraya*). Why is this so?
Because the *nakṣatra-putra* relies upon the *nakṣatra*, and the *nakṣatra* sustains the *nakṣatra-putra*, it does not scatter or perish.
As it is said:
among the five faculties, wisdom is the most excellent and is subsumed by wisdom.
Here, "wisdom" is a figurative expression for what is subsumed [by it].
Why is this? Because through the skillful means of wisdom (*prajñā-upāya*), the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are able to function and accomplish the great task.
As it is said:
"I gather my retinue by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as taught by the World-Honored One," and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, it is said that "not being separated" constitutes gathering, because one employs the skillful means of the four methods of attraction to ensure that the retinue does not become dispersed.
As it is said:
"Right awakening, right effort, and right mindfulness are subsumed under the aggregate of wisdom and the aggregate of concentration. Here, "subsumption" refers to conformity;
for right awakening and right effort conform to the aggregate of wisdom, while right mindfulness conforms to the aggregate of concentration.
As it is said:
"A doorframe holds the door, thread holds the garment, and a rope holds a bundle of firewood"—in these cases, "holding" (dhāraṇa) is what is meant by "grasping" (parigraha).
As it is said: "Laypeople and monastics grasp fields, wealth, robes, bowls, and so forth"—in these cases, "benefiting" (upakāra) is what is meant by "grasping."

Regarding the inclusion of dharmas and the inclusion of others' dharmas: sometimes they are included and sometimes they are not; there are reasons for including them and reasons for not including them.
As a verse says:
"Love arises because of an object; Hatred arises because of an object."
"When people give rise to attachment or aversion, there is nothing that does not have its cause in external phenomena.
As for "gathering phenomena" and "gathering one's own phenomena," every instance of gathering at all times has its underlying reason.
Regarding that which is subsumed at all times: there is nothing that is not so subsumed, for its own-characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) exists at all times. Why is this?
Because its own essence does not depend on any external cause.
When one contemplates the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena and subsumes them back into their own specific characteristics, what beneficial advantages are there?
The answer is:

one eliminates the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*), the notion of a collection (*piṇḍa-saṃjñā*), and is able to cultivate the notion of phenomena (*dharma-saṃjñā*) and the notion of differentiation (*prabhinna-saṃjñā*).

If sentient beings possess the notion of a self and the notion of a collection [of aggregates], they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion; because they give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, they are unable to escape birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

If one can eliminate the notion of a self and the notion of a collection, viewing form as being like scattered dust, and viewing non-form phenomena as neither preceding nor following one another, but rather as not coexisting, and if one views all conditioned phenomena as having the characteristic of dispersal like scattered sand, then the seed of the liberation door of emptiness will arise.

If one contemplates that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are empty and does not take pleasure in birth and death (*saṃsāra*), the seed of the liberation door of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*) arises.

If one does not take pleasure in birth and death and seeks *nirvāṇa*, the seed of the liberation door of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) arises. Based on the lower samādhi, the middle samādhi arises; based on the middle samādhi, the superior samādhi arises; and by relying on the superior samādhi, one is able to become free from the desires of the three realms (*tridhātu*).
When observing the phenomena of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇadharma*) and subsuming them back into the phenomena of specific characteristics, there is such a beneficial benefit:

the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) subsumes three latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). In summary, the view of a self-identity subsumes these three latent tendencies; the view of a self-identity exists within the three realms. The view of a self-identity in the desire realm subsumes the view of a self-identity in the desire realm, and so on, up to the view of a self-identity in the formless realm subsuming the view of a self-identity in the formless realm.

The grasping at precepts (*śīlavrata-parāmarśa*) subsumes six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*); doubt (*vicikitsā*) subsumes twelve underlying tendencies; the remaining [underlying tendencies] are subsumed as explained in the original sūtra.
Question: What is meant by "subsumption" (*saṃgraha*)?
The answer is:
An intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) exists, is real, and is obtainable in relation to itself; therefore, it is called "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*).

An intrinsic nature is not different from itself, an intrinsic nature is not external to itself, an intrinsic nature is not distant from itself, an intrinsic nature does not exclude itself, an intrinsic nature is not empty of itself, an intrinsic nature does not possess excess or increase in relation to itself, and an intrinsic nature is not non-existent in the past, not non-existent in the present, and not non-existent in the future; because an intrinsic nature includes itself, it is called inclusion.
It is not like grasping food with the hand or pinching clothing with the fingers that is called "inclusion" (*saṃgraha*).
Rather, when phenomena include their own essence, it is called inclusion; they do not include other things.
Do the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) include the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*)?
Are the three unwholesome roots subsumed within the three fetters?
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed?
Answer: Some say that a dharma which acts as a "grasper" (saṃgrāhaka) grasps another [dharma] but does not grasp its own self-substance (svabhāva).
This treatise is composed in order to further refute the intent of such a statement.
Do the three fetters (saṃyojana) include the three unwholesome roots (akuśalamūla), and do the three unwholesome roots include the three fetters?
Answer: They do not include one another.
The rest is explained at length as in the original sūtra. Regarding the question:
"How many existences (*bhava*) does the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) cause to continue?
it is asked:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
there are some who claim that the non-defiled mind causes continuity to exist, as the Vātsīputrīyas assert.
Question: For what reason does he make this statement? Answer:
According to the Buddhist sūtras, the sūtras state:

"The Bodhisattva dwells in right mindfulness when entering the mother’s womb, dwells in right mindfulness while staying in the mother’s womb, and dwells in right mindfulness when emerging from the mother’s womb."
To stop such a proponent’s intention and to clarify that it is solely by means of a defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-citta*) that existence continues, this treatise is composed.
A question is asked:
How does one reconcile the Buddha’s sūtras with the claim that existence continues solely by means of a defiled mind?
The answer is:
This teaching states that a non-inverted mind is called right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
All sentient beings enter the mother’s womb with an inverted mind, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas.
When the Bodhisattva enters his mother’s womb, he has this thought:
"This is my mother; this is my father.
He conceives maternal affection for his mother and paternal reverence for his father, entering the womb with an undistorted mind; therefore, it is called "right knowledge" (samyak-jñāna).

Furthermore, as for the reason for composing this treatise: some say that it is solely through the two fetters of craving (*rāga*) and aversion (*pratigha*) that existence continues its succession, as the Dārṣṭāntikas do.
Why do they make such a statement?
Answer: He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state that one enters the mother’s womb due to the conjunction of three factors:
First, the parents come together in one place with defiled intent;
second, the mother is free from illness and her fertile period has arrived;
third, the one who is to receive the body is present.
At that time, for one who has received a body, two kinds of minds alternate and manifest before them:
either that associated with desire or that associated with hatred.
This treatise was composed both to stop the intent of those who speak in such a manner and to clarify that all fetters cause the continuity of existence to persist.
Question: If this is so, how are the Buddhist sūtras to be reconciled? Answer:
In that teaching, it is said that there is a mind in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), but it is not said that there is a mind of continuity (*pratisaṃdhicitta*).

Alternatively, some say that in the evil realms, the mind continues by means of a mind of hatred (*vyāpāda-citta*), whereas in the human and heavenly realms, the mind continues by means of a mind of attachment (*anunaya-citta*).

In order to stop such proponents and to clarify that the thirty-six latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of sentient beings in the desire realm cause continuity to exist, as well as the thirty-one latent dispositions of the form realm and the thirty-one latent dispositions of the formless realm which likewise cause continuity to exist—in order to refute the positions of others and so forth, this treatise is composed.
Existence also has many names; as it is said here:
"The five aggregates, which are the basis for sentient beings to receive a body, are existence.
As it is stated:
When one dies in the desire realm and is reborn within the desire realm, does every existence (*bhava*) in the desire realm constitute a continuity?
Herein it is also explained that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are the basis for sentient beings to receive a body, are termed "existence."
As it is said:

"Being bound by the fetters (paryavasthāna), one causes the continuity of existence in hell. Here too, it is taught that the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) which constitute the locus where sentient beings receive a body are called "existence" (bhava).
As it is said:
When there is the continuity of existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), how many faculties resulting from karmic retribution (*vipākaja-indriya*) are initially acquired?
Herein, "existence" (*bhava*) is also explained as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) that constitute the locus of embodied birth for sentient beings.
As it is said that there are four types of existence—
prior-time existence, death-existence, intermediate existence, and birth-existence— it is also as described above in this context.

As it is said that when one abandons existence in the desire realm and causes the continuity of existence in the desire realm to arise again, all phenomena bound to the desire realm are extinguished and phenomena bound to the desire realm arise and manifest once more— it is also as described above in this context.
As it is asked, "What are the phenomena that exist?
the answer is: "The contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*)."
In this context, it is said that all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) constitute "existence" (*bhava*).

As it is said, "One should know that when *pratyaya* arises, consciousness (*vijñāna*) serves as its nutriment," here "existence" refers to the mind and its mental concomitants (*citta-saṃprayukta*) at the time of the continuity of birth.
As it is said, the Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there is karma that can cause the continuity of future birth, this is also called 'existence' (*bhava*).
In this context, the volition (*cetanā*) that creates future existence is termed "existence."

Regarding the statement that "clinging conditions existence" (*upādāna-pratyayo bhavaḥ*), the Abhidharmikas explain it thus: "In this context, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) at the time of [rebirth] are called 'existence' (*bhava*).
The Venerable Ghoṣaka explains it thus:
"The karma that creates future existence is called 'existence'."
As it is said, there are seven types of existence (*bhava*): first, existence as a hell-being;
second, existence as an animal; [and so forth].
3. The existence of hungry ghosts;
4. The existence of devas;
5. The existence of humans;
Sixth, karmic existence (*karmabhava*);
seventh, intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).

Herein it is taught that the cause of the five destinies and the direction toward the five destinies constitute "existence. Karmic existence within the five destinies is precisely the karma of the five destinies; this is the cause of the five destinies, while intermediate existence is the direction toward the five destinies.
As it is said: "What is existence in the realm of desire?
It is karma bound to the desire realm that, conditioned by grasping, is capable of producing future existence.
Herein, karma and the retribution of karma are being discussed, not the condition of grasping.

Question: If it is stated here that only karma and its retribution are discussed, without mentioning "clinging as a condition," how can this be reconciled with what is said in the Ten Gates? As it says:
Existence in the realm of desire is governed by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the realm of desire;
existence in the realms of form and formlessness is governed by all the underlying tendencies of the realms of form and formlessness.
While this may be so for the realm of desire, why is that?
The five types of karma to be abandoned in the desire realm are all capable of producing retribution.
How can it be that karma to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms is also capable of producing retribution?
The answer is:
The text for the ten gates should be stated as follows:
Existence in the realm of desire is that which is enslaved by all the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm;

existence in the realms of form and formlessness is that which is enslaved by the underlying tendencies abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the realms of form and formlessness, as well as by those underlying tendencies that pervade all [realms].
What is the intention behind not mentioning it?
The answer is:

herein, five kinds of abandoning minds (*prahāṇacitta*) can produce existence (*bhava*), causing existence to continue within the state of the "existence-factor" (*bhavāṅga*) and acting as its attendants; it is with this in mind that the statement was made.

Furthermore, there is another explanation: the "Chapter on the Ten Gates" speaks of karma and the retribution of karma, while the "Exegesis of the Chapter's Meaning" speaks of karma, the retribution of karma, and the conditions for grasping (*upādāna-pratyaya*).
Question: If this is so, how is this [contradiction] to be reconciled?
As it is said:
Why did that Venerable One establish the chapters first?
He wished to reveal the meaning of the "gates" (mukha).
What is meant by "the meaning of the chapters being established differently" and "the meaning of the chapters being explained differently"?
Therefore, it is better to follow what was stated previously. Question:
Why is it called "existence" (bhava)?
The answer is:
it is called existence because of arising and ceasing.
Question: If that is so, then the path one practices is also subject to arising and ceasing; could it therefore be considered existent? Answer:
If arising and ceasing could cause existence (*bhava*) to increase and expand, that would be existence;
yet although the Noble Path arises and ceases, it does not cause existence to increase and expand, but rather causes its destruction.
Furthermore, if arising and ceasing could cause the continuity, growth, and production of birth, aging, sickness, and death, that would be existence.
Although the Noble Path is subject to arising and ceasing, it is able to sever the continuity of existence and does not increase birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Furthermore, if arising and ceasing were the path leading to the origin of suffering, or the path leading to worldly birth and death, that would be "existence";
yet although the Noble Path is subject to arising and ceasing, it is the path leading to the cessation of the origin of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of worldly birth and death.

Furthermore, if arising and ceasing constitute the essence of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), the essence of perversion, the essence of craving, the essence of the underlying tendencies (anuśaya), and the basis for the footing of greed, hatred, and delusion—being a mixture of impurities, poisons, thorns, and dregs, and falling within the truth of the origin of suffering (samudayasatya) in existence—then this is "existence" (bhava).
The Noble Path is the opposite of this and is therefore not called "existence."
Furthermore, the meaning of "fearful" is the meaning of "existent. Question:
If that is so, is nirvāṇa existent, since it is fearful?
As it is said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that when ordinary, foolish people hear it said that nirvāṇa is without self and without 'other,' and that there is nothing whatsoever to be possessed, they give rise to a mind of fear toward these teachings."
The answer is:
If one fears existence, is that [fear] correct, or is it incorrect that one fears nirvana?
Furthermore, regarding phenomena that are to be feared, both ordinary persons and noble ones fear them alike.
Nirvana is feared only by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), not by noble ones (*ārya*).
Furthermore, it is called "existence" (*bhava*) because it is a vessel of suffering. Question:
This is also a musical instrument.
As it is said:
"Mahānāma, you should know that if form were exclusively suffering, devoid of any element of pleasure, and did not give rise to joy and happiness, sentient beings would not become attached to form."
Mahānāman! Because form is not exclusively suffering, but possesses a small portion of pleasure that can give rise to joy and happiness, sentient beings become stained by attachment to it.
It is also said:
There are three feelings: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
It is also said:
"What is required constitutes the equipment for the Path; the Path constitutes the equipment for Nirvana."
It is also said:
"The pleasure of what is required can produce the pleasure of the Path, and the pleasure of the Path can lead to Nirvana.
The answer is:
Although there is a small measure of pleasure within birth and death, suffering constitutes the greater portion;
because the portion of pleasure is so slight, it is designated as "the portion of suffering.

It is like a jar of poison: even if a single drop of honey falls into it, one does not call it a "honey jar" because of that single drop of honey, but rather a "poison jar" because the poison predominates.

The view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) causes the continuity of existence in the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) in one part, the continuity of existence in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) in another part, and the continuity of existence in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) in yet another part.

Since the view of a self-identity exists within the three realms, that which resides in the realm of desire causes the continuity of existence in the realm of desire; that which resides in the realm of form causes the continuity of existence in the realm of form; and that which resides in the formless realm causes the continuity of existence in the formless realm.
The same applies to the clinging to precepts and views, as well as doubt; the rest is explained in detail as in the original sūtra.
There are five kinds of continuity:
first, the continuity of the intermediate state (antarābhava);...
2. the continuity of birth;
3. the continuity of time;
4. the continuity of phenomena.
5. Momentary Continuity and Intermediate Existence Continuity.

Regarding intermediate existence continuity: immediately after the cessation of the aggregates of death (*cyuti-skandha*), the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) arises; because the intermediate existence follows upon the aggregates of death, it is called intermediate existence continuity.

Regarding the continuity of birth-existence (*upapatti-bhava*): when the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) ceases and the birth-state (*upapatti-skandha*) arises immediately thereafter, and the birth-state continues from the intermediate state, this is called the continuity of birth-existence.

Regarding the continuity of time: when the *kalala* stage ceases and the *arbuda* stage arises immediately thereafter, and the *arbuda* stage continues from the *kalala* stage, this is called the continuity of time.
Up until middle age, it ceases and subsequently arises in old age; old age continues from middle age—this is called the continuity of time (*kāla-saṃtati*).

As for the continuity of phenomena (*dharma-saṃtati*): after wholesome phenomena, unwholesome or neutral phenomena subsequently arise; unwholesome or neutral phenomena continue following wholesome phenomena; the same applies to the explanations of unwholesome and neutral phenomena. This is called the continuity of phenomena.

Regarding the continuity of moments: the moment produced immediately after a preceding moment arises, and the subsequent moment follows upon the preceding moment; this is called the continuity of moments.
These five kinds of continuity are all subsumed within two types of continuity, namely, the continuity of phenomena (*dharma-saṃtati*) and the continuity of moments (*kṣaṇa-saṃtati*).

Why is this so? Because the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the continuity of birth (*upapattibhava*), and the continuity of time are entirely comprised of the continuity of phenomena and moments.
Within the realms, there are five types of continuity in the desire realm;
four in the form realm, excluding the continuity of time;
and three in the formless realm, excluding the continuity of intermediate existence and the continuity of time.
Among the destinies (*gati*), the hellish destiny has four [types of continuity], excluding the continuity of time;
the remaining four destinies and the four modes of birth (*yoni*) have five types of continuity.
Herein, the treatise is composed based on two types of continuity: namely, the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the continuity of the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*).

Question: If the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies) cause the continuity of existence but are not *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts), and if they belong to the mental level (*manobhūmi*) rather than the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*),
why is it stated that sleep, restlessness-and-regret, craving born from nose-contact, and craving born from tongue-contact cause the continuity of the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*)?

Craving arises from eye-contact, craving arises from ear-contact, and craving arises from body-contact; these cause the two modes of existence to continue, with some entering the realm of desire (kāmadhātu) and some entering the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
Answer: This passage should be stated as follows:

The hindrance of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa*), the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*), and the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*) cause the continuity of the existence of desire (*kāmadhātu-bhava*); craving born from mental contact (*manas-saṃsparśa-jātā tṛṣṇā*) causes the continuity of the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka-bhava*); other hindrances and other types of contact that produce craving cannot cause the continuity of existence.
If it were not explained in this way, one should know that this explanation is incomplete.
Furthermore, because there is no severance, it is called a "continuity.
If one does not sever the hindrances, and does not sever the craving born of nose-contact or tongue-contact, then at the end of life, one will again be reborn in the desire realm.
If one does not sever the craving born of eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact, one will be reborn in the desire realm at the end of life.
Furthermore, there are three factors in the form realm that cause the continuity of existence:
first, non-severance;...
2. It can produce a fruit;
3. it causes existence to continue.

When [unwholesome states] reside within the five bodies of consciousness, those that are unwholesome possess two functions: first, they do not cease; second, they can produce a fruit, but they cannot cause existence to continue.
That which is indeterminate (avyākṛta) possesses one characteristic: it does not cut off [the continuity], cannot produce a fruit, and cannot cause existence to continue.
When it resides in the mental ground (manobhūmi), that which is unwholesome (akuśala) possesses three characteristics:
it does not cut off [the continuity], can produce a fruit, and can cause existence to continue.
The indeterminate [state] has two characteristics:
it does not interrupt the continuity of existence, yet it is unable to produce a fruit.
As for the unwholesome states that reside in the mental ground (manobhūmi) and the five groups of sensory consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya), they have two characteristics:
That which is uninterrupted and capable of producing a fruit, yet cannot cause existence to continue, is the indeterminate;
it possesses one characteristic: it is uninterrupted, yet it cannot produce a fruit nor cause existence to continue.
If these three factors exist, they can cause existence to continue.
By which samādhi is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) extinguished? Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
it was composed in order to manifest that when a Buddha appears in the world, he possesses such rare and wondrous powers.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
Outside Jambudvīpa, there is a path for the Wheel-turning Sage Kings (Cakravartin), one yojana in width, which is covered by the ocean waters.
When there is no Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin), there is no sentient being capable of surpassing him.

When a Wheel-Turning Sage King appears, the waters of the ocean recede by one yojana, and the path traversed by the Wheel-Turning Sage King manifests; it is then strewn with golden sand and sprinkled with sandalwood-scented water.
When a Wheel-Turning Sage King wishes to travel through the four continents with his fourfold army, he proceeds upon this path.
Likewise, when a Buddha does not appear in the world, there is no sentient being capable of traversing the fundamental ground.
Although there are sentient beings who have attained detachment from desire, they rely on peripheral paths and do not reach the fundamental path.

Only when the Ten-Powered Wheel-Turning Dharma King appears in the world does the fundamental path manifest; it is then strewn with the golden sand of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and sprinkled with the sandalwood perfumed water of morality, concentration, and wisdom.
The World-Honored One traverses upon it with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of sentient beings, proceeding toward the city of fearless nirvāṇa.
Therefore, wishing to manifest that the appearance of a Buddha in the world possesses such rare and wondrous power, this treatise is composed.

By what samādhi is the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) extinguished? It may be said to be by means of a certain path, it may be said to be by means of a certain antidote, or it may be said to be by means of a certain correct contemplation; all such explanations have the same meaning.
Cessation may also be called abandonment, it may be called dispassion, it may be called exhaustion, and it may be called liberation; such explanations as these all have the same meaning.
In the past, there were two great masters: the first was named Jīvaka and the second was named Ghoṣavarman.
The Venerable Jīvaka spoke thus: "What is spoken of here is ultimate abandonment, abandonment without remainder;
it pertains exclusively to noble ones and not to ordinary persons, for it is by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and not by the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*)."
The *Saptasaya-sūtra* (Seven Reliances Sūtra) is the root of this treatise.

The *Saptasaya-sūtra* speaks of the fundamental stage (*maulabhūmi*) but does not speak of the bordering stages; there is no one who, relying on the fundamental stage, becomes free from desire by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
The Venerable Ghoṣavarman spoke thus:

"In this context, what is taught is ultimate abandonment and abandonment without remainder; this applies both to ordinary persons and to noble ones, and occurs both through the mundane path and by means of the untainted path."
Question: If that is so, then the *Saptāśraya-sūtra* is not the root of this treatise, for the *Saptāśraya-sūtra* speaks exclusively of the roots. Answer:
For this reason, the Abhidharma illuminates the Sūtras just as a lamp does;
that which is not stated in the Sūtras is explained here,
and that which is not manifested in the Sūtras is revealed here.
Regarding other meanings contained within the Sūtra, they are explained here.
The explanations provided by both schools are equally well-justified.
The three fetters depend upon the four reliances and the *anāgamya* (unattained) stage.
"Relying on the four reliances" means relying on the four dhyānas.
"Relying on the threshold" (anāgamya) means relying on the threshold and the intermediate stages; this stage is named "threshold. Question:
Why is it called "the Not-yet-attained" (anāgamya)?
The answer is:

because one has not yet entered the fundamental stage (maulabhūmi), and although the fundamental stage has not yet become manifest, one is able to abandon desire; therefore, it is called the "Not-yet-attained" stage.
Question: That which has not yet reached the stage is not called a "basis.
Why, then, is this statement made?
"Is it based on the four dhyānas or on the *anāgamya*?
The answer is:
this text should be stated as follows:"
If [cessation] occurs both when one enters the four reliances and when one does not enter the four reliances,
what is the intention behind not mentioning this?
The answer is:
In order to restate the names of the four reliances (*catvāri pratisaraṇāni*), it is said:
"Either one attains cessation by entering the fundamental [dhyāna], or one attains cessation without entering the fundamental [dhyāna]."
It is like a person asking another man:
"Will your business be accomplished if you enter the city,
or will it be accomplished if you do not enter the city?"
The three fetters are found from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the desire realm, they depend on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*);
regarding the first dhyāna, they depend on the first basis (*prathama-āśraya*) and the threshold concentration.
The second dhyāna relies on two bases and the threshold concentration (anāgamya);
the third dhyāna relies on three bases and the threshold concentration;
the fourth dhyāna and the formless attainments rely on four bases and the threshold concentration.

Why is this so? The three fetters are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and must be definitively severed by means of that path. The path of seeing necessarily exists in six stages, namely: the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the four fundamental dhyānas.
If one attains right determination by relying on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*), then the three fetters are extinguished by means of the threshold concentration;
if one attains right determination by relying on the first dhyāna, then the three fetters are extinguished by means of the first dhyāna;
and if one attains right determination and the formless attainments (*ārūpya*) by relying on up to the fourth dhyāna, then the three fetters are extinguished by means of the fourth dhyāna.
In this context, the fourth dhyāna and the formless attainments (ārūpya) are mentioned; the three fetters (saṃyojana) depend upon the four dhyānas and the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
Greed, hatred, delusion, and the outflow of desire (kāma-āsava) depend upon the threshold concentration.
Why is this? Because when one is free from craving and desire, these phenomena are permanently severed.
If an ordinary person severs them, they do so by relying on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage.
The Noble One also relies on the *anāgamya* (not-yet-arrived) stage for abandonment.
Both the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) and the noble path (*āryamārga*) rely on the *anāgamya* stage for abandonment.
As for the contaminated [attainments], they either rely on seven stages or rely on the *anāgamya*.
The seven bases are the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments.
"Not-yet-reached" refers to the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*).
The contaminated [attainments] are obtainable from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding that sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one either relies on the "not-yet-arrived" (anāgamya) stage to become free from desire for it, or even relies up to the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana) to become free from desire for it; thus, there is the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the statement that the outflow-tainted [states] pertain to the seven stages and the threshold stage (*anāgamya*):
those belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna may rely on the first support or rely on the threshold stage;
those belonging to the stage of the second dhyāna may rely on the second support or rely on the threshold stage.
Up to the sphere of consciousness, one relies either on the six bases or on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
For the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one relies either on the seven bases or on the threshold concentration.
The outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava) relies either on the seven supports or on the threshold concentration (anāgamya).
The seven supports are the four dhyānas and the three formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti).
The threshold concentration refers to the preliminary stage (sāmantaka) and the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara).
The outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*) is found from the desire realm up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
That outflow of ignorance in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception either relies on the seven bases (*saptāśraya*) or relies on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
In brief, it is based on either the seven bases or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
If one is in the desire realm, it is based on the threshold concentration.
If one is in the first dhyāna, it is based on the first base or the threshold concentration.
Up to the sphere of consciousness, the outflow of ignorance relies on the six bases or the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*).
Regarding the spheres of nothingness and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the outflow of ignorance relies either on seven bases or on the threshold concentration.
The rest is explained at length as in the original sutra.
"If various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are past, have those fetters already bound [the person]?
He replied:
If a fetter is past, that fetter has already bound [the person].
It is the case that when all fetters are past, their acquisition (*prāpti*) is also past.
Is there any fetter that has already bound [the person] but is not past?
Answer: There are.
These are the fetters of the future and the present.
All fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the future and present may exist in the past.
When these fetters arise, they may proceed like a great bull walking in front, or like a calf following behind, or they may proceed together.
As for the great ox walking in front, the fetters arise first and attainment arises later;
as for the calf following behind, attainment arises first and the fetters arise later.
Regarding "those that coexist," it refers to the fetters being acquired simultaneously.
Herein, the *Vātsīputrīya* school's doctrine of "dharma-following" (*anugata*) is discussed.
If various fetters are yet to come into the future, will those fetters bind [the individual]?
Answer: Or, there are fetters that are future, yet those fetters are not bound [to the present].
This should be elaborated in full as four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
What is the case where a fetter exists in the future, yet that fetter does not bind?
The answer is:
regarding all future fetters that have been abandoned, fully understood, ceased, and vomited out, the mind of one who has severed those fetters never regresses from that state.

"Cutting off" refers to the knowledge of cutting off; "knowing" refers to knowing through wisdom; "extinguishing" refers to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); "vomiting out" refers to attaining liberation through the abandonment of non-liberation, and attaining realization.
Regarding one whose mind has severed the fetters therein and does not regress: this refers to an Arhat of the "non-regressive" type (*avinipātadharman*).

Having already severed, up to having already vomited out, the fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation in the future, those fetters shall never again bind him.
Why is this? Because he is of the nature of non-retrogression.

If he were an Arhat subject to retrogression, then as for the fetters of the three realms to be abandoned through the path of vision, which have already been severed and even cast out, those fetters would no longer bind him again.

The Anāgāmin is one who possesses the dharma of non-retrogression; having abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness, they have already severed, up to and including vomited out, the fetters to be abandoned through the path of vision within the three realms and the fetters of the eight stages to be abandoned through the path of cultivation. Those fetters shall never again bind them.

Up to the point where one has abandoned desire for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the first dhyāna, regarding those phenomena to be abandoned through the path of vision in the three realms and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm: their fetters have already been severed, up to having been vomited out, and they are no longer bound by them.

For one who is a non-retrogressive *sakṛdāgāmin*, the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms, as well as the six types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm, have already been severed and even vomited out; they will never again be bound by them.
The *srotāpanna* has already severed, up to having vomited out, the fetters of the future three realms to be abandoned through the path of vision; they are no longer bound by them.

An ordinary person of the non-retrogressive type, such as a bodhisattva and others who have abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness, has already severed, up to having vomited out, the fetters of the eight stages to be abandoned through the path of vision and the path of cultivation; they are no longer bound by them.
The same explanation applies even up to the single stage of being free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
How is it that a fetter (*saṃyojana*) is bound while that fetter does not exist in the future? Answer:
Regarding those fetters that have been past, already abandoned, already known, already ceased, and already vomited out—one necessarily falls away from that abandonment of fetters.

For an Arhat of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the fetters of the three realms that were to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, which have already been abandoned up to being vomited out—those fetters shall bind him again.

For a *parihāṇadharman* Anāgāmin who has abandoned desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) belonging to the eight stages have already been severed, up to being vomited out; yet those fetters are liable to bind him again.
The same applies even up to one who is free from the desires of the desire realm but not yet free from the desires of the first dhyāna.

Regarding an ordinary person who has fallen away from freedom from the desires of the sphere of nothingness, the fetters of the eight stages—whether abandoned through the path of seeing or the path of cultivation—that were already severed, up to already vomited out, those fetters shall bind them again.
The same explanation applies up to the point where one has abandoned desire for the desire realm but has not yet abandoned desire for the first dhyāna.
What kind of fetter exists in the future such that it will bind?
Answer: Regarding all future fetters that have already been severed, up to having been vomited out, one will certainly fall away from those fetters.
The detailed explanation is as in the case of the past.
What is the case where a fetter does not exist in the future, yet that fetter should not be said to bind?
The answer is:
those fetters that are past, already severed, and even already vomited out—those fetters will certainly not recur.
As explained in detail regarding the future, if various fetters are present, are those fetters currently binding?
The answer is: Yes.
If a fetter is present, that fetter binds now;
when various fetters are present, their acquisition is also present.
Is there any fetter that binds now, yet that fetter is not present?
Answer: There are;
namely, those fetters (saṃyojana) that are past and future.
Those fetters that are past and future can exist in the present and bind the past, just as the method of a great ox walking.
Regarding the present, it is like the behavior of a calf.
When one uses a certain path to sever the fetters of the desire realm, upon regressing from that path, does one again obtain those fetters?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
Some say there is no such thing as falling back from a state [of realization], just as the Vibhajyavādins, using a present analogy, have said:
"We see now that once a jar is broken, there remain only shards; it cannot be restored to its former state as a jar."
In this way, an Arhat uses the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) to destroy all afflictions so that none remain; they can never again become of the nature of affliction.
It is just like wood burned to ashes, which no longer has the utility of wood.

In this way, the Arhat burns away all afflictions with the fire of wisdom; since there are no longer any afflictions to function, based on this present analogy, it is said that there is no possibility of falling back.
To refute the intention of such proponents and to clarify that the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) possesses substantial reality:
if one were to say that there is no such nature of falling away, it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
There are two types of arhats: first, those subject to regression (parihāṇadharman), and second, those not subject to regression (aparihāṇadharman).
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras, which state:
"There are five causes and conditions by which a time-liberated (sāmayikī-vimukta) arhat regresses."
What are the five?
First, managing affairs;
second, extensive recitation.
Third, reconciling disputes;
fourth, traveling far;
fifth, long-term illness.
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras, which state:
"The Venerable Gauḍika attained arhatship; at that time he was one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), and six times he fell away from the fruit of arhatship."
On the seventh occasion, fearing that he would fall away from this Dharma, he took his own life with a blade.
To ensure that such a fault does not occur, it is taught that the nature of falling away (parihāṇadharman) possesses a real, determinate essence.
Question: If the dharma of falling back (parihāṇadharman) truly possesses a fixed essence, how do you reconcile this with the analogy for the present used by the Vibhajyavādins? Answer:
This need not necessarily be explained. Why is that?
Because this is neither Sūtra, nor Vinaya, nor Abhidharma.
One cannot use worldly, manifest matters to surpass the Dharma of the noble ones; the Dharma of the noble ones is distinct, and worldly dharmas are distinct.
If you wish to insist on reconciling them, what is your intention?
Answer: One should point out the fault in the analogy.
If the analogy has a fault, the meaning also has a fault.
Just as when a jar is broken, there remain shards of pottery,
when the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) of an Arhat are severed, do some fetters still remain or not?
If some fetters remain, he is called one who possesses fetters and is not called an Arhat.
If there are no remaining fetters (*anuśaya*), the meaning differs and the analogy differs.
For example, when wood has been burned and some ashes remain: when all the fetters of an Arhat have been exhausted, are there still remaining fetters, or are there no remaining fetters?
If there are remaining fetters (*saṃyojana*), one is not called an Arhat;
if there are no remaining fetters, the meaning differs and the analogy differs.

However, wood has no sense of being "burnt"; rather, once the subtle particles of wood have ceased after acting as the cause for the subtle particles of fire, and the subtle particles of fire have ceased after acting as the cause for the subtle particles of ash, it is for this reason that such a statement is made.
Wood is the cause of ash; since ash arises from wood, one forms the notion that the wood has been burned.
Yet once the wood is burned, there remains residual ash, which is not nothingness. Therefore, this analogy does not correspond to the intended meaning.

In this way, when the afflictions of an Arhat are exhausted, it is not that his fundamental nature does not exist; rather, it possesses characteristics and a substantial entity throughout the past and future lives. When those wholesome qualities that are contrary to the fetters have not yet arisen within that person's continuum, they are said to have "not severed the fetters.
When those wholesome qualities contrary to the fetters arise within that person's continuum, those fetters are said to be "severed."
When practicing the Noble Path in this manner, one does not cause the essence of the fetters to lack intrinsic nature.
Such is the marvelous quality of the Noble Path: it enables an Arhat to sever all fetters, yet it does not cause these fetters to be devoid of intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke thus:
"Afflictions are said to be 'abandoned' because they no longer function within the body;
it is like Devadatta not being present in a house—it does not mean that the nature of Devadatta is absent."
It is the same for them as well.
[The opponent] asks:
How does the Vibhajyavādin explain the sūtra cited by the Saṃmitīya?
The answer is:
They maintain this position:
an Arhat may fall away from the path, but does not fall away from the fruit.
Why is this so? Because the fruit is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*). Question:
If this is so, although one does not regress from the fruit, one regresses from the path; is such regression from the path not indeed a form of regression?
When one regresses from the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), does one then attain the path of learning (*śaikṣamārga*) or not?
If it were obtained, one should also say that there is a regression from the fruit;
if it were not obtained, there would be a great error.
To regress from the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga) without obtaining the path of learning (śaikṣamārga) would mean that at that time one is an ordinary person (pṛthagjana).
The Vibhajyavādins further maintain this position:
the *anuśaya* (latent proclivities) are the seeds of the *paryavasthāna* (outbursts). The *anuśaya* is not associated with the mind, whereas the *paryavasthāna* is associated with the mind.
The *anuśaya* is capable of producing the *paryavasthāna*; when the *paryavasthāna* manifests in the present, it is called "falling away" (*parihāṇi*).

Since the Arhat has already severed all latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), he cannot give rise to the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*); how then could he fall away by having an active outburst manifest?
For this reason, they maintain that there is no such thing as "falling away from the state of non-retrogression" (*aparihāṇadharma*).
It is well said thus:

when one speaks in this way, asserting that there is no "nature of falling away" (parihāṇadharman), this is the fruit of ignorance, the fruit of darkness, the fruit of folly, and the fruit of a lack of diligent application; yet the nature of falling away possesses both characteristics and substantial reality.
Therefore, this treatise is composed in order to refute the positions of others and to reveal our own position.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the state of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*)?

Answer: This is the nature of non-accomplishment (*aprāpti*), which is comprised within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) that are dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Within such dharmas, it is as stated:
Such dharmas as these are called formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
There is a distinction between "retrogression" (*hāni*) and "the dharma of retrogression. Retrogression refers to the state of non-accomplishment (*aprāpti*), as explained above.
The dharma of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*) consists of unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) and obscured-unspecified dharmas (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, it is like the difference between the schism of the Saṃgha (*saṃghabheda*) and the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha (*saṃghabhedāpatti*).

Schism in the Saṃgha is the nature of non-concordance; it is comprised within the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*) as an obscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) phenomenon.
The offense of schism is a false speech; it is accomplished when the Saṃgha becomes discordant, and the person who causes the schism accomplishes the offense.
Thus, the "falling away" is distinct and the "dharma of falling away" is distinct, as explained in detail above.

Furthermore, there are those who say that if the proclivities (*anuśaya*) arise, or if the fetters (*paryavasthāna*) manifest before one, this constitutes the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).
If this were the case, then the nature of falling away would be defiled (*kliṣṭa*).
Furthermore, there are those who say: "If a phenomenon conforms to the nature of decline, it possesses the nature of decline.
If one were to speak in this way, then all phenomena would possess the nature of decline. Why is this so?
Because all phenomena conform to the nature of retrogression,
the Venerable Buddhatīva stated: "Retrogression has no intrinsic nature."
Why is this so? Because although a practitioner originally possessed such various wholesome merits, they have regressed from and fallen away from those dharmas.
It is like a person whose wealth has been plundered by bandits; someone asks them:
"What is the essential nature of the wealth and goods you have lost?
He replied, "They have no essential nature."
If one's original wealth and possessions are plundered by thieves and taken away, what inherent nature remains?

It is just as if there were a person whose clothes were stolen by another; if someone were to ask him, "Now that you have lost your clothes, what is the essential nature of your body? [he would have no answer].
He replied: "It has no intrinsic nature. Why is this so?"
If this garment originally existed and someone were to rob it away, what nature would it have?
It is just as if there were a person whose garment was torn by another; someone else might ask him:
"Your garment is now torn; what is its essential nature?"
He replied: "There is no intrinsic nature. Why is that?"
If a garment was originally whole but has been torn by another, what inherent nature could it possess?
That case is likewise.
The commentary says:
It should be explained as stated above:
"The nature of falling away is non-accomplishment," and so forth, as extensively detailed. Question:
Is it that the defilements have already receded and then manifest, or do they manifest and thereby cause a regression?
If it were the case that one regresses because the defilements manifest, how would you reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*?
As it is said:
"The fetter of sensual desire arises due to three factors:
first, not severing and not understanding the underlying tendency of sensual desire."
Second, the manifestation of the full array of sensual desire;
third, improper reflection.
If one falls away when afflictions manifest, how is this scripture to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"There are five causes and conditions by which a parinirvāṇa-in-this-life (samayavimukta) arhat falls away.

If falling away occurs when afflictions manifest before one, how is this to be reconciled with what is stated in the *Samyuktabhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (or *Prakaraṇapāda*) regarding the *Vinaya-khandaka*?
As it is said:
"By means of a mind that is neither-learner-nor-non-learner, one falls away and gives rise to the acquisition of learner-dharmas.
How is it that an Arhat brings a defiled mind into manifestation? What kind of mind arises immediately prior to the defiled mind?
If one were to give rise to afflictions after having fallen away [from the attainment], how would one reconcile this with what is said in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*? As it says:

"At times the mind is distant, and at times the mind is rigid; because of being distant or rigid, at times the three envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) of the formless realm—namely, craving, pride, and ignorance—manifest before one, though it is mostly the envelopment of pride that arises."
