When the sixth path of non-obstruction ceases and the sixth path of liberation arises, at that time, that abandonment is called "abandonment," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth"; it is not called "knowledge of abandonment. It is called the fruit of the śramaṇa, namely the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin, but it is not called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder or nirvāṇa without remainder.

At that time, that which is abandoned through the path of vision within the three realms is called abandonment, called dispassion, called cessation, and called the knowledge of abandonment—referring to the knowledge of abandonment previously attained—and it is called the fruit of the ascetic life, namely the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin; however, it is not called the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder or the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

The five kinds of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm are of a single flavor; one attains liberation from them all at once. At that time, their abandonment is termed "abandonment," "freedom from desire," "cessation," and "truth," but it is not termed "knowledge of abandonment. It is called the fruit of the śramaṇa, namely the fruit of the sakṛdāgāmin, but it is not termed the realm of nirvāṇa with remainder or the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder.

When a Sakṛdāgāmin is about to attain the fruit of Anāgāmin and severs the seventh and eighth types of fetters, that severance is called "severance," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth"; it is not called "knowledge of severance," nor is it called a "fruit of the śramaṇa," nor is it called the realm of *sa-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* or *an-upādiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

When the ninth path of non-obstruction ceases and the ninth path of liberation arises, at that time, that abandonment is called "freedom from desire," "cessation," "truth," and "knowledge of abandonment"—specifically, the knowledge of abandonment consisting in the total exhaustion of the five lower fetters. It is called the fruit of the ascetic life, namely the fruit of the Non-returner (Anāgāmin), but it is not yet called the realm of nirvana with remainder or the realm of nirvana without remainder.

At that very moment, the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) within the three realms, as well as the nine types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm, become of a single flavor; one simultaneously realizes liberation and attains it. At that time, those abandonments are termed "dispassion" (*vairāgya*), "cessation" (*nirodha*), "truth" (*satya*), and "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*). This refers to the knowledge of abandonment previously attained regarding the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañcāvarabhāgīyasaṃyojana*). It is called the fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), namely the fruit of the non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), but it is not yet termed the realm of nirvana with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*) or the realm of nirvana without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣanirvāṇadhātu*).

When one is free from the desires of the first dhyāna and has severed one type of fetter up to nine types of fetters, at that time those severances are called "severance," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth"; they are not called "knowledge of severance," nor are they called "fruits of the śramaṇa," nor are they called the "realm of nirvāṇa with remainder" or "nirvāṇa without remainder."
This applies even up to the point of abandoning desire for the fourth dhyāna; the same explanation holds for severing one type of fetter up to severing eight types of fetters.

At the moment the ninth path of non-obstruction ceases and the ninth path of liberation arises, that abandonment is termed "abandonment," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth"; it is termed "knowledge of abandonment," specifically the knowledge of abandonment regarding the craving for form (*rūparāga-prahāṇa-jñāna*). However, it is not yet termed a "fruit of the ascetic life" (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), nor is it termed either "nirvāṇa with remainder" or the "element of nirvāṇa without remainder."

Having abandoned desire for the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one severs the eight kinds of fetters; at that time, those severances are called "severance," "freedom from desire," "cessation," and "truth," but they are not called "knowledge of severance," nor "fruit of the ascetic life," nor the "realm of nirvana with remainder" or "nirvana without remainder."

When the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) ceases and the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises, at that time nine kinds of fetters (saṃyojana) are severed. That severance is called "severance," "dispassion" (vairāgya), "cessation" (nirodha), and "truth" (satya); it is called the "knowledge of severance" (prahāṇajñāna), meaning the knowledge of the total exhaustion and severance of all fetters; it is called the "fruit of the śramaṇa" (śrāmaṇyaphala), namely the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala); and it is called the "nirvāṇa-element with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu), but it is not called the "nirvāṇa-element without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu).

At that time, the eight kinds of fetters—those abandoned through the path of vision in the three realms, those abandoned through the path of cultivation in the eight stages, and those abandoned through the path of cultivation in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—become of a single flavor; one simultaneously realizes liberation and attains it. At that moment, their abandonment is called "abandonment," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth"; it is called the "knowledge of abandonment," meaning the knowledge of the total exhaustion of all fetters; it is called the "fruit of the ascetic life," namely the fruit of Arhatship; and it is called the "realm of nirvana with remainder," but not the "realm of nirvana without remainder."

If an Arhat’s aggregates, elements, and sense bases no longer continue and he enters the realm of nirvana without remainder, at that time his abandonment is called "abandonment," "dispassion," "cessation," and "truth. The knowledge of abandonment attained therein is called "knowledge of abandonment" and the "fruit of the śramaṇa," namely the fruit of arhatship. This is not called the realm of nirvana with remainder, but is called the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Question: Since all abandonments (*prahāṇa*) are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), why is it that at times they are called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*) and at other times are not? Answer:
At that time, there are those for whom there are four matters or five matters, which are called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
As for the four matters: first, the destruction of both causes;
second, the attainment of liberation from both fetters.
Third, the attainment of untainted liberation;
fourth, the destruction of all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
As for the five matters, they consist of the aforementioned four matters and fifth, the permanent abandonment within the realms (*dhātu*).
In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there are four matters; in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are five matters.

When the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*) arises, at that time, non-harming does not share the same cause [as harming]. Although harming is abandoned through the vision of suffering, non-harming is abandoned through the vision of origin; thus, by not being bound by both simultaneously, one attains liberation.

Although one attains liberation from the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), one does not attain liberation from those abandoned through the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*).

Although one attains untainted liberation (*anāsrava-vimukti*), one does not eliminate the omnipresent latent tendencies (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). At that time, there is only one matter and not two; therefore, that abandonment is called "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), but it is not called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).

When the patience regarding the comparison of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) arises and the knowledge regarding the comparison of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is produced, at that time, non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) has both as its cause. Although it severs the causes to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), non-harming does not sever the causes to be abandoned by the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*); thus, while it severs the fetters (*bandhana*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering, it does not sever the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of origination. Even though the causes are severed, the simultaneous bond (*sahajāta-bandhana*) remains unsevered. Although the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are severed, the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of origination remain unsevered.

Although one attains the attainment of untainted liberation, one does not ultimately eradicate all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
At that time, because there are only two matters and not three, that abandonment is not called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).

When the patience regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) arises and the knowledge regarding the dharma of origination (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) is produced, at that time one destroys the causes associated with both [truths]. Previously, one destroyed the causes to be abandoned by the vision of suffering; now, one destroys the causes to be abandoned by the vision of origination, thereby attaining liberation from all fetters.

Previously, one attained liberation through the vision of what is to be abandoned by the truth of suffering; now, one attains liberation through the vision of what is to be abandoned by the truth of origin.

Upon attaining this untainted liberation, one also destroys all pervasive underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; at that time, it is termed the "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).

When the subsequent patience regarding the origin (*samudaye anvaya-kṣānti*) arises and the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin (*samudaye anvaya-jñāna*) is produced, at that time one destroys both types of causes: first, one destroys the causes to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*), and now one destroys the causes to be abandoned through the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*); thus, one attains liberation from both bonds.
Previously, one attained liberation from the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering; now, one attains liberation from the fetters abandoned through the vision of the origin [of suffering].

By attaining the acquisition of untainted liberation, one destroys all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. At that time, because four conditions are fulfilled, that abandonment is termed "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).

When the patience regarding the cessation of phenomena (nirodhadharma-kṣānti) arises and the knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena (nirodhadharma-jñāna) is produced, at that time one destroys the causes associated with both [truths]. Previously, one destroyed the causes to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of origination; now, one destroys the causes to be abandoned through the vision of cessation. Thus, one attains liberation from all fetters.

Previously, one attained liberation from the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering and the vision of the origin; now, one attains liberation from the fetters abandoned through the vision of cessation.

Upon attaining this untainted liberation, one destroys all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. At that time, because four conditions are fulfilled, that abandonment is termed "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).

With the cessation of the subsequent patience regarding cessation (*nirodhānvayakṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhānvayajñāna*) arises; with the cessation of the dharma-patience regarding the path (*mārgadharmakṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) arises; and with the cessation of the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*), the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) arises—the explanation is likewise for these cases.

Thus, what has been described is the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) pertaining to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there are five matters termed "knowledge of abandonment.

From the abandonment of one type of desire of the desire realm up to the abandonment of eight types of desire, at that time, one does not harm the co-existent cause; although the eight types of causes are abandoned, the lowest-of-the-low cause is not yet abandoned.
Why is this so? Because the nine kinds of fetters act as causes for one another, one remains bound and cannot attain liberation.
Although one may attain liberation from eight kinds of bonds, one cannot attain liberation from a single kind of bond.
Why is this? Because the nine kinds of fetters bind one to one another.

Although one attains the untainted liberation and eliminates all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one has not yet permanently departed from that realm.
At this time, there are only two things and not three; therefore, that cessation is not called "cessation through knowledge.

When the ninth type of fetter is severed, at that moment one eliminates both causes: having previously severed the eight types of causes, one now severs the lowest-of-the-low cause, thereby attaining liberation from all bonds.
Previously, one attained liberation from the eight kinds of fetters; now, one attains liberation from the lowest-of-the-low fetters.

By attaining the acquisition of untainted liberation, one destroys all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, achieving ultimate detachment from that realm—namely, detachment from the desire realm.
At that time, because there are five factors, that abandonment is called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
Having become detached from the desire of the first dhyāna, one abandons one kind of fetter up to eight kinds of fetters; the detailed explanation is as in the case of the desire realm.

When the ninth type is abandoned, the cause associated with harm is eliminated; having previously abandoned the eight types of causes, one now abandons the lowest-of-the-low cause, thereby attaining liberation from all bonds.
Having previously attained liberation from the eight types of bonds, one now attains liberation from the lowest-of-the-low bond, achieving the attainment of untainted liberation.

When one eliminates the pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), yet has not attained ultimate detachment from that realm, at that time there are only four factors and not five; therefore, that abandonment is not termed "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).
The same applies to the explanations for the second and third dhyānas.
Having abandoned desire for the fourth dhyāna, one may sever one type of fetter up to eight types of fetters; yet, because the causes and the bonds remain together, one does not attain liberation.

Although one attains the acquisition of untainted liberation and eliminates all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one has not yet definitively transcended that realm.
At this time, there are only two factors present and not three; therefore, that abandonment is not termed "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).
When severing the ninth type of fetter, one destroys both causes and attains liberation from both bonds.

One attains the acquisition of untainted liberation, destroys all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and achieves ultimate detachment from that realm.

At that time, because there are five factors, that abandonment is called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), namely, the knowledge of abandonment through the exhaustion of craving for form (*rūparāga*).

As it is with the departure from desire for the first dhyāna, so it is likewise taught for the departure from desire up to the third dhyāna, the departure from desire for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and even the departure from desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

When one becomes detached from the desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, at the moment of severing one type of fetter up to the eighth type of fetter, the cause and the bond are not severed simultaneously, and liberation is not attained simultaneously.

Although one attains the attainment of untainted liberation and eliminates all pervasive latent defilements (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), one has not yet definitively transcended that realm.
At this time, there are only two factors and not three; therefore, that abandonment is not termed "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).
When the ninth kind of fetter is severed, at that time one destroys both causes and attains liberation from both bonds.

One attains the acquisition of untainted liberation, destroying all pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and becomes ultimately detached from that realm.

At that time, due to five factors, that abandonment is called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*), namely, the knowledge of abandonment consisting in the total exhaustion of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojanakṣaya*). Question:

Is the love (*tṛṣṇā*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the four dhyānas what is called "knowledge of abandonment," or is it only the love to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the fourth dhyāna that is so named?
Answer: Some say that the abandonment of craving for the four dhyānas is called the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
Others say that the abandonment of the nine types of craving for the fourth dhyāna is called the knowledge of abandonment.
Furthermore, some say that only the abandonment of craving for the lowest of the low grades within the fourth dhyāna is called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*).
The critique states:
One should instead speak as follows:
The abandonment of all craving in the form realm that is to be severed through the path of cultivation is called "knowledge of abandonment" (*prahāṇajñāna*). Why is this so?

Because if one abandons even the lowest-of-the-low craving of the fourth dhyāna, then only when all craving in the form realm to be severed through the path of cultivation is exhausted is it termed "knowledge of abandonment."

Question: The abandonment of dharmas is the most supreme dharma; why is it that the attainment of the two abandonments is universally realized at the times of the fruits of *anāgāmin* and *arhat*? Answer:
At these two times, one attains the fruit while being ultimately detached from the realm;
however, when attaining the fruit of Srotāpanna or the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin, although one attains the fruit, one is not ultimately detached from the realm.
Although one who has abandoned the desire for the fourth dhyāna is ultimately separated from that realm, they have not yet attained the fruit.
When one attains the fruit of an Anāgāmin, one is ultimately separated from the realm; that is to say, one attains the fruit by becoming free from the desire of the desire realm.

When one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* and when one attains the fruit of *arhat*, one is ultimately detached from the realms; that is, one attains these fruits while being detached from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). When one attains the fruit of *arhat*, it is at that time [one is so detached].
Furthermore, at that time, when one has completely transcended the realm and severed the fetters of the lower and upper realms, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* and the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*;
however, when one has not yet completely transcended the realm and has not severed the fetters of the lower and upper realms, [these fruits are not attained].

When one is detached from craving for the form realm (*rūparāga*), although one is ultimately detached from that realm—meaning one is detached from the form realm—one has not yet completely severed the fetters of the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

When one attains the fruit of non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*), one is ultimately detached from that realm—meaning one is detached from the desire realm—and one has completely severed the fetters of the lower realms (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).

Upon attaining the fruit of arhatship, one is ultimately detached from the realms—meaning one is detached from the formless realm—and has ultimately severed the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, at that time, one is ultimately detached from the realms and has ultimately severed unwholesome and neutral afflictions (*kleśa*).
When attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna* or the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, one has not yet definitively transcended the realm, nor has one definitively severed unwholesome afflictions (*kleśa*).
When transcending the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), although one has definitively transcended that realm, one has not yet definitively severed indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) afflictions.
When attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*, one is ultimately detached from the realm—meaning detachment from the desire realm—and has ultimately abandoned unwholesome (*akuśala*) afflictions.
When attaining the fruit of *arhat*, one is ultimately detached from the realm—meaning detachment from the formless realm—and has ultimately abandoned indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) afflictions.

Just as it is with the unwholesome and the indeterminate, so too should one understand that the same applies to what has retribution and what lacks retribution, what produces two fruits and what produces one fruit, and what is associated with or dissociated from shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The explanation is likewise.
Regarding the nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), who relinquishes how many, and who acquires how many?
The answer is:
there are those who neither relinquish nor acquire any, such as ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Question: In this context, ordinary persons are neither questioned nor answered.
Furthermore, there are noble ones who neither abandon nor attain [the dharmas], such as those abiding in their original nature; those who are progressing toward excellence are also like this.

Just as when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) arises, at that time there is neither relinquishing nor obtaining.

When the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) arises, at that time as well there is neither relinquishing nor obtaining.

When the patience regarding the dharma of the origin (*samudaya-dharma-kṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge regarding the dharma of the origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) arises, at that time one attains one [fruit] and there is nothing to be relinquished.

When the subsequent patience regarding the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-kṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge regarding the origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) arises, at that time one attains one [fruit] and there is nothing to be relinquished.

When the patience regarding the cessation of phenomena (nirodhadharmakṣānti) ceases and the knowledge regarding the cessation of phenomena (nirodhadharmajñāna) arises, at that time one attains one [dharma] and there is nothing abandoned.

When the subsequent patience regarding cessation (nirodhānvayakṣānti) ceases and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (nirodhānvayajñāna) arises, at that time one attains one [dharma] and there is nothing abandoned.

When the acceptance of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*) ceases and the knowledge of the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) arises, at that time one attains one [knowledge] and there is nothing to be relinquished.

When the subsequent acceptance of the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) ceases and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) arises: if one is not yet free from desire, one attains one and there is nothing to be relinquished;

if one is already free from desire, one relinquishes five and attains one—namely, the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna*) obtained at the moment of the subsequent knowledge of the path, which is the knowledge of the exhaustion of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
When a noble one is free from the desires of the desire realm and has severed one up to eight types of fetters, there is no attainment or relinquishment.

When they sever the ninth type of fetter, at that time they relinquish six and attain one; this refers to the knowledge of the destruction of the five lower fetters (*pañca-avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana-kṣaya-jñāna*).
Having detached from the desire of the first dhyāna, one severs one to nine types of fetters, yet there is neither attainment nor relinquishment.
It is the same for the second and third dhyānas.
Having detached from the desire of the fourth dhyāna, one severs one to eight types [of fetters], yet there is neither attainment nor relinquishment.
When the ninth type is abandoned, one attains one [fruit] without relinquishing anything.
As it is with the first dhyāna, so it is with the second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness.
Having become detached from the desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one abandons one up to eight types of fetters, yet there is neither attainment nor relinquishment.
When the ninth type is abandoned, one relinquishes two and attains one, namely, the knowledge of the total destruction of all fetters.
This refers to the time of superior progress;
however, at the time of regression as well, there is both relinquishing and acquiring.
When an Arhat regresses by giving rise to afflictions of the formless realm, they relinquish one and acquire two.
When falling away due to the arising of afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one abandons one and acquires one.
When falling away due to the arising of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one abandons one and acquires six.
For an Anāgāmin who has detached from craving for the form realm, when falling away due to the arising of afflictions of the form realm, one abandons one but acquires nothing.
When one regresses due to the arising of afflictions of the desire realm, one abandons two and acquires six.
When an Anāgāmin who has not yet abandoned craving for the form realm regresses due to the arising of afflictions of the desire realm, one abandons one and acquires six.
When one falls away from the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin, there is neither abandonment nor attainment.
Among these nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*), how many are fruits of the dhyānas, and how many are fruits of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*)?
How many are fruits of the fundamental dhyānas, and how many are fruits of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the dhyānas?
How many are the fruits of the fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and how many are the fruits of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of the formless attainments?
How many are the fruits of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and how many are the fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)?
How many are the fruits of patience (*kṣānti*), and how many are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*)?
How many are the fruits of dharma-knowledge? How many are the fruits of subsequent knowledge?
How many are the partial fruits of dharma-knowledge? How many are the partial fruits of subsequent knowledge?
How many are the fruits of the mundane path? How many are the fruits of the untainted path?
As for how many are the fruits of dhyāna, the answer is:
nine are the fruits of dhyāna and its attendants.
As for how many are the fruits of the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), the answer is:
The second is the fruit of the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and their associated factors (*parivāra*).
Regarding how many are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), the answer is:
the Abhidharma masters speak as follows:
The fifth is the fruit of the fundamental dhyānas.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states that eight are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas.
As for how many are the fruits of the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) of dhyāna, the answer is:
nine; that is to say, they depend upon the preparatory stage of the first dhyāna, and not upon other preparatory stages.
As for how many are the fruits of the fundamental formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the answer is: [none].
1. Regarding how many are the fruits of the limit of the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the answer is:
one; namely, the limit of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), and not the limits of the other formless spheres.
How many are the fruits of the path of seeing? Answer:
Seven. How many are the fruits of the path of cultivation? Answer: [Seven].
3. How many are the fruits of patience?
One should explain that they are like those of the path of seeing.
Regarding how many are the fruits of knowledge (*jñāna*), one should explain it as in the case of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding how many are the fruits of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), the answer is: three.
As for how many are the fruits of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the answer is:
two. As for how many are the partial fruits of dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), the answer is: [two].
Sixth. How many are the fruits of the portion of subsequent knowledge? The answer is: five.
As for how many are the fruits of the mundane path, the answer is:
two. As for how many are the fruits of the untainted path, the answer is: [two].

9. If one becomes established in right determination by becoming detached from craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*), at what time is the knowledge of the destruction of that craving for form attained?
The Venerable Saṅghasena said:
It is attained when the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvayajñāna) is present before one. Why is this so?
Because the subsequent knowledge of the path is both the path leading toward [the fruit] and the path that constitutes the fruit itself.
One should not say that one who abides in a fruit is a candidate (*pratipannaka*). Since such a person has never,
even for a single moment, brought a path of candidacy (*pratipannaka-mārga*) into manifestation, why is it said that they possess the path of candidacy?

Furthermore, there is another explanation: when one is free from desire for the sphere of infinite space, at that time one cultivates untainted dhyāna in the future life, and at that time one attains the knowledge of the exhaustion of attachment to the realm of form.
This explanation also should not be so.

Why is that? At that time, one cultivates the future state of the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as an antidote, but does not cultivate the meditative absorptions of the form realm (rūpadhātu) as an antidote.

Furthermore, there is another explanation: when one is about to attain the fruit of arhatship and abides in the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the three realms become of a single flavor; one simultaneously realizes the attainment of liberation, and at that moment, one acquires the knowledge of the exhaustion of attachment to the form realm (*rūparāga-kṣaya-jñāna*).
The commentary states:
It should be explained thus:

when one necessarily gives rise to the path of superior fruit from that fruit so that it manifests before them, at that time one attains the knowledge of the abandonment of craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga-parikṣaya-jñāna*).

If one does not give rise to a superior path of fruition after [attaining] the fruition, and a person who has abandoned desire for the third dhyāna attains right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) based on a lower stage, then if they die and are reborn in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm, they should not be endowed with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
If that were the case, it would contradict what is explained in the Ten Gates (Daśamukha), as it says:
"Who possesses the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya)?"

Whether one is born in the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, or if an noble person (ārya) is born above the Śubhakṛtsna heaven, in order to avoid such faults, upon arising from the fruit, one must necessarily bring the path of the superior fruit into manifestation; at that time, one attains the knowledge of abandonment (prahāṇajñāna) regarding the exhaustion of craving for the form realm (rūparāga).
Do the nine knowledges of abandonment encompass all knowledges of abandonment, and do all knowledges of abandonment encompass the nine knowledges of abandonment?
Answer: All [knowledges] encompass the nine, but the nine do not encompass all.
Ninth, it is as explained herein.
"All" refers to these nine and all other abandonments.
"All" is numerous; "nine" is few.
All knowledge of abandonment subsumes nine types of knowledge of abandonment, yet what remains is still vast.
It is like a large vessel covering a small one; what remains is still vast.
This case is also like that.
What is not included?
The answer is:

for a disciple of the Blessed One who has fully realized the truths but has not yet abandoned desire, that which pertains to the desire realm and is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation is not included within the nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).

When a noble one abandons the desires of the desire realm, they sever the first type of fetter up to the eighth type of fetter; this severance is not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment (*navaprahāṇajñāna*).

Having already abandoned craving for the desire realm but not yet having abandoned craving for the form realm, the severance of the fetters abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of the form realm is not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment.

Having already abandoned craving for the form realm up to the fourth dhyāna, one abandons eight kinds of fetters; that abandonment is not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).

Having already become detached from craving for the form realm but not yet detached from craving for the formless realm, the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the formless realm are not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment.

Having abandoned the desires of the sphere of infinite space, up to the severing of the eight types of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—that severance is not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*). Question:

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the severance of the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms is not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment.
Why is this not explained here?
The answer is: it should be explained.
This passage should be stated as follows:
"All are subsumed within the nine, but the nine do not subsume all.
What is not subsumed?"
Answer:

When the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms are abandoned; however, those abandonments are not subsumed under the nine knowledges of abandonment.
The remainder is as explained above.
As for that which was not mentioned, what is its intended meaning?
The answer is:
The "abandonment" spoken of here is abandonment that exists and is abandoned by a person of wisdom.
Although that [other] is also abandonment, it is not abandonment that exists and is abandoned by a person of wisdom. Question:
Although this has been stated, it does not exhaustively clarify the meaning.
Why is this so? Because it does not state that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) undergo abandonment.
Answer: This is a brief explanation; it is stated in this way because it demonstrates the initial entry into the path.
There are eight types of persons:

Those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry, those who abide in the fruit of stream-entry; those who are candidates for the fruit of once-returning, those who abide in the fruit of once-returning; those who are candidates for the fruit of non-returning, those who abide in the fruit of non-returning; those who are candidates for the fruit of arhatship, and those who abide in the fruit of arhatship.
Question: There are eight types of persons; how many substantial entities (dravya) are there? Answer:
The Abhidharma masters state as follows:
there are eight types of persons, but their substantial entities are five.
Regarding those who are candidates for the fruit of stream-entry and those who have realized the fruit of arhatship, there are two names and two substantial entities.
Those who have realized the fruit of srotāpanna and those who are practicing toward the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin have two names but one substantial reality.
Those who have realized the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin and those who are practicing toward the fruit of anāgāmin have two names but one substantial reality.
Regarding those who have realized the fruit of *anāgāmin* and the stage leading toward the fruit of *arhat*, there are two names but one actual entity.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka states: "There are eight persons, thus there are eight names; there are eight actual entities."

He asserts this: when a person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna) abides in that fruit and does not progress further, he is called one who has accomplished the fruit of stream-entry;
if, however, he progresses further, he is called one who is realizing the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), having relinquished the fruit of stream-entry.

When a person who has attained the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmiphala) abides in that fruit and does not progress further, they are called a person who has accomplished the fruit of once-returning;
if, however, they do progress, they are called a person realizing the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), having relinquished the fruit of once-returning.
When a non-returner (anāgāmin) abides in the fruit of non-returning and does not progress further, they are called one who has attained the fruit of non-returning;
if they do progress, they are called one who is heading toward the realization of the fruit of arhatship, having relinquished the fruit of non-returning.
Why is this so? Because the distinctions among persons are explained by way of their faculties (*indriya*).
Therefore, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states as follows:
If one asks whether a person who has realized the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* should be said to have accomplished the fruit of *srotāpanna*,
the answer is:
they have not accomplished it.
"Furthermore, regarding one who is directed toward the realization of the fruit of Arhatship, should it be said that they have accomplished the fruit of Anāgāmin?
The answer is:
they have not accomplished it."
The commentary says:
Although there are eight names for these persons, there are only five actual entities.
This way of explaining is preferable:

Just as it is with names and entities, so too should one understand name-sets and entity-sets, name-differentiations and entity-differentiations, name-distinctions and entity-distinctions, name-separations and entity-separations, as well as the cognition of names and the cognition of meanings. It should be known that they are likewise.
Question: If there are eight persons and their bodies are eight, while the substantial entities are five, why is it said that there are distinctions among the eight persons? Answer:
Because they practice the noble path,

when a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) does not further advance toward the fruit of stream-entry, regarding that fruit of stream-entry, it is said to be "attained," "present in the body," "accomplished," and "manifestly active."

If one is progressing toward the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), at that time, abiding in the path directed toward the fruit of stream-entry is called "attainment" (*prāpti*); it is not yet present within the body, thus it is called "non-possession" (*asamanvāgama*) and does not manifest before one.
Regarding the path directed toward [the fruit], it is called "attainment," it is said to be "within the body," it is called "possession," and it is called "manifesting before one."

Furthermore, when one does not progress further toward the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala), at that time it is said that one has "attained" the fruit of non-returning, that it "resides within one," that one is "accomplished" in it, and that it is "manifestly present."

If one is progressing toward the fruit of *anāgāmin*, at that time, the state of being directed toward the fruit of *anāgāmin* is called "attainment" (*prāpti*); it does not reside within the person, and thus is called "accomplishment" (*samanvāgama*), yet it does not manifest before one.
Regarding the state of being directed [toward the fruit], it is called "attainment," it resides within the person, it is called "accomplishment," and it manifests before one.
Regarding the person who is currently realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*: how many of these nine knowledges of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*) does he possess, and how many does he not possess?
In this section, the person is taken as the chapter and the knowledges of abandonment as the gate.
Answer: Either they are not accomplished, or one, two, three, four, or five [are accomplished], as explained at length in the original sūtra.

translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman during the Northern Liang dynasty.

Translated by Gong Dao Tai and others. Chapter Three: On Persons (Pudgala-varga). Section One: The Chapter on the Causes (Hetu-kāṇḍa). Part One of Chapter Three: On Persons. There are two kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*): namely, those to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*) and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*).
There are two types in the desire realm, two types in the form realm, and two types in the formless realm.

Is it possible that one simultaneously attains the fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing and those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation?
...and so on, as explained at length; herein, the *upadeśa* (expository treatise) concerning the chapters and the interpretation of their meanings should be explained in detail. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
These afflictions act as a great bondage within birth and death; they bring no benefit and are perilous, like an enemy lying in ambush.

One undergoes great suffering and distress in the desire realm, and undergoes great suffering and distress in the form and formless realms. Revolving repeatedly within birth and death, one dwells in the dark and obscure place of the mother’s womb, oppressed by the raw and cooked intestines (*āma-koṣṭha* and *pakva-koṣṭha*). Not knowing how to investigate these fetters, one fails to know and see them as they truly are, and thus cannot eliminate them.
In order to make this known, it is like an enemy who remains hidden; if one does not know of his presence, he will cause harm, but if one knows him, one may avoid him.
It is the same with that [enemy-like state].
Therefore, one should reflect upon and examine various wholesome teachings so that they are never forgotten throughout all successive births.
As the Venerable Maitreya said at the time of his birth:
"There are two kinds of fetters: those to be abandoned by the path of seeing and those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation."
There are two types in the desire realm, two in the form realm, and two in the formless realm.
Question: For what reason do they speak such words at the time of birth?
The answer is:
While in the mother’s womb, being oppressed by manifold sufferings, he thinks to himself:
"For what reason do sentient beings repeatedly enter the mother’s womb and undergo such sufferings as these?"
Because of these two kinds of fetters, and in order to explain the faults and perils of these two fetters, as soon as he was born he spoke these words:
"There are two kinds of fetters; there are two in the desire realm," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: For what reason is it called a "seed" (*bīja*)? Answer:
In this context, it is said that a collection is a "seed" (gotra).
Just as a multitude of bhikṣus is called the "bhikṣu-seed" (bhikṣu-gotra) and a multitude of brahmins is called the "brahmin-seed" (brāhmaṇa-gotra), so too is this the case here.
What is called a "seed" (*gotra*) may also be called a "collection" (*rāśi*) or a "group" (*varga*); in actual meaning they are one and the same, though the names differ.
Is it attained all at once?
What is meant by "attained all at once"?
Answer: It is called "at one time" (ekasamaya) because it occurs instantaneously. How is this known?
The answer is:

There is a sutra that says King Prasenajit went to where the Buddha was and engaged in various discussions with the World-Honored One face-to-face. Sitting to one side, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard the śramaṇa Gautama speak in this way:"
In the past, future, and present, there has never been, nor will there ever be, any śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa capable of knowing and seeing all phenomena as they truly are.
To say that such knowledge and vision exists is impossible.
“Does the śramaṇa Gautama remember having said such a thing?
The Buddha replied to the king,
“I do not remember.”
The king spoke again:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!
There may be people in the world who do not properly grasp the meaning of the texts; what they hear at one time differs from what they say when explaining it to others."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will bear this matter in mind and explain it.
The Buddha replied to the king:
"I have indeed made such a statement:"
In the past, future, and present, there has never been anyone who could suddenly attain the knowledge and vision that realizes all phenomena as they truly are.
To say that one can suddenly attain such knowledge and vision is impossible.
All have gradually practiced the six pāramitās over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas before finally attaining realization; it is not known all at once.
For this reason, one knows that "attaining it all at once" refers to a single moment [of awakening].
Is it possible to simultaneously attain the fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of cultivation?
Answer: They are attained simultaneously.
An ordinary person who has become detached from desire does not fall away from that detachment.
Question: Who attains it instantaneously?
The answer is:

When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes detached from sensual desire, the fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) are collectively gathered into a single mass; like the method of mowing grass, these nine types of fetters are severed all at once.

By means of the lowest-lowest path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), one abandons the highest-highest fetter (*saṃyojana*); continuing in this manner up to abandoning the lowest-lowest fetter by means of the highest-highest path of non-obstruction.

For an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who possesses the lowest-lowest fetters, through the absence of desire for them, they suddenly attain the single type of fetter belonging to the desire realm that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
When one falls away from the lower or middle [stages], one suddenly acquires two types [of fetters].

This continues up until, when falling away from the highest-of-the-high fetters, one suddenly acquires the nine types of fetters belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of cultivation.

When one dies in the form realm or the formless realm and is reborn in the desire realm, an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) causes the fetters ranging from the lowest-of-the-low to the highest-of-the-high to arise and continue; they simultaneously acquire the nine kinds of fetters belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the path of vision and the path of cultivation.
Is it abandoned all at once?
Answer: It is abandoned.
When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes free from the craving for desire,
it is asked:
"Who abandons [it] all at once?"

Answer: When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes detached from sensual craving, the nine types of fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the desire realm—which are to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation—are collectively gathered into a single mass. This is like the method of mowing grass: the nine types of fetters are severed simultaneously. Specifically, the lowest-of-the-low path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) severs the highest-of-the-high fetter, continuing in this manner until the highest-of-the-high path of non-obstruction severs the lowest-of-the-low fetter.

Regarding those [defilements] bound to the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation—the lowest-of-the-low—is there simultaneous abandonment and gradual attainment? The answer is: no.
Why is this? Because one might first attain the abandonment of fetters severed by the path of seeing and later attain the abandonment of fetters severed by the path of cultivation;
or one might first attain the abandonment of fetters severed by the path of cultivation and later attain the abandonment of fetters severed by the path of seeing.
"That is impossible.
Is it abandoned gradually?
He replied:
Abandonment.

A disciple of the Blessed One first abandons the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and subsequently abandons the fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

The fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing are abandoned by means of the path of seeing; the fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation are abandoned by means of the path of cultivation.

Is it possible to attain all the fetters (saṃyojana) belonging to the realm of form (rūpadhātu), which are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) and the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), simultaneously?
Answer: They are attained simultaneously.
An ordinary person who has become detached from the craving for form may fall away from that state of desirelessness. Question:
Who attains [the fruit] all at once?
The answer is:

When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from the craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the realm of form that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) are collectively gathered into a single mass. This is like the method of mowing grass: nine types of fetters are severed simultaneously; by means of the lowest-of-the-low path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*), the highest-of-the-high fetter is severed, continuing in this manner until, by means of the highest-of-the-high path of non-obstruction, the lowest-of-the-low fetter is severed.

Regarding falling away from that state without desire: if one falls away by means of the lowest-of-the-low fetters bound to the form realm, one suddenly acquires one kind of fetter bound to the form realm that is to be abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation; if one falls away by the middle-of-the-low, one suddenly acquires two kinds; and so on, up to falling away by means of the highest-of-the-high fetters, one suddenly acquires nine kinds of fetters bound to the form realm that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

If one falls away from the lowest-of-the-low fetters of the desire realm up to the highest-of-the-high fetters, at that time one simultaneously acquires the nine types of fetters bound to the form realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, there are those who say that this passage should be stated as follows:
"An ordinary person, having become detached from craving for the form realm, falls away due to the fetters belonging to the Brahma-world level of the desire realm.
Such a statement should not be made.
Why is this? Herein, it is said that one attains the *dhātus* (elements) instantaneously, but it is not said that one attains the *bhūmis* (stages) instantaneously.

If one falls away from the fetters of the fourth dhyāna, or even from the fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), at that time one instantaneously attains the fetters associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

When one dies in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire or form realms (*kāmadhātu* or *rūpadhātu*), one simultaneously acquires the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the form realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) dies in the formless realm and is reborn within the desire or form realms, they cause the continuity of existence to arise through the fetters ranging from the lowest-of-the-low (*mṛdumṛdu*) to the highest-of-the-high (*adhimātrādhimātra*), thereby simultaneously acquiring the nine types of fetters belonging to the form realm that are to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of cultivation.
Is it abandoned all at once?
The answer is:
it is abandoned.
When an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) becomes detached from the craving for form (rūpa-tṛṣṇā),
it is asked:
who abandons [it] all at once?

Answer: When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from craving for the realm of form (*rūparāga*), the fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to the realm of form that are to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are collectively gathered into a single mass. This is like the method of mowing grass: nine types of fetters are severed simultaneously. By means of the lowest-of-the-low path of non-obstruction (*anantaryamārga*), one severs the highest-of-the-high fetter; thus, one suddenly abandons all the fetters belonging to the realm of form to be abandoned through the paths of vision and cultivation. Continuing in this manner until, by means of the highest-of-the-high path of non-obstruction, one severs the lowest-of-the-low fetter, one suddenly abandons all the fetters belonging to the realm of form to be abandoned through the paths of vision and cultivation.
"Is it attained gradually? He replied, "It is not."

Why is this? There is no case where one first attains the abandonment of what is severed by the path of seeing and subsequently attains the abandonment of what is severed by the path of cultivation; nor is there any case where one first attains the abandonment of what is severed by the path of cultivation and subsequently attains the abandonment of what is severed by the path of seeing.
Is it gradually abandoned?
The answer is:
it is abandoned.
The disciples of the World-Honored One first abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing, and subsequently abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Through the path of seeing, they abandon what is to be abandoned by the path of seeing; through the path of cultivation, they abandon what is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation.
Is it possible to abandon, all at once, the fetters belonging to the formless realm that are to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation?
Answer: No, it is not possible.

Why is this? Because one who suddenly attains [the fruit] is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and there is no ordinary person capable of completely severing the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

If, upon falling away from that state, one suddenly attains the fetters of the formless realm to be abandoned by the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), does one suddenly abandon them?
Answer: It is not abandoned. Why is this so?
One who abandons [them] all at once is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); yet there is no ordinary person who abandons the afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) all at once.
Is it attained gradually?
The answer is:

It is not so. Why is this? Because there is no case where one first attains the abandonment of the fetters severed by the path of seeing and later attains the abandonment of those severed by the path of cultivation, nor any case where one first attains the abandonment of those severed by the path of cultivation and later attains the abandonment of those severed by the path of seeing.
Is it gradually abandoned?
Answer: It is abandoned.
The disciples of the World-Honored One first abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing, and subsequently abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Through the path of seeing, they abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing; through the path of cultivation, they abandon the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
There is mundane practice (*laukika-caryā*). Question:

When an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes free from desire by means of the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*), they sever nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*); how many are abandoned through the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and how many are abandoned through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?

The Noble One severs the nine kinds of fetters by means of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*). How many are severed by the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and how many are severed by the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)? Answer:

Some say that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) severs the nine kinds of fetters, they do so through three paths of non-obstruction and three paths of liberation. That is to say: the lower-lower path of non-obstruction and the lower-lower path of liberation sever the upper three kinds of fetters; the lower-middle path of non-obstruction and the lower-middle path of liberation sever the middle three kinds of fetters; and the lower-upper path of non-obstruction and the lower-upper path of liberation sever the lower three kinds of fetters.
The Noble One is also like this.
Furthermore, there are those who say that an ordinary person severs the nine kinds of fetters through one path of non-obstruction and one path of liberation;
whereas a Noble One severs the nine kinds of fetters through nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.
Question: For what reason do ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) sever the nine kinds of fetters by means of one path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) and one path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*),
whereas noble ones (*ārya*) sever the nine kinds of fetters by means of nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation?
Answer: The path employed by ordinary persons is duller than the preceding dharma; it cannot observe, deliberate, or discern each part individually.
The path employed by noble ones is more sharp and vigorous than the preceding dharma; it can observe, deliberate, and discern each part individually.

Question: If one speaks in this way, it is intended to cause ordinary persons to descend while asserting that they are superior, and to cause noble ones to excel while asserting that they are inferior. Why is this so?
Ordinary persons sever the nine kinds of fetters by means of one path of non-obstruction and one path of liberation;
noble ones sever the nine kinds of fetters by means of nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.
If this were so, then ordinary persons would surpass the noble ones.
It would be like a person who has consumed much toxic medicine and vomits it all out at once—who could not do so?
The critique says:
It should be stated as follows:
An ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) severs the nine kinds of fetters through nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*);
the noble one (*ārya*) does likewise.
Question: If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) severs the nine kinds of fetters through nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*),
and if it is the same for a noble one (*ārya*), then what is the difference?
What is the difference between ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*)?
The answer is:

Ordinary persons regard the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) as a single aggregate. Like the method of mowing grass, they abandon these nine types of fetters simultaneously by means of the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) and the nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
The Noble One abandons the nine types of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the path by means of one path of non-obstruction and one path of liberation;
he abandons the nine types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation by means of nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation.
Ordinary persons and noble ones—this is what is meant by their distinction.
Question: When severing the fetters by means of the mundane path, how many skillful means are employed and how many meditative absorptions (dhyāna) are entered?
Answer: By means of three skillful means and by means of three entries into meditative concentration.
Through the first skillful means and the first entry into concentration, one abandons the three types of fetters belonging to the higher realms.
By means of the second skillful means and the second meditative absorption, one abandons the three types of fetters belonging to the intermediate realm.
By means of the third skillful means and the third meditative absorption, one abandons the three types of fetters belonging to the lower realm.
Question: Is it abandoned while emerging from meditative concentration, or is it abandoned without emerging from meditative concentration? Answer:

Some say that ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) abandon [defilements] without emerging from meditative concentration, whereas noble ones (*ārya*) abandon them either by emerging from concentration or without emerging from it.
Others say that ordinary persons abandon them either by emerging from concentration or without emerging from it, while noble ones abandon them only without emerging from concentration.
The commentary states:
It should be said that this matter is not fixed.
Ordinary persons may either not emerge from meditative concentration or may emerge from it; noble ones may either emerge from meditative concentration or not emerge from it;
ordinary persons may either emerge from meditative concentration or not emerge from it; and noble ones may, even without emerging from meditative concentration, sever the fetters.

Furthermore, there are those who say that one who has severed the fetters of the desire realm does not enter meditative absorption, whereas one who has severed the fetters of the form and formless realms may or may not enter meditative absorption.

Again, there are those who say that one who has severed the fetters of the desire realm may or may not enter meditative absorption, while one who has severed the fetters of the form and formless realms does not enter meditative absorption.
The commentary states:
This matter is not fixed.

One who has severed the fetters of the desire realm may either enter meditative absorption or not; one who has severed the fetters of the form and formless realms does not enter meditative absorption.

When one abandons the fetters of the desire realm without entering meditative absorption, and abandons the fetters of the form and formless realms—whether entering or not entering meditative absorption—it is said that this is the time of superior progress.

When an ordinary person regresses from having entered a lower fetter, they accomplish three types of lower fetters; when they regress from having entered a middle fetter, they accomplish six types of fetters; and when they regress from having entered a higher fetter, they accomplish nine types of fetters.

When a noble one (ārya) falls away from the attainment of the lowest-of-the-low fetters (mṛdumṛdu-saṃyojana), they possess the lowest-of-the-low fetters; continuing in this manner, when they fall away from the highest-of-the-high fetters (adhimātrādhimātra-saṃyojana), they possess all nine types of fetters.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) falls away from the attainment of the lowest-of-the-low fetters, and so on up to when they fall away from the highest-of-the-high fetters, they likewise possess all nine types of fetters.
The Noble One is as previously described. Question:

For what reason does an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) fall away due to the arising of the lowest-of-the-low fetters (saṃyojana), and so on, up to falling away due to the arising of the highest-of-the-high fetters, thereby accomplishing nine types of fetters?

When a noble one (ārya) falls away from the arising of the lowest-of-the-low fetters (mṛdumṛdu-saṃyojana), they possess the lowest-of-the-low fetters; when falling away from the arising of the middle-of-the-low fetters (mṛdumadhya-saṃyojana), they possess two kinds; and so on, up to when falling away from the arising of the highest-of-the-high fetters (adhimātrādhimātra-saṃyojana), they possess nine kinds of fetters?
Answer: Ordinary persons sustain themselves through mundane concentration, and that concentration is weak and inferior.
Noble ones sustain themselves through untainted concentration, and that concentration is firm and stable.
It should be stated thus:
ordinary persons die from taking poison.
The critique says:
One should state it thus:

when an ordinary person falls away from the attainment of the lowest-of-the-low fetters, they again become possessed of the lowest-of-the-low fetters; and so on, up to when they fall away from the highest-of-the-high fetters, they become possessed of all nine kinds of fetters.
Question: If that is so, what is the difference between ordinary persons and noble ones? Answer:

If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) undergoes regression by giving rise to the lowest-of-the-low fetters (saṃyojana), they become possessed of the lowest-of-the-low fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation; this continues up to the point where, by giving rise to the highest-of-the-high fetters, they undergo regression and become possessed of all nine types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

When a noble one falls away from the lowest-of-the-low fetters, they accomplish the lowest-of-the-low fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation; likewise, up until the point when they fall away from the highest-of-the-high fetters, they accomplish the nine types of fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, but do not accomplish the fetters to be abandoned by the path of vision.
Ordinary persons and noble ones—this is what constitutes their distinction.
Among those in the desire realm, noble ones possess three characteristics:
first, they pass away having attained ultimate detachment from desire.
2. Having regressed, one passes away;
3. Having gradually become free from desire, one passes away.
Ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) have two [such] cases.
First, passing away having attained ultimate freedom from desire;
second, passing away after having regressed.
Regarding noble beings in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are these two cases:
First, one dies having completely abandoned craving for form;
second, one dies having gradually abandoned desire without falling back. Why is this so?
In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are none who fall back.
Ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) possess one quality: they ultimately pass away having become free from craving for form, and do not fall back. Why is this?
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is no falling back, nor is there anyone who dies while gradually abandoning desire. Question:
For what reason do noble ones (*ārya*) die after gradually abandoning desire, whereas ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not?
Answer: The noble ones sustain themselves by means of the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*), and that path is firm and secure;
ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) sustain themselves by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), and that path is weak and inferior.
Furthermore, because noble ones have accomplished the factors of concentration and wisdom, they pass away while gradually severing the fetters;
because ordinary persons have not accomplished the factors of concentration and wisdom, they are unable to pass away while gradually severing the fetters.
Furthermore, because the noble ones have accomplished the factors of the untainted (*anāsrava*), they pass away while gradually severing the fetters;
because ordinary persons lack the factors of the untainted, they are unable to pass away while gradually severing the fetters.

Furthermore, noble ones possess both the power of karma and the power of the Path. By virtue of the power of karma, they are able to gradually sever the fetters before passing away; by virtue of the power of the Path, they are able to pass away having attained ultimate freedom from desire.
Ordinary persons lack the power of karma; thus, those who—relying on the strength of the power of the Path—attain ultimate freedom from desire before passing away, are liable to fall back.

Furthermore, among the noble ones (*ārya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are those who gradually abandon desire: if they sever three or four fetters (*saṃyojana*), they are called "those who go from family to family" (*kulaṃkula*); if they sever six fetters, they are called "once-returners" (*sakṛdāgāmin*); and if they sever seven or eight fetters, they are called "one-seeders" (*ekabījī*).

Therefore, among the noble ones, there are those who pass away while gradually abandoning desire. Among ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), however, there are none who pass away while gradually abandoning desire; therefore, among ordinary persons, there are no such who pass away while gradually abandoning desire.
The Venerable Saṅghasena said:
"There are also ordinary persons who pass away while gradually departing from desire; abiding in the mind of continuity, they again become possessed of the fetters previously severed."
The critique states:
One should not make such a statement; it is better as previously stated.

When one becomes free from desire by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), how many aspects (*ākāra*) does the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) possess, and how many aspects does the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) possess?
The answer is:
The path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) has three modes of activity, namely: the mode of coarseness, the mode of suffering, and the mode of coarse destruction.
The path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) has three modes of activity, namely: the mode of tranquility, the mode of excellence, and the mode of detachment.
Question: If there is coarse conduct within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), is there calm conduct within that path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
If there is painful conduct within the path of non-obstruction, is there sublime conduct within that path of liberation?

If there is the aspect of "coarseness and destruction" (audārikavibhāvanā) within the path of non-obstruction (ānantaryamārga), is there the aspect of "detachment" (vairāgya) within that path of liberation (vimuktimārga)?
The answer is:
some say that as asked, if there is the aspect of coarseness in the path of non-obstruction, there must be the aspect of tranquility (śamatha) in that path of liberation.
If the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga) involves painful practice, its corresponding path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) must involve sublime practice.
If the path of non-obstruction involves coarse and destructive practice, its corresponding path of liberation must involve practice of detachment.
The commentary states:
This matter is not fixed.
If there is coarse activity within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), then the three types of activity will successively manifest within that path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

If, within the path of non-obstruction (ānantarya-mārga), there are the three modes of practice—painful, coarse, and destructive—then within the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), these three modes of practice arise in succession.
Question: When one becomes detached from sensual desire by means of the mundane path (laukika-mārga), upon what dharma does the path of non-obstruction take as its object?
With respect to what phenomena do the paths of liberation take as their objects?
The answer is:
the nine paths of non-obstruction take the desire realm as their object, while the nine paths of liberation take the first dhyāna as their object.
Question: If that is so, the explanation in the Indriya-varga (Chapter on Faculties) is well-justified, as it asks:
"Is it possible that by contemplating dharmas of the form realm, one can know those of the desire realm?"
He replied: "I am able to know. [The Buddha asked:
"How is it that one does not engage in erroneous mental objects or erroneous conduct?"
If the application of the objects of focus is inverted, why does it not create obstacles or hindrances to the dharma of detachment?
The answer is:
even if the application of the objects of focus were inverted, it would still be unable to create obstacles or hindrances to the dharma of detachment.
Why is this? Because they have already well cultivated the dharma of detachment from that [realm] and have perfected the path.

It is just as when, within the Path of Seeing, after the forbearances and knowledges taking the desire realm as their object, the subsequent forbearances and knowledges taking the form and formless realms as their objects manifest before one.
When the patience and knowledge directed toward the form and formless realms have passed, the patience and knowledge directed toward the desire realm manifest before one.
Although there is thus a reversal in the sequence of the objects of focus, this does not constitute an obstacle or hindrance to attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*).
Why is this so? Because they have already well cultivated the path of vision and have fully accomplished the way;
it is the same for them as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*) and eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the desire realm as their object, while the final path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.

For example, when one becomes detached from craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) by means of the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), those nine paths of non-obstruction and eight paths of liberation take cessation or the path as their object, while the final path of liberation takes the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as its object.
It is the same for that case as well.

Furthermore, there are those who say: when one enters meditative absorption at the time of abandoning desire-attachment, having severed one type of fetter and remaining therein, one path of non-obstruction takes the desire realm as its object, while one path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.

If one dwells having already severed two kinds of fetters, those two paths of non-obstruction and one path of liberation take the desire realm as their object, while one path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.

If one dwells having severed up to eight kinds of fetters, those eight paths of non-obstruction and seven paths of liberation take the desire realm as their object, while the eighth path of liberation takes the first dhyāna as its object.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation all take the desire realm as their object.

For example, when one becomes free from the craving of the desire realm through the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of origination, the nine paths of non-obstruction and the nine paths of liberation take the desire realm as their object.
It is the same for that as well. Question:
If this is so, then one does not engage in erroneous practice, nor does one create obstacles or hindrances regarding the dharma of detachment from desire.
How is what is stated in the *Indriya-varga* to be reconciled?
For instance, it asks:
"Is it possible that by contemplating dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one can know those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?"
He replied:
"I am able to know.
He asked again:
This explains that when first observing and discerning, the practitioner first performs such discerning observation:
