"The desire realm is coarse; the first dhyāna is tranquility."
Question: How is the subsequent explanation in the Indriya-varga to be reconciled?
As it is said:
Is it possible that by contemplating the dharmas of the formless realm one can know the desire realm?
He replied:
"One cannot know it."
At that time, does the practitioner not first distinguish and observe that the desire realm is coarse and the formless realm is tranquil?
For what reason is it said that one cannot know this?
The answer is:
The practitioner also performs analytical observation, yet that which is observed is distant; one cannot become detached from desire by observing what is so distant.
Furthermore, some say that all nine paths of non-obstruction and nine paths of liberation take the first dhyāna as their object.
Question: If that is so, the explanation in the *Indriya-varga* (Chapter on Faculties) is thoroughly consistent, as it says:
"Is it possible that by contemplating dharmas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one can know those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?"
He replied: "I am able to know it;
nor is my application of the conditions erroneous."
What is it to take another place as the object and become free from desire for that other place?
The answer is:
if one takes another place as the object and becomes free from desire for that other place, there is no fault in this either.
Just as one who takes cessation and the path as objects through the knowledge of cessation and the path becomes free from the desires abandoned by [the paths of] suffering and its origin,
so it is in this case as well.
All that has been said is for the purpose of generating the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) in the disciples.

Regarding this point, it is best to explain that initially the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) take the desire realm as their object, while the nine paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the first dhyāna as their object.
Question: Within the path of non-obstruction, how many aspects (*ākāra*) are cultivated?
How many types of cultivation are practiced within the path of liberation?
The answer is:

when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from sensual desire, they cultivate three types of cultivation—coarseness (*audārikatā*), etc.—within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*). Within the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cultivate six types of cultivation, namely the three types beginning with coarseness and the three types beginning with tranquility (*śamatha*). Within the final path of liberation, they likewise cultivate these same six types of cultivation, as well as the immeasurable types of cultivation belonging to the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna; this remains the case even up to becoming detached from the craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

When a noble one (ārya) becomes detached from sensual desire, they cultivate nineteen modes of practice within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*): namely, the three modes such as "coarse" (*audārika*) and so forth, and the sixteen noble modes of practice that are both with and without outflows (*sāsrava-anāsrava*). Within the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cultivate twenty-two modes of practice: namely, the three modes such as "coarse" and so forth, the three modes such as "calm" (*śānta*) and so forth, and the sixteen noble modes of practice that are both with and without outflows. In the final path of liberation, they likewise cultivate these twenty-two modes of practice, and also cultivate the immeasurable modes of practice of the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna.

When a Noble One (ārya) becomes detached from the desire of the first dhyāna, they cultivate nineteen modes of practice within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*): namely, the three modes such as "coarseness" (*audārika*) and the sixteen noble modes (*āryākāra*), all of which are cultivated exclusively as untainted (*anāsrava*) and not as tainted (*sāsrava*). Within the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cultivate twenty-two modes of practice: namely, the three modes such as "coarseness," the three modes such as "calmness" (*śānta*), and the sixteen noble modes—all of which are cultivated exclusively as untainted and not as tainted. In the final path of liberation, they cultivate these same twenty-two modes, and additionally cultivate the immeasurable modes of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna.
The same applies up to the detachment from the craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Question:

Why is it that on the borders of the first dhyāna one cultivates both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) practices, whereas on the borders of the higher stages one cultivates only the uncontaminated and not the contaminated?
Answer: At the limit of the first dhyāna, there are both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) noble practices (*ārya-caryā*);

therefore, one cultivates them. In the limits of the higher stages, there are only contaminated practices and no uncontaminated noble practices; therefore, one cultivates only uncontaminated practices.

Furthermore, there are those who say that when an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) becomes detached from sensual desire, they cultivate nine mental applications during the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), namely: the three applications beginning with "coarseness" (*audārika*), loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). During the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cultivate twelve applications, which consist of the aforementioned nine plus the three applications beginning with "calming" (*śamatha*). In the final path of liberation, they likewise cultivate these twelve applications, and also cultivate the immeasurable applications of the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*) of the first dhyāna.

When a noble one (ārya) becomes detached from sensual desire, they cultivate twenty-five modes of practice during the path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*): namely, the three modes such as "coarseness" (*audārikatā*) and so forth; loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*); and the sixteen noble modes of practice, both with and without outflows (*sāsrava* and *anāsrava*). During the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they cultivate twenty-eight modes of practice: that is, these aforementioned twenty-five modes plus the three modes such as "calm abiding" (*śamatha*). In the final path of liberation, they likewise cultivate these twenty-eight modes, as well as the immeasurable practices of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*) and the first dhyāna.
The limits of the higher stages are as previously explained. Question:
For what reason does one cultivate such various practices at the limit of the first dhyāna, yet not cultivate them at the limits of the higher stages?
Answer: Because there are various roots of goodness at the limit of the first dhyāna, one cultivates such practices as these;
because the roots of goodness at the limits of the higher stages are few, one does not cultivate such practices as these.
Furthermore, because there are various afflictions in the desire realm, various remedies are required;
because there are no various afflictions in the higher stages, various remedies are not required.

Regarding the formations (saṃskāra) described here, which exist in the present and share the same concurrent activity, the same burden, and the same function, their objects of focus (ālambana) are as explained above.
As for those practiced in the future, what will be their objects of focus?

Answer: When one is detached from sensual desire, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—within the nine paths of non-obstruction take the desire realm as their object.
Those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—within the eight paths of liberation take both the desire realm and the first dhyāna as their objects.
Regarding the cultivation of the three modes of practice beginning with tranquility (*śamatha*), they take the first dhyāna as their object.
Regarding the cultivation of the three modes of practice beginning with coarseness (*audārikatā*) within the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), they take the three realms as their objects;

regarding the cultivation of the three modes of practice beginning with tranquility, they take everything from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) as their objects.

When one is free from the desires of the first dhyāna, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness (*audārikatā*), etc.—during the nine paths of non-obstruction take the first dhyāna as their object.
During the eight paths of liberation, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness, etc.—take both the first and second dhyānas as their objects;
those who cultivate the three modes of practice—calmness (*śāntatā*), etc.—take the second dhyāna as their object.
In the final path of liberation, those who cultivate the three modes of practice such as "coarseness" (audārikatā) take the three realms as their object;
those who cultivate the three modes of practice such as "calmness" (śāntatā) take the second dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as their object.
The detachment from the desire of the second dhyāna and the third dhyāna should be explained according to their respective characteristics.

When one detaches from the desire of the fourth dhyāna, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—within the nine paths of non-obstruction take the fourth dhyāna as their object.
Among the eight paths of liberation, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—take the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space as their objects;
those who cultivate the three modes of practice—stopping and so forth—take the sphere of infinite space as their object.

In the final path of liberation, those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—and the three modes of practice—calm abiding and so forth—take as their objects the sphere of infinite space up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Question: If, when one is free from desire for the fourth dhyāna, one practices the coarse and so forth aspects during the eight paths of liberation, and these take the fourth dhyāna and the sphere of infinite space as their objects, how is this to be reconciled with what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra*?
As it is said:
"Is there a mind bound to the formless realm that can know the realms of form and the formless?
The answer is:
"I do not know. He replied:
"In that context, it negates a single moment, but does not negate a long succession."
It is impossible for one to know both the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

When the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) arises and is present before one, whether that future practitioner takes the form realm as an object or the formless realm as an object, for this reason, they do not know both in a single moment; rather, they know them through a succession of many moments. Thus, these two explanations provide a thorough resolution.

When one is detached from the desire for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness (*audārikatā*) and so forth—during the nine paths of non-obstruction (*anantaryamārga*) take the sphere of infinite space as their object.

During the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), those who cultivate the three modes of practice—coarseness and so forth—take both the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) as their objects;
those who cultivate the three modes of practice—calmness (*śāntatā*) and so forth—take the sphere of infinite consciousness as their object.

In the final path of liberation, those who cultivate the three modes of conduct—coarseness and so forth—and the three modes of conduct—quiescence and so forth—take as their objects the sphere of infinite consciousness up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

One should explain this according to their characteristics: [the practitioner] is free from desire for the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness and free from desire for the Sphere of Nothingness. Question:

For what reason do the various practices cultivated within the dhyānas take all three realms as their objects, whereas the various practices cultivated within the formless attainments (ārūpya) take only the formless realm as their object?
Answer: Dhyāna can take all levels as its object; it can take its own level as an object, take lower levels as objects, and also take higher levels as objects.
The formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) cannot take all levels as their objects; they can only take their own level and higher levels as objects, but do not take lower levels as objects.

For this reason, the various practices cultivated within dhyāna can take the three realms as their objects, whereas the various practices cultivated within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) take only the formless realm as their object.

When the seeds of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (darśanamārga) that are bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are severed, into which fruit of the ascetic life (śrāmaṇyaphala) are they subsumed?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:

Regarding the various afflictions (*kleśa*), they were previously categorized by realm (*dhātu*) but not yet categorized by type (*prakāra*). Now, wishing to categorize them by type, this treatise is composed.

When the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are severed, by which fruit of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are they subsumed?
Answer: They are subsumed within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or they have no specific location.
Regarding the four fruits of śrāmaṇya: the stream-enterer is subsumed within the fruit of stream-entry, and so on, up to the arhat being subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding "having no place": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no place;
those who have abandoned desire and attained right determination have no place during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing;
and for those following the gradual sequence, there is no place during the two moments of mind within the path of seeing when seeing the truth of the path.

At such times as these, when the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing in the desire realm have been severed, and there is no place where the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation bound to the desire realm have not been severed, to which fruit do they belong?

Answer: The fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala) is subsumed under the state of a non-returner, and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala) is subsumed under the state of an arhat. A non-returner is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning, and an arhat is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding "having no locus": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no locus;
those who have abandoned desire and attained right determination have no locus for fifteen moments of mind.
A person of gradual attainment cannot say that there is no locus [for this fruit].

Why is this? At the moment of abandoning desire and craving, the final path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-saṃyojana*); when the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises, it is then subsumed within the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
The abandonment of the seeds of fetters belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*):
what fruit does this comprise? Answer: It is comprised within the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed location": for an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) at the time of abandoning attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*), there is no fixed location;
for one who has abandoned attachment to the realm of form and has attained right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*), there is no fixed location during the fifteen moments of mind.
One who follows the gradual path cannot say that there is no locus [for this abandonment].

Why is this? The subsequent patience regarding the Path (mārga-anvaya-kṣānti) definitively severs these fetters; when the subsequent knowledge of the Path (mārga-anvaya-jñāna) arises, that severance is then subsumed within the fruit.
To which fruit does the abandonment of the seeds of fetters abandoned through the path of cultivation pertaining to the form realm belong?
Answer: It is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship, or it has no specific location.
The Arhat is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding "having no locus": ordinary persons who have abandoned craving for the form realm have no locus.

When a person who has abandoned craving for the form realm attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), there is no locus when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) manifests.
For one who follows the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), when abandoning desire for the fourth dhyāna, there is no location for the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
When abandoning craving for the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), there is no location for the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) or the nine paths of liberation.
It is likewise even up to the time of abandoning craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

At the time of abandoning craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), during the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*) and the eight paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), as well as when the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) pertaining to the form realm have been severed and fully known, there is no locus [for those fetters].
To which fruit does the abandonment of the seeds of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) that are connected to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) belong?
Answer: It is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
In this context, it is not stated that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) have no place [among them]. Why is this?
There is no ordinary person who can be free from craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, one cannot say that there is no place for those who follow the gradual path. Why is this?

When the patience that conforms to the path (*mārgānvaya-kṣānti*) ultimately abandons these fetters, and when the knowledge that conforms to the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) manifests, that abandonment is subsumed under the fruit.
As for the abandonment of the seeds of fetters bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), under which fruit is it subsumed?
Answer: It is comprised solely within the fruit of arhatship.
Among these, there are no ordinary persons who have not yet abandoned desire.
Why is this? Because there is no ordinary person capable of being free from craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, one cannot say that a person following the gradual path lacks a locus [of attainment].

Why is this so? Because the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) ultimately severs these fetters; at the moment the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) arises, that severance is subsumed under the fruit, namely, the fruit of arhatship.
There are five kinds of fetters:
namely, those to be abandoned through the vision of suffering, up to those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation. Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
previously, it was analyzed that afflictions exist in two types within the realms, but the five types had not yet been analyzed; now, desiring to analyze them, this treatise was composed.
To which fruit does the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters abandoned through the vision of suffering belong?
The answer is:
it is comprised within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding those who have no fixed abode (*asthāna*), one should not speak here of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) attaining detachment from desire.

For a person of gradual attainment (*ānupūrvika*), at the moment of seeing suffering (*duḥkha-darśana*), it lasts for one mental moment; at the moment of seeing origin (*samudaya*), four mental moments; at the moment of seeing cessation (*nirodha*), four mental moments; and at the moment of seeing the path (*mārga*), three mental moments. During these times, the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering are severed; however, that severance is not included within the [four] fruits.
To which fruit does the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the origin belong?
The answer is:
it is included within the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above. Regarding "having no locus": herein, there is no ordinary person who attains freedom from desire.

For one who proceeds by stages, at the moment of seeing origination (*samudaya*), it lasts for one mental moment; at the moment of seeing cessation (*nirodha*), it lasts for four mental moments; and at the moment of seeing the path (*mārga*), it lasts for three mental moments. At that time, the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of origination are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are severed, in which fruit is that severance included?
The answer is:
it is included in one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
In this context, the ordinary person’s detachment from desire is not mentioned.

For one who proceeds through the stages, it takes the duration of one moment of mind to see cessation and three moments of mind to see the path; at that time, the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are severed, yet that severance is not included within the fruits of the śramaṇa.
When the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the path of seeing are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
The answer is:
the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
In this context, neither the ordinary person who has abandoned desire nor the practitioner following the gradual stages is mentioned.

Why is this? It is because these fetters are ultimately severed by the receptivity to subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*); when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) manifests, that very severance is subsumed within the fruit.
Regarding the abandonment of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattvaphala*).
In this context, neither ordinary persons who have abandoned desire nor those following the gradual path are mentioned. Why is this?

It is because the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) definitively severs these fetters; when the initial knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) manifests, that severance is subsumed within the fruit, namely, the fruit of arhatship.

There are nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*): the category of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of suffering; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of origin; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origin; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of the path; the category of fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path; and the category of fetters to be abandoned by the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again? Answer:

Previously, the afflictions were categorized according to their realms, being divided into two types and five types; however, their antidotes and the methods for abandoning them had not yet been distinguished. Now, desiring to distinguish these, this treatise is composed.
When the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or it has no specific location.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed location": for ordinary persons, there is no fixed location when they become free from desire;

for those who have become free from desire and have attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), it lasts for the duration of fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

For a person of gradual attainment, during the three moments of the mind that perceive suffering, the four moments that perceive origin, the four moments that perceive cessation, and the three moments that perceive the path, the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of suffering are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of the śramaṇa.
When the seeds of the fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvayajñāna*) are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under one of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding those who have no fixed station (*asthāna*), this does not refer here to ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) who have abandoned desire.

For a person following the gradual path (*ānupūrvika*), during the single moment of mind that sees suffering, the four moments of mind that see origination, the four moments of mind that see cessation, and the three moments of mind that see the path—at this time, the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Regarding the abandonment of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma (*dharmajñāna*) within the category of accumulation (*samudaya*), under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or there is no specific location for it.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed location": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no fixed location.
When those who have abandoned desire attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they have no fixed location during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

For one who proceeds by stages, the duration for seeing origination is three moments of mind, for seeing cessation four moments of mind, and for seeing the path three moments of mind. At that time, the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of origination are severed; however, those severances are not included within the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇya-phala*).

Regarding the abandonment of the seeds of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the origin (samudayānvaya-jñāna), under which fruit of the śramaṇa is that abandonment subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or there is no specific location [for its inclusion].
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding the absence of a specific location: herein, it is not stated that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) attain freedom from desire.

For one who proceeds by stages (anupūrvaka), the moment of one mind is for seeing origination (samudaya), four moments of mind are for seeing cessation (nirodha), and three moments of mind are for seeing the path (mārga). At that time, the seeds of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of origination (samudayānvayajñāna) are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma of cessation are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific location.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed location": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no fixed location.
When those who have abandoned desire attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they have no fixed location during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

For a person of gradual attainment, during the interval of three moments of seeing cessation and the interval of three moments of seeing the path, the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of cessation are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) are severed, under which fruit of abandonment is that severance subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the four fruits of the śramaṇa, or it has no specific location.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding the absence of a specific location: herein, the detachment from desire of ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) is not discussed.

For one who proceeds by stages (anupūrvaka), during the single moment of the mind that perceives cessation (nirodha-darśana) and the three moments of the mind that perceive the path (mārga-darśana), the seeds of the fetters (saṃyojana-bīja) to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna) are severed; however, those severances are not subsumed within the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the knowledge of the path (mārga-dharma-jñāna) are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed abode": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no fixed abode.
When those who have abandoned desire attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they have no fixed abode during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

For one who proceeds by stages (*ānupūrvika*), during the interval of two moments of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) abandoned by the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path (*mārgadharmajñāna*) are severed; that severance is not included within the fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
When the seeds of the fetters abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) are severed, to which fruit is that severance attributed?
Answer: The four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
In this context, neither ordinary persons who have abandoned desire nor those on the successive stages of the path are mentioned.

Why is this? It is because it is through the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) that these fetters are ultimately severed; when the subsequent knowledge of the path is present before one, their severance is subsumed within the fruit.
Regarding the abandonment of the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
In this context, neither ordinary persons who have abandoned desire nor those following the gradual path are mentioned. Why is this?

It is because the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) definitively severs these fetters; when the first knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) manifests, that severance is subsumed under the fruit, namely, the fruit of arhatship.
Question: Is it by means of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are severed, or is it by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*)?
If it is by means of the path of non-obstruction that the fetters are severed, how can this passage be reconciled?
As it is said:
regarding the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of suffering, up to the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the subsequent knowledge of the path.
If it were the path of liberation that abandons these fetters, how would one reconcile this with what is stated in the *Jñānaprasthāna*?
As it is said:
"Are those fetters that are abandoned through the vision of suffering also abandoned by the knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:
Those fetters abandoned by the patience regarding the suffering [of the truths]—are those fetters, up to those abandoned by the path of vision, also abandoned by the knowledge of the path?
Answer: Yes.
Question: Are the various fetters abandoned through the patience regarding the path? Answer:
It should be stated as follows:
The various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned by the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*). Question:
If this is so, then the explanation in the *Jñānaprasthāna* (or *Jñānakāṇḍa*) is thoroughly consistent.
How is what is stated in this text to be reconciled?
For example, it says:
"The seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the dharma-knowledge of suffering," and so forth, as explained at length.
Answer: This text should be stated as follows:

There are nine kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*), ranging from the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the receptivity to the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) up to the seeds of fetters to be abandoned by the receptivity to the dharma of the path (*mārga-dharma-kṣānti*).
If it is not so stated, what is the intention?
The answer is:
Patience (kṣānti) belongs to wisdom (jñāna) and is its retinue; therefore, that which is abandoned by patience is also said to be abandoned by wisdom.
It is just as when a person who belongs to a king performs some action, it is also called the "king's action.
It is the same in this case.
Furthermore, the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the fetters, while the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) maintains them so that they do not move.
If the path of liberation does not firmly sustain [the mind], then afflictions will arise once more as a source of harm.
It is like a person who first strikes an enemy down to the ground, and then another person comes to hold him firmly so that he cannot move.
If those who come later do not maintain [the practice] with respect, then resentment will arise again and become a source of harm.
It is like a person who drives an enemy out from within their house, and then another person comes and firmly closes the door.
Even if one person has driven out an enemy, if a subsequent person does not firmly close the door, the enemy will return and cause harm.
It is also like someone who first places a venomous snake in a jar, and later another person comes and securely seals its mouth.

Even if one person has previously been diligent, if those who come later do not keep their mouths firmly closed, the poisonous snake will emerge once more and become a source of calamity; it is just the same with them.
Furthermore, while the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) severs the fetters, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) possesses greater merit.
As explained in the *Indriya-skandhaka*, this point is analyzed in detail herein.
Furthermore, when the path of non-obstruction severs the fetters, the attainment of that severance arises simultaneously with liberation.
Because they arise simultaneously, the path of liberation is also called the severance of fetters.
Furthermore, while the path of non-obstruction severs the fetters, the path of liberation performs the same single task as the path of non-obstruction.
Because they perform the same function, the path of liberation is also called the severance of fetters (*saṃyojana*).
There are fifteen kinds of fetters:
the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm, up to the seeds of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The fetters of the form and formless realms are also like this.
Question: For what reason is this treatise composed once again?

Answer: Previously, the various afflictions were analyzed according to their two kinds and five kinds within the realms (*dhātu*), as well as their counteractive types (*pratipakṣa*); however, the specific types of the realms themselves had not yet been analyzed.
Now, because one wishes to analyze them, this treatise is composed.
To which fruit does the abandonment of the seeds of fetters belonging to the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering belong?
Answer: It belongs to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or it has no specific locus.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no fixed location": ordinary persons who have abandoned desire have no fixed location.
When those who have abandoned desire attain right determination (samyaktva-niyāma), they have no fixed location during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (darśana-mārga).

For a person of gradual attainment (*ānupūrvika*), during the three moments of the mind perceiving suffering, the four moments of perceiving origin, the four moments of perceiving cessation, and the three moments of perceiving the path, the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the desire realm are severed; however, that severance is not subsumed within the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

The fetters of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) to be abandoned by the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-heya*), by the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-heya*), by the vision of the path (*mārga-darśana-heya*), and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) should be explained according to their respective characteristics.

Regarding the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*) to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*), under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
Answer: There are four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there may be no location for them.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding "having no place": ordinary persons have no place when they are free from craving for form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*).
Those who are free from craving for form attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); within the fifteen moments of mind during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), they have no place.

For a person of gradual attainment (*ānupūrvika*), while observing suffering for the duration of one moment of mind, observing origin for four moments of mind, observing cessation for four moments of mind, and observing the path for three moments of mind—having no fixed location [for these durations]—at that time, the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering are severed; however, that severance is not included within the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).

The abandonment of the seeds of fetters belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—which are to be abandoned through the vision of origin, the vision of cessation, the vision of the path, and through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)—should be explained according to their respective characteristics.
Likewise, the abandonment of the seeds of the five types of fetters belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) should also be explained according to their respective characteristics.
Under which fruits is the abandonment of the view of a self-body subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the four fruits of śrāmaṇya, or there is no specific location for it.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
Regarding those who have no specific locus, it is not stated therein that ordinary persons (pṛthagjana) are free from desire.

For one who proceeds through the stages (*anupūrvaka*), during the single moment of mind when seeing suffering, the four moments of mind when seeing the origin, the four moments of mind when seeing cessation, and the three moments of mind when seeing the path, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned; however, that abandonment is not subsumed under the fruits of śrāmaṇya.

Just as with the abandonment of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the same explanation applies to the abandonment of the view of a self-identity among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and among the [five] views (*dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the abandonment of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
Answer: The four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya are as explained above.
In this context, neither ordinary persons who have abandoned desire nor those on the successive stages of the path are mentioned.

Why is this? Because it is through the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārgānvaya-kṣānti*) that these fetters are definitively severed; when the subsequent knowledge regarding the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) manifests, that very severance is subsumed within the fruit of the śramaṇa.

Just as with the abandonment of attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), the same applies in detail to the outflow of views (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*), the yoke of views (*dṛṣṭi-yoga*), the grasping of views (*dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa-upādāna*), the grasping of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-upādāna*), the fetter of precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the view of grasping within the bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*), the attachment to precepts and rituals among the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya*), the false view and the grasping of views among the [five] views, the latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) and the latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*), and the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) and the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*). The detailed exposition is likewise.
When the unwholesome roots of greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*), are abandoned, by which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed by the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of the Arhat (*arhattvaphala*), or else there is no specific locus.
The detailed explanation is as follows: it is like the abandonment of the seeds of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and meditation that are bound to the desire realm.

As with the outflow of desire (kāma-āsrava), so too for the outflow of existence (bhava-āsrava) and the outflow of ignorance (avidyā-āsrava); other afflictions that resemble them should be explained according to their respective characteristics.
Regarding the middle fetters, the fetters of doubt should be explained in detail as the abandonment of the types of fetters severed by the knowledge of the dharma regarding the path.
Regarding the higher fetters, they should be explained in detail as the abandonment of the types of fetters severed by the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms.
The abandonment of craving born from eye-contact, ear-contact, and body-contact—of what fruit is this comprised?
Answer: It is comprised of the fruit of arhatship, or it has no specific location.
The Arhat is subsumed under the fruit of arhatship.
Regarding "having no locus": ordinary persons who have abandoned craving for the Brahma world have no locus.

For those who have abandoned craving for the Brahma world and have attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), there is no locus during the fifteen moments of mind within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), nor during the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

When a person of gradual attainment (*ānupūrvika*) abandons craving for the first dhyāna, the final path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) abandons craving for the second dhyāna up to the abandonment of craving for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). This involves nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*) and nine paths of liberation. Upon abandoning craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are nine paths of non-obstruction and eight paths of liberation. At that time, the craving produced by contact of the eye, ear, and body is abandoned; however, that abandonment is not subsumed within the fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*).
Regarding the abandonment of the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*), as explained in detail in the section on the abandonment of the fifteen types of fetters (*saṃyojana*):
when the types of fetters abandoned by one who is approaching the realization of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) are abandoned, under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
Answer: There is no location. Why is this so?
Prior to the fruit of srotāpanna, there is no other fruit that can encompass its abandonment.

The srotāpanna is encompassed by the fruit of srotāpanna; the fruit of srotāpanna encompasses the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms.
Regarding the seeds of fetters abandoned by one who has realized the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, under which fruit are those abandonments subsumed?
The answer is:
they are subsumed under the fruit of *srotāpanna*, or there is no specific location [for them].
The fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) comprises the abandonment of the seeds of fetters (saṃyojana-bīja) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (darśanamārga) across the three realms.

Regarding those "without a specific location," for a person of gradual progression (anupūrvaka), the abandonment of the five types of fetters bound to the desire realm (kāmadhātu) does not constitute the fruit of stream-entry.
Why is this? Because it is the realization of the path of superior fruition (*viśeṣamārga*).
Just as the path of superior fruition is not subsumed under the category of "fruit," so too is abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
The Sakṛdāgāmin is subsumed under the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin.

The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin comprises the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms, as well as the abandonment of the six types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the desire realm.
Regarding the seeds of fetters severed by one who has realized the fruit of *anāgāmin*, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, or there is no specific location [for its inclusion].

The fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* comprises the abandonment of the seeds of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the three realms, as well as the abandonment of six types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm.
Regarding those without a fixed location, it comprises the abandonment of seven or eight types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm.
Regarding the seeds of fetters abandoned by one who has realized the fruit of Arhatship, under which fruit is that abandonment subsumed?
The answer is:
it is subsumed under the fruit of Anāgāmin, or there is no specific location.

The fruit of *anāgāmin* comprises the abandonment of the seeds of fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the three realms, as well as the abandonment of the nine types of fetters to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the desire realm.

Regarding those without a specific location: it includes the abandonment of the nine types of fetters from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the abandonment of the eight types of fetters in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Why is this so? Because it is the realization of the path of superior fruit (*viśeṣamārga*).
Just as the path of superior fruit is not subsumed under the category of "fruit," so too is that abandonment.
The Arhat is subsumed within the fruit of arhatship.
The fruit of arhatship comprises the exhaustion of all seeds of fetters (saṃyojana) abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation across the three realms. Question:
Just as one who has severed one kind of fetter up to five kinds of fetters is called a *srotāpanna* by virtue of having attained the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the Path, so too,
the severing of the five kinds of fetters bound to the desire realm is not subsumed under the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

When one has severed seven or eight kinds of fetters, attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and realizes the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*), they are called a *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Although they have severed those seven or eight kinds of fetters, such severance is not subsumed under the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.

When one is free from craving for the first dhyāna up to being free from craving for the sphere of nothingness, and attains right determination and the subsequent knowledge of the path, it is called the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).
He has severed the nine types of fetters of the first dhyāna, up to the nine types of fetters of the sphere of nothingness; yet these are not subsumed under the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
Why, then, is it said that a Srotāpanna is subsumed under the fruit of a Srotāpanna, a Sakṛdāgāmin under the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin, and an Anāgāmin under the fruit of an Anāgāmin?
Why is it not stated that [the place] does not exist?
The answer is:
this passage should be stated as follows:
The stream-enterer is subsumed under the fruit of stream-entry, or there is no specific location for it.
The once-returner is subsumed under the fruit of once-returning, or there is no specific location for it.
The non-returner is subsumed under the fruit of non-returning, or there is no specific location for it.
What is the intention behind not mentioning this?
The answer is:
this explanation concerns those who are bound by all fetters in their sequential order; it does not concern those who transcend them.

When a disciple of the Blessed One who is fully endowed with the vision of the truths has not yet abandoned desire-attachment, and has severed the seeds of the fetters belonging to the realm of desire that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation—under what fruit is that severance subsumed?
Answer: The fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin) may have no fixed location.
The fruit of the once-returner comprises the abandonment of the six types of fetters (saṃyojana) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) within the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Regarding "those without a locus," this refers to the abandonment of the seven or eight types of fetters (*saṃyojana*).

When one has already abandoned desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) but has not yet abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the seeds of the fetters belonging to the realm of form that are to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) are abandoned. To what fruit does that abandonment belong?
Answer: There is no location.
From the severing of the nine types of fetters of the first dhyāna up to the severing of the eight types of fetters of the fourth dhyāna, there is no location.

One who has already abandoned craving for the realm of form but has not yet abandoned craving for the formless realm—when the seeds of the fetters to be abandoned by the path of cultivation in the formless realm are severed, under which fruit is that severance subsumed?
Answer: It is not included in any [fruit].
The nine kinds of fetters of the sphere of infinite space are severed, up to and including the eight kinds of fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
which are severed without location. *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 34 [and] Scroll 35.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats and translated by the Northern Liang Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others.
Within the *Pudgala-varga* of the *Śīlaskandha*, there are the four fruits of the śramaṇa, namely: the fruit of srotāpanna, the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, the fruit of anāgāmin, and the fruit of arhat.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
Some say that the fruits of śramaṇaship are exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), as the Vātsīputrīyas maintain. Question:
For what reason do they make such a statement?
Answer: He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state that he addressed the bhikṣus:
I shall now explain the śramaṇa, the fruits of the śramaṇa, and the person who is a śramaṇa.
What is meant by "śramaṇa"?
The answer is:
The Eightfold Noble Path is called the śramaṇa.
What is called the fruit of the śramaṇa?
The answer is:
From the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of stream-entry?
The answer is:
This refers to the permanent severance of the three fetters.
What is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin?
The answer is:
The permanent severance of the three fetters and the attenuation of craving, hatred, and delusion—this is it.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmin)?
The answer is:
It is the permanent severance of the five lower fetters (pañca avarabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni). What is the fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
It is the permanent severance of craving, pride, delusion, and all fetters.
Who is a person of the śramaṇa?
The answer is:
One who accomplishes such dharmas as these is called a śramaṇa.
Because of this sūtra, it is said that the fruits of the śramaṇa are exclusively unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is in order to stop those who speak in such a manner, and also to clarify that the fruits of the śramaṇa are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned.
If the fruits of śrāmaṇya were exclusively unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and not conditioned (saṃskṛta), it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras.
The sūtras state:
"There are four paths of progress (pratipannaka) and those who abide in the four fruits."
One who abides in the fruit abides in the conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya, not in the unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya.
Question: At this time, one also abides in cessation.
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:

"He abides in cessation, seeking no further superior dharma; he does not claim to have attained what has not been attained, to have realized what has not been realized, or to have understood what has not been understood."

Answer: To speak of "abiding in cessation" does not mean abiding upon the elephant or horse as one who rides them; rather, it means that because one neither regresses nor advances from the state of cessation, one is said to abide in cessation.
In the Sūtras, the Blessed One has also spoken categorically regarding the conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya, as it is said:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that by making these five faculties superior, sharp, penetrating, and fully perfected, one shall attain the fruit of arhatship with both parts liberated (ubhayatobhāga-vimukta);
if they are less developed, one attains liberation through wisdom (prajñāvimukti), and so on, down to firm faith (śraddhādhimukta)."
Question: If the fruits of śrāmaṇya are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how are the Buddha’s sūtras to be reconciled? Answer:
The fruits of śrāmaṇya are both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet the Buddha’s sūtras speak only of the unconditioned. Question:
For what reason do the Buddha’s sūtras speak only of the unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya?
Answer: The Buddhist sūtras speak only of the fruits of the śramaṇa; they do not say that the path of the śramaṇa is itself the śramaṇa and also the fruit of the śramaṇa.
Furthermore, this sūtra speaks only of the fruits of the brāhmaṇa; it does not say that the path of the brāhmaṇa is itself the brāhmaṇa and also the fruit of the brāhmaṇa.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s sūtras state that the Brahma-faring (brahmacarya) is both the Brahma-faring itself and the fruit of the Brahma-faring.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s sūtras speak of a fruit; there is no path to a fruit that is itself the fruit, yet there is further fruit beyond it.
Furthermore, the Buddha’s sūtras speak of "separation" (*viveka*). There is no path of separation other than this; yet within this separation, there is further separation.
For this reason, desiring to refute the positions of others and to clarify our own position, we have composed this treatise, as explained at length.
The four fruits of śrāmaṇya: the fruit of stream-entry up to the fruit of arhatship.
What is the fruit of stream-entry?
The answer is:
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda*:
"The fruit of srotāpanna is of two kinds: conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the conditioned fruit of srotāpanna?"

Answer: When one realizes the fruit of *srotāpanna*, there are various trainings (*śaikṣadharma*) that have been attained, are being attained, and will be attained. Those already attained belong to the past, those being attained belong to the present, and those to be attained belong to the future; this is called the conditioned fruit of *srotāpanna*.
What is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*)?
The answer is:

at the time of realizing the fruit of stream-entry, the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) are abandoned—those already abandoned, those currently being abandoned, and those yet to be abandoned—as explained in detail above.
Question: It may be so that the Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), falls within the world, and has been attained, is being attained, or will be attained.
But how can it be so that cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), does not fall within the world, and yet has been attained, is being attained, or will be attained?
The answer is:
The *Puggalapaññatti* (Designation of Persons) Sūtra should state it thus:
"The various fetters are abandoned; they are now attained, now liberated, and now realized."
If it is not so stated, what is the intention?
The answer is:

this teaching is obtained within the body. That which has already been obtained is said to be obtained by the past body; that which is being obtained now is said to be obtained by the present body; and that which is to be obtained hereafter is said to be obtained by the future body.
As it is with the fruit of stream-entry, so too is the explanation for the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
The fruit of arhatship is of two kinds: namely, conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is the conditioned fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:

At the time of realizing the fruit of arhatship, all the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—whether already attained, currently being attained, or yet to be attained—are as explained in detail above.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* asks:
"What is the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala)?"
Answer: The fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is of two kinds, namely, conditioned (saṃskṛta) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
What is the conditioned fruit of stream-entry?
Answer: It is the acquisition of that fruit (phalaprāpti) and the acquisition of that acquisition (prāptiprāpti).
"Acquisition of the fruit" refers to the acquisition of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala).
"Attainment of attainment" refers to the attainment of that attainment.
It is called a "fruit" because it is attained; it is called "accomplishment" because it is attained by means of attainment.

The faculties of training, the powers of training, the precepts of training, the roots of goodness of training, and the eight factors of training—such dharmas of training as these are called the conditioned fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*).
What is the unconditioned fruit of stream-entry?
The answer is:
it is the permanent abandonment of the three fetters and the abandonment of all such factors of bondage.
The severance of the eighty-eight *anuśayas*, and likewise the severance of all such *anuśaya*-dharmas, is called the unconditioned fruit of *srotāpanna*.
What is the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*?
Answer: There are two kinds of the fruit of the once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin), namely the conditioned and the unconditioned, as explained in detail above.
The distinction here is that one gradually abandons craving, aversion, and delusion, as well as the phenomena associated with craving and aversion.
What is the fruit of the non-returner (anāgāmiphala)?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of the fruit of the non-returner, namely, the conditioned (saṃskṛta) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
The conditioned fruit of *anāgāmin* is as explained above.
As for the unconditioned fruit of *anāgāmin*: it is the permanent abandonment of the five lower fetters (*pañca avarabhāgīyāni saṃyojanāni*), the permanent abandonment of such dharmas of fettering;
and the permanent abandonment of the ninety-two proclivities (*anuśaya*), the permanent abandonment of such dharmas of proclivity. This is called the unconditioned fruit of *anāgāmin*.
What is the fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
the fruit of arhatship is of two kinds, namely, conditioned and unconditioned.
What is the conditioned fruit of arhatship?
The answer is:
the attainment of the fruit of arhatship, as well as the attainment of that attainment.
"Attaining the fruit" refers to the attainment by an arhat.
"Attaining the attainment" refers to the attainment of that attainment.
It is called a "fruit" because it is attained; it is called "accomplishment" because it is the attainment of that attainment.

The faculties of those beyond training, the powers of those beyond training, the precepts of those beyond training, the wholesome roots of those beyond training, and the ten dharmas of those beyond training—such various dharmas of those beyond training as these are called the conditioned fruit of arhatship.

What is the unconditioned fruit of arhatship? The answer is: the eternal severance of craving, conceit, ignorance, and all afflictions; emerging from all realms of existence; cutting off all paths of birth and death; extinguishing the three fires; having transcended the four floods; crushing and destroying all forms of pride; being free from thirsting craving; shattering the nest; the unsurpassed ultimate, the unsurpassed tranquility, and the unsurpassed peace—the nirvana where craving is exhausted and desire is absent. This is called the unconditioned fruit of arhatship.
"This is the essential nature of the fruits of śrāmaṇya," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained its essential nature and the reason for it, we shall now explain why it is called the "fruit of śrāmaṇya."
What is the meaning of "fruit of the śramaṇa"?
The answer is:
the noble path is called "śramaṇa," and because it is the fruit thereof, it is called the "fruit of the śramaṇa."

Question: The Noble Path is called "śramaṇa," and its fruit is the "fruit of the śramaṇa" (śrāmaṇyaphala). In this context, the eight patiences (kṣānti) within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) are named "śramaṇa," while the eight knowledges (jñāna) are the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa (saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala).
The abandonment of the eight kinds of fetters is the unconditioned fruit of the śramaṇa.
At the time of becoming free from desire for sensual pleasure, the nine paths of non-obstruction are called the śramaṇa;
the nine paths of liberation are the conditioned fruits of the śramaṇa, and the abandonment of the nine kinds of fetters is the unconditioned fruit of the śramaṇa.
This applies likewise up to the abandonment of desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, there are eighty-nine conditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya and eighty-nine unconditioned fruits of śrāmaṇya.
When distinguished by way of the world, eighty-nine are in the past, eighty-nine are in the future, and eighty-nine are in the present.
The *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* asks: "What are the dharmas that are results?"
Answer: All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
For however many moments of the Noble Path (*āryamārga-kṣaṇa*) there may be, there are that many conditioned fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇya-phala*).
However many modes of liberation there may be, there are that many fruits of the śramaṇa.
If one distinguishes them according to their presence in the body at each moment, then there are immeasurable and boundless fruits of the śramaṇa.
Why does the Buddha’s sūtra speak only of the four fruits of śrāmaṇya?
The answer is:
some say that this is the Tathāgata’s concise and essential teaching with intentional brevity (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita), spoken for the sake of those to be converted.
The Venerable Paśya said:
"The Buddha definitively knows the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and also knows their functional efficacy (*prabhāva*), which others do not know.
If the fruits of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are established through the sequential continuity of phenomena, he explains those fruits of śramaṇaship as being based on that sequential continuity."
Furthermore, at that time, it is easy to perceive and easy to designate, saying: "This is the fruit of stream-entry," up to "this is the fruit of arhatship";
however, the intermediate stages between these fruits are not easy to perceive nor easy to designate.
Furthermore, at that time, the practitioner experiences great joy and satisfaction regarding the fruit,
just as a farmer who has tended his fields for six months subsequently reaps a harvest of grain.
Upon the site of the accumulation, his mind was greatly joyful and at ease;
it was just so for him as well.
Furthermore, at that time, there were three reasons:
First, attaining the path never before attained;
second, relinquishing the path already attained;
third, severing afflictions so that they become of a single flavor.
Furthermore, at that time there are five matters:
first, attaining the path never before attained;
second, relinquishing the path already attained;
Third, the severance of afflictions is of one single flavor;
fourth, the instantaneous attainment of the eight knowledges;
fifth, the cultivation of the sixteen aspects.
Furthermore, at this time it is the state of rest.
Furthermore, at this time the task of severing the fetters is accomplished in every respect, and the skillful means of the path are perfected;
whereas during the intermediate stage of the fruit, the task of severing the fetters is not yet accomplished, nor are the skillful means of the path perfected.
Furthermore, at this time, there is space for the extensive cultivation of the fruits of the path, whereas in the interim, there is no room for the extensive cultivation of the path.
Moreover, at this time, the practitioner clearly discerns merit and fault; that which knows merit is the Path and its fruits, while that which knows faults is the dharma of birth and death.
Furthermore, at this time, the practitioner skillfully grasps the signs (*nimitta*).

For example, when a person walks along a road, they cannot skillfully grasp the signs of the four directions; however, if they sit in one place, they can skillfully grasp the signs of the four directions.
It is the same for him as well.
Furthermore, at that time, the practitioner possesses accompanying knowledge and vision;
it is like a person who, in the midst of a village, is robbed by others and lacks anyone to accompany him or provide knowledge and vision.
If one is robbed by others in a village, there are many followers who possess knowledge and insight.
Furthermore, at this time, the practitioner has previously extensively cultivated the path of skillful means, so that his footing is firm and secure.

Regarding the Srotāpanna fruit, for one who extensively cultivates the path of skillful means, this refers to the period of fifteen moments of mind within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), during which one previously cultivated giving, ethical discipline, the wisdom of hearing, the wisdom of reflection, and the wisdom of cultivation, as well as the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (laukikāgradharma) for the sake of liberation.
Regarding the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin who extensively cultivates the path of skillful means, it is as explained above.

Furthermore, among all virtues, there are those that are even more extraordinary: namely, the path of skillful means for detachment from the desire realm, the six paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the five paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Regarding the one who extensively cultivates the path of skillful means for the fruit of *anāgāmin*, it is as explained above.

Furthermore, among all wholesome qualities, there are those that are unprecedented: namely, the path of skillful means, the three paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the two paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) at the time of abandoning desire and craving.
Regarding the Arhat fruit, the extensive cultivation of the path of means is as explained above.

Furthermore, among all wholesome states, there are others that are unprecedented: the path of means, the nine paths of non-obstruction, and the nine paths of liberation involved in becoming detached from the desire of the first dhyāna; this description applies likewise up to becoming detached from the desire of the sphere of nothingness.

When one becomes detached from the desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, this refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), the nine paths of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), and the eight paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
Furthermore, at that time, the practitioner severs all factors of rebirth and brings all factors of rebirth to rest.

For a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), with the exception of the seven rebirths in the desire realm and one rebirth in each of the form and formless realms, all other rebirths attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).

For a Sakṛdāgāmin, with the exception of the two rebirths in the desire realm and one birth in each of the form and formless realms, all other rebirths attain non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

For an Anāgāmin, regarding each individual place of rebirth in the realms of form and formlessness, with the exception of the portion of one remaining birth, all other portions of rebirth attain non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
For an Arhat, all portions of rebirth attain non-analytical cessation.
Furthermore, at this time, the practitioner suddenly realizes the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation within the three realms.
A stream-enterer (srotāpanna) suddenly realizes the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms.

The Sakṛdāgāmin suddenly realizes the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms, as well as the six types of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the desire realm.

The Anāgāmin suddenly realizes the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing within the three realms, as well as the nine types of afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation within the desire realm.
The Arhat suddenly realizes the afflictions to be abandoned through the paths of seeing and cultivation within the three realms.
Furthermore, one who falls away from the fundamental fruit of śrāmaṇya does not die, whereas one who falls away from an intermediate fruit may die.
Furthermore, with reference to the five destinies (*gati*), the four fruits of śrāmaṇya are taught:

the fruit of srotāpanna corresponds to the realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts; the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin corresponds to a portion of the human realm; the fruit of anāgāmin corresponds ultimately to the human realm; and the fruit of arhat corresponds to the heavenly realm.
Furthermore, with respect to the four modes of birth:

the fruit of Srotāpanna corresponds to moisture-born and egg-born beings; the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin corresponds to a portion of womb-born beings; the fruit of Anāgāmin corresponds entirely to womb-born beings; and the fruit of Arhat corresponds to transformation-born beings.
Furthermore, it is in relation to two kinds of volition: first, the volition that severs the roots of goodness;
second, the volition that commits the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*).

The fruit of *srotāpanna* corresponds to the volition that severs the roots of goodness; the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* corresponds to the volition that commits the five heinous crimes; the fruit of *anāgāmin* corresponds to the retribution of those deeds; and the fruit of *arhat* corresponds to the aggregates (*skandha*) that receive that retribution.
Why is this so? Because the experience of retribution necessarily depends upon the aggregates (*skandha*).
Furthermore, it is because they correspond to the three sets of three phenomena.

The fruit of *srotāpanna* corresponds to the three fetters; the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* corresponds to the gradual attenuation of the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*); the fruit of *anāgāmin* corresponds ultimately to the three unwholesome roots and the outflow of desire; and the fruit of *arhat* corresponds to the outflows of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) and ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).
Furthermore, with respect to the four floods (*ogha*):

the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) corresponds to the flood of views (*dṛṣṭy-ogha*); the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*) corresponds to a small portion of the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*); the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*) corresponds entirely to the flood of desire; and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*) corresponds to the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).
The same applies to the yokes (*yoga*).
Furthermore, with respect to the four graspings (*upādāna*):

the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) opposes the grasping for views (*dṛṣṭy-upādāna*) and the grasping for precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa-upādāna*); the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) opposes a portion of the grasping for sensual desire (*kāma-upādāna*); the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) ultimately opposes the grasping for sensual desire; and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) opposes the grasping for self-theory (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*).
Furthermore, with respect to the five-and-three dharmas:

the fruit of *srotāpanna* corresponds to the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-āvaraṇa*) and three of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*); the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* corresponds to the remaining hindrances and a portion of two of the lower fetters; the fruit of *anāgāmin* ultimately corresponds to the remaining hindrances and the other two lower fetters; and the fruit of *arhat* corresponds to the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, with respect to the various views and the six groups of craving (ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya):

the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpatti-phala) is opposed to the five views; the fruit of once-returning (sakṛdāgāmi-phala) is opposed to a portion of the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) is ultimately opposed to the group of craving born of nose-contact and tongue-contact; and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala) is opposed to the remaining groups of craving.
Furthermore, with respect to the seven underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*):

the fruit of *srotāpanna* opposes the underlying tendencies of views and doubt; the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* opposes a portion of the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will; the fruit of *anāgāmin* completely opposes the underlying tendencies of sensual desire and ill-will; and the fruit of *arhat* opposes the remaining underlying tendencies.
Furthermore, with respect to the nine fetters (*saṃyojana*):

the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) opposes the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭisaṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśasaṃyojana*), and the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsāsaṃyojana*); the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*) opposes a portion of the fetter of ill-will (*pratighasaṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyāsaṃyojana*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsaryasaṃyojana*); the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*) ultimately opposes the fetter of ill-will, the fetter of envy, and the fetter of avarice; and the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*) opposes the remaining fetters.
Furthermore, with respect to the ninety-eight latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):

the fruit of *srotāpanna* corresponds to the latent tendencies to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) within the three realms; the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* corresponds to a small portion of those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the desire realm; the fruit of *anāgāmin* corresponds entirely to those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the desire realm; and the fruit of *arhat* corresponds to those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms.
