If consciousness were to cease from the feet and then arise again within the feet, such a thing would not even exist in the formless realm.
Question: Does the intermediate state (antarābhava) undergo transition?
Answer: There is no transmigration, that is to say, within the realms, the destinies, or the stations. Question:
If there were no transition of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) between realms, how would one account for the case of the monk of little learning?

It is heard that there was once a son of good family who left the household life to join the Buddha’s Dharma; he did not cultivate the means of extensive learning, yet dwelt in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*).

By the power of past causes, they are able to give rise to the mundane first dhyāna and claim it is the fruit of srotāpanna, up to giving rise to the mundane fourth dhyāna and claiming it is the fruit of arhat.

Throughout one's life, they claim to have attained what they have not attained, claim to have understood what they have not understood, and claim to have realized what they have not realized; they do not seek further progress on the path, nor do they aspire to attain what is not yet attained, understand what is not yet understood, or realize what is not yet realized.
Later, when his body breaks up and his life ends, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the fourth dhyāna manifests before him; at that time, he thinks:
"I have severed all conditions for rebirth; I should attain parinirvāṇa and should not be born again."
"What conditions have given rise to my current existence?
There is certainly no liberation.
If there were liberation, I should have attained it."
They then give rise to the false view that slanders *nirvāṇa*.

Because of this false view, their intermediate state (*antarābhava*) in the fourth dhyāna ceases immediately, and an intermediate state for the Avīci Hell manifests; at the end of their life, they are reborn in the Avīci Hell.
The answer is:
This refers to the transition occurring at the time of the preceding existence, not at the time of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
At the moment of death, the auspicious signs of the fourth dhyāna appear before him; having seen those signs, he then forms this thought:
"I have severed all conditions for rebirth and should enter parinirvāṇa.
By what cause has this auspicious sign arisen?
Surely there is no liberation."
If there were liberation, I should have attained it.
Thus he gave rise to the false view of slandering *nirvāṇa*.

Because he produced this false view, the auspicious signs of the fourth dhyāna vanished, and the auspicious signs of the Avīci Hell appeared before him. When his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn in the Avīci Hell.
For this reason, it is known that there is a transition from the previous state, but no transition via the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Question:
If there is no transition toward a destination (*gati*) by means of the intermediate state, how can the causal conditions for wholesome and unwholesome actions be reconciled?
I have heard that in the kingdom of Śrāvastī there were two men: one named Sukṛta (Good Conduct) and the other named Duṣkṛta (Evil Conduct).
As for Sukṛta, throughout his entire life he constantly practiced virtuous deeds and never committed unwholesome acts.
One who has practiced evil deeds constantly performs unwholesome actions and fails to perform wholesome ones throughout their life.
Because of wholesome karma from a previous existence, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a deva appears before them. At that moment, they think:

"Throughout my entire life, I have constantly performed evil deeds and failed to perform wholesome ones; I ought to be reborn in an evil realm and not in the heavens. By what cause, then, am I now born here in the intermediate state of a deva?"
He then thought to himself:
"There certainly is no retribution for good or evil deeds.
If there were, I ought to have received it."
He then gives rise to the false view that denies cause and effect.

Because of this false view, his intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a deva ceases, and an intermediate state for hell beings arises immediately; with the dissolution of the body at the end of life, he is reborn within the hells.

When a person who has practiced virtuous conduct approaches the end of life, because of unwholesome karma that will ripen as a subsequent retribution, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell manifests before them. They then think:

"Throughout my entire life I have constantly practiced virtuous conduct and never committed evil deeds; I ought to be reborn in a happy realm and not in an evil realm. By what cause and condition has this intermediate state of hell now arisen for me?"
He then thought to himself:
"This must surely be the fruit of unwholesome karma from my past lives, which has ripened in this present existence.

He immediately recollected the various wholesome deeds he had performed; as a great mind of goodness arose and became manifest before him, his intermediate state in hell vanished and his intermediate state in heaven appeared. With the dissolution of the body and the end of life, he was reborn in the heavenly realms.
The answer is:
All such instances involve the transition occurring during the previous existence, not during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

At the time of death, all sentient beings inevitably experience auspicious or inauspicious omens. If a sentient being has practiced much virtue, at the time of death they will mostly see fine halls, pavilions, gardens, bathing pools, and places for recreation.
Sentient beings who have frequently committed evil see many flames, swords, poisons, wolves, dogs, and burial mounds at the time of death.
When those who have practiced evil deeds die, because of the subsequent ripening of their wholesome karma, celestial omens appear before them. Having seen these, they think:

"Throughout my life I constantly practiced evil deeds and did not practice wholesome deeds; I ought to be reborn in the woeful realms and not in the heavens. By what cause, then, do these auspicious signs arise?"
They will certainly conclude that there is no retribution for good or evil karma,
and thus give rise to the false view of denying cause and effect.
Because they have produced such a false view, the auspicious signs of rebirth in heaven immediately vanish, and the ominous signs of hell arise instead.
When a practitioner of wholesome conduct dies, due to the ripening of subsequent evil karma, the omens of hell appear before them.
Having seen them, they think:

"Throughout my life I have always practiced wholesome conduct and not unwholesome conduct; I ought to be reborn in a happy realm and not in an evil destiny. By what cause, then, do these omens arise?"
"Surely this is the result of unwholesome karma from my past lives that has ripened in this birth.

He then recollected the various wholesome deeds he had performed; as a great mind of goodness arose and became manifest before him, the auspicious signs of hell vanished and the auspicious signs of the heavens appeared. When his body broke up and his life ended, he was reborn in the heavenly realms.

For this reason, both of these involve the transition of time during the stage of *pūrvakālabhava* (existence prior to death), not during the stage of *antarābhava* (intermediate existence). Question:
If there is no transition of place during the intermediate existence, how is the causal account of King Bimbisāra to be reconciled?
I have heard that King Bimbisāra once appeared before the Tuṣita Heaven, destined to be reborn there.
Passing over the summit of Mount Sumeru, he beheld the food consumed by the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, which was brilliant in color and perfect in fragrance and flavor. He then thought to himself:
"I shall first be born here, and afterwards I shall be born in the Tuṣita Heaven."

While he was forming this thought, his existence among the Tuṣita gods ceased and he was immediately reborn among the Four Great Kings; having ended his life there, he was born in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
Answer: This also refers to the transition occurring during the previous lifetime, not during the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
It was heard that King Bimbisāra was once bound by his nominal son Ajātaśatru, imprisoned, deprived of food and drink, and had the skin peeled from the soles of his feet with a knife.
At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain. Out of compassion, he emitted a radiance that shone upon her body through the window.
Encountering the Buddha’s light, her body attained peace and stability, and she gave rise to a mind of mindfulness of the Buddha, thinking:
"Now that I have met with such calamity, does the World-Honored One not turn his thoughts toward me?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing his thoughts, addressed Mahāmaudgalyāyana:
"Go to King Bimbisāra and speak these words:
'I have already performed all that I ought to do for Your Majesty.'"
"Even the Tathāgata cannot escape the karmic retribution of the evil destinies that you have determinedly incurred.

At that time, after Mahāmaudgalyāyana had heard these words from the Buddha, he immediately entered meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). By the power of his concentration, according to his intention, he vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa and emerged from the ground as if from the water of a spring or pond, standing before King Bimbisāra and speaking thus:

"Great King, you should know that the words of the Tathāgata are non-dual. With the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*) illuminating purity, he perceives deeply the law of cause and effect, and thus he has spoken these words:"
"O Great King, that which was to be done by me has all been accomplished.
I have delivered you from the karmic retribution of the evil destinies; even a Tathāgata cannot escape this.
Having spoken these words, he preached the Dharma for him."
At that time, King Bimbisāra, being distressed by hunger and thirst and unable to understand [the teaching], spoke these words:
"Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana!
Which among the devas has the most exquisite solid food?"
At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana spoke in succession, praising the food of the Four Great Kings.
When King Bimbisāra heard this, his body broke up and his life ended; he was reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings as the crown prince of Vaiśravaṇa, named Janarṣabha.
For this reason, it is known that the transition occurs at the time of the prior existence (*pūrvakālabhava*), not at the time of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
The Dārṣṭāntikas maintain this view, saying:
"The intermediate existence can undergo transition."
He asserts this: "All karmas can be transferred;
even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) can be transferred, let alone those of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
If the deeds of immediate retribution could not be transferred, then no one would ever be able to transcend the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*)."
Because there are those capable of transcending even the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it is known that even the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) can be diverted.
The critique states:
one should speak thus:
Within this intermediate state (antarābhava), there is no possibility of transition. Question:
For how long does one remain in the intermediate state?
Answer: For but a short time, not for long. Why is this so?
He seeks the locus for receiving a body within the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); therefore, he causes the continuity of existence (*bhava*) to arise swiftly.
Question: It may be granted that the conjunction of the dharmas through which sentient beings receive a body causes the continuity of existence to arise swiftly.

If the factors for receiving a body were not in conjunction—such as the father being in Kaśmīra while the mother is in China, or the father being in China while the mother is in Kaśmīra—how could one quickly cause the continuity of existence (bhava) to arise?

The answer is: One should observe these sentient beings; for some, the karma performed toward the mother can be transferred, while the karma performed toward the father cannot be transferred; for others, the karma performed toward the father can be transferred, while the karma performed toward the mother cannot be transferred; for others, the karma performed toward both parents cannot be transferred; and for others, the karma performed toward both parents can be transferred.

If the karmic action performed toward the mother can be transferred, while the karmic action performed toward the father cannot be transferred, then even a virtuous man who is fully endowed with dignified conduct, who has purely cultivated the holy life, and who maintains the five precepts, will necessarily go to another woman’s side and cause her to give birth to a rebirth-continuum.

If the karmic action performed toward the father can be transferred, while the karmic action performed toward the mother cannot be transferred, then even a woman who is perfectly endowed with dignified conduct, pure in her cultivation of the holy life, and maintains the five precepts, will inevitably go to another man and cause him to produce a rebirth-continuum.

If, regarding one's parents, the karma created is such that it cannot be transferred, then even though the recipient of the body has not yet died and the person has not yet attained what they sought, they will immediately give rise to the intention to depart.
Along that path, fire cannot burn them, blades cannot wound them, and poisons cannot harm them; they will surely reach that place of union and cause rebirth there through the continuity of existence.
Question: If sentient beings always possess a mind of desire, this may be so;
but if sentient beings only occasionally possess a mind of desire, how can this be?
Just as dogs have desire in autumn, bears have desire in winter, horses have desire in spring, and oxen have desire in summer—how could such things be possible?
Answer: Due to the karmic power of those sentient beings, they also give rise to desire at an improper time and achieve union, thereby causing their birth to continue.
Furthermore, some say that they are born among those who are similar to them.
Just as a dog has desire only occasionally while a jackal always has desire, one who was destined to be born among dogs is instead born among jackals.
Just as a brown bear has desire only occasionally while a black bear always has desire, one who was destined to be born among brown bears is instead born among black bears.
When horses occasionally have lustful thoughts while donkeys always have lustful thoughts, those who ought to be born among horses are born among donkeys.
When cattle occasionally have lustful thoughts while wild oxen always have lustful thoughts, those who ought to be born among cattle are born among wild oxen.
The Venerable Śamathadatta said:
"The lifespan of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is seven times seven days. The Venerable Revata said:
Among them are sentient beings whose lifespan lasts seven days, not exceeding one week. Why is this?
Because their bodies are weak and frail.
Question: If, upon reaching the seventh day, the conditions for rebirth are not harmonized, does that [intermediate state] undergo cessation? Answer: No.
Because it is not subject to cessation, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) can endure for a long duration.
The Venerable Buddhadeva stated: "The lifespan of the intermediate state is indefinite."
Why is this? Because the conditions for birth are not fixed.
Although the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) may achieve union, it does not achieve union with the place of birth; therefore, it causes [the being] to dwell there for a long time.
Question: What is the size of the form of the intermediate state (antarābhava)? Answer:
Its form is like that of a small child of five or six years of age.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"If its form is such as this, how can it give rise to such perverted perceptions—producing a mind of attachment toward the mother and a mind of resentment toward the father?"
The answer is:
Although its form is small, its faculties are sharp and acute.
It is like a painted image of an old man on a wall; although its form is small, it possesses the characteristics of old age.
Question: Does the form of the Bodhisattva in the intermediate state have a large or small size? Answer:

As previously described, there was at that time a youth whose form and other attributes were likewise adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; his body was of pure golden hue, and he was surrounded by a halo one fathom in width.
For this reason, when a bodhisattva dwells in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the radiance of his body illuminates ten billion four-continent worlds (*cāturdvīpaka*).
Question: If this is so, how do you reconcile this with the verse spoken by the Venerable Subhūti?
As it is said:
"His form was like that of a white elephant, with four feet and six tusks;
when he entered his mother’s womb, it was as if he were strolling through a pleasure garden."
He replied: "This need not necessarily be explained. Why is that?"
This is not found in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma;
it is a doctrine fabricated by oneself, which may be correct or incorrect, asserting existence where there is non-existence, or non-existence where there is existence.
If you insist on reconciling this, what is the underlying intention?
The answer is:
In the customs of that land, such a dream is considered auspicious; therefore, his mother saw this thing in a dream and wished to have it interpreted.
The physiognomists all declared it to be auspicious and virtuous.
Since the Bodhisattva had not fallen into the evil realms for ninety-one kalpas, by what cause did he assume the form of an animal to enter his mother’s womb?
Question: Is the intermediate state (antarābhava) endowed with all sense faculties, or is it not so endowed? Answer:
All faculties are complete.
Why is this? Because at the moment of initial birth in the intermediate state (antarābhava), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) all seek existence.
Furthermore, there are those who say that they do not possess all the sense faculties. One asks:
Which faculties do they lack?
The answer is:

Just as those who possessed incomplete sense faculties in the previous existence appear in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) accordingly—just as a reflection resembles its seal—the previous existence appears, and the intermediate state is likewise.
The commentary states:
It should be said that there is no one who does not possess all the sense faculties.
Why is this so? Because at the moment of birth in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), all six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) seek existence.
It is asked:
What is the manner of movement therein?
The answer is:
for those sentient beings who are destined to be born in hell, they move with their heads downward and their feet upward.
As the verse says:
"Those who fall into hell have their bodies all hanging upside down;
This is because they slandered the noble sages And those of pure conduct."
Those born in the four continents move horizontally, like birds flying through the air or like figures painted on a wall appearing to fly.
Those destined to be born in the heavens have their heads directed upward, like an arrow shot into the void.
Question: When the intermediate state being is born, does it possess clothing? Answer:
All beings born in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) possess clothing. Why is this?
Because the form realm is a realm of great shame and modesty (*hrī-apatrāpya*); just as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is always covered by robes, so too is the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
Among the sentient beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), many are born without clothing, with the sole exception of the Bodhisattva and the Bhikṣuṇī Śuklā.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the Bodhisattva in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is without clothing, whereas the Bhikṣuṇī Śuklā possesses clothing.
Question: For what reason is there no clothing for the Bodhisattva in his intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), while the Bhikṣuṇī Śuklā has clothing? Answer:
The bhikṣuṇī Śuklā offered a woolen cloth to the Saṃgha of the four directions.
It was asked:
"The segments of clothing offered by the Bodhisattva to the Saṃgha of the four directions were more numerous than the pieces of woven thread offered by the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā."
The answer is:
After the bhikṣuṇī Śuklā had offered a cotton cloth to the Saṃgha, she made this aspiration:
"May I always be provided with clothing in every place where I am born."

By the power of their aspirational prayers, they wear clothes at the moment of birth in the intermediate state; they continue to wear clothes upon entering and emerging from the womb, and as their bodies grow, their garments likewise increase in size.

Having conceived faith in the Buddha-dharma, he subsequently left the household life; using this very robe, he fashioned five kinds of garments and, through diligent cultivation of skillful means, attained arhatship. At the time of his parinirvāṇa, he wrapped his body in this very robe and performed the cremation.

All the wholesome dharmas practiced by a bodhisattva are dedicated toward unexcelled enlightenment; because they can produce a fruit that corresponds to its cause, they result in the attainment of the most supreme body among all sentient beings in their final existence.
Question: What do sentient beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) eat? Answer:
Some say that when there is food and drink, they eat it; otherwise, they survive by drinking water at rivers, ponds, or the water's edge.
A question is asked:
"If this is so, I have heard that just as one empties rice from a bag into a cauldron, the beings within the five realms of existence who are scattered throughout the world are likewise [dispersed]."
Of all the food and drink existing in the entire world, even that which is fit for dogs would not suffice to satisfy them, let alone for others.
Furthermore, their bodies are subtle and light while their food is coarse and heavy; were they to consume such food, their bodies would surely disintegrate.
If that is so, how does one sustain oneself?
The answer is:
by using fragrance as food.
If sentient beings possess merit, they sustain themselves by consuming pure food, drink, flowers, fruits, and fragrances.
Those without merit sustain themselves by consuming filth, impurities, and various foul odors.
Among these, there is that which is called *antarābhava*, also called *gandharva*, also called *bhavaiṣin*, and also called *manomaya*.
Question: For what reason is it called *antarābhava*?
Answer: Because there is birth in the interval between the two [existences], it is called "intermediate existence" (antarābhava). Question:
If that is so, would all other forms of existence that occur between two states of existence be called *antarābhava*?
The answer is:
if they occur between two states of existence but are not subsumed under the process of rebirth (*gati*), they are called *antarābhava*.
If that which exists between two states of existence (*bhava*) is subsumed under the category of "destiny" (*gati*), it is not called intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, if that which exists between two states of existence is subtle, difficult to clarify, difficult to see, and difficult to comprehend, it is called intermediate existence;
whereas other things, though existing between two states of existence, are coarse, easy to see, easy to clarify, and easy to comprehend, and are therefore not called intermediate existence.
Why is he called a gandharva?
The answer is:
because he sustains himself by means of fragrance, he is called a gandharva.
Why is it called "seeking existence"?
The answer is:
at the time of birth, one seeks existence by means of the six sense bases; therefore, it is called "seeking existence."
Why is it called *manomaya*?
The answer is:
because it arises from the mind (*manas*), it is called *manomaya*.
Sentient beings are either born from the mind, born from karma, born from retribution, or born from conjunction.
Those born from the mind refer to the various devas of the form and formless realms, as well as those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Those born from karma refer to sentient beings in the hells, as it is said:
"The sentient beings therein are bound by their karma.
Those born from retribution refer to birds.
Those born from conjunction refer to humans and the gods of the six desire realms.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"Because of the conjunction of three factors, one enters the mother's womb."
First, both parents possess a defiled mind and come together in one place;
second, the mother is free from illness and the season is appropriate;
third, the gandharva appears before them.
It is due to the conjunction of three factors: namely, the father, the mother, and the gandharva.
That the parents possess a defiled mind means that a mind of desire is present before them.
That they come together in one place means that they intend to unite sexually.
"Her mother is free from illness" means when her mother is joyful.
Regarding the Vinaya, it is said:
"The mother possesses a mind turbid with desire; just as rivers become turbid during the rainy season, so too is she."
Furthermore, there are no ailments such as wind, cold, or heat.
"Meeting the proper time" means meeting the time when a woman has her menses.
If the flow of menses is excessive, the womb is thin and an embryo will not form.
If the menstrual blood is insufficient, conception will not occur.
Only after the union of the father’s semen and the mother’s blood does the embryo form; this is called "meeting the proper time" and is also termed "possessing a body."
When a gandharva appears before one, it is the intermediate state (antarābhava) that appears; it may give rise to a mind of desire or a mind of aversion.
If it is a male, it conceives desire for the mother and aversion toward the father.
He thinks to himself:
"If this man were not here, I would have sexual union with this woman.
At that moment, he gives rise to such a perverted perception, seeing that person depart into the distance and seeing himself engaged in sexual union with this woman.

Regarding the vital essence produced by the union of the parents, [the intermediate being] perceives it as its own; having perceived it as its own, joy arises in the mind; because joy arises in the mind, one becomes deluded and faint; and because of this delusion and fainting, the intermediate state (antarābhava) becomes increasingly heavy and can no longer move.
At that time, he sees himself within his mother’s right flank, sitting with his face toward his mother’s back.
If it is a female, she conceives love for her father and resentment toward her mother.
He forms this thought:
"If this woman were not present, I would have sexual union with this man.
At that moment, he gives rise to such a perverted perception (*viparyāsa-saṃjñā*), seeing that woman depart into the distance, while seeing himself engaged in sexual union with this man.

Regarding the vital essence produced by the union of the parents, [the intermediate being] perceives it as its own; having perceived it as such, joy arises in its mind. Because joy arises in its mind, it becomes deluded and faint; because of this delusion and fainting, the intermediate state (antarābhava) becomes increasingly heavy and can no longer move.
At that time, he saw himself within his mother’s left flank, sitting with his face toward her abdomen.
All sentient beings enter the mother’s womb with such inverted perceptions, except for the Bodhisattva.
When a Bodhisattva enters the womb, he knows, "This is my mother; this is my father," and he conceives the perception of his mother as his mother and the perception of his father as his father.
Question: At what point does the intermediate state (antarābhava) enter the mother's body?
Answer: Some say that because it is without obstruction, one may enter it anywhere. Question:
If there were no obstructing conditions, one would not abide within the mother's body.
The answer is:
by the power of karma, one abides within the mother's body.
The commentary states:
It should be said that the intermediate state (antarābhava) enters the mother’s body through the birth canal.
For this reason, among twins, the one born later is considered the elder. Why is this so?
Because it was the first to enter the mother's womb.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"Only those with merit equal to that of their parents can receive conception.
It is asked:
It is like a wealthy and noble man approaching a poor and lowly woman, or a wealthy and noble woman approaching a base and lowly man; how, then, can conception occur?
The answer is:
at that time, she perceives the other person as noble and conceives the thought of them being honorable, while perceiving herself as base and conceiving the thought of her own lowliness.
A woman considers herself superior and views a man as inferior;
a noble woman approaches a lowly man, regarding him as superior and herself as base.
That man perceives himself as superior and others as inferior;
at that time, with such a conception, he is able to take conception because his merit is equal [to that of the mother].
Within a single mother's womb, there may be intermediate states (*antarābhava*) belonging to the five destinies (*gati*), such as those of dogs, jackals, fish, and frogs.
Question: If those in the intermediate state of hell exist within that belly, why are they not burned? Answer:
If one performs karmic actions, they will be burned; if one does not perform them, they will not be burned.
Furthermore, if one possesses such qualities as the observance of precepts, even if cast into hell, they cannot be burned. Why is this so?
Because they do not perform [further] actions, sentient beings in the hells are not necessarily burned beforehand; as stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"Sometimes, when a cold wind blows upon the sentient beings of the Saṃjīva Hell, they utter these words:"
"Beings live! Beings live! At that time, beings indeed come back to life.
For this reason, that intermediate state (*antarābhava*) need not be burned.

Question: If the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) cannot be obstructed by walls, mountains, forests, houses, tiles, or stones, does it nevertheless encounter mutual obstruction within the intermediate state itself? Answer:
Some say that they obstruct one another.
Question: If that is so, why is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) called "unobstructed"?
The answer is:
With the sole exception of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there are no obstructions among the others.
Furthermore, some say that within the intermediate state itself, beings do not obstruct one another.
Why is this so? Because there is no speech. Question:
Regarding the destination one travels to, is it the speed of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that brings one there, or is it the speed of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*)?
The answer is:
some say it is the speed of the intermediate state.
Why is this so? Because the power of karma is superior to the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*).
The commentary states:
One should say this:
the speed of the supernormal power of psychic travel is swift, not the speed produced by the force of karma. Question:
If this is so, why is it said that the power of karma surpasses the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*)?
The answer is:
One should understand that this is stated in reference to a specific matter where the power of karma surpasses the Buddha’s supernormal power.

It possesses the power of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*) to sustain all sentient beings; with the exception of the Buddha, Śāriputra lacks it, and with the exception of the Buddha and Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana lacks it.
Within that realm, there are no sentient beings, nor any incantations, spells, medicinal herbs, or drugs.

The Buddha, unlike a pratyekabuddha, is able to remain present and cause the continuity of rebirth to cease for them; for this reason, it is said that the power of karma surpasses the power of supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Question: Do those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) see one another as they pass from one to another?
Answer: Some say they see each other. To what extent do they see one another?
The answer is: those in hell see hell; animals see animals; hungry ghosts see hungry ghosts; humans see humans; and devas see devas.
Furthermore, there are those who say that those in hell see hell; animals see two realms; hungry ghosts see three realms; humans see four realms; and devas see all five realms.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the intermediate state (antarābhava) is not within the range of the human eye, but is within the range of the divine eye (divyacakṣus).
It is asked:
To what extent does the divine eye see?
Answer: Regarding the retribution of the divine eye of the Four Heavenly Kings, they see the lower realms, excluding their own level.
This continues up to the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, where they see the lower realms, excluding their own level.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the eyes of all beings in the desire realm cannot see the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), whereas the eyes of the form realm can see it. Question:
To what extent can the eyes obtained as retribution in the form realm see?
Answer: The eye obtained as retribution from the first dhyāna excludes seeing its own level and the lower levels.
This continues up to the fourth dhyāna, which excludes seeing its own level and the lower levels.
If one were to speak in this way, then there would be no one who sees beings within the fourth dhyāna.
The critique says:
One should speak as follows:

The eye obtained as a result of karmic retribution cannot see the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); however, if the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is purified, it can see the intermediate state, whereas if it is not purified, it does not see the intermediate state.
How is this known? The Buddhist scriptures state:

If a man or woman breaks the precepts and commits evil deeds, at the dissolution of the body after death, they will be born in such an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), whose color is like black woolen cloth or like the darkness of night; only those with the pure divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) are able to see it.

If a man or woman maintains the precepts and cultivates the holy life, at the dissolution of the body and the end of life, they will be born into such an intermediate state (*antarābhava*); their complexion is pure white like fine cotton cloth, and like the night when the bright moon shines. Only those with the purified divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) are able to see it.
As it is said, when King Vairūḍyaka confronted the evil Māra Devadatta, he entered the Avīci Hell with that very body.
Question: In cases such as these, does an intermediate state (antarābhava) exist or not?
Answer: There is.
It exists within a single moment.

The existence at death (cyuti-bhava) arises immediately into the intermediate existence (antarābhava), and the intermediate existence arises immediately into the existence at birth (upapatti-bhava); this occurs in a single kṣaṇa.
As it is said in the Sūtra, Śakra spoke this verse:
"Great Sage, you should know: while I am seated here..."
"I have regained my heavenly lifespan; I only pray that you will remember and uphold it. He asked:
"In this way, is there still birth and death?"
If there were death and birth, how could one experience the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
If there were no death and birth, how would this verse be reconciled?
As it is said:
"In this very seat, I have regained my heavenly life-span.
He replied:
"One should speak thus:"
"Neither born nor dying.
Question: If this is so, how is the verse to be understood?
Answer: This was said because [Śakra] had severed the causes and conditions for the evil realms.

When the Buddha preached the Dharma for Śakra, he attained the vision of the Truths and severed the causes and conditions for the evil realms; thus, having gained rebirth in the human or celestial realms according to his wish, he wished to return to the Buddha and spoke these words of affection:
"In this very seat, I have regained my celestial lifespan," and so forth, as extensively explained.
It is like a person within a prison who, having rescued another, dwells in a place of his own choosing.
When that person wishes to return to him, he speaks these affectionate words:
"That I have preserved my life is entirely due to your kindness; had it not been for you, I would have perished forever."
Furthermore, this was said for the purpose of removing the disease of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

The Buddha taught the Dharma to Śakra, removing the disease of the fetters to be abandoned through the path of vision, and causing him to abide in the foremost state of health, namely, the path and its fruit (*mārgaphala*).
He then turned back toward the Buddha and spoke these affectionate words:
"At this seat of mine," and so forth, as extensively explained.
It was like a physician with a compassionate heart who treats the illnesses of others, causing them to attain a state of health and security.
That person, wishing to return, would speak these affectionate words to the physician:
"Were it not for you, I would have perished forever in this place.
It is just the same with that [other person].
Furthermore, this was said because he had attained supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) and longevity (*āyus*).
As it is stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣu, what constitutes life?"
That is to say, the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) constitute his life-span.
The Buddha taught the Dharma for him, whereby he attained the life-span of psychic power.
Desiring to return to the Buddha, he spoke these affectionate words:
"I, while seated," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, this was said because he had attained the life-faculty of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Those who take wisdom as their life-force are the most excellent.
The Buddha taught them the Dharma so that they might obtain the root of the life-force of wisdom.
Desiring to return to the Buddha, he spoke these words of endearment:
"I was at this very seat," and so on, as extensively explained.
It is asked:
Did he originally lack the life-faculty of wisdom?
The answer is:
Although one originally possesses the life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*), it is still subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
Having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma and perceived the Four Noble Truths, one attains the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsravaprajñendriya*); therefore, this statement was made.
Furthermore, this was said in order to exclude five types of pseudo-signs of death.
When the gods are about to pass away, five pseudo-signs of death and five actual signs of death appear.
What are the five signs resembling death?
When the devas come and go, the jeweled necklaces upon their bodies produce the sounds of the five kinds of music;
these sounds then suddenly cease.
The bodies of the various devas emit radiance, yet they have no shadows;
some say that at this time the bodily light diminishes,
while others say that the bodily light is entirely extinguished and shadows of their own bodies appear.

The bodies of the devas are subtle, supple, and free from all impurities; when they enter the fragrant waters of the pool to bathe, upon emerging not even a single drop of water adheres to their bodies, just as [water does not cling] to a lotus leaf.
Yet, at this moment, drops of water do adhere to their bodies.

The various devas possess diverse, pure, and exquisite realms; their sensory faculties are swept away by these realms so that they do not abide in any single one. They revolve among these objects like a whirling firebrand, never remaining still for even a moment;
at such times, they must focus their attention exclusively upon a single realm.
The bodies of the various devas possess merit such that their eyes never blink;
at this moment, they blink.
Regarding the five signs of death, the Sūtra says:
When the lives of the gods—whether male or female—are about to end, five signs of death first appear:
first, their garments become soiled though they were not soiled before;
second, their flowers wither though they were not withered before.
Third, his armpits, which originally did not perspire, now sweat;
fourth, his body, which originally had no odor, now smells foul;
fifth, he who was formerly at ease in his seat is now no longer at ease.
The five signs resembling death can be removed, but the five signs of actual death cannot be removed.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru saw the five signs resembling death appear; before long, the five signs of actual death were about to manifest, whereupon he thought:
"Who can rescue me from such a perilous calamity?"
"Except for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, there is no one else capable of doing so.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was, and at that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma for him.
Because he had heard the Dharma, he removed the five signs of impending death and wished to return to the Buddha, speaking these words of affection:
"In this very seat," and so forth, as explained at length.

If one were to say that when performing karma whose retribution is experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*), one further obtains the eight faculties, such as vitality (*jīvita*), while remaining in that very seat.
Furthermore, there are those who say that at that time there was also death and birth.
A question is asked:
If this is so, how is the statement in the *Prajñapti-śāstra* to be reconciled?
As it is said:

when a male or female among the Trāyastriṃśa devas is first born, their body is like that of a five-year-old child, and they are suddenly manifested by transformation upon the laps of the various devas.
At that time, the gods, whether male or female, spoke thus:
"This is my son; this is my daughter.
Those born by transformation also spoke in this way.
"This is my father; this is my mother. He asked:
"At that time, did the various devas perceive such signs from Śakra?"
The answer is:
They all saw this and thought, "Now Śakra possesses great supernormal power; he has manifested his psychic powers before the World-Honored One."
Furthermore, among the gods, there are those possessing majestic power and virtue: first is named Indra, second is named Upendra, third is named Īśāna, and fourth is named Prajāpati.
Such gods of great majesty, just as they did when they were in their prime, have bodies at birth that are exactly like those of their youth;
for these gods born by transformation, there are no corpses.
The critique states:
It is better that there is no birth or death for them, as previously explained.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* says:
At the beginning of the kalpa, there were humans who transformed into belly-crawling insects and were called "belly-crawlers.
Those who transformed into three-handed beings were called "elephants.
For those whose bodies undergo such transformations, do they experience death and rebirth?
If such a thing exists, what is its nature?
If there were no death and rebirth, would a human being simply become an animal?
He replied:
One should speak thus:
there is neither death nor birth. Question:
If that were so, would humans immediately become animals?
He replied:
"Humans do not immediately become animals."
It is simply that the continuity of the animal body and the human body [occurs].

Furthermore, there are those who say: at the beginning of the kalpa, humans had forms resembling humans; later, because the times became corrupt, food and drink became foul, and because of an abundance of flattery and crookedness, the human form vanished and the form of an animal appeared before them. In reality, they were humans, but their forms were those of animals.
It is just as when, through the power of a spell, a person is transformed into a donkey; although his form is that of a donkey, he is in fact a human being.
It is the same with them. Furthermore, there are those who say that beings who die in the Ābhāsvara Heaven and are reborn here are actually animals whose forms resemble humans.
Later, because the times were degenerate, food and drink were poor, and because of much flattery and crookedness, the human form disappeared; they instead took on the forms of animals, such as frogs.
Their former bodies were complete, while their later bodies were likewise complete; their former bodies were round and black, while their later bodies were square and robust.
Furthermore, there are those who say that they undergo death and birth.
A question is asked:
If this is so, what then is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)?
Answer: The intermediate state (antarābhava) is subtle.
At the beginning of the eon, humans were born by transformation (upapāduka) and there was no death or birth.
The critique says:
One should state it thus:
there is neither death nor birth.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll Thirty-six and Scroll Thirty-seven.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.

Chapter Four: The Ten Gates, Section One of the Ten Gates of the *Prakaraṇapāda*. The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), the five aggregates (*skandha*), the five aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), and the six elements (*dhātu*).

There are two categories of phenomena: namely, material phenomena and immaterial phenomena; visible phenomena and invisible phenomena; resistant phenomena and non-resistant phenomena; tainted phenomena and untainted phenomena; conditioned phenomena and unconditioned phenomena.

There are three categories of phenomena: namely, past, future, and present phenomena; wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate phenomena; phenomena pertaining to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm; phenomena of those in training, those beyond training, and those who are neither; and phenomena abandoned through the path of seeing, abandoned through the path of cultivation, and phenomena not to be abandoned.
The four dharmas refer to the Four Truths, the Four Dhyānas, the Four Immeasurables, and the Four Formless Absorptions;
the Eight Liberations, the Eight Bases of Mastery, the Ten Totalities, the Eight Knowledges, the Three Samādhis, the Three Fetters, and so forth, up to the ninety-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*).

Regarding how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) the eye-faculty is driven by, and so on up to how many underlying tendencies the ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is driven by—
this chapter and its commentary should be explained here at length as an *upadeśa*.
The twenty-two faculties (*indriya*):

the eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, mind faculty, male faculty, female faculty, life faculty, faculty of pleasure, faculty of pain, faculty of joy, faculty of grief, faculty of equanimity, faculty of faith, faculty of energy, faculty of mindfulness, faculty of concentration, faculty of wisdom, faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," faculty of knowing, and faculty of one who has known.
Question: For what reason did that Venerable One establish twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) and compose this treatise? Answer:

The author of that treatise had such a desire and such an intention; he composed his discourse in accordance with that desire and intention, and it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
He intended to establish twenty-two faculties (*indriya*) in his treatise, and thus established twenty-two faculties according to his own intent.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one should not inquire here as to why that Venerable One established twenty-two faculties.
Why is this? Because the Buddha’s sūtras speak of twenty-two faculties.
The Buddhist sūtras are the fundamental source for this treatise, and this treatise also explains the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*).
That venerable one was unable to reduce one faculty from the twenty-two to speak of twenty-one, nor could he increase one faculty to speak of twenty-three.
Why is this so? Because the Buddha’s sūtras cannot be increased or decreased; there is nothing to be added to what is lacking, and nothing to be subtracted from what is superfluous.
Just as there is neither increase nor decrease, so too there is neither much nor little, neither benefit nor harm, and neither measure nor limit. It is the same for all these.
"Immeasurable" refers to the immeasurability of the meaning;
"boundless" refers to the boundlessness of the phrasing.
It is like the great ocean, which is both immeasurable and boundless: "immeasurable" means its depth is immeasurable, and "boundless" means its breadth is boundless.
The Buddha’s sutras are also like this.

For instance, although masters of treatises such as the Venerable Śāriputra—numbering hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas—composed hundreds of thousands of millions of treatises in order to explain the meaning of just two phrases of a Buddha’s sutra, even exhausting their enlightened nature, they were still unable to know its measure or reach its limit.
Question: Setting aside the author of this treatise,
for what reason do the Buddha’s sūtras speak of twenty-two faculties (indriyas)?
Answer: It is for the sake of those who are to be transformed.
When those to be transformed hear this teaching, they will attain increase and progress.
Furthermore, there are specific causes and conditions for each of these sutras. What are they?
The answer is:
The brahmin Jātiśroṇa went to where the Buddha was, and after exchanging various greetings with the World-Honored One, he sat to one side and said:
"There are many who speak of the faculties."
“How many faculties (indriya) does the śramaṇa Gautama teach?
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:
“I teach twenty-two faculties, namely, the faculty of the eye up to the faculty of one who has already known.”
The Tathāgata has taught the twenty-two faculties (indriya), which encompass the meaning of all faculties. O Brahmin!
If someone were to say:
"Regarding the faculties spoken of by the śramaṇa Gautama, I can refute them and speak of other faculties instead.
This is merely words, however, and lacks any reality.
If he were to question me further, I would not be able to know the answer; instead, I would only give rise to ignorance and delusion."
Why is this? Because it is not within his domain.

When a Brahmin questions the Buddha, if he should not inquire extensively into the causes and conditions of this sutra, should he instead have asked the Brahmin when he first approached the Buddha to inquire only about the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśati-indriya*), rather than asking about the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), sense bases (*āyatana*), the noble truths (*satya*), the fruits of asceticism (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), and so forth?
Answer: That brahmin asked only about what he doubted; what he did not doubt, he did not ask.
Furthermore, this brahmin was highly skilled at traversing various paths and delighted in testing others with his questions.
In order to inquire into the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*), one must pass through ninety-six varieties, for the purpose of knowing how many faculties are taught for each individual path.
For example, the Nirgranthas teach a single faculty, namely the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*); therefore, they do not drink cold water nor cut living grass.
Why is this so? Because one reckons that there is a life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) within external objects. Question:
Regarding what root non-Buddhists conceive of within external objects,
the answer is:
some say they conceive of the mental faculty (manas-indriya).
Furthermore, there are those who say that they reckon there is a life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Others say that non-Buddhists, among material things, reckon there is a mind-faculty (*manendriya*), which they call "things possessing faculties" (*sendriyadharma*);
and they reckon there is a life-faculty, which they call "things possessing life" (*sajīvadharma*).
Some reckon that there are two faculties, namely karma and the mind.
Others say that if the eye does not see forms and the ear does not hear sounds, this is called the noble cultivation of the faculties (*ārya-indriya-bhāvanā*).
As the *Pārasa* and others have stated thus. Question:
For what reason is it called *pārasa*?
Answer: This is the name of that person.
There is no difficulty regarding the name.
Why is this so? Because names are established that do not correspond to their actual meaning.

Furthermore, *Pārāśarya* is his clan name (*gotra*). Just as among the Brahmins there are various distinct clans—such as the Kauśika, the Vatsa, the Śāṇḍilya, and the Bhāradvāja—so too is the *Pārāśarya* clan.
Furthermore, if one is born from the lineage of a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, they are named *palaśa*, just as one born from a donkey and a horse is named a mule.
The evaluation states:
because this lineage is *palaśa*, he is therefore named *palaśa*.
He had a disciple, a young brahmin named Uttara, who went to where the Buddha was, exchanged greetings with the World-Honored One, engaged in various forms of conversation, and sat down to one side.
The World-Honored One asked,
"Does your teacher Pārāśarya teach the method for cultivating the faculties to his disciples?
The Māṇava replied:
"My teacher spoke of it.
The Buddha asked:
"How did he speak of it?"
Māṇava replied: "If the eye does not see forms and the ear does not hear sounds, this is called the noble cultivation of the faculties.
Then the Buddha challenged him, saying:
"If one does not see forms and yet is called a noble one who has cultivated the faculties, then a blind person would be such a noble one who has cultivated the faculties.
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Buddha, fanning him with a fan.
He further challenged the Māṇava, saying:
"If what you have said is true, then one who is deaf would be a holy person who has cultivated the sense faculties. Why is that?"
Because they do not hear his voice.
A question is asked:

Just as the Venerable Śāriputra and hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *nayutas* of great masters of treatises—only the Buddha alone is able to challenge their doctrines and render their established arguments ineffective.
For what reason did the Blessed One pose the first challenge, and the Venerable Ānanda the second?
And for what reason did the Blessed One not restrain the Venerable Ānanda?
The answer is:
The Buddha observed that Ānanda had a mark upon his throat and wished to ask a question.
When the Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he never interrupted anyone; even when it came to his disciples, he did not interrupt their questioning.

Furthermore, the Buddha knew that what Ānanda had spoken was identical to what he himself had taught, without any difference, addition, or omission; because there was no addition or omission, he did not restrain him.
Furthermore, if both the teacher and the disciple are capable of subduing [the opponent], this is called "skillful subduing.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to leave no further words for the non-Buddhists.
If the World-Honored One were to pose the first challenge and Ānanda did not pose the second challenge, that brahmin would return to his own assembly and say:
Although he is subdued by that teacher, he is not subdued by his disciples;
although he subdues our disciples, he is not subdued by our teacher.
If the World-Honored One raises the first challenge and Ānanda raises the second challenge, then the arrogant minds of the non-Buddhists will be shattered.
He thought to himself:
"If even a disciple can subdue me, how much more so the teacher?
Furthermore, he spoke thus in order to fulfill the intention of that brahmin.
That brahmin thought to himself:
"The śramaṇa Gautama is one whom no wrestler can subdue; he is one whom no one can refute in any debate; he is the most supreme among all debaters."
"In the past, there were no great masters of debate capable of subduing him, let alone us.
It would be appropriate for his disciples to engage in a dialogue with me regarding the principles of reasoning."
The Buddha constantly desires to fulfill the intentions of those he seeks to transform, acting in accordance with their thoughts.
Furthermore, the Buddha uses Ānanda as a witness to this principle, so that those non-Buddhists may develop faith and reverence toward him.

Ānanda was handsome in appearance and well-versed in the *Indra-vyākaraṇa* treatise; therefore, the World-Honored One wished to have Ānanda serve as a witness to this doctrine, so that those heterodox practitioners might develop faith and reverence for it.
Furthermore, [the Buddha] wished to manifest that his disciples were permitted to pose questions and challenges.
In the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), disciples are not allowed to raise such inquiries. Why is this?

If one permits disciples to pose challenging questions, it may at times cause the teacher to fall into a position of defeat; if the teacher falls into such a position of defeat, they will lose their offerings and support.

For instance, even when hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of great masters of debate, such as Śāriputra and others, set forth their challenges, there was still no one capable of equalling the Buddha, let alone surpassing him. Therefore, the Buddha-dharma does not cease because of the challenging questions posed by disciples.
Furthermore, it is to manifest the severing of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
This is why non-Buddhists do not permit their disciples to pose challenging questions; they think to themselves:
"Perhaps by means of this matter, I may obtain much gain and support."

The Buddha is not like this; even if he were to cause all people in the world to receive great gain and offerings, down to the point where there might be no one who gives the Tathāgata even so much as a hair’s breadth, the Tathāgata would never utter words of partiality.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest the completeness of what is taught within the well-expounded Dharma, being identical in view and without divergent intentions.
In the teachings of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), what the teacher says differs from what the disciple says, and the teacher’s understanding differs from the disciple’s understanding.
In the well-expounded Dharma, there is no such fault:
as it is for the teacher, so it is for the disciple;
as the teacher understands, so the disciple understands, for there is ultimately no difference between their words and meanings.

Therefore, because he wished to manifest that what is taught within the well-expounded Dharma is complete and identical to a single view without any difference in intent, the World-Honored One posed the first challenge and Ānanda posed the second challenge.
For this reason, he did not suppress the objection raised by Ānanda.
It is asked:
The non-Buddhists themselves make this statement:
If the eye does not see forms and the ear does not hear sounds, this is called the noble cultivation of the faculties (*āryendriyabhāvanā*).
The World-Honored One spoke with difficulty:
"If that were so, then those who are blind and deaf would be practicing the noble cultivation of the faculties."
If one merely follows the words of others, how can this be called a refutation?
The answer is:
when the Buddha makes such a statement, it is called a "great refutation"; it cuts off what others have said and is also termed a general exposition of the faults of all non-Buddhists.

If it is by not seeing forms with the eye and not hearing sounds with the ear that one is called a noble practitioner of the sense faculties, for what purpose have you left the household life, cast off ornaments, and practiced the holy life?
One who merely harms these two faculties is an *ārya*.

For this reason, the Buddha said it is called "the great difficulty"; it is the severing of what others have taught, and it is also called the general exposition of the faults of all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The Vaiśeṣika masters further explain five faculties, namely: the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As stated in the Sāṃkhya-sūtra, there are furthermore eleven faculties, namely: the five sensory faculties and the five active faculties.
The five faculties of sensation (vijñānendriya) refer to the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The five faculties of action (karmendriya) refer to the faculty of speech, the faculty of the hand, the faculty of the foot, the faculty of excretion, and the faculty of urination.
The eleventh is the faculty of mind (*manendriya*).

Some say there are one hundred and twenty faculties: namely, the two eye faculties, the two ear faculties, the two nose faculties, the tongue faculty, the body faculty, the mind faculty, the life faculty, the five feeling faculties, and the five faculties beginning with faith; thus, there are twenty such faculties.
There are twenty realms of the hells, twenty realms of animals, twenty realms of hungry ghosts, twenty realms of humans, twenty realms of devas, and twenty realms of asuras.

Furthermore, there are those who say that while the various non-Buddhists do not speak of one hundred and twenty faculties (*indriya*), they do speak of one hundred and twenty lords (*adhipati*), such as the Lord of Devas, the Lord of Nāgas, the Lord of Asuras, and the Lord of Humans.
With such sublime bodies as these, one passes through one hundred and twenty locations before finally attaining parinirvāṇa.

Upon hearing these words, that brahmin’s mind became increasingly doubtful; he did not know which was the truth—whether it was the teaching of a single faculty or the teaching of up to one hundred and twenty faculties.

Upon hearing that a prince had been born in the Śākya clan, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and eighty secondary characteristics, his body of pure golden hue, and a halo surrounding him one fathom in width—beholding which one could never tire—he was filled with wonder.

Having left the household life to seek the Way, he has attained all-knowing insight, is able to sever all doubts, bestows certainty upon all, and has reached the ultimate limit of all inquiry; I should go to question him.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was; having arrived, he paid his respects to the World-Honored One and related the matter in detail as above.
At that time, the brahmin Jātiśroṇa said to the Buddha:
"Śramaṇa Gautama!"
Regarding the explanation of the faculties (*indriya*), there are many; how many faculties are there?
Question: Why not ask in this way: [What are the faculties?]
Within each of the ninety-six paths, how many faculties (*indriya*) are taught?
The answer is:
although those brahmins are clever and wise, their nature is crooked and deceitful, and they harbor such thoughts:
"If I were to ask such a question, the śramaṇa Gautama would select the most excellent [answer] to explain.
The Buddha told the brāhmaṇa:

"There are twenty-two faculties (indriya), namely, from the eye faculty up to the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya). The Tathāgata teaches that these and other such faculties encompass the entire meaning of all faculties."
O Brahmin, if someone were to say:
"I can refute the faculties taught by the Śramaṇa Gautama and speak of other faculties," they would merely be speaking such words without any reality behind them.
If one were to ask in return, they likewise would be unable to know it, and instead would give rise to ignorance and delusion.
Why is this? Because it is not within their sphere of experience.
Question: For what reason is it further stated:
"If there be one who says... and so forth, as explained at length?

Answer: This is intended to stop that person’s prior assertions, whether they maintain there is only one faculty or even as many as one hundred and twenty faculties—all of which are not in accordance with reality.

Although I possess all-encompassing knowledge and vision, I cannot reduce one of the twenty-two faculties and speak of twenty-one, nor increase one and speak of twenty-three; how much less could those of external paths with limited wisdom, limited views, and false insight do so?

For this reason, that brahmin went to where the Buddha was and inquired only about the sense faculties (indriya), but did not ask about the aggregates (skandha), the elements (dhātu), the bases (āyatana), the noble truths (satya), the fruits of asceticism (śrāmaṇyaphala), dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), or the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma).
Question: Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), there are twenty-two names; how many distinct entities do they possess?
Answer: [To be continued...]
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), there are twenty-two names, but in terms of substantial entities (*dravya*), there are seventeen.
They state this as follows:

The five faculties have no separate entities apart from what are called the male faculty, the female faculty, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has already known.
Question: For what reason is it said that the male and female faculties have no separate entities?
The answer is:
He asserts that apart from the body-faculty (kāyendriya), there is no separate substantial entity for the male-faculty (puruṣendriya) or female-faculty (strīndriya).
As it is said:
What is the male faculty? Answer:
A portion of the body faculty.
What is the female faculty? Answer:
A portion of the body faculty.
Why do the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) have no separate substantial entities?
The answer is:
apart from the nine faculties, there are no further separate substantial entities for these three faculties.

The nine faculties are the mental faculty (*manendriya*), the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhādi*).

These nine faculties are at times called the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), at times called the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*), and at times called the faculty of "one who has known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*). When one is on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are called the faculty of desiring to know the unknown; when on the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), they are called the faculty of knowing; and when on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), they are called the faculty of one who has known.

Furthermore, within the bodies of those with firm faith and those with firm Dharma, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; within the bodies of those liberated through faith, those who have attained vision, and those who have realized through the body, it is called the faculty of "knowing"; and within the bodies of those liberated through wisdom and those liberated both ways, it is called the faculty of "having known."

Why is this so? Because the conjunction of nine faculties is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the conjunction of nine faculties is called the faculty of "knowing," and the conjunction of nine faculties is called the faculty of "one who has known."
For this reason, it is said that the three untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya) have no distinct substantial entities.
Therefore, while the faculties are said to be twenty-two in name, they exist as seventeen in substance.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta spoke thus:
"Regarding the twenty-two faculties, there are twenty-two names, but in terms of substantial entities, there are fourteen.

As previously stated, five faculties have no distinct entities; furthermore, it is said that three other faculties likewise lack distinct entities—namely, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*), and the concentration-faculty (*samādhīndriya*)."
Question: For what reason does he say that the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) has no separate entity? Answer:

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) belongs to the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra-skandha*). It is taught that this aggregate of formations dissociated from mind has no separate substantial entity (*dravya*).
For what reason, then, is it said that the equanimity faculty (*upekṣendriya*) has no separate substantial entity?
The answer is:
They assert that apart from painful feeling and pleasant feeling, there is no other distinct neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
If all that is felt is either painful or pleasant, how can that which is neither painful nor pleasant be called "feeling"?
Question: If that is so, how do you reconcile this with the Buddha’s sūtras?
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
There are painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
He replied:
They speak as follows:
Pleasant feeling is sometimes superior and sometimes inferior; sometimes wise and sometimes unwise; sometimes tranquil and sometimes not tranquil.
The same is true for painful feeling.

If one is moderate in pleasant feeling, moderate in painful feeling; if one lacks wisdom regarding pleasant feeling, lacks wisdom regarding painful feeling; or if one is tranquil regarding pleasant feeling, tranquil regarding painful feeling—this is called neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
This lack of determination does not reside within a single part; it is like doubt, for there is no certainty.
Question: For what reason is it said that the faculty of determination has no separate entity?
Answer: They state this:
apart from the mind, there is no separate faculty of concentration.
As it is said:
What is the faculty of concentration?
The answer is:
It is precisely this single mind.
Therefore, regarding those twenty-two faculties that are spoken of, while there are twenty-two names, in terms of substantial entity, there are only fourteen.
The Venerable Buddhadeva has stated as follows:
Regarding the twenty-two faculties (indriya), there are twenty-two names, but in terms of substantial entity (dravya), there is only one, namely the mental faculty (manas-indriya).

They explain that conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma) are divided into two parts: first, the part consisting of the four great elements (mahābhūta); [and second, the part consisting of derived matter].
2. The Mental Component.
Apart from the four great elements, there is no distinct derived matter; outside of the mind, there are no further enumerated dharmas.
They assert this as follows:
All material forms (*rūpa*) are distinctions of the four great elements; all immaterial faculties (*indriya*) are distinctions of the mind (*citta*).
Therefore, although twenty-two faculties are spoken of—possessing twenty-two names—in reality there is but one, namely the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The commentary states:
That which was explained previously is correct; there are twenty-two names and seventeen substantial entities.

As with names and entities, so it is with the designation of names as provisional and entities as provisional, the designation of names as distinct characteristics and entities as distinct characteristics, the designation of names as conceptualization and entities as conceptualization, and the knowledge of names and the knowledge of entities. It is likewise in all these cases.
"This is the essence of the faculties," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the nature of their essence, we shall now explain why they are called "faculties" (*indriya*).
What is the meaning of "faculty"?

Answer: The meaning of "majesty" (*vaśitā*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*); the meaning of "clarity" (*vidyā*) is the meaning of "faculty"; the meaning of "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is the meaning of "faculty"; the meaning of "delightful contemplation" (*pramodya-darśana*) is the meaning of "faculty"; the meaning of "excellence" (*jaya*) is the meaning of "faculty"; the meaning of "supremacy" (*agra*) is the meaning of "faculty"; and the meaning of "mastery" (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of "faculty."

Question: If the meaning of "root" (*indriya*) is the sense of "sovereign power" (*vaśitva*), then since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exercise sovereign power over one another, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) likewise exercise sovereign power over conditioned phenomena, it would follow that all such conditioned phenomena should be considered roots.
For what reason did the Buddha establish these twenty-two factors alone as faculties (*indriya*)?
The Venerable Vasu said:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, definitively knows the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and their functional powers (*śakti*), which others do not know."
If a phenomenon possesses the characteristic of a faculty (*indriya*), it is established as a faculty; if a phenomenon lacks the characteristic of a faculty, it is not established as a faculty.

Furthermore, regarding the condition of power (*prabhāva*), there may be that which is inferior, that which is superior, that which is decreasing, or that which is increasing. That which is superior or increasing is established as a faculty; that which is decreasing or inferior is a non-faculty phenomenon.

Furthermore, although conditioned phenomena possess mutual power, unconditioned phenomena also possess power over conditioned phenomena; however, this power is not like that of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). It is characterized by the absence of ignorance, the absence of differentiation, the absence of joyful observation, the absence of superiority, the absence of supremacy, and the absence of sovereignty.
Just as all sentient beings have conditions of mutual influence and power,

some being superior to others— such as King Yama over the beings in hell, the lion king among beasts, the village headman within the village, the king within his kingdom, the Cakravartin Sage-King over the four continents, the Lord of the Heaven of Sovereignty (Īśvara) over the desire realm, the Brahmā King over a thousand worlds, and the Buddha over the three realms.
The Buddha possesses such majestic power that he surpasses all sentient beings.

Likewise, although all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) possess a relative degree of majestic power among themselves, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) possess majestic power over conditioned phenomena, they do not equal the majestic power of the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), which possess the meaning of "clarity" up to the meaning of "mastery."
For this reason, the meaning of "power" (*vaśitā*), the meaning of "clarity" (*vibhūti*), and even the meaning of "mastery" (*aiśvarya*) is the meaning of "root" (*mūla*). Question:
If the meaning of power is the meaning of a root, in what respect does power exist?
The answer is:
The eye faculty exercises sovereign influence as a dominant condition in four ways:
first, it adorns the body; [and so forth].
Second, it protects itself;
third, it serves as the basis for visual consciousness and its associated mental factors;
fourth, it alone is capable of seeing forms.
Regarding "adorned with one's own body": although one may possess a wondrous body complete with all its limbs, if the faculty of sight is lacking, there will be no majesty.

Regarding "protecting one's own body": the faculty of sight can perceive whether forms are beautiful or ugly; by pursuing the beautiful and avoiding the ugly, it causes this body to endure for a long time.

Regarding its serving as the basis for visual consciousness and the mental factors associated with visual consciousness: visual consciousness and its associated factors arise depending upon the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
As for "the eye alone being able to see forms": it is the eye-faculty that can see forms, while the other twenty-one faculties cannot.
The faculty of hearing exercises its dominant influence as a condition in four ways:
first, by adorning the body; second, by protecting the body; [third, by perceiving sounds; and fourth, by serving as the basis for the consciousness of hearing].
Third, it serves as the basis for ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) and that which is associated with it;
fourth, it alone is capable of hearing sounds.

Regarding the adornment of the body: although one may possess a sublime body complete with all its limbs and members, if the faculty of hearing (*śrotrendriya*) is absent, there will be no majesty or authority.

As for protecting one's own person: the faculty of hearing can distinguish between pleasant and unpleasant sounds; one follows what is pleasant and avoids what is unpleasant, thereby causing this body to endure for a long time.
Regarding its serving as the basis for ear-consciousness and the mental factors associated with it: ear-consciousness and its associated factors arise depending upon the ear-faculty (*śrotrendriya*).
As for the ear-faculty being uniquely capable of hearing sound: it is the ear-faculty alone that can hear sound; no other twenty-one faculties are capable of doing so.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the eye-faculty protects the physical body and acts as a superior condition for exercising its majestic power.
As a verse says:
"Just as a person with clear vision Is able to avoid dangerous and evil paths;"
"In this world there are wise people who are able to remain far removed from all evils.
The faculty of hearing protects the Dharma-body, acting as a superior condition for its majestic power.
As it is said in verse:
"One who is learned can know the Dharma; one who is learned can distance themselves from [evil];
through learning one abandons what is meaningless; through learning one reaches Nirvana.

Furthermore, there are those who say that these two both protect the birth-body (*janmakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), acting as the superior conditions for manifesting their majestic power.
Protecting the birth-body is as explained above.
Regarding the protection of the dharma-body: through the faculty of the eye, one draws near to virtuous friends, thereby creating a superior condition of majestic power;
through the faculty of the ear, one hears the Dharma from them, thereby creating a superior condition of majestic power.
By associating with virtuous friends and hearing the Dharma from them, one is able to give rise to correct internal reflection and practice in accordance with the Dharma.
For this reason, the Sūtra says: "O Brahmin Brahmāyus!"
