The two faculties that are not impaired are the eye faculty and the ear faculty.
Question: For what reason are these two faculties said to be unimpaired among the collection of all faculties?
Answer: Because by means of these two faculties, one is able to enter the gateway of the Buddha-dharma when a Buddha appears in the world.
Furthermore, by means of these two faculties, one is able to understand and know the Buddha-dharma.
As it is said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that if one is unable to know the minds of others as they truly are, one should observe the Tathāgata through two ways:
first, by observing forms with the eye; second, by hearing sounds with the ear."
The faculties of nose, tongue, and body exercise sovereign power as conditions in four ways:
first, adorning the self; second, protecting the self; [third, experiencing objects; and fourth, serving as the basis for the mental faculty].
Third, it serves as the basis for olfactory consciousness, gustatory consciousness, tactile consciousness, and their associated mental factors;
fourth, the nose alone can smell odors, the tongue alone can perceive tastes, and the body alone can experience tangibles.

Regarding the adornment of one's own person: although one may possess a sublime body with all its limbs complete, if one lacks even a single one of these three faculties, one will have no majestic power.
One who protects oneself, by means of these three faculties, is able to consume morsel food so that the body may endure for a long time.
Why is this? Because morsel food consists of the sense bases of odor, flavor, and tangibility.
Regarding their serving as the bases for the three consciousnesses and their associated mental factors: it is by depending on these three faculties that the three consciousnesses are able to arise.
As for the olfactory faculty alone being able to smell odors: the olfactory faculty can perceive odors, whereas the other twenty-one faculties cannot.
Regarding the tongue-faculty alone being able to know tastes: the tongue-faculty alone is able to know tastes, which the other twenty-one faculties cannot.
Regarding the body-faculty alone being able to perceive tangibles: the body-faculty alone is able to perceive tangibles, which the other twenty-one faculties cannot.
The faculty of mind exercises sovereign influence as a dominant condition in two respects:
first, it causes the continuity of future existence; second, it exercises mastery over others so that they comply with one's will.
Regarding the continuity of future existence, as it is said, the Buddha told Ānanda:
If consciousness were not present in the mother's body, would name-and-form (nāmarūpa) form the kalala? He replied: "No."
Regarding mastery over causing others to comply, it is said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that the mind leads the world and gives rise to the world; wherever the mind arises, there it attains mastery."

Furthermore, there are those who say that the mental faculty (*manas*) exercises sovereign influence as a dominant condition in two respects: regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) and regarding the means of escape from them.
Regarding its sovereignty over the afflictions, it is said:
"Because the mind is afflicted, sentient beings are afflicted."
Regarding superiority in terms of the excellence of the outlet for emergence:
as it is said, "Because the mind emerges, sentient beings emerge.
As for the male and female faculties, they exercise sovereign influence as conditions in two respects:
First, distinct sentient beings;
second, differentiated sentient beings.

In ancient times, there were no men or women; because they were born from a small amount of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), there were then men and women, differing in their broad and long physical forms, as well as in their complexions, languages, clothing, and food and drink.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the male faculty and the female faculty exercise sovereign power as conditions in two locations: regarding afflictions and regarding the way out [of suffering].
Regarding the superiority in the location of afflictions, it is not because of the union of sexual desire that they are superior.
Why is this so? This must be the case here; there is no need to harbor doubt.

Those who possess male or female sexual organs are able to receive the precepts of evil, are able to sever their roots of goodness, thereby causing the seeds of goodness to cease to exist within this body, and are capable of committing the five deeds of immediate retribution.
Such matters as these cannot be performed by eunuchs, *paṇḍakas*, those without genitals, or those with dual genitals. Regarding the superiority of the state of renunciation:

if these two faculties are not impaired, one can receive the precepts of liberation (*vimukti-śīla*), can give rise to the precepts of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-śīla*) and the untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*), can become free from the craving for sensual desire, the craving for the realm of form, and the craving for the formless realm, and can produce the seeds of a Buddha, as well as the seeds of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*.
Such matters as these cannot be performed by eunuchs, those without sexual organs, or those with dual sexual organs.
The life-faculty exercises sovereign influence over two aspects:
first, it is said that there is a faculty; second, it causes the various faculties not to be severed.
As long as one lives, it is said that the faculties exist; once dead, it is said that the faculties do not exist.
As long as one lives, the faculties continue in succession; once dead, the faculties no longer continue in succession.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the life-faculty exercises sovereign influence as a dominant condition in four ways:
first, it causes this birth to continue;
second, it protects this birth.
Third, it can sustain this birth;
fourth, it causes this birth not to be interrupted.

Among the factors of affliction, the five faculties of sensation (vedanendriya) exercise a dominant influence as a conditioning cause. Because of sensation, sentient beings pursue their goals in the four directions, traveling upon paths of iron chains, hooks, and ropes; they climb high mountains and enter the great ocean, encountering immeasurable fears and hardships—namely, the hardship of surging waves and whirlpools, the hardship of the *śiśumāra* monster, the hardship of black winds and hurricanes, the hardship of submerged mountains, the hardship of drowning, the hardship of being stranded on sandbanks, the hardship of falling into the palaces of evil nāgas, and the hardship of falling into the realm of rākṣasas.
Such various pursuits as these are all causes for feeling (*vedanā*).
Question: How does untainted feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā*) exercise its dominant influence as a condition within the category of the afflictions (*kleśa*)?
Answer: When untainted feeling (*anāsrava-vedanā*) first arises through skillful means, it exerts a powerful influence as a dominant condition over the portion of afflictions (*kleśa*).

When a practitioner desires to give rise to untainted feeling, they must likewise seek out clothing, food, drink, and the necessities of life; therefore, it also exerts a powerful influence as a dominant condition within the portion of afflictions.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the faculty of sensation (*vedanendriya*) exerts a dominant influence as a condition in both the sphere of afflictions and the sphere of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Regarding how pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*) exerts a dominant influence as a condition in the sphere of afflictions, it is as stated: "Pleasant sensation is driven by craving.
Regarding how it exerts a dominant influence as a condition in the sphere of transcendence, it is as stated: "When the mind is happy, concentration arises."
Regarding how painful feeling acts as a potent condition within the category of afflictions: it is as stated that the latent tendency of malice (pratighānuśaya) drives one toward painful feeling.
Regarding how painful feeling acts as a potent and superior condition within the category of the means to liberation: it is as stated that suffering can give rise to faith.

When the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling acts as a dominant condition within the category of defilements, it is as stated: "the latent tendency of ignorance drives the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

When the neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling acts as a dominant condition within the category of renunciation, it is as stated: "one relies upon the six renunciations for the practice of contemplation."

Regarding how the five faculties, such as faith, exercise their sovereign influence within the category of the "factors conducive to emergence" (*nairyāṇika-bhāga*), it is said that one who possesses faith is able to draw near to virtuous persons.
As a verse also says:
"One who can believe crosses the stream, Transcends the ocean of negligence, And through diligence eliminates suffering."
"Wisdom reaches the other shore.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If my disciples take faith as a shield-board, they will be able to ward off the external enemies of unwholesomeness while practicing wholesome dharmas."
As the Buddha told Ānanda:
"Diligence can give rise to bodhi.
If my disciples possess a body of diligence, they are able to abandon unwholesome dharmas and practice wholesome dharmas."
As it is said:
"Mindfulness is a universal dharma; if my disciples guard the gate with mindfulness, they will be able to abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
As it is further said:

Concentration is the right path; non-concentration is the wrong path. A concentrated mind attains purity, whereas a non-concentrated mind does not; through concentration, one can know the arising and ceasing of the aggregates (*skandha*).
If my disciples can fully possess the garland of the three samādhis, they will be able to abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
As a verse says:
"Wisdom is supreme in the world; it leads those who can cultivate weary detachment, and by knowing things as they truly are, it can bring an end to the suffering of old age and death."

It is also said that wisdom is unsurpassed among all dharmas; it is also said, "Sisters, you should know that my disciples, by the power of wisdom, sever all fetters, latent tendencies, stains, and entanglements."
It is further said:
If my disciples are fully endowed with the city of wisdom, they are able to abandon unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas.

The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) excels as a powerful condition for seeing dharmas not previously seen. The faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) excels as a powerful condition for being able to eliminate faults regarding dharmas already seen. The faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) excels as a powerful condition for attaining happiness in the present life once faults have been eliminated.
Regarding these various faculties (*indriya*), they exercise sovereign power as conditions over these various phenomena (*dharma*).
The Venerable Ghoṣavarman stated: "In terms of ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*), it should be said that there is but one faculty, namely, the mental faculty (*manendriya*)."
Why is this so? The faculty of mind has three characteristics:
first, it is internal;...
Second, it pervades all places;
third, it is capable of having an object of perception.
That which exists internally is subsumed under the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*).
"Pervading all places" means it can be found from the Avīci Hell up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
"Capable of having an object" means it takes all phenomena as its objects.
The other faculties do not possess these three characteristics.

Although the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body are included among the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), they do not pervade all locations and are incapable of having an object of perception.
Although the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) pervades all locations, it is not included among the internal bases and is incapable of having an object of perception.

Apart from the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*), the other faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), although they possess objects of perception, are not included within the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*) and cannot pervade all locations.
The faculty of equanimity and the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), although they pervade all locations and possess objects of perception, are not included among the internal bases.

The three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) have no separate substantial entities; these three faculties are established based on the convergence of various faculties, as explained above. Question:
If this is so, for what reason are the remaining faculties designated as "faculties" (*indriya*)?

Answer: It serves as the support for the mental faculty (manas), it serves as its basis, it serves as affliction, it serves as the transcendence [of suffering], and it serves as the locus of transcendence.
What serves as the support?
Answer: The faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
Who acts as their support?
The answer is:
the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Who creates the afflictions?
Answer: It is the various faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*).
Who brings about the definitive departure [from suffering]?
Answer: The five faculties, beginning with faith.
Who establishes the state of definitive departure?
Answer: The path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning. Question:
By virtue of what factors are the male faculty and the female faculty designated as "faculties"? Answer:
By virtue of four factors.
First, it is capable of producing that which arises;
second, it is capable of generating desire and joy;
third, it is capable of subduing afflictions.
Fourth, it serves as the basis for defiled consciousness and its associated mental factors.
Regarding its capacity to produce: it gives rise to those born from a womb or from an egg.
Regarding its capacity to generate sensual pleasure: for one who engages in desire, pleasure arises here and pervades the entire body.
Just as when a noble one experiences the noble bliss born between the eyebrows, which pervades the entire body, so it is with this [bliss] as well.
For one who has suppressed the afflictions, [the afflictions] are severed for a brief moment.

That which can serve as the basis for the defiled consciousness and its associated factors is the other basis from which three kinds of consciousness arise—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
The basis for these two is solely that consciousness which is associated with and closely connected to defiled craving.
The Venerable Saṃghabhadra states:
"The six faculties, beginning with life, are the faculties in the ultimate sense."
The six faculties, such as life, refer to the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life.
Why is this so? Because these six are the fundamental basis of sentient beings.
Question: If that is so, for what reason are the remaining faculties designated as "faculties" (indriya)? Answer:
These six are the roots of sentient beings.
What serves as the seed for these roots?
Consciousness is the seed.
What causes its affliction? It is the five faculties of sensation (pañca-vedanendriya).
What causes its emergence from [suffering]?
This refers to the five faculties, beginning with faith.
From what are they liberated? They are liberated through the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.
For what reason are the male faculty and the female faculty called "faculties" (indriya)?
The answer is:
for sentient beings in the desire realm, sensual desire serves as the seed for their crops.
From what do they arise?
They all arise from the male faculty and the female faculty.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
The eight faculties, beginning with the life-faculty, are the faculties in the sense of ultimate reality.
These eight faculties are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, male faculty, female faculty, and life-faculty.
Why is this so? Because this is the root of sentient beings.
It is asked:
If that is so, for what reason are the remaining faculties designated as "faculties" (indriya)?
The answer is:
these eight are the fundamental bases of sentient beings.
What serves as the fundamental seed?
Who causes its afflictions? It is the five faculties of sensation (pañca-vedanendriyāṇi).
By what is one made to emerge from the essential [state]?
It is by the five faculties, beginning with faith.
From where does one emerge?
This refers to the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning. Question:

Since the atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya) pervade the entire body from the feet to the crown of the head, why is it that the body-faculty in this particular location is designated as the male-faculty (puruṣendriya) or female-faculty (strīndriya), and not in other locations?
The Venerable Sūmī said:
"It is by virtue of this location that one distinguishes between male and female. He asked:
If that is so, is a person with both sexual organs called both male and female?
The answer is:
such a person is not called male, nor is he called female.
Furthermore, this place is capable of producing and increasing both those who increase [in worldly merit] and those who are tranquil.
Those who increase are, for example, the six teachers such as Pūraṇa and others.
Those who are tranquil refer to the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"In this place, those capable of becoming sages can be born; those capable of becoming Munis can be born; those capable of becoming well-tamed can be born; and those capable of becoming well-dwelling together can be born."
The general explanation of the sense faculties has already been given; now they shall be explained individually one by one.
What is the eye faculty?
The answer is:
If the eye has already seen a form, is now seeing a form, or will see a form, as well as other parts thereof:
that which has already seen a form is the past eye; that which is now seeing a form is the present eye; and that which will see a form is the future eye.
Regarding "and other [faculties] belonging to that category," the detailed explanation is as in the case of the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*).
This applies likewise up to the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*).
What is the female faculty (*strī-indriya*)?
Answer: A small portion of the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*)?
Answer: A small portion of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
What is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*)?
Answer: It is the life-span within the three realms.
What is the faculty of pleasure?
Answer: Pleasurable sensation arises conditioned by contact.
Whether it pertains to the body or to the mind, the awareness of pleasure that is capable of endurance is called the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
What is the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*)?
The answer is:
when, due to contact, a painful sensation arises, and one experiences in the body a pain that is unbearable—this is called the faculty of suffering.
What is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*)?
The answer is:
when, based on contact, a pleasant feeling of joy arises, and one experiences this joy within the mind with a sense of endurance, this is called the faculty of joy.
What is the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*)?
The answer is:
when, conditioned by contact, a feeling of sorrow arises and one experiences within the mind an unbearable state of grief, this is called the faculty of sorrow.
What is the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)?
The answer is:

when contact gives rise to a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, whether it pertains to the body or to the mind, one perceives this neither-painful-nor-pleasant state as being neither tolerable nor intolerable; this is called the faculty of equanimity.
What is the faculty of faith?
The answer is:
it is the arising of faith toward wholesome dharmas that are secluded and tranquil.
If one has faith that this dharma is wholesome and faith that this discrimination exists, and thus accepts its reality and grasps its characteristics, such a pure mind is called the faculty of faith.

The faculty of energy (*vīryendriya*), the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*), and the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) are explained at length as in the original sūtra.
What is the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*)? Answer:

Not having seen the Truths and not having attained certainty regarding them, whatever faculty of wisdom and faculty of discernment one possesses, as well as the other faculties—namely, those of steadfast faith and steadfast dharma—who has not yet seen the Four Noble Truths but is destined to see them, this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñātāvyājñāsyāmīndriya).
"One who does not see persons" refers to one who does not see persons [who have realized] the truths.
"One who has not attained certainty" means one who has not attained certainty regarding the truths.
As for "the faculty of wisdom belonging to those in training," this refers to the faculty of wisdom itself.

The other faculties—namely, those of firm faith and firm dharma—consist of eight faculties when one has not yet seen the Four Truths but is about to see them; these are then called the eight faculties.
When these [eight] and others are combined, they are termed the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Question: Within that collection of faculties (*indriya-kalāpa*), why is the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) mentioned twice, while the other faculties are mentioned only once? Answer:
Because the name "ultimate" (paramārtha) is superior, the wisdom within that aggregate of faculties is also called "ultimate" and is likewise superior.
Furthermore, wisdom is designated as the "prior path.
As it is said:
Bhikṣus, you should know that when various wholesome dharmas arise, wisdom is their precursor and wisdom is their preceding sign; following this, there arises shame and dread of blame.
Furthermore, wisdom attains certainty regarding three matters:
first, it attains certainty regarding views.
Second, attaining certainty regarding the object;
third, attaining certainty regarding the phenomenon.
Those associated mental factors attain certainty regarding two phenomena:
One attains certainty regarding conditions and attains certainty regarding phenomena;
one does not attain certainty regarding views. Why is this so?
Because it is not the nature of seeing;

because it is not a dharma associated with or co-existent [with seeing] that attains a single determination—namely, the attainment of determination regarding the object—rather than a determination regarding the seeing itself, for it is not the characteristic of seeing; nor is it a determination regarding the condition, for it is not the dharma that conditions.
Furthermore, when afflictions are perceived with wisdom, they cannot remain for long.
It is like creatures that dwell in holes; if a person sees them, they immediately retreat back into their holes.
It is the same for that person as well.
Furthermore, if there is the illumination of wisdom within one's body, then the thieves of the afflictions cannot steal or plunder it.
It is just as when there is the light of a lamp inside a house, thieves cannot steal or plunder its contents.
It is also like this. Furthermore,
by means of wisdom one can illuminate all external phenomena,

just as the sun, the moon, medicinal herbs, mani jewels, and the palaces of the devas can illuminate a single realm (*dhātu*), a single sense-base (*āyatana*), a single aggregate (*skandha*), or a small portion of a single world-age (*kalpa*).

A small portion of one realm refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); a small portion of one base refers to the form base (*rūpāyatana*); a small portion of one aggregate refers to the form aggregate (*rūpaskandha*); and a small portion of one time refers to the present time.
Wisdom can illuminate the eighteen realms, the twelve bases, the five aggregates, the three periods of time, and unconditioned phenomena.
Furthermore, those without wisdom are bound, while those with wisdom are liberated.
Furthermore, when a Buddha appears in the world, those who enter the Buddha-dharma find their own delight through wisdom; for in the Buddha-dharma, understanding and insight are paramount.
It is like a person with eyes being able to reach a place of treasure; likewise, one who possesses the eye of wisdom can reach the place of the treasure of the Buddha-dharma.
For example, just as a blind person, though they may go to a place of jewels, sees nothing, so it is with a person of evil wisdom who enters the jewel-like realm of the Buddha’s Dharma.
Furthermore, wisdom is called the leader; it is also called the eye, the head, awakening, a factor of awakening, the path, and a factor of the path.
Furthermore, wisdom is called the eye, while the other factors conducive to enlightenment are called the blind.
It is like a multitude of blind people who are led by a single sighted person to travel upon the correct path.
It is the same for that as well.
Furthermore, wisdom is the sword that severs the afflictions,
as it is said:
Sisters, you should know that the noble disciple uses the sword of wisdom to sever all fetters, bonds, latent tendencies, stains, and entanglements.
Furthermore, wisdom is called the "hall of suchness."
As the Venerable Aniruddha has said: "Relying upon the precepts, I establish the precepts and ascend to the hall of unsurpassed wisdom.

Furthermore, wisdom is able to establish the specific and general characteristics of phenomena; it is able to understand specific characteristics, it is able to understand general characteristics, it is able to destroy delusion regarding intrinsic nature, and it is able to destroy delusion regarding conditions, thereby attaining non-perversion amidst all phenomena.
Furthermore, wisdom is that which all Buddhas love and respect.
The Buddhas do not love or respect people for their physical appearance, lineage, or wealth; rather, they love and respect those who possess wisdom.
Moreover, it is by virtue of wisdom that the Buddhas are distinguished from one another, and not by means of physical appearance, lineage, wealth, or the like.
For this reason, the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*) is explained twice, while the other faculties are explained once.
What is the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*)?

It refers to the faculty of wisdom and all other faculties belonging to those who are persons of vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), persons of certainty (*niyata*), and those in training (*śaikṣa*); as well as those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and those who have realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*). Having already seen the Four Truths and seeing them again, this is called the faculty of knowing.
One who sees refers to one who sees the various truths.
One who is resolved refers to one who is resolved regarding the various truths.
All wisdom that is in training and the faculty of wisdom are called the faculty of wisdom.

Regarding the remaining faculties, those employed by one liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), and one who has realized through the body (kāyasākṣin) consist of eight faculties; when they see the four truths and repeatedly see the four truths, these eight faculties are said to be present.
The collection of these nine faculties is called the faculty of one who knows (*ājñendriya*). Question:

Just as a person beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) may repeatedly perceive the Four Truths, so too does one of the "deteriorating" type (*parihāṇadharman*) reach the stage of the "remembering" type (*anurakṣaṇādharman*); the "remembering" type reaches the "protecting" type (*sthitākampya*); the "protecting" type reaches the "steadfast" type (*prativedhanādharman*); the "steadfast" type reaches the "progressive" type (*akopyadharman*); and the "progressive" type reaches the "immovable" type (*akopyadharman*).
Why is it that only those in training (śaikṣa) are mentioned, and not those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
The answer is:
although one should have mentioned those beyond training, their omission indicates that this teaching is incomplete (sāvaśeṣa).
Furthermore, if the beginning is spoken of, one should know that the end is also spoken of.
If the beginning is spoken of as "training" (*śaikṣa*), one should know that the end is spoken of as "beyond training" (*aśaikṣa*).
As it is with the beginning and the end, so it is with the initial entry and the completion of the crossing, as well as with skillful means and the ultimate goal.
Furthermore, one who abandons fetters never before abandoned and attains a fruit never before attained is said to be "seeing again.
Because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not abandon fetters never before abandoned nor attain fruits never before attained, they are not said to be "seeing again."
Furthermore, if one were to sever afflictions never before severed and attain liberation never before attained, this would be called "repeated seeing.
Although those beyond training (aśaikṣa) attain liberation never before attained, because they do not sever afflictions never before severed, it is therefore not so described.

Just as one attains liberation by severing afflictions, eliminates faults and cultivates merit, abandons the foul and evil while taking up the sublime and excellent, discards the meaningless while embracing the meaningful, and exhausts craving to experience the bliss of being free from affliction—know that it is likewise in this case.
Furthermore, to sever ignorance that has never before been severed and to attain wisdom that has never before been attained is called "repeated seeing.
Although those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have attained wisdom never before attained, they have not severed ignorance that has never before been severed—namely, defiled ignorance.
Because of such matters as these, it is said that only those in training (śaikṣa) who have realized the truths (satyadarśana) are emphasized, while those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are not.
How is the faculty of "having already known" (ājñātendriya) to be understood? Answer:

If an Arhat whose outflows are exhausted possesses the wisdom of one beyond training, the faculty of wisdom, and the various faculties employed for liberation and both liberation and analytical knowledge, which are able to produce happiness in the present life—this is called the faculty of "one who has known."
The wisdom and the faculty of wisdom possessed by an Arhat who has exhausted the outflows are called "liberation through wisdom.
As for the various faculties employed by an Arhat who is "doubly liberated" that are capable of producing happiness in the present life, these are said to be the eight faculties.
The collection of these nine faculties is called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*). Question:
Learners (*śaikṣa*) also possess happiness in the present life; why, then, is it spoken of only in relation to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)?

Answer: One should explain that just as the happiness of the present life for those beyond training (aśaikṣa) is taught, so too should the happiness of the present life for those in training (śaikṣa) be taught.
Furthermore, if the end is mentioned, it should be understood that the beginning is also mentioned.
When the ultimate is taught, one should know that the expedient means is also taught;
when the state beyond [suffering] is taught, one should know that the initial entry is also taught.
Furthermore, because the name itself is supreme, its meaning is also supreme.
If spoken of in terms of dharmas, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are superior to the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣa);
if spoken of in terms of persons, a person beyond training is superior to a person in training.
Furthermore, the tranquility and bliss possessed by a person beyond training is not obscured by afflictions (kleśa).
Although the practitioner possesses the bliss of tranquility, it is shrouded by afflictions.
Furthermore, if at the time of experiencing the bliss of tranquility it is expansive and vast, this is called "bliss in the present life."

Because the person in training (śaikṣa) has tasks to perform, when experiencing the bliss of tranquility (praśrabdhi-sukha), it is not expansive or vast; therefore, it is not called "bliss in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharma-sukha).
Because the person beyond training (aśaikṣa) has no tasks to perform, the experience of the bliss of tranquility is expansive and vast; therefore, it is called "bliss in the present life."
For example, as long as a king has not completely subdued his enemies, the happiness he enjoys is neither extensive nor vast.
It is the same in this case.
Furthermore, if there are no afflictions, one’s mental and verbal intentions are also fulfilled.
The Munis declare this to be happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*).
Furthermore, if one experiences happiness in the present life but does not experience happiness in the future, this is called happiness in the present life.
Because those in training (*śaikṣa*) experience happiness in the present life and also experience happiness in the future, it is not termed "happiness in the present life" alone.

Because of such matters as these, the tranquility and bliss of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) is called "bliss in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*), whereas the tranquility and bliss of a person in training (*śaikṣa*) is not so called.
Question: Are there Arhats who possess the three types of higher knowledge (*traividyā*)?
If it exists, why is it not mentioned here?
If it does not exist, how is this sutra to be reconciled?
As it says, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha:

"Bhagavān! Of these five hundred bhikṣus, how many possess the three knowledges (traividya), how many are liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), and how many are liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta)?
Thus he asked.
Does the Venerable Śāriputra know this matter?
If he knows it, why does he ask?
If he does not know it, how can he be said to have attained the perfection of a śrāvaka?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
the Venerable Śāriputra knows.
Question: If he already knows, why does he ask? Answer:
He asks intentionally despite already knowing,
as stated in the Vinaya: "The Buddha,
the World-Honored One, asked intentionally despite already knowing."
Furthermore, the Venerable Śāriputra asked for the sake of benefiting others.
Although the Venerable Śāriputra knew [the answer] himself, there were those in that assembly who did not know; because they lacked fearlessness, they were unable to question the Buddha.
The Venerable Śāriputra is free from such faults; he asks for the sake of benefiting others.
Furthermore, he asks because he wishes to explain general characteristics so that they may be distinguished.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for five hundred bhikṣus; having heard what the Buddha taught, they attained the fruit of arhatship, severed future existence, and fully met the Buddha’s expectations.
If sentient beings can attain arhatship and sever future existence, this is called the foremost way of meeting the World-Honored One’s expectations.
The Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Although all these venerable ones have attained arhatship and severed future existence, I do not know who among them has applied themselves with diligent skillful means."
He asks in order to explain such general characteristics so that they may be distinguished.

Furthermore, while the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has established five hundred bhikṣus and others in the fruits [of the path], Śāriputra asks in order to clarify the distinctions within those paths.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had caused five hundred bhikṣus and others to abide in unconditioned liberation; Śāriputra then asked his question because he wished to distinguish it from conditioned liberation.
Furthermore, he asks in order to reveal this treasury of merit so that the world may know it.

For example, just as a treasury of jewels buried beneath the earth is not seen by many people, so too this treasury of merit is covered by the soil of fewness of desires and contentment, such that no one in the world knows of it.
Furthermore, it is asked in order to inspire faith in the donor.
There are some donors who, during the four months of the summer retreat, provide the Sangha with all necessary requisites such as food and clothing.
He asked this so that the donor might know that what you have bestowed is for such pure fields of merit;
furthermore, it is the rule for the disciples of those venerable ones of pure conduct that disciples should ask questions and teachers should provide answers.
Furthermore, he asks in order to manifest his profound depth of seeking the Dharma by breaking through pride;
furthermore, he asks in order to destroy those who possess but little knowledge, who give rise to arrogance and take no pleasure in questioning others.
The Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:

"Of the wisdom I possess, there are sixteen parts, while that known by worldly people constitutes but one part; yet I still question others—how much more so should you, who possess little knowledge and insight, not ask?"
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest that one's own person is free from the stain of stinginess regarding the Dharma.
If a person is stingy with the Dharma, they do not even feel joy when seeing others ask questions, let alone when asked themselves.
Furthermore, this question is asked in order to stop slander.
Various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) spread such slander as this:
"The śramaṇa Gautama receives the Dharma at night from Upatiṣya and Kolita, and then teaches it to his disciples during the day."
If the Venerable Śāriputra were to join his ten fingers in palms-together salutation before the great assembly and question the Buddha, that slander would cease.
Furthermore, a disciple speaks of the wholesome Dharma, asking [the Buddha] so as to have it sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata.

For example, regarding all the official warrants and documents of a royal household, if they are not sealed with the king’s seal, they will not be accepted or trusted at the passes and fords they encounter;
however, if they are sealed with the king’s seal, they are accepted and trusted wherever they go.
If the wholesome dharmas spoken by such disciples are not sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata, then none among the fourfold assembly will have faith in or accept them within the bequeathed Dharma;
if they are sealed with the seal of the Tathāgata, then the fourfold assembly will all have faith in and accept the bequeathed Dharma.
Therefore, the disciple asks this with the desire to have it sealed by the seal of the Tathāgata.
He replies:
"One should speak thus:"
There are Arhats who possess the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā).
A question is asked:
Why are they not mentioned here?
Answer: This passage should be explained.
It should be stated as follows:
If one is an Arhat liberated by wisdom, doubly liberated, or possessing the three knowledges, they can produce the bliss of the present life.
Furthermore, this has already been explained within the previously stated meaning.

Regarding Arhats who possess the three knowledges—whether they are liberated by wisdom or both liberated—if one speaks of those liberated by wisdom, it should be understood that this already includes those liberated by wisdom who possess the three knowledges;
if one speaks of those both liberated, it should be understood that this already includes those both liberated who possess the three knowledges.
In the past, there were two masters of treatises: one named Śrīlāta and the other named Guṇavarmā.
The Venerable Śrīlāta exclusively praised wisdom (*prajñā*), while the Venerable Guṇavarmā exclusively praised the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
At that time, the Venerable Pārāśarya spoke thus:
"Wisdom is superior to the attainment of cessation. Why is this so?"
Wisdom (*prajñā*) has an object of focus, whereas the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) has no object of focus.
The Venerable Ghoṣavarma says: "The meditative attainment of cessation is superior to wisdom."
Why is this so? Because the attainment of cessation exists only among noble ones (*ārya*), whereas wisdom exists in both ordinary persons and noble ones.
Praising wisdom, it is said as follows:
If one possesses the three types of clear knowledge (trividyā) but does not possess the eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa), this is called "possessing the three types of clear knowledge.
If one possesses the three types of clear knowledge and also possesses the eight liberations, this is likewise called "possessing the three types of clear knowledge."
One who possesses the eight liberations but lacks the three types of supernormal knowledge is called "liberated both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
If one possesses one or two types of supernormal knowledge, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta). Why is this so?
Because wisdom excels the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
If one praises the attainment of cessation, one speaks thus:
"If one possesses the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*) but lacks the three knowledges (*vidyā*), this is called 'liberation through both' (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*)."
If one possesses the eight liberations and the three knowledges, they are also called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta).
If one possesses the three knowledges but does not possess the eight liberations, they are called "one with the three knowledges" (traividya).
If one possesses either one clear knowledge or two clear knowledges, they are called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñā-vimukta).
Why is this? Because their meditative absorption in cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is surpassed by their superior wisdom.
The efforts of these two [schools] are both in vain; what they have taught is of no benefit to the letter and of no benefit to the meaning.
Regarding the three types of knowledges (vidyā), some attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), while others do not.
If one has attained them, one is called "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta) and possesses the three knowledges (trividyā).
If one has not attained them, one is called "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta) and possesses the three knowledges.

Now, I shall again explain the reasons for the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya), the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya), and the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
Why is it called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"?
The answer is:

because that which was unknown is to be known, that which was undetermined is to be determined, and that which was unsevered is to be severed; for this reason, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

Question: If that which has not yet been known is to be known, that which has not yet been determined is to be determined, and that which has not yet been abandoned is to be abandoned—this is called the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown"—then at the moment the *duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti* arises, one contemplates the suffering of the five aggregates of the desire realm and attains certainty; subsequently, when the *duḥkha-dharma-jñāna* arises, one again contemplates the suffering of the five aggregates of the desire realm and attains certainty. At that time, would this not mean that having already known suffering, one knows suffering once more?
Why is it called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and not the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*)?
The answer is:

when the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) first contemplates the suffering of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) in the desire realm, it is not yet called "already known"; it is only with the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) that it is called "first known."

Furthermore, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) contemplates the five aggregates of the desire realm as being definitively suffering; this is not yet called "knowledge" (*jñāna*), for it is the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) that truly knows it.
It is by means of knowledge that there is definitive certainty, not by means of patience.

Furthermore, if one does not give rise again to the "faculty of the desire to know the unknown," is not obscured by the training of desiring to know the unknown, does not become attached to the higher while remaining in the lower, and attains mastery, this is called the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*).
Because it is the opposite of this, it is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya).
Why is it called the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya)?
The answer is:
The unknown is known, the undecided is decided, and the uneliminated is eliminated. Question:

If the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) is defined as that which has known what was unknown, decided what was undecided, and eliminated what was uneliminated, then when the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārgānvayakṣānti*) is present, with the exception of its own substance and its associated and co-arising factors, all other parts of the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) attain certainty.

Subsequently, when the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) arises, one first attains the designation "faculty of knowing" (*ājñendriya*) regarding those associated and co-existent phenomena; why then is it not called the "faculty of desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*)?
Answer: A foreign Dharma master says:
"The first moment of the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the path within the sixteenth mind is called the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga)."
Question: It is not this speaker who is being discussed here; rather, it is the fifteen moments of mind that constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
The Venerable Saṃghabhadra has stated as follows:

When the present *anvaya-kṣānti* (subsequent patience) manifests, there are immeasurable future *anvaya-kṣāntis*. One who cultivates those future [patiences] is able to attain certainty regarding the associated and co-existent dharmas at the moment of the present *anvaya-kṣānti*.
One should not speak in this way.
Why is that? Because the future path does not take what is conditioned as its object.
Question: If that is so, what is its meaning? Answer:

Because they constitute the majority, those who have attained certainty are many, while those who have not attained certainty are few; those who have attained certainty are like the great earth, whereas those who have not attained certainty are like a handful of soil.
The analogies are likewise: Mount Sumeru compared to a mustard seed, the great ocean compared to a single drop of water, and the expanse of space compared to the space occupied by a mosquito’s wing.

Furthermore, thereafter there is no longer any path of "the desire to know what is not yet known," nor is one again obscured by the cognition of "the desire to know what is not yet known. One does not cling to the higher realms while remaining bound to the lower, and one attains mastery; therefore, it is no longer called the faculty of "the desire to know what is not yet known."
Why is it called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*)?
The answer is:

having known, one no longer needs to know; having attained certainty, one no longer needs to seek certainty; having severed [the defilements], one no longer needs to sever them. This is called the faculty of one who has already known.

Question: If that which is known is no longer known, that which is determined is no longer determined, and that which is severed is no longer severed is called the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*), why is it that among these three factors of one who has already known, only one is uniquely named "Buddha"?

Answer: When the Buddha first attained the Way, he realized all dharmas through the contemplation of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), not the contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*).
When Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas first attain the Way, they realize all dharmas through the contemplation of general characteristics, not the contemplation of specific characteristics.
Furthermore, if wisdom knows itself, knows it universally, and knows it with certainty, it is called the Buddha’s wisdom;
although the wisdom of a pratyekabuddha knows itself, it does not know it universally nor with certainty;
and the wisdom of a śrāvaka is not even called "knowing itself," for it neither knows it universally nor with certainty.
Furthermore, if one realizes through dependent origination in all its aspects, one is called a Buddha;
although a Pratyekabuddha realizes through dependent origination, it is not in all aspects;
and a Śrāvaka does not realize through dependent origination in all aspects.

Furthermore, if wisdom pervades all that is known, awakening pervades all that is to be awakened to, practice pervades all objects of focus, the faculties pervade the meanings of the faculties, and the spheres of experience pervade all spheres, one is called a Buddha;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not so.
Furthermore, if that which is heard is not like a heavy burden, one is called a Buddha;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not so.
Furthermore, one who has eternally severed the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) for improper conduct within this body is called a Buddha.
The śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not so.
Furthermore, one who is able to reach the very bottom of the profound river of the twelve links of dependent origination is called a Buddha;
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are not so.
It is like three animals crossing a river—a hare, a horse, and an elephant.

The hare crosses by leaping; the horse sometimes crosses having reached the bottom and sometimes crosses without reaching the bottom; the fragrant elephant, however, always crosses with its feet treading upon the bottom.
As a rabbit crosses a river, so too do the śrāvakas cross the river of causes and conditions.
As a horse crosses a river, so too do the pratyekabuddhas cross the river of causes and conditions.
Just as a fragrant elephant crosses a river, so too does the Buddha cross the river of causes and conditions.
Furthermore, if one has eternally severed the two kinds of ignorance—namely, the defiled and the non-defiled—one is called a Buddha;
although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have severed defiled ignorance, they have not severed the non-defiled.

Furthermore, if one has eternally severed two kinds of doubt—namely, the doubt as to whether something is a person or a tree stump, and the doubt regarding the nature of the latent tendencies (anuśaya)—one is called a Buddha;
although Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have severed the doubt regarding the nature of the latent tendencies, they have not severed the doubt as to whether something is a person or a tree stump.

Furthermore, when the Buddha attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), his mind is liberated from two kinds of obstructions, namely the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction to liberation (*vimokṣāvaraṇa*); he is therefore called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if both the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrita*) are complete, one is called a Buddha.
Alternatively, there may be cases where the supported is complete while the support is incomplete, such as in the case of a wheel-turning sage king (*cakravartin*).
Alternatively, there is that which is based on both being complete and the basis being incomplete, such as the pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, relies on a basis where both are complete.
Just as it is with the basis, so too should one understand the vessel and its contents.
Furthermore, if three things are complete, one is called a Buddha:
first, physical form; second, lineage; and third, speech.
Furthermore, if one is complete in three things, one is called a Buddha:
First, the perfection of the vow;
second, the perfection of the fruit of merit;
third, the perfection of answering questions at will.
Furthermore, if one possesses the three forms of non-protection and the three unique applications of mindfulness, one is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if one’s speech is non-dual, possesses inexhaustible eloquence, and is never mistaken in its predictions, one is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if one well understands causes, well understands the timing, well understands characteristics, and well understands how to preach the Dharma for others, such a person is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if one possesses four kinds of knowledge:
first, the knowledge of fearlessness; [and so forth].
Second, non-attached wisdom; third, unimpaired wisdom;
fourth, non-retrogressive wisdom—one who possesses these is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if one knows various causes, knows various effects, knows various natures, and knows various remedial dharmas, this is called a Buddha.

Furthermore, if one attains liberation from the eight worldly dharmas, such that no one can fathom the limits of their virtue, and is able to act as a protector for all who face calamities and hardships—such a person is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if one possesses the eighteen unique qualities, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, great compassion, and the three unique foundations of mindfulness, this is called a Buddha.
Furthermore, if the mind of great compassion is profound, subtle, and pervasive throughout all places, one harbors no thoughts of enmity or hatred toward any sentient being.
It is "profound" because it has been accumulated over three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
It is subtle because it rescues sentient beings from the three types of suffering.
It pervades all places because it takes as its object sentient beings throughout the three realms.
It harbors no enmity or aversion toward any sentient being because it regards enemies, kin, and neutral parties with equal indifference.
For such reasons as these, it is stated in the *Triprakaraṇa* that one [of the aggregates] is established as the Buddha. Question:

For what reason are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body established as faculties (*indriya*) within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), while visible objects, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are not established as faculties?
Answer: They are not established as faculties because they lack the nature of a faculty.
Furthermore, if something is an internal sense base (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), it is established as a faculty; if it is an external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*), it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, if something acts as a basis, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*); if it acts as an object (*ālambana*), it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, if something belongs to the category of sentient beings, it is established as a faculty; if it is either sentient or non-sentient, it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, that which exists within one's own continuum is established as a faculty (*indriya*), while that which is not so determined is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, that which is utilized by oneself is established as a faculty, while that which is not so determined is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, that which is unique is established as a faculty (*indriya*), whereas that which is common is not so established. Question:

Within the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the sensation of pleasure is established as two faculties and the sensation of pain is established as two faculties; for what reason is the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure established as only one faculty?
The answer is:
When it should have been said that there are two faculties but was not so stated, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvasesa*).
Furthermore, it is intended to manifest various explanations and various literary styles, and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, there is the desire to manifest two gateways and two summaries, as explained at length.
Furthermore, regarding pleasant feeling, there are those who are wise and those who are unwise, and those who are fickle and those who are not fickle;
it is the same for painful feeling.
Within pleasant feeling, if one is not wise and not flighty, the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is established; if one is wise and flighty, the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya) is established.
It is the same for painful feeling.
Regarding the sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, a single faculty is established because it is neither unwise nor frivolous.

Furthermore, the function of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is distinct from the function of the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the same applies to the sensation of pain (*duḥkhavedanā*).
The function performed by neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is no different [from that of the other two].
Furthermore, it is because of the absence of mutual opposition among these phenomena:

pleasant feeling is opposed to painful feeling, and painful feeling is opposed to pleasant feeling; since neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling lacks such mutual opposition, it is established as a single faculty.
Question: For what reason is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) not established as a faculty (*indriya*)? Answer:
Since many dharmas do not constitute faculties (*indriya*), why is it that you ask specifically about perception (*saṃjñā*)? Question: The reason for this inquiry is as follows:

within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), only a small portion is established as faculties while the remainder is not; the aggregates of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) and consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) are entirely established as faculties; however, the aggregate of perception is neither entirely established as faculties nor is even a small portion of it so established. Therefore, one asks why the aggregate of perception is not established as a faculty.
Answer: Because it lacks the characteristic of a faculty (*indriya*), it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, a faculty is established by its own power and its own function, whereas perception (*saṃjñā*) is established by the power and function of another.
It is like a hired laborer who acts when instructed by another and does not act when not so instructed.
Only after one has experienced something that is felt, has something that is intended, and has something that is cognized, does one subsequently have something that is perceived.
Furthermore, because they are obscured by other factors:
wholesome perceptions are obscured by wisdom; for example, when a person’s recollections and thoughts are not delusory, people in the world say that this person possesses wisdom.
Unwholesome perceptions are obscured by perversions; for example, the perversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent.
The Venerable Susīma asked:
"For what reason is perception (*saṃjñā*) not established as a faculty (*indriya*)? He replied:
The meaning of "power" (*prabhāva*) is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) possesses little power. Question:
Perception also possesses power.
As it is said:
"All conditioned phenomena possess power through their mutual interaction."
Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) also possess power over conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*) are able to destroy afflictions (*kleśa*), whereas perception (*saṃjñā*) cannot. Question:
Perception (*saṃjñā*) can also destroy the afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said:

"When a bhikṣu cultivates and extensively practices the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), he eliminates all craving for sensual desire (*kāmarāga*) and craving for the realms of form and formlessness (*rūparāga* and *ārūpyarāga*)."
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"One first conceives a perception (*saṃjñā*), then grasps that perception, and then discriminates it; the essence of discrimination consists solely in grasping the perception. After the other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) have operated upon their respective objects, one subsequently grasps the perception and discriminates it."
Question: For what reason are the afflictions (*kleśa*) not established as faculties (*indriya*)? Answer:
Because they lack the characteristic of being a faculty (*indriya*), they are not established as faculties.
Furthermore, the meaning of "faculty" is the sense of "sovereign power" (*vaśitā*); since the sovereign power of the afflictions is slight, they are not established as faculties. Question:
Afflictions can cause one to sink into birth and death, distance oneself from nirvāṇa, and destroy all wholesome dharmas; how then can it be said that their power is slight?
The answer is:
because they are base and censurable phenomena, it is said that their power is slight.
Question: If that is so, for what reason is the faculty of afflicted sensation (kliṣṭa-vedanā) established as a faculty? Answer:
The afflictions possess great power, while the power of the afflictions is slight;
they are like prison wardens who, though their dwelling place be lowly, still associate with the noble and eminent.
Just as the various hell-wardens and gatekeepers, though they inflict bitter suffering upon people, possess no majestic power and are not permitted to associate with those of noble rank,
so too is it with them.
The Venerable Saṃghapāla said:

"If a dharma can be found within both those with desire and those without desire, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*); since afflictions are found only within those with desire, they are not established as faculties."
If one were to speak in this manner, then the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) would not be so. Why is this?
Because the faculty of sorrow can only be found within the human body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Knowing this, it is understood that the faculty of "one who has already known" (ājñātāvīndriya) can only be found within the human body of one free from desire;
therefore, what was stated previously is correct. Question:
For what reason are feeling (*vedanā*) established as faculties when it is wholesome, afflicted, or non-obscured-neutral;
yet wisdom (*prajñā*) is established as an faculty only when it is wholesome, while it is not so established when it is afflicted or non-obscured-neutral?

Answer: Among the factors associated with affliction (*kleśa*), sensation (*vedanā*) possesses superior functional power; thus, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*) across all categories—wholesome, defiled, and non-obscured neutral.

Regarding the factors of liberation (*nairyāṇika-dharma*), wisdom (*prajñā*) possesses superior functional power: wholesome wisdom can increase the factors of liberation, defiled wisdom can sever them, and non-obscured neutral wisdom neither increases nor diminishes them.

Question: Since both are factors of the aggregate of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), why is the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) established as a faculty, while the basis for receiving the body (*āśraya*) is not so established? Answer:
Because they lack the characteristic of being a faculty (*indriya*), they are not established as faculties.
Furthermore, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a maturation (*vipāka*); since all maturations arise from karma, the life-faculty is established as a faculty.
The locations where the body is received are not fixed; some are supports (*āśraya*) while others are maturations, and for this reason, they are not established as faculties.
Question: The meaning of "root" (*indriya*) is "supreme.
Since the cessation of extinction (*nirodha-nirvāṇa*) is supreme among all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, why is it not established as a root?
Answer: This is the point where the faculties (indriya) reach ultimate exhaustion; therefore, they are no longer established as faculties.
It is like a jar or a garment: when they have reached ultimate exhaustion, they are no longer called "jar" or "garment."

Furthermore, if a phenomenon functions within the world, is capable of grasping a fruit, is capable of performing an action, and is capable of cognizing an object, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*).
Nirvāṇa, being the cessation [of all things], is contrary to these characteristics; therefore, it is not established as a faculty.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is subject to arising and ceasing and possesses a cause, and thus constitutes a characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*), it is established as a faculty (*indriya*);
because cessation and nirvāṇa are contrary to these characteristics, they are not established as faculties.

Furthermore, the faculties (*indriya*) are established as such because they belong to causes, belong to conditions, and belong to what is produced; since *nirvāṇa* is contrary to these characteristics, it is not established as a faculty.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is that which is produced by birth, aged by aging, or destroyed by destruction, it is established as a faculty; *nirvāṇa* is not so.

Furthermore, the faculties (indriya) are established as such because they reside within the aggregates (skandha), belong to the world, are continuous with suffering, and possess characteristics of sequence—namely, the marks of prior, posterior, superior, middle, and inferior. Nirvāṇa is not like this.
Furthermore, regarding the term "supreme": because they are supreme among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are established as faculties (*indriya*);
because *nirvāṇa* is supreme among both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), it is not established as a faculty.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Thirty-seven [and] Volume Thirty-eight.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
Section on the Ten Gates of the *Khandaka*: the twenty-eighth chapter, the "Elements" (*dhātu*):
the eye element, the form element, and the eye-consciousness element, up to the mind element, the dharma element, and the mind-consciousness element.
The exposition of the elements (*dhātu*) is called both "concise" and "extensive.
The concise exposition refers to the teaching of the great sūtras, such as the *Mahā-nidāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
Regarding "extensive exposition": in the discourse on entering the sūtras, "entering" is called both a brief exposition and an extensive exposition.

Regarding "brief exposition": in the discourse on the elements (dhātu), it is a brief exposition; in the discourse on the aggregates (skandha), it is an extensive exposition. Furthermore, the aggregates are also called both a brief exposition and an extensive exposition.
The brief exposition refers to the discourse on "Entering the Dharma" (*dharmapraveśa-sūtra*);
the detailed exposition is as stated: "Whatever is felt, know that it is all suffering.
Such discourses as these are called detailed expositions.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the "elements" (dhātu) are called both the brief exposition and the detailed exposition; that is, it refers specifically to the elements and not to other phenomena. Why is this so?
Within the realms (*dhātu*), "mind" (*citta*) is the detailed explanation, while "mental factors" (*caitasika dharma*) are the brief explanation.
"Entrance" (*praveśa*) is also both a brief and a detailed explanation; that is, it refers specifically to entrance and not to other phenomena.
Why is this so? Within this context, "form" (*rūpa*) is explained extensively, while "mind" (*citta*) and "mental factors" (*caitasika*) are explained concisely.
The aggregates (*skandha*) are both explained concisely and extensively; that is, they are treated within the aggregates themselves, and not with respect to other phenomena.
Why is this so? Within the aggregates (*skandha*), form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are the brief exposition, while mental factors (*caitasika*) are the detailed exposition.
As it is said:
If there is anything that is grasped, one should know that it is all suffering.
This explanation is exclusively a brief summary.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "elements" (*dhātu*) is the extensive explanation, as it likewise encompasses all phenomena.
Although the *Mahā-nidāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* provide extensive explanations, they do not encompass all phenomena;
whereas the *Praveśa* encompasses all phenomena, yet it is not an extensive explanation.
Why is this so? Because the Dharma is taught therein;
the aggregates (skandhas) do not encompass all phenomena (dharmas).
Why is this? Because it encompasses all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) but does not encompass unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*);
furthermore, it is not an exhaustive exposition.
Why is this? Because it is a brief exposition.
As it is said:
If there is anything that is grasped, one should know that it is all suffering.
This is a brief exposition.

Regarding the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, the meaning of "extensive" and "brief" is as follows: it is not meant that teachings such as the gift of Dharma and the gift of material wealth are brief expositions, while the *Mahānidāna-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* are extensive expositions.

Regarding the phenomena to be known, the Blessed One first extensively explained the eighteen elements (dhātus); subsequently, he briefly explained the twelve bases (āyatanas) regarding those same phenomena to be known; and from within those twelve bases, excluding unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), he briefly explained the five aggregates (skandhas).
This is called the World-Honored One’s teaching in both its extensive and abbreviated forms.
Regarding these teachings spoken in such extensive and abbreviated ways, the Buddha told the Venerable Śāriputra:
"I have taught all dharmas, whether extensively or briefly."
Those capable of understanding and realizing [the Dharma] are difficult to find.
Because of this, through both extensive and concise expositions, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the World-Honored One:

"Whether the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma be extensive or concise, those who are able to understand and realize this jewel of the Dharma are like a dragon in the great ocean that manifests a massive body within the sea, ascends into the void, raises a great cloud that completely covers the sky, flashes lightning, and emits such thunderous sounds as these:"
"I shall now rain down.
Upon hearing these words, the medicinal herbs, grasses, and trees were all struck with terror and thought to themselves:
"If the dragon in the great ocean should let fall his rain, we shall all be submerged and destroyed."
At that time, the great earth, its mind free from doubt or fear and without any change in appearance, made this request:
"May you let fall rain for a hundred thousand years; I am fully capable of receiving it."

The World-Honored One is likewise; having cultivated his body of wisdom under the Buddhas Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and up to Kāśyapa, he ascends into the realm of empty space within the *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. There, with great clouds of compassion, he completely covers the world, flashes the lightning-light of wisdom, and utters the lion’s roar of selflessness, saying: "Śāriputra!"
Whether my teachings are extensive or concise, those capable of understanding them are difficult to find.
At that time, all those being transformed by the teaching felt fear upon hearing these words, with the sole exception of the Venerable Śāriputra.
The World-Honored One has taught all phenomena using names, phrases, and syllables never heard before; these we are unable to understand.
Yet the Venerable Śāriputra, who for sixty kalpas has increased his knowledge and vision like the earth, with a mind free from fear and without any change in expression, requested of the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, whether the Dharma you preach is extensive or concise, there are those capable of understanding this jewel of the Dharma."
Question: There are dharmas that are not within the sphere of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; for what reason did the Venerable Śāriputra make such a request to the Buddha? Answer:

What is known by the śrāvakas is not known by the Buddha, because the sphere of the śrāvakas is not the sphere of the Buddha, because the conduct of the śrāvakas is not the conduct of the Buddha, and because the faculties of the śrāvakas are not the faculties of the Buddha.
Furthermore, because the Buddha had granted permission for him to request [instruction], the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:

"The World-Honored One, in all that he speaks, always acts out of compassion; he discerns the capacity of his disciples as if examining a field, and when he rains down the rain of Dharma, his words are never in vain."
If one were to speak a single phrase and the person before me did not accept it, the Buddha would not speak it.
The World-Honored One, knowing that I possess such a vessel of the Dharma capable of receiving it, has therefore taught me this Dharma.
For this reason, the Buddha permitted [the request].
It is asked:

For what kind of disciples undergoing transformation does he teach the *dhātus* (elements), for what kind does he teach the *āyatanas* (bases), and for what kind does he teach the *skandhas* (aggregates)?
The answer is:

For those who are deluded regarding the elements (*dhātu*), one teaches the elements; for those who are deluded regarding the sense-bases (*āyatana*), one teaches the sense-bases; and for those who are deluded regarding the aggregates (*skandha*), one teaches the aggregates.
Furthermore, those who receive transformation may be beginners, those who have already practiced, or those who have long practiced. For beginners, one teaches the *dhātus*;
for those who have already practiced, one teaches the *āyatanas*; and for those who have long practiced, one teaches the *skandhas*.
The same applies to the teaching for those of inferior, middling, and superior faculties, as well as for those who delight in the extensive, the concise, or both the extensive and the concise.
Furthermore, for those who rely on their own nature and are arrogant and heedless, one teaches the *dhātus* (elements).
Why is this? Because the meaning of "nature" (*prakṛti*) is the meaning of "element" (*dhātu*).
For those who are arrogant and heedless due to their reliance on wealth, [the Buddha] teaches the entry [into the elements].
Why is this so? Because the meaning of "gate" (dvāra) is the meaning of "entry" (praveśa).
For those who are arrogant, negligent, and heedless due to their reliance on life, he teaches the aggregates (skandha).
Why is this? Because the aggregates (*skandha*) are said to be "slayers.
Furthermore, for those who are deluded regarding form and mind, the elements (*dhātu*) are taught.
Why is this? Within the *dhātus*, form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are explained in detail, while the mental factors (*caitasika dharma*) are explained in brief.
For those who are deluded regarding form, the *āyatanas* are taught.
Why is this so? Within this [teaching], form (*rūpa*) is explained in detail, while the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are explained in brief.
For those who are deluded regarding these mental factors, the aggregates (*skandha*) are taught.
Why is this so? Within the aggregates (*skandha*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are explained in detail, while form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are explained in brief.

Furthermore, the elements (*dhātu*) are taught for those who conceive of a self; the sense bases (*āyatana*) are taught for those who are deluded regarding the basis and the object; and the aggregates are taught for those who are arrogant about a self.
The Buddha taught the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense bases (āyatanas) for the sake of sentient beings who were thus ready to be transformed.
A question is asked:
"Regarding the eighteen elements, there are eighteen names; how many are there in terms of substantial entities?"
Answer: Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), there are eighteen names, but their actual substance is either seventeen or twelve.
If one speaks of the six groups of consciousness (*ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya*), then the mind element (*manodhātu*) does not exist.

Why is this so? Apart from the six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñāna-kāya), there is no further mental element (mano-dhātu); therefore, while eighteen elements are nominally established, in substance there are seventeen.
If one speaks of the mental element, then the six groups of consciousness do not exist as separate entities.
Why is this so? Because apart from the mind-element (manodhātu), there are no further six groups of consciousness (ṣaḍ-vijñānakāya).
Therefore, it is said that there are eighteen [elements], while in substance there are twelve.

Just as with the name and the substance—wherein both the name and the substance are provisional—even up to the knowledge of the name and the knowledge of the substance, the explanation is likewise. Question:
Regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātus*), if their substance is sometimes seventeen or sometimes twelve, how can they be established as eighteen?
Answer: The eighteen elements (dhātus) are established based on three factors:
first, by way of their support;
Second, by way of support;
third, by way of object.
The six elements are the supported, the six elements are the support, and the six elements are the objects.
The basis consists of the eye-element up to the mind-element.
The support consists of the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness.
The objects consist of visible forms up to mental phenomena.

Question: If the eighteen elements (dhātus) are established based on the supported, the support, and the object, then the final mind-moment of an Arhat would not constitute the mind-element (manodhātu). Why is this so?
Because it cannot produce consciousness.
The answer is:
That too is the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
The reason why consciousness does not continue further is that it is not by means of the mental element (*manodhātu*), but rather due to other factors.
If consciousness were to arise, [the mental element] would also be able to act as its support (*āśraya*).
There were eighteen [elements] in the past, and there will likewise be eighteen in the future and present.
Question: It may be so that there were eighteen elements in the past.
