That which is "capable of being sown" refers to the stage of the seed; that which is "capable of arising" refers to the stage of the sprout; that which is "capable of growing" refers to the stages of the stem, leaves, flowers, and fruit.

Regarding internal things, that which is "capable of being sown" refers to the *kalala* stage; that which is "capable of arising" refers to the *arbuda* stage; and that which is "capable of growing" refers to the stages of *peśī*, *ghana*, *praśākhā*, and *kharakha*.
Furthermore, the substance of spatial directions is form; because they are form, the various directions are designated.
Furthermore, the substance of a *yojana* is form; because it is form, the *yojana* is designated.
Furthermore, this sense-base (āyatana) can cover the other sense-bases, just like a turban or a hat; therefore, it is called the "form sense-base" (rūpāyatana).
Furthermore, if one speaks of twenty or twenty-one types [of form], these are designated as the form sense-base, whereas the remaining forms are not so.
The bases of sound, odor, and taste are explained at length as in the case of the elements and the sense-bases (*dhātu* and *āyatana*). Question:
Is the base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) so called because it is that which is touched, because its essence is tangibility, or because it is the object of contact?
If that which is tangible were the sense-base of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), then a minute particle (*paramāṇu*) could not touch another minute particle.

If the substance itself were tangible and thus named the sense-base of tangibles, then that substance would be matter derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and not the substance of tangibility itself.
If it were called the sense-base of tangibles because it is the object of tangibility, then it would also be the object of other numerical categories of phenomena (*dharma*).
Answer: It should be stated thus: it is called the "sphere of tangibility" (spraṣṭavyāyatana) because it is tangible.
Question: If that is so, then atoms cannot touch atoms. Answer:
This is conventional discourse. In conventional discourse, it is said thus:

that which is experienced by the eye is called "seen"; that which is experienced by the ear is called "heard"; that which is experienced by the nose is called "smelled"; that which is experienced by the tongue is called "tasted"; and that which is experienced by the body is called "touched."

Furthermore, because it arises conditioned by the body and conditioned by contact, bodily consciousness arises; since that [consciousness] takes as its object the real entity of the body, it is called "contact.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "One should say that there is no contact."
Why is this so? When the aggregation of form and contact occurs without interval, it is conventionally designated as "contact," yet there is no such thing as contact in an ultimate sense.
Furthermore, it is called the "contact-base" because it is capable of producing other bases and causing other bases to increase.
What is the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana)?

It refers to those phenomena that have been known by the mind, are currently being known by the mind, or will be known by the mind; as explained in detail regarding the elements (dhātu) and bases (āyatana).
Question: Since the essential nature of all twelve bases (*āyatana*) is *dharma*, why is only one base designated as "the *dharma*-base" (*dharmāyatana*), and not the others? Answer:
Although the essential nature of the twelve bases (*āyatana*) is *dharma*, the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) alone should be called "dharma.
Why is this? Just as the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have the essential nature of *dharma*, yet only the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*) is specifically named "dharma."
Just as the ten knowledges (*jñāna*), though their essential nature is *dharma*, are uniquely designated as "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*);

and just as the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), though their essential nature is *dharma*, the factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-bodhyaṅga*) is designated as "phenomena."
Among the six recollections, the recollection of the Dharma is called "Dharma.
Among the four foundations of mindfulness, the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena is called "Dharma.
Among the four kinds of unshakable confidence, unshakable confidence in the Dharma is called "Dharma."
The four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are called "dharmas" because they are unhindered.
The dharma of taking refuge in the Three Jewels is called "dharma" because one takes refuge in the Jewel of Dharma.
Furthermore, while other bases (*āyatana*) have two names, this [base] has only one name.
Furthermore, the other bases (*āyatana*) have specific names, whereas this base has a general name; it is named by virtue of being general.
Furthermore, because it can give rise to all phenomena, and because the arising of all phenomena occurs within it, it is called the "base of phenomena" (*dharmāyatana*).
Furthermore, all dharmas possess the characteristic of being sealed; because birth, old age, and impermanence reside therein, it is called the dharma-āyatana.
Furthermore, names manifest all dharmas; because names reside therein, it is called the dharma-āyatana.
Furthermore, the place from which all phenomena arise is called the *dharmāyatana*.
It is just as the place from which wind arises is called a "wind-hole"; it is the same in this case.
Furthermore, because the ability to comprehend the dharma of emptiness resides therein, it is called the *dharmāyatana*.
Question: If that is so, since the ability to conceive of a self and its phenomena is also included therein, can it be said that the "self" enters? Answer:
The conception of a self is unreal; the realization of emptiness is real.

Furthermore, the supreme reality is that which is eternally abiding and unchanging, not subject to destruction or extinction by birth, old age, and death—the nirvāṇa that exists therein. For this reason, it is called the *dharmāyatana* (the sphere of phenomena).

Furthermore, because it can discern general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), removing delusion regarding the substance of things as well as delusion regarding other conditions, and because the wisdom that does not grasp at false appearances resides therein, it is called the *dharmāyatana*.
Furthermore, because there are many phenomena within it, it is called the "dharma-entrance" (*dharmāyatana*).

These many phenomena refer to: material and immaterial phenomena; associated and dissociated phenomena; dependent and independent phenomena; active and inactive phenomena; objective and non-objective phenomena; and powerful and powerless phenomena.
Having already explained the individual natures of each of the sense bases (*āyatana*), we shall now investigate their sequential order.
For what reason did the Blessed One, among the internal bases, first teach the eye base up to the mind base, and among the external bases, first teach the form base up to the mental-object base?
Answer: It is because one wishes to ensure that the words and their meanings are consistent.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to ensure that the speaker is consistent, and that those who receive and uphold [the teaching] are likewise consistent.
Furthermore, because there is a distinction between the coarse and the subtle:
among the six internal bases (*āyatana*), the eye-base is coarse and is therefore mentioned first, while the mind-base is subtle and is therefore mentioned last.
Among the six external bases, the form-base is coarse and is therefore mentioned first, while the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*) is subtle and is therefore mentioned last.
Question: How are the six internal bases and the six external bases established?
Is it on account of the person (pudgala), or on account of phenomena (dharma)?
If one considers it from the perspective of phenomena (*dharma*), all phenomena are devoid of desire; how, then, can "internal" and "external" be established?
If one considers it from the perspective of the person (*pudgala*), in the sense of ultimate reality (*yathārtha-artha*), there is ultimately no person at all.
If there were no person, how could there be "internal" and "external"?
The answer is:
one should speak as follows:
The internal and external bases (āyatana) are established for the purpose of teaching the Dharma, yet they do not encompass all phenomena.
If a phenomenon can serve as the support (āśraya) for the six consciousnesses, it is an internal base; if it serves as the object-condition (ālambana), it is an external base.
Furthermore, the sense-faculties (*indriya*) are the internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), while the meaning of the faculties is the external bases (*bāhyāyatana*).
The same applies to the objects and the objective spheres (*viṣaya*).

However, these internal and external phenomena are not fixed: what is an internal base for me may be an external base for another, and what is an internal base for another may be an external base for me.
The Buddhist sūtras state that these six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) should be understood as internal phenomena (ādhyātmika-dharma). Question:
Since all phenomena should be understood as internal phenomena, why are only the six sense bases specifically said to be internal phenomena?
The answer is:
The World-Honored One wished to instruct his disciples in the practice of dhyāna within the internal dharmas.
As it is said:
One observes the internal faculties so that the mind does not take external objects as its focus.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to instruct all disciples so that they do not practice false dhyāna.
As it is said:

You should not practice false dhyāna by calculating permanence, bliss, self, and purity; rather, you should practice non-false dhyāna by calculating impermanence, non-self, suffering, and impurity, and by calculating causes, accumulations, existence, and conditions. You should observe existence through these eight noble practices.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to instruct his disciples in the practice of uncommon dhyāna.
As it is said:
"You should not practice common dhyāna methods, such as contemplating coarseness, contemplating suffering, contemplating the destruction of coarseness, or contemplating the excellence of cessation."

One should practice the uncommon dharma of meditation; one should contemplate [the body] as being like a disease, like an abscess, like an arrow piercing [the flesh], and that the body is constantly a source of affliction—impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One should observe existence by means of these eight factors.
Furthermore, this sutra speaks of observing internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*).

If one conceives of a self (*ātman*) regarding internal phenomena, one conceives of "mine" (*ātmīya*); having conceived of it, one then conceives of what belongs to that [self]. One has craving for the self, and likewise craving for what belongs to the self.
If one perceives a self, one also perceives what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*).
For the sake of nourishing this internal self, one seeks external objects of necessity.
The Buddhist sūtras speak of the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatana*); one should know that these are internal phenomena (*adhyātma-dharma*).
Question: What is the difference between the six bases (ṣaḍāyatana) and the six spheres of contact (ṣaṭ sparśāyatanāni)? Answer:
Some may say that there is no distinction;
whether one speaks of the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-spraṣṭavyāyatana*) or the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), although the names differ, there is no difference in meaning.
Furthermore, there are those who say that names themselves are the distinctions: this is called the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), and this is called the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Moreover, if there is something produced, it is called the sense-base of contact; if there is nothing produced, it is called the six sense-bases.
If one were to say this: that which is present is the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), while that which is past and future is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Furthermore, those six sense-bases that have already arisen are the sense-base of contact, while those six sense-bases that have not yet arisen are the six sense-bases.
If one were to speak thus: the past and present are the sense-base of contact (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), while the future is the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Furthermore, that which serves as the support for contact is called the sense-base of contact; that which serves as the support for the enumeration of phenomena is called the six sense-bases.

Furthermore, if it serves as the basis for the mind and mental factors, it is called the sense-base of contact; if it is empty and does not serve as the basis for the mind and mental factors, it is called the six sense-bases.
The Venerable Paśya said:
"Their substance is the six sense-bases (ṣaḍāyatana). When they serve as a basis for contact, they are called the six bases of contact (ṣaṭsparśāyatanāni).
It is like the substance of an alms-bowl being an alms-bowl; because a bhikṣu uses it, it is called a 'bhikṣu’s bowl'."
It is likewise for that.
The Venerable Pūrṇaśa said:
"The entry into essential nature is these six sense-bases; the entry into what is produced is these six contact-bases."
It is just as with an iron bowl: its essential nature is that of a bowl, yet because it is used to hold ghee, it is called an "iron bowl for holding ghee. Question: This case is also like that;
there are the six bases of feeling (*ṣaḍ-āyatanāni*), the six perceptions, the six volitions, and so forth. Why, then, are only the six bases of contact (*ṣaṭ-sparśāyatanāni*) specifically mentioned?
Answer: One should have explained the six bases of feeling (*ṣaḍ-vedanā-āyatana*) up to the six bases of volition (*ṣaṭ-cetanā-āyatana*).
That they are not mentioned here should be understood as indicating that this explanation is incomplete (*sāvasesa*).

Furthermore, because the designation "contact" (sparśa) is preeminent in meaning, if one speaks of the six bases of contact, it should be understood that this also refers to the six bases of feeling, and so on, up to the six bases of volition.

Moreover, contact is a mental factor associated with the mind; now, all mental factors arise from contact and manifest through the power of contact. For this reason, they are called the "bases of contact."
The Buddhist sūtras state:
"The six internal bases are this shore; the six external bases are the other shore.
A question is asked:
When the Buddha spoke of this shore and the other shore, by what dharma did he do so?
The answer is:
by way of the dharmas of proximity and distance.
Just as for a person by a river, that which is near is this shore and that which is distant is the far shore;
so too, among the mind and mental factors, that which is near is the basis (*āśraya*) and that which is distant is the object (*ālambana*).
Furthermore, it is because they have already crossed over the dharmas that were initially entered.
Just as for a person, the place where one first enters a river is this shore, and the place already crossed over is the other shore;
so too, regarding the mind and mental factors, the initial entry is like the basis (*āśraya*), and having already crossed over is like the object (*ālambana*).

Furthermore, the cessation and nirvana that is the "other shore" is a phenomenon (dharma) subsumed under the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*). Because it subsumes that phenomenon, the external sense bases are termed "the other shore.
As the Buddha’s sūtra states:
"The view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is this shore; the cessation of the view of a self-body is the other shore."
Question: What is the river in this context? Answer:

The mind and mental factors are like what is carried by a river: whether they belong to the category of sentient beings or the category of non-sentient beings, they are swept away into the great ocean.
In this same way, the minds and mental factors of sentient beings, being encompassed by their bases and objects of perception, are all swept away into the great ocean of birth and death.
The Buddhist scriptures state that there are eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Question:
This too is an *āyatana*; why then are only twelve *āyatanas* taught?
The answer is:
that [other] is also included within these twelve *āyatanas*.

The factors associated with and co-existent with those [meditative states] should be known as being entirely within the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) and the sense-base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:
"The four formless attainments are bases," ranging from the base of infinite space up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: For what reason did the World-Honored One say that the four formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti) are "bases" (sthāna)? Answer:
This is because one wishes to distinguish [the teaching] from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). The non-Buddhists reckon those [liberations] to be four kinds of liberation:
first, the bodiless;...
2. Boundless Intention;
3. Pure Accumulation;
4. Worldly Stūpa.

That which is bodiless is the sphere of infinite space; that which is boundless mind is the sphere of infinite consciousness; that which is a pure accumulation is the sphere of nothingness; and that which is a world-stupa is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
In order to distinguish [them] from non-Buddhists, he spoke thus:
"This is the place of birth; it is not liberation.
The Buddha’s sūtras speak of two places:
First, the realm of non-percipient beings;
second, the realm of neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient beings. Question:
For what reason do the Buddhist sūtras designate these two bases as "bases" (āyatana)?
The answer is:
because the Buddha wished to distinguish them from those of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
The non-Buddhists reckon these two places to be liberation, but the Buddha says they are merely places of rebirth and not liberation.
Furthermore, these places are subject to regression, yet the non-Buddhists reckon them to be liberation.
The Buddha taught that this place is where sentient beings fall back, because they return to birth within the various realms, births, and destinies.
Furthermore, this is a state of dispersion, yet non-Buddhists reckon it to be liberation.

The Buddha taught that these two places are states of dispersion; therein, sentient beings are dispersed throughout various realms, births, and destinies. Sentient beings in the realm of non-perception are dispersed within the desire realm, and sentient beings in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are dispersed into the lower stages.
Furthermore, because their lifespans are long and enduring, non-Buddhists reckon these states to be liberation.
Among all places where ordinary beings receive a body, none have a lifespan as long as that of the Sphere of Non-perception (*asaṃjñāyatana*), which lasts for five hundred great kalpas;
among all places of birth, none have a lifespan as long as that of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), which lasts for eighty thousand great kalpas.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"This is a place of rebirth, not liberation.
Furthermore, the Buddha stated that other places have two names:
First is the abode of sentient beings;
second is the station of consciousness.
These two locations are also designated by these two names.
First is called the abode of sentient beings;
second is called the location.
Furthermore, what the Buddha calls the abodes of sentient beings are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
If there are sentient beings who dwell in what is not a station of consciousness, the Buddha calls that place a "station.
As it is said in a sutra:
The Venerable Śāriputra went to where the Buddha was and spoke as follows:
The Blessed One has declared that the bases (*āyatana*) are unsurpassed; by "all" he means the twelve bases.

The Blessed One knows these phenomena with no remainder, and the Blessed One’s knowledge of the remainderless is unsurpassed; there is no ascetic or brahmin who possesses a realization that surpasses the Blessed One.
Question: How was the Venerable Śāriputra able to know that "all" refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*)? Answer:
Because one hears it from others, one is able to know this Dharma.
As stated in the Buddhist sutras:
"That which is called 'all' refers to the twelve bases (*āyatana*)."
The Venerable Śāriputra has attained indestructible faith and gives rise to respectful confidence toward what the Buddha has taught.
It is asked:
Does the Venerable Śāriputra know this Dharma because he hears it from others, rather than through his own direct realization?
Answer: There is also present wisdom by which one can know this. Why is that?
The Venerable Śāriputra is likewise able to know and see each of the twelve bases (āyatana) one by one.
It is asked:
The World-Honored One knows and sees each of the twelve bases one by one; the Venerable Śāriputra also knows and sees each of the twelve bases one by one.
"Bhagavān, what is the distinction between what you know and what the Venerable Śāriputra knows?
He replied:
"The Bhagavān knows and perceives each of the twelve āyatanas both by way of their general characteristics and their specific characteristics."

The Venerable Śāriputra knew and saw each of the twelve bases (āyatana), yet he could do so only through their general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) and not their specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa). Why was this?
Because there are further immeasurable meanings regarding the bases contained within the twelve bases; the Venerable Śāriputra required another to reveal them before he could understand them.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra knows and perceives each of the twelve bases (āyatana) by hearing them from others;
that which the World-Honored One knows, the Pratyekabuddhas know without a teacher.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One possesses all-knowledge and the knowledge of all modes;
the Venerable Śāriputra possesses all-knowledge, but does not possess the knowledge of all modes.
Furthermore, the Venerable Śāriputra knows this by means of the body of consciousness.
The Venerable Śāriputra reflects thus:
"The term 'all' refers to the bases and objects of the six consciousnesses."
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra knows this because of what has been taught without remainder:
the Buddha taught the twelve bases (*āyatana*), from the eye base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind base (*mano-āyatana*), with the base of mental phenomena (*dharma-āyatana*) mentioned last.
The Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"Whatever dharmas are not explicitly mentioned among the eleven bases (āyatana) must all be included within the base of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
Therefore, it is known by virtue of what has been taught without exception."
The five aggregates:
the aggregate of form up to the aggregate of consciousness. Question:
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
This is the Buddha’s scripture.
The Buddhist sūtras speak of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha), and so forth, up to their extensive exposition.
Although the sūtras do mention the five aggregates, they do not analyze them in detail.
The sūtras serve as the fundamental basis for this treatise; now, desiring to provide a detailed analysis, this treatise is composed.
What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"All that exists as form consists entirely of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and that which is derived from the four great elements."
Another sutra further states:
"What is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha)?
Whatever forms there are—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; coarse or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all such things are collectively termed the aggregate of form."
The same applies up to the explanation of consciousness (*vijñāna*).
The Abhidharmikas state as follows: "What is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*)?"
That is to say, the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the distinction between these three explanations?
The answer is:
Each [position] refutes the meaning of the others.
Question: As it is said in the Sūtra:
Whatever forms there are, all are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
What other meaning is intended here to be excluded?
The answer is:
The Buddha made this statement for the sake of future generations.
Knowing that in future ages there would be those who say that apart from the four great elements there is no further derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), he spoke thus.
In order to refute the views of those such as Buddhadeva, the Sūtra states: "Whatever form there may be,
all of it consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements."
As it is said:
"Whatever form there may be—past, future, or present; internal or external," and so forth, at length.
Within this context, what other meanings are being excluded?
Answer: At that time, there was a brahmin named Lohitaka who did not maintain that the past and future exist.
In order to refute his views, the World-Honored One spoke as follows:
Whatever form there is—past, future, or present; internal or external—and so forth, as explained at length.
As it is said:
"What is the aggregate of form?"
That is to say, the ten bases of form and the form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Herein, for what purpose and for what other reason is this stated?
The answer is:
In order to refute the position of the Dārṣṭāntikas,
[it is said that] the Dārṣṭāntikas do not maintain that the dharmāyatana possesses form; therefore, the Venerable Dharmatrāta spoke as follows:
Whatever forms there are, they are all the bases for the five consciousnesses and the objects of the five consciousnesses.
What, then, is meant by "form" that is neither the basis for the five consciousnesses nor the object of the five consciousnesses?
In order to stop the intention of those who speak thus,
that Venerable composed the Abhidharma treatise and made this statement:
"What is the aggregate of form?"
This refers to the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*) and the form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*). Question:
If the form within the base of mental objects possesses the characteristic of substantial reality, how are the words spoken by the Venerable Dharmatrāta to be reconciled?
Answer: One may say this:
all forms whatsoever are entirely the bases for the five consciousnesses and the objects of the six consciousnesses.

Although form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) is not the basis for the five consciousnesses nor their object, it is nevertheless the object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, although it is not the object of the five consciousnesses, its basis is the object of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
What is that upon which it depends?
It is the four great elements.
What is the aggregate of feeling?
This refers to the six groups of feeling:
feeling born of eye-contact, and feelings born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, so too is it stated in the Abhidharma.
What is the aggregate of perception?
It refers to the six classes of perception:
perception born of eye-contact, and perception born of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
As stated in the Buddha’s sūtras, so too it is stated in the Abhidharma.
What is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha)?
The answer is:
The Buddhist sūtras state that there are six groups of volition (*ṣaṭ cetanākāyāḥ*):
volition born of eye-contact, and volition born of contact with the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The Abhidharmikas explain it in this way:
The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is either associated (*saṃprayukta*) or dissociated (*viprayukta*), and so forth, as explained at length. Question:

For what reason did the Blessed One, among all the associated and dissociated formations within the aggregate of formations, designate only volition (*cetanā*) as the aggregate of formations, and not other associated or dissociated phenomena?
Answer: Because volition (*cetanā*) nourishes formations (*saṃskāra*), it is predominant; therefore, the World-Honored One said that volition is a formation.
Just as craving (*tṛṣṇā*) nourishes origination (*samudaya*), it is predominant; therefore, the World-Honored One said that among all outflows (*āsrava*), craving is origination.
That is also the case here.
Furthermore, the meaning of "formative activity" (saṃskāra) is the sense of "constructing"; it is the nature of volition (cetanā) that constructs.
What, then, is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha)?
This refers to the six groups of consciousness:
the group of visual consciousness up to the group of mental consciousness.
As it is stated in the Sūtras, so too is it explained in the Abhidharma.
"This is the essence of the aggregates," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the characteristics and the reasons for their existence, we shall now explain why they are called "aggregates" (*skandha*).
What is the meaning of "aggregate"?

Answer: The meaning of "accumulation" (caya) is the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha); the meaning of "abridgment" (saṃkṣepa) is the meaning of "aggregate"; the meaning of "heaping up" (rāśi) is the meaning of "aggregate"; the meaning of "totality" (samudāya) is the meaning of "aggregate. If one designates the world, it is the designation of aggregates; if one speaks with many words, the aggregate is expressed by those many words.

Regarding the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) as the meaning of "heaping up": all that exists as form—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—and so forth, as explained at length—all of this is heaped together to constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
This applies even up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*);
the brief explanation is likewise.

As for the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) being the meaning of "heap" (*rāśi*), it is like various miscellaneous items combined into a single heap; in the same way, the various types of form (*rūpa*) are combined into the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
The same applies up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Regarding the general meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*): as for the form that is the object of consciousness—whether past, future, or present; internal or external—and so forth, as explained at length—all such forms are collectively termed the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
This applies even up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Question:
Can past, future, and present form (*rūpa*) be gathered together?
Answer: It is possible to aggregate their names, but not to aggregate their substantial entities.
This applies even to consciousness in the same way.

Regarding the statement that "the designation of the three time periods is itself the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*)," this means that just as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is designated as having three time periods, so it is for each of the aggregates up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

Regarding the statement that "a plurality of words constitutes the word 'aggregate,'" this is like calling a great deal of wealth a "wealth-aggregate," a great deal of grain a "grain-aggregate," or a great many soldiers a "soldier-aggregate"; likewise, billions, millions, nayutas, and even infinitely distant instances of form are collectively termed the "form-aggregate."
This applies even up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). Question:
Can a single atom (*paramāṇu*) be established as the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*)?
Answer: Some say it cannot be established.
If one wishes to establish it, it must necessarily be accumulated.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the term "aggregate"] can be established on the basis of its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
If a single atom were not called an aggregate, then even a vast collection of them combined together would not be called an aggregate.
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
A single atom (paramāṇu), by virtue of not being an aggregate (skandha), is subsumed under one element (dhātu), one sense-base (āyatana), and one aggregate;
if it were considered an aggregate, it would be a mere fraction of one element, one sense-base, and one aggregate.
It is like a person who takes a single grain from a heap of grain, and another person asks him,
"What have you taken?
If that person does not point to the heap of grain, he says, "I took a single grain."
If one were to take a heap of grain, it would be said: "I am taking a single grain from the heap of grain.
Having thus explained the reason for the aggregates (*skandha*) as a whole, we shall now investigate their sequential order.
For what reason did the Blessed One first teach the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and subsequently teach the others up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*)?
Answer: It is because one wishes to ensure that the words and their meanings are in harmony.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to ensure that both the speaker is in harmony [with the truth] and the recipient who upholds it is likewise in harmony.
Furthermore, by way of being coarse or subtle:

among the five aggregates, the aggregate of form is coarse and is therefore explained first; among the four formless aggregates, the aggregate of sensation is coarse and is therefore explained next after the aggregate of form.

Question: Since feeling, like [other non-material phenomena], is not form and does not abide in a specific location, how can one establish the distinction between its coarse and subtle aspects? Answer:
It is because of what is performed.
As worldly people say:
"My hand experiences pleasure and pain," or "The head, feet, body, and all other parts likewise experience pleasure and pain."
In this manner, the explanation of form and feeling is likewise;
perception is subtler than feeling, so after feeling, perception is explained;
volitional formations are subtler than perception, so after perception, volitional formations are explained.
Consciousness is the most subtle and is therefore explained last. Question:
If the five aggregates (skandhas) possess the characteristic of conditioning (saṃskāra), then conditioning is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
“World-Honored One, for what reason is one aggregate designated as the ‘aggregate of formations’ (saṃskāra-skandha), while the others are not so designated?
He replied:
“Although all five aggregates possess the characteristic of being conditioned (abhisamskāra-lakṣaṇa), it is the aggregate of formations alone that receives the name ‘formations.’”
Just as among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), although their substance is entirely *dharma*, the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is specifically designated as "dharma";

and even regarding the Three Jewels and the three refuges, although their substance is *dharma*, the Jewel of Dharma (*dharmaratna*) and the Refuge in Dharma (*dharmasharaṇa*) are specifically designated as "dharma."
Thus, although the substance of these five aggregates is *saṃskāra*, they receive the designation "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, this aggregate has one name, while the remaining aggregates have two names.
Moreover, this aggregate has a common name, whereas the remaining aggregates have both common and uncommon names; it is by means of their uncommon names that they are designated.
Furthermore, because it can give rise to all phenomena, and because the arising of all phenomena occurs within it, it is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Furthermore, because the seals and marks of all phenomena—birth, old age, and impermanence—reside within it, it is called the aggregate of formations.
Furthermore, it is called the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) because names manifest therein; all phenomena have their names within it.
Furthermore, it is called the aggregate of formations because the ability to comprehend the dharma of emptiness resides therein.
Question: If that is so, since the ability to conceive of a self (*ātman*) and its phenomena (*dharma*) is also included therein, can it be called the "aggregate of self" (*ātmaskandha*)? Answer:
The calculation of a self is unreal; the realization of emptiness is real.

Furthermore, that which can differentiate general and specific characteristics, removes delusion regarding the substance of things and delusion regarding conditions, and wherein wisdom abides without grasping at false appearances—this is therefore called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Furthermore, because there are many phenomena within it, it is called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

These "many phenomena" consist of: associated and dissociated phenomena; dependent and independent phenomena; conditioned and unconditioned phenomena; objective and non-objective phenomena; and phenomena with functional efficacy and phenomena without functional efficacy.

Question: For what reason, among all the mental factors (caitasika-dharma), are perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) established separately as aggregates (skandha), while the remaining mental factors are established as the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha)?
The Venerable Vasu says:
The World-Honored One definitively knows the characteristics of dharmas and also knows their functional efficacy, which others cannot know.
If a dharma is capable of standing independently as a skandha, he establishes it as such; if it is not so capable, he establishes it only by combining it with others.

Furthermore, one wishes to adorn the meaning with various explanations and various phrases; if the meaning is adorned with various explanations and various phrases, then the meaning is easily understood.
Furthermore, there is the desire to see the two gates, the two summaries, and the two entries, as explained at length.

Furthermore, regarding all mental factors (caitta-dharma) present in this present gate, present summary, and present initial entry—whether they are of the nature of faculties (indriya) or not of the nature of faculties: if "feeling" (vedanā) is mentioned, it should be understood that those of the nature of faculties have already been mentioned;
if "perception" (saṃjñā) is mentioned, it should be understood that those not of the nature of faculties have already been mentioned.
Just as with the faculties and non-faculties, so too should one understand the cases of clarity and lack of clarity, having power and lacking power, and being strong and weak.

Furthermore, by means of these two factors, there is a distinction between the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); the distinctions within the form realm are explained by way of feeling (*vedanā*), while the distinctions within the formless realm are explained by way of perception (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, by means of these two factors, the practitioner gives rise to extreme suffering and affliction within the two realms: through sensation (*vedanā*), one gives rise to extreme suffering and affliction within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); and through perception (*saṃjñā*), one gives rise to extreme suffering and affliction within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Furthermore, because they are defiled by and attached to pleasant sensations through inverted perceptions, sentient beings undergo great suffering and affliction within saṃsāra.
Moreover, these two factors are the roots of conflict: sensation is the root of conflict regarding craving, and perception is the root of conflict regarding views.
Just as with the two roots of contention, so too should one understand the two afflictions, the two extremes, the two arrows, the two conceptual proliferations, and the two views.

Furthermore, these two dharmas alone receive the designation "abode of consciousness" (*vijñānasthiti*), while the remaining enumerated dharmas within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) also receive the designation "abode of consciousness.
Moreover, because the practitioner increases his aversion toward these two dharmas, he enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"By what means is the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) obtained?
How is the cultivation of the means for obtaining the attainment of cessation practiced?"
The answer is:
That beginner forms this thought:
"How may I not think of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), so that perception (saṃjñā) and feeling (vedanā) do not arise, and what has arisen is immediately extinguished?"
If one desires that what has not yet arisen does not arise and that what has already arisen is extinguished, this is called the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Question:
For what reason are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) not established as aggregates (*skandha*)?
Answer: Because they lack the characteristics of aggregates (*skandha*), aggregates are not established.
Furthermore, because this is the ultimate limit of aggregates, aggregates are not established.
Just as a jar or a garment at the point of their ultimate destruction are no longer called "jars" or "garments," so it is with this case as well.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is subject to arising and ceasing, possesses causes and conditions, and bears the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is established as an aggregate (*skandha*); because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack arising and ceasing, lack causes, and lack the characteristics of the conditioned, they are not established as aggregates.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon belongs to causes, belongs to conditions, and belongs to the combination of their operation, it is established as an aggregate (*skandha*); because unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) do not belong to causes, do not belong to conditions, and do not belong to the combination of their operation, they are not established as aggregates.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon conforms to worldly activity—being able to take up a fruit, being able to perform an action, and being able to cognize conditions—it is established as an aggregate (*skandha*);
since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) are contrary to these characteristics, they are not established as aggregates.
Furthermore, the aggregates (skandhas) conform to worldly activity, whereas unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) do not conform to worldly activity.
The aggregates are continuous with suffering, whereas unconditioned phenomena are not continuous with suffering.
The aggregates (skandhas) have before and after; unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) have no before or after.
The aggregates have superior, middling, and inferior; unconditioned phenomena have no superior, middling, or inferior.
Furthermore, the essence of the unconditioned is not form (rūpa), nor is it called form; likewise, its essence is not consciousness (vijñāna), nor is it called consciousness.

Furthermore, the aggregates (skandhas) are established because they arise from others; since unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) do not arise from others, they are not established as aggregates.
For such reasons as these, unconditioned phenomena are not established as aggregates.
In the sūtras, the World-Honored One has spoken of the five aggregates:
the aggregate of precepts, the aggregate of concentration, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation. Question:
If this were so, there would be ten aggregates (*skandha*).
Why, then, are five aggregates taught?
The answer is:
These latter five aggregates are included within the former five aggregates:
the aggregate of precepts is contained within the aggregate of form, and the remaining four aggregates are contained within the aggregate of formations; therefore, they are said to be five.
The Sūtra further states:
The Venerable Ānanda spoke thus:
"From the Buddha, I have received eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (dharmaskandhas); from the bhikṣus, I have received twenty thousand aggregates of Dharma."
Question: Since there are so many such aggregates (skandhas), for what reason did the Blessed One teach only five aggregates? Answer:
Although there are many such aggregates (*skandha*), they are nonetheless included within the five aggregates.
Some say that the essence of the Buddha’s speech is vocal action (*vākkarman*); others say its essence is name (*nāman*).
If its essence is said to be vocal action, it is subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha);
if its essence is said to be name (nāman), it is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha). Therefore, it is included within the five aggregates.
Question: What is the measure of a dharma-skandha? Answer:
Some say, as stated in the *Dharmaskandha-śāstra*:
"Six thousand stanzas constitute the measure of one *dharmaskandha*; the same applies to all other *dharmaskandhas*."

Furthermore, there are those who say that as the Blessed One has taught the four foundations of mindfulness through various modes of expression, this constitutes the measure of one aggregate of dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
The same applies to the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold path.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka stated:
"Five hundred thousand, five thousand five hundred and fifty verses constitute the measure of one *dharma-skandha*.
The critique says:
It should be stated thus:
there are eighty thousand modes of conduct among sentient beings, and the Buddha taught eighty thousand remedial dharmas in response.
Those who receive transformation enter into the Buddha-dharma by means of these eighty thousand dharmas; these are precisely the eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas*.
The five aggregates of clinging:
the aggregate of clinging to form, and the aggregates of clinging to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Question:
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
This is the Buddha’s sūtra.
The Buddhist sūtras speak of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), and so forth, in detail.
Although the sūtras mention the five aggregates of clinging, they do not provide an extensive analysis; because we now wish to provide such an extensive analysis, this treatise is composed.
What is the aggregate of grasping at form (*rūpôpādānaskandha*)?
The answer is:

if form is with outflows (*sâsrava*) and is grasped (*upātta*), and if, in relation to that form—whether past, future, or present—one gives rise to desire, gives rise to craving, gives rise to anger, gives rise to delusion, or gives rise to fear, and thus gives rise to such mental afflictions (*citta-kleśa-dharma*).
That which gives rise to desire and gives rise to craving is thirst; that which gives rise to anger is anger; that which gives rise to delusion is ignorance.
Regarding that which gives rise to fear, some may say it should not be so stated.
Why is this? Because the nature of the afflictions previously described is itself fear. Question:
If that is so, what is the essential nature of fear?
The answer is:
some say it is the nature of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Why is this so? Because sentient beings who conceive of a self are constantly afraid; if one speaks of the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it should be understood that fear has already been spoken of.
Furthermore, there are those who say its essential nature is craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Why is this so? Because those who practice craving are constantly afraid; thus, if one speaks of craving, one should know that fear has already been spoken of.
Furthermore, there are those who say its essential nature is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Why is this so? Because the deluded are constantly afraid; thus, if one speaks of delusion, one should know that fear has already been spoken of.
The critique states:
One should speak of fear.
Why is this? Because the essential nature of fear is distinct.
Fear is a mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*), associated with the mind.
Among such phenomena, these and other similar factors are called mental factors.
Question: Where does this fear exist? Answer:
This occurs in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), not in the form or formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*). Question:
If there is no fear in the form realm, how is this reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
As it is said:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that when the beings born earlier in the Ābhāsvara Heaven saw those born later, fear arose in their minds, and they comforted them, saying:
'Great Sages, do not be afraid!'"
"We have repeatedly seen [fires] that burned the Brahma palaces extinguish right there.
How is the meaning of the verse to be reconciled? As the verse says:"
"I have heard from the long-lived devas that those who possess exquisite form and renown may harbor fear and distress in their hearts, like a deer dreading a lion. He replied:
In this context, it is said that disenchantment (*nirveda*) is fear (*bhaya*). Question:
What is the distinction between disenchantment and fear?
Answer: The names themselves constitute the distinctions; that is called "disgust" (nirveda) and that is called "fear" (bhaya).
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:
If it occurs in the desire realm, it is called fear; if it occurs in the form realm, it is called weary detachment.
That which arises amidst afflictions is fear; that which arises amidst roots of goodness is weary detachment.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
To give rise to doubt regarding that which is unbeneficial and to desire to be free from it is fear (*bhaya*).
Once one has attained freedom from it, yet the mind still experiences agitation, this is revulsion (*nirveda*).
Fear and revulsion—this is what constitutes the distinction. Question:
Who possesses this fear?
"Is this an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) or is this a noble one (ārya)?
He replied:
"Some say that this is an ordinary person and not a noble one."
Why is this so? Because the Noble Ones have already abandoned the five fears. The five fears are:
1. Fear of not being able to make a living;
2. Fear of ill repute;
3. Fear of the great assembly.
4. Fear of death; 5. Fear of the evil realms.
The commentary states:
One should say this:
both ordinary persons and noble ones fear. Question:
"Does the Noble One not already abide free from the five fears?
He replied:
"Although he is free from such fears as those, he still possesses momentary fear."
Question: Which noble ones experience fear?
Are they those in training (śaikṣa) or those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
Answer: They are both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Those in training are the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), and the non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Those who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas,
with the sole exception of the Buddha,
the World-Honored One. Why is this so?

The Blessed One is free from fear, doubt, and such mental afflictions as the bristling of body hair; this refers to those universal underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) directed toward form and those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
What is the aggregate of grasping at feeling (*vedanopādānaskandha*)?
The answer is:
if feeling is with outflows (*sāsrava*) and is grasping (*upādāna*), it is explained in detail as in the case of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The distinction here is that, taking those feelings as objects, there are both pervasive and non-pervasive latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As it is with feeling, so it is for perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"This is the essence of the aggregates of clinging," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the reason for their essential nature, we shall now explain why they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*).
What is the meaning of "aggregates of clinging"?
Answer: It is called the aggregate of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) because it arises from grasping; it is called the aggregate of grasping because it can produce grasping.
Furthermore, it is called the aggregate of grasping because it evolves from grasping; it is called the aggregate of grasping because it can evolve grasping.
Furthermore, they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) because they are able to undergo clinging; they are called "aggregates of clinging" because they are able to receive clinging.
Furthermore, they are called "aggregates of clinging" because they grow from clinging; they are called "aggregates of clinging" because they are able to cause clinging to grow.
Furthermore, it is called the "aggregate of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*) because it is extensive due to clinging, and because it is capable of extensively grasping;
thus it is called the aggregate of clinging. Furthermore, it is called the aggregate of clinging because it belongs to clinging, just as a person who belongs to a king is called a "king's man."
It is the same with that: there is no self within it.
If someone asks about the aggregates:
"To whom do you belong?
The aggregate (skandha) should answer:
"I belong to grasping (upādāna)."

Furthermore, when grasping arises within the aggregates, it causes them to arise; when it abides, it causes them to abide; and when it impels, it causes them to impel without decay or loss—this is called the "aggregates of grasping.
Furthermore, because grasping causes the aggregates to grow, develop, and expand, this is called the "aggregates of grasping."
Furthermore, because they increase and provide benefit within the aggregates (*skandha*), they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*).
Furthermore, because clinging gives rise to greedy attachment within the aggregates—just like dust and grime—they are called "aggregates of clinging."

Furthermore, because one takes up the aggregates (*skandha*) and the mind gives rise to attachment and delight toward them—just as fish and other creatures delight in water—they are called "aggregates of clinging" (*upādānaskandha*).
Furthermore, because clinging is the house, the dwelling place, and the foundation for these aggregates, they are called "aggregates of clinging."

Because these aggregates give rise to various afflictions and impurities—namely craving, views, pride, ignorance, doubt, and anger—and because they resemble grasping (*upādāna*), they are called the aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*).

As for what is called the "grasping aggregates of the desire realm," the "grasping aggregates of the form realm," and the "grasping aggregates of the formless realm"—these do not destroy the realms nor do they destroy the stages, yet they destroy the body.
Because of grasping at "self," the aggregates of others are called "aggregates of grasping" (upādānaskandha);
because of grasping at "others," one's own aggregates are called "aggregates of grasping.
If one does not destroy the body [of self], then all external objects would not be called "aggregates of grasping."
Why is this? Because within those external objects, there are no appropriated aggregates (*upādāna-skandha*). Question:
What is the difference between the aggregates (*skandha*) and the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*)?
The answer is:
the very names constitute the difference; these are the aggregates, and these are the appropriated aggregates.
Furthermore, the aggregates (*skandha*) are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*), whereas the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*) are exclusively with outflows.
Furthermore, the aggregates subsume the three truths, while the appropriated aggregates subsume two truths.
Furthermore, when the aggregates are subject to censure, they cause the person to increase their censure; when they are praised, they cause the person to receive that praise in tranquility.
The aggregates of grasping (*upādānaskandha*) are those that increase the person's experience of censure at the very moment they receive censure;
this is the distinction between the aggregates (*skandha*) and the aggregates of grasping.
The six elements (*ṣaddhātu*):
The earth element, the water element, the fire element, the wind element, the space element, and the consciousness element.
Question: For what reason did the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra compose this treatise based on the six elements?
The answer is:

That venerable one has such an inclination and such an intention; he composes his treatise according to that inclination and intention, yet it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Since his intention was to compose the treatise based on the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), he composed it based on the six elements.
Furthermore, one should not inquire why that Venerable One established his treatise based on the six elements. Why is this?
Because this is a Buddhist scripture.

The Buddhist sūtras speak of the eighteen elements (*dhātus*); among these eighteen elements, the Buddha speaks of six elements. These six elements subsume the eighteen elements, as well as five elements and a portion of four elements.
That which comprises the five elements refers to the eye-consciousness element and the consciousness elements of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

Regarding the portions of the four elements: the space element comprises a portion of the form element; the earth, water, fire, and wind elements comprise portions of the tangible-object element; and the consciousness element comprises portions of the mind-element and the mental-consciousness element.
What are the minor portions of these two?
The answer is:

These two realms consist of both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*); they include the contaminated but do not include the uncontaminated. Therefore, they comprise only a minor portion.
The five elements and a portion of four elements subsume the six elements. Question:
For what reason does the Buddha, among the eighteen elements, speak of the six elements?
Answer: It is for the sake of those who are to be transformed.

Among those to be transformed regarding the sphere of wisdom, some may be entirely ignorant, while others may be partially ignorant. For those who are partially ignorant, one teaches the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*); for those who are entirely ignorant, one teaches the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

Furthermore, among those who receive the Buddha’s transformation, there are those with sharp faculties and those with dull faculties; for those with sharp faculties, he teaches the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*), and for those with dull faculties, he teaches the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*).

Furthermore, among those who receive the Buddha’s transformation, there are those who progress rapidly and those who progress slowly; for those who progress rapidly, he teaches the six elements, and for those who progress slowly, he teaches the eighteen elements.

Furthermore, among those who receive the Buddha’s transformation, some prefer brevity while others prefer detail. For those who prefer brevity, he teaches the six elements; for those who prefer detail, he teaches the eighteen elements.

Furthermore, in order to manifest the gateway, regarding all elements (dhātu)—whether they are of the nature of form or not of the nature of form—it should be known that when the five elements are taught, those elements of the nature of form have already been taught; and when the element of consciousness is taught, those elements not of the nature of form have already been taught.

Just as with the form and formless [realms], so too should one understand the visible and the invisible, the resistant and the non-resistant, the associated and the dissociated, the dependent and the independent, the active and the inactive, the functional and the non-functional, and the objective and the non-objective.

Furthermore, the six elements can generate, nourish, and grow the bodies of the form and formless realms: "generation" refers to the consciousness element; "nourishment" refers to the earth, water, fire, and wind elements; and "growth" refers to the space element.

Furthermore, these six elements are able to grasp, maintain, and increase the bodies of the form and formless realms: that which grasps is the consciousness element; that which maintains is the earth, water, fire, and wind elements; and that which increases is the space element.

Furthermore, these six elements are the root of sentient beings; they are the root of sentient beings in all places; they are the root of sentient beings from time immemorial; and they are the root of sentient beings, whether possessing conceptual differentiation or lacking conceptual differentiation.

Regarding the fundamental nature of sentient beings: for those in the desire and form realms, from the state of birth-existence up to the state of death-existence, these six elements never exist at a time when they lack power and function.

Regarding the fundamental nature of sentient beings in all places: from the existence at birth until the existence at death, there are no sentient beings in the desire realm or the form realm for whom these six elements ever lack power or function.

Since beginningless time, this has been the fundamental nature of sentient beings; there is no prior limit to sentient beings, nor is there any sentient being who proceeds from the existence of birth to the existence of death, for these six elements never lack their functional power and efficacy.

Regarding that which has differentiation and that which is without differentiation as the fundamental nature of sentient beings: when sentient beings can be differentiated as male or female, such as during the stages of *peśī*, *ghana*, and *praśākhā*, these six elements also possess functional efficacy;
when sentient beings cannot be differentiated as male or female, such as during the stages of *kalala*, *arbuda*, and *peśī*, these six elements likewise possess functional efficacy.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"It is by depending on these six elements that one enters the mother's womb.
For such reasons as these, the six elements are taught among the eighteen elements."
What is the earth element? The answer is: solidity.

Generally speaking, it is solidity; yet there are immeasurable distinctions of solidity. There is solidity within internal phenomena that differs from solidity within external phenomena. Regarding the difference in solidity within internal phenomena: this refers to the solidity of the various parts of the body, such as hair, body hair, nails, teeth, thin skin, thick skin, flesh, sinews, veins, bones, heart, spleen, kidneys, liver, lungs, the raw stomach (āmāśaya), the cooked stomach (pakvāśaya), the stomach, excrement, hands, feet, and so forth.
Within the category of internal dharmas, the feet are firm and the hands are firm.
Why is this? Because it is with the feet that sentient beings walk.
If one were to travel by means of hands, the sinews, blood, and flesh of the hands would quickly perish and be exhausted.
Such are the various sentient beings with bodily parts, each of whom possesses its own excellence.

Among external phenomena, those that are solid refer to such things as the earth and mountains, large and small stones, trees, copper, iron, white tin, lead, pewter, gold, silver, lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, and conch shells.
All such internal and external solidities are collectively termed the characteristic of solidity (*khakkhaṭa-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the water element (*ab-dhātu*)?
The answer is: moisture (*sneha*).
In brief, this is moisture, yet there are immeasurable distinctions of moisture: the moisture of internal phenomena is distinct from the moisture of external phenomena.

Regarding the moisture within internal phenomena, it refers to tears, sweat, mucus, saliva, fat, marrow, spittle, bile, pus, blood, brain-fluid, lymph, and urine—such as these are the moistures of the internal.
Regarding moisture among external phenomena, this refers to the moisture found in springs, ponds, rivers, the four oceans, the water wheel [of the world-system], and so forth.
All such internal and external forms of moisture are collectively termed the water element (*abdhātu*).
What is the fire element?
The answer is: heat.
In brief, this is heat, yet there are immeasurable distinctions within it: the heat within internal phenomena is distinct from the heat within external phenomena.
Regarding the heat within internal phenomena, it is able to warm this body, cause the food and drink one consumes to be digested and matured, and bring peace and stability to the body.
When it increases, it is called a feverish disease.

Among external phenomena, "heat" refers to such things as the fire of torches, lamps, and candles; the fires that burn cities and villages; the fires of *maṇi* jewels, medicinal herbs, and gunpowder; the fire of the sun’s radiance; the fires of the radiance from the palaces of the various devas; and the *pāṭala* fire, and so forth.
Some say that the fire of internal phenomena is hot, whereas the fire of external phenomena is not. Why is this?
If food and drink are placed in a copper or iron cauldron and heated over a fierce fire, they cannot cause the color of the food to change as it does when consumed within the belly.
The heat within such internal and external phenomena is collectively termed the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
What is the wind element (*vāyudhātu*)?
The answer is:
Lightness and movement.

In summary, this is lightness and movement; yet the characteristics of lightness and movement have immeasurable distinctions, differing in the case of internal phenomena and differing in the case of external phenomena.

Among internal phenomena, those that are light and mobile include: the upward-moving wind, the downward-moving wind, the wind residing in the ribs, the wind residing in the abdomen, and the wind residing in the back; as well as the piercing-needle wind, the cutting-knife wind, the grinding wind, the winds of inhalation and exhalation, and the winds of the various limbs and joints.

Regarding wind among external phenomena: it includes the winds of the four directions; winds with dust and winds without dust; pervasive winds and non-pervasive winds; small winds and great winds; the vāḷavāta (tornado) wind; the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*), and so forth.
All such internal and external winds are collectively termed the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
What is the space element (*ākāśa-dhātu*)?
The answer is:
The Buddhist scriptures state:

the space within the eyes, the space within the ears, the space within the nose, the space within the mouth, the space within the throat, the space within the heart, and the space at the sides of the heart; the place where food and drink enter and reside, and the place where the consumed food and drink descend and remain—these are called the element of space (ākāśadhātu).
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
"What is the space element?
It is the form at the edge of accumulated form."

Regarding "the matter at the edge of accumulated matter," this refers to the matter at the edge of a wall, the edge of a tree, the space through which one moves within a window opening, or the matter between the fingers.
Furthermore, others say that this passage should be stated as follows:
"What is the element of space?"
Answer: It is not possible to remove form from its boundaries.

There are two kinds of form: that which can be removed and that which cannot be removed. That form which can be removed belongs to the category of sentient beings; that which cannot be removed belongs to the category of non-sentient beings.

This space-element is the color of boundaries that cannot be obstructed, namely: the color at the edges of walls, the space between trees, the space between leaves, and the color at the edges of windows and passageways.
The Śramaṇas of Kaśmīra, in their ancient Abhidharma, have stated as follows:
"Bones also possess the space element (*ākāśadhātu*); likewise, muscles, sinews, blood, skin, day and night, light and darkness, and visible forms also possess the space element."
Question: Does visual consciousness arise with that as its object? Answer: Yes.
Some may say that it does not arise. Why is this?
It is called a "condition" (pratyaya) because it is capable of being an object of cognition; that consciousness does not [arise] by virtue of being produced.
Furthermore, there are those who say it arises.
A question is asked:
For what reason does it not manifest clearly?
Answer: By day it is obscured by light, and by night it is obscured by darkness; therefore, it does not appear clearly. Question:
What is the difference between space (*ākāśa*) and the space element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
The answer is:
space is not matter (*arūpa*), whereas the space element is matter (*rūpa*).
Space is invisible; the space element is visible.
Space is non-obstructive; the space element is obstructive.
Space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); the space element is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Question: If space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), how is this reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"The Tathāgata strokes empty space with his hand. O bhikṣus!
Does the World-Honored One stroke the unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛtadharma) with his hand?
They replied: [No.]
In this context, it is said that the space-element is space.
As stated in another sutra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know: if a painter or a painter’s apprentice were to say this:"
"I can paint various colors in the midst of space," and so forth, as explained at length.
Herein, it is said that the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*) is space itself. As a verse says:
“Deer return to the forest; birds return to the void; phenomena return to conceptual differentiation;
Arhats return to cessation.
Herein, it is also stated that the realm of space is the void.
Furthermore, as a verse says:
"Space leaves no trace, and among outsiders there are no true śramaṇas.
The ignorant and small-minded engage in conceptual proliferation, but for the Tathāgata, such things do not exist."
In this context, it is also stated that the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) is space; elsewhere, too, one asks about space and answers with the space element.
As the *Prakaraṇapāda* says: "What is space?"
Answer: It is because space does not obstruct form that it allows form to pervade everywhere. Question:
Why is it that one asks about space yet answers with the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*)?
The answer is:
the space-element is coarse while space is subtle; [the answer is given] because one wishes to manifest the subtle dharma by means of the coarse dharma.
Question: How is it known that space exists?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra replied:
Because the Buddha has spoken of it, we know that space exists. Question:
One knows that space exists because one hears others speak of it.
"It is not known through direct knowledge.
He replied:
"It is indeed known through direct knowledge."
If there were no space, there would be no room to contain things.
Because there is room to contain things, we know that space exists; because there are places of obstruction and non-obstruction, we know that space exists.
Furthermore, because of the presence of obstruction and non-obstruction, one knows that space exists: where there is obstruction, it is not space; where there is no obstruction, it is space.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"Space is unknowable, because it is not a dharma that can be known. Why is this so?"
Space is neither form nor formlessness; it is neither that nor this.
What is called "space" is merely a conventional designation and a conceptual construction. Question:
What does space do? The answer is: Space is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and performs no action;

however, it serves as a proximate sovereign condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for the various spatial realms (*ākāśadhātu*). The various spatial realms serve as proximate sovereign conditions for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). The four great elements serve as proximate sovereign conditions for derived matter with resistance (*sapratigha-rūpa*). Derived matter with resistance serves as a proximate sovereign condition for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
Having thus refuted these successive and sequential phenomena, one might say that space does not exist; however, space actually possesses an essential nature and characteristics.
What is the element of consciousness?
The answer is:
The five groups of consciousness and the contaminated mental consciousness. Question:
Why is the uncontaminated mental consciousness not mentioned among the elements?

Answer: If a phenomenon can cause existence (*bhava*) to increase, it is established as an element (*dhātu*); because untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) is contrary to this, it is not established as an element.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon can cause the continuity, increase, birth, aging, sickness, and death of existence, it is established as an element; because untainted mental consciousness (*anāsravamanovijñāna*) is contrary to this, it is not established as an element.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is of the nature of the origin of suffering or the path [leading to it], and is thus a path of birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is established as a constituent element (*dhātu*); because the untainted mental consciousness (*anāsrava-manovijñāna*) is contrary to these, it is not established as a constituent element.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon has as its essential nature the inversion of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), craving, or latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); if it serves as a foundation for greed, hatred, and delusion; if it is stained, mixed with poison, thorny, turbid, fallen into existence, or fallen into the truth of the origin of suffering—such things are established as elements (*dhātu*). Because uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) is the opposite of these, it is not established as an element.
The Venerable Sūmīta said:
For what reason is untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) not established as a constituent element (*dhātu*)?
He replied:
This realm arises from that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*); uncontaminated consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) does not arise from that which is with outflows.
Furthermore, this realm can produce that which is with outflows; uncontaminated consciousness does not produce that which is with outflows.
Furthermore, those who conceive of a self do so within the [six] elements (*dhātu*); there is no one who conceives of a self within untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*).
Moreover, the six elements are conventionally designated as a "person," whereas untainted consciousness is not conventionally designated as a person.
Furthermore, the term "element" (*dhātu*) refers to phenomena that entail retribution; untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-vijñāna*) is not termed a phenomenon that entails retribution.
Furthermore, it is by taking this element as an object that one enters the mother's womb, whereas one does not enter the mother's womb by taking untainted consciousness as an object.
Furthermore, these six elements are dharmas that are beginningless, whereas untainted consciousness (*anāsravavijñāna*) is not a dharma that is beginningless.

The Venerable Buddhadeva stated: "These six elements constitute the constituent parts of the person (*pudgalāvayava*), whereas untainted consciousness does not constitute a constituent part of the person."
Question: What is the distinction between these three: the aggregates (skandha), the bases of grasping (upādānaskandha), and the elements (dhātu)? Answer:
The names themselves constitute their differentiation: this is called an aggregate (*skandha*), this is called an appropriation-aggregate (*upādānaskandha*), and this is called an element (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, that which is conventionally designated as conditioned is an aggregate; that which is conventionally designated as tainted is an appropriation-aggregate; and that which is conventionally designated as a sentient being is an element.

Furthermore, that which is preeminent in its activity is the aggregate (*skandha*); that which is preeminent in the growth of its activity is the appropriation-aggregate (*upādānaskandha*); and that which is preeminent in the continuity of birth is the element (*dhātu*).
These are called the distinctions between the aggregates, the appropriation-aggregates, and the elements.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Thirty-nine [and] Volume Forty.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
From the *Prakaraṇapāda*, Chapter Ten on the Ten Gates, Part Four:
Two Dharmas—Form-dharmas and Formless Dharmas.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
This is for the purpose of stopping the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*) and for the purpose of manifesting the rarity of wisdom.
To stop the view of a person: these phenomena of form and formlessness are ultimately devoid of a person.
To manifest the rarity of wisdom: it is because those who are intelligent and wise understand all phenomena by means of these two methods.
Why is this so? Because these two dharmas are able to encompass all dharmas.
For this reason, this treatise is composed.
What are the material phenomena (rūpadharma)? Answer:
They consist of ten bases (āyatana) and a portion of one base.
The ten bases (*āyatana*) are: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible object.
The partial portion of one base refers to the mental-object base (*dharmāyatana*).
What are the formless phenomena (*arūpadharma*)?
Answer: One base refers to the mind-base (manāyatana); one portion of another base refers to the mental-object-base (dharmāyatana). Question:
What are called material phenomena (rūpadharma)?
What are called immaterial phenomena (arūpadharma)? Answer:
If a phenomenon is named "form" and its substance is form, it is form;
if a phenomenon is not named "form" and its substance is not form, it is non-form.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon has as its substance the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements, it is form.
If a phenomenon has an essence that is neither the four great elements nor produced from the four great elements, it is formless (*arūpa*).
Furthermore, if the four great elements serve as its cause and its essence is derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), it is form;
if a phenomenon does not have the four great elements as its cause and its essence is not produced from the four great elements, it is formless.
