Furthermore, if a phenomenon can be produced, produced further, or increased, it is form (*rūpa*);
that which is contrary to this is the formless (*arūpa*).
The Venerable Sthavira Sumati said:
Among these, what is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*)? The answer is:

the sense of coming gradually is the characteristic of form; the sense of perishing gradually is the characteristic of form; the sense of having a location is the characteristic of form; the sense of obstruction is the characteristic of form; and the sense of being constantly subject to diminution as if traveling with an enemy is the characteristic of form.
Furthermore, there are three meanings that constitute the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*):
there is form that is visible and resistant; there is form that is invisible and resistant; and there is form that is invisible and non-resistant.

The characteristic of being subject to appropriation and rejection is the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); furthermore, the characteristic of resistance (*pratighāta*) is the characteristic of form. Question:
Past and future matter, subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), and unmanifest matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*) should not be considered form.
Answer: That too is form (*rūpa*), because it possesses the characteristic of form.
Past form has already been obstructed; future form will be obstructed. Although a single atom (*paramāṇu*) cannot obstruct, when they aggregate, they can obstruct.
Although unmanifest form (avijñapti-rūpa) is non-obstructive, its basis is obstructive.
What is this basis? It refers to the four great elements (mahābhūta).
Because the four great elements possess resistance, they also possess resistance.
For example, when a tree moves, its shadow also moves accordingly.
Furthermore, the quality of being removable is the characteristic of form (*rūpa*).
Furthermore, there is the meaning of a single characteristic, which is the characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*).
The characteristic of form in the eye is distinct, and so on, up to the characteristic of form within the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) being distinct. The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
The characteristic of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) is that which is obstructive and destructible; that which is contrary to this is the characteristic of the formless (*arūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Question:
Why is "form" not mentioned among the ten bases (*āyatana*), whereas it is included within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*)?
The answer is:
If form were to last for a moment and possess the nature of atoms, it would be included within the ten bases (*āyatana*);
however, although form within the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) lasts for a moment, it does not possess the nature of atoms, and for this reason it is not so described.
Furthermore, if form were the basis for the five consciousnesses and the object of the five consciousnesses, it would be explained among the ten bases (*āyatana*);

however, in the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*), form is neither the basis for the five consciousnesses nor the object of the five consciousnesses, and for this reason it is not mentioned there.
Question: Are the forms (*rūpa*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) more numerous, or are the forms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) more numerous? Answer:
If categorized by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*), the forms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are more numerous. Why is this?

Because the forms of the desire realm constitute two entire sense bases and a portion of nine sense bases, whereas the forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) constitute only a portion of nine sense bases.
If categorized by their essential nature, matter (*rūpa*) predominates in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Why is this? As it is said in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
The body of a Ābhāsvara deity transforms into the body of a Mahābrahmā deity, and even the body of an Akaniṣṭha deity likewise transforms into something greater.
There are two kinds of phenomena: visible phenomena and invisible phenomena.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
To stop people’s views and to manifest the rarity of his wisdom, it has been explained at length as above.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the reason this treatise was composed is to refute the intentions of those who conflate [the meanings].
Some say that all phenomena (*dharma*) are visible.
For instance, the Venerable Ghoṣaka and others—Ghoṣaka spoke thus:
"All phenomena are visible, because they are the objective domain of the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*)."
To stop such proponents from their views and to clarify that dharmas are both visible and invisible, this treatise is composed.
What are the visible dharmas?
Answer: One base, namely the base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
What is the invisible dharma?
Answer: The eleven bases (āyatana). Question:
Why is it that among the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*), one is said to be visible while the others are not?
The answer is:
because the base of form is coarse and perceptible; this is explained in detail as in the section on the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

The sense-base of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) consists of twenty kinds, namely: long, short, square, round, beautiful, ugly, high, low, blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, darkness, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist.
Furthermore, there is another teaching that enumerates twenty-one types: the twenty types as previously described, plus the single type of color which is space.
Among these twenty types of color, how many possess color but lack shape, and how many possess both color and shape?
Answer: Eight kinds of material form are formless, namely blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness; the remaining twelve kinds of material form possess shape.

Furthermore, there are those who formulate four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*): either there is matter (*rūpa*) without form (*saṃsthāna*), or there is form without matter, and so on, elaborating extensively upon these four propositions.
That which is matter without form refers to these eight types: blue, yellow, red, white, light, shadow, brightness, and darkness.
"Having form but being colorless" refers to the body possessing the color of action (*karmarūpa*).
"Having both color and form" refers to the twelve kinds [of forms], namely: long, short, square, round, beautiful, ugly, high, low, cloud, smoke, dust, and mist.
"Formless and shapeless" means that if there is form, it has neither color nor shape.
Question: In what sense can this be understood?
What is the meaning of "unseeable"? The Venerable Sūmīta said:
Because that which is visible exists as "this" and "that," it is the meaning of "visible."
It is "invisible" because it does not exist as either this or that; such is the meaning of "invisible.
The Venerable Buddhadeva stated:
"That which is the domain of the eye and the range of the eye's activity—this is the meaning of 'visible'."
That which is contrary to this is the meaning of "unperceivable. Question:
Are the reflections in a vessel of water or in a mirror real, or are they unreal?
The Dārṣṭāntikas say it is not real. Why is this?
The mirror does not enter into the face, nor does the face enter into the mirror; how, then, can it be real?
The Abhidharmikas say that this is real.
Why? Because this visible object-base (rūpāyatana) serves as the objective condition for visual consciousness.
Question: Since the face does not enter into the mirror and the mirror does not enter into the face, how can this be real? Answer:
It is taught that various types of produced matter constitute the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*), but it is not said that a single type of produced matter does so.

For example, water arises by depending on the moon, a moonstone, and a vessel; likewise, fire arises and performs the function of fire by depending on the sun, a sunstone, and dry cow dung. It is not that these things lack actual reality.
Just as fire arises from the friction of wood and the labor of a person, and thus possesses the function of fire rather than being devoid of its reality;

so too, because of the conditions of the mirror and the face, an image arises within the mirror, which truly possesses the function of an image capable of producing visual consciousness, rather than being devoid of its reality.
Is the sound that is heard real, or is it unreal?
The proponents of similes (aupamika) say it is unreal. Why is this so?
Just as sound arises in a single moment, that very same moment the sound ceases; how, then, could it possibly reach the point of producing an echo?
The Abhidharmikas say that this is the reality.
Why is this so? Because this is the domain of the ear and is cognized by ear-consciousness. Question:
If, at the very moment a sound arises, that same momentary sound ceases, how could it possibly reach the point of producing an echo?
The answer is:
we speak of various kinds of sounds arising as the "sound-base" (śabdāyatana), not of a single kind of sound arising.

Just as sound is produced by the contact of various factors such as the tongue, teeth, lips, breath, and throat, which can then give rise to auditory consciousness— and this is not without a real basis—
so too is that [the case].
Two dharmas:
obstructive dharmas and non-obstructive dharmas. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
it is intended to refute the views of others and to manifest the rarity of such wisdom, as explained in detail above.
What are the dharmas with resistance?
The answer is:
the ten bases of form, namely the five internal bases and the five external bases.
What are the non-resistant dharmas?
The answer is:
two bases, namely the mind base (manāyatana) and the dharma base (dharmāyatana).
There are three kinds of resistance (sapratigha):
first, resistance as obstruction (āvaraṇapratigha);
second, resistance as object (viṣayapratigha).
Third, resistance as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratighāta*).
Regarding resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratighāta*): for example, when one hand strikes another hand, they mutually obstruct each other;
when a stone strikes a stone, they mutually obstruct each other. Such cases as these are called resistance as obstruction.
Obstruction by way of objective field (*viṣayapratighāta*) refers to cases such as the eye being obstructed by visible forms; this is called obstruction by way of objective field.
Obstruction by way of object (*ālambanapratighāta*) refers to cases such as the mind and mental factors each experiencing their respective objects; this is called obstruction by way of object.
There are three kinds of resistance (*pratigha*); herein, the discussion is based on the resistance of obstruction (*āvaraṇa-pratigha*).
Question: How many bases (*āyatana*) does this resistance of obstruction pertain to?
Answer: Some say that the obstruction of one base refers to the base of touch (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*), while the other bases are not touched.
Others say that it obstructs five bases: among the internal bases, it obstructs the body-base (*kāyāyatana*); among the external bases, it obstructs the bases of visible form, odor, taste, and touch.
If one were to say that the five sense-bases (pañcāyatana) obstruct one another: when striking hand with hand, it is five striking five;
when striking a stone or similar object with the hand, it is five striking four;
and when striking stone with stone, it is four striking four.
When striking the hand with a stone, four [elements] strike five.
Furthermore, some say that it obstructs the formless bases (*arūpyāyatana*), excluding the sound base (*śabdāyatana*).
If one strikes the eye with the hand, is this not an obstruction?
The commentary states:
It should be said that they obstruct the ten bases (āyatana).
If sound were not obstructed by the auditory faculty (*śrotra-āyatana*), then sound would lack the quality of accumulation.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:

"The eye is invariably related to visible form, and visible form is invariably related to the eye; and so on, up to: the mind is invariably related to mental objects (*dharma*), and mental objects are invariably related to the mind."

Regarding that, the Venerable [Vasumitra], in composing his treatise, stated that there is resistance by way of the object (*ālambana-pratighāta*). There are eyes that are unobstructed in water but obstructed on land, such as those of fish and the like;
and there are eyes that are unobstructed on land but obstructed in water, such as those of human beings and the like.
There are those who encounter no obstruction in water and no obstruction on land, such as the man Māndhātṛ and the aquatic rākṣasas.
Those who encounter obstruction both in water and on land are all cases other than those mentioned above.
There are eyes that are unobstructed at night but obstructed during the day, such as those of owls and other similar creatures;
there are those that are unobstructed during the day but obstructed at night, such as those of human beings and others.
Those that are unobstructed by day and night are such as deer, horses, mongooses, cats, and so forth.
Those that are obstructed by day and night are all things other than those mentioned above.
Among these, which ones possess resistance (*sapratigha*)?
What is non-resistant?
The answer is:
if accumulated atoms are resistant, then non-accumulated atoms are non-resistant.
Furthermore, that which possesses various distinct characteristics is "with resistance" (sapratigha); that which lacks various distinct characteristics is "without resistance" (apratigha).
Furthermore, that which has the characteristic of being obstructed or concealed is "with resistance"; that which lacks the characteristic of being obstructed or concealed is "without resistance."
Furthermore, if that which has the characteristic of being accumulated is resistant, that which has the characteristic of not being accumulated is non-resistant.
Furthermore, if that which possesses large physical dimensions is resistant, that which lacks large physical dimensions is non-resistant.
Furthermore, that which can be removed is "with resistance" (sapratigha), while that which cannot be removed is "without resistance" (apratigha).
The Venerable Pāṣa said:

"If there are distinct characteristics, there is obstruction; if there is obstruction, there is accumulation; if there is accumulation, there are constituent parts and segments, and thus it can be removed; if it can be removed, it is with resistance."
That which is contrary to this is non-obstructive (*apratigha*).
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra says:
that which possesses the characteristic of differentiation and the characteristic of obstruction is obstructive;
That which lacks the characteristic of distinctness and lacks the characteristic of obstruction is "without resistance" (apratigha). The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"That which can be removed is 'with resistance' (sapratigha); that which cannot be removed is 'without resistance'."
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"If it is of the nature of an accumulation of atoms, possesses form that can be designated as long or short, and is also capable of producing sound, then it is 'with resistance' (sapratigha)."
The accumulation of the nature of subtle atoms is called the eight bases (*āyatana*).
That which possesses form and can be designated as long or short is called the base of form (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is also capable of producing sound is called the base of sound (*śabdāyatana*).
That which is the opposite of the above is non-obstructive (*apratigha*). The Venerable Vāmalakṣya said:
"The aggregation of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) is obstructive; that which is contrary to this is non-obstructive."
Two dharmas:
contaminated dharmas and uncontaminated dharmas. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
it is intended to refute the views of others and to manifest the rarity of such wisdom; the detailed explanation is as stated above.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the purpose for composing this treatise is to refute the views of those who hold conflicting opinions.
For example, the Mahāsāṃghika school asserts:
"The Buddha’s body is exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*)."
Question: Why did he make this statement? Answer:
He relies upon the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"The Tathāgata is born in the world and grows in the world, yet he transcends the world and is not defiled by the world."
They assert this:
"If the Buddha has appeared in the world yet is not defiled by the world, then one knows that the Buddha's body is exclusively without outflows (*anāsrava*).
To stop such proponents from speaking thus, and also to clarify that the Buddha's body possesses outflows (*sāsrava*), [the text states]: "The Buddha’s body is with outflows."
If the Buddha’s body were without outflows (*anāsrava*), the woman Anupamā would not have conceived feelings of attachment toward the Buddha’s body.
The rest is explained in detail as in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Miscellaneous Section).
What are phenomena with outflows (*sāsrava-dharma*)?
Answer: Ten bases (āyatana) and a portion of two bases—namely, the mind base (manāyatana) and the mental-object base (dharmāyatana)—are untainted (anāsrava).
What are the untainted phenomena?
Answer: A small portion of two bases, namely the mind base (manāyatana) and the phenomena base (dharmāyatana). Question:
Why are they called "dharmas with outflows" (*sāsrava*) and "dharmas without outflows" (*anāsrava*)?
The answer is:
if a dharma can increase *bhava* (existence), it is with outflows; that which is contrary to this is without outflows.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon can cause the continuity of existence and can increase birth, aging, sickness, and death, it is with outflows (*sāsrava*); that which is contrary to this is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
This is explained at length, and so forth.
If a phenomenon falls within the truths of suffering and its origin, it is with outflows (*sāsrava*); that which is contrary to this is without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The Venerable Revata said: "What is the characteristic of being with outflows?"
What is the characteristic of the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
The answer is:
that which arises from the outflowing (sāsrava) has the characteristic of being outflowing.
That which does not arise from outflows (*āsrava*) is the characteristic of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, that which can produce the characteristic of outflows is with outflows;
that which cannot produce the characteristic of outflows is outflow-free.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"If a locus can give rise to outflows (āsrava), it possesses the characteristic of being with-outflow (sāsrava);
if a locus cannot give rise to outflows, it possesses the characteristic of being without-outflow (anāsrava)."
Two dharmas:
conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
to refute the views of people and to manifest the rarity of wisdom, as explained extensively above.
What are conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*)?
The answer is:
the eleven bases (*āyatana*), and a small portion of one base, namely the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
The answer is:
a small portion of one base (*āyatana*), namely, the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).
Question: For what reason are they called conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas? Answer:
If a phenomenon has arising and ceasing, has a cause, and possesses the characteristics of the conditioned, it is a conditioned phenomenon;
that which is contrary to these is an unconditioned phenomenon.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon belongs to causes, belongs to conditions, belongs to what is produced, or belongs to a combination of factors, it is a conditioned phenomenon.
That which is contrary to this is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is that which is produced by arising, that which is maintained by duration, or that which is aged by aging, it is a conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomenon;
that which is contrary to this is an unconditioned phenomenon.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon proceeds through the world, capable of accumulating results, capable of cognizing conditions, and capable of performing functions, it is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma);
that which is contrary to this is an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma).

Furthermore, if a phenomenon falls within the world, resides within the aggregates, is a continuity of suffering, possesses a before and after, and has superior, middling, or inferior grades, it is a conditioned phenomenon;
that which is contrary to these characteristics is an unconditioned phenomenon.
The Venerable Sūmī said: "What are the characteristics of the conditioned?
He replied:
The characteristic of the world (*loka-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of the aggregates (*skandha-lakṣaṇa*) are the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*).
What is the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*)? Answer:
That which is not the characteristic of the world and not the characteristic of the aggregates is the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"If there is arising and ceasing by reason of sentient beings, that is the characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)."
If one does not regard sentient beings as having arising or ceasing, this is the mark of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
There are three categories of phenomena: past phenomena, future phenomena, and present phenomena.
What are past phenomena?
Answer: The five aggregates of the past.
What are future dharmas?
The answer is:
the five aggregates (skandhas) of the future.
What are present phenomena?
The answer is:
the five aggregates of the present.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [To be provided].
This is for the purpose of refuting the intention of those who hold combined views. For example, the Dārṣṭāntikas assert:
"The world is eternal; conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
When conditioned phenomena proceed through the world, it is like objects moving from one vessel to another, or like many people going from one house to another;
so too do all conditioned phenomena proceed through the world.
To stop such an interpretation and to clarify that formations (*saṃskāra*) are themselves the world (*loka*), and the world is itself formations, the Mahādhātuvarga thus states:
"What dharma is designated by the name 'world'?"
The answer is:
These are words concerning practice.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the reason this treatise was composed is to stop the delusions of those who claim that the past and future do not exist within the world, and who maintain that the present is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma.

This also clarifies that the past and future possess the characteristic of real existence. If the past and future did not exist, then there would be no such things as accomplishment or non-accomplishment.
It would be like a second head, a third hand, or a thirteenth sense-base, for which there could be neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment.
If the past and future did not exist, then there would be no accomplishment or non-accomplishment.
Since there is accomplishment and non-accomplishment, one knows that the past and future must necessarily exist as real entities.
If one were to say that the past and future do not exist, then one should speak as follows:

Regarding that past [action], if it produced a cause at the time of the present, should its fruit be said to exist in the past, should it be said to exist in the future, or should it be said to exist in the present?
If it existed in the past, one should say that the past exists; one should not say that the past does not exist.
To say that the past does not exist is incorrect.
If one says it exists in the future, one should say that there is a future; one should not say that there is no future.
If one says there is no future, this is not the case.
If one says it exists in the present, then cause and effect would coexist.
If cause and effect were to coexist, this would contradict what is stated in the verse, as it says:
"Evil deeds do not bear fruit immediately, Just as milk does not turn into curd at once;
The fool treads on fire hidden beneath ashes, Yet his feet are not burned at that very moment.

If the fruit does not exist in the past, future, or present, then there is no fruit. If there is no fruit, then there is no cause—just like a second head, a third hand, a sixth sense-faculty (*āyatana*), or a thirteenth base (*dhātu*).
If cause and effect exist but do not reside in the past, future, or present, they would be permanent, like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If the effect exists in the present time, where could its cause be said to reside?
Is it in the past, is it in the future, or is it in the present?
If it is in the past, it is as explained above;
if it is in the future, it is also as explained above.
If it exists in the present, it is also as explained above.

If it does not exist in the past, future, or present, then it has no cause; if there is no cause, then there is no fruit—just like a second head, a third hand, a sixth aggregate, or a thirteenth base.
If cause and effect were not situated within the three periods of time, they would necessarily be eternal, like unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Furthermore, if the past and the future did not exist, there would be no dharma of renunciation (*pravrajyā-dharma*).
As a verse says:
"If one says there is no past, then there is no Buddha of the past;
if there is no Buddha of the past, then there is no dharma of renunciation."
Furthermore, if the past and the future did not exist, then one would always be speaking falsehoods.
As a verse says:
"If one says there is no past, yet speaks of the number of years [of monastic life],"
"Then at all times, because it is eternal, it would be a false statement.
Furthermore, if the past and future did not exist, then the present would not exist either.
Why is this so? Because there is the past and the future, one designates the present.
If the three periods of time did not exist, then conditioned phenomena would not exist; and if conditioned phenomena did not exist, unconditioned phenomena would likewise not exist.
Why is this so? Because it is due to the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are designated.
If both conditioned and unconditioned phenomena did not exist, then no phenomena whatsoever would exist.
If all phenomena did not exist, there would be no liberation or transcendence.
To avoid such an error, it is taught that the past and future possess the characteristic of real existence.

Therefore, in order to refute the positions of others, to manifest my own position, and to clarify the meaning of the correspondence with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), I have composed this treatise.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the world?
The answer is:
The five aggregates of the past, the future, and the present—these constitute the essential nature of the world (*loka*), as explained at length.
Having already explained the reason for its essential nature, we shall now explain why it is called "the world."
What is the meaning of "world" (*loka*)?
The answer is:
the meaning of "passing away" (*gati*) is the meaning of "world."
Question: All conditioned phenomena neither come nor go; that which comes does not go, and that which goes does not come.
Furthermore, if something were to come, its place of origin would necessarily be empty.
Why is this? Because it comes from that place;
if there were a goer, it would obstruct the place of going.
Why is this? Because one has gone to that place.
Therefore, the Venerable Sthavira Sumati spoke these verses:
"All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) have no characteristic of coming, because they consist of momentary instants;
they have no characteristic of going, nor do they abide.
If conditioned phenomena neither come nor go, how can there be the three times?
Answer: Because of their activity.
If conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have no activity, they are called "future."
If there is something being performed, this is called the present;
if that which was performed has already ceased, this is called the past.
If the eye has not yet seen a form, this is the future; seeing a form is the present; and when seeing has already ceased, it is the past.
Question: If that is so, how can the present portion of the eye perform its function? Answer:
Because it acts as a similar cause:
if it does not manifest, it does not act as a similar cause for that which is future;
if it manifests, it acts as a similar cause for that which is future.
This applies even to the mind in the same way.
Just as form that has not yet acted as an obstruction is future, that which acts as an obstruction is present, and that which has already ceased after acting as an obstruction is past.
Just as feeling that has not yet arisen is future, feeling that has arisen is present, and feeling that has arisen and ceased is past.
This applies likewise to feeling up to perception, formations, and consciousness.

Furthermore, if a dharma has not yet taken or given its fruit, it is future; if it is taking or giving its fruit, it is present; and if it has already ceased after taking or giving its fruit, it is past.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon has neither grasped nor bestowed its fruit of support or its fruit of retribution, it is future; if it has grasped its fruit of support and its fruit of retribution but has not yet bestowed them, it is present; if it has grasped its fruit of support and its fruit of retribution and they have already ceased, it is past.
Furthermore, if a dharma has not yet produced its similar cause or its pervasive cause, it is future; if it has produced them, it is present; and if they have already ceased, it is past.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon has not yet arisen and has not yet ceased, it is the future; if it has already arisen but has not yet ceased, it is the present; if it has arisen and already ceased, it is the past. The same applies to the explanations of: that which has not arisen and is not destroyed;

that which has already arisen but is not destroyed; and that which has already arisen and is destroyed; as well as that which has not arisen and is not separated [from its characteristics]; that which has already arisen but is not separated; and that which has already arisen and is separated.

Furthermore, if a dharma has not yet produced the three characteristics of the conditioned, it is future; if one has already been produced and two are currently being produced, it is present; if all three have already been produced, it is past.

Furthermore, if a dharma has not yet performed its four conditions, it is future; if it is performing its four conditions, it is present; and if it has already performed its four conditions and ceased, it is past.

Furthermore, if a dharma acts as a cause for dharmas of all three time periods, it is past; if it acts as a cause for dharmas of two time periods, it is present; and if it acts as a cause for dharmas of one time period, it is future.
Furthermore, if a dharma is the fruit of the three time periods, it is future; if it is the fruit of two time periods, it is present; if it is the fruit of one time period, it is past.
Furthermore, the present is designated by means of the past and the future, but the present is not designated by means of the present itself, because there is no fourth time-period.
The future is designated by means of the past and the present, but the future is not designated by means of the future itself, because there is no fourth time-period.
The past is designated by means of the future and the present; it is not designated by means of the past itself, because there is no fourth time-period.
Is everything that is past also form?
The answer is:
There may be that which belongs to the past but does not belong to form, and so on, elaborated extensively as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding that which belongs to the past but does not belong to form: the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the past are what belong to form.
That which does not belong to the past belongs to the future and the present.
That which belongs to the past and also belongs to matter refers to that which belongs to past matter.

That which does not belong to the past and does not belong to form refers to that which belongs to the four aggregates of the future and present, as well as that which belongs to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Just as one constructs four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) for form, one likewise constructs four propositions for each of the [other] aggregates up to consciousness;

and just as one constructs five sets of four propositions for the past, one likewise constructs five sets of four propositions for the future and present. Thus, there are fifteen sets of four propositions.
If all that belongs to form, does it entirely belong to the various spatial divisions? Answer:
If it belongs to the various spatial divisions, it entirely belongs to form.
Is there any form that exists but does not exist as spatial divisions? Answer: There is.
Regarding past and future form, present atoms, and unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*):
if one were to possess all of these, would they not all be entirely devoid of spatial dimensions and parts?
Answer: If that which is possessed is entirely not possessed by any spatial direction or part,
could there be something that is not possessed by any spatial direction or part yet is not possessed?
Answer: There is.
It includes all past and future form, present atoms, unmanifested form (*avijñaptirūpa*), and that which belongs to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
As it is with feeling (vedanā), so it is for perception (saṃjñā), mental formations (saṃskāra), and consciousness (vijñāna). Are all forms (rūpa) entirely obstructive? Answer: No.
If that which is obstructive is entirely comprised of matter (rūpa), is there any matter that is not obstructive?
The answer is: Yes.
There is. This includes past and future form, present atoms, and unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Are all sensations that exist fully understood?
Answer: If all that is perception (*saṃjñā*) were feeling (*vedanā*),
could there be any feeling that is not perception?
Answer: There are;
namely, feelings of the past and future.
As it is with feeling (*vedanā*), so it is for perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Question:
Is it that which has already arisen or that which has not yet arisen?
If that which has already arisen has arisen, why do the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) not undergo reversal?
If that which has not yet arisen has arisen, why do the conditioned phenomena not exist where they were previously non-existent?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
by way of a causal condition, that which has already arisen arises; by way of a causal condition, that which has not yet arisen arises.
Regarding "that which has already arisen arises because of conditions": it arises because all phenomena abide in their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Regarding "that which has not yet arisen arises because of conditions": it arises because all future phenomena are, by nature, unarisen phenomena.
Question: Does it arise as the world, or does it arise within the world?
If it arises as the world, why is it that when one dharma arises, all dharmas do not arise?
If the arising of a single dharma were the arising of all dharmas, then the world would be destroyed.
If they arise within the world, how is it that their activity does not differ from the world?
He replied:
It should be stated thus:
"The world arises because of a thing; it arises within the world because of a thing.
As for "the world arises because of a thing," this is because at the very moment of a single kṣaṇa of arising, that itself constitutes the world.
Regarding the statement "that which is born in the world exists by way of conditions": it is born in a single moment within the future, because other moments have not yet been born. Question:
Does that very dharma which arises perish as that same dharma, or does a different dharma arise while a different dharma perishes?
If that which arises is the very same dharma that ceases, does the future dharma arise and the future dharma itself cease?
Or, if another dharma arises and another dharma ceases, does it mean that when form arises, feeling ceases?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
by reason of a certain thing, that very phenomenon arises and that very phenomenon ceases; by reason of a certain thing, another phenomenon arises and another phenomenon ceases.

Regarding the statement that "by reason of this phenomenon, that phenomenon arises and ceases": when form arises, it is form that ceases; and so on, up to when consciousness arises, it is consciousness that ceases.
Regarding the statement that "by reason of this phenomenon, other phenomena arise and cease": those of the future world arise, while those of the present world cease.
Question: Does it arise from its own part (*svabhāga*) or does it arise from another part (*parabhāga*)?

If it arises from its own part, how is it that what previously lacked its own part now possesses its own part, and what previously lacked a substantial entity (*dravya*) now possesses a substantial entity?
If it arises from another part, how is it that a dharma does not abandon its own essence?
The answer is:
one should state it thus:
It is not produced from itself, nor is it produced from another; rather, having arisen according to the nature of its own dharma, it ceases.
Question: Since the future world decreases and the past world increases, why is it not established that there is increase and decrease in these two periods?
The Venerable Sūmī said:
"In order to increase the calculation of past and future worlds, is there an increase or decrease?
If one does not increase the calculation of past and future worlds, why say that past and future worlds have increase and decrease?"
Furthermore, the past and future are immeasurable and boundless; it is said that they neither increase nor decrease.

For example, if one were to take a hundred thousand jars of water from the ocean, the ocean would not diminish; if one were to pour a hundred thousand jars of water into it, it would not increase, because the waters of the ocean are immeasurable.
It is likewise for that [present].
Furthermore, future phenomena do not decrease because they have neither arisen nor ceased; past phenomena do not increase because they have already arisen and ceased.
Furthermore, future phenomena do not decrease because they have not yet arisen and are not destroyed; past phenomena do not increase because they have already arisen and are destroyed.
Furthermore, future dharmas do not diminish because they have not yet arisen and have not yet departed; past dharmas do not increase because they have already arisen and have already departed.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "If dharmas move through the world, why is it not said that there is increase and decrease?"
It is simply that phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and cease when those causes and conditions disperse. Question:
Do the past and future exist as accumulated entities, like present walls, trees, mountains, and cliffs?
Is it scattered in various places?
If it were accumulated, how could the donor’s effort not be rendered fruitless?
And how could it lack a specific location?
Why is it not eternal? Why is it not perceived by direct observation?
If [the king] were dispersed in various places, how could one say that there was a past king named Mahāsudarśana, a city named Kuśāvatī, and an assembly hall named Sudharmā?
It is also said that there were Buddhas from Vipaśyin down to Kāśyapa.
How then can it be said that there will be a future city named Kukkuṭa and a future Buddha named Maitreya?
How is it that the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) contemplates past events, while the knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) contemplates both past and future events?
And how is it that things do not exist having previously been non-existent, nor do they exist having once existed and then ceased?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
Some say that accumulation is like present walls and so forth.
Question: If that is so, how is it that this is not something performed by the donor, and yet their merit is not in vain? Answer:
Because of other views:
if one does not cultivate [the path], the merit does not manifest; if one cultivates the merit, it then manifests. Question:
Why is it that there is no location?
The answer is:
if there were a location, what further fault would there be?
Why is it not eternal?
The answer is:
because there is momentary impermanence.
Why is it not manifest?
The answer is:
if it has not yet become an object for the group of the five consciousnesses, it is not manifest; if it has already become so, it is manifest.
The commentary states:
One should say this:
that which is present is an accumulation, while that which is future and past is dispersed throughout various places.
Why is this so? Because it is included among the categories of dharmas (*dharmasaṃkhyā*). Question:
If that is so, how can one speak of the past?
The answer is:
one speaks of the past as it was when it was originally present.
How is it said that the future exists?
The answer is:
as when that which is future is about to become present.
What is the past that constitutes the objective domain of the knowledge of recollecting former existences (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna) and the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna)?
The answer is:
because it is that which has been experienced.
Just as previously experienced syllables are arranged in sequence to form phrases that clarify meaning,
so too does the sequential recollection of previously experienced events give rise to knowledge and vision.
What is the future object of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)? Answer:
It is as with the past; it is known by means of inferring its characteristics based on the present.
It is just as a farmer knows [the state of his field] through comparison.
How is it that what was not originally present now exists, and having existed, returns to non-existence?
The answer is:
This cannot be reconciled.

Within the Sarvāstivāda school, there are four types of masters: first, those who maintain that things (dharmas) are distinct; [the others being those who maintain they are identical, those who maintain they are both, and those who maintain they are neither].
Second, the difference in the teaching of characteristics;
third, the difference in the time of the teaching;
fourth, the difference in the teachings themselves.

Those who propound the theory of the difference in states (*avasthānyathāvādin*) say: when a phenomenon (*dharma*) proceeds through the world, its state changes while its essence (*svabhāva*) does not change.
For example, when gold or silver vessels are broken and remade, although their shapes differ, their color remains unchanged.
It is also like when milk turns into curd: although its fragrance and flavor change, its color does not.
In this way, when a future dharma reaches the present, although it relinquishes its status as a future dharma, it does not relinquish its essence;
when a present dharma reaches the past, although it relinquishes its status as a present dharma, it does not relinquish its essence.
Those who propound the theory of distinct characteristics say:
when a phenomenon exists in the present, it possesses its past characteristic, yet it does not lack its future and present characteristics;
a future phenomenon possesses its future characteristic, yet it does not lack its past and present characteristics.
Present phenomena possess the characteristics of the present, yet this does not mean they lack the characteristics of the past and future.
It is like a person who loves the beauty of one woman; it does not mean that he lacks love for the beauty of other women.
It is the same in this case as well.
Those who speak of the difference in time say:
when the Dharma circulates through different periods, different names arise due to the difference in time, but its essence does not differ.
It is like counting sticks: the first placed down is called one; when turned once, it is called ten; when turned again, it is called a hundred; and so on up to a thousand or ten million.
Although the counting stick is but one, it receives various names because it is moved to different positions.
It is the same for that [time] as well.
To speak of "the three times" in this manner is called speaking without confusion; it is because of what has been performed that the three times exist.

If a phenomenon has not yet performed its function, it is called the future; if it has already performed its function, it is called the present; and if its function has already ceased, it is called the past.
Those who propound the theory of difference (*anyathānyathika*) say:
"When a dharma proceeds through time, it receives different names due to its prior and subsequent states.
It is like a single woman who is called both 'daughter' and 'mother'; she is called a daughter because she has a mother, and she is called a mother because she has a daughter."
When such dharmas circulate in the world, their distinction arises from preceding and succeeding births; it is not a distinction of time or a distinction of essence.
To speak otherwise would be called "confusion. Why is this so?
One lifetime consists of three lifetimes.

Within the past lifetime there are three lifetimes: the two moments (kṣaṇa) preceding and following the past are called the past and the future, while the central moment of the past is called the past.
The same applies to the present and future worlds as well. Question:
Who are the four great masters among the Sarvāstivādins?
The first is Dharmatrāta, the second is Ghoṣaka, the third is Vasumitra, and the fourth is Buddhadeva. There are three categories of phenomena:
wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, and indeterminate phenomena.
What are wholesome phenomena?
The answer is:
the five wholesome aggregates and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
What are unwholesome dharmas?
The answer is:
the five unwholesome aggregates (skandhas).
What are the indeterminate dharmas?
The answer is:
the five aggregates that are indeterminate, as well as space and analytical cessation.
Why are they called wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate?
A detailed explanation is as given in the Chapter on the Unwholesome.
There are three dharmas:
Dharmas bound to the desire realm, dharmas bound to the form realm, and dharmas bound to the formless realm.
What are dharmas bound to the desire realm? Answer:
The five aggregates bound to the desire realm.
What are the phenomena bound to the form realm? Answer:
The five aggregates bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-saṃprayukta-skandha*).
What are the phenomena bound to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-saṃprayukta-dharma*)? Answer:
The four aggregates bound to the formless realm.
Why are they called phenomena bound to the desire realm, bound to the form realm, and bound to the formless realm?
The detailed explanation is as above.
Three categories of phenomena:

phenomena of those in training (*śaikṣadharma*), phenomena of those beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*), and phenomena that are neither of those in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma*).
What are phenomena of those in training?
Answer: One studies the five aggregates.
What are the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma)?
Answer: The five aggregates of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What are the dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training?
Answer: They are the five aggregates with outflows (sāsrava) and the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta).
Why are they called "in training" (śaikṣa), "beyond training" (aśaikṣa), and "neither in training nor beyond training" (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa)?

Answer: One is called "in training" (śaikṣa) because one trains to sever greed by means of the path of non-greed; one is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa) because one does not need to train to sever greed by means of the path of non-greed. Why is this so?
Because they have already been cultivated previously.
That which is contrary to this is called "neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
The same explanation applies to non-hatred and non-delusion.
Furthermore, by means of the path of non-craving (*anaiṣa-mārga*), one trains to sever craving; that which is not the essence of craving is training (*śaikṣa*).
By means of the path of non-craving, one trains to sever craving, thereby excluding the path of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-mārga*);
as for that whose essence is not craving, it excludes the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*).
Because the path of non-craving does not involve training in the abandonment of craving—since one has already trained in it previously—it is non-craving by nature;
thus, it is the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Since the path of non-craving does not involve training in the abandonment of craving, it excludes the essential nature of the path as being craving; and since it is not craving, it excludes the mundane path (*laukikamārga*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Furthermore, the learner’s abandonment of afflictions and the learner’s vision of the true truths constitute "learning"; as for the non-learner’s abandonment of afflictions, it is not "learning" because they have already been abandoned previously.
One who has seen the Truths is a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*) because they have already seen them previously.
That which is contrary to this is neither-a-learner-nor-a-non-learner (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, the learner (*śaikṣa*) abandons two types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*), namely, the seeking of sensual desire (*kāma-paryeṣaṇā*) and the seeking of existence (*bhava-paryeṣaṇā*).
One trains to abandon two types of seeking and fulfills one type of seeking, namely the seeking for the holy life (*brahmacarya*); this is the training of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
One does not train to abandon two types of seeking because they have already been abandoned;
one does not train to fulfill one type of seeking because it has already been fulfilled; thus, this is the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.

Furthermore, if within one’s continuum there is the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions (*kleśa*), yet the untainted dharma (*anāsrava-dharma*) is also obtainable, then the abandonment of afflictions by a learner (*śaikṣa*) constitutes being a learner;
if within one’s continuum there is no acquisition of afflictions and the untainted dharma is obtainable, the non-learning abandonment of afflictions constitutes being a non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Furthermore, no untainted (anāsrava) dharma can be found apart from craving;
the learner’s abandonment of craving is what constitutes being a learner.

When one has already abandoned craving for existence and there are untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas to be attained, yet one does not train in the abandonment of craving, this is the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naivaśaikṣa-naivāśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, that which is subsumed under the path of seeing and the path of cultivation is "in training" (śaikṣa); that which is subsumed under the path of no-more-learning is "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
The same explanation applies to the three stages and the three faculties.
Furthermore, those untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) which can be found within the persons of five types are "in training" (*śaikṣa*). These five types of persons are:

the one of steadfast faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), the one of steadfast dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the one liberated through faith (*śraddhāvimukta*), the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), and the one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*); these are those in training.
If untainted dharmas are found within the persons of these two types, they are those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
These two types of persons are the one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) and the one liberated independent of time (*asamayavimukta*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Furthermore, if uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas are obtainable within the persons of the seven [types of] individuals, these are learners (*śaikṣa*).
The seven individuals refer to those in the four stages of approach (*pratipannaka*) and those abiding in the three fruits (*phalastha*).
If untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) can be found within the body of a single person, that person is one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
A "single person" here refers to one who abides in a single fruit (*eka-phala*).
That which is contrary to this is neither-in-training-nor-beyond-training (*naiva-śaikṣa-naivāśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, if untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are obtainable within the bodies of those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), they are "of the training"; if untainted phenomena are obtainable within the bodies of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are "beyond training. That which is contrary to these is "neither of the training nor beyond training" (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*).
Three categories of phenomena:
phenomena to be abandoned by the path of seeing, phenomena to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, and phenomena not to be abandoned.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned by the path of seeing?
Answer: If a dharma is abandoned through firm faith, firm practice of the Dharma,
and the various patiences, what is that?

Answer: The eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), along with their associated factors (*saṃprayuktadharma*) and the co-arising factors that originate from them, are called the factors abandoned through the path of seeing.
What are the phenomena to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path? Answer:
Those phenomena which are abandoned by one who has seen the tracks of training through the cultivation of the path.
What are these? The answer is:

the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanāmārga*), as well as the factors associated with them, the bodily and vocal actions arising from them along with their co-arising factors, and non-defiled outflowing factors (*sāsrava-dharma*); these are called the factors abandoned through the cultivation of the path.
What are the dharmas that are not to be abandoned? Answer:
The untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.

Question: For what reason are they called dharmas abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*), and dharmas not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)? Answer:
The detailed exposition is as above.
The Four Truths are:
the truth of suffering, the truth of the origin, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path.
Question: For what purpose is this treatise composed? Answer:
This is the Buddha’s sūtra.
The Buddha’s sūtra teaches the Four Noble Truths, from the truth of suffering up to the truth of the path.
Although the Buddha’s sūtra speaks of the Four Noble Truths, it does not analyze them in detail.
The Buddhist sūtras are the fundamental basis for this treatise; now, desiring to provide a detailed analysis of them, this treatise is composed.
Question: What is the essential nature of the Truths (satya)?
The answer is:
The Abhidharma states as follows:

the five aggregates of clinging are the truth of suffering; contaminated causes are the truth of origination; analytical cessation is the truth of cessation; and the dharmas of those in training and those beyond training are the truth of the path.
The Dārṣṭāntikas explain it as follows:

name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the truth of suffering; afflictions and karma are the truth of origination; the exhaustion of afflictions and karma is the truth of cessation; and concentration and wisdom are the truth of the path.
The Vibhajyavādins maintain this position:
the eight aspects of suffering are both suffering and the Truth of Suffering, while other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are suffering but not the Truth of Suffering;

craving for future existence (*punarbhava-tṛṣṇā*) is both origination and the Truth of Origination, while other forms of craving and other contaminated phenomena are origination but not the Truth of Origination.

The exhaustion of craving for existence after rebirth is cessation; it is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*). The exhaustion of other cravings and other tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) is cessation, but not the truth of cessation.

The eightfold path of training (*śaikṣa-aṣṭāṅga-mārga*) is the path; it is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). Other phenomena of training and all phenomena beyond training (*aśaikṣa-dharma*) are the path, but not the truth of the path.
If it is as you have said, then an Arhat accomplishes two truths—namely, the truth of suffering and the truth of cessation—but does not accomplish the truth of origination. Why is this so?
The craving for future existence is the Truth of Origination, because the Arhat has already abandoned the craving for future existence.
He does not possess the Truth of the Path; why is this so?
They assert that the eight factors of the path in training constitute the Truth of the Path, because they have already been abandoned at the time an Arhat attains the fruit.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:

"Whether they belong to one's own aggregates or to the aggregates of another, whether they are included among the category of sentient beings or not, all such things are suffering and the Truth of Suffering."
When the practitioner perceives suffering, they perceive it as the suffering of their own body, not the suffering of another's body, nor that which does not belong to the category of sentient beings.

Why is this so? Because the meaning of "suffering" is the sense of being oppressed; since the suffering of another's body or that which is not of the category of sentient beings is not oppressive, it is not [what is meant by] suffering.
For this reason, the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* states as follows:
"Suffering that afflicts one's own body does not arise from suffering in another's body, nor does it afflict without being caused by one's own or another's body."
If there were no self-body, what would be oppressed by the suffering of another’s body or by the suffering of that which is not classified as a sentient being?

If the cause of suffering within one's own body, and the causes of suffering—whether classified as sentient beings or not—within another’s body, constitute "origination," then this is the Truth of Origination.

When the practitioner contemplates origination, they perceive the cause of suffering within their own person, but do not perceive the cause of suffering in the persons of others, nor do they perceive the cause of suffering in that which is not included among the category of sentient beings.

Whether it be the exhaustion of suffering within one's own person, the exhaustion of suffering within the persons of others, or the exhaustion of suffering in both the category of sentient beings and that which is not the category of sentient beings—this is cessation; this is the Truth of Cessation.

When the practitioner perceives cessation, they perceive it as cessation within their own body, not as the cessation of another's body, nor as the cessation of that which is not included among sentient beings.

Whether it be the counteractive agent of one's own body, or that of another's body, or the counteractive agent of what is included among sentient beings or what is not included among sentient beings—this is the Path; this is the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).

When a practitioner perceives the Path, they perceive the path of antidote within their own person, not within another’s person, nor the path of antidote belonging to that which is not reckoned as a sentient being (*asattvasaṃkhyāta*). The Abhidharmikas state:

whether it be suffering in one's own person, suffering in another's person, or suffering in that which is reckoned as a sentient being or not reckoned as a sentient being—when the practitioner perceives suffering, they perceive all such suffering.
Question: When a practitioner perceives suffering, they perceive it as a pressing and urgent suffering.
Suffering within the bodies of others, as well as suffering not categorized among sentient beings, is not pressing; why, then, does the practitioner perceive them when perceiving suffering?
The answer is:
Although that suffering is not immediately oppressive, it is a point of delusion where wisdom should arise;
it is a point of doubt where certainty should arise.
Furthermore, regarding this point of censure, one should give rise to faith and reverence.
Who could say that the suffering within another's body— the suffering not categorized as a sentient being— is not oppressive?
If one is struck by another, is that not oppressive?
If wood or stones fall from the sky onto one’s body, is that not oppressive?

Whether it be caused by the aggregates (skandhas) of one's own body, the aggregates of another's body, or the aggregates of sentient or non-sentient beings—all such causes are collectively "origination" (samudaya), and this is the Truth of Origination. When the practitioner perceives origination, they perceive all of these as origination.

Whether it be the exhaustion of suffering within one's own body, or the exhaustion of suffering in the bodies of others, or among sentient beings and non-sentient things—this is cessation; this is the truth of cessation. When the practitioner perceives cessation, they perceive this cessation in its entirety.

Whether it be the aggregates of one's own body as an antidote, or the aggregates of another's body, or those belonging to sentient beings or non-sentient things, when these are exhausted through their respective antidotes, this is the Path; this is the Truth of the Path. When the practitioner perceives the Path, they perceive this Path in its entirety.
"This is the essential nature of the truths," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the reason for its essential nature, we shall now explain why it is called "truth" (*satya*).
What is the meaning of "truth"?
Answer: The meaning of "reality" (satya) is the meaning of "truth. The meanings of "thoroughness," "suchness," "non-perversion," and "non-alteration" are the meanings of truth. Question:

If the meaning of "truth" (satya) consists in being real, being examined, being as-it-is, being non-erroneous, and being non-different, then why are space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) not also established as truths? For they too possess the qualities of being real, up to and including being non-different.
Answer: If a phenomenon is suffering, the cause of suffering, the cessation of suffering, or the remedy for suffering, it is established as a Truth (satya).
Space and analytical cessation are neither suffering, nor the cause of suffering, nor the cessation of suffering, nor the remedy for suffering; therefore, they are not established as Truths.
As with suffering, so too it is when speaking of the aggregates (*skandha*), illness, an abscess, an arrow, a calamity, and a heavy burden.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is like this shore, the other shore, a river, or a raft, it is established as a Truth (*satya*);
since space and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) are neither this shore, nor the other shore, nor a river, nor a raft, they are not established as Truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon is suffering, the cause of suffering, the path, or the fruit of the path, it is established as a Truth (satya).
Space and analytical cessation are the opposite of these; therefore, they are not established as Truths.
Furthermore, if a phenomenon possesses both cause and fruit, it is established as a Truth (satya);
because space (ākāśa) and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) lack cause and fruit, they are not established as Truths.

Furthermore, because space and analytical cessation are untainted (anāsrava), they are not the Truths of Suffering or Origination; because they are indeterminate (avyākṛta), they are not the Truth of Cessation; and because they are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they are not the Truth of the Path.

Furthermore, because this dharma does not function within the world, the three truths are not established; because it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is not established.
Furthermore, because this dharma is not an aggregate (*skandha*), the three truths are not established; because it is not wholesome (*kuśala*), the truth of cessation is not established.

Furthermore, because this dharma does not accompany the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), the three truths are not established; because it is not wholesome (*kuśala*), the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is not established.

Furthermore, if a dharma were to be established as a truth by being the object (*ālambana*) of false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) or untainted right view (*anāsrava-samyag-dṛṣṭi*), this dharma is not the object of false view or untainted right view, and therefore it is not established as a truth.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is established as a Truth (satya) because it serves as an object-condition for ignorance (avidyā), this phenomenon is not established as a Truth because it does not serve as an object-condition for ignorance.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon is established as a Truth because its essence is the departure from afflictions (kleśa), this phenomenon is not established as a Truth because it is not the departure from afflictions.

Furthermore, if a phenomenon can produce revulsion, renunciation, and sympathetic joy, it is established as a Truth (*satya*); because this phenomenon cannot produce revulsion, renunciation, and sympathetic joy, it is not established as a Truth.
Question: If the meaning of "Truth" is that which is non-erroneous, then that which is erroneous should not be subsumed under the category of Truth.
Why is this? Because its nature is that of perversion.
He replied:
Perversion is established on account of certain factors, while being subsumed under the truths on account of other factors.
Perversion is established by way of three factors:
first, its active engagement, because it is intense;...
The second is false;
the third is exclusively inverted.
Because these dharmas possess a real intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the category of truths.
Furthermore, to conceive the impermanent as permanent, suffering as happiness, the impure as pure, and the non-self as self constitutes inversion.
Because these phenomena possess causes and effects, they are subsumed within the Truths.
Question: If the meaning of "not different" constitutes the meaning of "truth," then false speech should not be subsumed under truth. Why is this so?
False speech is so called because one utters words different from the truth with the intent to deceive another.
The answer is:
false speech is established on account of one matter, yet it is subsumed under the category of truth on account of another matter.
False speech is established because one deceives others with words that differ from reality; since it possesses substantial existence, it is subsumed under the truths.
Furthermore, false speech is established by claiming to have seen what was not seen, heard what was not heard, known what was not known, and cognized what was not cognized.
Because this dharma possesses both cause and fruit, it is subsumed under the category of truth (*satya*).
Therefore, the meaning of "real" (*bhūta*) is the meaning of "truth," and so forth, as explained at length.
[The opponent] asks:
How are the Four Noble Truths established?
Is it by way of their essential nature, or by way of cause and effect, or by way of the time of their realization?
If they were established by way of their essential nature, there would be only three truths.
Why is this so? Without suffering there is no origin, and without origin there is no suffering; cessation is the second truth, and the path is the third truth.
If one considers them in terms of cause and effect, there ought to be five truths:
Suffering can be called both cause and effect; the Path can also be called both cause and effect; Cessation is the fifth.
If one considers them from the perspective of the time of their realization, there should be eight truths:
the practitioner first perceives the suffering of the desire realm, and subsequently perceives that of the form and formless realms.
First one sees the causes and conditions of the formations of the desire realm, and subsequently those of the form and formless realms;
first one sees the cessation of the formations of the desire realm, and subsequently those of the form and formless realms;
first one sees the path that serves as the antidote to the formations of the desire realm, and subsequently those of the form and formless realms.
Answer: It should be stated thus:
the Truths are established by way of cause and effect.
Question: If that is so, there ought to be five truths. Answer:
Because they are explained collectively, there are not five separate truths or paths.
Whether cause or fruit, they are collectively termed "suffering" (*duḥkha*); cessation and the path are collectively termed the "exhaustion of birth, aging, sickness, and death. Question:
Whether it be the cause or the fruit of suffering, it is also the path of the accumulation of suffering and the path of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
The answer is:
because the modes of practice differ.
Regarding the meaning of suffering having a fruit, one practices four modes of contemplation: namely, suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self.
Regarding the meaning of suffering having a cause, one practices four modes of contemplation: namely, cause, origin, existence, and condition.

The Path also possesses the sense of cause and the sense of fruit. Regarding the sense of fruit: it consists of practicing one kind of fourfold practice, namely, the path (*mārga*), suchness (*tathatā*), the track (*padavyañjana*), and the vehicle (*yāna*).
Furthermore, the Four Noble Truths are established by virtue of three factors: first, by way of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); [the others being]...
Second, by means of cause and effect;
third, by means of generating faith through refutation.
Regarding their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the essential nature of the Four Truths consists of both the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).
Regarding cause and effect: the nature of that which is with outflows (sāsrava) possesses both cause and effect.
That which has an effect is the Truth of Suffering (duḥkhasatya); that which has a cause is the Truth of Origination (samudayasatya).
The nature of that which is without outflows (anāsrava) likewise possesses both cause and effect, as well as cases where there is an effect but no cause.
That which possesses both cause and fruit is the Truth of the Path; that which possesses fruit but lacks cause is the Truth of Cessation. Question:
For what reason is that which has the nature of being outflowing (sāsrava) and possesses fruit established as one Truth, while that which possesses cause is established as another Truth?
Is the uncontaminated essence established as a single truth because it possesses both cause and fruit?
The answer is:
It is so that by refuting [false views], faith may arise.
The essential nature of the outflows gives rise to two kinds of denial: claiming that there is no suffering and no origin;
and it gives rise to two kinds of faith: claiming that there is suffering, an origin, and a path.
Furthermore, regarding both cause and fruit, it gives rise to one kind of denial: claiming that there is no path.
One gives rise to a single kind of faith, saying that the Path exists.
For these three reasons, the Four Truths are established.
Furthermore, they are established as the Four Noble Truths by virtue of the time when the truths are seen.
Question: If that were so, there should be eight truths. Answer:
Whether it be suffering of the desire realm or suffering of the form and formless realms, when seeing suffering, one contemplates it through the four aspects, beginning with "suffering.

Whether it be the cause of formations in the desire realm or the cause of formations in the form and formless realms, when seeing the origin, one contemplates it through the four aspects, beginning with "origin."

When the formations of the desire realm cease, or the formations of the form and formless realms cease, at the time of seeing their cessation, these are collectively the four aspects beginning with cessation (*nirodha*).

When the antidotes to the formations of the desire realm arise, or the antidotes to the formations of the form and formless realms arise, at the time of seeing the path, these are collectively the four aspects beginning with the path (*mārga*).
Therefore, because one practices them collectively at the time of seeing the truths, there are only four truths and not eight.
Question: What are the characteristics of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path?
The Venerable Paśya said:

"The characteristic of oppression is the characteristic of suffering; the characteristic of existence is the characteristic of origination; the characteristic of tranquility is the characteristic of cessation; and the characteristic of proceeding is the characteristic of the path."
The Venerable Sūmī said: The characteristic of transformation is the characteristic of suffering;

the characteristic of being able to transform is the characteristic of origination; the characteristic of cessation is the characteristic of extinction; and the characteristic of abiding in transformation is the characteristic of the path.

Furthermore, the transformation of the body of existence is the characteristic of suffering; that which can transform the body of existence is the characteristic of origination; the exhaustion of the transformation of the body of existence is the characteristic of cessation; and proceeding toward the transformation of the body of existence is the characteristic of the path.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "The entities that constitute the truths are called the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
Their substance is like heated iron that, having been long in contact with fire, has become the same color as the fire."
The three types of suffering combined with the five aggregates of clinging are likewise thus; this is the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Karma arising from afflictions that causes cyclic existence is the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*).
When afflictions and karma are destroyed and one no longer undergoes further existence, this is the Truth of Cessation.
To cultivate ethical discipline and meditative concentration, and to observe arising and ceasing with wisdom so as to be able to sever the causes of existence, this is the Truth of the Path.
A verse in the Buddhist scriptures says:
"There is but one truth, not two; yet sentient beings harbor doubts regarding it.
They propound various truths, and thus no true śramaṇa is found among them."
Question: There are four truths; for what reason is one truth taught?
Venerable Vaśa replied:
The single truth refers to the truth of suffering; there is no second truth of suffering.
There is one truth of origination; there is no second truth of origination.
There is one truth of cessation; there is no second truth of cessation.
There is one truth of the path, and no second truth of the path.
Furthermore, the "one truth" refers to the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), because it stands in contrast to the various forms of liberation imagined by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Those non-Buddhists postulate various types of liberation:
There is liberation of the formless body, liberation of the boundless mind, liberation of the pure aggregate, and mundane liberation.

Liberation of the formless body is the sphere of infinite space; liberation of the boundless mind is the sphere of infinite consciousness; liberation of the pure aggregate is the sphere of nothingness; and mundane liberation is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"This is the locus of receiving a body, not liberation;
true liberation is solely the extinction of nirvana."
Furthermore, the "one truth" refers to the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), as it stands in contrast to the various paths [proclaimed by others].

Non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) postulate many kinds of paths, namely: the path of not eating food, the path of lying on ashes, the path of serving the sun and moon, the path of eating wind or fruit, the path of nakedness, the path of lying on thorns, and the path of wearing tattered rags.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"This is not the path; this is a false path, a path upon which virtuous persons do not rely.
The true path is the Noble Eightfold Path."
Furthermore, there is one truth, namely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), because it can bring an end to the suffering of the body.
There is another single truth, namely the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), because it can bring an end to the suffering of the evil realms.
The Buddhist scriptures speak of two truths, namely the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Question: What is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
and what is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)?

Answer: Some say that two of the truths belong to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), namely the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) and the truth of the origin [of suffering] (*samudaya-satya*). Why is this so?
Because worldly phenomena are contained within these two truths,
just as the coming and going of men and women and all present activities are entirely contained therein.
The two truths are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), namely the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that three truths are conventional truths—namely, the truths of suffering, origin, and cessation.
Why is this? Because the Buddha taught that the truth of cessation is a provisional designation, as it is the city of the further shore.
The one truth is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), namely the truth of the path (mārga-satya).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the truth of the path is also conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya). Why is this so?
The Buddha said that the Truths of the Path are also mere designations, just like the terms "śramaṇa" and "brāhmaṇa.
The commentary states:
One should speak as follows:
