Just as a gatekeeper does not allow others to enter, so it is with this.
Furthermore, in order to counteract these phenomena, the practitioner cultivates the path of the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, because the practitioner abhors this dharma, they completely abandon the first dhyāna.
Moreover, because this dharma does not exist in the higher stages and is therefore not practiced there,
for these reasons the Buddha taught the cessation of vitarka and vicāra.
"Internal faith" (*adhyātma-śraddhā*) means that "internal" refers to the mind and "faith" refers to the faculty of faith; because the mind has faith in this Dharma, it is called internal faith.
The Venerable Sthavira Saṃgharakṣita said:

"Applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) disturb the concentrated mind; if applied and sustained thought are extinguished, the mind becomes pure, and thus it is called internal purity (*adhyātma-prasāda*)."
Just as water is called "clear" when it is free from waves, so too is this the case.
Defiled joy causes the concentrated mind to become turbid; when that [joy] is extinguished, the mind becomes pure, just as turbid water is called "pure" when it becomes clear.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta said:

When a practitioner enters the second dhyāna, his mind of that dhyāna becomes expansive, characterized by faith and joy; he is able to endure it for a long time, delights in observing those dharmas, and his mind remains unmoving, dwelling in one place.
There is this locus and there is this essential nature: "I have attained the mind of the second dhyāna.
As for "abiding in one place," it is because the mind operates solely within a single gateway.

The mental activities of the desire realm operate through six doors; those of the first dhyāna operate through four doors; and those of the second dhyāna operate through one door; therefore, it is said that the mind abides in a single place.
"Without applied thought and sustained thought" means that applied and sustained thought have already ceased.
Regarding "born of concentration," a question is asked:
Since the first dhyāna also possesses concentration, why is it said that the second dhyāna is "born of concentration" while the first dhyāna is not?
Answer: Because the clarity, purity, excellence, and subtlety of the second dhyāna-concentration surpass those of the first dhyāna-concentration.
Furthermore, within the second dhyāna, concentration arises from concentration, is nurtured by concentration, and manifests subsequent to concentration.
"Concentration" refers to the first dhyāna; this concentration of the first dhyāna is the "first concentration," which manifests immediately after an unconcentrated mind.
An "unconcentrated mind" refers to a mind belonging to the desire realm.

Furthermore, in the first dhyāna there are both concentrated and unconcentrated minds; there are inward-directed minds and outward-directed minds, which may take external phenomena as their object or internal phenomena as their object.
The second dhyāna is characterized solely by concentration, solely by an inward-directed mind, and solely by taking internal phenomena as its object.
Furthermore, the second dhyāna extinguishes the root of sound.
The root of sound refers to applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), as it is said:
One who possesses vitarka and vicāra is able to produce vocal sounds; this does not occur in the absence of vitarka and vicāra.
Furthermore, in the second dhyāna, such things do not exist.
Moreover, the second dhyāna is described as the "noble silence" (ārya-tūṣṇīmbhāva).
As the Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Do not despise the second dhyāna; this is the noble silence of the sages.
For this reason, he spoke of the second dhyāna-concentration and did not speak of the first dhyāna.
Regarding "joy and bliss": joy is the faculty of joy (*somanassindriya*), and bliss is the bliss of tranquility (*passaddhisukha*).
Furthermore, joy is subsumed under the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), while bliss is subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

One who enters the second dhyāna, having attained and accomplished the five wholesome aggregates of the second dhyāna, is said to have "entered the second dhyāna," being "detached from joy and dwelling in equanimity," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: Just as when one is detached from the desire of the second dhyāna, one is entirely detached from all phenomena of the second dhyāna,
why does the World-Honored One speak only of detachment from joy (*prīti*)?
Answer: As the Buddha said, "being detached from joy," one should know that this already describes the method for departing from the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is because joy is difficult to sever, difficult to eliminate, and difficult to transcend.
Furthermore, because joy (*prīti*) is heavy and possesses many faults;
furthermore, when this dharma is separated from craving for the second dhyāna, it frequently creates obstacles, preventing the continuity of the dharma that leads to the departure from desire.
Just as a gatekeeper prevents others from entering, so too is this [the case].
Furthermore, in order to counteract these phenomena, the practitioner cultivates the path of the three dhyānas.
Furthermore, because the practitioner detests this dharma, he completely abandons the second dhyāna.
Moreover, this dharma does not exist in the higher stages and is therefore not practiced there.
For these reasons, the Buddha taught that one dwells in equanimity, detached from joy.
Regarding "one who possesses mindfulness and wisdom experiences pleasure with the body," "body" here refers to the mental body (*manokāya*).
Furthermore, when it is said that the mind experiences pleasure, it causes the physical body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to experience pleasure as well.
Regarding that which the noble ones have taught should be abandoned: what they have taught for others is that which should be abandoned by oneself.
Question: If all stages [of dhyāna] are entirely taught by the noble ones as things to be abandoned, why does the Buddha specifically state that only the third dhyāna should be abandoned?

Answer: Because the path of the third dhyāna contains many obstacles; there are obstacles from its own stage as well as obstacles from other stages. Regarding the obstacles from the paths of other stages:

the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna causes one to be overwhelmed and become flighty, just as a rākṣasa might cause a practitioner to regress from the desire for the state of detachment from the second dhyāna.

Regarding obstacles on the path of the stages: in the stage of the third dhyāna, there is the most supreme bliss among all births and deaths; because the practitioner gives rise to craving and attachment for it, they do not seek the dharmas of detachment belonging to the higher stages.
Therefore, those who teach the Path explain the points of obstruction for beginners.
On the path of the third dhyāna, there are many obstructions; namely, the joy (*prīti*) of the second dhyāna. You should cultivate right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*);
when you are detaching from the desire of the second dhyāna, do not be swept away by that joy.
Regarding the obstacles of one's own stage, this refers to the most excellent pleasure within all of birth and death.
You should eliminate attachment to it with right wisdom and seek the dharma of detachment belonging to the higher stages.
It is like a merchant who, for the sake of novice merchants who do not know the dangers of various regions, describes the obstacles they may encounter:

"In this city there are many brothels, gambling dens, drinking houses, and places of deception; you should keep far away from them, lest others deceive you and plunder your wealth until it is utterly exhausted."
It is the same for him as well.

One who dwells in mindfulness and delights in entering the third dhyāna, if they achieve the five aggregates of the wholesome third dhyāna, this is called "entering the third dhyāna by abandoning pleasure," and so forth, as explained at length.
Question: When one becomes detached from the desire of the third dhyāna, one completely abandons all dharmas of the third dhyāna.
Why, then, is it said that one only abandons pleasure?
Answer: As the Buddha taught the abandonment of pleasure, one should know that he has thereby already explained the method for abandoning the third dhyāna.
Furthermore, it is because pleasure is difficult to sever, difficult to eliminate, and difficult to transcend.
Furthermore, because this pleasure is heavy and possesses many faults;
furthermore, when this pleasure is separated from craving for the third dhyāna, it frequently creates obstacles that prevent the continuity of the factors for detachment.
Just as a gatekeeper does not allow others to enter, so it is with this.
Furthermore, in order to counteract these states, the practitioner cultivates the path of the fourth dhyāna concentration.
Furthermore, because the practitioner abhors this dharma, he completely abandons the third dhyāna.
Moreover, because this dharma does not exist in the higher stages, it is not practiced there.
For these reasons, the Buddha said: "Having abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain."
Question: When one becomes detached from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the practitioner has already severed the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
Why, then, is it said that the faculty of suffering is severed when one becomes detached from the desires of the third dhyāna?
The answer is:
In this context, that which has already been abandoned is called "abandoned," and that which is distant is called "near," just as one who has already arrived is said to be "arriving.
As it is said:
"Great King, from where have you come?
"He has already come; that is what is meant by 'come'.
Herein, it is said that "having already come" is called "come"; the rest is explained in detail as above.
This is also like that: what has been severed is called "severed," and what is distant is called "near.
Furthermore, it is because the paired dharmas (*yuganaddha-dharma*) are said here to be ultimately severed.
Suffering and pleasure are a pair; although suffering and pleasure are severed at the time one becomes free from desire and craving, pleasure is not ultimately severed.
Having become detached from the desire for the third dhyāna, one completely abandons pleasure (*sukha*).

Furthermore, that which abandons pleasure is the pleasure of the third dhyāna; that which abandons suffering (*duḥkha*) refers to the primary mind and its associated mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) associated with it.
Furthermore, the "abandonment of pleasure" refers to the third dhyāna; the "abandonment of suffering" refers to the inhalation and exhalation of breath in the third dhyāna.
To the noble ones, the perception of suffering arising from inhalation and exhalation is more intense than the suffering experienced by ordinary worldlings in the Avīci Hell.
Furthermore, the "abandonment of pleasure" refers to the bliss of the third dhyāna, while the "abandonment of suffering" also refers to the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
As it is said:
"Because it is impermanent, it is suffering."

Regarding the phrase "first extinguishing sorrow and joy": when one is detached from sensual desire, the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is extinguished; when one is detached from the desire of the second dhyāna, the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) is extinguished. Therefore, it is said that "sorrow and joy are first extinguished."
Regarding "neither-painful-nor-pleasant," it is said to be neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Regarding "feeling equanimity," it is said to be the practice of equanimity.
Regarding "pure mindfulness," he asks:
The untainted mindfulness (*anāsrava-smṛti*) of the lower stages is also pure; why then is it said that the mindfulness of the fourth dhyāna alone is pure?
The answer is:

the mindfulness of the fourth dhyāna is called pure because it is free from eight factors—namely, suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), and inhalation and exhalation.
Furthermore, that mindfulness is free from internal and external obstacles.

In the three lower dhyānas, there are internal and external obstacles: in the first dhyāna, the internal obstacle is the fire-like vitarka and vicāra, while the external obstacle is being burned by fire;
in the second dhyāna, the internal obstacle is the water-like prīti, while the external obstacle is being swept away by water.
The internal obstacles of the third dhyāna are like the inhalation and exhalation of breath; the external obstacles are being dispersed by the wind.
In the fourth dhyāna, there are no internal or external obstacles.
Furthermore, because mindfulness is not lost in the fourth dhyāna,
whereas the third dhyāna is subject to calamities and mindfulness therein is subject to loss;
since mindfulness in the fourth dhyāna is not affected by calamities, there is no loss of mindfulness.
Furthermore, because there are those who are without afflictions but have suffering,

those who have mindfulness but have afflictions yet no suffering, those who have mindfulness and are without both afflictions and suffering, and those who have mindfulness and possess both afflictions and suffering.
That which is without affliction but possesses suffering refers to untainted mindfulness within the third dhyāna.
That which is without suffering but possesses affliction refers to tainted mindfulness within the fourth dhyāna.
That which is neither afflicted nor suffering refers to untainted mindfulness within the fourth dhyāna.
That which possesses defects and afflictions refers to the tainted mindfulness (*sāsrava-smṛti*) within the third dhyāna as well as the mindfulness pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, because its basis is pure:
the body that serves as the basis for the fourth dhyāna is luminously pure, like the light of a lamp; and because its basis is luminously pure, that mindfulness is also luminously pure.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is the basis of fulfillment, the most excellent ground among all bases, and the dharma for reaching the other shore.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is the central basis, just as there are three stages of outflow-free (anāsrava) states above it and three stages of outflow-free states below it.
Furthermore, the fourth dhyāna is the universal basis for the immovable concentration (*āniñjya-samādhi*).
Moreover, the fourth dhyāna is extensive in two respects: first, it is extensive in its locus;
second, it is extensive in its roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Furthermore, in the fourth dhyāna stage, bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges attain right determination and realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
All bodhisattvas rely entirely upon the fourth dhyāna to attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Furthermore, practitioners of the three types of vehicles all rely upon the fourth dhyāna to enter right determination, attain the fruit, and exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).
The three types of practitioners refer to the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
Furthermore, it is because the four great elements of the fourth dhyāna are most excellent and its form and color are most excellent.
Furthermore, within the fourth dhyāna, the knowledge that recollects past lives can take as its object everything from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna itself.
For such reasons, the Buddha taught that the mindfulness in the fourth dhyāna is called "pure."
Regarding one who enters the fourth dhyāna: if they achieve the five aggregates of the wholesome fourth dhyāna, this is called entering the fourth dhyāna.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"The faculty of sorrow is extinguished by the first dhyāna; the faculty of suffering is extinguished by the second dhyāna."

Question: Since both faculties are extinguished at the time one becomes detached from desire, why does the Buddha say that the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is extinguished in the first dhyāna and the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is extinguished in the second dhyāna?
Answer: The Buddha taught the dharma of transcendent counteractives (*atikrāntapratipakṣa*).
Although suffering is abandoned when one becomes free from the desires of the desire realm, that counteractive is not called "transcendent."
If one is separated from the desire for the first dhyāna at the time of its antidote, that antidote is called "transcendence. Who is this antidote?
The answer is:
The first dhyāna is such.
Furthermore, herein the nature of its defects is explained:
although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is severed at the time of detachment from sensual desire, one does not transcend its underlying nature.
What is its nature?
The answer is:
it is the aggregate of consciousness.
Furthermore, herein the basis for the aforementioned [distinction] is explained:
when one is free from desire for the realm of sensuality (*kāmadhātu*), although the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is severed, one does not transcend its basis;
when one is free from desire for the first dhyāna, one transcends its basis.
Who is the basis? The answer is: it is the collection of consciousnesses.
Furthermore, it is stated herein that vitarka and vicāra are suffering.
The noble ones conceive of vitarka and vicāra as suffering even more intensely than sentient beings endure the sufferings of hell.
As the Buddha’s sūtra says:

"Kuṇḍadhāna, you should know that these four superior mental states certainly bring about happiness in the present life; a bhikkhu practicing meditation should know how to enter them and how to emerge from them.
Kuṇḍadhāna, you should know that these four formless, peaceful liberations are what a bhikkhu practicing meditation should explain to others."
Question: For what reason is it said that for the dhyānas one "knows," while for the formless attainments (ārūpya) one "should explain them to others"? Answer:
Because dhyāna is a coarse, manifest, and clearly perceived phenomenon, the practitioner of dhyāna may arise from it and then desire to enter it again.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"If you wish to enter, you may do so at will."

The formless attainments are subtle, not easily perceived, and not clearly understood; thus, when a practitioner of meditation arises from a formless attainment, they may have no desire to enter it again.
The Buddha spoke thus:
"If you do not wish to enter it again, you should explain to others the method for emerging from and entering concentration, lest you forget this dharma."
Furthermore, because dhyāna possesses various dissimilar qualities,
a practitioner of dhyāna, having emerged from it, may wish to enter it again.
Thus the Buddha spoke:
If you wish to enter, enter as you please.

In the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are no diverse or dissimilar phenomena; thus, once a practitioner of meditation has emerged, they may have no desire to re-enter. For this reason, the Buddha spoke these words:
"If you do not wish to re-enter, you should explain to others the method for emerging from and entering into concentration, lest you forget this teaching."
Furthermore, because there are many merits and benefits within dhyāna, the practitioner of dhyāna may, after emerging from it, wish to enter once more; for this reason, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to enter, enter as you please."

The formless attainments do not possess many virtues or great benefits; thus, when a practitioner of dhyāna emerges from those attainments, they do not wish to enter them again. For this reason, the Buddha said:
"If you do not wish to enter them, you should explain them to others so that you do not forget or lose this Dharma."

Furthermore, regarding the dharma of the universal illumination of dhyāna, it can take its own stage as an object and also take the stages above and below as objects. When a practitioner of dhyāna has emerged and wishes to enter again, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to enter, enter according to your will."

The formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are not all-illuminating dharmas; they can take their own level as an object and also take higher levels as objects, but they cannot take lower levels as objects.
When a practitioner of dhyāna has arisen from that attainment and does not wish to enter it again, for this reason the Buddha spoke thus:
"If you do not wish to enter [it] again, you should explain it to others so that you do not forget this dharma."
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"The four dhyānas have four beneficial advantages, while the four formless attainments have one beneficial advantage. Question:
For what reason does the Buddha say that the four dhyānas have four beneficial advantages, while he says that the four formless attainments have only one beneficial advantage?
Answer: The various answers previously stated should be explained here in detail.
Furthermore, there are two differences.
The answer is:
first, because dhyāna has three types—namely, with vitarka and vicāra, without vitarka but with vicāra, and without vitarka or vicāra—there are four kinds of wholesome benefits.
The formless attainments possess only the absence of vitarka and vicāra; thus, they have one beneficial quality.

Second, because dhyāna possesses various faculties—namely, the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya)—it has four beneficial qualities.
In the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), there are no various faculties; there is only the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*). Therefore, there is one wholesome benefit.
Question: What is the distinction between the wholesome benefits of the dhyānas?
Answer: "Name" refers to differentiation; that is called dhyāna, and that is called wholesome benefit.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of dhyāna:
They are wholesome, defiled, or non-obscured neutral; however, the wholesome aids are exclusively wholesome.
Furthermore, dhyāna is either with outflows (sāsrava) or without outflows (anāsrava); the wholesome aids are exclusively without outflows.
Furthermore, dhyāna is associated with the realm of form (rūpadhātu) or dissociated from it, whereas wholesome benefit (kuśalārtha) is exclusively dissociated.

Furthermore, dhyāna is of the nature of training (śaikṣa), beyond training (aśaikṣa), or neither-training-nor-beyond-training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), whereas wholesome benefit is exclusively of the nature of training or beyond training.
Furthermore, dhyāna is [to be abandoned] by the path of seeing, by the path of cultivation, or not to be abandoned; wholesome benefit (*kuśalārtha*) is exclusively not to be abandoned.
This is the distinction between dhyāna and wholesome benefit.
As the Buddha’s sūtra says:
The four dhyānas are the couch.
Question: For what reason did the Buddha say that the four dhyānas are the couch?
Answer: Because it is a superior inclusion.
"Superior" means superior to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
"Compendium" means to gather all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, it is because it shows the place of rest for the noble ones who are weary of the path of birth and death;
just as one who is exhausted from traveling on a road finds rest by sitting upon a couch or seat.
In this way, the noble ones, weary of the path of birth and death, obtain rest by sitting upon the seat of the four dhyānas.
The Buddhist sūtras state:
"The four dhyānas are a cool breeze."
Question: For what reason does the Buddha say that the four dhyānas are a cool breeze? Answer:
Because it can eliminate and arrest the heat of afflictions and karma:
through the coolness of the first dhyāna, one arrests the heat of the afflictions and karma of the desire realm;
through the coolness of the second dhyāna, one arrests the heat of the first dhyāna.
By means of the coolness of the third dhyāna, one stops the heat of the second dhyāna;
by means of the coolness of the fourth dhyāna, one stops the heat of the third dhyāna.
Thus it is said in the Buddha’s sūtras:
The four dhyānas are food.
Question: For what reason do the Buddhist sūtras state that the four dhyānas are food?
Answer: It is for the sake of fulfilling the Dharma-body (dharmakāya).
For example, all food and drink from a village that is sent toward a city is for the purpose of nourishing the bodies of the people within that city.
All the roots of goodness within such meditative concentrations are for the purpose of nurturing the Dharma-body.
As the Buddha’s sutras state:
"O Brahmin, you should know that the fourth dhyāna is the ultimate path."
Question: For what reason does the Buddha reject the third dhyāna and declare the fourth dhyāna to be the ultimate path? Answer:

When that brahmin heard that the Buddha possessed all-knowing vision, and further heard that the Tathāgata had attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of the fourth dhyāna, and that he taught the fourth dhyāna to be the ultimate path, he thought to himself:
"If the śramaṇa Gautama teaches that the fourth dhyāna is the ultimate path, then he must certainly possess all-knowing vision."
He then proceeded to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, he inquired about this matter.
Knowing what was in his mind, the Buddha set aside the third dhyāna and taught that the fourth dhyāna is the ultimate path.
Having heard this, that person gives rise to a mind of certainty, thinking: "There must certainly exist a Brahmin who possesses all-knowing vision.
This is also called the conduct of the Tathāgata, and it is also called the Dharma manifested by the Tathāgata.

For example, when a wild elephant in the summer season sees the ground covered with lush, verdant grass and various lotus ponds, its heart leaps with joy; it digs into the earth with its tusks and then firmly plants its feet.
The Tathāgata is likewise; by means of the practice of equanimity within the four dhyānas, he excavates the ground of the knowable and establishes the feet of wisdom.
The path of the Tathāgata is that which abides in śamatha.
That which the Tathāgata practices is dwelling in vipaśyanā;
that which the Tathāgata manifests as practice is dwelling in both.
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:
The four dhyānas are abodes of bliss.
Question: For what reason did the Buddha say that the four dhyānas are abodes of bliss?
Answer: Because they are easy to produce as joy.
The fundamental dhyānas are joy because they are easy to produce; the various access concentrations and the formless attainments are suffering because they are difficult to produce.
What makes it difficult to be born [there]?
The answer is:
because one is bound by the afflictions and karma of the desire realm.

The *anāgamya-dhyāna* (preliminary concentration) is difficult to bring into manifestation; it is like a person whose hands are tightly bound behind their back, who must exert great effort before they can free themselves.

Likewise, because one is bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one must exert great effort for the path of that stage to arise and manifest. Some bring forth the path of that stage through the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), while others do so through mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*). Those who employ the contemplation of impurity [do so] as follows:
Some may practice the meditation on the white-bone contemplation for ten or twelve years, yet some are able to cause that stage to arise before them while others are not.

As for those who practice mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), they may constantly count the inhalations and exhalations for ten or twelve years, yet some are able to cause that stage to manifest before them while others are not.

Having already severed craving for sensual desire, without expending much effort, the first dhyāna arises and becomes manifest. One thought-moment ceases and another distinct thought-moment arises and becomes manifest; the coarse mind ceases and the subtle mind arises and becomes manifest; the mind accompanied by vitarka ceases and the mind accompanied by vicāra arises and becomes manifest.
It is like a person splitting wood with wood; much effort and exertion are required before it can finally be split.

In the same way, when the first dhyāna occurs, one mind ceases and another mind manifests; the coarse mind ceases and the subtle mind manifests; the mind accompanied by *vitarka* (applied thought) ceases and the mind accompanied by *vicāra* (sustained thought) manifests. That much effort and exertion are likewise required.
If one is free from desire for the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna arises and manifests before one without requiring much effort;
likewise, if one is free from desire for the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna arises and manifests;
and if one is free from desire for the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna arises and manifests—all in the same manner.

Question: If one leaves behind desire for the fourth dhyāna and brings the sphere of infinite space (ākāśāyatana) into manifestation, this likewise does not require much effort; why, then, is it not called the "path of ease" (sukha-mārga)?
The answer is:
because the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are subtle,
some say that there are no formless attainments.
Just as the householder Lāḷudāyin went to the Venerable Ānanda and spoke thus:

"I am a layperson who for a long night has delighted in and been attached to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; upon hearing the teaching on the formless attainments, my mind was struck with fear, as if standing at the edge of a deep pit."
How is it that sentient beings lack form?
Furthermore, it is because they experience pleasure while moving.
For example, suppose two people both wish to reach a certain destination; one travels by land and the other by water.
Although both reach the same destination, those who travel by water find joy, while those who travel by land find suffering.

Likewise, when boundless sentient beings attain freedom from desire, whether they rely on the fundamental dhyānas or on the various access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), although all have attained freedom from desire, those relying on the fundamental dhyānas find joy, while those relying on the access concentrations and formless attainments find suffering.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of pleasure within the realm of suffering: namely, the pleasure of sensation (*vedita-sukha*) and the pleasure of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).

Within the third dhyāna, there are these two kinds of pleasure; although the pleasure of sensation is absent in the fourth dhyāna, the pleasure of tranquility is extensively present and superior to the pleasure of sensation.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
first, the pleasure of those who have long resided [therein], and second, the pleasure of guests.
As for the pleasure of those who have long resided, it is like one dwelling in dhyāna when that dhyāna manifests before them.
As for "joy of guests," it is like when one dwelling in dhyāna brings forth the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) so that they manifest before one.
Furthermore, because within this [state] there can be found the joy of not harming sentient beings.
As it is said:
"If one does not afflict or harm others, this is called happiness.
Furthermore, when the fundamental dhyāna arises and manifests before one, the four great elements throughout the entire body become supple.
When the various preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) manifest, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the mind become supple and soft.

Furthermore, some say that when the various preparatory stages manifest, the four great elements of the entire body also become supple and soft, though not to the same extent as when the fundamental dhyānas (*mauladhyāna*) manifest.

For example, suppose two people bathe in the same pool: one remains at the edge while the other enters into it. Although both are bathing, the one who has entered into the water causes the four great elements to be more thoroughly moistened and nourished.
It is the same for that as well.
Furthermore, because two dharmas coexist in one place and arise together,
these two dharmas are concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
In the preparatory and intermediate dhyānas, wisdom is predominant and concentration is slight;
in the formless absorptions, concentration is predominant and wisdom is slight;
in the fundamental dhyānas, concentration and wisdom arise in equilibrium.
Furthermore, there are two factors that arise simultaneously.
These two factors are concentration (*samādhi*) and diligence (*vīrya*).
Although diligence is predominant in all stages, because of the power of the fundamental dhyānas, these two factors arise in equal measure when they manifest.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of abandonment:
that which requires much effort and that which does not require much effort.

If there is anything to be abandoned in the various access concentrations (*sāmantaka*) and formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), it requires much effort; if there is anything to be abandoned in the fundamental dhyānas (*maula-dhyāna*), it does not require much effort.

It is like two people riding horses who both arrive at the same destination; one rides a well-trained horse and the other rides an untrained horse. Although they both reach the same place, the one riding the well-trained horse exerts little effort, whereas the one riding the untrained horse exerts much effort.

When these sentient beings become detached from desire, they do so either by relying on the fundamental dhyānas or by relying on the various peripheral formless attainments. If they rely on the fundamental dhyānas, they do not require much effort; however, if they rely on the various peripheral formless attainments, they must exert much effort.
Furthermore, it is because one attains peace and happiness when practicing the path.

For example, it is like many people crossing a river; whether by means of a bundle of grass, an air-filled bag, a boat, or a ship, although they all cross from this shore to the other shore together, only those who cross by means of a ship do so with peace and happiness.
It is the same for that [attainment].
For these reasons, the Buddha’s sūtras state that fundamental dhyāna is a dwelling in happiness (*sukha-vihāra*).
As it is with dwelling in happiness, so it is with dwelling in contact (*sparśa-vihāra*) and dwelling in pleasant contact (*sukha-sparśa-vihāra*).
The four immeasurables are loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Question: For what reason are the immeasurables taught in the sequence following the dhyānas?
Answer: Because the immeasurables arise from within dhyāna.
Furthermore, because the immeasurables are secondary merits within dhyāna.
For this reason, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are explained following the dhyānas.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these immeasurables?

Answer: Compassion (*maitrī*) and loving-kindness (*karuṇā*) are the wholesome roots of non-ill-will (*avyāpāda*); they act as antidotes to ill-will and consist of the associated and co-existent factors that turn toward it.

Their essential nature consists of four aggregates (*skandha*) or five aggregates; those belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) consist of four aggregates, while those belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) consist of five aggregates.
Question: Both of these are the wholesome root of non-ill will (*avyāpāda*), which serves as an antidote to ill will (*vyāpāda*).
As for loving-kindness (*maitrī*), what kind of ill will does it counteract?
What kind of malice (*vyāpāda*) does compassion (*karuṇā*) counteract?
The answer is:
malice, which may consist of either the desire to kill sentient beings or the desire to strike sentient beings.
If one wishes to kill sentient beings out of anger, loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the antidote;
if one wishes to strike sentient beings out of anger, compassion (*karuṇā*) serves as the antidote.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of anger:
First, one becomes angry toward those who deserve anger; second, one becomes angry toward those who do not deserve anger.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) serves as the antidote for anger toward those who deserve it, while compassion (*karuṇā*) serves as the antidote for anger toward those who do not deserve it.
Joy is the faculty of joy (*somanasyendriya*); it takes as its object the associated and co-existent dharmas that revolve [with it].

Its substance consists of four aggregates (*skandha*) or five aggregates: in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) it consists of four aggregates, and in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) it consists of five aggregates.
Question: If the essence of joy (*prīti*) is the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*), how is one to reconcile this with what is stated in the *Prakaraṇa*? As it says:
What is joy (*prīti*)?
The answer is:

it consists of the feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) associated with joy, as well as the bodily and vocal actions (*kāya-vāk-karman*) arising from them, and the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) arising from them; this is called joy.
If one has already received [a precept], should one receive it again?
The answer is:
The text of the *Prakaraṇa* should state it as follows:
"Perception, mental formations, and consciousness associated with joy," and so forth, as explained at length;
"feeling" should not be mentioned therein. What is the intention behind its omission?
The answer is:
This is because the reciter has made an error.
Furthermore, the *Prakaraṇa* states:

"The essence of the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); although they are not associated with feeling (*vedanā*), they are associated with other enumerated factors (*dharmāḥ*)."
Furthermore, some say that joy has its own intrinsic nature; it is a mental factor (caitta) associated with the mind.
Others say that it is the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), which is found within the collection of mental factors.

Some say that this is the faculty of joy (*sukhendriya*), from which equanimity (*upekṣā*) subsequently arises; this is the wholesome root of non-attachment (*alobha*), which counteracts attachment and takes up the associated and co-existent dharmas of its turning back.
Its substance consists of four aggregates or five aggregates; in the desire realm it consists of four aggregates, while in the form realm it consists of five aggregates.
This is its immeasurable essential nature.
Having explained its essential nature, what are its characteristics?

Answer: The essential nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic is itself the essential nature; one cannot abandon the essential nature of all phenomena and speak of characteristics separately.
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:

The aspect of benefiting others is loving-kindness (*maitrī*); the aspect of removing what is not beneficial is compassion (*karuṇā*); the aspect of sympathetic joy is joy (*muditā*); and the aspect of relinquishment is equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Having already explained the essential characteristics of these immeasurables, I shall now explain why they are called "immeasurable."
What is the meaning of "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*)?
The answer is:
it is called immeasurable because it serves as the antidote to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Question: If the antidote to conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) is immeasurable, there are two kinds of conceptual proliferation:
first, the proliferation of craving (*tṛṣṇā-prapañca*), and second, the proliferation of views (*dṛṣṭi-prapañca*).
By what immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are which conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) countered? Answer:
The immeasurables cannot sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*); rather, one uses the immeasurables to counteract craving (*tṛṣṇā*), or one uses the immeasurables to counteract views (*dṛṣṭi*).
If one takes its direct antidote, compassion is the direct antidote to [wrong] views.
Why is this? Sentient beings who follow the path of views mostly delight in anger and hatred.
Generosity is the direct antidote to craving.
Why is this? Sentient beings who act out of craving mostly delight in mutual intimacy.
Furthermore, they are called "immeasurable" because they serve as antidotes to the dharma of heedlessness (*pramāda*).
Heedlessness consists of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
What is its direct antidote?
It refers to the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, it is called "joy" (*prāmodya*) because it is a place where the noble ones (*ārya*) sport;
just as a wealthy person has various places for recreation, such as gardens, parks, courtesans, and hunting, which are called places of joy.
It is likewise in this case.
As for the realms (*dhātu*), it exists within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

As for the stages (*bhūmi*), it is obtainable within the ten stages of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*); that is to say, within the four fundamental dhyānas, the preparatory stages of the dhyānas (*dhyānāntara*), the desire realm, and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
Joy exists in three stages: the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are those who say that compassion does not exist in the first or second dhyānas. Why is this?
The joy (*prīti*) of the first and second dhyānas is an attachment to its own level;
the faculty of joy (*prītīndriya*) functions as a state of elation, whereas sorrow (*daurmanasya*) functions as a state of dejection.
If there were sorrow in the first or second dhyāna, then within a single mental complex (*citta-kalāpa*), there would be both a state of elation and a state of dejection.
Question: Are there no untainted (anāsrava) practices of disenchantment in the first and second dhyānas?
Answer: [Yes].
The untainted practice of revulsion is the contemplation of reality; as one follows this contemplation of reality, joy arises in the mind. As joy arises, one desires to know further.
It is like a person digging the earth for the sake of treasure: as they dig, they obtain the treasure, and having obtained it, they desire to dig even more.
That too is likewise; it is not an empty contemplation.
The critique says:
one should speak thus:
The first dhyāna and the second dhyāna possess compassion (*karuṇā*).
Its basis is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). As for their practice:

loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is the practice of happiness; compassion is the practice of suffering; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the practice of rejoicing; and equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the practice of relinquishment.
As for "condition" (ālambana), it refers to conditions that take the desire realm, conditioned aggregates (saṃskāra), or sentient beings as their object.

Regarding the five aggregates and two aggregates of sentient beings in the desire realm: if one takes as an object sentient beings who abide within one's own mind, then one is taking the five aggregates as an object; if one takes as an object sentient beings who abide within the minds of others or those who are mindless, then one is taking the two aggregates as an object.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the immeasurables of the first dhyāna take the desire realm as their object;
the immeasurables of the second dhyāna take the desire realm and the first dhyāna as their objects;
and the immeasurables of the third dhyāna take the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna as their objects.
The immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna take as their objects the desire realm, the first, second, and third dhyānas.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the immeasurables of the first dhyāna take as their objects the desire realm and the first dhyāna, and so on, up to the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna taking as their objects the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, there are those who say that loving-kindness takes as its object the desire realm and the first, second, and third dhyānas.
Why is this? Because loving-kindness is a practice of bliss, and within the desire realm and the three dhyānas, there exists the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*).
Compassion takes the desire realm as its object. Why is this?
Because compassion involves the practice of suffering, and within the desire realm there is the experience of painful sensation (*duḥkhavedanā*).
Joy takes the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna as its objects.
Why is this? Because joy functions as the practice of rapture, and the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna possess the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
It relinquishes the objects of the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this? Because it is the practice of relinquishing and the practice of letting go, and because relinquishment exists from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
The commentary says:
It is better as stated previously.
The immeasurables take the desire realm, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), and sentient beings as their objects.
As for the foundations of mindfulness, they are all accompanied by the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
As for wisdom (*prajñā*), it is all accompanied by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
As for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is not accompanied by meditative concentration.

As for the faculties (*indriya*), they are collectively associated with three faculties, namely: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
As for the time periods (*adhvan*), these are the past, future, and present.

Regarding those conditioned by the three periods of time: those in the past are conditioned by the past; those in the present are conditioned by the present; and those in the future—whether they are destined not to arise or destined to arise—are both conditioned by all three periods of time.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object; the unwholesome and the indeterminate take all three types as their objects.
Regarding those bound to the three realms and those not so bound: these are bound to the desire realm and the form realm.
Regarding those conditioned by the three realms and those unconditioned: that which is conditioned by the desire realm pertains to the desire realm.
Regarding those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: these are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.

Those conditioned by what is in training (*śaikṣa*), what is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and what is neither in training nor beyond training, have as their object that which is neither in training nor beyond training.

Those [factors] abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya*), those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*), and those not to be abandoned (*aprahātavya*)—these are abandoned through the path of cultivation.

Regarding those [factors] abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and those not abandoned: they take as their object that which is abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Regarding those that take names (*nāman*) as their object and those that take meanings (*artha*) as their object: they take both as their object.
Regarding those that take one's own body, another's body, or that which is neither as their object: these take another's body as their object.

Regarding whether this is attained through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya-prāpta*) or attained through skillful means (*upāya-prāpta*): it is both attained through the abandonment of desire and attained through skillful means.

As for attainment through the abandonment of desire: one who abandons the desires of the desire realm attains the first dhyāna; one who abandons the desires of the first dhyāna attains the second dhyāna; one who abandons the desires of the second dhyāna attains the third dhyāna; and one who abandons the desires of the third dhyāna attains the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding those who attain the detachment from the four dhyānas, is this a new attainment or a former attainment? It is both a new attainment and a former attainment.
For a noble one (ārya) in their final existence and for ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), it is both a new attainment and a former attainment;
for other ordinary persons, it is only a former attainment.
Regarding those attained through skillful means (*upāya*), they manifest before one by virtue of such means.

The Buddha does not cause [the Dharma] to manifest through skillful means; the Pratyekabuddha causes it to manifest through inferior skillful means; and the Śrāvaka causes it to manifest through either middling or superior skillful means.
Question: How does one give rise to the immeasurables? Answer:

Regarding the generation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) based on the classification of beings as kin: when a practitioner wishes to arouse a mind of loving-kindness, they categorize all sentient beings into three groups:
first, those who are kin; second, those who are enemies; and [third, those who are neutral].
Third, there is the category of those who are neither friends nor enemies.
Furthermore, the category of friends is divided into three types— namely, inferior, middling, and superior—
and the category of enemies is likewise divided in the same way.
Those who are neither kin nor enemies constitute only one category.

Within the category of superior kin, there are those to whom one owes a profound debt of gratitude, namely: parents, preceptors (upādhyāya), teachers (ācārya), and other venerable persons who are practitioners of pure conduct (brahmacārin) endowed with wisdom.
Regarding those sentient beings, one first forms a favorable view:
"May all these sentient beings attain happiness.

This mind is firm and difficult to subdue because, since beginningless time, one has constantly habituated oneself to an evil mind toward sentient beings; thus, even toward those sentient beings who have shown such profound kindness, one is still unable to cause a wholesome mind to abide.
Furthermore, one must forcibly turn this mind back and cause it to abide in that dharma.
It is like a person striking the point of an awl with a mustard seed; it is extremely difficult to keep it fixed there.
However, if one practices the striking without ceasing, it will eventually become stable.
It is the same for them as well.

If one can contemplate these superior kinsmen among sentient beings and cause them all to attain happiness, one next contemplates those who are middling kinsmen, and then those who are inferior kinsmen.

If one can first contemplate all those who are one's kin and cause them all to attain happiness, next contemplate those who are neither kin nor enemies, next contemplate those of lesser enmity, next contemplate those of middling enmity, and finally contemplate those of supreme enmity, wishing for them all to attain happiness.

If one can contemplate all sentient beings in this way, causing them all to attain happiness just as one does for one's superior kin, and regarding even those who are superior enemies without any distinction, then one has achieved success.
The same applies to loving-kindness, compassion, and sympathetic joy.
Equanimity arises toward sentient beings who are neither friends nor enemies. Why is this so?

Toward those who have been abandoned as kin, a mind of affection arises; toward those who have been abandoned as enemies, a mind of resentment arises. Therefore, one first abandons sentient beings who are neither kin nor enemies; next, one abandons minor enemies; next, one abandons middling enemies; and finally, one abandons major enemies.
Why is this? Because a mind of anger is easy to dispel, whereas a mind of affection is not.
Next, one abandons inferior relatives; next, one abandons middling relatives; next, one abandons superior relatives.
If one can cultivate such contemplation of equanimity toward all sentient beings, the mind will become impartial and free from discrimination, just like a scale.
Just as one views a forest without making distinctions, so too should one view all sentient beings; this is the accomplishment of the mind of equanimity.
Question: What kind of person is able to give rise to the immeasurables?
What kind of person is unable to give rise to the immeasurables?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of people:
first, those who delight in seeking out the faults of others; second, those who delight in seeking out the virtues of others.
If one delights in seeking out the faults of others, one cannot give rise to the immeasurables. Why is this?
Because such a person seeks out even the faults within the body of an Arhat.
What fault, what unreality, or what defilement exists that I should censure?
If one delights in seeking the virtues of others, then one can give rise to the immeasurable. Why is this so?
One seeks out even the slightest goodness in those who have severed their roots of virtue. Question:
Since those who have severed their roots of virtue possess no virtues whatsoever, how can one seek goodness in them?

Answer: Although there is no present goodness, there is the retribution of past wholesome karma, which causes one’s body to be upright and handsome, to be born into a noble clan, to possess majestic authority in speech, and to be learned and eloquent.
Perceiving such signs as these, one gives rise to wholesome thoughts:
"That conduct is excellent; it has such a fruit and retribution.
A question is asked:
Regarding these four immeasurables, do they arise exactly as described, or are they different from what was described?
The answer is:
some say they arise exactly as described.

Why is this so? Because the practitioner first desires to benefit sentient beings, and the mental state of benefiting sentient beings is loving-kindness (maitrī); therefore, the World-Honored One spoke of the mind of loving-kindness first.

Next, one eliminates that which is non-beneficial; this aspect of eliminating the non-beneficial is compassion (*karuṇā*). For this reason, the World-Honored One taught compassion immediately after loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

If one bestows benefit and eliminates the non-beneficial, joy subsequently arises; this aspect of joy is sympathetic joy (*muditā*). For this reason, the World-Honored One taught sympathetic joy immediately after compassion.
Next, one relinquishes sentient beings; this relinquishing aspect is "equanimity" (upekṣā). For this reason, the World-Honored One taught equanimity last.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the practitioner first gives rise to loving-kindness (maitrī), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā) while setting aside compassion (karuṇā), and subsequently gives rise to loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Why is this? First, one removes what is unbeneficial for sentient beings; afterwards, one bestows what is beneficial. Next, one gives rise to equanimity and joy;
finally, one gives rise to equanimity. The Venerable Saṅghapāla said:
These two immeasurables mutually govern one another;
if compassion arises first, joy must necessarily arise next. Why is this so?
Compassion (*karuṇā*) is sorrowful concern, while joy (*muditā*) is gladness.
If one first gives rise to joy, compassion will necessarily arise next. Why is this so?
Joy is agitation; compassion restrains it.
The critique says:
one should speak thus:
The immeasurables do not necessarily arise exactly as described. Why is this?

Among practitioners, some first give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and proceed up to equanimity (*upekṣā*), while others first give rise to equanimity and proceed up to loving-kindness; some may attain loving-kindness but not the others, and some may even attain equanimity but not the others.

There are immeasurable [attainments] following the direct order and reverse order, as well as the direct and reverse leaps; just as it is with the liberations, the bases of mastery, and the totalities, so too is it with these.
Question: Can compassion (maitrī) successively give rise to sorrow (karuṇā), joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā)?
Answer: Yes.
The *Samādhi-skandhaka* states:
"What is the mental recollection of the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*)? It answers:
The Joy of Sentient Beings...
and so on, up to: What is the samādhi of mental recollection of relinquishment?
The answer is:
Sentient beings abandon it.
Some say that this passage refers to co-nascent formations (*sahaja-saṃskāra*).
Others say it refers to formations as sequential conditions (*anantara-pratyaya-saṃskāra*).
If it is said that these arise simultaneously, then loving-kindness can sequentially give rise to compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
If it is said that they function as sequential conditions, then loving-kindness cannot sequentially give rise to compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Question: If one does not give rise to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of the first dhyāna stage, can one give rise to the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage?
And so on, up to: if one does not give rise to the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage, can one give rise to the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage?
Answer: Some say that it is not possible. Why is this so?

The immeasurables of the first dhyāna stage are the basis for the skillful means of the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage, and so on, up to the point that the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage are the basis for the skillful means of the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it is possible;
if a practitioner attains mastery over a particular stage, they can, by relying on that stage, bring forth immeasurable [attainments] into manifestation.
Question: Is it faster for one to be reborn in the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) of the second dhyāna stage after having been in the immeasurables of the first dhyāna stage?
And so on, up to being reborn in the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage after having been in the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage?
Is it faster for one to be reborn from the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage into the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage,
and so on down to the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage, than to be reborn from the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage into the immeasurables of the first dhyāna stage?
The answer is:

The immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage arise more swiftly than those of the first dhyāna stage; likewise, up to the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage, they arise more swiftly than those of the third dhyāna stage.

The immeasurable [state] of the non-first-dhyāna stage is not as swift as the immeasurable [state] of one subsequently born in the second-dhyāna stage; this continues up to the immeasurable [state] of the non-third-dhyāna stage, which is not as swift as the immeasurable [state] of one subsequently born in the fourth-dhyāna stage.
It is like a person who first studies the Brāhmī script and later studies the Khaṛoṣṭhī script quickly;
it is not the case that one who first studies the Khaṛoṣṭhī script and later studies the Brāhmī script learns it quickly. Question:
Can the immeasurables of the first dhyāna stage successively give rise to the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage?
And so on, up to whether the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage can successively give rise to the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage?

Answer: Some say that the immeasurables of the first dhyāna stage can successively produce the immeasurables of the second dhyāna stage, and so on up to the immeasurables of the third dhyāna stage, which successively produce the immeasurables of the fourth dhyāna stage.
Furthermore, there are those who say it is not possible.
Why is this? The immeasurables must necessarily rely on skillful means (*upāya*), and skillful means must necessarily be similar to that of one's own stage (*svabhūmi*).
Through skillful means, one arouses loving-kindness, up to and including equanimity.
There are three kinds of contemplation:
first, contemplation of specific characteristics;...
2. Contemplation of general characteristics;
3. Contemplation of empty characteristics.

As for contemplation of specific characteristics: it is like contemplating that earth has the characteristic of solidity, water has the characteristic of moisture, fire has the characteristic of heat, and wind has the characteristic of motion.
The contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is, for example, like the simultaneous contemplation of the sixteen noble practices (*ārya-prakāra*).

The contemplation of empty characteristics (*śūnya-lakṣaṇa*) is, for example, the simultaneous contemplation of the immeasurable aspects of impurity, mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*); among the three types of contemplation, this is the contemplation of empty characteristics.
Question: When a practitioner contemplates the happiness of sentient beings, by means of what kind of happiness does he cause them to be happy? Answer:
Some say it is by means of the bliss of the third dhyāna. Why is this?
Because the bliss of the third dhyāna is the most supreme bliss among all of saṃsāra.
If one were to say that without having arisen in the third dhyāna, one could not give rise to the immeasurable [state], there are others who say:

having previously attained the bliss of the third dhyāna in past lives, by means of the knowledge of recollecting past lives belonging to the level of the third dhyāna, one contemplates that bliss and causes sentient beings to experience bliss through that very bliss.
If one were to say this: if one does not attain the knowledge of recollecting past lives belonging to the stage of the third dhyāna, then one cannot give rise to the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*).

Furthermore, there are those who say that by means of the pleasures recently experienced—such as the pleasure of food and drink, the pleasure of riding, the pleasure of clothing, and the pleasure of bedding—one causes sentient beings to experience joy through such characteristics of pleasure.
The Venerable Sūmī said:
"By what kind of happiness does the practitioner cause sentient beings to be happy?
He replied:
If sentient beings possess happiness, then by means of such characteristics one causes those sentient beings to be happy.
If one were to speak in this way, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) would be unable to take all sentient beings as its object.
Why is this? It is because not all sentient beings necessarily possess happiness.
Furthermore, sentient beings possess the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); by means of such characteristics, they cause sentient beings to experience happiness.
If one were to speak in this way, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) would be unable to take all sentient beings as its object. Why is this?
Because it is not possible for the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) to manifest at all times for all sentient beings.

Furthermore, sentient beings possess the pleasure of food and drink, the pleasure of vehicles, the pleasure of clothing, and the pleasure of bedding; by means of such characteristics of pleasure, they cause sentient beings to experience joy.
If one were to speak in this way, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) would be unable to take all sentient beings as its object. Why is this?
Because it is not necessarily the case that all sentient beings can attain such happiness.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"One perceives happiness through what is known and seen, grasps such a sign, and causes sentient beings to be happy with a mind of compassion.
This is as when, during the time of original skillful means, one dwells either in dependence upon a village or in dependence upon a city."

During the forenoon, if he enters a city or village to beg for alms, he may see sentient beings experiencing pure pleasure, either traveling on elephants, horses, or carriages, or wearing earrings, pearl rings, or various necklaces to adorn their bodies, appearing just like the sons of gods.

Or one may see those who experience nothing but suffering, such as those without clothing or food and drink, with disheveled hair and cracked hands and feet, carrying broken ceramic vessels to beg from the houses of others.

Having grasped such signs of sentient beings experiencing pleasure and pain, he quickly returns to his dwelling to wash his feet. Seated upon his seat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), he makes his body and mind supple; with no obstruction in body and no obstruction in mind, he contemplates the previously grasped signs of those sentient beings who are happy, constantly ensuring they obtain happiness;
and for those sentient beings who are suffering, he ensures they obtain the happiness he previously beheld.
Question: Since not all sentient beings being observed actually attain happiness,
how is it that this contemplation is not a perversion?
Answer: Because it is wholesome, it is not a perversion.

It arises from a mind of benefit, from a wholesome mind, from a mind of compassion, and from a mind of correct contemplation; because it is associated with roots of goodness and associated with shame and remorse, it is not a perversion.
There are two kinds of inversion:
first, inversion of essence; second, inversion of object.
Although that contemplation is an inversion of object, it is not an inversion of essence.
The Venerable Sūmī said:
It is not by dwelling in loving-kindness that one brings happiness to sentient beings; rather, this dharma serves as a skillful means to restrain anger and sever the fetters.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
This contemplation should be called non-perverted. Why is that?
Because it is incompatible with ill will (*vyāpāda*), the Buddha’s sūtras state:

"If one possesses a mind of loving-kindness that is without enmity, without ill will, and without harm, and skillfully cultivates this mind so that it becomes vast and immeasurable— thus contemplating one direction until it is full, and likewise the second, third, fourth, upper, and lower directions— one contemplates all places and all sentient beings everywhere with a mind of loving-kindness."
Question: This loving-kindness takes sentient beings as its object; why, then, is it said to "fill" one direction? Answer:
This scriptural passage should be stated as follows:

"If, with a mind of loving-kindness that is without enmity, without ill-will, and without harm, one skillfully cultivates this mind so that it becomes vast and immeasurable, and thus contemplates the beings of the eastern direction, the beings of the southern, western, and northern directions, and so forth, as extensively explained."
What is the intention behind not speaking [of them]?
The answer is:
herein, sentient beings are spoken of by way of their locations, just as one points to an object within a vessel by indicating the vessel itself.
Regarding "observing all places and all sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness," it is asked:
Is this immeasurable meditation performed by way of spatial divisions, or by way of sentient beings?
If one were to take this literally and limit it to specific sections, how would one reconcile this with such statements as:
"With a mind of loving-kindness, one contemplates all sentient beings in all places"?
If it is by means of sentient beings, why is it not obtained at the edge of the ocean of sentient beings?
The answer is:
some say it is because of its spatial dimensions.
Question: If this is so, how can the following statement be reconciled?
As it is said:
One contemplates all places and all sentient beings with a mind of loving-kindness.
The answer is: there are two kinds of "all": [the all of space and the all of sentient beings].
There is "all-in-all" and there is "partial all"; here, it refers to partial all.
Furthermore, some say it is so called because of sentient beings.
Question: If that is so, why is it not the case that one does not fail to reach the shore of the ocean of sentient beings? Answer:
If one can obtain the ocean of sentient beings by means of this matter, what fault would there be?

One can indeed obtain the ocean of sentient beings because it is taken as a whole (*sāmānya*) and not as individual characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*); for example, all sentient beings are comprised within the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), and outside of these four modes of birth, there are no further sentient beings.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha’s immeasurability extends to the limits of all sentient beings, whereas the immeasurability of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas is limited by spatial dimensions.

Again, there are those who say that the immeasurability of both the Buddha and the pratyekabuddhas extends to the limits of all sentient beings, whereas the immeasurability of the śrāvakas is limited by spatial dimensions.
The critique says:
One should state it thus:
this matter is not fixed.
Why is this? This is the contemplation of empty marks.
Some reach the limit of sentient beings, while others do so by means of spatial divisions.
Question: Does one contemplate the happiness of a single sentient being, or does one contemplate the happiness of many sentient beings? Answer:
When first arising, one contemplates many sentient beings.
Why is this? Because "immeasurable" is a condition that gathers conditions upon the dharmas of sentient beings.
When it is later perfected, it takes as its object both a single sentient being and many sentient beings.
As the Buddha’s sūtra says: "O bhikṣus!"
Because I cultivated a mind of loving-kindness for seven years, I did not return to this world for seven kalpas of cosmic dissolution and formation.
When the world was dissolving, I was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven;
when the world was forming, I was born in the empty Brahma-world.
I was once the Great Brahmā King, the most honored among all Brahmās with none superior to me, attaining sovereign mastery over a thousand worlds.
Thirty-six times, I was Śakra, the Lord of Devas.

Furthermore, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he served as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, commanding the fourfold army and always subduing sentient beings through the True Dharma; he perfected the seven treasures, and so forth, as extensively described.
The "middle seven years" refers to seven rainy seasons.
In ancient times, during a favorable period, the Bodhisattva was the king of a central kingdom where the climate was very hot.
Not far from the city there was a forest; its terrain was high and cool, and it was fully endowed with flowers, fruits, plants, trees, and flowing streams.
During the heat of summer, the people of the cities and villages all abandoned their dwellings and flocked to that forest, each cultivating their respective practices.

The Bodhisattva did likewise; leaving the city under the guard of other men, he went into the forest and, at a high, prominent, and secluded spot, detached himself from the desires of the desire realm and gave rise to the four immeasurables.
During the four months of the summer rains, he dwelt in the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
Once the summer heat had passed and the weather turned cool, the people left those groves and returned to their dwellings, each attending to their respective occupations.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also left the grove and returned to the palace city.
Out of compassion, he established a great Dharma sacrifice and cultivated meritorious deeds through giving, bestowing gifts upon śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, laborers, and travelers on the road.
To those who came seeking, he gave food, drink, clothing, ointments, dwellings, bedding, elephants, horses, chariots, and lamps.
In this manner, he went to that forest six times.
Some say that after seven rebirths as a bodhisattva, when his life-span is exhausted and he passes away, he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Others say that when the world undergoes destruction, at the end of his life, he is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Therefore, among the seven rains, it is termed "seven years.
Question: This may be so if one is born in the Brahma-world or among the Ābhāsvara devas.
Why is this? Because it is that fruit and because it is bound to the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
As for the statement that one becomes Śakra or a universal monarch (cakravartin), how could that be possible?
Are the immeasurables also experienced as retribution within the desire realm?
The answer is:

when a bodhisattva gives rise to the three stages of the immeasurables—namely, the stage of the desire realm, the stage of the first dhyāna, and the stage of the second dhyāna—they are so experienced.
Receiving immeasurable retribution of the desire realm, one becomes a wheel-turning sage king or Śakra;
receiving immeasurable retribution of the first dhyāna stage, one becomes a Great Brahmā King;
receiving immeasurable retribution of the second dhyāna stage, one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven.

Furthermore, in the desire realm there are immeasurable minds for emerging from and entering into meditative absorption; because they receive the retribution for these minds of entering and emerging from absorption, they become wheel-turning sage kings (*cakravartin*) or Śakra;
and because they receive immeasurable retribution, they are born in the Brahma-world among the Ābhāsvara devas.
Furthermore, in the desire realm there are immeasurable skillful means; because they experience the retribution of such skillful means, they become universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) or Śakras;
and because they experience immeasurable retribution, they are born in the Brahma-world among the Ābhāsvara devas.

Furthermore, the desire realm is the seed-sphere for all roots of goodness. All roots of goodness, up to and including the meditative absorption of cessation, possess analogous dharmas; because they receive corresponding retributions for immeasurable roots of goodness, one becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King or Śakra;
and because one receives immeasurable retributions, one is born into the Brahma-world or among the Ābhāsvara devas.
Furthermore, by virtue of the retribution for practicing the dharma of sacrificial offerings, he became a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
by virtue of the retribution for upholding the precepts, he became Śakra;
and by virtue of the retribution for cultivating the immeasurables within that grove, he was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven of the Brahma World.

Furthermore, this sutra speaks of three kinds of meritorious action (puṇyakarman), namely: the meritorious action of giving (dāna), the meritorious action of ethical discipline (śīla), and the meritorious action of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
As that sutra says: "O bhikṣus!"
By virtue of the retribution of my three types of action, I have been endowed with great majesty and power.
These three types of action are giving, meditative concentration, and ethical discipline.

Giving refers to the meritorious action of generosity; meditative concentration refers to the meritorious action of cultivating samādhi; and ethical discipline refers to the meritorious action of cultivating śīla.
By virtue of the karmic retribution of the merit of giving, one becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King;
by virtue of the karmic retribution of the merit of observing the precepts, one becomes Śakra;
and by virtue of the karmic retribution of the merit of cultivating meditative concentration, one is born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven within the Brahma World.

The Buddhist scriptures speak of three kinds of meritorious action (*puṇyakarman*): namely, the meritorious action of giving (*dāna*), the meritorious action of ethical discipline (*śīla*), and the meritorious action of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
What is the meritorious action of giving?
If one gives material things to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, even as little as a lamp for illumination, this is called the meritorious action of giving (*dāna-puṇya-karma*).
What is the meritorious action of ethical discipline (*śīla-puṇya-karma*)?

Refraining from killing and having no further desire to kill, not stealing, not engaging in sexual misconduct, not speaking falsely, and likewise not drinking intoxicants—this is called the meritorious action of ethical discipline.
What is the cultivation of meritorious action through concentration?
It is as previously explained in detail: constantly maintaining a mind of loving-kindness that is without enmity, without ill will, and without harm.
The same applies to the cultivation of the minds of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; this is called the cultivation of meritorious action through concentration.

Question: For what reason are only the immeasurables among the wholesome roots of the form and formless realms described as the meritorious action of cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhāvanā-kuśala-karma*), and not other wholesome roots of the form and formless realms?

Answer: Worldly people regard that which brings benefit as a conception of merit; however, among all the roots of goodness within the realms of form and formlessness that seek to benefit others, none is equal to the Immeasurables.
Furthermore, worldly people conceive the idea of merit regarding the fruits of merit, because they are capable of producing vast fruits of merit.
As a verse says:
"Fire cannot burn merit; The wind cannot blow it away."
Even the waters that can float the great earth cannot sweep it away;
nor can kings or thieves, despite employing every means,
ever plunder the merit of men and women.
"The treasury of merit is most secure; it shall never be lost. Question:
If non-merit likewise cannot be burned by fire, why do you speak only of merit?
Answer: Although non-merit does not burn itself, it burns the fruit of non-merit;
the immeasurable fruit has not been burned by fire, will not be burned by fire, and is not being burned by fire now.
The Buddha’s sutra says:
"O bhikṣus! The disciples of Sunidha, who were perfect in their training at all times, were reborn in the Brahma-world after the dissolution of the body and the end of life."

Alternatively, those who never find satisfaction in their training, at the dissolution of the body after death, are reborn among the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, or the Nirmāṇarati gods, or the Tuṣita gods, or the Yāma gods, or the Trāyastriṃśa gods, or the Cāturmahārājika gods; or they are reborn into such families as the great Kṣatriya clans, the great Brāhmaṇa clans, or the great householder families—places where wealth is abundant, treasures are many, and storehouses overflow with riches.
Question: If that were so, then Sūnīta would be superior to the Buddha, the World-Honored One. Why is this?
