The disciples of Sunidha who were at all times satisfied in their training, upon the dissolution of the body after death, were reborn in the Brahma-world.
Those who were at all times unsatisfied in their training, upon the dissolution of the body after death, were reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations, as explained in detail above.
The disciples of the Blessed One who are at all times satisfied in their training will be reborn in the heavens or attain nirvana;
those who are at all times unsatisfied in their training, upon the breakup of the body after death, will be reborn in the evil realms.
Answer: Regarding this matter, one should not say that the Buddha is inferior. Why is this so?
Just as the World-Honored One’s youngest disciple, Srotāpanna, surpassed the body of Sunīda;
this was precisely when the Buddha, while practicing the bodhisattva path, was known by the name Sunīda.
Question: Is the World-Honored One superior when practicing the bodhisattva path, or when having attained buddhahood? Answer:
One should understand the purpose of that sutra and for what reason it was spoken in such a manner.
Sunītha taught the dharma of the Brahma-abodes to his disciples so that they might be reborn in the Brahma-heaven.

It is said that those disciples of the Sunīta who have fulfilled their training at all times, who practice with diligence and are able to give rise to the dharmas of the Brahma-abodes, will, upon the dissolution of the body after death, be reborn in the Brahma-world.

If those who exert diligence in practicing the dharmas of the Brahma-abodes fail to achieve [liberation], they may be reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, or even among human beings.
Yet in ancient times, people were so virtuous that they attained rebirth in the heavens without relying on immeasurable skillful means;
how much more so for one who exerts diligence in the most supreme roots of goodness for the sake of the immeasurable—how could such a person not be born among gods or humans?
The Blessed One has taught the disciples the precepts for attaining liberation and achieving nirvāṇa, saying, "You should train in these teachings.
Among these teachings, those disciples of the Blessed One who do not break, pierce, or transgress the regulations shall be reborn in the heavens and attain nirvāṇa.
"Those disciples of the Blessed One who violate the established rules within this training, upon the dissolution of the body after death, will be reborn in the woeful states.
For this reason, this sutra states that 'immeasurable' constitutes the fulfillment of the training."
At that time, Sunīdha thought to himself:
"I ought not to dwell in the same place as these disciples.
I should cultivate the supreme loving-kindness and be reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas."
At that time, Sunīta cultivated the loving-kindness of the second dhyāna stage; when his body perished and his life ended, he was reborn among the Ābhāsvara gods.
It is asked:
Since Sunīta was a bodhisattva who was close to the Buddha, he should not have possessed stinginess regarding the Dharma.
For what reason did he teach the disciples the method for being born in the Brahma-world, while he himself was born in the Ābhāsvara Heaven?
The answer is:
because he observed that the faculties (*indriya*) of those disciples were of a limited capacity.

Furthermore, those brahmins have long directed their minds toward the Brahmā world; as they gradually draw closer to being reborn there, he therefore teaches them the method for rebirth in the Brahmā world.

Furthermore, when there is no Buddha in the world, there is no one capable of giving rise to the immeasurables of the second, third, or fourth dhyāna stages, with the sole exception of Bodhisattvas who are close to Buddhahood.

Question: Since the higher stages are immeasurable, luminous, pure, and superior, why is it said that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the second dhyāna stage is called "supreme loving-kindness"? Answer:
Because the loving-kindness (*maitrī*) of the second dhyāna stage is superior to the loving-kindness of the first dhyāna stage;
furthermore, because its loving-kindness toward śrāvakas is more excellent, it is superior;
moreover, because this loving-kindness is superior to that which was previously practiced, it is superior.

Furthermore, when there is no Buddha in the world, there are none capable of giving rise to the immeasurables of the third or fourth dhyāna stages; yet, by the power of the Buddha, the disciples of the Buddha are able to give rise to loving-kindness (*maitrī*) belonging to those respective stages based upon them.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka has stated:
"That loving-kindness of the two stages does not belong to ordinary persons;
by the power of the Buddha, the disciples of the Buddha are able to give rise to that loving-kindness."
Question: For what reason are they called the "Brahma Abodes" (brahmavihāra)? Answer:
Because the Brahma-world exists at the beginning and possesses [these qualities] in their entirety;

whereas the *anāgamya* dhyāna, though existing at the beginning, does not possess them in their entirety, and the second dhyāna, though possessing them, does not exist at the beginning; only the first dhyāna exists at the beginning and possesses them in their entirety.
Furthermore, they are called "Brahma-abodes" (brahmavihāra) because they are the opposites of what is non-Brahma-like.
By "non-Brahma-like" is meant the afflictions of the desire realm, as these [abodes] serve as their direct antidotes.
Furthermore, they are called Brahma-abodes because they are the opposites of non-Brahma-like conduct.
Non-Brahma-conduct refers to sexual desire within the realm of desire.
What is its direct antidote?
It is the four Brahma-abodes.
Furthermore, because it can be found within the body of one who practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), it is called a "Brahma-abode" (*brahmavihāra*).
Furthermore, the Blessed One is Brahma; because he manifests and explains that Brahma, it is called a "Brahma-abode."
Furthermore, it is called a Brahma-abode because it is explained in the Brahma-sound and the Brahma-language.
Furthermore, it is called a Brahma-abode because all Brahmās practice this dharma and thereby attain rebirth in the Brahma-world.
Question: What is the distinction between the Brahma-vihāras and the apramāṇas? Answer:
Some say there is no distinction. Why is this?
Because the four Brahma-abodes are themselves the four immeasurables, and the four immeasurables are themselves the four Brahma-abodes.
Furthermore, there are those who say that names themselves are the distinctions: this is called the Brahma-abodes (brahmavihāra), and this is called the immeasurables (apramāṇa).
Moreover, they are called Brahma-abodes in contrast to what is non-Brahma, and they are called immeasurables in contrast to conceptual proliferation (prapañca).

Furthermore, the body of one who practices the holy life (brahmacarya) may be called a "Brahma-abode" (brahmavihāra), while the body of one free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca) may be called "immeasurable" (apramāṇa).
Furthermore, because it counteracts what is not the holy life, it is a Brahma-abode; because it counteracts negligence (pramāda), it is immeasurable.
Furthermore, that which exists in the Brahma-world is the Brahma-abode (*brahmavihāra*); that which exists in the higher stages is the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*).
Furthermore, that which relies on the Brahma-world in the stage of "not-yet-arrived" (*anāgamya*) is the Brahma-abode; that which exists in the higher stages is the immeasurable.

Furthermore, that which exists prior to reaching the Brahma-world is both a Brahma-abiding (*brahmavihāra*) and is called immeasurable (*apramāṇa*); that which exists in the higher stages is exclusively immeasurable.
Furthermore, that which has been previously attained is a Brahma-abiding; that which has not yet been attained is immeasurable.

Furthermore, that which is practiced within our own school (the Inner Way) is the Brahma-abode and is also called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); that which is practiced among the outsiders (the Non-Buddhists) is merely "immeasurable.
Furthermore, that which is common [to both] is the Brahma-abode; that which is uncommon is the immeasurable.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka stated:
"The Brahma-abodes are common dharmas, because they are shared by both ordinary persons and noble ones.
The Immeasurables are uncommon dharmas of non-negligence, because they are not shared by ordinary persons and noble ones."
The Brahma-abodes and the immeasurables (apramāṇa) are what constitute the distinction.
The Buddhist sūtras state that four types of persons obtain Brahma-merit (brahmapuṇya).
What are the four?
If a person, at a place where no stūpa has previously been erected, is able to erect a stūpa there for the relics of the Tathāgata, this is called the first Brahma-merit.

Furthermore, if a person is able to establish a monastery for the Noble Assembly on a site where no such monastery for the Noble Assembly has previously been established, this is called the second Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, if one causes the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples who have been divided to reunite, this is called the third Brahma-merit.
Furthermore, if a person can cultivate the four dharmas of the Brahma-abodes, this is called the fourth Brahma-merit.
The Dārṣṭāntikas speak thus:
"This sūtra was not spoken by the Tathāgata, nor are these four [types of merit] Brahma-merit. Why is this so?"
Since the retributions for these four sites are not equal,

if a person erects a great stūpa at the places where the Tathāgata was born, attained enlightenment, turned the wheel of Dharma, or entered parinirvāṇa, and another person gathers small stones to pile them into a stūpa, are the merits of these two equal and without difference?
If one person builds a great vihāra, such as the Jeta Grove, the Bamboo Grove, or the Tamaśa Grove vihāras, and another person builds a single-story room, is their merit equal and without difference?
If one reconciles a monastic community that has been split by Devadatta, or reconciles a community at Kauśāmbī that is embroiled in strife, is the merit of these acts equal and without distinction?
The four Brahma-vihāras are taught in the Tathāgata’s sūtras, and they are also "Brahma-merit."
The Abhidharmikas state as follows:
"This sutra was spoken by the Tathāgata, and it is also a source of Brahma-merit.
[An opponent] asks:
Why are these retributions not equal?
The answer is:
because that which was performed [to bring them about] was equal.
If a person, at a site where no stupa has previously been erected, erects a great stupa for the sake of the Tathāgata, the Great Brahmā;
or if a person, at a site where no stupa has previously been erected, erects a small stupa for the sake of the Tathāgata, the Great Brahmā.
Because the purpose is the same, there is no difference in their merit.

Whether one builds a monastery for the Saṅgha where none exists, or reconciles a schism among the disciples of the Tathāgata so that they are united again—both acts are performed for the sake of the holy life (brahmacarya); thus, this "merit of the holy life" is equal and without distinction.
Because these three objectives are identical, their merit is equal and without distinction.
Furthermore, because they are similar: if a person cultivates the four immeasurables with the desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

If one erects a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata in a place where no stūpa has previously been built, it is likewise for the purpose of benefiting immeasurable sentient beings. Why is this so?

Because of these stūpas of the Tathāgata, hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings shall make offerings to them with incense, flowers, music, powdered incense, ointments, banners, flags, canopies, and various other ritual implements.

Because of these matters, one gives rise to wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind; through the causes and conditions of planting [seeds] in a noble family, one possesses great majesty and virtue, abundant wealth and many treasures, a handsome and upright appearance that people delight to behold, and may plant the causes and conditions for becoming a Wheel-Turning King, or plant the causes and conditions for Śakra, or plant the causes and conditions for a Māra King, or plant the causes and conditions for a Śrāvaka, or plant the causes and conditions for a Pratyekabuddha, or plant the causes and conditions for a Buddha.

If one cultivates the immeasurables with the desire to benefit immeasurable sentient beings, or if one establishes monasteries and dwellings for the noble Saṃgha in places where they have never before been established, this too is for the benefit of immeasurable sentient beings.

Why is this? Because hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, as disciples of the Tathāgata, provide various kinds of food and drink for one day, seven days, half a month, or a full month; they hold *pañcavārṣika* assemblies and regular gatherings, and also provide them with beds, seats, and medicinal requisites according to their needs. This enables the bhikṣus to recite the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma and contemplate their meaning, thereby giving rise to the stages of impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the levels of heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*). They enter into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), attain the fruits [of the path], become free from desire, and exhaust all outflows (*āsrava*).

Because of this matter, one plants the causal conditions for noble lineages, possessing great majesty and virtue, abundant wealth and many treasures, a handsome appearance that people delight to behold; or one plants the causal conditions for becoming a Wheel-Turning King, or the causal conditions for Śakra, or the causal conditions for a Māra King, or the causal conditions for a Śrāvaka, or the causal conditions for a Pratyekabuddha, or the causal conditions for a Buddha.

Just as one cultivates immeasurable benefit for immeasurable sentient beings, so too do the disciples of the Tathāgata reconcile those who have been divided, likewise desiring to benefit immeasurable sentient beings.

Why is this? If the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples were to be divided, those who ought to enter into right determination would not enter it; they would not attain the fruit, would not become free from desire, would not exhaust their outflows, would not teach others, and would neither receive nor recite the scriptures. At such a time, they would be unable to contemplate the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, nor would they be able to plant the causal conditions for the paths of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Buddhas. This would cause the Wheel of Dharma to cease throughout the trichiliocosm, even reaching as far as the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, where beings would harbor divergent thoughts.

If the Sangha has been split, one should cause them to be reconciled; those who ought to enter the fixed determination of correctness (samyaktva-niyāma) may enter it, and even up to the Śuddhāvāsa deities, there shall be no dissension.
Because of such corresponding deeds, these are all merits of Brahmā (brahma-puṇya).
Furthermore, if one erects a stūpa containing the relics of the Tathāgata at a site where no stūpa has previously been established, it is called "Brahma-merit" for four reasons:
first, one relinquishes great wealth and generates vast faith;
second, one causes many sentient beings to plant roots of goodness.
Third, completing the construction;
fourth, enshrining the relics of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, if there is no monastery or dwelling for the noble community of the Tathāgata’s disciples, and one establishes a monastery for the first time, it is also called a "Brahma-merit" due to four causes:
First, by relinquishing great wealth, one generates great faith;
second, one causes many sentient beings to plant roots of goodness;
third, one brings all things to ultimate completion.
Fourth, for those who have no support, one acts as their support; for those who have no dwelling place, one provides them with a dwelling place.
Furthermore, if one reconciles a schism within the community of the Tathāgata’s disciples, it is also called "Brahma-merit" due to four factors:
first, abstaining from the four types of verbal misconduct.
2. To practice the four kinds of wholesome verbal karma;
3. To eliminate unrighteousness;
4. To cultivate the dharma of reverence.
If one cultivates the four immeasurables, they are also termed "Brahma-merit" for four reasons:
first, being free from hatred and attachment;
second, severing all hindrances.
3. Because that fruit exists;
4. because it is bound by that. Question:
What is the measure of Brahma-merit?
The answer is:
some say that if the retribution of a meritorious deed can result in the body of a Wheel-Turning Sage King, the measure of Brahma-merit is likewise the same.
Furthermore, some say that if the retribution of meritorious karma can result in the body of Śakra, the measure of Brahma-merit is likewise.
Others say that if the retribution of meritorious karma can result in the body of the King of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, the measure of Brahma-merit is likewise.
Furthermore, some say that if the retribution of meritorious karma can result in the body of a Brahmā King, the measure of Brahmā-merit is likewise the same.
Others say that because of the power of the meritorious karma of all sentient beings, the world is restored to formation; the measure of Brahmā-merit is likewise the same.

Furthermore, there are those who say that, with the exception of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the measure of Brahma-merit is equal to all the wealth, nobility, and meritorious karma possessed by all other sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the measure of Brahma-merit is equal to the merit obtained by the Brahmā King when he invited the Buddha.
The critique states:
the measure of Brahma-merit is immeasurable and boundless; all that has been said above are merely words of praise for Brahma-merit.
Question: When does one obtain Brahma-merit upon the Brahma King’s invitation of the Buddha? Answer:
Some may say that when one has resolved to go and invite the Buddha,
one should not speak in this manner. Why is that?
How can one obtain merit without having performed an action?
Furthermore, there are those who say that one obtains Brahma-merit at the time of inviting the Buddha;
this too should not be asserted.
Why is this? When Brahmā invited the Buddha, it was a desire-realm non-obscured neutral state of mind; a non-obscured neutral state of mind cannot produce karmic retribution.
The commentary states:
It should be explained in this way:

After the Brahmā King had invited the Buddha and returned to his own palace, the Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma on account of the Brahmā King’s invitation; the five bhikṣus and eighty thousand devas all attained the vision of the Truth (dṛṣṭi-prāpti).
This sound was heard as far as the Brahma Heaven; having heard this sound, the Brahmā King conceived faith and reverence, thinking:
"Because I invited the Buddha, the Buddha has turned the Wheel of Dharma, enabling others to obtain such benefits."
At that time, one attains Brahma-merit.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 42. *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 43.

translated during the Northern Liang dynasty by the Indian śramaṇa Buddhavarman, together with Dao Tai and others.
From the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Shi men pin), Chapter Seven: As it is said:

If one enters the meditative concentration of loving-kindness, fire cannot burn them, weapons cannot wound them, poison cannot harm them, water cannot sweep them away, and they cannot be killed by others.
Question: For what reason does one who has entered the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) not suffer from water, fire, weapons, or poison, nor get killed by others?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra replied:
Because the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) is a dharma of non-harming, no one can harm that which is itself non-harming.
Furthermore, because that concentration possesses great majestic power (*mahānubhāva*), all the gods of majestic power come to protect it, so that harm cannot prevail.
Furthermore, the dharma of meditative concentration and the dharma of inconceivable supernormal powers are likewise so.
Moreover, when entering that concentration, one does not abide in one's own mind; he who does not abide in his own mind neither dies nor is born.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

"When a practitioner enters the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm pervade this body and become a single unity, just like a stone; therefore, there is nothing that can harm it."
Question: Are these concentrations of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) harmed by harmful factors (*vihethaka-dharma*)?

If they are harmed, why is one not harmed by harmful factors when entering the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), yet is harmed when entering the concentrations of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity?
If it is not [the case that] "not harming," why is this not stated here?
The answer is:
It should be stated as follows:
Non-harming.
Question: If that is so, why is it not mentioned here?
Answer: When that which ought to be said is not said, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, what has already been stated is included within what was previously taught.
If one speaks of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), it should be understood that compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) have already been spoken of as well.
Furthermore, because this is the initial entry into the skillful means (*upāya*), as it is with loving-kindness, so it is with compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Furthermore, when entering the meditative absorptions of compassion, joy, or equanimity, although the factors of harm cannot cause injury, upon emerging from these states, the body experiences pain;
this is not the case with loving-kindness.
Moreover, when entering the meditative absorptions of compassion, joy, or equanimity, although the factors of harm cannot cause injury, they still break through the skin and flesh.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is not like this.

Furthermore, when one enters the meditative absorptions of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*), one cannot be harmed; however, during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of these, one can be harmed.
During the preparatory stage of loving-kindness, no one is able to cause harm.

It is said that there was once a person who had attained the skillful means of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) pertaining to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). When he violated the king’s law, people bound him and brought him before the king, saying:
"This man has violated the king’s law; he should be subjected to punishment."
At that time, the king was riding an elephant and holding a spear, intending to go out of the city for a stroll. He then recited a scripture:
"Whatever sins a person has committed, the king should slay them with his own hand.
At this, the king became enraged and immediately hurled the spear at that man.
Seeing that the king was enraged, the man gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
Because of this mind of loving-kindness, the iron stake turned back and fell to the ground not far from the king's body.
When the king saw this, fear arose in his heart, and he questioned the man:
"What methods or arts do you possess?
The man replied to the king:
"I possess no methods or arts. Because I saw the King’s anger, compassion arose within me; by virtue of that compassionate mind, he did not harm me."
For this reason, one knows that the skillful means of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cannot be harmed by injury.
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:

"By practicing and widely disseminating the mind of loving-kindness, one can sever anger; by practicing and widely disseminating the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one can sever suffering; by practicing and widely disseminating the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one can sever discontent; by practicing and widely disseminating the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one can sever sensual desire and anger."
Question: Do the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) serve to sever the fetters (*saṃyojana*)?
If they can sever them, how is one to reconcile this with what is stated in the *Samādhivarga* (The Chapter on Concentration)?
As it is said:
"What fetters does loving-kindness sever?
The answer is:
It has no location.
Regarding compassion, joy, and equanimity, which fetters and bonds do they sever? Question:
There is no such place.
If it cannot be severed, how is this sūtra to be reconciled?
The answer is:
One should say this:
the immeasurable cannot sever the fetters. Question:
If this is so, then what is stated in the *Samyuktabhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (the *Viniścaya-skandha*) is thoroughly consistent.
How is this sutra to be interpreted?
The answer is:
This sutra speaks of "momentary abandonment.
There are two kinds of abandonment:
first, momentary abandonment; second, ultimate abandonment.
Because it is severed for a brief moment, the Buddhist sūtras speak of "severance";
because it is severed ultimately, the Abhidharma speaks of "non-severance.
Both of these explanations are thoroughly consistent with reason.

Just as there is momentary abandonment and ultimate abandonment, abandonment with fragments and abandonment without fragments, abandonment with shadows and abandonment without shadows, abandonment with remainder and abandonment without remainder, abandonment through restraint and abandonment at the root—it should be understood that it is likewise in these cases.
Question: If there are no immeasurable or uninterrupted fetters (*anantaryasaṃyojana*), how can other sūtras be reconciled?
For example, it is said:

If a bhikṣu cultivates the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) and does not progress further toward other dharmas, he will certainly attain the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmiphala*).
This applies likewise up to the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The answer is:
In this context, the Buddha taught that the untainted noble path is loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

The World-Honored One has sometimes said that the noble path is perception (*saṃjñā*), or feeling (*vedanā*), or mind (*manas*), or realization (*sākṣātkriyā*); or he has said it is faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; or he has said it is a raft, or a stone, or water, or a flower, or compassion, kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity (*maitrī-karuṇā-muditā-upekṣā*).
Where is it said that this is "perception" up to "flower"?
The detailed explanation is as found in the *Kṣudraka-vastu*.

Furthermore, one constantly maintains a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and constantly contemplates a mind of loving-kindness; for the sake of seeking a mind of loving-kindness, one becomes detached from sensual desire, whether one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) or a noble one (*ārya*).

If it is an ordinary person who, having already abandoned sensual desire, attains the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*), and later enters into right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) to attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*;
or if they enter into right determination without having previously abandoned sensual desire, they will attain either the fruit of *srotāpanna* or the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*.
The reason one attains the fruit of Anāgāmin is due to the power of the concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*).
If a noble one (*ārya*) is free from sensual desire and attains the concentration of a loving mind, they likewise attain the fruit of Anāgāmin.
For this reason, the Buddha spoke thus:
"A bhikṣu who cultivates the concentration of loving-kindness attains the fruit of anāgāmin;
however, the immeasurable [state] alone cannot sever the fetters."
As it is with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), so it is with compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
"By practicing and widely disseminating the mind of loving-kindness, one abandons ill-will; by practicing and widely disseminating the mind of equanimity, one abandons sensual desire and ill-will."
Question: What kind of ill-will does loving-kindness (*maitrī*) eliminate?
What kind of ill-will does equanimity (*upekṣā*) eliminate?
Answer: There is anger that desires to kill another, and there is anger that desires to strike another.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cuts off the anger that desires to kill another, while equanimity (*upekṣā*) cuts off the anger that desires to strike another.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of ill-will:
either ill-will directed toward an object where it is appropriate, or ill-will directed toward an object where it is inappropriate.
Loving-kindness (*maitrī*) abandons ill-will toward objects where it is appropriate, while equanimity (*upekṣā*) abandons ill-will toward objects where it is inappropriate.
Such forms of hatred as these are severed by loving-kindness (*maitrī*); such forms of hatred as these are severed by equanimity (*upekṣā*).
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:

"By cultivating and widely disseminating the perception of impurity (*aśubha-saṃjñā*), one severs sensual desire; by cultivating and widely disseminating the mind of equanimity, one severs sensual hatred."
Question: What kind of craving does the perception of impurity sever?
What kind of craving does the mind of equanimity sever?
The answer is:
There are two kinds of craving:
first, craving for sensual desire; second, craving for objective realms.
The perception of impurity cuts off sensual desire and craving; the mind of equanimity cuts off craving for sense objects.
Furthermore, there is craving for color and craving for shape: the perception of impurity cuts off craving for color, and the mind of equanimity cuts off craving for shape.
Furthermore, there is craving for contact and craving for deportment. The perception of impurity cuts off craving for contact, and the mind of equanimity cuts off craving for deportment.
Through the perception of impurity, such cravings as these are severed; through the mind of equanimity, such cravings as these are severed.
The Buddhist scriptures state:

By cultivating the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness conjoined with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one can attain detachment, attain freedom from desire, attain cessation, and relinquish birth and death.
The same is taught for the states of compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Question: Immeasurability (*apramāṇa*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is without outflows (*anāsrava*). How can a dharma with outflows and a dharma without outflows coexist?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:

Because the immeasurables (apramāṇa) tame the mind and, once it has become upright and serviceable, subsequently give rise to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), and because these factors of enlightenment arise again after the immeasurables have arisen, it is said that they are associated only with outflowing phenomena (sāsrava-dharma).
Question: Among the immeasurables, which is the most excellent? Answer:
Some may say that loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is superior. Why is this?
Because loving-kindness is a dharma of non-harming.
Furthermore, there are those who say that compassion is superior.
Why is this? It is because it is out of compassion that the Buddha preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind of joy (*muditā*) is superior. Why is this?
Because joy severs the states of non-joy and lack of delight.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the mind of equanimity is superior. Why is this?
Because equanimity is able to sever sensual desire and ill will.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "Equanimity is supreme. Why is this so?"
It is by means of two matters:
first, that which is performed; second, tranquility.
As for that which is performed, it is the cultivation and widespread dissemination of the mind of equanimity, which severs desire, attachment, and ill-will.
"Quiescence" means not discriminating among sentient beings.
Question: Why is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) mentioned, but not great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), or great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*)?
Answer: It should be explained that all the merits contained within the bodies of all Buddhas should be called "great."
Why is this? Because the Buddha possesses immeasurable compassion and a mind intent on benefiting sentient beings;
however, you should not have asked such a question.
Why is this so? If compassion were identical to great compassion, such a question could be asked;
however, because ordinary compassion is distinct from great compassion, such a question should not be asked.
Question: If compassion (*karuṇā*) is distinct from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), what is the difference between compassion and great compassion? Answer:
The names themselves constitute the distinction: this is called compassion (*karuṇā*), and this is called great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
Furthermore, compassion is the wholesome root of non-hatred (*adveṣa*), while great compassion is the wholesome root of non-delusion (*amoha*).
Furthermore, ordinary compassion (*karuṇā*) exists in the four dhyānas, whereas great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) exists only in the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, while ordinary compassion is possessed by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and buddhas alike,
great compassion is possessed by the Buddha alone.
Furthermore, compassion (*karuṇā*) is subsumed under the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), whereas great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) is not subsumed under the immeasurables.
Furthermore, compassion is the antidote to the unwholesome root of ill-will (*vyāpāda*), while great compassion is the antidote to the unwholesome root of delusion (*moha*).
Furthermore, compassion takes the desire realm as its object, whereas great compassion takes the three realms as its object.

Furthermore, compassion takes as its object those sentient beings who are afflicted by the sufferings of the desire realm, while great compassion takes as its object those sentient beings who are afflicted by the sufferings of the three realms.

Furthermore, compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are afflicted by the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who are afflicted by the three types of suffering.
Furthermore, compassion takes as its object sentient beings who suffer bodily pain; great compassion takes as its object sentient beings who suffer both bodily and mental pain.
Furthermore, regarding compassion (*karuṇā*): ordinary compassion pities sentient beings but cannot rescue them;
great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) pities sentient beings and is able to rescue them.
It is like two people sitting by a river when someone is being swept away by the water.
One person raised his hand and said:
"This man has lost [his way],
and we cannot save him."
The second person rolls up his robes and enters the water to rescue that individual and enable them to emerge from the water.
Compassion and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) are likewise so.
The Venerable Revata said:
What is the difference between compassion (*karuṇā*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
The answer is:
the first is called compassion, and the second is called great compassion.
Furthermore, there is a distinction in their essential nature:
one is the essence of the wholesome root of non-ill will, and the other is the essence of the wholesome root of non-delusion.
Furthermore, there is a distinction in their stages: compassion resides in the four dhyānas, while great compassion resides in the fourth dhyāna.
The rest is explained in detail as above.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "Great Compassion is the Buddha;

it resides in the fourth dhyāna; it is an uncommon quality (āveṇika-dharma); it is profound, remote, and subtle, pervading all places; and toward all sentient beings, there is neither enemy nor friend."
The compassion (*karuṇā*) of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas cannot take the form and formless realms as its object.
This is what distinguishes ordinary compassion from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Question:
Why is it called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā)?
The answer is:
because it rescues and delivers sentient beings from great suffering, it is called Great Compassion.
"Great suffering" refers to the sufferings of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals.

Furthermore, because it rescues sentient beings from the great mire of greed, hatred, and delusion, and establishes them upon the level path of the fruits [of the spiritual life], it is called "great compassion."
Furthermore, it is for the sake of bringing about great benefit for all sentient beings.

Because sentient beings perform wholesome deeds of body, speech, and mind, they plant the causes and conditions for noble lineages, possessing great majesty and power, abundant wealth and many treasures, and upright and handsome physical forms; or they plant the causes and conditions for becoming a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), Śakra, or the Heavenly King Maheśvara; or they plant the causes and conditions for the paths of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, or Buddha—all of these are due to the power of Great Compassion.

Furthermore, it is called "great compassion" because it is attained through the Great Dharma; it is not like the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which are attained by giving to others a single fast, a single teaching, or a single meal.
Because he practices great giving, bestowing all beloved things upon all people in all places, it is called Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Furthermore, it is called Great Compassion because it is attained through great skillful means (*upāya*); it is not like the Śrāvaka path, which is attained after practicing the path of skillful means for sixty *kalpas*, nor like the Pratyekabuddha path, which is attained after practicing skillful means for a hundred *kalpas*. The Buddha attains it by practicing hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities over three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*; therefore, it is called Great Compassion.

Furthermore, it is called "Great Compassion" because it abides in reliance upon a great body; it is not like the path of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, which is attained by relying on a body with deficient faculties.

If the body possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man, is adorned with the eighty secondary signs, and has a bodily radiance extending one fathom, such that one never tires of beholding it—because one abides within such a body, it is called Great Compassion.
Furthermore, it is called "great compassion" (mahākaruṇā) because it is the opposite of great pleasure.

The Buddha possesses profound, pure, and luminous unshared dharmas; yet he relinquishes such dharma-pleasures and traverses hundreds of thousands of millions of Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*) to preach the Dharma for others, all by the power of great compassion. Therefore, it is called great compassion.
Furthermore, because he causes great beings to perform what is difficult to perform, it is called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā).

The World-Honored One may manifest as a lion, or manifest as a woman, or manifest as a wrestler, or manifest as a musician, or manifest as a beggar; he takes Nanda by the arm and leads him throughout the five destinies. Whether near or far before Aṅgulimāla, he brings about the perfection of those sentient beings who possess superior shame and remorse. For the sake of transforming women, he reveals his private organ, displays the mark of lightness and agility, and extends his tongue to cover his face up to the hairline.
The manifestation of such difficult-to-accomplish deeds is entirely due to the power of great compassion (mahākaruṇā); therefore, it is called "great compassion.
Furthermore, it is because he can move the mountain of great equanimity (mahopekṣā).
The Buddha possesses two kinds of unique qualities (āveṇikadharma): first, great compassion; second, great equanimity.
If the Tathāgata were to dwell in exclusive great equanimity, such a thing would not be possible, for it is spoken of through conceptual differentiation.
Even if all sentient beings were ablaze, like fire consuming a heap of wood, the Tathāgata would still not regard them as such.

When the Tathāgata abides in his unique great compassion (*asādhāraṇa-mahākaruṇā*) and beholds sentient beings undergoing suffering and affliction, his body—though as firm as that of Nārāyaṇa—trembles like the leaves of a plantain tree; therefore, it is called "great compassion."
As stated in the Vinaya:
"The Buddha taught the Dharma to sentient beings with universal loving-kindness.
A question is asked:
The Buddha extends universal compassion to all sentient beings; do these beings not thereby attain happiness?

If they do attain happiness, why is it that those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and all other sentient beings beset by suffering and calamity do not likewise leave their suffering behind and attain happiness?
If one does not obtain pleasure, how is this verse to be reconciled?
As the verse says:
"When spirits and ghosts approach a person with malicious intent,"
"Though no poisonous harm has yet been inflicted, my mind already harbors terror.
If even a ghost coming with an evil intent can produce suffering, how much more so would the Tathāgata’s benevolent mind not produce joy?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
it is able to cause sentient beings to experience happiness.
Question: If that is so, the meaning of the verse is well-established.
Yet, why do those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, and all sentient beings afflicted by suffering and calamity not escape their pain and attain happiness?
The answer is:
The Buddha observes the karma of sentient beings; some can be transformed, while others cannot.
Those who can be transformed are rescued through his compassion.
If it cannot be transformed, then loving-kindness (*maitrī*) cannot save them.
Furthermore, there are those who say that it cannot cause sentient beings to experience happiness.
[The opponent] asks:
If this were so, how would one reconcile the statement in the Vinaya?
For it says: "The Buddha, with universal compassion, preached the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."

Answer: The Buddha’s universal compassion is manifold; he may manifest supernatural powers, or manifest things beloved by others, or give medicinal herbs to others, or touch them with the *kalaviṅka* bird, or cover them with the shadow of peace and bliss.
Regarding those with supernormal powers: it was heard that once, when the Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a meal.
At that time, during the forenoon, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered Rājagṛha together with the bhikṣus.
At that time, because King Ajātaśatru had associated with the evil friend Devadatta, he gave wine to the elephant Dhana-pāla to make him wild and reckless, intending to harm the Tathāgata.
At that time, the Tathāgata raised his right hand and its five fingers, which transformed into five lion kings.
When the elephant saw them, fear arose in its heart, and it sought to flee back.
Looking behind him, he saw a great deep pit; looking to his left and right, he saw a great high mansion; looking up into the sky, he saw a large square stone from which flames were issuing.
He looked again in all four directions and saw fierce flames everywhere, yet only at the feet of the World-Honored One did he perceive coolness.
Having seen this, the elephant’s intoxicated mind was awakened.
At that time, the World-Honored One extinguished the five lion roars, whereupon [the elephant] immediately approached and rubbed the World-Honored One’s feet with its trunk.
The World-Honored One, with his hands adorned by the marks and signs of excellence, stroked the top of its head and preached the Dharma to it in the language of elephants:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; all dharmas are without self; nirvāṇa is the dharma of quiescence."
"You should give rise to a mind of faith and reverence toward me, and you shall be liberated from this animal body.
Upon hearing these words, the elephant ceased eating and drinking, and his life immediately came to an end.
Because of his pure mind, he was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Again, assuming a celestial body, he came to where the Buddha was; the Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and having attained the vision of the Truths, he returned to his heavenly palace.
At that time, everyone said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal loving-kindness extends even to the Dānavas.
In this context, "universal loving-kindness" refers to the supernormal power (ṛddhi).
In other instances as well, he manifested supernormal powers through universal loving-kindness.
It was heard that the World-Honored One, while traveling through the country of the Mallas, arrived at the city of Pāpā and stayed in the Sālavana grove.
When the Mallas of Pāpā heard that the Buddha was there, they immediately gathered for a council, saying:
"We must all go together to the place where the Buddha is; whoever does not go shall be fined five hundred pieces of gold."
At that time, there was a wrestler named Rocaka who lacked faith in the Buddha. Possessing great power and abundant wealth and treasures, he had no desire to go to the Buddha and thought to himself:
"I could offer five hundred measures of gold;
however, it would be improper to go against my relatives."
Then all the Mallas went together at once to the place where the Buddha was; having arrived, they prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, Ānanda saw the Malla Roca and said to him, "Welcome, Roca; come see the Buddha."
The World-Honored One is the field of merit for the world; before long, he shall pass into extinction within the grove of the twin śāla trees.
His body is upright and possesses little guile or crookedness. He said to Ānanda:
"I have come now not to see the Buddha, but merely to visit my kinsmen."
He related these previous events to Ānanda.
At that time, Ānanda took Roca by the arm and went before the Buddha, saying to him:
"This Roca, a strongman, does not have faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will preach the Dharma for him, so that he may give rise to faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected:
"This Roca Malla is one who acts out of craving and is deeply attached to sensory objects; if I were to preach the Dharma directly to him, he would not believe or understand it."
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One manifested his supernormal powers and, right there, conjured a pit of boiling excrement, foul-smelling and impure, from which flames burst forth.
A voice arose and spoke these words:
"If the Malla Roca had not received the Dharma from the Buddha and given rise to faith, upon the dissolution of the body after death, he would have been reborn here."

At that time, when the Malla saw and heard these matters, his heart was filled with great terror; he sat before the Buddha, who preached the Dharma for him, whereupon he immediately gave rise to faith and took refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus.
At that time, everyone said that the World-Honored One’s universal compassion extended even to the Malla Lūśa.
In this context, "universal compassion" refers to his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Regarding "manifesting things beloved by others," it is heard that once when the Buddha was staying in the Mahādeva Āmra Grove in the kingdom of Vaiśālī, there was a Brahmin woman named Vāsisthā who had recently lost six sons.
Out of longing for his son, he ran about frantically with an emaciated body until he reached the Mahādeva-āmra grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma, surrounded by an immeasurable multitude of hundreds of thousands of followers.
Such is the nature of the Dharma: one who is deranged shall surely regain right mindfulness upon seeing the Buddha.
At that time, because he had seen the Buddha, Vāsiṣṭha regained his right mindfulness; filled with shame and remorse, he sat with his body bent forward.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"You may give the robe to Vāsitha; I shall preach the Dharma for him.
Ānanda immediately gave him the robe.
Then Vāseṭṭha, having put on his robes, paid homage to the Buddha and sat down.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"Even if as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for him, he would ultimately fail to believe or understand it because of his grief and distress."
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One used his supernormal powers to manifest six sons.
When the woman saw these sons, she thought to herself:
"It was for the sake of these sons that my heart was filled with grief and distress; now that I have seen my children, I am free from sorrow once more."
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma to him according to what was appropriate, and he attained the vision of the Truths.
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal loving-kindness extends even to Vāsava."
In this context, "universal loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) refers to manifesting that which is beloved by others.
Elsewhere, it is called universal loving-kindness because it manifests that which is beloved by others.
It is heard that when the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī, there was a certain brahmin in Śrāvastī whose rice fields were ripe and about to be harvested; he sent one of his sons to guard them.
At that time, heaven sent down hail that damaged his rice paddies and also took the life of his son.
Because the rice paddies were ruined and his son had perished, the Brahmin ran about naked and frantic until he reached the Jeta Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma, surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands.
Such is the nature of the Dharma: when one who is deranged beholds the Buddha, they necessarily regain right mindfulness.
At that moment, because he had seen the Buddha, the brahmin regained his right mindfulness and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One reflected thus:
"Even if as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges were to preach the Dharma for him, he would ultimately never believe or understand it because of his grief and distress.
Out of compassion, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested a rice field and his beloved son.
Having seen him, the man thought to himself:
"I was filled with grief and affliction because of my beloved son who was tending the rice fields; now that I have seen him, I am no longer afflicted by sorrow."
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to them according to what was appropriate for each, and they attained the vision of the Truths.
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal compassion extends even to the Brahmins."
Regarding "universal loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) herein, it means manifesting things that others hold dear.
As for "giving medicinal herbs to others," it is heard that once the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and arrived at the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva) in the Abode of Sages (Ṛṣipatana).
At that time, there was a householder in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Mahāsenaka, whose wife was named Mahāsenī.
At that time, the householder and his wife invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, pledging to provide all necessary requisites and assets.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had taken a purgative medicine, which provoked a wind disorder (vāta-vyādhi). The physician prescribed that he should be treated with meat broth.
The bhikṣu then went to inform Mahāseni of this matter.
At that time, Mahāseni ordered a servant to take money and buy meat to make a broth for the bhikṣu.
On that day, King Brahmadatta had given birth to a son; filled with joy, he issued a proclamation that no living beings were to be killed.
At that time, the maidservant searched throughout the city of Vārāṇasī for meat but could find none, so she returned and informed her mistress.
Then Mahāseni thought to herself:
"I have invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and I shall provide them with all necessary provisions and requisites."
If that sick bhikṣu does not obtain meat, he may die because of this illness.
He further reflects:
"When the World-Honored One was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, he repeatedly gave his own flesh as a gift for the sake of others' lives."
"Now I too should follow the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas by giving my own flesh to another.
He immediately entered a quiet room, took up a sharp knife, cut the flesh from his own thigh, and gave it to the maidservant, instructing her to prepare a meat broth to give to the sick bhikṣu.
Then the maidservant, following the instructions, prepared a matured meat broth and offered it to the sick bhikṣu.
At that time, because the bhikṣu did not reflect upon it, he immediately consumed it, and his ailment was instantly cured.
At that time, Mahāseni’s body was racked with pain, and she could not remain still in one place.
Then Mahāsena entered from outside; not seeing his wife, he asked the members of the household: "Where is Mahāseni now?"
The family members replied:
"He is currently inside the house; his body is in pain and he cannot remain still in one place.
They then related the aforementioned events in detail.
At that time, Mahāsenā became exceedingly enraged and spoke these words:
"The śramaṇa sons of the Śākya do not know the proper occasion, nor do they possess contentment."
"Although the donors are immeasurable, the recipients should know moderation.
We must go and inform the World-Honored One of this matter.
They then proceeded to the Buddha's dwelling.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands as he preached the Dharma.
The World-Honored One’s exquisite form brought joy to all who beheld it; upon seeing the Buddha, the householder’s hindrance of anger was immediately removed, and his heart was filled with joy.
He then thought: "I ought not to report this matter to the Buddha now; rather, I shall invite the Buddha and the Sangha to my home and speak of it then."
He immediately prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and sat to one side.
When the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, he rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept a meal at my home."
At that time, the World-Honored One accepted the invitation by remaining silent.
Knowing that the Buddha had granted his permission, Mahāsenā prostrated before the Buddha and withdrew.
Returning home, he immediately prepared various kinds of delicacies and all necessary provisions during the night. At dawn, he arranged the seats and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The food and drink are prepared; may the Blessed One know the time.

Then, during the first part of the day, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his bowl, and accompanied by the community of bhikṣus, entered the house of Mahāsenā and sat upon the seat that had been spread out.
Knowing [the answer], the Buddha asked: "Where is Mahāśrīṇi now?
Her husband replied:
"He is currently inside the house, his body in pain and unable to find comfort.
The Buddha told the householder,
"Go and tell your wife that the World-Honored One summons her."

The World-Honored One, being well-versed in the dharma of internal dependent origination and likewise well-versed in the dharma of external dependent origination, used his supernormal powers to go to Mount Gandhamādana, where he took the medicinal incense for healing wounds and gave it to Mahāśrāvaka Mahāseni; upon its application to the wound, it was immediately healed, and the flesh, hair, skin, and color at that site were restored to their former state.
At that time, Mahāsenā went to his wife Mahāsenī and said to her,
"The World-Honored One is calling for you.
His wife then replied:
"Householder, you should know that the supernatural power of the World-Honored One is inconceivable.
You said to me: 'The World-Honored One calls for you.'"
After this period of time, the wounds upon my body healed and returned to their former state.
At that time, the husband and wife redoubled their faith and reverence; together they went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, and sat to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One taught the Dharma according to what was appropriate, and all attained the vision of the Truths.
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal compassion extends even to Mahāśāṇava."
In this context, "universal loving-kindness" refers to giving medicinal herbs to others;
it also includes giving medicine to others in other circumstances.
It is heard that King Prasenajit once severed the hands and feet of a thief and cast him away into a ditch.
At that time, during the early part of the day, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
When the bandits saw the Buddha, they raised their voices and cried out:
"We are now in dire distress; we pray that you will have compassion for us."

The World-Honored One, being well-versed in the internal law of dependent origination as well as the external law of dependent origination, used his supernormal powers to go to Mount Gandhamādana and fetch medicinal incense for treating wounds; he applied it to the man’s wound, and the pain was immediately relieved. He also preached the Dharma to those bandits according to their needs, and they immediately attained the vision of the Truths.
The people of the world all say:
"The World-Honored One extends his universal compassion even toward thieves.
In this context, "universal compassion" refers to giving medicinal herbs to others.

Regarding the account of the touch with the *kalaviṅka* feather: it was heard that when the Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, the Tathāgata dwelt on one side of the mountain while Devadatta dwelt on the other side.
At that time, Devadatta suffered from a headache; he could not sleep day or night and was extremely distressed.

Ānanda then reported this in detail to the Buddha. Thereupon, the Tathāgata extended his arm like the trunk of an elephant king, pierced through Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, and touched Devadatta’s head with his hand as soft as *kāliṅga* cotton, speaking these words of sincerity:
"In my heart toward Rāhula and Devadatta, there is no increase or decrease."
"If these words are truthful, Devadatta’s headache shall be cured.
Because of these truthful words, Devadatta’s headache was immediately cured.
At that time, Devadatta thought to himself:
"Whose hand is this?
Knowing it was the Buddha's hand, he spoke these words:
"How wonderful, Siddhārtha!"
He was well-versed in medical arts and could thus support himself.
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal compassion extends even to Devadatta."
In this context, universal loving-kindness is illustrated by the incident of the Kalinga touch.
In other places as well, there was a Kalinga touch.
It is reported that while the Blessed One was touring the lodgings, he arrived at a certain room where a sick bhikṣu was unable to rise or move, lying amidst excrement and filth.
Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he cried out in a loud voice:
"World-Honored One!
I am now without refuge and without protection."
The Buddha said to the sick bhikṣu:
"Did you not go forth into homelessness for the sake of the World-Honored One who transcends the three realms?
He replied:
"So it is," the Buddha said to the sick bhikṣu.
"You have gone forth for my sake; why do you say that you are without support and without refuge?"
"Sick bhikṣu! When you were not ill, did you ever attend to and care for other sick bhikṣus?
He replied:
"No," the Buddha told the sick bhikṣu,
"it is because you did not tend to others that you have now been brought to such a state."

At that time, the World-Honored One removed his own outer robe, raised the sick bhikṣu from the grass matting, scraped the filth from his body with a bamboo splinter, washed him with white clay paste, while Śakra poured water over him.

At that time, the World-Honored One cleared away his filth, plastered the dwelling anew, washed the soiled garments, spread fresh grass, fed him with half of his own meal, and further stroked the crown of his head with his hand, which was as soft as kāliṅga cloth.
At that time, the suffering of the sick bhikṣu was immediately dispelled; the Buddha preached the Dharma to him according to his needs, and he attained the fruit of arhatship.
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal compassion extends even to this sick bhikṣu."
Regarding "universal loving-kindness" herein, it refers to the touch of a kalaviṅka bird.
Regarding "being covered by the shadow of peace and happiness," it is heard that the Buddha once walked together with the Venerable Śāriputra in one place.
At that time, there was a bird who, being driven by intense fear, sought the shadow of Śāriputra; yet it remained fearful, its whole body trembling.
It then moved into the shadow of the Buddha, whereupon its fear was immediately dispelled, and it ceased its trembling.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra joined his ten fingers in palms-together salutation and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
This bird was terrified and trembling within my shadow, yet it ceased its fear and trembling while remaining in the shadow of the World-Honored One."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"You have practiced the mind of non-killing for sixty kalpas, whereas I have practiced the mind of non-killing for three asaṃkhyeya kalpas."
The people of the world all say:
"The World-Honored One’s universal loving-kindness extends even to the birds.
Herein, "universal loving-kindness" means to cover them with the shadow of peace and happiness.
Other places as well were shrouded by the shadow of peace and bliss.

It was heard that the foolish King Vairūḍya destroyed the city of Kapilavastu, which was like a celestial palace, and cut off the lives of all the Śākyas. He took five hundred Śākya women back to the kingdom of Śrāvastī; together they ascended a high tower, and he addressed the Śākya women with self-praise:
"The Śākyas were valiant and strong, yet their hearts were filled with arrogance; I have now slain them."
The women replied:
"The reason we killed you was because you were bound by the precepts.
At that time, the king became enraged:
The Śākyas still harbored prideful thoughts;
he immediately cut off the hands and feet of five hundred Śākya women and threw them into the moat of the city, causing them extreme suffering.
Each of the Śākya women thought to herself:
"We are suffering and distressed; O World-Honored One, will you not have compassion for us?
The Buddha, knowing what was in the minds of these women, out of his great compassionate heart, went to their location and gave rise to a conventional thought:
"Śakra may cover these women with his garments."
At that time, Śakra, knowing the Buddha’s thought, immediately covered these women with celestial garments.
The Buddha emitted a radiance that pervaded all the women; because their bodies were touched by the Buddha’s light, their suffering and pain were instantly removed.

He also preached the Dharma to them according to their needs, and at that time, all the Śākya women attained the vision of the Truth (dṛṣṭasatya). When their bodies perished and their lives ended, they were reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three (Trāyastriṃśa).
The people of the world all said:
"The World-Honored One’s universal compassion extends even to these Śākya women."
Regarding "universal loving-kindness" (*sabbamaitrī*) herein, it refers to covering [all beings] with the light of peace and happiness.
As stated in the Buddha’s sutras:
"The retribution for practicing and extensively disseminating a mind of loving-kindness does not exceed the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*)."
When one practices and extensively disseminates the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), its retribution does not exceed the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
When one practices and extensively disseminates the mind of sympathetic joy (*muditā*), its retribution does not exceed the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
When one practices and extensively disseminates the mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*), its retribution does not exceed the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Question: It may be granted that the retribution for loving-kindness (*maitrī*) does not exceed the Heaven of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*). Why is this so?
Because that fruit is bound to that realm.

As for the other three immeasurables, which are wholesome roots bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta-kuśalamūla*), can their retribution be experienced in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The answer is: No.
The meaning and significance of this shall be revealed only when Maitreya descends to be born.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the Venerable Śamathadeva was able to know this meaning, but because he had entered meditative absorption at that time, the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra did not inquire about it.

Furthermore, there are those who say that for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings, the World-Honored One has described the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) by means of the term "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*).
If the formless attainments are described using the term "immeasurable," those who are being transformed will find it easier to awaken to and understand them.
Just as those to be transformed must hear and understand liberation through specific names in order to attain awakening, the Buddha accordingly explains liberation using specific names.

Furthermore, there are other teachers who explain the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) that serve as antidotes to the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) using the name "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*); the factors of enlightenment that serve as antidotes to the third dhyāna using the name "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*); the antidote to the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) using the name "compassion" (*karuṇā*); the antidote to the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) using the name "sympathetic joy" (*muditā*); and the antidote to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) using the name "equanimity" (*upekṣā*).
Furthermore, there are those who say it is because they are similar:
the practice of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the practice of joy (*muditā*) involve pleasant feelings, which can be obtained from the desire realm up to the third dhyāna;

whereas the practice of compassion (*karuṇā*) involves painful feelings, as in the form realm where one suffers the pain of having hands, feet, ears, noses, or heads severed, and in the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) where one reviles form.
Practicing with joy, when consciousness arises and manifests in the sphere of infinite consciousness, the mind is filled with much joy.
Practicing with equanimity and relinquishing the sphere of nothingness is called the contemplation of equanimity.
It is on account of such similar circumstances that this statement is made.
Furthermore, it is because one delights in dwelling in that state.

Alternatively, there may be one who delights in contemplating loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); yet, because of that mind of loving-kindness, they seek detachment from desire, and although the first dhyāna arises and becomes manifest, their mind does not find joy therein. Having a residual seeking-mind, they are unable to settle the attention.
It is likewise when, having detached from the desire of the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna arises and manifests.

If, having detached from the desire of the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna arises and manifests, one then gives rise to the feeling of joy and bliss without further seeking, and is able to cause the mind to abide.

Alternatively, because one delights in the mind of compassion, one becomes detached from sensual desire and even detached from the desire for the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna arises before them; the detailed explanation is as above.
If, having detached from craving for the fourth dhyāna, the sphere of infinite space manifests before him, his mind does not find joy; the detailed explanation is as above.
If, having detached from craving for the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness manifests before him, his mind finds joy; the detailed explanation is as above.
Or there may be one who delights in the mind of equanimity; because of this mind of equanimity, they seek to depart from desire and craving.

This continues until, having departed from craving for the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness manifests before them, yet their mind feels neither joy nor pleasure, as explained in detail above.

If one becomes detached from craving for the sphere of infinite consciousness and the sphere of nothingness manifests before them, the mind then experiences joy and happiness; this is explained in detail as above.
Therefore, because one dwells in that state with happiness, it is described in such a manner.
Furthermore, it is spoken thus for the sake of conformity:
arising from the third dhyāna, the faculties of the desire realm and the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
From the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the sense-faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and benefited, thereby conforming to the third dhyāna.

From the concentration of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*), the sense-faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and benefited, thereby conforming to the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*).
From compassion, the sense-faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the concentration of the sphere of infinite space.
From the concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sense-faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the mind of joy.

From the mind of joy, the sense faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
From the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness, the sense faculties of the desire realm arise; the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the mind of equanimity.
From the mind of equanimity arise the faculties of the desire realm; the four great elements are moistened and nourished, conforming to the meditative absorption of the sphere of nothingness.
Therefore, because they conform [to it], this statement is made.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of counteracting the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).

The non-Buddhists form the notion of liberation regarding the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti), asserting: "There is no body; there is the infinite, pure collection of mind, which is the world and the shrine."
Because they hold such views regarding non-Buddhists, the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are described by the term "immeasurable.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka stated:
"Non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the dharma of cessation; they reckon the formless attainments to be cessation."

For the sake of those outside the [Buddhist] fold, the Buddhist scriptures state that the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) are both not liberations (*vimokṣa*), and are thus equal and without distinction.
The four formless attainments are:

the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
Question: For what purpose is this treatise composed? Answer:
This is to refute the intention of those who hold such views,
such as the Vibhajyavādins, who assert that there is form within the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
Pūrvavideha says: "In the formless realm, there is no form. He asks:
On what sūtras does the Vibhajyavāda rely when it asserts that there is form within the formless realm?
Answer: It relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddhist sūtras state:
"Name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.
Since there is consciousness in the formless realm, there must also be name-and-form therein.
Other sūtras also state:
"Life-force, warmth, and consciousness—these three phenomena always accompany one another and are never separated; they do not disperse to reside in different locations."
Since the formless realm possesses life-force (*jīvita*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), it should likewise possess warmth (*uṣman*).
Furthermore, another sutra states:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if one were to exclude form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and yet say there is coming and going, birth, death, or abiding—that statement should not be made. Because consciousness exists within the formless realm, there must also be a locus for the abiding of consciousness."
Furthermore, it presents a difficult objection:

if there were no form in the formless realm, then for one who dies in the desire or form realms and is reborn in the formless realm, their form would have to be severed after twenty thousand kalpas, or forty thousand kalpas, or sixty thousand kalpas, or eighty thousand kalpas.
If one dies in the formless realm and is reborn again in the desire or form realms, having long since severed form, it resumes its continuity with form once more.
Likewise, upon entering the realm of nirvana without remainder, although formations have long since been extinguished, they should likewise resume their continuity with formations.
In order to avoid such faults, it is said that there is form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Question:
Upon what sūtra does the Saṃmitīya school rely when asserting that there is no form in the formless realm?
Answer: It is based on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
Tranquil liberation transcends the sphere of form; thus one realizes the formless meditative attainments with the body.
If one speaks of formless meditative attainments that transcend the sphere of form, it should be understood that these are formless within the formless realm.
Other sūtras also state:

"By means of form, one becomes free from desire; by means of the formless, one becomes free from form; being free from all mental factors and free from all conditioned activities, one enters the nirvāṇa of cessation."
If it is said that one leaves the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) to enter the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one should know that in the formless realm there is no form.
As stated in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*:

"Whether there is form, or feeling, or perception, or consciousness—one should contemplate these phenomena as a disease," and so forth, as extensively explained in the discourse on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).
The Sūtra says:
"If there is feeling, if there is perception, if there are formations, or if there is consciousness, one should contemplate these phenomena as a disease," and so forth, as explained at length.
If one speaks of dhyāna, one speaks of form; if one speaks of the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), one does not speak of form.
For this reason, it is known that the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is without form.
This also refutes the objection regarding "excess."

If there were form in the formless realm, then one could not designate the sequential cessation of phenomena; if there were no sequential cessation of phenomena, there would be no ultimate cessation of phenomena; and if there were no ultimate cessation of phenomena, there would be no liberation or means of deliverance.
In order to avoid such faults, it is said that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is without form (*arūpa*).
Thus, one teaching asserts that the formless realm possesses form, while another teaching asserts that the formless realm is without form. Between these two teachings, which is superior?
Answer: That which is taught by the Vaitulika regarding the formless realm being formless is superior. Question:
How does the theory of *yuktavādin* (the rationalist) reconcile it with the sūtras upon which the theory of *vibhajyavādin* (the analyticalist) relies?
The answer is:
those sūtras are of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), they are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*), and they possess an underlying intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Question: What meaning in that sutra remains unclarified, what meaning is merely conventional (prajñapti), and what further intention does it possess? Answer:

In the Buddha’s sūtras, some speak of the dharmas of the desire realm, some speak of the dharmas of the form realm, some speak of the dharmas of the formless realm, some speak of the dharmas of both the desire and form realms, some speak of the dharmas of both the form and formless realms, some speak of the dharmas of all three realms, and some speak of dharmas that do not belong to the three realms.

Regarding the teaching on the phenomena of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is as when one speaks of the three realms: namely, the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the realm of ill-will (*vyāpādadhātu*), and the realm of harm (*vihiṃsādhātu*).
There are three types of applied thought (*vitarka*): the thought of desire (*kāmavitarka*), the thought of ill-will (*vyāpādavitarka*), and the thought of harm (*vihiṃsāvitarka*).
There are three perceptions:
the perception of desire, the perception of ill-will, and the perception of harm.
Regarding the teaching of the dharmas of the form realm, it is as when the four dhyānas are taught.
To speak of the dharmas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is as when one speaks of the four formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
To speak of the dharmas of the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*) is as stated in this sutra.
