To speak of the dharmas of both the form and formless realms is as when one speaks of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or as when one speaks of *mauneya*.

To speak of dharmas pertaining to the three realms is, for example, as with the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm; or the existence of desire, the existence of form, and the existence of the formless.

To speak of dharmas not pertaining to the three realms is, for example, as when it is said: "I shall now explain nirvāṇa and the dharmas that lead to nirvāṇa"; or as when it is said: "name-and-form conditions consciousness."
It should be understood that this explains the phenomena of the desire realm and the form realm. Why is this so?
Because there is form in the desire and form realms, name-and-form serves as the condition for consciousness.
Because there is no form in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), it is said that consciousness acts as the condition.
This is what is meant by "this [text] accords with that sūtra.

If one were to follow what is stated in that sūtra—wherein it says that the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are the condition for contact (sparśa)—then since contact exists in the formless realm, the six sense bases should also exist there.
As the Sūtra says:
"Life-force, warmth, and consciousness always follow one another and are never separated," and so forth, as explained at length.
This Sūtra also speaks of the dharmas of the desire realm and the form realm.
Why is this so? Because the realms of desire and form possess warmth, these three factors—vitality, warmth, and consciousness—constantly accompany one another and are never separated.
In the formless realm, there is no warmth; therein, the two factors of vitality and consciousness constantly accompany one another and are never separated.
This refers to that sūtra.
If it were as stated in that sūtra, that sūtra says:
"These three dharmas always follow one another; they are not separated from each other, nor do they disperse to remain in different places."

Furthermore, this dharma can be designated as existing in a distinct location—either within the aggregates (skandhas), within the elements (dhātus), or within the sense bases (āyatanas). Regarding its presence within the aggregates:
warmth is the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), life-force is the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha), and consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha).
Regarding those within the *dhātus*: warmth is the *spraṣṭavya-dhātu* (tangible object element); life-force is the *dharma-dhātu*; and consciousness is the seven *citta-dhātus*.
Regarding those within the *āyatanas*: life-force is the *dharma-āyatana*; warmth is the *spraṣṭavya-āyatana*; and consciousness is the *manas-āyatana*.

For this reason, those dharmas can be designated as existing in different locations; therefore, one should not rely exclusively on what is stated in that sutra, but should instead understand its underlying meaning.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

"Bhikṣus, you should know that if one were to say that there is coming and going, birth and death, or abiding, apart from form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, such a statement should not be made."
This sutra also speaks of the dharmas of the desire realm and the form realm. Why is this?
Because there is form in the desire and form realms, consciousness abides depending upon these four dharmas.
Because there is no form in the formless realm, consciousness abides by means of three factors.
This is consistent with that sutra.
If it were as stated in that sutra, other sutras would also say:
All sentient beings subsist by depending on food.
Is there also edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) in the form and formless realms?
If so, how can one resolve the difficulty regarding the fault [of those realms] being subject to exhaustion?
Answer: This need not necessarily be resolved. Why is that?
"This is not found in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma.
If you insist on reconciling it, what is your intention?
He replied:
According to my doctrine, form continues into form, form continues into the formless, the formless continues into the formless, and the formless continues into form.
As for "form continuing into form," it is like one who dies in the desire realm or the form realm and is reborn again in the desire realm or the form realm.
The continuity of form into the formless realm refers to those who, at the end of their lives in the desire or form realms, are reborn in the formless realm.
The continuity of the formless into the formless realm refers to those who, at the end of their lives in the formless realm, are reborn again in the formless realm.
Regarding "one who continues from the formless [realm] into the realm of form": this refers to one who dies in the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms. Question:

If that is so, then as with one who dies in the desire or form realms and is reborn in the formless realm—where the cessation of form may occur after twenty thousand kalpas, or forty thousand kalpas, or sixty thousand kalpas, or eighty thousand kalpas—[is it not the same here?]

If one who has passed away from the formless realm is reborn again in the desire or form realms, such that after a long period of severance of form it continues once more with form, then likewise, for one who has entered the realm of nirvana without remainder and whose formations have been extinguished for a long time, those formations should also continue once more.
Answer: There are two kinds of abandonment:
temporary abandonment and ultimate abandonment.
If it is severed for a brief moment, it continues again; if it is severed forever, it does not continue.
Question: How do the Vibhajyavādins reconcile their position with the sūtras upon which the Sarvāstivādins rely?
The answer is:
They say that this sutra is of provisional meaning (neyārtha), is merely a conventional designation (prajñapti), and possesses an underlying intention (saṃdhāya-bhāṣita).
Question: What meaning remains unclarified, what is the provisional designation, and what is the underlying intention? Answer:

He says this: "The Sūtra states that 'transcending the realm of form, one enters the formless' because one transcends coarse form and enters subtle form; there is indeed form in the formless realm, but it is subtle."
The Sūtra states that the Form Realm is distinguished from the Desire Realm because it possesses form;
yet, since the Formless Realm is distinguished from the Form Realm, the Formless Realm should likewise possess form.
Question: If it is argued that the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) is called "detached from the desire realm" because it is free from the matter of the desire realm, this may be so.

However, the Form Realm is called "detached from desire" because it is free from desire; yet, since there is no desire within the Form Realm itself, this [argument] is not tenable, nor does it accord with the scriptures.
The *Dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Ārūpya-samādhi-sūtra*, and the discourse on the refutation of difficulties cannot provide a resolution [to this].

However, what the Vibhajyavādins state is that it is the fruit of ignorance (*avidyā*), the fruit of darkness, the fruit of delusion (*moha*), and the fruit of a lack of diligent application of skillful means (*upāya*).
Some claim that there is form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), yet the formless realm is devoid of form.

Therefore, this treatise is composed in order to refute the positions of others, to reveal one's own position, and to explain the meaning of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in accordance with reality.

This treatise was composed not to refute the positions of others nor to establish one's own position, but solely because one desires to explain the characteristics of phenomena according to their true meaning.
The four formless attainments are:
the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
What is the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*)? The *Prakaraṇa* states:
"What is the sphere of infinite space?"

Answer: There are two kinds of the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana): that which is born of meditative concentration (samādhi), and the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness produced therein; these are called the sphere of infinite space.

As it is with the sphere of infinite space, so it is for the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; the explanation is likewise.
"Concentration" refers here to the formless concentrations.

"Birth" refers to birth in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as well as the non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness that arise therein; these constitute the retribution of the formless.
A Buddhist sūtra asks:
"What is the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*)?"

Transcending all perceptions of form, with the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance and non-attention to perceptions of diversity, one enters the sphere of infinite space; this is called the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).

Question: The perception of form is a perception associated with visual consciousness, which has already been transcended when one leaves the desire for the first dhyāna. Why, then, is it said here that one transcends the perception of form?
Answer: In this context, the term "fault" (dosa) refers to that which serves as the basis for a fault.
There are two kinds of faults:
First is the transgression of the basis; second is the transgression of the objective basis.

When one is free from desire for the first dhyāna, there is the transgression of the basis of the perception of form; when one is free from desire for the fourth dhyāna, there is the transgression of the objective basis of the perception of form.
Furthermore, this refers to that which transcends the objects of practice.
There are two kinds of transcendence:
first, transcendence of what is to be abandoned; second, transcendence of active manifestation.

When one is free from desire for the first dhyāna, one transcends the ideation of form that has already been abandoned; when one is free from desire for the fourth dhyāna, one transcends the ideation of form currently active.
Furthermore, this explains the states of abiding and dwelling.
There are two kinds of faults:
first, the fault of desire for sensual pleasure; second, the fault of attachment to a dwelling place.

When one is detached from the desires of the first dhyāna, one transcends the desire for the perception of form; when one is detached from the desires of the fourth dhyāna, one transcends the dwelling place of the perception of form.
Furthermore, when one is born into the fourth dhyāna, because of the presence of visual consciousness, the craving for forms arises and manifests before one.
For this reason, it is said that "all perceptions of form have been transcended."
Regarding the phrase "the cessation of the perception of resistance" (*sapratigha-saṃjñā*), a question is asked:
The perception of resistance is the perception associated with the consciousnesses of the ear, nose, tongue, and body.

Among these, some are ceased at the time of detachment from desire, while others are not ceased at the time of detachment from desire. For what reason, then, is it said that "herein the perception of resistance is ceased"?
The answer is:
All that was previously stated in response should be fully explained here as well.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "perception of resistance" (pratighasaṃjñā) refers to perception associated with ill-will (vyāpādasaṃprayuktasaṃjñā).
Question: When one is detached from desire and craving, the perception of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*) ceases; why, then, is it said here that the perception of resistance ceases? Answer:
Because the objects for which they were performed have ceased.
All those objects for which [the thoughts] were performed that could give rise to perceptions of anger are entirely extinguished when one becomes detached from the desire of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding "the absence of various perceptions and discursive thoughts": what are these various perceptions and discursive thoughts?
This refers to the various discursive perceptions within the fourth dhyāna.
Question: For what reason are they called "various perceptions"?
Answer: This perception takes various bases as its object.
That which is defiled takes ten bases as its object; that which is non-defiled takes twelve bases as its object.
Question: For what reason is it said that there is no mental application of diverse perceptions? Answer:
Various perceptions create extreme obstacles when one seeks to depart from the desire for the fourth dhyāna, preventing the continuity of the factors that lead to dispassion.
It is just as a gatekeeper prevents others from entering; so too is this the case here.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke thus:
"One should not contemplate various perceptions; one should abandon desire for the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), it is asked:
Why is it called the Sphere of Infinite Space?
Is it by virtue of its own essence (*svabhāva*), or by virtue of its object (*ālambana*)?
If it were by virtue of its own essence, then since its essence consists of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*), it would not be "infinite space."
If it is by way of conditions, then it conditions the Four Noble Truths, space, and analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The answer is:
one should state it thus:
It is neither by way of its own essence nor by way of conditions, but rather by way of skillful means (*upāya*). As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"By what skillful means does one seek the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space?"
The answer is:

A beginner, whether contemplating the emptiness at the top of a wall, the emptiness at the top of a tree, or the emptiness above a house, having grasped such signs of emptiness, contemplates this space.

Forming such a conception and conducting such an observation, one gives rise to that meditative absorption by taking emptiness as its object; therefore, it is called the "absorption of the sphere of infinite space.
Furthermore, according to the nature of phenomena, the first stage beyond form must be designated as the "sphere of infinite space."

The practitioner first contemplates the higher realms of form and becomes detached from the desires of the lower realms of form. When becoming detached from the desires of the fourth dhyāna, they contemplate the four aggregates of the sphere of infinite space as being detached from the desires of the fourth dhyāna; therefore, they form the perception of space therein.

It is like a person climbing a tree: as they ascend, they let go of the lower branches; when they reach the treetop where there are no more branches above, they then form the perception of space. It is the same for him.
Furthermore, it is called the "sphere of empty space" because it is based upon that [space].
Why is this so? Because even when one arises from that meditative concentration, there remains a residual basis.
It is said that there was once a bhikṣu who attained the concentration on empty space. Rising from that concentration, he reached out to touch the void.
Another bhikṣu asked him: "What are you seeking?"
He replied,
"I seek my own body. The bhikṣu said:
Your body remains upon the bed.

As for "entering the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-samādhi*): if one attains mastery over the four aggregates (*skandha*) that are virtuous and associated with the sphere of infinite space, this is called "entering.
What is the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*)?
Transcending the sphere of infinite space, one enters the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness; this is called the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*).
Question: Why is it called the sphere of infinite consciousness?
Is it by way of its own substance (*svabhāva*), or by way of its object (*ālambana*)?
If it is by way of its own substance, that substance consists of the four aggregates (*skandha*).
If it is by way of its object, then it takes the Four Noble Truths, space (*ākāśa*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) as its objects.
Answer: It is neither by way of its own essence nor by way of its object, but solely by way of skillful means (*upāya*).
As it is said in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
How does one seek the concentration of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana-samādhi*) through skillful means?
The answer is:

the beginner grasps the pure eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mental consciousness; having grasped these signs, they contemplate and examine consciousness. By observing consciousness through skillful means, the concentration of the sphere of consciousness arises.
Furthermore, because of the remaining substrate (*upādi*), consciousness rejoices upon arising from the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi*).

As for "entering," if one attains the accomplishment of the four aggregates (*skandha*) that are wholesome within the meditative absorption of the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is called "entering."
What is the sphere of nothingness?
The answer is:
having transcended the sphere of infinite consciousness, perceiving that there is nothing further, one enters the meditative absorption of nothingness.
Question: What is it that does not exist? Answer:
In that state, there is no self and no what belongs to a self. Question:
Is it the case that throughout all stages there is entirely no self and no what belongs to a self?
The answer is:

Although in all stages there is no self and nothing belonging to a self, the vision of non-self makes my own view weak, thin, and meager, resulting in little suffering and no power; it is not like the contemplation of non-existence.
Furthermore, because it is impermanent therein, lacking constancy and unchangingness, it is called "non-existent.
Furthermore, because it is without concealment, without support, and without refuge, it is called "non-existent."
Furthermore, "nothingness" (ākiṃcanya) is so called because there is no limit to its practice; since nothing exists therein, it is named "nothingness.
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra says:
This meditative concentration is named "nothingness" because it is a dharma that belongs to nothing.
As it is said: "I do not belong to them, nor do they belong to me"; therefore, it is called 'nothingness' (ākiṃcanya).
As for 'entering': if one achieves the four aggregates of the wholesome sphere of nothingness, this is called 'entering'.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"The sphere of nothingness is equanimity.
A question is asked:
Why does the Buddhist scripture state that the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
The answer is:
the Noble Path is equanimity; since this is the final stage attainable, it is therefore called equanimity.
The Venerable Sūmīta said: "Infinite conduct is coarse contemplation;
because one attains tranquility by being free from that joy, it is called equanimity (upekṣā).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
Furthermore, one no longer attends to infinite conduct; with the mind devoid of active power, one abides in equanimity (*upekṣā*).
What is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*)?
The answer is:
Transcending the sphere of nothingness, one enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: For what reason is it called the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception?
Answer: There is no characteristic of clear perception, nor is there a characteristic of clear non-perception.
As for the absence of a characteristic of clear perception, it means there is no such thing as the characteristic of the seven meditative attainments (samāpatti).

Regarding "neither clearly perceived nor characterized by perception": it is like the state of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) or the state of non-perception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti), yet it lacks their characteristics.
Because that perception is dull, foolish, indistinct, and uncertain, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
"Entry" refers to attaining the accomplishment of the four wholesome aggregates of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; this is called entry.
In the desire realm and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, there are no untainted (anāsrava) states.
Question: For what reason is there no untainted (anāsrava) [attainment] in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana)? Answer:
"It is not its field implement," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, because there is a fundamental basis for existence (*bhava-mūla*).
There are two such fundamental bases:
The first is the desire realm (kāmadhātu), and the second is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
Because the untainted path (anāsravamārga) possesses fundamental antidotes (mūlapratipakṣa), it does not reside in the same location as these two.
Furthermore, it serves as an antidote to the two extremes.
There are two kinds of extremes:
first, the desire realm; second, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Because the untainted path counteracts the two extremes, it abides in the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the desire realm is an indeterminate realm; it is neither a stage of detachment from desire nor a stage of cultivation.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is dull, indistinct, uncertain, and not sharp;
the Noble Path is concentrated and sharp.

Furthermore, in the desire realm, restlessness (*auddhatya*) predominates; in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), meditative concentration (*samādhi*) predominates; and in the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), both concentration and wisdom (*prajñā*) predominate.
Furthermore, the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is indeterminate, like doubt, whereas the Noble Path is determinate.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"Dhyāna" is called "entering," while the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamādhi*) are called "transcending.
A question is asked:
Question: For what reason do the Buddhist sūtras refer to the formless absorptions (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) as "transcending" [the form realm], but not the dhyānas?
Answer: The Buddhist sūtras also speak of the dhyānas as "transcending."
As stated in the *Udāyi-sūtra*: "O Udāyin!
A bhikṣu, detached from desires and unwholesome states, with directed thought and sustained evaluation, enters the first dhyāna, which is born of detachment and characterized by joy and bliss."
Udayin! I also declare that this dharma is indeterminate, it is subject to cessation, and it is a fault.
This applies even up to the fourth dhyāna; the explanation is likewise for all of them.
Question: In one sutra, the Buddha says that dhyāna is a fault; in many other sutras, it is said that the formless attainments (ārūpya-samādhi) are faults. Answer:

Because the dhyānas possess various dissimilar characteristics, they are not termed "defects"; because the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) lack such various dissimilar characteristics, they are said to be "defects."

Furthermore, since the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) frequently describe many virtues and beneficial advantages, they are not termed "defects"; however, because the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samādhi*) lack such numerous virtues and beneficial advantages, they are termed "defects."

Furthermore, dhyāna is coarse and directly perceptible, and thus is not called a "transgression" (ādīnava); because the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti) are subtle and difficult to perceive, they are said to be transgressions.
Furthermore, dhyāna is a universally illuminating dharma, as it takes the higher stages, the lower stages, and its own stage as objects; therefore, it is not called a transgression.
Although the formless attainments take their own stage and the higher stages as objects, they do not take the lower stages as objects; therefore, they are said to be transgressions.

Furthermore, because the dhyānas involve coming and going with restless movement, one who is born in the desire realm neither dies nor is reborn there; by means of the power of the *ṛddhipāda*, they reach the fourth dhyāna, and from within the fourth dhyāna, they likewise return to the desire realm. Because it appears as though they cannot transcend these realms, it is not called "transcending.
Since the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are devoid of coming and going, they are said to be "transcending."
Furthermore, because the dhyānas possess internal disturbances,
there is the manifestation of states from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna, and the manifestation of states from the fourth dhyāna down to the desire realm;
since there are no intermediate states (*antarābhava*) in the formless realm (*ārūpya*), it is said to have transcended them.

Furthermore, when one arises in a higher dhyāna, the mind belonging to a lower stage manifests before one; this is not called "transcending," just as the mind that produces transformations within the *vijñānakāya* is not so termed.
However, when one arises in a formless absorption (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the mind of a lower stage does not manifest; therefore, it is said to be "transcending."
Furthermore, when dhyāna arises in a higher stage, there is a continuity of dharmas from the lower stage, just as the mind of transformation within the *vijñānakāya* is not considered "transcendent";
however, since no such continuity of dharmas from a lower stage exists when formless attainments (*ārūpya-samādhi*) arise in a higher stage, they are said to be "transcendent."
For these and other such reasons, it is said that the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are subject to faults, whereas the dhyānas are not.

In the Sphere of Infinite Space, the lifespan is twenty thousand kalpas; in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, it is forty thousand kalpas; in the Sphere of Nothingness, it is sixty thousand kalpas; and in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, it is eighty thousand kalpas.
Question: For what reason do the birthplaces in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) either increase their lifespan twofold or not? Answer:
Because they possess such a degree of causal power for retribution, they experience such a degree of retribution.
Furthermore, in the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, there is both the practice of boundlessness and other practices as well.
In the sphere of infinite space, twenty thousand kalpas are the retribution for the practice of infinity, and twenty thousand kalpas are the retribution for other practices.
In the sphere of infinite consciousness, twenty thousand kalpas are the retribution for the practice of infinity, and twenty thousand kalpas are the retribution for other practices.
In the higher stages there is no practice of the "boundless" (appamāṇa), and therefore there is no retribution.

Furthermore, because the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness possess both concentration and wisdom—the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Space yields a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas as its retribution, and wisdom yields a lifespan of ten thousand kalpas as its retribution;
the concentration of the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness yields a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas as its retribution, and wisdom yields a lifespan of twenty thousand kalpas as its retribution.
Because wisdom is slight in the higher realms, the retribution is also slight.

Furthermore, in the birthplaces of the formless realm, twenty thousand kalpas constitute the fixed lifespan; because they are free from desire, the lifespan increases by twenty thousand kalpas for each successive level.

In the sphere of infinite consciousness (vijñānānantyāyatana), twenty thousand kalpas constitute the fixed lifespan, while another twenty thousand kalpas constitute the lifespan for those who have abandoned desire for the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana).

In the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), twenty thousand kalpas constitute the fixed lifespan, while forty thousand kalpas constitute the lifespan for those who have abandoned desire for both the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness.

Twenty thousand kalpas is the fixed lifespan in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; sixty thousand kalpas is the lifespan for those who have abandoned desire for the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness.
The eight liberations:
contemplating forms as forms is the first liberation;
being internally percipient of no form while contemplating external forms is the second liberation;
The third liberation is the realization through bodily witness of the pure liberation;

the fourth liberation is the transcendence of all perceptions of form, the cessation of perceptions of sensory resistance, and the non-attention to perceptions of diversity, entering the sphere of infinite space;
the fifth liberation is the transcendence of the entire sphere of space, entering the sphere of infinite consciousness.
Transcending the sphere of infinite consciousness and entering the sphere of nothingness is the sixth liberation;
transcending the sphere of nothingness and entering the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the seventh liberation;

transcending the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and entering the cessation of perception and feeling, realizing it through bodily witness and attaining its perfection, is the eighth liberation.
Question: What is the essential nature of liberation? Answer:

The first liberation, the second, and the third liberation are the wholesome root of non-attachment; they serve as the antidote to grasping through attachment. Their corresponding mental states revolve around the four aggregates in the desire realm and the five aggregates in the form realm. The liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception consist of the four aggregates.
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception is subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*).
This is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of liberation; this is explained at length.
Having already explained its essential nature and the reason for it, we shall now explain why it is called "liberation."
What is the meaning of liberation?
The answer is:
the meaning of turning one's back on and abandoning [defilements] is the meaning of liberation.
Question: If the meaning of turning away and abandoning is the meaning of liberation, then from what place does the mind turn away and abandon in order to attain liberation? Answer:

The first liberation and the second liberation involve turning away from the mind of attachment to form; the third liberation involves turning away from the mind of impurity; the liberation of the sphere of infinite space involves turning away from the factors of the lower stages, and so on, up to the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, which likewise turns away from the factors of the lower stages; and the liberation of the cessation of feeling and perception turns away from all minds that take objects as conditions. Therefore, the meaning of "turning away" is the meaning of "liberation."
The Venerable Sumanas said: "The meaning of liberation is the meaning of being released from attachment.
Because the mind is released from and purified of the afflictions, it is called 'liberation'."
The Venerable Buddhadeva said: "Because one attains liberation through the contemplation of conceptualized emptiness, it is called 'liberation.
As for the realms: the first, second, and third liberations are situated within the realm of form (rūpadhātu)."

The liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness—those that are with outflows (sāsrava) belong to the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), while those that are without outflows (anāsrava) are unconditioned by any realm;
the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling belong to the formless realm.

Regarding the "stages" (bhūmi): the first liberation and the second liberation exist in the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the first and second dhyānas; furthermore, there are similar roots of goodness in the higher stages as well, yet they are not established as liberations.
Why is this? To counteract attachment to the forms of the desire realm, the first dhyāna’s liberation through impurity is established;
to counteract attachment to the forms of the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna’s liberation through impurity is established.
Because there is craving for the formless realm in the second dhyāna, the liberation of the impure is not established in the third dhyāna;
because there is craving for the formless realm in the third dhyāna, the liberation of the impure is not established in the fourth dhyāna.
Although there are similar wholesome roots in the stages below the fourth dhyāna that correspond to the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa), they are not established as liberations. Why is this?
Because the pure liberation counteracts the impure and is not overwhelmed by the impure.
If one were to establish the pure liberation (śubha-vimokṣa) within its own respective stage, it would be overcome by the impure.
The liberation of the sphere of space (ākāśāyatana-vimokṣa) resides in the sphere of space. Question:
Regarding the dharmas of the sphere of infinite space, which among them are liberation and which are not liberation?
The answer is:
When one becomes free from desire for the fourth dhyāna, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and eight liberations.
At the time of death, the wholesome state of the sphere of infinite space is not a liberation; other wholesome states of the sphere of infinite space are liberations.
Regarding the liberation of the sphere of consciousness, it resides in the sphere of consciousness. Question:
Among the phenomena of the sphere of consciousness, what constitutes liberation?
What is not liberation?
The answer is:
at the time of departing from desire for the sphere of infinite space, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and eight liberations.
At the time of death, the wholesome sphere of consciousness is not liberation; other wholesome spheres of consciousness are liberation.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness exists within the sphere of nothingness.
Question: Regarding the dharmas of the sphere of nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana), which are liberation and which are not liberation?
Answer: When one is free from desire for the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), there are nine non-obstructions (*anantarya*) and eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
At the time of death, the wholesome state of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) is not a liberation; other wholesome states of the sphere of nothingness are liberations.
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception exists within the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: Among the phenomena of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, what constitutes liberation?
What is not liberation?
The answer is:
at the time of abandoning desire for the sphere of nothingness, there are nine paths of non-obstruction and eight liberations.
At the time of death, wholesome non-percipient-non-non-percipient attainment is not liberation; other wholesome non-percipient-non-non-percipient attainments are liberation.
The cessation-of-ideation-and-feeling liberation resides within the non-percipient-non-non-percipient realm.
Regarding the basis: the first, second, and third liberations are based on a body belonging to the desire realm;
the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling is based on a body belonging to either the desire or form realms.
The remaining liberations depend on bodies belonging to the three realms.

In the practice of the first and second liberations, the practitioner practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); in the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), he practices the contemplation of purity; in the four formless liberations (*ārūpya-vimokṣa*), he practices sixteen aspects or other aspects; and in the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*), no aspect is practiced.
Regarding "object-condition" (ālambana): the first liberation and the second and third liberations take the desire realm as their object.
What phenomena do they take as objects?
The answer is:

The liberation of the sphere of infinite space takes as its object the sense-base of form; it takes as its objects the four formless spheres, their causes, their cessation, all portions of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and subsequent knowledge that is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) take as their objects all of space, whether characterized by unity or diversity.

The liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*) takes as its objects the three formless realms, their causes, their cessations, all portions of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the non-analytical cessation associated with subsequent knowledge.
The three formless attainments (*ārūpya*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) take as their objects all of space, whether characterized by a single aspect or diverse aspects.

The liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*) takes as its objects the two formless spheres, their causes, their cessations, all portions of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and the non-analytical cessation associated with subsequent knowledge.
The two formless [liberations] and non-analytical cessation take as their objects all of space, whether characterized by unity or diversity.

The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception takes as its objects the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, its causes, its cessation, all portions of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and non-analytical cessation associated with subsequent knowledge.
The first formless attainment is not analytical cessation; it takes all space as its object, whether in a single aspect or diverse aspects.
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception has no object.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness: the first liberation, as well as the second and third liberations, are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The four formless liberations are associated with the four foundations of mindfulness.

Regarding the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception: if it is by way of the foundations of mindfulness as application or the foundations of mindfulness as nature, it does not coincide with that [liberation];
if it is by way of the foundation of mindfulness as object, it is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
The wise one, in the first liberation and the second and third liberations, possesses them together with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

In the liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness, they possess them together with six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is accompanied by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception is not accompanied by knowledge.

Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*): the first liberation, the second and third liberations, the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception are not accompanied by concentration.

The liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness are either associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*) or not associated with meditative concentration.
As for the faculties (*indriya*): the first liberation and the second liberation are associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*) is not associated with any faculty (*indriya*).
The remaining liberations are associated with one faculty, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
Regarding the "worlds": those that exist in the three times and take the three times as their object are the first, second, and third liberations.

The past [objects] take the past as their object; the present [objects] take the present as their object; those of the future that are destined to arise take the future as their object, while those not destined to arise take all three periods of time as their object.
The four formless liberations take the three periods of time and the non-temporal (the unconditioned) as their objects.
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception has no object of focus.
Regarding what is wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate: that which is wholesome takes the wholesome as its object;

that which is unwholesome takes the unwholesome as its object; and that which is indeterminate—namely, the first liberation and the second and third liberations—takes the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate as their objects.
The four formless liberations take the wholesome and the neutral as their objects.
The liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling has no object.

Regarding those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound: three are bound to the realm of form, two are bound to the formless realm, and among the remaining three, those with outflows are bound to the formless realm while those without outflows are unbound.

Regarding those conditioned by the three realms’ fetters and those that are unfettered: three conditions pertain to the fetters of the desire realm; four conditions pertain to the fetters of the formless realm and those that are unfettered; one does not condition them at all.

Regarding those that are trainee (*śaikṣa*), non-trainee (*aśaikṣa*), or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: five are neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee, and three are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.

As for those conditioned by what is trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: three are conditioned by the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee, four are conditioned by all three types, and one is unconditioned (*anālambana*).

Regarding those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), those abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), and those not abandoned: five are abandoned by the path of cultivation; as for the three, if they are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are abandoned by the path of cultivation, but if they are without outflows (*anāsrava*), they are not abandoned.

Regarding those abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), as well as those not abandoned: three conditions are abandoned by the path of cultivation; four conditions are of three kinds [abandoned by both paths or not abandoned]; one has no object of perception (*ālambana*).

Regarding "conditions that take names as objects" and "conditions that take meanings as objects": three conditions take meanings as objects; four—if it is said that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) possesses names—then they take names as objects and take meanings as objects; if it is said that it lacks names, then they take meanings as objects; one has no object of perception.

Regarding those conditioned by one's own body, another's body, and non-body dharmas: the first liberation takes as its object one's own body and another's body; the second and third liberations take another's body as their object; the four formless liberations take as their objects one's own body, another's body, and non-body dharmas; and one [liberation] has no object.

Regarding whether these are attained through skillful means (*upāya*) or attained through the abandonment of desire (*vairāgya*): the liberation through the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) is attained through skillful means; the others are attained both through the abandonment of desire and through skillful means.

If it is in the first dhyāna, it is attained at the time of abandoning desire for the desire realm; and so on, up to if it is in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is attained at the time of abandoning desire for the sphere of nothingness.
Regarding "attaining through skillful means," it means that [the path] manifests by means of skillful means.

For a Buddha, it does not manifest by means of skillful means; for a Pratyekabuddha, it is by means of inferior skillful means; and for a Śrāvaka, it is by means of either middling or superior skillful means.

Regarding what is "already attained" and what is "not yet attained": the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*) is not yet attained; the remainder is both already attained and not yet attained.
The Buddhadharma of the sages is that which ordinary beings have fundamentally attained yet never before realized; other ordinary beings have merely attained what they already possessed.
The eight liberations (aṣṭavimokṣa) are explained in detail as above.

Regarding the first liberation—contemplating form as form—it consists of manifesting the cultivation of the perception of internal form while not being separated from the characteristics of internal form, and then contemplating external forms as blue, or as pus, or as bloated, or as swollen, or as bones, or as skeletons. This is called the first liberation.

Regarding "the first" (*ādi*): it is called "the first" because its numerical position is at the beginning; it is called "the first" because its meaning conforms to the sequence and is situated at the beginning.

Furthermore, it is called "the first" because its numerical position is at the beginning when entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in sequence; it is called "the first" because its meaning conforms to the sequence and is situated at the beginning when entering meditative absorption.
When one who is liberated enters this meditative concentration, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness are called liberation.

Regarding "one who, having no perception of internal form, perceives external forms": not manifesting the cultivation of internal form-characteristics and being detached from the perception of internal form, one perceives external forms as blue, as explained in detail above; this is called the second liberation.
The second meaning, the meaning of liberation, is also as explained above. Question:

When contemplating external forms, does one also contemplate the internal perception of formlessness at that time, or does one contemplate the internal perception of formlessness only after having contemplated external forms?
If, when observing external forms, one also observes the internal perception of formlessness, how can a single mind take two dharmas as its object?
If it can take two dharmas as its object, it could likewise take many dharmas as its object.
If one contemplates external forms and then further contemplates internal non-perception of form, how can this be reconciled with what is said here:
"Having no perception of internal form, one contemplates external forms"?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
when one contemplates external forms, at that time one does not contemplate internal non-perception of form.
Question: If that is so, how are the statements made here to be reconciled?
For example, it is said:
"Internally perceiving no marks of form, one contemplates external forms. Answer:
Because the practitioner has formed such a mental resolve, they speak in this way.
The practitioner forms such a resolve:
"I shall not contemplate internal form, but shall contemplate only external form.
Because he has formed such a resolve, the Buddha spoke these words.
Furthermore, it is said here that because the practitioner first performs analytical observation, the Buddha made this statement.
Moreover, it is because the meaning is fixed:
if one observes internally with the perception of formlessness, one then necessarily observes external forms.
If one contemplates external forms, one must necessarily contemplate the internal absence of the perception of form.
Furthermore, this section explains the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and the skillful means (*upāya*).
The internal absence of the perception of form is the skillful means for the roots of goodness, while contemplating external forms is the fulfillment of those roots of goodness.
Furthermore, "having no perception of internal form" refers to the mind; "observing external forms" refers to the object of focus.
To personally realize and accomplish the liberation of the pure is called the third liberation.
Question: Regarding the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*), does one contemplate form as being form, or does one, having no perception of internal form, contemplate external forms?
If one contemplates form as being form, what is the distinction between the first liberation and the third liberation?
If one who lacks the perception of internal form contemplates external forms, what is the difference between the second liberation and the third liberation?
The answer is:
it should be stated as follows:
"Having no perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms. Question:
If this is so, what is the difference between the second liberation and the third liberation?
The answer is:
The names themselves constitute the distinctions; thus, this is called the second liberation and this is called the third liberation.
Furthermore, the second liberation is in the first dhyāna, while the third liberation is in the fourth dhyāna.

Furthermore, the second liberation exists within the bodies of both those of the inner path and those of the outer paths, whereas the pure liberation exists only within the bodies of those of the inner path.
Furthermore, the second liberation practices impure conduct, while the third liberation practices pure conduct.
Furthermore, the second liberation serves as the antidote to craving for form (*rūparāga*), while the third liberation serves as the antidote to [the perception of] impurity (*aśubha*).
Moreover, the second liberation is attained with little effort and little exertion, whereas the pure liberation (*śubhavimokṣa*) is attained through much effort and much exertion.
Furthermore, regarding the second liberation: its essence is luminous and pure while its object is not luminous and pure; its essence is sublime while its object is not sublime;
the liberation of purity has an essence that is sublime and an object that is sublime, and an essence that is luminous and pure and an object that is luminous and pure.
The pure liberation takes the pure as its object. Question:
For what reason does the practitioner contemplate the pure as the object within the pure liberation?
The answer is:
It is for the purpose of testing one's roots of goodness.
The practitioner forms this thought:
I practiced the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and afflictions did not arise.

Not yet knowing whether this root of goodness was fulfilled, I further tested myself by contemplating purity (*śubha-bhāvanā*); afflictions likewise did not arise, whereby I knew that the root of goodness had already reached fulfillment.
Furthermore, because the practitioner contemplates impurity, the mind becomes weak; because the mind is weak, one is unable to cultivate superior and progressive roots of goodness.
Furthermore, pure contemplation causes the mind to rejoice and leap forward, enabling the cultivation of superior and progressive roots of goodness.

It is like a bhikṣu dwelling among cemeteries who, because he constantly contemplates corpses, finds his mind weak and inferior; unable to cultivate superior roots of goodness, he goes from his dwelling to pure, exquisite rivers, ponds, and groves to contemplate the various excellent and wonderful things of the world. His heart becomes joyful and exultant, and only then can he give rise to superior roots of goodness.
It is the same for him as well.

Furthermore, when a practitioner performs the contemplation on impurity, his mind is constantly sorrowful and distressed; since there is no time of joy, he is unable to cultivate superior and progressive roots of goodness.
If one abandons the mind of impurity through pure contemplation, one is able to cultivate superior and progressive roots of goodness.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest the firmness of one's own mind that one forms this thought:
My mind is firm and steadfast; even when practicing the contemplation of purity, afflictions do not arise.
Furthermore, I wish to manifest that my roots of goodness possess great power and efficacy.
Thus, I reflect further:
These roots of goodness possess great power and efficacy; even when encountering pure phenomena, they do not give rise to afflictions.
Furthermore, it is because he wishes to manifest the firmness of his own mind and to demonstrate that these roots of goodness possess great power and efficacy.
He thinks to himself:
"My mind is firm and my roots of goodness possess great power; even when contemplating pure objects, afflictions do not arise.
Furthermore, the liberation of purity cannot be produced by ordinary worldlings.
If a practitioner delights in purity and cleanliness, they have come from the Maṇu-māra heaven.
It is heard that once there was a bhikṣu who, at the time of sunset, went to the Buddha’s dwelling and requested a room from the Buddha.
At that time, the Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Seek a dwelling for this bhikṣu.
Then, Ānanda showed the bhikṣu a room.
That bhikṣu said to Ānanda:

"You should thoroughly sweep and sprinkle this room, hang silk banners and canopies, scatter various kinds of flowers, burn many varieties of famous incense, spread soft bedding, and arrange fine pillows."
At that time, Ānanda went to inform the World-Honored One of these matters in detail.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Whatever that bhikṣu requires, provide it all in full."
At that time, Ānanda immediately prepared everything for him.

Then the bhikṣu entered this room, sat upon the seat, and during the first watch of the night, he gave rise to the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*). By means of this sequence, he attained the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*), became an arhat, and acquired the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
At dawn, by means of his supernormal power, he suddenly departed.
At that time, Ānanda went to the bhikṣu’s dwelling early in the morning; upon entering the room, he saw only the dignified and well-arranged seat, but the man himself was not there.
Having seen this, he went to where the Buddha was and said to the Buddha:
"That bhikṣu has prepared his seat with great solemnity, yet I do not know where he has gone.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
Do not give rise to a contemptuous mind toward that bhikṣu.

Last night, that bhikṣu gave rise to the pure liberation, attained the exhaustion of outflows, became an arhat, and acquired the supernormal powers; by means of his supernormal power, he suddenly departed.
Ānanda, you should know that this bhikṣu delights in purity and cleanliness; he has come from the Maṇusya-deva heaven.
If he had not obtained such a pure dwelling, bed, seat, and bedding, he would not have been able to give rise to these roots of goodness.

For this reason, it is known that the pure liberation cannot be produced by ordinary persons; rather, it can only be produced by those who dwell in the delight of purity and have come from the Mānuṣottara Heaven.
The third meaning, the meaning of liberation, is as explained above.

The liberations of the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are explained in detail as the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
The liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*), the sphere of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*),
and the eighth meaning of liberation should be explained in detail as previously stated.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 43.
The Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Fascicle 44.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Northern Liang Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman.
Translated by Goudai and others, from the *Khandaka*, Chapter Ten on the Ten Gates, Part Eight. Question:

For what reason are the remaining wholesome roots within the dhyānas established as liberations (*vimokṣa*), whereas all [wholesome roots] within the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) are established as liberations?
Answer: Because dhyāna is coarse and is clearly perceived through direct observation, the other roots of goodness are established as liberation;
because the formless attainments (ārūpya-samādhi) are subtle, not clearly perceived, and not distinct, they are all established as liberation.
Furthermore, because there are various dissimilar roots of goodness within the dhyānas, other roots of goodness are established as liberations;
because the formless attainments lack such various dissimilar roots of goodness, they are all established as liberations.
Furthermore, because the dhyānas possess many meritorious virtues and beneficial qualities, the other roots of goodness are established as liberation;
whereas because the formless attainments lack such manifold meritorious virtues and beneficial qualities, they are all established as liberation [from the realm of form].
Furthermore, dhyāna is able to illuminate universally; it takes the higher stages as its object, as well as the lower stages and its own stage, and other wholesome roots therein establish liberation.

The formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) cannot illuminate universally; they can take the higher stages and their own stage as objects, but do not take the lower stages as objects. Therefore, liberation is established only for them in their entirety.

Furthermore, the liberations within the dhyānas are with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the liberations within the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are both with and without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Thus, from this discussion, further inquiry arises:
for what reason are the liberations within the dhyānas exclusively with outflows, while those within the formless attainments are both with and without outflows?
Answer: The four types of answers previously mentioned should be explained here.

As for the remaining answer regarding identity and difference: the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and liberations (*vimokṣa*) are conceptual observations, whereas the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and liberations are actual observations.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"Liberation is called direction.
Question: [Why is this so?]
Why does the Buddha say that liberation is called a "direction"?
The answer is:
for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Those who are to be transformed must hear the teaching of the name "direction" (dis) before they can attain awakening and understanding; therefore, the Buddha teaches liberation by means of the term "direction.
As other sūtras state: "The Truth (satya) is called 'direction'."
There are those to be transformed who must hear the name "Truth" before they can attain awakening and understanding; for this reason, the Buddha spoke of the name "Truth.
This case is also like that. Question:
What similarity do liberation and direction possess?
The answer is:
they share eight similarities.
There are eight liberations and likewise eight directions.
Question: There should be ten directions, namely the four cardinal points, the four intermediate points, and the zenith and nadir.
Why are eight taught?
The answer is:
because it is like the method for training an elephant, there should be eight.
The method for training an elephant requires directing it toward the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate points; one cannot cause it to face upward or downward.
Just as an elephant is trained by means of these directions, so too is liberation attained through skillful means.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke thus:
"There are three matters concerning the taming and liberation of an elephant that are common to both, and three matters that differ.
As for what is common: first, because it is methodical, the dragon-elephant can be tamed."
Liberation is likewise: because obstacles are removed, sentient beings are able to attain liberation.
Second, it is like a tamed dragon or elephant; when it has set out for one direction, it cannot proceed toward another.
The Dharma for liberating sentient beings taught by the Buddha is also like this: when one attains liberation, there is neither duality nor multiplicity.
It is like a tamed dragon or elephant; when it moves toward one direction, it is far removed from all other directions.
The World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma for liberation to sentient beings is likewise: when one liberation manifests before one, the other liberations recede.
As for the three distinct matters, the first is like taming a dragon or an elephant; if it does not proceed toward its proper direction, it cannot be tamed.
The Buddha taught the Dharma of liberation, which abides in one place without moving toward anything else, yet enables sentient beings to attain the Dharma of liberation.
Second, it is like a tamed dragon or elephant that, once directed toward a single direction, cannot move toward any other direction.
The Dharma of liberation taught by the Buddha is not like that; he can, in a single moment, expound the eight liberations so that all sentient beings attain awakening and understanding.
Third, it is like a tamed dragon-elephant: when it moves toward one direction, it leaves all other directions far behind.

The Dharma of liberation taught by the Buddha is not otherwise; for the sake of all sentient beings, he teaches a single method of liberation, yet employs skillful means to bring all other methods of liberation into close proximity.
Furthermore, herein is explained the most excellent method of taming.
It is heard that King Prasenajit of Kosala once commanded his elephant-trappers to capture wild elephants, saying:
"If you catch an elephant, come and inform me."
At that time, having heard the king’s command, the elephant hunters immediately captured a wild elephant and came to inform the king, saying:
"Your Majesty, please be informed that we have now captured a wild elephant."
Upon hearing these words, the king commanded the elephant trainer to tame the wild elephant, saying:
"If you can successfully tame it, then come and inform me.

At that time, the elephant trainer, having received the king's command, proceeded to tame the wild elephant using various harsh and painful methods, until he was able to subdue it just like a previously trained elephant.
At that time, the elephant trainer, knowing that the elephant had been well-trained, came and addressed the king, saying:
"Great King, you should know that the elephant previously commanded to be trained is now well-trained.
Great King, you should know that this is the time."
At that time, King Prasenajit was riding this elephant together with an elephant trainer when they went out to the fields for a hunt.
Seeing a herd of female elephants, the king’s lustful desire flared up, and he galloped toward the herd.
At that time, the elephant trainer sought to turn the animal back and restrain it, yet despite exhausting all his skillful means, he could not make it turn back.
The king and the trainer climbed down from the tree and thus managed to save their own lives.
He returned to the palace and said to the elephant trainer:
"You have made me ride an untamed elephant.
Is this the proper way to act?"
Then the elephant trainer addressed the king, saying:
"I only pray that Your Majesty will not look upon me with anger or reproach.
This elephant is truly tamed; I shall cause Your Majesty to verify this matter later."
When the elephant’s lustful mind had subsided, it returned to the royal palace.
Then the elephant trainer led the elephant before the king, placed a glowing red-hot iron ball upon its head, and spoke into its ear:

"This is the final method for training you so that you remain unmoved; if you can endure this, it will be well, but if you cannot endure it, we shall once again train you in succession with the previous methods of harsh discipline."
Upon hearing these words, the elephant remained as motionless as a mountain.
Then, hot iron balls scorched the elephant’s head like birch bark being burned.
When the king witnessed this unprecedented marvel, he immediately commanded the elephant trainer to remove the iron balls.
The elephant trainer said to the king:
"Since you can now train an elephant to such an extent, why was it not so before?
The elephant trainer replied to the king:
"I am able to train the body, but I cannot train the mind.
Then the king again asked the elephant trainer:
"Is there anyone in the world who can train the mind?"
Then the elephant trainer replied to the king, saying:
"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who dwells at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī; he is skilled at taming the bodies and minds of sentient beings."
At that time, King Prasenajit thought to himself,
"I wish to see the Buddha.
He immediately mounted his original state elephant together with the elephant trainer and proceeded to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a retinue of hundreds of thousands as he preached the Dharma.
Seeing King Prasenajit approaching, the World-Honored One employed skillful means appropriate to him to preach the Dharma for the king—a realm beyond the knowledge of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"It is like an elephant trainer who, having well-trained an elephant, leads it toward one direction—whether east, west, south, or north."
One who trains oxen is skilled at training oxen; one who trains horses is skilled at training horses, each leading them toward a single direction.
As explained in detail above, monks, you should know that the Unsurpassed Tamer of Men is skilled at training people so that they may proceed toward all directions.
What is the direction?
It is the contemplation that "form is form," and so forth, up to the detailed exposition on liberation.
For this reason, it is known that this sutra speaks of the most excellent tamer.
The Sūtra says:
A certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”

There is the element of light, the element of purity, the element of the sphere of infinite space, the element of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the element of the sphere of nothingness, the element of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the element of cessation.
“World-Honored One!
For what reason are these various elements established?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

Because of darkness, the realm of light is established; because of impurity, the realm of purity is established; because of form, the realm of the sphere of infinite space is established; because of limitation, the realm of the sphere of infinite consciousness is established; because of existence, the realm of the sphere of nothingness is established; because of the substantial body, the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is established; and because of the cessation of the substantial body, the realm of cessation is established.
Question: For what purpose did that bhikṣu question the Buddha,
and for what purpose did the Buddha answer that bhikṣu?
The answer is:

That bhikṣu questioned about the meaning of the eight liberations using indirect terminology, and the Buddha likewise answered regarding the meaning of the eight liberations using indirect terminology.
"Clarifying the realms" refers to the first two liberations.
The realm of purity is the liberation of purity.
The realm of the sphere of infinite space is the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
The realm of the sphere of infinite consciousness is the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness.
The sphere of nothingness is the liberation of the sphere of nothingness.
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Regarding the "element of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*), it is the liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā-vimokṣa*). Question:
For what reason did that bhikṣu ask the Buddha about the meaning of the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) by using indirect phrasing?
Answer: That bhikṣu has few desires and is content; he conceals his wholesome qualities because he does not wish to display his own merits to others. Question:
Why did the Buddha teach the eight liberations using concealed terminology?
The answer is:
because he wished to fulfill the aspirations in the minds of those bhikṣus.
That bhikṣu thought to himself:
"It would be excellent if the Buddha were to explain the eight liberations to me using concealed terminology.
Since the Buddha fulfills the wishes of others and thoroughly understands their faculties and natures, he spoke using concealed terminology because of what that bhikṣu had thought.

Bhikṣus, you should know that the element of light constitutes the first two liberations. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of darkness," "darkness" refers to the craving for form within the desire realm; the first two liberations are their antidotes, and these two liberations are established on account of that craving for form.

Regarding the establishment of the "pure realm" (śubhadhātu) on account of the impure: the impure refers to the first two liberations (vimokṣa); the pure liberation is their antidote, and it is established as such because of them.

Regarding the establishment of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśāyatana*) on account of form (*rūpa*): form refers to the fourth dhyāna, and the liberation of the sphere of infinite space is its antidote; it is for that reason that the liberation of the sphere of infinite space is established.

Regarding the establishment of the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*) because of its limit: the limit is the sphere of infinite space; the liberation of the sphere of consciousness is its antidote, and it is established as such on account of that [limit].
Question: Why is the sphere of infinite space called "the limit"? Answer:
The limit of form (*rūpa*) is the boundary of form; therefore, it is called a "boundary" (*anta*).

As for the establishment of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-dhātu*) on the basis of "that which exists": that which exists is the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), because there is the practice of the infinite.
The liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*) is its antidote; it is established as such because of that [antidote].

Regarding the establishment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-dhātu*) by way of the "actual body" (*bhūtadeha*): the actual body refers to the sphere of nothingness, and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is its antidote; it is established as such because of that [antidote].

The element of cessation is established by means of the cessation of the actual body; the cessation of the actual body is termed the liberation of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, while the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception is its antidote. It is on account of that [antidote] that the liberation characterized by the cessation of sensation is established.
Question: Why is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception called the "body of actual cessation"? Answer:

The actual body is the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is its antidote; therefore, it is called "cessation.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, that bhikṣu rejoiced and followed it with faith, and further asked the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what concentration are the element of clarity (*vidyā-dhātu*) up to the element of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*) attained?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The element of clarity up to the element of cessation are attained by means of the concentration of practice (*caryā-samādhi*)."
Some say that the bhikṣu asks about attaining the stages in succession;
others say that the bhikṣu asks about the abandonment [of defilements].

If it is said that the bhikṣu asks about attaining the stages in succession, then his practice of concentration extends from the limit of the first dhyāna up to the limit of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).

Regarding the limit of the first dhyāna: by abandoning desire and craving, one attains the first and second liberations. Regarding the limit of the fourth dhyāna: by abandoning the desires of the third dhyāna, one attains the pure liberation.
Regarding the limit of the sphere of infinite space: by abandoning the desires of the fourth dhyāna, one attains the liberation of the sphere of infinite space.
Regarding the limit of the sphere of consciousness: having abandoned desire for the sphere of infinite space, one attains liberation in the sphere of consciousness.
Regarding the limit of the sphere of nothingness: having abandoned desire for the sphere of consciousness, one attains liberation in the sphere of nothingness.
Among these, the remaining two are the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained through the concentration of superior practice."

Regarding the concentration of supreme practice (*abhibhvāyatana-samādhi*): it is at the limit of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*). By means of the concentration of supreme practice, one becomes detached from the desire for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and attains the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The realm of cessation is attained through the meditative absorption of the station of the extinction of perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-samāpatti*).

As for the meditative absorption of the extinction of perception and feeling, it is the meditative absorption of the station of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samāpatti*). Why is this so?
Because the mind remains in that state both during entry into and emergence from meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

If one explains it in this way, when that bhikṣu asks about "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*), he is referring to the practice of concentration as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*); therefore, he is able to become detached from the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Among these, the remaining are the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the liberation of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Monks! The liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is attained through the meditative concentration of superior practice.
The concentration of superior practice is the untainted antidote.

Since the mundane path may decline and regress from detachment from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one therefore employs the untainted antidote to abandon desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The realm of cessation is attained through the cessation of the substantial body.
This cessation of the substantial body is the nirvana of extinction.
Because it is the nirvana of extinction, one cultivates the meditative attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.

Regarding the statement that "the bhikṣu establishes the element of light because of darkness": "darkness" refers to the darkness of the objective sphere; the first two liberations are their antidotes.

Furthermore, there are those who say that this bhikṣu, having abandoned desire for the three realms, questioned the Buddha using the concealed mode (*saṃvṛta-lakṣaṇa*) in both broad and abbreviated forms; the Buddha likewise answered him using the concealed mode in both broad and abbreviated forms, as he too had abandoned desire for the three realms.
The "sphere of clarity" (*vidarśanā-dhātu*) is the manifestation of being currently free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
The "sphere of purified skillful means" (*upāya-śuddha-dhātu*) is a brief manifestation of being free from desire for the realm of desire.
The "sphere of the base of infinite space" (*ākāśānantyāyatana-dhātu*) is a brief manifestation of being free from desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

The sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception are the extensive manifestations of detachment from the desire for the formless realm.
The sphere of cessation is the concise manifestation of detachment from the desire for the formless realm.

Regarding the statement that "a bhikṣu establishes the realm of light because of darkness," "darkness" refers to craving for the five sublime sensual pleasures; the first two liberations are their antidotes.
The parable-makers speak thus:
that bhikṣu asked about the eight kinds of meditative concentration using indirect phrasing, and the Buddha also explained the eight kinds of meditative concentration using indirect phrasing.
