But if it is said that bodily and vocal formations arise at the moment of emerging from the attainment of cessation, how can this be?

Why is this? It is because one arises from the fourth dhyāna and enters the bodily formations (*kāyasamskāra*) of the third dhyāna, and so on, down to arising from the second dhyāna and entering the verbal formations (*vāksaṃskāra*) of the first dhyāna, and so on, until birth.
Why is it said that when emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one gives rise to bodily and vocal formations?
The answer is:

there are two types of emergence from the attainment of cessation—the near and the distant. In the case of the near, one gives rise to mental formations; in the case of the distant, one gives rise to bodily and vocal formations.
Furthermore, from the arising of the cessation attainment (*nirodhasamāpatti*) up to the first dhyāna, all are termed "the time of arising from the cessation attainment.
Why is this so? Because by virtue of the cessation attainment, one arises from those various stages.
He asked again: "Āyuṣman!
When a bhikṣu arises from the meditative attainment of cessation, what does his mind accord with?"
Toward what does the mind turn?
Into what does the mind descend? He spoke thus:
"Upāsikā Viśākhā! When a bhikṣu arises from the attainment of cessation, his mind inclines toward detachment, his mind turns closer to detachment, and his mind tends toward entering into detachment.
[She] asked:
In this context, what is "separation"?
The answer is:
some say it is the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

If one speaks thus, there are two factors in the conventional mind of one who has emerged from this meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*): they accord with detachment, they turn toward detachment, and they are on the verge of entering detachment;
first, by way of aspiration, and second, by way of the object-condition (*ālambana*).

When an outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*) upon emerging from meditative absorption is associated with the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*), there is one factor that accords with detachment: it takes [the object] as its condition, but not through a directed mental aspiration.

When it is associated with the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) or the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*), it neither takes [the object] as its condition nor does it involve a directed mental aspiration.
Furthermore, there are those who say that Nirvana is extinction apart from this.

If one were to say that Nirvana is extinction apart from this, then even upon emerging from meditative absorption with a conventional mind, there would be no directed thought, no object of focus, and no [states of] detachment by conformity, detachment by proximity, or detachment by imminent entry.

If an untainted [consciousness] is associated with the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, or the knowledge of the path, it has no object regarding the aspiration for liberation from existence.
If it is associated with the knowledge of cessation, it does have an object regarding the aspiration for liberation from existence.
Furthermore, there are those who say that apart from this cessation concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*), there is also a cessation that is *nirvāṇa*.

If one were to make such a claim—that apart from this cessation concentration there is also a cessation that is *nirvāṇa*—then regarding the conventional mind upon emerging from concentration and the untainted mind associated with the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, its origin, and its path, taken together, there are two factors that accord with detachment, approach detachment, and incline toward entry into detachment: first, by means of the directed mind (*citta-ākṣepa*);
second, by means of the object-condition (*ālambana*).
"One who accords with the Way has one thing that conforms to detachment, approaches detachment, and inclines toward entering detachment; they have a directed mind, yet no objective conditions.
He asked again: "Āyuṣman!"
When a bhikkhu arises from the attainment of cessation, how many contacts does he experience?
He said this: "Uppāsikā Visākhā!"
There are three types of contact:
first, immovable contact; second, the contact of nothingness;
[and third, the contact of neither-perception-nor-non-perception].
3. The Contact of Signlessness. Question:
What are the contact of immovability, the contact of nothingness, and the contact of signlessness?
The Venerable Sūmī said:

“The sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness are the contact of immovability; the sphere of nothingness is the contact of nothingness; and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is the contact of signlessness.”
Furthermore, emptiness is the contact of immovability; wishlessness is the contact of non-existence; signlessness is the contact of signlessness.
Furthermore, the sphere of nothingness is the contact of immovability, the contact of non-existence, and the contact of signlessness.
That which is untainted (*anāsrava*) is the contact of immovability;
because it is subsumed under the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is the contact of nothingness;
because it takes nirvāṇa as its object, it is the contact of signlessness (*animitta*).
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:

When a bhikṣu arises from the attainment of cessation, if it is a mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception that arises and no other dissimilar mind arises, it should be said that he contacts the contact of signlessness.
If it is a dissimilar mind belonging to the sphere of nothingness, one should say it contacts the contact of nothingness.
If it is a dissimilar mind belonging to the sphere of consciousness, one should say it contacts the immovable contact.
The same explanation applies to the other five attainments of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*). Question:
Just as one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in successive order, does one also emerge from the attainment of cessation in successive order?
The answer is:
one enters according to sequence, but does not emerge according to sequence;
one emerges according to sequence, but does not enter according to sequence.
Just as it is not as easy to wake up in sequence as it is to fall asleep in sequence,
so too is it not as easy to fall asleep in sequence as it is to wake up in sequence;
such is the case here as well.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Forty-four [and] Volume Forty-five.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
From the *Prakaraṇapāda* (Shi-men-pin), Chapter Nine: As it is said:

"If one attains this concentration, by relying on this concentration and establishing this concentration, one will no longer undergo future birth, old age, sickness, death, suffering, its origin, and its cessation."
Question: This concentration cannot sever the fetters (saṃyojana).
Why, then, is this statement made?
"If one attains this concentration," and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer is:
one should examine this matter to determine for what reason it occurs.
If a practitioner who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) emerges from that state, they form this thought:
"This is a momentary cessation;

for a brief moment, the mind and mental factors did not function, and it was so still and sublime. How much more so would it be when there is ultimate cessation, where the mind and mental factors never again function?"
For this reason, they immediately sever the afflictions and enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.

If an *aśaikṣa* who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) arises from that concentration, he forms such a thought, and so on, until for this reason he relinquishes the aggregates (*skandhas*) and enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
For this reason, it is said: "If one attains this concentration," and so forth, up to "one will no longer undergo suffering or give rise to its accumulation.
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:

There are those who enter meditative absorption with a vow but emerge from it without a vow; there are those who enter meditative absorption without a vow but emerge from it with a vow; there are those who enter meditative absorption with a vow and emerge from it with a vow; and there are those who enter meditative absorption without a vow and emerge from it without a vow.
Regarding entering meditative absorption with a formal resolve but emerging from it without one: it is like someone who forms this thought,
"May I enter the attainment of cessation," yet does not form the thought [to emerge].

It causes me to emerge from the extinction attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). It gives rise to the four types of existence-perception attainments (*bhava-saṃjñā-samāpatti*); if any one of them manifests before me, I am able to emerge from that attainment.
If any one of the four types of existence-perception attainments manifests before me, this is called entering the attainment by making a vow and emerging from the attainment without making a vow.
Regarding "entering meditative absorption without forming a vow and emerging from it with a vow": it is like someone who does not form the thought,
"May I enter the attainment of cessation," but instead forms this thought:
"May I emerge from the attainment of cessation.

He gives rise to one of the four types of ideation-attainments of existence; when one of these manifests before him, he enters the attainment of cessation and emerges from the attainment of cessation.

By giving rise to one of the four types of ideation-attainments of existence and manifesting it before him, this is called "entering the attainment without making a vow and emerging from the attainment by making a vow."
Regarding "entering meditative absorption through a formal resolve and emerging from meditative absorption through a formal resolve," it is like someone who forms this thought:
"May I enter the attainment of cessation; may I emerge from the attainment of cessation."

One gives rise to the four types of meditative attainments involving perception of existence (*bhavasaṃjñāsamāpatti*); if any one of them manifests before one, one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and emerges from the attainment of cessation.

When one gives rise to the four types of meditative attainments involving perception of existence and any one of them manifests before one, this is called entering the attainment by making a vow and emerging from the attainment by making a vow.
There are those who enter meditative absorption without forming a wish and emerge from it without forming a wish; this is just as when someone does not form the thought:
"May I enter the attainment of cessation" or "May I emerge from the attainment of cessation."

When one gives rise to the four types of perception of existence (*bhavasaṃjñā*) and brings any one of them to presence, one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and emerges from the attainment of cessation.

When one gives rise to the four types of perception of existence and brings any one of them to presence, this is called entering the meditative absorption without making a vow and emerging from the meditative absorption without making a vow.
Question: It may be that one enters meditative absorption through a formal vow and emerges from it through a formal vow;
however, what is meant by entering and emerging from meditative absorption without the desire to do so?
Answer: This refers to those who wish to enter meditative absorption at will and wish to emerge from meditative absorption at will.
However, regarding entry into and emergence from meditative absorption, there are those who possess mastery and those who do not.
Therefore, the *Prajñapti-śāstra* states as follows:

"There are those whose minds attain mastery when entering meditative absorption but do not attain mastery when emerging from it; there are those whose minds attain mastery when emerging from absorption but do not attain mastery when entering it; there are those whose minds attain mastery both when entering and emerging from absorption; and there are those whose minds do not attain mastery either when entering or emerging from absorption."

If one attains mastery over the mind upon entering meditative concentration but lacks mastery over the mind upon emerging from it, this is because one has not made a vow to enter concentration but has made a vow to emerge from it.

If one attains mastery over the mind upon emerging from meditative concentration but lacks mastery over the mind upon entering it, this is because one has not made a vow to emerge from concentration but has made a vow to enter it.

One who has mastery over the mind when entering meditative concentration and mastery over the mind when emerging from it does not form a wish to enter concentration nor does he form a wish to emerge from it.

One who lacks mastery over the mind when entering meditative concentration and lacks mastery over the mind when emerging from it forms a wish to enter concentration and forms a wish to emerge from it.
For this reason, it is said:
those who have entered meditative concentration all desire to enter concentration; those who have emerged from meditative concentration all desire to emerge from concentration. Question:
In this context, what is described as the four meditative attainments of non-perception?
The answer is:
they are the four formless [attainments].
Question: For what reason are the four formless attainments (ārūpyas) called the four meditative absorptions of existence (bhavasaṃjñāsamāpattis)? Answer:

Regarding the four formless attainments, one can perform the "reverse-order attainment" (*pratiloma-anuloma-samāpatti*) and the "reverse-leap attainment" (*pratiloma-vyutkrānta-samāpatti*) in relation to the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

If, upon emerging from that attainment, one gives rise to the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and subsequently gives rise to the mind of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), this is the reverse-order attainment.
If one gives rise to the mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), this is the reverse leap concentration (*vyutkrāntakasamādhi*).

If, upon emerging from that concentration, one gives rise to the mind of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) and subsequently gives rise to the mind of the sphere of infinite consciousness, this is the reverse sequential concentration (*anulomavyutkrama-samādhi*).
If one gives rise to the mind of the sphere of infinite space, this is the reverse leap-concentration (*vyutkrāntaka-samādhi*).
For this reason, it is said that the four formless attainments are the four meditative states with perception (*saṃjñā-samāpatti*).
As the Sūtra says:

One who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation cannot be burned by fire, cannot be swept away by water, cannot be wounded by a blade, cannot be harmed by poison, and cannot be killed by another.

Question: For what reason is one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) unable to be burned by fire, unable to be swept away by water, unable to be wounded by a blade, unable to be harmed by poison, and unable to be killed by another?
The Venerable Sūmīpa said:
"This concentration is a state of non-harming.
If one enters this concentration, harm cannot cause injury."
Furthermore, because this concentration possesses great majestic power, the deities of majestic virtue constantly guard it.
Moreover, the realms of each dhyāna and the realms of the bases of supernormal power (*ṛddhipāda*) are inconceivable.
Furthermore, this concentration is without mind; that which is without mind neither dies nor is born.
The *Saṃjīva-sūtra* provides the causal basis for this argument.
It is heard that in the past there was the Buddha Kakusandha, who had two great and virtuous disciples: one named Vīra and the other named Saṃjīva.

At that time, the Venerable Śāṇakavāsin had extensively taught and transformed many people within a certain city. He entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) at a place frequented by many people on the outskirts of that city.
Then, cowherds, shepherds, wood-gatherers, and travelers who saw him all thought to themselves:
"This Great Virtuous One has died while sitting upright; we should take cow dung and dry firewood to cremate him and then depart."
Just as he had thought, he took dry firewood and cow dung, burned them, and departed.

At that time, the Venerable Sañjīva arose from the meditative absorption of cessation early in the morning; he quickly shook out his saṃghāṭī robe and, during the first part of the day, donned his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for alms.
At that time, the cowherds, shepherds, wood-gatherers, grass-cutters, and travelers who saw him all said this:
"This venerable one died sitting upright yesterday; we burned him with dry wood and cow dung and left him, yet now he has come back to life again."
The people of that time all called him "Revived.
The reason he did not burn his body was because it was protected by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*);
the reason his robes did not burn was because they were sustained by the power of supernormal faculties (*ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that the reason his body was not burned and his robes were not consumed was entirely due to the power of his meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Therefore, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* serves as the scriptural source for this treatise.
As it is said in the *Nidāna*:
"One who gives to a person who has emerged from the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) obtains a reward in the present life.
Question: Why is this so?
Why is it that giving to one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation yields a reward in the present life?
The answer is:
this need not necessarily be explained.
Why is this so? Because this teaching is not found in the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Abhidharma;
it is merely a causal explanation, which may be either correct or incorrect.
If one must insist on reconciling this, what is the underlying meaning?
The answer is:
although one does not receive retribution in the present life, one receives manifold retributions [in future lives].
Question: For what reason does giving to one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation result in either a reward in the present life or a great reward? Answer:

If one gives food to those who have attained the cessation of perception and feeling (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is as if one were giving food to those who have arisen from the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis. Why is this so?

Because one who wishes to enter this meditative absorption first arouses a wholesome mind of the desire realm, then successively enters the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), and finally enters the cessation of perception and feeling in succession.

When wishing to emerge from this meditative absorption, one successively gives rise to the mind of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception from that absorption down to the first dhyāna, and then successively gives rise to a wholesome mind of the desire realm.
Because the practitioner cultivates such merits within their own person, they obtain rewards in the present life, or even manifold rewards, for giving food.

Furthermore, when arising from this meditative concentration, their deportment—such as moving in and out, speaking, putting on robes, and receiving food and drink—is tranquil; consequently, faithful brāhmaṇas and householders develop a mind of reverence and respect, bestowing upon them clothing, food, and other necessities, whereby they obtain rewards in the present life, or even manifold rewards.
Furthermore, this meditative absorption gives rise to a sense of rarity.

If people hear that a certain bhikṣu has attained the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), they conceive an extreme sense of rarity; consequently, brahmins and householders with faith offer him robes, food, and other necessities with a pure mind, thereby obtaining rewards in the present life or even manifold rewards.
Furthermore, if one gives food to one who has arisen from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is called giving food to a person who does not eat.

One who has entered the attainment of the perception of existence (*saṃjñisamāpatti*), although not consuming edible morsel-food (*kabaḷīkārāhāra*), nevertheless consumes the contaminated foods of contact (*sparśāhāra*), volition (*manosañcetanāhāra*), and consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*).

Although one who enters the untainted concentration (anāsrava-samādhi) does not consume the four kinds of tainted food (sāsrava-āhāra), they sustain the body by means of untainted contact (sparśa), volition (manasikāra), and consciousness (vijñāna).

One who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), however, lacks these four kinds of food and likewise does not sustain the body by means of untainted contact, volition, or consciousness. Therefore, giving to one who has arisen from the attainment of cessation is equivalent to giving food to one who does not eat; such a gift yields a reward in the present life, or even a great reward.
Furthermore, if one gives food to those who have arisen from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is as if giving food to those who have returned from nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because this meditative attainment resembles nirvāṇa.

Just as when one enters *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, all mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) do not arise, and all conditioned phenomena with objects (*sālambana-dharma*) are extinguished;
this meditative concentration is likewise so. Therefore, those who give food to such a person obtain rewards in the present life, or else they obtain manifold rewards.

Not only does one obtain a reward in the present life for giving food to those who have entered the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti), but one also obtains a reward in the present life for giving food to five kinds of persons:
first, those emerging from the meditative absorption of cessation;
second, those emerging from a mind of loving-kindness (maitrīcitta); [and so forth].
Third, arising from the state of non-contention;
fourth, arising from the path of vision;
fifth, arising from the attainment of the knowledge of exhaustion.
Furthermore, giving food to five kinds of persons yields great reward:
first, giving to one's father;
second, giving to one's mother;... [and so forth].
Third, giving to the sick;
fourth, giving to those who preach the Dharma;
fifth, giving to those near Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Question: Is this meditative concentration the karma that creates the place of rebirth, or is it the completing karma? Answer:
This is the ripening karma (*pūrṇakarma*), not the formative karma (*abhisamskāra-karma*).
Why is this so? Because formative karma must possess the nature of karma, whereas that [ripening karma] does not possess the nature of karma.
Question: Does this concentration result in reward in the present life, reward in the next birth, or reward in a subsequent life? Answer:
This meditative absorption can only result in rebirth in a future life; it cannot yield a reward in the present life. Why is this?
Because one cannot give rise to this absorption while in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: In what place is the retribution for this meditative concentration received? Answer:
Regarding the four aggregates that constitute the retribution of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception:
if one accomplishes the attainment of cessation, does one also accomplish the retribution of the attainment of cessation?
The answer is: Yes.
Or, one may achieve the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) but not the retribution for the attainment of cessation; this is elaborated in full as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the case of achieving the attainment of cessation but not its retribution: it refers to one born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) who has attained the attainment of cessation, or one who, having attained the attainment of cessation, does not fall away from it, yet is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and has not yet experienced the retribution of that attainment.

One who has attained the retribution of the attainment of cessation but has not attained the attainment of cessation itself, falls away from that attainment of cessation and is reborn in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, where they experience the retribution of the attainment of cessation.

One who accomplishes the attainment of cessation and also accomplishes the retribution of the attainment of cessation is one who, having attained the attainment of cessation without falling back from it, is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and experiences the retribution of the attainment of cessation.

One who neither possesses the attainment of cessation nor possesses the retribution for the attainment of cessation is one who is born within the desire realm or the form realm and does not attain the attainment of cessation;

or one who is born in the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, or the sphere of nothingness, and either falls away from having attained the attainment of cessation or never attains it; or one who is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and does not receive the retribution for the attainment of cessation.
If one falls away from the *nirodha-samāpatti*, does one also fall away from the fruit of Arhatship?
The answer is:
one may fall away from the *nirodha-samāpatti* without falling away from the fruit of Arhatship; thus, one should elaborate fully upon the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding one who falls away from the attainment of cessation but does not fall away from the fruit of arhatship: a trainee (śaikṣa) may fall away from the attainment of cessation; an arhat may fall away from the attainment of cessation, yet such a falling away is not due to a lack of mastery, nor does it result in the manifestation of active fetters.
Regarding those who fall from the fruit of arhatship but do not fall from the meditative attainment of cessation: the arhat liberated by wisdom (prajñā-vimukta) falls;

one who had attained the attainment of cessation during the stage of training (śaikṣa) gives rise to the fetters of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception at the time of being beyond training (aśaikṣa).

Regarding those who fall away from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and also fall away from the fruit of arhatship: one who attains the attainment of cessation during the stage of training (*śaikṣa*) may fall away from it due to the arising of fetters (*saṃyojana*) belonging to a lower realm when they reach the stage of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa*);
one who attains the attainment of cessation during the stage of no-more-training may fall away from it due to the arising of fetters belonging to any one of the three realms.
Regarding those who do not fall back from the concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) nor from the fruit of arhatship: this excludes the aforementioned cases.

There are six types of arhats, namely: those subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), those subject to mindfulness (*cetayitadharman*), those subject to guarding (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), those abiding in equanimity (*sthitākampya*), those capable of progress (*prativedhanādharman*), and the immovable (*akopyadharman*).
Are all Arhats of the "subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman) type necessarily both-liberated (ubhayatobhāgavimukta)?
Are all Arhats who are both-liberated necessarily of the "subject to regression" type?
And so on, up to: are all Arhats of the "immovable" (akopyadharman) type necessarily both-liberated?
If all Arhats who are liberated through both parts are necessarily immovable?
The answer is:
some are Arhats subject to falling away who are not liberated through both parts; thus, one should elaborate fully using the four permutations.

An Arhat of the "subject to regression" (parihāṇadharman) type is not one liberated both ways (ubhayatobhāgavimukta), for no Arhat of the subject to regression type attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

An Arhat of the "liberated both ways" type is not of the subject to regression type; such an Arhat—ranging from the "mindful of the Dharma" (dharmānusārin) up to the "immovable" (akopyadharman)—attains the meditative absorption of cessation.

The Arhat of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is also one liberated both ways (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), for the Arhat of the nature of falling away attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

The Arhat who is neither of the nature of falling away nor one liberated both ways—ranging from the Arhat of the nature of mindfulness (*cetana-dharman*) up to the immovable Arhat (*akopyadharman*)—does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation.
Just as there are four permutations for an Arhat of the "regressive" (parihāṇadharman) type, so too are there five and four permutations respectively for each of the other five types of Arhats.
Just as there are six types of Arhats on the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), there are likewise six types of spiritual lineages (gotra) on the stage of learning (śaikṣabhūmi).
Are all those who train in the dharmas subject to regression necessarily body-witnesses?
If they are body-witnesses, are they all those who train in the dharmas subject to regression?
And so on, up to: are those who train in the immovable nature necessarily body-witnesses?
If one who has realized through the body (*kāyasākṣin*) is necessarily one who trains in the nature of immovability (*akopyadharman*), the answer is:
it may be that one who trains in the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) is not one who has realized through the body; thus, the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) are to be elaborated at length.

Regarding those who are of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and are learners (*śaikṣa*) but not body-witnesses (*kāyasākṣin*): learners of the nature of falling away do not attain the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

Regarding those who are body-witnesses but not of the nature of falling away: learners from those of the nature of remembering the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) up to those of the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*) attain the attainment of cessation.
One who is of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*) and is also a bodily witness (*kāyasākṣin*) is one who has attained the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

One who is not of the nature of falling back and is also not a bodily witness is one who, from the stage of being mindful of the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*) up to the stage of immovability (*akopyadharman*), has not attained the attainment of cessation.

Just as one constructs four propositions regarding those of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) who train, so too should one construct five or four propositions for each of the other five natures (*gotra*) who train in the same way.
Furthermore, if a dharma serves as an immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*) to the mind, is it also an uninterrupted condition (*anantara*)?

Answer: Regarding the statement that "some dharmas serve as the immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) for the mind but do not constitute its immediate succession (*anantara*)," this is explained at length through four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

That which serves as the immediate antecedent for the mind but does not constitute its immediate succession refers to all moments of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) except for the first moment of entry, as well as the mind emerging from absorption; these are the cases in question.

That which is immediately following the mind but not a sequential stage of the mind refers to the first moment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), as well as the arising, abiding, and impermanence during moments when the mind is present.
That which is both a sequential stage of the mind and immediately following the mind refers to the first moment of meditative concentration and moments when the mind is present.

That which is neither a mental sequence nor a mental immediate antecedent refers to all other moments of meditative concentration—excluding the first moment of concentration and the arising, abiding, and impermanence during states with mind—as well as the arising, abiding, and impermanence of the mind emerging from concentration.
If a dharma is a mental succession (*cittānantara*), is it also necessarily an immediate succession (*anantarya*)?
The answer is:
some dharmas are mental successions but not immediate successions; this is elaborated at length into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is sequential to the mind but not immediately contiguous to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) refers to the first moment of absorption and moments when the mind is active.

That which is immediately contiguous to absorption but not sequential to the mind refers to the arising, abiding, and impermanence of all moments of absorption except for the first moment, as well as the arising, abiding, and impermanence of the mind upon emerging from absorption.

Regarding the statement that "this mind is both sequential and immediate": this refers to all moments other than the first moment of meditative absorption and the moments of mind during the state of absorption, as well as the mind upon emerging from absorption.

That which is neither a mental succession nor the immediate sequence of meditative concentration refers to the first moment of concentration and the arising, abiding, and impermanence of other states accompanied by mind.
This applies extensively to the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭāv abhibhvāyatanāni*) and so forth.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*)? Answer:
This root of goodness of non-greed serves as the antidote to greed.
If it is associated with grasping and revolves [within the realms], in the desire realm it consists of four aggregates, and in the form realm it consists of five aggregates.
The reason for their essential nature has already been explained; now it shall be explained why they are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
What is the meaning of "base of mastery"?
The answer is:
They are called "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) because they master objects and master afflictions.
Although practitioners may not be able to completely master all objects, they do not give rise to afflictions toward those objects; therefore, they are called bases of mastery.
As the Blessed One said:
"Because they excel over this place, they are called 'spheres of mastery' (abhibhvāyatana).
As for 'realm' (dhātu), it refers to the realm of form (rūpadhātu)."

Regarding the stages (*bhūmi*): the first four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) belong to the stages of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna.
The latter four spheres of mastery belong to the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
As for the supporting body, it is a body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
As for the object-condition (*ālambana*), it takes the desire realm as its object.
What is the object of this condition?
Answer: It takes the form-base (rūpāyatana) as its object.
Does it take all the form-bases of the desire realm as its object?
Answer: It takes all as its object. Question:
If that were so, how would one reconcile this with the Sūtra? As it says:
"The Venerable Aniruddha was staying in a monastery in the kingdom of Śrāvastī."
Four *manāpa* goddesses approached the Venerable Aniruddha and spoke these words: "Venerable Aniruddha!
We are *manāpa* goddesses who have attained mastery over four things; we can assume whatever form we desire at will for our own enjoyment."
If she desires garments or necklaces, she can create them at will for her own enjoyment.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha thought to himself:
"I should now contemplate this woman with the perception of impurity."

He then gave rise to the perception of impurity associated with the first dhyāna, yet he could not overcome it; this continued until he gave rise to the contemplation of impurity associated with the fourth dhyāna, still unable to overcome it.
He further thought: "Because this form is mixed, I cannot overcome it."
"If it were of a single color, I would be able to defeat you.
Having thought this, he said to her: "Sister!"
"Those of you who have attained mastery over the four elements, all turn yourselves blue and come here!
They all turned blue, yet they were still unable to prevail.
He then thought again:
If one were to transform this form, one might even overcome it.
He spoke to him again, saying:
"Come as a yellow color."
They all became yellow;
the red color likewise could not overcome it.
At that time, Aniruddha again thought to himself:
The white [deity] conformed to the perception of impurity, thinking, "If I appear as white, perhaps I may prevail.
He then spoke to him again,
saying, "Come, appearing as white!"
They were all white in color, yet they could not outshine it.
At that time, the Venerable Aniruddha, knowing that these various colors were so exquisite as to be unsurpassable, closed his eyes and sat.
At that time, the goddess thought to herself:
"Now this venerable one is unable to remember us.
Having realized this, she suddenly vanished from sight.
The Venerable Aniruddha did not surpass his object, nor did his object surpass the Venerable Aniruddha.
It was just as if two strong wrestlers were wrestling and neither could overcome the other; so it was with him.
How is this statement to be reconciled?
The answer is:
although the Venerable Aniruddha was not superior, others of sharp faculties—such as the Buddha’s disciples Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana—were indeed superior.
Question: Is it possible to practice the contemplation of impurity regarding the Buddha’s body? Answer:
It can be accomplished;
only a Buddha can do so, not other śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?

The Buddha’s body is pure and stainless; no one who practices the contemplation of impurity can conceive of the Buddha’s body as impure, yet only the World-Honored Buddha himself can perform the contemplation of impurity upon his own body.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of contemplation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*):

first, the contemplation of the defects of form (*rūpa-doṣa*), and second, the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). The contemplation of the defects of form cannot be applied to the Buddha’s body; however, the contemplation of the defects of form can serve as the basis for the contemplation of dependent origination.
The rest is explained in detail as in the section on the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*.
As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), they are all associated with the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
As for being accompanied by knowledge (*jñāna*), they are all accompanied by conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
As for samādhi, it does not coexist with [other] samādhis.
As for the faculties (*indriya*), taken collectively, they are associated with two faculties, namely the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

The past, future, and present constitute the three periods of time. Regarding those conditioned by the three periods: that which is past is conditioned by the past; that which is future and destined to arise is conditioned by the future, while that which is not destined to arise is conditioned by all three periods; and that which is present is conditioned by the present.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object; the unwholesome and the indeterminate both take all three types as their objects.

Those bound to the three realms take what is bound to the form realm as their object; those bound to the three realms as well as those that are unbound take what is bound to the desire realm as their object.
Those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee are the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
Those conditioned by the trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee are conditioned by the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.
That which is abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned, is abandoned by the path of cultivation.
That which takes as its object what is abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned, takes as its object what is abandoned by the path of cultivation.
Regarding "conditioned by names" and "conditioned by meanings," these are conditions of meaning.

As for "conditioned by one's own body, another's body, or what is not the body": the first two conditions pertain to one's own body and another's body, while the remaining ones pertain to another's body.
Regarding "attained through detachment and attained through skillful means": this refers to attainment through detachment as well as attainment through skillful means.

One who attains the first dhyāna does so by becoming detached from the desires of the desire realm; one who attains the second dhyāna does so by becoming detached from the desires of the first dhyāna; and one who attains the fourth dhyāna does so by becoming detached from the desires of the third dhyāna.
Arising and manifesting through skillful means is attainment by means of skillful means.
The Buddha does not arise and manifest through skillful means; the pratyekabuddha arises through inferior skillful means; and the śrāvaka arises through either middling or superior skillful means.
Regarding "that which was previously attained or not yet attained": for a noble one in their final birth, it is that which was previously attained;
for other ordinary persons, it is that which was previously attained. For [others], it is that which was not yet attained.
The eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*):
possessing the perception of internal forms, one contemplates external forms.
"Possessing the perception of internal forms" means contemplating the forms of one's own body, cultivating the perception of form, and not being separated from that perception of form.
Regarding the contemplation of external forms: one contemplates a small amount of external form, whether beautiful or ugly.
"Small" has two types:
first, smallness of the object; second, smallness of mastery.
Those who delight in beautiful colors do not spoil or destroy the colors blue, yellow, red, and white.
Those who delight in unattractive colors do spoil and destroy the colors blue, yellow, red, and white.

One who gives rise to superior knowledge and vision regarding these colors severs craving for desire and transcends craving for desire; by taking these aforementioned colors as an object, they attain mastery over them—this is called "superior."
It is like a great householder or a great householder’s son who, in employing servants, possesses complete mastery over them.
That [meditative state] is likewise; this is called the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
"First" means that it is designated as the first because it stands at the beginning of the sequential enumeration.
Furthermore, as for entering that meditative absorption in successive order, it is called "initial" because it is the first entry.
Regarding the "bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*): when one enters this absorption, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are called the bases of mastery.
As with the first sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), so it is with the second;

the difference is that whereas previously one contemplated the small, now one contemplates the large. There are two kinds of "large": [Note: The source text provides the structural outline for the second *abhibhvāyatana* without listing the specific types of "large" objects.]
First, multiplicity of objects; second, multiplicity of mastery.
The rest is as explained above.
Internally perceiving no form, one contemplates external forms.
"Having no perception of internal forms" means not cultivating the perception of internal forms and being free from the perception of forms, one contemplates external forms as limited.
The rest is explained at length as above; this is called the third *abhibhvāyatana* (sphere of mastery).
As with the third sphere of mastery, so it is with the fourth;
the difference is that while the third contemplates few beautiful and ugly forms, the fourth contemplates many [forms] while internally maintaining the perception of no-form.
One contemplates external forms as previously described.
Regarding the contemplation of blue forms, one cultivates this understanding:
all forms whatsoever, whether concise or extensive, are entirely contemplated as blue.
Just as when the eye-consciousness observes and the eye-consciousness ranges over its objects, the mental consciousness subsequently arises, observing blue color, blue luster, and blue shadow;
likewise, being internally without perception of form, one observes externally blue color, blue luster, and blue shadow.
One who has produced superior knowledge and superior vision severs craving for desire and transcends desire; this is called being superior to form.
Taking prior forms as an object, they attain mastery over them all.
Just as a great householder and his sons, having commanded their servants, possess complete mastery over them, so it is with this.
When one who has such a perception gives rise to such a perception and brings it before oneself, this is called the fifth sphere of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
The fifth meaning is explained at length as above.
As it is with the color blue, so it is for yellow, red, and white; the explanations are likewise. Regarding the specific differences:

for the yellow *abhibhvāyatana*, one should cite the simile of the *kaṇaka* flower; for the red, one should cite the simile of the *pāṇḍu-jīvaka* flower; and for the white, one should cite the simile of the *uśanas* star.
Question: Among these four kinds of form (*rūpa*), which is the most excellent?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:
White is most excellent; worldly people also say it is an auspicious color.
Just as among the four directions the east is the most superior and is likewise called auspicious by the world, so too is this the case.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
"One who contemplates the color white has a pure mind and does not succumb to the tendency toward sleep.
This is explained at length regarding the ten universal bases (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and so forth.
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the ten spheres of totality (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*)? Answer:
The eighth is the wholesome root of non-attachment, which serves as the antidote to attachment.

If it functions in association with grasping, its nature consists of four aggregates or five aggregates; specifically, if it belongs to the desire realm, it consists of four aggregates, and if it belongs to the form realm, it consists of five aggregates. In the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness, its essential nature consists of four aggregates.
"This is the essential nature of all bases (kṛtsnāyatana)," and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the reason for its essential nature, we shall now explain why it is called "all bases."
What is the meaning of "all bases" (*sarvatraga*)?
The answer is:
they are called "all bases" for two reasons.
First, by way of being uninterrupted; second, by way of being vast.
As for "uninterrupted," there is no location or ground upon which it rests;
yet it takes water as its object just as it took earth as its object.
If one takes water as the object, or fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, white, the sphere of infinite space, or the sphere of infinite consciousness as the object, the absence of deficiency is likewise.
As for "vast," it means taking earth as the universal object, and so on, up to taking consciousness as the universal object.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
That which takes all things as its object without exception is called "all-bases" (*sarvatraga*).
As for the realms: eight belong to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and two belong to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding the stages: eight [of the bases] are in the stage of the fourth dhyāna; the base of infinite space and all the bases of totality are in the stage of the base of infinite space; and the base of infinite consciousness and all the bases of totality are in the stage of the base of infinite consciousness.

Why is this? Because the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) within the stage of the fourth dhyāna can enter the latter four spheres of mastery (*abhibhv-āyatana*), and the latter four spheres of mastery can enter the eight spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

The pure liberation takes a pure object as its condition; it cannot distinguish whether [the object] is beautiful or ugly, yet it can distinguish superior locations such as blue, yellow, red, and white, though it cannot make them infinite.
The universal bases (kṛtsnāyatana) can make blue, yellow, red, and white infinite.
Upon what does this form depend?
It depends upon the four great elements.
Therefore, one next contemplates infinite earth, infinite water, infinite fire, and infinite wind.
From what is this vastness produced?
Because of cognition, one knows that form and so forth depend upon space; therefore, one next contemplates the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Upon what does that cognition depend?
Based upon consciousness (*vijñāna*), one therefore next contemplates infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantya*).
Since consciousness has nothing further upon which to rely, no further spheres (*āyatana*) are established.
Regarding the bodies that serve as their bases: the first eight depend on bodies within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the latter two depend on bodies within all three realms.
The practitioner does not practice practice.
As for conditions, there are eight conditions pertaining to the desire realm.
What phenomena of the desire realm do they condition?
Answer: It takes the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) as its object;
two take the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) as their objects.

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): eight are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), while the final two are associated with the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding wisdom (*prajñā*): all are associated with conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*): it is not associated with meditative concentration.
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*), they are associated with the single faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).

Those belonging to the past, future, and present constitute the three time periods. Eight [faculties] take the three time periods as their objects: those in the past take the past as their object; those in the future that are destined to arise take the future as their object, while those destined not to arise take all three time periods as their object; those in the present take the present as their object; and the latter two take all three time periods as their objects.

Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object; the unwholesome and the neutral take the three types [wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral] as their objects through eight conditions, while two take the wholesome and neutral as their objects.
Regarding those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound: eight are bound to the form realm, and two are bound to the formless realm.
Regarding those conditioned by the three realms and those unconditioned: eight are conditioned by the realm of desire, and two are conditioned by the formless realm.

As for those that are in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), and those that are neither in training nor beyond training (*naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa*), these belong to the category of being neither in training nor beyond training.

Regarding those conditioned by what is in training, what is beyond training, and what is neither in training nor beyond training: that which is conditioned by what is neither in training nor beyond training and is abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned, is abandoned by the path of cultivation.

Regarding those [factors] abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), those abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and those not abandoned: eight are abandoned through the path of cultivation; two are abandoned through both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
That which takes names as its object (*nāmalambana*) and takes meanings as its object (*arthālambana*) is what takes meanings as its object.
Regarding those conditioned by one's own body, another's body, or the non-body dharma: eight are conditioned by another's body, and two are conditioned by both one's own body and another's body.

As for "attained through the abandonment of desire" and "attained through expedient means": these refer to attainment through the abandonment of desire and attainment through expedient means; "attainment through the abandonment of desire" means it is attained at the time of abandoning desire.
Regarding those attained through skillful means (*upāya*), they are attained by performing skillful means.

For a Buddha, [the path] does not manifest through skillful means; for a Pratyekabuddha, it is through inferior skillful means; and for a Śrāvaka, it is either through middling or superior [skillful means].
"This is what was originally attained but never before attained" means that it is both originally attained and never before attained.
For the sages of the inner path and for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), it is both originally attained and never before attained; for other ordinary persons, it is simply originally attained.
Question: What are the skillful means (upāya) in all circumstances? Answer:
Fourth, when it is fulfilled by means of visual consciousness, one enters into the sense-sphere of visible forms characterized by blue, yellow, red, and white;
fourth, when it is fulfilled by means of tactile consciousness, one enters into the sense-sphere of tangibles characterized by earth, water, fire, and wind.
Furthermore, some say that seven [elements] take eye-consciousness as their means, excluding the sphere of wind.
Others say that eight [elements] take eye-consciousness as their means.
Question: Since wind exists everywhere, how can it take visual consciousness as its means? Answer:
Visual consciousness also apprehends the wind-sphere as having such characteristics, namely: whether there is dust or no dust, and the *vairambha* winds and so forth that fill all places.
Regarding the sphere of space, one takes space as the means; regarding the sphere of consciousness, one takes consciousness as the means.
The ten universal bases (*daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni*). What are the ten?
One contemplates that above, below, and in all directions, there is no deficiency and no limit.
"Superior" refers to the upper direction; "inferior" refers to the lower direction; "all sides" refers to the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions.
"Without deficiency" means unmixed.
"Immeasurable" means having no boundaries.
This is called the first of the *kṛtsnāyatana*s (bases of totality).
It is called "first" because it stands at the beginning in the sequential enumeration;
furthermore, it is called "first" because it is the initial entry when entering this meditative absorption in regular succession.
Regarding "all bases" (kṛtsnāyatana): when entering this meditative absorption, the wholesome form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness constitute these all-bases.
This applies up to the base of consciousness; the explanation for all bases is likewise the same.

As for the difference: among the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the sphere of totality of space and the sphere of totality of consciousness do not mention the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
A question is raised:
it may be so that the eight spheres of totality take as their objects the upper, lower, and peripheral directions.
Why is this? Because their objects of focus possess spatial location.
Since the objects of focus for the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness have no spatial location, how could there be upper, lower, or peripheral directions?
The answer is:
One should say that the eight *kṛtsnāyatanas* (totalities) possess upper, lower, and lateral boundaries, whereas the two *kṛtsnāyatanas* lack upper, lower, and lateral boundaries.
If one speaks in this manner, what is the intended meaning?
Answer: This is because those who practice this meditative absorption do so at the upper and lower limits.

For example, among humans, practicing the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) in all its aspects is "lower," while among the gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*), practicing the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) in all its aspects is "upper. The same explanation applies to other directions.
Question: For what reason are there no liberations (vimokṣa), no spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and no spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) in the third dhyāna? Answer:
"It is not its field tool," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, in order to counteract attachment to form within the desire realm, the first dhyāna establishes liberation;
in order to counteract attachment to form within the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna establishes liberation.

Because there is craving for the formless (*ārūpya*) in the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna does not establish liberation (*vimokṣa*); since the third dhyāna lacks liberation, it likewise lacks the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Why is this? Because one enters the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) by means of liberation, and enters the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana) by means of the spheres of mastery.
Furthermore, it is because [the former] is remote and because [the latter] is not subtle.
The third dhyāna is distant from the desire realm and inferior to the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, because it is like the third formless attainment:

in the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness there is the practice of boundlessness; in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception there is the meditative attainment of cessation; whereas in the sphere of nothingness there is neither the practice of boundlessness nor the meditative attainment of cessation.
Just as the wholesome roots are diminished in the third formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), so it is with the third dhyāna.

Furthermore, because the third dhyāna contains the most excellent experience of pleasure among all births and deaths, practitioners are largely attached to that pleasure; consequently, they are unable to give rise to the superior bases of liberation (*vimokṣa*) in all places.
Question: If that is so, why are there immeasurable merits such as the supernormal powers (abhijñā)? Answer:
Not all that arises necessarily possesses all virtues.
If that stage were devoid of the immeasurables and the supernormal powers, that stage would be a void stage, lacking in virtue.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
One who has entered the meditative absorption on earth (*pṛthivī-samādhi*) forms this thought:
"The earth is myself; I am the earth; my absorption and the earth are non-dual and indistinguishable."
It is the same for all other spheres as well. Question:
If one attains all the spheres, must one necessarily be free from desire for the third dhyāna?
If one reckons the earth as the self, this must be the view of a self in the body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) belonging to the stage of the fourth dhyāna, reckoning the stage of the fourth dhyāna as the self.
Since all [such views] take the desire realm as their object, how can this be possible?
Answer: Here, that which is indeterminate is described as determinate.
Just as one who is not a śramaṇa is called a śramaṇa, and one who is not a brāhmaṇa is called a brāhmaṇa, so it is in this case as well.
Furthermore, this refers to what was previously attained.
For example, even though a king may have lost his kingdom and his wealth and status, he is still called a "king.
This is likewise the case here: although one has previously attained this meditative concentration and subsequently lost it, it is described in this way because it was once attained.

Furthermore, he is one who enters concentration swiftly; having regressed from that concentration, he gives rise to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the desire realm, reckoning the stage of the desire realm as "I. He quickly returns to detachment from desire and gives rise to [attainments] in all stages, again taking the desire realm as his object.

Just as Devadatta was able to enter meditative absorption quickly, he used his supernormal powers to transform himself into a small child with hair shorn in five patterns and wearing golden necklaces, rolling about and playing in the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru.
Again, he manifested this sign so that Prince Ajātaśatru would know that this was the great sage Devadatta.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru took him up, fondled and kissed him, and spat into his mouth.
Because of his greed for gain and offerings, he swallowed their spittle.
Therefore, the World-Honored One said to Devadatta:
"You are like a corpse that eats spittle."
When he consumed the saliva, he lost his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

Because he had quickly entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he soon attained freedom from desire (*vairāgya*); he then transformed his own body and returned once more to roll and play upon the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru.
Furthermore, the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) conceives of the stage of the fourth dhyāna as "I," and in all instances, it likewise contemplates the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
Question: In all instances, [the object] takes the desire realm as its condition.
Answer: There are also those that take the fourth dhyāna as their object.
If one were to speak in this way, then all [meditative states] would also take the fourth dhyāna as their object.
Question: If that is so, the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are purely white; how then can they perceive blue, yellow, and red colors? Answer:
They assert: "The bodies of the gods in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are purely white in color, whereas non-sentient things possess blue, yellow, and red colors.
This assertion should not be made; for if the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) were associated with all stages, such a fault would ensue.
How can there be associated and co-existent dharmas that take either the desire realm or the body-view (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) of the fourth dhyāna as their object, yet are not associated with all stages?
Furthermore, how is it that one person is called both "one who conceives a self" and "one who has attained meditative concentration"?
Because it gives rise to the view of a body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), it is called "reckoning as self" (ātmagrāha);
because it arises in all places, it is called "attaining concentration" (samādhi).

The view of a body reckons the stage of the fourth dhyāna as the self, while the object of "all places" (sarvatra) is the desire realm; since these do not occur simultaneously, this sūtra is well-explained.

There is the concentration on earth (*pṛthivī-samādhi*) and the universal concentration on earth (*pṛthivī-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*), and so on, up to the concentration on white (*avadāta-samādhi*) and the universal concentration on white (*avadāta-kṛtsnāyatana-samādhi*). Question:
What is the difference between the concentration on earth and the universal concentration on earth?

Answer: The *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) is fixed in the four *dhyāna* stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), whereas the *sarvatra-dhātu-samādhi* (the concentration of all places) is fixed in the fourth *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, skillful means (*upāya*) constitutes the concentration, while fulfillment constitutes the "all places."
Furthermore, this meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has as its fruit the [mastery of] all bases (*sarvabhūmi*).
Furthermore, while this [concentration] is partial, the [mastery of] all bases is universal.
The distinction lies between the concentration on a specific stage (*bhūmi-samādhi*) and the concentration on all bases of that stage (*sarvabhūmi-sarvāyatana-samādhi*).
Question: What is the difference between the liberations (vimokṣa), the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana), and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana)? Answer:
The names themselves constitute the distinctions: this is called liberation, this is called the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and this is called the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, inferior roots of goodness are liberation; middling roots of goodness are the bases of mastery; and superior roots of goodness are the bases of totality.

Furthermore, limited roots of goodness are liberation; abundant roots of goodness among the many are the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); and immeasurable, supreme roots of goodness are the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, the cause is liberation, the fruit is the spheres of totality, and both cause and fruit are the spheres of mastery.

Furthermore, the meaning of "turning away" (*prātikūlya*) is liberation (*vimokṣa*); the meaning of "superior object" (*viśiṣṭālambana*) is the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*); and the meaning of "pervasive object" (*sarvatrālambana*) is the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Furthermore, the liberation of the mind is liberation; the meaning of "overcoming afflictions" is the bases of mastery; and the meaning of being "unimpaired and pervasive" is the spheres of totality.
Furthermore, if one attains liberation, it does not necessarily mean one has attained the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) or the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*);
if one attains liberation and the spheres of mastery, it does not necessarily mean one has attained the spheres of totality;
however, if one attains the spheres of totality, one will necessarily attain liberation and the spheres of mastery.
Why is this so? Because liberation can enter the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of mastery can enter the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Liberation, the spheres of mastery, and the spheres of totality—these are called the distinctions.
There are eight knowledges:

knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
What is knowledge of phenomena, up to and including knowledge of the path?
The detailed explanation is as given in the original sūtra. Question:
For what reason does that Venerable One employ the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) in this treatise?
The answer is:
That Venerable One had such a desire, such an inclination, and such an intention that he composed this treatise by means of the eight knowledges (*aṣṭajñāna*).
In accordance with his desire and intention, and without contradicting the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he established the eight knowledges and composed the treatise.
In other places as well, treatises are composed by establishing eight knowledges (*jñāna*), as explained in the *Samādhijñāna-vastu* (Chapter on Concentration and Knowledge).

Alternatively, one may wish to compose a treatise based on two knowledges, in which case two knowledges are established, as explained in the *Jñāna-vastu* (Chapter on Knowledge) regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*);
or as explained in the *Indriya-vastu* (Chapter on Faculties) regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Within the *Samādhivarga*, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are established.
Alternatively, one might wish to treat the subject according to four knowledges and thus establish four knowledges, as explained in the *Indriyavarga*:
"If it is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), is it the untainted knowledge of suffering (*anāsrava-duḥkhajñāna*)?"
Furthermore, if it is path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*), is that path untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)?
Alternatively, if one intends to treat this as a discourse on the ten knowledges, one establishes the ten knowledges according to what is known therein.
For example, just as a potter, knowing how to place a lump of clay upon the wheel, produces various objects according to his desire without impairing his skill, so too is that Venerable One:

by means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, he eliminates the faults of what is to be known and composes treatises according to his desire, never contravening the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa). Thus it is.
Furthermore, one should not inquire why that venerable one established eight knowledges. Why is this?
Because this is a Buddhist scripture.
The Buddhist scriptures speak of eight knowledges (*jñāna*), from the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Since the scriptures are the fundamental source for this treatise, that Venerable One composed it based upon these eight knowledges.

That venerable one lacks the power [to understand] that among the eight knowledges, by subtracting one knowledge it is called seven knowledges, and by adding one knowledge it is called nine knowledges.
Why is this? Because there is no such increase or decrease in the Buddha’s sūtras.
That which has no increase is such that there is nothing to be diminished;
that which has no diminution is such that there is nothing to be increased.
As with neither increase nor diminution, there is neither benefit nor loss, and it is immeasurable and boundless.
"Immeasurable" refers to immeasurable meaning;
"boundless" refers to boundless phrasing.
It is like the waters of the great ocean, which are both immeasurable and boundless: "immeasurable" means its depth is immeasurable, and "boundless" means its breadth is boundless.
The sūtras of all Buddhas are likewise immeasurable and boundless; "immeasurable" refers to the immeasurability of their meaning, and "boundless" refers to the boundlessness of their phrasing.

For instance, although masters of treatises such as the Venerable Śāriputra and hundreds of thousands of others composed hundreds of thousands of nayutas of treatises in an attempt to explain the meaning of just two phrases from a Buddha’s sūtra, they were unable to reach the limit or the further shore of those two phrases despite exhausting their intellectual capacities and turning back in defeat.

Question: If the Buddhist sūtras are the fundamental source for this treatise, then within the sūtras various types of knowledge (*jñāna*) are taught: sometimes two kinds of knowledge are mentioned, as in the "Two Dharmas";
sometimes four kinds of knowledge are mentioned, as in the "Four Dharmas."
In some instances eight knowledges (*jñāna*) are taught, as in the "Eight Dharmas";
in others, ten knowledges are taught, as in the "Ten Dharmas.
For what reason did that Venerable One, amidst these various types of knowledge, compose this *Anuśaya-skandha* based specifically upon eight knowledges?
Answer: Among these eight knowledges, it is taught that all knowledges are subsumed.
Although two knowledges also subsume all knowledges, those are merely brief explanations.
Although the ten knowledges encompass all forms of knowledge, this is a detailed exposition.
Furthermore, regarding those knowledges that are repeatedly cultivated and repeatedly brought into manifestation, it is based upon these knowledges that this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, these eight knowledges possess both the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*) and the nature of vision (*darśana*).
Although the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) possess the nature of knowledge, they do not possess the nature of vision.
Furthermore, if a wisdom that can be found within the persons of both those with desire and those free from desire were to exist, one would base this treatise upon it.
However, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) can only be found within the persons who are free from desire.
Furthermore, if a wisdom is obtainable within the person of one in training (śaikṣa) or one beyond training (aśaikṣa), it is on the basis of this wisdom that the treatise is composed.
The knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) are obtainable within the person of one beyond training.

Just as with those in training and those beyond training—those who have done what was to be done and those who have not yet done so, those who have laid down the heavy burden and those who have not yet laid it down, those who have attained their own benefit and those who have not yet attained it, those who still seek and those who do not—it should be known that the case is likewise.
That Venerable One may have formulated his argument based on a single cognition occurring within a single moment, as stated in the *Saṃyukta-āgama*:
"Is there a single cognition that knows all phenomena?"
The answer is:
I do not know.
If one were to construct this treatise based on the ten knowledges (daśajñāna), this treatise would not be established.
If one were to compose this treatise based on nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or even one moment of cognition, this treatise would not be established;
even if one were to compose it based on a single moment of cognition lasting for two kṣaṇas, this treatise likewise would not be established.

Why is this? At the first moment of cognition, it does not know its own associated and coexistent factors; at the second moment, it knows the factors associated and coexistent with the preceding cognition.
Because the discussion therein is based on a single cognition occurring within a single moment, the answer states that [the Buddha] does not know.

Alternatively, it is said that a single cognition encompasses all cognitions, namely *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena); this is not like *dharmajñāna* in the sense that its essence is the phenomenon itself.
Some say that all knowledge is subsumed within two types of knowledge, such as contaminated and uncontaminated knowledge, bound and liberated knowledge, or fettered and unfettered knowledge.

Others say that all knowledge is subsumed within three types of knowledge, such as knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
Some say that all knowledge is subsumed within four types of knowledge, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds to the first three.
Others say that all knowledge is subsumed within five types of knowledge, such as conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
Some say that six knowledges encompass all knowledges, with the first five knowledges further augmented by the knowledge of others' minds.
Others say that seven knowledges encompass all knowledges, excluding the knowledge of others' minds.
Some say that the eight knowledges (*jñāna*) encompass all knowledge, with the addition of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*). Question:

If the eight knowledges encompass all knowledge, there are yet other eight knowledges—namely, the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*), the knowledge of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇajñāna*), the knowledge of birth and death (*saṃsārajñāna*), the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). How are these encompassed?
Answer: Although there are further eight knowledges, these too are subsumed within these [same] eight knowledges. Why is this so?
Because these eight knowledges are entirely contained within the preceding eight knowledges. Question:
How are these eight knowledges included within the preceding eight knowledges?
Answer: "Abiding" (sthiti) refers to the cause of all phenomena; the fruits of the three realms—superior, middling, and inferior—abide within the cause.
If one knows this wisdom, it is called the wisdom of the cause (hetu-jñāna).
The knowledge of causes consists of the nature of four knowledges:

conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of origination. The knowledge of cessation consists of the nature of four knowledges: conventional knowledge, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and the knowledge of nirvana.

Regarding conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and knowledge of birth and death (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna*), the masters of the old Abhidharma—the Śramaṇas of Kaśmīr—state as follows:
these are but a single knowledge, namely, conventional knowledge.
The Venerable Vāmalaka has already stated this:
the knowledge of birth and death is of the nature of four knowledges, namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of suffering.
The commentary states:
It should be explained thus:
this is the knowledge of equality (samatājñāna).

Regarding the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna), some say it is called the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows because it is attainable within the person whose outflows have been destroyed.
If one explains it in this way, its nature consists of the ten knowledges.
