Some say that the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) is the knowledge that takes the state of the destruction of the outflows as its object.

If this is asserted, then the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows possesses the nature of four knowledges: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna), and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna).
The Sthavira Abhidharmikas, the śramaṇas of Kaśmīra, maintain this view:
"This is a single knowledge.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains this view:
These are six knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of others' minds.
It is not the knowledge of others' minds. Why is this so?
The knowledge of others' minds takes present phenomena as its object;
it is not the knowledge of cessation. Why is this so?
The knowledge of cessation takes unconditioned phenomena as its object.
The critique states:
one should speak thus:
This is the knowledge of equality; the knowledge of aspiration is the knowledge of equality.
Some say it is of the nature of eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising. Why is this so?
The knowledge of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) is of the nature of vision (*darśana*), whereas those two types of knowledge are not of the nature of vision.
The critique states:
One should speak thus:

The knowledge of aspiration (praṇidhijñāna) is one single knowledge; the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) consist of six knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and the knowledges of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
For these reasons, the eight knowledges encompass all knowledge.
The Venerable Saṃghasena said: "One should speak of a single knowledge, namely, decisive knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*)."
Why is this so? Because the meaning of "determination" (niścaya) is the meaning of "knowledge" (jñāna).
That determination exists as both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), as bound (baddha) and liberated (mukta), and as fettered (saṃyukta) and unfettered (asaṃyukta).
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*); it is bondage and fetter.
Untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) is liberation and non-fettering.

That which is either the antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or the antidote to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*), or specifically the antidote to the desire realm, is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*).
If it is the antidote to the form and formless realms, it is subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
These three knowledges, when they cognize the minds and mental factors of others, constitute the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
The untainted, determinate knowledge consists of either the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering, up to the four modes of contemplation regarding the path.

If one contemplates through the four modes regarding suffering, it is the knowledge of suffering; likewise, if one contemplates through the four modes regarding the path, it is the knowledge of the path.
Question: If that is so, there would be only three types of knowledge: dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). Answer:
Thus, there are only three knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Question: If this is so, how are the eight knowledges established?
The answer is:
by virtue of five matters; first, as an antidote;
second, as a skillful means.
Third, by way of its own essence;
fourth, by way of activity;
fifth, by way of the activity of conditions.
The antidote consists of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*).
The skillful means consists of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The essential nature consists of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The practitioner possesses the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin [of suffering]. Why is this so?
Because these knowledges function through different objects of focus.
Knowledge of cessation and knowledge of the path have the same object but different modes of activity. Why is this?
Because these two knowledges have different objects and different modes of activity.
For these five reasons, eight knowledges are established.
The Venerable Vāmalakṣya said:
"The eight knowledges are established in order to counteract four kinds of delusion."

There are four kinds of delusion: delusion regarding the elements (*dhātu*), delusion regarding the mind (*citta*), delusion regarding phenomena (*dharma*), and delusion regarding the truths (*satya*).
To counteract delusion regarding the elements, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) are taught;
to counteract delusion regarding the mind, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is taught.
Because it counteracts delusion regarding phenomena (*dharma*), it is called conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*);
because it counteracts delusion regarding the truths (*satya*), it is called the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path.
This is the essential nature of knowledge, and so forth, as explained at length.
Having already explained the nature and reason [for its existence], we shall now explain why it is called "wisdom" (jñāna).
What is the meaning of "wisdom"?
The answer is:
The meaning of "ascertainment" (niścaya) is the meaning of "knowledge" (jñāna). Question:
If the meaning of ascertainment is the meaning of knowledge, then knowledge associated with doubt would not be knowledge.
Why is this? Because it is not determinate. He replied:
Wisdom associated with doubt is also knowledge; however, because doubt possesses functional power within that aggregate, it is called an "aggregate of doubt.
This is like a person who has much craving being called "one of craving-disposition," even though they are not devoid of hatred and delusion;
because craving possesses functional power, they are termed "one of craving-disposition."
It is the same for that [person].
The same applies to those who act out of hatred and those who act out of delusion.
The Dārṣṭāntikas (Exemplifiers) speak as follows:
If the mind possesses wisdom, there is no lack of wisdom; if the mind is resolute, there is no hesitation; if the mind is coarse, there is no subtlety.
Furthermore, this is said as a critique of the Abhidharmikas:
"In your exposition of the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), it is like various kinds of grasses and trees growing together in one place without distinct characteristics."

Within a single mind, there is wisdom and non-wisdom; neither wisdom nor non-wisdom; hesitation and certainty; neither hesitation nor certainty; and coarseness and subtlety, as well as neither coarse nor subtle.
The Abhidharmikas further state:

"When my dharmas arise, they arise as an aggregate within a single moment of mind; there is wisdom and non-wisdom, neither wisdom nor non-wisdom, certainty and hesitation, neither certainty nor hesitation, and the coarse, the subtle, and neither coarse nor subtle."
Wisdom is knowledge; non-wisdom is ignorance (*avidyā*); that which is neither wisdom nor ignorance consists of other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*).
Hesitation is doubt (*vicikitsā*); decisiveness is discernment (*prajñā*); that which is neither decisive nor hesitant consists of other mental states and mental factors.
The coarse is *vitarka* (applied thought), the subtle is *vicāra* (sustained thought), and that which is neither coarse nor subtle consists of other dharmas.
Furthermore, some say that it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*) for two reasons:
first, because of its decisiveness; second, because of its appropriateness.
To know suffering up to knowing the path is called "certainty" (*niyama*); because it brings satisfaction to oneself and others, it is called "satisfactory" (*yogya*).
Having thus explained in general the reasons for the various types of knowledge, I shall now explain them individually. Why is this so?
Why is it called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna)?
The answer is:
because its essence is phenomena, it is therefore called knowledge of phenomena.
Question: Other types of wisdom are also, in their essence, dharmas; why then are they not called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna)? Answer:
Although other forms of knowledge have "dharma" as their essence, it is specifically *dharmajñāna* (knowledge of phenomena) that is called "dharma.

For example, although the eighteen *dhātus* have "dharma" as their essence, the twelve *āyatanas* have "dharma" as their essence, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) have "dharma" as their essence, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) have "dharma" as their essence, the fourfold unshakable confidence (*aveṇika-prasāda*) has "dharma" as its essence, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have "dharma" as their essence, and the three refuges and Three Jewels (*triratna*) have "dharma" as their essence; yet it is only the *dharmadhātu*, the *dharmāyatana*, the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-bodhyaṅga*), the mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), the dharma of unshakable confidence, the dharma of analytical knowledge, and the dharma of the Jewel of Dharma that are designated as "dharma."
Thus, although the substance of these ten knowledges is dharma, the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is named "dharma.
Furthermore, the knowledge of phenomena has one name, while the remaining knowledges have two names.
The knowledge of phenomena is a common name, whereas the remaining knowledges are both common and uncommon names; they are spoken of by means of their uncommon names.

Furthermore, it is called "knowledge of phenomena" (dharmajñāna) because one first knows the phenomena, and it is called "subsequent knowledge" (anvayajñāna) because one subsequently knows the phenomena.

Furthermore, that knowledge associated with the initial attainment of faith in the phenomena is called "knowledge of phenomena," while the subsequent attainment of faith in the phenomena is called "subsequent knowledge."

Furthermore, it is called "knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñāna*) because it directly perceives phenomena; it is called "subsequent knowledge" (*anvayajñāna*) because it arises subsequently to that direct perception.
Furthermore, the desire realm abounds in various non-dharmic afflictions, such as anger, resentment, guile, deceit, negligence, and harmfulness—all of which are non-dharmic.
Who is their immediate antidote?
It is the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna).
Because such non-dharmic afflictions do not exist in the realms of form and formlessness, it is called subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).

Furthermore, if wisdom is comprised within six stages and takes one stage as its object, it is dharma-knowledge; if wisdom is comprised within nine stages and takes eight stages as its object, it is inferential knowledge.

Furthermore, if a cognition is comprised within six stages and takes those six stages as its object, it is dharma-knowledge; if a cognition is comprised within nine stages and takes those nine stages as its object, it is subsequent knowledge.

Furthermore, if knowledge serves as the antidote to the eighteen elements (dhātus), the twelve bases (āyatanas), and the five aggregates (skandhas), it is dharma-knowledge; if knowledge serves as the antidote to fourteen elements, twelve bases, and five aggregates, it is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).

Furthermore, if a wisdom that serves as the antidote to the five aggregates (skandhas) that are wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate is dharma-knowledge; if a wisdom that serves as the antidote to the five aggregates that are wholesome or indeterminate is subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna).

If knowledge that serves as the antidote to those who practice for merit, non-merit, or the imperturbable is dharma-knowledge; if knowledge that serves as the antidote to those who practice for merit or the imperturbable is subsequent knowledge.

Furthermore, if knowledge that serves as the antidote to craving for edible food and craving for sensual desire is dharma-knowledge; if knowledge that serves as the antidote to craving for meditative concentration is subsequent knowledge.
Why is it called the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:
because it knows the minds of others, it is called the knowledge of others' minds.
Question: Since one also knows the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) of others, why is it called only "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: [Because]...
Regarding the aspiration of the mind:
the practitioner forms this aspiration, thinking,
"May I know the minds of others."
If one knows the minds of others, one also knows their numerical states.
It is just as when someone thinks to themselves:
"May I see the king."
When one sees the king, one also sees the king’s attendants;

it is the same for that [dharma]. Furthermore, this dharma receives its name through various factors: either by way of its own essence (*svabhāva*), or by way of its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), or by way of its means (*upāya*), or by way of its association (*saṃprayoga*), or by way of its basis (*āśraya*), or by way of its activity (*caryā*), or by way of its object (*ālambana*), or by way of the activity and its object (*caryā-ālambana*).
In terms of their intrinsic nature, they are like the aggregates (*skandha*), the truths (*satya*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).

In terms of their antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), they are like dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); if it acts as an antidote to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called dharma-knowledge, and if it acts as an antidote to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*), it is called subsequent knowledge.
"By means of skillful means" refers to such states as the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the five present samādhis, and the knowledge of others' minds.
"By means of association" refers to what is taught in the *Bhāgala Sūtra*:
"What is the dharma of pleasant feeling?"
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated with pleasant feeling,
how could it be a phenomenon of painful feeling?
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated with painful feeling,
how can it be a phenomenon associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling?
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā),
its bases are the eye-consciousness up to the mind-consciousness.
If it arises in dependence on the eye, it is called eye-consciousness, and so on up to if it arises in dependence on the mind, it is called mind-consciousness.
As for the practitioner, this is the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of the origin [of suffering]. Why is that?
This wisdom differs in its mode of activity (*ākāra*) but is identical in its object (*ālambana*).
Alternatively, regarding the object: it is the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*). Regarding the mode of activity and the object:
it is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).
Why is this? Because their practices differ and their conditions also differ.
Furthermore, it is because the meaning of the name is superior.
Within this collection, which is the most preeminent?
The mind is the most preeminent.
It is like when a king arrives, his retinue also arrives, yet one simply says, "The king has arrived."
It is the same for that as well.
For the rest, the detailed explanation is as given in the *Kṣudraka-vastu* regarding the locus of the mind (*citta-sthāna*).
Why is it called "equal knowledge" (*samājñā*)?
Answer: It is called "conventional knowledge" (saṃvṛti-jñāna) because worldly people practice this knowledge equally,
such as the coming and going of men and women, and the various phenomena currently practiced by worldly people.
Question: Since it also takes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-dharma*) as its object, why is it called "worldly knowledge" (*loka-jñāna*)? Answer:
Because it occurs for the most part, it mostly takes conventional phenomena (*saṃvṛti-dharma*) as its object and only rarely takes ultimate reality (*paramārtha-dharma*).
Furthermore, this knowledge lacks the characteristics of ultimate reality; it is called "worldly knowledge" because it is what is commonly designated by many people.
It is just as when many people establish a king; although he is not of royal lineage, because he is established by many people, he is also called a king.
This case is likewise.
Furthermore, this wisdom is a conventional designation.
Why is this so? Because this wisdom exists entirely within all persons, all sentient beings, and in all places.
Furthermore, this wisdom is the basis upon which delusion relies and the ground upon which delusion stands.
Moreover, this wisdom is that which is appointed,
just as one appoints a senior elder (sthavira) or a disciplinarian (karmadāna).
The proponents of the *Śabdavāda* (Exponents of Phonetics) say:
"This knowledge is called 'knowledge of equality' (*samatājñāna*) because it is covered by ignorance (*ajñāna*), just as objects within a vessel are said to be 'covered objects.
Why, then, is it called 'knowledge of suffering' (*duḥkhajñāna*) up to 'knowledge of the path' (*mārgajñāna*)?"
Answer: Because of the determination of the antidote and the determination of the object of focus.
This applies even up to the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
Furthermore, they are termed the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge of the path because their bases are determined and their antidotes are determined.

Furthermore, they are termed the knowledge of suffering because they consist of the four aspects of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and so on, up to being termed the knowledge of the path because they consist of the four aspects of the practice of the path (*mārga-pratipatti*).

Question: If there are the four modes of practice regarding suffering up to the four modes of practice regarding the path within tainted wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*), are these the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)? Answer:

If one practices the four aspects of the truth of suffering and the four aspects of the path to cessation, and possesses certainty regarding the truths, this is termed knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Although wholesome contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) may practice the four aspects of suffering up to the four aspects of the path, because it lacks certainty regarding the truths, it is not termed knowledge of suffering up to knowledge of the path.
Furthermore, if one practices the four modes regarding suffering, up to the four modes regarding the path, afflictions will arise again.

Furthermore, if one practices the four modes regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, then seeing is no longer called "not seeing," and knowing is no longer called "not knowing. Having attained a state of certainty, one is not obscured by ignorance, doubt, or wrong views.

Although wholesome contaminated wisdom engages with the four aspects such as suffering and so forth, it still does not truly see, it still does not truly know, and it remains obscured by ignorance, doubt, and false views.

Furthermore, if one practices the four modes of contemplation, such as the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha*), they are able to diminish and destroy [existence]; this constitutes the knowledge of suffering up to the knowledge of the path regarding existence.

Although wholesome contaminated wisdom (*sāsravakuśalaprajñā*) practices the four modes of contemplation of suffering up to the four modes of contemplation of the path, it increases and nourishes that which remains in existence; the answer is as explained in the *Saṃyuktāgama* (Miscellaneous Section).

Furthermore, if one practices the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering and so forth, but does not practice the four modes of contemplation regarding origin, cessation, and the path, this is the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*). If one practices the four modes of contemplation regarding origin and so forth, but does not practice the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering, cessation, and the path, this is the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*). If one practices the four modes of contemplation regarding cessation and so forth, but does not practice the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering, origin, and the path, this is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*). If one practices the four modes of contemplation regarding the path, but does not practice the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering, origin, and cessation, this is the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*).

Wholesome contaminated wisdom may practice the four aspects such as suffering and so forth, or it may also practice the four aspects such as origin, cessation, and the path; it may practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspect of origin, or practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspect of cessation, or practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspect of the path; it may practice the aspect of origin while also practicing the aspect of cessation, or practice the aspect of origin while also practicing the aspect of the path, or practice the aspect of cessation while also practicing the aspect of the path; it may practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspects of origin and cessation, or practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspects of origin and the path, or practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspects of cessation and the path; it may practice the aspect of origin while also practicing the aspects of cessation and the path; or it may practice the aspect of suffering while also practicing the aspects of origin, cessation, and the path.
When practicing in this manner, one should say that this is the knowledge of suffering, up to and including the knowledge of the path.
Furthermore, if one practices the four modes of contemplation regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, these are not identical to the single bond of suffering and its origin.
Although wholesome contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) operates upon the four aspects of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, it is bound by the same fetter as suffering and origin.
Question: Since cessation and the path are not bound by the same fetter, why is there no establishment of "knowledge of cessation" (*nirodha-jñāna*) or "knowledge of the path" (*mārga-jñāna*)?
Answer: Because it does not abide in the middle at the beginning, it likewise does not abide in the middle at the end. Regarding the realms (*dhātu*):

that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) within the knowledge of others' minds is bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*); that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) is bound to the three realms; the others are unbound.
As for the stages (bhūmi): dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) resides in six stages, namely, the preliminary stage (anāgamya), the intermediate stage (dhyānāntara), and the four fundamental dhyānas.
The knowledge of comparison (anvaya-jñāna) resides in the nine stages.
Of the six stages mentioned above, the three formless stages (ārūpya-dhātu) exclude the stage of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The knowledge of others' minds (paracitta-jñāna) resides in the four fundamental dhyāna stages.

Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) exists in eleven stages: the desire realm, the threshold concentration (anāgamya), the intermediate concentration (dhyānāntara), the four fundamental dhyānas, and the four formless stages.

As for the remaining types of knowledge, if they belong to the category of dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), they exist in six stages; if they belong to the category of subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), they exist in nine stages.
Regarding the bodies upon which they rely: dharma-knowledge relies on a body of the desire realm;
knowledge of others' minds relies on bodies of the desire and form realms;
and subsequent knowledge and conventional knowledge rely on bodies of all three realms.

As for the remaining [knowledges], if they belong to the category of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), they depend on the body of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); if they belong to the category of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), they depend on the bodies of all three realms.
Regarding their practice, the practitioner practices the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*) through both dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge.
If the knowledge of others' minds is untainted (*anāsrava*), it proceeds through the four modes of practice; if it is tainted (*sāsrava*), it does not proceed through those modes.
Conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) proceeds through sixteen modes, and there are also instances where it does not proceed through them.

The knowledge of suffering proceeds by way of the four aspects beginning with "suffering as conditioned by formations" (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā); the knowledge of origination proceeds by way of the four aspects beginning with "origination"; the knowledge of cessation proceeds by way of the four aspects beginning with "cessation"; and the knowledge of the path proceeds by way of the four aspects beginning with "path."
Regarding their objects: dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge take the Four Truths as their objects;
knowledge of others' minds takes the mind and mental factors as its object;
conventional knowledge takes all phenomena as its object.

The knowledge of suffering takes the truth of suffering as its object; the knowledge of origination takes the truth of origination as its object; the knowledge of cessation takes the truth of cessation as its object; and the knowledge of the path takes the truth of the path as its object.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness, the knowledge of others' minds consists of three foundations of mindfulness, excluding the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
The knowledge of cessation is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); the remaining knowledges are the four foundations of mindfulness.
"Knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to wisdom itself.
Regarding the samādhis: dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) are associated with the three samādhis.

If the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) is untainted (anāsrava), it is associated with the path-samādhi and the wishless (apraṇihita) samādhi; if it is tainted (sāsrava), it is not associated with any samādhi.
Conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) does not coexist with the samādhis.

The knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna) coexists with two samādhis; the knowledge of origin (samudayajñāna) coexists with the samādhi of the wishless regarding origin; the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna) coexists with the samādhi of signlessness; and the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna) coexists with the samādhi of the wishless regarding the path.
Regarding the faculties (*indriya*): conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is associated with five faculties.
Generally speaking, the remaining knowledges are associated with three faculties.

Those pertaining to the past, future, and present constitute the three time periods (*adhvan*). Knowledge that takes the three time periods as well as the non-temporal (*adhvan-mukta*) as its objects consists of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge.
The knowledge of others' minds takes as its object both the three periods of time and non-temporal phenomena (*adhvanirapekṣa-dharma*).

That which pertains to the past takes the past as its object; that which pertains to the present takes the present as its object; and that which pertains to the future—whether it is destined not to arise or destined to arise—takes the three periods of time or the future as its object respectively.
The knowledge of cessation takes non-worldly phenomena as its object.
The remaining knowledges take the three periods of time as their objects.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate: conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) is of these three kinds, while the remaining knowledges are wholesome.

Regarding the objects of knowledge as wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral: subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) takes the wholesome and the neutral as its objects; the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna) take the wholesome as their objects;
the remaining knowledges take all three types as their objects.

Regarding those that are bound to the three realms and those that are unbound: among the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is bound to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu-pratisaṃyukta*), while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is unbound.
The conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is bound to all three realms.

The remaining knowledges are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*). Regarding those that take as their object both what is conditioned by the three realms and what is unconditioned: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) takes as its object what is conditioned by the desire realm and what is unconditioned; the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) takes as its object what is conditioned by the form and formless realms and what is unconditioned; the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) takes as its object what is conditioned by the desire and form realms and what is unconditioned; conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) takes as its object what is conditioned by the three realms and what is unconditioned; the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*) and the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*) take as their object what is conditioned by the three realms; and the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*) take as their object what is unconditioned.

Regarding those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: the knowledge of others' minds consists of these three types; conventional knowledge is neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee;
and the remaining knowledges are both trainee and non-trainee.

Regarding those conditioned by the trainee, the non-trainee, and that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) take all three types as their objects; the knowledge of suffering, origin, and cessation take that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee as their object; and the knowledge of the path takes both the trainee and the non-trainee as its objects.

Regarding those [knowledges] that are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), or not abandoned: among the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is abandoned by the path of cultivation, while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is not abandoned; conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) is abandoned by both the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, and the remaining knowledges are not abandoned.

Regarding those [objects] that are abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, and conventional knowledge take all three types as their objects; suffering-knowledge and origin-knowledge take those abandoned by the path of seeing and the path of cultivation as their objects; while cessation-knowledge and path-knowledge take those not abandoned as their objects.

Regarding those that take names as their object and take meanings as their object: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, and knowledge of origin take both names and meanings as their objects; the remaining knowledges take meanings as their objects.

Regarding those that take as their object one's own body, another's body, or what is not a body: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, and conventional knowledge take as their objects one's own body, another's body, and what is not a body; other-mind knowledge takes as its object another's body; the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, and the knowledge of the path take as their objects one's own body and another's body; and the knowledge of cessation takes as its object what is not a body.
If the knowledge of suffering is the practice of the practice of suffering?
Or if the practice of the practice of suffering is the knowledge of suffering? Answer:
Alternatively, there is the knowledge of suffering that does not practice the contemplation of the suffering of conditioned existence; this is elaborated at length as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is the knowledge of suffering but does not practice the contemplation of the suffering of conditioned existence: it is the knowledge of suffering that practices the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of emptiness, and the contemplation of non-self.
One who practices asceticism but lacks the knowledge of suffering practices the dharma associated with the suffering of asceticism while lacking that knowledge of suffering.
One for whom the knowledge of suffering also practices asceticism is one whose knowledge of suffering practices asceticism.

Regarding "neither the knowledge of suffering nor the practice of the suffering of conditioned formations": if one takes up this very lineage, one practices the contemplation of impermanence, emptiness, and non-self, which are dharmas associated with the knowledge of suffering;
if one does not take up this lineage, it excludes all such matters as mentioned above.
The same applies to the statements regarding those who have practiced asceticism and those who shall practice asceticism.

Just as there are three or four propositions concerning asceticism, there are likewise three or four propositions concerning the practice of impermanence, the practice of emptiness, and the practice of non-self.

Just as there are twelve sets of four propositions regarding the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), there are likewise twelve sets of four propositions each for the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*); together, these comprise forty-eight sets of four propositions.
There are four reasons why it is called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna):
first, because it knows the dharma for the first time;
second, because it perceives the dharma directly.
Third, it is the knowledge of reality;
fourth, it is the knowledge of equanimity.
There are four matters termed inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*):
1. To infer the effect by means of the cause;
2. to infer the cause by means of the effect;
3. to infer the mind by means of bodily and verbal conduct.
4. One knows through the comparison with what has been taught.

The Buddha possesses four factors called the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): namely, cause (*hetu*), immediate succession (*anantara*), object-condition (*ālambana*), and sovereign power (*ādhipatya*).
This knowledge likewise possesses these four factors, and the objects of this knowledge also possess these four factors: namely, cause, immediate succession, object-condition, and sovereign power.
There are four matters termed "equality of names":
first, equality by way of names;
second, equality by way of fetters.
Third, by means of the provisional and so forth;
fourth, by means of attachment and so forth.
There are four matters termed suffering:
First, by means of burning affliction;
second, by means of birth;
third, by means of bodily sensation.
Fourth, by death. If one practices these four matters with wisdom, this is called the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*).
There are four matters called the origin (*samudaya*):
First, by means of karma;
second, by means of afflictions;
third, by means of craving.
Fourth, by means of ignorance.
If wisdom operates upon these four matters, it is called the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
There are four matters termed cessation (*nirodha*): first, the fruit of the śramaṇa, which is the abandonment of the three fetters (*trisaṃyojana*).
The second fruit consists of the abandonment of the three fetters and the attenuation of craving, hatred, and delusion;
the third fruit consists of the abandonment of the five lower fetters;
and the fourth fruit consists of the abandonment of all fetters.
If wisdom practices these four modes of conduct, it is the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).
There are four matters termed the Path (*mārga*):
first, all that is undertaken by those in training (*śaikṣa*), from the eighth stage up to the final stage.
2. Subduing enemies; 3. Contemplating one's past deeds;
4. Approaching the exhaustion of outflows.
If wisdom practices these four modes of conduct, it is called the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna).
There are four matters termed the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna):
first, the non-apprehension of views.
2. Not practicing emptiness;
3. lacking the knowledge of others' minds;
4. being slow in skillful means.
There are four matters termed the knowledge of non-arising:
first, knowing the cause;
second, knowing the fruit.
Third, knowing one's own self;
fourth, by means of others.

The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) should be spoken of as a single knowledge, namely, dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*); this is not like [the case of] dharma-knowledge [in the sense that it is so called] because its essence is the Dharma.
The ten knowledges should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely, determinative knowledge (*niścaya-jñāna*). Why is this?
Because the meaning of determination is knowledge.
The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely, knowledge (*jñāna*).
The objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) are also one knowledge, namely, the attachment that arises from examining and ascertaining the objects of knowledge.
The nine knowledges should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*), because they are subsumed under the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*).
The ten knowledges should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), because it fulfills all aspirations.
The ten knowledges should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), because it is found within the person who has exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*).
The ten knowledges should be spoken of as one knowledge, namely the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), because it does not regress further.
There are three samādhis:
emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), and signlessness (*animitta*).

One should speak of one samādhi, as in the case of concentration (*samādhi*) among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), such as the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and right concentration. One should speak of two kinds of samādhi:
namely, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), or the bound (*baddha*) and the liberated (*mukta*).
One should speak of four samādhis, namely: those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, and those that are unbound.

One should speak of five samādhis, namely: those bound to the desire realm, those bound to the form realm, those bound to the formless realm, those of the learner (śaikṣa), and those of the non-learner (aśaikṣa).
Whether considered in terms of their presence within the body or in terms of moments, there are immeasurable samādhis.
Why, then, does the Blessed One establish only three samādhis among these one samādhi and immeasurable samādhis?
The answer is:
For three reasons: first, by way of antidote;
second, by way of aspiration.
3. Regarding the antidote by way of the object of focus (*ālambana*):
this is the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). The concentration on emptiness is the proximate antidote to the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*).

The view of a self-identity functions through the modes of "I" and "mine," whereas the concentration on emptiness functions through the modes of emptiness and non-self. By what mode of activity does it act as the antidote to which mode of activity?
The answer is:

One counteracts the practice of the self (*ātman*) by means of the practice of non-self (*anātman*), and one counteracts the practice of "mine" (*ātmīya*) by means of the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Furthermore, the practice of non-self counteracts the five types of views regarding the self, while the practice of emptiness counteracts the fifteen types of views regarding "mine."
Furthermore, the practice of selflessness serves as the antidote to the view of a self, while the practice of emptiness serves as the antidote to the view of what belongs to a self.

Furthermore, the practice of selflessness serves as the antidote to attachment to the view of a self, while the practice of emptiness serves as the antidote to attachment to the view of what belongs to a self.
Furthermore, that the aggregates (*skandha*) are not the self is the practice of non-self (*anātma-gati*); that there is no self within the aggregates is the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā-gati*).
Furthermore, that the eye is not the self is the practice of non-self; that there is no self within the eye is the practice of emptiness.
This applies likewise to the mind as well.
Furthermore, the emptiness of intrinsic nature is the practice of non-self; the emptiness of that which is practiced is the practice of emptiness.
That which is directed toward the mind is wishlessness; because the directed mind does not wish for existence, it is called wishlessness.
Question: Does one also direct the mind toward the Path without aspiring for it? Answer: No.
One should not ask such a question. Nor is it that one does not direct the mind toward or aspire for the Path; rather, there is a specific reason why one does not aspire for the Path.

Although the Noble Path is non-existent (*anupalabdha*), it relies upon existence (*bhava*); the practitioner directs the mind so as not to aspire for the aggregates (*skandha*), yet the Noble Path relies upon the aggregates; one does not aspire for the world (*loka*), yet the Noble Path relies upon the world; one does not aspire for suffering (*duḥkha*), yet the Noble Path continues in succession with suffering.
Question: If this is so, for what reason do the sages cultivate the Path? Answer:
Because they wish to reach nirvana,
the practitioner reflects thus:
"Apart from the Noble Path, is there any other means by which one may reach nirvana?"
Knowing that nothing further exists, one cultivates the path because of the desire to reach nirvāṇa.
The object of focus is the signless (animitta) object; it is signless because the ten signs of phenomena are absent.
The ten signs refer to form, sound, odor, taste, touch, male and female characteristics, as well as the three conditioned characteristics.
Furthermore, the aggregates (skandhas) are signs; because those [signs] are extinguished by taking the aggregates as their object, they are signless (animitta).

The world is a mark; the past and future are marks; the inferior, middling, and superior are marks. Because it does not take the world as an object, does not take the past and future as objects, and does not take the inferior, middling, and superior as objects, it is signless.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the three samādhis also practice the practices.
The emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) practices two practices, namely the practice of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the practice of non-self (*anātman*).

The wishlessness samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) practices ten practices, namely the eight practices of the origin and the path, as well as the practices of impermanence (*anitya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*).
The practice of the signless samādhi consists of four modes of activity, namely, the cessation of the four modes of activity.
Furthermore, some say that the three samādhis serve as antidotes:

the emptiness samādhi is the proximate antidote to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); the wishlessness samādhi is the proximate antidote to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); and the signless samādhi is the proximate antidote to doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The *Prajñapti-śāstra* states:
"The emptiness samādhi is emptiness, not wishlessness or signlessness;
the wishlessness samādhi is wishlessness, not emptiness or signlessness."
The signless samādhi is signless, yet it is not emptiness or wishlessness. Why is this?
The sphere of activity of the emptiness samādhi is not that of wishlessness or the signless; the same applies to wishlessness and the signless as well.
Furthermore, it is said that the emptiness samādhi is wishlessness, and wishlessness is the emptiness samādhi; the signless is itself the signless, and is neither emptiness nor wishlessness.
Question: Why is it that two samādhis are of the same essence, while one samādhi is of a different essence? Answer:
By means of these two samādhis, one simultaneously attains the antidote to a single category of phenomena.

Regarding "attaining simultaneously": if one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), then during the four moments of mind that perceive suffering (*duḥkha*), one cultivates the future wishlessness samādhi (*apraṇihita-samādhi*).

If one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) by relying on the wishless concentration (*apraṇihita-samādhi*), then during the four moments of mind that perceive suffering, one cultivates the future emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).
Regarding the "counteracting of one kind of dharma," these two concentrations both counteract the dharmas to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
Furthermore, it is said that the samādhi of emptiness consists of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness. What is emptiness?
Within this, there is nothing permanent or immutable; it is empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self.
What is wishlessness?
This samādhi does not wish for attachment, does not wish for aversion, does not wish for delusion, and does not wish for future existence.
What is meant by "signless"?
The answer is:
this samādhi is signless because it is devoid of form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.
The wishless is both wishless, empty, and signless.
What is meant by "wishless"?
This samādhi does not wish for craving, hatred, or delusion, nor does it wish for future existence.
What is emptiness? This samādhi is empty and lacks permanence, up to and including the absence of self and what belongs to a self.
What is signlessness?
This samādhi has no characteristic of form, nor even of touch.
This signless samādhi is signless, it is empty, and it is wishless.
In what way is it signless?
This samādhi has no characteristic of form, up to and including no characteristic of tangibility. How is it empty?
This samādhi is without permanence, up to and including being without self or what belongs to a self.
What is wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)?
This samādhi does not wish for craving, and so forth, as explained at length.
This is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this samādhi, and so forth, as explained at length.
The nature and reason for its existence have already been explained; now it shall be explained why it is called *samādhi*.
What is the meaning of *samādhi*?
The answer is:
It is called samādhi for three reasons:
first, by way of correctness;
second, by way of gathering.
Third, by means of continuity.

"Correct" refers to the fact that since beginningless time, afflictions, evil conduct, and inverted false views have disturbed and afflicted the mind and its mental factors; therefore, that which causes them to become upright and correct is entirely due to the power of samādhi.

Regarding "concentration" (*saṃgraha*): since beginningless time, the mind and mental factors have been scattered among forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and phenomena; therefore, to concentrate them so they do not scatter and cause them to abide upon a single object is entirely due to the power of samādhi.

Regarding continuity: when the mind and mental factors arise in the formless attainments, a wholesome mind arises in succession to a defiled or neutral mind; a defiled or neutral mind arises in succession to a wholesome mind; and a neutral mind arises in succession to a wholesome or defiled mind. That one is able to abandon these two types of minds and cause only the wholesome mind to continue in succession is entirely due to the power of samādhi.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 45 [and] Fascicle 46.

Furthermore, it is called samādhi due to three factors:
First, rectifying one's own mind;
second, planting the seeds of roots of goodness;
third, ensuring that the mind remains upright in continuous succession.
Furthermore, there are three reasons why it is called samādhi:
first, not following after objects;
second, upholding various wholesome dharmas.
Third, it enables various wholesome states of mind to abide within a single object of focus.
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra said:
For what reason is it called *samādhi*?
Answer: It is that which enables various wholesome states of mind to abide within a single object of focus;
the rest is as explained above. The Venerable Buddhadeva says:
Samādhi has many names: there is samādhi of wholesome dharmas, samādhi of unwholesome dharmas, samādhi of indeterminate dharmas, and the nine successive samādhis.
In this context, the mind being in right samādhi is called "samādhi.
Regarding its realm (*dhātu*): that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is bound to the three realms; that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is unbound.
Regarding its stage (*bhūmi*): that which is with outflows exists in eleven stages; that which is without outflows exists in nine stages.

Regarding the basis of the body: for one who practices based on a body belonging to the three realms, the emptiness [samādhi] has two modes of practice, the wishlessness [samādhi] has ten modes of practice, and the signlessness [samādhi] has four modes of practice.

Regarding their objects: the outflowing (sāsrava) emptiness samādhi takes all things as its object, while the non-outflowing (anāsrava) emptiness samādhi takes the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya) as its object; wishlessness takes the [remaining] three truths as its object, and signlessness takes the truth of cessation (nirodha-satya) as its object.

Regarding the foundations of mindfulness: the samādhis of emptiness and wishlessness constitute the four foundations of mindfulness, while the samādhi of signlessness constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

As for the knowledges: the samādhi of emptiness is associated with four knowledges, namely, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*);
the samādhi of wishlessness is associated with seven knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*).
The signless samādhi is associated with four knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and the knowledge of cessation.
Regarding "samādhi," that which is the root of samādhi, in summary, is associated with the three roots.
The past, future, and present constitute the three periods of time (*trikāla*).

Regarding those dharmas that take the three periods as their object: the samādhi of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) takes as its object both the dharmas of the three periods and those that are not of the periods; the wishless (*apraṇihita*) takes the three periods as its object; and the signless (*animitta*) takes what is not of the periods as its object.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object;
the unwholesome and the neutral take the three types [of emptiness, wishlessness, and signlessness] as their objects; and the signless takes the wholesome as its object.
Regarding those that are bound to the three realms and those that are not bound: some are bound to the three realms, while others are not bound.

As for those that take as their object both what is bound to the three realms and what is not bound: the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi), when with outflows (sāsrava), takes as its object both what is bound to the three realms and what is not bound; when without outflows (anāsrava), it takes as its object only what is bound to the three realms. The wishlessness samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) takes as its object both what is bound to the three realms and what is not bound. The signlessness samādhi (animitta-samādhi) takes as its object only what is not bound.
Regarding those that are trainee, non-trainee, or neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee—these are the three types.

As for those conditioned by the trainee, the non-trainee, or the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee: the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi), when with outflows (sāsrava), conditions all three types; when without outflows (anāsrava), it conditions the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee. The wishlessness samādhi (apraṇihita-samādhi) conditions all three types. The signlessness samādhi (animitta-samādhi) conditions the neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee.

Regarding those [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, and not abandoned: those that are contaminated (*sāsrava*) are abandoned by the path of cultivation; those that are uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are not abandoned.

Regarding those that take as their object [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned: the emptiness concentration (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), when contaminated, takes all three types as its object; when uncontaminated, it takes [those] abandoned by the path of seeing and abandoned by the path of cultivation as its object. The wishlessness concentration (*apranihita-samādhi*) takes the three types as its object; the signlessness concentration (*animitta-samādhi*) takes the non-abandoned as its object.

Regarding "conditioning by name and conditioning by meaning": the emptiness and wishlessness [samādhis] take both meaning and name as their objects; the signlessness [samādhi] takes meaning as its object.

Regarding "conditioning one's own body, another's body, and that which is not the body": the impure (sāsrava) emptiness samādhi takes these three types as its objects; the pure (anāsrava) [emptiness] and the wishlessness [samādhi] take one's own body and another's body as their objects; the signlessness [samādhi] takes that which is not the body as its object.
If one who possesses the emptiness samādhi necessarily practices the practice of emptiness?
The answer is:
there are cases where one possesses the emptiness samādhi but does not practice the practice of emptiness; thus, one should elaborate upon this in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
One who practices the emptiness samādhi without practicing the contemplation of emptiness practices the contemplation of non-self within the emptiness samādhi.
One who practices the contemplation of emptiness without the emptiness samādhi practices the contemplation of emptiness in accordance with the dharmas associated with the emptiness samādhi.
Regarding those who practice the emptiness samādhi by practicing the path of emptiness: they practice the path of emptiness through the emptiness samādhi.
Regarding those who neither [practice] the emptiness samādhi nor the path of emptiness: if they grasp this very lineage, they practice the dharma associated with the emptiness samādhi of non-self;
if they do not grasp this lineage, it is as previously described.
The same applies to what has already been practiced and what is yet to be practiced.
Just as there are four propositions regarding the practice of emptiness within the emptiness-samādhi, the same applies to the practice of non-self within the emptiness-samādhi.
The wishless (*apraṇihita*) consists of thirty-four phrases, and the signless (*animitta*) consists of twelve sets of four phrases, totaling forty-eight sets of four phrases.
Question: What is the difference between samādhi and the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*)?
Answer: Samādhi is both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava), whereas the gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha) are exclusively without outflows. Question:
Why is it that while samādhi can be both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), the gates of liberation (vimokṣamukha) are exclusively without-outflows?
The answer is:
the gates of liberation should not be with-outflows; they should not be fetters (bandhana).
Question: Is one established in the gates of liberation by attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), or by the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*)?
If it were by attaining right determination, then the concentration associated with the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) should necessarily be a gate of liberation.
If it were by means of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), then the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) would have to be a door to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
The answer is:
one should state it thus:
Because one has attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and because one has exhausted the outflows (*āsrava*), it is called a gate of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*). Why is this so?
Attaining all noble paths is termed "determination," and the total exhaustion of everything is termed "exhaustion of outflows."

Just as one attains the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti) immediately following the supreme mundane dharmas (laukikāgra-dharma), one attains [the patience regarding] the origin (samudaya) immediately following suffering, the cessation (nirodha) immediately following the origin, and the path (mārga) immediately following cessation.

Regarding the exhaustion of outflows: one may exhaust the outflows of the three realms by relying on the emptiness samādhi, or exhaust the outflows of the three realms by relying on the wishlessness samādhi, or exhaust the outflows of the three realms by relying on the signlessness samādhi.
Question: For what reason are they called "gateways to liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*)? Answer:
Because it is like the method of a shield.

For example, just as a combatant holding a shield in front severs the heads of his enemies, so too the practitioner at that time holds the liberation-door of the shield before him, severing the enemies that are the afflictions; he brings about their falling off and establishes them upon the ground of non-attainment.
As it is said:

"Certainty is the right path; uncertainty is the wrong path. A concentrated mind attains liberation, whereas an unconcentrated mind does not. One who possesses concentration can know the arising and ceasing of the aggregates."

The *Prajñapti-śāstra* explains emptiness in detail, namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, conditioned emptiness, unconditioned emptiness, beginningless emptiness, essential emptiness, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of the ultimate truth, and the emptiness of emptiness.
Question: For what reason does the *Prajñapti-śāstra* explain emptiness in detail? Answer:
Because emptiness is the direct antidote to the twenty types of satkāyadṛṣṭi,
the Buddha’s sūtras state:
"If a noble disciple is fully endowed with the garland of the three samādhis, they can sever unwholesome dharmas and cultivate wholesome dharmas."
Question: For what reason are the three samādhis called a "garland"? Answer:
Because of its exquisite beauty, people of the world give rise to a heart of joy and aspiration;
it is like when, in one's youth, a flower garland is bound upon the head, whether male or female, a heart of love and reverence arises.
The practitioner is likewise: if they bind on the garland of samādhi, gods and worldly people will conceive love and respect for them.
Furthermore, it is like a person who binds a flower garland upon their head; the wind will not dishevel their hair.
Virtuous One, if one binds this garland of flowers of samādhi, the wind of restlessness cannot disturb them.
It is like a flower: if it is bound together to form a garland, its utility is greatly increased.

All merits are likewise; if they are tied together to form a garland, they have many uses: one can thereby attain right determination, realize the fruits [of the path], become free from desire, and exhaust all outflows.
Furthermore, just as worldly people form the notion of a garland from flowers that have been strung together,
so too do the noble ones form the notion of a garland by binding all meritorious qualities with the three samādhis.
It is also like people in the world who, by successively stringing together flowers, conceive the idea of a garland.
So too it is with the noble ones (ārya): they fix their minds successively upon a single object and likewise conceive the idea of a garland.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"The samādhi of emptiness is the dwelling place of the Elder. Question:
Why is it said that the emptiness samādhi is the dwelling place of the elders?
The answer is:
because most elders dwell in this state.
Within the three realms, the Buddha is the most virtuous elder (*sthavira*), followed by the *pratyekabuddha*.
Because the Venerable Śāriputra constantly dwells in this place, it is called "the dwelling place of the elder."
Furthermore, emptiness is a unique teaching within our own school.
Within our school, all are elders (*sthavira*), whereas all those of other schools are but youths.
Even among our own school, those who are eight years old are considered elders.
Why is this? Because they have accomplished the Dharma of the Elder;
among the outsiders, even those who are eighty years old are all but youths.
Why is this? Because he has accomplished the qualities of youth.
It is asked:
Do the various non-Buddhists possess the wishless and the signless?
The answer is:
although they lack the fundamental [realization], they possess that which resembles it.

Coarse conduct resembles the wishless (*apraṇihita*), and the practice of cessation resembles the signless (*animitta*); if even these resemble [the stages] from emptiness (*śūnyatā*) up to the wishless, how much more so their fundamental states?
Furthermore, because they can give rise to the dharmas of the Elder (*sthavira*), emptiness is called the dwelling place of the Elder.
The Dharma of the Elder consists of the Path and its fruit.
Who is able to give rise to it?
It is emptiness that is able to give rise to it.
Furthermore, because they abide securely in the dharma of profound discernment, the dwelling place of an Elder is called "emptiness.
If sentient beings do not attain the samādhi of emptiness, their dispositions are frivolous and restless;
if they attain the samādhi of emptiness, their dispositions become as immovable as a mountain.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka spoke thus:

"If one understands the dharma of liberation, then one's disposition is examined and certain; one whose disposition is examined and certain is called an Elder (sthavira). For this reason, it is said that emptiness is the dwelling place of the Elder."

Furthermore, when the practitioner dwells in the dharma of emptiness, whether things are agreeable or disagreeable, good or bad, beneficial or not beneficial, and whether they are matters of worldly pleasure or matters of worldly suffering, their mind does not waver amidst these circumstances.
It was previously heard that when the Venerable Śāriputra’s mother passed away, his co-resident disciple returned to lay life.
The bhikṣu Dīrghadanta, who harbored a constant sense of resentment and aversion toward the Venerable Śāriputra, thought to himself:
"I should now go and inform him of this inauspicious matter."
At that time, the bhikṣu Dīrghadanta went to the Venerable Śāriputra and spoke these words:
"Venerable sir, you should know that your mother has passed away and your co-resident disciple has returned to lay life."
The Venerable Śāriputra replied thus:
"The passing away of my mother is the nature of this physical body.
My disciple returning to lay life is the way of ordinary worldlings."
At that time, the bhikṣu Dīrghadanta thought to himself:
"Although the Elder Śāriputra has spoken thus, his mind must surely harbor something different.

Then, on the following morning, for this very reason, the Venerable Śāriputra dressed in his robes and took up his bowl to enter the city of Śrāvastī for alms. Having finished his meal by begging from house to house, he returned to his dwelling. After putting away his robe and bowl and washing his feet, he placed his sitting mat (niṣadana) over his shoulder and went from the Jeta Grove to the Ārāma-śānta Grove. There, in the open air during the day, he sat beneath a tree and formed this thought in his mind:
Is there anything in this world of lovely and exquisite forms that, when it changes, decays, and perishes, would cause me to give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress?
Upon thorough examination, I see that there is nothing such as that.
At that time, as evening fell, the Venerable Śāriputra returned from the Andhavana forest to the Jeta Grove.
At that moment, the Elder Ānanda was walking up and down near the gate of his dwelling in the vihāra; seeing the Venerable Śāriputra approaching, he asked him:
"Venerable Śāriputra!"
"From where have you come? Śāriputra replied,
"I have come from the Andhavana forest."
He asked again:
"Venerable Śāriputra!
In the Andhavana forest, in which samādhi do you mostly abide?"
Śāriputra replied: "He dwells in the samādhi of vitarka and vicāra.
Ānanda asked again:
"What are the applied thought and sustained thought with which you dwell? Śāriputra replied:
"During the day, while in the Andhavana forest, I have had such an applied thought:"
"In this world, there are indeed lovely and exquisite forms," and so forth, as extensively described.
Ānanda asked: "Venerable Śāriputra!"
"What do you think? Does such form exist? Śāriputra replied:
"No. Ānanda spoke again to the Venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"You have often said this:"
If a Buddha did not appear in the world, we would die blind. The Buddha is a lovely and wondrous form;
if he were to undergo change, decay, and pass away, would you not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, pain, and distress?
The Venerable Śāriputra replied:
"Even if the World-Honored One were to undergo transformation, decay, and extinction, I would not give rise to sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or distress.
I have only this thought:"
"The World-Honored One will swiftly enter parinirvāṇa; the eye of the world will swiftly perish.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Venerable Śāriputra!

You have skillfully eliminated the view of self, the view of what belongs to self, and the conceit of "I am," cutting them off at their root so that they will never grow again, just like the head of a tāla tree when severed.
Although the Tathāgata possesses a form that is most lovely, if it were subject to change, decay, and dissolution, what cause would there be for sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction?

Therefore, when a practitioner dwells in that Dharma, their mind does not waver in the face of the agreeable or disagreeable, the pleasant or unpleasant, the beneficial or non-beneficial, or matters of worldly enjoyment and matters of worldly suffering.
For this reason, it is called "Emptiness," the dwelling place of the Elder.
It is further said:
The Venerable Śāriputra was staying in a forest in the kingdom of Kośala.
At that time, there was also a brahmin named Agivaka living in that forest, not far from the Venerable Śāriputra.

When the people were holding a four-month festival, the brahmin went into the village, drank much fine liquor, and ate his fill of pork; he then returned to the forest where he resided, carrying the remaining meat and a bottle of wine.
Seeing the Venerable Śāriputra sitting beneath a tree, he conceived a sense of contempt, thinking:
"He and I are both renunciants; yet I am now in extreme comfort, while that bhikṣu is in extreme suffering."
He then spoke in verse:
"I drank rice wine, And secretly brought back a jar of it;
The grasses and trees upon the mountains and the earth, To my eyes, appeared like heaps of gold."
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra thought to himself:
"This one is like a deceased brahmin who has recited such a verse to me.
I, too, should now recite a verse."
Then the Venerable Śāriputra spoke this verse:
“I have drunk the wine of signlessness, And have further stolen the empty bottle;
The grasses, trees, and mountains upon the earth— I view them as nothing more than a mass of spittle.”
In this verse, the Venerable Śāriputra utters a lion’s roar by means of the three gates of liberation.
When he says, "I drink the wine of signlessness," this refers to the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*).
Furthermore, "secretly holding an empty bottle" refers to the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).
Regarding the grasses and trees upon the earth and mountains as being like a glob of spittle refers to the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).

The signless (*animitta*) is spoken of by many names: sometimes it is said that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the signless; sometimes it is said that the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) is the signless; sometimes it is said that the immovable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*) is the signless; sometimes it is said that the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) is the signless; and sometimes it is said that the signless itself is the signless.
Regarding the statement that emptiness is signlessness, as it is said in a sutra:
There was a bhikṣu who attained the concentration of the signless mind.
That bhikṣu had dull faculties and did not know what merit this concentration possessed, nor what its fruit and retribution were.
He reflected thus: "Who knows the meritorious fruit and retribution of this meditative concentration?
He then further thought:
Venerable Ānanda, praised by the Buddha and revered by all fellow practitioners of the holy life, you must certainly know the merits and the fruits of this meditative concentration.
"I should now go and ask about such matters.
He further thought:
"The Elder Ānanda well understands the characteristics of things."
If I go to question him, he will in turn question me:
"Have you attained this concentration? If I answer:
Yes, it is so.
That bhikṣu is one of few desires and conceals his own virtues; as one who speaks the Dharma, he does not wish to manifest his own merits.
If he were to answer:
It is not permitted.
This constitutes lying in the presence of others.
If one speaks otherwise or answers improperly, it constitutes harassing a senior bhikṣu.
"I have never from the past troubled the senior bhikṣus; now I should simply follow behind them so that, if they preach this Dharma to others, I may hear it."
At that time, that bhikṣu followed after Ānanda for six years, yet he still did not hear [the Dharma] being explained to others.
Then the bhikṣu asked the Elder Ānanda:

"If a person attains the concentration of the signless mind, the mind neither increases nor decreases; it abides in a state difficult to attain, like water remaining still. Because it has already come to rest, it is liberated; because it is already liberated, it abides."
"What merit is there in this emptiness spoken of by the World-Honored One, and what is its fruit and retribution?
At that time, the Elder Ānanda asked that bhikṣu:
"Have you attained this meditative concentration?"
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"Just as I feared, the question has now been asked.
He then remained silent.
At that time, Ānanda spoke as follows:
"If a bhikṣu, in the concentration of the signless mind, neither increases nor decreases," and so on, as extensively explained.
The Buddha taught that the fruit of this concentration is the attainment of all-knowing vision, the ability to generate wisdom, and the cultivation of the path to exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*).
"You, too, shall before long attain this Dharma.
'Neither increasing' means severing the view of self;
'neither decreasing' means severing the view of what belongs to the self."
The five views of "self" and the fifteen views of "mine" are also like this.
That which does not increase is saṃsāra;
that which does not decrease is nirvāṇa.
Regarding "dwelling in the practice that is difficult to attain": this practice is difficult to attain because it requires great effort and much activity.
As for "staying still like water," it is, for example, like water flowing from its source that stays in one place and no longer flows elsewhere.
Thus, when that concentration abides in a single object and no other object, because it abides, it is "liberation by its own nature.
Because it is liberated, it abides; this is "liberation within the body."
In this context, emptiness is explained as signlessness;
elsewhere, signlessness is also explained as emptiness.
As it is said in the *Dharmamudrā-sūtra*:
"If one abandons the perception of form while observing form," and so forth, as extensively explained.

The characteristic of a sentient being is the characteristic of an objective sphere; if that bhikṣu perceives phenomena as empty, he eliminates the characteristic of a sentient being and no longer perceives the characteristics of male or female within the objective sphere.
Therefore, the Venerable Ghoṣaka has said: "The characteristic of sentient beings is the characteristic of the objective sphere (*viṣaya-lakṣaṇa*).
If one possesses this practice of emptiness, one does not perceive the characteristic of male or female within that objective sphere."
Regarding the statement that the path of vision (darśanamārga) is signless (animitta), it is as said: "Maudgalyāyana!
Did the brahmin Tiṣya not say that the person of the sixth stage practices the signless?"
How does the sixth type of person practice the signless?
The answer is:
the sixth type of person who practices the signless consists of those with firm faith and those with firm Dharma.
Why is this so? Because they are signless (*animitta*); they cannot be enumerated, nor can it be easily known whether they exist here or there.

This applies to the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), and so on, up to the subsequent patience regarding the path (*mārga-anvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Question: For what reason is the path of seeing (darśanamārga) called "signless" (animitta)? Answer:
This path is the swift path, for it is a path that does not give rise to expectations.
That the immovable liberation of mind is signless is as it was said:
"O Elder Gavampati!"
Greed is a sign; hatred and delusion are signs; the immovable liberation of mind is the supreme signlessness (*animitta*).
Question: For what reason is the immovable liberation of mind called signless?
Answer: Defilements are the signs (*nimitta*).

That mind is not covered by defilements, not destroyed by them, does not cling to what is above while remaining below, and is not subject to impurity; therefore, the liberation of the immovable mind is called signless (*animitta*).
Regarding the designation "signless" for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, it is as stated:
"I frequently practice the signless concentration of mind through many merits.
A question is asked:
Why is the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception called the concentration of signlessness?
The answer is:
because the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is characterized by delusion, lack of sharpness, and lack of decisiveness.
It is just like doubt: there is neither a clearly perceived characteristic of having perception nor a clearly perceived characteristic of non-perception.
To speak of "signlessness" as signlessness is as explained herein.
The Sūtra says:
The Buddha was staying in the country of Śrāvastī, residing in the Eastern Monastery, the Hall of Migāra’s Mother.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān! Once, at one time, the Bhagavān was staying at the village of Micchakā among the Śākyas.
From the Bhagavān I heard this teaching:"
"I now dwell frequently in the samādhi of emptiness.
Have I correctly received, upheld, and recollected what has been thus spoken?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
As you have said, you have well received and retained [this teaching], exactly as I have spoken it, without any difference. He asked:
"If one has well received and retained it, one should not give rise to doubt."
If one harbors doubts, it cannot be called "properly upholding.
The answer is:
It is precisely because of this matter that it is called "properly upholding."
Why is this? Because they do not give rise to wrong views, do not propagate them to others, and do not completely forget them. Question:

Just as the Elder Ānanda, who possesses great learning and retains all that has been taught by the Omniscient One— the eighty-four thousand clusters of Dharma— stores them within the vessel of right mindfulness,
for what reason do you give rise to doubt regarding even a single phrase?
Answer: When hearing this Dharma, his mind was filled with grief and distress.
The killing of the Śākyas was the causal condition for this discourse.
Just as when the foolish King Virūḍhaka slaughtered the Śākyas, Ānanda entered the city of Kapilavastu accompanied by a single bhikṣu.
This city, which was originally like the cities of the devas, at that time resembled nothing but a cemetery.

All the towers, battlements, and parapets, as well as the various windows and casements, were completely destroyed; the clear springs and ponds were all fouled and turbid.
