Geese, mandarin ducks, peacocks, parrots, and mynas, driven by the smoke and fire, all flew up into the void. The young men and women all wept as they followed after Ānanda, saying these words:
"Venerable Ānanda!"
"My mother has passed away;
my father has passed away;
both my parents have passed away."
At that time, the Elder Ānanda again went to Sūkarakhata, where he stayed in the brahmin’s monastery.
There, the foolish King Virūḍhaka had buried half the bodies of the Śākyas of Kapilavastu underground; he ground them with iron filings and killed seventy-seven thousand noble sages.
At that time, having witnessed this event, Ānanda was overcome with extreme grief and distress.

Yet the World-Honored One’s faculties remained unchanged; his mind dwelt in peace, immovable as a mountain. He skillfully governed his mind, like one holding an oil-filled bowl while subduing the five sense-faculties, or like a horse looking straight ahead as it enters the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, the Elder Ānanda observed that the World-Honored One’s facial complexion was serene and joyful; having seen this, he thought to himself:
"When my own kinsmen were separated from me and my birthplace was destroyed, the World-Honored One did not experience such [distress]."
"I am now afflicted with suffering and distress, yet the World-Honored One’s mind is as unmoving as a mountain.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing what Ānanda was thinking, addressed him, saying:
"It is because I dwell frequently in the samādhi of emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi)."
Your mind dwells in the perception of a village, while mine dwells in the perception of an araṇya;
you dwell in the state of perceiving kinsmen, while I dwell in the perception of ordinary people;
you form the perception of sentient beings, while I form the perception of the fulfillment of the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that Ānanda and the bhikṣus were unable to practice the Path, led the bhikṣus on a gradual journey until they reached the Migāramātupāsāda monastery to the east of Śrāvastī.

At that time, the Elder Ānanda’s grief and distress were further extinguished; he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha as described in detail above.
For this reason, when Ānanda asked about this matter, his mind was filled with sorrow and distress.
He heard what the Buddha said:
"I constantly abide in the samādhi of emptiness."
For this reason, doubt arises.
He asks: "The Buddha said that I dwell much in emptiness."
"In what emptiness does one abide?
The answer is:
"Some say that one abides in the emptiness of non-activity."

Why is this? Because there is no practice that does not accord with the dharma of the four modes of deportment; when walking, the other three modes of deportment are empty, and it is likewise when in the other modes of deportment.
The commentary states:
One should say that it abides in the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Why is this? It is because one contemplates only the nature of dharmas. Therefore, Ānanda!
If a bhikṣu wishes to dwell extensively in emptiness, he should contemplate villages and sentient beings while maintaining the perception of an araṇya.
At that time, all the bhikṣus had this thought:
"This dharma of dwelling in emptiness is a unique quality of the Buddha."
To eliminate the doubts in the minds of the bhikṣus, the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"If a bhikṣu wishes to dwell extensively in the samādhi of emptiness, he should eliminate perceptions of villages and sentient beings, and dwell in the perception of an araṇya."
Question: For what reason did the Buddha tell the bhikṣus to eliminate these two perceptions? Answer:
Because the bhikṣus give rise to suffering and distress due to these two perceptions,

Ānanda! If a bhikṣu eliminates the perception of the village and the perception of sentient beings, and dwells in the perception of the forest hermitage, he should cultivate the perception of earth, and so on, up to the perception of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Question: For what reason does the World-Honored One, at all times, eliminate the perception of the lower and teach the perception of the higher, rather than teaching its fundamental basis? Answer:
This teaching is the ancient Dharma; all Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, have taught the Dharma in this very same way.
Furthermore, it is intended to ensure that what is spoken is not disordered.
If the World-Honored One were to speak of the superior perception without first eliminating the inferior perception, then the teaching would be disordered.
The Buddhas teach the Dharma without any confusion.
Furthermore, it is because they wish to avoid the fault of redundant teaching.
If the Blessed One were to speak of a higher perception without first eliminating the lower perception, that would constitute redundant teaching.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, does not delight in speaking at length.
Furthermore, this concentration is a concise and essential teaching.
If the World-Honored One were to explain the fundamental principles in their entirety at all times, the scriptural text would be too voluminous.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to manifest the path of debate.
Regarding the path of debate, whatever is spoken must have its words firmly established.
If one repeatedly revises what was previously stated, then the path of debate is destroyed.
The Buddha is a teacher who is beyond opposition, for he is well-versed in the way of debate.
Question: By speaking of the "notion of a village," what is being manifested?
Even up to the description of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, what is being manifested?
The answer is:

the perception of a village manifests the perception of Kapilavastu; the perception of sentient beings manifests the perception of the Śākyas; and the perception of an araṇya manifests the perception of the Nyagrodha monastery as well as the perception of the places where the bhikṣus practice the path.
Regarding the perception of earth: it is the perception that matter is subject to disintegration. Why is this so?
Because matter exists, there is the cutting off of hands, feet, ears, and noses.

The perception of suffering and emptiness is the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the perception of emptiness, up to and including the direct realization of the perception of neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Furthermore, the perception of the village consists of fifteen views of "mine," the perception of sentient beings consists of five views of "self," and the perception of the forest hermitage is the samādhi of emptiness.
The perception of earth is the object of focus (*ālambana*); its respective antidotes are the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Furthermore, the perception of the village is the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) of the desire realm; the perception of sentient beings is the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*) of the desire realm; and the perception of the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) is the perception of the stages of the first and second dhyānas, as well as the third and fourth dhyānas; their respective antidotes are the formless attainments.
Furthermore, the perception of a village is the desire realm.
Why is this so? Because the desire realm is designated by the name "village."
As a verse says:
"If one has subdued the thorns of the village, there will be no abuse, binding, or harm;
with mind unmoved by suffering or pleasure, such a person is called a bhikṣu."
The perception of sentient beings is the first dhyāna.
Why is this? Because within it there exist distinctions of honor and kinship.
The perception of the forest retreat is the second dhyāna. Why is this?
Because the second dhyāna is the noble and holy dharma of silence.
The perception of earth is the fourth dhyāna.
Why is this? Because within it there are the spheres of mastery (abhibhvāyatana) and the spheres of totality (kṛtsnāyatana).
Ānanda, those various antidotes are the formless attainments.
This is called entering the emptiness of the ultimate: namely, the exhaustion of outflows, attaining liberation of mind without requiring great effort.
Question: How is it that some attain liberation through much exertion, while others attain liberation without much exertion? Answer:
Those liberated by occasion (*sāmayikī-vimukti*) require much effort, whereas those liberated independent of occasion (*asamayikī-vimukti*) do not require much effort.
Furthermore, the five types of *arhat*s are said to require much effort, while the immovable (*akopya*) *arhat* does not require much effort.

Liberation attained by relying on the preparatory stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, or the three formless attainments is called "requiring much effort"; liberation attained by relying on the fundamental dhyānas is called "not requiring much effort."
Furthermore, there are three samādhis, namely: the emptiness-of-emptiness samādhi, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness samādhi, and the signlessness-of-signlessness samādhi.
What is the emptiness-of-emptiness samādhi?
Answer: As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:

"If a bhikṹṣu contemplates that conditioned formations associated with outflows and grasping (*sāsrava-upādāna-saṃskāra*) are empty, then within these conditioned formations associated with outflows and grasping, there is no phenomenon that is permanent or immutable; they are empty, selfless, and devoid of what belongs to a self (*anātman* and *anātmīya*)."

While reflecting in this way, there further arise minds and mental factors; one contemplates that the mind of the preceding reflection is empty, containing within it no permanent or unchanging dharma—empty, without self, and without what belongs to a self.

It is, for example, like a person who wishes to burn ten logs, a hundred logs, or a thousand logs, piling them together as a heap and setting fire to them. Standing by the side with a long pole, if any among them should fall and not burn, he gathers them back with the long pole;
once he knows the wood is already burned, he throws the long pole he was holding into the fire as well.
The practitioner is likewise: first they contemplate that conditioned formations associated with outflows and grasping are empty, as explained in detail above.
What is the wishless wishless samādhi?
The answer is:

If a bhikṣu contemplates that conditioned formations associated with outflows and grasping are impermanent and subject to change, when he reflects in this way, further moments of mind and mental factors arise; he then contemplates that the preceding mind of reflection is likewise impermanent and subject to change.
Just as when a person burns wood—as explained in detail above—so too it is with the bhikṣu:
he contemplates that conditioned formations associated with outflows and grasping are impermanent, and so forth, as explained in detail. This is called the wishless of the wishless.
What is the signless-signless samādhi?
The answer is:
if a bhikṣu contemplates the dharma of cessation—this is the sublime detachment, namely, the exhaustion of craving, the fading away of desire, cessation, and nirvāṇa.

While contemplating in this way, there further arise minds and mental factors; one observes that even the mind of the preceding contemplation is likewise quiescent and extinguished, as explained at length above. This is called the emptiness of the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*).
Next, one gives rise to the *śūnyatā-śūnyatā-samādhi*, which contemplates that emptiness itself is empty, and that even your emptiness is empty.

One gives rise to the *apraṇihita-samādhi* by contemplating that the five aggregates of clinging are impermanent; subsequently, one gives rise to the *apraṇihitāpraṇihita-samādhi* by contemplating that the preceding *apraṇihita-samādhi* is also impermanent, and that even your *apraṇihita* is impermanent.

The signless samādhi contemplates the quiescent extinction of nirvāṇa; subsequently, it gives rise to the signless-signless samādhi, which contemplates that the preceding signless samādhi is a non-enumerated extinction (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Your signless samādhi is also a non-enumerated extinction because it is devoid of the three marks, and thus it too is quiescent extinction.
For example, when a caṇḍāla burns a corpse, he holds a long pole in his hand and walks around its perimeter.
If anything falls into it, he should gather it together with this pole.
Knowing that it has been consumed, one likewise casts a long pole into the fire. The samādhi of emptiness is also like this:

one contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as empty; subsequently, one gives rise to the samādhi of the emptiness of emptiness and contemplates that even the samādhi of emptiness is empty. You, too, are empty.
The same applies to the teachings on wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and signlessness (*animitta*). Question:
How does one attain these samādhis?
Answer: Some say it is acquired at the edge of the path of seeing, like the conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) at the edge of the path of seeing.
Others say it is acquired when one becomes free from the desires of the desire realm, like the mind of transformation (nirmāṇacitta).
The commentary states:
It should be explained thus:
if one is to attain samādhi, when one is free from the desire for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the preparatory application (prayoga) manifests before one.
Question: After how many types of knowledge does this samādhi arise and manifest before one? Answer:

Fourth, regarding the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna), and knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna): taken collectively, they follow four knowledges;
as for the desire realm, they follow three knowledges—namely, the knowledge of phenomena, the knowledge of suffering, and the knowledge of cessation.

In the realms of form and formlessness, there are likewise three types of knowledge following [the path]: subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*).

If these belong to the desire realm, the three samādhis such as the "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) are subsumed under the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya-dhyāna*); they arise and manifest immediately after the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
The sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is subsumed under the sphere of nothingness; it arises and manifests immediately after the untainted path.
As for the others, they arise and manifest immediately after the untainted path of their own respective levels.
As for the realms, they exist within the three realms.
As for the stages, they exist within the eleven stages.
As for the supporting body, it relies upon a body belonging to the desire realm.

Regarding the practitioner, there are two modes of practice for emptiness (*śūnyatā*), while for the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) there is only one mode, which is exclusively the practice of emptiness. Question:
For what reason does emptiness have two modes of practice, whereas the emptiness of emptiness has only one?
Answer: Because it arises subsequent to the practice of emptiness and the emptiness-samādhi.
Furthermore, this practice is contrary to existence and is able to relinquish birth and death.
This root of goodness is able to perceive even the untainted as a fault; how much more so, then, saṃsāra?
Question: For what reason does it not practice the contemplation of non-self?
The answer is:
If one perceives that all phenomena are without self but does not perceive emptiness, although one may feel weary of and seek to leave saṃsāra, the mind will not be victorious.
If one perceives that all phenomena are empty, then the mind that feels weary of and seeks to leave saṃsāra will be victorious.
Just as a person walking alone on a road does not feel great distress, yet feels great distress when parting from a companion, so it is with this case as well.
The practice of wishlessness involves ten practices, whereas the practice of the wishlessness of wishlessness involves only the practice of impermanence. Question:
Why does the practice of wishlessness involve ten practices, while the practice of the wishlessness of wishlessness involves only the practice of impermanence?
Answer: Because it arises subsequent to the practice of impermanence and the practice of wishlessness.
Furthermore, this practice is contrary to existence (*bhava*) and is able to relinquish birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
This root of goodness is able to perceive even the untainted path as a source of suffering; how much more so, then, the cycle of birth and death.
Why, then, does one not practice asceticism?
The answer is:
One does not practice such conduct while failing to contemplate the Path.
Why, then, do you not practice the cultivation of such conduct?
The answer is:
If one practices the contemplation of formations such as arising and so forth, one is then observing the Noble Path, because this is a dharma characterized by continuity.
Why does one not practice the four modes of contemplation beginning with the path?
The answer is:
If one practices the path and so forth, it is then appropriate for the noble path and is not termed a fault.
The four modes of signless practice are the signless, the signless-signless, and the practice of cessation.
Question: For what reason does the practice of signlessness involve the four practices, while the practice of the signlessness-of-signlessness involves only the practice of cessation? Answer:
Because [the practice] exists within the movement of practicing signlessness (*animitta*) and arises subsequently.
Question: For what reason does one not practice the path of cessation (*nirodha*)?

Answer: There are two kinds of cessation: analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation through impermanence (*anityatā-nirodha*). It is not known for which kind of cessation [the text] refers.
For what reason, then, would one not practice sublime conduct?
Answer: The *Prakaraṇa* states: "What is the sublime Dharma?"
The untainted (anāsrava) and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) dharmas:
those are dharmas within that [state], and for this reason one does not practice sublime conduct (sucarita). Question:
Why does one not practice the practice of detachment?
The answer is given in the *Prakaraṇa*: [it says:]...

What is the dharma that is dissociated? The answer is: wholesome precepts bound to the desire realm; wholesome meditative absorptions of renunciation belonging to the form and formless realms; the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); and analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Among these, there is no single object of perception for them, namely: emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*).
Some say it takes as its object the final moment of the Noble Path;
some say it takes as its object the five aggregates co-arising with that final moment of the Noble Path;
others say it takes as its object the Noble Path throughout one's entire life.
Some say that the noble path of a single lifetime is associated with the five aggregates;

the object of "signless-signless" is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). As for the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this refers to the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
"Knowledge" (jñāna) is associated with conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
"Concentration" (samādhi) is concentration itself.
"Faculties" (indriya), taken collectively, are associated with three faculties.
The "world" (*loka*) refers to the three periods of time.
That which takes the world as its object consists of emptiness-of-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness (*apraṇihitāpraṇihita*).

If one were to say that it takes the final moment of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) as its object: those [moments] in the past and present take the past and future as their objects; the first [moment] about to arise takes the present as its object; and the remaining future moments take all three periods of time as their objects.

If one were to say this: regarding the noble path that takes a single lifetime as its object, both the emptiness-of-emptiness and the wishlessness-of-wishlessness take the three periods of time as their objects, whereas the signlessness-of-signlessness takes what is non-temporal as its object.
Regarding the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the indeterminate: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object;
the unwholesome and the indeterminate take emptiness-emptiness and wishlessness-wishlessness as their objects for the wholesome, while signlessness-signlessness takes the indeterminate as its object.
"Bondage" refers to bondage within the three realms.
That which takes as its object both what is bound to the three realms and what is not bound takes as its object that which is not bound.
Regarding those that are "in training," "beyond training," or "neither in training nor beyond training": these are [the category of] neither in training nor beyond training.

Regarding those conditioned by the trainee, the non-trainee, and that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee: emptiness-emptiness and wishlessness-wishlessness are conditioned by the non-trainee; signlessness-signlessness is conditioned by that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee.
Regarding those [factors] abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned: these are abandoned by the path of cultivation.
Regarding those that take as their object what is abandoned by the path of seeing, abandoned by the path of cultivation, or not abandoned: they take as their object what is not abandoned.
To take names as conditions and meanings as conditions is to take meanings as conditions.

To take one's own body, another's body, and that which is not the body as conditions: emptiness-emptiness takes one's own body as its condition; wishlessness-wishlessness takes that which is not the body as its condition; and signlessness-signlessness takes that which is not the body as its condition.
Question: From where does this samādhi arise? Answer:

Regarding those who arise in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) rather than the form or formless realms: this occurs within the human destiny (*manuṣyagati*) and not in other destinies; among humans, it occurs in the three continents and not in Uttarakuru; and it is possible for both those relying on a male body and those relying on a female body.
Ghoṣavarman spoke thus: "It is only in Jambudvīpa and not in other regions; it relies on a male body and not a female body. Why is this so?"
These roots of goodness rely upon a firm and strong body; the female body is inferior and weak.
Evaluation: As stated previously, this is correct.
Why is this so? Because men attain mastery over their minds and mastery over meditative concentration, and women likewise attain mastery over their minds and mastery over meditative concentration.
Regarding whether one is a person in training or a person beyond training, such a person is one beyond training.
Regarding whether one is liberated by occasion or not liberated by occasion, such a person is one not liberated by occasion.
Why is this so? What kind of person is able to give rise to this meditative absorption?

It is one who possesses mastery over concentration and is liberated through faith with no afflictions within their body; it is not one who lacks mastery over concentration nor one who does not have no afflictions within their body.
One who has attained mastery over meditative concentration (samādhi) may still possess afflictions within their body;
one liberated by time (samayavimukta), though free from afflictions within the body, does not attain mastery over meditative concentration.
In the body of one liberated at non-specific times, there are no afflictions, and one has attained mastery over meditative concentration. Question: What is this samādhi?
Is it the first moment, or is it the subsequent continuity?
If it is the first, what is the purpose of the others?
If it is the subsequent continuity, how can this be reconciled with what is taught regarding the collection of consciousnesses (*vijñānakāya*)?
As it is said:

Is there any phenomenon that is conventional, with outflows, comprised within the aggregates of grasping, arising from within, produced by wisdom, wholesome, bound to the desire realm, arising immediately after the noble path, taking the uncontaminated as its object, and is an uncommon dharma shared only by noble ones and not by ordinary persons?
Answer: There are;
namely, the emptiness-of-emptiness, the wishlessness-of-wishlessness, and the signlessness-of-signlessness bound to the desire realm. Answer:
One should say: it is the first moment. Question:
If that is so, what are the subsequent moments?
The answer is:
they are similar to those roots of goodness.
Furthermore, there are those who say that the entire continuum is [the person].
A question is asked:
If this were so, how would one reconcile what is stated in the *Vijñānakāya*?

Answer: The first [type] takes the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as its object through the sequence of the Noble Path; the others, although not following the sequence of the Noble Path, also take the uncontaminated as their object. Question:
At what time does this samādhi manifest?
The answer is:
at the time of parinirvāṇa.

When an Arhat desires to enter parinirvāṇa, having emerged from the Noble Path, he brings this samādhi into manifestation; having emerged from this samādhi, he immediately enters parinirvāṇa, never again arising, and never again arising in the Noble Path.
The commentary states:
It should be explained thus:
having attained this samādhi, whenever one wishes to employ it, it immediately arises and manifests before one.
Question: After the Noble Path has arisen, this samādhi manifests; does the Noble Path arise again and manifest after this samādhi? Answer:
Some say that it does not arise.
Why is this? Because this samādhi harbors aversion toward the Noble Path.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the mind] can arise.
It is asked:
If it can arise, how can it be called "hating the Noble Path"?
The answer is:
Although this samādhi may indeed loathe the Noble Path, it does not loathe it as the Noble Path loathes it.
Even after the Noble Path has arisen, one may still give rise to a tainted (sāsrava) mind; how much more so would one not give rise to an untainted (anāsrava) mind after this concentration?
However, while the noble path arises in succession to this meditative absorption, this absorption does not arise in succession to the untainted (anāsrava) mind;
thus, this absorption is exclusively tainted (sāsrava). Question: Why is this absorption exclusively tainted?
Answer: Because they have not severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Question:
For what reason does the Noble One cultivate this concentration?
The answer is:
it is cultivated for four reasons; first, because he desires to dwell in the happiness of the present life.
Second, because they desire to sport;
third, because they desire to observe their original deeds;
fourth, because they desire to enjoy the noble Dharma.
Furthermore, this concentration is a supreme dharma because the noble ones desire to dwell within it.
*Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Chapter on the Eightfold Path, First: The Buddha said: "A practitioner in training (*śaikṣa*) accomplishes eight paths of training (*śaikṣamārga*).
An Arhat whose taints are exhausted (*kṣīṇāsrava*) and whose holy life is established accomplishes ten paths of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*)."
Regarding the eight types of training paths for a trainee (*śaikṣa*), how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?

Regarding the ten types of non-training paths (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) of an Arhat whose taints are exhausted and whose holy life is established, how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Regarding this chapter and the explanation of its meaning, the *upadeśa* (instructional treatise) should be explained here in detail. Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?

Answer: This is to stop the foolish talk within the world that claims there is no accomplishment of the past and future lives, and to counter the view that asserts the present life is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma. It also clarifies that the formations (*saṃskāra*) of the past and future are accomplished as truly existent dharmas; for if the formations of the past and future were not truly existent, then there would be neither the accomplishment nor the non-accomplishment of those past and future formations.

Just as there can be no such thing as a second head, a third hand, a sixth sense-faculty (*āyatana*), or a thirteenth base (*āyatana*)— neither their accomplishment nor non-accomplishment being possible—
yet because past and future formations (*saṃskāra*) are accomplished, one knows that past and future formations are substantially existent dharmas.
Furthermore, there is another explanation for why this treatise was composed: some claim that "possession" (*prāpti*) is not a substantially existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*).
For instance, the Dārṣṭāntika Venerable Buddhadeva stated:
"Possession has no essence; it is not a substantially existent phenomenon."
Why is this so? If sentient beings do not depart from those phenomena, it is called "accomplishment.
However, that which is not departed from is a conceptual, relative, and composite phenomenon, lacking any substantial reality.
Just as five fingers gathered together are called a "fist," whereas when scattered they are not a fist;
so too, if sentient beings do not depart from those dharmas, it is called "accomplishment," but if they depart from those dharmas, it is not called accomplishment.
Question: For what reason does he speak in this way? Answer:
He relies upon the Buddhist sūtras.
The sūtras state that a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) possesses seven treasures.
Does he thereby accomplish the qualities of another's body and the qualities not included among sentient beings?
If a Wheel-Turning King were to possess the Wheel Jewel and the Divine Jewel, he would destroy the essence of the Dharma.
Why is this? Because they are both included within the category of sentient beings and yet are not included within the category of sentient beings.
If one possesses the elephant-treasure and the horse-treasure, then the realms of rebirth are destroyed. Why is this?
Because they belong both to the human realm and to the animal realm.
If one possesses the Jewel of the Woman, it will destroy the body. Why is this?
Because it is both a male body and a female body.
If one achieves the status of a minister of the treasury or a minister of the military, then karma is destroyed. Why is this?
Because such a person is both noble and base.
In order to prevent such an error, it is said that the "established" (siddha) lacks substantial reality.
Furthermore, to stop the intention of those who speak thus, it is also clarified that the "established" does possess substantial reality.
If it were established that there is no substantial entity, it would contradict this sutra.
As it is said:

"The seeker (śaikṣa) accomplishes the eightfold path of training; the Arhat with outflows exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava), whose holy life is established, accomplishes the tenfold path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa)."

When an Ārya brings a tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*) into manifestation, he possesses [that mind] of the past, future, and present; however, because he lacks the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), he does not possess it [in that state].
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras, such as the one which says:
"This person possesses wholesome dharmas, and also possesses unwholesome and neutral dharmas."
When wholesome dharmas manifest, one should not be possessed of unwholesome or neutral dharmas;
when unwholesome dharmas manifest, one should not be possessed of wholesome or neutral dharmas.
When an indeterminate dharma is present, one would then be separated from wholesome and unwholesome dharmas and thus should not be said to possess them.
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras, which state:
"A bhikṣu who possesses seven dharmas dwells much in joy and happiness in the present life; if he applies skillful means, he will certainly be able to exhaust the outflows."
There is no bhikṣu who accomplishes all seven dharmas; if among these seven dharmas even one single dharma arises and becomes manifest, he then accomplishes that one dharma.
If any other dharma arises and becomes manifest, he does not accomplish [any of] the seven dharmas.
Furthermore, this contradicts other sūtras, which state:
"The Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers.

There is no one who is a Tathāgata who is not endowed with the ten powers; whether he is endowed with even a single power or not, when the Tathāgata brings forth each individual power from among the ten so that it manifests before him, he is then said to be endowed with that particular power.
Why is this so? Because within a single moment, two types of wisdom cannot manifest simultaneously, much less many.
If other dharmas arise and manifest, then [the power] is not accomplished.

Furthermore, there is another fault: one could say that an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is free from the fetters of the three realms, and one could say that a person free from the fetters of the three realms is an ordinary person.

Regarding the claim that an ordinary person is free from the fetters of the three realms: when an ordinary person’s wholesome or non-obscured neutral mind is present, they do not possess the past, future, or present fetters of the three realms; thus, they would have to be a person who has abandoned desire for the three realms.

If one who has abandoned desire for the three realms were an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), then at the time when an Arhat brings forth wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) or non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds, they would not possess past, future, or present uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas; and because they would not possess uncontaminated dharmas, they ought to be an ordinary person.
In order to prevent such faults, it is said that "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is a truly existent phenomenon (*dravyasat*). Question:
If accomplishment is a truly existent phenomenon, how do you explain the sūtra cited by the Dārṣṭāntikas?
Answer: Because a wheel-turning monarch obtains sovereign mastery over the seven treasures as he desires, the World-Honored One says they are "accomplished.

Furthermore, some say that the reason this treatise was composed is that some explain accomplishment (*samanvāgama*) as a truly existent dharma (*dravyasat*), while non-accomplishment (*asamanvāgama*) is not a truly existent dharma.
To stop such proponents from speaking thus, it is also clarified that what is not established is not a truly existent phenomenon.
If that which is not established is not truly existent, then establishment itself is also not truly existent.

Why is this so? Because accomplishment is designated based on non-accomplishment; it is just as there is darkness because of light, day because of night, and heat because of cold—likewise, accomplishment exists because of non-accomplishment.
Furthermore, non-attainment and attainment are two dharmas that are closely related as opposites.
Just as greed and non-greed, hatred and non-hatred, and delusion and non-delusion are two dharmas that are closely related as opposites, so too are these two.
Furthermore, if that which lacks substantial reality were not established, then there would be no provision for the dharma that severs the afflictions. Why is this so?
When the Noble Path arises, it severs the afflictions; it is not like grinding incense with a stone.
Because one attains the abandonment of afflictions and the realization of liberation at the moment the Noble Path arises, it is called "the abandonment of afflictions.
Furthermore, there is another explanation for why this treatise was composed: some say that the Noble Path is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), as the Vībhāṣā-vādins state:
"The Noble Path is an unconditioned dharma."
He speaks thus:
"The path to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is a single, eternally abiding dharma; whenever Buddhas appear in the world, they all fully awaken to this path."
For example, it is like a magnificent carriage of elephants and horses that many people ride in succession; although the individuals differ, the carriage remains one and the same.
In this way, the path of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is a single, eternal reality. All Buddhas who appear in the world awaken to this very path; though the Buddhas differ, their path is eternally one.
Question: For what reason did he speak in such a manner? Answer:
Based on the Buddhist sūtras,
the sūtras state:
"I have attained the ancient path previously realized by the seers of the past."
Because the Buddha taught that this path is an ancient dharma, he said it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
To refute those who speak in such a manner, he also clarifies that the path exists within the world.
If the Way were in the world, it would necessarily be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Why is this so?
Because there is no unconditioned dharma that exists within the world.
If one were to claim that the Path is an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*), it would contradict this sutra.
As it is said:
The upāsikā Viśākhā went to the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinna and asked her as follows:
"Is the Path conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
He replied: "Upāsikā Viśākhā!"
The Path is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), not unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Question:
If the Path is conditioned and not unconditioned, how do you reconcile this with the sūtra spoken by the Vibhajyavādins?
Answer: It is called the "ancient path" because five factors are identical.
First, they are identical in terms of skillful means (*upāya*).
2. By sameness of ground;
3. by sameness of practice;
4. by sameness of objective sphere.
Fifth, by the sameness of what is performed.
Regarding the sameness of skillful means: just as one Buddha fulfills the six pāramitās over three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, so it is for all Buddhas.
Regarding the identity of stage: their path is entirely contained within the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
Regarding the identity of practice: they fully practice the sixteen aspects.
Regarding the identity of object: they all take the four noble truths as their cognitive objects.
Regarding "those whose actions are the same": just as one Buddha extinguishes afflictions through the Way, so it is for all Buddhas.
This principle should be applied to that sūtra.
If one does not rely on the underlying meaning but takes the literal words as they appear in the sūtra, then it is as stated within this very sūtra.
I have passed through old cities and old villages; are these cities and villages unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas?
Although one speaks of them as "old" cities and villages, they are not unconditioned.
The Way is also like this: although one speaks of an "old path," it is not unconditioned.
As it is said in verse:
"If desire is severed without remainder, Like a lotus flower amidst the water;
A bhikṣu detached from both this and that, Is like a snake shedding its old skin."
"Is a snake's slough an unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)?
Although such a snake's slough is said to be 'old,' it is not unconditioned.
The Way (*mārga*) is likewise."

Therefore, in order to refute the positions of others, to manifest one's own position, and also to explain the meaning that accords with the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), this treatise is composed.
As for the "eightfold," it refers to right view up to right concentration.
Regarding "accomplishment," one asks:
Who accomplishes? Is it the accomplishment of the Dharma, or the accomplishment of the person?
If phenomena are accomplished, then all phenomena are without desire; how, then, can they be accomplished?
If a person accomplishes them, that person cannot be found within the ultimate meaning.
If there were no person, how could [these] be accomplished?
The answer is:
one should state it thus:
One accomplishes what is neither dharma nor non-human.
Within the ultimate reality (paramārtha), there is accomplishment and non-accomplishment, yet there is no one who accomplishes or does not accomplish.
Within the ultimate reality, there is bondage and liberation, yet there is neither one who is bound nor one who is liberated.
There are afflictions and there is the way out of them, yet there is neither affliction nor one who goes out;
there is birth and there is death, yet there is neither birth nor one who dies;
there is karma and there is the retribution of karma, yet there is neither one who performs karma nor one who receives its retribution.
There is the Path and the fruit of the Path, yet there is no one who cultivates the Path or realizes the fruit of the Path.
Within the ultimate sense (*tattvārtha*), there is accomplishment and non-accomplishment, yet there is no one who accomplishes or fails to accomplish.
Some say that the dharmas are accomplished. He asks:
If that is so, when the eye-base is accomplished, are the eleven bases also accomplished, and are the eleven bases also accomplished when the eye-base is accomplished?
Answer: If one were to say that the eye-base (cakṣur-āyatana) accomplishes the eleven bases, and the eleven bases accomplish the eye-base, there would be no fault.
Critique: [This is not so].
One should say this: there is the accomplishment of that which is neither *dharma* nor *pudgala*.
However, when the four or five aggregates arise, there is such a similar acquisition (*prāpti*) that it is termed "accomplishment" or "non-accomplishment."
The Venerable Revata said:
All phenomena are devoid of desire.
Within phenomena that are devoid of desire, what is there to be accomplished or not accomplished?
Question: If that is so, how are the Buddhist scriptures to be reconciled?
For example, it is said:
"This person accomplishes both wholesome and unwholesome dharmas.
Answer: "This is merely the Tathāgata’s conventional discourse according to worldly usage; it possesses no ultimate reality."
Question: What is the meaning of "accomplishment" (*siddhi*)?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra replied:
The meaning of non-interruption is the meaning of accomplishment. Question:
If that is so, then do ordinary persons bound by all fetters accomplish everything because they do not interrupt any phenomena?
Answer: No. Because those dharmas cannot be apprehended.
Furthermore, the meaning of "not abandoning" is the meaning of "accomplishing. Question:
If that is so, when a trainee (śaikṣa) does not abandon the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), does he accomplish those dharmas?
He replied:
"No, because those dharmas have not been attained.
The Venerable Buddhadeva said:
The meaning of "attaining without losing" is the meaning of "accomplishment.
If one attains those dharmas and does not lose them, this is called accomplishment. Question:
Why is one called a "learner" (śaikṣa)?
Is one called a learner because they study the dharmas,
or is one called a learner because they have attained the dharmas of a learner?
If one who trains in the factors of training is themselves a trainee (*śaikṣa*), how is the statement in the *Samyukta-āgama* (or *Vibhaṅga*) to be reconciled? As it says:
"The trainee abides in his own nature."
If one who has attained the Dharma of training were merely a learner (*śaikṣa*), how would the Buddhist sūtras be interpreted?
As it is said:
The Buddha addressed Śivaka:
One is called "in training" (śaikṣa) because one trains in the dharmas of training.
The answer is: it should be stated thus:
One is called a "learner" (śaikṣa) because one studies the dharmas of learning. Question:
If that is so, then one has thoroughly mastered the Buddha’s sūtras.
How is what is taught in the *Samādhivarga* to be reconciled?
The answer is:
therein it is said that one is called a "learner" (*śaikṣa*) because they have attained the dharmas of a learner.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one is called a "learner" (śaikṣa) because they have attained the dharmas of a learner.
A question is asked:
If this were so, what would be the explanation for the *Sūtra* while the exposition in the *Samādhivarga* (Chapter on Concentration) is already well-justified?
The answer is:
The Buddhist sūtras state that one does not abandon the aspirational mind nor does one abandon skillful means.
If a practitioner dwells in a wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral state of mind, yet does not abandon the mind directed toward nirvāṇa, they are therefore called a "learner" (śaikṣa).
It is like a person resting by the side of a road who is asked by another,
"Where do you intend to go?
and that person replies:
Suppose a person intends to go in a certain direction;
because they have not abandoned the intention to depart, they are said to be "going" even while remaining stationary. It is the same with that [mind].
Regarding the "tracks of training" (*śaikṣa-pada*): A question is asked:

Since the tracks of no-more-training (*aśaikṣa-pada*) are more luminous, pure, and sublime than the tracks of training, why is it that only the tracks of training are mentioned, and not the tracks of no-more-training?
Answer: When something that ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that this explanation is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).

Furthermore, while this explanation begins with those who have first entered the Dharma, it has already stated what pertains to the learner (*śaikṣa*); it should also be understood as stating what pertains to the non-learner (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, because their respective activities differ:
those in training (śaikṣa) excel in the activity of the path of realization (mārga), while those beyond training (aśaikṣa) excel in the activity of liberation (vimukti).

Just as the actions of a king and his ministers differ from one another—the king excels in his deeds through his noble status and subduing power, while the minister excels in his deeds through wielding weapons and engaging in battle.
It is the same for that [learner].
Furthermore, the path of training (śaikṣamārga) is able to sever the afflictions (kleśa), just as weapons are able to defeat enemies, whereas the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) is not so.
Furthermore, the path of training is able to act as both the means for severing the afflictions and the actual severance of the afflictions, whereas the state of no-more-learning is not so.
Furthermore, the meaning of "repeated practice" is the meaning of "the path-traces" (*mārga-pada*). Because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) do not practice repeatedly, they are not called "traces.
When a person in training (*śaikṣa*) accomplishes the eight kinds of path-traces, how many are accomplished in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present?
Answer: It is if one relies on the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra.
The samādhi with vitarka and vicāra refers to the threshold concentration (anāgamya) and the first dhyāna.
Question: What is the basis (āśraya) in this context? Answer:
Some say that it is the basis because they arise simultaneously.
Others say that the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is the basis.
The critique states:
One should speak thus:
it is called "dependent" because this dharma arises based on those two stages.
There are four kinds of "initial":
1. The first moment of attaining right determination;
2. The first moment of attaining the fruit;
3. The first moment of transforming the faculties.
Fourth, the beginning of detachment from desire;
the beginning of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) refers to attaining right determination based on those two stages;
the beginning of attaining the fruit refers to first attaining the fruit of training (*śaikṣa-phala*) based on those two stages.

Regarding the first instance of the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*): based on those two stages, one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).

Regarding the first instance of the departure from desire (*vairāgya*): by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), one departs from desire, and based on those two stages, the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) first arises and becomes manifest.
In this context, the treatise is composed based on four types of initialities.
It explains that training occurs as the vision of the present manifests according to its characteristics. Question:
If a learner (śaikṣa) should give rise to a view that is neither of a learner nor of one beyond learning (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣa), why is it said that only the learner’s view of a learner manifests?
The answer is:
It should be stated as follows:
If the vision of one in training (śaikṣa-dṛṣṭi) manifests before them but is not mentioned [in that context],

it should be understood that a person in training necessarily gives rise to the vision of one in training, and does not give rise to a vision that is neither of one in training nor of one beyond training (naiva-śaikṣa-nāśaikṣa-dṛṣṭi).
As it has been said, when the various initial moments manifest, there is no past. Why is this?
Because not a single moment has yet undergone arising and ceasing.
If there is arising and ceasing, one abandons the eight future attainments due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties, and cultivates the eight present attainments.
If they have ceased and are not abandoned, that "ceasing" refers to impermanent cessation;
as for "not abandoning," the abandonment of the Noble Path is of three kinds:
First, the attainment of the fruit;
second, falling away;
third, the transformation of the faculties.
If one does not attain the fruit, does not regress, and does not transform the faculties, then having ceased in dependence upon that stage, it arises again and manifests before one.
Question: For what reason does it arise again and manifest after having ceased in dependence upon that stage?
The answer is:
The practitioner, relying on that stage, achieves victory in battle against the common afflictions and destroys the hostile enemies of the fetters;
because he remembers their kindness, they arise once more and manifest before him.

It is like a person who, having donned armor and grasped weapons to fight an enemy, and having achieved victory, subsequently—out of gratitude for that [victory]—frequently maintains and repairs his weapons and keeps them concealed so that they do not fall into ruin.
It is the same for that [concentration] as well. Furthermore, it manifests again due to four reasons:
first, because of the desire to experience happiness in the present life;
Second, because he desires to sport;
third, because he desires to observe what was previously done;
fourth, because he desires to enjoy the noble Dharma.
At the moment of the second *kṣaṇa* of training, eight [factors] are accomplished as past; these are those that arose and ceased in the preceding *kṣaṇa*.
Eight are accomplished as future; these are those cultivated in the future.
Eight factors are accomplished when the present [knowledge] is manifest before one;
that which has ceased is not abandoned.
If, relying on the concentration without applied thought and sustained thought (*avitarkāvicāra-samādhi*), the learner’s vision is manifest before one, eight factors are accomplished in the past.

Regarding those that arise and cease in the stage characterized by both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought): eight are accomplished in the future and are thus cultivated for the future;
seven are accomplished in the present and are thus present before one, with the exception of *samyagbodhi* (right awakening).
Why is this? Because there is no perfect enlightenment within the stages.
Once that [enlightenment] has ceased, it is not abandoned.

When one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the vision of training (*śaikṣa-darśana*) manifests, one accomplishes eight factors of the past—namely, those that arise and cease in stages characterized by both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*);
one accomplishes eight factors of the future—namely, those cultivated in the future;

and one accomplishes four factors of the present—excluding right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*), right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), right speech (*samyag-vāc*), right action (*samyak-karmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*), because these do not exist in that stage.
Once that has ceased, they are not abandoned.

If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or if a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) arises and becomes present, one accomplishes eight [factors] of the past—namely, those produced in stages with directed thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra-bhūmi*);
and one accomplishes eight [factors] of the future—namely, those cultivated for the future.
In the present, it does not exist.

If one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), at that time there is no mind; for only one who possesses a mind can cultivate the path. If a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) arises and manifests before one, that mind is with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Here, only the untainted paths (anāsrava-mārga) are discussed.
If one relies on the concentration without applied thought and without sustained thought (avitarka-avicāra-samādhi), this refers to the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Question: Why is the intermediate dhyāna not mentioned here? Answer:
That which should have been stated but was not stated, one should know that this explanation is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, because it has already been included within what will be stated later. Why is this so?
There are no other distinct types, as they are identical to the types of the second, third, and fourth dhyānas.
Regarding their meaning, it is as previously explained.
There are four kinds of the first [dhyāna], as previously explained.
When the training-insight (śaikṣa-darśana) manifests before one, it is as previously stated.
In the first moment, one does not possess the past [insight], as previously explained.
One possesses eight future [factors] and seven present [factors], as previously explained.
Once that has ceased, it is not abandoned, as previously explained. Furthermore,

when one relies on the samādhi without vitarka and without vicāra, and the vision of training manifests before them, at the second moment, seven factors are accomplished in the past— these being those produced by the stage of no-vitarka and no-vicāra—
and eight are accomplished in the future, with seven in the present, as previously explained.
Having ceased that [state], one does not abandon it;

relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the vision of training (*śaikṣa-darśana*) manifests before one. Seven [factors] are accomplished in the past—namely, those arising and ceasing in the stage without vitarka and without vicāra—and eight are accomplished in the future, while four are accomplished in the present, as previously explained.

Having ceased that [thought], he does not abandon it as he enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*). If he gives rise to a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*), it is as previously explained.
Having ceased that [mind], he does not abandon it.

Based on the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra, when the vision of training manifests, seven [factors] are accomplished in the past; for one born in a stage without vitarka and vicāra, eight are accomplished in the future and eight in the present, as previously explained.

If one relies on the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the names of these formless attainments are the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*), and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
"Relying" is as previously explained.
"Initial" refers to the four kinds of initial [states], as previously explained.
In this context, the discussion is based on the initial stage of detachment from desire, not the initial attainment of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). Why is this?
Because there is no one who attains right determination by relying on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
This is not the first attainment of the fruit.
Why is this? Because there is no one who attains the fruit of training (śaikṣaphala) by relying on the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamādhi).
This is not the initial stage of the transformation of faculties. Why is this?
Because there is no one who transforms the roots of training while relying on a formless absorption.

When one has abandoned the desires of the lower stages by means of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*) and subsequently, based on that stage, first brings the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) into presence, at the initial moment one possesses eight future and four present factors, as previously explained; there are none past.
Question: Just as mundane formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) do not arise without mundane dhyānas, and untainted (*anāsrava*) formless attainments do not arise without untainted dhyānas;

and just as mundane dhyāna is the gateway upon which mundane formless attainments depend as their preparatory means (*upāya*), and untainted dhyāna is the gateway upon which untainted formless attainments depend as their preparatory means—why is it said that there is no past [of these]?
Answer: Among the *mārgākāras*, some belong to the dhyāna stages and some belong to the formless (*ārūpya*) stages.
Although those belonging to the dhyāna stages have already arisen, those belonging to the formless stages have not yet arisen; therefore, there are none that are past.
"Cessation" refers to the cessation of impermanence.
"Not abandoning" means that there are three ways of abandoning the Noble Path, as previously explained.
Based on that stage, the arising and ceasing of the Noble Path arises again and manifests in the present.
Question: For what reason does the noble path that arises based on those stages (bhūmi) arise again and manifest in the present? Answer:
Because of the recollection of their kindness, the detailed explanation is as above.
In the second moment, four are accomplished in the past; these are those that arise and cease based on the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
Eight are accomplished in the future; these are those cultivated for the future.

Regarding the four factors that are accomplished in the present and arise as manifest in the present: these exclude right view, right speech, right action, and right livelihood, because they do not exist in that stage.
Once that has ceased, it is not abandoned.

If one enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or if a mundane mind (*laukikacitta*) arises and becomes manifest, four [factors] are accomplished in the past, eight are accomplished in the future, and none exist in the present, as previously explained.
When that has ceased, one does not abandon it.

Relying on the samādhi with applied thought and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), the vision of training manifests before one. Four are accomplished in the past; this is for those who give rise to cessation based on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Eight are accomplished in the future; this is for those who practice cultivation in the future.
"Eight [attainments] accomplish the present; these are those that give rise to the present.
Question: Can the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) successively give rise to the samādhi with directed thought and evaluation (savitarka-savicāra)?
Answer: No. This teaching explains the sequential order; it does not explain a fixed, absolute order.
This teaching speaks of conformity, not of fixed conformity.
Once that has ceased, it is not abandoned.

Based on the samādhi without vitarka and vicāra, when the vision of training manifests before one, four [factors] are accomplished in the past; this refers to those who give rise to cessation based on the formless attainments.
Question: Regarding the statement that there are eight past [factors] which depend on the samādhi with vitarka and vicāra for their arising and ceasing, why are only four mentioned? Answer:
In this context, all instances refer exclusively to the initial arising and ceasing.
Eight are accomplished in the future; these are those cultivated in the future.
Seven are accomplished in the present; these are those that arise in the present. This excludes Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), because it does not exist in those stages.
Question: What kind of trainees (śaikṣa) are being discussed here? Answer:
In this context, it is explained that one enters all meditative absorptions through a sequential process of training.

Just as one ascending a stone staircase does so step by step, one first enters the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*), next enters the concentration without directed thought and sustained evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*), next enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), next enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and finally arises with a conventional mind (*saṃvṛti-citta*) to speak.

If such a practitioner first enters the concentration with directed thought and sustained evaluation (*savitarka-savicāra-samādhi*), then enters the concentration without directed thought and sustained evaluation (*avitarka-avicāra-samādhi*), then enters the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), and finally enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), yet does not give rise to worldly thoughts nor speak [of these stages], such a practitioner is not so described.
The remainder is as explained in the *Prakīrṇaka-vastu* (Miscellaneous Chapter) regarding the person, in the parable of the twelve-limbed dependent origination and the beautiful woman.
There are four kinds of paths:
first, the path of suffering with sluggish wisdom;
2. The path of painful progress with swift wisdom;
3. The path of pleasant progress with slow wisdom;
4. The path of pleasant progress with swift wisdom.
Question: One should speak of a single path—namely, the path that exhausts suffering, the path that exhausts birth and death, and the path that exhausts old age and death.
Or one should speak of two paths: first, the path that exhausts form (*rūpa*), and second, the path that exhausts name (*nāman*).
One should speak of three paths: first, the path that exhausts the desire realm; second, the path that exhausts the form realm; and third, the path that exhausts the formless realm.
One should also speak of five paths, namely, the path that exhausts the form [aggregate], up to the path that exhausts the consciousness [aggregate].
One should speak of eleven paths, namely, the path for the exhaustion of old age and death, up to the path for the exhaustion of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*).
If considered either in terms of their presence within a continuum or in terms of individual moments (*kṣaṇa*), then there are immeasurable and boundless paths.
For what reason does the Blessed One extensively explain four paths within a single path, and briefly explain four paths within immeasurable and boundless paths?
How are these four paths established?
Answer: It is by way of three matters:
first, by way of the stage (bhūmi).
Second, by means of the faculties;
third, by means of the persons.
Taken together, they are summarized by these three matters.
This should be understood by way of two factors: either by way of the stage (*bhūmi*) and the faculty (*indriya*), or by way of the stage and the person (*pudgala*).

Regarding "by way of the stage and the faculty": the path practiced by a person of dull faculties based on the *anāgamya*, the intermediate (*dhyānāntara*), or the three formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) is called "painful progress with sluggish wisdom" (*duḥkhā pratipat dhandhābhijñā*).
Based on this very stage, the path practiced by those of sharp faculties is called the "path of swift wisdom through suffering.
Based on the fundamental dhyānas, the path practiced by those of dull faculties is called the "path of slow wisdom through ease."
Based on this very dhyāna, the path practiced by those of sharp faculties is called the "path of ease with swift wisdom.
This is what is meant by "by way of stage and by way of faculty.

As for "by way of stage and by way of person," the path practiced by those of firm faith, those liberated through faith, and those liberated by time—relying on the *anāgamya*, the intermediate dhyāna, and the three formless attainments—is called the "path of difficulty with sluggish wisdom."
Based on this very stage, the path practiced by those of steadfast dharma, those who have attained vision, and those liberated at any time is called the "path of swift wisdom and ease.
Based on the fundamental dhyānas, the path practiced by those of steadfast faith, those liberated through faith, and those liberated by time is called the "path of easy progress and slow wisdom."

Relying precisely upon this dhyāna, it is the path practiced by those who possess firmness in the Dharma, those who have attained vision, and those liberated at any time; this is called the path of ease with swift wisdom.
This is designated according to both the stage and the person.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 46 [and] Fascicle 47.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
*Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra*, Chapter Eight: The Section on the Eightfold Path (Part One). Question:
What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the four paths?

Answer: These are the natures of the five aggregates or four aggregates; if they exist in the stages of dhyāna, they are five aggregates, and if they exist in the formless absorptions (ārūpyasamādhi), they are four aggregates.
This is the essential nature of the four paths, characterized by the marks of self and the divisions of things.
Having already explained the nature and reason [of the path], we shall now explain why it is called the "path" (*mārga*).
What is the meaning of "path"?
To proceed toward the correct principle is the meaning of "path"; to proceed toward the city of Nirvāṇa is the meaning of "path."
Regarding the path of sluggish wisdom (*duḥkhā pratipad*): A question is asked:
"The untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is not a painful feeling (*duḥkhā vedanā*), nor is it associated with painful feeling; why then is it called 'painful'?
The answer is:

The paths of the peripheral formless realms are called suffering because they are difficult to generate, whereas the paths of the fundamental dhyānas are called happiness because they are easy to generate.
Why are the paths of the peripheral formless realms difficult to generate?
Answer: Because they are bound by the afflictions and karma of the desire realm, one must exert great effort to give rise to the *anāgamya* dhyāna.
It is like a person who, being bound, can only free themselves with great exertion; it is the same for that [attainment].

There are some who, by practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), are born in that realm; there are others who, by practicing mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*), are born in that realm.

Among those who practice the contemplation of impurity, some constantly contemplate white bones for ten years or twelve years; among them, some are able to be born in that realm, while others are not.

Regarding the practitioner of *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), if they constantly count the breaths for ten or twelve years, some may be able to be reborn in that stage, while others may not.
Having already become detached from sensual desire, one does not require much effort to cause the first dhyāna to manifest before one.

The factors of the first dhyāna differ: the various minds and mental concomitants cease, and other minds and mental concomitants arise. The coarse mind ceases and the subtle mind arises; the mind associated with *vitarka* (initial application) ceases, and the mind associated with *vicāra* (sustained application) arises.
It is like a person splitting wood with an axe; much effort must be exerted before it finally splits. The first dhyāna is likewise:

distinct mental states and their concomitants cease, and distinct mental states and their concomitants arise; coarse mind ceases, and subtle mind arises; mind accompanied by *vitarka* (applied thought) ceases, and mind accompanied by *vicāra* (sustained thought) arises.
Having already become free from desire for the first dhyāna, one brings the second dhyāna into manifestation without much effort.
The same applies to the third and fourth dhyānas. Question:

Having detached from the desire for the fourth dhyāna, one does not exert much effort to bring the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) into manifestation; why, then, are they called the "path of suffering"?
The answer is:
the formless attainments are subtle phenomena (*sūkṣma-dharma*).
There are some who claim that there is no formless absorption (*ārūpya-samādhi*). For example, the householder Tāpasa went to the Venerable Ānanda and asked him this question:
"Venerable Ānanda!"

I am a householder who has long delighted in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles; upon hearing it said that there are formless beings, my heart was struck with terror, as if I were standing on the brink of a great abyss.
Why is it said that sentient beings have no form?

Fundamental dhyāna is the path of bliss. It is like two people who both arrive at the same destination; one travels by waterway and the other by land. Although they both reach the same place, the one who traveled by waterway finds it pleasant, whereas the one who traveled by land does not.

It is the same for all sentient beings who become free from desire: whether they rely on the various peripheral formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) or on the fundamental dhyānas, although both achieve freedom from desire, the joy belongs to those relying on the dhyānas, not to those relying on the peripheral formless attainments.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bliss, and for this reason it is called "bliss": namely, the bliss of sensation (*vedanā-sukha*) and the bliss of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-sukha*).

In the third dhyāna, both the bliss of tranquility and the bliss of sensation are present; in the fourth dhyāna, although the bliss of sensation is absent, the bliss of tranquility is abundant, surpassing the two kinds of bliss found in the other stages.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of bliss, and for this reason it is called "bliss": namely, innate bliss (*paurāṇa-sukha*) and adventitious bliss (*āgantuka-sukha*).
Innate bliss refers to when one dwells in dhyāna and dhyāna arises and manifests before one.
Adventitious bliss refers to when one dwells in dhyāna and the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) arise and manifest before one.
Other teachers explain the characteristics of the bliss of dhyāna as they are extensively described above in the section on the four dhyānas.
Question: For what reason is it called "slow"?
Answer: Because one who has attained this path cannot reach the city of Nirvāṇa quickly, it is called "slow. Question:
Why is it called "swift"?
The answer is:
because by attaining this path, one can swiftly reach the city of Nirvana; therefore, it is called swift.

Question: If that which does not arrive quickly is called "slow" and that which arrives quickly is called "swift," then there are those liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who arrive more swiftly than those with vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*). If a person liberated through faith exerts diligent effort while a person with vision does not, then the one liberated through faith will arrive more swiftly than the one with vision.
As a verse says:
"Between the heedful and the heedless, between those who sleep and those who are awake, it is like swift and slow horses: the one who starts first arrives first."

"It is just as if two people were to travel to the same destination together: one riding a swift horse and the other riding a slow horse; although he rides the slow horse, because he set out first, he will arrive at his destination before the other."
Thus, the person liberated through faith who practices with diligent effort attains nirvana first;
the person attained through vision, because they do not practice with diligent effort, attains nirvana later.
Answer: Herein, it speaks of one who practices balanced diligence (*samyak-pradhāna*).
If one practices balanced diligence, the one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) arrives first.
Question: These four paths have the nature of the four aggregates or the five aggregates; for what reason are they called "wisdom"? Answer:
Although this path is by nature composed of four or five aggregates (*skandha*), it is called the "Path of Wisdom" (*prajñāmārga*) because wisdom is predominant therein.
It is just as the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), though it is by nature composed of five aggregates, is called the "Path of Seeing" because seeing is predominant therein.
The knowledge of the limits (*prāntakoṭika-jñāna*) has the nature of the five aggregates or four aggregates; it is called "knowledge" because knowledge predominates therein.
The diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) has the nature of the five aggregates or four aggregates; it is called "concentration" because concentration predominates therein.
The four paths are likewise of the nature of five aggregates or four aggregates; they are called the "path of wisdom" because wisdom is predominant therein.
What is the path of slow progress with wisdom?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
The bhikṣu who feels revulsion toward the five aggregates of clinging—this is called the path of sluggish wisdom regarding suffering. Question:
This path takes the four noble truths as its object; why then did the Blessed One speak only of it taking the truth of suffering as its object?

Answer: One should explain that when it is said that [the teaching] takes the Four Noble Truths as its object but does not explicitly state so, one should know that this statement is incomplete (*sāvasesa*).

Furthermore, since this teaching was initially introduced for those entering the Dharma by explaining the taking of the Truth of Suffering as its object, one should know that it also explains the taking of the other Truths as objects.
Furthermore, the Buddhist sūtras speak of the four paths of skillful means (*upāya*), but do not speak of the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the four paths.
Within these paths of skillful means, one performs such contemplations of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇā*) regarding the arising of phenomena (*saṃudaya-dharma*).
The Sūtra further states:
"What is the path of sluggish wisdom?
The answer is:"
This refers to the dull five faculties (pañcendriya) not subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas.
What is the path of swift wisdom regarding suffering?
The answer is:
This refers to the five faculties that are sharp but not included within the fundamental dhyānas.
What is the path of pleasant progress with slow wisdom?
The answer is:
This refers to the dull five faculties (pañcendriya) subsumed under the fundamental dhyānas (mauladhyāna).
What is the path of joy and swift wisdom?
The answer is:
This refers to the five faculties (indriya) that are beneficial and subsumed within the fundamental dhyānas. Question:
Since this path has the nature of either the five aggregates (skandha) or the four aggregates, why is it described only as these faculties?
Answer: Herein, that which is most excellent is taught; the nature of the five faculties is skillful means, for they are able to accomplish great matters. Question:
Is there such a thing as one of medium capacity? If there is, why is it not mentioned here?
If there is not, how can this be reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
As it is said:
"All sentient beings are born according to the world and grow according to the world; among them there are those of inferior faculties, those of middling faculties, and those of superior faculties."
Regarding those of superior faculties, their afflictions are subtle and thin, making them easy to transform; yet, if they do not hear the Dharma, they will fall away and lose their roots of goodness.
The answer is:
one should speak thus:
There is no such thing as a person of middling faculties. Why is this?
Because there are two kinds of seeing the path (darśanamārga):
First, the path of firm faith; second, the path of firm Dharma.
Within the path of cultivation, there are also two types:
first, the path of liberation through faith; second, the path of vision.
Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), there are also two types:
first, the path of occasional liberation (*samayavimuktimārga*); second, the path of non-occasional liberation (*asamayavimuktimārga*).
Because there is no third path, there is no one of intermediate faculty (*madhyendriya*).
Question: If this is so, how are the Buddhist sūtras to be reconciled? Answer:
Among those who undergo transformation and perceive the Noble Truths, some do so at the beginning, some in the middle, and some at the end.
Those at the beginning are called those of sharp faculties; those in the middle are called those of medium faculties; and those at the end are called those of dull faculties.

Furthermore, among those who receive transformation and perceive the Noble Truths, there are those who are near, those who are distant, and those who are neither near nor distant. Those who are "near" possess sharp faculties, such as Kauṇḍinya and others;
those who are "distant" possess dull faculties, such as Subhadra and others;
and those who are "neither near nor distant" possess middling faculties, such as Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and others.
Furthermore, there are those who say that there are individuals of middling faculties. Question: Why are these not mentioned here?
Answer: This has already been explained within what was previously stated.
When the inferior faculty is discussed, the middling faculty is included within the superior faculty.
When the superior faculty is being discussed, the intermediate faculty is included within the inferior faculty.
For this reason, the Venerable Ghoṣaka made this statement:
"Where does the intermediate faculty reside?"
Answer: It is within the lower [category]. Why is this so?
That which is superior among the middle is called "middle.
Furthermore, it is situated above the middle. Why is this so?
That which is inferior, middling, or superior is called "middle.
Furthermore, both are present within the two [categories].
The critique states:
It is well said thus. Why is this?
The Buddha is one whose nature is firm;
