If one attains a wholesome mind of the formless realm while not yet being free from desire for the form realm, one possesses the defiled wisdom abandoned through the path of cultivation in the form and formless realms, the wholesome wisdom of view in the form and formless realms, the non-obscured neutral wisdom of the desire and form realms, and the untainted wisdom of view.

Having already become detached from the desire realm of form, one accomplishes the defiled wisdom abandoned through the path of cultivation in the formless realm, the wholesome wisdom of seeing in the realms of form and formlessness, the non-obscured neutral wisdom in the realms of desire and form, and the untainted wisdom of seeing.

An Arhat born in the realm of form (rūpadhātu) possesses wholesome vision and wisdom pertaining to the realms of form and formlessness, non-obscured neutral vision and wisdom pertaining to the realms of desire and form, and untainted vision and wisdom.

For one born in the formless realm who is an Anāgāmin, the retributive mind does not manifest; yet they possess the defiled wisdom abandoned through the path of cultivation in the formless realm, as well as the wisdom of right view and the untainted wisdom of vision.
If a resultant mind (*vipākacitta*) manifests, one accomplishes non-obscured neutral wisdom (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-prajñā*).
The remainder is as previously explained.

For an Arhat born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), a resultant mind does not manifest; rather, they accomplish the wholesome formless-realm seeing-wisdom (*ārūpya-kuśala-darśana-prajñā*) and untainted seeing-wisdom (*anāsrava-darśana-prajñā*).
If a mind of retribution manifests, one accomplishes non-obscured neutral wisdom.
The rest is as previously explained.
If it is abandoned by seeing, is that wisdom also abandoned?
Answer: It is so.
If it is abandoned by wisdom, is it also abandoned by vision?
Answer: It is so.
If it is abandoned through vision, is it also abandoned by wisdom?
Answer: It is so.
If it is abandoned by wisdom, is it also abandoned by vision?
Answer: It is so.
If it is abandoned by wisdom (*jñāna*), is it also abandoned by insight (*prajñā*)?
Answer: It is so.
If it is abandoned by wisdom (*prajñā*), is it also abandoned by knowledge (*jñāna*)?
Answer: It is so.
Who is it that cuts off views through wisdom?
Answer: This refers to an Arhat.

Regarding those who have abandoned [defilements] to a greater or lesser extent: an Anāgāmin who has already detached from the desire of the sphere of nothingness has abandoned the wisdom of insight that abandons the defilements of the three realms to be eliminated by the path of seeing, as well as those of the eight stages to be eliminated by the path of cultivation.

Up to and including the Anāgāmin who has not yet abandoned the desires of the first dhyāna, there is the wisdom of insight that abandons the desires of the three realms to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
For the Srotāpanna and Sakṛdāgāmin, there is the wisdom of insight that abandons the views of the three realms to be abandoned through the path of seeing.

For one who possesses firm faith and firm realization of the Dharma, when the knowledge of suffering has arisen but the knowledge of origin has not yet arisen, they abandon the wisdom of views to be abandoned by seeing suffering within the three realms;

continuing in this manner until the knowledge of cessation has arisen but the knowledge of the path has not yet been reached, they abandon the wisdom of views to be abandoned by seeing suffering, origin, and cessation within the three realms.

An ordinary person who is detached from the desire for the sphere of nothingness possesses the wisdom that perceives the [defilements] to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation belonging to the eight stages;

likewise, an ordinary person who is detached from the desires of the desire realm possesses the wisdom that perceives the [defilements] to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation belonging to one stage.
Are all right views the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena? Question:
For what purpose is this treatise composed?
Answer: The preceding treatise is the fundamental basis for this treatise.
The preceding work made this statement:
What is view? What is knowledge? What is wisdom?
Yet he does not state: "Are all right views the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of phenomena?
This is because what was previously stated constitutes the fundamental basis of this treatise; it is now composed in order to provide a detailed exposition thereof.
Within this Abhidharma, there is this definitive characteristic:
if the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) are taught after the factors of the path (mārgāṅga), one should know that the factors of the path are exclusively untainted (anāsrava);
if the factors of the path are taught after the factors of enlightenment, one should know that the factors of the path are both tainted (sāsrava) and untainted.

Since the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are taught after the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) herein, it should be understood that the factors of the path are both with outflows (*sāsrava*) and without outflows (*anāsrava*).

Alternatively, there may be right view that is not the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-sambodhyaṅga*), and so forth; one should construct the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) in detail.
That which is right view but not the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena refers to mundane right view. Why is this so?
Because the factors of enlightenment are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*).

That which is the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) but is not right view is the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna). Why is this so?
Because they lack the characteristic of viewing.

That which is right view and is also the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena refers to all other untainted wisdoms (*anāsravaprajñā*) apart from the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). What, then, is that?
This refers to the various patiences (kṣānti) within the path of seeing, the eight knowledges of the learner (śaikṣa), and the right view of the adept (aśaikṣa).
Why is this so? Because they possess the characteristic of seeing and the characteristic of awakening.
That which is neither right view nor the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena consists of all things except those mentioned above.

Regarding those factors that have already been established by name and designated, they constitute the first, second, and third phrases; regarding those that have not yet been established by name or designated, they constitute the fourth phrase.
What is this? It refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) as expressed in these four propositions:

the wholesome wisdom of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), whether with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), constitutes the first three propositions; the remaining formations associated (*saṃprayukta*) or dissociated (*viprayukta*) with the mind constitute the fourth proposition; and the remaining four aggregates (*skandha*) along with unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) also constitute the fourth proposition. This is called "excluding the aforementioned matters."
Are all correct knowledges (*samyagjñāna*) the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
Some correct knowledges are not the factor of enlightenment consisting in the investigation of phenomena; thus, one should elaborate the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) in full.
That which is right knowledge but not the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena refers to conventional right knowledge. Why is this?
Because it lacks the characteristics of an awakening factor.

As for the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) that is not right knowledge (samyagjñāna), it refers to the eight patiences (kṣānti) within the path of seeing (darśanamārga). Why is this so?
Because they lack the characteristic of knowledge.

That which is both right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and the factor of awakening consisting in the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasaṃbodhyaṅga*) is, with the exception of the various patiences (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), all other untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*). What is that?
The eight knowledges of those in training and those beyond training: why is this so?
Because they possess the characteristics of knowledge and the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment.

Regarding that which is neither right knowledge nor the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena: excluding the aforementioned matters as previously explained, the difference here is that it includes all wholesome wisdom belonging to the mental consciousness level (*manobhūmi*) and the five sensory consciousness levels (*pañcavijñānakāyabhūmi*), whether they are with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*).
Question: Why are the other factors of enlightenment not questioned? Answer:
One should also ask this question:
"Is right effort the factor of enlightenment of energy?
The answer is:
If the factor of enlightenment of energy is also right effort, is there any right effort that is not the factor of enlightenment of energy? Answer: Yes.
There is; it is mundane right effort (*laukika-samyak-pradhāna*).
The remaining factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) should also be questioned in this same way.
What is the intention behind not questioning them?
Answer: One should know that what has been stated here and there is incomplete.
Furthermore, regarding the mention of "beginning" and "end" herein: the beginning is right view, and the end is right knowledge.
Just as it was when first entering, so it is for the exit, the preparatory means (*upāya*), and the ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā*).

Furthermore, if the meaning were to be fully expressed through the fourfold logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*), it would be explained; however, where there is only the "consequent phrase" (*pṛṣṭha-pada*), it is not explained here.
Furthermore, this is the *Jñāna-vastu* (Chapter on Knowledge). Regarding those phenomena whose nature is the wisdom of vision (*darśana-prajñā*), they are analyzed in detail herein.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present, how many awakening factors and how many path factors (*mārgāṅga*) are present?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]
There is a teaching that phenomena arise sequentially and not simultaneously.
As the Dārṣṭāntika Buddhadeva has stated:
"Phenomena arise sequentially; they do not arise all at once."
It is just as when many people travel along a narrow path: one goes out and another enters; two cannot proceed side by side at the same time, much less a multitude.
In this way, conditioned phenomena each arise from their own characteristic of arising (*jāti-lakṣaṇa*); what power could there be for them to arise simultaneously?
Question: Why does he make this statement? Answer:
He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras, which state:
"If the mind is weak and inferior, it is the wrong time to cultivate the three factors of enlightenment— namely, the enlightenment factors of tranquility, concentration, and equanimity."
At this time, one should cultivate three factors of enlightenment: namely, the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*).
If the mind is agitated, cultivating these three factors of enlightenment—namely, investigation of phenomena, energy, and joy—is inappropriate for that occasion;
at such a time, one should cultivate three other factors of enlightenment: namely, tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If the Buddha’s sūtras state that three factors of enlightenment are "timely" and three factors of enlightenment are "untimely," one should know that dharmas arise sequentially as they occur, rather than arising all at once.
Furthermore, other sūtras are cited, such as when the Venerable Śāriputra spoke thus:
"Venerable elders, you should know that I have attained mastery over the seven factors of enlightenment according to my will."
In the first watch of the day, when I wish to dwell in such factors of awakening, I am able to dwell therein as I please;
likewise, in the middle watch and the last watch of the day, when I wish to dwell in such factors of awakening, I am able to dwell therein as I please.
Based on what is taught in these two sūtras, one knows that when dharmas arise, they do so in succession and not all at once.
To refute the intention behind such a statement, it is also clarified that dharmas arise simultaneously.
Question: If dharmas arise simultaneously rather than arising sequentially, how is this reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
For instance, it is said:
Regarding the cultivation of the three factors of enlightenment, three are timely and three are untimely.
The answer is:
this sutra teaches that when dharmas arise, they arise simultaneously; it is not the case that they do not arise at one time.
Why is this so? If there were two or three factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyadhamma) within the mind, they would arise simultaneously once the Dharma is clarified, rather than sequentially.
It is asked:

Since these factors that assist the path are cultivated without deficiency according to their respective stages, why is it said that at this time one cultivates three factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) while [at other times] three factors of enlightenment are not cultivated?
Answer: The factors of enlightenment consist of two parts:
first, the part of concentration; second, the part of wisdom.
When the factors of concentration and the awakening factors are present before one, the three awakening factors belonging to the category of wisdom are then untimely.
Why is this? Because the power and function of the factors of concentration are predominant at that time.
At this time, one should cultivate the three factors of enlightenment.
Contrary to what was stated above, the same applies to the explanation of the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, there are those who enter the Noble Path through concentration (*samādhi*), and those who enter the Noble Path through wisdom (*prajñā*).

If one enters the noble path through concentration, it is the appropriate time to cultivate the three factors of enlightenment belonging to concentration, while it is the inappropriate time to cultivate the three factors of enlightenment belonging to wisdom.

If one enters the noble path through wisdom, it is the appropriate time to cultivate the three factors of enlightenment belonging to wisdom, while it is the inappropriate time to cultivate the three factors of enlightenment belonging to concentration.
How then should one interpret the sūtra spoken by the Venerable Śāriputra?
The answer is:

The Venerable Śāriputra thoroughly understood the mental and physical characteristics associated with emerging from and entering meditative absorption. If he wished to enter such factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) during the first watch of the day, he could do so at will and with mastery; the same was true for the middle and final watches of the day. It is in this sense that he made such a statement.

Furthermore, this sutra speaks of the factors of enlightenment (bodhyanga) in three stages: the stage with directed thought and sustained thought (savitarka-savicāra), the stage without directed thought but with sustained thought (avitarka-vicāramātra), and the stage without directed thought and without sustained thought (avitarka-avicāra).

If one wishes to enter the factors of enlightenment of the stage with directed thought and sustained thought during the first part of the day, those of the stage without directed thought but with sustained thought during the middle part of the day, and those of the stage without directed thought and without sustained thought during the latter part of the day, all may do so according to their preference; therefore, it is said thus.

Furthermore, it is said herein that three faculties are associated with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*), namely: the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are all associated with the factors of enlightenment.

If one wishes to associate the factors of enlightenment with the faculty of pleasure during the first part of the day, with the faculty of joy during the middle part of the day, and with the faculty of equanimity during the latter part of the day, one may do so as one pleases; therefore, this statement was made.

The same applies to the explanation of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) associated with emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as those associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), and the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi). The Dārṣṭāntikas state:

"In this context, the factors of enlightenment are said to pertain to seven stages, namely, the factors of enlightenment belonging to the four fundamental dhyānas and the three formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti)."

Within these seven stages, if one wishes to enter the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) of the first dhyāna stage up to the stage of nothingness during the morning, or to enter the factors of enlightenment of the first dhyāna stage up to the stage of nothingness during the midday or the afternoon, one is able to do so at will; therefore, this statement was made.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the reason this treatise was composed is to refute various assertions: some claim that while there is joy (*prīti*) in the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) of the form realm, there is no ethical discipline (*śīla*); others claim that correct awakening (*samyagbodhi*) exists in the higher stages; and still others claim that ethical discipline exists within the formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is for the purpose of stopping such views that this treatise was written.
When the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is present, how many awakening factors and path factors (*mārgāṅga*) are present? Answer:

If, based on the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-dhyāna*) with applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), the learner’s awakening factor of mindfulness is present, then six awakening factors and eight path factors are present.
The six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are present.
This is said with the intention that within the meditative absorptions (dhyāna) that suppress all extremes, there is joy but no precepts. Question:
If the preparatory concentration (anāgamya-dhyāna) is without applied thought (vitarka) and sustained thought (vicāra),
why is it said that one relies upon the preparatory concentration that possesses applied and sustained thought?
The answer is:
One should say this:
if it relies on the *anāgamya* dhyāna concentration, one should say that it possesses both vitarka and vicāra.
What is the intended meaning behind saying this?
Answer: It is because one wishes to enable those who harbor doubts to attain certainty.
As it is said in the Mahābhūta-skandhaka:
The various stages above [the first dhyāna] are also called "not yet reached" (*anāgamya*).
Some, upon hearing the term "not yet reached," claim it refers to the "not yet reached" stage of the higher grounds.
However, if it is described as having both applied and sustained thought (*savitarka-savicāra*), one should know that it must refer to the "not yet reached" stage of the first dhyāna.

If, relying on the first dhyāna, one brings the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) to presence while training, seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) are present;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
If, based on the intermediate dhyāna, the factors of enlightenment of mindfulness are present for one in training, six factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path are present;
for one beyond training, six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
If one speaks in this way, it stops the notion that there is a perfectly awakened one (samyaksambuddha) in the higher stages.
As it is with the intermediate dhyāna, so it is with the third and fourth dhyānas as well.
If, relying on the second dhyāna, the training practitioner brings the awakening factor of mindfulness into manifestation, seven awakening factors and seven path factors are manifested;
for the one beyond training, seven awakening factors and eight path factors are manifested.

If one relies on a formless absorption (ārūpya-samāpatti), when the enlightenment factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) manifests for a trainee (śaikṣa), six enlightenment factors and four path factors (mārgāṅga) manifest;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), six enlightenment factors and five path factors manifest.
If one speaks in this way, it stops the intention of asserting that there is morality in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Regarding those factors obtained within all stages and all untainted minds (*anāsravacitta*)—namely, the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)—the explanation is likewise as for the factor of mindfulness (*smṛtibodhyaṅga*).
What are they? They are the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena (*dharma-vicaya*), energy (*vīrya*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), concentration (*samādhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
When right view, right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration, and the awakening factor of joy (*prīti*) are present, how many awakening factors and path factors (*mārgāṅga*) are present?

Answer: If, relying on the first dhyāna, the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) manifests for one in training (śaikṣa), then seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path (mārgāṅga) manifest;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path manifest.

If, relying on the second dhyāna, the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) manifests for one in training (śaikṣa), then seven factors of enlightenment and seven factors of the path (mārgāṅga) manifest;
for one beyond training (aśaikṣa), seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path manifest.
When the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiyā dhammā) are present, how many factors of enlightenment and how many factors of the path (maggaṅgāni) are present?
The answer is:
if one relies on the threshold concentration (anāgāmya-dhyāna), when the enlightenment of a trainee (śaikṣa) is present, six factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present.
Six factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present for one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If, relying on the first dhyāna, a factor of right awakening is present for one in training (śaikṣa), then seven factors of enlightenment and eight factors of the path are present;
for one beyond training, seven factors of enlightenment and nine factors of the path are present.
Question: Why is there no joy among the extremes and the middle? Answer:
Because those who have abandoned desire for some objects but not others can still give rise to [the feeling] as it manifests before them, they cannot produce joy.
It is like a person bound in many places; as long as there are places where they are bound and places where they are not yet freed, they cannot experience joy.
It is the same for that [higher stage] as well. Question:
For what reason is there no perfect enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) in the higher stages?
The answer is:
"Because it is not its field or its implement," and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, one seeks a higher stage (*bhūmi*) in order to eliminate discursive thought (*vitarka*); if there were discursive thought in the higher stage, one would not apply the means (*upāya*) of the lower stage to seek that higher stage.
If a dharma exists both in a lower stage and in a higher stage, then there can be no sequential cessation; if there is no sequential cessation, then there is no ultimate cessation. Why is this so?
By means of sequential cessation, one can reach ultimate cessation.
If there were no ultimate cessation, there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, if right awakening exists where there are bodily and vocal actions, then because higher stages lack bodily and vocal actions, there would be no right awakening there.
Question: For what reason is there no morality in the formless realm? Answer:
"Because there is no field or vessel," and so forth, as explained at length.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of abandoning morality that one seeks the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); if there were morality in the formless realm, then sentient beings of the lower stages would not employ skillful means to seek the formless realm.
If a dharma exists both in a lower stage and in a higher stage, then there can be no sequential cessation; if there is no sequential cessation, then there is no ultimate cessation. Why is this so?
Successive cessation leads to ultimate cessation;
if there were no ultimate cessation, there would be no liberation.
Furthermore, precepts are a portion of form (*rūpa*); in the formless realm (*ārūpya*), there is no form.
Precepts are composed of the four great elements, yet in the formless realm there are no four great elements.
Question: Since there are no untainted (anāsrava) four great elements, why is there untainted precept?
Answer: Untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are not untainted by virtue of the power of the four great elements; rather, they are untainted by virtue of the power of the mind.

Furthermore, precepts serve as the antidote to unwholesome precepts (*duḥśīla*); since there is no unwholesome precept in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no [untainted] precept there either.
Why is this so? Because immoral conduct exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The desire realm is distant from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) by way of four things:
First, by distance of the basis;
second, by distance of the range of activity;
third, by distance of the object of focus.
Fourth, by way of remoteness through counteraction (*pratipakṣa-dūratā*).
These are the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*):

the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*), the four right endeavors (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*), the four bases of power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the five powers (*pañca balāni*), the seven factors of awakening (*sapta bodhyaṅgāni*), and the eightfold path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārgaḥ*).
The Buddha taught that there are not thirty factors of the path to enlightenment; rather, the seven factors of awakening are the factors of the path to enlightenment. How is this known?
A sutra states:
A certain bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was staying. Upon arrival, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding what is called a ‘factor of enlightenment’ (bodhyaṅga), for what reason is it named a factor of enlightenment?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"These seven factors that assist the path are therefore called the limbs of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*); namely, the limb of mindfulness, the limb of investigation of phenomena, the limb of energy, the limb of joy, the limb of tranquility, the limb of concentration, and the limb of equanimity."
For this reason, it is known that the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are the factors conducive to the path (*mārga-parivāra-dharma*). Question:
There are thirty-seven factors conducive to the path; why did the Blessed One say that only the seven factors of enlightenment are the factors conducive to the path?
The answer is:
In accordance with what that bhikṣu asked, the Buddha taught that the seven factors of enlightenment are dharmas that assist the path.
If that bhikṣu had asked about the four foundations of mindfulness, the Buddha would likewise have taught that the four foundations of mindfulness are dharmas that assist the path.
Furthermore, that sutra speaks exclusively of the untainted factors conducive to enlightenment (*anāsrava-bodhipakṣadharma*), whereas others are not so determined.

For example, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are of two kinds—namely, tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted—and this extends even to the limbs of the path (*mārgāṅga*), which are likewise both tainted and untainted.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the Buddha taught the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), but because a long period of time elapsed, they were lost. As Dharadatta stated:
"The factors of enlightenment should be spoken of as having one branch, up to thirty-seven branches, just like the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
As it is also said in the *Anaxoropama-sūtra* (The Simile of the Axe Handle):
"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that are untainted (*anāsrava*).
If one takes up the definitive cultivation of the path, these are the seven factors of awakening (*saptabodhyaṅga*)."
If one takes [the position] that it is not determinate,
then there are six types of factors. Why is this so?
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are of two kinds: with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava); this applies likewise even to the factors of the path (mārgāṅga).
Question: The factors that assist the path (bodhipakṣadharma) are said to have thirty-seven names; how many distinct entities (dravya) do they possess?
Answer: The factors that assist the path (bodhipakṣadharma) are thirty-seven in name, but eleven or twelve in substance.
If one says they are all contained within the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), there are seven names for the factors of enlightenment, and their substance is likewise seven.
The four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and right view are all entirely contained within the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena.
The four right endeavors, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and right effort are all entirely contained within the factor of enlightenment of energy.

The four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the faculty of concentration (*samādhindriya*), the power of concentration (*samādhibala*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) are all entirely contained within the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*).

The faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*), the power of mindfulness (*smṛtibala*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) are all entirely contained within the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*).

The remaining [factors] include the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*), and among the branches of the path (*mārgāṅga*) there are right speech (*samyagvāk*), right action (*samyakkarmānta*), and right livelihood (*samyagājīva*).

If one were to say that all these are included within the branches of the path, yet maintain that apart from right speech and right action there is no further right livelihood, then while the name "eightfold path" would consist of eight, its substance would consist of only seven.
If one asserts that right livelihood exists separately from right speech and right action, then there would be eight members of the path in name and eight in substance.

However, the four foundations of mindfulness, the faculty of wisdom, the power of wisdom, and the factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena are all entirely contained within right view.
The four right endeavors, the faculty of energy, the power of energy, and the factor of enlightenment of energy are all contained within right effort.
The four bases of psychic power, the faculty of concentration, the power of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration are all contained within right concentration.
The faculty of mindfulness, the power of mindfulness, and the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness are all contained within right mindfulness.
As for the remaining faculties, there is the faculty of faith; among the factors of enlightenment, there are joy, tranquility, and equanimity.
For this reason, the factors conducive to the path (bodhipakṣadharma) are said to have thirty-seven names, while their substance consists of eleven or twelve.

As it is with the names and the substance, so it is with the number of names and the number of substances; as it is with the difference of names and the difference of substance, so it is with the difference of the characteristics of names and the difference of the characteristics of substance; and knowing the names and knowing the substance is likewise.
"This is the essential nature and the dharma-nature of the factors conducive to awakening," and so forth, as explained at length.
Why are they called "factors conducive to awakening"?
What is the meaning of "conducive to awakening"?

Answer: The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are awakening (*bodhi*). These various dharmas accord with that [awakening], assist that [awakening], and are its constituent parts; because their functional power is superior, they are called the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
The reason for the factors conducive to enlightenment has already been explained in general; now, the reasons for each one shall be explained individually.
Why are they called "foundations of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
The answer is:
The meaning of "discriminating the aggregates" is the meaning of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

"Aggregates" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*); if one wishes to discriminate them, it should be done by means of the foundations of mindfulness. The meaning of "burning away" is the meaning of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*). The meaning of "accumulation" and the meaning of "dharmas" is the meaning of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). The meaning of "predominance and excellence" is the meaning of the faculties (*indriya*). The meaning of "indestructibility" is the meaning of the powers (*bala*). The meaning of "awakening and knowing" is the meaning of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*). The meaning of "seeking and searching" is the meaning of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Having already explained the reasons for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) separately, we shall now separately explain the reasons for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
Why are they called "factors of enlightenment"?
Is it because they cause awakening that they are called factors of enlightenment, or is it because they are themselves factors of enlightenment that they are so called?
If they are called factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) simply because they are awakening, then one is a factor of enlightenment while the other six are not.
If they are called factors of enlightenment because they are factors of enlightenment, then the six are factors of enlightenment while the one is not.
Answer: It should be stated thus: they are called factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) because they consist of awakening.
Question: If that is so, then one is correct and the other six are incorrect. Answer:
All these dharmas are entirely portions of that dharma and entirely conform to that dharma; because their functional power is preeminent, they are called limbs of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
Furthermore, there are those who say they are called limbs of enlightenment because they are themselves the limbs of enlightenment.
Question: If that is so, then six [of the positions] are correct and one is incorrect. Answer:

The factor of enlightenment of the investigation of phenomena (*dharma-vicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is both awakening (*bodhi*) and a factor of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*); the others are only factors of awakening.
Why, then, are they called "factors of the path" (*mārgāṅga*)?
Are they factors of the path because they are the seeking [itself], or are they factors of the path because they are the factors for that seeking?
If one considers seeking to be a factor of the path, then one is correct and seven are incorrect.
If one considers that which seeks to be a factor of the path because it is a factor of seeking, then seven are correct and one is incorrect.
Answer: It should be stated thus:
they are branches of the path because they involve seeking and investigation.
Question: If that is so, then one is correct and seven are incorrect. Answer:
All these factors are portions of that [noble] dharma and conform to it; because their functional power is preeminent, they are called "limbs of the path" (*mārgāṅga*).
Furthermore, some say they are limbs of the path because they are limbs for seeking and searching.
Question: If that is so, then seven [of these] are correct and one is incorrect. Answer:
Right view is both seeking and a factor of seeking; the others are factors of seeking.

Just as the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena is both awakening and a factor of awakening, just as right concentration is both dhyāna and a factor of dhyāna, and just as abstaining from eating at improper times is both the fast and a factor of the fast, so too is right view: it is both seeking and a factor of seeking.
Having already explained individually the reasons for each of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), we shall now seek their sequential order.
Why are the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) taught first, and why are the eight branches of the path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) taught last?
Answer: Because it accords with the sequential order of verbal expression.
Furthermore, when the Buddha speaks in accordance [with this order], the questioner finds it easy to receive.

Furthermore, the four foundations of mindfulness are like one who has eyes to see, while the other factors conducive to enlightenment are like the blind; they prevent one from falling into unwholesome states.
It is like a group of many blind people who, when led by one with sight, are not allowed to fall onto a wrong path.
It is the same for him as well.

Furthermore, by means of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), he is able to clearly discern the general and specific characteristics of phenomena; he destroys delusion regarding the substantiality of things and delusion regarding conditions, grasping the true nature of phenomena without allowing it to increase or decrease.

Furthermore, the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) possess ever-increasing power from the stage of initial awakening through to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). The right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) possess ever-increasing power from the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) upwards. The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) possess ever-increasing power from the stage of "summit" (*mūrdhan*) upwards. The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) possess ever-increasing power from the stage of "patience" (*kṣānti*) upwards. The five powers (*pañcabala*) possess ever-increasing power from the stage of "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) upwards. The factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), while the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are predominant within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).

Question: Why is it that the path factors (*mārgāṅga*) are predominant in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the awakening factors (*bodhyaṅga*) are predominant in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*)? Answer:
The meaning of "going" (gati) is the meaning of "path" (mārga), because within the path, one proceeds with extreme swiftness.

The meaning of "awakening" (bodha) is the meaning of "limb of awakening" (bodhyaṅga), because within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), there are nine kinds of awakenings through which one awakens repeatedly.

Question: If these are the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), why did the Blessed One first speak of the factors of awakening and later of the factors of the path?
Answer: Because it accords with the sequential order of verbal expression.
Furthermore, when the Buddha speaks in accordance [with this sequence], the questioner finds it easy to receive [the teaching].
Furthermore, because he wishes to gradually increase one factor at a time, he first teaches four dharmas, followed by five, seven, and eight dharmas.
Moreover, it is because he wishes to gradually bring about the essential dharma and to progressively augment it.

Having already explained the general sequence of the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*), we shall now explain each of the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) individually.
Why is mindfulness (*smṛti*) taught first among the factors of awakening, followed by the others up to equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
Answer: Because it accords with the sequential order of verbal expression.
Furthermore, when the Buddha speaks, he accords with [the truth], so that the questioner may easily receive [the teaching].
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

"One who has already seen the Truths is able to fulfill the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment by means of the power of mindfulness regarding what was previously attained; therefore, the Buddha taught the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness first."
As the Sūtra says:

When the practitioner correctly contemplates this dharma and mindfulness is present before them, they do not give rise to delusion or confusion, and are thus able to fulfill the cultivation of the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

By the power of mindfulness, they are able to discern, select, and deliberate upon dharmas, and are thus able to fulfill the cultivation of the awakening factor of discrimination of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because one is able to select, discern, and deliberate upon the Dharma, one practices diligence, thereby fulfilling the cultivation of the awakening factor of diligence (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Having practiced diligence, there arises a joy of unmixed flavor, thereby fulfilling the cultivation of the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Because of joy, the body and mind experience pliancy and bliss, thereby enabling the fulfillment of the cultivation of the awakening factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Because of the bliss of concentration and pliancy, the mind becomes concentrated, thereby enabling the fulfillment of the cultivation of the awakening factor of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

Because the mind is concentrated, and because one dwells in equanimity free from desire and sorrow, one is able to fulfill the cultivation of the awakening factor of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Question:
For what reason does the Blessed One first teach right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) among the factors of the path, and subsequently [teach] everything up to right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*)?
Answer: Because it accords with the sequential order of verbal expression.
Furthermore, when the Buddha speaks in accordance [with this order], the questioner easily receives the teaching.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
One who has already seen the truths is able to cultivate the factors of the path by means of right view.
As it is said:
By virtue of right view, one is able to cultivate the factors of the path.
As it is said:
"By virtue of right view, one is able to give rise to right resolve, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration."
The sequence of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) has already been explained; now the stages (*bhūmi*) shall be explained.
In which stage are there how many factors conducive to enlightenment?
The answer is:
The preliminary dhyāna (anāgamya) has thirty-six factors, excluding joy (prīti).
The first dhyāna has thirty-seven.
The intermediate dhyāna has thirty-five, excluding joy and right awakening (samyak-saṃkalpa).
In the second dhyāna there are thirty-six factors, excluding right enlightenment.
In the third and fourth dhyānas there are thirty-five, excluding joy, right enlightenment, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
In the formless attainments there are thirty-two, excluding joy, right enlightenment, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.

The stages (*bhūmi*) have already been explained; now we shall explain their manifestation. At the time of manifestation, how many factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) from which stage manifest simultaneously?
The answer is:
based on the *anāgamya* (preliminary) dhyāna, there are thirty-six; when they manifest simultaneously, there are thirty-three, excluding three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Why is this? Because their objects of focus (ālambana) are each distinct, one cannot even give rise to two [mental applications] at once, let alone many.
In the first dhyāna, there are thirty-seven factors; thus, thirty-four appear simultaneously, with the three applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) also excluded.
In the intermediate dhyāna, there are thirty-five factors; thus, thirty-two appear simultaneously, likewise excluding the three applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
As it is with the intermediate dhyāna, so it is with the third and fourth dhyānas as well.
In the second dhyāna, there are thirty-six [factors]; thus, thirty-three manifest simultaneously, as three of the applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are also excluded.
In the formless realms, there are thirty-two; thus, twenty-nine manifest, as three applications of mindfulness are likewise excluded.
Having already explained those that are present before one, we shall now explain their common and distinct characteristics.
If something is a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), is it also a factor of the path (mārgāṅga)?
The answer is:
Or, there are factors that are limbs of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) but not limbs of the path (mārgāṅga); this is elaborated at length as a fourfold permutation (catuṣkoṭi).
Those that are limbs of enlightenment but not limbs of the path are the limbs of enlightenment of joy (prīti), tranquility (praśrabdhi), and equanimity (upekṣā).
Those that are factors of the path but not factors of enlightenment are right view, right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Those that are both factors of enlightenment and factors of the path are all other factors conducive to enlightenment, excluding faith.
That which is neither a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) nor a factor of the path (mārgāṅga) is faith (śraddhā). Question:
For what reason is joy (prīti) established as a factor of enlightenment?
Answer: The meaning of "awakening" (bodha) is the meaning of "factor of awakening" (bodhyaṅga); joy (prīti) is conducive to the factors of awakening. Question:
What is the factor of enlightenment of joy that is conducive [to awakening]?
The answer is:
if one repeatedly awakens to the object as it truly is, then joy arises; if joy repeatedly arises, then one awakens to the object as it truly is.
It is like a person digging the earth who finds treasure; because he has found treasure, he digs further, and by digging further, he finds more.
It is the same for him. Question:
Why is joy (*prīti*) not established as a factor of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
The answer is:
the meaning of "going" (*gati*) is the meaning of a factor of the path, and joy does not accord with going.
Question: For what reason does joy not follow along? Answer:
If one repeatedly delights [in a state], one dwells therein and does not depart.
It is like a person traveling on a road who, if they repeatedly stop to rest, desires to stay and does not go on;
it is the same for that person.
Question: For what reason are tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? Answer:

The meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*) is the meaning of the "factors of awakening" (*bodhipakṣa*). Tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are in conformity with the factors of awakening. Question:
In what way do tranquility and equanimity conform to the factors of awakening?
Answer: If one attains pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) regarding all things, then one can realize the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) as it truly is. Question:
Why are tranquility (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) not established as factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
The answer is:
the meaning of "going" (*gati*) is the meaning of the factors of the path; tranquility and equanimity do not conform to going.
Question: For what reason do *praśrabdhi* (tranquility) and *upekṣā* (equanimity) not follow along? Answer:
Relaxation (*praśrabdhi*) and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are incompatible with departure (*niḥsaraṇa*).
Just as walking and standing, or sleeping and waking, are mutually exclusive, so too are these. Question:
For what reason did the Perfectly Awakened One establish the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)?
The answer is:
the meaning of "going" (*gati*) is the meaning of the factors of the path; for through perfect awakening, one is able to set forth right view and thus emerge from birth and death.
Just as a person can reach their destination by striking an ox with a staff, so it is in this case.
Question: For what reason did the Perfectly Awakened One not establish factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: Because the nature of perfect awakening is active, while the nature of the factors of awakening is quiescent. Question:
Why are right speech, right action, and right livelihood established as factors of the path?
The answer is:
the meaning of "going" is the meaning of a factor of the path; because right speech, action, and livelihood serve as the hub for the chariot of the path.
Question: For what reason are right speech, action, and livelihood not established as factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*)? Answer:
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood are factors of the path, not the path itself.
Furthermore, right speech, right action, and right livelihood are dissociated, without support, without activity, and without an object; the factors of enlightenment are the opposite of these.
Question: Why is faith not a factor of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) or a factor of the path (mārgāṅga)? Answer:

When first entering the Dharma, because the power of faith is predominant, one who has already entered the Dharma cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).

Furthermore, regarding the methods for transcendence (*nairyāṇika-dharma*), there are those that are complete and those that are incomplete. Those methods for transcendence that possess the characteristics of the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), factors of enlightenment, and the path are called "complete"; the opposite of these is called "incomplete."

If they do not fulfill the characteristics of the factors of emergence (*niḥsaraṇa-dharma*), but possess the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and lack the characteristics of the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), they are established as factors of enlightenment, such as joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

If they lack the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment but possess the characteristics of the factors of the path, they are established as factors of the path, such as right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*) and right speech, action, and livelihood (*samyag-vāk-karmāntājīva*).

If the factors of renunciation are fulfilled and possess the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), they are established as factors of enlightenment and factors of the path, just like other factors of enlightenment and factors of the path.

If they do not fulfill the factors of renunciation and lack the characteristics of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*), the factors of enlightenment and the factors of the path are not established; faith is an example of this.
Question: For what reason is the mind (*citta*) not established as an auxiliary factor of the path?
Answer: Because they lack the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

Furthermore, while the mind possesses efficacy toward both the afflictions and the methods for their transcendence, the factors conducive to enlightenment possess efficacy specifically toward the methods for transcendence.
Furthermore, while the mind takes both general and specific characteristics as its objects, the factors conducive to enlightenment take only general characteristics as their objects.
Furthermore, just as the afflictions are mental concomitants (*caitta*) and not the mind itself, their antidotes are likewise mental concomitants and not the mind itself.
If it is said that one is called "concentrated" because the mind is fixed, this refers to concentration among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Question:

For what reason is the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) established as a factor conducive to enlightenment among the three faculties, while the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) are not?
Answer: Because they lack the characteristics of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), they are not established as such.
Furthermore, the practice of the factors conducive to enlightenment is intense and sharp, whereas those two faculties are dull and their practice is not sharp.

Furthermore, the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is obscured by the pleasure of tranquility (*praśrabdhisukha*), and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is obscured by the equanimity of formations (*saṃskāropekṣā*); therefore, they are not established as factors conducive to the path (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
Question: For what reason are the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) not established as factors conducive to the path?
Answer: There are also those who maintain this position.
For example, as the Vibhajyavādins say:
There are thirty-one factors that aid the path.
Question: I am not asking about those who speak in such a manner.
The answer is:
The factors conducive to the Path (bodhipakṣadharma) possess two superior qualities among householders and renunciants:
first, superiority of the initial resolve; second, superiority in practice and realization.
Among renunciants, the noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) excel in two respects:
first, excellence in aspiration; second, excellence in practice.
Among householders, they excel in one respect, namely, excellence in aspiration, but not in excellence in practice.

Just as Śakra sits upon a seat of various flowers, surrounded by twelve nayutas of celestial maidens, with sixty thousand musicians known as "Abiding in the Noble Lineage" (Āryavaṃśasthita), who merely harbor the aspiration for it but do not practice its observance.
It is the same for King Bimbisāra and others, as well as for the householder Sudatta and others.
If one were to say that delighting in abandonment is diligence, this is precisely the factor of awakening of diligence.
The *Pakaraṇa Sūtra* states:
"What is the awakening factor of mindfulness?
The answer is:"

The noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; endowed with indestructible knowledge, this constitutes mindfulness of enlightenment, which he recollects repeatedly, recollects in succession, and never forgets or loses.
This is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.

Furthermore, if a noble disciple perceives birth and death as a source of suffering and perceives nirvana as supreme and wondrous, he maintains mindfulness for the sake of enlightenment, and so forth, as explained at length.
This is called the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*).
When an Arhat contemplates the mind of liberation, this is called the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
This applies likewise up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
What is right view?
The answer is:

when a noble disciple contemplates suffering as suffering, up to contemplating the path as the path; this discernment through investigation that is able to grasp its characteristics, which is awakening, clarity, vision, and wisdom—this is called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

If a noble disciple perceives birth-and-death as a fault and peril, and perceives nirvāṇa as supreme and sublime—this is the analytical discernment, and so forth, as explained at length; this is called the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*).
When an Arhat contemplates the liberation of his own mind, this is the analytical observation; [and so on], as explained at length, this refers to the faculty of "having known.
The same applies up to right concentration.

Question: For what reason is it called "mindfulness of enlightenment" (*bodhyanusmṛti*) within the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), but not mentioned among the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*)? Answer:
When something that ought to be said is not said, one should know that this teaching is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).
Furthermore, it is because [the author] wishes to manifest diverse phrasings and diverse explanations;
if the text is adorned with various modes of expression, the meaning will be easily understood.
Furthermore, this is because one wishes to manifest two gateways, two summaries, two initial methods of entry, two reflections, and the fact that both are universally applicable.

This is just as it was explained in the context of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) where they are termed "mindfulness of enlightenment" (*bodhi-smṛti*), and likewise in the context of the factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) where they are termed "right view of enlightenment" (*bodhi-samyagdṛṣṭi*).
Just as it is not stated that [right view] among the factors of the path is "enlightenment" (bodhi), the same applies to the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga).
Furthermore, it was previously stated that the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) constitute enlightenment.

Within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the power and function of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are superior; because the path of cultivation is proximate to the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), they are designated as "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) among the factors of enlightenment, but not among the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*).
The Sūtra states:

"One cultivates the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity, for the sake of tranquility, for the sake of dispassion, and for the sake of Nirvāṇa. Question:

The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) is with outflows (*sāsrava*), whereas the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*) are without outflows (*anāsrava*). How can these two—those with outflows and those without outflows—occur together?
The Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra says:

First, one uses the contemplation of impurity to cause the mind to become compliant, supple, upright, patient, and masterful; subsequently, the factors of enlightenment arise and manifest; and after the factors of enlightenment, the contemplation of impurity arises once again.

Because the awakening factors (bodhyaṅga) move the contemplation of impurity (aśubhabhāvanā), it is said thus; yet there is nothing therein that is both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava).
The Buddha’s sūtra states:
"The noble disciple, with a single mind and attentive ears, listens to the Dharma; he is able to sever the five hindrances (pañcanīvaraṇa) and fully cultivates the seven awakening factors."
Question: If it is the concentrated mind that can sever the fetters, and not the unconcentrated mind—
and this belongs to the mental faculty (*manobhūmi*) rather than the five groups of sensory consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*)— why is it stated as follows?
"Listen to the Dharma with a single-minded focus on your ears," and so forth, as explained at length.
The answer says:
This explains the principle of phenomena arising in successive succession.

From auditory consciousness, wholesome mental consciousness arises next; from wholesome mental consciousness, that which arises from hearing arises next; from that which arises from hearing, that which arises from reflection arises next; from that which arises from reflection, that which arises from cultivation arises next; and by means of that which arises from cultivation, one abandons the afflictions.
Furthermore, this explains the principle of continuity.
It is said that because the wholesome mental consciousness continues with the wholesome auditory consciousness, it is able to sever the afflictions.
A question is asked:
If it is the path of non-obstruction (*ānantaryamārga*), it can sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) but cannot fulfill the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*);
if it is the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), it can fulfill the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment but cannot sever the afflictions.
The answer is:
The Buddha spoke thus because he was referring to factors that are closely associated.
Are all factors that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness also associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena?

Answer: There are cases where [a factor] is associated with the awakening-factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) but not with the awakening-factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga), and so forth, as elaborated in the four permutations (catuṣkoṭi).
That which is associated with the awakening-factor of mindfulness but not with the awakening-factor of investigation of phenomena is the awakening-factor of investigation of phenomena itself.
Why is this so? For three reasons, a self-nature does not associate with itself:
first, because two types of wisdom cannot arise simultaneously.
Second, because [the factors] do not coexist before and after;
third, because all dharmas, excluding their own substance, act as conditions for other dharmas.

That which is associated with the factor of enlightenment of investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness.
Why is this? Because of the nature of seeking, a self-essence does not associate with itself, as previously explained.
Those phenomena that associate with the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena [are as follows].
Regarding those associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*):
what are they? The answer is:

those which are concomitant within the same aggregate as the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, excluding their own self-nature (*svabhāva*), and all other factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena.
What are they? They are the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) and the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
If one is in a state characterized by both initial and sustained application (*savitarka-savicāra*), then there is initial application, sustained application, and the mind.

Those factors not associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena are all other mental states and mental concomitants, matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
In this context, the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is primarily discussed, with nothing else being mentioned.

Other factors—namely, tainted minds and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*)—constitute the fourth category.

As it is with the awakening factor of mindfulness and the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena, so too should it be explained for the awakening factors of energy, rapture, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity, as well as right effort and right concentration.
Are all phenomena that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness also associated with the awakening factor of joy?
[The answer] should be elaborated in full as four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The awakening factor of mindfulness exists in all stages and in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), whereas the awakening factor of joy exists in all untainted minds but not in all stages.
Therefore, one can formulate four propositions.

Regarding that which is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness but not with the awakening factor of rapture: within the aggregate associated with both the awakening factor of rapture and the awakening factor of mindfulness, the essence of the awakening factor of rapture is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, yet it is not associated with the awakening factor of rapture itself.
Why is this? It is because, for three reasons, a self-entity does not associate with itself, as previously explained.
As for those other factors that do not associate with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but do associate with the factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), what are they?

Answer: The factors associated with the factor of awakening of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga) within the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna (dhyānāntara), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (ārūpya), are not associated with the factor of awakening of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Why is this? Because there is no joy (*prīti*) within those stages.
It is associated with the factor of awakening of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), but not associated with the factor of awakening of mindfulness (*smṛtisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 48 [and] Volume 49. Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.

In the eighth chapter of the *Jñānaprasthāna*, the Section on the Eightfold Path, Part Two: The factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-sambodhyaṅga*) is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-sambodhyaṅga*). Within the aggregate (*skandha*) that co-exists with the factor of enlightenment of joy, the essence of the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, but it is not associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness itself.
Why is this? It is because of three reasons that a self-entity does not associate with itself, as previously explained.

Regarding its association with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and also with the joy factor of enlightenment (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), this excludes those factors already associated with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because they are numerous, they are excluded.

Furthermore, within the aggregate of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the joy factor of enlightenment (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of both the mindfulness and joy factors of enlightenment, as well as all other mental concomitants (*caitasika*), are entirely associated with these two.

What is that? It refers to the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), those stages where there is initial application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*), and those instances where the mind is not associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛtisambodhyaṅga*) or the awakening factor of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*).
What is the factor of mindfulness that does not associate with the factor of joy?

It refers to the essence of the factor of mindfulness within the preliminary stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), which does not associate with the factor of mindfulness itself.
Why is this? For three reasons, as previously explained, the intrinsic nature does not associate with itself;
nor does it associate with the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Why is this? Because there is no joy (*prīti*) within those stages.
As for the other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), what is stated here exhaustively refers to all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), with nothing else remaining.

There are other contaminated mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asamskrta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-samskāra*) that constitute the fourth category.

As it is with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), so it is for the awakening factor of mindfulness in relation to right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and right resolve (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).
Are those phenomena that are associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness also associated with right mindfulness? Answer: Yes.
If one is associated with right mindfulness, is one also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness? Answer: It is so.

As with the awakening factor of mindfulness, so it is for the awakening factors of investigation of phenomena, energy, tranquility, concentration, and equanimity; the same applies to right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
Are all phenomena that are associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena also associated with right view?
Answer: If a phenomenon is associated with right view, it is also associated with the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena.
Are there any phenomena that are associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) but are not right view (samyagdṛṣṭi)? Answer:
Yes; there are phenomena associated with the awakening factor of investigation of phenomena that are not subsumed under right view.
What are those? They are the factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Are all factors associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right effort (*samyak-vyāyāma*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one is associated with right effort (*samyak-pradhāna*), is one also associated with the awakening factor of energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: It is so.
Are those dharmas that are associated with the awakening factor of concentration also associated with right concentration?
Answer: It is so.
If one is associated with right concentration, is one also associated with the factor of enlightenment of concentration?
Answer: It is so.
Are those dharmas that are associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy also associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility?

Answer: Sometimes it is associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not associated with the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*); thus, one should formulate four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Joy exists in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) but does not exist in all stages (*bhūmi*); tranquility exists in all untainted minds and also exists in all stages.

Regarding that which is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): the factor of enlightenment of tranquility is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy; within the aggregate that coexists with the factor of enlightenment of joy, the essence of the factor of enlightenment of tranquility is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, but it is not associated with itself, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility.
Why is this? It is because of three reasons that a self-essence cannot correspond with itself, as previously stated.

Regarding that which corresponds with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but does not correspond with the awakening factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): within the aggregate where both the awakening factor of joy and the awakening factor of tranquility are gathered together, the essence of the awakening factor of joy corresponds with the awakening factor of tranquility.
Why is this? Because, for three reasons, a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated.
What, then, are those factors that are associated with the factor of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not associated with the other factors of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

This refers to those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), which are associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility but not with the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Why is this? Because there is no joy (*prīti*) within that stage.

Regarding those associated with the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) and also associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), one must exclude the awakening factor of tranquility itself and whatever is associated with it.
Why is this? Because they are numerous, they are excluded.

Among those factors that coexist with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) and the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), all other mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), excluding their own self-nature (*svabhāva*), are associated with both.

What is that? It refers to the nine universal ground factors (mahābhūmika) and the nine wholesome universal ground factors (kuśalamahābhūmika), which are accompanied by vitarka and vicāra when in a state with both vitarka and vicāra, as well as those mental states associated neither with the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) nor with the factor of tranquility (praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga).
Regarding the factor of tranquility (*passaddhi-sambojjhaṅga*) that is not associated with the factor of joy (*pīti-sambojjhaṅga*), what is it?

It refers to the essence of the factor of tranquility within the preliminary stage (*anāgāmya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), which is not associated with the factor of joy.
Why is this? Because there is no joy (*prīti*) within that stage.
Furthermore, it is not associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Why is this so? It is because, for three reasons, a self-essence cannot act upon itself, as previously explained.
As for the remaining minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*) are fully included herein; there are no others.

There are other contaminated mental states and mental factors, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind; such dharmas as these are not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), nor are they associated with the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*).

As with the enlightenment factor of joy and the enlightenment factor of tranquility, so too it is for the enlightenment factors of joy, equanimity, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration; the explanation is likewise.
Are all dharmas that are associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Joy exists in all untainted minds (*anāsrava-citta*), but not in all stages (*bhūmi*);
right view exists in all stages, but not in all untainted minds. Therefore, four great permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.

Regarding that which is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy but not with right view: right view is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy; within the aggregate of factors coexisting with the factor of enlightenment of joy, the essence of right view is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, but it is not itself associated with right view.
Why is this? Because of three reasons, as previously stated, a self-essence cannot be associated with itself.
What, then, are those other factors associated with the factor of joy that are not associated with right view?

Within the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna, among the collection of factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the factor of the awakening-factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) is not associated with right view. Why is this so?
Because it belongs to that same aggregate.

Regarding "that which is associated with right view but is not the factor of joy": the factor of joy is associated with right view; within the aggregate that coexists with right view, the essence of the factor of joy is associated with right view, but it is not [itself] associated with the factor of joy.
Why is this? It is because, for three reasons, a self-entity cannot correspond with itself, as previously stated.
What, then, are those other factors associated with right view that are not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?

This refers to the factors associated with right view in the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*); these are not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), because joy is absent in those stages.
