Regarding those factors associated with both the joy factor of enlightenment (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) and right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*):

excluding right view itself, what are the other mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) that are associated with the joy factor of enlightenment—excluding the joy factor of enlightenment—and are also associated with right view?

This refers to the eight universal mental factors and the ten wholesome universal mental factors; when they exist in a stage characterized by both initial and sustained application of thought, they are accompanied by both initial and sustained application of thought, as well as by a mind that is neither associated with the factor of joy nor with right view.
Right view is not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). What, then, is it?

In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), the essence of right view is not associated with the factor of joy.
Why is this? Because there is no joy within that stage;
it is not associated with right view.
Why is this? Because of three reasons, as previously explained, a self-essence cannot be associated with itself.
Furthermore, the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) is not associated with right view; what, then, is it associated with?

In the first dhyāna and the second dhyāna, the factor of joy within the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) constitutes the essence of the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*), but it is not associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Why is this?
Because it is a composite of other factors.
It is not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Why is this?
It is because of three reasons; as previously stated, a self-essence cannot be associated with itself.
What are those other mental states and mental factors? They are:

the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), as well as matter (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).

As with the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) and right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), so it is said regarding the factor of enlightenment of joy and right awakening (samyaksaṃbodhi): right awakening with respect to right view is explained in the same way.
What is mundane right view (laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi)?
What is mundane right knowledge?
Why was this treatise composed?
The answer is as follows:
The preceding treatise serves as the fundamental basis for this present treatise.
That preceding treatise states as follows:
"What is meant by 'view'?"
What is knowledge (*jñāna*)?
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)?
Yet, one does not engage in such a discussion:
What is mundane right view? What is mundane right knowledge?
Since the preceding treatise serves as the foundation for this present treatise, this work is now composed in order to provide a detailed analysis.

Furthermore, there is another explanation for why this treatise was composed: some say that not all wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is of the nature of view (dṛṣṭi).
For example, as the Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"What is that [wholesome wisdom]?"
This refers to the mind at the time of death that gives rise to the subsequent five consciousnesses and is capable of initiating bodily and vocal actions.
Question: For what reason is it said that those who give rise to the subsequent five consciousnesses do not possess the nature of vision?
Just as the five consciousnesses are incapable of discrimination, so too is the mental consciousness that arises immediately following them incapable of discrimination.
For what reason is it that that which can initiate bodily and vocal karma does not possess the nature of vision?
Answer: Seeing operates within, while that [mind] operates externally.
For what reason is the mind at the time of death not seeing?
Answer: Seeing that there is power and influence, his wisdom is weak and inferior. Question:
He asks: How is it that this accords with the Buddha’s sūtras, which state:
"When a person is about to die, wholesome mental states and mental factors arise together with right view"?
He replies:
They maintain this position:
"The Buddha spoke of the 'preceding moment of consciousness at the time of death,' not the 'consciousness at the very moment of death.
To refute the intent of those who speak thus, and to clarify that all tainted wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness is of the nature of *dṛṣṭi* (view), this treatise is composed.
What is mundane right view?
The answer is:
wholesome, out-flowing wisdom associated with the mental consciousness.

What is that? It refers to that which is associated with impure contemplation; that which is associated with mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*), the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and the stages of heat (*ūṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the highest mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*); and that which is associated with the dhyānas, the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).
Worldly right view is more vast than the waters of the four great oceans; herein, only the coarse aspects have been briefly explained.
What is worldly right knowledge?
The answer is:
What is that tainted, wholesome wisdom associated with the mental consciousness?
The answer is:
The wholesome wisdom associated with impure contemplations, up to and including mundane right knowledge, is more vast than the waters of the four great oceans.
And what is that wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses? What is it?
Regarding "associated with wholesome eye-consciousness," up to "associated with wholesome body-consciousness":
what is the wisdom associated with wholesome eye-consciousness?
The answer is:

When one sees one’s parents, Buddhas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, or other objects of veneration, there arises wisdom associated with wholesome visual consciousness and wholesome auditory consciousness. What is this?

Answer: Just as hearing the words of the Buddha or the words of one’s parents and other venerable persons gives rise to wholesome ear-consciousness, so too do the other three wholesome consciousnesses not arise in ordinary persons;
they can only arise in those who practice the meditation on the nature of morsel food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
The essential nature has already been explained; now the characteristics of their similarities and differences shall be explained.
If it is mundane right view, is it also mundane right knowledge?
The answer is:
If it is mundane right view, it is also mundane right knowledge.
Is there anything that is mundane right knowledge but not mundane right view?
Answer: Yes.
Yes; it is the wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
Does mundane right view subsume mundane right knowledge, or does mundane right knowledge subsume mundane right view?
Answer: Mundane right knowledge (samyagjñāna) subsumes mundane right view (samyagdṛṣṭi), but mundane right view does not subsume mundane right knowledge.
What is not subsumed?
This refers to wholesome wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses.
If one possesses mundane right view, does one also possess mundane right knowledge?
The answer is: Yes.
Thus it is.
If one is accomplished in mundane right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), is one also accomplished in mundane right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
Who is endowed with mundane right view and mundane right knowledge?
The answer is:
Regarding those who do not sever their roots of goodness:
in general, they are called "those who do not sever their roots of goodness," yet there are various distinctions among them.

Some merely accomplish the wholesome views and knowledge of the desire realm; some merely accomplish those of the form realm; some merely accomplish those of the formless realm; some accomplish those of both the desire and form realms; some accomplish those of both the form and formless realms; and some accomplish the views and knowledge of all three—the desire, form, and formless realms.
For this reason, speaking generally, those who have not severed their roots of goodness vary in degree.
If one severs mundane right view, does one also sever mundane right knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one abandons conventional right knowledge (*saṃvṛti-samyagjñāna*), does one also abandon conventional right view (*saṃvṛti-samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
Answer: It is so.
Who severs mundane right view and right knowledge?
Answer: An Arhat.
Generally speaking, this refers to an Arhat; as for other persons, there are varying degrees.

If one is free from desire for the sphere of nothingness, there is right view and right knowledge regarding the abandonment of the eight stages; up to being free from desire for the realm of desire, yet not yet free from desire for the first dhyāna, there is right view and right knowledge regarding the abandonment of one stage.
Therefore, speaking generally, these are the Arhats; as for others, they exist in varying degrees.
Question: For what reason is this called "conventional" (saṃvṛti)?
Is it because of its being subject to destruction that it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti), or is it because it is the basis for the establishment of craving that it is called "conventional"?
If it were because of being subject to destruction that it is called conventional, then the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) would also be subject to destruction and should therefore be conventional.
If one says that the mundane is so called because it is the basis for this greed, it is likewise the basis for hatred and delusion.
The answer is:
one should speak thus:
Because it is characterized by destruction, it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti).
A question is asked:
If that is so, then the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) is also characterized by destruction; it should therefore also be conventional.
Answer: If one destroys [the defilements], one increases existence (*bhava*).
Although the untainted path (*anāsravamārga*) destroys them, it does not increase existence; rather, it causes existence to diminish.
Furthermore, while destruction can cause the continuity of existence (*bhava*)— characterized by birth, aging, sickness, and death— to persist,
the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), though it involves destruction, is able to sever existence so that birth, aging, sickness, and death do not continue.
Furthermore, if one destroys the path leading to the accumulation of suffering, that is the path leading to birth, aging, sickness, and death.
Although the untainted path is also destroyed, it is the path leading to the cessation of the accumulation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of birth, aging, sickness, and death.

Furthermore, that which destroys this body—the locus for the underlying tendencies of attachment and craving, the foundation for greed, hatred, and delusion, and that which is firmly established within the nature of suffering and its origination as being mixed with impurities, poisons, faults, and dregs—is the conventional;
the Noble Path, being the opposite of this, is not called conventional.
Furthermore, there are those who say that "conventional" (saṃvṛti) refers to the basis upon which craving stands. Question:
If that were so, it would also be the basis upon which hatred and delusion stand.
Answer: If it is said that greed is a basis for standing, it is likewise a basis for standing for anger and delusion. Question:
If it is conventional, is it also disintegrating?
The answer is:
some things are conventional but not disintegrating; thus, one should elaborate extensively on the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is conventional but not subject to destruction consists of the two outflows (āsrava) of the past and future.
That which is subject to destruction but not conventional is the present Truth of the Path (mārgasatya).
That which is both subject to destruction and conventional consists of the two outflows of the present.

"Neither that which is subject to destruction nor that which is conventional" refers to the Noble Truth of the Path (mārga-satya) of the past and future, as well as all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma).
As the Sūtra states:
The Elder Śāriputra went to the place where the Buddha was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is that which is called ‘the conventional’?
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
Because it is subject to disintegration, it is called "conventional" (saṃvṛti).
He asked again:
"What is this disintegration?"
The Buddha told Śrimitri:
"The eye-base is subject to disintegration, and so on, up to the mind-base which is subject to disintegration. He asked:
Why did the World-Honored One say that this is conventional truth?
He replied: It is for the sake of those to be converted.

Because those who are to be transformed must hear and enter into this conventional reality (saṃvṛti) in order to attain awakening and understanding, the Buddha taught that one enters this conventional reality.
Question: What is the difference between "destruction" (bhaṅga) and this?
Answer: "Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) refers to impermanence at the moment of a single instant (*kṣaṇa*); "disintegration" (*vibhava*) refers to impermanence at the time of the body's dissolution.
Furthermore, destruction is subtle impermanence, while disintegration is coarse impermanence.
Furthermore, it destroys the impermanence of internal phenomena and ruins the impermanence of external phenomena.
Furthermore, it destroys the phenomena categorized as sentient beings and ruins the phenomena categorized as non-sentient beings.
What is untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*)?
What is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)? Question:
For what purpose was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
the preceding treatise serves as the fundamental basis for this treatise.
The preceding treatise states as follows:
What is view? What is knowledge?
What is wisdom? It does not state: "What is untainted vision?"
What is untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*)?
Since the preceding treatise serves as the foundation for this treatise, this work is composed in order to provide a detailed analysis thereof.
Furthermore, because one wishes to explain the methods of direct antidotes, it first asks: what is mundane right view (*laukika-samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
What is mundane right knowledge?
What phenomenon is its direct antidote?
It is said that this treatise is composed because [mundane right knowledge] consists of untainted vision and wisdom.
What is untainted vision?
The answer is:
other untainted wisdom not included within the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising.
What are these? They are the eight patiences within the path of seeing, the eight knowledges of the learner, and the right view of the one beyond training.
What is untainted knowledge?
Answer: It is all untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā) other than the various patiences (kṣānti) within the path of seeing (darśanamārga). What, then, is that?
These are the eight knowledges of those in training and those beyond training.
Having already explained their essential nature, we shall now discuss their characteristics of similarity and difference.
Are all untainted views untainted knowledge?
The answer is:
There are cases where it is untainted vision (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) but not untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and so forth, as elaborated in the four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
That which is untainted vision but not untainted knowledge refers to the various patiences (*kṣānti*) within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Why is this? Because that possesses the characteristic of view (dṛṣṭi) but lacks the characteristic of knowledge (jñāna).
This untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) which is not untainted view is precisely the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣaya-jñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpāda-jñāna).
Why is this so? Because that is the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna*) and lacks the characteristic of view (*dṛṣṭi*).

This "outflow-free view" (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) which is also "outflow-free wisdom" (*anāsrava-jñāna*) refers to all other outflow-free discernment (*prajñā*), excluding the various patiences (*kṣānti*) within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*), as well as the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
What is that? It is the eight knowledges of one in training and the right view of one beyond training. Why is this so?
That which is both a characteristic of view (*dṛṣṭi-nimitta*) and a characteristic of knowledge (*jñāna-nimitta*),
yet is neither untainted view (*anāsrava-dṛṣṭi*) nor untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), excludes the aforementioned matters.
Having excluded those dharmas that have already been established, designated, or spoken, the remainder— those not yet established, designated, or spoken— constitute the fourth alternative.

What is that? The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) constitutes these four propositions; all untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) constitutes three propositions; those characterized by being with-outflow (*sāsrava*), having an object (*sālambana*), and having the nature of knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) constitute [the first three]; the remaining formations associated or dissociated [with mind], the other four aggregates, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) constitute the fourth proposition. This is called "excluding as many things as have been mentioned above."
The same applies to the inclusion [of the categories].
If one accomplishes untainted vision (anāsrava-dṛṣṭi), does one also accomplish untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna)?
Answer: Yes.
If one accomplishes untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna), one also accomplishes untainted vision (anāsrava-dṛṣṭi).
Is there any case where one accomplishes untainted vision but does not accomplish untainted knowledge?
Answer: Yes.

There is [possession] at the time of abiding in the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*). Question: The established rule concerns the possession of attainment (*prāpti*), not the abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
Question: Why is "abandonment" not mentioned? Answer:

If one speaks without being prolix regarding the phrasing, that Venerable Kātyāyanīputra did not compose his analysis of the phrasing for even a single moment; however, if what is spoken were prolix regarding the phrasing, it would be like summarizing the entirety of the words and meanings of the waters of the four great oceans.
Furthermore, [defiled phenomena] are abandoned because they possess defilement (*mala*), whereas untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not abandoned because they lack defilement. Question:
If untainted phenomena are not abandoned, how do you reconcile this with the Buddha’s sūtras?
As it is said: "O Bhikṣus!
If you understand the Dharma through the parable of the raft, even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."

The answer is: There are two kinds of abandonment: first, abandonment through the removal of craving (*tṛṣṇā-prahāṇa*); second, abandonment through relinquishment (*tyāga-prahāṇa*). Here, it refers to abandonment through relinquishment.

Although untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) lack abandonment through the removal of craving, they do possess abandonment through relinquishment; it is because of this abandonment through relinquishment that this statement is made.

The bhikṣus had abandoned the noble path and exhausted their outflows; yet, because they remembered [the Buddha’s] kindness, they repeatedly brought the noble path back into presence, thereby undergoing various bodily sufferings, such as headaches and other pains.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke thus:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that whatever was to be accomplished by the Noble Path has already been accomplished; you should now abandon this path and enter into nirvāṇa."
It is like a person who, having crossed a river by means of a raft, continues to carry it on his head or shoulders out of gratitude for its kindness.
Others say to him: "O man!..."
"What ought to be done by means of this raft has all been accomplished; you should now abandon it and go as you please.
It is the same with that [Dharma]. What is this Dharma?
What is non-Dharma?
The answer is:
the teachings of our own school are Dharma; the teachings of external schools are non-Dharma.

The teachings of our own school accord with emptiness, accord with selflessness, and accord with nirvana; since even these teachings should be relinquished, how much more so the verbal expressions of non-Buddhists, which cause the continuity of existence and lead to the succession of birth, aging, sickness, and death?
Furthermore, that which consists of the proper upholding of the collection of names, phrases, and syllables is the Dharma; that which consists of the improper upholding of them is not the Dharma.
If even one who properly upholds the collection of names, phrases, and syllables must relinquish [them], how much more so one who improperly upholds the collection of names, phrases, and syllables?
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

"That which is correctly upheld is called the Dharma; that which is not correctly upheld is called non-Dharma. Since it increases birth and death, it should be abandoned—how much more so that which is non-Dharma."
The Venerable Paśya said:
"To view things correctly is the Dharma; to view them incorrectly is non-Dharma.
Even the Dharma viewed correctly should be relinquished, how much more so that which is viewed incorrectly?"
Furthermore, shame and remorse are the Dharma; lack of shame and remorse are non-Dharma.
The three roots of goodness are the Dharma; the three unwholesome roots are non-Dharma.
The four foundations of mindfulness are the Dharma; the four perversions are non-Dharma.
The five faculties are the Dharma; the five hindrances are non-Dharma.
The six recollections are the Dharma; the six groups of craving are non-Dharma.
The seven factors of enlightenment are the Dharma; the seven latent tendencies are non-Dharma.
The eightfold noble path is the Dharma; the eightfold wrong path is non-Dharma.
The nine successive attainments are the Dharma; the nine fetters are non-Dharma.
The ten paths of wholesome action are the Dharma; the ten paths of unwholesome action are non-Dharma.
If even such dharmas as these should be abandoned, how much more so those that are non-dharmas.
Chapter Two: Knowledge of Others' Minds (*Paracittajñāna*) from the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Section on Knowledge (*Jñāna-kāṇḍa*). What is the knowledge of others' minds?
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
Regarding these chapters and the meaning of their explanations, the *Upadeśa* (Expository Treatise) should be explained here in detail.
A question is asked: For what reason did the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra compose this treatise based upon two types of knowledge?
The answer is:

That venerable one had such a desire and such an intention; he composed his treatise in accordance with that desire and intention, and it does not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

His intention was to compose the treatise based on two types of knowledge (*jñāna*), and thus he discussed those two knowledges—namely, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) and the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*)—because he intended to discuss these two knowledges.

In other places as well, treatises are composed based on two knowledges; for example, in the *Indriya-varga*, there is a discussion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).

In other places as well, treatises are composed based on two knowledges; for example, in the *Samādhi-varga*, there is a discussion of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

In other places, the intention is to discuss the four knowledges (*jñāna*), and the treatise is composed on the basis of these four knowledges. For example, in the *Indriya-varga*, there is a discussion regarding the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path, as it is said:
"If it is the knowledge of suffering, is it the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of suffering?"
Furthermore, if path-knowledge (*mārga-jñāna*) is knowledge of the path that is untainted (*anāsrava*), one intends to discuss the eight knowledges elsewhere;
thus, this treatise is composed based on those eight knowledges, as explained in the *Anuśaya-varga*, the *Samādhi-varga*, and the *Jñāna-varga*.
In other places, the intent is to discuss the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*), and thus the treatise is composed based on those ten knowledges. As it is said:
"By how many knowledges is the eye-faculty known?
It is like a skilled potter who first prepares a pliable lump of clay and places it upon the wheel, then fashions various vessels according to his intention.

That venerable one was likewise; by observing the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) through the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection (*śrutamayī-prajñā* and *cintāmayī-prajñā*), he severed his ignorance regarding the objects of cognition. Therefore, when composing treatises according to his own inclination, he did not contravene the characteristics of phenomena.

Furthermore, these two types of knowledge are, by nature, wisdom acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), because they are obtained through the means of detachment from desire; they are also, by nature, the fruit of the fourfold and fivefold dhyānas, which constitute the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, these two types of knowledge have as their essence the nature of wisdom and the vision of the nature of phenomena.

Moreover, each of these two knowledges takes a single time period as its object: the knowledge of others' minds takes the present time period as its object, while the knowledge of recollecting past lives takes the past time period as its object.
If one were to say that the knowledge of recollecting past lives is both with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava), one should instead say:
"Because these two types of knowledge are both with-outflows and without-outflows."
What is the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:
it is that wisdom which is cultivation, the fruit of cultivation, produced from cultivation, and attained without being lost.
"Cultivation" refers to the essence of cultivation.
"The fruit of cultivation" refers to the fruits of the fourfold and fivefold dhyānas.
"Arising from cultivation" means arising through the practice of cultivation.
"Not losing what has been attained" means not abandoning what has been attained. Question:
Why does it not speak of what has already been attained or what will be attained, but speaks only of attaining now?

Question: When another person’s mind takes form as its object through vitarka and vicāra, does the knowledge of others' minds also know that form which is the object of that other mind?
Answer: [It does not.]
The scriptural text of the foreign Dharma Master states as follows:

"If wisdom knows the mental states and mental factors of another person's mind present before one, as well as their untainted mind (anāsrava-citta), this is called the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)."
Question: Why do the śramaṇas of Kaśmīra not make such a statement? Answer:
One should also speak in this manner; what is the intention behind not doing so?
The answer is:

when one speaks of that which is perceived, observed, and practiced, one describes its essential nature (*svabhāva*), rather than describing the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) that serve as the objects of perception, knowing them as they truly are.
"Mind" refers to the mental factors (*caitasika*), and "phenomena" refers to those enumerated phenomena; one who knows them as they truly are is said to know their objective sphere.
One should speak of a single "knowledge of others' minds," which refers to the supernormal power of knowing others' minds.
It should be explained as twofold, namely: knowing the outflowing and the non-outflowing, as well as the bound and liberated, the fettered and the unfettered.
It should be explained as threefold, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.
It should be explained as fourfold, namely: the fruits of the four dhyānas.
It should be stated as sixfold: namely, the contaminated (sāsrava) of superior, middling, and inferior grades, and the uncontaminated (anāsrava) of superior, middling, and inferior grades.
It should be stated as eightfold: namely, the contaminated and uncontaminated states of the four dhyānas.
It should be stated as ninefold: namely, from the lowest-of-the-low (mṛdu-mṛdu) up to the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra).
One should say there are twelve, meaning that within each of the four dhyānas there are three types—namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
One should say there are eighteen, meaning there are nine with outflows (sāsrava) and nine without outflows (anāsrava).
One should say there are twenty-four: the contaminated states of the first dhyāna are threefold and the uncontaminated states are threefold, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, which is likewise.
One should say there are thirty-six: that is, the first dhyāna has nine types, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, which has nine types.
One should say there are seventy-two types: in the first dhyāna, there are nine types of impure (sāsrava) and nine types of pure (anāsrava), and so it is up to the fourth dhyāna.
Whether considered in terms of their presence within a body or in terms of moments (kṣaṇa), there are immeasurable and boundless instances of the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna).
In this context, the treatise is composed based on a general exposition of one type of knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Question: What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Having already explained the reason for its essential nature, we shall now explain why it is called the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*).
Answer: It is called the knowledge of others' minds because it knows the minds of others. Question:
Question: Since one also knows the factors of number (saṃkhyā-dharma), why is it called only "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: Because it takes the mind as its primary object.

When a practitioner sets their mind on diligently cultivating skillful means with the desire to know the minds of others, they do not set their intention upon the numerical categories [of dharmas], yet they nonetheless know those numerical categories; therefore, it is called the "knowledge of others' minds" (paracittajñāna).
It is like a person who seeks an audience with a king, not seeking an audience with the king’s retinue; yet when they see the king, they also see the retinue.

It is just so in this case. Furthermore, each designation for phenomena has its own specific reason: it may be established by way of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or by way of its antidote (*pratipakṣa*), or by way of its means (*upāya*), or by way of association (*saṃprayoga*), or by way of its basis (*āśraya*), or by way of its range of activity (*gocara*), or by way of its object (*ālambana*), or by way of both its activity and its object.
Regarding its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it refers to such wisdom as that concerning the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four truths (*catuḥ-satya*).
The detailed explanation of the remaining interpretations is as stated above.

Regarding its realm (*dhātu*), that which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) is bound to the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu-yukta*), while that which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) is unbound (*apratisaṃyukta*).
Question: For what reason is there no knowledge of others' minds in the formless realm? Answer:
"Because it is not his field," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the knowledge of others' minds arises dependent upon form; in the formless realm, there is no form.
As for the "stages," these refer to the stages of the four fundamental dhyānas, and do not reside in the peripheral formless stages.
Question: Among the various limits (antāḥ), why is there no knowledge of others' minds? Answer:

This is the supernormal power (*abhijñā*); if there is a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) capable of producing the fruit of supernormal power, then this knowledge exists. This is because such a concentration does not exist within the intermediate states (*antara*).
Question: By what means does the mind of the intermediate dhyāna know the knowledge of others' minds?
The answer is:
Some say it is known by those in the stage of the first dhyāna;
others say it is known by those in the stage of the second dhyāna.
The commentary says: It should be stated thus:
it is known by those belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna.
Why is this so? Because these are the dharmas of a single stage (*bhūmi*).

As for the basis: for one who practices with a body belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the untainted (*anāsrava*) practitioner performs the four modes of practice such as the path (*mārga*), whereas the tainted (*sāsrava*) practitioner does not.

Regarding the objects of focus for the practice: those in the stage of the first dhyāna take as their object the desire realm and the first dhyāna; those in the stage of the second dhyāna take as their object the desire realm up to the second dhyāna; those in the stage of the third dhyāna take as their object the desire realm up to the third dhyāna; and those in the stage of the fourth dhyāna take as their object the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna.
The knowledge of others' minds does not know the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Question:
For what reason does the knowledge of others' minds not know the formless realm?
Answer: The knowledge of others' minds does not know the dharmas of higher stages.

The knowledge of others' minds belonging to the first dhyāna does not know the mind of the second dhyāna, and so on, up to the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the third dhyāna, which does not know the mind of the fourth dhyāna.

Question: When one born in the desire or form realms brings forth an immaterial-sphere concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*) so that it is present before them, can the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) know their mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*)?
Answer: [It cannot.]
I do not know. Why is this? If it is thus when [the fruit] is present, it is likewise when [the cause] is present.
The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) here refer to three foundations of mindfulness, excluding the foundation of mindfulness of the body.

The knowledges (jñāna) refer to four knowledges, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna).
Regarding samādhi: that which is untainted (anāsrava) is associated with the path of wishlessness (apraṇihita), whereas that which is tainted (sāsrava) is not so associated.

Regarding the faculties (indriya): it is universally associated with three faculties, namely, the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya), the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya), and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
As for "worlds," they exist within the three periods of time.

Regarding conditions pertaining to the three periods: those of the past condition the past; those of the present condition the present; those of the future that do not arise condition all three periods; and those of the future that will certainly arise condition the future.
Regarding the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral: the wholesome takes the wholesome as its object; the unwholesome and the neutral take all three types as their objects.
As for those bound to the three realms and those that are unbound: the contaminated (*sāsrava*) are bound to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), while the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) are unbound.
"Conditioned by that which is bound to the three realms and that which is unbound" means being conditioned by the desire realm, the form realm, and the unbound.
"Those who are in training, those who have completed their training, and those who are neither in training nor have completed their training" refers to these three types.
Regarding those conditioned by the trainee (śaikṣa), the non-trainee (aśaikṣa), and that which is neither trainee nor non-trainee: all three types serve as conditions.

As for those abandoned through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga-prahātavya), those abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya), and those not abandoned: the contaminated (sāsrava) are abandoned through the path of cultivation, while the uncontaminated (anāsrava) are not abandoned.
Regarding those that are not abandoned by the path of seeing or the path of cultivation, they all take the three types as their objects.
As for "taking names as objects" or "taking meanings as objects," this refers to taking meanings as objects.
Regarding those that take as objects one's own body, another's body, or that which is neither, these take another's body as their object.
Regarding "attaining detachment through these skillful means": these skillful means are themselves detachment.
One attains the first dhyāna by becoming detached from the desires of the desire realm, and so on, up to attaining the fourth dhyāna by becoming detached from the desires of the third dhyāna.

As for skillful means (*upāya*): for a Buddha, skillful means manifests; for a Pratyekabuddha, it does not manifest through skillful means; and for a Śrāvaka, it manifests either through inferior, middling, or superior skillful means.
Question: What is the skillful means for the knowledge of others' minds? Answer:
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:

"A beginner first grasps the characteristics of his own body, thinking: 'If the body has such-and-such a form, then the mind has such-and-such a state; if the mind has such-and-such a state, then the body has such-and-such a form.'"

Having apprehended the physical characteristics of one's own body, one also apprehends the physical characteristics of another's body; if another's body possesses such a form, then it possesses such a mind, and if it possesses such a mind, then the body possesses such a form.
Having grasped such signs, he reflects:
"What is this sentient being observing now? What is it discriminating?
While reflecting in this way, he knows it as it truly is: "This sentient being is thinking thus; it is discriminating thus."
This is called the knowledge of others' minds.
The *Saṃparigraha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* also says:
"What is the skillful means of the knowledge of others' minds?"
Answer: One contemplates the five aggregates of clinging as suffering, empty, impermanent, and non-self; such contemplation constitutes untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Question:
If the knowledge of others' minds takes the four truths as its object, why is it said that it only takes the truth of suffering as its object?
The answer is:
one should know that when it is said that [the knowledge of others' minds] takes all [truths] as its object but this is not stated, this teaching is incomplete (sāvaśeṣa).

Furthermore, this explains the initial application for entering the Dharma; if one speaks of the knowledge conditioned by suffering, it should be understood that this also includes the knowledge conditioned by the other [truths]. Question:
What is the difference between the former application and this latter application?
Answer: The previously explained skillful means extend from the contaminated (*sāsrava*) to the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), whereas the skillful means here explained are exclusively uncontaminated.
Furthermore, these subsequent skillful means are superior, sublime, luminous, and pure, excelling those preceding skillful means.
Question: If the eye does not see forms, can it know the minds of others? Answer:
One can know it,
because one hears its sound with the ear.
If the eye does not see forms and the ear does not hear sounds, would one be able to know another's mind?
Answer: Yes, one knows it because one smells its fragrance with the nose.
If the eyes, ears, and nose do not see forms, hear sounds, or smell fragrances, can one still know the minds of others?
The answer is:
Yes, one knows, because one knows tastes with the tongue.
If one does not see forms, hear sounds, smell odors, or know tastes, can one still know the minds of others?
Answer: Yes, one knows [the other's mind] because of physical contact.
If one does not see forms and so forth, and the body does not perceive touch, can one still know another's mind?
Answer: Some say that [the Buddha] did not know. Why is this?
Because the knowledge of others' minds is dependent upon form (*rūpa*).
The critique states:
One should speak as follows:
One does not know [the minds of others] during the stage of preparation (*upāya*), but one can know them at the time of fulfillment. Question:
For what reason does the knowledge of others' minds arise based on form (*rūpa*) during the stage of preparation?
Answer: Because one enters the subtle by means of the coarse.
At the time of the skillful means (*upāya*) of the knowledge of others' minds, it takes oneself as its object; at the time of fulfillment, it does not take oneself as its object.
Question: For what reason does the knowledge of others' minds take oneself as its object during the stage of skillful means, yet not take oneself as its object when it is perfected? Answer:
The knowledge of others' minds does not take as its object the objects or spheres of activity of another's mind.
If the knowledge of others' minds were to take as its object the objects or spheres of activity of another's mind, it could also be called the knowledge of one's own mind.

Regarding the fifteen types of tainted mental states and mental factors previously acquired: there are three kinds in the desire realm—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and likewise, there are three kinds up through the fourth dhyāna.

The impure knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna knows the three types of mind and mental factors of the desire realm, as well as the impure minds and mental factors of the stages below the first dhyāna.
The middling [level] knows the three types of the desire realm and the two types—lower and middling—of the first dhyāna.
The superior [level] knows the three types of the desire realm and the three types of the first dhyāna.
As with the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna, those of superior capacity know fifteen kinds.
Just as there were originally fifteen kinds of outflow-tainted minds that had previously arisen, there are likewise fifteen kinds of outflow-tainted minds that have never before been attained.

The untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is of twelve kinds: there are three types in the stage of the first dhyāna—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—and this is likewise for each stage up to the fourth dhyāna.
An untainted mind in a lower stage of the second dhyāna knows the untainted minds in the lower stages of the first dhyāna, and it also knows [the untainted minds of] the second dhyāna itself.

The inferior [level] knows the second dhyāna; the middling knows both the inferior and middling types of the first and second dhyānas; the superior knows all three types—inferior, middling, and superior—of the first and second dhyānas, and knows from the second dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna. The superior [level] knows twelve kinds of untainted (anāsrava) minds and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma).

Question: Why is it that an impure knowledge of others' minds directed toward a lower level knows the three types [of mind] of that lower level as well as those of its own lower level, whereas an impure knowledge of others' minds directed toward a lower level knows the mental states and mental concomitants of that lower level as well as those of its own lower level, but not those of the middle or upper levels?
Answer: Impure mental states and their associated mental factors are distinct, and pure mental states and their associated mental factors are distinct.
Within a single body, there may be three types of impure and pure mental states and their associated mental factors, distinguished by way of their faculties (indriya).
If one possesses inferior faculties, then there are no middling or superior faculties; likewise, if one possesses superior faculties, then there are no middling or inferior faculties.
The knowledge of others' minds does not know those of a higher stage, superior faculties, or superior persons.

Regarding "superior stages": the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna does not know the mind and mental factors of the second dhyāna stage, and so on, up to the point where that belonging to the third dhyāna stage does not know the mind and mental factors of the fourth dhyāna stage.
Regarding superior faculties: one with a lower faculty does not know the mind and mental factors of those with middle or superior faculties through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Regarding superior persons: one who is still in training (*śaikṣa*) does not know the mind and mental factors of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) through the knowledge of others' minds.
Question: Does the knowledge of others' minds possessed by all those beyond training (aśaikṣa) fully know the mind and mental factors (citta-caitasika-dharma) of those still in training (śaikṣa)?
Answer: No.
They do not know it.
One liberated by occasion does not know the mind of one who has attained vision, and one who has attained vision does not know the mind of one liberated by occasion. Why is this?
Because those with vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) possess superior faculties, they are superior to those liberated by time (samayavimukta). Question:

When a person in training (śaikṣa) brings forth the mind of the second dhyāna into the present, and a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) brings forth the mind of the first dhyāna into the present, do these minds mutually cognize one another?
He replied: "I do not know. Why is this?"
The person beyond training (aśaikṣa) excels the person in training (śaikṣa), and the person in training excels the person beyond training in terms of their stage.

When a śrāvaka brings forth the mind and mental factors of the second dhyāna into the present, and a Buddha brings forth the mind and mental factors of the first dhyāna into the present, do they mutually know one another?
He replied: "I do not know. Why is this?"
The Buddha excels the śrāvakas in terms of faculties, while the śrāvaka excels the Buddha in terms of stages.
In the desire realm, there are four types of transformative minds (*nirmāṇacitta*), namely those which are the fruits of the first dhyāna up to the fourth dhyāna.
Does the knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of the first dhyāna know these four types of mind?
The answer is:
some say that it does know them.
Why is this? Because these are all states of mind belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that one knows only the fruit of the first dhyāna, while the others are not known.
Why is this so? Just as one who does not know the cause cannot know the fruit, so too,

regarding the Buddha’s untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and his previously unattained tainted mind (*sāsrava-citta*), there is no one capable of knowing them through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
Having already possessed a mind with outflows (*sāsrava-citta*), the Buddha desires that others know it, and they know it.

If the Buddha desires that those of dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*) know it while those of sharp faculties (*tīkṣṇa-indriya*) do not, then those of dull faculties know it and those of sharp faculties do not.
If the Buddha wishes for Sāvadā to know while Śāriputra does not, then Sāvadā knows and Śāriputra does not.
If he wishes for animals to know while humans do not, then the animals know and the humans do not.
How is this known? There is a sutra that says:
When the Buddha was staying at the Kiṅka Monastery in the city of Nadīkāśyapa, many bhikṣus placed their bowls in the open air, and the bowl of the World-Honored One was likewise in the open air.
At that time, a monkey came down from a śāla tree and approached the place where many alms bowls were kept.
Fearing that the bowls might be broken, the bhikṣus all gathered together to ward it off.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do not prevent this monkey; it will not break your bowls.
Thereupon, the monkey took the World-Honored One’s bowl, slowly returned to climb up a tree, filled it with flowing honey, and offered it to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it because it was mixed with insects.
At that time, the World-Honored One gave rise to a mundane thought, wishing to remove the insects.
Then the monkey, immediately understanding the Buddha’s intention, withdrew to one side and removed the insects from the honey before returning to the World-Honored One.
The World-Honored One did not accept it because it had not been purified.
The World-Honored One then gave rise to a mundane thought:
"If this monkey were to purify it with water, I would then accept it."
At that time, the monkey immediately understood the Buddha’s mind and purified [the honey] with water.
Because it was thus purified, the Buddha accepted it.
Then, because the World-Honored One had accepted his honey, the monkey felt immeasurable joy in his heart; he leaped for joy and began to dance as he retreated, falling into a pit and dying.
He was reborn among humans, left the household life to join the Buddha’s Dharma, and attained the path of Arhatship, becoming known as Māṭhava Sāttha.
Because of this matter, the Venerable Pāveyya composed a verse in praise of the Buddha:
“If one wishes to let gods and humans know the Buddha’s mind, He is able to know everything according to their thoughts.”
"If one enters the profound and wondrous meditative concentrations of the various dhyānas, there is no one who can know the Buddha's mind.
It is asked: Does the Buddha possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) such that he can know the Buddha's own mind?
Answer: Some say that it is not obtained. Why is this?
Because there are not two Buddhas in the world.
Furthermore, there are those who say that [the Pratyekabuddha] attains it because he is capable of taking it as an object, though it does not arise before him.
A Pratyekabuddha who appears alone in the world, like the horn of a *ṛkṣa* deer, is no different from a Buddha.

If one were to say this, then among those who have appeared in the world, there are those with the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) directed toward the mind of a pratyekabuddha; they can take it as an object and can also cause it to arise and manifest before them.
Śrāvakas possess the knowledge of others' minds that cognizes the minds of Śrāvakas; they are able to take such minds as objects and are able to bring them forth into manifestation.

However, regarding the uncontaminated minds of a Buddha, his never-before-attained contaminated minds, and the minds belonging to the formless realm, there is no knowledge of others' minds capable of cognizing these minds.
Sentient beings may either arise or cease.

Regarding those who arise—namely, sentient beings born in the desire realm or the form realm, as well as ordinary persons born in the formless realm—will they necessarily attain the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: One should obtain it for two reasons: first, by virtue of being able to take it as an object; second, by virtue of its manifest activity.
As for those who have ceased—that is, noble ones born in the formless realm or those who have entered nirvana—would they still possess the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: It should not be attained.
Furthermore, there are those who say it should be attained because it can serve as an object of cognition (*ālambana*), but not by way of its manifest activity.
The critique states:
One should not say that [it] will be attained.
If it does not manifest before one, one should certainly say that it is not attained; one should not say that it is attained when it does not manifest before one.
There are objects of experience known by the Buddha’s knowledge of others' minds, which are objects of experience not known by Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas.
This is known by the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, but not known by Śrāvakas.
There is a sphere that is known by the knowledge of others' minds of Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that within the Snowy Mountains there are places where monkeys cannot go, nor can humans go."
There are places where monkeys can travel but humans cannot;
there are places where both monkeys and humans can travel.
The Snowy Mountains are like the realm [of practice]; the monkey is like a pratyekabuddha; and the human is like a śrāvaka.
This meaning shall now be clarified. There are fifteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) perceives similar dharmas: it knows the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as contaminated and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as uncontaminated; it knows what has already been attained as already attained and what has not yet been attained as not yet attained; it knows the portion of dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣa*) as the portion of dharma-knowledge and the portion of subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna-pakṣa*) as the portion of subsequent knowledge.

Regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), a Śrāvaka perceives two moments of mind during the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); a Pratyekabuddha perceives four moments; and a Buddha perceives them one by one in succession. Why is this so?
Pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas manifest through skillful means (*upāya*), whereas Buddhas do not manifest through skillful means.

When a practitioner enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they apply skillful means; when a śrāvaka enters it, they apply skillful means for the sake of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).

When a practitioner has already entered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), a Śrāvaka who has given rise to the mental state of the "knowledge-part" (*dharmajñāna-bhāga*) of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) can know two moments of mind in that practitioner, namely: the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmakṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).
When the practitioner enters the stage of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), the śrāvaka applies the preparatory means for the subsequent-knowledge mind that knows the minds of others.

Once the practitioner has entered the stage of subsequent knowledge, the śrāvaka gives rise to the desire for the subsequent-knowledge mind that knows the minds of others to manifest; through the subsequent-receptivity to suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*), he then attains the subsequent-knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*).

The practitioner performs the preparatory application for the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), while the pratyekabuddha performs the preparatory application for the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) as a portion of the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*).

Once the practitioner has entered the path of seeing, the pratyekabuddha brings forth the knowledge of others' minds as a portion of the knowledge of phenomena so that it becomes present, thereby knowing two moments of the practitioner's mind: namely, the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmakṣānti*) and the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñāna*).

When the practitioner enters the stage of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-pakṣa*), the pratyekabuddha employs the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) belonging to the stage of subsequent knowledge as a preparatory means.

Once the practitioner has entered the stage of subsequent knowledge, the pratyekabuddha gives rise to the desire for the supernormal knowledge of others' minds belonging to the stage of subsequent knowledge to manifest before him; through this, he knows the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*), and subsequently knows the subsequent patience regarding cessation (*nirodhe 'nvaya-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodhe 'nvaya-jñāna*).
The Buddha does not employ expedient means for all his meritorious qualities to manifest before him.

Just as a practitioner gives rise to the vision of the path (*darśanamārga*) one by one in succession as it manifests, the World-Honored One knows them one by one in succession through his knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
The Buddha knows the three kinds of paths through both their general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) and their specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).

The Pratyekabuddha also knows the three kinds of paths; he knows the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha paths through both their general and specific characteristics, but he knows the Buddha-path only through its general characteristic and not through its specific characteristics.

The śrāvaka also knows the three kinds of paths; regarding the path of the śrāvaka, he knows it through both its general and specific characteristics, whereas regarding the paths of the pratyekabuddha and the Buddha, he knows them only through their general characteristics, not their specific characteristics.
Question: When a śrāvaka perceives the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), does he also perceive the path of the pratyekabuddha and the Buddha?
If he does perceive them, why is it that the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) does not know them?
If one does not see [the Buddha], how can one obtain unshakable faith directed toward him?
The answer is:
One should explain it in this way:
[The interlocutor] sees this and asks:
"If that is so, why does the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) not know [them]?"
Answer: This is because the knowledge of others' minds is known through its specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*),

whereas it is by means of general characteristic wisdom (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-jñāna*) that one knows the minds and mental factors (*citta-caitasika-dharma*) of all sentient beings through the knowledge of others' minds belonging to even a single sentient being.
Does "knowing the time" mean knowing the essence of feeling, or does it mean knowing the various moments of feeling?
If it were merely knowing the essence of feeling, how could one know those other feelings that have not been perceived?
If one knows the various sensations of each moment (*kṣaṇa*), how is it that one's own body is not manifold?
If the body were manifold, then the essence of the knowledge of one's own and others' minds would consist of twenty-one types of knowing the sensation of a single sentient being in a single moment.
As it is with the experience of one moment, so it is with all other moments of experience.
As it is with the moment of experience, so it is with all other moments of mind and mental factors.
Just as the mental states and mental factors of one sentient being are so, those of all other sentient beings are likewise.

Since the mental states and mental factors known by my knowledge of others' minds are many, and since all sentient beings possess mental states and mental factors as numerous as mine, their supporting bodies should also be numerous.
Answer: It should be stated thus:
one knows the essence of feeling.
Question: If that is so, how does one know those other sensations that are not known? Answer:
If one knows other feelings, that is impossible; when knowing, one knows only that which is known.
Furthermore, there are those who say that one knows feelings moment by moment (*kṣaṇa*).
A question is asked:
If this is so, why is it that one's own body is not manifold?
The answer is:
what fault is there in being manifold?

Why is this? Just as my own substance of knowledge of others' minds possesses twenty-one kinds [of aspects] by which it knows the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, so too does the substance of the knowledge of others' minds belonging to all sentient beings possess twenty-one kinds [of aspects] by which it knows my mind and mental factors.
Therefore, there is no fault. Question:
Does the knowledge of others' minds take the past as its object, the future as its object, or the present as its object?
Answer: It takes the present as its object. Question:
If that were so, how would one reconcile what is stated in the Sūtra?
For example, it says:
"Past and future dharmas are known by nine knowledges."
Answer: The original sutra should have stated:
"Past and future dharmas are known by eight knowledges, excluding the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of others' minds."
What is the intention behind not stating [this]? It is stated in accordance with conditions (*pratyaya*).

Regarding the past, it takes the past as its condition; regarding the future, it takes the future as its condition. If it were as previously stated, the knowledge of others' minds would know three moments: namely, the present moment, that which has just ceased, and that which is about to arise.
The sūtra should have stated it thus: Question:
Does the knowledge of others' minds take one dharma as its object, or does it take many dharmas as its object?
If [the mind] takes only a single dharma as its object, how is the statement in the Sūtra to be reconciled? As it says:
"One knows a mind with desire, as it truly is, to be a mind with desire."
If one simultaneously knows desire and also knows the mind, would this not be knowing multiple dharmas?
Furthermore, how are the explanations in other sūtras to be reconciled?
For example, it is said:
When the World-Honored One recollects, he thoroughly knows the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of monks.
If he takes many dharmas as his object, how is it that their essence constitutes the three foundations of mindfulness?
Answer: It should be stated thus:
it takes a single dharma as its object.
Question: If that is so, how are the Buddha’s sūtras to be reconciled?
For instance, it is said:
To know, as it truly is, a mind possessed of desire.
The answer is:
because the mind is associated with desire, it is called "a mind possessed of desire. One might know the desire but not the mind, or one might know the mind but not the desire.
It is like observing a soiled garment: if one observes the soil, one does not observe the garment; if one observes the garment, one does not observe the soil.
That case is also like this.
How, then, are other sūtras to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"When the World-Honored One brings [the past] to mind, he fully knows the thoughts in the minds of the Saṃgha.
He replied:
He knows them through the knowledge of characteristics by analogy, not through the knowledge of others' minds.

The World-Honored One, having observed the mind of one bhikṣu abiding in the path of tranquility with the knowledge of others' minds, subsequently knows the minds of all the bhikṣus to be likewise through the knowledge of characteristics by analogy.

Furthermore, some say that the World-Honored One does not know [the minds of others] through the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), nor does he know them through the knowledge of signs (*anvayajñāna*), but rather knows them through the knowledge resulting from resolve (*praṇidhijñāna*).

Others say that the World-Honored One does not know them through the knowledge of others' minds, the knowledge of signs, or the knowledge resulting from resolve; rather, when the World-Honored One attains the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), he attains for the first time the unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) mind and mental factors of the desire realm. Without entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and without manifesting supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), at the moment of recollection, he fully knows the minds of the entire community of monks (*bhikṣusaṃgha*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that one knows many dharmas.
It is asked:
If this is so, how is it that their substance constitutes the three foundations of mindfulness?

Answer: At the time of the initial application of skillful means, these are the three applications of mindfulness; when fully perfected, they are the application of mindfulness to phenomena through universal objectification (*sarvālambana-dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*). Evaluation:
It should be stated as follows: All knowledge of others' minds takes a single dharma as its object; it is a contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

It takes the present as its object, takes another person as its object, and takes both mind and mental factors (*citta-caitasika*) as its objects. It does not exist within the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), but exists within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). It is not associated with the samādhis of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or signlessness (*animitta*), nor is it subsumed under the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*) or the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*). Knowledge of others' minds does not exist within the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The Dharma should be thus.
What is the knowledge of recollecting past lives?
The answer is:

If a wisdom is cultivated, is the fruit of cultivation, arises from cultivation, and is attained without being lost—by means of this wisdom one recollects such characteristics of countless past lives; this is called the knowledge of recollecting former existences.
Regarding the questions and answers herein, they are explained in detail as in the case of the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*).
What is meant by "such characteristics" and "such appearance"?
The answer is:
That which has such characteristics is the prior-time existence (*pūrvakālabhava*); that which has such appearance is the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, there are those who say that such characteristics belong to the intermediate existence, while such appearance belongs to the prior-time existence.
Why is this? Because previously there were things that could be pointed out, such as the distinct appearances of these: a kṣatriya, a brāhmaṇa, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, as stated in the sūtra.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If there are such characteristics and such appearances that can be designated, it is called the 'form-body' (rūpakāya).
If there were no such characteristics or such appearances to be designated, would there still be contact through resistance (pratigha-sparśa)?"
He replied: "No. That sutra states:
The internal bases (ādhyātmikāyatana) are the characteristics (lakṣaṇa), and the external bases (bāhyāyatana) are the appearances (ākṛti).
Furthermore, there are those who say that in that sutra, the internal bases are the appearances and the external bases are the characteristics. Why is this so?
Because they are internal bases (*ādhyātmikāyatana*), the various distinctions among the characteristics of consciousness are explained.
As it is said:
"Excluding the aforementioned matters."
There is no such characteristic within this; therefore, it is excluded.
As it is said:
"If one enters the first dhyāna by means of such a characteristic and such a mark."
Such characteristics are the skillful means; such appearances are the objects of focus.
As the verse says:
"If one accomplishes the eight knowledges and the sixteen aspects,"
"Just like Jāmbūnada gold, no one can speak of its faults.
Herein, wisdom is described by means of its characteristics.
"Countless past births" refers to the sphere of the knowledge that recollects former lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).

One should speak of the knowledge of past lives as being attained in a single moment; it is called the supernormal power of recollecting past lives, the clarity of recollecting past lives, and the power of recollecting past lives.
One should further speak of two types: namely, that which has already been attained and that which has not yet been attained.
It should be said that there are three, namely:
superior, middling, and inferior. It should be said that there are four, namely: the fruit of the first dhyāna up to the fruit of the fourth dhyāna.
It should be said that there are six: three types already obtained and three types not yet obtained, namely: superior, middling, and inferior.

It should be stated that there are eight; for the stage of the first dhyāna there are two kinds, namely, those already attained and those not yet attained, and so it is likewise up to the stage of the fourth dhyāna.
One should say there are nine, namely from the lowest-of-the-low up to the highest-of-the-high.
One should say there are twelve: the first dhyāna has three types, namely high, medium, and low, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, which is likewise.
One should say there are eighteen, namely nine kinds that have already been attained and nine kinds not yet attained.
One should say there are twenty-four: in the first dhyāna there are six kinds, namely three kinds already attained and three kinds not yet attained; this applies likewise up to the fourth dhyāna.
One should say there are thirty-six: there are nine types in the first dhyāna, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, which is likewise.
One should say there are seventy-two: there are nine types previously attained in the first dhyāna and nine types not yet attained, and so on up to the fourth dhyāna, which is likewise.
Whether it be in terms of existing throughout one's entire life or in terms of a single moment, there are immeasurable and boundless instances of knowledge of past lives;
herein, for the sake of brevity, the discussion is conducted by referring to this knowledge of past lives as "a single instance."
Question: What is the essential nature of the wisdom that recollects past lives? Answer:
Its essential nature is wisdom; because the power of mindfulness is predominant, it is called "knowledge of past lives.
Just as the essential nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is wisdom, yet they are called "foundations of mindfulness" because the power of mindfulness is predominant.
Just as the essential nature of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*) is wisdom, it is called "mindfulness of breathing" because the power of mindfulness is predominant.
Likewise, the essential nature of mindfulness of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) is wisdom, and it is called "mindfulness of past lives" because the power of mindfulness is predominant.

Excluding the perception of form, the essential nature of the perception of the realm of infinite space is wisdom; because the power of perception is predominant, it is called the "perception of the realm of infinite space.
Likewise, the essential nature of the knowledge of recollecting past lives is wisdom; because the power of mindfulness is predominant, it is called the "knowledge of recollecting past lives."
"This is the essential nature of the knowledge of recollecting past lives," and so forth, as explained at length.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 49; *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Scroll 50.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats;
translated by the Northern Liang Indian *śramaṇa* Buddhabhadra together with Daotai and others.

The Second Part of the Second Chapter on the Knowledge of Others' Minds in the Jñāna-varga. Having already explained the essential nature (*svabhāva*) and the reasons [for its existence], we shall now explain why it is called the "knowledge of recollecting past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
Answer: It is called the knowledge of recollecting past lives because it recollects the aggregates (*skandha*) of previous existences.
As for "realm" (*dhātu*), it refers to the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Question: For what reason is there no knowledge of past lives within the formless realm? Answer:
"Because it is not its cause," and so forth, as explained at length.
Furthermore, the knowledge that recollects previous lives arises dependent on form; since there is no form in the formless realm, such knowledge does not exist there.
As for its stage, it resides in the stages of the four fundamental dhyānas, not within the various peripheral formless attainments.

Why is this so? Because if there is a state of meditative concentration that serves as the basis for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), then in that state there is the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*).

Since such a basis for supernormal powers does not exist within the various limitative states (*antagrāha*) or the formless realms (*ārūpya*), there is no knowledge of recollecting past lives therein.
Question: By means of which stage does one who possesses the knowledge of recollecting past lives recollect the intermediate dhyānas? Answer:
Some say it is by means of the first dhyāna; others say it is by means of the second dhyāna.
The critique states:
one should speak thus:
Regarding those in the first dhyāna:
why is this so? Because they belong to the same stage (bhūmi).
As for the "body as the basis," it relies upon the bodies of the desire and form realms.
As for the "practitioner," there is no place of practice.

As for the "object of focus," one uses the mindfulness of past lives in the first dhyāna to know the five aggregates of previous births in the first dhyāna and the desire realm; likewise, one in the fourth dhyāna knows the five aggregates of previous births from the desire realm up to the fourth dhyāna, but does not know those of the formless realm.
Question: For what reason does the knowledge that recollects past lives not know the formless realm? Answer:
The wisdom that recollects past lives does not know the dharmas of higher stages.

One in the first dhyāna does not know the five aggregates of the past lives of the second dhyāna, and so on, up to one in the third dhyāna who does not know the five aggregates of the past lives of the fourth dhyāna.
In the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), there is no knowledge of recollecting past lives. Question:

When one born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu) brings forth a formless absorption (ārūpyasamādhi) into the present, is it possible to know past lives through that knowledge?
He replied: "I do not know. Why is this?"
As it is with not knowing the fruit, so it is with the cause. Question:
If the knowledge that recollects past lives does not know the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), how is this reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
As it is said:

"The Blessed One, throughout his countless past births in various places—whether born in the realm of form or the formless realm, or with perception or without perception—is able to recall all such characteristics of those countless past births."
Question: What is said to be form (rūpa)?
And what is not form?
Answer: "Form" refers to that which exists in the previous time; "formlessness" refers to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Question:
If that were the case, then even śrāvakas would be able to know it; what difference would there be from the Buddha?
Furthermore, some say that "form" refers to the desire realm and the form realm, while "formlessness" refers to the formless realm.
Question: If that is so, how does the World-Honored One know the formless realm? Answer:
[One] knows by means of inferential characteristics (*anvaya-nimitta*).
A question is asked:
"If that is so, since Śrāvakas can also know by means of inferential characteristics, what difference is there between them and the Buddha?"
The answer is:
Just as non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) contemplate past lives, if they do not perceive [a being] within the desire realm or the form realm, they declare that it has been annihilated.

When śrāvakas contemplate past lives, if they do not perceive [a being] within the desire or form realms for more than twenty thousand kalpas, they say that this sentient being has been born in the sphere of empty space (ākāśāyatana), yet that sentient being may still have not exhausted their lifespan in the higher stages.

If one does not see them after forty thousand kalpas have passed, it is said that these beings are born in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*); yet those beings may have been reborn in the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), or they may still have their lifespan remaining in a higher stage.

If one does not see them after sixty thousand kalpas have passed, it is said that these beings are born in the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*); yet those beings may have been reborn three times in the Sphere of Infinite Space, or once or half a time in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, or they may still have their lifespan remaining in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

If one does not see them after eighty thousand kalpas have passed, it is said that these beings are born in the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception; yet those beings may have been reborn four times in the Sphere of Infinite Space, twice in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, or once or half a time in the Sphere of Nothingness.

World-Honored One, when the Blessed One wishes to observe the formless realm, he contemplates the minds of sentient beings at the moment of death as they pass away from the desire and form realms; he knows that such a being is born in the sphere of infinite space, such a being is born in the sphere of infinite consciousness, such a being is born in the sphere of nothingness, and such a being is born in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. He also knows which beings will complete their full lifespan and which beings will not complete their lifespan.

If one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the desire or form realms, observing the mind at the time of birth, they know that this sentient being died from the sphere of infinite space, or even from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they know whether this sentient being has exhausted their lifespan there, or whether this sentient being has not exhausted their lifespan there.
The non-Buddhists’ inferential knowledge based on signs perceives things as being subject to annihilation;
the knowledge based on signs known by the śrāvakas may correspond to the actual state of things or may not correspond to it;
