Furthermore, there are those who exhaust the fetters of the three realms through the samādhis of emptiness, suffering, origination, and wishlessness; and there are those who exhaust the fetters of the three realms through the samādhis of signlessness, the path, and wishlessness. If one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the samādhis of emptiness, suffering, origination, and wishlessness, one cultivates three kinds of wisdom; if one exhausts the fetters of the three realms through the samādhis of signlessness, the path, and wishlessness, one cultivates two kinds of wisdom.
Furthermore, some enter the noble path through concentration, while others enter the noble path through wisdom. Those who enter the noble path through concentration cultivate three kinds of wisdom.

The same applies to the explanations regarding the path of concentration-wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā-mārga*), the path with more concentration or more wisdom, the path suitable for concentration or the path suitable for wisdom, dull faculties or sharp faculties, and the power of conditions (*pratyaya-bala*) or the power of causes (*hetu-bala*).

Furthermore, there are those who cultivate the mind through meditative concentration and attain liberation through wisdom, cultivating two kinds of wisdom; and there are those who cultivate the mind through wisdom and attain liberation through meditative concentration, cultivating three kinds of wisdom.

Furthermore, there are those who attain inner tranquility of mind but do not attain the dharma of insight-wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*); there are also those who attain both inner tranquility of mind and the dharma of insight-wisdom. The former cultivates two kinds of wisdom, while the latter cultivates three kinds of wisdom.
Furthermore, if a person accomplishes four dharmas, it is truly rare:
first, to draw near to virtuous friends;
second, to hear the Dharma from them.
Third, internal right reflection;
fourth, practice in accordance with the Dharma.
If one accomplishes the first two types of dharmas, one cultivates two kinds of wisdom; if one accomplishes the latter two types of dharmas, one cultivates three kinds of wisdom.

Furthermore, there are those who hear much Dharma from others, and there are those who engage frequently in internal correct reflection. Those who hear much Dharma from others cultivate two kinds of wisdom; those who engage frequently in internal correct reflection cultivate three kinds of wisdom.

Some have a predominance of the wholesome root of non-attachment, while others have a predominance of the wholesome root of non-delusion. Those with a predominance of the wholesome root of non-attachment cultivate two kinds of wisdom; those with a predominance of the wholesome root of non-delusion cultivate three kinds of wisdom.
"My births have been exhausted"—this is called the knowledge of exhaustion;
"the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence"—this is called the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "My births have been exhausted and the holy life has been established"—this is called the knowledge of exhaustion;
"what was to be done has been accomplished and there will be no further existence"—this is called the knowledge of non-arising.
Furthermore, "my births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished"—this is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
"There will be no further existence"—this is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Question: There is no Arhat who, after the moment of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), gives rise to the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), let alone many such moments.
Why, then, is it said that "my births are exhausted, the holy life has been established, and what was to be done has been accomplished" constitutes the knowledge of exhaustion?
Answer: Although it is but a single moment, there are three aspects to it; therefore, this statement is made.
The Venerable Vasu said:

To speak in this manner is not to speak of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), nor to speak of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), nor to speak of the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*); rather, this is a statement of praise for the Arhat:
"For the Arhat, birth is exhausted, the holy life is established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence."
Furthermore, "my births have been exhausted" refers to the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna);
"the holy life has been established" refers to the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna);
"what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna).
"Not subject to further existence" is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Furthermore, "my births have been exhausted" is called the knowledge of the origin;
"the holy life has been established" is called the knowledge of the path.
"Having done what was to be done" refers to the knowledge of cessation;
"no further existence is to be undergone" refers to the knowledge of suffering.
The same applies to the statement regarding the realization of exhaustion.
Furthermore, "my births have been exhausted" refers to the abandonment of the origin [of suffering];
"the holy life has been established" refers to the cultivation of the path;
and "what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the realization of cessation.
"Not subject to further existence" is said to be the knowledge of suffering.
Furthermore, "my births have been exhausted" is said to be the abandonment of the cause;
"the holy life has been established" is said to be the cultivation of the path.
"Having done what was to be done" refers to the attainment of the fruit;
"no further existence is to be undergone" refers to the knowledge of the essence.
Furthermore, "my births have been exhausted" refers to the knowledge of origination (*samudaya-jñāna*).
"The holy life has been established" refers to the knowledge of the path;
"what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to the knowledge of cessation;
"there is no further existence" refers to the knowledge of suffering.
Furthermore, "my births are exhausted" refers to the wishlessness regarding the origin [of suffering];
"the holy life has been established" refers to the wishlessness regarding the path;
"what was to be done has been accomplished" refers to signlessness.
"Not being subject to further existence" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
Question: Why is it called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*)?

Is it because the object-condition (*ālambana*) has ceased that it is called "knowledge of cessation" (*kṣayajñāna*), or is it because the afflictions have ceased within the body that it is called "knowledge of cessation"?
If it were because the object-condition has ceased that it is called "knowledge of cessation," then the knowledge of extinction (*nirodhajñāna*) should also be "knowledge of cessation."

If one were to define "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*) as that which arises within the body when afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted, then the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) would also have to be considered knowledge of exhaustion.
The answer is: it should be stated thus:
It is called the knowledge of destruction (*kṣayajñāna*) because it arises within the body when the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted. Question:
If that is so, then the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) and the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) should also be the knowledge of destruction.
Answer: If a wisdom exists at the very beginning and is present in all [stages], it is called the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Although the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) is present in all [stages], it does not exist at the beginning.
The knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) does not exist at the beginning, nor is it possessed by all;
whereas the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) exists at the beginning and is possessed by all. Question:
Beyond the sixteen noble practices, is there further untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*)?
The question and answer regarding this are explained in detail as in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Miscellaneous Section).
What is the "clear knowledge of one in training" (*śaikṣa-vidyā*)?
What is the knowledge of one in training (śaikṣajñāna)?
What is the clear vision of one beyond training (aśaikṣavijjā)?
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna)?
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: [As follows:]

The world takes various worldly treatises as its notion of illumination, yet it does not recognize true illumination. Desiring to stop those who speak in such a manner, and also to clarify the meaning of true illumination, this treatise is composed.
Furthermore, there is another explanation: the reason this treatise was composed is that it is based upon the Buddha’s sūtras.
A sūtra states:
The Buddha addressed a householder:

Just as you have seen the Four Noble Truths through the wisdom of one in training, the vision of one in training, and the clarity of one in training, so too has this youth Yaśas now seen the Four Noble Truths through the wisdom of one beyond training, the vision of one beyond training, and the clarity of one beyond training; he will no longer dwell in a householder’s home to enjoy the pleasures of the five senses.
Although the Buddha’s sūtras contain such statements, they do not provide extensive analysis.
Since the Buddha’s sūtras constitute the fundamental basis for this treatise, and because one now wishes to provide extensive analysis, this treatise has been composed.
What is the training in clear knowledge?
The answer is:
it is the training in wisdom.
What is the knowledge of one in training?
The answer is:
it consists of the eight knowledges of one in training.
What is the clear knowledge of one beyond training?
The answer is:
it is the wisdom of one beyond training.
What is the knowledge of one beyond training (aśaikṣajñāna)?
The answer is:
it consists of the eight knowledges of one beyond training, namely, the four knowledges of phenomena (dharmajñāna) and the four subsequent knowledges (anvayajñāna).
This is the essence of clarity (*vidyā*); [the reason for this] has been explained at length. Now it shall be stated: why is it called "clarity"?
What is the meaning of "clarity"?
The answer is:
The meaning of "clearly cognizing" (*vijñāna*) is the meaning of "clarity. Question:
If the meaning of clearly cognizing is the meaning of clarity, then wholesome contaminated wisdom (*kuśala sāsravā prajñā*) also clearly cognizes; is that, too, the meaning of clarity?
The answer is:

If one’s awareness and cognition of the Four Noble Truths is clear, and ultimately clear, such that no further delusions arise—this is explained in detail as in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Miscellaneous Section).
Question: If wholesome contaminated wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*) is not called "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*), how is this reconciled with the Buddha’s sūtras?
For example, it is said:
The one beyond training possesses three kinds of clear knowledge (*vidyā*):

the clear knowledge of the realization of recollecting past lives, the clear knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth, and the clear knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Answer: It is called "clarity" (vidyā) because it possesses a slight degree of distinctness.
What constitutes this slight degree of distinctness?
Because it is contrary to the afflictions and is not mixed with them, it is called "slight clarity" (*parīttābhā*).
Furthermore, because these two types of clarity can produce and accord with the outflow-free clarity (*anāsravābhā*) that realizes the true meaning, they are called "clarity" (*ābhā*).
Therefore, the Venerable Sthavira Vasumitra stated:
"The first true meaning of untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-vidyā*) is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*).
The other two knowledges are called 'knowledges' because they can give rise to this [third] knowledge."
Furthermore, through the clear knowledge and realization of recollecting past lives, one knows the phenomena that increase in the prior limit;
through the clear knowledge and realization of birth and death, one knows the phenomena that increase in the subsequent limit;
and through the clear knowledge and realization of the exhaustion of outflows, one knows the phenomenon of the tranquility of nirvana.
The Venerable Buddhadeva also spoke thus:

"By means of the clear knowledge and realization of recollecting past lives, one knows the dharma of the continuity of causes and effects in the past, wherein these sentient beings have passed away from that place and been reborn here;

by means of the clear knowledge and realization of birth and death, one knows the dharma of the continuity of causes and effects in the future, wherein these sentient beings, having performed such karma, shall be born in that place."

The realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā*) consists in knowing that these sentient beings can exhaust the causes and effects of the outflows through such a path; this is called the first light of ultimate reality.
Furthermore, through the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, one’s conscious awareness clearly perceives the events of the past;
through the clear realization of the knowledge of birth and death, one’s conscious awareness clearly perceives the events of the future;
and through the clear realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, one’s conscious awareness clearly perceives unconditioned nirvana.
Furthermore, the clear knowledge and realization of recollecting past lives removes the darkness of ignorance regarding the past;
the clear knowledge and realization of birth and death removes the darkness of ignorance regarding the future;
and the clear knowledge and realization of the exhaustion of outflows removes the darkness of ignorance regarding nirvana.
Question: For what reason are three among the six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) established as "clear knowledges" (vidyā), while the other three are not? Answer:

The supernormal power of the body is a craft; the supernormal power of the divine ear merely hears sounds; and the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds takes specific characteristics as its object. These three types of higher knowledge can lead to the dharma of disenchantment and detachment, can cause one to abandon birth and death and accord with wholesome dharmas, and can lead to the attainment of nirvana.

Question: How can these three types of supernormal knowledge (tisro vidyāḥ) accord with the dharma of revulsion and detachment, enable one to abandon birth and death and accord with wholesome dharmas, and lead to the attainment of nirvāṇa?
Answer: Through the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives, one perceives the events of the past and gives rise to great weary detachment;
through the clear realization of the knowledge of birth and death, one perceives the events of future lives and gives rise to great weary detachment.

By means of revulsion and detachment, one realizes the knowledge and vision of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānadarśana*), being able to practice correct contemplation and sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, one realizes the knowledge and vision of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānadarśana*), knowing the various causes of the continuity of the past;

and one realizes the knowledge and vision of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānadarśana*), seeing the future aggregates (*skandha*) of all sentient beings as scattered atoms, thereby giving rise to great revulsion and detachment.
The clear realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*) enables one to practice correct contemplation and sever the afflictions.

Furthermore, the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*) allows one to know the events of decay and suffering within one's own past existence, giving rise to great revulsion;

the clear realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyāvidyā*) allows one to see the events of decay and suffering within the bodies of others in the future, giving rise to great revulsion.

By means of disenchantment, one realizes the knowledge and vision of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānadarśana*), being able to practice correct contemplation and sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, through the realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānadarśana*), one eliminates delusion regarding existence;
through the realization of the knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñānadarśana*), one eliminates delusion regarding sentient beings.
The clear realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows removes delusion regarding phenomena.
Furthermore, the clear realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives counteracts the view of eternalism;
the clear realization of the knowledge of birth and death counteracts the view of nihilism.
The realization through the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣayajñānasākṣātkriyā) counteracts the two extremes and abides in the Middle Way.
Furthermore, the realization through the knowledge of recollecting past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyā) can give rise to emptiness (śūnyatā);
the realization through the knowledge of birth and death (cyutyupapādajñānasākṣātkriyā) can give rise to wishlessness (apranihita).
The realization of the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows can give rise to the signless (*animitta*).

For these reasons, these three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*) accord with the dharma of wearying detachment; they enable one to abandon birth and death, accord with wholesome dharmas, and reach *nirvāṇa*.
The *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* states:

There are three kinds of clear knowledges (*vidyā*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), namely: the clear knowledge of the realization of the wisdom of recollecting past lives, the clear knowledge of the realization of the wisdom of birth and death, and the clear knowledge of the realization of the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
What is the realization through direct knowledge of the recollection of past lives belonging to one beyond training?
The answer is:
the wisdom of one beyond training that knows the birth and death of all sentient beings as a process of continuous succession.
What is the realization of the knowledge of birth and death of one beyond training?
The answer is:
the knowledge beyond training that knows the various karmas performed by sentient beings themselves.
What is the realization of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows for one beyond training?
The answer is:
the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows belonging to one beyond training.
Question: It may be granted that the clear knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) is called "beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
However, since the other two clear knowledges are neither "in training" (śaikṣa) nor "beyond training," why are they also described as the clear knowledges of one beyond training?
Answer: The *Saṃyuktāgama* (or *Dharmasaṃgraha-sūtra*) should state this:
"Those who have attained the stage of no-more-learning possess the three types of higher knowledge (*vidyā*)."
What is the intention behind not stating this?
The answer is:

Although these two types of clear knowledge (vidyā) are neither-learner-nor-non-learner, they are also called "non-learner" because they can be attained within the personhood of one who is a non-learner.
As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"There are two kinds of samādhi:
first, that which is noble (*ārya*); second, that which is not noble."
The noble samādhis are of three kinds:
first, wholesome with outflows; second, without outflows; and third, non-obscured indeterminate.
Wholesome samādhis with outflows are called "noble" by virtue of being wholesome, not because they are without outflows.
The untainted (anāsrava) samādhi is called "noble" (ārya) because it is wholesome and because it is untainted.
As for the non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta) samādhi, which is neither wholesome nor untainted, it is nevertheless called "noble" because it can be found within the bodies of noble ones (ārya).
It is the same for him as well. Question:
For what reason is "clear knowledge" (vidyā) established within the person of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), but not established within the person of one in training (śaikṣa)?
Answer: Because its meaning is superior.
If we speak in terms of dharmas, the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) are superior to the dharmas of one in training (śaikṣadharma).
If we speak in terms of persons, those beyond training (aśaikṣa) are superior to those still in training (śaikṣa).
Furthermore, it is called "clarity" (vidyā) because it is unmixed with ignorance (avidyā).
The wisdom within the person who is still in training is not called clarity because it is mixed with ignorance.
The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows within the body of a Tathāgata has four aspects:
first, it is called supernormal power (*abhijñā*); second, it is called clear vision (*vidyā*).
Third is power;
fourth is manifestation.

"Pervasive" refers to the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*); "clarity" refers to the clarity of the destruction of the outflows; "power" refers to the power of the destruction of the outflows; and "manifestation" refers to the manifestation of teaching the Dharma.
The knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows possessed by Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who have attained no-more-learning has three aspects:
first, the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows;
second, the clear vision of the exhaustion of outflows.
Third is the manifestation of non-power.
Within the Tathāgata’s body, there are three aspects to the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of birth and death:
first, they constitute supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
The second is clarity;
the third is power, not manifestation.
The knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of birth and death possessed by Pratyekabuddhas and Arhats who are Śrāvakas have two characteristics:
This is supernormal power (*abhijñā*), this is clear knowledge (*vidyā*); it is not a power (*bala*), nor is it a manifestation (*prātihārya*).

Whatever knowledge of past lives and knowledge of birth and death exists within the person of one in training (*śaikṣa*) is, in a single sense, supernormal power; it is not clear knowledge, nor is it a power, nor is it a manifestation.
Question: Is the wisdom established as a power within the body of a Tathāgata distinct from the wisdom within the bodies of Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas?
Answer: [It is.]
The meaning of being unobstructed is the meaning of power (*bala*).
Because the wisdom of *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas* is obstructed by ignorance, it is not power.
It was heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the Venerable Śāriputra were once walking together along a path.
A sentient being came to where he was, and the Buddha said to Śāriputra:
"You should observe this sentient being: in past lives, where did you dwell together with this sentient being?"

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra attempted to observe his past lives through the knowledge of recollecting former existences while in the first dhyāna, but he did not know them; he continued in this manner until he attempted to observe his past lives through the knowledge of recollecting former existences while in the fourth dhyāna, yet still did not know them.
He immediately arose from concentration and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I observe these sentient beings, yet none of them can see the place from which they have come.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

The wisdom and vision possessed by pratyekabuddhas surpass those of you all; furthermore, surpassing even the wisdom and vision of pratyekabuddhas, [I know] that this sentient being has come from such-and-such a world to be born here.
Later, at another time, the World-Honored One was again walking in meditation with Śāriputra in a certain place.
At that time, a person passed away; having seen this, the World-Honored One said to Śāriputra:
"You should observe where this person has been reborn."

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra first used the divine eye of the first dhyāna to observe him, but could not see him; he proceeded even as far as using the divine eye of the fourth dhyāna to observe him, yet still could not see him.
He immediately arose from his concentration and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have observed this person with my divine eye, yet I do not know where he has been reborn.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
Beyond the sphere of knowledge accessible to Pratyekabuddhas, there is a certain land where this person was born.
It may be asked:
while it is indeed appropriate that the Tathāgata’s wisdom regarding past lives and his wisdom regarding birth and death are supreme and sublime.
Just as the Buddha possesses the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), so it is for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
For what reason is the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows established as a power (*bala*) for the Buddha, but not for the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas?
Answer: The Tathāgata’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) is likewise supreme and wondrous.
All the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows within the Tathāgata’s body is by nature fierce and sharp; if it takes afflictions as its object, those afflictions are immediately severed.

Because the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*) of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas is not sharp and intense, they must repeatedly take afflictions as their object before those afflictions are severed.
It is like two men cutting down a tree: one is brave and strong and uses a sharp axe, while the other is of inferior character and uses a blunt axe.
Although both are cutting down trees, it is the one who is courageous and uses a sharp axe who works quickly, not the one of inferior nature who uses a dull axe. It is the same in this case:

it is not called a "power" because of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (āsravakṣayajñāna) possessed by oneself; rather, it is called a power because it enables those sentient beings to attain the destruction of the outflows.

The World-Honored One knows that some sentient beings can exhaust the outflows through painful and slow superknowledge, while other sentient beings can exhaust the outflows through pleasant and swift superknowledge; for this reason, it is called a power.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifty-two.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle Fifty-three.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
Chapter Two: The Knowledge of Others’ Minds within the Section on Wisdom (Jñāna-vastu), Part Five. Question:

Of these six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), how many are clear knowledges (*vidyā*) but not manifestations (*prātihārya*), how many are manifestations but not clear knowledges, how many are both clear knowledges and manifestations, and how many are neither clear knowledges nor manifestations?
Answer: The two that are clarity (*vidyā*) but not manifestations (*prātihārya*) are the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of birth and death.
The two that are manifestations but not clarity are the supernormal power of the body and the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds.
That which is both clear knowledge (*vidyā*) and a manifestation is the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
That which is neither clear knowledge nor a manifestation is the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*). Question:
Regarding these six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), why are three considered manifestations (*saṃdarśana*) and three not manifestations?
The answer is:
that which causes others to develop faith and joy, to conceive a sense of wonder, and to enter into the Dharma is called a manifestation.
The three supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are not like this.
If one were to say, "With my divine ear I hear sounds, with my divine eye I see forms, and I am able to know the events of countless past lives," [it would be incorrect].
Everyone harbored doubts,
wondering whether this matter was false or true.
It was heard that once a lay devotee invited Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta and his assembly of disciples to his home for a meal.
When the Nirgrantha Jñātiputra had entered his house, he smiled.
The householder asked him, "The Great Teacher has long since abandoned all manner of frivolous play; for what reason do you smile now?"
The Master replied to him, saying:
"Can you now hear all the sublime teachings contained within my Dharma?
At that time, the lay devotee asked with earnest persistence, and the Master then answered:
"On the banks of the Nairañjanā River there were two monkeys who fought incessantly; they suddenly fell into the river and were carried away by the current.
This is why I laughed.
At that time, the householder spoke these words:
"The Great Master’s divine eye is truly rare; how clear and pure it is!
At that time, the various Nirgranthas each sat upon their own mats.
As the food was served in succession, they placed the rice over the soup when serving their teacher, while the other Nirgranthas placed the soup on top.
All the other Nirgranthas ate at the proper time,
but their teacher alone did not eat.
The householder asked:
"Great Master!
Why do you not eat today?
The Master replied to him, saying:
"This rice has no soup; that is why I do not eat it.
At that time, the householder said to the teacher, "Your divine eye is so exceptionally clear and pure!
You see a monkey by the side of the Nairañjanā River falling into the river, yet you do not see the soup at the bottom of my bowl?"

For this reason, three of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are not manifestations; they cannot cause others to develop faith and joy or to conceive a sense of wonder so that they enter the Buddha-dharma.

However, by means of the power of the body (*kāyābhijñā*), one can cause a single body to become many, and many to return to being one; through such various transformations reaching as high as the Brahma-world, one causes many sentient beings to conceive a sense of wonder.
If there are those who know the dharmas contemplated in the minds of others, they say to them:
"You have such a thought; you have made such a reflection.
This is entirely in accordance with their minds and not at variance with them, causing many sentient beings to conceive a sense of wonder toward the Buddha-dharma.

If one preaches the Dharma for others, causing them to distance themselves from dust and leave behind defilement so as to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye, one also causes many sentient beings to conceive a sense of rare wonder toward the Buddha-dharma.
For this reason, the three [supernormal powers] cause others to believe and rejoice, giving rise to a sense of wonder as they enter the Buddha-dharma.
Question: What kind of person should be manifested with these supernatural transformations?
For what kind of person should one not manifest supernatural transformations?
The answer is:
for one who is entirely faithful or for one who is entirely faithless, one should not manifest supernatural transformations.
If there are those who are neither certain in their faith nor certain in their lack of faith, one should manifest supernormal transformations for them to lead them into the Buddha-dharma.
How is this known?
A sutra states:
The Buddha was staying at the Pāpaliya mango grove in the city of Nāgakaṇḍa.

At that time, there was a son of a householder named Śivadata who went to where the Buddha was, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
This city of Nāgagandha is prosperous, flourishing, and teeming with a vast population, who moreover possess great faith and reverence for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

We pray that the World-Honored One would permit a single śramaṇa to manifest various supernormal transformations—the dharmas of a superior person—before the multitude of people in this land, so that the people of Nāgagandha may redouble their faith and reverence toward the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The Buddha told the householder’s son:
"I do not instruct my disciples in this way:
'Wherever you go and come, manifest various supernormal transformations and the qualities of a superior person before others.'"
"I have made this statement for the sake of my disciples:
'You should conceal wholesome dharmas and disclose unwholesome dharmas.
At that time, the son of a householder again addressed the Buddha, saying:"
"Bhagavān! Seeing what fault or peril do you not allow your disciples to manifest supernatural transformations, yet instead make this statement:
'Conceal wholesome dharmas and disclose unwholesome dharmas'?"
The Buddha told the son of a householder:
"There are three kinds of manifestations:
first, the manifestation of supernormal powers; second, the manifestation of knowing the minds of others; and third, the manifestation of preaching the Dharma."
What is called the manifestation of supernormal powers?
Son of a householder!

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas manifest various kinds of miraculous transformations—such as making one body into many bodies, or many bodies into one body, even attaining mastery over their bodies up to the Brahma world.
Those with faith see this and speak to those who lack faith, saying:

"I have seen śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas manifest various supernatural transformations: making one body into many bodies and many bodies into one body, even attaining mastery over bodies as far as the Brahma-world."
At that time, those who lacked faith said to those with faith:
"What is so extraordinary about what you have seen?
There is a mantra called Gandhara; if someone receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, they too can manifest various supernatural transformations."
"Son of a householder!
What do you think?
Is such a person of no faith not indeed censuring those who have faith?"
The householder’s son said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One,
I truly feel resentment and reproach.”
Furthermore, son of a householder!
If a śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa speaks of what another person is thinking in their mind, saying:
"You have such a thought; you have such a reflection."
All of this is exactly as he said, without any falsehood.
A believer hears what was spoken by the previous non-believer and says:
"I have seen śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who know the dharmas thought in the minds of others," and so forth, as extensively described.
At that time, those who did not believe said:
"What is so extraordinary about you seeing this?
There is a mantra called *kṣaṇika*; if one receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, one can know the thoughts and dharmas in the minds of others," and so forth, as explained at length.
"Son of a householder!
You should know that because of such faults and disadvantages, I do not permit my disciples to manifest various supernatural transformations; rather, I say this to you:
'You should conceal your wholesome dharmas.'"

One who has confessed their evil dharmas, because of this matter, possesses either absolute faith or absolute lack of faith; for such a person, one should not manifest various supernatural transformations.
However, for one who is intermediate—neither definitively faithful nor definitively faithless—one should manifest supernatural transformations to cause them to enter the Buddha-dharma.
Question: For what reason is it called "manifestation" (saṃdarśana)? Answer:
It is called "manifestation" because it follows the manner of a gatekeeper.
Just as a gatekeeper manifests internal matters so that outsiders may know them, and manifests external matters so that those within may know them.
To manifest internal matters so that outsiders may know them is as it is said:
"The King is now within, bathing, eating, and beholding various precious jewels.
To manifest external matters so that those within may know them is as it is said:
"Now, a person from such-and-such a country and such-and-such a village, bearing such-and-such credentials, stands outside the gate.
For this reason, according to the rule of a gatekeeper, it is called 'manifestation' (nidarśana)."
The Buddhist sūtras state:

A bodhisattva arouses supernormal powers and attains clear vision during the first watch of the night; arouses supernormal powers and attains clear vision during the middle watch of the night; and arouses supernormal powers and attains clear vision during the final watch of the night.
Question: For what reason does the Bodhisattva arouse the supernormal powers and clear knowledges during the first, middle, and last watches of the night? Answer:
This is the sequential practice of the Dharma for bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Furthermore, regarding the arising of supernormal powers and clear vision during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, it is because one desires to make this body a vessel fit for the Dharma.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to make what is to be accomplished clear and distinct;
furthermore, it is because one wishes to establish a firm footing that supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) arise, and because one wishes to illuminate from afar that clarity (*vidyā*) arises.
Furthermore, they are like the path of unimpeded liberation (*anantarya-vimukti-mārga*): thus, supernormal powers are like the path of non-obstruction, and clarity is like the path of liberation.

Furthermore, they are illustrated by the analogy of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*): the supernormal power of penetration (*abhijñā*) is like the path of seeing, while the supernormal power of clarity (*vidyā*) is like the path of cultivation.

Furthermore, they are illustrated by the analogy of wholesome contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-kuśala-dharma*), uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*), both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, and neutral phenomena (*avyākṛta-dharma*): two of the supernormal powers are wholesome and contaminated—namely, the supernormal power of the body (*kāya-ṛddhi*) and the supernormal power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*);
one supernormal power is uncontaminated—namely, the supernormal power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*).
One supernormal power (abhijñā) is both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava), namely the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds;
two supernormal powers are non-obscured neutral (anivṛtāvyākṛta), namely the supernormal powers of the divine eye and the divine ear.
Furthermore, it is for the purpose of successively subduing the hosts of Māra.

It is heard that when the Bodhisattva was practicing austerities, he realized this was not the path; he then rose from that practice and accepted sixteen servings of milk-rice from the brahmin sisters Nandā and Nandabalā, thereby restoring strength to his body.
Receiving grass from a virtuous man, he went beneath the Bodhi tree and personally spread the grass; then, sitting cross-legged with his body folded like the Nāga King Sāgara, he made this vow:
"I shall not rise from this seat until all outflows are exhausted."
At that time, the earth and heavens shook in six ways like a ship upon the great ocean; even the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven trembled like a *khaṭṭhāri* leaf.
Then the Māra King thought to himself:
"For what reason is this palace trembling in such a manner?"

Upon observation, he realized that this bodhisattva was sitting cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree and had established a firm vow; he then departed from his own palace, went to where the bodhisattva was, and spoke these words:
"Arise, O Kṣatriya!"

At this time, sentient beings are turbid, evil, and stubborn; you will not be able to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. You should properly remain in the position of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), and I shall offer you the seven treasures.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Māra:
"What you have just said is like the talk of a child.

One might cause the sun, moon, and stars to fall; one might cause the mountains, forests, and the great earth to remain suspended in space; but for me to rise from this seat without having exhausted all outflows—that is impossible."
At that time, Māra the Evil One spoke again to the Bodhisattva:
"Since you do not accept my gentle and pleasant words now, I shall manifest a scene of great terror for you to behold."
At that time, having spoken these words, the Evil Māra rained down various flowers and returned to his own palace.
He announced to all the devas of the six heavens of desire:
"You all must take up various weapons and implements for combat; I now have an enemy beneath the Bodhi tree."
Not long after the Māra had departed, the Bodhisattva then thought to himself:
"If one should not treat even an ordinary person with contempt when contending with them, how much less so one who is the most honored within the realm of desire?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva carefully and thoroughly contemplated the path of detachment from desire; he swiftly abandoned the desires of the desire realm and gave rise to the supernormal power of the first dhyāna, manifesting various kinds of paired forms.

Those among the hosts of Māra who came in the form of birds were transformed into the likeness of raccoons and cats; those who came in the form of raccoons and cats were transformed into the likeness of dogs; those who came in the form of dogs were transformed into the likeness of leopards; those who came in the form of leopards were transformed into the likeness of tigers; those who came in the form of tigers were transformed into the likeness of lions; those who came in the form of lions were transformed into swords and spears; those who were flames were turned into rain; and those who were rain were turned into parasols.
They themselves transformed their own bodies within a palace of lapis lazuli to shield their bodies but not their eyes, and they also transformed this great earth so that it could produce sound.
Having thus manifested these corresponding phenomena, he further thought:
"Have I ever created obstacles for those practicing the Path?

He then gave rise to the wisdom of past lives and saw that throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of past eons, he had never created obstacles for those practicing the Path; rather, he had benefited them by providing all manner of requisites for their practice.
Again, he thought: "What wholesome karma have I performed?
What wholesome karma has the evil Māra performed?"
I saw Māra the Evil One holding a great and boundless sacrificial assembly.
Compared to the assembly held by Māra, I shall hold one a hundred thousand million times greater.
Even the merit from the act of giving performed by Māra does not equal mine, let alone the merit from his observance of the precepts and cultivation of meditative concentration.
At that time, by the power of his merit, the Bodhisattva sat upright and majestic.
Then, the Evil Māra led an army of thirty-six billion demons, all assuming various hideous appearances and forms, and approached the foot of the Bodhi tree.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Māra:
"You shall hold one limitless assembly of giving.
To whatever extent you hold this limitless assembly of giving, I shall further double it by a factor of hundreds of thousands of millions."
Māra said to the Bodhisattva:
"I take you as my witness for this sacrificial assembly.
Who is your witness?"

At that time, the Bodhisattva pressed the ground with his hand, adorned with the marks and signs of excellence, and a great sound issued forth; upon hearing this sound, Māra’s army was instantly shattered.
At that moment, by means of the divine eye born of karmic retribution, the Bodhisattva could see forms within one *yojana* but could not hear their sounds;
he then activated the supernormal power of the divine ear, whereby he could hear sounds beyond one *yojana* even though he could not see their forms.
Next, he developed the supernormal power of the divine eye; although he saw forms and heard sounds, he did not know what was being thought in their minds.

Next, he developed the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, whereby he knew that the followers of Śakra were filled with joy, while the followers of Māra were filled with sorrow and affliction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further thought to himself:
"For what reason has the Evil Māra conceived this evil intent?
It is entirely due to the possession of the five desires."
Attachment to the five desires arises entirely from afflictions; for this reason, one gives rise to the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
Therefore, it is said that in order to successively subdue Māra, one brings forth the supernormal powers and clear visions (*abhijñā-vidyā*) during the first, middle, and last watches of the night.
When seeing suffering, what kind of indestructible clarity (avetyaprasāda) is first attained?
When seeing the origin, cessation, and the path, what kind of indestructible clarity is first attained? Question:
For what reason was this treatise composed?
The answer is:
Some say that one realizes the truths all at once, rather than realizing them through a gradual sequence.
As for the Vibhajyavādins,
it is asked:
For what reason do they speak in this way?
Answer: He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
The Buddha’s sūtras state:
If one has no doubt regarding suffering, one likewise has no doubt regarding the origin, cessation, and path.

If it is said that one has no doubt regarding suffering and likewise no doubt regarding the origin, cessation, and path, does this not mean that one perceives the truths simultaneously rather than sequentially?
This is said to refute the views of such proponents and to clarify the sequential realization of the truths.
If the realization of the truths were simultaneous rather than sequential, it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said:
The householder Sudatta went to where the Buddha was and asked him this:
"World-Honored One!"
"Is it that one perceives the truths all at once, or does one perceive the truths in succession?
The Buddha told the householder:
"One perceives the truths in succession; it is not that one perceives the truths all at once."
It is like the method of climbing a four-rung ladder. Question:
If the vision of the truths occurs sequentially rather than simultaneously, how do you reconcile this with the sūtra cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
The answer is:
That scriptural passage should state it thus:
"If one has no doubt regarding the Path, one likewise has no doubt regarding suffering, its origin, and its cessation."
What is the intention behind not stating what should have been stated?
The answer is:
the Buddha spoke of those who have attained the fruits [of the path].
If one person attains the fruit, they have no doubt regarding the Four Truths.
Furthermore, this sutra speaks of those who do not engage in doubt;
since such a person, having seen suffering, ultimately does not engage in doubt, it is for this reason that this statement is made.
The Venerable Buddhadeva spoke thus:
"When a practitioner first enters the path of seeing, this is termed 'faith in all aspects' (sarvatragādhimokṣa) in its technical sense.
He was asked:
That Venerable One spoke of the sequential realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*), not of their simultaneous realization; for what reason did he make this statement?
The answer is:
one should understand what he intended by that statement.

For they say this: when a practitioner is at the stage of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), there is no further interval of abiding; one necessarily attains all forms of faith.
It is like a clay vessel placed upon a three-storied house and thrown to the ground: even before it has reached the ground, its destruction is already certain by definition.
It is the same with this [treatise].

Therefore, desiring to refute the positions of others, desiring to clarify one's own position, and also desiring to explain the meaning that accords with the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), this treatise was composed.
The dharmas of one beyond training within the Buddha’s body are called the Buddha; the untainted faith that takes them as its object is called indestructible faith in the Buddha.

All three faculties present in the body of a Pratyekabuddha, and all two faculties and the three truths present in the body of a Bodhisattva, are called the Dharma; if one has untainted faith taking these as its object, it is called indestructible faith in the Dharma.

All the dharmas of training and the dharmas beyond training within the bodies of śrāvakas—if one takes them as an object and possesses untainted faith (anāsrava-śraddhā), this is called indestructible faith in the Saṃgha.
Untainted ethical discipline (anāsrava-śīla) is the ethical discipline beloved by the Noble Ones.
When one perceives suffering, what kind of faith is first attained?
The answer is:
one attains faith in the Dharma, specifically regarding the dharma of suffering.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"One has faith in the phenomena that are defects regarding the Truth of Suffering, and faith in the phenomena that are virtues regarding the Truth of Cessation.
When one perceives the Truth of Origination, what kind of faith is obtained first?"
Answer: To attain the Dharma is, in itself, to gather the Dharma.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
One perceives the phenomena of defects within the Truth of Origination (samudaya-satya), and perceives the phenomena of merit within the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
When perceiving cessation, what kind of faith is first attained?
The answer is:
Regarding the attainment of the Dharma, it occurs precisely at the moment of the cessation of dharmas.
A question is asked:
When a practitioner perceives the three truths, they attain two kinds of indestructible purity (*aveccappasāda*), namely faith and morality.
Why is it that only faith is mentioned and not the precepts?
The answer is:
when something ought to be stated but is not, one should know that this teaching is incomplete.
Furthermore, herein it is not asked how many types of indestructible purity one may attain; rather, it is asked what serves as the object-condition for attaining indestructible purity.
Because pure ethical discipline is a dharma that lacks an object-condition, it is therefore not mentioned.
If one asks what kind of faith is first attained at the time of the Path of Seeing,
the answer is:
one attains unshakable faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
The foreign Dharma masters explain it thus:

when the faculty of faith (śraddhendriya) manifests during the three moments of seeing the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya), there are the four forms of unshakable confidence (avetyaprasāda) which comprise the corresponding associated and concomitant dharmas.
If that faith takes as its object the dharmas of one beyond training within the body of a Buddha, it is called indestructible faith in the Buddha;
if it takes as its object the three faculties within the body of a Pratyekabuddha or the two faculties of a Bodhisattva, it is called indestructible faith in the Dharma;
if it takes as its object the dharmas of training and beyond training within the body of a Śrāvaka, it is called indestructible faith in the Saṃgha.
Taking up these precepts of turning back [from evil] is called "the precepts beloved by the Noble Ones.
One should not follow what the foreign Dharma masters say;
the Śramaṇas of Kaśmīra speak as follows:
That faith takes all phenomena as its object collectively and is free from conceptual discrimination; this is called "unwavering faith in phenomena.
When that faith alone manifests in the present, there is immeasurable cultivation of future faith, which constitutes the cultivation of faith for the future.
If there is one who takes the Buddha’s dharmas of no-more-learning as an object, this is called the unshared indestructible faith directed toward the Buddha;
if there is one who takes the three faculties of the pratyekabuddha or the two faculties of the bodhisattva as an object, this is called the unshared indestructible faith directed toward the Dharma;
if there is one who takes the śrāvaka’s dharmas of training and no-more-learning within the Saṃgha as an object, this is called the unshared indestructible faith directed toward the Saṃgha.

There are those who take as their object the dharmas of no-more-learning within the body of a Buddha, the three faculties within the body of a pratyekabuddha, or the two faculties within the body of a bodhisattva;
there are those who take as their object the dharmas of no-more-learning within the body of a Buddha, or the dharmas of training and no-more-learning within the body of a śrāvaka;

and there are those who take as their object the three faculties within the body of a pratyekabuddha, the two faculties within the body of a bodhisattva, or the dharmas of training and no-more-learning within the body of a śrāvaka.

There may be those who take as their object the dharmas of one beyond training within the body of a Buddha; the three faculties within the body of a Pratyekabuddha; the two faculties within the body of a Bodhisattva; or the dharmas of training and beyond training within the body of a Śrāvaka.

All such instances constitute unshakable faith in the Dharma that takes all phenomena as its common object; one also attains the "precepts cherished by the Noble Ones" (*āryakānta-śīla*) which can be redirected.
This is just as it was during the three moments when the Truth of the Path was seen; the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) is likewise so.

Regarding the difference: at that time, the practitioner cannot cultivate [the knowledges] during the three moments of seeing the Truth of the Path; rather, they cultivate faith in the preceding three truths during those moments.

Question: It may be granted that since the essence of Cessation and the Path is purity and the locus of purity, one can attain the "unshakeable purities" (akopya-prasāda) upon seeing them. However, [how is this possible for the other truths?]
The essence of the truth of the origin of suffering is neither pure nor a locus of purity. Why is this?
Because it consists of afflictions, unwholesome conduct, false views, and inverted dharmas.
How does one attain unshakable faith (aveccappasāda) at the time of seeing?
The answer is:
one attains unshakable faith through two factors: first, that which is trustworthy; second, that which is worthy of pursuit.

Regarding the attainment of unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*) in the truths of cessation and the path, there are two aspects; for this reason, they are both to be trusted and to be sought after.
Regarding the attainment of unshakable confidence in the truths of suffering and its origin, there is only one aspect: it is to be trusted, but not to be sought after.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:
"If one is oppressed by suffering and its origin, then one regards cessation and the path as supreme.
It is just as when a person is oppressed by a violent windstorm and regards their house as supreme and wonderful; so it is in this case."

A person of firm conviction attains indestructible purity regarding the path of firm conviction through two factors: first, that it is trustworthy; second, that it is worth seeking. Regarding the path of firm dharma, there are likewise two factors.

Regarding the person of fixed nature in the path of fixed dharma, there are also two aspects: first, that which is trustworthy, and second, that which is to be sought. In the case of the person of fixed nature in the path of fixed conviction, it is only trustworthy and not something to be sought.

The path of liberation through faith, the path of vision, the path of occasional liberation, the path of non-occasional liberation, the path of the śrāvaka, the path of the pratyekabuddha, and the path of the Buddha are taught according to their respective characteristics.
Question: If one has faith that the dharmas beyond training exist within Śāriputra’s body, is this indestructible faith in the Dharma or is it indestructible faith in the Saṅgha?
If it refers to the Dharma, it refers to the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) within the bodies of those śrāvakas.
If it refers to the Saṃgha, Śāriputra alone is not the Saṃgha.
He replied:
It should be said that this is the Saṃgha. Question:
If that is so, how can a single person be the Saṃgha?
Answer: If one speaks in terms of the Dharma, it is the Saṃgha; if one speaks in terms of persons, it is not the Saṃgha.

When, by relying on the *anāgamya* dhyāna, one attains what was previously unattained and the indestructible confidence in the Buddha (*buddhāveśambhāsa*) manifests before one, there are two present: namely, [confidence] in the Buddha and in the precepts; and four future.
If that which was previously attained arises and becomes manifest, there are two in the present and none in the future.
This is likewise stated for all stages up to and including reliance on the fourth dhyāna.

If, by relying on the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one attains what was not previously attained and the unshakable confidence in the Buddha (*buddhāveṇika-prasāda*) becomes manifest, there is one in the present—namely, faith in the Buddha—and four in the future.
If that which was previously acquired arises and manifests in the present, there is one in the present and none in the future.
Question: How are the indestructible purities (akṣayaprasāda) established?
Is it by way of its own essence, or by way of its object?
If it were by way of its own essence, there would be two kinds, namely faith and ethical discipline.
If it were by way of its object, there would be three kinds, namely the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Why is this? Because precepts have no objective referent (*ālambana*).
He replied:
One should say this:
it is by way of its own essence and also by way of its object.
Its own essence is ethical discipline; its object is faith.
Just as with the object of one's own nature, so too is it said regarding the Three Jewels of one's own nature and the threefold refuge of one's own nature.
This is the essential nature of the indestructible purities (*akṣayaprasāda*), and so forth, as explained at length.
The reason for their essential nature has already been explained; now it shall be explained why they are called "unbreakable.
What is the meaning of "unbreakable purity" (*akopya-prasāda*)?
The answer is:
Because they are attained through various modes of contemplation and various forms of deliberation, they are called "unshakable purity" (*aveccappasāda*).
Furthermore, because they cannot be destroyed, they are called "unshakable purity."
Because no śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world is able to refute it in accordance with the Dharma, it is called "unwavering confidence."
Furthermore, this faith cannot be severed; therefore, it is called "unshakable purity" (*aveccappasāda*).
There is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa capable of severing it in accordance with the Dharma, as explained in detail above.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka said:

"If one does not contemplate and understand the Buddha’s Dharma in its various aspects, nor investigate and weigh it in its various aspects, it will be like an unmoored boat upon the water—light, fickle, and easily destroyed."
Being the opposite of the aforementioned, it is not frivolous or easily corrupted; therefore, it is called "unbreakable purity" (*aveccappasāda*). Question:

For what reason did the World-Honored One first speak of unbreakable purity toward the Buddha, and so on, until finally speaking of unbreakable purity toward the Dharma and the Saṅgha, and concluding with unbreakable purity toward the precepts?
Answer: If one speaks in this way, the words and their meaning will be in harmony; it will be easy for the speaker to explain and easy for the listener to understand.
Furthermore, the Buddha is likened to a physician, the Dharma to freedom from illness, the Saṅgha to those who nurse the sick, and the precepts to excellent medicine.
Furthermore, because the Buddha is able to expound the Dharma, he is placed at the beginning.
What Dharma does the Buddha expound?
It is for this reason that faith follows next.
For whom was the Dharma taught?
The Dharma was taught for the Saṃgha; this is why faith in the Saṃgha follows [faith in the Dharma].
For what reason is it called the Saṃgha?
One is called a *saṃgha* because of the precepts; therefore, the precepts follow next.

Furthermore, because they can show the path to sentient beings, one first has faith in the Buddha; because they can lead one to the city of *nirvāṇa*, one next has faith in the Dharma; because they are like good companions, one next has faith in the *saṃgha*; and because they are like provisions for the journey, the precepts follow next.
Furthermore, faith in the Buddha is like a boatman; faith in the Dharma is like the further shore; faith in the Saṅgha is like fellow passengers; and faith in the precepts is like the boat.
As the Buddha’s sūtras state:
"These precepts beloved by the noble ones are unbroken, unperforated, unblemished, and unstained, and are praised by the wise."
Question: Why is the morality beloved by the noble ones called "unbroken and unpierced" and "unmixed with impurity and evil"?
A detailed explanation is as given in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Miscellaneous Khandas).
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll 53 [and] Scroll 54. Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman together with Daotai and others during the Northern Liang dynasty.
From the *Jñānavastu*, Chapter on the Knowledge of Others' Minds, Part Six: The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If there are sentient beings who can believe in and delight in what you have said, you should, out of a heart of compassion, teach them the four kinds of indestructible purity (*catur-avetyaprasāda*), so that they may dwell securely and practice this Dharma."
It is explained at length as set forth in the sūtras. Question:
For what reason did the World-Honored One speak this sūtra?
The answer is:
For one who wishes to preach the Dharma, this is to demonstrate the conditions for listening to the Dharma.
When a Dharma-preacher does not know for whom it should be preached and for whom it should not be preached, their mind becomes timid and weak.
Regarding this, the Buddha spoke thus: "You should not speak lightly."
If there are sentient beings who can believe and delight in what you have said, only then may you speak it for them.
Furthermore, wishing to explain the Dharma of repaying kindness, the Buddha preached this sutra.
The Sūtra says that the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If a person were to carry their father on one shoulder and their mother on the other for a hundred years, traveling everywhere, it would still not be called repaying the kindness of one's parents."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If one leads one's parents who lack faith to establish faith; preaches wholesome precepts to those who lack them; teaches generosity to those who are stingy; and instructs those who lack wisdom to cultivate wisdom—only then can it be called repaying the kindness of one's parents."

Question: Among all the wholesome dharmas within the teachings of the Buddhas, one should instruct people in them all; why then is it said that one specifically teaches only the four types of indestructible faith (*avetyaprasāda*)?
Venerable Vaspa replied:
In this context, the Blessed One speaks of the Noble Path by the name "unshakable confidence" (aveccappasāda).

All noble paths consist either of associated factors (sampayutta-dhamma) or concomitant factors (sahajāta-dhamma); if one speaks of faith, one refers to the noble path as an associated factor, and if one speaks of virtue, one refers to the noble path as a concomitant factor.
Furthermore, this teaching provides a brief and essential introduction for initial entry into the Dharma.

Regarding all the Buddha-dharmas and all wholesome dharmas—whether they are material (*rūpa*) or immaterial (*arūpa*)—if one speaks of ethical discipline (*śīla*), it should be understood that all wholesome dharmas of a material nature have already been explained; if one speaks of faith (*śraddhā*), it should be understood that all wholesome dharmas of an immaterial nature have already been explained.

As it is with material phenomena and non-material phenomena, so too should one understand the cases of the associated and the dissociated, those with a basis and those without a basis, those with activity and those without activity, those with functional power and those without functional power, and those with an object and those without an object.

Furthermore, regarding all wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*), whether they are of the nature of faculties (*indriya*) or not of the nature of faculties: if one speaks of faith (*śraddhā*), it should be understood that wholesome phenomena of the nature of faculties have already been explained; if one speaks of ethical discipline (*śīla*), it should be understood that wholesome phenomena not of the nature of faculties have already been explained.
Furthermore, based on the four kinds of unshakable confidence (*aveccappasāda*), the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*) are established.
Moreover, these four unshakable confidences possess two characteristics:
first, the characteristic of being unshakable; second, the characteristic of purity.
Regarding the "unimpaired characteristic": untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) is not impaired by non-faith, and untainted precept (*anāsrava-śīla*) is not impaired by non-precept.
Within the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), faith is the characteristic of purity; within the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), precept is the characteristic of purity.
Furthermore, it is to demonstrate the skillful means for ceasing the fear of the miserable realms and poverty:
ethical discipline can cease the fear of the miserable realms, and faith can cease the fear of poverty.
Although untainted faith and precepts are unobstructed, they do not arise without being caused by tainted faith and precepts.
Furthermore, it is because one wishes to lead those who follow external paths and are receptive to transformation so that they may enter the Buddha-dharma.

"Monks, there may be relatives who have been converted by non-Buddhist teachers. Because they were personally influenced by those outsiders, they praise the Buddha's Dharma and disparage the teachings of the non-Buddhists, thereby inciting anger in others and causing them to distance themselves further from the Buddha's Dharma."
The Buddha then said:
"You lack the power and the fearlessness; you do not know the faculties, minds, and conducts of sentient beings.
If you have a heart of compassion for those people, you should teach them the four kinds of indestructible purity."
If one attains the four kinds of unshakable confidence, the mind will not waver. Why is this?
A bhikṣu should know that the four great elements can be made to change.
If a person attains the four kinds of unshakable faith (*avetyaprasāda*), they will not undergo change.
Question: Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely immutable, why is it said specifically that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not change?
Answer: It is because the four dharmas are clarified by means of the four dharmas.
Furthermore, the practitioner first contemplates the unchanging characteristic of the four great elements, and subsequently perceives the unchanging characteristic in all phenomena.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that the four great elements (mahābhūta) are eternal, whereas the Buddha teaches that the four great elements are not eternal dharmas.
If the four great elements were eternal as the non-Buddhists claim, then an eternal dharma could be made to undergo transformation.
If it were possible for my disciples who have accomplished the four kinds of unshakable confidence to undergo change, such a thing could never occur.
Furthermore, the four great elements are able to sustain and cause the successive growth of the phenomena of birth and death.
The Buddhist scriptures state:
"Faith is the trunk of the great elephant.
A question is asked: [Why is this so?]
Why does the Buddha say that faith is the trunk of a great elephant?
The answer is:
because it is able to grasp what is to be taken.
Just as an elephant has hands with which it can grasp things both animate and inanimate,
so too does a noble disciple who possesses the hand of faith have the capacity to grasp wholesome qualities.
The Buddhist sūtras state:
When a noble disciple accomplishes unwavering confidence in the Buddha and dwells frequently in this dharma, at that time they have first accomplished unwavering confidence in the Buddha.
The devas rejoiced greatly in their hearts and spoke thus:

"Just as we have been born here because we achieved and dwelt extensively in unwavering confidence in the Buddha, so too shall the noble disciples who have achieved unwavering confidence in the Buddha be born here after the dissolution of the body at the end of life, to dwell together with us."
The same applies to the accomplishment of unshakable confidence in the Dharma, unshakable confidence in the Saṅgha, and unshakable confidence in the precepts. Question:
Those devas had previously accomplished all four types of unshakable confidence while still in this world.
For what reason do some among the devas praise the indestructible purity regarding the Buddha, while others even praise the indestructible purity regarding the precepts?
The answer is:

among sentient beings, there are those who, for the sake of the indestructible purity regarding the Buddha, diligently apply skillful means and enter the Buddha-dharma; and there are those who, for the sake of the indestructible purity regarding the precepts, diligently apply skillful means and enter the Buddha-dharma.

If there are devas who, for the sake of unwavering confidence in the Buddha, diligently apply skillful means to enter the Buddha-dharma, they praise unwavering confidence in the Buddha; likewise, if there are devas who, for the sake of unwavering confidence in the Dharma, the Sangha, and unwavering purity of ethical discipline, diligently apply skillful means to enter the Buddha-dharma, they praise unwavering confidence in the Dharma, the Sangha, and unwavering purity of ethical discipline.
Furthermore, among the devas, some take pleasure in contemplating the Buddha, while others take pleasure in contemplating the precepts.

Those who take pleasure in contemplating the Buddha praise the indestructible clarity of faith in the Buddha; likewise, those who take pleasure in contemplating the precepts praise the indestructible clarity of faith in the precepts.
The Buddhist scriptures state that King Ajātaśatru achieved rootless faith (*amūlaka-śraddhā*).
A question is asked:
All conditioned phenomena possess roots; why, then, is it said that King Ajātaśatru’s faith is rootless?
The answer is:
this faith lacks the root of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
As it is said:
faith associated with unshakable knowledge takes the path of seeing as its root.
Because that [faith] lacks the root of the path of seeing, it is said to be "rootless," yet there exists a faith similar to the path of seeing that serves as its root.
Furthermore, because they lack the roots of wholesome merit that constitute untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), they are said to be "rootless.

Untainted faith takes untainted wisdom and untainted roots of wholesome merit as its roots; since these individuals neither attain untainted wisdom nor untainted roots of wholesome merit, they can only attain a faith that resembles the untainted.
Furthermore, King Ajātaśatru had not long ago made offerings to the Buddha, nor had he drawn near to virtuous bhikṣus, yet he attained such faith.

When he saw the World-Honored Buddha from atop a multi-storied pavilion or upon an elephant or horse, he immediately advanced toward the Buddha and threw his body to the ground, yet his body felt no pain.
This is the power of rootless faith, which is also due to the majestic spiritual authority of the Buddha; therefore, it is called "rootless faith.
Furthermore, this faith has no similar cause; there is no dharma that can serve as a similar cause for that faith.

Regarding suffering, there is the perversion of perceiving it as pleasure—the perversion of mind and the perversion of view;
regarding non-self, there is the perversion of perceiving it as self—the perversion of mind and the perversion of view;
regarding the impure, there is the perversion of perceiving it as pure—the perversion of mind and the perversion of view.
Eight are abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), and four are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Regarding the eight abandoned through the path of seeing: they consist of the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, and the inversion of views;
and the inversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, and the inversion of views.

The inversion of perceiving a self where there is no self consists of both an inversion of perception and an inversion of view; the inversion of perceiving purity where there is impurity likewise consists of an inversion of perception and an inversion of view.

These four are abandoned through the path of cultivation: the mental inversion of reckoning the impermanent as permanent, the mental inversion of reckoning suffering as pleasure, the mental inversion of reckoning what is not-self as self, and the mental inversion of reckoning the impure as pure.
Those [defilements] to be abandoned by the path of seeing are ultimately abandoned when the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) is present.
Those to be abandoned by the path of cultivation are ultimately abandoned when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is present.
Question: Why does he speak in this way? Answer:
He relies on the Buddha’s sūtras.
In the sūtras, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These are the four perversions: perversion of perception, perversion of mind, and perversion of view," and so forth, as explained at length.
Based on this sūtra, the twelve inversions are taught.
To bring such a speaker’s intention to rest through two matters, a question and answer are formulated.
If one were to ask as follows:
Regarding these four perversions, how many are abandoned and how many are not abandoned by a Srotāpanna?
This serves to stop the intention behind the statement that there are twelve [perversions].
If one were to answer as follows:
The statement that the *srotāpanna* has completely severed [the defilements] refers to the intention that they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). Why is this so?
Because within the path of cultivation, there are no such dharmas as those to be abandoned by the *srotāpanna*.
If there were twelve kinds of perversions (*viparyāsa*) that were also to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtras.
As it is said, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If there are those who are perverted by the four perversions, you should know that they are all foolish, petty worldlings (*bāla-pṛthagjana*)."
Why is this so? Because ordinary beings contemplate the phenomena of birth and death without seeing their beginning or end, like examining the entrails of a dog.
If a Buddhist sūtra speaks of four [noble truths], one should know that there are no twelve [links of dependent origination] therein.
If it is said that these are all merely foolish, ordinary worldlings, one should know that they are not what is abandoned through the cultivation of the path. Question:
If there are only four inversions, how do you reconcile this with the sūtra cited by the Vibhajyavādins?
Answer: Because perception and mind are closely associated with inversion, they are also called "inversions. Question:
The dharmas of enumeration, such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, are also closely associated with inverted dharmas; why then are they not called "inverted"?
The answer is:
because these two are dharmas of conventional discourse.
The world generally says of such a person:
"This person has a perversion of mind and a perversion of perception," yet they do not say they have a perversion of feeling or a perversion of volition.
Question: What is the essential nature of perversion (*viparyāsa*)? Answer:
Their essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*). Question:
If the essential nature of these perversions is wisdom, then among these five views, how many are perversions and how many are not?
Answer: Two and a half views are inversions, while two and a half views are not inversions.

Those two and a half views that are inversions refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the eternalist view within the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the "two and a half views that are not inverted," these refer to wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the attachment to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and among the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Question:
For what reason are two and a half views inverted, while the other two and a half views are not inverted?
The answer is:
It is a perversion for three reasons: first, because it is intense; second, because it involves false grasping; and third, because it is a one-sided perversion.
Although the view of annihilationism, which is subsumed under wrong view and extreme views, is both intense and one-sidedly perverted, it does not involve false grasping.
Why is this so? Because it exclusively destroys the substance of things.
Although the clinging to precepts and rituals is both fierce and sharp and is a false grasping, it is not invariably a perversion of nature.
Why is this? Because there is a slight resemblance.

There are paths of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that can bring about detachment from the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and there are paths of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) that can bring about detachment from the form realm.
