The answer is:

The factors associated with the concentration of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-samādhi*) and the signless concentration (*animitta-samādhi*), which are not subsumed under nor dissociated from the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), are: form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth category.

As it is with the emptiness samādhi (śūnyatā-samādhi) in relation to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), so it is also for the emptiness samādhi in relation to the faculty of "knowing" (ājñendriya) and the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya).
If a dharma is associated with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), is it also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
This should be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is associated with the emptiness samādhi but not with the awakening factor of mindfulness: the awakening factor of mindfulness should [arise] in relation to the emptiness samādhi; within the aggregate of factors co-arising with the emptiness samādhi, the essence of the awakening factor of mindfulness is associated with the emptiness samādhi, yet it is not itself associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness.
Why is this? Because a self-essence cannot correspond with itself, as previously stated.

Regarding that which is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*): the concentration on emptiness should relate to the awakening factor of mindfulness; within the aggregate of factors co-arising with the awakening factor of mindfulness, the essence of the concentration on emptiness is associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness, but it is not associated with the concentration on emptiness itself.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, a self-essence cannot correspond with itself;
furthermore, it does not correspond with other factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are dissociated from the emptiness samādhi.
What is that? It refers to the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness within the collection [of mental states] concurrent with the wishless and signless samādhis.

As for those associated with the emptiness samādhi and also with the awakening factor of mindfulness: excluding the awakening factor of mindfulness associated with the emptiness samādhi (which is excluded because it is predominant), there are all other mind and mental factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness concurrent with the emptiness samādhi.

What are they? The answer is: the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the mental application (*vitarka*) and sustained application (*vicāra*) that follow the respective stages.

Regarding "neither associated with the emptiness samādhi nor with the mindfulness factor of enlightenment": within the collection [of mental factors] that is not associated with the emptiness samādhi and is co-present with the wishless and signless samādhis, the essence of the mindfulness factor of enlightenment is not associated with the emptiness samādhi, because it belongs to a different collection.
It is not associated with the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness. Why is this?
Because a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.

All other mental states and mental concomitants (*citta-caitasika-dharma*), with the exception of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) and its remaining factors, as well as the remaining tainted mental states and mental concomitants, matter (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from the mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Such dharmas as these constitute the fourth category.

Just as with the concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) in relation to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), so it is for the concentration on emptiness in relation to the factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmavicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), energy (*vīrya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*), equanimity (*upekṣā-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), right effort (*samyagvyāyāma*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*).
If a dharma is associated with the emptiness samādhi, is it also associated with the factor of awakening that is joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
This should be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is associated with the emptiness samādhi but not with the factor of awakening that is joy: the factor of awakening that is joy should [be analyzed] in relation to the emptiness samādhi; within the collection [of factors] co-arising with the emptiness samādhi, the essence of the factor of awakening that is joy is associated with the emptiness samādhi, but not associated with the factor of awakening that is joy itself.
Why is this? Because a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated;
furthermore, it is because [the factors] are associated with the emptiness samādhi, which is not associated with the factor of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga).

What is that? It consists of the dharmas associated with the emptiness samādhi within the preparatory dhyāna (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

Regarding "that which is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga) but not with the concentration on emptiness (śūnyatā-samādhi)": the concentration on emptiness should be applied to the factor of enlightenment of joy; within the aggregate associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, the essence of the concentration on emptiness is associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy, but it is not associated with the concentration on emptiness itself.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, a self-nature cannot correspond with itself;
furthermore, it refers to those factors associated with the awakening factor of joy that are not associated with the samādhi of emptiness.
What is that? It is the factors associated with the awakening factor of joy within the collection [of mental states] concurrent with the wishless and signless samādhis.

Regarding those concurrent with both the emptiness samādhi and the awakening factor of joy: excluding the emptiness samādhi concurrent with the awakening factor of joy, and excluding the awakening factor of joy concurrent with the emptiness samādhi, it consists of the remaining mind and mental concomitant factors concurrent with both the emptiness samādhi and the awakening factor of joy.

What are they? The answer is: the eight universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal mental factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the mental application (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) that follow the respective stages.

Regarding "neither associated with the emptiness samādhi nor with the joy factor of enlightenment": this refers to the joy factor of enlightenment that is not associated with the emptiness samādhi; within the collection [of mental factors] concomitant with the wishless and signless samādhis, the essence of the joy factor of enlightenment is not associated with the emptiness samādhi, because it belongs to a different collection.
It is not associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga). Why is this?
Because a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.
The emptiness samādhi that is dissociated from the factor of enlightenment of joy— what is that?

It is the essence of the emptiness samādhi within the aggregate of the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate dhyāna, the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), which does not associate with the emptiness samādhi.
Why is this? Because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated.
Furthermore, it is not associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*).
Why is this so? Because within that stage there is no joy (*prīti*).

Furthermore, all other mental states and mental factors—including those in the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, the three formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), and the clusters associated with the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and signless (*animitta*) samādhis—as well as all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors, matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth alternative.

As it is with the emptiness samādhi (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) in relation to the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), so it is also with the emptiness samādhi in relation to right awakening (*samyag-bodhi*).
If a dharma is associated with the emptiness samādhi, is it also associated with the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: If it is associated with the emptiness samādhi, it is also associated with the factor of awakening of concentration.
Is there anything that is associated with the factor of awakening of concentration but not associated with the emptiness samādhi?
Answer: There are.
These are the factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration that are not subsumed within the emptiness samādhi.
What is that? It is the factors associated with the awakening factor of concentration within the meditative absorption that is the conjunction of wishlessness and signlessness.
Just as the emptiness samādhi relates to the awakening factor of concentration, so too does the emptiness samādhi relate to right concentration.
As it is with the *śūnyatā-samādhi*, so too is the explanation for the *apraṇihita-samādhi* and the *animitta-samādhi*. The difference lies in the *apraṇihita-samādhi*.
Regarding the *animitta-samādhi*, it is likewise in relation to the factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), and right resolve (*samyaksaṃkalpa*).

If a dharma is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), but is not associated with the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) or the faculty of having known (ājñātāvīndriya), is it also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛtisambodhyaṅga)?
This is elaborated at length in a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) but is not associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): it refers to the awakening factor of mindfulness subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. Within the aggregate of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the essence of the awakening factor of mindfulness is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but is not associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness itself.
Why is this? Because a self-entity cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated.

Regarding those factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," these are the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that? The answer is:

among the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness within the aggregate of the faculty of knowing and the faculty of one who has known, there are factors that do not correspond with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because they belong to a different aggregate.

Regarding "associated with the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and also associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga)": these are the factors associated with the awakening factor of mindfulness that are subsumed under the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown. What are they?
Answer: The eight faculties and those mental factors associated with them that are not themselves faculties.

Regarding "not associated with the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and also not being the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment (smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga)": this refers to the factor of mindfulness-enlightenment that is not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that? The answer is:

within the aggregate of both the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the essence of the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because it belongs to a different aggregate.
One does not practice in association with the awakening factor of mindfulness. Why is this?
Because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.

And other mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*); furthermore, there is no untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), nor any other tainted (*sāsrava*) minds and mental factors, nor form (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), or formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth category.

Just as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" relates to the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, so too does the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" relate to the factors of enlightenment of discrimination of phenomena, energy, and concentration, as well as to right view, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. It is likewise for all such cases.
If a dharma is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), is it also associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga)?
[This should be expanded into four permutations.

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" but not with the factor of enlightenment of joy: the factor of enlightenment of joy subsumed within the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—that is, the essence of the factor of enlightenment of joy within the aggregate associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"—is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but is not associated with the factor of enlightenment of joy.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, a self-essence cannot be its own self-essence;

furthermore, it includes those factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are not subsumed under and are dissociated from the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
What are these? The answer is:

the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) within the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), the intermediate stage (*dhyānāntara*), and the third and fourth dhyānas, do not correspond to the awakening factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*).
Why is this? Because that stage lacks joy (*prīti*).

As for those associated with the factor of awakening of joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*) but not with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), the factors associated with the factor of awakening of joy are not subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that? The answer is:

among the factors associated with the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) and the faculty of having known (ājñātāvīndriya), those factors associated with the factor of joy (prītisaṃbodhyaṅga) are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (ājñāsyāmīndriya), because they belong to a different category.

Regarding "that which is associated with the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown' and also with the factor of joy within awakening": this refers to those phenomena associated with the factor of joy that is subsumed under the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. What, then, are these?
Answer: It refers to the eight faculties and their associated mental factors that are not themselves faculties.

Regarding those that are neither associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" nor associated with the factor of joy in enlightenment (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*): this means that the factor of joy in enlightenment is neither subsumed by nor associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that? The answer is:

within the aggregate of both the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), the essential nature of the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*) does not correspond with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*), because it belongs to a different aggregate.
Nor is it associated with the factor of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*). Why is this?
Because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated.

And what are those other mental states and mental factors associated with the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) that are not included within and are dissociated from the factor of joy (*prītisaṃbodhyaṅga*)?
Answer: [They are as follows:]

Within the preliminary concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), the third and fourth dhyānas, and the three formless attainments (*ārūpya*), all contaminated (*sāsrava*) mental states and mental factors, as well as matter (*rūpa*), unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*), that exist within the aggregate of the faculty of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Such dharmas constitute the fourth alternative (*catuṣkoṭi*).

If a dharma is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), is it also associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*)?
This should be expanded into four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) as far as possible.

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) but not with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): the awakening factor of tranquility should be [considered] in relation to the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; within the aggregate (*kalāpa*) that co-exists with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the essence (*svabhāva*) of the awakening factor of tranquility is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but it is not associated with itself as the awakening factor of tranquility.
Why is this? Because a self-nature cannot be associated with itself, as previously stated.

Regarding that which is associated with the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) but not with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), it refers to those factors associated with the factor of tranquility that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."
What is that? The answer is:

among the collection of factors associated with both the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvindriya*), those factors associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) that are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) [constitute it], because they belong to a different collection.

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and also associated with the awakening factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*): it refers to those phenomena associated with the awakening factor of tranquility and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown. What are they?

Answer: The ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the nine wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the mental factors of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) according to their respective stages.

That which is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and also not associated with the factor of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) refers to the factor of tranquility that is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

What is this? It refers to the factor of the enlightenment constituent of tranquility (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) within the aggregate of both the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), which does not associate with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), because it belongs to a different aggregate.
Nor is it associated with the factor of enlightenment of tranquility. Why is this?
Because a self-substance cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.

And other mental states and mental concomitants; furthermore, there is no untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*), but rather other tainted minds and mental concomitants (*sāsrava-citta-caitasika-dharma*), as well as form (*rūpa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Such dharmas as these constitute the fourth category.

Just as the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" relates to the awakening factor of tranquility, so too does the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" relate to the awakening factor of equanimity.
If a dharma is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), is it also associated with perfect enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*)?
This should be expanded into four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" but not with perfect enlightenment: as for the entity of perfect enlightenment, within the aggregate of the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the essence of perfect enlightenment is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," yet it is not associated with [itself as] perfect enlightenment.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, a self-nature cannot be associated with itself;
furthermore, it is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," but rather associated with the faculty of "perfect enlightenment."
What is that? It is the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) within the intermediate dhyāna and the third dhyāna.

Regarding those associated with perfect enlightenment (*samyagbodhi*) but not with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," these are factors associated with perfect enlightenment but not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown."

What is that? It refers to those factors associated with right awakening within the aggregate of the faculty of knowing (ājñendriya) and the faculty of one who has known (ājñātāvīndriya), which are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya), because they belong to a different aggregate.

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya) and is also associated with perfect enlightenment (samyagbodhi): these are the factors associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" and with perfect enlightenment. What are they?
Answer: The ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), and the contemplation of the mind (*cittanidhyapti*).

That which is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and is also not [associated with] perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) means that it is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," nor is it associated with perfect enlightenment.

What is this? It is the essence of perfect enlightenment within the aggregate of both the faculty of knowing and the faculty of having known, which is not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," because it belongs to a different aggregate.
Nor is it associated with perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.

And as for the remaining mind and mental factors: "the remainder" refers to all contaminated (sāsrava) mind and mental factors, matter (rūpa), unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta), and formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra) that exist within the aggregate of the faculty of knowledge (ājñendriya) and the faculty of having known (ājñātāvīndriya) during the intermediate dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the three formless absorptions (ārūpyasamāpatti).
Such dharmas as these constitute the fourth alternative.

As it is with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*), so too are the explanations for the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) and the faculty of having known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
The difference is as follows:
If a dharma is associated with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*), is it also associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*)?
This should be elaborated at length as a fourfold permutation (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of one who has already known but not with right view: the right view subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known; within the aggregate associated with the faculty of one who has already known, the essence of right view is associated with the faculty of one who has already known, but is not associated with right view.
Why is this? Because, as previously stated, a self-nature cannot be associated with itself;
furthermore, it should be known that [the faculty of having already known] is not associated with other right views, but is associated with [other] dharmas.
What is that? The answer is:

within the aggregate of both the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), it is associated with the faculty of having already known (*ājñātendriya*), but not associated with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), because it belongs to a different aggregate.

Regarding "associated with right view but not associated with the faculty of one who has already known": this refers to those factors associated with right view that are not subsumed under the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*). Furthermore, the factors associated with right view within the same assembly as the faculty of one who desires to know (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) or the faculty of knowing (*ājñendriya*) are not associated with the faculty of one who has already known, because they belong to a different assembly.

Regarding that which is associated with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) but not with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*): it refers to those dharmas associated with both the faculty of one who has already known and right view.
What are they? The answer is: [the dharmas of the stage of arhatship].

The eight faculties, as well as their associated non-faculty mental states and mental factors, are neither associated with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*) nor are they right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Regarding right view not included within the faculty of one who has already known: within the aggregate associated with the faculty of "desiring to know what is not yet known" (*ājñāsyāmīndriya*), the essence of right view is not associated with the faculty of one who has already known, because it belongs to a different aggregate.
It is not associated with right view.
Why is this? Because a self-essence cannot be associated with itself, as previously explained.

And other mental states and mental concomitants; all untainted phenomena without exception; and the remaining tainted mental states and mental concomitants, as well as matter, unconditioned phenomena, and formations dissociated from mind.
Such dharmas as these constitute the fourth category.
The remaining associated factors are as explained in the preceding chapter.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 58.
Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Scroll 59.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred Arhats.
Translated by the Northern Liang Indian Śramaṇa Buddhavarman.
Translated by Kung Tao-t’ai and others. Chapter Four of the Section Corresponding to the *Jñāna-skandha*, Part Three. There are forty-four essential natures of knowledge (*jñāna-svabhāva*):

the essential nature of knowing old age and death; the essential nature of knowing the origin of old age and death; the essential nature of knowing the cessation of old age and death; and the essential nature of knowing the path leading to the cessation of old age and death. This applies likewise up to the knowledge of formations (*saṃskāra*).
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed? Answer:
This is a Buddhist sutra.
In this sutra, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"I shall now expound the essence of forty-four types of knowledge; you all should listen with single-minded attention."
The Buddha taught this sūtra without providing extensive analysis.
Since the Buddha’s sūtras constitute the foundation for this treatise, this treatise has been composed in order to provide such extensive analysis.
Question: If the Buddha’s sūtras are the foundation of this treatise, for what reason did the World-Honored One preach these sūtras? Answer:
The World-Honored One has attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* by means of such gates of expedient paths; he now wishes to demonstrate these gates of expedient paths to his disciples:
"If you do not abandon these gates of expedient paths, you shall before long attain the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*)."
It is like a wealthy and noble elder who, having accumulated wealth through such skillful means, further desires to instruct his sons and grandsons with these same skillful means:
"You should not abandon such skillful means; before long, you shall obtain immeasurable wealth and treasures."
It is the same for that as well.
What are the forty-four entities of knowledge?

Knowledge of aging and death is one entity of knowledge; knowledge of the origin of aging and death is the second entity of knowledge; knowledge of the cessation of aging and death is the third entity of knowledge; and knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death is the fourth entity of knowledge.

Knowing the cause of old age and death involves four types of wisdom; likewise, up to knowing the cause of existence, there are also four types of wisdom. Thus, eleven sets of four constitute forty-four types of wisdom.
Question: Why is it not said that the essence of wisdom consists in the knowledge of non-existence? Answer:
When something that ought to be stated is not stated, one should know that this statement is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).

Furthermore, if it were the case that a member of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) which acts as a cause for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is what is meant by the "essence of knowledge" (*jñānasvabhāva*), then although ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed a member of dependent origination, it does not act as such a cause.
Furthermore, as for the four dharmas, they establish the essence of knowledge; ignorance is not so established because it possesses three types of meaning.
Knowledge of old age and death consists of four knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of suffering, and conventional knowledge.

The knowledge of the origin of old age and death consists of four knowledges: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), knowledge of the origin (samudaya-jñāna), and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).

The knowledge of the cessation of old age and death consists of four knowledges: namely, the knowledge of phenomena, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna), and conventional knowledge.
The knowledge of the path leading to the cessation of aging and death consists of four knowledges: namely, dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, and conventional knowledge.

Just as there are sixteen knowledges in knowing the existence of aging and death, there are likewise sixteen knowledges in knowing the existence of birth, and so on, up to the knowledge of formations.

If analyzed according to the body and the moments, they are immeasurable and boundless; however, within this context, there are forty-four essential natures of knowledge by way of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*), the truths (*satya*), and the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).
Question: Of these forty-four types of wisdom, how many exist in the past, how many in the future, and how many in the present? Answer:
Some belong to the past, some to the future, and some to the present.
How many conditions pertain to the past, and how many to the future and the present? Answer:
Thirty-three conditions pertain to the three periods of time; eleven conditions pertain to non-temporal phenomena (*adhva-dharma*).

According to what is stated in the *Saṃyukta-āgama* (Miscellaneous Khandhas), three conditions pertain to the past: namely, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of the origin of suffering (*samudaya-jñāna*), and the knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*nirodha-jñāna*).
Three conditions pertain to the future: namely, knowing aging and death, knowing the origin of aging and death, and knowing birth.

Sixteen conditions pertain to the present: namely, knowing birth and knowing the origin of birth; knowing existence and knowing the origin of existence; knowing grasping and knowing the origin of grasping; knowing craving and knowing the origin of craving; knowing feeling and knowing the origin of feeling; knowing contact and knowing the origin of contact; knowing the six sense bases and knowing the origin of the six sense bases; knowing name-and-form and knowing the origin of name-and-form; and knowing consciousness.
Eleven [factors] have the three time periods as their conditions; eleven have non-time periods as their conditions.
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*), and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The answer is:
Some are entirely with outflows (sāsrava), and some are entirely without outflows (anāsrava).
How many have outflows as their object (ālambana), and how many have no outflows as their object? Answer:
Twenty-two [factors] have outflows as their object; twenty-two have the outflow-free as their object.
How many are conditioned, and how many are unconditioned? Answer:
All are conditioned; there is no wisdom that is unconditioned.
How many conditions are for the conditioned? How many conditions are for the unconditioned? Answer:
Thirty-three conditions pertain to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and eleven conditions pertain to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

This wisdom, by its very nature, cannot attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), nor can it realize the fruit, nor abandon desire, nor exhaust the outflows (*āsrava*). It is a dharma originally attained by the noble ones (*ārya*) which arises and manifests for the sake of sport, for the sake of contemplating what was originally accomplished, for the sake of experiencing happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*), and for the sake of enjoying the noble dharmas.
There are seventy-seven entities of wisdom.
Question: For what purpose was this treatise composed?
Answer: This is a Buddhist scripture.
The Buddhist scriptures state:

I shall now explain the essence of the seventy-seven knowledges: namely, the essence of the knowledge that birth is the condition for aging-and-death; the essence of the knowledge that there is no aging-and-death without birth as its condition; and so on, as explained at length.
As for why the Buddha taught this sutra, it is as previously explained.
What is the essence of the seventy-seven knowledges?
The answer is:

To know that birth is the condition for old age and death is the essence of the first wisdom; to know that it is not the case that there is old age and death without birth as a condition is the essence of the second wisdom; to know that past birth was once the condition for old age and death is the essence of the third wisdom; to know that it is not the case that there was no past birth as a condition for old age and death is the essence of the fourth wisdom; to know that future birth will be the condition for old age and death is the essence of the fifth wisdom; to know that it is not the case that there will be no future birth as a condition for old age and death is the essence of the sixth wisdom; and to know the wisdom of the stability of phenomena—that these phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, born from causes and conditions, subject to exhaustion, subject to cessation, and subject to dispassion—and to know such phenomena is the essence of the seventh wisdom.

Just as there are seven types of wisdom regarding old age and death, and likewise seven types of wisdom regarding birth, these eleven sets of seven types of wisdom constitute seventy-seven types of wisdom.
Question: Why is it not stated here that one knows the essence of wisdom which has ignorance as its condition? Answer:
That which ought to be stated but is not stated, one should know that such a statement is incomplete (*sāvaśeṣa*).

Furthermore, if it were the case that a member of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpādāṅga*) functions as a cause for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṭa*), then the essence of knowledge (*jñāna-svabhāva*) would be so stated; however, although ignorance (*avidyā*) is indeed a member of dependent origination, it does not function as a cause [for conditioned phenomena].

Knowing that birth is the condition for old age and death constitutes the essence of four types of knowledge: namely, dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and origin-knowledge (samudayajñāna).
It is not the case that there is no essence of knowledge regarding old age and death that does not take birth as its object.
Why is this further statement made?
The answer is:
there are two kinds of arguments: first, establishing one's own position; second, establishing the position of another.

"Establishing one's own statement" refers to how a disciple of the Buddha establishes their own statement according to the principles of the Buddha-dharma, just as a disciple of a non-Buddhist school establishes their own statement according to the principles of that non-Buddhist school.
As in the case of the *yuktavādin*, one establishes one's own statement by means of the meaning of being a *yuktavādin*;
as in the case of the *vibhajyavādin*, one establishes one's own statement by means of the meaning of being a *vibhajyavādin*.

Regarding "definitive speech": it is like a disciple of the Buddha definitively speaking to a disciple of a non-Buddhist, or a disciple of a non-Buddhist definitively speaking to a disciple of the Buddha;
or as a Yuktavādin definitively speaking to a Vibhajyavādin, or a Vibhajyavādin definitively speaking to a Yuktavādin.
Some may say that this was stated merely for the sake of dialectical discussion and does not refer to actual phenomena.
To ensure that this meaning is definitively established as having such a factual basis, it is therefore said:
"There is no aging and death that does not arise conditioned [by birth]."

This knowledge consists of four knowledges, namely: dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), and knowledge of the origin [of suffering] (samudayajñāna).
Together with the preceding, there are eight knowledges.

The knowledge that knows past births as having served as the conditions for old age and death has four knowledges as its essence—namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, conventional knowledge, and knowledge of the origin—and together with the preceding, there are twelve knowledges in its essence.

The knowledge that [the past] was not non-contingent upon old age and death in previous births is, in its essence, four types of knowledge as previously explained; together with the preceding, there are sixteen types of knowledge in their essential nature.

The knowledge that future birth will serve as the condition for aging and death has four knowledges as its essence, as previously explained; including the preceding, there are twenty knowledges in total.

The knowledge that it is not the case that aging and death will not occur conditioned by future birth has four knowledges as its essence, as previously explained; including the preceding, there are twenty-four knowledges in total.
The knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), and so forth as extensively explained, together with the preceding [knowledge], constitutes twenty-five essential natures of wisdom.

Just as there are twenty-five essential natures of wisdom for knowing that old age and death have existence (*bhava*) as their condition, there are likewise twenty-five essential natures of wisdom for knowing that formations (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition.

If one analyzes them according to the person and the moment, there are immeasurable and boundless bodies of wisdom; herein, by way of the factors of existence (*aṅga*), the time periods (*adhvan*), the truths (*satya*), and the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*), seventy-seven bodies of wisdom are established.
Question: Why is the essence of the knowledge that knows the present not explained? Answer:
Some may say that birth is the condition for old age and death, and that there is no old age and death without birth as a condition; this refers to the essence of knowledge of the present.
One who knows the past knows the past, and one who knows the future knows the future.
Furthermore, there are those who say: "One knows that birth is the condition for old age and death; it is not the case that there is old age and death without birth as a condition.
This is called knowing the three periods of time: one knows the past as the past, and one knows the future as the future.
Question: How much of this wisdom exists in the past, and how much in the future and present? Answer:
Some are entirely in the past, some are entirely in the future, and some are entirely in the present.
How many have the past as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), how many have the future as their object-condition, and how many have the present as their object-condition?

Answer: If, as it has been said, birth is the condition for old age and death, and there is no old age and death without the condition of birth—this refers to the essence of the knowledge that knows the present. Twenty-two conditions pertain to the past, twenty-two to the future, twenty-two to the present, and eleven to the three periods of time.

If one were to say that birth is the condition for old age and death, and that there is no old age and death without birth as a condition—this being said by one who understands the essence of the knowledge of the three periods of time—then twenty-two conditions pertain to the past, twenty-two conditions pertain to the future, and thirty-three conditions pertain to all three periods of time.
How many are with outflows (sāsrava) and how many are without outflows (anāsrava)? Answer:
Some are entirely with outflows, while others are entirely without outflows.
How many take the contaminated (*sāsrava*) as their object, and how many take the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) as their object? Answer:
All take the contaminated as their object.
How many are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and how many are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
The answer is:
all are conditioned; there is no essence of wisdom that is unconditioned.
How many conditions are conditioned (*saṃskṛta*)? How many conditions are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)? Answer:
All conditions are conditioned.
"The essence of this wisdom cannot attain right determination," and so forth, as extensively explained.
Furthermore, there is the "wisdom of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), and so forth, as extensively explained.
The "wisdom of the stability of phenomena" is the wisdom that knows causes.
Why is this so? Because "abiding" is called the cause;
it is because the fruits—superior, middling, and inferior—of the three realms abide therein.
If one knows this wisdom, it is called the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa).

This wisdom consists of four types of knowledge: namely, the knowledge of phenomena (dhammañāṇa), subsequent knowledge (anvayañāṇa), conventional knowledge (sammutiñāṇa), and the knowledge of origination (samudayañāṇa).

Furthermore, there are those who say: "If one wishes to know the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*), this is called knowing the knowledge of the stability of phenomena; to know that knowledge is the knowledge of the path (*maggañāṇa*). Question:
If this is so, how is this teaching to be reconciled?
As it is said:
"This is the dharma of exhaustion, the dharma of cessation, the dharma of desirelessness, and the dharma without outflows; it is not the dharma of non-desire.
The answer is:
This passage should be stated as follows:
"This is the nature of exhaustion, the nature of cessation"; one should not say it is "the nature of dispassion.
What is the intention behind not stating it so?
Answer: It is because one wishes to censure the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas.
As the Sūtra says:
Suśīma, you should know that first there is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), and subsequently there is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Question: Among these, what is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena?
What is the knowledge of nirvāṇa?
The answer is:

the knowledge that understands the increase of birth and death is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna); the knowledge that understands the cessation of the increase of birth and death is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, knowing the twelve links of dependent origination is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna); knowing the cessation of the twelve links of dependent origination is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Knowing the knowledge of suffering and its origin is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena; knowing the knowledge of cessation and the path is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
If one explains it in this way, it effectively accounts for the fact that the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) occurs first, followed by the knowledge of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, there are those who say that the knowledge of suffering, its origin, and the path is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena, while the knowledge of cessation is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Question: If that is so, then the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dharmasthitijñāna*) would exist first, followed by the knowledge of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇajñāna*).
How can this statement be reconciled?
Answer: There are also instances where the knowledge of nirvāṇa occurs later.

Furthermore, the knowledge regarding the middle among the extremes is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), while the fundamental knowledge regarding the middle is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
How is this known?
A sutra states:
"A great multitude of heterodox brahmins gathered in one place and engaged in this discussion:"
Hearing these words, [they thought], "Before the śramaṇa Gautama appeared in the world, we were respected, honored, and provided for by kings, ministers, brahmins, and householders."
"Now that the śramaṇa Gautama has appeared in the world, he has stripped us of our reputation and material gains.
It is as if the rising sun causes fire to lose its light.
What skillful means should we now employ to regain our fame and profits? and so forth, as extensively described.
Again, they thought:
"The śramaṇa Gautama possesses no extraordinary virtues; he merely knows the sūtras and śāstras well and has a handsome countenance.
We do not rely on physical appearance; if we simply know the sūtras and śāstras, we can likewise regain our reputation and material gains," and so forth, as extensively explained.
They spoke again, saying:
"Who among this assembly is capable of going forth within the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama and secretly mastering the Dharma, so that we may receive, uphold, read, and recite it?"
They further spoke these words:

"Now the brahmin Susīma is firm in his resolve; he is capable of leaving the household life within the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama and secretly receiving the teachings, so that we may receive, uphold, read, and recite them."
They all went immediately to Suśīma and reported the aforementioned matter to him in detail.
At that time, Suśīma consented for two reasons: first, out of affection for his kinsmen and retinue; second, due to the causal conditions of their roots of virtue.
At that time, Susīma departed from Rājagṛha and went to the Bamboo Grove.
There, a great number of bhikṣus were pacing back and forth in walking meditation near the gate of the vihāra.
At that time, Susīma saw the bhikṣus from afar; he immediately went to them and spoke these words:
"Bhikṣus, you should know that I wish to practice the pure life of brahmacarya within the Dharma of the śramaṇa Gautama."
Then the bhikṣus took Suśīma to the place where the World-Honored One was and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This brahmin Suśīma now wishes to leave the household life within the Dharma of the World-Honored One, receive full ordination, and practice the way of a bhikṣu."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You may grant Suśīma the going forth and bestow upon him full ordination.
Thereupon, the bhikṣus immediately granted him the going forth and bestowed full ordination.
At that time, Suśīma was intelligent and wise, with firm power of mindfulness; before long, he had read and recited the Tripiṭaka.
Having gained a slight understanding of its meaning, he thought to himself:
"If I wish to benefit my kinsmen, now is precisely the right time."
Emerging from the Bamboo Grove, he was about to proceed toward Rājagṛha.
"The World-Honored One possesses all-illuminating eyes that protect the Dharma; who could possibly steal it?
At that time, five hundred bhikṣus went to the place of Susīma.
Some said, "These bhikṣus were created by the Buddha through his transformative power.
Others said, "They are actual bhikṣus.
Then the bhikṣus went to Suśīma’s place and all spoke these words:
"Suśīma, you should know that for us, birth is exhausted, what was to be done has been accomplished, the holy life is established, and there will be no further existence.
At that time, Suśīma asked the bhikṣus:
"Did you attain the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the first dhyāna?"
He replied: "No.
Can one attain the exhaustion of outflows by relying on the second, third, or fourth dhyānas, or by the peaceful liberations that transcend form and the formless?"
He replied,
"No. Then Suśīma spoke again as follows:
"Since you have not attained the exhaustion of outflows by relying on meditative concentration, who would believe you?
At that time, the bhikṣus all said:
"We are those liberated through wisdom."
At that time, Suśīma did not understand the liberation through wisdom;
he thought, "If my kinsmen were to ask about this matter, I would not know.
For this reason, he returned to the place where the Buddha was and related all these matters to the Buddha in detail.
The Buddha replied:
"Suśīma, you should know that first there is the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena (dharmasthitijñāna), and subsequently there is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
Suśīma again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I do not now know which is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) and which is the knowledge of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told Suśīma:
Whether you know it or not, such is the nature of the Dharma: first there is the knowledge of the abiding of phenomena, and subsequently there is the knowledge of Nirvana.
Those bhikṣus first exhaust their outflows by relying on the preparatory dhyāna (anāgamya), and only afterwards do they give rise to the fundamental dhyānas.

For this reason, one knows that the knowledge of the extremes and the middle is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna), while the fundamental knowledge of the middle is the knowledge of nirvana.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna), does one also accomplish inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna)?
The answer is:
If it is attained.
What constitutes attainment?
If the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is present before one,
and one possesses that subsequent knowledge, does one also possess the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)? Answer:
It is so. Why is this? Because the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is attained first.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained and not lost.
What is meant by "attained and not lost"?
It refers to one who has already abandoned craving for the desire realm and does not regress from that state of detachment.
Furthermore, if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: If it is attained.
What constitutes attainment?
If the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) is present before one,
and if one possesses the knowledge of the dharma, does one also possess conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna)? Answer:
Thus it is.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also accomplish dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna)? Answer: No.
If it is attained,
how is it attained? It is when the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (duḥkha-dharma-jñāna) is present before one.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the knowledge of suffering, does one also achieve the knowledge of phenomena? Answer: Yes.
Why is this? Because these two knowledges are attained simultaneously.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also accomplish the knowledges of origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If one has attained it.
Furthermore, if one accomplishes the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path, does one also accomplish the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna)?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
Because the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) is attained first.
If one possesses the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: Yes.
If one attains it and does not lose it—
what does "attaining it and not losing it" mean?
It means that having already become free from craving for sensual desires, one does not regress from that freedom from desire.
If one achieves the knowledge of others' minds, does one also achieve inferential knowledge?
Answer: If one has attained it.
What constitutes "attainment"?
It is when the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is present before one.
If one has attained the subsequent knowledge, does one also attain conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also accomplish inferential knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: If it is attained, it is as previously explained.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of inference (*anvaya-jñāna*), does one also accomplish the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: It is so.
If one achieves the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), does one also achieve subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*)?
Answer: If it is attained, it is as previously explained.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of inference (anvaya-jñāna), does one also accomplish the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If it is attained, it is as previously explained.
Furthermore, if one accomplishes the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path, does one also accomplish subsequent knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds, does one also accomplish conventional knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), does one also accomplish the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: If it is attained and not lost, it is as previously explained.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds, does one also accomplish the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If one has attained them,
and if one accomplishes the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, does one also accomplish the knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: If it is attained and not lost, it is as previously explained.
If one accomplishes conventional knowledge (*samvṛti-jñāna*), does one also accomplish the knowledge of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If one has attained them,
and if one accomplishes the knowledge of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, does one also accomplish conventional knowledge?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of suffering, does one also accomplish the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path?
Answer: If one has attained them,
even if one accomplishes the knowledge of origin, cessation, and the path, does one also accomplish the knowledge of suffering?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
Because the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) is attained first.
If one possesses the knowledge of origination (samudaya-jñāna), does one also possess the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) and the knowledge of the path (mārga-jñāna)?
Answer: Yes.
If one has attained [it], and if one has accomplished the knowledge of cessation and the knowledge of the path, does one also accomplish the knowledge of origination? Answer: Yes.
Thus it is. If one is accomplished in the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), is one also accomplished in the knowledge of the path (*mārga-jñāna*)?
The answer is:
If one has attained it—
specifically, if one accomplishes the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)— does one also accomplish the knowledge of cessation (nirodhajñāna)?
The answer is:
Thus it is.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future [knowledge of phenomena]?
Answer: Yes.
Thus it is.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past and future phenomena? Answer:

When attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the two moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the four moments when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the four moments when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the three moments when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or Arhat (*arhat*). When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or when one who is liberated transforms their faculties to become immovable (*akopyadharman*), at the moment they have already produced the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*): if they possess the future knowledge of the dharma (*anāgata-dharmajñāna*), do they also possess the past [knowledge of the dharma]?
The answer is:
If it has ceased and is not lost, it is as previously explained.
If it does not cease at that time, or if it ceases and is then lost, then it is not established.
At what time does one possess the future knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not the past?
The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), for the duration of a single thought-moment; or upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), when the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, or that which previously arose has been lost due to the attainment of the fruit; and so on, up until the case of one liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) who transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*), where that which previously arose has been lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties.
If one has attained the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past, has one also attained it regarding the present?
Answer: If it is manifest before one.

How does it manifest? It manifests when one has not yet given rise to the patience (*kṣānti*) of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) or conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), or when one is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
At what time is one endowed with the past and present *dharma-jñāna*?

Answer: Upon attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Once the knowledge of the dharma of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has arisen and is present before one, this continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) at the stage of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*), one becomes immovable (*akopya*), and the knowledge of the dharma of cessation has arisen and is present before one.
If one has attained present *dharmajñāna*, has one also attained it in the past?
The answer is: if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one has attained it.
At what time does one attain present *dharmajñāna* and also attain it in the past?
Answer: As previously stated,
if time were not subject to cessation, or if it ceased and was thereby lost, then [the argument] would not be established.
At what time is one accomplished in the present knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not in the past? The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); at the moment of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna*), during the single thought-moment; when the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, or when that which arose previously has been lost due to the attainment of the fruit; and when the knowledge of phenomena arises and is present before one. This continues until, in the case of one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*), they transform their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*), whereupon the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena that had not yet arisen, or that which arose previously, is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of faculties, and the knowledge of phenomena arises and is present before them.
If one accomplishes the future knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifested in the present.
At what time is one accomplished in the future and present *dharmajñāna*?
The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single-moment duration of seeing the Truth of Suffering, the single-moment duration of seeing the Truth of Origination, the single-moment duration of seeing the Truth of Cessation, and the single-moment duration of seeing the Truth of the Path; at the moment of attaining the fruit of *srotāpanna* when *dharmajñāna* arises and manifests before one; and so on, until the time of liberation through time (*samaya-vimukta*) transforms the faculties (*indriya*) to become immovable (*akopya*), when *dharmajñāna* arises and manifests before one.
If one has attained present dharma-knowledge, has one also attained it in the future? Answer: Yes.
Why is this so? If one accomplishes the present knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), one necessarily accomplishes it in the future.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena, does one also accomplish it in the future and the present?
Answer: It is accomplished in the future, and in the present if it is currently manifest.
At what time is the knowledge of the dharma of the three periods of time accomplished?
The answer is:

When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Once the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has arisen and is present before one, this continues until the stage of occasional liberation (*samayavimukti*) transforms its faculties (*indriya*) into the immovable (*akopya*), at which point the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation has already arisen and is present before one.
If one accomplishes the future and present knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also accomplish it in the past?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one accomplishes it, as previously explained regarding time.
If it were not extinguished, or if having been extinguished it were lost, then it would not be accomplished.
At what time is one accomplished in the future and present knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), yet not accomplished in the past?

Answer: When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) in the duration of a single moment of mind. That which has previously arisen and ceased is lost upon attaining the fruit; when the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) arises and becomes present, and so on until the liberation-by-time (*samaya-vimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya*) to become immovable (*akopya*), that which has previously arisen and ceased is lost due to attaining the fruit and transforming the faculties; then the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation arises and becomes present.
If one accomplishes the future knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish it in the past and present?
The answer is:

one may accomplish the future knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing it in the past or present; or accomplish it in the past without accomplishing it in the present; or accomplish it in the present without accomplishing it in the past; or accomplish it in both the past and the present.

Regarding the accomplishment of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) pertaining to the future but not the past or present: if one has acquired the knowledge of phenomena that has not yet ceased, or if it has ceased and been lost, it does not manifest before one.
If one has attained dharma-knowledge, this clarifies that there is a future.
If it has not yet ceased, or if having ceased it is lost, this clarifies that there is no past.
If it does not manifest before one, this clarifies that there is no present.
At what time is one accomplished in the future knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), yet not accomplished in the past or present?

It does not exist within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), because one has attained the fruit, the previously arisen knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*) is lost; thus, the knowledge of phenomena does not arise as a present manifestation.

Even when one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, if they have not yet given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), that which arose previously is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of faculties; thus, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) does not manifest before them.

Regarding that which is past but not present: if the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of non-arising (*anvayajñāna*) is not manifest before one, then if the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena has already arisen, it is evident that there is a past [state].
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) does not arise and is not present before one, then there is no manifestation of the present.
If one has attained [the knowledge of phenomena] in the past, one necessarily attains it in the future.
At what time does one attain the past and future knowledge of phenomena, yet not attain it in the present?
Answer: As previously stated regarding the accomplishment of the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) pertaining to the past and future:
as for that which is present but not past, when the knowledge of phenomena arises and is present before one, it has not yet ceased; or, even if it had ceased, it would have been lost.
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises and is present before one, it clarifies that the present exists.
If [the knowledge] has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased and is lost, it clarifies that the past does not exist.
If one possesses the present, one necessarily possesses the future.
At what time does one accomplish the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the future and present, but not the past?
Answer: It is as previously stated regarding the time when one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena regarding the future and present.
Regarding the past and the present: if one does not lose the knowledge of the dharma of arising and ceasing, the knowledge of the dharma of arising manifests before one.
If one does not lose the knowledge of the dharma of arising and ceasing, then it is clear that the past exists.
When the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) arises and is present, it clarifies that the present exists.
If one possesses [the knowledge of phenomena] in the past and present, one necessarily possesses it in the future.
At what time does one possess the knowledge of phenomena across the three periods?
Answer: As previously stated regarding the accomplishment of the knowledge of dharmas of the three times:
if one accomplishes the knowledge of dharmas of the past and present, does one also accomplish that of the future?
Answer: It is so.
If one accomplishes the present knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish it in the past and future?

Answer: One accomplishes it in the future; as for the past, if it has already ceased but is not lost, or if it has not yet ceased, or even if it has ceased but is lost, then one does not accomplish it.
At what time is the knowledge of the dharmas of the three periods of time accomplished?
Answer: It is at the time previously described for accomplishing the knowledge of the dharmas of the three periods of time.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) pertaining to the past and future, does one also accomplish it in the present?
The answer is:
if it is manifest before one, it is as previously explained.

Just as with the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), there are six propositions; the same applies to the knowledge of inference (*anvayajñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), the knowledge of origin (*samudayajñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodhajñāna*), and the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñāna*).
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 59. *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, Fascicle 60.
Composed by Kātyāyanīputra; explained by five hundred arhats and translated by the Northern Liang Indian *śramaṇa* Buddhabhadra together with Daotai and others.

The Fourth Part of the Fourth Chapter on Correspondence in the *Jñānavastu*: If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) regarding the past, does one also possess it regarding the future?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
If one accomplishes the past, one necessarily accomplishes the future.
At what time does one accomplish the knowledge of others' minds regarding both the past and the future? Answer:
Those born in the desire realm who have abandoned the desires of the desire realm, as well as those born in the form realm;

and if a learner (*śaikṣa*) has already produced the untainted knowledge of others' minds regarding the arising and ceasing [of states] in the desire and form realms, but at the end of life is reborn in the formless realm without yet having attained the fruit of arhatship.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the future, does one also accomplish it in the past?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one accomplishes it, as previously explained regarding time.
If it has not been extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, then it is not accomplished.
This does not occur for those born in the desire realm or the form realm.

However, if one has already produced the knowledge of others' minds that has been extinguished within the desire or form realms, and then at the end of life is reborn in the formless realm and attains the fruit of Arhatship there, at that time the knowledge of others' minds that was previously extinguished is not produced; because of the attainment of the fruit, what was previously produced is lost.

If a noble one, while in the desire or form realms, does not give rise to the untainted knowledge of others' minds regarding cessation, and subsequently dies to be reborn in the formless realm, they possess only the future knowledge of others' minds, but not the past.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds in the past, does one also attain it in the present?
Answer: If it is manifested in the present.
How does it manifest? It manifests when no other knowledge arises, when no receptivity (*kṣānti*) arises, and provided one is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
If one possesses the present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the past?
Answer: It is so.
At what time does one achieve the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and the present?
Answer: One born in the realm of desire or the realm of form brings the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) into manifestation.
If one possesses the future knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
What does "present before one" mean?
Answer: It occurs when no other knowledge (*jñāna*) or receptivity (*kṣānti*) arises, or when it manifests while one is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
At what time does one accomplish the future and present knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: One born in the desire realm or the form realm brings the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) into manifestation.
If one possesses the present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess it in the future?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
If one accomplishes the present [knowledge], one necessarily accomplishes the future.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the past, does one also accomplish it in the future and the present?
Answer: It is accomplished in the future, and it manifests in the present if it is present before one.
What does "manifesting in the present" mean?
As previously stated:
At what time does one achieve the knowledge of others' minds regarding the three periods of time?
The answer is:
When one is born in the desire realm or the form realm, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) arises and is present before them.
If one possesses the future and present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess the past [knowledge of others' minds]?
Answer: It is so.
At what time is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the three times accomplished?
Answer: As previously stated.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the future, does one also accomplish it in the past and the present?
Answer: One may possess the knowledge of others' minds in the future but not in the past or present; or possess it in the past but not in the present; or possess it in both the past and the present.
At what time is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) accomplished with respect to the future, but not with respect to the past or the present?
Answer: Among those born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu), such a case does not exist.

If a practitioner, while in the desire or form realms, does not produce the untainted knowledge of others' minds regarding their cessation, and dies to be reborn in the formless realm without having attained the fruit of Arhatship;

or if they have produced the knowledge of others' minds regarding their cessation, and die to be reborn in the formless realm and attain the fruit of Arhatship—at those times, they possess only the future [knowledge] and the past [knowledge], but not the present.

Those born in the desire realm who have abandoned craving for sensual pleasures; those in whom the knowledge of others' minds does not arise when present before them; those born in the form realm in whom the knowledge of others' minds does not arise when present before them; and those trainees (*śaikṣa*) who, having already produced the untainted knowledge of others' minds that is subject to cessation, die and are reborn in the formless realm without yet having attained the fruit of Arhatship—these constitute the past and present [cases].
When one is born in the desire realm or the form realm, the knowledge of others' minds arises and is present before them.
If one possesses past knowledge of others' minds and present knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess future [knowledge of others' minds]?
Answer: It is so.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of others' minds regarding the three periods of time?
Answer: As previously stated regarding time:
if one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the present, does one also accomplish it in the past and future?
Answer: It is so.
At what time does one achieve the knowledge of others' minds regarding the three periods of time?
