Answer: As previously stated regarding time:
if one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the past and future, does one also possess it of the present?
Answer: If it is present before one.
What does "being present before one" mean?
Answer: As previously stated.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the past and so forth, does one also accomplish that of the future?
He replied: "It is so. Why is this?"
Because all sentient beings fully accomplish the knowledge of the past, future, and so forth.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of the future and so forth, does one also accomplish that of the past?
The answer is:
Thus it is.
If one accomplishes past knowledge and so forth, does one also accomplish present [knowledge]?
The answer is:
If it manifests before one,

how does it manifest? It manifests when one does not give rise to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), does not give rise to receptivity (*kṣānti*), and is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
If one achieves the knowledge of the present and so forth, does one also achieve that of the past? The answer is: Yes.
The rest is explained at length as in the original sūtra.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge, does one also accomplish past inference-knowledge? Answer:
If, having been extinguished, it is not lost, then it is accomplished.
At what time are the past dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge accomplished?
The answer is:

Upon attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* during four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and three moments of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). Having already produced the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) regarding cessation, even if one subsequently transforms the faculties to become "immovable" (*akopya*) through timely liberation (*samayavimukta*), if the previously produced knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation has not ceased, or if it has ceased and is then lost, it is no longer accomplished.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (dharmajñāna) but not accomplished in subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: At the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattiphala) and the fruit of arhatship (arhattvaphala).
When one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, such a thing does not occur.
Why is this? Because at that time, there is already the presence of inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of the dharma regarding the past, yet not accomplished in the subsequent inferential knowledge regarding the past?

Answer: At the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the two moments of mind when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); and at the time of attaining the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. When the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has already arisen, inferential knowledge has not [yet] arisen; that which arose previously is lost because of the attainment of the fruit.

It is the same for one who has attained the fruit of *anāgāmin* as a faith-liberated (*śraddhādhimukta*) practitioner, when they transform their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become one liberated by vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
Furthermore, if one accomplishes past subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), does one also accomplish past dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: If, having been extinguished, it is not lost, then one possesses it.
At what time does one possess past subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) but not possess past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: This does not occur within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga). Why is that?

Because within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) one first attains the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), at the time of attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), although the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñāna-nirodha*) has already arisen, the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*anvayajñāna-nirodha-dharma*) does not arise. That which arose previously is lost upon the attainment of the fruit. This applies even up to the case of one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) who transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopyadharman*); although the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of phenomena has already arisen, the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of phenomena does not arise, and that which arose previously is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)?
Answer: If it has been attained.
At what time does one accomplish the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past (*atīta-dharma-jñāna*) and also accomplish the subsequent knowledge regarding the future (*anāgata-anvaya-jñāna*)?

Answer: At the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*): during the single mind-moment of seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); during four mind-moments of seeing the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*); during four mind-moments of seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and during three mind-moments of seeing the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). This applies to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), as well as to one who, having already produced the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), subsequently transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) from occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) to the immovable state (*akopya*). In these cases, the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation has already been produced.
If one has attained future subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna), does one also attain past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it.
At what time is one accomplished in the future knowledge of inference (anvaya-jñāna) and also accomplished in the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: At the same time as previously described.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is future subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) accomplished, yet past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is not accomplished?
Answer: In the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga), such a thing does not exist.

From the attainment of the fruit of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up to the transformation of faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) from "timely liberation" (samayavimukta) to "unshakable" (akopya), one does not give rise to the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (kṣayajñāna).
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*), does one also accomplish present subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
Answer: If it is present before one.
How does it become manifest?
It becomes manifest when no other knowledge arises, when no patience (*kṣānti*) arises, and when one is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*).
At what time does one possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and also possess present subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*)?
The answer is:

Upon attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Suffering, the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination, and the single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having already given rise to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) arises and becomes manifest. This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) from "timely liberation" (*samaya-vimukta*) to "unshakable" (*akopya*), having already given rise to the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation, the subsequent knowledge arises and becomes manifest.
If one achieves present subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), does one also achieve past dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished but not lost, then one achieves it, as previously explained regarding the time periods.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is present subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) accomplished, while past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is not accomplished?
Answer: Such a thing does not exist within the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

One who has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* loses it because they have already previously arisen the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) before the knowledge of the cessation [of suffering] arises; thus, the subsequent inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) manifests. This continues until one who is liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopyadharman*); having previously arisen the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena, they lose it because they have attained the fruit and transformed their faculties, and thus the inferential knowledge manifests.
If one accomplishes past *dharmajñāna*, does one also accomplish past and present *anvayajñāna*?
The answer is:

one may accomplish past *dharmajñāna* without accomplishing past and present *anvayajñāna*; or [accomplish] the past but not the present; or [accomplish] the present but not the past; or [accomplish] both the past and the present.

One who has accomplished past dharma-knowledge but has not accomplished past or present inferential knowledge is one for whom dharma-knowledge of cessation has already arisen and ceased, while inferential knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, and inferential knowledge does not arise as a present manifestation.
At what time is one accomplished in past dharma-knowledge but not accomplished in past and present subsequent knowledge?
The answer is:

it is impossible for one who has attained the fruit of Srotāpanna or Arhat, or one who, being liberated by occasion (samayavimukta), transforms their faculties to become immovable (akopya), to be in such a state.

When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) for the duration of a single moment of mind, one attains the fruit of Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*) or Non-returner (*anāgāmin*). When one who is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) transforms their faculties to become one who has attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they have already produced the knowledge of cessation regarding the dharma (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), but have not yet produced the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*). That which was previously produced is abandoned because of the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties; thus, the subsequent knowledge of cessation does not arise as a present manifestation.

Regarding those that are past but not present: these are the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) that have already arisen and ceased, yet whose subsequent knowledge has not arisen to manifest before one.
At what time does one possess past dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge, while not possessing present subsequent knowledge?
Answer: As previously stated. Regarding that which is present but not past:

when the knowledge of the dharma has already arisen and ceased, and the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) arises and is present before one, [the object] has not yet ceased; or, even if it had ceased, it would have been lost.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and present inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not in past inferential knowledge?
Answer: As previously stated.

Regarding "the past and the present": when the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) have already arisen and ceased, and subsequent knowledge has arisen and is present before one, at what time does one possess the past knowledge of phenomena as well as the past and present subsequent knowledge?
The answer is:

When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at the moment of seeing the Truth of Origination for a single mental instant, and at the moment of seeing the Truth of Cessation for a single mental instant, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having already given rise to the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna*), the subsequent knowledge arises and becomes manifest. This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) from occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta*) to immovability (*akopya*), having already given rise to the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation, the subsequent knowledge arises and becomes manifest.
If one has attained the knowledge of inference (anvaya-jñāna) regarding the past and present, does one also attain the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) regarding the past?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one has attained it.
At what time is one accomplished in the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the past and present, and also accomplished in the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) of the past?
Answer: As previously stated.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the past and present accomplished, while the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) of the past is not accomplished?
Answer: Such a thing does not exist within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

Having attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, one has already produced the subsequent knowledge of cessation (nirodha-anvaya-jñāna); when this subsequent knowledge of cessation arises and is present before one, the previously arisen knowledge of the dharma of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna) is lost because of the attainment of the fruit. This applies even up to the case where one who is liberated by time (samayavimukta) transforms their faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) to become immovable (akopyadharman); the explanation is likewise.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future and present subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish the past knowledge of phenomena without accomplishing the future and present subsequent knowledge; or accomplish it with the future but not the present; or accomplish it with both the future and the present.

One who has accomplished past dharma-knowledge but not future or present inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is one who has already arisen and ceased dharma-knowledge without losing it, yet has not yet attained inferential knowledge.
At what time does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge but not future or present inferential knowledge?
Answer: One attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) for the duration of a single moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Regarding the phrase "and the future, but not the present": although the Dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) that has already arisen and ceased is not lost, the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) is attained but does not arise as a present manifestation.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and future inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not in present [knowledge]?
Answer: As previously stated.

Regarding "and those of the future and present": when the dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) that has already arisen and ceased is not lost, the subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) arises and is present before one.
At what time does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge while also accomplishing future and present subsequent knowledge?

Answer: Having attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at the moment of seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) for a single thought-moment, at the moment of seeing the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*) for a single thought-moment, and at the moment of seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*) for a single thought-moment, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). Once the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has arisen and the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises and is present before one, this applies even up to the case where one who is liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*); it is likewise so.
If one has attained the future and present knowledge of inference (anvaya-jñāna), does one also attain the past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it.
At what time does one accomplish future and present subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), while also accomplishing past dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: As previously stated.
If it is not extinguished, or if, having been extinguished, it is lost, then it is not accomplished.
At what time is future and present subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) accomplished, while past dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) is not accomplished?
Answer: Such a thing does not exist within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

From the attainment of the fruit of Srotāpanna up until the transformation of faculties (indriya-saṃcāra) from "timely liberation" (samaya-vimukta) to "unshakable" (akopya), that which has not yet arisen is lost because of the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of faculties; rather, it is the knowledge of cessation (nirodha-jñāna) that arises first, and when inferential knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) subsequently manifests before one, [the former] is lost.
If one accomplishes past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish past and future subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna)? Answer:

One may accomplish past dharma-knowledge but not past and future subsequent knowledge; or accomplish future [subsequent knowledge] but not past [dharma-knowledge]; or accomplish both past and future [subsequent knowledge] while accomplishing past dharma-knowledge.

Regarding one who possesses the knowledge of the past and future but not the inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*): they have already arisen and do not lose the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), yet they have not yet attained inferential knowledge.
At what time is one accomplished in the past *dharma-jñāna* but not in the past and future inferential knowledge?
Answer: One attains right determination (samyaktva-niyāma) at the moment of a single thought when seeing the Truth of Suffering.

Regarding the statement that this pertains to the future and not the past: although the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) that has already arisen and ceased is not lost, the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) is not yet extinguished; even if it were to cease, it would be lost.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and future subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), but not in the past?
The answer is:

at the moment of a single thought when attaining right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*) upon seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*); when attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*) or the fruit of arhatship (*arhattvaphala*); and when an arhat of occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*). There is no other such occasion.
Why is this? Because inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) was previously attained.

When one who has attained the fruits of *sakṛdāgāmin* or *anāgāmin*, being liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become one who has seen the truth (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), they have already produced the knowledge of cessation regarding phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), but have not yet produced the inferential knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*). That which was previously produced is lost because of the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties.
Regarding the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the past and future: once the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) has arisen and ceased, the subsequent knowledge is not lost.
At what time does one achieve the past *dharma-jñāna* as well as the subsequent knowledge of the past and future?

Answer: One attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) during four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and three moments of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). At that time, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having already produced the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna-anvayajñāna*), and continuing until the transformation of faculties from occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) to immovability (*akopya*), one has already produced the knowledge of the dharma and subsequent knowledge regarding cessation.
If one has attained the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the past and future, does one also attain the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) of the past?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it, as previously explained regarding the timing.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) of the past and future accomplished, while the dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) of the past is not accomplished?
Answer: This does not occur within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga). Why is this so?

Because the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) is acquired prior [to the subsequent knowledge], when one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), the subsequent inferential knowledge of cessation (*anvayajñāna-nirodha*) has already arisen, whereas the inferential knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*anvayajñāna-nirodha-dharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen. That which arose previously is lost because the fruit has been attained; this applies likewise up to the case where one who is liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopyadharman*).
If one accomplishes the past dharma-knowledge, does one also accomplish the past, future, and present subsequent knowledge?
The answer is:
there are five propositions regarding this.
Regarding the question of one who has accomplished the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not the inferential knowledge (*anvayajñāna*) of the past, future, or present,
the answer is as previously stated.
Regarding the case of accomplishing the future [inferential knowledge] but not the past or present, the answer is:
Regarding what was previously stated concerning the past and future not being the present, the answer is:
as previously stated.
Regarding "those of the future and present, but not the past," the answer is:
as previously stated.

Regarding "those of the past, future, and present," it refers to the knowledge of phenomena already arisen and ceased, and the inferential knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*); when inferential knowledge arises, it is manifested before one.
At what time does one who has accomplished the knowledge of the dharma regarding the past also accomplish the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the three times?
The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the single-moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), and during the single-moment of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); upon attaining the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*); up until the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) from occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta*) to immovability (*akopya*); and when, having already arisen, the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation and subsequent knowledge have arisen, and the subsequent knowledge manifests before one.
If one possesses the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) of the past, future, and present, does one also possess the dharma-knowledge (*dharma-jñāna*) of the past?
Answer: As previously stated.
If one has attained past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also attain past knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains the past.
At what time does one accomplish the knowledge of past dharmas (*atīta-dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*)? Answer:

For a person who has abandoned sensual desire (*vītarāga*) and attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), it occurs at the moment of two mental instants when seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); four mental instants when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*); four mental instants when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and three mental instants when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). This also applies upon attaining the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or Arhatship (*arhat*). Furthermore, for a person who has abandoned sensual desire and is liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) who transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become one with vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*), or one who is temporarily liberated (*samayavimukta*) who transforms their faculties to become immovable (*akopyadharman*), once they have already arisen the knowledge of past dharmas and the knowledge of others' minds—provided these do not cease, or if they were to cease and are subsequently lost, they are no longer accomplished.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not in the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)? Answer:

For a person who has not yet abandoned desire and attachment, at the moment they attain right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*): during the two moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), the four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*), the four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), and the three moments of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*); and when attaining the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) or Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*); and when a person who has not yet abandoned desire and attachment, being liberated through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*), transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become one who sees by insight (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*)—at these times, the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding that which has already arisen and ceased has been produced.
If one has attained past knowledge of others' minds, does one also attain past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If it has been extinguished but not lost, then one attains it, as previously explained regarding time.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is past knowledge of others' minds accomplished, yet not the knowledge of dharmas? Answer:

When a person who is free from desire for the realm of form attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at the moment of two mental instants upon seeing the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), they attain the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmin*) or the fruit of Arhatship (*arhat*). This is because, even if the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, or if it has already arisen, the attainment of the fruit causes [the previous state] to be lost.

One who has attained liberation through faith by being freed from desire for the realm of form transforms their faculties to become one who attains vision; one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become one who is immovable. If they have not yet produced the knowledge of the cessation of suffering, or even if they have produced it, it is lost due to the transformation of their faculties.
If one does not produce the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) regarding the desire realm, yet at the end of life is reborn in the form realm;

or if, regarding both the desire and form realms, one has already produced the untainted knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) regarding cessation but has not produced the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena, and at the end of life is reborn in the formless realm without having attained the fruit of Arhatship.
Regarding an ordinary person born in the desire realm who is free from craving for sensual desires, or an ordinary person born in the form realm:
if they have attained the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) pertaining to the past, do they also attain the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) pertaining to the future?
Answer: If one attains it and does not lose it, then one accomplishes it.
How does one attain it and not lose it?
If one has become free from desire and does not regress from that freedom from desire,
at what time does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge and also accomplish future knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: As previously stated regarding time:
if one possesses future knowledge of others' minds, does one also possess past dharma-knowledge?
Answer: If that which has already ceased is not lost, then it is accomplished, as previously explained regarding time.
If it has not ceased, or if having ceased it is lost, then it is not accomplished.
At what time does one possess future knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) but not possess past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)? Answer:

When a person who has abandoned desire for the realm of sensuality attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the two moments of mind at the time of seeing the Truth of Suffering; or when one attains the fruit of Non-returner (*anāgāmiphala*) or the fruit of Arhatship (*arhattvaphala*), provided that the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodhadharmajñāna*) has not yet arisen, or if it has arisen, it is lost due to the attainment of the fruit.

One who has attained liberation through faith by being freed from desire for sensual pleasures transforms their faculties to become one of "view-attainment"; one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become one of "immovability. This occurs before the knowledge of the cessation of suffering has arisen; even if it had arisen, it is lost due to the transformation of the faculties.

If one has not yet produced the knowledge of cessation regarding the phenomena of the desire realm at the time of death and is reborn in the form or formless realms, or even if such knowledge were to arise there, one would immediately attain the fruit of arhatship in that very state.
Regarding an ordinary person born in the desire realm who is free from desire, or an ordinary person born in the form realm:
if they have attained past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), have they also attained present knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: If it is present before one.
What does "being present before one" mean?
If no other knowledge arises, no patience (*kṣānti*) arises, and it is not a state of mindlessness, then [the knowledge] manifests before one.
At what time does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge while accomplishing present knowledge of others' minds?

Answer: One who has attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, up to one who, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), becomes immovable (*akopya*) by means of occasional liberation (*samaya-vimukta*), having already given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), which now manifests before them.

If one gives rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) regarding the desire realm and, at the end of life, is reborn in the form realm where the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) manifests before them:
if they possess the present knowledge of others' minds, do they also possess the past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If [the dharma] has ceased but is not lost, then it is accomplished, as previously explained regarding time.
If it has not ceased, or if it has ceased and is then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is one accomplished in the present knowledge of others' minds but not accomplished in the past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: Within the Path of Seeing, such a case does not exist.

Having attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, up to the point where one who is liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become unshakable (*akopya*), they have not yet given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*). Even if such knowledge were to arise, it is lost because of the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties; thus, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) arises and becomes manifest.

If one does not give rise to the knowledge of cessation regarding the phenomena of the desire realm, but at the end of life is reborn in the form realm and gives rise to the knowledge of others' minds as it manifests before them—or even if cessation itself manifests—one attains the fruit of arhatship therein.

When the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) arises and is present before one, ordinary persons born in the desire realm (kāmadhātu) or the form realm (rūpadhātu) likewise have the knowledge of others' minds arise and be present before them.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also attain the past and present knowledge of others' minds?

Answer: One may possess past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) without possessing past or present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna); or possess it in the past but not in the present; or possess it in both the past and the present.

Regarding one who has accomplished the knowledge of phenomena pertaining to the past but not the knowledge of others' minds pertaining to the past or present: this refers to one who has already produced and subsequently ceased the knowledge of phenomena, but has not produced the knowledge of others' minds, or if it was produced and ceased, it has been lost, such that the knowledge of others' minds does not arise as a present manifestation.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (atīta-dharma-jñāna), yet not accomplished in the knowledge of others' minds regarding the past and present?
Answer: As previously stated, it is at the time when one has not yet abandoned desire and attachment.

Regarding "and [those] past but not present": the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) has already arisen and ceased; the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is not lost, yet the knowledge of others' minds does not arise and manifest, as previously explained.
As for "different," it refers to the case where the knowledge of others' minds does not arise and manifest.

Regarding "past and present," it means that although the dharma-knowledge has already arisen and ceased, the knowledge of others' minds is not lost, and thus the knowledge of others' minds arises and manifests in the present.
At what time does one accomplish past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and also accomplish past and present knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
The answer is:
there is no such case within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Having attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*, one has already produced the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), and the knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna*) now manifests before them.

This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one who is liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) becomes immovable (*akopya*); having already produced the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena, the knowledge of others' minds now manifests before them.

If, having already produced the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (nirodha-dharma-jñāna) regarding the desire realm, one dies and is reborn in the form realm, and before attaining the fruit of arhatship, the knowledge of others' minds (para-citta-jñāna) arises and becomes present.
If one has attained the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) regarding the past and present, does one also attain the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) regarding the past?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it, as previously explained at the time [of its attainment].
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the past and present accomplished, yet the knowledge of dharmas (dharmajñāna) of the past is not?
Answer: Such a thing does not occur within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

Regarding the fruit of Non-returner (anāgāmiphala), before the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (kṣayajñāna) has arisen, the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) arises and becomes manifest.
Even until one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, before the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena has arisen, the knowledge of others' minds manifests.

Or, if one does not give rise to the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena within the desire realm but dies and is reborn in the form realm, the knowledge of others' minds manifests; even if the knowledge of the destruction [of phenomena] had arisen [previously], upon being reborn in the form realm and attaining the fruit of Arhatship, the knowledge of others' minds manifests.
When an ordinary person born in the desire realm or the form realm brings the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) to presence,
if they have attained the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) in the past, do they also attain it in the future and present?
Answer: There are three propositions here.
Regarding the case of one who has attained past *dharmajñāna* but has not attained future or present *paracittajñāna*, the answer is as previously stated.

Regarding "and [attaining] the future but not the present": this refers to one who has already arisen and ceased the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) without losing it, and who has attained the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) but does not bring it into present manifestation.
At what time is one accomplished in the past knowledge of phenomena and the future knowledge of others' minds, but not the present?

Answer: A person who has abandoned craving for the realm of desire attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*). At the moment of seeing the Truth of Suffering, it lasts for two moments of mind; at the moment of seeing the Truth of Origination, four moments of mind; at the moment of seeing the Truth of Cessation, four moments of mind; and at the moment of seeing the Truth of the Path, three moments of mind. They attain the fruit of *anāgāmin*, and even up to the point where one with occasional liberation (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*), having already given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*) does not arise as a present manifestation.

If one gives rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena regarding the desire realm and, at the end of life, is reborn in the form realm, but has not yet attained the fruit of Arhatship, the knowledge of others' minds will not arise and manifest before them.
If one is born in the formless realm and has not yet attained the fruit of arhatship,
such that the dharma-knowledge of cessation— which has already arisen and ceased— is not lost, and the knowledge of others' minds arises and is present before them.
At what time does one accomplish the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) as well as the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) in the future and present?
The answer is:
as previously stated, it is at the time when one accomplishes the knowledge of others' minds in the past and present.
If one achieves the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) in the future and present, does one also achieve the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) in the past?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one achieves it, as previously explained regarding the time periods.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished, as previously stated.
If one accomplishes past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also accomplish past and future knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*)?
Answer: There are three propositions here.
Regarding the case of one who has attained past *dharmajñāna* but not past or future *paracittajñāna*, the answer is as previously stated.

Regarding "possessing the future [knowledge] but not the past": the knowledge of dharma (*dharmajñāna*) has already arisen and ceased, while the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) has not yet arisen or has already ceased; even if it had ceased, it would have been lost.
At what time does one possess both the past knowledge of dharma and the future knowledge of others' minds?
Answer: This does not occur for those born in the desire realm or the form realm.

If one gives rise to the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena regarding the desire or form realms, yet does not give rise to the untainted knowledge of the cessation of others' minds, and then dies to be reborn in the formless realm without having attained the fruit of Arhatship; [in such a case, this would occur].
Regarding those who possess the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) of the past and future, the answer is:
as previously stated.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds of the past and future, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) of the past?
Answer: As previously stated.
If one has attained past knowledge of dharmas (dharmajñāna), does one also attain past, future, and present knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna)?
Answer: There are four propositions here, explained according to their characteristics.
If one possesses the knowledge of others' minds (paracittajñāna) pertaining to the past, future, and present, does one also possess the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) pertaining to the past?
Answer: If, having ceased, it is not lost, then it is accomplished, as previously explained regarding time.
If it does not cease, or if, having ceased, it is lost, then it is not accomplished, also as previously explained.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the past conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)? Answer: It is so.
At what time does one accomplish both the knowledge of the past (*atīta-dharma-jñāna*) and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*)?
The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during the two moments of mind when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the four moments of mind when seeing the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*), the four moments of mind when seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), and the three moments of mind when seeing the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*); and upon attaining the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*), up until the point of attaining liberation through time (*samayavimukta*) and transforming the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopya*), at which point the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*kṣaya-jñāna*) has already arisen.
If one accomplishes the knowledge of past [phenomena] and so forth, does one also accomplish the knowledge of past phenomena?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one accomplishes it, as previously explained regarding the time.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is the knowledge of the past and so forth accomplished, while the knowledge of the dharma of the past is not accomplished?

Answer: For all ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those who have attained right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at the moment of two mental instants when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), they attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpanna-phala*). This continues up until the time-released (*samaya-vimukta*) practitioner transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*); as long as the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) has not arisen, [the attainment is maintained]. Even if it were to arise, because one attains the fruit and transforms the faculties, [the previous state] is lost.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna)? Answer: Yes.
At what time are the past dharma-knowledge and the future conventional knowledge accomplished?
Answer: As previously stated.
If one has attained future conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna), does one also attain past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna)?
Answer: If it has already ceased and has not been lost, then one attains it, as previously explained.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished, as previously explained.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the present conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna)?
Answer: If it is present before one.
What does "being present before one" mean?

If one does not give rise to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*), does not give rise to patience (*kṣānti*), and is not in a state of mindlessness (*acittaka*), then [these knowledges] manifest in the present.
At what time does one accomplish past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*) as well as present conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*)?
Answer: Such a thing does not exist within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

From the attainment of the fruit of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna) up until the point when one of the "timely-liberated" (samayavimukta) transforms their faculties (indriya-parāvṛtti) to become "unshakable" (akopya), the knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna) has already arisen and ceased, and the subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna) arises and manifests before them.
If one achieves present conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*), does one also achieve past dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one achieves it, as previously explained regarding the time periods.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is present conventional knowledge (samvṛtijñāna) accomplished while past dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) is not accomplished?
Answer: Such a thing does not exist within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

Upon attaining the fruit of Srotāpanna, that which has previously arisen and ceased is lost because the fruit has been attained; subsequently, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) arises and becomes manifest.

Even until the time when one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, before the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (kṣayajñāna) arises, that which arose previously is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties; thus, conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) arises and becomes manifest.
The remaining secondary characteristics are explained extensively through seven propositions.
If one possesses past *dharmajñāna*, does one also possess past *duḥkhajñāna*?
The answer is:
If, having been extinguished, it is not lost, then it is accomplished.
At what time is the past *dharmajñāna* and *duḥkhajñāna* accomplished? Answer:

Having attained right determination, one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* during two moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Suffering, four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Origination, four moments of mind when seeing the Truth of Cessation, and three moments of mind when seeing the Truth of the Path.

Even when one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, if the dharma-knowledge and suffering-knowledge that have already arisen have not yet ceased, or if they have ceased but are subsequently lost, then these are not accomplished.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of phenomena regarding the past (*atīta-dharma-jñāna*) but not accomplished in the knowledge of suffering regarding the past (*atīta-duḥkha-jñāna*)?
Answer: There is no such case within the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).

Having attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to the point of transforming the faculties (*indriya*) from "timely liberation" (*samayavimukta*) to "unshakable" (*akopya*), one has already given rise to the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation, origination, and the path (*nirodha-samudaya-mārga-dharma-jñāna*); however, the knowledge of phenomena regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) has not yet arisen. That which had previously arisen is lost because of attaining the fruit and the transformation of the faculties.
If one has attained the knowledge of past suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), does one also attain the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past suffering and the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)?
Answer: As previously stated.
If [the afflictions] have not been extinguished, or if they were extinguished but have subsequently been lost, then one is not accomplished in them.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past suffering (*atīta-duḥkha-jñāna*) but not accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*atīta-dharma-jñāna*)?
Answer: There is no such case within the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

Having attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*, up to the point of attaining *samayavimukta* and transforming one's faculties (*indriya*) into those of an *akopyadharman*, one has already given rise to the subsequent knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*nirodhe 'nvajñāna*), but has not yet given rise to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodhe dharmajñāna*). Even if it were to arise, because one attains the fruit and transforms the faculties, it is lost.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer: Yes.
At what time does one who has attained the knowledge of the dharma regarding the past also attain the future knowledge of suffering? The answer is:

at the moment of attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), during two moments of mind when seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); four moments of mind when seeing the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*); four moments of mind when seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*); and three moments of mind when seeing the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). This applies from the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*) up until the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) of one liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) into the immovable state (*akopya*), at which point the knowledge of the dharma regarding cessation has already arisen.
If one has attained the future knowledge of suffering, has one also attained the past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: If it has been extinguished and not lost, then one has attained it.
At what time does one accomplish future knowledge of suffering and also accomplish past knowledge of phenomena?
Answer: At the time previously described.
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is future knowledge of suffering accomplished, yet past knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) is not accomplished?

Answer: When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna-phala*) in the duration of a single moment of mind. That which has not yet arisen—the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*)—is lost upon the prior arising [of the fruit], because one has attained the fruit. This applies even up to the case of one liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) who transforms their faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) to become immovable (*akopya*); that which has not yet arisen—the knowledge of cessation—is lost upon the prior arising [of the transformation], because one has both attained the fruit and transformed the faculties.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)? Answer:
If it is present before one.
How does it manifest? It manifests when no other knowledge arises, when no patience (*kṣānti*) arises, and when one is not in a state of mindlessness.
At what time does one possess both the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?

Answer: When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), in the duration of a single moment of mind, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*), one who is liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) becomes immovable (*akopya*); having already given rise to the knowledge of the destruction of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) arises and becomes present.
If one has attained present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), does one also attain past knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*)?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one attains it, as previously explained regarding the time [of its occurrence].
If it is not extinguished, or if, having been extinguished, it is lost, then it is not accomplished.
At what time is the present knowledge of suffering accomplished, while the past knowledge of phenomena is not accomplished?

Answer: When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), in the duration of a single moment of mind, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one who is liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*) becomes immovable (*akopya*). Because of attaining the fruit and transforming the faculties, that which has not yet arisen—the knowledge of the cessation of phenomena (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*)—is lost even before it arises. This is because of the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties.

When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) arises and is present before one, if one possesses the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), does one also possess the past and present knowledge of suffering?
The answer is:
there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) in this regard.

Regarding the case of one who has accomplished past *dharmajñāna* but does not accomplish past or present *duḥkhajñāna*: if *dharmajñāna* has already arisen and ceased without being lost, then one accomplishes it;
however, if *duḥkhajñāna* has not yet arisen, or if it arose and was subsequently lost, and *duḥkhajñāna* does not arise and manifest in the present, then one does not accomplish it.
At what time does one possess the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) but not possess the past and present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Answer: Within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), such a case does not exist.

Having attained the fruit of Srotāpanna, one has already given rise to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (nirodha-dharma-jñāna), but has not yet given rise to the cessation-knowledge of suffering (nirodha-duḥkha-jñāna). Even if it were to arise, it would be lost because of the attainment of the fruit; thus, the cessation-knowledge of suffering does not manifest before one.

Even when one who is liberated by occasion transforms their faculties to become immovable, having already given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of formations, they have not yet given rise to the knowledge of the cessation of suffering; or, even if they have given rise to it, because they attain the fruit and transform their faculties, they lose it, and thus the knowledge of the cessation of suffering does not manifest before them.

Regarding those that are past but not present: this refers to having already arisen the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), yet the knowledge of suffering does not presently manifest.
At what time is one accomplished in the past knowledge of phenomena and the knowledge of suffering, but not accomplished in the present knowledge of suffering?

Answer: Upon attaining right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), at the moment of seeing the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), it takes one mental moment; at the moment of seeing the truth of origin (*samudaya-satya*), four mental moments; at the moment of seeing the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*), four mental moments; and at the moment of seeing the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*), three mental moments, one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*). Having already produced the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), the knowledge of suffering does not arise again as a present manifestation. This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-parāvṛtti*) in the case of one liberated by time (*samaya-vimukta*), one becomes immovable (*akopya*); having already produced the knowledge of phenomena regarding cessation and the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of suffering does not arise again as a present manifestation.

Regarding that which is present and not past: if the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*) has already arisen and ceased but is not lost, while the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen—or if it arose but was subsequently lost—then the knowledge of suffering arises and is present before one.
At what time is one accomplished in the knowledge of past phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), but not in the past?
Answer: There is no such case within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).

Having attained the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpattiphala*), up to the point where one who is liberated by time (*samayavimukta*) transforms their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) to become immovable (*akopya*): once the knowledge of the cessation of formations (*saṃskāranirodha-jñāna*) has arisen, but the knowledge of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodha-jñāna*) has not yet arisen—then that which previously arose and ceased is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of the faculties; subsequently, the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) arises and becomes manifest.

Regarding "past and present": one has already produced the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering is now manifest before one.
At what time does one possess both past *dharmajñāna* and past and present *duḥkhajñāna*?

Answer: When one attains right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and perceives the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), in the space of a single moment of mind, one attains the fruit of Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). This continues until, through the transformation of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) from "timely liberation" (*samaya-vimukta*) to "unshakable" (*akopya*), one has already given rise to the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) and the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*), and the knowledge of suffering now manifests before one.
If one has attained the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) regarding the past and present, does one also attain the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*) regarding the past?
The answer is:
if it has been extinguished and not lost, then one has attained it, as previously stated regarding the time [of its occurrence].
If it is not extinguished, or if it is extinguished and then lost, it is not accomplished.
At what time is the knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-jñāna) of the past and present accomplished, while the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) of the past is not accomplished?
Answer: Such a thing does not occur within the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).

From the attainment of the fruit of Srotāpanna up to the transformation of faculties (indriyasaṃcāra) from the "timely-liberated" (samayavimukta) to the "unshakable" (akopya), once the subsequent knowledge of cessation regarding suffering (duḥkhe 'nvayajñāna) has arisen, if the dharma-knowledge of cessation (nirodhe dharmajñāna) has not yet arisen, then that which arose previously is lost due to the attainment of the fruit and the transformation of faculties; thus, the subsequent knowledge of cessation regarding suffering manifests before one.
If one accomplishes the past knowledge of phenomena (dharmajñāna), does one also accomplish the future and present knowledge of suffering (duḥkhajñāna)?
Answer: One accomplishes it in the future; as for the present, it is accomplished if it is currently manifest. The remaining cases should be explained according to their respective characteristics.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), does one also attain the past and future knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
Answer: One attains it in the future; as for the past, if it has been extinguished and not lost, one attains it. The remaining cases are explained according to their respective characteristics.
If one has attained the past knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), has one also attained the past, future, and present knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhajñāna*)?
The answer is:
there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) here, which are explained according to their characteristics.

Just as *dharma-jñāna* forms seven propositions with respect to *duḥkha-jñāna*, so too does *dharma-jñāna* form seven propositions with respect to *samudaya-jñāna*, *nirodha-jñāna*, and *mārga-jñāna*.

Past *dharma-jñāna*, past *anvaya-jñāna*, and past *paracitta-jñāna* form seven propositions; this continues up to *mārga-jñāna* forming seven propositions in the same manner. The remaining details are explained at length as in the *Anuśaya-skandhaka*.
The *Ekavyavahārika* school distinguishes six or seven great births; the answer is as in the *Prajñapti-prakaraṇa* (the *Śīla-skandha*).

**Preface to the Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume 60.** Composed by Shi Daoyan. As for this *Vibhāṣā*, it is the ultimate destination of the Tripiṭaka and the compass for the ninefold canon. Once the compass is established, the masses of the deluded are corrected; once the destination is proclaimed, the chariot of heterodoxy halts its course.

More than six hundred years after Śākyamuni’s radiance had departed, there were five hundred arhats in North India who considered that the divine torch had long been hidden and the sacred beacon had lost its brilliance; thus, sentient beings were shrouded in darkness and a profound dream had begun. Although the eminent Kātyāyanīputra had previously composed the *Abhidharma* to rescue the declining era, later worthies who sought its fundamental principles found themselves embroiled in disputes between Confucian and Mohist-like factions, with right and wrong entangled in chaos. Consequently, they clarified their spirits and cultivated contemplation to investigate and select the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). They composed the *Vibhāṣā* to suppress heterodox views and establish the correct doctrine, whether by employing exceptional arguments or by providing critical evaluations. Its principles are profound and vast, and its literary expressions are elegant and extensive; among the eminent and accomplished scholars of the Western Regions, there are none who do not rely upon it to mirror their minds and use it to clarify their insights.
Yet the profound waves silently drench, about to reach all distant lands; however, principle does not operate in a vacuum, for its propagation depends upon man.

The Great Juqu, King of Hexi, possessed a celestial mind vast and expansive, setting his sincerity upon a sublime reliance. Although his traces were entangled in worldly affairs, his spirit dwelt in the realm of the mysterious. Thus, he was able to harmonize mountain retreats with the imperial court, and palaces with forest wilds. This caused the deep-seated recluses to cast down their staffs and the mountain-dwelling hermits to come to the palace gates; those who had stilled their minds ascended the hall, and the guests of the profound entered the inner chambers.
Since his sincere devotion was already manifest, a profound resonance with the principles arose beyond expectation.
There was a śramaṇa named Daotai, whose talent was innate and whose vital energy was profound yet lucid; he was extensively learned in rare curiosities and had traveled far to consult foreign texts.

In the past, as the various scriptures of the Han lands were already complete and the profound teachings had been roughly elucidated, the only areas yet unrefined were the Tripiṭaka and the nine divisions of the canon.

Therefore, I took up my staff and braved the perils, traveling as far as the west of the Pamirs, where I mastered the Sanskrit texts, inherited their lofty principles, and obtained over one hundred thousand verses of the original Sanskrit manuscripts.
Once he reached the territory of Liang, the King immediately wished to have him proclaim and translate [the scriptures].
However, fearing that his own understanding might not yet be exhaustive, the King set aside his seat with humility and waited expectantly for further clarification and excellence.
The Indian śramaṇa Buddhamitra traveled extensively to propagate the teachings and eventually arrived at the region of Liang.
He was profoundly enlightened and possessed vast learning; his spiritual mind was deep and far-reaching, and his diligent study and profound contemplation were utterly unfathomable.

In the middle of the fourth month of the year Yichou, at the Xianyu Monastery within the inner garden of Liangcheng, he requested that the translation be transmitted. Over three hundred people, including the śramaṇas Zhisong and Daolang, who were experts in the principles and flavor of the teachings, examined the text and evaluated the meaning, ensuring that the essence remained faithful to the original intent; they eliminated redundancies to reach the reality of the text, resulting in a style that was plain yet not crude.

The King repeatedly halted his carriage to cultivate their profound aesthetic sensibilities, ensuring that the compositions were logically sound and that even a single phrase conveyed deep significance.
By the seventh month of the year Dingmao, the work was completed, comprising one hundred fascicles in total.
When the realm of Liang was submerged and its distant borders fell into ruin, the original texts of the scriptures produced there were nearly all lost.

Now, the King of Liang’s faith is profound; he probes the depths of the subtle mysteries and thus constantly seeks out new and extraordinary teachings, aspiring to rare and marvelous news. He has therefore transcribed sixty fascicles of previously extant texts and sent them to the Song court for promulgation among those who have not yet heard them. It is his hope that the beauty of daily renewal shall flourish in this present age, and that the rise of his blessings and sovereignty shall extend to future generations.

Having been granted the slight fortune of participating as a junior listener at the end [of these teachings], my sincere joy at this encounter prevents me from remaining silent; I have thus roughly illustrated contemporary events to bequeath them to future sages.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, the bhikṣu Dharmottara composed the four-fascicle *Abhidharmahṛdaya*.
Furthermore, Kātyāyanīputra composed the Abhidharma, consisting of eight *skandhas* (sections) in forty-four chapters.
Later, five hundred arhats composed the *Vibhāṣā* to provide a detailed commentary on these eight *skandhas*. When it was translated by Juqu Jingsheng, it comprised one hundred large fascicles.
After Daowu defeated the Juqu [rulers], he collected the scattered fragments and obtained sixty fascicles.
Later generations divided these into one hundred and ten fascicles; however, only the *Śaikṣa-vastu* (釋三揵度) remains, while the *Prātimokṣa-vastu* (五揵度) has been completely lost.
Preface to the *Vibhāṣā* (Great Commentary)
